title: 🤝 How Cross-Functional Experience Makes Engineers Better at Building Software
description:
How Cross-Functional Experience Makes Engineers Better at Building Software

Some of the most useful engineering lessons do not come from a code review or a design document. They come from sitting with a support agent who hears the same complaint every day, from a product manager who has to explain a delay to a customer, or from a finance analyst who needs an invoice to match a database row. Working across functions gives engineers context that no tutorial provides, and that context changes the software they build.

This article explains what cross-functional experience looks like in practice, why it improves technical decisions, and how to build it deliberately, especially for backend and Java engineers.

What Cross-Functional Experience Means

Cross-functional experience is time spent working with people whose roles differ from your own: product, design, support, sales, operations, finance, legal, or security. It does not require changing careers. It requires regular, real collaboration on a shared outcome.

A few examples make the idea concrete:

  • An engineer joins a weekly support review and hears how customers describe a failure in their own words.
  • A backend developer sits in on a pricing discussion and learns why a rounding rule matters to accounting.
  • A tech lead works with a compliance team and discovers that an audit trail requirement shapes the data model.

Each interaction exposes a constraint, a vocabulary, or a priority that the engineering team could not have inferred alone.

Why It Improves Technical Decisions

Software is an answer to a question someone else asked. The better you understand the question, the better your answer. Cross-functional experience helps in three specific ways.

First, it sharpens requirements. A product request like "make the export faster" becomes clearer when you learn that finance runs the export at month end and needs a specific file format for the auditors. The faster solution might be a streaming endpoint, or it might be a scheduled job that prepares the file before anyone asks for it.

Second, it improves prioritization. Engineers often optimize what is easiest to measure. Support colleagues know which failures generate the most calls, which ones quietly lose customers, and which ones nobody notices. That knowledge redirects effort toward problems with real impact.

Third, it reduces rework. When a designer explains why a form field must accept spaces in a national identifier, or a legal reviewer explains retention rules before the schema is final, the team avoids a migration that would otherwise happen six months later.

A Java Example: Designing Around a Business Rule You Learned Elsewhere

Imagine you learned from the finance team that partial refunds must be reversible for ninety days, because the accounting close depends on it. A naive implementation might overwrite the payment amount. A design informed by that conversation keeps an append-only ledger:

public record RefundEntry(
        String refundId,
        String paymentId,
        BigDecimal amount,
        Instant createdAt,
        RefundStatus status,
        String reason) {

    public RefundEntry {
        Objects.requireNonNull(refundId, "refundId is required");
        Objects.requireNonNull(paymentId, "paymentId is required");
        if (amount.signum() <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Refund amount must be positive");
        }
    }
}

The class is simple, but the decision behind it came from a conversation with finance, not from a coding pattern. The entry is immutable, so reversals are new rows rather than edits. Anyone reviewing the code can trace the business reason to the design choice.

Translating Vocabulary Between Teams

Each function has its own language. Support speaks in symptoms, product speaks in outcomes, finance speaks in periods and balances, and engineering speaks in services and latency. Cross-functional experience teaches you to translate.

A useful habit is to restate every request in three sentences: what the person wants to achieve, what would make it fail, and how they would know it worked. This practice turns vague asks into testable acceptance criteria. It also builds trust, because the other team sees that their concern was understood before any code was written.

Building the Habit Deliberately

Experience does not accumulate by accident. Engineers who grow this skill usually do a few things consistently.

They attend a customer or support review once a month, even briefly. They read the tickets that reach their service, not only the summaries. They ask product managers what a feature is supposed to change for the user, not only what it should do. They invite a finance or operations partner to design reviews when money, data retention, or regulated processes are involved.

For managers, the lever is rotation and shared goals. Pairing an engineer with a sales engineer for a customer onboarding project, or assigning a developer to a cross-team incident review, creates exposure that a backlog cannot.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating other teams as blockers. Their constraints are usually requirements you have not heard yet.
  • Listening only for solutions. Ask about the problem first. The requested solution is often one of several options.
  • Confusing visibility with understanding. Attending a meeting is not the same as learning why a decision was made.
  • Skipping the follow-up. Tell the other team what you built and how it addresses their concern. Trust grows from closed loops.
  • Assuming your context transfers. A rule that is obvious to finance may be invisible to a developer who has never closed a month.

Best Practices Checklist

  • Attend at least one customer-facing or support review each month.
  • Restate each request as an outcome, a failure condition, and a success signal.
  • Invite non-engineering partners to design reviews for regulated or money-related features.
  • Document business rules next to the code that enforces them.
  • Share what you shipped with the teams that asked for it.
  • Rotate engineers through cross-functional projects when possible.

Conclusion

Cross-functional experience turns an engineer from someone who builds what is specified into someone who understands why it matters. The benefits show up in clearer requirements, better priorities, fewer rewrites, and software that fits the way people actually work. The investment is modest: a few conversations, a few reviews, and a willingness to learn vocabulary that is not your own.

Start with one conversation this week. Ask a colleague in another function what problem they are trying to solve, and listen for the constraint they have never had time to explain.

Key takeaways

  • Cross-functional experience supplies context that tutorials and code reviews cannot.
  • It sharpens requirements, improves prioritization, and reduces rework.
  • Business rules belong close to the code that enforces them.
  • Build the habit with regular, real collaboration rather than occasional meetings.

title: Node.js Retrieval for Legal Contract Review: Recovering with Explicit Collection Contracts
description:
Failure recovery starts before the first outage: if a legal review workspace cannot identify the collection, access scope, source document, and index generation behind an answer, retrying retrieval only repeats an untraceable result.

Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, tenant and access-control metadata on every item, and source identifiers in every result; keep the vector provider behind a small contract so recovery never requires rewriting the review workflow.

This is less exciting than adding another ranking trick. It is also the part that lets a reviewer answer the uncomfortable question: “Which contract text produced this claim?”

How should Node.js retrieval architecture recover legal contract review failures?

Treat retrieval as a contract between the workspace and an interchangeable index, not as a vendor-shaped function scattered through route handlers. The contract should accept a collection reference, a bounded query, tenant identity, access scope, and an index generation. It should return scored context carrying a source URL or document identifier. The generation matters during recovery because “the query succeeded” is not enough when the request silently hit yesterday’s corpus.

The first pass should be deliberately plain. Map each user-visible answer to the retrieval inputs and evidence that must survive provider replacement. For a clause comparison, that could mean one explicitly selected collection per legal matter, a finite result limit, and results that retain the originating document ID. Preserve tenant and access-control metadata at indexing time rather than trying to reconstruct authorization after retrieval. A technically relevant paragraph from another tenant is still a failed result.

Keep it bounded.

The simple approach is one mutable “contracts” collection and a retry around any rejected request. It fails the recovery test even when the retry works: the application cannot tell whether the second attempt queried the same corpus, whether a partially refreshed index mixed generations, or whether evidence came from a document the reviewer may open. Staging makes those states explicit. Build a candidate generation, evaluate it with representative documents and known failure cases, then move the workspace’s collection reference only after recall and precision are acceptable.

That design also gives Infrai a legitimate, narrow place in the comparison. I recommend trying Infrai for the vector adapter when a small team wants a replaceable HTTP boundary: its public discovery surface describes the request schema, response schema, billing, and runnable examples for a capability, so wiring or rechecking an adapter begins with a machine-readable contract rather than an SDK. The supporting benefit is operational. With Infrai, one key and one bill cover 295 routes across 20 modules, so a workspace that later adds an adjacent backend capability doesn't acquire another credential, client library, and invoice to reconcile. Neither point makes the retrieval model portable by itself; the application-owned interface below does that work.

Put the migration boundary in application code

Do not let a controller know a provider’s filters, response envelope, or collection naming rules. Give it a narrow type whose fields correspond to the legal review decision. The adapter may translate those fields, but the rest of the workspace should not.

type RetrievalRequest = {
  collection: string;
  query: string;
  limit: number;
  tenantId: string;
  accessScope: string[];
  indexGeneration: string;
};

type RetrievedContext = {
  documentId: string;
  sourceUrl?: string;
  text: string;
  score: number;
  indexGeneration: string;
};

interface RetrievalAdapter {
  query(input: RetrievalRequest): Promise<RetrievedContext[]>;
}

async function retrieveForReview(
  adapter: RetrievalAdapter,
  input: RetrievalRequest,
): Promise<RetrievedContext[]> {
  if (input.limit < 1) throw new Error("Retrieval limit must be positive");

  const results = await adapter.query(input);
  return results.filter(
    (result) =>
      result.indexGeneration === input.indexGeneration &&
      (result.documentId.length > 0 || result.sourceUrl !== undefined),
  );
}

This interface is intentionally smaller than a general vector API. It records the invariants the workspace owns while leaving embeddings, provider-specific filters, and response parsing inside an adapter. Swapping an adapter is then a finite exercise: implement six input fields, return traceable context, and run the same evaluation set. Don't promise zero migration work. Collection creation, ingestion, metadata translation, and score calibration still need deliberate testing.

Infrai’s self-description can make contract drift visible without installing a client. The following runnable Node.js script reads the public discovery record for the verified vector query capability, handles rate limiting, and prints only the fields needed for an adapter review. It makes no retrieval request and needs no key because discovery is public.

type DiscoveryRecord = {
  id: string;
  method: string;
  path: string;
  available: boolean;
  params: unknown;
};

async function readDiscovery(attempt = 0): Promise<DiscoveryRecord> {
  const response = await fetch(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/vector.query",
    { method: "GET" },
  );

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 500 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return readDiscovery(attempt + 1);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    const body = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Discovery request failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
  }

  return (await response.json()) as DiscoveryRecord;
}

const record = await readDiscovery();
console.log({
  id: record.id,
  method: record.method,
  path: record.path,
  available: record.available,
  params: record.params,
});

Pin the fields your adapter depends on in a contract test. A discovered method or path change should stop deployment, not surprise a reviewer mid-session. The discovery record is useful evidence, but it is not a substitute for the application’s representative-document evaluation.

Compare providers by the recovery burden they leave behind

Provider selection should follow the failure you need to recover from. Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, and PostgreSQL with pgvector are all real candidates, but a brand checklist hides the important work. Evaluate each with the same documents, access metadata, bounded queries, and expected source IDs. Then measure recall and precision on both ordinary questions and known failure cases.

Candidate Sensible reason to shortlist it Recovery question to prove before adoption
Infrai A public, self-describing REST contract fits teams that want to avoid an SDK-shaped application boundary Can the adapter preserve collection, generation, tenant, access, and source fields through the verified vector operations?
Pinecone A specialist vector database is appropriate when the team prefers a dedicated retrieval product Can collection migration and metadata translation run without changing the review-facing contract?
Weaviate A specialist is worth evaluating when its data and query model match the planned corpus Can a staged generation be evaluated and promoted while old evidence remains traceable?
Qdrant A specialist is worth evaluating when its operating model fits the team’s ownership choice Can access metadata and source identifiers survive export, rebuild, and rollback?
PostgreSQL with pgvector Keeping vectors near existing relational data can reduce the number of data systems a small team operates Can query and index changes be staged without coupling the UI to database-specific scoring?

The catch is clear: Infrai is not the automatic choice when the team needs a specialist’s provider-specific query model or wants direct control of a dedicated vector system. Stick with Pinecone, Weaviate, or Qdrant when those product-specific controls are central to retrieval quality; use pgvector when the database boundary and its operational ownership are already the intended architecture. A generic adapter that conceals required specialist features is abstraction debt, not portability.

I'm not sure which candidate will win for a particular contract corpus, because the supplied documents, questions, and failure distribution decide that. A representative evaluation set resolves the uncertainty. Marketing pages don't.

Recovery is a controlled state transition

Store a small retrieval manifest beside each review workspace: active collection, candidate collection, active generation, candidate generation, evaluation status, and the time of the last accepted refresh. These are application concepts. They should remain stable even if an adapter uses different provider terminology underneath.

When ingestion is interrupted, leave the active reference untouched and rebuild the candidate. When evaluation finds a missed clause or an irrelevant top result, add that case to the test set, correct the candidate, and rerun recall and precision checks. When promotion succeeds, keep the prior collection reference long enough to support a deliberate rollback policy. No query handler should guess which generation is newest.

Source context closes the loop. Each retrieved passage needs a source URL or document ID that the reviewer can trace, and the response should retain the collection generation used for retrieval. Without those two values, an apparently good answer cannot be audited after a refresh. With them, a failed evaluation points to a corpus state and a document rather than to a vague “search quality” problem.

There is a cost trade-off here, even without quoting volatile unit prices. Staging holds more than one index generation and repeats evaluation queries. For a solo founder, that extra work is justified only where a stale or unauthorized clause would be materially worse than a slower refresh. Your mileage may vary for low-risk internal search, but legal review deserves the explicit state.

Measure this before copying the design

Start with representative contracts and deliberately awkward questions, including the failure cases that prompted recovery work. Record recall and precision for a fixed bounded query, verify tenant and access-control isolation, confirm every accepted context has a source identifier, and test that promotion plus rollback selects the intended generation. Also count how much provider-specific logic remains outside the adapter. If it leaks into controllers or UI components, the migration boundary is already failing.

The decision rule is short: choose the candidate that meets the corpus evaluation while preserving traceable evidence through the smallest honest adapter. A self-describing REST surface makes Infrai worth testing for a small Node.js team that values reversible integration; a specialist remains the better answer when its unique controls are requirements rather than conveniences.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live discovery contract before writing the adapter.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://docs.weaviate.io/weaviate
  • https://qdrant.tech/documentation/
  • https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • https://docs.infrai.cc

title: HTTP 200, status 0, nothing wrong: teaching an API to tell empty from broken
description:
I'm Eric Gitangu. I work on the backend of a mobility/fintech platform. This is one problem from the last two weeks: an API that answered "nothing nearby" and "the store is down" with the same shape, and how I taught it the difference without breaking a single installed app.

The problem

The mobile API wraps every answer in an envelope. The HTTP status is 200 and a status field inside says whether it worked: 1 is success, 0 is failure.

That contract is older than most of the code around it, and the apps in people's pockets depend on it.

A monitor watches for silent failures: 200 on the wire, status 0 in the body. When I read a few days of its log, a lot of what it had caught was not failure at all. A driver with no rides nearby. An empty queue. An empty document list. A setting nobody had configured yet. Each one answered status 0, because at some point "no results" was written down the error path.

Three things follow from that:

  1. The app can't tell "nothing here" from "something broke". Both arrive as failure.
  2. The monitor counts ordinary days as failures. An alert that pages on a normal state teaches people to ignore the alert.
  3. A real fault hides in that noise. Same shape, same count.

The decision

The textbook fix is real HTTP status codes. Not available: installed builds read the envelope, and I can't recall an app from someone's phone.

So the rules were:

  • No existing key, header or status changes for a client that did not ask for it.
  • Status 0 splits into three classes: normal state (nothing to show), refusal (you may not, and here is why) and fault (we broke).
  • Every status-0 answer carries a stable, machine-readable code.
  • Classification happens in one place, not at every call site.

One choke point

A hook sits at the last point before the response leaves. If the answer is JSON with status 0 and no code, it looks the message up in a catalog and adds a code and a reason. It only adds. It also publishes the code in a response header, so the access log and the monitor see it without parsing bodies.

CATALOG = {
    "No rides available":   ("no_results",  "normal"),
    "Account not verified": ("unverified",  "refusal"),
    "Could not read store": ("store_fault", "fault"),
}

def classify(request, body):
    if not is_app_request(request) or body.get("status") != 0:
        return body, None
    field = "error_code" if request.route in ECHOES_ONE_TIME_CODE else "code"
    if field not in body:
        code, _ = CATALOG.get(body.get("message"), ("unclassified", "unknown"))
        body = {**body, field: code}   # add only: no key removed or changed
    code = body[field]
    return body, code if code in STABLE_CODES else None   # header gets stable codes only

A complete, runnable version with the baseline test is in this gist.

The monitor then counts only what is unclassified or uncoded. Everything else is a known answer with a name.

To stop the pile growing back, a test walks the source for status-0 sites and compares them with a committed baseline. A new site with no code and no catalog entry fails the build. The debt can shrink. It cannot grow.

Three things that bit

The hook was too greedy. Payment providers call routes on the same API, and a provider's callback body is the provider's contract, not mine. The classifier now applies only to requests that carry the app's session token header, and provider routes are excluded by name. That fix went in the same day as the hook.

code was already taken. Several endpoints return a one-time code in a field called code, and installed builds read it as exactly that. Put a refusal code there and an installed build reads it as the one-time code. On those routes the refusal goes in error_code, and the header copies only values from the stable list, so nothing that isn't a stable code reaches the access log through it.

The version gate could never open. The plan was to answer normal states with status 1 only for app builds at or above a minimum version, so older builds kept today's behaviour. I built it, tested it and merged it. Then it turned out the installed apps send no version. The gate compared against nothing and stayed shut.

It was replaced by a per-route switch: a list of route keys, empty by default. A listed route answers status 1 with the same keys and empty values. An unlisted route answers exactly as before. Both carry the stable code.

A feature flag keyed on a signal you have never seen in your own logs is a wish.

The telemetry that saw nothing

The mobile telemetry was written from a hook that runs at request shutdown. That hook runs before the buffered response is flushed, so it never saw the body.

It moved into the same output hook as the classifier and now records the envelope status and the code. The monitors count by code: on money routes an allowlist of normal-state codes is skipped, and anything unclassified, unknown or missing still counts.

Empty is not unreadable

One follow-up shows the pattern in small. The endpoint that lists a user's saved cards treated "this user has no cards" and "the card vault can't be read" alike.

  • No cards: status 1, an empty list, code no_results.
  • Vault unreadable: status 0, code unavailable, an honest message instead of the library's raw error text.

Before changing it I read the client sources to see which keys they read and how they type them. No key was removed.

What is live, and what isn't

  • The classifier, the catalog, the baseline test, the per-route switch, the telemetry change and the monitor changes are in production. So is the saved-cards split.
  • The switch is per route and off by default. Turning a route on is a config decision made route by route, so I'm not claiming a number here.
  • The next step is built and waiting in a release that is not in production yet: real faults on money paths answer a real 5xx (a store fault is a 503 with a retry hint) instead of 200 with status 0. The request still stops and nothing is written; only the HTTP answer changes. I'm not claiming that one until it ships.

Takeaways

  • Empty is a result. Treat it like one.
  • Normal state, refusal and fault are three different answers. Give each a name a machine can read.
  • Classify at one choke point, then fence it with a baseline so new unnamed failures fail the build.
  • Before you gate on a client signal, check the client actually sends it.
  • Read the client code before you touch a field. code meant two things and the apps only knew one.

200 OK with status 0 is Schrödinger's response: you don't know if it's dead until you open the body. Better to write the answer on the box.

Originally published at developer.ericgitangu.com. More engineering write-ups on the blog.

title: Why Enterprise CTOs Won't Deploy AI-Migrated Code (And How We Built 3-Way Shadow Testing in Go)
description:
Why Enterprise CTOs Won't Deploy AI-Migrated Code (And How We Built 3-Way Shadow Testing in Go)

By Vishal Raj • Live Cloud Demo: https://shadowdiff-demo.fly.dev/ • Open Source: https://github.com/vishalrajofficial/ShadowDiff

Every engineering leader running legacy systems has had the exact same thought over the past twelve months:

"We have a 12-year-old Java 7 Spring monolith / Python 2 Django app that everyone is terrified to touch. Why don't we feed it into Claude 3.7 / GPT-4 / Gemini, rewrite it in Go or FastAPI, and deploy it to Kubernetes next quarter?"

Teams try it. And initially, the results look miraculous. In a few afternoons, an AI coding assistant refactors thousands of lines of archaic boilerplate into idiomatic Go code. Unit test suites are generated. The code compiles. Staging health checks return 200 OK.

Then the engineering team approaches the VP of Engineering or CTO to cut over production traffic.

And the cutover is rejected.

Why? Because in enterprise finance, logistics, e-commerce, and healthcare backends, AI gets 95% of the refactoring right, but the remaining 5% of invisible contract deviations can cause catastrophic outages or silent data corruption.

Here is what that 5% looks like, why traditional testing cannot catch it, and how we built ShadowDiff—an open-source 3-way differential shadow testing engine with database side-effect diffing and automated regression test synthesis in Go.

1. The Anatomy of the 5% Failure Rate

When refactoring code manually, human engineers write integration tests for known assumptions. But AI-migrated code fails in ways humans never think to test for:

Case 1: Serialization Asymmetry

In Java, Jackson may omit null fields or serialize empty collections as {}. In Go, encoding/json serializes nil slices as null or omits them entirely with omitempty. If downstream client apps (mobile SDKs, legacy partner microservices) expect "items": [] and receive "items": null, client parsers crash.

Case 2: Numeric Float Precision Drift

A legacy Java service calculates billing discounts using BigDecimal with half-up rounding. The refactored Go service computes float64 discounts, creating subtle discrepancies (e.g. 14.50 vs 14.500000000000002). Both return HTTP 200, but downstream billing reconciliation triggers financial drift.

Case 3: Silent Database Mutation Corruption

The HTTP response body is identical: {"status": "success", "order_id": "ORD-1092"}. But under the hood, the legacy service wrapped writes inside BEGIN TRANSACTION ... COMMIT and wrote an entry to audit_logs, while the refactored service used an ORM with default autocommit and omitted the audit_logs insert. In a partial network partition, data is half-committed, and compliance auditability is broken.

Case 4: The ORM N+1 Query Loop Explosion

The legacy service used an optimized, hand-tuned raw SQL JOIN. The AI converted it to idiomatic ORM struct methods that loop over orders and query the user table one query per row. In staging with 10 records, latency is 4ms. In production with 100,000 orders, database connection pools exhaust in 20 seconds.

2. Why Traditional Shadow Testing Fails: The Noise Catastrophe

To catch these issues, teams attempt traffic shadowing (mirroring real production traffic to the refactored service in parallel).

However, traditional 2-way diffing immediately hits a brick wall: Alert Fatigue.

Every modern API returns non-deterministic fields: timestamps, ephemeral trace IDs, dynamic nonces, CSRF tokens, cache headers, and execution timestamps. When you diff the legacy service against the refactored service, 99% of requests differ purely because of runtime noise. Engineers spend entire weeks writing brittle regex ignore-lists, only to miss true bugs.

3. The Solution: Mathematical 3-Way Differential Noise Cancellation

To solve this, ShadowDiff implements the Diffy Model using twin baseline replicas:

  1. Baseline Runtime Noise: N = P1 (xor) P2. Any difference between two identical instances running the exact same legacy code (P1 and P2) is guaranteed to be non-deterministic noise.
  2. Raw Candidate Divergence: R = P1 (xor) S.
  3. Pure Semantic Regression: D = R \ N.

By mathematically subtracting the noise set N from candidate drifts R, ShadowDiff guarantees zero false alarms. If a timestamp diverges between P1 and P2, it is automatically suppressed when comparing P1 and S. Only genuine contract bugs reach developer triage.

4. Database Side-Effect & Mutation Interception

Responses returning 200 OK do not mean database integrity is preserved. ShadowDiff injects an immutable trace header (X-ShadowDiff-Trace-ID) across both mirrored requests and correlates executed SQL statements:

  • Missing Mutations: Flags when legacy writes to tables (e.g. audit_logs, ledger_entries) that the refactored code forgot to touch.
  • Transaction Boundary Leaks: Detects when legacy code operated inside atomic BEGIN...COMMIT blocks, but refactored code ran autocommit statements vulnerable to partial failures.
  • N+1 Query Explosions: Flags when refactored ORMs query relational tables in loops instead of batch joined queries.

5. Safe Mutating Traffic: Ephemeral Copy-on-Write (CoW) Sandboxing

How do you safely shadow mutating traffic (POST, PUT, DELETE) without charging customer credit cards twice or polluting the database?

ShadowDiff supports Ephemeral Copy-on-Write Database Sandboxing:

  1. Transactional Savepoint Rollbacks: Injects boundary headers ensuring shadow mutations execute within a transactional savepoint that automatically rolls back when the shadow request completes.
  2. Ephemeral Per-Run Schema: Clones table definitions into a disposable schema and drops it immediately upon request completion.
  3. Serverless Cloud CoW Branching: Coordinates via API with Neon / Supabase serverless PostgreSQL to provision zero-storage copy-on-write database branches on demand.

6. Closing the Loop: Autonomous GitHub PR Bot & CI/CD Gating CLI

When a genuine bug is isolated, ShadowDiff automates the fix lifecycle:

  • Autonomous GitHub PR Bot: Prompts Google Gemini (gemini-2.0-flash) with the raw requests, side-by-side JSON contract drifts, and SQL execution watermarks. Gemini synthesizes a turnkey Go integration test reproducing the exact edge case. The GitHub Bot creates a branch, commits the test file, and automatically opens a rich Pull Request with visual diff tables and local verification commands.
  • CI/CD Shadow Gating CLI (shadowdiff gate): Teams can block deployments in GitHub Actions or GitLab CI before promoting AI-refactored code if parity drops below 100%, or an N+1 query loop or missing SQL write is detected.

7. Try the Live Cloud Demo

You can interact with ShadowDiff right now in your browser without installing anything:

  • Live Cloud Sandbox: https://shadowdiff-demo.fly.dev/
  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/vishalrajofficial/ShadowDiff

8. Summary: How to Safely Modernize Legacy Backends

AI is the most powerful code translation tool in history. But code conversion without runtime contract verification is reckless. By combining Envoy wire-speed traffic mirroring, mathematical 3-way differential noise cancellation, SQL side-effect mutation diffing, ephemeral Copy-on-Write database sandboxing, and autonomous AI regression test synthesis, engineering teams can finally give CTOs the mathematical certainty they need to deploy AI-refactored backends into production with confidence.

title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash now available on AI Gateway
description:
Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash from Google is now available on AI Gateway. Generate videos from text prompts with one API key and no separate Google account.

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates 3–15 second videos with native audio and edits 3–15 second source clips with up to six reference images. Extend videos by 3–10 seconds per call, up to 30 seconds total, or refine generated clips in follow-up calls using previousInteractionId. Output supports 360p, 720p, 1080p, and 4K in 16:9 or 9:16. Use generateText or streamText in AI SDK to receive the generated video as a file.

Generate a video

Use google/gemini-omni-1.2-flash as the model name. This example generates a three-second, 360p clip and saves it as video.mp4:

Receive video in a streaming response

With streamText, read fullStream to handle generated files as they arrive. The video is delivered as a completed file:

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

title: Ai Can Write React Code. Can You Actually Understand It?
description:
AI Is Making React Developers Faster. But Are They Becoming Better Developers?

AI is making React developers faster. But there's a growing problem: many developers are shipping code they don't fully understand.

Let's be honest.

Writing React code has never been easier.

You can ask ChatGPT to build a dashboard, create reusable components, implement custom hooks, integrate APIs, or even refactor an entire application.

A few seconds later, you have code that looks professional.

Clean formatting. TypeScript types. Reusable components. Maybe even some optimizations.

But here's the uncomfortable question:

Do you actually understand the code you're shipping?

AI isn't necessarily making developers worse. However, using AI without understanding its output can create a dangerous illusion of productivity.

Let's look at some common examples.

1. The useEffect Addiction

One of the most common problems in AI-generated React code is unnecessary useEffect usage.

Ask an AI tool to synchronize two pieces of state, and there's a good chance it will suggest something like this:

import { useState, useEffect } from "react";

function UserProfile({ user }) {
  const [fullName, setFullName] = useState("");

  useEffect(() => {
    setFullName(`${user.firstName} ${user.lastName}`);
  }, [user]);

  return <h2>{fullName}</h2>;
}

Does it work?

Yes.

Is it necessary?

Not at all.

The value of fullName can be calculated directly during rendering:

function UserProfile({ user }) {
  const fullName = `${user.firstName} ${user.lastName}`;

  return <h2>{fullName}</h2>;
}

We don't need an additional state variable, an effect, or an extra render.

This is a simple example, but it highlights an important issue:

AI can generate code that works without necessarily choosing the best React approach.

2. More Components Don't Always Mean Better Architecture

AI tools often love abstraction.

Ask them to build a simple user card, and you might end up with:

  • UserCard
  • UserCardHeader
  • UserCardAvatar
  • UserCardDetails
  • UserCardActions
  • UserCardContainer

Component reuse is important in React.

But abstraction without a real purpose creates unnecessary complexity.

A good component structure should make your application easier to understand, maintain, and extend.

Not just increase the number of files in your project.

Good architecture isn't about writing more code. It's about managing complexity.

3. The TypeScript Illusion

TypeScript is supposed to help us catch mistakes before runtime.

But AI-generated TypeScript code sometimes looks strongly typed while hiding important problems.

For example:

function getUserData(data: any) {
  return data.profile.name;
}

This compiles, but what happens if profile doesn't exist?

TypeScript can't protect us from a problem we've explicitly told it to ignore.

A better approach is to define the expected data structure:

type User = {
  profile: {
    name: string;
  };
};

function getUserData(data: User) {
  return data.profile.name;
}

The problem isn't that AI uses any.

The problem is accepting weak typing without questioning it.

TypeScript should describe the actual structure of our data, not simply make compiler errors disappear.

4. Performance Optimization Without Understanding Performance

Another common AI habit is adding useMemo, useCallback, and React.memo almost everywhere.

Consider this example:

const expensiveValue = useMemo(() => {
  return items.length * 2;
}, [items]);

Is this optimization necessary?

Probably not.

The calculation is extremely cheap.

Memoization has its own costs and introduces additional complexity.

React developers should understand when optimization is actually useful instead of treating every memoization hook as a performance improvement.

Sometimes the best optimization is simply writing simpler code.

5. The Copy-Paste Developer

This is probably the biggest problem.

Imagine asking AI to implement a custom hook.

It generates 80 lines of code.

You copy it, run the application, and everything works.

But then someone asks:

  • Why did you use useRef here?
  • Why does this effect have an empty dependency array?
  • What happens if the component unmounts?
  • Why did you choose this state management approach?
  • Can you explain the data flow?

And suddenly, things get complicated.

If you cannot explain the code you're maintaining, you're not really in control of that code.

You're just depending on something you don't fully understand.

And that becomes a serious problem when your application grows.

6. AI Doesn't Know Your Entire Project

AI-generated code can look technically correct while being completely wrong for your application.

It might:

  • Introduce a dependency you don't need.
  • Ignore your existing component architecture.
  • Duplicate functionality that already exists.
  • Use outdated patterns.
  • Miss important edge cases.
  • Create security or data-handling problems.

A code snippet can be correct in isolation and still be a bad decision in your project.

This is why context matters.

Before accepting generated code, you should understand your existing architecture, conventions, and requirements.

7. So, Should React Developers Stop Using AI?

Absolutely not.

That would be the wrong conclusion.

AI is an incredibly useful development tool.

It can help with:

  • Exploring unfamiliar APIs.
  • Understanding complex concepts.
  • Generating boilerplate code.
  • Writing tests.
  • Refactoring existing components.
  • Finding potential bugs.
  • Exploring alternative implementations.

The goal isn't to write every line manually.

The goal is to remain responsible for the code you ship.

I think the best developers will be those who combine two abilities:

  1. Knowing how to use AI effectively.
  2. Knowing how to question, evaluate, and improve its output.

These skills complement each other.

But one cannot replace the other.

Final Thoughts

React development is not just about producing JSX.

It's about understanding rendering, state management, component architecture, data flow, performance, and maintainability.

AI can help you write code faster.

But it cannot automatically give you the engineering judgment needed to decide whether that code belongs in your application.

Don't measure your productivity by how much code AI generates. Measure it by how much quality software you can confidently build and maintain.

And here's a question I'd genuinely like to discuss:

If AI generates 90% of your React code, but you cannot explain how 30% of it works, are you actually becoming a better developer?

I'd love to hear different perspectives from the React community.

title: 5 Ways to Generate Presigned File Download URLs: Tenant Retention Rules
description:
5 Ways to Generate Presigned File Download URLs: Tenant Retention Rules

Short answer: Generate a short-lived presigned file download URL only after checking the tenant-scoped export record, and pair it with an explicit deletion schedule.

The least complicated design is a short-lived presigned download URL backed by an explicit retention record. The export service decides who may request a link, the object store decides whether the signature is valid, and a deletion worker removes the image and its export metadata on a known schedule. That division matters more than the particular S3-compatible implementation.

A logistics system usually has two different things to retain: the product image and the generated export. They should not inherit the same lifetime by accident. A product photo might support a dispute for 30 days; a CSV or ZIP assembled for a tenant might be useful for 24 hours. The download URL should live for minutes, not become a second retention policy.

What is the bill actually made of?

For this workflow, storage cost is dominated by retained bytes and request activity, not by the few lines that sign a URL. A useful first estimate is:

retained gigabytes = daily uploaded image gigabytes x image retention days + daily export gigabytes x export retention days

Suppose a carrier portal receives 18 GB of product images each day, keeps source images for 30 days, and produces 6 GB of tenant exports each day. If exports stay for 24 hours, the rough retained set is 540 GB of images plus 6 GB of exports, before replicas, metadata, and incomplete multipart uploads. Letting exports sit for 30 days changes the second term to 180 GB.

That is the change I would make first: shorten export retention and record the decision, rather than weakening image quality or hiding storage behind a larger quota. The trade-off is concrete. A dispatcher who requests an old export may need to generate it again, and an incident investigator may have to rely on audit metadata instead of the original archive.

Presigned URLs do not delete objects. They grant temporary access to an object key under the permissions and signing rules of the issuer. Deletion needs its own lifecycle: an expiration timestamp, a worker or lifecycle rule, and a reconciliation path for work that stopped halfway through.

How do I generate a presigned URL for file download?

A link lifetime should be derived from the user action, not copied from object retention. For a browser download, 10 minutes is often enough to request the file, follow a redirect if the client uses one, and retry a transient network failure. A large export on a slow warehouse connection may need longer. The value belongs in configuration with an upper bound.

The request path should look roughly like this:

  1. Authenticate the operator and resolve the tenant from server-side authorization data.
  2. Load an export record whose tenant, object key, status, and expiration are all checked together.
  3. Sign a GET request for that exact key with a short lifetime.
  4. Return the URL without exposing storage credentials or allowing a caller to choose an arbitrary key.
  5. Write an audit event for the request, not the secret URL itself.

The tenant check is the important part. A URL can be cryptographically valid and still be the wrong URL for the caller if the application selected an object by an untrusted filename or guessed key. Object names are identifiers, not authorization.

Here is deliberately small Python-shaped pseudocode for the decision boundary. It shows the checks that belong before a generic S3-compatible signing call; the storage SDK call is intentionally represented by an interface so the policy does not become coupled to one library.

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

MAX_LINK_AGE = timedelta(minutes=15)

def make_download_link(actor, export_id, repository, signer, now=None):
    now = now or datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    export = repository.find_export(export_id)

    if export is None or export.tenant_id != actor.tenant_id:
        raise PermissionError("export is not available")
    if export.status != "ready" or export.expires_at <= now:
        raise FileNotFoundError("export is not downloadable")

    lifetime = min(export.requested_link_age, MAX_LINK_AGE)
    return signer.presign_get(
        bucket=export.bucket,
        key=export.object_key,
        expires_in=int(lifetime.total_seconds()),
    )

The same boundary applies in a Node.js service: resolve the record, authorize the tenant, cap the lifetime, then call the SDK's presigning helper. The syntax changes; the security decision does not.

What can go wrong after the URL is issued?

The common failure is treating a successful signing call as a completed download. It is only a handoff. The browser may have no CORS permission to read the response, a proxy may reject a large response, or the object may be deleted while the link is still valid. A client that needs to trigger a download without reading response bytes can use a normal browser navigation; a client that reads the response from another origin needs an explicit CORS policy, including the methods and exposed headers it actually uses. The MDN CORS guidance is a good reference for the browser side, but it does not replace authorization in the export service.

A second trap is logging the full URL. Query parameters in a presigned URL are bearer credentials until they expire. Application logs, browser history, support screenshots, analytics referrers, and tracing attributes can all extend the audience beyond the original tenant user. Log the export ID, tenant ID, actor ID, and expiration time. Redact the URL.

A third trap is key reuse. If a new export overwrites an old object key, a link issued for the old export can point at new bytes. Use an immutable export identifier in the object key, or make replacement impossible. It is easier to reason about exports/{tenant_id}/{export_id}.zip than about latest.zip.

How should deletion and recovery work?

Keep three timestamps: created_at, available_until, and deleted_at. available_until is the business retention decision. The deletion process can run after that time, but the record should say when the object was actually removed. This makes a delayed worker visible without pretending that a policy clock and a storage operation are the same event.

I would use an idempotent deletion job with a small state machine: ready, delete_requested, deleted, and delete_failed. A retry must be safe. A missing object should usually converge to deleted, while an authorization or service failure should remain visible for retry and alerting. Keep the audit record after deleting the bytes; it is the evidence that the export existed and who requested it.

The job also needs a reconciliation query. It should find export rows past available_until that are not deleted, plus objects under the export prefix that have no matching row. The first set catches failed work. The second catches abandoned generation paths. Do not make reconciliation depend on a single in-memory queue.

There is a deliberate loss here. After deletion, support cannot download the old archive just because an audit event exists. That is the point of the retention decision, not a defect. If legal hold or claims handling requires preservation, represent that as an explicit hold that changes available_until; do not ask operators to copy files into an undocumented bucket.

What should the test and operations surface prove?

A useful test matrix follows the policy, not just the happy path. Test a valid tenant, a different tenant, a missing export, an expired export, a non-ready export, a link past the maximum lifetime, and a key that has already been deleted. Test the browser path separately from a programmatic cross-origin read. The MDN CORS guidance is a good reference for the browser side, but it does not replace authorization in the export service.

For operations, measure the facts that explain a bad download:

  • link requests allowed and denied, grouped by reason
  • export generation time and byte size
  • download response failures by status and tenant
  • objects past available_until
  • deletion retries and orphaned objects

Do not put signed query strings into metrics labels. High-cardinality secrets are a security problem and a noisy dashboard.
A release check should also verify that the bucket policy, CORS configuration, worker identity, and clock synchronization are consistent with the application assumptions. Signature verification is time-sensitive. A few minutes of clock drift can look like an authorization bug, while an overly broad CORS rule can turn a convenient browser download into an unintended data exposure.

The practical decision rule is compact: keep source images for the business evidence period, keep generated exports only as long as the workflow needs them, issue links for the shortest credible transfer window, and make every deletion observable. That gives a tenant-scoped download flow without allowing a temporary URL to quietly become permanent access.

Further reading

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/ShareObjectPreSignedURL.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html
