title: Your Database Isn't Slow, It's Waiting: 5 Counter-Intuitive Truths About PostgreSQL Lock Contention
description:
Your Database Isn't Slow, It's Waiting: 5 Counter-Intuitive Truths About PostgreSQL Lock Contention

When database latency spikes suddenly, backend engineers routinely jump to standard performance troubleshooting: analyzing execution plans, looking for missing indexes, or trying to refactor seemingly expensive queries. However, this reflex often misdiagnoses the true underlying bottleneck.

The core reality of database performance is that a struggling database often isn't performing complex, CPU-intensive calculations at all—it is simply waiting on a locked resource. Relational databases rely on locks to maintain data consistency during concurrent updates. When these locks are held longer than expected, incoming queries stall, creating a perception of poor execution performance.

Understanding the mechanics of PostgreSQL lock contention, distinguishing waiting states from active execution, and knowing how to diagnose lock dependencies are essential skills for maintaining scalable systems. This article explores five counter-intuitive truths about PostgreSQL lock contention, common diagnostic traps, and operational strategies for prevention.

Takeaway 1: Your "Slow Query" Might Not Be Doing Any Work At All

When a transaction updates a record in PostgreSQL, it acquires a row-level lock to prevent concurrent modifications from corrupting data. As long as that initial transaction remains open, the lock stays active.

There is a fundamental difference between slow query execution and lock contention:

  • Slow Query Execution: The database engine is actively using system resources (CPU, I/O) to process work, such as scanning large tables or performing complex joins.
  • Lock Contention: The query has been sent to the database, but execution cannot proceed because it is waiting for a conflicting lock held by another transaction to be released.

When Transaction A updates a customer record and holds the row lock, subsequent requests—such as Transaction B and Transaction C attempting to update or execute conflicting operations on that same record—are forced to queue up. This creates a cascading backlog of stalled requests.

Crucially, lock contention does not mean that every query touching the table—or even the specific row—will block. PostgreSQL's Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) architecture ensures that standard read operations (SELECT) do not block on row update locks, and write operations do not block non-conflicting reads. Contention arises strictly when concurrent operations request incompatible lock modes on the same database target—such as multiple concurrent UPDATE or DELETE statements targeting the same tuple, or explicit row-locking clauses like SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.

"A slow query is not always doing expensive work. Sometimes it is simply waiting for someone else's transaction to finish."

Developers frequently misdiagnose lock contention because traditional latency metrics measure elapsed execution time from request start to completion. Because a waiting query remains open while stalled, execution time metrics register it as "slow," masking the reality that the query spent its entire lifespan dormant, waiting for an upstream lock release rather than executing database operations.

Takeaway 2: The Silent Killer Called "Idle in Transaction"

One of the most dangerous states for a PostgreSQL session to enter is state = 'idle in transaction'.

In PostgreSQL, idle in transaction means a backend process has executed a BEGIN statement and potentially run one or more queries, but it is currently waiting for the application client to send the next command. No active SQL queries are being processed on the database server during this pause.

Consider a common production incident sequence:

  1. Transaction A opens a database transaction (BEGIN) and executes an UPDATE on a row, successfully acquiring a row-level lock.
  2. Before sending a COMMIT or ROLLBACK, the application logic performs non-database work—such as executing an external API call, running complex application code, or hitting an unhandled error/pause.
  3. While the application is paused or stalled, the database connection sits in an idle in transaction state. Even though the database session is executing zero queries and consuming virtually no CPU, it continues to hold all acquired row-level locks. Subsequent transactions (Transaction B, Transaction C) attempting to modify the same resource immediately stall, building up latency across the application stack.

Takeaway 3: Increasing Connection Pools Can Make the Incident Worse

When latency rises and requests begin timing out, a common operational impulse is to scale up the application's database connection pool to handle the backlog. During a lock contention incident, this reaction is a trap that often exacerbates the failure.

It is vital to distinguish between these two failure modes:

  • Connection Pool Exhaustion: The application runs out of available database client connections because all pool connections are actively serving legitimate traffic.
  • Lock Contention: Database connections are stalled behind a single blocking transaction that holds a required lock.

When lock contention is the root cause, adding more connections to the pool does not speed up processing. Instead, it simply opens more pathways for incoming application requests to enter the database, attempt the conflicting operation, and join the waiting queue behind the primary blocking process.

Rather than resolving the issue, expanding the pool causes:

  • Rapid occupation of newly added connections.
  • Compounded latency as more application worker threads stall.
  • Cascading application-level timeouts across dependent services.

Takeaway 4: PostgreSQL Has Built-In Detectives for Unmasking Blockers

PostgreSQL provides system views and diagnostic functions to inspect active session states and expose lock contention: pg_stat_activity and pg_locks.

High-Level Inspection with pg_stat_activity

The pg_stat_activity system view offers real-time insight into process states across backend engines. Key fields include:

  • pid: The process ID of the backend session.
  • state: The current status of the session (e.g., active, idle in transaction).
  • query_start: The timestamp when the currently executing query began.
  • xact_start: The timestamp when the current transaction started.
  • wait_event_type & wait_event: Indicates if and why a backend is waiting (e.g., wait_event_type = 'Lock').
  • query: The text of the most recent or currently active query.

Deep Lock Inspection with pg_locks

While pg_stat_activity shows session status, pg_locks exposes the exact lock hierarchy and resource targets. pg_locks details every lock held or awaited by active processes, categorized by locktype (such as relation, tuple, or transactionid), lock modes (e.g., RowExclusiveLock acquired during updates versus AccessExclusiveLock acquired during schema migrations), and the Boolean status granted.

When diagnosing complex lock trees, joining pg_locks with pg_stat_activity allows database architects to map explicit target dependencies. By filtering for records where granted = false, engineers can identify blocked processes, trace their required target resource (relation or tuple), and match it to the session where granted = true for that exact resource and conflicting lock mode.

Query 1: Identifying Blocking and Blocked Sessions 

SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocking_pids, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;

Query 2: Tracking Idle Transactions Holding Locks 

SELECT pid, state, xact_start, now() - xact_start AS transaction_duration, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
ORDER BY xact_start;

Takeaway 5: Session Termination Is a Last Resort, Not a Solution

When a blocking process brings down database throughput, forcefully terminating the backend session (e.g., via pg_terminate_backend) is often attempted. However, session termination carries distinct architectural risks and must not be treated as a default operational fix.

Risks of Terminating Sessions

  • Transaction Rollbacks: Terminating a session forces an immediate rollback of the active transaction, which can leave application workflows in inconsistent or uncoordinated states.
  • Application-Side Consequences: The client application communicating over that connection receives sudden connection errors, potentially leading to unhandled retries or broken state machines.

Prevention Strategies and Operational Safeguards

Rather than relying on manual intervention during outages, production environments should enforce operational safeguards:

  • Keep Transactions Short: Scope transactions strictly to essential database operations to minimize lock hold duration.
  • Remove External Logic from Transactions: Avoid making external API calls or executing non-database application logic inside open database transactions.
  • Explicit Transaction Termination: Ensure client application code paths guaranteed execution of explicit COMMIT or ROLLBACK commands under all conditions, including error states.
  • Configure Transaction Timeouts: Use built-in database timeouts to automatically mitigate abandoned transactions. Specifically, configure idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to automatically terminate sessions that remain idle within an open transaction beyond a specified threshold.
  • Proactive Monitoring: Instrument continuous monitoring for transaction age, lock wait counts, and blocking sessions before they escalate into outages.
  • Establish Operational Protocols: Create strict, documented procedures before manually terminating any database backend process.

Conclusion: The Mental Shift Every Engineer Needs

Managing relational database performance effectively requires a fundamental distinction between query execution efficiency and concurrency management. Adding indexes and rewriting SQL queries will not resolve system slowdowns if the database spends its time waiting on concurrent lock holders.

Before writing a new index or refactoring query logic during a latency incident, engineers should adopt a simple diagnostic step:

Before optimizing a slow query, check whether it's actually waiting for a lock.

Originally published on gokairo.dev.

title: A stab at superpowers
description:
I've been using AI workflows to build applications for a little over one year now. I decided, for the first time, to use a pre-baked industry methodology: superpowers.

Superpowers caught my attention because it resembles how I currently work with AI. I plan my work and chunk it down into smaller deliverables, which I execute through tdd.

I have a few dimensions I wanna assess out of this experiment:

  • the end result feature correctness and UX;
  • the generated code;
  • cost, both time and tokens;
  • ergonomics: how I feel about this workflow;

Running the experiment

I used my agentic hobby project, conveyor, as the guinea pig for this. Conveyor is a TUI that lets me see which stage of the SDLC my iterations are: Pull Request, merge queue, merged or deployed. A feature it lacks is tabs. I wanna be able to cycle through PRs I wrote and PRs I need to review, for instance.

To keep it simple, this iteration focused on adding tabs just for the PRs column.

I gave two distinct Claude Code sessions running Sonnet 5.5 on medium the same initial prompt:

Let's plan a feature: tabs. Right now each column shows a fixed view based on its config. I would like to add the ability of having multiple configs for each column, and you'd cycle through them by pressing a key that defaults to . I'm ok breaking the current tab behaviour. I envision these tabs appearing at the top of the column. The currently selected one gets a visible highlight.

Both got the PR through the automatic review cycle without any further interaction with me, and in about 40 minutes I had two working versions of the same feature. I was excited to try them out!

Artifacts & Results

Artifact Current workflow Superpowers
Issue/plan https://github.com/piacsek/conveyor/issues/79 https://github.com/piacsek/conveyor/issues/80
Pull request https://github.com/piacsek/conveyor/pull/82 https://github.com/piacsek/conveyor/pull/81
Screenshot
Cost Current workflow Superpowers
Build wall time 41min 42min
Token cost - main session 104.9k 196.7k
Token cost - subagents 483k 1.28M
Token cost - total 587.9k 1.477M

My thoughts

Both implementations worked first time! And both of them kept retrocompatibility with the existing configuration schema.

However, I must say that I'm intrigued. My current workflow beat superpowers in all the dimensions I was interested in analysing: it basically took the same time for almost a third of the token cost to produce an outcome I enjoyed more.

  • UI: I don't like the tab number showing up, it's confusing since it's so close to the PR count above;
  • Code: I prefer the Tab abstraction over the View one - it clicks faster in my mind;
  • Ergonomics: To my surprise, my current workflow asked me more questions than superpower's brainstorming skill: 5x1 - I felt more in the loop;

I wasn't expecting such one-sided result. If you've used superpowers, please comment how you operate it! I'm interested in experimenting more with it.

Thank you for reading, have a great day!

title: Storybook for Beginners: Build Your UI Components in Isolation
description:
Storybook is a tool that lets you build and test your UI components one at a time, outside your app. Instead of clicking through five screens to see a button in its loading state, you open Storybook, pick the button, and switch it to loading with one click. It turns UI development from a maze into a catalogue.

The idea is simple: every component gets a story, which is a small file that renders the component with specific props. A button gets stories for its default, disabled, loading, and large variants. A card gets stories for short text, long text, and no image. You see them all in one place, in a browser, with controls to change the props live.

A first Storybook story looks like this:

// Button.stories.js
import { Button } from './Button';

export default {
  title: 'Components/Button',
  component: Button,
};

export const Primary = {
  args: { label: 'Save', primary: true },
};

export const Disabled = {
  args: { label: 'Save', disabled: true },
};

Open Storybook and you can flip between Primary and Disabled, change the label in the controls panel, and see the result instantly. That is the whole workflow — and it is dramatically faster than testing components inside a full app.

Storybook also helps your team. Designers can browse the component catalogue without running the app. New developers can see every variant of every component in one place. And you can add accessibility checks and visual regression tests on top, so a change that breaks a component's look gets caught automatically.

The limits are honest. Storybook adds setup and maintenance — you have to write stories, and keep them in sync with your components. For a tiny project with three components, it is overkill. And it does not replace real testing: a component that looks right in isolation can still break when it is used in a real page.

Start today with one step: pick your most-used component, write two stories for it — the normal case and one edge case — and open Storybook. When you see both variants side by side, you will understand why teams that use it never go back.

title: From a Static Site to Multi-Region DR: 12 AWS Reference Architectures, Explained
description:
Most AWS diagrams I find online fall into one of two groups. Some are simple enough to fit on a slide but skip the details that break in production. Others are complete reference architectures with forty icons and no clear starting point.

I wanted something in between, so I built a catalog of 12 AWS reference architectures. It starts with a static site and grows one concern at a time until it reaches multi-region disaster recovery. Each diagram is a single self-contained HTML page with the services involved, the numbered information flow, comments on the parts that are easy to misread, and one practical note to consider before you build it.

  • 🌐 Live catalog: https://josesaid.github.io/aws-architecture-diagrams/
  • 💻 Source: https://github.com/josesaid/aws-architecture-diagrams

This article walks through the 12 architectures, explains why each one exists, and shows two of them as Java infrastructure code with the AWS CDK.

The problem: knowing which services go together

AWS has more than 200 services. Learning what each one does is the easy part. The hard part is knowing which services go together for a specific problem and in what order a request moves through them.

That gap shows up in familiar ways:

  • A static site ends up with a public S3 bucket because nobody explained Origin Access Control.
  • An SQS consumer processes the same message twice because the visibility timeout is shorter than the Lambda timeout.
  • A RAG assistant gives poor answers because the embeddings at query time come from a different model than the ones used during ingestion.
  • A disaster recovery plan exists on paper, but nobody defined the RTO and RPO, so nobody can say whether it is good enough.

None of these are exotic. They are what happens when you know the services but not how they fit together. Each diagram in the catalog targets one of these combinations and calls out the detail that tends to go wrong.

How each diagram is structured

Every page follows the same layout so you can compare them quickly:

  1. Summary: one paragraph describing what the architecture solves.
  2. Services: the AWS services involved, as chips.
  3. Diagram: the services, with numbered arrows for user traffic and dashed lines for configuration (for example, ACM providing a certificate to CloudFront).
  4. Comments: what the diagram simplifies and why.
  5. Information flow: the numbered steps a request follows, one service at a time.
  6. Note to consider: the operational detail that usually causes trouble.

The pages are plain HTML and CSS with no build step and no framework, so they load instantly and can be hosted anywhere. The catalog itself runs on GitHub Pages.

The 12 architectures

1. Static HTML site

Route 53 → CloudFront (ACM certificate) → private S3 bucket with OAC.

The baseline. Route 53 resolves the domain, CloudFront serves the site over HTTPS, and S3 stores the files in a bucket that only CloudFront can read. Users never reach the bucket directly.

Note to consider: if users see old content after a deploy, CloudFront is serving cached objects. Create an invalidation or wait for the TTL to expire.

2. Layered security for a static site

Diagram 1 + AWS WAF + AWS Shield + AWS KMS.

The same site with protection layers. WAF evaluates every request against managed rules (OWASP, bots, rate limits), Shield Standard mitigates DDoS attacks at no extra cost, OAC keeps the bucket private, and KMS encrypts the objects at rest.

Note to consider: WAF is billed per Web ACL, per rule and per million requests. Start with managed rules and a rate limit, and review the logs before adding custom rules.

3. Automated deployment (CI/CD)

Source bucket → CodePipeline → CodeBuild → site bucket + CloudFront invalidation.

A code change triggers the pipeline. CodeBuild installs dependencies, runs the tests and builds the site, then publishes it and invalidates the cache. Using two separate buckets, one for the source and one for the published site, prevents uncompiled code from going live.

Note to consider: if the tests fail, the previous site stays live. Turn on S3 versioning so you can roll back quickly.

4. Dynamic site with ALB, ECS and RDS

CloudFront → ALB → ECS Fargate (private subnets) → RDS, with static files from S3.

The first architecture with server-side logic. CloudFront splits the traffic: dynamic requests go to the load balancer and static assets come from S3. Only the ALB is exposed, and RDS has no public access.

Note to consider: the RDS security group should accept traffic only from the ECS security group. Multi-AZ keeps the database available when an availability zone fails.

5. Serverless site with login and API

Amplify Hosting + Cognito + API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB.

Cognito issues JWT tokens, API Gateway validates them with a Cognito authorizer, and Lambda only runs business logic on top of DynamoDB. No servers to patch.

Note to consider: define Cognito user groups from the start so you can control permissions without changing the authentication code later.

6. Asynchronous processing with SQS

API Gateway → SQS (+ dead-letter queue) → Lambda → DynamoDB, with notifications via SNS.

Requests are accepted fast and processed later. If Lambda is slow or fails, messages wait in the queue instead of being lost. Messages that keep failing go to a dead-letter queue.

Note to consider: the SQS visibility timeout must be longer than the maximum Lambda execution time. Otherwise the same message gets processed twice. The Java section below shows how to set it.

7. Events and orchestration with Step Functions

API Gateway → EventBridge → Step Functions → Lambda (validate, charge) → Aurora Serverless v2.

EventBridge decouples the producer of an event from its consumers. Step Functions stores the state of each execution and retries failed steps with backoff, so the order workflow stays easy to audit.

Note to consider: Standard workflows suit long-running, auditable processes. Express workflows cost less for high volumes of short executions, but they do not keep execution history the same way.

8. Real time with AppSync and DynamoDB Streams

AppSync (GraphQL) → DynamoDB → Streams → Lambda → AppSync subscriptions.

Changes reach every connected client without polling. AppSync manages the WebSocket subscriptions for you.

Note to consider: subscriptions are billed per connection and per message. Use subscription filters so each client receives only the events it needs.

9. Data and analytics on a data lake

Applications → Data Firehose → S3 (data lake) → Glue Catalog → Athena → QuickSight.

Firehose batches the records into S3, Glue keeps the table catalog, Athena queries the files with SQL, and QuickSight builds the dashboards. Organize the bucket in layers (raw and curated) and partition by date, because Athena charges for the data it scans.

Note to consider: validate the partitions and the Glue schema before building dashboards. A badly defined table returns wrong results without raising an error.

10. Generative AI with RAG on Amazon Bedrock

API Gateway → Lambda → OpenSearch Serverless (vector search) → Bedrock, with documents ingested from S3.

The model does not know your documents. Lambda retrieves the relevant chunks from OpenSearch and sends them to a Bedrock model together with the question. Embeddings must come from the same model during ingestion and at query time.

Note to consider: cost grows with the amount of context you send. Limit the number and size of the retrieved chunks.

11. Managed Kubernetes with EKS

Route 53 → ALB (created by the AWS Load Balancer Controller) → EKS pods → RDS/Aurora, images from ECR.

AWS manages the control plane, and the pods run on worker nodes in private subnets. An Ingress resource creates the ALB for you.

Note to consider: set CPU and memory requests and limits on every pod. Without them, the scheduler cannot spread the load well, and one pod can starve the others.

12. Multi-region and disaster recovery

Route 53 failover + health checks → ECS in us-east-1 (primary) and us-west-2 (secondary) → Aurora Global Database.

Route 53 sends traffic to the primary region while its health checks pass and fails over to the secondary when they do not. Aurora Global Database replicates the data across regions, typically with under one second of lag.

Note to consider: define your RTO and RPO before you choose a strategy. Active-active lowers RTO but roughly doubles compute cost. Pilot light or warm standby cost less but take longer to recover.

From diagram to code: two architectures in Java with the AWS CDK

A diagram is only useful if you can build it. The AWS CDK lets you define the same infrastructure in Java, so the security decisions in the diagram live in typed, reviewable code.

Diagram 1: a private bucket behind CloudFront with OAC

A common mistake is to make the bucket public and point CloudFront at the S3 website endpoint:

// ❌ Common mistake: public bucket, reachable without CloudFront
Bucket site = Bucket.Builder.create(this, "SiteBucket")
        .publicReadAccess(true)
        .blockPublicAccess(BlockPublicAccess.BLOCK_ACLS)
        .websiteIndexDocument("index.html")
        .build();

Anyone can then skip CloudFront, and with it your WAF rules, your HTTPS redirect and your caching. The diagram's version keeps the bucket fully private and lets only CloudFront read it through Origin Access Control:

import software.amazon.awscdk.Stack;
import software.amazon.awscdk.StackProps;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.cloudfront.BehaviorOptions;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.cloudfront.Distribution;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.cloudfront.ViewerProtocolPolicy;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.cloudfront.origins.S3BucketOrigin;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.s3.BlockPublicAccess;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.s3.Bucket;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.s3.BucketEncryption;
import software.constructs.Construct;

public class StaticSiteStack extends Stack {

    public StaticSiteStack(Construct scope, String id, StackProps props) {
        super(scope, id, props);

        // ✅ Private bucket: no public access, TLS only, versioned for rollbacks
        Bucket site = Bucket.Builder.create(this, "SiteBucket")
                .blockPublicAccess(BlockPublicAccess.BLOCK_ALL)
                .encryption(BucketEncryption.S3_MANAGED)
                .enforceSsl(true)
                .versioned(true)
                .build();

        // CloudFront reads the bucket through Origin Access Control (OAC).
        // The CDK adds the bucket policy that allows only this distribution.
        Distribution.Builder.create(this, "SiteCdn")
                .defaultBehavior(BehaviorOptions.builder()
                        .origin(S3BucketOrigin.withOriginAccessControl(site))
                        .viewerProtocolPolicy(ViewerProtocolPolicy.REDIRECT_TO_HTTPS)
                        .build())
                .defaultRootObject("index.html")
                .build();
    }
}

Versioning on the bucket is what makes the "roll back quickly" note in diagram 3 possible.

Diagram 6: an SQS consumer that does not process messages twice

The duplicate-processing bug from diagram 6 usually looks like this:

// ❌ Common mistake: default visibility timeout (30 s) with a 60 s Lambda.
// While Lambda is still working, the message becomes visible again
// and a second invocation picks it up.
Queue orders = new Queue(this, "Orders");

The fix is to make the visibility timeout clearly longer than the function timeout (AWS recommends at least six times) and to add a dead-letter queue for messages that keep failing:

import software.amazon.awscdk.Duration;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.lambda.Code;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.lambda.Function;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.lambda.Runtime;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.lambda.eventsources.SqsEventSource;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.sqs.DeadLetterQueue;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.sqs.Queue;

// Messages that fail 3 times are kept here for 14 days for inspection
Queue dlq = Queue.Builder.create(this, "OrdersDlq")
        .retentionPeriod(Duration.days(14))
        .build();

Function worker = Function.Builder.create(this, "OrderWorker")
        .runtime(Runtime.JAVA_21)
        .handler("com.example.orders.OrderWorker::handleRequest")
        .code(Code.fromAsset("target/order-worker.jar"))
        .memorySize(1024)
        .timeout(Duration.seconds(30))
        .build();

// ✅ Visibility timeout = 6 x the Lambda timeout
Queue orders = Queue.Builder.create(this, "Orders")
        .visibilityTimeout(Duration.seconds(180))
        .deadLetterQueue(DeadLetterQueue.builder()
                .queue(dlq)
                .maxReceiveCount(3)
                .build())
        .build();

// Report partial batch failures so one bad message
// does not force the whole batch to be retried
worker.addEventSource(SqsEventSource.Builder.create(orders)
        .batchSize(10)
        .reportBatchItemFailures(true)
        .build());

With reportBatchItemFailures turned on, the handler returns only the IDs of the messages that failed:

public class OrderWorker implements RequestHandler<SQSEvent, SQSBatchResponse> {

    @Override
    public SQSBatchResponse handleRequest(SQSEvent event, Context context) {
        List<SQSBatchResponse.BatchItemFailure> failures = new ArrayList<>();
        for (SQSEvent.SQSMessage message : event.getRecords()) {
            try {
                process(message.getBody()); // must be idempotent: SQS is at-least-once
            } catch (Exception e) {
                failures.add(new SQSBatchResponse.BatchItemFailure(message.getMessageId()));
            }
        }
        return new SQSBatchResponse(failures);
    }
}

Even with the right timeout, SQS standard queues deliver at least once, so process should be idempotent. For example, use the order ID as a conditional write key in DynamoDB.

Best practices across the 12 diagrams

A few rules repeat across the catalog:

  • Expose one entry point. CloudFront, the ALB or API Gateway faces the internet. Buckets, containers and databases stay private.
  • Separate intake from processing. Queues (diagram 6) and event buses (diagram 7) let you absorb spikes and retry failures without losing requests.
  • Treat configuration as part of the architecture. OAC, security groups, visibility timeouts and pod limits are not details to fix later. They decide whether the design works.
  • Know what you pay for. WAF rules, Athena scans, AppSync connections and Bedrock context all scale with usage. Each diagram's note points out the main cost driver.
  • Decide RTO and RPO before you design for resilience. Multi-AZ, multi-region and active-active are answers to different questions.

Conclusion

The catalog is meant as a map: start with the static site, add security and CI/CD, move to containers or serverless, then add asynchronous processing, events, real time, analytics, generative AI, Kubernetes and multi-region resilience as the problem requires.

Key takeaways:

  • Learn AWS services in combinations, not one by one.
  • Each architecture has one detail that usually breaks it. Learn that detail early.
  • Infrastructure as code in Java with the CDK turns those details into code you can review.

Browse the diagrams at https://josesaid.github.io/aws-architecture-diagrams/. The source is on GitHub. Which architecture would you add as number 13?

title: Two Tests Passed for 18 Days Over a Line That Crashed. Here's the Test That Caught It.
description:
I build a desktop options trading tool with Claude Code. Everything runs in a sandbox account. On Nov 13 it threw this:

AttributeError: 'Front' object has no attribute '_say'

How it hid for 18 days

The trading window is handed a small Front object that stands in for the engine. On Oct 26, a change had the window call self.engine._say(...) in two places:

  • in the constructor, when the configured screen can't be found
  • in a check that runs every 1.5 seconds and moves the window back if it drifts off its screen

Front never got a _say.

Two tests covered the change. Both opened ui.py and checked that the call was in the file. It was, so both passed on every run for 18 days.

On Nov 13 the window was moved off its screen, the check fired, and the call crashed. The constructor path would have been worse: with that monitor unplugged, the window would not have opened at all.

Why the tests missed it

A test that searches source text proves the text is there. It never runs the line. Python only looks up self.engine._say when that line executes, and in this window it executes in two rare situations.

The test, written first

Before touching the fix, the new test went in, and it had to fail on the old code. Its first check walks ui.py's syntax tree, collects every attribute the window reads from self.engine, and asserts each one exists on Front. Here's a minimal version of the idea:

import ast

def attrs_read_from_engine(path):
    tree = ast.parse(open(path, encoding="utf-8").read())
    names = set()
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
        if (isinstance(node, ast.Attribute)
                and isinstance(node.value, ast.Attribute)
                and node.value.attr == "engine"
                and isinstance(node.value.value, ast.Name)
                and node.value.value.id == "self"):
            names.add(node.attr)
    return names

def test_front_has_everything_the_window_uses():
    from ticket import Front
    missing = sorted(n for n in attrs_read_from_engine("ui.py")
                     if not hasattr(Front, n))
    assert not missing, f"Front is missing: {missing}"

If your stand-in sets attributes in __init__, check an instance instead of the class.

The second check makes sure _say hands the message only to the page that's on screen.

Old code: 0 passed, 2 failed. Then the fix, six lines on Front. New code: 4 passed.

The first check covers the whole type. The next time anyone, human or AI, adds a call the stand-in doesn't support, the suite fails the same day.

The check you can copy

Search your suite for tests that read source files as text. Each one only proves some code exists. Swap it for a test that builds the real object and calls it, or one that checks the real type has everything its caller uses.

Follow the loop

This bug is now in my AI's mistake log under "a test that skips the real path." Each round of the loop goes up on YouTube first, with which piles grew.

Subscribe to Dr_Delta on YouTube

Have you found tests like this in your own suite? Tell me in the comments.

title: When the agent writes the patch, who audits the tests?
description:
In the METR randomized trial published in July 2025, sixteen experienced open-source developers worked on 246 real issues in their own repositories. Half the tasks allowed AI tools, half did not. The AI-allowed tasks took 19% longer. Before the study the same developers expected a 24% speedup, and after living through the slowdown they still believed they had been sped up by 20%.

That gap between what happened and what the developers felt is the most useful result in the paper, and it is not really about coding speed. It is about measurement. People are bad at knowing whether a tool helped, and the tool is now producing the thing that tells them.

Apply that to tests and you get the quiet failure nobody is writing postmortems about yet. The agent writes the code. The agent writes the tests. The agent runs the suite and reports green. Every step is plausible, the diff is clean, and the review takes four minutes because the checks passed.

The ways a test suite gets laundered

None of these require an adversarial model. They are the shortcuts a model takes when the goal is "make the suite pass," which is the goal you wrote in the prompt.

A new test that asserts the code's current behavior instead of the intended behavior. It passes on the first run, it has a nice name, and it would pass if the function returned zero for everything.

A snapshot that got regenerated. -u is one keystroke away and the resulting diff is unreviewable by construction, which is the whole reason it slips through.

A broad except or a try/except: pass inserted in the module, converting a real failure into silence that the test reads as success.

An assertion loosened from equality to truthiness. assertEqual(total, 41.50) becomes assertIsNotNone(total). Both are green. Only one is a test.

A deleted case, or a skipped one with a TODO. The count of tests stays roughly stable so nobody notices.

A timeout raised from 2s to 30s, which hides a performance regression behind a green check.

Every one of these shows up in the diff as a small, defensible line. That is what makes it survive review: nothing looks wrong in isolation, and reviewers anchor on the code file being the interesting part.

Coverage is not the control you think it is

Coverage measures whether a line executed, not whether anything was verified. A test that calls a function and asserts nothing gives you 100% coverage of that function and zero protection. An agent optimizing for coverage will produce exactly that, because it is the cheapest way to satisfy the metric you put in the prompt.

The metric is the problem. If you tell an agent "increase coverage to 85%," you have defined success as execution, and the model will deliver execution.

Mutation testing on the changed lines

The cheapest real signal I have found is mutation testing scoped to the diff. Take the changed lines, mutate them (flip a comparison, change a constant by one, negate a boolean, remove a return), and check whether the test suite notices. If a mutant survives, the tests around that line do not actually verify it.

Running mutation testing on a whole repository is too slow to put in CI. Running it on the diff is not:

# Python: mutate only the files this PR touched
git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD -- '*.py' \
  | xargs mutmut run --paths-to-mutate {} --tests-dir tests

Stryker does the same for JavaScript with --mutate limited to changed files, PIT with --targetClasses for Java. The report is a number: what fraction of injected faults did the suite catch. A patch with 40% mutation score is a patch with tests that exist and do not verify.

This catches the laundered test directly, because a test that asserts nothing kills no mutants. It also catches the deleted case and the loosened assertion, which coverage never will.

One piece of evidence to require

Every AI-assisted pull request should carry a failing-before proof for the behavior it claims to fix.

The mechanics are simple: run the new test against the code from before the patch, and attach the failure. In git terms, stash the source change, keep the test, run it, capture the output. Then unstash and run it again. The artifact is a diff of two test runs, and it takes the model four seconds to produce if you ask for it in the same session.

git stash push -- src/            # source change only
npm test -- --testPathPattern changed.behavior
git stash pop
npm test -- --testPathPattern changed.behavior

If the test passes both times, it does not test the change. Whatever else is true about the patch, the verification is decorative. That single check invalidates most of the laundered-test patterns in one step, and unlike a coverage threshold it cannot be satisfied by writing more nothing.

Separate the two capabilities

Here is the part that is an architecture decision rather than a process one. The agent should not be able to edit tests and source in the same commit with the same approvals.

Split them. A code change lands with tests unchanged, or a test change lands with code unchanged and a reviewer who is explicitly looking at it. CODEOWNERS on the tests directory is the mechanism, and "tests modified in this PR" as a required label is the signal. It is a five-line policy that makes the failure mode visible instead of silently green.

The agent can still propose test changes. It just cannot be the only witness to its own work.

The honest version of the productivity story

METR's follow-up work in early 2026 suggests developer experience has improved since that first trial, with an estimated speedup among returning participants, while also warning that selection effects make the number unreliable. I believe the newer estimate is closer to reality than the old one. I also think the perception gap is still there, and it matters more now that the tool writes the tests as well as the code.

You cannot feel your way to "the tests verify the change." You can measure it. Mutation score on the diff, a failing-before artifact, and test files that a different person signed off on. Three checks, none of them expensive, all of them boring, which is what a control is supposed to look like.

title: Static Analysis Gates: PHPStan, TypeScript Strict & Coverage in CI
description:
A client's Laravel team asked me why their AI-assisted pull requests kept passing review and then failing in production. One example: a generated service method returned ?Order and the controller called $order->total without a null check. Tests covered the happy path only. The reviewer skimmed 400 lines of plausible code and approved it. PHPStan at level 6 would have flagged that exact line in under a second. They had PHPStan installed, but nobody ran it in CI because the first run produced 1,800 errors and the team gave up.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every config against PHPStan 2.x, Larastan 3, TypeScript 5.6, Vitest 2 and GitHub Actions. I am a Principal Software Engineer in Karachi with 9+ years across PHP/Laravel, Vue, Node and .NET microservices, and through Loop Origin I maintain production SaaS codebases where a growing share of code is AI-assisted.

📚 Series Navigation — Maintaining AI-Written Code in Production

  • Part 1: Reviewing AI-Generated Pull Requests: A Checklist That Catches Real Bugs
  • Part 2: Characterization Tests Before You Refactor AI-Written Code
  • Part 3: Hallucinated Packages & Dependency Drift in AI-Assisted Code
  • Part 4 (This Post): Static Analysis Gates: PHPStan, TypeScript Strict & Coverage in CI
  • Part 5: Decision Records So AI Context Doesn't Rot
  • Part 6: Measuring AI Coding Impact With DORA Metrics, Not Vibes

Related earlier posts: Config & Feature Flags That Quietly Diverged Across Environments · Synthetic Checks & SLOs for the Paths Nobody Clicks

How do you add static analysis gates to a codebase with lots of AI-written code?

Direct answer: Start with a baseline so existing errors do not block anyone, then fail CI only on new problems. Run PHPStan (with Larastan for Laravel) at a realistic level, turn on TypeScript strict gradually per folder, and require coverage on changed lines rather than a global percentage. Raise the bar in small steps each sprint, and never let AI-generated code add to the baseline.

Why AI-written code needs machine gates

Human reviewers get tired; type checkers do not. Assistants are good at producing code that looks right and passes the test they also wrote. The bugs that slip through are usually the boring kind static analysis is built for: nullable values used as non-null, wrong argument types, unreachable branches, undefined array keys, and methods called on the wrong model. A gate catches those in seconds and frees the reviewer to think about design, which is where Part 1's checklist puts the human effort.

Gate What it catches Typical runtime Blocking rule I use
PHPStan + Larastan Null misuse, wrong types, undefined methods/properties 20–90 s No new errors vs baseline
TypeScript strict Implicit any, unchecked nulls, unsafe indexing 10–60 s Strict folders must compile clean
ESLint (typed rules) Floating promises, unsafe any flows 15–60 s No new errors in changed files
Diff coverage Untested new branches Depends on suite 80%+ of changed lines covered
Global coverage Overall trend Same Report only, never block

Gate 1: PHPStan with a baseline

Install Larastan and generate a baseline that records today's errors so the build goes green immediately:

composer require --dev larastan/larastan
vendor/bin/phpstan analyse --generate-baseline

# phpstan.neon
includes:
    - vendor/larastan/larastan/extension.neon
    - phpstan-baseline.neon

parameters:
    level: 6
    paths:
        - app
        - routes
    reportUnmatchedIgnoredErrors: true
    treatPhpDocTypesAsCertain: false

reportUnmatchedIgnoredErrors matters: when someone fixes a baselined error, the build tells them to remove it from the baseline, so the file only ever shrinks. Pick a level you can hold; level 6 is a solid start for most Laravel apps, and you can move to 8 once nullable handling is tidy.

The rule I add to the PR template: AI-assisted changes may never add entries to phpstan-baseline.neon. If the generated code fails analysis, fix the code. A CI check enforces it:

# ci/baseline-guard.sh
set -euo pipefail
git fetch origin main --depth=1
added=$(git diff origin/main -- phpstan-baseline.neon | grep -c '^+\s*-\s*message' || true)
if [ "$added" -gt 0 ]; then
  echo "::error::PR adds $added PHPStan baseline entries. Fix the code instead."
  exit 1
fi

Gate 2: TypeScript strict, one folder at a time

Turning on strict for a large Vue or Node codebase at once produces hundreds of errors. Instead, keep the main config permissive and add a strict config that covers folders you have cleaned:

// tsconfig.strict.json
{
  "extends": "./tsconfig.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "noImplicitOverride": true,
    "noEmit": true
  },
  "include": ["src/services/**/*", "src/composables/**/*", "src/api/**/*"]
}

// package.json scripts
"typecheck": "vue-tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json",
"typecheck:strict": "vue-tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.strict.json"

Every sprint, add one folder to include. New folders start strict from day one. noUncheckedIndexedAccess is the flag that catches the most AI-written bugs in my experience, because generated code loves items[0].id without checking the array is non-empty.

Gate 3: diff coverage instead of global targets

A global "80% coverage" rule pushes people, and assistants, to write shallow tests for easy code. Diff coverage asks a better question: are the lines this PR changed actually exercised?

# .github/workflows/quality.yml
name: quality
on: pull_request
jobs:
  php:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with: { php-version: '8.3', coverage: pcov }
      - run: composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist
      - run: vendor/bin/phpstan analyse --no-progress --error-format=github
      - run: bash ci/baseline-guard.sh
      - run: vendor/bin/pest --coverage-clover=coverage.xml
      - run: pip install diff-cover
      - run: diff-cover coverage.xml --compare-branch=origin/main --fail-under=80
  js:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run typecheck && npm run typecheck:strict
      - run: npx eslint . --max-warnings=0

diff-cover reads Cobertura or Clover style reports and compares them with the git diff. For Vitest, configure the cobertura reporter and run the same command on its output.

Rolling it out without a revolt

  1. Week 1: add the gates in report-only mode and share the numbers.
  2. Week 2: block on new PHPStan errors and the baseline guard.
  3. Week 3: block on strict folders and diff coverage at 60%.
  4. Monthly: raise diff coverage by 5–10 points and the PHPStan level by one when the baseline is small.

Keep total CI time under ten minutes or people will start bypassing it. Cache Composer and npm, and run PHP and JS jobs in parallel.

Diagnostic checklist

  • [ ] PHPStan + Larastan run on every PR with a committed baseline
  • [ ] reportUnmatchedIgnoredErrors enabled so the baseline only shrinks
  • [ ] CI fails if a PR adds baseline entries
  • [ ] tsconfig.strict.json exists and covers at least one real folder
  • [ ] noUncheckedIndexedAccess enabled in strict folders
  • [ ] Diff coverage enforced; global coverage reported, not enforced
  • [ ] Gates documented in the PR template, including the AI-assisted rule
  • [ ] Total CI runtime under ten minutes

FAQs

What PHPStan level should a Laravel app start at?

Generate a baseline at level 5 or 6 so the build is green on day one, then raise the level once the baseline is small. Starting at max with a giant baseline just hides problems.

Won't a baseline hide real bugs forever?

Only if nobody looks at it. Track its size as a metric, fix a few entries each sprint, and the unmatched-error setting stops it from growing quietly.

Can I ask the AI assistant to fix PHPStan errors?

Yes, and it is one of the better uses of an assistant. Review the fixes carefully: assistants sometimes silence errors with @phpstan-ignore or loose mixed types instead of fixing the cause. Ban both in review.

Is 80% diff coverage realistic?

For most business logic, yes. Allow exceptions for generated files, migrations and config, and exclude them in the coverage config rather than lowering the number.

Do these gates slow the team down?

In my experience they speed reviews up, because reviewers stop hunting for type mistakes. The first two weeks feel slower; after that, fewer hotfixes more than make up for it.

Can Loop Origin set these gates up for us?

Yes. We add them as part of our Laravel development and maintenance work; see pricing for typical engagements.

Next in this series, Part 5 covers decision records so AI context doesn't rot.

  • Website: Loop Origin
  • LinkedIn: Loop Origin
  • X: Muhammad Ali Mughal (@AliMughal887)
  • GitHub: Loop Origin (@LoopOrigin)

title: Vercel Sandbox snapshot creation is now up to 10x faster
description:
Vercel Sandbox now creates snapshots up to 10x faster. Median time to snapshot is under 0.4 seconds, down from 4.4 seconds. Snapshot restore speed has also improved by 50% from 500ms to 250ms at p50.

Snapshots are now able to write and restore by re-using frames within the Vercel Hive Snapshot (VHS) format. VHS now indexes data in a more efficient way which means that more read and write operations can be done in parallel. Snapshots can now restore more of your Sandbox base image in parallel with user data, leading to overall faster operations.

Persistent sandboxes, the default, snapshot automatically when a session stops and resume from the latest snapshot. This applies to all new snapshots, with nothing to configure. Existing snapshots keep the previous format.
