title: Why Did My Python List Change? Understanding References and Copies
description:
Why Did My Python List Change? Understanding References and Copies

You create a list, assign it to another variable, and change one item. Then you discover that your original list has changed too.

If that has surprised you, the key is understanding what assignment does in Python.

Let’s work through a few examples, starting with a simple shopping list.

1. Assignment does not create a copy 

shopping = ["milk", "bread", "eggs"]
backup = shopping

backup.append("coffee")

print(shopping)
print(backup)

Output:

['milk', 'bread', 'eggs', 'coffee']
['milk', 'bread', 'eggs', 'coffee']

Despite its name, backup is not a separate list.

This statement:

backup = shopping

binds another name to the same list. Calling append() through either name changes that shared object.

You can check whether two names refer to the same object using is:

print(shopping is backup)

Output:

True

The lesson: Giving a list another name does not duplicate it.

2. Changing a list differs from reassigning a variable

Now consider this example:

shopping = ["milk", "bread"]
backup = shopping

backup = ["coffee"]

print(shopping)
print(backup)

Output:

['milk', 'bread']
['coffee']

Why did shopping stay unchanged this time?

The statement:

backup = ["coffee"]

creates a new list and makes backup refer to it. It does not modify the original list.

Compare these two operations:

Operation Effect
backup.append("coffee") Changes the list that backup refers to
backup = ["coffee"] Makes backup refer to a different list

When tracing Python code, ask: Does this line change an existing object, or change which object a name refers to?

3. Use a copy when you need a separate list

For a flat list of strings, the copy() method provides the separation we wanted:

shopping = ["milk", "bread"]
backup = shopping.copy()

backup.append("coffee")

print(shopping)
print(backup)

Output:

['milk', 'bread']
['milk', 'bread', 'coffee']

You can also create a shallow copy of a list using a full slice:

backup = shopping[:]

Both approaches create a new outer list. But “shallow” matters when the list contains other lists.

4. A shallow copy can still share nested lists

Suppose you keep scores in a nested list:

scores = [[10, 20], [30, 40]]
backup = scores.copy()

backup[0][0] = 99

print(scores)
print(backup)

Output:

[[99, 20], [30, 40]]
[[99, 20], [30, 40]]

The outer lists are separate, but they contain references to the same inner lists.

We can check both levels:

print(scores is backup)
print(scores[0] is backup[0])

Output:

False
True

Changing an element inside a shared inner list affects what both outer lists display.

However, replacing an entire item in the copied outer list behaves differently:

scores = [[10, 20], [30, 40]]
backup = scores.copy()

backup[0] = [99, 20]

print(scores)
print(backup)

Output:

[[10, 20], [30, 40]]
[[99, 20], [30, 40]]

Here, we replaced a reference in backup. We did not modify the shared inner list.

5. Copy nested data when independence is required

For this nested-list example, deepcopy() also copies the inner lists:

from copy import deepcopy

scores = [[10, 20], [30, 40]]
backup = deepcopy(scores)

backup[0][0] = 99

print(scores)
print(backup)

Output:

[[10, 20], [30, 40]]
[[99, 20], [30, 40]]

Use deep copying when the nested mutable data needs to be independent. It is not necessary for every list: a shallow copy may provide exactly the behaviour you need.

6. Watch out for repeated nested lists

The same reference issue appears when building a grid:

grid = [[0, 0]] * 3

grid[0][0] = 1

print(grid)

Output:

[[1, 0], [1, 0], [1, 0]]

The multiplication repeats references to one inner list. It does not create three independent rows.

Create each row separately instead:

grid = [[0, 0] for _ in range(3)]

grid[0][0] = 1

print(grid)

Output:

[[1, 0], [0, 0], [0, 0]]

The list comprehension creates a new inner list on each iteration.

A useful habit when reading Python code

Whenever a question involves lists, pause at assignments and modifications:

  • Does another variable refer to the same list?
  • Was a shallow copy created?
  • Are any inner lists still shared?
  • Is the code modifying an object or reassigning a name?

Predict the output first, then run the example. Explaining why the result occurs is more useful than memorising it.

For further reading, see the official Python documentation on shallow and deep copying.

Free PCEP practice test

Preparing for PCEP? I create Python learning resources through AM Academy, and you can access my free practice test here: https://www.udemy.com/course/python-pcep-30-03-certification-practice-tests-2026/?couponCode=FREE-COURSE-PCEP. This is an independently created preparation resource, not an official Python Institute exam.

title: Private Object Storage Uploads in 2026 — Signed Document Download URLs by Deadline
description:
Short answer: retain signed customer-support documents in a private bucket, keep ownership and the deletion deadline in the application database, and issue a short-lived signed URL only after each download is authorized. Infrai is worth trying for that narrow upload-and-presign boundary when a team wants plain REST calls without installing and maintaining a storage SDK; it is not the compliance archive.

The deciding quantity is effective cost over the document's full life, not a storage unit price. Count upload and inspection calls, retained bytes, downloads and egress, the database state that makes deletion reproducible, cleanup execution, reconciliation, and the engineering burden of another client library and credential. A design that makes the initial PUT easy but leaves an operator unable to prove deletion is cheap only on the first invoice.

For a support system, the record might be a signed agreement.pdf or authorization.docx. Its object key can be users/user_4821/documents/doc_91a7/original.pdf, but the database must separately hold user_4821, doc_91a7, the content type, a digest, and delete_at. Object metadata is a display aid, not an ownership index: server-side listing can filter by key prefix, not by metadata.

What belongs in the retention cost ledger?

Start with one workload row per document class rather than one blended storage estimate. Record average object size, uploads, HEAD checks, signed downloads, average retention days, egress, replacements, and deletion attempts. Then add two labor terms that vendor calculators tend to omit: integration upkeep and reconciliation. The latter is the recurring work needed to compare database intent with stored reality, find an expired object that remains, or find an active database row whose bytes are absent.

The exercise changes the decision. Suppose support agents review some signed records repeatedly while most are never reopened. Storage duration may be a minor term; download egress and authorization traffic may dominate the active subset. I'm not sure which term will dominate in a particular queue without its access logs, so I would not rank providers from a hypothetical average. Measure the distribution, especially its long tail.

This is also where Infrai has a concrete operational argument. Its storage capability is exposed through a plain REST API, so any service able to send HTTP can use it without adopting a provider SDK or tracking a client-library release line. The supporting benefit is consolidation: one key and one billing surface can cover this storage boundary and other backend capabilities, reducing credential and invoice reconciliation work. Neither point removes object storage, egress, database, or deletion-job costs; they remove specific integration work.

No magic here.

The ledger should charge failed business operations even when every storage request behaves correctly. A support agent can authorize a download just as the retention worker begins deletion; two replacement requests can target the same logical document; a database commit can succeed before an upload is visible to the rest of the application flow. These are coordination boundaries. Treating them as a provider selection problem hides the system that must actually resolve them.

How should private object storage handle signed document download URLs?

The central invariant is: a caller receives a signed download URL only while the database says the caller may read the document and the deletion deadline has not passed. Keep the bucket private because public or public-read access is unavailable, and never persist a presigned URL as though it were the document's permanent address. It is a bearer capability with a limited life.

Three more invariants make the retention story auditable:

  1. The database, not object metadata, is authoritative for owner, logical document identity, current object key, retention state, and deletion deadline.
  2. A replacement receives a new document identity or passes through a database-serialized state transition. There is no object versioning and no If-Match conditional write protection, so concurrent overwrite is not a safe compare-and-swap mechanism.
  3. Deletion is a recorded workflow: mark the row due, attempt object deletion, verify the resulting state, append an audit event, and retry from durable state when the workflow is interrupted.

Exactly once is an accounting property here, not a promise that a network call runs once. Give each business transition a stable operation id, persist it with the document row, and make a repeated worker execution converge on the same terminal state. A 429 is routine backpressure; it should cause bounded exponential delay, honoring Retry-After, rather than a tight retry loop or a second logical operation.

Lifecycle policy can provide a backstop when deadlines are day-granular, but its minimum is one day. It cannot express an hour-level deletion obligation. Abandoned multipart fragments also lack an automatic cleanup rule, which means a workload using multipart upload must account for its own abort and reconciliation process. These details belong in the operating bill because each requires execution, observation, and an audit trail.

Which boundary should own retention and deletion?

The options are not interchangeable. This table compares the boundary that a customer-support service would actually own, rather than pretending that a common API shape makes governance features equivalent.

Option Sensible fit Hidden operating work Retention or deletion boundary
Amazon S3 directly A team that needs a specialist storage relationship and provider-native governance controls Operate its SDK or HTTP signing, credentials, policies, and separate billing reconciliation Evaluate provider-native versioning and immutable-retention controls against the compliance rule
Google Cloud Storage directly An organization committed to GCS and its surrounding cloud controls Maintain a GCS-specific integration and include its access and egress behavior in the workload model Prefer this route when GCS coverage or organization-level cloud policy is mandatory
Cloudflare R2 directly A team that wants to contract with and configure R2 without an intermediary API Own the provider integration, credentials, and migration path Validate the required retention controls directly; S3 compatibility does not itself prove governance equivalence
Infrai storage A service that values a plain REST boundary, one key, and consistent backend conventions The application still owns deadline state, reconciliation, and exact deletion scheduling Private signed access fits; object lock, versioning, cross-region automatic replication, and metadata search do not

My recommendation is deliberately conditional: try Infrai for private document transfer and signed delivery when SDK upkeep and cross-service credential reconciliation are meaningful costs, while the application is already responsible for authorization and an auditable deletion workflow. Its public, self-describing discovery surface is useful during integration because request schemas and runnable examples can be inspected without a key. The catch is that this choice is not suitable for write-once regulated records that require provider-enforced immutability, automatic cross-region replication, or recovery from accidental overwrite; use a specialist storage product with the required control instead. Stick with Google Cloud Storage when direct GCS coverage is a hard platform requirement, since GCS is not among the covered storage vendors.

Public hosting is out too. There is no public/public-read ACL, and public_url remains null, so a permanent public link, static website, or image-hosting design needs a different product. Browser-direct upload also requires a CORS decision before selection; do not assume that an S3-compatible bucket makes every browser flow portable.

Can the signed-access critical path stay small and auditable?

Yes. The following Go program requests a ten-minute download capability for an object that has already been uploaded under the owner-scoped key. The full URL and explicit POST method are intentional: they make the reviewed route visible, while url.PathEscape protects each variable path segment in a production helper. The returned signed URL must be used without the Infrai Authorization header.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    route := "/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
    route = strings.Replace(route, "{bucket}", url.PathEscape("support-private-docs"), 1)
    route = strings.Replace(route, "{key}", url.PathEscape("users/user_4821/documents/doc_91a7/original.pdf"), 1)
    endpoint := "https://api.infrai.cc" + route
    body := []byte(`{"expires_in":600}`)

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "POST", endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "download-doc_91a7-agent_204")

        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 250 * time.Millisecond
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("presign request %s: %s", res.Status, data))
        }

        fmt.Println(string(data))
        return
    }

    panic("rate limit retries exhausted")
}

The program prints the response rather than inventing a response field that is not established here. In the service, bind the presign event to the authenticated actor, doc_91a7, the expiry request, and the storage request id in an append-only application audit record. Do not log the signed URL itself; the audit fact is that access was granted, not the reusable bearer capability.

There is a subtle cost boundary around HEAD calls. They can help reconcile the expected key before issuing access, but making every download perform redundant storage inspection increases request count and latency. If database state and the deletion worker have a strong reconciliation loop, reserve HEAD for state transitions and exception handling. If another writer can mutate the bucket outside the application, inspect more aggressively and charge those calls to the governance model. Your mileage may vary because that boundary depends on who else holds credentials.

Why reject a public bucket or overwrite-in-place design?

A public bucket fails the authorization model before cost enters the discussion. An opaque filename is not access control, a copied permanent link cannot be recalled at the support application's deadline, and public_url is unavailable in this storage surface anyway. Signed delivery keeps each grant time-limited and makes the application authorization check unavoidable.

Overwrite in place is the more tempting mistake — and the more expensive one to investigate. Without object versioning or conditional If-Match writes, two valid workers can race and leave only the last bytes at a key, while both business requests appear successful in separate logs. Assign a new docId for a replacement, store the new key beside a stable logical case id, and change the current pointer through a serialized database transaction. That adds a row and a state transition; it also preserves which PDF an agent saw, which digest was signed, and which object must be deleted on which deadline.

For immutable financial or compliance evidence, reject this application-enforced pattern. A storage system with object lock or another external WORM control is the valid choice even if its SDK, policy review, and separate invoice make the effective bill larger, because recoverability and tamper resistance are requirements rather than optional cost optimizations.

For ordinary customer-support agreements whose policy permits application-enforced deletion, close the decision record with measurable acceptance criteria: every active row resolves to one private key; every download has an authorization and audit event; every expired row reaches a verified terminal deletion state; replacement never mutates historical identity; and the monthly review accounts for retained bytes, operations, egress, integration upkeep, and reconciliation labor. If this boundary fits the system, start with the Infrai storage documentation and inspect the discovery schema before implementing the call.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: Building a REST API with Laravel and React: A Beginner-Friendly Guide
description:
Building a REST API with Laravel and React: A Beginner-Friendly Guide

Modern web applications often separate the frontend and backend to make development more organized, flexible, and maintainable.

One popular combination is Laravel for backend development and React for frontend development.

In this article, we'll explore how these two technologies work together to create a simple full-stack application.

1. Understanding the Architecture

Before writing code, it's important to understand the responsibilities of each technology.

Laravel (Backend)

Laravel handles:

  • API endpoints and routing.
  • Database operations.
  • Authentication and authorization.
  • Business logic.
  • Request validation.

React (Frontend)

React handles:

  • User interfaces.
  • Forms and user interactions.
  • Displaying data from the API.
  • Managing application state.
  • Communicating with the backend.

The general workflow looks like this:

React → HTTP Request → Laravel API → Database

The response then travels back to React, where the data can be displayed to the user.

2. Creating a Laravel Project

First, create a new Laravel application:

composer create-project laravel/laravel backend

Navigate into the project:

cd backend

Start the development server:

php artisan serve

Your Laravel application will typically be available at:

http://127.0.0.1:8000

3. Creating an API Endpoint

Let's create a simple API endpoint that returns a list of users.

Open your routes/api.php file and add:

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::get('/users', function () {
    return response()->json([
        'success' => true,
        'message' => 'Users retrieved successfully',
        'data' => [
            [
                'id' => 1,
                'name' => 'John Doe',
                'email' => 'john@example.com',
            ],
            [
                'id' => 2,
                'name' => 'Jane Doe',
                'email' => 'jane@example.com',
            ],
        ],
    ]);
});

This endpoint returns JSON data that can be consumed by a frontend application.

4. Connecting React to Laravel

Now let's create a React application.

npm create vite@latest frontend -- --template react

Install the dependencies:

cd frontend
npm install

Inside your React application, open src/App.jsx and add:

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

function App() {
  const [users, setUsers] = useState([]);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

  useEffect(() => {
    fetch("http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/users")
      .then((response) => {
        if (!response.ok) {
          throw new Error("Failed to fetch users");
        }

        return response.json();
      })
      .then((result) => {
        setUsers(result.data);
      })
      .catch((error) => {
        console.error(error);
      })
      .finally(() => {
        setLoading(false);
      });
  }, []);

  if (loading) {
    return <p>Loading users...</p>;
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>User Management</h1>

      {users.map((user) => (
        <div key={user.id}>
          <h2>{user.name}</h2>
          <p>{user.email}</p>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;

This example demonstrates how React can request data from Laravel and display the returned users.

5. Understanding CORS

When your frontend and backend run on different origins, browsers may block requests unless the backend allows them.

This is where Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) comes in.

Laravel provides CORS configuration through its application configuration.

Make sure your frontend origin is allowed in the backend configuration before testing API requests.

Avoid allowing every origin in production unless your security requirements explicitly justify it.

6. Improving the Application

Once the basic connection works, you can start adding real application features:

  • User registration and login.
  • CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete).
  • Form validation.
  • Database integration using MySQL.
  • API authentication.
  • Pagination and filtering.
  • Error handling.

For larger applications, organizing your Laravel code into controllers, models, requests, services, and API resources can make the project easier to maintain.

7. Best Practices

Here are some practices worth following when developing a Laravel and React application:

  1. Keep frontend and backend responsibilities separate.
  2. Validate incoming data on the backend.
  3. Never expose sensitive credentials in frontend code.
  4. Use environment variables for configuration.
  5. Handle API errors properly.
  6. Keep your components reusable.
  7. Use Git to track changes and collaborate with other developers.

Final Thoughts

Building a full-stack application becomes easier when you understand how the frontend and backend communicate.

Laravel provides a powerful backend foundation, while React makes it possible to create dynamic and interactive user experiences.

You don't need to master everything immediately. Start with a simple API, connect it to React, and gradually introduce more advanced features.

The best way to understand full-stack development is to build something yourself.

Have you tried combining Laravel and React in a project? What challenges did you encounter? Let's share our experiences and learn together!

title: Playwright Email Fixtures Need Better Failure Evidence
description:
Email tests rarely fail because an email is completely absent. More often, the test sees the wrong message, reads the inbox too early, or loses the evidence that would explain what happened. A temp mail generator can provide a useful isolated fixture, but isolation alone does not make an end-to-end test diagnosable.

This is the workflow I use when a Playwright email test is flaky: define the expected states, capture the first useful evidence, and make every retry explain what changed. The goal is not to add more waits. It is to make the failure tell us which boundary broke.

The failure is often a missing state, not a missing email

Consider a signup test that requests a verification code. The test opens an inbox and waits for a message with the subject “Verify your account.” It passes locally, then fails in CI with “message not found.”

That message hides several different failures:

  • The signup request never completed.
  • The message was sent to a previous fixture address.
  • The inbox API returned an older message first.
  • The email arrived after the polling deadline.
  • The code was present, but the selector matched the wrong element.
  • The test found the message but failed while parsing its body.

Each case needs a different fix. A longer timeout only makes some of them slower. The first diagnostic step is to record the boundary events: fixture created, address submitted, request accepted, message observed, code extracted, and verification completed.

Model the fixture as a state ledger

I prefer a small state ledger over a single waitForEmail() helper. The ledger gives each transition a timestamp and a compact detail value without storing the whole mailbox contents in every log line.

type EmailState =
  | "fixture-created"
  | "address-submitted"
  | "message-observed"
  | "code-extracted"
  | "verified"
  | "expired";

const states: Array<{ name: EmailState; at: string; detail?: string }> = [];

function mark(name: EmailState, detail?: string) {
  states.push({ name, at: new Date().toISOString(), detail });
}

The ledger should be attached to the test result when a step fails. Do not log the verification code itself; record its source message ID, subject, and age instead. This keeps the artifact useful without turning a CI report into a copy of the inbox.

A state ledger also catches an easy-to-miss problem: the first clue are often in the order of events. If message-observed occurs before address-submitted, the test may be reading a stale message or sharing a fixture across workers.

Build a diagnostic Playwright helper

The helper should poll for a message using a stable identity, not a broad text match. A good identity usually combines the fixture address, a test-run token, and a bounded age. Subject text can be part of the check, but it should not be the only check.

async function waitForVerification(page: Page, token: string) {
  const deadline = Date.now() + 30_000;

  while (Date.now() < deadline) {
    const message = await readLatestMessage();
    if (message && message.runToken === token) {
      mark("message-observed", message.id);
      const code = extractCode(message.text);
      if (!code) throw new Error(`Message ${message.id} has no code`);
      mark("code-extracted", message.id);
      return code;
    }

    await page.waitForTimeout(1_000);
  }

  mark("expired", `token=${token}`);
  throw new Error("Verification message did not arrive before the deadline");
}

In the real helper, keep the polling interval and deadline configurable. Capture one sanitized response summary on timeout: message count, newest message timestamp, and the requested token. That is usually enough to tell whether delivery or matching failed.

If a selector is involved, prefer a role or a data attribute that the application owns. Avoid a selector such as text=123456; another message can contain the same number. Playwright is very good at reporting selector failures, but only when the test gives it a stable target.

Keep the mailbox boundary explicit

The mailbox is an external dependency even when it is created by a test service. Give each worker a unique address or run token, and clean it up after the test. Also separate the browser timeout from the email delivery timeout. They measure different things and should produce different errors.

When documenting fixtures, search terms can be messy. Someone may write tepm mail com or temp gamil com in a failure ticket. Keep those phrases in troubleshooting notes if they help search older incidents, but do not turn them into selectors or production validation rules. The phrase temp mail mail can likewise appear in an imported test description without being a reliable fixture identifier.

For privacy-sensitive flows, review what the fixture service retains and who can access it. These privacy notes for email checks are a useful reminder that test data still deserves a boundary and a deletion policy.

A repeatable CI failure checklist

When the test fails, check the evidence in this order:

  1. Identity: Was the same address or run token used from setup through message lookup?
  2. Application event: Did the signup request return the expected status before polling began?
  3. Delivery: Did any message arrive within the deadline, even if it had an unexpected subject?
  4. Matching: Did the message contain the current token, or was it stale?
  5. Parsing: Was the message body format different from the local fixture?
  6. Browser state: Did the page navigate, reload, or lose the verification form while waiting?
  7. Artifact quality: Can another engineer replay the relevant inputs from the CI artifact?

If the failure is intermittent, save a small replay pack with the state ledger, sanitized message metadata, request correlation ID, and the final page screenshot. An approach based on replay packs for easier debugging works well because it preserves the facts without asking a developer to guess which retry was meaningful.

Questions that help classify the failure

Should I increase the email timeout first?

No. First determine whether the message arrived late, arrived under a different identity, or was never requested. Increase the deadline only when delivery latency is the known cause, and keep the failure artifact so the new budget remains visible.

Is a temp mail generator suitable for every test?

It is useful for isolated signup and verification scenarios, especially when each run gets a unique fixture. It is less suitable for tests that need long-term mailbox history, guaranteed retention, or sensitive production-like data. In those cases, a controlled fake mail adapter may be more predictable.

What makes an email test reliable?

Reliable tests have unique identity, explicit states, bounded polling, stable selectors, sanitized evidence, and cleanup. They also fail at the first broken boundary. That last part matters most: a test that says “verification failed” is hard to repair, while one that says “message arrived for the previous run token” points directly to fixture isolation.

The practical rule is simple: treat email as a sequence of observable states, not a single asynchronous event. Once Playwright records that sequence, flaky failures become smaller QA problems with evidence instead of mysterious red builds.

title: Pulse: Heart Rate Zones From the Watch to the Trainer's Screen
description:
A spin class with a screen on the wall showing every rider's heart rate zone is the kind of feature studios pay a lot for. It usually means a vendor's hardware, a vendor's app and a monthly fee per location. Underneath, it's three hard integrations: reading a watch or a chest strap in real time, getting that reading off the phone fast enough to matter, and doing it on iOS and Android, which store health data in two completely different places.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Pulse is a studio template where that's already done, in one Java project you own the source of. The member's phone records the class, the trainer's phone shows the room. You can generate it from the Initializr as Fitness studio, under your own name and package, and the source is MIT-0.

Download the trainer video.

From the wrist to the wall

When a member checks into a class, the app asks for permission once, then opens a workout session that collects heart rate. On iOS that's a HealthKit workout, which also brings in a paired Apple Watch; on Android it's Health Connect. It's the same code on both:

Health.getInstance().getStore().requestAuthorization(
        HealthAccess.write(HealthDataType.WORKOUT),
        HealthAccess.read(HealthDataType.HEART_RATE),
        HealthAccess.write(HealthDataType.HEART_RATE)).onResult((asked, refused) -> {
    WorkoutConfiguration config = new WorkoutConfiguration()
            .setActivityType(WorkoutActivityType.CYCLING)
            .setTitle("Morning Spin")
            .addCollectedType(HealthDataType.HEART_RATE);
    Health.getInstance().getWorkouts().startSession(config).onResult((workout, failed) -> {
        if (workout != null) {
            workout.addListener(workoutListener);
            workout.start();
            pairStrap(workout);
        }
    });
});

Chest straps over Bluetooth

Plenty of members train with a chest strap instead of a watch, and the strap is more accurate anyway. Every strap on the market speaks the standard Bluetooth Heart Rate profile, so Pulse scans for that profile, connects to the first one it finds and feeds it into the same workout session, which means the strap's beats end up in the member's health history too:

HealthSensors sensors = Health.getInstance().getSensors();
sensors.startScan(new SensorScanSettings()
        .addProfile(HealthSensorProfile.HEART_RATE)
        .setTimeoutMillis(20000), new SensorDiscoveryListener() {
    public void sensorDiscovered(HealthSensor sensor) {
        SensorSessionOptions options = new SensorSessionOptions()
                .setAutoReconnect(true)
                .setWorkoutSession(workout);
        sensors.connect(sensor, HealthSensorProfile.HEART_RATE, options)
                .onResult((strap, failed) -> {
                    if (strap != null) {
                        strap.addListener(strapListener);
                    }
                });
    }

    public void scanFailed(HealthException error) {
    }
});

Auto reconnect matters more than it looks. A strap drops off for a second whenever someone wipes their chest, and you don't want the trainer's screen to lose them for the rest of the class.

A strap reports every beat. A watch, through the platform, reports running statistics instead, so Pulse reads whichever one it has:

public void sensorSample(SensorSession session, HealthSample sample) {
    if (sample instanceof QuantitySample
            && HealthDataType.HEART_RATE.equals(sample.getType())) {
        beat((int) Math.round(((QuantitySample) sample)
                .getValue(HealthUnit.COUNT_PER_MINUTE)));
    }
}

public void workoutStatisticsUpdated(WorkoutSession session, HealthDataType type) {
    HealthQuantity average = session.getStatistic(HealthDataType.HEART_RATE,
            AggregateMetric.AVERAGE);
    if (average != null) {
        beat((int) Math.round(average.getValue(HealthUnit.COUNT_PER_MINUTE)));
    }
}

Zones on the trainer's screen

beat() sends the reading to the studio's backend. The server keeps only the latest reading per member, in memory, and turns it into a zone: the reading's share of 220 minus the member's age, in fifths starting at 50%. Zone 1 is a warm-up, zone 5 is everything they've got. The trainer's phone gets the zones over a live channel, so the room view updates as people push, and a trainer can see who's coasting and who needs to back off.

Individual readings are never written to the database. A reading matters for a few seconds; the workout, which is kept, arrives whole when the class ends, and it's also saved to the member's own HealthKit or Health Connect store.

Reading history back

Past workouts, including ones recorded by other apps, feed the member's progress screen. One query works on both platforms:

SampleQuery query = new SampleQuery().addType(HealthDataType.WORKOUT)
        .setTimeRange(HealthTimeRange.lastDays(14)).setLimit(30)
        .setSortDescending(true);
Health.getInstance().getStore().readSamples(query).onResult((samples, failed) -> {
    // turn workouts into visits, minutes and points
});

Workouts become points, streaks and badges, and friends can send kudos, which is the part that keeps people coming back in January.

Health data is regulated data

Heart rate is health data. In the EU it's special-category data under GDPR, in the US it can fall under HIPAA depending on who holds it, and Apple and Google both have their own rules for apps that read HealthKit or Health Connect, including what you may store and what you must disclose. Pulse is built to stay on the right side of that by default: it asks only for the types it uses and keeps live readings out of the database. The implementor's guide lists what you still have to do yourself before you ship, and you should read that part with whoever handles your privacy policy.

The rest of the studio

Health is the part this post is about, but Pulse is a whole studio app. The server decides which roles an account has, so the same install becomes a member app at home and a trainer app on the coach's phone:

Members book classes, join waitlists, add their kids to a household, and walk in with a door pass: a QR code that rotates, so an old screenshot stops working, or an NFC tap.

Download the member video.

Owners get the desktop from the same codebase: takings, busy hours, under-filled classes, members who are about to churn, plans and pricing, campaigns, staff shifts and billing with a dunning ladder for failed cards.

Download the owner video.

Try it in two commands

The simulator has no watch or strap, so the dev backend plays demo heart rates into the live view. It runs in a dev profile with an in-memory database, text messages and pushes printed to the console and simulated card payments:

CN1_PROFILE=dev backend/server.sh run
mvn verify -Psimulator -DskipTests -Dcodename1.platform=javase

Log in with the demo accounts from the guide (owner@pulse.example, trainer@pulse.example, desk@pulse.example) to see each role.

The user's guide walks through every screen, and the implementor's guide explains billing, the door pass, health and what to change to make it your studio's app.

title: I shipped a VPN app on iOS, Mac, Android and Windows without writing a VPN protocol
description:
I build mobile apps for a living, mostly on iOS. This year I shipped a VPN called Privalune on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Android and Windows. I did it alone, and the only reason that was possible is one decision I made early: I would not write or bundle a VPN protocol.

Every platform I target already ships an IKEv2 client. So the apps are remote controls. They hand the operating system a server and a login, and the OS runs the tunnel.

This post covers how that works on each platform, what the backend looks like, and where the approach hurts.

The numbers
iOS, iPadOS and Mac: about 7,400 lines of Swift (SwiftUI)
Android: about 4,200 lines of Kotlin (Jetpack Compose)
Windows: about 3,350 lines of TypeScript, CSS and Rust (Tauri 2 + Preact)
Backend: seven Supabase Edge Functions and five SQL migrations
Website: static HTML, 92 pages in six languages

None of those codebases contains cryptography or packet handling.

iOS and Mac: NEVPNManager

On Apple platforms the system VPN is NEVPNManager, the "Personal VPN" API. You fill in an IKEv2 profile, save it, and ask the system to start it. iOS shows its own permission prompt the first time.

The part I like most is on-demand rules. This is the whole "protect me on public Wi-Fi automatically" feature:

enum AutoProtect {
    static func rules(trustedNetworks: [String]) -> [NEOnDemandRule] {
        var rules: [NEOnDemandRule] = []

        if !trustedNetworks.isEmpty {
            let stayOff = NEOnDemandRuleDisconnect()
            stayOff.interfaceTypeMatch = .wiFi
            stayOff.ssidMatch = trustedNetworks
            rules.append(stayOff)
        }

        let connectOnWiFi = NEOnDemandRuleConnect()
        connectOnWiFi.interfaceTypeMatch = .wiFi
        rules.append(connectOnWiFi)

        return rules
    }
}

The system evaluates those rules even when the app is not running. I wrote no background code for it.

Two things I learned the hard way:

The Simulator cannot run a VPN. I added a simulated tunnel with realistic timing so I could build the whole UI, including the connect animation and the Live Activity, without a device in my hand.
Mac came almost free. The iPhone and iPad app runs on Apple silicon Macs through the App Store, so Mac users get the same binary. Intel Macs are not covered.
Android: the platform VPN profile

Most Android VPN apps implement VpnService and ship their own protocol stack. Since Android 11 there is another option: Ikev2VpnProfile with VpnManager. You build a profile, the system asks the user for consent once, and Android runs the tunnel.

The flow is: prepare() saves the profile and may return an Intent for the consent screen, then start() brings the tunnel up. To know the real state, I listen for networks with TRANSPORT_VPN instead of trusting my own flags.

The cost is a minimum of Android 11. For a new app in 2026 I accepted that.

Windows: Tauri, PowerShell and the RAS API

The Windows app is Tauri 2 with a Preact front end. The Rust side is about 340 lines and does three things:

Creates a per-user VPN profile with PowerShell's Add-VpnConnection. Per-user means no administrator prompt.
Dials and hangs up through the Win32 RAS API, using the windows crate. The password goes straight into the API call, so it never appears on a command line where other processes could read it.
Translates Windows error codes into sentences a person can act on:

let message = match code {
    691 => "The VPN login was refused. Please try again.",
    13801 => "Windows couldn't verify the server's certificate. Please try another location.",
    809 | 13806 | 13820 => "This network seems to block VPN connections. Try another Wi-Fi or mobile hotspot.",
    868 => "The server's address couldn't be found. Check your internet connection.",
    _ => "Couldn't connect. Please try again or pick another location.",
};

I do not own a Windows PC. A friend ran the first builds for me, and I tested it myself later. That made the error table far more important than I expected: "Error 809" in a screenshot told me exactly what happened on his network.

The backend: small functions, one source of truth

The backend is Supabase Edge Functions, written in TypeScript for Deno:

servers returns the location list. It is cached for 30 minutes, and if the upstream call fails it serves the last good list instead of an error.
vpn-credentials checks that the caller has Premium and returns a VPN login.
devices links up to 10 devices to one subscription.
A webhook keeps subscription state in sync with RevenueCat, which is my single source of truth for "is this person Premium" across Apple, Google and web purchases.

On infrastructure, to be clear about what I did and did not build: the free server is a VPS I configured as a VPN server myself. It meters the daily free time on the server side, and the app only mirrors the countdown. The paid locations come from an infrastructure provider's network through their API. I did not rack servers in 55 countries.

No accounts in the apps

I did not want a sign-up screen between a person and the connect button. So the apps have no login.

Someone who buys on the website receives a Premium key by email. Typing that key into any of the apps links the device, up to 10 per subscription. Each linked device gets a random token, and the database stores only its hash.

The trade-off is support. With no account, "I lost my key" has to be solved by email, so the website has a small dashboard where buyers sign in with a one-time code and see their key again.

The website is plain HTML

No framework. A shell script copies files into dist/ for Cloudflare Pages. Small Python scripts generate the repetitive pages, and translations live in one JSON file per language, keyed by text segment, so changing an English sentence tells me exactly which translations are stale.

One environment variable, LAUNCHED, switched the site from a holding page to the full site on launch day.

What this approach costs
One protocol. IKEv2 only. Some networks block it, and I cannot fall back to something that looks like normal web traffic.
Less control. I get the features each OS exposes and nothing more.
Windows trust. My installer is not code-signed yet, so Windows warns people before running it. That is the next thing I am fixing.
Android 11 and later only.

What I got in return: four small apps that one person can maintain, no native crypto to audit, and tunnels run by code that Apple, Google and Microsoft maintain.

Try it

Privalune is free to start with no account: privalune.com. If you only want to see what websites can read about your connection, the What's my IP page works without installing anything.

I would like to hear from anyone who has shipped on the platform IKEv2 clients, especially about handling networks that block it.
