Total 6 capabilities 17 charged calls 354 rows $0.019516

Eight more calls failed and cost nothing. The section on failed calls covers them. The company page gives enough for the size sentence of a brief.

Field Wayfair Snowflake Mercado Libre
Employees on the page 12,876 12,030 70,342
Followers 458,919 1,447,139 3,621,004
Founded 2002 2012 not returned
Headquarters Boston, MA "The Cloud", US Buenos Aires
Company IDs in job_search_url 1 5 2

The profile also has a job_search_url field. The job searches below depend on it. The LinkedIn data API page lists all LinkedIn capabilities. See company profile, company posts, jobs and job detail for parameters.

Company posts: the same 20 posts can cover 9 days or 286 days

In this test, linkedin/company_posts returned 20 posts per company. By posted_at, Snowflake's 20 posts fall between November 6 and November 15, a 9-day span. All 20 are in the last 30 days. Wayfair's 20 run from September 29 to November 13, a 45-day span, with 12 in the last 30 days.

Mercado Libre's 20 posts run from January 22 to November 4, a 286-day span. Only one is in the last 30 days: the third-quarter results post on November 4. The call count and cost are the same for all three companies. The density of recent news differs by an order of magnitude.

After each call, we sort the posts by posted_at, newest first. Then we cut at October 17 and put the rest in an "older" column. A script does this step, so the model gets a list that is already sorted and cut. The model does not have to decide which post is newer. The cut removed 8 older posts for Wayfair, 0 for Snowflake and 19 for Mercado Libre. These are the "older" segments in the chart above.

We also coded post text with keyword rules. One post can count in more than one group. Wayfair's 12 recent posts include 5 on stores and logistics, 5 on people and culture, 3 on AI, 3 on events and 2 on results. The median like count is 78. The top post, with 417 likes, marks the co-founder and CEO joining a home furnishings hall of fame.

Snowflake's 20 posts include 15 on AI. The median like count is 53. The top post, with 259 likes, announces same-day availability of Claude Fable 5.2 on Cortex AI on November 10. This kind of spread tells a proposal writer what the client stresses in public this month. The proposal can open from that angle.

Mercado Libre shows a different lesson. For a company that posts rarely, company posts are poor value. Its only recent post covers the third quarter. Net revenue and financial income reached $10.75 billion, up 45% year on year, with 94 million unique active buyers. The same numbers are on its investor relations site and in its press release. For clients like this, skip posts and save $0.002319 per brief.

Hiring signal one: a company name as keyword pulls in other employers

The keyword parameter of linkedin/jobs accepts a keyword or a full LinkedIn job search URL. We first tried the obvious form: the company name as keyword, the United States as location, and 50 results. The Wayfair search returned 50 roles, all from Wayfair. The Snowflake search returned 50 roles, and only 12 were Snowflake's own.

The other 38 came from 17 employers. Snowflake is also the name of a data platform. These employers want data engineers who know Snowflake.

Employer in the "Snowflake" keyword results Roles
First Citizens Bank 8
Tata Consultancy Services 7
Anblicks 3
Six employers with 2 each (incl. Franklin Templeton, Salesforce, Slack) 12
Eight employers with 1 each (incl. Capital One, SoFi, a university) 8
Snowflake itself 12

linkedin/company_profile returns job_search_url, a job search link filtered by company IDs. Snowflake's link holds 5 company IDs, for the main page and related pages. Mercado Libre's holds 2.

We passed the Snowflake link unchanged as keyword. All 50 roles came back as Snowflake's own, all posted on or after October 25. The Mercado Libre call through remote MCP also returned 50 of 50.

LinkedIn's help center confirms that job search can filter by company. It also says the order considers your search activity and that search shows up to 1,000 results. So the same keyword can give a different top 50 for a different person or at a different time.

We also compared the two Snowflake searches. Of the 12 Snowflake roles from the keyword search, only 1 was in the 50 roles from the filter URL. That role was a software engineer for virtualization. Together, the two searches found 61 different Snowflake roles. So each top 50 is only a slice of the open roles. A proposal can state a share, but not a total.

The shares were close in the two samples. In the keyword set, 7 of 12 roles were engineering and AI, which is 58%. In the filter URL set, 32 of 50 were, which is 64%. So "most Snowflake hiring is for engineers" is a safe sentence. "Snowflake is hiring for 50 roles" is not.

This step costs almost nothing. A profile call costs $0.000556, and a jobs call costs the same. The saving is time spent removing other employers. It also prevents a bad sentence in the proposal, such as "you are hiring data engineers at scale", when the roles belong to someone else.

Hiring signal two: what the role mix says, and where it misleads

With clean lists, we put each role into one group by keywords in its title. The groups were sales and presales, engineering and AI, stores and operations, product, marketing, analytics, finance and HR and legal, and other. We wrote the rules after we looked at the raw Wayfair and Snowflake lists, and we did not change them after that.

The rules run in order, and the first match wins. A title with words such as sales, account executive, solution engineer, venta or comercial goes to sales. A title with store, retail, warehouse or operations goes to stores. A title with engineer, scientist, software or AI goes to engineering. A title with no match goes to other.

The three companies look very different. Wayfair has 29 of 50 roles in stores, warehouses and operations. That matches its posts about new stores. On October 7 it announced its 11th store, in Cherry Hill, New Jersey. On November 12 it announced a second New York store in the Buffalo area for 2028, at 96,000 square feet.

Snowflake has 32 of 50 roles in engineering, data engineering and research, plus 7 product roles. Its 8 sales roles include Spanish-speaking and French-speaking sales development representatives and an enterprise account executive for Norway. You can read that as growth in Europe and Spanish-speaking markets. Mercado Libre has 26 of 50 roles in sales. Most are Mercado Pago field sales, payment terminal and direct sales roles in Chile and Mexico.

Here are Wayfair's six "sales" roles. Three are "Assistant Store Manager of Sales", "Assistant Manager, Retail Sales" and "Assistant Store Manager, Retail Sales". These are store management roles. The sales rule runs before the stores rule, so "Retail Sales" matched sales first. Only three relate to business customers. They are a commercial go-to-market role for Wayfair Professional, a B2B sales strategy analytics manager and a sales compensation analyst.

A team that sells to Wayfair's business buying side could read "six sales roles" as fast B2B growth. Read each title, and the claim shrinks by half.

A job detail call can confirm one signal. We called linkedin/job_detail for the Wayfair commercial role, ID 4487569684, posted November 4. It cost $0.001194. The description says Wayfair Professional is the company's B2B business. It is "a multi-billion dollar business serving 1M+ active customers" in office, interior design, contractor and property management. The role owns go-to-market strategy for property management and works from the Boston headquarters four days a week.

A team that sells office furniture procurement software or property sector data can quote this in a proposal.

Read the job data with care in four more places. Wayfair's 50 rows hold only 45 distinct titles, and Mercado Libre's 50 hold only 38. The same role appears once per city. Remove duplicates by title, or by title and location, before you count roles. The choice depends on whether you want to talk about functions or headcount.

Wayfair's oldest role dates from May 27, and only 23 of its 50 rows are from the last 30 days. Long-running roles dilute "recent hiring".

The applicant_count column also needs care. Wayfair has 26 rows at exactly 25 and 2 at 200. Snowflake has 21 rows at 200. We think these are display buckets such as "first 25 applicants" or "over 200 applicants", so they are not exact counts. Salary is common in US rows: 45 of Wayfair's 50 have it. Only 1 of Mercado Libre's 50 Latin American rows has a salary.

News and web search: check every date

google_news/search with a one-month window returned 20 rows per company. All 60 rows across the three companies had a date, and all fell within 30 days. Wayfair's 20 included 5 from Yahoo Finance plus CNBC, CBS and several Buffalo local stations. The topics were third-quarter results, the Buffalo store and the late-October Way Day sale.

Snowflake's 20 included 11 from Yahoo Finance and 7 from Snowflake's own press releases and blog. For Mercado Libre we searched in Spanish for Mexico. Two of the 20 rows used "mercado libre" in the sense of "free market" and had nothing to do with the company. A person had to remove them. See the Google News API and news search pages for parameters.

News set Rows Within 30 days Largest source Company's own pages Off-topic
Wayfair, US, English 20 20 Yahoo Finance, 5 0 0
Snowflake Inc, US, English 20 20 Yahoo Finance, 11 7 0
Mercado Libre, Mexico, Spanish 20 20 Milenio, 3 0 2

web/search results were messier. We searched " news November 2026" for 10 rows each. Wayfair's 10 included 3 with no date, 1 with only "1 year ago", and a layoffs story from August 22, 2022. Snowflake's 10 included 1 with no date and 2 with only "days ago". The field note already warns that published_at for web search can be missing or wrong.

That matches what Google says about its own results. Google estimates the date in search results from several signals on the page. If the page does not mark its date clearly, the estimate can be wrong. See the web data API and web search pages for parameters.

So we split the work between the two sources. News search answers "what happened this month", and its dates can be used directly. Web search finds primary pages, such as investor relations pages and original press releases. We open each page, check the date and the numbers, and only then quote it.

If a model takes the August 2022 layoffs story as recent news, a November 2026 proposal will say "you are cutting staff". The story is more than four years old.

Writing the section: two sample "our understanding" drafts

We built two sample drafts from the data above. In the first, we write to Wayfair's corporate purchasing team. In the second, we write to Snowflake's sales operations team. Each sentence ends with a source ID in brackets: a post ID, a role ID, or a source and date for news. A model wrote the drafts under fixed rules. One rule mattered most: a sentence without a source ID does not go into the draft.

Wayfair draft. Your third-quarter 2026 revenue was $3.4 billion, up 9.7%, with US revenue up 11.4% and 22.2 million active customers (investor relations, November 4). Your store rollout is speeding up. In October you announced your 11th store in Cherry Hill (post 7513659797682982912, October 7, older than 30 days). On November 12 you announced a second New York store in the Buffalo area for 2028 (post 7526750679131062272). Of your 50 open roles, 29 are in stores, warehouses and operations.

Wayfair Professional, your business customer unit, serves more than 1 million active business customers and is hiring a commercial lead for property management (role 4487569684, November 4). You use AI at scale inside the company. More than 1,600 engineers use an AI coding tool (post 7526313811780472832, November 11). AI has validated more than 11 million product specs and resolves more than 41,000 supplier tickets each month (post 7524124393464217600, November 5).

Snowflake draft. At Expedition on November 3, you launched Business Ontology and Cortex AI Gateway, so AI agents can work inside governed data and permissions (press release, November 3; post 7524576411794194432, November 6). On November 10 you made Claude Fable 5.2 available the same day in private preview on Cortex AI (post 7525739668739497984). A post on November 14 proposed "cost per correct, governed outcome" as the way to measure AI spend (post 7527181045956349952).

In hiring, 32 of your 50 recent open roles are in engineering, data engineering and research. Your sales roles include Spanish-speaking and French-speaking representatives and a Norway account executive (company-filter URL, pulled November 16 at 00:31 Singapore time). Your third-quarter results come out on December 2 (press release, November 2). Any budget-cycle point in the proposal should take that date into account.

Fact in the draft Source type Source ID Date Within 30 days
Wayfair Q3 revenue $3.4 billion, up 9.7% Investor relations investor.wayfair.com Q3 results 2026-11-04 Yes
Wayfair 11th store in Cherry Hill Company post 7513659797682982912 2026-10-07 No, flagged
Wayfair Buffalo store in 2028 Company post 7526750679131062272 2026-11-12 Yes
Wayfair Professional, 1M+ active business customers Job detail 4487569684 2026-11-04 Yes
1,600+ Wayfair engineers use an AI coding tool Company post 7526313811780472832 2026-11-11 Yes
Snowflake Business Ontology and AI Gateway Press release snowflake.com press release 2026-11-03 Yes
Snowflake adds Claude Fable 5.2 Company post 7525739668739497984 2026-11-10 Yes
Snowflake Q3 results on December 2 Press release snowflake.com press release 2026-11-02 Yes

Neither draft quotes a web search row. In this test, web search only helped us find the investor relations page and the press releases. We opened those pages, checked them, and quoted the pages themselves.

Keep client-supplied material apart from public data

A proposal writer usually holds three kinds of material at once. There is the RFP and its attachments, there are notes from discovery calls, and there is public data like the data above. The first two come from the client and often carry confidentiality terms. The third is open to anyone.

If you mix all three in one prompt and ask for "recent context", two problems are common. The model can present a private remark from a call as "public reports say". It can also blend a public number with a number the client gave verbally, so neither source matches.

Aspect Public data Client-supplied material
Examples Company posts, open roles, press releases, earnings RFP, attachments, call notes, client emails
Storage A separate folder in the proposal project, filed by pull time Responsive project attachments, under project permissions
How it reaches the model Only structured results with source IDs A separate pass, marked "client-supplied, do not quote externally"
How the proposal cites it "In your November 12 announcement" "As stated in your requirements document"
Can it appear in material for third parties Yes, with the source No, unless the contract allows it
Expiry Flag after 30 days; drop from the section after 90 days The client's latest version wins

We follow three rules. First, the pass that pulls public data gets no client material in its prompt. A reviewer then reads the draft next to the client material and can see where each sentence came from. Second, every sentence carries a source ID. Client sentences use "file name and page", and public sentences use a post, role or URL. The two formats look different, so a mix-up is easy to see.

Third, never put client material into the parameters of an outside search or data API. For example, do not search the news for an unreleased project name that a client mentioned on a call. That sends confidential information to a third party.

Personal data needs its own line. Company posts and job pages sometimes name employees, for example a warehouse manager in a feature post. A proposal does not need any of those names. When you must refer to a person, use the job title, for example "your CFO said in a November interview with Bloomberg".

On November 10, 2026, the European Data Protection Board adopted version 2.0 of its guidelines on legitimate interest as a legal basis. A controller must assess and document three conditions before processing. The interest must be legitimate. The processing must be necessary. The person's rights must not override the interest.

Account research that collects only company-level facts avoids most of this work. This is a work habit, not legal advice. Ask your own counsel about specific cases.

Where hiring signals mislead

Case Example in this test Effect How to avoid it
Company name is also a skill Keyword "Snowflake": 38 of 50 roles from other employers Other employers' hiring is credited to the client Use job_search_url from the profile
Store roles with "Sales" in the title 3 of Wayfair's 6 "sales" roles are store managers B2B sales growth looks bigger than it is Read each title after the rule runs
Same role in many cities Wayfair: 45 titles in 50 rows; Mercado Libre: 38 in 50 Headcount looks bigger Remove duplicates by title, or title and location
Roles that stay open for months Wayfair's oldest is May 27; only 23 rows are recent A steady state looks like a new move Use the last 30 days, or compare with last month
Applicant counts are display buckets Wayfair: 26 rows at 25; Snowflake: 21 rows at 200 A bucket looks like demand Treat as a rough signal; keep it out of the proposal
Affiliates counted together Snowflake's filter URL holds 5 company IDs Subsidiaries and acquired teams blend into the parent Split by company_name if needed
Hiring is not buying Mercado Libre's 26 sales roles are mostly field sales It looks like a buyer of sales tools Hiring shows direction; budget needs other evidence

Mercado Libre has 26 sales roles in its 50. By business line, Mercado Pago has 15, Fintech has 7, and Mercado Ads and Marketplace have 2 each. By country, Chile has 14 of the 26 and Mexico has 9. Mercado Libre is hiring Mercado Pago field sellers in large numbers. You can read that as a push for offline merchants in Chile and Mexico. It does not mean the company will buy a CRM or sales training.

Keep "what the client is doing" apart from "what the client needs from us". The second claim needs the client's own words, from the RFP or a call. That brings us back to the previous section: those words are client material and go in the other column.

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on November 3 that job openings were about 7.5 million in September. On November 12, Indeed Hiring Lab published quarterly reports on tech and retail hiring. Retail seasonal postings grew faster than in the same period of earlier years. Before you compare one company's role count with figures like these, check the scope. National data estimates all postings across channels. Our data is the top 50 open roles of one company on one platform at one moment.

One remote MCP round trip: tools/list and tools/call

Inside an assistant, all of these calls run through one tool. At 00:33 Singapore time we sent a tools/list request to https://api.everyinfra.com/mcp. The tool list included everyinfra_list_capabilities for the catalog, everyinfra_call_api for any capability, and everyinfra_get_job for async jobs. The tool description says the catalog covers 106 platforms and 574 capabilities. Then we used everyinfra_call_api to pull Mercado Libre's open roles, with the filter URL from its profile as the parameter.

# The tools/call sent at 00:33:36 Singapore time (the key comes from an environment variable only)
curl -s https://api.everyinfra.com/mcp \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $EVERYINFRA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"everyinfra_call_api",
       "arguments":{"platform":"linkedin","action":"jobs",
       "params":{"keyword":"https://www.linkedin.com/jobs/search?geoId=92000000&f_C=14226%2C107272452","limit":50}}}}'

A remote MCP call sent at 00:33 Singapore time on November 16, 2026. The response holds 50 roles and the charge for the call. EveryInfra remote MCP response, November 16, 2026, 00:33 SGT, screenshot

The content field of the response holds a JSON text. Its results hold 50 roles, and billing shows a charge of $0.000556, the same as a direct REST call. In the MCP specification, tools/list lets a client discover the tools on a server, and tools/call runs one. JSON Schema describes tool inputs and outputs.

Remote servers use Streamable HTTP, with one endpoint for POST and GET. The authorization section of the spec recommends OAuth 2.1 for HTTP transports and also allows other methods. Our call used a bearer token, as defined for OAuth 2.0 in RFC 6750. Setup details are on the MCP server page.

Setup in Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Responsive (configuration examples)

The four setups below are configuration examples. Each one follows the vendor's help center. We tested only the tools/list and tools/call requests that we sent with curl in the previous section. We did not test the setup in Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot or Responsive.

A Claude custom connector connects from Anthropic's cloud to your MCP server, so the server must be reachable from the public internet. On Team and Enterprise plans, an owner adds the connector and each member connects on their own. Connectors inherit each user's permissions in the connected system.

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "everyinfra": {
      "url": "https://api.everyinfra.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" }
    },
    "responsive": {
      "url": "https://<tenant>.rfpio.com/oa/v1/mcp"
    }
  }
}

This configuration connects one assistant to two servers. EveryInfra supplies public data. Responsive supplies internal answers and takes the write-back. The Responsive entry uses OAuth, as its help center describes, so the config holds no key. The first use opens a sign-in page.

In ChatGPT, the OpenAI help center explains how to add a custom MCP server in settings. The Responsive example for ChatGPT uses OAuth, and its save tool is save_project_question_response. In Copilot Studio, the Microsoft docs say to add a new tool and choose Model Context Protocol. You enter a server name, a description and a URL. Authentication can be none, API key or OAuth 2.0. Copilot Studio supports only the Streamable transport and dropped SSE after August 2025.

To add EveryInfra to Responsive as an outside connector, the help center steps are as follows. Open Organization Settings, then Responsive AI, then MCP Connectors, then Add New. Enter a name and a description, such as "Look up public company pages, company posts, open roles and news, with dates and source links". Enter https://api.everyinfra.com/mcp as the URL. Choose API key, choose Request Header, and change X-API-Key to Authorization. Enter Bearer and the key as the value, and check the Request Preview before you save.

Responsive then discovers the tools and turns all of them on. An admin can keep only everyinfra_call_api and everyinfra_list_capabilities. The help center also gives the lookup order. Responsive AI checks the content library first, then outside sources, and the MCP server last, unless the prompt names a tool. So the prompt should say "use everyinfra_call_api to query linkedin/jobs".

Whatever the setup, write the rules into the prompt. Sort by date and keep the last 30 days. Give each sentence a source ID. Remove duplicate roles by title. Use web search only to find original pages. The snippet below holds our sort and cut logic. A model can follow it as an instruction, and a script can run it.

from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta
cut = datetime(2026, 11, 16, tzinfo=timezone.utc) - timedelta(days=30)
posts = sorted(resp["results"], key=lambda p: p["posted_at"], reverse=True)   # sort newest first
recent = [p for p in posts if datetime.fromisoformat(p["posted_at"]) >= cut]
older = [p for p in posts if datetime.fromisoformat(p["posted_at"]) < cut]    # separate column, not in the brief
seen, jobs = set(), []
for j in job_resp["results"]:
    key = (j["title"].strip().lower(), j.get("location"))                     # one row per title and city
    if key not in seen:
        seen.add(key); jobs.append(j)

What a sales proposal AI agent pays for research per proposal

One client brief, with one call per capability, costs the following. Company page $0.000556, posts $0.002319, open roles $0.000556, job detail $0.001194, news $0.000792 and web search $0.001389. The total is $0.006806. If you quote three job details, add two more detail calls for a total of $0.009194.

At 100 proposals a year, the data cost is about $0.68. Model costs come on top and depend on the assistant you use. Prices follow the pricing page and the price_usd of each capability in the catalog. In this test, the charged_usd of all 17 calls matched the catalog prices.

Option Calls per client Cost per client 100 proposals
Lean: profile, roles, news 3 $0.001904 about $0.19
Standard: one call per capability 6 $0.006806 about $0.68
With job details: quote 3 roles 8 $0.009194 about $0.92
Client that rarely posts: no posts 5 $0.004487 about $0.45

We measured time from the call log. From the first request at 00:18:57 to the last at 00:34:21, the test took 15 minutes and 24 seconds. For the first 4 minutes, we waited on rate limits for the shared key. Between 00:24 and 00:29, eight async calls failed and we retried them. After we changed to sync mode, 11 charged calls ran from 00:29:42 to 00:34:21. That is 4 minutes and 39 seconds, or about 25 seconds per call.

We did not time the model draft or the human check, so we give no number for them. In the check, open the source for every number that goes into the proposal: revenue, store count and role count.

The 8 failed calls: async mode returned 503 and cost nothing

Eight calls failed in this test. We sent linkedin/company_posts and web/search in async mode ("mode":"async") twice each for Wayfair and Snowflake. All eight returned HTTP 503. The posts calls said the data was unavailable for now. The web search calls reported an internal error while preparing the request.

The posts responses had a billing object with charged set to false and an amount of 0. They also had a refund status. The web search responses had no billing object, and next_steps said "Not charged". No call in either group was charged. We switched to synchronous mode, and all four calls succeeded with 20 or 10 rows each.

Capability Mode Attempts Result Charged
linkedin/company_posts async 2 each for Wayfair and Snowflake 4 × 503 $0
web/search async 2 each for Wayfair and Snowflake 4 × 503 $0
linkedin/company_posts sync 1 each for Wayfair, Snowflake, Mercado Libre 20 rows $0.002319 each
web/search sync 1 each for Wayfair and Snowflake 10 rows $0.001389 each

To diagnose, we first called company posts in sync mode with the catalog's example parameter, the company "google". It returned 10 posts for $0.002319. That confirmed the capability worked, and then we went back to our companies. The check is included in the 17 charged calls.

If an assistant hits a 503 halfway, the model may say "no recent activity found". That sentence in a proposal would be false.

When the API cannot get results, it returns 503 and charges nothing. The response has retryable and retry_after. For the posts calls, retry_after was 60 seconds with up to 2 retries. For the web search calls, it was 30 seconds with 1 retry. Tell the model in the prompt that 503 means "retry after retry_after, or use sync mode". It must never mean "the company has no recent news".

Industry moves: proposal tools added MCP this month

Two weeks before the Responsive fall release, QorusDocs launched QPilot Workspace on October 27, 2026. Its press release says MCP connectors link it to Microsoft Copilot, Claude and ChatGPT. It also cites the company's survey: 68% of respondents saw proposal volume rise.

AdExchanger reported in November that TIME's ad sales team uses an AI agent to read RFPs and draft proposals. The story mentions an MCP server. AutoRFP published a November post on using Claude connectors for RFPs.

Over a longer span, Anthropic released MCP on November 25, 2024. The latest spec version is dated 2025-11-25. Responsive's spring release (2026-05-13) and fall release (2026-11-10) are 181 days apart. The spring release cites a Gartner prediction. By 2027, 80% of AI agent interaction with SaaS apps will run through SaaS-hosted MCP servers, up from less than 5% in 2025.

The 2025 State of Strategic Response Management report from Responsive and APMP has one useful number. 75% of organizations say buyers demand faster responses and more personalization under tighter budgets.

APMP splits winning business into a pre-bid capture stage and a bid and proposal stage. Analysis of client objectives, challenges and history belongs to the capture stage. Writing starts after the RFP arrives. So do account research during capture, before the RFP. When you write, refresh only the last week.

Limits: what this method cannot do

First, public data shows what a client does, not what it needs. Hiring, posts and news are things the client chose to say in public, with a PR filter. The "our understanding" section can use them. The "your challenges" section must rest on what the client said in the RFP and in calls.

Second, each call returned 20 posts and 50 roles. For companies that post and hire a lot, that is only a slice. "You are hiring for 50 roles" is wrong. "Among roles posted in the last 30 days" is right.

Third, LinkedIn's official API does not cover this kind of reading. Microsoft's documentation describes the Community Management API for pages where you hold an admin role. Reading posts, posting and analytics apply only to organizations you manage. In proposal work, you need the client's page, and you are not its admin.

Fourth, a person must review every draft. Our drafts follow fixed rules, and the rules miss some cases, such as odd job titles or a post that covers two topics. Only a person catches those. Fifth, this article is not legal advice. Ask your own counsel about cross-border use of public data and about quoting third-party reporting in proposals.

Get started

Step one: get an API key from the EveryInfra quickstart. Call linkedin/company_profile for a client you know well and note the job_search_url in the response.

Step two: pass that URL to linkedin/jobs. Then call linkedin/company_posts and google_news/search. Sort the results by date, keep the last 30 days, and read them yourself. Confirm that no other employer's roles slipped in.

Step three: connect the remote MCP server in your assistant. Put the rules from step two in the prompt. Sort, cut, remove duplicates, cite a source ID and retry on 503.

Step four: with Responsive, use the "Responsive as server" direction and connect both servers in one assistant. As an alternative, an admin can add an outside connector under MCP Connectors in Responsive. Check the Request Preview before you save.

Step five: before the proposal goes out, a person checks three kinds of numbers in the client section. These are revenue and results, store or employee counts, and role counts.

For more ways to read hiring data, see job posting data as buying signals. For another case of public data in a business tool through remote MCP, see ActiveCampaign MCP: subject lines and segments from real reviews.

FAQ

What is the Responsive MCP server, and what can it do in an assistant?

The Responsive MCP Server connects ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Claude to approved answers and project data in Responsive. Its capability page says users can draft and save responses to project questions, add comments and complete reviews. Available actions vary by assistant and user permissions. The fall release on November 10, 2026, extended the server from lookups to these actions.

Can Responsive (responsive io MCP) connect to an outside data source?

Yes. A help article covers connecting outside MCP servers to Responsive AI. An admin adds the server under MCP Connectors in Organization Settings.

Authentication supports API keys, in a header or a query parameter, and OAuth 2.0. Responsive discovers the tools on its own. The MCP client feature is part of Responsive AI, and the help article says to contact Responsive support to enable it. It does not say which plans include it.

What does data cost for a sales proposal AI agent?

In our test, one client brief with one call per capability costs $0.006806. Profile, roles and news alone cost $0.001904. For 100 proposals a year, the range is $0.19 to $0.92, depending on which calls you make. Model costs come on top and depend on your assistant and plan.

Can I use ChatGPT as a sales proposal AI agent?

Yes. ChatGPT supports custom MCP servers, and Responsive documents a ChatGPT setup. The method is the same as in Claude: connect two servers in one assistant, one for public data and one for Responsive. Put the rules for sorting, duplicates and source IDs in the prompt. Assistants differ a little in how they call tools. On first use, ask the assistant to list the parameters of each tool call, and check them.

How does this fit with client records in Salesforce?

Opportunity records, contacts and call notes in Salesforce are client material. They go in the client-supplied column and stay out of the public-data prompt. After you pull public data, you can write fields such as company size, headquarters and recent role count back to the CRM account record. Add the pull date, and pull again after 30 days.

How often should I refresh hiring data?

Pull once when you write the proposal. If news breaks in the last week before you submit, refresh the news only. In this test, all 50 Snowflake roles were posted on or after October 25, so roles change fast. Wayfair has long-running store roles, with the oldest from May 27. For a quarterly account review, pull roles once a month and compare the mix by function. The change tells you more than a single count.

title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen in a React chat: the migration details that actually matter
description:
Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen (gemini-4-hydrogen) on November 12, 2026. It's the fast, cheaper model in the Gemini 4 family, sitting below Carbon and Argon. It's on the free and paid tiers of the Gemini API and AI Studio, and the paid price is flat across the whole context window: $1.50 per 1M input tokens and $7.50 per 1M output tokens (thinking tokens count as output).

Google's launch post says that compared with Gemini 3.8 Flash it finishes tasks 2.5x faster at its default setting and more than triples Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores (57% vs. 18.2%). Those are Google's numbers. I haven't benchmarked them myself.

What I did test is the boring part: wiring Hydrogen into a streaming React chat with the Vercel AI SDK, and checking what actually goes over the wire. A few details in the migration guide are easy to miss.

What changed for developers

From the official "What's new in Gemini 4 Hydrogen" guide:

  • Four thinking levels: low, medium, high (the default) and a new xhigh. minimal is rejected with an error.
  • One unified window: input, thinking and output share 1,048,576 tokens. A single request still caps at 65,536 output tokens, streaming or not. To go longer you use background execution or client-side continuation.
  • Sampling params are gone: remove temperature, top_p and top_k. In-range values are ignored, and out-of-range values return a 400.
  • No explicit caching: cachedContents / caches.create aren't supported. Implicit caching runs automatically on prompts of at least 4,096 tokens and discounts cached input by 95%.
  • Thought signatures matter: if you manage history yourself with generateContent, send prior model turns and thought signatures back unchanged.

The guide also suggests running your evals at all four levels and picking the lowest level that meets your quality bar. That's good advice for a chat UI, where latency is most of the user experience.

SDK support

@ai-sdk/google 4.0.119 added the gemini-4-hydrogen model ID and the xhigh thinking level (see the package changelog). I used ai@7.0.173 with @ai-sdk/google@4.0.121.

The route handler 

// app/api/chat/route.ts
import { streamText, convertToModelMessages, type UIMessage } from 'ai';
import { google } from '@ai-sdk/google';

export const maxDuration = 60;

type Level = 'low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh';

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { messages, level = 'medium' }: { messages: UIMessage[]; level?: Level } =
    await req.json();

  const result = streamText({
    model: google('gemini-4-hydrogen'),
    messages: await convertToModelMessages(messages),
    // No temperature/topP: Hydrogen ignores them (out-of-range values return a 400).
    providerOptions: {
      google: { thinkingConfig: { thinkingLevel: level, includeThoughts: true } },
    },
  });

  return result.toUIMessageStreamResponse({ sendReasoning: true });
}

I default to medium because Google's own table recommends it for responsive chat and interactive coding. high is the API default, though, so if you omit the level you pay for more thinking than a chat turn usually needs.

The client

A plain useChat component that shows reasoning in a collapsible block and lets the user pick the thinking level for each message:

'use client';
import { useState } from 'react';
import { useChat } from '@ai-sdk/react';

export function Chat() {
  const [input, setInput] = useState('');
  const [level, setLevel] = useState<'low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh'>('medium');
  const { messages, sendMessage, status, stop } = useChat();

  return (
    <div className="mx-auto flex max-w-2xl flex-col gap-4 p-4">
      {messages.map((m) => (
        <div key={m.id} className={m.role === 'user' ? 'self-end' : 'self-start'}>
          {m.parts.map((part, i) =>
            part.type === 'reasoning' ? (
              <details key={i} className="text-sm text-muted-foreground">
                <summary>Thinking</summary>
                <p className="whitespace-pre-wrap">{part.text}</p>
              </details>
            ) : part.type === 'text' ? (
              <p key={i} className="whitespace-pre-wrap">{part.text}</p>
            ) : null,
          )}
        </div>
      ))}
      <form
        className="flex gap-2"
        onSubmit={(e) => {
          e.preventDefault();
          if (!input.trim()) return;
          sendMessage({ text: input }, { body: { level } });
          setInput('');
        }}
      >
        <select value={level} onChange={(e) => setLevel(e.target.value as typeof level)}>
          <option value="low">low</option>
          <option value="medium">medium</option>
          <option value="high">high</option>
          <option value="xhigh">xhigh</option>
        </select>
        <input className="flex-1 border px-2" value={input} onChange={(e) => setInput(e.target.value)} />
        {status === 'streaming' ? (
          <button type="button" onClick={stop}>Stop</button>
        ) : (
          <button type="submit" disabled={status === 'submitted'}>Send</button>
        )}
      </form>
    </div>
  );
}

Swap the raw elements for shadcn Button, Select and Collapsible if that's your stack. The data flow stays the same.

How I tested it (and what I didn't)

To be upfront: I didn't call the live API for this post. I ran the code above on Node 24 with a custom fetch that records the outgoing request and replies with a fake SSE stream. That checks the wiring, not the model's quality or speed. Here's what it showed:

  1. The request is right. It hits models/gemini-4-hydrogen:streamGenerateContent?alt=sse with thinkingConfig: { thinkingLevel, includeThoughts: true }. The UI stream comes back as reasoning-start / reasoning-delta / reasoning-end followed by text-* parts, which is exactly what the details block renders.
  2. temperature is still forwarded, with no warning. Passing temperature: 0.2 put "temperature": 0.2 in generationConfig, and result.warnings was empty. Per Google's guide the server ignores in-range values, so this won't break anything. But if your shared config sets something out of range, you'll get a 400 and the SDK won't have warned you. I'd strip sampling params for Hydrogen.
  3. thinkingLevel: 'minimal' passes through unchanged. The provider's types still allow it for older models, so a config copied from a Gemini 3 app will type-check and then fail at the API. Search your code for minimal.
  4. The portable reasoning option maps correctly. reasoning: 'xhigh' became thinkingLevel: 'xhigh' on Hydrogen. On gemini-4-argon, the SDK downgraded it to high and raised a compatibility warning, which matches the changelog note that xhigh maps only for Hydrogen.

Honest limits

  • The speed and benchmark figures above are Google's, not mine.
  • xhigh costs more and responds more slowly, and Google warns it can overthink simple prompts. Don't make it the default in a chat box.
  • Thinking tokens are billed as output at $7.50/1M, so includeThoughts plus high on every turn adds up. Log usage.outputTokenDetails.reasoningTokens, which the SDK exposes, and watch it.
  • If you rely on explicit context caching for a big system prompt, that path is gone. Check whether implicit caching (prompts of 4,096+ tokens) covers your case.

Sources

  • Google: Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen (Nov 12, 2026)
  • Google AI Studio docs: What's new in Gemini 4 Hydrogen
  • Vercel AI SDK: @ai-sdk/google changelog (4.0.119)

If you'd rather not hand-roll the reasoning, tool-call and message components, Cuelark UI has shadcn-style ones built for this kind of stream.

Call Google Cloud APIs from streaming gateways

title: Architecting Scalable E-Commerce & Booking Platforms with React, Django REST & PostgreSQL (Sub-Second TTFB Architecture)
description:
Architecting Scalable E-Commerce & Booking Platforms with React, Django REST & PostgreSQL (Sub-Second TTFB Architecture)

Engineering scalable, mission-critical web applications—whether high-volume e-commerce engines, patient healthcare booking portals, or multi-tenant SaaS platforms—requires a disciplined decoupling of presentation and business logic. When off-the-shelf monolithic page builders buckle under high concurrency and database strain, senior engineering teams rely on the battle-tested power of React, Django REST Framework (DRF), and PostgreSQL.

In this technical architectural teardown, the engineering team at UCDREAMS breaks down the complete production blueprints for building sub-second TTFB, enterprise-grade web applications.

1. High-Performance Decoupled Architecture

Modern web application performance relies on strict separation of concerns:

[ Browser / Native App ]
       │  (HTTPS / HTTP/2 / WebSockets)
       ▼
[ Cloudflare / Fastly Edge CDN ] ────► Static Asset Cache & Geo-Routing
       │
       ▼ (Reverse Proxy / SSL Termination)
[ NGINX Edge Gateway & Rate Limiter ]
       │  (Gunicorn / Uvicorn WSGI/ASGI)
       ▼
[ Django REST Framework (DRF) Application Tier ]
       ├── Redis Enterprise (Query Cache, Session Store & Celery Queue)
       └── PostgreSQL High-Availability Cluster (PgBouncer Connection Pooling)

Key Architectural Tenets:

  1. Stateless JWT & HTTP-Only Refresh Tokens: Maximum horizontal scalability across multi-region container clusters without session affinity bottlenecks.
  2. PgBouncer Connection Pooling: Managing thousands of concurrent transactional connections with sub-millisecond query allocation.
  3. Redis Read-Through Caching: Eliminating duplicate database roundtrips for catalog metadata, inventory lookups, and user access control lists (ACLs).

2. Production Django REST Framework Optimization

Default Django ORM configurations often suffer from the classic N+1 query dilemma. In enterprise e-commerce and booking applications, unoptimized queries can rapidly exhaust database connection limits.

Eliminating N+1 Queries with select_related and prefetch_related 

# models.py - High-Performance E-Commerce Schema
from django.db import models
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model

User = get_user_model()

class BookingOrder(models.Model):
    user = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='orders')
    reference_id = models.CharField(max_length=32, unique=True, db_index=True)
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20, default='PENDING', db_index=True)
    total_amount = models.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True, db_index=True)

    class Meta:
        indexes = [
            models.Index(fields=['status', 'created_at']),
        ]

class BookingItem(models.Model):
    order = models.ForeignKey(BookingOrder, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='items')
    service_sku = models.CharField(max_length=64, db_index=True)
    quantity = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=1)
    unit_price = models.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2)

# views.py - Optimized DRF ViewSet with Sub-50ms Query Execution
from rest_framework import viewsets, permissions
from rest_framework.response import Response
from django.core.cache import cache

class BookingOrderViewSet(viewsets.ReadOnlyModelViewSet):
    permission_classes = [permissions.IsAuthenticated]

    def get_queryset(self):
        # 1-Query execution combining order, customer profile, and item lines
        return (
            BookingOrder.objects.filter(user=self.request.user)
            .select_related('user')
            .prefetch_related('items')
            .order_by('-created_at')
        )

3. Sub-Second Core Web Vitals on React Frontends

For consumer-facing booking and checkout flows, Core Web Vitals directly impact search engine visibility and checkout conversion rates:

  • Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): Under 1.2s through prioritized edge hero rendering and WebP/AVIF compression.
  • Interaction to Next Paint (INP): Under 50ms via non-blocking asynchronous state dispatch and optimistic UI updates.
  • Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): Zero shift with fixed aspect-ratio containers and server-driven skeleton loaders.

4. Real-Time State Sync via WebSockets

For live seat reservations, inventory countdowns, and concurrent booking locks, polling is an anti-pattern that creates unnecessary server load. We leverage Django Channels with Redis backends to broadcast state updates:

// React Live Booking Hook
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export function useLiveBookingState(orderId) {
  const [status, setStatus] = useState('SYNCING');

  useEffect(() => {
    const ws = new WebSocket(`wss://ucdreams.com/ws/orders/${orderId}/`);

    ws.onmessage = (event) => {
      const data = JSON.parse(event.data);
      if (data.type === 'STATUS_UPDATE') {
        setStatus(data.status);
      }
    };

    return () => ws.close();
  }, [orderId]);

  return { status };
}

5. Live Showcase: The UCDREAMS Ecosystem

At UCDREAMS, our engineering teams put these full-stack principles into daily practice:

  • UCDREAMS Web Development Services: Hand-crafted, semantic, lightweight container architectures delivering guaranteed 95+ PageSpeed scores.
  • UCDREAMS In-Browser Tools Hub: 100% client-side, zero-server utilities including P2P WebRTC large file transfer (FileShareOnline), AI cutout background removal (Image Background Remover), and office document editors (DOCX Web Editor).
  • UCDREAMS Multiplayer Games Hub: 60FPS real-time canvas games powered by low-latency state synchronization (Paper War and Ludo Classic).

title: The Security Bugs That Look Fine in Code Review
description:
I recently finished 41 secure-coding labs across TypeScript, Java and C#. The biggest lesson was not about exotic exploits. The bugs that cause real damage usually look like perfectly reasonable code, and they pass review because every line makes sense on its own.
Here are five patterns that stood out, each with the one-line habit that prevents it. The examples use TypeScript and NestJS, but the ideas apply everywhere.

  1. Checking who you are, but not whose data it is Authentication answers "who is this?" Authorization answers "can they touch this object?" Many APIs do the first and forget the second. This is the classic broken object-level authorization (IDOR) bug. // Looks fine, but any logged-in user can read any invoice return this.invoices.findOne({ where: { id } });

// Scope the query to the owner
return this.invoices.findOne({ where: { id, ownerId: user.id } });
Habit: every query that loads something by ID should also be scoped to the caller, or go through an explicit permission check.

  1. Trusting a token because it "verifies" A token that passes signature verification is not automatically a token you should accept. Pin the algorithm, the issuer and the audience, and check expiry. jwt.verify(token, publicKey, { algorithms: ['RS256'], issuer: 'https://auth.example.com', audience: 'my-api', }); The same applies to identity headers set by a gateway. If your service trusts x-user-id, make sure nothing outside the gateway can set it. Habit: decide exactly what a valid token must contain, and reject everything else.
  2. Race conditions in business logic Imagine a voucher with a quota of one. Two requests arrive at the same moment, both read remaining = 1, and both succeed. Nothing was "hacked"; the logic simply was not atomic. // Read, check, then write: two requests can both pass the check const v = await repo.findOne({ where: { id } }); if (v.remaining > 0) { v.remaining--; await repo.save(v); }

// Let the database do the check and the write in one statement
const res = await db.query(
'UPDATE vouchers SET remaining = remaining - 1 WHERE id = $1 AND remaining > 0',
[id],
);
if (res.rowCount === 0) throw new ConflictException('Quota exhausted');
Habit: anything involving money, quotas or inventory needs an atomic update or a transaction with the right isolation.

  1. Webhooks that can be replayed Verifying a webhook signature proves it came from the sender. It does not prove it is new. An attacker who captures one valid request can send it again. Check the signature, check the timestamp is recent, and store event IDs so each one is processed once. Habit: signature plus timestamp plus idempotency key. All three.
  2. Letting clients decide which fields to set Mass assignment happens when you pass a request body straight into your model and a client adds "role": "admin". In NestJS you can reject unknown fields globally: app.useGlobalPipes( new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true }), ); Habit: define the fields a client may send, and drop or reject everything else. A small checklist Before I open a pull request now, I ask: • Is this query scoped to the caller? • Is every token or header I trust actually verified, and only for what it should prove? • Can two requests at once break this rule? • Could a captured request be replayed? • Can a client set a field it should not? Over to you Which of these have you seen in a real codebase? And what is the one security habit you wish you had learned earlier? I would love to hear it in the comments. I am a software engineer working with NestJS, TypeScript, Python and Soroban. You can find my work on GitHub at github.com/OthmanImam.
