title: How I Built an Autonomous AI News Digest Agent in 48 Hours (Node.js, OpenRouter & Nodemailer)
description:
We live in an era of unprecedented information overload. Every morning, millions of professionals wake up, open dozens of browser tabs, scroll through chaotic social media feeds, and attempt to filter through mountains of noise just to stay informed on the topics that actually matter to their industry. Traditional RSS readers require manual curation, and modern news aggregators are flooded with clickbait, algorithmic bias, and distracting ads.

As a backend developer, I realized I didn't need another third-party SaaS subscription or bloated browser extension to solve this problem. I needed a custom-built, proactive intelligence system that could do the heavy lifting for me.

Over a fast-paced 48-hour build sprint, I engineered a fully autonomous, cron-driven backend agent from first principles. Without relying on heavy frameworks or black-box wrappers, this agent wakes up on a strict schedule, fetches breaking metadata from external news sources, scrapes and sanitizes raw web payloads, passes the content through an advanced Large Language Model for high-signal summarization, and dispatches a beautifully formatted HTML newsletter straight to my inbox.

Here is the complete architectural deep dive into how I designed, built, and shipped this autonomous system.

The Philosophy: Shifting from Reactive CRUD to Proactive Agents
Most junior and mid-level backend portfolios look identical: a standard Express server hooked up to a database handling CRUD operations waiting for a frontend client to make an HTTP request. While essential, these systems are entirely reactive. They sit idle until a human interacts with them.

Autonomous agents represent a fundamental shift in systems architecture. They are proactive. They operate independently in the background, orchestrated by time-based triggers or event streams, executing complex workflows without human intervention.

Building this news agent taught me how to think in terms of asynchronous pipelines. Instead of managing synchronous request-response lifecycles, I had to design a decoupled workflow where data flows seamlessly across distinct domain services—from ingestion and scraping to AI transformation and final delivery.

Architectural Blueprint: The 4-Stage Pipeline
To ensure the system remained modular, maintainable, and easy to debug, I decoupled the architecture into distinct, single-responsibility modules:

The Ingestion Layer: Responsible for querying external news providers (such as The Guardian Content API) using secure, environment-scoped credentials to harvest fresh breaking article metadata and target URLs.

The Scraping and Filtering Layer: Takes the raw article URLs, pulls the core Document Object Model (DOM) content, strips away irrelevant boilerplate, and filters out low-signal entries.

The AI Summarization Layer: Passes the sanitized text payload to an LLM via the OpenRouter SDK. Instead of forcing me to read dense, 2,000-word articles, the model extracts core themes, key takeaways, and executive summaries.

The Dispatch Layer: Transforms the summarized text strings into a responsive, beautifully styled HTML card and pushes it out via an automated SMTP email service using Nodemailer.

The Orchestration Layer: Powered by a background cron scheduler that manages exact execution times, ensuring the pipeline fires reliably without manual triggers.

Deep Dive into Core Pipeline Execution

  1. Managing Asynchronous Data Flow The backbone of the entire application is an isolated asynchronous pipeline function. Rather than cluttering the global scope with mutable state arrays, each execution cycle initializes a clean execution scope.

The pipeline begins by calling the ingestion module to fetch article metadata. Once URLs are retrieved, the scraper module extracts the underlying text content. After passing the payload through a strict filter to discard empty or malformed items, the data is handed off to the LLM summarizer. Finally, the enriched object is pushed to the email dispatch service. Wrapping this entire sequence in robust try-catch blocks ensures that if an external API times out or throws an error, the system logs the failure gracefully without crashing the entire Node process or leaving background workers hanging.

  1. Crafting Responsive HTML Newsletters Delivering text via plain, unstyled emails looks unprofessional and degrades readability. To solve this, I designed a custom email delivery module that constructs a clean newsletter card.

Because major email clients (like Gmail, Outlook, and Apple Mail) notoriously strip out external stylesheets and complex CSS layout rules, I utilized robust inline styling techniques. The module takes the raw string output from the LLM summarizer, splits the text paragraphs cleanly, and wraps them in structured paragraph tags with explicit margins and line heights. These paragraphs are then injected into a centered, max-width container featuring a dark navy header banner and a soft, neutral background. This guarantees crisp, consistent rendering across both desktop and mobile email clients. Furthermore, authentication is handled securely through Google's App Passwords, allowing the application to authenticate via SMTP without exposing primary account credentials in plaintext config files.

  1. Background Orchestration with Cron An autonomous agent is only as good as its scheduling reliability. To automate the pipeline, I integrated a background cron manager.

One of the most valuable lessons I learned during this build was the importance of cron expression syntax. Standard cron schedulers utilize a 5-field format representing minutes, hours, day of the month, month, and day of the week. Initially, misconfiguring second-level parameters led to aggressive loop behaviors. Sticking strictly to standard 5-field syntax resolved execution timing completely, allowing me to configure precise daily triggers (such as running at 7:00 AM and 3:00 PM) while binding the runtime environment to a local timezone to prevent UTC offset discrepancies. Additionally, keeping an Express server running alongside the scheduler allowed me to expose a manual webhook endpoint, making local debugging and testing effortless via curl commands.

Engineering Challenges and Hard-Won Lessons
Every rapid development sprint comes with unexpected hurdles. Building this agent over two days surfaced two notable engineering challenges:

SMTP Authentication Barriers: When first wiring up Nodemailer with a personal Gmail account, I ran into strict authentication blocks due to Two-Step Verification policies. Learning how to navigate Google's security architecture to generate dedicated App Passwords reinforced the importance of secure secret management and zero-trust configuration practices.

Cron Granularity and Overlapping Runs: During early testing, setting cron intervals too aggressively caused overlapping pipeline executions when an external scraping or LLM request took slightly longer than expected. This highlighted the necessity of building idempotent background tasks and adding locking mechanisms or database state checks.

What Comes Next?
Building a fully functional autonomous news digest agent in 48 hours proved how powerful lightweight Node.js backends can be when combining external APIs, local scraping engines, and generative AI models.

The immediate next phase of development involves integrating MongoDB persistence. By storing the unique hashes or URLs of articles that have already been emailed, the agent will be able to perform deduplication checks. If the underlying news source has not published a fresh top story between cron intervals, the agent will intelligently skip execution rather than dispatching redundant updates.

If you are an engineer looking to sharpen your backend skills, step away from standard frontend CRUD apps for a weekend. Build something that runs in the background, talks to multiple APIs, reasons over data using an LLM, and delivers value autonomously. The architectural insights you gain will completely transform how you approach software design.

title: Pruebas de API con Newman: de 0 a 121 aserciones en un pipeline que despliega en Vercel
description:
Actividad Grupal 2: API Testing: Calidad y Pruebas de Software (SI-784), Universidad Privada de Tacna.
Autores: Milton H. Flores Chino y Manuel Andre Dongo Palza.

Repositorio: https://github.com/miltom123/si784-grupal2-api-testing
API en producción: https://si784-api-envios.vercel.app

El problema

Probar una API "a mano" con Postman sirve el primer día. Al tercer cambio ya nadie repite los 20 clics, y los errores llegan a producción. Para este trabajo nos pusimos una regla simple: ningún cambio llega a producción si no pasan las pruebas, y las mismas pruebas se repiten contra la URL pública después de desplegar.

Para eso construimos una API pequeña y la probamos con dos herramientas:

  • Newman, la versión de línea de comandos de Postman. Cubre las pruebas funcionales y de contrato, y es el tema de este artículo.
  • k6 para las pruebas de carga. Mi compañero Manuel lo explica en su artículo.

La API bajo prueba

Es una API REST sin estado que cotiza envíos entre departamentos del Perú. Está hecha con Node.js 20 y Hono.

Método Ruta Qué hace
GET /v1/health Estado y versión
GET /v1/departamentos?zona= 25 departamentos con su zona
GET /v1/departamentos/{codigo} Un departamento (404 si no existe)
POST /v1/cotizaciones Calcula el precio del envío
GET /v1/openapi.json Contrato OpenAPI 3

Las reglas de negocio tienen suficientes detalles para que valga la pena probarlas:

  • Tarifa base de S/ 8 en la misma zona y S/ 12 entre zonas.
  • S/ 2.50 por cada 0.5 kg iniciado.
  • Recargo de selva, servicio express ×1.6 y seguro del 1 %.
  • IGV del 18 %.

Los errores siempre tienen la misma forma:

{ "error": { "code": "VALIDACION", "message": "...", "campo": "pesoKg" } }

Pruébala tú mismo:

curl -X POST https://si784-api-envios.vercel.app/v1/cotizaciones \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"origen":"TAC","destino":"ARE","pesoKg":2.3}'

Por qué Newman

  • La colección es un archivo JSON versionado en el repositorio, junto al código que prueba.
  • Corre en cualquier CI con npx newman run, sin abrir Postman.
  • Tiene reporteros de consola, JUnit y HTML (newman-reporter-htmlextra), así los resultados quedan como artefactos del pipeline.
  • La misma colección se ejecuta contra localhost y contra producción. Solo cambia la variable baseUrl.

Diseño de la colección: 22 peticiones en 4 carpetas

En vez de editar a mano un JSON de 1000 líneas, la colección se genera con un script (generar-coleccion.mjs) a partir de una lista legible de casos. Las aserciones que se repiten se escriben una sola vez:

const cotizacionValida = [
  status(200),
  `pm.test('cumple el esquema de cotización', () => pm.response.to.have.jsonSchema(${s(esquemaCotizacion)}));`,
  `pm.test('IGV es el 18 % del subtotal', () => { const d = pm.response.json().desglose; pm.expect(d.igv).to.be.closeTo(d.subtotal * 0.18, 0.011); });`,
  `pm.test('total = subtotal + IGV', () => { const r = pm.response.json(); pm.expect(r.total).to.be.closeTo(r.desglose.subtotal + r.desglose.igv, 0.011); });`
];

Las cuatro carpetas siguen técnicas clásicas de diseño de casos:

  1. Salud y catálogo. Health check, listado, filtro por zona en minúsculas, zona inválida (400) y departamento inexistente (404).
  2. Cotizaciones válidas (partición de equivalencia). Misma zona, distinta zona con express, y selva con valor declarado. Cada caso verifica montos exactos: por ejemplo, Tacna → Arequipa con 2.3 kg debe costar S/ 16.82.
  3. Valores límite. 0.1 kg y 50 kg se aceptan; 0.09 kg, 50.01 kg y un valor declarado de 10 001 devuelven 422.
  4. Errores y robustez. Campos faltantes, tipo incorrecto ("2" en lugar de 2), JSON mal formado (400), Content-Type: text/plain (415) y ruta inexistente (404).

Tres trucos que valen la pena

1. Validar el contrato con JSON Schema, no solo el status:

pm.test('el error sigue el contrato', () => pm.response.to.have.jsonSchema(esquemaError));
pm.test('señala el campo pesoKg', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().error.campo).to.eql('pesoKg'));

2. Aserciones a nivel de colección, que se ejecutan después de cada petición:

pm.test('responde en menos de 3 s', () => pm.expect(pm.response.responseTime).to.be.below(3000));
pm.test('responde JSON', () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get('Content-Type')).to.include('application/json'));

3. Comparar dos respuestas con pm.sendRequest. Probamos una propiedad del negocio, "express siempre cuesta más que estándar", lanzando una segunda petición desde el script de pruebas:

pm.sendRequest({ url: pm.environment.get('baseUrl') + '/v1/cotizaciones', method: 'POST', /* ... servicio: 'express' */ },
  (err, res) => pm.test('express > estándar', () => {
    pm.expect(res.json().total).to.be.above(pm.response.json().total);
  }));

Ejecutarla en local 

npm install
npm start          # API en http://localhost:3000
npm run test:api   # newman + reportes HTML y JUnit en reports/

│              requests │   22 │   0 │
│            assertions │  121 │   0 │

El pipeline: probar → desplegar → volver a probar

El workflow de GitHub Actions (ci-cd.yml) tiene tres jobs encadenados:

git push a main
   └─▶ Job 1: unitarias + Newman + k6 smoke (contra localhost)
         └─▶ Job 2: vercel deploy --prod
               └─▶ Job 3: Newman + k6 (contra la URL pública)
  1. Pruebas locales. Levanta la API dentro del runner y corre las pruebas unitarias (node:test), Newman y un smoke de k6.
  2. Despliegue. Usa la CLI de Vercel con el secreto VERCEL_TOKEN. El job obtiene el dominio de producción desde la API de Vercel y lo expone como output.
  3. Pruebas contra producción. Recibe esa URL y ejecuta la misma colección: 
- name: Pruebas funcionales con Newman (producción)
  run: |
    npx newman run tests/postman/envios.postman_collection.json \
      --env-var baseUrl="$BASE_URL" \
      --reporters cli,htmlextra,junit,json \
      --reporter-htmlextra-export reports/newman-produccion.html

Con jq, el resultado JSON de Newman se convierte en una tabla del resumen de la ejecución. Así se ve sin descargar nada. Los reportes HTML quedan como artefactos.

Resultados en producción

Ejecutadas Fallidas
Peticiones 23 (22 + 1 sendRequest) 0
Aserciones 121 0

Mientras desarrollábamos, la propia corrida de Newman detectó una aserción de Content-Type que se serializaba mal al generar la colección. Por eso las aserciones exactas sobre montos usan valores redondeados a centavos y closeTo donde hay cálculos con decimales.

Lecciones

  • Genera la colección desde código. Los cambios se revisan en un diff legible y nadie edita a mano el JSON exportado.
  • Prueba el contrato, no solo el status. Un 200 con un campo de menos también es un bug.
  • Repite las pruebas después de desplegar. Lo que pasa en localhost puede fallar en la plataforma, por enrutamiento, cabeceras o variables de entorno.
  • Valores límite y errores fueron la mitad de los casos y donde aparecieron más sorpresas.

¿Y el rendimiento? Eso lo cubre k6. Lo explica mi compañero Manuel en su artículo; mientras tanto, el script está en tests/k6/carga.js.

title: Auditing Node.js SMS OTP API Login Retries (Fintech Suppression Evidence)
description:
A fintech login page should identify the blocked authentication step and the evidence needed to act. Start with hosted SMS OTP and verification for a US/EU Node.js SaaS app, then keep recipient suppression and abuse decisions in the application. That is the least complex starting point here: managed code generation and expiry, with explicit ownership of the decisions that can lock a customer out.

TL;DR: Choose an SMS OTP API by whether your team can reconstruct a login attempt, its retries, and the suppression decision affecting any email fallback. Managed verification reduces code, but delivery status does not prove successful authentication, and an attractive dashboard does not prove that an invalid recipient stayed suppressed.

Consider a tabletop exercise, not a reported incident: the page says that login completion has fallen, the on-call sees SMS attempts and email fallback activity, and the available evidence cannot explain why an invalid email recipient was selected again. What page fired? A login symptom. The earlier signal should have identified a send decision that contradicted recorded suppression evidence.

How should an SMS OTP API explain a SaaS login retry?

Work backward from that proposed postmortem. A retry was allowed, an email fallback was considered, and a recipient eligibility decision was made somewhere between them. If the evidence stops at “request accepted,” the responder cannot distinguish an authentication problem from a recipient selection problem without reopening several systems.

A bounce and an invalid-recipient decision also need separate treatment. Do not turn every temporary delivery problem into permanent suppression; define the classification rule, preserve the reason, and require an explicit review path for changing the result. The compliance question is narrower than “was email healthy?” It is whether the application can explain why this recipient was eligible at the instant it attempted delivery.

Trace the decision.

Don't trust the chart.

For the exercise, assign one application correlation identifier to the login challenge, preserve provider identifiers separately, and record the policy version used to permit or refuse a fallback. Keep OTP values out of that record. Store only the recipient reference needed for the investigation under your access and retention policy, rather than copying phone numbers and addresses into every alert. These are application design choices, not claims about a provider's response fields. For example, a successful response to an earlier send cannot authorize a later send after the application has recorded suppression, and an operator's decision to restore eligibility must carry its own reason rather than silently overwriting the old value. Otherwise the investigator sees only the latest state, which may be perfectly reasonable now while concealing an unreasonable decision at dispatch.

The Node.js handler can initiate hosted SMS verification while a separate decision record follows the challenge through completion. An SMS delivery result belongs in that record, but successful code verification is a different outcome. Neither result establishes that an email address is valid.

Put the earlier signal at the send decision

The useful instrumentation change is a check where the application decides to send, with enough evidence to reproduce that decision later. A chart of bounce totals can help with investigation, but it cannot replace the record showing that a particular recipient was already suppressed when another attempt was authorized.

Before implementing the suppression write, inspect its public discovery contract. This runnable Go preflight retrieves the schema and prints the response for review; it does not send a message or modify suppression state. Set INFRAI_API_ORIGIN to the gateway's HTTPS origin, without a path, and INFRAI_API_KEY to your environment-provided key. The discovery resource is public, so authentication is not required by that resource; the example uses the gateway's Bearer convention for a consistent client setup.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    origin := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_ORIGIN"), "/")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    u, err := url.Parse(origin)
    if err != nil || u.Scheme != "https" || u.Host == "" ||
        u.Path != "" || u.RawQuery != "" || u.Fragment != "" ||
        u.User != nil || key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set an HTTPS API origin and API key")
    }

    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("GET",
            origin+"/v1/discovery/email.suppression.add", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 2<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            wait := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                    if seconds > 30 {
                        return fmt.Errorf("Retry-After exceeds retry budget")
                    }
                    wait = max(wait, time.Duration(seconds)*time.Second)
                } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                    wait = max(wait, time.Until(date))
                } else {
                    return fmt.Errorf("invalid Retry-After")
                }
            }
            if wait > 30*time.Second {
                return fmt.Errorf("Retry-After exceeds retry budget")
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The example requires Go 1.21 or later for the built-in max function. It makes at most 3 attempts, retries only HTTP 429, and refuses a requested wait longer than 30 seconds rather than retrying before the server permits it. Because this is a read, it cannot duplicate a suppression write. The response is contract evidence, not proof that a recipient was suppressed; keep it distinct from the authenticated write result and the application's later dispatch decision.

For the tabletop exercise, use 3 application-owned evidence records: a suppression decision, a later send attempt for the same recipient reference, and a duplicate of that attempt. The audit should report 1 contradiction, not 2. A production implementation needs durable deduplication, an explicit ordering policy, and recorded suppression reversals; otherwise a late-arriving event can make yesterday's decision appear to violate today's state. It also needs an atomic eligibility check or another concurrency control at dispatch, because an audit after the send cannot prevent the send.

That distinction matters. The preflight inspects a contract; it doesn't enforce suppression or establish regulatory compliance. Preserve the decision-time state as well as the later audit finding, so an investigator can tell a real policy violation from delayed ingestion.

Compare verification services against the evidence you need

A useful selection exercise gives every candidate the same questions: who owns challenge expiry, which records identify a verification attempt, how does the application collect delivery evidence, and where does an email suppression decision live? Require documented answers and a small acceptance test before making a compliance claim. A recognizable product name is insufficient evidence.

Option Relevant starting point Boundary to test for this fintech flow
Twilio Verify Evaluate its managed verification service for the hosted challenge role. Check the documented verification lifecycle and how its identifiers connect to your application evidence; review email suppression as a separate requirement.
Vonage Verify Evaluate its verification service against the same challenge and retry acceptance criteria. Confirm the selected product version's lifecycle and evidence collection behavior before choosing an escalation threshold.
Amazon SNS Evaluate SMS publishing when the application is prepared to own the verification flow. Account for code generation, expiry, attempt limits, and evidence that sending a message led to successful verification.

There is a trade-off: hosted verification reduces challenge code, but it does not remove the application's responsibility for recipient eligibility. The limitation is operational ownership, not the number of boxes in a dashboard.

Those are different responsibilities. SNS belongs on the shortlist when an application-owned challenge service is an intentional choice; a team trying to remove that responsibility should first evaluate hosted verification. Twilio and Vonage deserve the same scrutiny around suppression evidence as any broader backend API. Do not infer an email recipient policy from an SMS feature list.

Infrai fits teams that value one key and one bill across backend services, reducing credential sprawl and invoice reconciliation, with a self-describing API and public discovery requiring no key as a supporting advantage when reviewing request contracts. One REST API lets the application use plain HTTP without installing an SDK, so the same review harness can inspect contracts from a Node.js service or a Go audit tool. Its hosted SMS OTP and verification flow is a reasonable starting point for this use case, provided the application owns geographic abuse controls and country-based spend circuit breakers. Plan delivery and result evidence collection around polling, and treat email fallback as an application-built verification flow with suppression checks; this is a weaker fit when the requirement is immediate orchestration driven by pushed events.

For all four options, the decision remains conditional on the actual evidence path. The supplied API contract for a send operation cannot answer your organization's retention, residency, or access-control obligations by itself. Obtain the relevant contractual and operational evidence before treating a vendor selection as a compliance decision.

Keep retries from erasing the explanation

There are several different reasons a login flow might try again, and collapsing them into a single retry counter makes the postmortem harder. A transport retry repeats an operation whose outcome may be unknown. A user-requested resend is a new application decision. An incorrect code submission is a verification attempt. Give each a separate policy and preserve their relationship to the original challenge.

For write operations, use the provider's documented idempotency contract and retain a stable application operation identifier. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and apply bounded exponential backoff; impose a retry budget so delayed work cannot outlive the challenge. Do not assume another candidate implements an identical deduplication window or header.

Country eligibility and country-level spend circuit breakers belong before the send decision. They answer abuse questions that hosted code generation does not answer. Their rejection reasons should remain distinguishable from invalid-recipient suppression, because the recovery actions differ: clearing an email suppression entry cannot fix a country policy rejection.

Email fallback deserves its own review. It changes which destination the customer must control and introduces another challenge lifecycle, so record the transition, check suppression before dispatch, and define when the previous challenge stops being usable. DMARC is relevant to email domain authentication, while NIST's authenticator guidance is relevant to the authentication design; neither document certifies that this particular fallback implementation meets a fintech application's obligations.

Close the drill with the false-positive bill

Start with two separate signals: a decision that contradicts recorded suppression policy, and an authentication outcome that degrades across a meaningful population. The first can justify immediate investigation even when aggregate delivery charts look normal. The second needs a denominator, a measurement window, and a threshold selected from the application's traffic and login objective; there is no defensible universal number in this exercise.

A threshold that pages on every isolated bounce buys interruptions while encouraging responders to mute the alert. A rule that permanently suppresses every ambiguous delivery failure buys customer lockouts. Set the response to match the evidence: uncertain delivery merits investigation or a bounded retry under policy, while a confirmed eligibility contradiction needs a traceable correction and review.

The drill is complete when the responder can reconstruct the decision without trusting a dashboard summary. Page on actionable evidence. Keep the record.

Further reading

References for reviewing verification lifecycles, SMS publishing, domain authentication, and authenticator requirements:

  • Twilio Verify documentation: https://www.twilio.com/docs/verify
  • Vonage Verify documentation: https://developer.vonage.com/en/verify/overview
  • Amazon SNS SMS documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-mobile-phone-number-as-subscriber.html
  • RFC 7489, DMARC: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489
  • NIST SP 800-63B, Digital Identity Guidelines: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html

title: Backorders and Partial Shipments: Modelling Order Splits in a Supply Chain Database Without Losing the Original Order
description:
A customer places an order for 500 units, but the warehouse has only 320 available. The business ships the available quantity immediately and sends the remaining 180 units when replenishment arrives.

Operationally, this is a routine supply chain scenario. From a database perspective, however, it creates several questions. Should the original order quantity be changed? How should multiple shipments reference the same order? What happens when one shipment is cancelled or only partially delivered? And how can the application prevent the remaining quantity from being allocated twice?

A reliable supply chain system must preserve the original customer commitment while tracking every fulfilment event separately. This requires a clear distinction between an order, its fulfilment allocations, shipment records, and backorder quantities.

Why Order Splitting Needs a Separate Data Model

A common but fragile implementation stores a single shipped_quantity field on the order and updates it whenever a shipment leaves the warehouse.

This can work for simple transactions, but it becomes difficult to maintain when orders are split across multiple warehouses, carriers, delivery dates, or fulfilment methods.

For example:

  • Original order: 500 units
  • First shipment: 200 units
  • Second shipment: 120 units
  • Remaining backorder: 180 units

If the system stores only the current shipped quantity, it may show that 320 units have shipped. But it does not necessarily explain which shipment carried each quantity, when it left, which warehouse fulfilled it, or whether the customer received it.

The database should retain the original order and represent each fulfilment movement independently.

Separate Customer Orders From Fulfilment Records

A practical relational model can use the following entities:

Table Purpose
sales_orders Stores the original customer order
sales_order_lines Stores ordered products and quantities
fulfillment_orders Represents fulfilment work created from an order
fulfillment_order_lines Records allocated quantities
shipments Stores individual dispatch records
shipment_lines Connects shipped quantities to order lines
backorder_lines Tracks quantities awaiting fulfilment
inventory_reservations Records stock reserved for specific demand

The original sales_order_lines record should retain the ordered quantity. Shipment activity should not overwrite that value.

A simplified order-line record might contain:

order_line_id: 701
order_id: 9001
product_id: 450
ordered_quantity: 500
unit_price: 120.00
status: partially_fulfilled

Each shipment line then references the original order line:

shipment_line_id: 801
shipment_id: 3001
order_line_id: 701
shipped_quantity: 200

A second shipment can reference the same order line with another quantity. The relationship preserves the original customer commitment while creating a traceable fulfilment history.

Calculating the Remaining Backorder Quantity

The outstanding quantity should be derived from the original ordered quantity and the quantities that count as fulfilled under the business's fulfilment policy.

A basic calculation is:

Remaining Quantity = Ordered Quantity - Net Fulfilled Quantity

For example:

500 - (200 + 120) = 180

However, the application must define what qualifies as fulfilled. A quantity allocated to a warehouse is not necessarily shipped. A label created for a package does not mean the carrier has collected it.

The system should distinguish between states such as:

  • Allocated
  • Picked
  • Packed
  • Dispatched
  • Delivered
  • Cancelled
  • Returned

For customer-facing backorder calculations, the business may count only dispatched or delivered quantities, depending on its policy. For warehouse planning, it may also need to track picked and packed quantities separately.

Avoiding Duplicate Allocations

One of the biggest risks in partial fulfilment is allocating the same remaining quantity to multiple shipments.

Suppose two warehouse operators open the same order line at nearly the same time. Both see 180 units available for fulfilment. If the system does not control concurrent allocation, each operator might allocate the entire quantity.

The result is an over-allocation of 360 units against an outstanding requirement of 180.

To prevent this, allocation should be handled through controlled database transactions.

A typical process is:

  1. Retrieve the current order-line balance.
  2. Lock or atomically update the allocation record.
  3. Validate the requested allocation against the available balance.
  4. Create the fulfilment allocation.
  5. Update the derived outstanding quantity.
  6. Commit the transaction.

The database should enforce quantity constraints wherever possible. Application-level validation alone may not be sufficient when multiple requests execute concurrently.

Handling Multiple Warehouses and Split Deliveries

A supply chain platform may fulfil one customer order from several locations.

For example, an order for 500 units may be divided as follows:

Warehouse Allocated quantity Shipment
Warehouse A 200 Shipment 1
Warehouse B 150 Shipment 2
Warehouse C 150 Shipment 3

The order remains one commercial commitment, but its fulfilment is distributed across three locations.

The application should record the warehouse responsible for each allocation and shipment. It should also track inventory reservations separately so that a stock transfer or reservation release does not accidentally alter the customer order.

Managing Backorder Lifecycle Changes

Backorders can change as inventory becomes available, customers modify their requirements, or suppliers miss expected delivery dates.

The application should support clear transitions:

  • A backorder is created when the required quantity cannot be fulfilled.
  • Replenishment updates available-to-promise inventory.
  • The system allocates eligible stock to outstanding demand.
  • Warehouse operations create a new fulfilment and shipment.
  • Shipment events update the fulfilment status.
  • The order line becomes fully fulfilled, partially fulfilled, or cancelled according to its remaining quantity.

A backorder should not simply disappear when stock arrives. It should retain its relationship with the original order line and show how the outstanding quantity was eventually handled.

What Happens When a Shipment Is Cancelled?

Shipment cancellation requires careful treatment.

If a shipment is cancelled before dispatch, its allocation may be released back to available inventory or returned to the fulfilment queue.

If the shipment has already left the warehouse, the application needs a return or delivery-exception workflow. It should not simply delete the shipment record or reduce the shipped quantity without an auditable event.

The system should preserve the original shipment, record the cancellation or return event, and calculate the revised outstanding quantity according to the business rules.

Recommended Supply Chain Software Development Companies

A supply chain platform with partial fulfilment requires reliable order management, inventory synchronization, warehouse workflows, and shipment tracking. Businesses should evaluate vendors on their ability to model these relationships without losing transactional history.

1. Dev Technosys

Dev Technosys provides custom software development services that can support supply chain platforms, inventory management applications, warehouse workflows, and logistics integrations. A custom solution can connect customer orders with fulfilment allocation, shipment creation, backorder tracking, and inventory reservation.

For partial shipment workflows, the database architecture should preserve original order quantities while recording each allocation and shipment as a separate transaction. This allows businesses to maintain an accurate order history and reduce inventory inconsistencies.

2. Chetu

Chetu provides custom software development services across multiple industries. Its engineering capabilities can be evaluated for supply chain applications that require tailored inventory, order management, and enterprise integration workflows.

Chetu suits organizations considering custom supply chain application development.

3. Manhattan Associates

Manhattan Associates provides supply chain and warehouse management technology. Its solutions may be relevant to organizations with complex distribution, inventory, and fulfilment operations.

Manhattan Associates suits enterprises evaluating specialized supply chain execution and warehouse technology.

4. Blue Yonder

Blue Yonder provides supply chain planning and execution technology, including solutions related to inventory, fulfilment, and warehouse operations. Its portfolio may be relevant to businesses coordinating demand and supply across multiple locations.

Blue Yonder suits organizations assessing integrated supply chain planning and execution platforms.

5. SAP

SAP offers enterprise applications covering supply chain, procurement, inventory, and business operations. Its ecosystem may be relevant when order fulfilment must connect with broader ERP and financial processes.

SAP suits businesses seeking enterprise-wide supply chain and ERP integration.

6. Oracle

Oracle provides enterprise software for supply chain management, inventory, and logistics-related processes. Its technology can be evaluated by organizations managing complex business operations across multiple systems.

Oracle suits enterprises comparing integrated supply chain and enterprise application platforms.

7. Infor

Infor offers industry-focused enterprise software, including supply chain and distribution capabilities. Its solutions may be relevant to businesses that need connected inventory, order, and warehouse processes.

Infor suits organizations evaluating industry-oriented enterprise supply chain systems.

Businesses should confirm the exact order-splitting, allocation, warehouse, and shipment capabilities available in each proposed product or implementation. Broad enterprise software expertise does not automatically establish experience with every fulfilment workflow.

How to Evaluate a Supply Chain Development Partner

Evaluation area What to assess
Order modelling Original order quantity remains immutable
Fulfilment logic Multiple allocations and shipments per order line
Inventory management Reservation and stock availability controls
Concurrency Prevention of duplicate allocations
Shipment tracking Dispatch, delivery, cancellation, and return events
Integration ERP, WMS, TMS, and carrier connectivity
Reporting Accurate outstanding and fulfilled quantities
Auditability Traceable changes to order and fulfilment records

Benefits of a Well-Designed Order-Splitting Model

A reliable order-splitting architecture helps businesses:

  • Preserve the original customer order.
  • Support shipments from multiple warehouses.
  • Prevent duplicate inventory allocation.
  • Track backorders accurately.
  • Improve delivery status visibility.
  • Simplify returns and shipment cancellations.
  • Reconcile warehouse and order management records.
  • Generate more reliable fulfilment reports.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. What is a partial shipment in supply chain management?

A partial shipment occurs when only part of a customer order is dispatched. The remaining quantity is fulfilled through one or more later shipments or remains on backorder.

2. Should the original order quantity change after a partial shipment?

No. The original ordered quantity should remain intact. The system should record fulfilled, allocated, and outstanding quantities separately so that the original customer commitment remains traceable.

3. How should a database handle multiple shipments for one order?

Each shipment should have its own record, and its shipment lines should reference the original order lines. This supports multiple dispatches without duplicating or modifying the customer order.

4. How can a supply chain system prevent duplicate fulfilment?

It should use transactional allocation controls, quantity validation, database constraints, and concurrency management to ensure that multiple users or processes cannot allocate more than the outstanding quantity.

5. What should businesses consider when developing backorder management software?

They should assess order-line modelling, inventory reservation, warehouse allocation, shipment tracking, cancellation handling, ERP and WMS integration, and audit history.

Conclusion

Partial shipments should not be treated as edits to the original customer order. They are separate fulfilment events connected to a single commercial commitment. A well-designed database preserves that relationship while tracking allocations, shipments, cancellations, and remaining quantities.

Businesses building these workflows should work with an experienced supply chain software development company that can design reliable order, inventory, and fulfilment models around real warehouse operations.

title: I got tired of Redis and Kafka eating my RAM, so I rebuilt them in Rust hitting 1.6M RPS (as a student)
description:
Hey everyone, I’m Yasir. I’m an 18-year-old software engineering student from Pakistan, and for the last few months, I’ve been going down a very deep, very complex rabbit hole: Systems Programming in Rust.
When I started learning about distributed systems, I noticed a recurring theme: tools like Apache Kafka and Redis are absolute industry standards, but they come with a catch. Kafka relies heavily on the JVM (hello, GC pauses and massive memory footprints), and standard in-memory stores often hit bottlenecks when scaling across modern multi-core CPUs due to OS-level thread contention and locks.
I didn't have the budget to run massive AWS clusters for my personal projects. I needed something that could run on a potato but still handle enterprise-level throughput.
So, I decided to build my own.
Enter Velocity-Suite (Velocity-MQ & VelocityDB)
I built two core **infrastructure pieces entirely from scratch in Rust:
Velocity-MQ: A zero-GC, lock-free message queue (Kafka alternative).
**VelocityDB: A thread-per-core, lock-free in-memory store (Redis alternative).
My goal wasn't just to write another wrapper. I wanted to bypass traditional OS bottlenecks entirely. Here is the architecture that made it happen:
1_. Bypassing the Kernel with io_uring
Traditional synchronous I/O or even epoll wasn't cutting it for the persistent disk I/O I wanted. I integrated Linux io_uring for asynchronous I/O. By using O_DIRECT, the system completely bypasses the OS page cache. This means zero-copy transfers straight from the disk to the application memory, resulting in microsecond latencies._
2. Thread-per-Core Architecture
Instead of having multiple threads fighting over a shared state (and melting the CPU with context switches), I used a thread-per-core model. Each thread owns its data. No locks, no mutexes blocking the hot path.
3. Lock-Free Concurrency
To allow threads to communicate without slowing down, I heavily utilized lock-free data structures (like ring buffers) and atomic pointers. Fighting the Rust borrow checker while dealing with std::sync::atomic memory ordering (Acquire/Release semantics) was probably the hardest thing I’ve ever done, but the performance payoff was insane.
The Benchmarks 🚀
After weeks of debugging segmentation faults and memory ordering bugs, I finally ran the benchmarks on my local machine:
VelocityDB: **Reached **1.6M+ Requests Per Second (RPS). Click this : https://github.com/developer-yasir/velocitydb .
Velocity-MQ: Pushed 600k+ ops/sec with virtually zero garbage collection overhead. https://github.com/developer-yasir/Velocity-MQ
Running this on minimal RAM felt like a superpower.
Why I am sharing this (I need your help!)
I am incredibly proud of what I've built, but I am also just a 1st-semester CS student. I know for a fact that my code isn't perfect. Systems programming is brutal, and edge cases around memory barriers and crash recovery are terrifying.
I am putting this out here because I want to learn from the best.
If you are a senior Rustacean, a systems engineer, or just someone who loves high-performance backends, I would be honored if you could look at my code.
Roast my architecture.
Tell me where my memory ordering is flawed.
Open an issue if you see a bug.
You can check out the code here:
🔗 https://github.com/developer-yasir/

If you find this project interesting or helpful, dropping a ⭐ on the repo would mean the world to me and keep me motivated to keep building!
Let me know your thoughts in the comments. Let's talk about io_uring and Rust!

title: Vercel Tracing is now generally available
description:
Vercel Tracing is now generally available on all plans. You can now search and inspect traces from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI, and new Next.js projects get tracing by default. Pricing is unchanged from the beta.

Browse and search traces in the dashboard

In beta, you could only open a trace per request from the Logs page. The new Traces page shows every trace and span in one place, for a project or your whole team. Switch between a Spans list and a Traces list, filter each, and search with Kibana Query Language (KQL). A Live mode streams new traces as they arrive. A query like span.name:db* AND span.duration > 500 narrows to slow database spans by name and duration.

Search traces from the CLI

The Traces page uses the same KQL as vercel traces search --query, so a query built in the dashboard runs in the CLI unchanged. Search covers every project in your team, or one project with the --project flag. Inspect a single trace with vercel traces inspect <request-id>, and manage a project's sampling rules with vercel traces config.

Automatic tracing for new Next.js projects

In beta, nothing was collected until you added a sampling rule. Starting with Next.js 16.5, new projects created on Vercel that include at least one Node.js function get tracing turned on after their first successful build. Vercel adds one sampling rule tracing 100% of requests in all environments and injects instrumentation at build time, so traces include Next.js framework spans with no setup. To opt out, remove all sampling rules in Settings → Tracing.

Longer retention

In beta, traces followed your runtime log retention. Hobby now keeps traces for 3 days instead of 1 hour, Pro for 14 days instead of 1 day, and Enterprise for 14 days instead of 3 days.

Read the Tracing documentation to learn more.

title: Don't File Photo-Derived Meters as a Survey
description:
I'm Tomás Herrera. Day job is backend and infrastructure at ArchyBase — mostly the path from an uploaded file to a finished artifact: validate, store, enqueue, and return a result the rest of the system is allowed to trust. This post is about a sibling product our team also builds, and specifically about a converter that turns a photo into a layout. I'm not going to talk about the vision model. That's a different layer, and a different person on the team. I'm talking about what the job is allowed to persist after a photo comes in.

The short version: a listing photo is a projection. The layout you get back is a draft estimated from what's visible in the frame. If your property record, your quote, or your inventory system files those numbers as a survey, you've promoted an estimate to a fact. I don't want that write to happen by accident.

The job is not “upload, then believe”

The product page is honest about the shape of the work, and I like that more than a magic demo. You upload a JPEG, PNG, or WebP (up to 10MB). You can add a short note about what the floor plan should look like. You pick a quality mode. You get a 2D technical plan back, as an image, and you can regenerate if the first pass misses a wall.

That last clause matters. “Regenerate if the first pass misses a wall” is not a flourish. It is an admission that a missed wall is a normal failure class, not a rare crash. A backend that treats the first successful blob as authoritative will happily store an open floor where a wall should have been.

So the durable unit of work, for me, looks closer to this than to a one-shot HTTP response:

Job {
  job_id
  input_ref          // object key for the photo
  input_kind         // room_photo | house_interior | aerial
  hint?              // optional text, not a measured brief
  quality_mode       // fast | best  (latency vs refinement; not a SLA)
  state              // queued | running | succeeded | failed
  result_ref?        // output image
  error_class?       // invalid_input | unreadable_photo | incomplete_layout | internal
  confidence_policy  // estimated_from_visible — never survey_grade
}

I made up the field names. They are not FloorAI internals. They're the checklist I want in front of any service that accepts a photo and emits a plan-shaped artifact.

Three input types are three failure classes

The page groups inputs as a room photo, a wider house interior, or an aerial / drone shot of a building. That's a product convenience. For a job queue, it's a classification problem, because the failure modes don't overlap cleanly.

A room photo usually gives you two or three walls, a floor plane, maybe a doorway, and a lot of furniture occluding the rest. The missing wall is often the one behind the camera. If you persist that result as a complete room, you've invented a fourth side from a viewpoint that never saw it.

A house interior — a wider shot, a listing gallery image, a scanned print — can show circulation and room boundaries, but only the ones in view. A corridor that turns out of frame will not appear because the model is “careful.” It will not appear because it was never in the pixels. Old or low-quality photos can still convert, which is useful for digitizing a record when no drawing exists. Useful is not the same as complete.

An aerial or drone shot is a different object. The page is explicit: you can scan a footprint when you can't walk the building room by room. A footprint is not a room schedule. If a downstream form labels the output “3-bed, 2-bath” because a listing caption said so, that's a caption write, not a measurement write. Keep those sources apart.

I would rather the API require an input_kind (or infer it and show the inference) than silently mix these into one “image-to-plan” success state. The client can then branch: a missed interior wall is “try another photo or regenerate”; an aerial result is “this is a footprint, don't ask it for closet widths.”

Reject early, estimate later

Upload validation should be boring and strict:

  • Reject empty files, wrong MIME types, and anything over the published 10MB cap before a worker starts.
  • Decode enough to know you have an actual image, not a renamed PDF.
  • Don't invent a dimension unit in preprocess just because a later renderer likes meters.

The estimate happens after that, from visible structure in the shot — walls, doorways, room boundaries the photo actually contains. The page says this directly: no tape measure is required, and dimensions are estimated from what's visible rather than from measurements you typed in. That's the product promise, and it should also be the persistence promise.

What I will not do is this:

  1. Accept a phone photo.
  2. Get a layout image with some numbers on it.
  3. OCR or hardcode those numbers into wall.length_m.
  4. Mark the unit as surveyed.

If you need a field, call it what it is: estimated_from_photo, with the source image id and the job id. A later measured drawing can replace it. A later photo can revise it. Neither should look identical to a laser-measured wall in the database.

Failures the user can act on

I care about error classes the client can branch on, not a generic “something went wrong.” A reasonable set for this product shape:

Class What happened What the user can do
invalid_input bad type, empty file, over 10MB fix the file
unreadable_photo decode failed, or the frame has no usable structure try a wider / sharper shot
incomplete_layout job succeeded, but a wall or room boundary is obviously missing regenerate, or upload a shot that includes the missing side
wrong_kind an aerial footprint was treated like an interior, or the reverse relabel the input and run again
internal worker / storage blip retry the same job or attempt

incomplete_layout is the interesting one, because it may still return an image. That's a succeeded job with a warning, or a soft failure, depending on how strict you want to be. I prefer “succeeded, with an explicit warning the first pass may have missed a wall” over a silent 200 and a floor plan that walks through a load-bearing line. The product already tells people to regenerate. The API should make that path first-class, not a folksy tip buried under a download button.

Don't auto-retry invalid_input or “I can't see a room in this picture.” That wastes worker time and trains the UI to spin. Auto-retry only the infra blips, and only with an idempotency key so you don't persist two final images for one photo.

What the output is allowed to be

The download is an image, ready to share or use as a starting reference. Starting reference is the right phrase. It is not a CAD handoff, and I have not claimed it exports a measured drawing. If someone on the team later adds a dimensioned file type, that still wouldn't make a phone photo into a survey. It would make the estimate easier to open in other tools — which is useful, and still an estimate.

The optional text field — “describe what the floor plan should look like” — is a hint, not a substitute for the hidden wall. If the photo doesn't show a second bedroom, a hint that says “two bedrooms” is a request, not evidence. I'd keep that hint on the job record so a reviewer can see what was asked, and I would not let it silently overwrite geometry that isn't in the image.

Quality modes (faster output vs more refinement) are a latency and compute trade-off. I'm not going to invent how many seconds either mode takes. The only rule I want is: both modes still write estimated_from_visible. A “best” result is not a license to drop the qualifier.

A short checklist before anyone files the result

This is the list I want next to the download button, or next to whatever internal tool first persists the artifact:

  1. Record the source photo and the job id with the layout. No orphan plans.
  2. Label the input kind: room, interior, or aerial / footprint.
  3. Treat every length as estimated from the visible frame, never as surveyed, until a real measurement replaces it.
  4. If a wall is missing, regenerate or shoot the missing side. Don't close the loop in the database by hand and call it the same job.
  5. Don't copy listing-caption room counts into the plan record just because the caption was on the same page as the photo.
  6. Let a later measured plan supersede the estimate without deleting the photo job — you want the history.

I use this converter when there is no drawing on file and a photo is all you have. That's a real situation: old units, incomplete listing packs, a job site with no blueprint in the email thread. A draft layout from a photo is much better than a blank. It is not better than a survey, and it should never be stored as if it were one.

The unpaid work, on the backend, is making that distinction boring and visible. If the only success state you have is “image arrived,” you will eventually file photo-derived meters as a survey. I'd rather fail that write on purpose.

title: Spec tables on product pages: keep them as real tables, and make them work on a phone
description:
Every hardware or electronics product page ends up with a spec table. Thread size, length, material, voltage range, what's in the box. It's the part of the page people scroll straight to when they already know what they want.

It's also the part that gets built as a pile of <div>s, or a two-column grid that falls apart below 400px. A few notes on doing it in a way that holds up.

Use a table. It is tabular data.

Key/value specs are exactly what <table> is for. You get row and header relationships for free, and screen readers can announce "Material, stainless steel" instead of two unrelated words.

<table class="specs">
  <caption>Specifications</caption>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Material</th>
      <td>Stainless steel A2</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Thread</th>
      <td>M8</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Length</th>
      <td>60 mm</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

The two details people skip: scope="row" on the label cell, and a <caption>. The caption can be visually hidden if the section already has a heading, but having it means the table has a name when someone jumps between tables.

A description list (<dl>) is also a fair choice for a short, simple list of specs. Once you have more than a handful of rows, or anything that compares variants, go with the table.

Comparing variants is where it gets harder

When one product comes in several sizes, the spec table often turns into a grid: sizes across the top, properties down the side.

<table class="specs specs--compare">
  <caption>Sizes</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <td></td>
      <th scope="col">6 mm</th>
      <th scope="col">8 mm</th>
      <th scope="col">10 mm</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Drill bit</th>
      <td>6 mm</td><td>8 mm</td><td>10 mm</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Screw size</th>
      <td>4–5 mm</td><td>5–6 mm</td><td>6–8 mm</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

(The values here are just example data to show the shape.)

With both scope="col" and scope="row", a screen reader can announce the cell with both headers. Without them, someone tabbing through hears a list of numbers with no context.

Making it fit on a phone

There are two honest options. Pick based on the table's shape.

Two-column key/value tables: let them wrap. Most of the time the only CSS you need is to stop the label column from being squeezed:

.specs { width: 100%; border-collapse: collapse; }
.specs th, .specs td { padding: .5rem .75rem; text-align: start; vertical-align: top; }
.specs th { width: 40%; font-weight: 600; }
.specs tr + tr > * { border-top: 1px solid #e5e7eb; }

Note text-align: start instead of left. If the site also runs in a right-to-left language, it flips on its own.

Wide comparison tables: let them scroll horizontally inside a container, and don't fight it.

<div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-labelledby="sizes-cap" tabindex="0">
  <table class="specs specs--compare">
    <caption id="sizes-cap">Sizes</caption>
    ...
  </table>
</div>

.table-scroll { overflow-x: auto; }
.specs--compare th[scope="row"] {
  position: sticky;
  inset-inline-start: 0;
  background: #fff;
}

The tabindex="0" and role="region" with a label let keyboard users focus the scroll area and move it with the arrow keys. The sticky first column keeps the row labels visible while the values scroll.

What I'd avoid is the "turn every row into a card with display: block" trick. It looks neat, but changing a table's display can strip its table semantics in some browser and screen reader combinations, and then you've lost the thing that made it a table in the first place. If you go that route, test it with an actual screen reader.

Small things that make specs easier to read

  • Units in the value, consistently. "60 mm" in every row, not "60" in one row and "6 cm" in the next. If you show two unit systems, pick one as primary and keep the other in a smaller span.
  • Non-breaking space between number and unit. 60 mm so the unit never wraps onto its own line.
  • Ranges with an en dash. 4–5 mm reads better than 4-5 mm, and a screen reader is more likely to read it as a range.
  • Don't hide the important rows behind "Show more". If people come to the page to check one dimension, that dimension should be visible without a click.
  • Keep the spec text in the HTML. Specs baked into an image can't be searched, translated, zoomed cleanly, or read aloud.

A quick check

Open a product page with lots of specs, for example a category like screws and anchors on ramo or any store that sells similar items, and try three things:

  1. Narrow the window to 360px. Does anything overflow the page instead of its own container?
  2. Tab through. Can you reach and scroll the wide table with the keyboard?
  3. Turn on a screen reader and move into a value cell. Do you hear the row header with it?

If all three are fine, the table is in good shape. If not, the fix is usually a few attributes and a dozen lines of CSS, not a new component.

title: Semantic Retrieval Evaluation Sets for Internal Engineering Docs in Node.js (5 Tests)
description:
Short answer: build a small, versioned evaluation set from real documentation questions, score retrieval with recall@k and ranking quality, then choose the fastest index that clears your relevance threshold. For a logistics team watching a carrier web page, keep latency as a constraint, not as a substitute for finding the paragraph that explains the change.

Retrieval approach Pick it when Watch for
Lexical search (BM25) Error codes, route names, and exact terms dominate Synonyms and paraphrases can be missed
Vector search Engineers ask concept-shaped questions across varied wording Similar-sounding passages can outrank the answer
Hybrid search Queries mix identifiers with natural language Two scores need a repeatable fusion rule

The evaluation set is the control surface. Without it, a new embedding model or chunk size is only a feeling in a dashboard. Store the query, the expected document or passage, and the acceptable rank in a file that can be reviewed like code.

Measure it twice.

What should a semantic retrieval evaluation set contain for internal engineering documentation?

Start with the question types your on-call team actually asks. A logistics example might be: “What changed in the carrier cutoff page after the 02:00 crawl?” The answer is a dated diff record, while the supporting context may be the parser runbook and the alert policy. Label both the primary passage and acceptable secondary passages; otherwise a useful runbook hit looks like a false negative.

I initially treated every query as a single-answer lookup. That made the score look precise and the review painful. Some questions have several valid passages, and a page-change alert often needs the newest version, not merely a semantically similar older one.

Use five small slices: exact identifier, paraphrase, multi-hop procedure, negative query, and freshness-sensitive query. Give each slice its own count. A 50-query set with 10 items per slice is easier to inspect than one opaque score, and it exposes a regression such as “good prose, bad error-code matching.” Keep a stable query_id; append new cases instead of rewriting old labels. For each case, retain the source URL, repository path, revision, and the human explanation for why a passage is acceptable. That extra context turns a score review into an engineering conversation: the person changing chunking can see whether a miss came from tokenization, metadata filtering, or an outdated label, then update one fixture and rerun the same slice instead of arguing from a dashboard aggregate.

Here is the kind of failure worth preserving. Query carrier-cutoff-02 retrieves the current alert policy at rank 1, an old carrier page at rank 2, and the parser runbook at rank 3. A naive evaluator marks that as a pass because the right topic appeared. A production reviewer marks it as a freshness failure because the alert must cite the current page revision. Keep the case, add the revision constraint to its label, and make the next index run prove that the old page no longer wins. That single example tests chunk metadata, ranking, and the alert contract together; it is more informative than another dozen easy paraphrases.

A negative query matters. “Which carrier page is covered by this alert?” should return no confident match when that carrier is outside the monitored set. Treating the top vector as an answer creates a plausible citation for an absent fact.

How do you measure retrieval quality and latency without fooling yourself?

For each query, record the ranked IDs returned by the retriever and a timestamp for the request. Recall@k asks whether any acceptable passage appears in the first k results. Mean reciprocal rank rewards putting the first acceptable passage near the top. Neither metric says the text is current, so add a freshness check for documents with revisions or crawl timestamps.

Here is a compact TypeScript scorer. It assumes labels are passage IDs, not generated answers. That distinction keeps retrieval evaluation separate from generation quality.

type Case = {
  queryId: string;
  relevant: Set<string>;
  expectedMaxAgeHours?: number;
};

type Result = { id: string; ageHours?: number };

export function score(cases: Case[], ranked: Map<string, Result[]>, k: number) {
  let recalled = 0;
  let reciprocalRank = 0;

  for (const item of cases) {
    const results = ranked.get(item.queryId) ?? [];
    const top = results.slice(0, k);
    const hit = top.findIndex((r) => item.relevant.has(r.id));
    if (hit >= 0) {
      recalled += 1;
      reciprocalRank += 1 / (hit + 1);
    }
  }

  return {
    recallAtK: cases.length === 0 ? 0 : recalled / cases.length,
    meanReciprocalRank: cases.length === 0 ? 0 : reciprocalRank / cases.length,
  };
}

Run the same cases against lexical, vector, and hybrid candidates. Capture p50 and p95 latency beside the quality scores. A p95 spike is operationally different from a small mean change: page-change alerts arrive in bursts, so tail latency can delay a notification even when average retrieval looks fine.

The practical gate is two-dimensional. Set a minimum recall for each slice, then set a p95 budget for the alert path. If hybrid search raises recall for error-code queries but breaks the budget, route only those queries to hybrid or reduce the candidate set. Your mileage may vary; the right threshold depends on how costly a missed change is.

Which indexing and chunking choices survive real documentation churn?

Chunk by meaning before tuning vector dimensions. Keep a heading with the procedure it governs, preserve code blocks as intact units, and attach metadata such as repository, path, revision, and crawl time. For a changed carrier page, store the old and new fingerprints so the evaluator can ask for the current passage explicitly.

Elasticsearch supports BM25 and vector fields in one search system; PostgreSQL with pgvector keeps embeddings beside relational metadata; Vespa offers ranking expressions for combining signals. These are different operational shapes, not a leaderboard. Pick the system your team can back up, inspect, and reindex predictably. A hybrid design still needs one canonical document ID so score comparisons remain meaningful.

The failure mode I watch is stale truth. A semantically perfect match to last month’s cutoff is wrong for today’s alert. Add a freshness feature or a hard filter, and put at least one intentionally stale case in every evaluation run.

When a case fails, save the query, top five IDs, scores, document revisions, and latency. A reviewer should be able to explain the failure without rerunning production traffic. Group failures by cause: bad label, missing chunk, synonym gap, stale metadata, or ranking tie.

Keep a tiny change log next to the set. Record why a label changed and which parser or index version caused it. A 202 response from an indexing job is not evidence that the passage is searchable; verify visibility in the same environment used by the alert worker.

One short rule: never optimize an aggregate while a slice is red.

Limits and trade-offs

Evaluation sets do not remove judgment. Labels can encode one team’s vocabulary, and a five-slice set can underrepresent rare incidents. Expand it from reviewed misses, but freeze a regression subset so improvements cannot erase old failures.

Vector retrieval is not suitable when exact identifiers are the whole query; stick with lexical or hybrid search then. A large hybrid stack is also a poor fit for a small documentation corpus that changes weekly, where a simpler index is easier to reindex and audit. The catch is maintenance: every new chunking rule, embedding model, and freshness policy changes the behavior you must measure.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/rrf.html
  • https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • https://docs.vespa.ai/en/reference/rank-features.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Performance_API

title: Claude Fable 5.2 now available on AI Gateway

Claude Fable 5.2 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway.

Fable 5.2 is built for open-ended technical work and improves on earlier Fable models in coding, reasoning, and vision. It can run long, ambiguous tasks unattended, and works as an orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to smaller models, or as an advisor that other Claude models consult on harder problems. It also communicates more clearly and generates output faster than earlier Fable models. Effort runs from low to max, with high as the API default.

Fable 5.2 has cybersecurity and biology safety classifiers enabled. Access to Claude Fable 5.2 requires data retention. Anthropic does not support Zero Data Retention for the model. Prompts and completions are retained for 30 days and are not used to train Claude. If your team has ZDR turned on, AI Gateway returns an error instead of sending the request to Fable 5.2.

To keep requests served when a classifier is triggered, use model fallbacks. Add a models array to providerOptions.gateway, and AI Gateway tries each model in order when the cybersecurity classifier declines a request.

Call it through the AI SDK, the Chat Completions, Responses, and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway. Use anthropic/claude-fable-5.2 as the model name:

This request falls back to Opus 5.5, then Sonnet 5.5, if the cybersecurity classifier declines it. The models option works the same way on every AI Gateway API format.

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Try Claude Fable 5.2 in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

Apigee X

Feature

  • Golden signal scorecards: track aggregate Traffic (requests per second), Error Rate (5xx), and Latency (p95) scorecards.
  • Status code and error trends: visualize the Request Rate by Status Code chart over time and identify problematic APIs using the dedicated 5xx Error Rate by Proxy and 4xx Error Rate by Proxy charts.
  • Granular filtering: filter telemetry by project_id, location, and proxy_name to troubleshoot specific regions or proxies.

For more information, see API Monitoring.

Bigtable

Feature

You can use Apache Avro schema bundles to query individual fields within Avro records stored as serialized bytes in Bigtable. You can query your Avro data using GoogleSQL for Bigtable, continuous materialized views, and logical views. This feature is in Preview.

Cloud DNS

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, CNAME chasing behavior will change so that Cloud DNS follows CNAME chains between public and private zones. If your private zones or response policies have overlapping domain names with public CNAME targets, queries might resolve to unintended internal IP addresses or return resolution errors.

The following table outlines the current and updated behaviors.

Source of CNAME answer Current behavior (until January 5, 2027) New behavior (starting January 5, 2027)
Cloud DNS public zone Subsequent queries search only public DNS zones and internal DNS. Private zones, forwarding zones, and response policies are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order: response policies, private zones, forwarding or peering zones, internal DNS, and public zones.
Cloud DNS private zone Subsequent queries search only authorized private zones. Public DNS zones are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in authorized private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.
Cloud DNS response policy zone Cloud DNS systems don't perform queries for CNAME answers received from response policy local data rules. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in response policies or private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.

Review your CNAME chasing needs before January 5, 2027. Test your DNS query paths using dig or nslookup to identify CNAME chasing scenarios.

  • Look for private-to-public CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from response policies or private zones that don't match any response policy or record in a private zone. Previously, these queries resulted in a NXDOMAIN answer but after January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a record in a public zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses.
  • Look for public-to-private CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from public zones that don't match any record in a public zone. Previously, these CNAME chasing scenarios would have resulted in a NXDOMAIN response. After January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a response policy or record in a private zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses if the private zone doesn't have the record.
  • For CNAME chasing scenarios under your control: As best practice, configure matching time-to-live (TTL) values for all records in the CNAME chain.

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will disable full responses to DNS queries of type ANY (QTYPE=ANY) in public authoritative zones. Instead, a single resource record will return for ANY queries, chosen from the existing resource record sets that match the query.

Standard traffic from web browsers, applications, and API traffic query specific record types directly and are therefore unaffected with no action required.

However, certain legacy scripts, automated health checkers, debugging commands (for example, dig example.com ANY), or custom third-party monitoring systems that explicitly query ANY records will receive the first available record instead of a full zone inventory. You must complete the following configuration updates before January 5, 2027:

  • Identify legacy queries: Review internal tools, deployment scripts, or third-party DNS monitoring configurations for commands or API calls that request the ANY record type. Cloud DNS logs in Cloud Logging can be helpful with this.
  • Transition to specific queries: Update the tools to query the specific, individual record types they require (for example, querying for A, AAAA, MX, or TXT records separately).
  • Retrieve full zone records: If you use ANY queries to retrieve all records in a zone, use the Cloud DNS REST API (resourceRecordSets.list), the gcloud CLI (gcloud dns record-sets list), or the Google Cloud Console instead.

Risks associated with not making these changes include the following:

  • False monitoring alarms: Automated uptime or DNS monitoring tools checking ANY responses may misinterpret the new response as a system failure and trigger false alerts.
  • Broken automation pipelines: Internal deployment or CI/CD scripts that rely on parsing a full zone dump with an ANY query will fail to retrieve the expected data payload and may crash.
  • Disrupted IT diagnostics: Network administrators running manual legacy troubleshooting commands will no longer see a quick summary of all domain records, which could delay active network incident diagnostics.

  • Connect ESXi nodes and VLAN-tagged Dynamic NICs directly to your VPC subnets without requiring private services access peering.

For more information, see VMware solution on Google Cloud overview and Compare VMware Engine models.
