title: Website Redesign Rfp Template
description:
Designing an Effective Website Redesign RFP Template: Avoiding Common Pitfalls

In the digital age, a well-crafted Request for Proposal (RFP) is essential for initiating a successful website redesign project. It serves as the cornerstone document, setting the tone and direction for the entire endeavor. A strong RFP not only attracts the right talent but also ensures that the project aligns with your organization's strategic goals. However, many organizations fall short by relying on generic templates that fail to capture the essence of their unique needs.

Why Standard Templates Often Fall Short

  1. Lack of Specificity: Generic templates often lack the depth required to address the unique challenges and opportunities of your organization. Without specific details, potential vendors may struggle to propose tailored solutions that meet your exact requirements.

  2. Insufficient Context: Many standard RFPs fail to provide adequate context about the project. This includes the organization's mission, target audience, and the intended outcomes of the redesign. Without this information, vendors may not fully grasp the project's scope, leading to misaligned proposals.

  3. Poor Prioritization: Generic templates often do not prioritize objectives effectively. This can result in proposals that address less critical aspects of the project while overlooking more important ones, potentially derailing the project's success.

Engineering Takeaways for an Effective RFP

To create an RFP that stands out and yields high-quality proposals, consider the following actionable insights:

  1. Tailor the RFP to Your Organization's Needs: Customize the RFP to reflect your organization's unique challenges, goals, and brand identity. This specificity will help attract vendors who can offer solutions that resonate with your vision.

title: Making a static file tool site work offline with a service worker
description:
A static website doesn't have to stop working when the internet connection disappears.

I wanted PocketPDF to keep working after its first load, including when someone opens it somewhere with no connection.

That meant building an offline strategy around a service worker.

The important distinction is that a service worker isn't just a way to cache the homepage. It needs to understand which resources are essential, which can be downloaded later, and which should never be stored.

Start with the application shell

The first thing I wanted available offline was the application itself.

That includes the HTML, CSS, JavaScript needed to navigate the site, and the basic resources required to open the tools.

These are relatively small files and make sense to precache.

The vendor libraries are another important part of the application shell.

If a tool depends on a local JavaScript library, having the interface cached but not the library doesn't help much.

For example, a PDF tool needs its PDF-related dependencies available before it can perform the operation.

Don't download everything immediately

There is a difference between caching a resource and downloading every resource during the first visit.

Some libraries are large and only needed by particular tools.

I use lazy loading for heavy dependencies, so someone opening a basic image utility doesn't need to download a PDF engine.

The service worker can cache these resources when they are first requested.

The general idea looks something like this:

const CACHE_VERSION = "pocketpdf-v3";
const SHELL_FILES = [
"/",
"/css/style.css",
"/js/core.js",
"/js/tools-index.js"
];

self.addEventListener("install", event => {
event.waitUntil(
caches.open(CACHE_VERSION)
.then(cache => cache.addAll(SHELL_FILES))
);
});

self.addEventListener("fetch", event => {
const request = event.request;

if (request.method !== "GET") return;

event.respondWith(
caches.match(request).then(cached => {
return cached || fetch(request);
})
);
});

This is a simplified example, not the complete production caching strategy. In practice, I also need to handle cache updates, failed requests, and different resource types.

What should not be cached blindly

One mistake with service workers is treating every request as something worth storing.

I avoid blindly caching API responses because they can contain changing or user-specific information.

I also avoid caching the service worker core itself as an ordinary application asset. The browser needs to be able to fetch and install an updated worker when I release changes.

Caching the worker incorrectly can make updates difficult to deliver.

The same applies to dynamic content. A cached response might be outdated even when the user expects fresh information.

Stale caches are a real maintenance problem

This is probably the most frustrating part.

You fix a bug, deploy the updated JavaScript, open the website, and the browser continues using an older cached file.

The code is correct on the server, but the user is still executing the previous version.

Versioned cache names help:

const CACHE_NAME = "pocketpdf-v4";

When the version changes, the new worker can populate a new cache and old caches can be cleaned up during activation.

However, changing a cache name alone isn't a complete update strategy. The worker lifecycle, existing tabs, and resource loading all need to be considered.

I have to be particularly careful when changing vendor libraries because an old cached application file combined with a new dependency can create unexpected problems.

What offline actually means for the user

After the initial visit and the necessary resources have been cached, the tools can continue working without an internet connection.

Someone on a plane can open the site and merge two PDFs, provided the relevant application files and dependencies have already been downloaded.

OCR has an additional requirement: its Tesseract WebAssembly engine and language data need to be downloaded before the first offline OCR session.

That is an important distinction. Offline support doesn't mean every possible resource is magically available before it has ever been requested.

Why I bothered

I didn't want PocketPDF to depend on a permanent connection just to run JavaScript that is already stored in the browser.

A static site, local processing, lazy loading, and service worker caching work well together.

There are still edge cases to handle, especially around updates and large dependencies, but the result is a tool collection that can keep working after the first load.

The project is available at https://pocketpdf.site

title: ElevenLabs on AI Gateway
description:
Vercel and ElevenLabs are partnering to bring 14 ElevenLabs models to AI Gateway. To celebrate the launch, all ElevenLabs models are 50% off on AI Gateway for the first 14 days, through November 9th.

AI Gateway supports six different types of ElevenLabs audio models:

  • Speech to text: Transcribe recordings or caption live audio as people speak.

  • Streaming text to speech: Start playing audio while a language model is still writing its reply, so users don't have to wait for the full answer.

  • Realtime voice agents: Let users talk to your app and listen to it respond out loud in a single live session. Useful for support lines, tutors, and in-app assistants.

  • Music: Describe a track in plain text and get back a finished song or instrumental at the length you need.

  • Sound effects: Generate game and interface sounds, or ambience that loops cleanly, from a short description.

  • Multi-voice dialogue: Voice a whole conversation in one call, with a different voice for each speaker.

All of these audio models are accessible through a single gateway API key. Your app or agent can transcribe what a user says, reason over it with your choice of hundreds of models, then answer in an ElevenLabs voice. You can also create soundtracks with generated music and sound effects.

Every request lands in the same usage, cost, and trace views as your other AI Gateway traffic.

Model types

AI Gateway gives you access to 14 ElevenLabs models, spanning speech to text, realtime voice, and music.

Speech and transcription

Scribe v2 Realtime turns a user's speech into text while they are still talking. A language model of your choice then writes the answer. Eleven Flash v2.5, a low-latency ElevenLabs voice model, reads that answer aloud as it streams in, so the user hears the reply begin before the model finishes writing it.

Because each step is its own model, you can swap the transcription, language, or speech model without touching the rest of the pipeline.

In the example below, a user asks whether they’ll make a connecting flight. The text model combines flight status and gate distance to answer, then the speech model delivers the response.

Realtime voice agents

Eleven Realtime v1 Max and Eleven Realtime v1 Mini run the whole spoken conversation in one model, which suits conversations where users expect natural back-and-forth, like a support call or an in-app assistant. Both models take the user's audio in and speak a reply back over a single WebSocket session, so there's no separate transcription or speech step to wire up.

Eleven Realtime hears “Can I change the delivery address for my order?” and responds “I can help with that. What’s your order number?” over one WebSocket session.

In the browser, connect with the useRealtime hook from @ai-sdk/react, which handles the WebSocket connection, microphone capture, and audio playback. In the hook's sessionConfig, set an ElevenLabs voice ID and turnDetection: { type: 'semantic-vad' }. These models support semantic voice activity detection (VAD) to decide when the user has finished speaking, but they don't support server-vad. The realtime guide walks through the full browser setup.

Music and sound effects

Music v2.5 and Music v2 compose original music from a text description. Name a genre, a mood, or the instruments you want, and the model returns a finished track at the length you ask for, with or without vocals. For more control, you can lay out a song section by section and give each section its own style and length.

Sound Effects v2 works the same way for shorter sounds, such as footsteps, a door slamming, or rain that loops under a game level.

All three models use generateSpeech, with text describing the sound you want instead of words to read aloud. This example requests a 30-second track:

Multi-voice dialogue

Eleven v4, Eleven v4 Turbo, and Eleven v3 perform a script with several speakers in a single request. You assign a voice to each line, and each change of voice starts a new turn. A two-host podcast or a scene with a full cast comes back as one continuous recording, so there are no separate clips to stitch together.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

The AI Gateway audio docs have examples across the ElevenLabs models. Browse all audio models on AI Gateway, and try ElevenLabs at 50% off until November 9th.

title: My falsifier was measuring my laptop
description:
I ship small engines twice: once in Python as an oracle, once in JavaScript so a
stranger can play with one in a browser without installing anything. The rule is
that the port must agree with the oracle exactly — not approximately, not
within tolerance. Zero tolerance.

That rule needs a falsifier: a frozen fixture generated from the oracle and
committed, plus a script that recomputes everything and diffs it against the
frozen file. On the economic-threshold page that is 250 states and 4,270
compared values, including a Monte Carlo bank (n=8000, seed=20261113).

It was green on my laptop every time I ran it. The first CI run after deploying
turned it red.

This post is about three checks that lied to me, and the one habit that caught
them: measure the difference before naming the cause.

Defect 1 — the fixture recorded who measured 

RC 5 · el oráculo se movió

CI runs Python 3.12.13; my laptop runs 3.9.6. The interesting conclusion is
also the wrong one: the oracle is not deterministic across interpreters. So I
measured instead of concluding.

  • Oracle under 3.9.6 → fixture 102,715 bytes
  • Oracle under 3.12.13 → fixture 102,717 bytes

Two bytes. A recursion over the two JSON trees puts both failures in one leaf:

/procedencia/python    "3.9.6"  ->  "3.12.13"

And the number that settles it: of the 4,270 values the fixture claims to
compare, 4,270 are identical, bit for bit. Every boundary state, every
preset, every value on the frontier band. Nothing numeric moved.

The fixture recorded who measured inside the bytes it compared:

{
  "estados": [ "... 250 states, 4270 values ..." ],
  "procedencia": { "python": "3.9.6" }
}

procedencia.python is a statement about the observer. The contract is about
the subject — the numbers. By putting the observer inside the compared region, a
correct oracle failed on a different interpreter.

This is worth naming precisely, because it is not "a flaky test". The oracle was
right. The page was right. The falsifier was answering the wrong question: it
asked "did the environment change?" and reported the answer as "did the math
change?"

The fix, and the part that matters more

Split the compared region from the metadata:

CAMPOS_DEL_OBSERVADOR = ("procedencia/python",)

def _sujeto(datos):
    """Lo que se compara: el sujeto, sin el estado del observador."""
    sujeto = copy.deepcopy(datos)
    sujeto.pop("procedencia", None)
    return sujeto

# --check compares the subject on both sides
if serializa(_sujeto(congelado)) != serializa(_sujeto(datos)):
    return RC_ORACULO_MOVIDO

The obvious version stops there, and that version has a second defect waiting: a
file that silently excludes a field is indistinguishable from a file that
silently excludes the wrong field. An unstated exemption is the same class of
error as a lie.

So --check prints its exemption on every run:

RC 0 · fixture congelado == oráculo (102715 bytes) · fuera del sujeto: procedencia/python=3.9.6

There is no state in which the tool excludes something and does not say so.

Pin both halves

A fix tested only in the direction it was written is not tested. The test pins
the exemption and its boundary:

def test_el_check_ignora_solo_al_observador(...):
    # 1) change the interpreter -> still RC 0, and the field is named
    # 2) change the Monte Carlo seed -> RC 5, naming the contract that moved

Change the observer and the check stays green. Change the subject and it goes
red, with a reason. Without that second assertion, "ignore procedencia" would
be indistinguishable from "ignore anything inconvenient".

Defect 2 — a hang that had already printed its failure

The suite also drives the real page through a headless runtime and mutates it,
asserting that each mutation is caught. On macOS 26.5.2 / node 24.15.0, about 2%
of those runs never returned:

sample <pid>
  Builtins_JSEntryTrampoline
  node::Environment::Exit
  NodePlatform::Shutdown
  WorkerThreadsTaskRunner::Shutdown()      <- stuck here, after printing the failure

The failure had already been printed. The process just would not die. Measured:
3 hangs in 150 runs of a mutated page, 0 in 200 of the pristine one, 0
in 200 of node -e 'process.exit(1)'.

The mitigation is one retry with a UserWarning — plus the check that keeps it
honest: two consecutive timeouts still fail. A retry that also swallows a
real hang is not a mitigation, it is a mute button.

The claim is not "it never hangs". The claim is "a hang costs one retry, not a
red build" — and since it has already fired once on a real run, the docs say
exactly that.

The rule I added afterwards — and the false green inside it

Publishing four demos made the next gap obvious. Three of the four pages proved
their thesis and never said what they do not prove. For a project whose
whole argument is "publish the negative result as a result", that is a
credibility gap, not a rendering gap.

So the house rule became: no page ships without a block declaring its limits, in
both languages. Each page now carries two, and they are not decorative. This one
is from the field classifier:

reader drift compares two readers of this same code. If both share the same
wrong definition of the invariant, the drift is zero and the error stays
invisible: zero drift proves the two paths agree, not that the class is right.

And the rule is enforced, not requested:

$ python3 tools/verificar_limites.py
demo/clasificador-de-campos            limites=2  OK
demo/nulo-con-dientes                  limites=2  OK
demo/piso-de-deteccion                 limites=2  OK
demo/umbral-economico                  limites=2  OK
README.md                              cita la regla
README.es.md                           cita la regla
RC 0 · 4 páginas declaran lo que no prueban, en todos sus idiomas

Delete a limit while still declaring data-limites="2" and it fails closed:

  ✗ demo/piso-de-deteccion: declara 2 límites y publica 1
  ✗ demo/piso-de-deteccion: publica 1 límite(s) y el mínimo es 2: un límite único no distingue el alcance de la excusa
RC 1 · 2 fallo(s): una página que no declara su límite no es un instrumento

Then I tried to write this paragraph, and the paragraph was false

I was about to publish "the limits contract fails closed", which is a claim, not
an observation. So I ran the mutation that the sentence depends on:

<!-- <li data-t="lim1">The floats are not bit-exact and this page does not
     claim they are: x**2 in CPython routes to the system libm …</li> -->

$ python3 tools/verificar_limites.py
...
RC 0 · 4 páginas declaran lo que no prueban, en todos sus idiomas

RC 0. A limit wrapped in an HTML comment — present in the file, invisible to
every reader — counted as published. The verifier extracted <li> elements from
the raw body, and the comment markers sat outside the <li>, so the element
was still there and its text was still substantive. Commenting the whole
<section id="limites"> did not register either.

The cause is embarrassingly simple, and it is the same cause as defect 1: the
check was reading the observer's view of the document (what a findall sees)
instead of the reader's view (what a person sees). Stripping <!-- … --> from
the whole document before counting anything closed all three shapes.

The other half of the defect is in the test bank: it covered commenting the text
inside a <li> — the half of the problem that was easy to imagine. The half
that mattered was the one outside the quote marks.

Two new mutations, and I checked that each one is a real falsifier by reverting
the fix in a throwaway copy:

FAILED tests/test_limites.py::MutacionesTests::test_la_seccion_entera_comentada_no_cuenta
FAILED tests/test_limites.py::MutacionesTests::test_un_limite_entero_comentado_no_cuenta
2 failed, 15 passed

Green with the fix, red without it. Without that second run, "the test passes"
would have meant nothing more than "the test agrees with the code I just wrote".

What generalises

  1. A fixture that fails on a correct implementation teaches people to ignore fixtures. The cost of a false red is not the red — it is the credibility you spend next time.
  2. Separate the observer from the subject, and print what you excluded. Compiler versions, OS, machine, timestamp, user: all of them describe who measured, not what was measured. HTML comments, rendering, and scroll position are observers too.
  3. If you cannot make a check fail on purpose, it is not a check. Every verifier here is paired with a mutation that must produce a non-zero exit — and the mutation is re-run with the fix removed, because a mutation that passes in both directions is measuring nothing.
  4. A test bank covers exactly the failures its author imagined. The gap is never in the case you wrote; it is in the neighbouring one. Enumerate the shapes the defect can take — text inside the tag, tag inside the comment, comment around the section — not just the one in front of you.
  5. Measure the difference before naming the cause. "Not deterministic across interpreters" was one command away from being refuted. If I had written it in the commit message first, it would have become the story.

Go try to break them

Four engines. Each page ships its frozen fixture — every state, every compared
value — plus a script that recomputes the browser engine and diffs it against
that file. The check runs in the public repo, against a fixture generated from
the Python oracle. The oracle itself lives in a private repository for three of
the four, and those fixtures say fuente_publica: false with a reproducible
local command rather than a link that would 404:

  • Classifier of electromagnetic fields — six components of an antisymmetric tensor, classified into the algebraic types of Cl(1,3), with the invariants that do not move under a frame change.
  • Does your null have teeth? — a permutation test is a null only for the invariant it destroys: which invariant dies, and which one survives, under each of five resamplers.
  • The detection floor — a gate that judges a field with a constant ε is not choosing a precision, it is choosing between two blindnesses; the operator's truncation floor depends on the node and is measured without ground truth.
  • The threshold — p_min = C/V and expected value for repeated attempts, with the Monte Carlo bank behind the closed form.

Hub: alexisromtz-lab.github.io/auditor-toolkit

Each page also tells you, in English and Spanish, what it does not prove — and
a script fails the build if that block ever disappears. If you find a state where
the browser and the oracle disagree, that is the bug report I want.

title: PageSpeed mobile: como levei um site HTML estático de 64 para 97
description:
Não sou programador. Sou corretor de planos de saúde e sócio de uma corretora, e cuido pessoalmente dos nossos sites. Nesta semana passei alguns dias mexendo na performance de quatro sites em HTML estático, e o resultado me surpreendeu: o pior deles saiu de 64 para 97 no PageSpeed Insights mobile.

Vou contar o que fiz, na ordem, com os números reais. Se você tem um site feito a partir de um template pronto (desses com Bootstrap, jQuery e uma dúzia de plugins), é bem provável que o seu tenha os mesmos problemas.

Transparência: fiz esse trabalho com ajuda de IA (Claude), que escreveu os scripts e conferiu cada etapa comigo. As decisões, os testes e os números são dos meus sites.

O incômodo: o WordPress estava mais rápido que o HTML puro

Nosso site principal, de planos da Amil Saúde, roda em WordPress com plugin de cache e marca 94 no mobile. Já os sites menores, feitos em HTML estático, que em teoria deveriam voar, estavam entre 63 e 79.

Não fazia sentido, não é mesmo? HTML puro não tem banco de dados, não tem PHP, não tem nada. O problema não era o tipo de site. Era tudo o que o template carregava sem usar.

O caso deste artigo é um site sobre a linha Amil Black (a linha topo da operadora, que substituiu o antigo Amil One em março de 2026). Ele estava assim no PageSpeed mobile:

  • Desempenho: 64
  • LCP (Largest Contentful Paint): 7,4 s

Sete segundos para o maior elemento aparecer na tela de um celular. Muita gente desiste antes disso.

Passo 1: descobrir o que o template carregava de graça

Abri o <head> e o fim do <body> da home. Esta era a lista de scripts, carregada em todas as páginas:

<script src="plugins/jQuery/jquery.min.js"></script>
<script src="plugins/bootstrap/bootstrap.min.js"></script>
<script src="plugins/magnific-popup/jquery.magnific.popup.min.js"></script>
<script src="plugins/slick/slick.min.js"></script>
<script src="plugins/filterizr/jquery.filterizr.min.js"></script>
<script src="https://maps.googleapis.com/maps/api/js?key=..."></script>
<script src="plugins/google-map/gmap.js"></script>
<script src="plugins/syotimer/jquery.syotimer.js"></script>
<script src="plugins/aos/aos.js"></script>
<script src="plugins/swiper/swiper.min.js"></script>
<script src="js/script.js"></script>
<script src="js/menu-black.js"></script>

O site não tem mapa, não tem carrossel, não tem contador regressivo, não tem galeria com filtro. O único script que realmente fazia alguma coisa era o último, menu-black.js, que é o menu.

No CSS, a mesma história: Bootstrap completo, Slick, Slick Theme, Themify Icons e Font Awesome 4.5 vindo de uma CDN.

Uma curiosidade: em outro dos sites, o script.js do template tinha um trecho de CSS colado no final do arquivo. Isso é erro de sintaxe, então o script nunca executou, provavelmente durante anos, e ninguém percebeu. Era peso puro.

Como tirar sem quebrar nada

Antes de apagar qualquer coisa, tirei print de página inteira de todas as páginas, no desktop (1280 px) e no celular (390 px), com o Playwright. Depois de cada mudança, tirei os prints de novo e comparei pixel a pixel.

Para comparar, usei uma tolerância pequena (diferença maior que 24 em algum canal de cor), porque gradientes de fundo às vezes variam um pouco entre uma renderização e outra e geram "diferença" que o olho não vê.

Também conferi três coisas que print não mostra:

  1. Erros de JavaScript no console (pageerror no Playwright).
  2. O menu: o mega menu no hover do desktop e o hambúrguer no celular.
  3. O botão "voltar ao topo".

Esse terceiro item me pegou. O botão dependia do script.js antigo, que era jQuery. Tirei o jQuery e precisei de um substituto. Foram seis linhas de JavaScript puro, no arquivo do menu que já existia:

document.addEventListener('click', function (e) {
    var b = e.target.closest ? e.target.closest('.back-to-top') : null;
    if (!b) return;
    e.preventDefault();
    window.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: 'smooth' });
});

Resultado: 11 scripts a menos por página, além dos CSS de Slick, Slick Theme e Font Awesome.

Passo 2: PurgeCSS no Bootstrap

Mesmo sem os plugins, o bootstrap.min.css tinha 141 KB, e o site usa uma fração disso: o grid, alguns utilitários e o collapse do menu.

Usei o PurgeCSS, passando como conteúdo todos os HTML e os JS que sobraram:

import { PurgeCSS } from 'purgecss';
import fs from 'fs';

const result = await new PurgeCSS().purge({
  content: ['site/*.html', 'site/js/*.js'],
  css: ['site/plugins/bootstrap/bootstrap.min.css'],
  safelist: {
    standard: ['show', 'collapse', 'collapsing', 'fade', 'active', 'open'],
    greedy: [/^modal/, /^dropdown/, /^navbar/, /^nav-/]
  }
});

fs.writeFileSync('site/plugins/bootstrap/bootstrap.min.css', result[0].css);

A safelist é a parte importante. Classes que o JavaScript adiciona na hora (como show no menu aberto) não aparecem no HTML, e o PurgeCSS apagaria essas classes se você não avisar.

  • Bootstrap: 141 KB → ~26 KB
  • Themify Icons: 18,6 KB → ~1 KB (o site usa meia dúzia de ícones)

💡 Dica: depois de purgar, coloque um ?v=4 (ou qualquer número novo) no link do CSS. Sem isso, quem já visitou o site continua com o arquivo antigo em cache e você fica achando que algo deu errado.

Passo 3: a imagem do LCP (aqui estava o 7,4 s)

O maior elemento da primeira tela era a imagem principal da home: um PNG de 399 KB.

Convertida para WebP, com uma versão menor para o celular:

  • amil-black-hero.webp (700 px): 24,9 KB
  • amil-black-hero-400.webp (400 px): 11,6 KB 
<link rel="preload" as="image" href="images/amil-black-hero.webp"
      imagesrcset="images/amil-black-hero-400.webp 400w, images/amil-black-hero.webp 700w"
      imagesizes="(max-width: 575px) 88vw, 532px" fetchpriority="high">

<img src="images/amil-black-hero.webp"
     srcset="images/amil-black-hero-400.webp 400w, images/amil-black-hero.webp 700w"
     sizes="(max-width: 575px) 88vw, 532px"
     width="700" height="525" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async"
     alt="Mulher sorrindo segurando o cartão do plano Amil Black">

O width e o height evitam que a página "pule" quando a imagem chega (é o CLS). O sizes diz ao navegador que, no celular, a imagem ocupa 88% da largura da tela, então ele baixa a versão de 400 px.

E aqui encontrei o erro mais curioso de todos. Outra imagem, uma foto que fica no meio da página, estava marcada com fetchpriority="high":

<img src="images/amil-black/amil-black.jpg" alt="..." fetchpriority="high">

Ou seja: o navegador baixava com prioridade máxima uma foto que o visitante só vê depois de rolar a tela, competindo com a imagem que realmente importava. Troquei por loading="lazy" e converti essa foto também para WebP, em três tamanhos.

💡 Dica: procure fetchpriority="high" no seu site inteiro. Deve existir no máximo um por página, e só na imagem do LCP.

Aproveitei para reescrever os alt das imagens. Se a imagem tem texto escrito nela (banner, chamada), o alt deve dizer o que está escrito, não só descrever a cena.

Passo 4: as fontes do Google sem travar a página

O style.css do template começava a carregar as fontes assim:

@import url("https://fonts.googleapis.com/css?family=Open+Sans:400,600,700|Poppins:300,400,500,600,700|Work+Sans:400,500,600|Roboto:100,200,300,400,500,600,700,800,900");

Isso é ruim por dois motivos:

  1. @import dentro do CSS é uma cadeia: o navegador baixa o style.css, só então descobre o @import, só então vai ao Google. Tudo isso antes de pintar o texto.
  2. Quatro famílias e 20 pesos. O site usa duas famílias e três pesos.

Tirei o @import e coloquei no <head> de cada página:

<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
<link rel="stylesheet"
      href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Open+Sans:wght@400;600;700&family=Poppins:wght@400;600;700&display=swap"
      media="print" onload="this.media='all'">
<noscript>
  <link rel="stylesheet"
        href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Open+Sans:wght@400;600;700&family=Poppins:wght@400;600;700&display=swap">
</noscript>

O truque do media="print" faz o navegador baixar a fonte sem bloquear a renderização. Quando termina, o onload aplica a fonte na tela. O display=swap mostra o texto com a fonte do sistema enquanto isso.

Passo 5: gzip e cache no .htaccess

O servidor é Apache (hospedagem compartilhada comum). Sem nenhuma configuração, ele não comprimia nada e não dizia ao navegador por quanto tempo guardar os arquivos.

<IfModule mod_deflate.c>
  AddOutputFilterByType DEFLATE text/html text/css text/plain text/xml
  AddOutputFilterByType DEFLATE application/javascript application/json
  AddOutputFilterByType DEFLATE application/xml image/svg+xml font/woff2
</IfModule>

<IfModule mod_expires.c>
  ExpiresActive On
  ExpiresByType image/webp "access plus 1 year"
  ExpiresByType image/jpeg "access plus 1 year"
  ExpiresByType image/png  "access plus 1 year"
  ExpiresByType font/woff2 "access plus 1 year"
  ExpiresByType text/css   "access plus 1 month"
  ExpiresByType application/javascript "access plus 1 month"
  ExpiresByType text/html  "access plus 0 seconds"
</IfModule>

Tudo dentro de <IfModule>: se o módulo não existir no servidor, o bloco é ignorado e o site não cai com erro 500.

HTML com cache zero é de propósito: assim, quando eu atualizo uma página, o visitante vê a versão nova na hora. Imagens e fontes quase nunca mudam e podem ficar um ano em cache. CSS e JS têm o ?v= para forçar a atualização quando eu mexo neles.

No site de Brasília, só esse passo levou a nota de 78 para 89. Foi o ajuste com melhor custo-benefício de todos.

O resultado

Métrica (mobile) Antes Depois
Desempenho 64 97
First Contentful Paint — 1,1 s
Largest Contentful Paint 7,4 s 2,6 s
Total Blocking Time — 0 ms
Cumulative Layout Shift — 0,001
Speed Index — 2,7 s
SEO — 100

Não anotei todas as métricas do "antes", só a nota e o LCP. Fica a lição: tire print completo do PageSpeed antes de começar.

Fiz o mesmo processo nos outros três sites:

O que ainda falta

  • LCP de 2,6 s: está um pouco acima do verde, que vai até 2,5 s. No print do PageSpeed, o banner de cookies cobre boa parte da tela do celular, e desconfio que ele esteja sendo contado como o maior elemento. É o próximo teste.
  • Acessibilidade em 85: provavelmente é o contraste do texto dourado sobre o fundo preto e a ordem dos títulos. Ajuste fino, mas importa.

Checklist para o seu site

  • Liste os scripts e CSS de cada página: para cada um, pergunte "o que quebra se eu tirar?". Em template pronto, a resposta costuma ser "nada".
  • Tire prints antes e depois: de todas as páginas, desktop e celular. Compare automaticamente.
  • Purgue o Bootstrap: com uma safelist para as classes que o JavaScript adiciona.
  • Ataque a imagem do LCP: WebP, srcset, preload e fetchpriority="high" só nela.
  • Procure fetchpriority errado: um por página, no máximo.
  • Tire o @import de fontes do CSS: carregue só as famílias e os pesos que você usa, sem bloquear.
  • Configure gzip e cache: sempre dentro de <IfModule>.
  • Coloque ?v= nos arquivos alterados: para o cache não esconder a sua mudança.

Se você tem um site parado em 60 e poucos no mobile, comece pela imagem do LCP e pelo .htaccess. São os dois passos que mais mexeram na nota aqui.

Ficou alguma dúvida, ou você já passou por algo parecido com template pronto? Me conta nos comentários.

title: Migrating Media Gallery from Electron to Native Rust GUI to Reduce Overhead and Improve Scrolling
description:
Benchmarking Electron vs. Rust GUI Performance Bottlenecks

When evaluating the transition of a massive local media gallery from an Electron frontend to a native Rust GUI framework, developers frequently run headfirst into a fundamental misconception: that dropping the Chromium runtime eliminates performance overhead. In reality, performance for collections scaling past one hundred thousand items is dictated by memory bandwidth limits, thread contention, and layout recalculation mechanics rather than runtime branding. Analyzing the bottlenecks reveals distinct structural failure points across both architectures.

Memory Overhead and Process Architecture: Electron wraps applications in a multi-process model where every window and iframe spins up a distinct Chromium instance complete with a dedicated V8 isolate, Blink rendering engine, and GPU command buffer. For a media gallery maintaining tens of thousands of thumbnail references, Electron’s JavaScript heap bloats rapidly due to DOM node object allocations, CSS style declaration trees, and V8 garbage collection pauses. When scrolling rapidly through a masonry grid, the V8 garbage collector is forced to sweep massive generations of discarded DOM wrapper objects, causing unpredictable micro-stutters. Conversely, native Rust frameworks eliminate JavaScript bridging overhead, but memory profiles diverge wildly based on design model:

  • Immediate-Mode (e.g., egui): Re-evaluates the entire widget tree every single frame. Storing state for 100,000 items requires either continuous allocation churn or manual clipping hacks, pushing CPU caches to their limits as the CPU constantly re-fetches off-screen layout structs.
  • Retained-Mode (e.g., GTK4, Slint): Maintains a persistent scene graph. Memory overhead stays flat relative to visible items, but complex custom masonry layouts demand aggressive item recycling to prevent heap fragmentation.

Layout Recalculation and DOM vs. Native Math: In Electron, layout recalculation relies on Blink's highly optimized, multi-threaded CSS engine. While powerful, style invalidation cascades can trigger expensive layout reflows across the entire flex or grid container whenever a thumbnail loads or a filter changes. If virtualization is imperfect, the layout engine wastes cycles calculating geometry for off-screen nodes. In native Rust toolkits, the performance equation shifts depending on layout flexibility:

  • The Immediate-Mode Trap: Frameworks like egui lack native, high-performance masonry layout widgets. Implementing a multi-column dynamic aspect-ratio masonry grid requires calculating explicit bounding boxes for every item on every frame. If the frame budget is 16.6ms for 60fps, evaluating 100,000 items sequentially on the main thread causes CPU thread starvation, driving CPU core temperatures up and triggering thermal throttling on laptops.
  • The Retained-Mode Advantage: GTK4 provides battle-tested native list and grid view widgets with built-in hardware recycling and differential layout passes, bypassing redundant math for non-visible nodes.

Thread Constraints and Texture Upload Synchronization: The primary bottleneck in large media galleries is rarely the language runtime divide, but rather CPU-to-GPU texture transfer synchronization and image decoding throughput. In Electron, asynchronous image decoding happens in worker threads, but uploading decoded bitmap buffers to the GPU through Chromium's rendering pipeline introduces multi-process IPC serialization costs. In native Rust architectures, disk I/O, SQLite metadata queries, and image decoding are cleanly offloaded to background thread pools via non-blocking message-passing channels. However, if the UI thread blocks synchronously on GPU texture uploads (glTexImage2D or Vulkan equivalents) during rapid scroll bursts, the event loop freezes, dropping frames and leaving blank cells.
Metric / Vector Electron + TS (Current) Immediate-Mode Rust (e.g., egui) Retained-Mode Native (e.g., GTK4)
Layout Calculation Cost High CSS reflow overhead; mitigated by Blink's mature flex/grid layout heuristics. Severe CPU thrashing; forces manual layout math on every frame for virtualized lists. Low; incremental layout passes restricted strictly to visible bounding viewports.
Memory Footprint High; inflated by V8 isolates, DOM node trees, and garbage collection overhead. Low baseline, but vulnerable to cache thrashing if immediate states are mismanaged. Optimized; persistent scene graph with predictable heap utilization.
Scroll Fluidity under Load Smooth hardware acceleration, but vulnerable to JS garbage collection frame drops. Prone to micro-stutters during rapid scroll bursts due to full-frame re-evaluations. Extremely high native frame rates with robust item recycling and native Vsync locking.

Strategic Decision Rule: If a personal project's existing Rust backend already communicates cleanly with the TypeScript frontend via asynchronous channels, migrating the UI to an immature native Rust framework trades away decades of mature browser layout flexibility for marginal rendering gains. Rule of thumb: If the target GUI framework lacks a robust, virtualized masonry widget out of the box, do not rewrite. Optimize the existing stack or adopt a mature retained-mode framework like GTK4 only when the maintenance friction of the hybrid bridge demonstrably halts feature expansion.

Comparative Analysis of egui, Iced, Slint, and GTK4 for Masonry Layouts

Transitioning a high-performance local media gallery managing tens to hundreds of thousands of images from an Electron stack to a native Rust GUI requires confronting fundamental architectural trade-offs. The core engineering challenge lies in rendering a dynamic, multi-column masonry layout with varied aspect ratios while sustaining ultra-low-latency scrolling, real-time filesystem change monitoring, and asynchronous GPU texture uploads. Evaluating egui, Iced, Slint, and GTK4 reveals stark contrasts in how immediate-mode and retained-mode engines handle layout calculation costs, memory bandwidth limits, and thread contention.
Framework Architecture Model Virtualization & Masonry Support Failure Mode & Risk Mechanism
egui Immediate-Mode Non-existent natively; requires manual bounding-box clipping hacks per frame. CPU Thread Starvation: Re-evaluating 100,000 items every frame triggers severe allocation churn and CPU cache thrashing, causing micro-stutters and thermal throttling.
Iced Elm-based Retained/Hybrid Maturing widget ecosystem; custom multi-column variable-aspect grids demand manual layout math. Layout Thrashing: Lack of built-in item recycling for complex asymmetric grids forces full-pass layout recalculations during rapid scroll bursts.
Slint Declarative Retained-Mode Structured markup language with flat memory footprints, but limited high-throughput masonry components. Ecosystem Maturity Gaps: Complex dynamic asynchronous thumbnail injection and VRAM texture eviction require low-level binding workarounds.
GTK4 Retained-Mode Native Production-grade via GtkGridView and list item factory recycling pipelines. C-FFI Boundary Friction: Interfacing Rust backends with GTK's object model introduces boilerplate and C-FFI overhead, though rendering performance remains optimal.

Analyzing the physical mechanics of rendering exposes why immediate-mode engines falter under heavy media workloads. In an immediate-mode framework like egui, the entire widget tree is re-evaluated on every single frame. When a user scrolls rapidly through 100,000 image nodes, the CPU is forced to compute layout constraints for off-screen elements sequentially. This creates extreme allocation churn on the heap, exhausts L3 cache lines, and starves the UI thread. The observable effect is severe input latency, dropped frames, and visible blank cell placeholders as the event loop locks up during full-frame re-evaluations.

Conversely, retained-mode architectures mitigate these bottlenecks through persistent scene graphs and item recycling. Among the native Rust-compatible options, GTK4 stands out as the most battle-tested choice due to its differential layout passes and robust hardware-accelerated view recycling. Instead of recalculating coordinates for unrendered nodes, GTK4 restricts layout math strictly to visible bounding viewports, maintaining a flat memory footprint relative to visible items rather than total dataset size. However, developers adopting GTK4 must accept the friction of bridging a Rust backend to a C-based object system via FFI, trading away pure-Rust ergonomics for hardware-accelerated stability.

When assessing GPU texture caching capabilities across these frameworks, the primary performance bottleneck shifts from layout math to texture upload synchronization. Regardless of whether a gallery uses egui, Iced, Slint, or GTK4, synchronous texture uploads executed directly on the UI thread during rapid scroll bursts will freeze the event loop. To achieve zero-stutter scrolling, the chosen framework must support asynchronous texture streaming, where decoded thumbnails are uploaded to GPU memory via auxiliary worker threads. While GTK4 handles this cleanly via native GSK rendering nodes, immediate-mode frameworks struggle to coordinate asynchronous texture readiness with single-pass frame execution, leading to visual tearing and stuttering.

Framing this migration through decision dominance principles yields a clear engineering directive:

  • Choice Error: Assuming that rewriting a hybrid stack into a pure Rust immediate-mode GUI will automatically cure performance bottlenecks caused by unoptimized layout algorithms or synchronous texture uploads.
  • Optimal Solution: If a native rewrite is strictly required, GTK4 is the only candidate offering production-ready virtualized grid recycling out of the box, whereas egui and Iced will trap the project in endless custom layout boilerplate.
  • Decision Rule: Do not rewrite a hybrid stack solely to drop the Chromium runtime if the target GUI framework lacks a robust, virtualized masonry widget out of the box. Migrate to a mature retained-mode framework like GTK4 strictly when hybrid bridge maintenance friction halts feature expansion; otherwise, targeted optimization of the existing Electron or Tauri stack remains the more pragmatic and computationally efficient path.

Async Decoding Pipelines and Framework Recommendation

When engineering a high-performance local media gallery handling upwards of 100,000 items, the primary performance bottleneck is rarely the JavaScript-versus-Rust runtime divide. Instead, it is the collision between memory bandwidth limits, thread contention, and CPU-to-GPU texture synchronization. Moving away from an Electron stack without addressing these underlying data flows merely shifts the bottleneck from a V8 garbage collection pause to immediate-mode CPU thread starvation.

Designing the Asynchronous Decoding and Texture Pipeline

To eliminate UI stutter during rapid scroll bursts, disk I/O, SQLite metadata queries, and heavy image decoding must be strictly decoupled from the main UI thread. A naive implementation that executes synchronous texture uploads via glTexImage2D or Vulkan equivalents will block the event loop, freezing rendering and dropping frames into blank cell placeholders.

The optimal architectural mechanism relies on a non-blocking message-passing pipeline powered by Tokio and cross-thread channels:

  • Worker Offloading: A dedicated Tokio worker pool handles asynchronous filesystem monitoring and batch image decoding in background threads, keeping the main event loop entirely free of blocking system calls.
  • Asynchronous Texture Streaming: Decoded raw pixel buffers are dispatched through bounded channels (tokio::sync::mpsc) to an auxiliary worker thread responsible for staging and uploading textures to GPU memory asynchronously.
  • Incremental Viewport Culling: The UI thread receives only lightweight texture handles and layout metadata, restricting layout calculations strictly to visible bounding viewports and recycling off-screen nodes.

Comparative Framework Benchmarks and Failure Modes

Evaluating native Rust GUI frameworks against a high-throughput, multi-column masonry layout reveals stark operational divergences under heavy load:
Framework Evaluation Model Primary Failure Mechanism Observable Impact
egui Immediate-Mode (Full tree re-evaluation every frame) Heap allocation churn and L3 cache line exhaustion from evaluating 100,000 items per frame. Severe CPU thread starvation, thermal throttling, input latency, and micro-stutters during rapid scroll bursts.
Iced Elm-based Retained/Hybrid Lack of native item recycling for complex asymmetric masonry grids forces full-pass layout thrashing. Unpredictable frame drops and high layout calculation overhead during dynamic viewport resizing.
Slint Declarative Retained-Mode Ecosystem maturity gaps for high-throughput masonry components require low-level binding workarounds. Manual VRAM texture eviction management leads to heap fragmentation and pipeline stalls.
GTK4 Production-Grade Retained-Mode Native C-FFI interop friction introduces boilerplate when interfacing Rust backends with GObject models. Minimal rendering overhead; robust item factory recycling maintains a flat memory footprint relative to visible items.

Decision Dominance and Final Recommendation

Developers frequently commit a foundational choice error: assuming that rewriting a hybrid stack into a pure-Rust immediate-mode GUI will automatically eliminate performance bottlenecks. In reality, frameworks like egui force manual per-frame bounding-box clipping hacks, turning the CPU into a brute-force layout engine that constantly thrashes memory caches.

The Optimal Solution: GTK4 is the sole Rust-compatible candidate offering production-ready virtualized grid recycling out of the box via GtkGridView and built-in hardware recycling pipelines. It maintains a persistent scene graph and restricts layout math strictly to visible bounding viewports.

Migration Rule: If the target GUI framework lacks a robust, virtualized masonry widget out of the box, do not rewrite a hybrid stack solely to drop the Chromium runtime. Migrate to GTK4 strictly when hybrid bridge maintenance friction halts feature expansion; otherwise, targeted optimization of the existing Electron or Tauri stack—bolstered by a Tokio-driven async decoding pipeline—remains computationally superior and practically pragmatic.

title: Gaming Image Transformations: Missing Names Fail the Build Before Deployment
description:
Storage and cache budgets constrain how many compressed image variants a gaming marketplace can retain, so a provider migration needs a release check for the transformation names the application actually uses. TL;DR: list existing transformations in CI, assert that every name referenced by the application exists, and fail the build if one is missing. Keep those names as constants in one module. A matching name establishes a dependency; it doesn't establish equivalent image output.

What page fired, and what should have failed earlier?

Consider a hypothetical production review: a marketplace release references three image transformations for game listings, but the deployment target contains only two. Stop the release before a player requests the missing variant. This is an illustrative scenario, not an observed outage. My review question would be specific: what page fired, and did it identify a missing dependency or merely report an aggregate image error rate? A green dashboard doesn't answer that question.

Stop the release.

The invariant is small enough to inspect: every transformation name referenced by the release must exist in the environment that will serve it. For a Node.js application, export the required names from its constants module and pass them to an independent CI assertion. The implementation below uses Go. The application can remain JavaScript; the release contract is a set of names rather than an imported provider SDK.

I recommend trying Infrai for this marketplace's transformation inventory check when consolidating backend services under one key and one bill would reduce credential and invoice handling. Its public, self-describing API supplies request and response schemas, so the integration can translate the provider inventory into application-owned names without guessing its response fields. That supports a concrete migration boundary: replace the inventory adapter, preserve the application identifiers and assertion, and revalidate image outputs separately. It does not promise interchangeable image processors.

Keep the release contract smaller than the rendering contract

Use three illustrative constants: listing_card, listing_detail, and seller_preview. These are names to configure in your own environment, not built-in transformations or verified account inventory. During the build, export the constants from the same module the application imports. Don't maintain a second handwritten list in CI; that list can stay green while application code adds a dependency the gate has never checked.

The inventory read is a cheap dependency check. It should reject missing names, malformed responses, and unsuccessful requests. It should not create missing transformations or silently substitute another name, because provisioning and verification have different jobs: one changes the environment, while the other determines whether this release can use it. Bind the credentials to the actual deployment target. Finding the same three strings in another account proves nothing about readiness here.

Names are necessary.

They are also insufficient. Before a provider migration, compare actual outputs on a representative set of game listing assets against application requirements for dimensions, format, visual quality, and retained variants. MDN's image format guide helps explain format choices; it doesn't establish that a particular quality setting meets the marketplace's storage budget. No measured compression advantage or cost savings is claimed here. The storage and cache decision is how many outputs the application elects to retain and serve, and a name-existence check cannot make that decision for you.

Compare the exit path before choosing the entry point

Evaluate candidates against the same requirement: can the integration produce a trustworthy inventory for the deployment target while application identifiers remain stable? Product concepts need explicit translation. A named transformation, a rendering URL, and an image variant shouldn't be treated as equivalent merely because all three can participate in an image workflow.

Option Documentation to evaluate Fit and migration boundary
Cloudinary Named image transformations and the Admin API Evaluate for a specialist transformation workflow; map both names and settings before accepting equivalent behavior.
imgix Rendering API and URL parameters Evaluate when URL-driven image rendering fits delivery; the appropriate release check may validate parameters instead of a named inventory.
Cloudflare Images Image variants and delivery documentation Evaluate when its variant model fits the marketplace; translate those concepts rather than equating labels across providers.
Infrai Transformation listing and public capability schemas Evaluate when image operations belong within a broader backend API under one key and one bill; output validation remains separate.

A specialist is the better choice when its documented image workflow is the requirement the team needs, and consolidating other backend integrations adds little value. Conversely, Infrai's REST API needs no SDK for this check, which removes a provider library dependency from the build utility. That benefit is concrete, but bounded: the HTTP request and response mapping still need maintenance when changing providers.

There is a tradeoff. An adapter adds code, and the release now depends on obtaining a valid inventory. Accept that dependency deliberately; otherwise a missing name can first become visible on a real user's image request. Neither integration style proves superior latency, image quality, or storage efficiency without testing the workload.

How can CI list existing transformations and assert required names?

Save the program below as gate.go. Supply INFRAI_API_KEY through the CI secret mechanism, set NAMES_POINTER to the JSON Pointer identifying the inventory array in the documented response, and set NAME_FIELD if its entries are objects rather than strings. An empty pointer selects a top-level array. These environment variables are local adapter configuration, not API parameters or claims about the response schema. Obtain their values from the public capability schema rather than guessing a data or name field.

Run go run gate.go listing_card listing_detail seller_preview for the illustrative names, replacing the arguments with the output of the application's constants module in the real build. The program makes one read-only API call, validates the configured mapping, and exits with status 1 on a missing name. It uses only the standard library. There are no creation retries or write operations to make idempotent.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func inventory(key string) ([]byte, error) {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("GET",
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/image/transformation/list", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 8<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 60 {
                    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry delay exceeds CI budget")
                }
                if d := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; d > delay {
                    delay = d
                }
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if d := time.Until(date); d > delay {
                    delay = d
                }
            }
            if delay > 60*time.Second {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry delay exceeds CI budget")
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("inventory HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("inventory retry budget exhausted")
}

func namesFrom(body []byte, pointer, field string) (map[string]bool, error) {
    var value any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &value); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if pointer != "" {
        if !strings.HasPrefix(pointer, "/") {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("NAMES_POINTER must start with /")
        }
        for _, token := range strings.Split(pointer[1:], "/") {
            token = strings.ReplaceAll(strings.ReplaceAll(token, "~1", "/"), "~0", "~")
            switch node := value.(type) {
            case map[string]any:
                value = node[token]
            case []any:
                index, err := strconv.Atoi(token)
                if err != nil || index < 0 || index >= len(node) {
                    return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid array index in NAMES_POINTER")
                }
                value = node[index]
            default:
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("NAMES_POINTER does not resolve")
            }
        }
    }
    entries, ok := value.([]any)
    if !ok {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("configured inventory value is not an array")
    }
    names := make(map[string]bool)
    for _, entry := range entries {
        if field != "" {
            object, ok := entry.(map[string]any)
            if !ok {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("expected an inventory object")
            }
            entry = object[field]
        }
        name, ok := entry.(string)
        if !ok || strings.TrimSpace(name) == "" {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("expected a nonempty transformation name")
        }
        names[name] = true
    }
    return names, nil
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" || len(os.Args) < 2 {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY and pass required names as arguments")
    }
    body, err := inventory(key)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    existing, err := namesFrom(body, os.Getenv("NAMES_POINTER"), os.Getenv("NAME_FIELD"))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var missing []string
    for _, required := range os.Args[1:] {
        if strings.TrimSpace(required) == "" {
            return fmt.Errorf("required transformation name is empty")
        }
        if !existing[required] {
            missing = append(missing, required)
        }
    }
    if len(missing) > 0 {
        return fmt.Errorf("missing transformations: %s", strings.Join(missing, ", "))
    }
    fmt.Println("all required transformation names exist")
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Make a nonzero exit status block deployment. For a controlled check, require a name you have deliberately omitted from a test environment: the gate should identify it and fail. Then restore the expected inventory and verify the passing path. Those are proposed acceptance checks, not reported production results.

The retry budget is four attempts, with a 20-second HTTP timeout per attempt and a 60-second ceiling on each retry wait. A longer server-requested wait fails this build rather than retrying before the requested time. Review those local policy choices against the pipeline's deadline. The response body limit is 8 MiB; a response that cannot be decoded within that limit fails the check instead of becoming a partial successful inventory.

Where this check stops helping

If an existing transformation changes compression behavior without changing its name, this gate will pass. Output checks must cover that separate risk. If the chosen provider has no persistent named transformations, validate the configuration the integration actually uses instead of forcing it into this abstraction. An inventory read is also a point-in-time observation; coordinate configuration changes with deployments.

For this marketplace, verify the names, validate the rendered assets, and review retained variants against the storage and cache budget. Keep the checks distinct enough that the on-call engineer can tell which requirement failed without reverse-engineering a dashboard. The reversible part is the application naming contract and assertion. The provider adapter and evidence of acceptable output still need review during migration.

Sources

References for checking the format and integration boundaries:

  • MDN, Image file type and format guide
  • Cloudinary, Image transformations
  • Cloudinary, Admin API
  • imgix, Rendering API
  • Cloudflare Images, Variants

If the shared backend boundary fits your marketplace, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Mintu v0.2.3: Building Desktop Automation, Apple-Style Spring Physics, and Safe Evaluators with Tauri & Rust
description:
Introduction

With the release of Mintu v0.2.3, our open-source Dynamic Island desktop companion advances from a passive interface into an active, automated desktop assistant.

Built with Tauri v2, Rust, and TypeScript, Mintu runs locally with offline models (via llama.cpp) or connects to modern cloud providers. This release tackles core user experience pain points, desktop automation, and runtime security.

What We Built in v0.2.3

1. Real Desktop Automation

Users can now delegate OS-level tasks directly to the model:

  • VS Code Code Generation (create_code_file): Instruct the pet to write scripts in Python, TypeScript, Rust, or HTML and immediately launch them in VS Code.
  • Media Integration (play_spotify & search_youtube): Direct playback commands for songs, albums, and video tutorials.
  • Desktop Guidance (desktop_guide): Screen guidance and cursor positioning via native Win32 APIs (SetCursorPos).

2. Solving the Streaming Auto-Scroll Problem

In real-time token streaming interfaces, unconditionally setting scrollTop = scrollHeight traps the user at the bottom of the viewport.

In v0.2.3, we introduced user scroll intent detection:

  • The scroll area tracks upward displacement (distanceFromBottom > 50).
  • If the user scrolls up to inspect previous code snippets or responses, token streaming updates the DOM without dragging the viewport down.
  • When the user scrolls back to the bottom or submits a new message, automatic following resumes.

3. Apple-Inspired Spring Morph on Music Events

Whenever media playback starts or a track changes, the island applies spring physics velocity impulses:

  • springWidth and springHeight expand fluidly before settling into equilibrium.
  • A radial background glow samples the dominant tones of the active track's album cover art.

4. Expanded Model Catalog

  • Local: Qwen 2.5 Coder 1.5B for local code authoring and DeepSeek-R1 Distill Qwen 1.5B for step-by-step reasoning.
  • Cloud: Anthropic Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Google Gemini 2.0 Flash, DeepSeek-R1 Reasoner, and OpenAI o3-mini.
  • Every catalog entry now indicates tool-calling compatibility so users know which models can execute desktop actions.

5. Comprehensive Security Hardening

  • Replaced all legacy new Function math execution with a pure, recursive-descent math parser supporting operators (+, -, *, /, %, ^, **), unary signs, and division-by-zero protection.
  • Hardened file sandboxing to strictly use Rust internal directories.
  • Enabled production Content Security Policy (CSP) blocking external eval.

Open Source & Community

Mintu is free and open-source under the MIT license.

  • GitHub: github.com/HuseynDeveloper/Mintu
  • v0.2.3 Release: github.com/HuseynDeveloper/Mintu/releases/tag/v0.2.3

title: Exploring Global Air Pollution Trends with Python and Pandas
description:
python #datascience #dataanalytics #environment

Air pollution is a major environmental health concern.

I wanted to understand how air quality differs between countries and how pollution levels changed over time.

This led me to build my Global Air Quality Analysis project.

Project Overview

The project explores annual PM2.5 exposure data for 87 countries between 2010 and 2019.

PM2.5 refers to fine particulate matter with a diameter of 2.5 micrometres or less.

The analysis uses data attributed to the World Health Organization's Global Health Observatory, accessed through Our World in Data.

My Analytical Process

The project follows a workflow covering data cleaning, validation, country comparisons, trend analysis and visualisation.

Using Python, Pandas, NumPy and Matplotlib, I explored questions such as:

  • Which countries had the highest reported exposure?
  • How did average exposure change between 2010 and 2019?
  • Which countries showed improvements?
  • How did regional trends differ?

Selected Results

The repository reports the following dataset findings:

Indicator Result
2010 average PM2.5 35.3 µg/m³
2019 average PM2.5 31.7 µg/m³
Highest 2019 value Kuwait, 64.1 µg/m³
Lowest 2019 value Bahamas, 5.2 µg/m³
Largest reported improvement China, −9.0 µg/m³

These figures describe the analysed dataset and its averaging method. They should not automatically be interpreted as population-weighted global exposure estimates.

Understanding the Limitations

One important detail is that the project uses the historical WHO guideline of 10 µg/m³ for annual PM2.5 exposure.

The WHO updated its annual guideline to 5 µg/m³ in 2021.

The dataset also contains modelled national estimates rather than continuous direct measurements from every location.

National averages can hide substantial differences between cities, rural areas and seasons.

What I Learned

This project helped me practise translating environmental datasets into understandable visualisations.

It also highlighted why analytical conclusions need to explain their data sources, time periods and limitations.

Future Work

I would like to explore newer observations, uncertainty intervals and comparisons between urban and rural exposure.

GitHub: https://github.com/tasnem-tech/global-air-quality-analysis

How do you communicate uncertainty when presenting environmental data?
