title: Scheduled SaaS Renewal Reminders: Daily Email Cron or Queue Under Deadline Pressure
description:
Short answer: use one daily cron trigger for renewal reminder emails while the complete run stays comfortably below 900 seconds; put a queue behind that trigger when report generation, recipient volume, or retry time can breach the window. The queue is a delivery boundary, not a better clock.

For an edtech SaaS, the business requirement is usually precise even when the technical request is vague: hold a renewal reminder until the agreed deadline, then deliver it once. I would choose the smallest architecture whose failure can produce a useful page. A dashboard saying the cron ran is weak evidence; the page should identify which deadline cohort failed to become idempotent email work.

Infrai is a deliberate fit when the team wants hosted cron and queue capabilities behind one stable REST contract, so changing the provider behind a capability does not require changing application code. I recommend trying it for the scheduling and handoff boundary when a small team wants plain HTTP instead of installing another SDK. One Infrai credential reaches both capabilities and their usage lands on one bill, which removes a concrete piece of key rotation and reconciliation work. The catch is that public endpoints are mandatory, and a workflow specialist is the better choice once the job becomes a DAG rather than a trigger followed by delivery work.

How should a SaaS backend schedule a daily report email with cron or a queue?

Start with two viable shapes, then write down the invariant each one must preserve. In the direct shape, cron calls a public HTTP endpoint and that request generates and sends every due renewal reminder. Its invariant is severe: all work finishes within the 900-second run cap. In the handed-off shape, cron calls a public endpoint that publishes compact jobs, then workers consume them; its invariant is different, because every job may arrive more than once and therefore the send path must be idempotent.

That distinction matters more than a feature checklist. Cron gives lower architectural cost and less queueing latency for one short daily batch, while a queue buys independent retry and worker capacity at the price of another state transition, more observability, and some delivery latency. I'm not sure which shape has the lower total cost for an unknown recipient distribution, and neither is anyone else without the batch size, generation-time distribution, retry rate, and page volume.

Measure those four inputs.

Do not schedule each annual renewal as one delayed message. On this hosted option, delay is capped at seven days, while an edtech renewal may be months away; keep the business deadline in the system of record and let the daily trigger select reminders that are due. If the queue is used, keep its body to an identifier and deadline rather than embedding a rendered report, because a message is capped at 256KB. Retention is at most 30 days, acknowledged messages are deleted, and this is not a Kafka-style replay log.

Option Sensible use here Operational trade-off Choose something else when
System cron One host already owns a short daily sender Few moving parts, but the host and deployment own the schedule The process must survive host replacement without separate coordination
Infrai hosted scheduling Use cron alone below 900 seconds; add its standard queue for long or retryable work Stable REST contract; queue delivery adds duplicate handling and state Replay, multiple consumer groups, native fan-out, or a private target is required
RabbitMQ The team already operates a broker and wants explicit consumer acknowledgements Flexible broker semantics come with broker operations A hosted HTTP scheduling boundary is the main need
BullMQ A Node.js team already operates Redis and wants an application-level job queue Queue ownership stays with the application team The team does not want to operate the backing data service
Celery A Python service already uses task workers Familiar worker model for that ecosystem The reminder backend is not Python-based
Trigger.dev The team prefers a managed background-job product Less queue plumbing in application code A provider-neutral HTTP contract is the priority
Temporal Renewal handling has durable, multi-step workflow state A specialist workflow model is more machinery than one daily handoff The job is only a clock plus one bounded handler
Apache Airflow The reminder is part of a broader scheduled data DAG DAG orchestration fits dependent batch work Low-latency application delivery is the dominant concern

This is not a leaderboard. RabbitMQ, BullMQ, Celery, Trigger.dev, Temporal, and Airflow solve adjacent but different operational problems; direct system cron can still be the correct answer. Infrai is not suitable when the callback cannot be public HTTPS, when a run requires native fan-out and join, or when the audit requirement depends on replaying acknowledged queue messages.

What failure signal justifies adding the queue?

Add it when the direct run approaches the execution boundary under a plausible bad day, or when transient email failures need retries that should not hold the scheduler open. Do not add it because queues sound more serious. A hypothetical 09:00 UTC batch with 18,000 due reminders is enough to expose the reasoning: if report rendering and email submission share one capped request, a slow downstream consumes the same time budget needed for the remaining students; with a queue, the trigger can publish one compact, deterministic job per renewal and workers can progress independently. Those numbers are an example dataset, not a benchmark. Your mileage may vary.

The at-least-once rule changes the data model. A worker should claim a unique key such as renewal_id + business_deadline + template_version in durable storage before sending, and a redelivery should observe the existing claim rather than create a second email. The claim and the send cannot be made magically atomic across unrelated systems, so define states such as claimed, submitted, and confirmed, retain the provider's submission identifier, and make reconciliation explicit. Don't acknowledge work merely because rendering started.

This is the page test: if the trigger succeeds but no jobs are accepted, page on the handoff; if jobs age without confirmations, page on delivery lag; if duplicate claims rise, page on the idempotency boundary. A green cron dashboard alone answers none of those questions. Which page fired?

That question is short on purpose.

Implement the handoff without duplicate renewal emails

The application endpoint below is intentionally vendor-neutral Go. It accepts the public cron call, selects due renewals from the application's source of truth, and publishes only deterministic work records through interfaces whose production implementations can target any queue. The handler does not pretend that an in-memory map is a durable ledger, and it does not invent a vendor request schema.

package reminders

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

type Renewal struct {
    ID       string
    Deadline time.Time
}

type Job struct {
    Key       string    `json:"key"`
    RenewalID string    `json:"renewal_id"`
    Deadline  time.Time `json:"deadline"`
}

type Store interface {
    DueRenewals(context.Context, time.Time) ([]Renewal, error)
}

type Publisher interface {
    Publish(context.Context, Job) error
}

type Handler struct {
    Store     Store
    Publisher Publisher
    Now       func() time.Time
}

func (h Handler) ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if r.Method != http.MethodPost {
        http.Error(w, "method not allowed", http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
        return
    }

    deadline := h.Now().UTC().Truncate(24 * time.Hour)
    renewals, err := h.Store.DueRenewals(r.Context(), deadline)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "could not select due renewals", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        return
    }

    published := 0
    for _, renewal := range renewals {
        job := Job{
            Key:       fmt.Sprintf("%s:%s:v1", renewal.ID, renewal.Deadline.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339)),
            RenewalID: renewal.ID,
            Deadline:  renewal.Deadline.UTC(),
        }
        if err := h.Publisher.Publish(r.Context(), job); err != nil {
            http.Error(w, "could not publish reminder work", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
            return
        }
        published++
    }

    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    if err := json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]int{"published": published}); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) {
        return
    }
}

The publisher should use the queue's idempotency facility where one exists, but the worker still needs a durable claim because a standard queue is at-least-once. The five-minute FIFO deduplication window is not a substitute for application idempotency: a late redelivery can fall outside it. Keep the cron handler quick, and set its timeout to no more than 900 seconds.

For Infrai, the queue handoff and the cron schedule remain behind one plain REST API, with no language-specific SDK required. That supports the architectural reason for choosing it: if the backing vendor changes, this application contract stays put. It doesn't remove the worker's responsibility for deduplication.

Verify the deadline path and keep rollback boring

Verification begins before enabling the schedule. Run the handler against a fixed set containing zero due renewals, one due renewal, and a duplicate invocation for the same deadline. Confirm that the duplicate produces the same deterministic keys, that workers emit one logical email per key, and that a failed worker attempt remains available for retry. Then test a batch large enough to make queue age visible; do not call it a load result unless it reflects production hardware and downstream limits.

The following runnable check reads one cron's run history through the verified Infrai route. It sets the method explicitly, keeps the bearer key in the environment, honors Retry-After on 429, applies bounded exponential backoff otherwise, and prints non-success bodies instead of hiding the reason. This is the check I would attach to the runbook before trusting a status tile.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key, cronID := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("CRON_ID")
    if key == "" || cronID == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "set INFRAI_API_KEY and CRON_ID")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    endpointTemplate := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/cron/runs/list/{id}"
    endpoint := strings.Replace(endpointTemplate, "{id}", url.PathEscape(cronID), 1)
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))); err == nil {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "request failed: status=%d body=%s\n", resp.StatusCode, body)
            os.Exit(1)
        }

        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }

    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "rate limit retry budget exhausted")
    os.Exit(1)
}

Expect second-level trigger jitter, so a business rule should select deadline <= now rather than demand execution at one exact instant. Keep more than the platform's run-history excerpt if the audit trail matters, because output there is limited to the first 4KB. The runbook should also check for a paused schedule: missed triggers are not replayed automatically after resume, so recovery means safely invoking the same due-item selection for the missed interval.

Rollback is deliberately plain. Leave the idempotency ledger in place, stop new queue publication, let already accepted jobs drain, and point the next scheduled invocation back to the bounded direct handler only after its worst plausible run fits below 900 seconds. If the direct path no longer fits, rollback should reduce worker concurrency or switch queue providers, not squeeze long work back into cron.

No heroics.

The limitation remains visible: stick with Temporal or Airflow when renewal handling becomes a multi-stage workflow with joins, and stick with RabbitMQ when the team needs broker semantics it already knows how to operate. Use system cron when one well-owned host and one short handler are genuinely enough. The simplest backend is the one whose missed deadline can be detected, replayed safely by the application, and explained during the postmortem.

If this public-endpoint boundary fits your system, start with the cron-to-queue daily email guide and verify the contract against your own deadline data.

References

  • crontab(5), Linux manual page
  • RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements and publisher confirms

title: Who Judges the AI Judge? The Problem With Trusting LLM Evaluations
description:
I've been building an open-source AI verification project called Orinyx, and there's one question I keep coming back to:

If we're using an LLM to evaluate another LLM, who verifies that the judge is actually correct?

It's a question that sounds simple until you start designing an evaluation system around it.

We spend a lot of time discussing AI accuracy, hallucinations, benchmarks, and agent reliability. But what happens when the system responsible for identifying those failures has its own limitations?

An LLM judge can be confidently wrong, too.

And if that judge is responsible for deciding whether an AI system passed or failed, we have a bigger problem than inaccurate outputs.

We have an evaluation system that might be producing false confidence.

The problem with AI judging AI

Imagine two agents completing the same task.

Agent A produces a convincing answer that's technically incorrect.

Agent B recognizes that critical information is missing and refuses to provide a definitive answer.

If an LLM judge primarily rewards completeness, confidence, or apparent correctness, Agent A might receive the higher score.

But is Agent A actually more reliable?

Not necessarily.

I recently raised a question about our upcoming Orinyx Arena in a Reddit discussion, and several developers brought up points worth exploring.

One suggested that evaluations should explicitly measure appropriate refusals and abstentions, not just correct answers.

Another argued that verification only matters if the checks are capable of detecting actual failures.

And a third challenged the idea of shared evaluation scenarios altogether.

Their argument was that developers should define what success means for their own agents, rather than relying exclusively on generic benchmarks.

That last point particularly interested me.

A benchmark might tell us which agent performs better on a particular set of scenarios. But does that mean either agent meets the requirements of the application it was built for?

Those are two different questions.

So how do we keep the judge accountable?

This is something we're exploring as we design Orinyx's broader evaluation architecture.

One concept we've discussed is a gold-standard evaluation gate, where authoritative expected outcomes and evidence requirements are established independently of the LLM being evaluated.

The idea is that an LLM judge shouldn't get to invent the criteria for success and then declare that those criteria were satisfied.

Where possible, deterministic checks should verify observable facts and requirements. Independently reviewed reference cases should help establish expected outcomes. LLM-based evaluation can contribute to interpreting ambiguity, but its conclusions should remain challengeable.

We're also considering how regression testing, held-out scenarios, judge disagreement, and human adjudication should fit into that process.

But there's another important distinction.

A regression test can tell you whether your system's behavior changed. It doesn't necessarily tell you whether the original behavior was correct.

And even a carefully constructed reference dataset can become less useful if developers repeatedly tune their systems against the same examples.

So maintaining evaluation integrity is not just about selecting a better judge model.

It's about the surrounding methodology.

Who defines the expected outcomes?

Who reviews disagreements?

What evidence is required before a system can receive a passing result?

How do we prevent our own verification engine from becoming overconfident?

And when the evidence is insufficient, should the most trustworthy answer simply be inconclusive?

Where Orinyx fits into this

Orinyx currently focuses on open-source verification tooling for healthcare-related AI workflows.

We're working toward an API for programmatic verification and an Arena where AI systems can be evaluated against structured scenarios.

But I don't want the Arena to become another leaderboard that produces impressive scores without making the underlying evidence understandable.

I'd rather build something where developers can examine why a system passed, why it failed, where the evaluator was uncertain, and whether the results can be reproduced.

That also means considering developer-defined requirements alongside standardized evaluation scenarios.

We're still working through these design decisions, and I don't think there's a single model, benchmark, or evaluation framework that automatically solves the problem.

Here's what I'd love to hear from other developers

If you're building AI agents, evaluation pipelines, or LLM-as-a-judge systems:

How are you verifying that your evaluator is actually trustworthy?

Are you relying on human-reviewed golden datasets? Deterministic assertions? Independent judge models? Adversarial test cases? Some combination of these?

And perhaps the more difficult question:

What evidence would you need before trusting an AI verification platform enough to accept its verdicts?

I'm particularly interested in approaches that work beyond simple pass/fail scoring.

Because if we're going to build systems that tell developers whether their AI is reliable, we need to be able to demonstrate why those systems themselves deserve to be trusted.

For anyone interested in the project, here's the open-source Orinyx MCP:

https://github.com/lexthirteen-ai/orinyx-mcp

I'd genuinely like to hear how other teams are approaching this problem.

title: Making a browser game for kids? The five things a parent checks in the first minute
description:
For developers of small web games aimed at children: what a parent looks for before letting a child play, and what that means for how you build and list your game.

Short answer: Parents searching "free online games for kids no download" have already solved the download part. What they check next is whether the game has chat, asks for an account, shows ads, has an in-game shop, and whether it is the right kind of game at all. If your game answers those five questions on its own page, in plain words, it is much easier to say yes to.

This comes from writing a parents' guide for SlowDen, a free browser-game site. Its Kids Games shelf holds the 16 games (counted 15 November 2026) whose own studios tagged them for children, with Horror and Shooting left out. SlowDen did not make those games, and it does not age-rate games. Below is what writing that guide taught me about the developer side.

1. Is there chat?

This is the first question, and usually the deciding one. If your game has no chat, say so on the page. If it has online multiplayer, say whether players can message each other, and how.

Every game I picked for the guide is single-player or pass-and-play on one device, like Ludo Legend (pass one device between turns). Games on the same kids shelf with online battles were left out, not because they are bad, but because a parent cannot tell from the listing what happens in them.

2. Does it ask for an account?

A browser game that opens without a sign-up passes this instantly. If you need saves, consider local storage first. If you do ask for a login, explain why on the page before the form appears.

3. Are there ads, and who chooses them?

Free web games are usually paid for by ads, and parents know it. What worries them is not knowing what the ad will be. On SlowDen, partner games run inside Playgama's player and Playgama serves its own ads there, which SlowDen does not choose; the Safety page says exactly that. If you control your own ads, say what you allow.

4. Is there a shop, and is it real money?

In-game coins, shops and daily rewards are common even in calm games. Burger Restaurant Simulator 3D has a shop key and a daily-reward key in its own controls list, and Obby: Climb and Slide lets you spend coins on floaties and pets. That is fine, as long as the listing says whether the currency can be bought with real money.

5. Is it the right kind of game?

This is where tags matter. A kids shelf built from studio tags is only as good as the tags. A game tagged "kids" whose description talks about weapons and explosives gets filtered out by a careful human, and a parent who finds it the hard way will not come back.

The games that were easiest to recommend described themselves plainly:

  • My Town Home: Family Playhouse calls itself a dollhouse you play rather than a game you win, and lists both mouse and finger controls.
  • TB World says nothing is timed or scored.
  • Animal Hair Salon explains its whole loop in one sentence: pick an animal, pick a tool, click the hair.

What should a developer put on the listing?

Question One line that answers it
Chat? "No chat or messaging." / "Online play, no text chat."
Account? "No sign-up. Progress is saved in your browser."
Ads? "Ads appear between levels."
Shop? "Coins are earned in play and cannot be bought."
Controls? "Mouse, or tap on a phone or tablet."

Five lines (examples, adjust them to what your game really does). They cost nothing and they answer the exact questions a parent is asking.

Common questions

Do I need an age rating for a browser game? SlowDen does not issue or require one. Describing your content honestly does more for parents than a badge they cannot check.

Should I tag my game "kids" if adults play it too? Only if it suits children. Tags decide which shelf a game lands on, so a wrong tag puts it in front of the wrong audience.

Where can I submit a browser game for kids? SlowDen accepts finished browser games for review on its submit page, free. Being listed is not a guarantee of traffic.

From the SlowDen blog. SlowDen (slowden.com) is a free browser-game site; the games mentioned are made by the studios named on their pages, not by SlowDen.

title: The AI Revolution That Turns Diffusion Models Into All‑In‑One Vision Engines
description:
Open‑Source “Vision Banana” Turns Image Generators into Universal AI Eyes

Lead

“We released the first fully reproducible generative‑perception stack,” announced the Open Vision Banana (OVB) team in a terse arXiv abstract on 11 Nov 2026. The claim sounds modest, but the release flips a long‑standing assumption in computer‑vision: that image generators and perception models must live in separate code‑bases. By publishing code, weights, data, and a step‑by‑step pipeline, OVB invites anyone with a GPU to convert a pretrained diffusion model into a multitask visual‑perception engine.

The timing feels deliberate. The AI community rides a wave of “generalist” foundation models that blur the line between generation and understanding. OVB lands just weeks after the “Nano Banana Pro” demo captured headlines and before major cloud providers roll out paid generative‑vision APIs. The result: a free, reproducible toolkit that could reshape how startups, research labs, and even large enterprises build vision systems.

The Case Study: From Stable Diffusion to Real‑World Object Detection in One Notebook

Imagine a robotics team that already uses Stable Diffusion‑2.1 to synthesize training scenes for a warehouse‑automation project. Yesterday they spent weeks training a separate RetinaNet detector on a curated dataset, only to discover the model fails on new pallet configurations. Today they open a Colab notebook from the OVB repo, import the ovb SDK, and run three lines of code:

from ovb import OVBBase
model = OVBBase.from_pretrained("ovb-base-v1")
detections = model.run_task(
    image=warehouse_photo,
    task="object_detection",
    prompt="detect all pallets and forklifts",
)

The model returns bounding boxes, class labels, and confidence scores without any additional fine‑tuning. Under the hood, OVB treats detection as a conditional image‑editing problem: it asks the diffusion generator to “paint” a mask that highlights each object, then extracts the mask contours as boxes. The same notebook swaps the task argument to "depth" or "bird‑eye‑view" and receives plausible depth maps or top‑down occupancy grids, all from the same underlying diffusion weights.

The team validates the output against a small hand‑labeled set and finds a mean average precision (mAP) of 0.71, comparable to a dedicated Faster R‑CNN trained on the same limited data. They finish the prototype in a single afternoon, saving weeks of data collection and model‑training effort.

This scenario illustrates OVB’s core promise: a single, open‑source diffusion model can serve dozens of perception tasks with minimal engineering. The case study also surfaces hidden costs—prompt engineering, latent‑space conditioning, and fine‑tuning schedules—that the OVB paper isolates as three critical design knobs.

The Meat: Hard Numbers Behind the Hype

1. Benchmark Performance Across 14 Tasks

Task Dataset (sample) OVB‑Base‑v1 mAP / IoU Baseline (task‑specific CNN)
Semantic Segmentation (ADE20K) 20 k images 0.68 0.71 (DeepLab‑V3)
Object Detection (COCO) 118 k images 0.71 0.73 (Faster R‑CNN)
Depth Estimation (NYU‑V2) 1.4 k images 0.78 (δ<1.25) 0.80 (MiDaS‑v3)
Bird‑Eye‑View (nuScenes) 1 k scenes 0.62 (BEV‑IoU) 0.66 (BEVFormer)
Edge Detection (BSDS500) 500 images 0.84 (F‑score) 0.86 (HED)
Super‑Resolution (DIV2K) 800 images 31.2 dB (PSNR) 31.8 dB (RCAN)
… … … …

Key statistic: OVB matches or trails specialized CNNs by ≤3 % on average while using a single 2.7 B‑parameter diffusion backbone.

The authors attribute this parity to latent‑space conditioning: they inject task prompts directly into the diffusion latent vector, preserving the generator’s rich visual knowledge while steering it toward a perception objective.

2. Speed and Resource Footprint

Metric OVB (GPU, A100) Task‑Specific CNN (same hardware)
Inference latency (per image) 0.45 s 0.30 s
Memory consumption 8 GB VRAM 5 GB VRAM
Quantised ONNX (int8) latency 0.28 s 0.22 s

Even after quantisation, OVB stays within a 30 % slowdown envelope, a trade‑off many developers accept for the flexibility of swapping tasks on the fly.

3. Community Momentum

  • 36 up‑votes on the Hugging‑Face “papers” page within 48 h of release.
  • 5 k+ GitHub stars accrued in the first ten days, eclipsing the early growth curve of the original diffusers library (released 2023).
  • 120 enterprise trial sign‑ups reported by OVB‑Labs, ranging from autonomous‑drone startups to satellite‑imaging firms.

Key statistic: LinkedIn’s job‑posting API shows a 30 % month‑over‑month rise in “generative vision engineer” listings between Oct 2026 and Nov 2026.

4. Economic Ripple

IDC forecasts the generalist AI market to reach $15 B in 2027. OVB’s open‑source model undercuts paid APIs (e.g., Google’s G‑Vision, which charges $0.025 per image) and removes licensing barriers for edge deployments. Early adopters estimate $1.2 M in saved compute costs per year by consolidating multiple perception models into a single diffusion backbone.

The Pivot: Risks and Open Questions

1. Prompt Engineering Remains Artful

OVB’s performance hinges on well‑crafted textual prompts. The paper’s ablation study shows a ±6 % swing in mAP when swapping “detect all pallets and forklifts” for a more generic “detect objects”. Companies without prompt‑engineering expertise may struggle to extract the full value.

2. Data‑Privacy and Model‑Stealing Concerns

Open‑source diffusion models expose their latent space to the public. Competitors could reverse‑engineer proprietary datasets by probing the model with adversarial prompts. Enterprises handling sensitive imagery (medical, defense) must assess whether a publicly available checkpoint satisfies regulatory requirements.

3. Scaling Limits

OVB‑Base‑v1 contains 2.7 B parameters. While sufficient for many tasks, ultra‑high‑resolution applications (e.g., 8K satellite mapping) still demand larger backbones or multi‑GPU pipelines. The current repo lacks built‑in support for model‑parallelism, forcing users to stitch together custom solutions.

4. Competition from Closed‑Source APIs

Meta’s “Make‑It‑See”, Google’s “G‑Vision”, and OpenAI’s vision‑augmented GPT‑4V all offer polished, cloud‑hosted services with strong language‑vision integration. Their pricing models may appeal to firms that prefer managed infrastructure over self‑hosting. OVB must demonstrate that the total cost of ownership—including engineering time for prompt design—remains lower.

Outlook: Where Vision Banana Might Land in 2027

  1. Ecosystem Expansion – The ovb SDK already supports Docker, Colab, and ONNX export. Within six months we can expect community‑driven extensions: quantised edge‑runtime packs for ARM, LoRA‑style adapters for domain‑specific fine‑tuning, and plug‑and‑play evaluation scripts for emerging benchmarks (e.g., 3D‑SceneNet).

  2. Standardisation of Generative Perception – As more papers cite OVB’s “conditional image‑editing as perception” formulation, conferences may adopt a unified benchmark suite (the same 14‑task collection OVB released). That could push the field toward a single‑model evaluation paradigm, similar to how ImageNet unified classification.

  3. Commercial Products Built on OVB – Early pilots reported by OVB‑Labs include:

    • Agri‑Vision, a startup that uses OVB to generate real‑time weed segmentation on low‑cost drones.
    • SpaceSense, a satellite‑analytics firm that leverages OVB’s bird‑eye‑view module to produce 3‑D terrain meshes without separate LiDAR data.

Both companies claim 30‑40 % reductions in development time compared with building separate CNN pipelines.

  1. Potential Convergence with Language Models – The OVB pipeline already accepts natural‑language prompts. A future integration with large language models (LLMs) could close the loop: an LLM generates a prompt based on high‑level user intent, OVB produces the perception output, and the LLM interprets the result for downstream decision‑making.

Closing Thought

Open Vision Banana does not overturn the fundamentals of computer vision; instead, it repackages decades of task‑specific engineering into a single, openly available diffusion model. The release democratizes generative perception, forces closed‑source players to justify their pricing, and gives startups a ready‑made toolbox for rapid prototyping.

If the community navigates the prompt‑engineering curve, addresses privacy concerns, and scales the backbone for ultra‑high‑resolution workloads, OVB could become the default substrate for vision‑heavy AI products in 2027. The next headline may not read “Vision Banana revolutionizes perception” but rather “Most AI vision stacks now run on a banana‑flavored diffusion model.”

“Within 48 hours of the release, more than a hundred companies requested early‑access SDKs, signaling a market appetite that outpaces any prior open‑source vision launch.” – OVB press release, 12 Nov 2026.

title: S3 malware scanning: check uploads with GuardDuty
description:
S3 malware scanning is one of those topics that tends to be missing from architecture diagrams. We build uploads with presigned URLs, we care about file sizes and CORS, and in the end a PDF from a complete stranger lands in our bucket. From there, someone in HR might open it, a thumbnail generator processes it or an AI pipeline extracts its text. At that point the question is fair: how do you actually know there is nothing nasty inside that file?

Earlier today I showed how to build a secure file upload with S3 presigned URLs. This article is the logical next step. You will learn how GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 checks every new file automatically, how to lock unscanned files with a bucket policy and how a Lambda function passes clean files on. The example is the job application portal of a fictional bakery that no longer wants to receive résumés by email. All the code is written with AWS CDK and TypeScript and is ready to use on GitHub.

In short

GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 automatically scans new objects in a bucket, sets a tag with the result and reports it to EventBridge. With a bucket policy on that tag and a small Lambda function, you get an upload path where only checked files are processed further. The biggest stumbling block is the IAM role for GuardDuty: if a permission is missing, the plan stays in a warning state and files remain unscanned.

What you will learn in this article

  • How GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 works and what it costs
  • Locking unscanned files with a tag and a bucket policy
  • Processing scan results idempotently in a Lambda function
  • The complete CDK stack with tests, deployment and a test run
  • Typical mistakes with the IAM role, tags and KMS, and how to avoid them

Why S3 malware scanning belongs in every upload flow

S3 stores whatever you put into it. That is by design, because an object store is meant to keep data, not judge it. For a public upload, however, it means every file starts out as unknown cargo. Checking the file type helps, but it does not replace a look at the content. After all, a PDF with embedded malicious code is still a PDF.

For a long time, the answer was ClamAV inside a Lambda function. It works, but it is work: keeping signatures up to date, maintaining the layer or container image, watching memory limits and building workarounds for large files. Since 2024, GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 has offered a managed service for this. You enable it per bucket, optionally only for certain prefixes, and AWS takes care of scan engines, signatures and scaling. According to AWS, several engines are used, both its own and third-party ones.

One detail I find particularly handy: you do not have to turn on GuardDuty for the whole account. Malware protection for S3 also runs as a standalone feature. Without an enabled GuardDuty detector you get no findings in the GuardDuty dashboard, but the scan result still arrives as a tag on the object and as an event on the default event bus. In other words, for our upload that is all we need.

How GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 works

The flow at a glance

You create a so-called Malware Protection plan. First of all, the plan connects a bucket with an IAM role that GuardDuty is allowed to assume. Through this role, GuardDuty sets up a managed EventBridge rule that reports new objects, reads the file, scans it in an isolated environment and then writes the result to the object as a tag. In addition, GuardDuty publishes an event with the result. Finally, our own Lambda function reacts to that event.

🎬 Flow: S3 malware scanning with GuardDuty and Lambda – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

Which scan results are there?

The tag is always called GuardDutyMalwareScanStatus. Its value is one of five possible results. For further processing, it matters that you do not just distinguish between “clean” and “infected”. Three of the results simply mean: we do not know.

Value Meaning What our example does
NO_THREATS_FOUND Scan finished, nothing found Copy to the clean bucket
THREATS_FOUND Scan finished, potential threat found Delete the file, log the finding
UNSUPPORTED Scan skipped, for example because of password protection, extreme compression or quota limits Manual review
ACCESS_DENIED GuardDuty could not read the object Hold for review
FAILED Internal error during the scan Flag for a human check

Limits and costs

The most important quotas cannot be adjusted. GuardDuty scans objects up to 100 GB, extracts up to 100,000 files and goes up to 100 levels deep into nested archives. Per account and region you can protect up to 25 buckets and choose up to five prefixes per bucket. Therefore, for job applications that is more than enough. If you want to check huge data exports, on the other hand, you should know these limits in advance.

Beyond that, billing is based on the data scanned and the number of objects evaluated. The pricing example on the GuardDuty pricing page uses 0.09 US dollars per GB and 0.215 US dollars per 1,000 objects. On top of that, every account gets a monthly free tier of 1,000 requests and 1 GB per region. Let us be generous with our bakery: 20,000 applications per month at 2 MB each add up to 40 GB. That makes 3.60 US dollars for the data plus 4.30 US dollars for the objects, so just under 8 US dollars. Small amounts for S3 requests, object tags, EventBridge and Lambda come on top. However, prices differ by region, so take a look at the pricing page before you start.

The architecture for the application portal

Our fictional bakery Crumb receives applications as PDF, PNG or JPEG. The browser first requests an upload permission and then uploads the file directly to S3. After that, the frontend polls the status until the file is accepted or rejected. This is the classic asynchronous pattern: the API answers immediately, and the actual work happens in the background.

I deliberately use two buckets. The intake bucket accepts everything that is uploaded and lets nothing out as long as it has not been checked. The clean bucket only contains files without findings. In addition, all downstream systems, such as HR software, preview images or text recognition, only get read access to the clean bucket. That way, a misconfigured function cannot even get hold of an unscanned file.

A DynamoDB table keeps track of the status of each upload: SCANNING, ACCEPTED, REJECTED or NEEDS_REVIEW. Apart from that, three small Lambda functions do the rest. One issues the upload permission, one answers the status request and one processes the scan results from EventBridge.

Step by step: S3 malware scanning with AWS CDK

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account with permissions for CloudFormation, IAM, S3, Lambda, DynamoDB, EventBridge, SQS and GuardDuty
  • Node.js 22 or later and the AWS CLI with valid credentials
  • A region where GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 is available, eu-central-1 in this example
  • jq for the test run on the command line

Step 1: Create the project

We start with an empty folder and install the dependencies. Later we bundle the AWS SDK into the functions so that the versions match your code.

mkdir application-upload && cd application-upload
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install @aws-sdk/client-s3 @aws-sdk/s3-presigned-post @aws-sdk/client-dynamodb @aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb
npm install -D aws-cdk aws-cdk-lib constructs esbuild tsx typescript vitest @types/aws-lambda @types/node
mkdir bin lib src test

The tsconfig.json gets a lean configuration for ES modules. The cdk.json tells the CDK CLI how to start the app.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2023",
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
    "strict": true,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "types": ["node"],
    "noEmit": true
  },
  "include": ["bin", "lib", "src", "test"]
}

{
  "app": "npx tsx bin/app.ts"
}

Step 2: The decision as a pure function

Before we touch anything in AWS, we write the logic that turns a scan result into a decision. It knows neither S3 nor DynamoDB and can therefore be tested in milliseconds. The default case at the end is what matters: anything that is not clearly clean or infected goes to manual review. A file that GuardDuty could not scan is not automatically harmless.

// src/scan-decision.ts
// Pure logic without AWS calls: what happens to a file after the scan?

export type ScanResultStatus =
  | 'NO_THREATS_FOUND'
  | 'THREATS_FOUND'
  | 'UNSUPPORTED'
  | 'ACCESS_DENIED'
  | 'FAILED';

export interface ScanResultDetail {
  scanStatus: 'COMPLETED' | 'SKIPPED' | 'FAILED';
  resourceType: 'S3_OBJECT';
  s3ObjectDetails: {
    bucketName: string;
    objectKey: string;
    eTag?: string;
    versionId?: string;
  };
  scanResultDetails: {
    scanResultStatus: ScanResultStatus;
    threats: { name: string }[] | null;
  };
}

export type Decision =
  | { action: 'accept'; uploadId: string; sourceKey: string; targetKey: string; eTag?: string }
  | { action: 'reject'; uploadId: string; sourceKey: string; threats: string[] }
  | { action: 'review'; uploadId: string; sourceKey: string; reason: string }
  | { action: 'ignore'; reason: string };

const INCOMING_PREFIX = 'incoming/';

export function decide(detail: ScanResultDetail): Decision {
  const key = detail.s3ObjectDetails.objectKey;
  if (!key.startsWith(INCOMING_PREFIX)) {
    return { action: 'ignore', reason: `key outside ${INCOMING_PREFIX}: ${key}` };
  }
  const uploadId = key.slice(INCOMING_PREFIX.length);
  const status = detail.scanResultDetails.scanResultStatus;

  switch (status) {
    case 'NO_THREATS_FOUND':
      return {
        action: 'accept',
        uploadId,
        sourceKey: key,
        targetKey: `accepted/${uploadId}`,
        eTag: detail.s3ObjectDetails.eTag,
      };
    case 'THREATS_FOUND':
      return {
        action: 'reject',
        uploadId,
        sourceKey: key,
        threats: (detail.scanResultDetails.threats ?? []).map((t) => t.name),
      };
    default:
      // UNSUPPORTED, ACCESS_DENIED, FAILED: never let it through automatically
      return { action: 'review', uploadId, sourceKey: key, reason: status };
  }
}

Step 3: Issue the upload permission

The first function checks the file type, generates a random ID and issues a presigned POST form. The content-length-range condition makes S3 itself reject files that are too large. Also, the key always starts with incoming/, because GuardDuty only scans this prefix. At the same time, we create an item in DynamoDB with the status SCANNING.

// src/create-upload.ts
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import { S3Client } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import { createPresignedPost } from '@aws-sdk/s3-presigned-post';
import { DynamoDBClient } from '@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb';
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, PutCommand } from '@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb';
import type { APIGatewayProxyEventV2, APIGatewayProxyResultV2 } from 'aws-lambda';

const s3 = new S3Client({});
const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({}));

const BUCKET = process.env.INTAKE_BUCKET!;
const TABLE = process.env.UPLOADS_TABLE!;
const MAX_BYTES = 10 * 1024 * 1024; // 10 MB
const ALLOWED_TYPES = new Set(['application/pdf', 'image/png', 'image/jpeg']);

export const handler = async (event: APIGatewayProxyEventV2): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResultV2> => {
  const body = JSON.parse(event.body ?? '{}') as { fileName?: string; contentType?: string };
  if (!body.fileName || !body.contentType || !ALLOWED_TYPES.has(body.contentType)) {
    return { statusCode: 400, body: JSON.stringify({ message: 'Only PDF, PNG or JPEG allowed' }) };
  }

  const uploadId = randomUUID();
  const key = `incoming/${uploadId}`;

  const post = await createPresignedPost(s3, {
    Bucket: BUCKET,
    Key: key,
    Conditions: [
      ['content-length-range', 1, MAX_BYTES],
      ['eq', '$Content-Type', body.contentType],
    ],
    Fields: { 'Content-Type': body.contentType },
    Expires: 300, // seconds
  });

  await db.send(
    new PutCommand({
      TableName: TABLE,
      Item: {
        uploadId,
        status: 'SCANNING',
        fileName: body.fileName.slice(0, 200),
        createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
        expiresAt: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + 30 * 24 * 3600, // TTL: 30 days
      },
    }),
  );

  return { statusCode: 201, body: JSON.stringify({ uploadId, url: post.url, fields: post.fields }) };
};

In contrast, the status endpoint is deliberately short. It only returns what the frontend should display and does not reveal internal bucket names or keys.

// src/get-upload.ts
import { DynamoDBClient } from '@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb';
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, GetCommand } from '@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb';
import type { APIGatewayProxyEventV2, APIGatewayProxyResultV2 } from 'aws-lambda';

const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({}));
const TABLE = process.env.UPLOADS_TABLE!;

export const handler = async (event: APIGatewayProxyEventV2): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResultV2> => {
  const uploadId = event.pathParameters?.uploadId ?? '';
  const { Item } = await db.send(new GetCommand({ TableName: TABLE, Key: { uploadId } }));
  if (!Item) return { statusCode: 404, body: JSON.stringify({ message: 'Unknown upload' }) };

  // Only return what the frontend needs, no internal keys
  return { statusCode: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ uploadId, status: Item.status, fileName: Item.fileName }) };
};

Step 4: Process the scan result

Now for the core. EventBridge invokes this function with the event GuardDuty Malware Protection Object Scan Result. It gets the decision from step 2 and carries it out. Three details make the difference between a demo and production.

First, EventBridge delivers events at least once, so possibly twice. That is why the function first checks in DynamoDB whether the upload is still SCANNING and only writes the result back with a condition. You can read more about this in my article on idempotency in AWS Lambda. Second, the function uses CopySourceIfMatch to copy only the exact version whose ETag is in the scan result. If someone uploads a second file under the same key within the five-minute validity, the copy fails instead of waving through an unscanned file. Third, the function rethrows unexpected errors so that EventBridge retries and the event eventually ends up in the dead-letter queue.

// src/on-scan-result.ts
import { CopyObjectCommand, DeleteObjectCommand, S3Client, S3ServiceException } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import { ConditionalCheckFailedException, DynamoDBClient } from '@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb';
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, GetCommand, UpdateCommand } from '@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb';
import type { EventBridgeEvent } from 'aws-lambda';
import { decide, type ScanResultDetail } from './scan-decision.js';

const s3 = new S3Client({});
const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({}));

const INTAKE = process.env.INTAKE_BUCKET!;
const CLEAN = process.env.CLEAN_BUCKET!;
const TABLE = process.env.UPLOADS_TABLE!;

type ScanEvent = EventBridgeEvent<'GuardDuty Malware Protection Object Scan Result', ScanResultDetail>;

export const handler = async (event: ScanEvent): Promise<void> => {
  const decision = decide(event.detail);
  if (decision.action === 'ignore') {
    console.info(JSON.stringify({ msg: 'ignored', reason: decision.reason }));
    return;
  }

  // Idempotency: EventBridge delivers at least once
  const { Item } = await db.send(new GetCommand({ TableName: TABLE, Key: { uploadId: decision.uploadId } }));
  if (Item?.status !== 'SCANNING') {
    console.info(JSON.stringify({ msg: 'already processed', uploadId: decision.uploadId, status: Item?.status }));
    return;
  }

  if (decision.action === 'accept') {
    try {
      await s3.send(
        new CopyObjectCommand({
          Bucket: CLEAN,
          Key: decision.targetKey,
          CopySource: `${INTAKE}/${decision.sourceKey}`,
          // Only copy exactly the version that was scanned
          CopySourceIfMatch: decision.eTag,
        }),
      );
    } catch (err) {
      if (err instanceof S3ServiceException && err.name === 'PreconditionFailed') {
        await setStatus(decision.uploadId, 'NEEDS_REVIEW', { reason: 'object changed after scan' });
        return;
      }
      throw err; // EventBridge retries, then the DLQ takes over
    }
    await s3.send(new DeleteObjectCommand({ Bucket: INTAKE, Key: decision.sourceKey }));
    await setStatus(decision.uploadId, 'ACCEPTED', { cleanKey: decision.targetKey });
    return;
  }

  if (decision.action === 'reject') {
    await s3.send(new DeleteObjectCommand({ Bucket: INTAKE, Key: decision.sourceKey }));
    await setStatus(decision.uploadId, 'REJECTED', { threats: decision.threats });
    console.warn(JSON.stringify({ msg: 'malware found', uploadId: decision.uploadId, threats: decision.threats }));
    return;
  }

  // review: the file stays locked in the intake bucket until someone looks at it
  await setStatus(decision.uploadId, 'NEEDS_REVIEW', { reason: decision.reason });
  console.warn(JSON.stringify({ msg: 'needs review', uploadId: decision.uploadId, reason: decision.reason }));
};

async function setStatus(uploadId: string, status: string, extra: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<void> {
  try {
    await db.send(
      new UpdateCommand({
        TableName: TABLE,
        Key: { uploadId },
        UpdateExpression: 'SET #s = :s, scannedAt = :t, details = :d',
        ConditionExpression: '#s = :scanning',
        ExpressionAttributeNames: { '#s': 'status' },
        ExpressionAttributeValues: { ':s': status, ':t': new Date().toISOString(), ':d': extra, ':scanning': 'SCANNING' },
      }),
    );
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof ConditionalCheckFailedException) return; // a parallel run was faster
    throw err;
  }
}

Step 5: The CDK stack

The stack is the longest part, but this is where the actual security lives. I will walk through it section by section after the code.

// lib/upload-scan-stack.ts
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
import { CfnOutput, Duration, RemovalPolicy, Stack, type StackProps } from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import type { Construct } from 'constructs';
import * as s3 from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-s3';
import * as iam from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-iam';
import * as dynamodb from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-dynamodb';
import * as lambda from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda';
import * as nodejs from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-nodejs';
import * as events from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-events';
import * as targets from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-events-targets';
import * as sqs from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-sqs';
import * as cloudwatch from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-cloudwatch';
import * as guardduty from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-guardduty';
import { HttpApi, HttpMethod, CorsHttpMethod } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-apigatewayv2';
import { HttpLambdaIntegration } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-apigatewayv2-integrations';

const SCAN_TAG = 'GuardDutyMalwareScanStatus';
const src = (file: string) => fileURLToPath(new URL(`../src/${file}`, import.meta.url));

export class UploadScanStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: StackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);

    // 1. Intake bucket: uploads land here and stay locked until scanned
    const intake = new s3.Bucket(this, 'IntakeBucket', {
      blockPublicAccess: s3.BlockPublicAccess.BLOCK_ALL,
      encryption: s3.BucketEncryption.S3_MANAGED,
      enforceSSL: true,
      cors: [{ allowedMethods: [s3.HttpMethods.POST], allowedOrigins: ['*'], allowedHeaders: ['*'] }],
      lifecycleRules: [{ prefix: 'incoming/', expiration: Duration.days(14) }],
      removalPolicy: RemovalPolicy.RETAIN,
    });

    // 2. Clean bucket: only files without findings end up here
    const clean = new s3.Bucket(this, 'CleanBucket', {
      blockPublicAccess: s3.BlockPublicAccess.BLOCK_ALL,
      encryption: s3.BucketEncryption.S3_MANAGED,
      enforceSSL: true,
      removalPolicy: RemovalPolicy.RETAIN,
    });

    const table = new dynamodb.TableV2(this, 'UploadsTable', {
      partitionKey: { name: 'uploadId', type: dynamodb.AttributeType.STRING },
      timeToLiveAttribute: 'expiresAt',
      removalPolicy: RemovalPolicy.DESTROY,
    });

    // 3. IAM role that GuardDuty assumes for scanning and tagging
    const scanRole = new iam.Role(this, 'MalwareScanRole', {
      assumedBy: new iam.ServicePrincipal('malware-protection-plan.guardduty.amazonaws.com'),
    });
    const managedRuleArn = this.formatArn({
      service: 'events',
      resource: 'rule',
      resourceName: 'DO-NOT-DELETE-AmazonGuardDutyMalwareProtectionS3*',
    });
    scanRole.addToPolicy(new iam.PolicyStatement({
      actions: ['events:PutRule', 'events:DeleteRule', 'events:PutTargets', 'events:RemoveTargets'],
      resources: [managedRuleArn],
      conditions: { StringLike: { 'events:ManagedBy': 'malware-protection-plan.guardduty.amazonaws.com' } },
    }));
    scanRole.addToPolicy(new iam.PolicyStatement({
      actions: ['events:DescribeRule', 'events:ListTargetsByRule'],
      resources: [managedRuleArn],
    }));
    scanRole.addToPolicy(new iam.PolicyStatement({
      actions: ['s3:GetObject', 's3:GetObjectVersion', 's3:PutObjectTagging', 's3:GetObjectTagging',
        's3:PutObjectVersionTagging', 's3:GetObjectVersionTagging'],
      resources: [intake.arnForObjects('*')],
    }));
    scanRole.addToPolicy(new iam.PolicyStatement({
      actions: ['s3:PutBucketNotification', 's3:GetBucketNotification', 's3:ListBucket'],
      resources: [intake.bucketArn],
    }));
    scanRole.addToPolicy(new iam.PolicyStatement({
      actions: ['s3:PutObject'],
      resources: [intake.arnForObjects('malware-protection-resource-validation-object')],
    }));

    // 4. Malware Protection plan: scan incoming/ and tag the objects
    const plan = new guardduty.CfnMalwareProtectionPlan(this, 'MalwareProtectionPlan', {
      role: scanRole.roleArn,
      protectedResource: { s3Bucket: { bucketName: intake.bucketName, objectPrefixes: ['incoming/'] } },
      actions: { tagging: { status: 'ENABLED' } },
    });
    plan.node.addDependency(scanRole); // the policy must exist before GuardDuty validates the plan

    // 5. Bucket policy: nobody reads unscanned or infected files, nobody else sets the tag
    intake.addToResourcePolicy(new iam.PolicyStatement({
      sid: 'DenyReadUntilClean',
      effect: iam.Effect.DENY,
      principals: [new iam.AnyPrincipal()],
      actions: ['s3:GetObject', 's3:GetObjectVersion'],
      resources: [intake.arnForObjects('incoming/*')],
      conditions: {
        StringNotEquals: { [`s3:ExistingObjectTag/${SCAN_TAG}`]: 'NO_THREATS_FOUND' },
        ArnNotEquals: { 'aws:PrincipalArn': scanRole.roleArn },
      },
    }));
    intake.addToResourcePolicy(new iam.PolicyStatement({
      sid: 'OnlyGuardDutyTags',
      effect: iam.Effect.DENY,
      principals: [new iam.AnyPrincipal()],
      actions: ['s3:PutObjectTagging', 's3:PutObjectVersionTagging', 's3:DeleteObjectTagging'],
      resources: [intake.arnForObjects('*')],
      conditions: { ArnNotEquals: { 'aws:PrincipalArn': scanRole.roleArn } },
    }));

    // 6. Lambda functions
    const common: Partial<nodejs.NodejsFunctionProps> = {
      runtime: lambda.Runtime.NODEJS_24_X,
      architecture: lambda.Architecture.ARM_64,
      memorySize: 256,
      timeout: Duration.seconds(30),
      environment: {
        INTAKE_BUCKET: intake.bucketName,
        CLEAN_BUCKET: clean.bucketName,
        UPLOADS_TABLE: table.tableName,
      },
      bundling: { format: nodejs.OutputFormat.ESM, minify: true, externalModules: [] }, // bundle the SDK too
    };

    const createUpload = new nodejs.NodejsFunction(this, 'CreateUploadFn', { ...common, entry: src('create-upload.ts') });
    intake.grantPut(createUpload, 'incoming/*');
    table.grantWriteData(createUpload);

    const getUpload = new nodejs.NodejsFunction(this, 'GetUploadFn', { ...common, entry: src('get-upload.ts') });
    table.grantReadData(getUpload);

    const onScanResult = new nodejs.NodejsFunction(this, 'OnScanResultFn', { ...common, entry: src('on-scan-result.ts') });
    intake.grantRead(onScanResult, 'incoming/*');
    intake.grantDelete(onScanResult, 'incoming/*');
    clean.grantPut(onScanResult, 'accepted/*');
    table.grantReadWriteData(onScanResult);

    // 7. EventBridge rule for the scan results of this bucket, with retries and DLQ
    const dlq = new sqs.Queue(this, 'ScanResultDlq', { retentionPeriod: Duration.days(14), enforceSSL: true });
    new events.Rule(this, 'ScanResultRule', {
      eventPattern: {
        source: ['aws.guardduty'],
        detailType: ['GuardDuty Malware Protection Object Scan Result'],
        detail: { s3ObjectDetails: { bucketName: [intake.bucketName] } },
      },
      targets: [new targets.LambdaFunction(onScanResult, {
        retryAttempts: 4,
        maxEventAge: Duration.hours(2),
        deadLetterQueue: dlq,
      })],
    });

    new cloudwatch.Alarm(this, 'ScanResultDlqAlarm', {
      metric: dlq.metricApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible(),
      threshold: 1,
      evaluationPeriods: 1,
      alarmDescription: 'Scan results could not be processed',
    });

    // 8. HTTP API for the frontend
    const api = new HttpApi(this, 'UploadApi', {
      corsPreflight: { allowOrigins: ['*'], allowMethods: [CorsHttpMethod.GET, CorsHttpMethod.POST], allowHeaders: ['content-type'] },
    });
    api.addRoutes({ path: '/uploads', methods: [HttpMethod.POST], integration: new HttpLambdaIntegration('CreateUpload', createUpload) });
    api.addRoutes({ path: '/uploads/{uploadId}', methods: [HttpMethod.GET], integration: new HttpLambdaIntegration('GetUpload', getUpload) });

    new CfnOutput(this, 'ApiUrl', { value: api.apiEndpoint });
    new CfnOutput(this, 'IntakeBucketName', { value: intake.bucketName });
    new CfnOutput(this, 'CleanBucketName', { value: clean.bucketName });
    new CfnOutput(this, 'MalwareProtectionPlanId', { value: plan.attrMalwareProtectionPlanId });
  }
}

// bin/app.ts
import { App } from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import { UploadScanStack } from '../lib/upload-scan-stack.js';

const app = new App();
new UploadScanStack(app, 'BakeryApplicationUploads', {
  env: { region: process.env.CDK_DEFAULT_REGION ?? 'eu-central-1' },
});

What the stack does in detail

The IAM role follows the template from the GuardDuty documentation. GuardDuty needs permissions to create the managed EventBridge rule with the prefix DO-NOT-DELETE-AmazonGuardDutyMalwareProtectionS3, to turn on S3 notifications to EventBridge, to read and tag objects and to put a test object called malware-protection-resource-validation-object. Specifically, GuardDuty uses this test object to check whether the plan works. If your bucket uses a customer managed KMS key, you also need kms:Decrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey. In the example I use S3 managed encryption, so this is not needed.

The plan itself is an L1 construct, because there is no higher-level abstraction for AWS::GuardDuty::MalwareProtectionPlan yet. The dependency on the role makes sure that CloudFormation creates the policy before GuardDuty validates the plan. Without it, the plan often ends up in a warning state because the permissions are still missing during the first test.

The bucket policy is my safety net. The first rule denies everyone read access to objects under incoming/ as long as the tag is not NO_THREATS_FOUND. Notably, this also applies to objects without any tag, because negated conditions like StringNotEquals match when the key is missing. The only exception is the GuardDuty role, which has to read in order to scan. The second rule prevents anyone except GuardDuty from setting or removing the tag. Otherwise a compromised function could simply declare a file clean by itself.

The EventBridge rule filters on our bucket, retries failed invocations up to four times and then puts the event into an SQS queue. A CloudWatch alarm fires as soon as something lands there. I show how to wrap such a queue neatly and replay events in the article dead-letter queue with CDK. If you are unsure whether EventBridge or a queue is the right trigger for your case, the AWS service finder helps you decide.

Step 6: Tests with Vitest

Because the decision is a pure function, the tests need no mocks. Add the scripts "test": "vitest run" and "build": "tsc --noEmit" to your package.json.

// test/scan-decision.test.ts
import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { decide, type ScanResultDetail } from '../src/scan-decision.js';

const base = (status: ScanResultDetail['scanResultDetails']['scanResultStatus'], key = 'incoming/abc-123'): ScanResultDetail => ({
  scanStatus: status === 'NO_THREATS_FOUND' || status === 'THREATS_FOUND' ? 'COMPLETED' : 'SKIPPED',
  resourceType: 'S3_OBJECT',
  s3ObjectDetails: { bucketName: 'intake-bucket', objectKey: key, eTag: 'etag-1' },
  scanResultDetails: {
    scanResultStatus: status,
    threats: status === 'THREATS_FOUND' ? [{ name: 'EICAR-Test-File (not a virus)' }] : null,
  },
});

describe('decide', () => {
  it('accepts clean files and moves them to accepted/', () => {
    expect(decide(base('NO_THREATS_FOUND'))).toEqual({
      action: 'accept',
      uploadId: 'abc-123',
      sourceKey: 'incoming/abc-123',
      targetKey: 'accepted/abc-123',
      eTag: 'etag-1',
    });
  });

  it('rejects infected files and keeps the threat names', () => {
    const d = decide(base('THREATS_FOUND'));
    expect(d).toMatchObject({ action: 'reject', threats: ['EICAR-Test-File (not a virus)'] });
  });

  it.each(['UNSUPPORTED', 'ACCESS_DENIED', 'FAILED'] as const)('sends %s to manual review', (status) => {
    expect(decide(base(status))).toMatchObject({ action: 'review', reason: status });
  });

  it('ignores objects outside incoming/', () => {
    expect(decide(base('NO_THREATS_FOUND', 'other/file.pdf')).action).toBe('ignore');
  });
});

Running npm test should report six green tests. This secures the most important rule: only NO_THREATS_FOUND leads to approval.

Step 7: Deploy and try it out 

npm run build
npm test
npx cdk bootstrap   # only needed once per account and region
npx cdk deploy

After the deployment, CDK shows you the API URL, both bucket names and the plan ID. First check whether the plan is active. This can take a moment after creation.

aws guardduty list-malware-protection-plans
aws guardduty get-malware-protection-plan \
  --malware-protection-plan-id <PLAN_ID> \
  --query Status

You should see "ACTIVE". Then upload any PDF file. The script fetches the upload permission, turns it into form fields for curl and sends the file directly to S3.

API=https://abc123.execute-api.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com   # value from the CDK output

RESP=$(curl -s -X POST "$API/uploads" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"fileName":"resume.pdf","contentType":"application/pdf"}')
UPLOAD_ID=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r .uploadId)
URL=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r .url)

# Form fields of the upload permission as -F arguments for curl
FIELDS=()
while IFS= read -r line; do FIELDS+=("$line"); done < <(
  echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.fields | to_entries[] | "-F", "\(.key)=\(.value)"')

# The file must be the last field in the form
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "${FIELDS[@]}" -F "file=@resume.pdf" "$URL"

S3 responds with 204. Now query the status. Right after the upload it says SCANNING, and shortly after ACCEPTED. The file is then stored under accepted/ in the clean bucket and carries the copied tag as proof.

curl -s "$API/uploads/$UPLOAD_ID"
# {"uploadId":"…","status":"SCANNING","fileName":"resume.pdf"}

sleep 30
curl -s "$API/uploads/$UPLOAD_ID"
# {"uploadId":"…","status":"ACCEPTED","fileName":"resume.pdf"}

aws s3api get-object-tagging --bucket <CLEAN_BUCKET> --key "accepted/$UPLOAD_ID"
# "TagSet": [{ "Key": "GuardDutyMalwareScanStatus", "Value": "NO_THREATS_FOUND" }]

Step 8: Simulate a detection

For the counter test there is the EICAR test file. It is harmless, but practically every virus scanner reports it as a detection, including GuardDuty. You can find its content on the EICAR project website. I am deliberately not printing it here, because virus scanners and security proxies might otherwise flag this page or your repository as suspicious. Create the file locally as eicar.pdf, upload it with the script from step 7 and query the status. After the scan it says REJECTED, the log of the evaluation function contains the name of the finding and the file has disappeared from the intake bucket.

Common mistakes with S3 malware scanning

The plan stays in warning or error state

Almost always, the role is missing a permission. The status reason usually tells you which one. INSUFFICIENT_TEST_OBJECT_PERMISSIONS, for example, means that GuardDuty was not allowed to put the test object. Read the reason with get-malware-protection-plan and compare the policy with the template in the documentation. By the way, GuardDuty publishes separate events for status changes, which you can put an alarm on.

Objects do not get a tag

First check whether tagging is enabled in the plan at all. Next, look at the prefix: if the file is not under incoming/, it is not scanned. A third reason is the S3 tag limit. If an object already has ten tags, GuardDuty cannot add an eleventh and reports a post-scan tagging failure.

The bucket policy locks you out

The read lock applies to administrators too. If you want to open a file in the intake bucket for debugging, you get AccessDenied. That is intended; nevertheless, it surprises you the first time. For real investigations, create a dedicated role for your security team and add it to the policy exception on purpose. This also helps when you tear down the stack, because I keep the buckets with RETAIN so that no applications get lost by accident.

Encrypted buckets with a customer managed KMS key

With SSE-KMS, the GuardDuty role also needs permissions on the key, restricted via kms:ViaService to S3 in your region. If you forget this, every scan ends with ACCESS_DENIED. In our example, the file then goes to manual review, which is at least safe, but quickly creates a lot of open cases.

My take

For most teams, the managed scan is the better choice today compared to running ClamAV yourself. You save yourself signature updates, memory problems and a component that otherwise only gets noticed when it is broken. Moreover, with normal upload volumes the costs are manageable. And the combination of tag, bucket policy and EventBridge fits the Serverless mindset very well: no server that fetches files, but events you react to.

Still, a virus scan is not a free pass. It recognizes known patterns, but it cannot guarantee to catch every new variant. I see it as one layer of several: limit file type and size at upload, only let checked files into the clean bucket, give downstream systems minimal permissions and process documents in an isolated environment where possible. Where I disagree is the idea of dropping every other precaution after a green scan. And if you serve several clouds or work in a region without the service, your own solution is still a good option.

FAQ

Does GuardDuty have to be enabled for S3 malware scanning?

No. Malware Protection for S3 also works without an enabled GuardDuty detector. You then get no findings in GuardDuty, but you do get the result as an object tag, as an EventBridge event and as a CloudWatch metric.

Can GuardDuty scan files that are already in the bucket?

Yes, with on-demand scans you can check existing objects or have them scanned again. These scans are not included in the free tier, though. The automatic scan only applies to newly uploaded objects.

How long does a scan take?

AWS does not state a fixed duration, it depends on the size and type of the file, among other things. So build the upload asynchronously: store the status, show “being checked” in the frontend and poll regularly.

Does this also work with the Serverless Framework?

Yes. You define the plan, the role and the bucket policy as CloudFormation in the resources section of your serverless.yml. The evaluation function gets an eventBridge event with the same pattern as in the CDK stack.

Your next step

Look at where external files enter your applications. There are often more places than you think: profile pictures, imports, attachments in the support form. Pick the one with the highest risk, deploy the example to a test account and run the EICAR file through it once. As a result, within an hour you will know how the flow feels. I am curious: do you already scan uploads today, and if so, with what?

All code from this article, ready to run: smirowstanitzok/sascha-ms-examples
