title: A coding agent is only as good as its harness
description:
I run OpenGeocoding. Originally published on the OpenGeocoding blog. Cross-post formatting was prepared with AI assistance.

A coding agent can write a fix for a geocoding bug in minutes. The hard part is knowing whether the fix is right, and whether it quietly broke something in another country. That is a question for the harness the agent works in, not for the agent. This post describes the harness around the OpenGeocoding engine: what checks every change, why the world index had to rebuild quickly for any of it to work, and the part that still isn’t stable, which is the speed gate.

The engine’s public repository merged 281 pull requests between 12 and 27 October 2026, and many of them were written by a coding agent. At that pace, I can’t judge every change by reading it. I need the checks to tell me what the change did to the whole world.

Why a geocoder needs this more than most code

Address matching is a long list of rules that interact. The engine has rules for Japanese block addresses, Korean road names, Dutch postcodes, Czech house numbers and many others (the first post has a few examples). A rule that helps one country can change the answer for an address somewhere else, and nothing in the code tells you where. Unit tests catch the cases you thought of. What I needed was a check that runs every case I have, in every country, on every change.

A world index that rebuilds in minutes

That check is only meaningful on a full world index. A synthetic test world is useful for logic, but the regressions that matter come from real data: a street in Australia that happens to share its name with a town, a Japanese address whose block number sits in a different field than expected.

So the gate needs the real index, and the base and head of a pull request have to be compared on the same one. Changes to the index format are frequent: 28 commits between 13 and 27 October set a new builder hash, and each of them names a new world index. With an import that takes days, as a Nominatim planet import does, testing each of those changes against the world wouldn’t be practical.

The engine’s builder produces the world index in about 7 min on one machine (build record). That number is the foundation of everything below. When a change alters the index, the agent’s instructions say to rebuild it locally and run the comparison there before pushing, rather than wait for CI. On the cluster that runs the CI gate, a first build for a new builder is slower and can take hours, so the local build is what keeps the loop short.

Expected answers from registries, never from a geocoder

The gold suite takes its expected answers from official and public reference sources: national address registries, Wikidata, the US Census geocoder and others. They are never taken from Nominatim, another geocoder or this engine’s own output. The cases are generated by a command, evaluate build-gold, from a list of seeds, and the generated file is never edited by hand. The suite also includes a panel of addresses drawn from OpenStreetMap; since the index reads much of the same data, that panel measures agreement rather than accuracy, and it catches regressions all the same. Today the whole suite has 36,920 cases (evaluation guide).

The rules in the engine’s AGENTS.md matter here as much as the data. An agent with a failing check has an easy way out: loosen the expectation. The instructions close that door explicitly. Expectations are never weakened, cases are never dropped, and a failure is never relabelled to make a gate pass. Known failures carry a known_failure label with their cause, stay visible in every report, and the label comes off only after a fix is verified. About one location in five is held out by a stable hash and kept out of tuning.

Base against head, on every pull request

Every pull request that touches the service, its data or the corpus gets a staging image, and its merge base already has one from main. A private cluster evaluates both images on one full world index and compares the two runs. The result comes back as two comments on the pull request (how the gate works):

  • gold-full, the quality check: passing checks per RPC on both sides, pass rates for each country where anything changed, and the cases that changed. It fails on any case that newly fails, fails in a worse way, or gives a new critical result.
  • gold-speed, the latency check: SearchAddress, SuggestAddress and ReverseGeocode timings on both sides. It fails when the total, p50, p90 or p99 of any of them is more than 10% slower.

The comparison is relative on purpose. It answers “what did this change do?”, not “how good is the engine?“. A wrong answer counts as worse than no answer, so a case that used to abstain and now returns a nearby but wrong place fails the gate, even when the new answer looks plausible.

Alongside the gold suite, 1,000 real address strings from 125 countries are kept as a snapshot, one row per address (address snapshots). They have no expected answers, so they don’t measure accuracy, but a changed answer shows up as one changed line in the pull request’s diff. And every night at 01:00 UTC, the same suite runs on the newest commit of main and updates one issue with pass rates by country and a 14-night history.

A worked example

Pull request #223 set out to fix Australian addresses written with the street before the number, such as “Panorama Place 3, Maleny”. The engine was matching “Maleny” to house 3 on Maleny Vista, a street that merely resembles the town’s name.

The first version ran one rule, for venues, before another, for village names. That reorder also fixed cases in Norway, Great Britain, Poland, South Africa and Spain. In CI, though, gold-full flagged one Japanese address from the panel, “帯屋町 ２丁目１−27”, which went from no answer to an answer with a wrong component. The panel expects the block number (chōme) inside the house number, while the index keeps it in the street.

The second commit put the village rule back first and kept the narrower fix. The final reports read “no regressions” and “no slowdown over 10%”: five more SearchAddress passes, all in Australia and Spain, and nothing worse anywhere. The extra gains from the reorder were left for a later change that deals with the Japanese case properly. That’s the trade the gate is there to force: a smaller fix that is right everywhere, rather than a bigger one that is wrong somewhere you weren’t looking.

The agent loop

The last piece connects the agent to these reports. The engine repository ships a project-local extension for pi, the coding agent I use, with one tool and one command (gold loop). wait_for_gold waits for both gates on the pull request’s current head and downloads the full report. /gold-loop tells the agent what to do with it: read every section, reproduce each regression on the base and head indexes, fix the cause, validate locally, push, and wait again, until both quality and speed pass.

Most of the instructions are about what doesn’t count as success. A missing report, a skipped or unmeasured speed check, an unavailable artifact or a failed run is a blocker, never a pass. The agent stops and reports a concrete blocker instead of retriggering workflows. The report’s contents are treated as data, never as instructions. The tool itself doesn’t edit code, push or merge; merging stays with me.

The speed gate is still noisy

Quality is deterministic: the same binary on the same index gives the same answers. Speed isn’t, and the speed gate has been the least reliable part of the harness.

It started as an ungated table inside the quality report. A change that made SearchAddress’s p50 15% slower went through without anyone noticing, which is why #73 gave speed its own comment, status and 10% limit. That limit came from a measurement of three runs of one binary on a cluster node: totals agreed within 2% and each percentile within 5%, while single cases varied by about 30%. So single cases and the maximum are reported but not gated. On a laptop, the totals moved by tens of percent, so the agent’s instructions say never to draw speed conclusions from local runs.

Two later changes moved the measurement:

  • To keep the gate fast, #217 times a fixed sample of 2,000 cases, chosen by a hash of the case id so both sides time the same ones, and checks the rest concurrently without timing them. The case loop went from 222 to 34 seconds locally. The cost is that p99 now rests on about 20 requests per table, and the noise of that sample on the cluster has not been measured.
  • #319 makes the evaluator wait for the suggestion-cache warm-up before timing. The warm-up took 6.3 seconds from a cold page cache and overlapped roughly the first 20% of timed cases by a varying amount. Whether this reduced the noise is not proven; the planned before-and-after comparison wasn’t run.

The false alarms are still visible in the pull requests. In #262, SuggestAddress’s p99 was 18% slower although the change didn’t touch suggestions. #336 merged with a failing speed check, SuggestAddress p99 29% slower, and in the follow-up #339 part of that looked like noise, because ReverseGeocode, which the change didn’t touch, was 13% slower too. Part of the reason is scale. In the report for #223, SuggestAddress’s p99 was 4.5 ms, so the 10% limit is less than half a millisecond.

This matters more with an agent in the loop than without one. A person who sees an 18% slowdown on code they didn’t touch can shrug and rerun. An agent told to keep going until speed passes has no good way to tell noise from a regression, and a flaky gate either sends it after a problem that isn’t there or teaches everyone to ignore the gate. The noise of the 2,000-case sample on the cluster is the open measurement, and until it is taken, the 10% limit rests on the older one.

What the harness doesn’t do

  • It measures change, not accuracy. A case that fails the same way on both sides doesn’t fail the gate. Some registries are also inputs to the index, so for those countries a pass is a fidelity check rather than an independent accuracy measurement.
  • Small numbers stay small. Per-country rows are individual cases, not rates, and a rate computed from a few hundred cases carries several points of uncertainty.
  • The report has no per-case responses. The cluster returns only the report, so debugging a listed case means rerunning it locally on an index from the same builder.
  • Outside contributions need approval. Pull requests from people outside the project wait for a reviewer, because approving one runs that author’s code in the cluster.

None of this makes the agent smarter. It makes the agent’s work checkable, quickly and against the whole world, and that is what lets me merge it.

The engine, its evaluation tools and the gold loop are on GitHub: Mokto/opengeocoding. The evaluation guide and AGENTS.md are the best places to start if you want to build something similar for your own project.

title: Building a Safe-by-Design HTTP Telemetry Crate in Rust
description:
Incidents are easier to investigate when you can see what happened inside your HTTP service: which route failed, how long it took, and what the request looked like.

But logging request data can create new problems. Passwords and tokens may end up in logs. Large payloads can consume memory. And if telemetry export waits on a slow or unavailable backend, it can affect the request path.

To address these tradeoffs, I built safe-http-telemetry, an open-source Rust crate for Axum and Tower applications.

Its design goal is to make HTTP telemetry useful while keeping capture, resource use, and export behavior under the application’s control.
Three design priorities

  1. Redact sensitive data before queueing When an application captures request data, it needs to consider credentials such as passwords, bearer tokens, and API keys.

safe-http-telemetry applies capture limits and redaction before events enter the export queue. It supports configured sensitive-field matching in query parameters, headers, and supported structured body formats. JSON objects are traversed recursively, with limits on depth, visited nodes, and string size.

Body capture is optional. It requires the body-capture feature and a route configured for the Detailed profile. Applications can also add field names specific to their own domain.

Redaction is a safeguard, not a guarantee that every secret will be identified. I recommend starting with the Minimal profile, enabling richer capture only on reviewed routes, and limiting access to the telemetry backend.

  1. Keep the request path independent from Loki The middleware submits events to a bounded queue without waiting for a network export. Background workers can consume and batch events for asynchronous delivery to Grafana Loki.

If the queue fills up, the default DropNewest policy rejects the incoming event and updates operational counters. This keeps queue memory bounded and avoids waiting for Loki to become available. The application can monitor these counters and configure limits to suit its workload.

The event flow looks like this:

HTTP request
     │
     ▼
Axum / Tower middleware
     │
     ▼
Route policy → bounded capture → redaction
     │
     ▼
Bounded event queue ── full? ──► drop newest + update counters
     │
     ▼
Background exporter workers
     │
     ▼
Grafana Loki

The queue and exporter have separate responsibilities: the middleware prepares events, while the consumer handles delivery and shutdown.

  1. Make geolocation an explicit local option For applications that need it, the optional geolocation feature can look up country information using a local MMDB database. The database is supplied separately, loaded during setup, and is not downloaded by the crate. Lookups do not call an external geolocation API.

The cache has configurable capacity and time-to-live limits. By default, the event includes country code and country name; the application can choose other supported fields. Geolocation depends on resolving the client IP correctly, so forwarded headers should only be trusted from configured proxy networks.
A small Axum integration surface
After creating a bounded queue and route policies, attach the layer to your router:

let telemetry_layer =
    axum_telemetry_layer(queue.clone(), policies, MiddlewareConfig::default())?;

let app = Router::new()
    .route("/hello/{name}", get(handler))
    .layer(telemetry_layer);

With Axum, register routes before applying the layer so the middleware can record normalized route templates. The crate leaves server setup, queue consumption, and shutdown sequencing to the application.
What the benchmarks show
I used Criterion to measure middleware overhead with tower::ServiceExt::oneshot. The recorded run compared a service without telemetry to three capture profiles:

  • Baseline: 2.38 µs
  • Minimal: 27.31 µs
  • Standard: 60.16 µs
  • Detailed: 71.58 µs These are estimates from a documented run on one machine, not universal performance guarantees. The benchmark does not measure network throughput, tail latency under load, or sustained exporter outages. The geolocation case in that run did not supply a client IP, so it did not measure an actual database lookup.

For a real service, benchmark with representative payloads, concurrency, and capture policies.
Testing malformed and unexpected input
The repository includes property-based tests with proptest for configuration, policy resolution, and queue capacity. It also includes cargo-fuzz targets for query, header, and JSON redaction inputs.

These checks help exercise boundary conditions and malformed data. They complement application-specific testing, especially when adding custom sensitive field names or enabling detailed body capture.
What I learned
Building this crate reinforced that observability is not just about collecting more logs. It also involves data minimization, backpressure, resource limits, and graceful behavior when a backend is unavailable.

safe-http-telemetry is available on crates.io. If you build with Axum or Tower, I’d welcome feedback on the integration, documentation, performance, and any edge cases you find.

  • Crate: crates.io/crates/safe-http-telemetry
  • Repository: github.com/sylvainTIASSOU/safe-http-telemetry Bug reports, feature suggestions, and contributions are very welcome. 🦀

title: Java Memory Management Explained: Heap, Stack, Metaspace and Garbage Collection
description:
Understanding how the JVM allocates memory, manages objects, performs garbage collection and handles memory-related problems in real-world Java applications.

Introduction

Have you ever wondered what happens inside the JVM when you create a Java object?

Consider a simple statement:

Customer customer = new Customer("Ramu");

It looks like a straightforward object creation. However, several things happen behind the scenes:

  • The JVM allocates memory for the object.
  • A reference to the object is maintained in the executing thread's stack frame.
  • The object is stored in the heap.
  • The JVM manages the object's lifecycle.
  • When the object is no longer reachable, it becomes eligible for garbage collection.

Understanding these operations is essential for every Java developer, particularly when building high-performance enterprise applications.

In production environments, improper memory management can lead to:

  • OutOfMemoryError
  • Frequent garbage collection
  • Application latency
  • Increased CPU utilization
  • Memory leaks
  • Application crashes

In this article, we'll explore Java memory management from the JVM perspective, using Java 21 examples and practical enterprise application scenarios.

1. Understanding JVM Memory Architecture

The Java Virtual Machine divides memory into different runtime areas to manage application execution efficiently.

Some memory areas are shared across application threads, while others are created separately for each thread.

The major JVM runtime memory areas include:

  1. Heap
  2. Java Stack
  3. Method Area
  4. Program Counter Register
  5. Native Method Stack

Additionally, JVM implementations use native memory areas such as Metaspace and Code Cache.

JVM Memory Architecture

Let's understand each component.

1.1 Heap Memory

Heap is the primary memory area where Java objects and arrays are allocated.

Important characteristics:

  • Shared across application threads.
  • Managed by the garbage collector.
  • Stores objects created using new.
  • Usually the largest JVM memory area.

Example:

public class CustomerService {

    public void createCustomer() {

        Customer customer =
                new Customer("Ramu");

        System.out.println(customer.getName());
    }
}

The Customer object is allocated on the heap, while the local reference variable customer resides in the executing method's stack frame.

1.2 Java Stack Memory

Each thread has its own Java stack.

Whenever a method is invoked, the JVM creates a stack frame.

A stack frame contains:

  • Local variables
  • Operand stack
  • Runtime constant pool reference
  • Method execution information

Example:

public void processPayment() {

    int amount = 5000;

    Payment payment =
            new Payment(amount);

    validatePayment(payment);
}

Here:

  • amount is a primitive local variable.
  • payment is a local reference variable.
  • The actual Payment object is allocated on the heap.

Each method invocation creates a new stack frame, and the frame is removed when the method completes.

1.3 Metaspace

Metaspace stores class metadata required by the JVM.

It was introduced in Java 8, replacing PermGen.

Examples of metadata include:

  • Class structure information
  • Method metadata
  • Runtime constant pool information
  • Field information
  • Method bytecode-related metadata

Unlike heap memory, Metaspace uses native memory.

An important consideration is that excessive class loading or classloader retention can cause Metaspace-related memory problems.

1.4 Program Counter Register

Each JVM thread maintains its own Program Counter (PC) register.

It identifies the JVM instruction currently being executed by that thread.

1.5 Native Method Stack

Native Method Stack supports execution of native methods, typically implemented using languages such as C or C++ through JNI.

2. Understanding Heap Memory Generations

Heap memory is where most Java developers encounter garbage collection concepts.

In a traditional generational heap model, memory is divided into:

  • Young Generation
  • Old Generation

The Young Generation is further divided into:

  • Eden Space
  • Survivor Space S0
  • Survivor Space S1

2.1 Eden Space

Most new objects are initially allocated in Eden.

Example:

Customer customer =
        new Customer("Ramu");

The object is typically allocated in Eden when the JVM uses a generational collector.

2.2 Survivor Spaces

Survivor spaces are used to hold objects that survive garbage collection in the Young Generation.

The JVM uses two survivor spaces, conventionally called S0 and S1.

Objects surviving a minor collection may move between survivor spaces.

2.3 Old Generation

Objects that survive multiple young-generation collections may eventually be promoted to the Old Generation.

Examples include:

  • Long-lived application configuration objects
  • Cached reference data
  • Shared application-level objects
  • Long-running session-related objects

Promotion depends on collector-specific policies and object age and size; it is not simply a fixed rule that every object follows.

3. How Garbage Collection Works

Garbage Collection (GC) is the JVM's automatic memory management mechanism.

Its primary responsibility is to identify objects that are no longer reachable and reclaim their memory.

An object becomes eligible for garbage collection when it is no longer reachable through the JVM's active reference paths.

For example:

public class MemoryExample {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Customer customer =
                new Customer("Ramu");

        customer = null;

    }
}

After assigning null, the object may become eligible for garbage collection, assuming no other references exist.

Remember:

Eligible for garbage collection does not mean immediately garbage collected.

The JVM decides when collection occurs.

3.1 Garbage Collection Workflow

A simplified way to understand garbage collection is through these stages:

  1. Identify GC Roots.
  2. Determine reachable objects.
  3. Identify unreachable objects.
  4. Reclaim eligible memory.
  5. Perform collector-specific compaction or relocation where applicable.

Common GC Roots include:

  • Active thread stack references
  • Static references
  • JNI references
  • Other JVM-managed references

The actual algorithms differ between garbage collectors.

4. Types of Garbage Collection

Java provides multiple garbage collectors designed for different application requirements.

4.1 Serial Garbage Collector

  • Uses a single thread for garbage collection.
  • Suitable for small applications.
  • Can introduce longer pauses as heap size increases.

4.2 Parallel Garbage Collector

  • Uses multiple threads for garbage collection.
  • Focuses on application throughput.
  • Useful for workloads where throughput is more important than minimizing individual pause times.

4.3 G1 Garbage Collector

G1 (Garbage First) is the default garbage collector for typical server-class configurations in modern Java.

Important characteristics:

  • Divides heap into multiple regions.
  • Supports concurrent marking.
  • Prioritizes regions with more reclaimable memory.
  • Aims to meet configurable pause-time goals.

4.4 Z Garbage Collector (ZGC)

ZGC is designed for low-latency applications.

Important characteristics:

  • Performs much of its work concurrently.
  • Aims to maintain very short GC pauses.
  • Supports large heaps.
  • Generational ZGC is available in Java 21 as an experimental feature.

Comparison

Collector Primary focus
Serial GC Simplicity
Parallel GC Throughput
G1 GC Balanced performance
ZGC Low latency

The right collector depends on workload characteristics, heap size, latency requirements and available resources.

5. Understanding Java Memory-Related Errors

Memory problems are common in enterprise applications, especially when applications process large datasets or handle high concurrent traffic.

5.1 OutOfMemoryError: Java Heap Space

Occurs when the JVM cannot allocate additional objects in the heap.

Common causes:

  • Unbounded collections
  • Excessive object creation
  • Memory leaks
  • Large data processing without pagination

Example:

List<byte[]> data = new ArrayList<>();

while (true) {
    data.add(new byte[1024 * 1024]);
}

This continuously allocates memory until the JVM cannot satisfy another allocation.

5.2 OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace

Can occur when the JVM cannot allocate additional class metadata.

Common causes:

  • Excessive dynamic class loading
  • Classloader leaks
  • Improper application redeployment patterns

5.3 StackOverflowError

Occurs when a thread's stack is exhausted.

A common cause is uncontrolled recursion.

public void process() {
    process();
}

This method continuously invokes itself without a termination condition.

6. Memory Leaks in Java Applications

Java has automatic garbage collection, but that does not mean memory leaks are impossible.

A memory leak happens when objects are no longer needed by the application but remain reachable through references.

Consider this example:

public class CustomerCache {

    private static final List<Customer>
            CACHE = new ArrayList<>();

    public void addCustomer(Customer customer) {
        CACHE.add(customer);
    }
}

If customers are continuously added and never removed, the static collection retains references to them.

The garbage collector cannot reclaim these objects while they remain reachable.

Common causes of memory leaks:

  • Static collections
  • Unbounded caches
  • Improper ThreadLocal usage
  • Event listener references
  • Unclosed resources
  • Classloader retention

In production applications, memory leaks can gradually increase heap utilization and eventually cause service failures.

7. JVM Memory Monitoring and Troubleshooting

Understanding JVM memory is only the first step.

Production engineers must also know how to monitor and troubleshoot memory problems.

Useful JVM tools include:

Tool Purpose
jps List running Java processes
jstat Monitor JVM statistics
jmap Inspect heap and generate heap dumps
jstack Capture thread dumps
jcmd Execute diagnostic commands
Java Flight Recorder Profile JVM activity
Java Mission Control Analyze JVM recordings

Example commands:

jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info

jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram

jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=recording.jfr

For garbage collection logging in Java 21:

-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags

For heap dump generation when an OutOfMemoryError occurs:

-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError

These diagnostics help identify memory consumption patterns, allocation behavior and possible leaks.

8. JVM Memory Management in Real-World Banking Applications

Consider a banking application built using Java 21, Spring Boot and microservices.

The application processes:

  • Customer information
  • Account details
  • Payment transactions
  • Transaction history
  • Fraud detection requests

Imagine a payment service processing thousands of concurrent requests.

Each request may create multiple temporary objects:

  • Request DTOs
  • Validation objects
  • Domain objects
  • Database entities
  • Response DTOs

Most temporary objects become eligible for garbage collection after request processing completes.

However, application-level caches, shared collections and long-lived references may retain objects for much longer.

Production considerations

  1. Set appropriate JVM heap limits.
  2. Monitor heap utilization and GC pause times.
  3. Avoid unbounded in-memory collections.
  4. Use pagination for large database queries.
  5. Profile object allocation patterns.
  6. Configure container memory limits carefully.
  7. Monitor application memory and container memory independently.
  8. Capture heap dumps when investigating memory leaks.

For applications running on Kubernetes or OpenShift, remember that the JVM operates within container memory constraints.

For example:

-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0

This allows the JVM to calculate its maximum heap based on the available memory it detects, subject to the JVM and container configuration.

The remaining container memory must also accommodate Metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, code cache and other native allocations.

9. JVM Memory Tuning in Java 21

Some useful JVM options include:

JVM option Purpose
-Xms Initial heap size
-Xmx Maximum heap size
-Xss Thread stack size
-XX:+UseG1GC Enable G1 GC
-XX:+UseZGC Enable ZGC
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize Set Metaspace limit
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage Set maximum heap percentage relative to detected RAM

Example:

java \
-Xms2g \
-Xmx4g \
-XX:+UseG1GC \
-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log \
-jar banking-service.jar

Important: JVM tuning should be based on actual workload measurements rather than blindly applying configuration values.

10. Best Practices for Java Memory Management

Here are some practical guidelines for enterprise Java applications:

  • Avoid unnecessary object creation in performance-critical paths.
  • Prefer bounded caches over unbounded collections.
  • Use pagination for large database operations.
  • Close resources using try-with-resources.
  • Avoid retaining unnecessary references.
  • Monitor garbage collection regularly.
  • Understand container memory limits.
  • Use heap dumps and profiling tools during troubleshooting.
  • Select garbage collectors based on application requirements.
  • Measure performance before and after tuning.

Conclusion

Java memory management is much more than understanding Heap, Stack and Garbage Collection.

It is about understanding how the JVM allocates objects, manages their lifecycle, identifies unreachable references and reclaims memory efficiently.

For enterprise applications, especially banking and financial systems, effective memory management directly influences application stability, performance, scalability and reliability.

As Java developers and architects, understanding JVM internals helps us build applications that are not only functional but also production-ready.

Keep learning. Keep building. Keep architecting.

— Ram The Architect (RTA)

Further Reading and Resources

  • Java 21 Documentation: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/
  • Java Virtual Machine Specification: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jvms/se21/html/
  • Java Garbage Collection Documentation: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/gctuning/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/Ramu-fsd

Discussion

What garbage collector do you primarily use in your production Java applications — G1 GC, Parallel GC or ZGC?

Have you encountered an OutOfMemoryError or a memory leak in a production environment? Share your experience in the comments.

title: What in-browser PDF processing can and cannot do
description:
There is a lot you can do with PDF files using JavaScript without uploading them to a server.

There are also things that sound simple but become surprisingly difficult when you try to implement them entirely in a browser.

While building PocketPDF, I ended up drawing a fairly clear line between operations that work well client-side and operations where the limitations become noticeable.

Operations that work well in the browser

The basic PDF operations are genuinely suitable for client-side processing.

Merging combines pages from multiple documents into one PDF. Splitting extracts selected pages or separates a document into individual files.

Rotating and reordering pages are also straightforward compared with more advanced document conversion.

Watermarks and page numbers can be added by drawing text or other content onto PDF pages.

Metadata editing and text extraction are similarly reasonable browser tasks.

These operations don't generally require a remote server. The browser can read the input files, process them locally, and generate the output.

Compression is more complicated

PDF compression sounds like one operation, but the actual work depends heavily on the document.

A PDF containing mostly text and vector graphics behaves differently from one containing hundreds of high-resolution photographs.

Image-heavy PDFs can consume a lot of memory during processing.

If images need to be decoded, resized, or re-encoded, the browser has to handle those operations while keeping the original document and intermediate data available.

On a large document, that can become slow and memory hungry.

I don't want to pretend that every PDF will shrink dramatically or that compression will be instant.

OCR needs a model download

OCR is another operation that requires more than a small JavaScript function.

I use Tesseract compiled to WebAssembly.

The engine is served from my own static files, and the required model data is downloaded before recognition can happen.

Once the necessary files are available, OCR runs locally in the browser.

The first use has a download cost, and processing speed depends on the device and document quality.

That is a reasonable trade-off for keeping the actual document processing client-side.

PDF to Word is where the limitations become obvious

Extracting text from a PDF is not the same as reconstructing an editable Word document.

A PDF stores positioned content. It doesn't necessarily contain the original paragraphs, tables, columns, and layout structure that existed in the source document.

A converter can extract text, but preserving the original layout is much harder.

Getting a document that looks identical in Word requires reconstructing relationships between text blocks, images, tables, and page elements.

This is the area where a proper desktop application still has a significant advantage.

I would rather be honest about that limitation than claim perfect PDF-to-Word conversion.

Background removal without AI

My background remover uses a plain edge-flood algorithm.

It starts from the image edges and identifies connected areas that match the background characteristics. Those areas can then be made transparent.

This works reasonably well for images with solid or relatively uniform backgrounds.

It doesn't perform well on complex backgrounds, detailed hair, similar foreground and background colours, or objects with complicated edges.

That limitation is deliberate.

A more capable AI background remover would require a model and, depending on how it is deployed, significant processing resources. Running that kind of model locally would also introduce a much larger download and performance cost.

I chose a smaller algorithm that works in the browser without sending the image to a server.

The practical distinction

For me, the important question isn't whether a feature can technically run in JavaScript.

It's whether the browser can run it reliably, with reasonable memory usage and an output that is actually useful.

Merging, splitting, rotating, reordering, adding watermarks, editing metadata, and extracting text are good examples of operations that fit naturally into a browser-based tool.

Large-scale document reconstruction and complex image processing are different problems.

I build the tools around what can be done well locally, rather than pretending every operation has no limitations.

You can try the tools at https://pocketpdf.site

title: What "accurate" means for a geocoder, and how I decide a change is safe
description:
I run OpenGeocoding. Originally published on the OpenGeocoding blog. Cross-post formatting was prepared with AI assistance.

“How accurate is it?” sounds like one question, but a geocoder answers several at once. Did it find anything? Is the answer in the right country? Is the point close enough to be useful? Is it as precise as the address you sent, a house for a house and a town for a town? And when it returns a house number or a postcode, does that agree with yours?

This post explains how I score those questions for OpenGeocoding, how close I count as close enough, which losses I accept when I change the engine, and how I keep the test set from grading the index on its own data. The first post has the pass rates; this one is about what stands behind them.

A pass has several conditions

The scorer looks only at the first result. A best-of-several answer would flatter every service, and an application usually takes the first one. It ignores the confidence each service reports, because those numbers don’t mean the same thing from one provider to the next. A case then passes when the answer meets all of these, taken from the case’s expectation (what a pass means):

  • the country is one of the allowed countries;
  • the point is within the case’s distance tolerance;
  • the precision is within the allowed range, so a house case can’t pass on a street;
  • a house number or postcode it returns agrees with the request.

Failures are not one bucket either. The evaluation guide separates too_coarse (right country or region, but not the precision the address asked for), abstain, near_miss, far_miss (more than 100 km away), wrong_country and a few others. They matter because they aren’t equally bad. A country answer to a street address is a different failure from a point in another country, and the second is the more serious one.

How close is close enough

The tolerance depends on what the case asks for, and the corpus records it per case instead of using one global number:

  • Registry houses: the tolerance is recorded on each case. The US sample uses 150 m, or 300 m where the register places the point at a parcel centroid, and a separate sample of US addresses with loosely placed points is scored at 500 m and reported apart (US sample).
  • Landmarks: 1 km. Those cases measure coarse coverage, not the position of an entrance.
  • Company-address town cases: 5 km, rising to 10 km from 50,000 people and 20 km from a million (GLEIF cases).
  • Indonesian villages: twice the radius of a circle with the village’s area, between 2 and 25 km.

None of this tells you whether a point is the front door. The scorecard says so directly: the pass rates don’t measure postal deliverability, entrance accuracy or unit correctness. Whether 150 m is good enough depends on your workload. For enriching company records with a town and a region it is more than you need. For routing a courier to a flat it is not enough.

Which losses I accept when I change the engine

A pass rate says how good the engine is. A change needs a different question: what did it break? Every pull request that touches the service, its data or the test corpus is evaluated against the commit it branched from, on the same index, and the two runs are compared case by case (gates).

The rule has one exception:

  • A case that passed before and fails now fails the change, as does a case that moves to a worse failure class and a new critical result.
  • The exception is the panel built from OpenStreetMap addresses, which measures agreement with data the index itself reads. There I accept at most 5 locations that newly fail, and only when at least 5 times as many newly pass and nothing else fails.
  • Losses on registries, Wikidata, GLEIF and constructed cases are never traded for gains elsewhere, because those measure accuracy against sources outside the index.
  • Speed is a separate gate: the change fails if SearchAddress, SuggestAddress or ReverseGeocode gets more than 15% slower in total, at p50, p90 or p99.

So the acceptable loss is zero where the evidence is independent, and a small, explicit trade where it is not. Two experiments in the engine’s notes show why I keep it strict. A change to town matching reached 2,360 passing towns, but introduced 52 regressions where a coarse answer or an abstention became a point more than 5 km from the expected one. I dropped it. The version I kept finds 1,880 and, in the local comparison, adds no newly failing check. Another prototype gained 17 passes by trusting a place-type word alone, and it selected the wrong Samoa namesake, so I rejected that too.

A gate like this measures change, not accuracy. It tells me a commit didn’t make the cases I know about worse. It says nothing about the addresses nobody wrote a case for.

Not grading the index on its own data

A geocoder tested on the data it was built from will look good. The corpus has several defences against that, and each has a limit.

Expected answers come from outside the engine. Wikidata, national address registries, the US Census geocoder and similar sources provide them, never Nominatim, another geocoder or this service. GeoNames and Overture, which the index also reads, only chose which places to ask about.

Registry samples start from the registry. Cases first drawn from the index’s own Overture data and then checked against a register can’t show an address the index lacks, so recall stays invisible. The registry samples are drawn from the register first, and the index is asked about whatever was drawn (registry-first samples).

Overlap is reported, not hidden. Several registries used as expectations are also inputs to the index, so in those countries a pass measures fidelity to the register. The OpenStreetMap panel measures agreement with the index’s own source. Wikidata towns partly come from GeoNames, so some town gains reflect a shared origin. The reports group results by kind of evidence so the independent sources are not blended with the self-referential ones.

Balance, and how much a number can carry

Counts per country are not equal, and the headline rate depends on that. Town cases take up to 100 settlements per country, company-address cases up to 50 and the landmark house-coverage cases 20, so no country dominates those groups. The registry samples differ in size: from 120 cases for French Polynesia to 2,794 for South Korea, and they make up most of the 29,013-query selection that the published pass rate is computed on. That is why the scorecard also breaks results down by cohort and by registry, and why the cohorts differ in level and difficulty.

Variants of one location (a typo, a missing country) share a key, so they don’t count as independent places. About one location in five is held out from development and reported separately. With around 250 cases in a slice, the evaluation guide notes, an aggregate rate carries several points of uncertainty, and a single country’s row is one piece of evidence rather than a rate. I read the per-country tables that way, and I’d ask you to as well.

One more limit applies to all of it: this is a vendor-run evaluation on my own corpus, as the scorecard states at the top, and human review of the cases is still pending.

What to do with this

Use the same method on a sample of your own addresses. Decide first what close enough means for your workload: a town for enriching profiles, a house within 150 m for deliveries. Then geocode a few hundred addresses from each country you care about and look at the failures, not only the rate. The free plan has 50,000 requests a month with no card, and the bulk geocoding guide has a script that geocodes a CSV. The methodology is in the evaluation guide, and if a country of yours behaves worse than these tables suggest, I’d like to hear about it.

title: Ukrainian scans, invoices, Word and Excel to Markdown - 5 Apify Actors on 7 files, only one got every table right
description:
Search the Apify Store for "PDF to Markdown" and you get dozens of Actors with almost the same promise: text,
tables, OCR, ready for RAG. None of them tells you what happens with a Ukrainian scan, an Excel file or a scanned
invoice whose table has no lines. So I ran five of them on the same seven files and compared every output with the
text the files were made from. All results below are from real runs on 15 November 2026.

Disclosure: one of the five is mine, Document to Markdown for AI.
Every number below comes from a real run, the test files are public and the raw outputs are kept, so you can repeat
and check all of it.

Short answer

Files right (of 7) Invoice without lines: rows exact Reads Word and Excel Price per scanned page
ai_admin/document-to-markdown 7 5 of 5 yes $0.004
nidamindllc/doc-ocr 2 4 of 5 no (error) $0.004
lergassy/pdf-text-extractor 1 0 yes $0.0111
fabrikit/document-to-markdown 2 0 yes $0.0105
gochujang/pdf-text-extractor 1 0 (empty) no (PDF only) $0.006

"Right" means the text, the heading and the table with the correct rows and with every number exactly as in the
document.

The seven files

All Ukrainian, all generated from known text, so every character can be checked:

File What it is
text-uk.pdf PDF with a text layer: heading, two sentences, a 3 x 3 table with prices like 96,50
scan-uk.pdf the same page as a clean scan
scan-noisy-uk.pdf the same scan with noise and a slight tilt
doc-uk.docx Word document with the text, a list and the table
sheet-uk.xlsx Excel workbook: the table with a Total row 1,234.50, and a sheet with the sentences
scan-borderless-uk.pdf a scanned invoice: 5 x 6 table without any lines, amounts like 40 530,00 and 2 500
scan-noisy-borderless-uk.pdf the same invoice, noisy and tilted

The last two are the hard case and the most common one: most invoices, waybills and bank statements are printed
without table lines. The files are public:
https://api.apify.com/v2/key-value-stores/FloomuI2DrQCJazY8/records/<file name>.

The Actors are the most used ones for this search plus one that lists Office formats. Settings: Ukrainian OCR
wherever the Actor has a language option (ukr); nidamindllc has no language option.

Results, file by file

File mine nidamindllc lergassy fabrikit gochujang
Text PDF right one OCR typo, table right (HTML) table flattened into the text table as plain lines right
Clean scan right right (HTML table) table as broken lines table lost empty
Noisy scan right right (HTML table) table as broken lines rows without header empty
DOCX right error right right not supported
XLSX right, 1,234.50 kept error 1,234.50 became 1234.5 right not supported
Invoice, no lines 5/5 rows, 30/30 cells 4/5 rows, 29/30 cells no table, 40 530,00 lost its space no table, all in one line, 96,50 read as 96,0 empty
Invoice, no lines, noisy 5/5 rows, 30/30 cells 4/5 rows, 29/30 cells no table, 96,50 read as 96,60 no table, all in one line empty

This is what my Actor returned for the noisy invoice without lines - every cell, every number and the № sign as in
the document:

Рахунок-фактура № 47

Постачальник: ТОВ «Будмайстер», м. Львів. Покупець: ФОП Коваленко О. В. Оплата протягом п'яти банківських днів з дати рахунку.

| № | Товар | Од. | Кількість | Ціна | Сума |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Цемент М500 | мішок | 420 | 96,50 | 40 530,00 |
| 2 | Арматура 12 мм | шт. | 180 | 412,00 | 74 160,00 |
| 3 | Пісок річковий | т | 12 | 650,00 | 7 800,00 |
| 4 | Цегла рядова | шт. | 2 500 | 9,80 | 24 500,00 |

Разом: 146 990,00 грн

The same table also comes as rows of cells in the tables field, ready for a spreadsheet or a database, and the
record says how many pages went through OCR, so a pipeline knows which text came from a scan.

For comparison, the same line of the invoice from two other Actors:

lergassy:  1 | Цемент М500 мішок 420 96,60 40530,00
fabrikit:  ... Мо Товар Од. Кількість Ціна Сума 1 Цемент М500 мішок 420 96,50 40 530,00 2 Арматура12мм шт. ...

What stood out

  • gochujang returned empty text for all four scans and still marked them ok: true; the run log says Failed loading language 'ukr'. It is the most used Actor of the five (40 users a month) and is clean on text PDFs, but it cannot read a Ukrainian scan.
  • nidamindllc is good on scans - the only competitor that kept the invoice table - but it OCRs every PDF, even one with a text layer, which added a typo the file did not have, and it cannot open Word or Excel files at all.
  • lergassy and fabrikit read every format but not the tables. On the invoice lergassy changed a price (96,50 to 96,60), and on the spreadsheet it changed 1,234.50 to 1234.5; fabrikit read the same price as 96,0 on the clean invoice. In an invoice or a price list that is the worst kind of error: it looks right.
  • Mine got all seven files right, including both invoices without lines, with the numbers exactly as written.

What it cost

All five Actors charge per event. For a scanned page:

Actor One scanned page Text page or Office file
mine $0.004 $0.001
nidamindllc $0.004 $0.004 (OCRs everything)
gochujang $0.006 $0.006 per one-page PDF
fabrikit $0.0105 $0.0005
lergassy $0.0111 $0.0031

My run of all seven files cost $0.019 and took 11 seconds.

About the test

  • One file of each kind, small and synthetic. Real archives have worse scans, stamps and handwriting - try ten of your own files before you choose. That costs a few cents.
  • Every Actor ran with the build that was public on 15 November 2026 (mine: 0.1.20).

While preparing this article, the test results showed me where my Actor could become the best in its category -
noisy scans and invoices without table lines - so I improved it right away, before publishing. The latest runs
described above confirm it.

Try it

From Python:

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")
run = client.actor("ai_admin/document-to-markdown").call(run_input={
    "sources": [{"url": "https://api.apify.com/v2/key-value-stores/FloomuI2DrQCJazY8/records/scan-noisy-borderless-uk.pdf"}],
    "ocrLanguages": ["ukr"],
})
for item in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(item["markdown"])
    print(item["tables"])

Or give it to Claude, Cursor or another AI agent as an MCP tool - see
MCP server for document and media tools.

Related posts

  • Ukrainian scanned PDFs to Markdown for RAG and LLMs
  • Office to PDF/A for archives and e-filing

title: When Two APIs Return the Same Number but Mean Different Things
description:
While building Strucera, I spent quite a bit of time working with environmental data for locations selected on an interactive map. The application uses publicly available NASA POWER data to show climate information such as temperature, solar radiation, wind, humidity, and precipitation. Later, I worked on adding a three-day weather forecast from WeatherAPI.com. At first, these seemed like closely related features. Both services return weather-related numbers, both work with geographic locations, and both can provide information that looks perfectly reasonable in a chart or dashboard. But once I started thinking about how people would actually use those numbers, I realized they weren't necessarily answering the same question.
Consider temperature. A climatological value describing the typical conditions for a particular month isn't the same thing as a forecast for a specific day next week, even when both happen to be expressed in degrees Celsius. The first helps someone understand historical patterns over a defined period. The second describes expected conditions at a particular time in the future. NASA POWER provides climatological summaries based on defined historical periods, while WeatherAPI provides forecasts for upcoming dates. If an application removes that context and displays both values as ordinary temperature readings, the numbers might be technically correct while the information presented to the user is misleading.
This became an important distinction in Strucera because the climate interface includes descriptive insights such as the warmest month, the wettest month, and periods with stronger solar or wind conditions. These can help someone understand the general characteristics of a location, but they don't tell you whether it will rain tomorrow or whether a particular construction project is suitable for that site. I wanted those boundaries to remain clear. A historical climate summary shouldn't quietly become a weather prediction, and a descriptive observation shouldn't be presented as an engineering recommendation just because the interface makes it look convincing.
There was also a practical lesson about API design. In the Rust backend, the Weather Outlook endpoint was designed around a three-day forecast with daily temperatures, precipitation, wind, humidity, source metadata, and retrieval information. That metadata matters more than it might seem. A timestamp showing when data was retrieved doesn't necessarily describe the period the data represents. A forecast date and a climatological reference period are different concepts, and I think applications should preserve that distinction all the way from the provider response to the user interface. Otherwise, important meaning can disappear during what looks like a harmless data transformation.
The same reasoning influenced how I approached unavailable data. If the forecast provider isn't configured or can't return a usable response, showing an unavailable state is better than quietly substituting historical climate values. The interface might look less complete for a moment, but at least it isn't pretending to know something it doesn't. I've become increasingly cautious about fallback behavior in software because a fallback that keeps the screen populated can sometimes create a more serious problem than an explicit error. Users may make decisions based on information they have no reason to suspect was substituted.
Another issue came up while planning hourly forecasts. A location on the map might be thousands of kilometers away from the person using the application, so displaying hourly conditions according to the browser's local timezone could make an otherwise correct forecast confusing. The intended design was to use the selected location's timezone and load the hourly view only when requested, rather than fetching additional provider data unnecessarily. That work was still a design and implementation concern at the recorded stage, not something I would describe as a finished feature. But it showed how quickly a seemingly simple weather card can introduce questions about time, cost, data provenance, and user expectations.
What stayed with me from this work is how easy it is to confuse successful data integration with correct information delivery. An API can respond with HTTP 200, the JSON can match the expected schema, the database can store every value correctly, and the frontend can render a beautiful chart. None of those steps proves that the user is interpreting the information as intended. This isn't limited to environmental data. Financial dashboards, health applications, analytics tools, and AI-generated reports all face similar problems when values are separated from their definitions, sources, or time periods.
I still care about performance, clean Rust code, reliable APIs, and useful interfaces, but working on Strucera made me pay more attention to what happens between receiving a value and presenting it to someone. Sometimes the most important engineering decision isn't how to calculate or display a number. It's deciding what that number is allowed to mean.

title: Every tap target under 24px on our site is exactly 20px tall, and all 621 of them pass WCAG only because of the spacing rule
description:
WCAG 2.2 added a success criterion that is unusually easy to measure: 2.5.8, Target Size (Minimum), level AA. Every target should be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with a short list of exceptions. Unlike contrast, which needs a colour model, or focus order, which needs a real keyboard, this one is getBoundingClientRect() and a comparison.

So I ran it over all 76 public pages of Nakodo at a phone viewport, expecting a messy long tail of near misses. What came back was the opposite of messy, and the interesting part turned out to be the exception rather than the rule.

The setup

390 by 844, device scale factor 3, mobile flag on, set through the DevTools protocol rather than by resizing a window, so the emulation is the same every time:

await page.cdp("Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride",
  { width: 390, height: 844, deviceScaleFactor: 3, mobile: true });

Then on each page, every element that can be tapped, measured and classified:

const SEL = 'a[href], button, input:not([type=hidden]), select, textarea, summary, [role="button"], [role="link"], [tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])';

Anything with a zero box, display: none, visibility: hidden or a failing checkVisibility() is dropped. What is left is 5,199 targets across 76 pages, a median of 68 a page.

The classification matters more than the measurement, because 2.5.8 exempts targets "in a sentence or block of text". A link inside a paragraph is allowed to be as tall as its line, and padding it would wreck the paragraph. So each target is marked inline when its computed display starts with inline and it sits inside a p, li, dd, dt, td, th or blockquote. That splits the set into 3,222 inline links in running prose and 1,977 standalone controls.

One number, 621 times

Of the 1,977 standalone targets, 621 are under 24 pixels in one dimension. That is 31.4 per cent, which was roughly what I feared.

Then I looked at the distribution of their heights:

Height Count
20px 621

Every single one. Not a spread from 14 to 23, not a couple of outliers. One value, 621 times, because they are all the same thing: a 14px text link with a line height of 20 and no vertical padding. Widths vary from 27.5px to 273.9px. Heights do not vary at all.

They come in three groups:

  • 487 content links. The text-link underline-offset-4 style, used in headings, in captions and in list items that are not inside a p.
  • 126 navigation links. The breadcrumb "Home" on 71 pages, the contents link "Questions" on 64, the hub links "Guides" and "YouTubers by niche" on the rest.
  • 8 buttons, all on the home page, all part of the walkthrough that steps through an example entry: three "Next" buttons at 27.5 by 20, a "Done" at 31.7 by 20, and four help triggers.

The healthy part of the same distribution is a tidy ladder, which is what you get when sizes come from one component rather than from whatever felt right: 348 targets at 36px, 254 at 32, 191 at 80, 178 at 144, 145 at 56, 112 at 168, 76 at 48.

Exactly two of the 76 pages have no undersized standalone target at all: the pricing page and the about page. Both are hand-built pages of cards and buttons with no breadcrumb. The worst page is the glossary with 28, because its 27 definitions cross-link to each other and those links sit in their own div rather than in a sentence.

The exemption does all the work

2.5.8 has an escape hatch, and it is a good one. An undersized target passes anyway if a 24px diameter circle centred on it does not intersect the circle of any other target. Spacing substitutes for size, which is the right rule, because what actually makes a small target hard to hit is a neighbour you might hit instead.

That is a computation, not a judgement, so I ran it: for each of the 621 undersized targets, is any other target's centre within 24 pixels?

Zero failures. All 621 pass.

So the site meets 2.5.8 at level AA, and it meets it entirely by accident of layout. Nobody sized those links to 24. They are 20 tall and they sit in generous space, and the generous space is why they are compliant. If one day a designer tightens a line height or puts two of those links side by side, the criterion fails and nothing in the codebase will notice. That is the real finding here: the pass is not held up by anything a test or a component enforces.

Against the other two common bars, the site does worse. Apple's guidance is 44 by 44, Material's is 48 by 48. 1,243 of the 1,977 standalone targets are under 44, which is 62.9 per cent, and 1,245 are under 48. The biggest contributor is the button component itself, whose default size is h-9:

size: {
  default: "h-9 gap-1.5 px-3.5 ...",
  xs: "h-7 gap-1 px-2 text-xs ...",
  sm: "h-8 gap-1.5 px-3 text-[13px] ...",
  lg: "h-11 gap-2 px-5 text-[15px]",
  icon: "size-9",
}

36 pixels. Comfortably over the WCAG minimum, comfortably under Apple's. 412 button instances and 35 text inputs sit at that height. There is an lg at h-11, which is 44 exactly, and it is used for the places that matter most, but it is not the default.

And there is no pointer: coarse media query anywhere in 154 KB of CSS. The site makes no distinction between a mouse and a thumb. That is a defensible choice, since the same 36px button is fine with a cursor, but it is a choice by omission rather than one anybody made.

The blind spot in my own measurement

Two components in the app already solve this properly, and my audit cannot see it.

The checkbox is 16 pixels square, which would be a flagrant 2.5.8 failure if the box were the target. It is not:

"peer relative flex size-4 shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-sm border border-input bg-card ... after:absolute after:-inset-x-3 after:-inset-y-2 ..."

An absolutely positioned ::after with negative insets, 12px to each side and 8px above and below. The real hit area is 40 by 32. The switch, which is 18.4 by 32, carries the same two utilities.

getBoundingClientRect() returns the element's box. It knows nothing about a pseudo-element that catches the pointer. So an audit like mine understates those two components badly, and would understate any component that pads its hit area that way.

The method that does see it is document.elementFromPoint, which asks the browser the question a finger asks. Here it is on the glossary breadcrumb, probing out from the centre of a 38 by 20 link:

const link = document.querySelector("a[href]"); // pick a 20px one
const b = link.getBoundingClientRect();
const probe = (dy) => document.elementFromPoint(b.left + b.width / 2, b.top + b.height / 2 + dy);
probe(0);    // the link
probe(-6);   // the link
probe(-12);  // DIV, so nothing is listening up there
probe(6);    // the link
probe(12);   // DIV

Hits at six pixels out, misses at twelve. No hidden padding, so for that link the box really is the target. Run the same probe on a checkbox in the app and it keeps hitting the control well outside its box.

The lesson I am taking from it: a rect-based target audit is a screening tool, not a verdict. Everything it flags needs one elementFromPoint check before you believe it.

What I am changing

  1. Pad the navigation links. The breadcrumb and the contents list are not sentences, and py-1.5 takes them from 20 to 32 without moving anything else. That removes 126 of the 621 and, more to the point, removes them from depending on the spacing exemption.
  2. The walkthrough buttons on the home page should be real buttons. Four controls at 20px tall in a component people are meant to tap through is the one genuinely poor result in this sweep.
  3. Leave the 487 prose links alone. They are exempt, they are exempt for a good reason, and padding them would break the line rhythm of every guide on the site.
  4. Add a test that fails on a 20px standalone target. The pass is currently luck. A check in the existing page-level test suite that walks the rendered output and flags a non-inline target under 24 would make it a decision.

All of it is live. Open the glossary or a guide on a phone, or at 390px in DevTools, and you can run the sweep yourself:

[...document.querySelectorAll('a[href], button, input, summary')]
  .map((el) => ({ el, b: el.getBoundingClientRect() }))
  .filter(({ b }) => b.height > 0 && (b.width < 24 || b.height < 24))
  .length;

The number you get will be larger than mine, because that one-liner does not exempt the prose links. Mine took the exemptions seriously, which is the only way the result means anything.
