title: wtfi3: Who Is Talking to Whom on My WiFi
description:
A router's admin page lists the devices on the network and stops there. I wanted the other half: who each one is talking to. Wireshark answers that, but I wanted something I could leave open in a tab.

wtfi3 is one Go binary. Point it at an interface, open http://localhost:8080, and it draws which device talks to which service, which of those are trackers, and how many bytes are moving right now.

  • Source: https://github.com/kanywst/wtfi3
  • Install: brew install kanywst/tap/wtfi3 or go build -o wtfi3 ./cmd/wtfi3 (needs libpcap)

All screenshots here come from make demo, which serves the dashboard on synthetic household traffic. None of it is my network.

Metadata, not payloads

Nothing is decrypted. What wtfi3 reads is what is already in the clear:

  • IP and MAC addresses, with the vendor looked up in an embedded copy of the IEEE OUI list
  • bytes and packets per flow (source, destination, protocol, port)
  • DNS responses: which client asked for which name, and the answer
  • the SNI hostname in a TLS ClientHello on port 443 or 8443

The SNI parser is about a hundred lines in internal/tlsmeta/sni.go: walk the record header, skip the random, session id, cipher suites and compression methods, then look for extension 0x00. That is enough to know a device is on www.youtube.com, not which video.

Trying it without root

-r replays a pcap and needs no root. The repo has a generator for a six-packet capture: a phone and a TV doing a TLS ClientHello and a DNS lookup each.

go run hack/gensample.go sample.pcap
./wtfi3 -i nosuch0 -r sample.pcap -listen 127.0.0.1:18080
curl -s 127.0.0.1:18080/api/state

I gave it a nonexistent interface on purpose so it would not read my real one. The log says so:

WARN offline mode: interface unavailable, LAN attribution limited iface=nosuch0
INFO dashboard serving addr=127.0.0.1:18080 spoof=false
INFO finished replay; dashboard still serving (Ctrl-C to quit) addr=127.0.0.1:18080

/api/state, trimmed to the interesting fields:

"flows": [
  {"src": "192.168.0.20", "dst": "93.184.216.34", "proto": "tcp", "dst_port": 443,
   "bytes": 1584, "packets": 2, "sni": "www.youtube.com"},
  {"src": "192.168.0.31", "dst": "140.82.121.4", "proto": "tcp", "dst_port": 443,
   "bytes": 984, "packets": 2, "sni": "api.netflix.com"},
  ...
],
"dns": [
  {"client": "192.168.0.31", "name": "api.netflix.com", "type": "A", "answer": "44.242.61.10"},
  {"client": "192.168.0.20", "name": "www.youtube.com", "type": "A", "answer": "142.250.196.142"}
],
"devices": null

devices is empty because a device is a host inside one of the capture interface's on-link prefixes, and with no interface there are none. Flows and DNS do not depend on that. On a live interface the same packets fill in the device rows.

The browser gets the same JSON over Server-Sent Events, once a second, from /api/stream.

Naming the trackers

Raw flow tables tell you app-measurement.com. The Simple view tells you Google Analytics. The dictionary is 26 regexes in internal/web/index.html, covering ad networks, analytics, attribution SDKs, crash reporters, and IoT and smart TV telemetry (tuyaus.com is Tuya cloud, samsungacr.com is Samsung TV telemetry). Every pattern is anchored at a label boundary, and there is deliberately no catch-all for telemetry or metrics, because that cannot tell a third party from the device vendor's own servers.

Each device card gets a tracker badge: green for 0, amber for 1 to 4, red for 5 or more. A device that joins more than 20 seconds after startup is flagged NEW for 90 seconds. Everything already there at startup is the baseline.

The Detailed view drops the interpretation and shows the tables:

Seeing other devices

On a switched network your machine only receives its own unicast plus broadcast and multicast. Passive mode shows exactly that. To see the TV's flows you have to sit between it and the gateway, so wtfi3 has an ARP-spoof mode:

sudo ./wtfi3 -i en0 -spoof -i-own-this-network

-spoof alone refuses to run. With both flags it ARP-scans the subnet every 30 seconds, poisons each target and the gateway every 2 seconds, turns on IP forwarding, and on exit sends the real MACs back three times to restore the caches. Forwarding goes through net.inet.ip.forwarding on macOS and /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward on Linux, and goes back to whatever it was before. The gateway is the default route on the interface you capture on, not just the first default route the host has.

A relayed packet crosses the capture interface twice (target to me, me to gateway), so in spoof mode only the leg addressed to my MAC is counted. Otherwise every byte would show up double.

This is an active man-in-the-middle. Run it on a network you own.

The dashboard leaks too

The dashboard shows every device's DNS names and destinations with no password, so it binds to 127.0.0.1 by default. Loopback alone is not enough: a web page in the same browser can reach it through DNS rebinding. So while it is bound to loopback, any request whose Host is not localhost, 127.0.0.1 or ::1 gets a 403:

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H 'Host: evil.example' 127.0.0.1:18080/api/state
403

-listen 0.0.0.0:8080 still works and logs a warning. An SSH tunnel is the better way to open it from another machine.

Source and issues: https://github.com/kanywst/wtfi3

title: 🤝 Why "Customer-Facing" Matters: Building Software That Meets People Where They Are
description:
Why "Customer-Facing" Matters: Building Software That Meets People Where They Are

Engineers love internal details: the database schema, the retry policy, the service mesh. Customers never see any of it. They see one thing: whether the screen loads, whether the payment goes through, whether the error message tells them what to do next. The phrase customer-facing describes exactly that boundary, and understanding it changes how we design, test, and talk about our work.

This article explains what customer-facing means, why it deserves deliberate attention in Java and backend teams, and how to make customer-facing decisions concrete in code, APIs, and team practices.

What "Customer-Facing" Really Means

A customer-facing system or behavior is anything a customer can directly perceive or act on. That includes obvious surfaces like a mobile app or a web checkout, but it also includes:

  • The API contract that a partner integrates against
  • The error messages a user reads when something fails
  • The latency of a response that a person is waiting for
  • The notifications, invoices, and emails that arrive in their inbox
  • The support process a customer follows when they need help

The opposite term, internal, describes systems that customers never touch: batch jobs, data pipelines, internal dashboards. Both matter, but they deserve different trade-offs. A nightly reconciliation job can tolerate a retry that takes an hour. A checkout cannot.

Why the Distinction Changes Decisions

When a team forgets which parts of a system are customer-facing, priorities drift. Engineers optimize what they can measure internally, such as CPU usage or service count, while the customer experiences something else entirely: a spinner that never stops, or a confusing failure message after a successful charge.

Explicitly labeling customer-facing work helps in three ways.

First, it sets service level objectives where they matter. A customer-facing endpoint might target a p99 latency under 300 milliseconds and 99.9 percent availability, while an internal report might accept a much slower, less available path.

Second, it sets the bar for failure behavior. A customer-facing failure should degrade gracefully: show cached data, queue a request for later, or explain what happened in plain language. An internal failure can simply fail loudly and page someone.

Third, it shapes who is in the room during design. Customer-facing decisions benefit from product, support, and design input early, not after the API is already published.

Designing Customer-Facing APIs in Java

For Java backends, customer-facing usually means a REST or GraphQL API that other teams and partners depend on. Treat the contract as a product. Breaking changes hurt people you may never meet.

A few practices make that concrete. Version your endpoints and never remove a field without a deprecation period:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/orders")
public class OrderController {

    private final OrderService orderService;

    public OrderController(OrderService orderService) {
        this.orderService = orderService;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> getOrder(@PathVariable String id) {
        return orderService.findById(id)
                .map(order -> ResponseEntity.ok(OrderResponse.from(order)))
                .orElseGet(() -> ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
}

Notice that the controller returns a dedicated OrderResponse rather than the internal entity. That separation lets you change the persistence model without breaking the customer contract.

Error handling is just as visible. A global handler can translate internal exceptions into stable, customer-readable responses:

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(PaymentDeclinedException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handlePaymentDeclined(PaymentDeclinedException ex) {
        ApiError error = new ApiError(
            "PAYMENT_DECLINED",
            "Your payment could not be processed. Please check your card details or try another method.",
            ex.getCorrelationId()
        );
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.PAYMENT_REQUIRED).body(error);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handleUnexpected(Exception ex) {
        // Log the full stack trace internally; never leak it to the customer.
        ApiError error = new ApiError(
            "SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE",
            "Something went wrong on our side. Please try again in a few minutes.",
            UUID.randomUUID().toString()
        );
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE).body(error);
    }

    public record ApiError(String code, String message, String correlationId) {}
}

The correlation ID does double duty. The customer can quote it to support, and your team can find the matching log entries in seconds. That single field often turns a frustrating support ticket into a fast fix.

Latency Is a Customer Feature

Customers do not experience averages. They experience the slowest moment of their session. For customer-facing paths, track percentiles, not means, and set explicit budgets.

Timeouts belong in the design, not as an afterthought. If a downstream fraud check usually takes 80 milliseconds, decide in advance what happens when it takes two seconds. Fail open with a review queue, fail closed with a clear message, or serve a cached decision. Each option is a product decision wearing an engineering costume.

CompletableFuture<FraudDecision> fraudCheck = fraudClient.evaluateAsync(order)
        .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
        .exceptionally(ex -> FraudDecision.REVIEW_LATER);

Here the customer is not blocked by a slow dependency. The trade-off is explicit, documented, and easy to revisit.

Communicating Failure Honestly

Customer-facing communication includes what happens when things go wrong. Silence is worse than a clear, honest message. Customers tolerate delays when they know what is happening and when to expect an update.

Good practices include status pages that match reality, emails that confirm what was done and what remains pending, and idempotency keys so retries never charge a card twice. That last point deserves emphasis. A customer who clicks "pay" twice because the page froze should never be billed twice. Idempotent endpoints protect both the customer and the business.

Testing From the Customer's Point of View

Unit tests verify code. Customer-facing tests verify journeys. Build a small set of end-to-end scenarios that mirror real user actions: sign up, place an order, receive a confirmation, request a refund. Run them against a production-like environment on every release.

Contract tests matter just as much for partners. Tools such as Spring Cloud Contract or Pact let you publish the expectations partners depend on and fail the build before a breaking change ships. The customer never sees the failed build, which is the point.

Making "Customer-Facing" a Team Habit

Start by listing your customer-facing surfaces in a single document. For each one, record the owner, the target latency, the expected availability, the failure message, and the support path. Review this list in planning meetings, the same way you review security or cost.

Invite support engineers and account managers into incident reviews. They hear the customer's words directly, and their stories often reveal problems that dashboards miss. A ticket that says "the app keeps logging me out" points to a session issue no metric flagged.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating every endpoint the same. A checkout and an admin report do not need identical reliability budgets.
  • Leaking internals. Stack traces, database errors, and service names in responses confuse customers and expose your architecture.
  • Breaking contracts silently. Renaming a field can cost a partner a weekend.
  • Measuring only averages. A healthy mean can hide a painful p99.
  • Forgetting the message. A technically correct error that tells the customer nothing useful is still a bad experience.

Best Practices Checklist

  • Label every customer-facing surface and assign an owner.
  • Set latency and availability targets per surface, measured at percentiles.
  • Return stable, human-readable error codes with a correlation ID.
  • Version APIs and deprecate before removing anything.
  • Make write operations idempotent.
  • Decide timeout behavior with product input, not just engineering defaults.
  • Keep end-to-end journey tests and partner contract tests in the pipeline.
  • Include support and account teams in incident reviews.

Conclusion

Customer-facing is not a marketing label. It is a reminder that every design decision eventually reaches a person who is trying to get something done. The clearer we are about which parts of our systems customers touch, the better we can choose our trade-offs, our error messages, and our priorities.

Start small. Pick one customer-facing journey this week, map every system it touches, and ask what the customer would see if each one failed. The answers will tell you where to invest next.

Key takeaways

  • Customer-facing means anything a customer can perceive or act on, including APIs and error messages.
  • Explicit labels change priorities for latency, failure behavior, and design input.
  • Stable contracts, honest errors, and idempotent writes protect customers and the business.
  • Measure percentiles and test complete journeys, not only components.

title: Cutover Needs a No-Go: Microsoft, Workday, the FAA, and Starship Flight 15
description:
These four events landed in the same mid-November 2026 window. Nothing public connects them, and I am not suggesting a link.

What they share is a lesson about gates, verification and change discipline. Things fail at cutovers, at tests that touch production, and in old infrastructure that is finally being changed. One of the four shows the opposite pattern: an automated no-go that refused to proceed.

I build MigrateForge in Coimbatore: a system that moves PHP applications to Java 21 / Spring Boot and keeps cutover blocked until recorded user journeys match on both sides. That is not a claim that it would have prevented any of these incidents. It is about applying the same discipline to a software cutover.

Microsoft 365: the checker was in the failure path

Starting shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday, 12 November, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint Online and Copilot were disrupted for a large part of a day, with knock-on effects for organisations that depend on them. CNBC reported that engineers were still restoring service nearly 24 hours later, and that Microsoft said on Saturday, 14 November, that it had addressed the underlying issue and restored service to the remaining affected customers and regions.

Microsoft's first public account was not a traffic surge. A portion of its infrastructure was under elevated load across multiple regions because servers had become unexpectedly unavailable. As Ars Technica quoted from Microsoft's status updates, the company pointed to "a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable," which then strained the machines that remained. Recovery was slow in part because early fixes did not hold: some servers brought back online became unresponsive again once they received traffic.

Microsoft later said the disruption stemmed from "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade." CNBC reported that the company had not detected malicious activity and would issue a full report once its assessment was complete. Until that post-incident report is published, the upgrade wording is Microsoft's stated cause, not a finished root-cause analysis.

Two points matter for anyone planning a cutover.

First, a health check is a gate. If the gate fails in a way that removes healthy capacity, the rest of the system inherits the error. "The dashboard is green" is not evidence if you have not tested the checker.

Second, a workflow that lives inside someone else's cloud inherits that cloud's outages. MigrateForge is local-first: source code stays on the client's machines, and only AI requests leave. When an AI provider is down, translation runs end PAUSED or ENVIRONMENT_INVALID and resume later with nothing lost. Capture, replay, parity verification, security sweeps and evidence reports need no AI call. Several recent nights spent $0 while still producing verified waves.

Workday: a disaster-recovery test reached production

On the evening of Friday, 13 November, Workday placed all WD1 production tenants into maintenance. The company's Community Status Page notice, quoted in full by Washington University IT, said:

While validating the weekly Maintenance Window for Disaster Recovery tenants, we have identified that tenanted services within the DR Site unexpectedly connected to Production databases. As a result, this has left data in an inconsistent state that can cause errors accessing tenants or jobs/integrations/tasks to fail with missing transaction error messages.

Florida Atlantic University's IT status page reported the same pattern that night: an issue involving the disaster-recovery environment had left production data inconsistent, and production was taken offline as a precaution. FAU said users could not access the system or complete normal business activities; Washington University had to collect time by hand for staff who could not clock in. FAU said production was available again at 10:30 a.m. on Saturday, 14 November; Washington University marked the unplanned outage resolved later that afternoon, with some updates between systems still delayed. Restoration times varied by tenant. Workday has not, in public, said how many customers were affected, and a detailed root-cause report is still outstanding.

A disaster-recovery test is supposed to prove you can survive a failure. Here the test became the failure, because the recovery copy was not isolated from live databases. For a migration, the analogue is direct. If your verification environment can write to production, or if a rehearsal shares state with the live system, you are not testing. You are touching the data you are trying to protect.

The FAA: a copper-to-fiber cutover flooded the network

On Friday, 13 November, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop after communication issues hit multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers. The Verge reported that the stop went out at 3:44 p.m. ET and was lifted at 8:15 p.m. ET, a little over four hours later.

The next day, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy gave the Department's account. At a remote FAA site, contractor L3Harris was replacing discontinued copper telecommunications lines with fiber, moving from TDM to IP. A router involved in that work "started flooding other routers": more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. That disrupted communications with aircraft and radar feeds. Controllers and pilots then grounded more than 3,500 flights. Once the stop lifted, more than 8,000 flight operations resumed that night.

Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford have described the underlying telecom as a 1980s-era TDM network. Officials said they do not believe the event was a cyber attack. They have not yet determined whether the fault was installer error or a faulty router.

The airspace shutdown was itself a gate: when the data going to controllers was inconsistent, traffic stopped. The expensive part was that the inconsistency showed up in operation, during a change that was supposed to be routine, rather than in a rehearsal that could refuse to proceed.

Starship Flight 15: the no-go fired

The contrast is Starship Flight 15.

On Friday, 13 November, Super Heavy lifted off from Starbase, Texas. SpaceX's flight recap says the booster's boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass, with the root cause of that early cutoff still under investigation. During coast, the booster's guidance, navigation and control system triggered an automated abort, diverted to an offshore landing in the Gulf of Mexico, hovered, cut its engines, and the flight termination system triggered.

About 22.5 hours after liftoff, on Saturday, 14 November, the ship returned to the same pad and was caught by the tower for the first time.

SpaceX commentator Dan Huot corrected an earlier remark on the Saturday webcast: "It was not a GNC issue that caused us not to come back. GNC triggered that abort; it was doing what it was supposed to do." It had detected that the booster "was not in the place that it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch."

The catch is the new part. The gate is old. A no-go that fires automatically, against a written criterion, is how you keep a bad state from becoming a worse one. Most software migrations have no such gate. A rewrite looks done, someone switches traffic, and production is where you find out.

What a migration gate has to do

If you are moving a business-critical PHP application to Java 21 and Spring Boot, the question is the same one that GNC answered: are we where we need to be to proceed?

MigrateForge's answer is behavioural, not ceremonial:

  1. Record real user journeys on the existing PHP system.
  2. Replay them against both the legacy PHP and the new Spring Boot application.
  3. Compare HTTP responses, database writes and outgoing API calls.
  4. Keep cutover blocked until they match.

The output is standard Spring Boot. Every wave ships an evidence report. The work is local-first, as above: code stays on the client's machines.

This is the product today for plain PHP and CodeIgniter 3. Laravel is next.

What the benchmarks actually show

These are benchmarks, not client projects.

  • WA Blast Pro, my own production multi-tenant WhatsApp SaaS (plain PHP): waves 1–2, 572 fixtures, all matching.
  • InvoicePlane v1.7.2 (open-source, CodeIgniter 3.4): waves 1–2, 286 fixtures, all matching.

In total: 4 waves, 858 fixtures, 100% parity, 0 write-effect diffs and 0 HIGH findings.

First-pass parity, before hand fixes, was 82%, with 9.7 hand fixes per 1,000 PHP lines. The gate held until the rest was closed.

We also test the checker, by planting known bugs. The self-test catch rate was 57.14% on WA Blast Pro wave 1 and 35.89% on InvoicePlane wave 1. That is not 100%, and it is why we publish it next to the parity numbers. A checker you have not tested is the Microsoft lesson in miniature.

Before release, verification caught a delete that would also have removed a client's invoices and payments, a page missing its login check, data visible across tenants, and a skipped cashback payout. It also found defects in the original PHP applications.

Full evidence is at migrateforge.com/proof.

A starting point

If you run a PHP estate and a Java cutover is on the horizon, the free migration report is ₹0: size, risks, an indicative wave plan and a price range, with no source code required. It is on migrateforge.com.

For a comparison of manual rewrites, AI coding agents and parity-gated replay, see the earlier piece: PHP to Java 21 Migration in 2026: Manual Rewrite vs AI Coding Agents vs Parity-Gated Replay.

title: Miktam Bible | Part 3 — Reading Plans and Reminders That Follow Your Progress
description:
Reading plans fail in a very particular way: you miss a day, the app keeps nagging about Day 1, and you give up. Miktam Bible v1.2.1 rebuilt the planner and its notifications around what you have actually read.

🔔 Reminders that know where you are

  • Mark today's reading as done and today's pending reminder is cleared; the next one is scheduled for tomorrow's reading.
  • Notifications show the next unread day, for example "Day 4: Genesis 10–12", instead of being stuck on Genesis 1–3.
  • Finish early and the planner shows a completion banner with a Read Ahead button for tomorrow.

🌅 Verse of the Day at midnight

A daily notification at 12:00 AM delivers the Verse of the Day. It always matches the verse on the Home screen for that date, and it uses its own Android notification channel so it is delivered reliably.

⏰ Pick your own time

Fixed reminder slots are gone. Choose any hour and minute (with ±5-minute steppers) and AM or PM, or use a preset. Tap the reminder time on an active plan to change it on the fly.

📅 Real curricula, not repeated passages

Every built-in plan now follows a real schedule:

Plan Pace
Navigators 4-track 365 days, four daily readings (Gospels, Law/History, Psalms/Wisdom, Epistles)
CSB 90-day sprint the whole Bible, about 13 chapters a day
6 months whole Bible about 6–7 chapters a day
3 months New Testament Matthew to Revelation
2 months New Testament sprint about 4–5 chapters a day
1 year sequential Genesis to Revelation

Preview the first five days before you start, and browse the full schedule with All / Pending / Completed filters.

  • A crash when opening some chapters (an infinite re-render loop) is fixed.

title: How to Tune Go Checkout Uptime Alerts — Free Pingdom Alternatives
description:
For free uptime monitoring alternatives to Pingdom, start with UptimeRobot for external checks and Healthchecks.io for completion heartbeats. Get the logistics checkout operator a page that identifies the failed customer outcome; a searchable exception record supplies the context needed to act. Imagine the page says only “checkout unavailable,” while the operator needs to distinguish an unreachable backend from a running service that cannot complete an order. That is a design exercise, not a reported incident.

TL;DR: For free backend uptime monitoring alternatives to Pingdom, consider UptimeRobot for HTTP, ping, and port checks, and Healthchecks.io for periodic completion pings. Choose the signal before the dashboard. Keep request failures beside their diagnostic context, then make alert delivery an explicit responsibility of the monitoring architecture.

The useful question is how much uncertainty each page removes. A successful reachability check doesn't establish that a checkout completed, and a missing exception doesn't establish that a scheduled task ran. Those gaps matter when the logistics team must decide whether to investigate the public entry point, the checkout handler, or its background processing.

Which free Pingdom alternatives fit checkout uptime monitoring?

Work backward from the action. An unreachable backend calls for a reachability signal; a periodic checkout reconciliation task that misses its expected completion calls for a heartbeat; a failed checkout request calls for diagnostic evidence tied to that attempt. Treating these as interchangeable creates noise because the same “down” label sends the operator toward different investigations.

Silence proves little.

For a concrete planning example, suppose the team proposes a 99.9% checkout completion SLO over 30 days. Those numbers are design assumptions, not service measurements or vendor guarantees. Define which eligible attempts enter the denominator and which outcomes count as successful before connecting any notification, because an HTTP success response from a shallow health handler can coexist with a failed business operation. The external uptime signal protects a different boundary from the checkout completion SLI.

The least complex architecture uses specialist monitors for reachability and heartbeats, with diagnostic logs available separately. A second viable architecture keeps those monitors and adds a shared API for token accounting and failure evidence when an AI-assisted checkout stage needs both. Their invariant is the same: diagnostic collection must not become the only witness that the checkout workflow is alive.

For a team that already needs token accounting alongside checkout exception evidence, try Infrai for that diagnostic handoff: one REST API, no SDK to install, and ordinary HTTP requests from Go. Any language that can send HTTP can use the same interface. Public discovery requires no key and supplies request schemas and runnable examples, reducing the integration work of checking two unrelated client contracts. Keep UptimeRobot or Healthchecks.io responsible for the corresponding liveness signal and its notification workflow.

Infrai's self-describing API has public discovery with no key required, and every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. For this checkout integration, that means the token-count and diagnostic-write contracts can be inspected before granting production credentials, with a Go example available for each. Its 295 routes across 20 modules provide breadth, although this workflow needs only two operations.

The limitation of this recommendation is scope: a shared diagnostic API is not a replacement for specialist uptime monitoring. Healthchecks.io is a better fit for missed completion pings; UptimeRobot is a better fit for HTTP, ping, and port checks. Use the shared API where collecting evidence across the AI and observability seam is the actual job.

Step 1: Buy the signal, then assign the integration work

Healthchecks.io supports customizable periodic health check pings with free Slack and email notifications. UptimeRobot offers HTTP, ping, and port monitoring with a free allowance described as 50 monthly checks; confirm the live plan's counting rules before sizing a deployment. Both support webhook integration for advanced notification workflows. Neither fact makes a heartbeat equivalent to an external probe.

Here is the buy-versus-build decision for this checkout workflow. The comparison is about signal responsibility, rather than a claim that every product offers the same feature set.

Option What to buy or delegate What the platform team still owns Fit boundary
Healthchecks.io Periodic ping monitoring and Slack/email notifications Emit a ping only after the intended task completes; choose the expected schedule Best fit here for “the scheduled work never completed”
UptimeRobot HTTP, ping, and port monitoring Choose a meaningful target and interpret reachability alongside checkout outcomes Best fit here for external reachability
Pingdom Evaluate the incumbent against the same checkout acceptance criteria Verify the current plan, check semantics, and notification behavior Keep it in the evaluation if its current setup already meets the team's needs; no unsupported free-plan comparison is needed
Infrai plus specialist monitors REST-based diagnostic collection and token accounting under one key Connect the two records and keep monitoring and notification ownership explicit Useful when the diagnostic handoff reduces integration work; specialist monitors remain the choice for liveness

The free alternatives answer the original selection question directly. The fourth row answers a narrower operating question: where should evidence from an AI-assisted checkout stage go when the operator needs to understand the failure behind the page?

Capacity planning starts with the number of distinct signals, not the number of services. As an illustrative inventory, 8 services with 3 independently meaningful external checks need 24 check definitions, before any staging environments or heartbeat jobs enter the count. That is arithmetic for a proposed deployment, not a statement about a provider's billing units. Inventory the signals first, then check the live allowance and delivery expectations.

For the alternative stack named OpenAI + Sentry + Datadog, budget for three service signups and three sets of service credentials. The integration design would also need glue to carry the checkout context between token accounting, exception evidence, and telemetry. A common key reduces credential handling; it doesn't establish that two separate HTTP operations represent the same checkout attempt.

One vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface are the costs of the combined approach. That concentration belongs in the platform roadmap decision.

Step 2: Attach token accounting to the failure evidence

For an AI-assisted stage in logistics checkout, the useful handoff is the token-count operation's actual response becoming part of the diagnostic record for the failed attempt. Don't invent a correlation identifier just to make a demo look connected. Preserve the first response in the second request's diagnostic content, and retain the application's existing checkout context according to its data-handling policy.

The following Go program makes that handoff with the same key and base URL. Save it as checkout-evidence.go and run it with go run checkout-evidence.go after setting the environment variables described below. It has no third-party dependencies.

Two inputs are deliberately explicit: TOKEN_COUNT_BODY is a complete JSON request matching the current token-count schema, and LOG_INGEST_TEMPLATE is a complete JSON log-ingest request matching its current schema. Put the literal string __TOKEN_RESPONSE__ inside the template's schema-approved diagnostic text value. Copy the current request shapes from public discovery or the documentation; don't assume a field named message, model, or tokens exists merely because another API uses it. The program checks that the marker occurs exactly once and embeds the complete token response there as JSON-escaped text.

Also set INFRAI_API_KEY and a stable CHECKOUT_EVENT_KEY for this diagnostic event. Reuse the event key if rerunning the same event, and use a different one for a different event. The two operations receive distinct idempotency keys derived from that stable event key.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
const marker = "__TOKEN_RESPONSE__"

func required(name string) string {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" {
        panic("missing environment variable: " + name)
    }
    return value
}

func post(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key, path, eventKey string, body []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, baseURL+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", eventKey)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if requested := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                if requested := time.Until(when); requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s returned %d: %s", path, resp.StatusCode, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func run() error {
    key := required("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    eventKey := required("CHECKOUT_EVENT_KEY")
    tokenBody := []byte(required("TOKEN_COUNT_BODY"))
    template := required("LOG_INGEST_TEMPLATE")
    if !json.Valid(tokenBody) || !json.Valid([]byte(template)) {
        return fmt.Errorf("both request inputs must be valid JSON")
    }
    if strings.Count(template, marker) != 1 {
        return fmt.Errorf("log template must contain the marker exactly once")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 90*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    tokenResponse, err := post(ctx, client, key, "/ai/tokens/count", eventKey+":count", tokenBody)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    escaped, err := json.Marshal(string(tokenResponse))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    logBody := []byte(strings.Replace(template, marker, string(escaped[1:len(escaped)-1]), 1))
    if !json.Valid(logBody) {
        return fmt.Errorf("place the marker inside a JSON string value")
    }
    result, err := post(ctx, client, key, "/logs/ingest", eventKey+":evidence", logBody)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    fmt.Println(string(result))
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The acceptance criterion is concrete: the log request must contain the exact response returned by the token-count operation, and the program must return a nonzero exit status if either operation fails. A status error includes the service's response body so the caller can identify a rejected input. Handle that output as operational data rather than copying it into a public incident channel.

There is a common integration trap here. Sharing authentication doesn't give separate calls a shared request identity. Embedding the first response preserves the evidence actually returned, including any metadata it contains, without asserting an undocumented token-response field or promising a distributed trace. The program uses bounded exponential backoff for rate limits and honors a longer Retry-After; the overall deadline caps its work. Keep this diagnostic operation off the checkout's critical response path and give its caller an explicit failure policy.

This is an evidence collector. The external monitor and heartbeat still determine when the operator gets a page.

Step 3: Rehearse the page and count its false positives

Before enabling escalation, test three distinct cases in a controlled environment: an unreachable check target, a withheld completion ping, and a checkout failure whose diagnostic record includes the token-count response. The first should exercise external monitoring, the second should exercise the scheduled-work signal, and the third should exercise evidence collection. These are proposed acceptance tests, not measurements of any provider.

Then test a healthy checkout with a delayed diagnostic write. Decide in advance whether the evidence delay deserves a ticket or a page; otherwise an auxiliary collection problem can consume the same response budget as a customer-facing outage. The distinction should survive a busy shift.

Thresholds have an operating cost even when the monitor has a free allowance. As an illustrative exercise, if 12 checks each generate 2 unactionable pages a week, the rotation receives 24 interruptions before a real checkout failure arrives. Tightening every threshold can increase that burden; loosening every threshold can delay detection. Review the resulting pages against the checkout SLO and require each escalation to name an action an operator can take.

Choose the specialist-only architecture when reachability and missed completions answer the operational question. Add the shared diagnostic API when token accounting and exception context make the page materially easier to resolve. The false-positive cost is the final acceptance criterion: a monitor that repeatedly wakes someone without changing the next action is consuming attention the real checkout incident will need.

Further reading

References for the signal distinctions and the monitoring evaluation:

  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • UptimeRobot
  • Pingdom
  • OpenTelemetry logs signal concepts

If the shared diagnostic boundary fits your checkout workflow, start with the current schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Cómo desarrollé y desplegué una aplicación web con React, Firebase Firestore y GitHub Actions
description:
Introducción

Cuando desarrollamos una aplicación web, normalmente nos concentramos en que tenga una buena interfaz y que sus funciones trabajen correctamente. Sin embargo, una aplicación completa también necesita almacenar información, proteger los datos de sus usuarios y estar disponible desde Internet.

En este proyecto decidí desarrollar TaskFlow, una aplicación web para gestionar tareas personales utilizando React y Firebase Cloud Firestore como base de datos NoSQL. La idea fue construir un sistema sencillo, pero que permitiera trabajar con datos reales, implementar autenticación y automatizar su publicación en la nube.

Además, quería comprobar cómo funcionaba un proyecto que no dependiera de una base de datos relacional tradicional como MySQL o SQL Server. Por eso elegí Firestore, que permite almacenar información mediante colecciones y documentos.

El desarrollo también me permitió trabajar con GitHub, Firebase Hosting y GitHub Actions, herramientas que se complementan para llevar una aplicación desde mi computadora hasta un entorno público.

  1. ¿Qué es TaskFlow y qué problema resuelve?

TaskFlow es una aplicación web que permite registrar, organizar y realizar seguimiento de tareas personales.

La necesidad que busca resolver es bastante común: cuando tenemos varias actividades pendientes, podemos perder el control de cuáles ya terminamos, cuáles estamos desarrollando y cuáles todavía no hemos comenzado.

Para solucionar esto, implementé las siguientes funcionalidades:

  • Registro e inicio de sesión mediante correo electrónico y contraseña.
  • Creación de tareas con título, descripción y fecha límite.
  • Visualización de todas las tareas registradas.
  • Modificación de la información de una tarea.
  • Clasificación mediante los estados pendiente, en proceso y completada.
  • Eliminación de tareas que ya no necesitamos.
  • Filtrado de las tareas según su estado.
  • Almacenamiento de la información en Firebase Firestore.
  • Separación de las tareas según el usuario autenticado.

Aunque se trata de una aplicación relativamente pequeña, reúne funcionalidades que también podemos encontrar en sistemas de gestión más grandes.

  1. Tecnologías utilizadas

Para desarrollar el proyecto utilicé distintas herramientas, cada una con una función específica.

Tecnología Función
React Construcción de los componentes de la interfaz
Vite Entorno de desarrollo y compilación
JavaScript Lógica y funcionalidades del sistema
CSS Diseño visual y adaptación a diferentes pantallas
Firebase Authentication Registro e inicio de sesión de usuarios
Cloud Firestore Almacenamiento de los documentos NoSQL
Git y GitHub Control de versiones y repositorio público
GitHub Actions Automatización de la compilación y despliegue
Firebase Hosting Publicación de la aplicación en Internet

Elegí React porque permite construir interfaces mediante componentes y actualizar los elementos visuales cuando cambian los datos.

Por otro lado, Firebase me permitió trabajar con una base de datos alojada en la nube, sin tener que instalar y administrar un servidor de base de datos propio.

3. ¿Por qué utilicé una base de datos NoSQL?

Una de las decisiones principales del proyecto fue utilizar Cloud Firestore.

A diferencia de una base de datos relacional, donde normalmente organizamos la información en tablas, filas y columnas, Firestore utiliza colecciones y documentos.

Por ejemplo, en TaskFlow creé una colección llamada tareas. Dentro de ella, cada tarea se almacena como un documento con su propio identificador.

Un documento tiene una estructura similar a la siguiente:

{
  "titulo": "Primera tarea NoSQL",
  "descripcion": "Comprobar la conexión con Firebase",
  "estado": "Pendiente",
  "fecha": "2026-11-20",
  "creada": "2026-11-14T23:08:15.890Z",
  "usuarioId": "identificador_del_usuario"
}

En este caso, el documento almacena la información de una tarea sin que tengamos que definir previamente una tabla SQL.

Algo importante es que Firestore también permite trabajar con consultas, reglas de seguridad y actualizaciones en tiempo real.

Esto fue especialmente útil en TaskFlow, porque las tareas pueden mostrarse nuevamente en la interfaz cuando se produce un cambio en la base de datos.

Organización de los datos

La estructura utilizada fue:

Cloud Firestore
└── tareas
    ├── Documento 1
    │   ├── titulo
    │   ├── descripcion
    │   ├── estado
    │   ├── fecha
    │   ├── creada
    │   └── usuarioId
    │
    └── Documento 2
        ├── titulo
        ├── descripcion
        ├── estado
        ├── fecha
        ├── creada
        └── usuarioId

Cada documento tiene un identificador generado por Firestore. El campo usuarioId permite relacionar las tareas con la cuenta que las creó.

  1. Creación del proyecto con React y Vite

Comencé el desarrollo desde Visual Studio Code, utilizando Node.js y npm para gestionar las dependencias.

Primero ejecuté:

npm create vite@latest taskflow -- --template react

Después ingresé a la carpeta e instalé las dependencias:

cd taskflow
npm install

Para iniciar el servidor de desarrollo utilicé:

npm run dev

Con esto pude abrir la aplicación desde el navegador mediante una dirección local como:

http://localhost:5173/

Al principio aparecía la pantalla predeterminada de Vite. Posteriormente la reemplacé por la interfaz de TaskFlow.

Diseño de la interfaz

Busqué que la aplicación tuviera una apariencia sencilla y organizada. Para ello desarrollé un panel con menú lateral, tarjetas de estadísticas, formulario de registro y listado de tareas.

También incorporé colores diferentes para representar los estados:

  • Pendiente: color naranja.
  • En proceso: color azul.
  • Completada: color verde.

La intención fue que el usuario pudiera identificar rápidamente el avance de sus actividades sin tener que ingresar a cada una.

  1. Conexión de React con Firebase

Una vez terminada la interfaz, el siguiente paso fue conectar la aplicación con los servicios de Firebase.

Primero creé el proyecto taskflow-nosql desde Firebase Console y registré una aplicación web.

Después instalé el SDK de Firebase:

npm install firebase

Dentro de la carpeta src creé un archivo llamado firebase.js, encargado de inicializar Firebase y exportar los servicios utilizados.

La estructura principal es la siguiente:

import { initializeApp } from 'firebase/app';
import { getFirestore } from 'firebase/firestore';
import { getAuth } from 'firebase/auth';

const firebaseConfig = {
  // Configuración de la aplicación web
  // proporcionada por Firebase Console
};

const app = initializeApp(firebaseConfig);

export const db = getFirestore(app);
export const auth = getAuth(app);

Con esta configuración preparé dos servicios: db, para acceder a Cloud Firestore, y auth, para trabajar con Firebase Authentication.

Un detalle importante es que la configuración del cliente no debe confundirse con las claves privadas de una cuenta de servicio. Estas últimas nunca deben publicarse en un repositorio.

6. Implementación del registro e inicio de sesión

Antes de conectar todas las tareas a Firestore, consideré necesario implementar autenticación.

Para ello habilité el método de correo electrónico y contraseña en Firebase Authentication.

Después desarrollé un componente llamado AuthGate.jsx, encargado de comprobar si existe una sesión activa.

Para registrar usuarios utilicé:

import {
  createUserWithEmailAndPassword,
  signInWithEmailAndPassword,
  signOut
} from 'firebase/auth';

Por ejemplo, para registrar una cuenta se utiliza:

await createUserWithEmailAndPassword(
  auth,
  correo,
  password
);

Y para iniciar sesión:

await signInWithEmailAndPassword(
  auth,
  correo,
  password
);

De esta manera, el usuario primero debe autenticarse para acceder al panel de tareas.

Durante esta implementación encontré un error relacionado con una API Key que Firebase no reconocía. Después de revisar el mensaje de error, recuperé la configuración original desde Firebase Console y corregí el archivo de conexión.

Esta experiencia me permitió entender que, cuando un servicio externo falla, resulta importante revisar el código específico del error en lugar de modificar varias partes de la aplicación sin saber cuál es el problema.

  1. Implementación de las operaciones CRUD en Firestore

Una vez configurada la autenticación, conecté las principales funcionalidades de TaskFlow con Cloud Firestore.

Las operaciones CRUD permiten crear, consultar, actualizar y eliminar información.

Crear una tarea (CREATE)

Para registrar una tarea utilicé la función addDoc():

await addDoc(collection(db, 'tareas'), {
  titulo: formulario.titulo,
  descripcion: formulario.descripcion,
  fecha: formulario.fecha,
  estado: formulario.estado,
  usuarioId: usuario.uid,
  creada: new Date().toISOString()
});

Cuando el usuario presiona el botón de crear tarea, los datos se envían a Firestore y se genera automáticamente un documento.

Consultar las tareas (READ)

Para recuperar las tareas implementé una consulta filtrada mediante el identificador del usuario.

const consulta = query(
  collection(db, 'tareas'),
  where('usuarioId', '==', usuario.uid)
);

Además, utilicé onSnapshot() para escuchar los cambios en tiempo real.

onSnapshot(consulta, (snapshot) => {
  const tareas = snapshot.docs.map((documento) => ({
    ...documento.data(),
    id: documento.id
  }));

  setTareas(tareas);
});

Esto permite que el listado se actualice cuando Firestore informa de cambios, sin tener que recargar manualmente toda la aplicación.

Actualizar una tarea (UPDATE)

Para editar las tareas utilicé updateDoc():

await updateDoc(
  doc(db, 'tareas', idTarea),
  {
    titulo: nuevoTitulo,
    descripcion: nuevaDescripcion,
    estado: nuevoEstado
  }
);

Con esta operación podemos modificar el contenido de un documento existente, manteniendo su identificador.

También utilicé esta función para cambiar el estado de una tarea a completada.

Eliminar una tarea (DELETE)

Finalmente, implementé la eliminación mediante deleteDoc():

await deleteDoc(
  doc(db, 'tareas', idTarea)
);

Antes de eliminar, la aplicación solicita una confirmación al usuario.

De esta manera, TaskFlow cuenta con las cuatro operaciones CRUD conectadas directamente con una base de datos NoSQL.

  1. Seguridad de la información

Además de registrar usuarios, fue necesario proteger las tareas almacenadas en Firestore.

Para ello configuré reglas de seguridad basadas en Firebase Authentication.

La lógica principal consiste en comprobar que el usuario esté autenticado y que el campo usuarioId del documento coincida con su identificador.

Una regla utilizada para consultar tareas fue:

allow read: if request.auth != null
  && resource.data.usuarioId == request.auth.uid;

También configuré restricciones para crear, actualizar y eliminar documentos.

En la actualización se comprueba tanto la propiedad actual como que el documento mantenga el mismo propietario.

Estas reglas permiten establecer un primer nivel de separación entre usuarios. Para una versión de producción más exigente también sería recomendable validar los campos, tipos de datos y tamaños de los documentos.

9. Publicación del código en GitHub

Después de desarrollar y probar la aplicación, utilicé Git para controlar las versiones y publicar el código fuente.

Inicialicé el repositorio local:

git init

Después preparé los archivos y registré los cambios:

git add .
git commit -m "Version inicial de TaskFlow con React y Firebase"

Finalmente conecté el repositorio local con GitHub y publiqué los archivos en la rama principal.

git branch -M main
git push -u origin main

También configuré .gitignore para evitar incluir carpetas innecesarias como node_modules y archivos privados de entorno.

El repositorio público contiene el código de la aplicación y permite revisar cómo se implementaron las funcionalidades.

Repositorio del proyecto:

https://github.com/fm2021072628/taskflow-nosql-firebase

  1. Despliegue de la aplicación en Firebase Hosting

Una vez publicado el repositorio, el siguiente objetivo fue hacer que TaskFlow estuviera disponible desde Internet.

Para ello utilicé Firebase Hosting, un servicio que permite alojar aplicaciones web.

Primero instalé Firebase CLI:

npm install -g firebase-tools

Después inicié sesión:

firebase login

Configuré Hosting para utilizar la carpeta dist, porque allí Vite genera los archivos de producción.

Para compilar la aplicación ejecuté:

npm run build

Y posteriormente:

firebase deploy --only hosting

Firebase confirmó que los archivos se habían cargado y que la nueva versión estaba publicada.

Finalmente obtuve la dirección pública:

Aplicación desplegada:

https://taskflow-nosql.web.app

Gracias a esto, TaskFlow dejó de depender de mi computadora y pasó a estar disponible mediante una dirección web pública.

  1. Automatización del despliegue con GitHub Actions

Una de las partes más interesantes del proyecto fue automatizar la publicación.

Inicialmente, cada vez que necesitaba actualizar la aplicación, debía ejecutar manualmente los comandos de compilación y despliegue.

Aunque este procedimiento funciona, no resulta tan práctico cuando realizamos cambios constantemente.

Por eso decidí integrar GitHub Actions con Firebase Hosting.

¿Cómo funciona la automatización?

El proceso es el siguiente:

  1. Modifico el código de TaskFlow en Visual Studio Code.
  2. Registro los cambios mediante Git.
  3. Envío los cambios a la rama main de GitHub.
  4. GitHub Actions detecta la actualización.
  5. Se ejecuta el flujo configurado para compilar y publicar la aplicación.
  6. Firebase Hosting recibe la nueva versión.

Para preparar la automatización utilicé:

firebase init hosting:github

Este comando generó archivos de configuración dentro de:

.github/
└── workflows/
    ├── firebase-hosting-merge.yml
    └── firebase-hosting-pull-request.yml

El primero permite desplegar cuando se incorporan cambios a la rama principal. El segundo permite trabajar con versiones de vista previa para solicitudes de extracción.

Problema durante la configuración

No todo funcionó en el primer intento.

Durante la integración, Firebase mostró un error relacionado con una cuenta de servicio de Google Cloud que no podía encontrar.

Para resolverlo revisé la sección de IAM, confirmé la existencia de la cuenta de servicio creada para GitHub Actions y configuré los permisos necesarios para Firebase Hosting.

Después repetí la configuración y Firebase consiguió generar los archivos del flujo de trabajo.

Finalmente envié esos archivos al repositorio mediante Git.

Resultado de la automatización

Al ingresar a la pestaña Actions del repositorio, pude observar una ejecución de GitHub Actions asociada al despliegue de Firebase Hosting.

La ejecución finalizó correctamente y apareció una marca verde, con una duración registrada de aproximadamente 50 segundos.

Esto confirmó que el flujo de automatización se había ejecutado sin errores.

Automatización del proyecto:

https://github.com/fm2021072628/taskflow-nosql-firebase/actions

12. Pruebas realizadas

Durante el desarrollo realicé distintas pruebas para comprobar las funcionalidades principales.

Prueba Resultado observado
Registro de tareas Se creó un documento en Cloud Firestore
Consulta de tareas Las tareas aparecieron en la interfaz
Edición Se modificó el título, la descripción y el estado de una tarea
Cambio de estado Se visualizaron los estados pendiente, en proceso y completada
Autenticación Se implementó el registro y acceso con Firebase
Compilación Vite generó correctamente la aplicación de producción
Despliegue Firebase Hosting confirmó la publicación
Automatización GitHub Actions mostró una ejecución exitosa

Estas pruebas permitieron comprobar la integración entre React, Firebase y GitHub.

Sin embargo, todavía quedan mejoras que podrían incorporarse, como ampliar las pruebas de seguridad entre diferentes cuentas y optimizar el tamaño del JavaScript generado.

13. Dificultades encontradas y soluciones

Durante el desarrollo aparecieron algunos problemas que considero importantes mencionar porque forman parte del aprendizaje.

Error en la configuración de Firebase. Al principio, Firebase Authentication rechazaba la API Key. Lo solucioné recuperando la configuración correcta desde Firebase Console.

Diferencia entre almacenamiento local y NoSQL. Inicialmente las tareas se guardaban en el navegador mediante localStorage. Después sustituí ese almacenamiento por operaciones con Firestore, permitiendo trabajar con documentos almacenados en la nube.

Errores al configurar GitHub Actions. La integración automática presentó problemas de autorización y de cuentas de servicio. Para solucionarlos tuve que revisar la configuración de Google Cloud IAM.

Advertencia durante la compilación. Vite informó que uno de los archivos JavaScript generados era relativamente grande. La compilación terminó correctamente, pero esta advertencia señala una oportunidad de optimización futura.

Estas dificultades me ayudaron a comprender mejor la relación entre el código de una aplicación y los servicios que necesita para funcionar.

14. Posibles mejoras del proyecto

Aunque TaskFlow ya cuenta con las funcionalidades principales, todavía se podrían incorporar mejoras.

Por ejemplo, sería útil agregar prioridades a las tareas, implementar búsqueda por palabras clave y mostrar estadísticas más detalladas sobre las actividades completadas.

También podría mejorarse la interfaz de autenticación, incorporando recuperación de contraseña y verificación de correo electrónico.

Desde el lado técnico, sería recomendable ampliar las validaciones de Firestore, realizar pruebas automatizadas y optimizar el tamaño de los archivos de producción.

Estas mejoras permitirían convertir TaskFlow en una herramienta más completa y preparada para un mayor número de usuarios.

15. Conclusiones

Desarrollar TaskFlow me permitió comprender que crear una aplicación web no consiste únicamente en diseñar pantallas o programar botones. También es necesario pensar en dónde se almacenarán los datos, cómo se protegerán y de qué manera se publicará el sistema.

Uno de los aprendizajes principales fue trabajar con una base de datos NoSQL como Cloud Firestore. A través de sus colecciones y documentos pude implementar operaciones CRUD sin tener que construir una base de datos relacional tradicional.

Otro aspecto importante fue la integración de Firebase Authentication, porque permitió incorporar el concepto de usuarios autenticados y separar sus tareas mediante identificadores.

Finalmente, GitHub Actions me ayudó a comprender cómo funciona la automatización dentro del desarrollo de software. En lugar de depender completamente de comandos manuales, es posible preparar un flujo que ejecute tareas de compilación y despliegue cuando se actualiza el repositorio.

En general, este proyecto me permitió aplicar diferentes conocimientos en una sola aplicación: desarrollo frontend, bases de datos NoSQL, autenticación, control de versiones, servicios en la nube y automatización.

Lo que más destaco es que pude pasar de una aplicación que inicialmente funcionaba solo en mi computadora a un sistema publicado en Internet, con almacenamiento en la nube y un flujo de despliegue automatizado.

title: Building a Production-Grade Streaming AI-Agent Chat Workspace with Shadcn UI & React
description:
Most AI chat tutorials stop at a basic <input> box and a unstyled <div> list. When you ship a real AI-Agent Workspace to production, users immediately expect multi-thread conversation history, smart auto-scrolling that doesn't hijack manual reading, syntax-highlighted markdown blocks with one-click copy hooks, and clean attachment trays.

Here is the core frontend architecture pattern to keep a React + TypeScript + Shadcn UI streaming chat interface responsive at 60fps.

1. Non-Intrusive Auto-Scroll During Token Streaming

When an LLM streams tokens rapidly, forcing scrollIntoView() on every chunk locks the user out of scrolling up to read earlier paragraphs. Track whether the user is near the bottom before auto-scrolling:

import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from "react";

export function useSmartChatScroll(dependency: unknown) {
  const containerRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const [shouldAutoScroll, setShouldAutoScroll] = useState(true);

  const handleScroll = () => {
    const el = containerRef.current;
    if (!el) return;
    const distanceFromBottom = el.scrollHeight - el.scrollTop - el.clientHeight;
    setShouldAutoScroll(distanceFromBottom < 80);
  };

  useEffect(() => {
    if (shouldAutoScroll && containerRef.current) {
      containerRef.current.scrollTop = containerRef.current.scrollHeight;
    }
  }, [dependency, shouldAutoScroll]);

  return { containerRef, handleScroll };
}

2. Memoizing Message Bubbles to Prevent Re-Render Lag

During active streaming, only the last message in the array changes on each token. Wrap completed message components in React.memo so React doesn't re-parse heavy markdown syntax across 50 historical messages every 20 milliseconds.

3. Collapsible Multi-Thread Sidebar & Dark-Mode Tokens

Using Shadcn UI CSS variables (--background, --card, --muted, --border) paired with a collapsible drawer keeps desktop workspaces spacious while adapting cleanly to mobile viewports without layout shift.

title: I built an open-source debugging lab for Android emulators and iOS simulators
description:
When I debug a mobile app I end up with six tools open: Logcat, the Instruments window, Android Studio's profilers, a proxy like Charles, a terminal full of adb shell and xcrun simctl, and a text editor to read some database I pulled off the device. Every one of them knows a slice of what the emulator knows, and none of them talk to each other.

So I built EmuLabZip: one open-source app that connects to your running Android emulators and iOS simulators and brings all of that into one window. It is written in Rust, ships as a desktop app (Tauri + Svelte) and as a command line tool, and nothing gets installed on the device.

What it does

You start an emulator or boot a simulator, and it shows up. There is no setup on the device and nothing to add to your app. From there:

  • Logs from logcat and the iOS unified log in one table that stays smooth at thousands of lines per second, with level, tag, text, regex and per-app filters.
  • Performance and memory: CPU, memory, frame rate, janky frames and battery for the app you pick, memory snapshots you can diff by category, and Android heap dumps with a built-in leak finder.
  • Network: a debugging proxy that decrypts HTTPS, with mocks, breakpoints, throttling, GraphQL and gRPC decoding.
  • Storage: browse an app's files and open SQLite, SharedPreferences, property lists, MMKV, Realm and more in place.
  • Crashes: crashes, native crashes and ANRs with their stacks, readable when you give it your R8 mapping.txt, source map or dSYM.
  • Sessions: record a whole run (logs, requests, crashes, screen video, touches) into one file you can open later, compare, or collect from CI.

Why Rust, and why no agent on the device

EmuLabZip does not inject anything into your app. It speaks the public interfaces of each platform: for Android it has its own async client for the ADB host protocol (no need to shell out to adb for every call), and for iOS it drives xcrun simctl. The Android and Apple code lives in separate crates behind one Backend trait, so the desktop app and the CLI use exactly the same code.

That also means it keeps working when Xcode or Android Studio update, because it depends on interfaces they have to keep.

The same data in a terminal

Everything the app shows is also a command. Start a device, then:

emulabzip devices
emulabzip logs
emulabzip mem com.example.app
emulabzip net --har capture.har
emulabzip crashes --app com.example.app

Each command prints tables for people and --json for scripts. The same engine runs in CI: emulabzip ci records a session around your test command and exits with its exit code, so a pipeline behaves as before and you get a file to open when something fails. I will write about that in a later post.

And it talks to AI assistants

EmuLabZip includes an MCP server (emulabzip mcp). Connect Claude, Cursor or VS Code and the assistant can read your logs and crashes, follow the traffic live, drive the screen and record a session. It cannot wipe or rewrite anything unless you start the server with --allow-writes, and then each change asks you first. There is a post about that too.

Try it

The desktop app has installers for macOS, Windows and Linux. The command line tool installs with Cargo:

cargo install --git https://github.com/LuisPeixoto/EmuLabZip emulabzip-cli

Then start an emulator or simulator and run emulabzip devices.

  • Website and documentation: emulabzip.luispeixoto.dev
  • Getting started guide: emulabzip.luispeixoto.dev/docs/getting-started/
  • Source code and releases (MIT): github.com/LuisPeixoto/EmuLabZip

If something breaks or is missing, tell me in an issue. It is a one-person project and the roadmap follows what people need.

Also in Portuguese: Criei um laboratório de debug open source para emuladores Android e simuladores iOS

title: Your cron job will fire twice. Design for it.
description:
Every tutorial for scheduled work has the same shape. A cron expression, a route handler, a loop over users, a call to an email API. It runs on the author's machine for two days and then it ships.

Then production happens. The platform retries a 502 that actually succeeded. A deploy lands mid-run and two workers process the same batch. The retry after a rate limit sends the digest a second time. A customer forwards the duplicate to support, and someone writes a ticket titled "we got this twice," and that is the first time anybody thinks about delivery semantics.

Cron is a trigger, not a scheduler. The moment your work leaves the process, you are in at-least-once territory, and at-least-once means duplicates are not an edge case. They are the contract.

Make the duplicate impossible, not unlikely

The fix is not a sent_at column you check before sending, because check-then-send has a race and you will find it at 3 a.m. with two workers that both read null.

The fix is a unique constraint that decides the winner atomically, before any side effect:

import pg from "pg";
const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

async function claim(eventId) {
  const { rowCount } = await pool.query(
    `insert into processed_events (event_id, claimed_at)
     values ($1, now())
     on conflict (event_id) do nothing`,
    [eventId]
  );
  return rowCount === 1; // true only for the first caller
}

if (!(await claim(event.id))) return; // someone else has it, or we already did

Two details matter more than the code. The key must come from the event, not from a timestamp or a random UUID you generate at send time, and it must be stable across retries. If your queue redelivers with a fresh ID, the constraint does nothing for you. And on conflict do nothing returning rowCount = 0 tells you the event was already claimed, which is exactly the information you need to skip quietly instead of erroring.

For the recurring job itself, the same idea applies at the job level. A single-flight lock beats a if (running) return flag in memory, which does nothing when you run three replicas:

const { rows } = await pool.query(
  `select pg_try_advisory_lock(hashtext('nightly-digest')) as locked`
);
if (!rows[0].locked) return;
try {
  await runDigest();
} finally {
  await pool.query(`select pg_advisory_unlock(hashtext('nightly-digest'))`);
}

Bound the concurrency or drown

The other half of this problem is what happens when your provider pushes back. A loop over ten thousand users with await inside is slow but polite. A loop with Promise.all is fast and gets you a 429 within seconds, and then the retry storm makes it worse.

Bound the in-flight requests, and treat 429 as an instruction rather than an error:

import pLimit from "p-limit";
const limit = pLimit(4); // provider allows ~5 concurrent, leave headroom

async function sendWithRetry(payload, attempt = 0) {
  try {
    return await limit(() => post("/v1/messages", payload));
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.status === 429 && attempt < 5) {
      const retryAfter = Number(err.headers.get("retry-after") ?? 0);
      const backoff = retryAfter * 1000 || 2 ** attempt * 1000;
      await sleep(backoff + Math.random() * 250); // jitter
      return sendWithRetry(payload, attempt + 1);
    }
    throw err;
  }
}

Three things in there that get skipped in tutorials. Retry-After is honored when the server sends it, because the server knows better than your exponential curve. Jitter is added, because identical backoff across workers synchronizes them into a thundering herd. And there is an attempt cap, because a permanent failure should land in a dead letter queue where a human sees it, not in an infinite loop that burns your quota.

Cap it, then route it. A row in a failed_jobs table with the last error and the payload hash is worth more than any amount of clever retry logic, because it makes the failure visible instead of ambient.

Don't enqueue from inside the transaction you can still roll back

One pattern bites every team once. You write to the database and publish to the queue in the same handler. The write commits, the publish fails, and the work is lost. Or the write rolls back after the publish, and the consumer acts on a record that does not exist.

Use an outbox: write the event to a table in the same transaction as the state change, then have a separate poller publish and mark it sent. It costs one table and one query per tick, and it converts a distributed consistency problem into a local one.

create table outbox (
  id          bigserial primary key,
  topic       text not null,
  payload     jsonb not null,
  created_at  timestamptz not null default now(),
  sent_at     timestamptz
);
create index on outbox (id) where sent_at is null;

The poller claims rows with for update skip locked, which lets you run it on every replica without coordination. That is the whole trick, and it is the same trick as the idempotency key: let the database decide who wins.

The test that would have caught it

Before any of this, write the test that fails on the tutorial version of the code.

Fire the same event twice into your handler with the same event ID. Assert that exactly one email exists in the fake provider, that the second call returns 2xx, and that no error is thrown. Then add the harder one: two concurrent calls with the same ID, awaited together, asserting one send. That second test is the one that proves your constraint is doing the work instead of your application logic.

Both run in about fifty milliseconds. Neither requires a queue, a fake clock, or a staging environment.

What you actually owe the reader

The "cron plus webhook" post is not wrong because it is simple. It is wrong because it teaches a delivery model that does not exist. Nobody gets exactly-once across a network boundary, and the tutorials that skip that sentence are the reason the same digest goes out twice to a customer who has already unsubscribed once.

Write the duplicate test first. Put the unique index in before the feature ships. And when someone asks why there is a processed_events table that seems to do nothing, tell them it is the part of the system that keeps the rest of it honest.

title: Why "it works on my machine" isn't enough for open-source QA
description:
When you build an open-source testing framework, you reach a point where the code is done, the tests are passing, and the features are implemented.

For a lot of developers, that's the end of the line. "It works on my machine. I'm done."

But for a framework to be truly valuable to a client, that is only the halfway point. The code existing is not the same thing as the code being reliable.

I've been building Praman, an open-source QA engine in Python. The test suite just crossed 910 passing tests. The API automation, browser sessions, configuration, and reporting are all implemented. But as I look at my roadmap, I realize the hardest work is still ahead: proving it actually works in the real world.

Here is why building a framework for real clients requires a different mindset.

When you build a feature, it's easy to mark it as "done" in your head. But a QA framework requires independent validation.

If I build a wheel and test it locally, that proves the wheel builds. It doesn't prove that a developer in a different environment can install it, import it, and run a test without it breaking. To prove that, I have to build the wheel, spin up a completely isolated Python 3.12 environment, install the wheel from scratch, and run an external client smoke test.

Only then is the packaging "done."

Phase 5 of my roadmap is AI-assisted testing. It's the most exciting part. I want to build LLM integration, failure analysis, and suggested fixes.

But I am deliberately not starting it yet.

If I introduce an AI agent that analyzes failures, but my JSON failure reports are inconsistent, the AI will give me bad analysis. If I add LLM code generation, but my isolated installation tests aren't passing, the AI will generate tests that don't run.

You cannot build advanced AI features on top of a shaky foundation. The execution, reporting, and evidence systems have to be bulletproof first.

I created a "Foundation Release Candidate" checklist for the next milestone. It doesn't just ask "does the code exist?" It asks:

  • Does the latest wheel build and install independently?
  • Do the external client tests pass?
  • Are failure screenshots and redaction verified?
  • Does the latest hosted GitHub Actions run succeed?

If any of these are false, the foundation isn't ready.

A passing test suite is a great milestone. It means you have 910 examples of your code doing the right thing. But a reliable framework is not just about the tests you write. It's about isolated client installation, clean CI pipelines, and documenting exactly what has been verified.

If you are building a tool for other developers, don't just ask if it works on your machine. Ask if it works on theirs.

You can see the current progress and the roadmap on the repository: https://github.com/pranromumu/praman
