title: De 360 formas de escribir un archivo, sólo una escribe
description:
Fecha: 2026-11-14 · Base medida: el gate de pre-vuelo de este repositorio, con la precedencia leída de su propio código y una tabla de 360 estados precalculada.
Origen de las cifras: la tabla viaja dentro de la página publicada; cualquiera puede abrirla y contar.

El problema no es el código de salida: es el orden

Un pre-vuelo que bloquea escrituras suele presentarse como una lista de comprobaciones. La nuestra tiene 13 códigos de salida y 12 posiciones de guarda, y esa diferencia de uno ya dice algo: dos códigos (11 y 19) comparten posición porque describen el mismo hecho visto desde dos lados —la huella ya habita el destino— y sólo se distinguen por si el blob es el contratado.

Lo que casi nunca se documenta es la precedencia. Sobre un archivo que git ignora, ¿qué se informa: que está sucio o que está fuera de perímetro? Depende del orden, y el orden casi siempre vive en la cabeza de quien lo escribió.

En este repositorio el orden se publica en el propio gate, en una línea:

20 -> 29 -> 10 -> 31 -> 14 -> 23 -> 11/19 -> 12 -> 13 -> 24 -> 15 -> 0

Traducido: primero la aridad de la tupla, después la divergencia de rama, después si el destino existe, después si el universo está vacío, después si hay árbol git, después si el archivo está ignorado, y sólo entonces el desfase del blob.

Seis preguntas, 360 estados

El formulario interactivo pregunta seis cosas:

# pregunta opciones
1 la tupla de pre-vuelo 2
2 el estado del destino 3
3 el estado del árbol git 5
4 el blob del disco frente al contrato 2
5 la huella en el destino 3
6 las líneas frente al contrato 2

2 · 3 · 5 · 2 · 3 · 2 = 360. El simulador no ejecuta el gate: tiene la tabla precalculada y responde qué guarda dispara primero para cada una de las 360 combinaciones.

De las 360, exactamente una llega al permiso terminal. El reparto medido:

código qué informa estados
20 uso incorrecto: aridad, argumento inválido o TARGET no absoluto 180
31 universo vacío — destino sin bytes con LINEAS_PRE > 0 48
10 el destino no existe: es un alta 48
29 divergencia de rama: la base es caduca 36
23 el TARGET está ignorado por git y fuera del perímetro 12
14 el destino no vive en un árbol git 12
11 la huella ya habita el destino y el blob es el contratado 8
19 la huella habita el destino pero el blob no es el contratado 8
12 blob distinto al contrato 4
13 estado sucio por cambios ajenos al TARGET 2
15 líneas distintas al contrato 1
0 pre-vuelo correcto 1

La mitad de los estados son un error de llamada. Eso no es un detalle: si la mitad de los usos falla en la aridad, el problema no es el gate, es su interfaz.

Por qué el 23 va antes del 12

Hay una decisión en ese orden que vale la pena aislar. Un archivo ignorado por git y sin perímetro declarado está prohibido, con independencia de que su blob coincida o no con el contrato.

Si el gate midiera primero el desfase, el mensaje sería «tu blob cambió» y alguien lo leería como «actualiza la tupla». Sería un gate que mide para autorizar sobre un objeto que no puede autorizar. El orden es entonces parte del contrato, no un detalle de implementación: por eso se publica y por eso el simulador lo lee del código en vez de tenerlo escrito a mano.

Lo que no se puede simular, se declara

El código 24 —el índice declara un bit de frescura (assume-unchanged, skip-worktree), así que git status --porcelain devuelve vacío aunque el disco haya cambiado— está en la lista, tiene su posición (la 10) y no aparece nunca en la tabla de 360.

La razón es que assume-unchanged no es una pregunta de este formulario. Hay dos salidas posibles: inventar un estado donde ese código dispare, o declararlo. El artefacto lo declara, en un campo aparte:

{"codigo": 24, "motivo": "el bit de frescura del indice no se pregunta en este formulario"}

Un cero en una tabla se lee como «no ocurre». Y 24 sí ocurre: ocurre en el mundo real, todos los días, cuando alguien marca un archivo como assume-unchanged para que git status deje de molestarle. Un simulador que lo omitiera en silencio mentiría por omisión.

La página se deriva, no se teclea

El detalle que hace todo esto mantenible: el HTML no es texto escrito a mano. Se genera a partir de dos fuentes —la línea de orden y la tabla de la taxonomía— y cada bloque viaja con el identificador del objeto git de su fuente en el momento de generar.

Eso da una propiedad concreta: si el gate cambia y la página no se regenera, un comparador lo dice con los dos identificadores a la vista, y el despliegue se detiene. La página publicada es el sujeto de la medición, no una copia de la idea.

Y no hay ninguna llamada de red: la tabla de 360 estados va embebida en el documento. Se puede abrir sin conexión.

Pruébalo

El simulador está en línea y es de una sola página:

https://indice-rc.vercel.app/simulador.html

Mueve los seis controles y mira qué guarda dispara primero. Si encuentras una combinación donde el resultado te parece injusto, ese es exactamente el punto: el orden se puede discutir, pero ahora está a la vista.

title: Fixing a Concurrency Bug an Architect Caught in My Flink-Qdrant Connector
description:
The connector nobody had built yet

Apache Flink didn't have an official SQL connector for Qdrant, the vector database. I use both — Flink for streaming pipelines, Qdrant for the embedding store downstream — so I built flink-connector-qdrant to close that gap: a Flink SQL sink that upserts points into Qdrant directly from a streaming job, no glue code in between.

It shipped, people started using it, and then an architect reviewing it on LinkedIn pointed out something I'd missed.

The bug

My upsert path stored a version number per point so that if the same ID arrived twice, the connector could tell which write was newer and keep that one. Straightforward, except for one thing: storing a version number alone doesn't guarantee atomic ordering under concurrent writers.

Picture two parallel sink tasks racing on the same point ID. Writer A has version 5, writer B has version 6. There's no guarantee B's write lands after A's just because its version number is higher — depending on timing, A can still land last and silently overwrite the newer data. A bare version field tells you which value should win; it doesn't make the database enforce that when two writes are in flight at the same time.

That's a real data-correctness bug, not a style nit. In a streaming sink, "newer data wins" is the whole point of upserts.

The fix

I added an opt-in version-field option: when configured, the connector deduplicates by highest version within a batch before the Qdrant write goes out, instead of trusting Qdrant to sort it out writer by writer. Same version field the architect was looking at, but the ordering guarantee now lives on my side of the wire, where I actually control it.

I shipped it as three separate commits — a fix for the dedup logic, a feat for the opt-in config surface, and a docs commit explaining when to turn it on — instead of squashing it into one. Reviewing a bug fix is easier when you're not also reviewing a new feature flag in the same diff, and it meant the person who raised the issue could actually see the fix land commit by commit rather than taking my word for it.

The other repo

Same week, I pushed multi-cluster support into apache-flink-mcp-server — it lets AI assistants talk to a Flink cluster over MCP (Model Context Protocol), but until now it only knew about one cluster at a time, which doesn't match how anyone actually runs Flink. It also picked up its listing on the Glama MCP directory.

Neither of these projects is glamorous. They're the kind of infrastructure that's only interesting when it's wrong. But getting real review from someone who actually reads the code, and being able to turn that into a fix the same week, is the part of open source that's worth writing about.

If you're running vector search behind a Flink pipeline, or you want an AI assistant that can actually see what's happening in your Flink cluster, both repos are open for issues and PRs.

title: Account Recovery Hardening: The Side Door Next to Your Passkey
description:
A SaaS team I worked with rolled out passkeys last spring and celebrated a big drop in password-reset tickets. Three months later, a review of their support logs showed something uncomfortable. Their "lost my passkey" flow sent a magic link to the account email, the link stayed valid for seven days, it could be reused, and changing the email address did not require any re-authentication. Sign-in had become very strong. Recovery was still the weakest version of their old password reset. Attackers rarely break the front door when there is an unlocked side door right next to it.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every snippet against current OWASP Forgot Password and Authentication guidance, NIST SP 800-63B, Laravel 11 and Node 22. I am a Principal Software Engineer in Karachi with 9+ years across PHP/Laravel, Vue, Node and .NET microservices, and I build the free developer tools at PixelValut. Everything here is about hardening recovery in an app you own.

📚 Series Navigation — Passkeys & Session Hardening for Web Apps

  • Part 1: Rolling Out Passkeys Without Locking Users Out
  • Part 2: Session Lifecycle Hardening: Rotation, Timeouts & Server-Side Revocation
  • Part 3: CSRF in 2026: SameSite, Fetch Metadata & Origin Checks
  • Part 4 (This Post): Account Recovery Hardening: The Side Door Next to Your Passkey
  • Part 5: Protecting Login Endpoints: Credential-Stuffing Signals & Adaptive Rate Limits
  • Part 6: Step-Up Authentication for Sensitive Actions

Related earlier posts: Browser Secrets That Leak: Token Storage, Quotas & Outbound Controls · OAuth 2.1, OIDC ID Tokens & PKCE Forensics

How do you secure account recovery when users sign in with passkeys?

Direct answer: Treat recovery as a sign-in method with the same strength as your weakest factor. Use single-use, high-entropy tokens stored only as hashes, expire them in 15–30 minutes, give the same response whether or not the account exists, rate-limit per account and IP, notify every existing channel, revoke sessions after recovery, and add a cooldown before sensitive changes.

Why recovery is the real security boundary

Your account is only as strong as the easiest path into it. With passwords, that path was usually phishing. With passkeys, phishing gets much harder, so the easiest path moves to recovery: email links, SMS codes, support desk overrides and "change email" forms. If any of those accepts less proof than a passkey, that is now your effective security level.

The goal is not to make recovery impossible. Users do lose phones. The goal is to make recovery slower, louder and more auditable than normal sign-in, so a real owner gets back in and an impostor gets noticed.

Recovery methods compared

Recovery method Strength Main risk User friction When I use it
Second registered passkey (another device) High User never registers one Low Always prompt after first passkey
Single-use recovery codes (printed/stored) High Lost or stored in plain notes Medium Offer at enrolment, require confirmation
Email magic link Medium Mailbox compromise, long-lived links Low With short expiry + notifications + cooldown
SMS code Low–medium SIM swap, interception Low Avoid as sole factor; secondary signal only
Support desk / ID check Varies Social engineering of agents High Last resort, with scripted verification

The single most effective change is getting users to register a second passkey or save recovery codes at enrolment. Every account that has one rarely needs the weaker paths at all.

Building a safe recovery token

Most recovery bugs I find are in token handling. The token should be random, single-use, short-lived and never stored in plain text.

Node (Express) example:

import crypto from 'node:crypto';

const TOKEN_TTL_MS = 20 * 60 * 1000; // 20 minutes

export async function issueRecoveryToken(db, userId) {
  const raw = crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url'); // 256 bits
  const hash = crypto.createHash('sha256').update(raw).digest('hex');

  // Invalidate any earlier unused tokens for this user
  await db.query('UPDATE recovery_tokens SET used_at = now() WHERE user_id = $1 AND used_at IS NULL', [userId]);
  await db.query(
    'INSERT INTO recovery_tokens (user_id, token_hash, expires_at) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)',
    [userId, hash, new Date(Date.now() + TOKEN_TTL_MS)]
  );
  return raw; // only ever sent in the email, never logged
}

export async function consumeRecoveryToken(db, raw) {
  const hash = crypto.createHash('sha256').update(raw).digest('hex');
  const { rows } = await db.query(
    `UPDATE recovery_tokens SET used_at = now()
     WHERE token_hash = $1 AND used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now()
     RETURNING user_id`,
    [hash]
  );
  return rows[0]?.user_id ?? null; // atomic: second use returns null
}

The UPDATE ... RETURNING makes consumption atomic, so two requests racing with the same link cannot both succeed. Storing only the SHA-256 hash means a database leak does not hand out working links. You can sanity-check your hashing output with a hash generator while debugging, using test values only.

Laravel: the built-in password broker already hashes tokens and expires them. Tighten the defaults in config/auth.php:

'passwords' => [
    'users' => [
        'provider' => 'users',
        'table' => 'password_reset_tokens',
        'expire' => 20,   // minutes, default is 60
        'throttle' => 120, // seconds between requests per user
    ],
],

For a passkey "add a new device" recovery flow, reuse the same broker pattern rather than inventing a second token system.

Same response, every time

The recovery form should never tell a stranger whether an account exists:

app.post('/recover', recoverLimiter, async (req, res) => {
  const user = await findUserByEmail(req.body.email);
  if (user) {
    const token = await issueRecoveryToken(db, user.id);
    await sendRecoveryEmail(user, token);
  }
  // Identical body, status and similar timing either way
  res.status(202).json({ message: 'If that account exists, we sent a link.' });
});

Send the email from a queue job so response time does not reveal whether a message was actually sent.

After recovery: limit the blast radius

Getting back in should not immediately unlock everything. After a successful recovery I apply four rules:

  1. Revoke all other sessions and refresh tokens. Part 2 of this series covers server-side revocation.
  2. Notify every channel on file, including the old email if it was changed, with a clear "this wasn't me" link.
  3. Start a cooldown (for example 24–72 hours) before changing email, adding payout details, exporting data or removing other passkeys.
  4. Log the event with timestamp, IP range and user agent so support can review it later.

When checking cooldown windows and token expiry in logs, a Unix timestamp converter saves a lot of mental arithmetic.

The support desk is part of your auth system

Many real account takeovers go through a helpful support agent. Give agents a script: verify through existing channels, never change the email and the recovery method in the same ticket, and require a second agent for overrides on high-value accounts. Record every manual override as an auth event, not just a ticket note.

Diagnostic checklist

  • [ ] Every user is prompted to add a second passkey or save recovery codes at enrolment.
  • [ ] Recovery tokens are at least 128 bits of randomness, single-use and stored as hashes.
  • [ ] Tokens expire in 30 minutes or less and earlier tokens are invalidated on reissue.
  • [ ] The recovery endpoint returns the same response whether or not the account exists.
  • [ ] Recovery is rate-limited per account and per IP.
  • [ ] All sessions are revoked after recovery and every channel is notified.
  • [ ] Sensitive changes have a cooldown after recovery.
  • [ ] Support overrides are scripted, logged and reviewed.

FAQ

If users have passkeys, why keep email recovery at all?

Because people lose devices and not everyone syncs passkeys. Removing email recovery entirely tends to push users to support, which is often weaker. Keep it, but make it short-lived, noisy and followed by a cooldown.

Are SMS codes acceptable for recovery?

As a secondary signal, sometimes. As the only factor, I avoid them because of SIM-swap risk. NIST classes SMS as a restricted authenticator for this reason.

How long should a recovery link last?

I use 15–30 minutes. Long enough to switch to an email app, short enough that an old email in a compromised mailbox is useless.

Should recovery codes be hashed too?

Yes. Store them like passwords, using a slow hash such as bcrypt or Argon2, and mark each one used after a single redemption.

Does a cooldown annoy legitimate users?

Slightly, and that is the trade-off. Explain it clearly in the UI ("For your safety, email changes are paused for 48 hours after recovery"). Most users accept it when they understand why.

What should I monitor?

Spikes in recovery requests, recoveries followed quickly by email or payout changes, and many recovery requests from one IP range. Those patterns usually show an attack before customers report it.

Next in this series, Part 5 covers protecting login endpoints with credential-stuffing signals and adaptive rate limits.

  • YouTube: PixelValut (@pixel-valut)
  • TikTok: PixelValut (@pixelvalut007)
  • GitHub: Muhammad Ali Mughal (@ali111887)
  • LinkedIn: Muhammad Ali Mughal

title: Deploy a Node.js API to Ubuntu with PM2, Nginx, MySQL and Let's Encrypt
description:
Deploying a Node.js API for the first time usually goes wrong in the same places: an env file that crashes the app on startup, a PM2 restart loop, DNS that isn't there yet when certbot runs. This guide walks through the full setup in order, with a filled-in example for every step and a troubleshooting table built from real errors.

What you'll have at the end

  • Your API running under PM2, restarting on crashes and on reboot
  • Nginx in front of it as a reverse proxy
  • HTTPS from Let's Encrypt, renewing automatically
  • A MySQL database with its own user
  • A firewall that only lets in SSH, HTTP and HTTPS

It works for any environment: staging, production, UAT or a fresh server.

How to use this guide

The stack is Node.js, PM2, Nginx, MySQL, Let's Encrypt and a DNS A record. Fill in the worksheet first. Each step then shows the command with <placeholders>, followed by an example using the sample values below. Never write real secrets into notes or guides: keep them in a password manager.

Placeholder Meaning Example value used in this guide
<app> App name, also the PM2 process name orders-api
<env> Environment, the value of NODE_ENV staging
<env-file> Env file the app reads for <env> .env.staging
<server-ip> Server public IP (curl -4 ifconfig.me) 203.0.113.10
<ssh-user> Linux user that runs the app ubuntu
<app-dir> Folder the app lives in /home/ubuntu/orders-api
<port> Local port the app listens on; must be free 4000
<api-domain> Public domain for the API api-staging.example.com
<ui-origin> Frontend URL allowed by CORS https://staging.example.com
<git-host> Git provider host bitbucket.org
<repo> Repository path acme/orders-api.git
<branch> Branch to deploy main
<node-version> Node major version from package.json engines 24
<db-name> / <db-user> Database and its dedicated user orders_staging / orders_app
<build-command> Compiles the app npm run build
<migration-command> Applies database migrations npm run migration:run
<seed-command> Creates first-login data npm run seed:admin
<start-file> Compiled entry file dist/server.js
<health-path> Health-check URL path api/v1/health

Before starting, find your app's real values for the last six rows in its README or package.json.

Before you start

Most setup delays come from missing access or missing values, not from the commands. Collect these before you touch the server.

  • SSH access to the server, and an SFTP client such as FileZilla as a fallback
  • Admin on the git repository, to add a read-only deploy (access) key for the server
  • Access to the DNS provider for the domain (for example AWS Route 53), to add the A record
  • Access to the server firewall or cloud security group, with ports 22, 80 and 443 open
  • Database admin access on the server, to create the database and its user
  • A free port: sudo ss -ltnp | grep <port> prints nothing
  • The app's full list of environment variables (usually .env.example), with a value for every required one
  • New random secrets for this environment, each from openssl rand -hex 32; never reuse another environment's secrets
  • Credentials for every third-party service the app calls in this environment (cloud storage, SMS, email, CAPTCHA, payment and so on), or a decision to use the app's fake provider where it allows one
  • Seed data the app needs for its first login, such as an admin user

Step-by-step setup

Do the steps in order: each needs the one before it. DNS must resolve before HTTPS, and the env file must pass the app's checks before PM2 runs it.

Step 1. Install the software

Skip what is already installed. Check with node -v, pm2 -v, nginx -v and mysql --version.

curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.40.1/install.sh | bash
source ~/.bashrc
nvm install <node-version>
npm install -g pm2
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y git nginx mysql-server certbot python3-certbot-nginx

Example:

nvm install 24
node -v        # v24.x.x
pm2 -v         # 6.x.x

Step 2. Create the database and its user 

CREATE DATABASE <db-name> CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;
CREATE USER '<db-user>'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY '<strong-password>';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON <db-name>.* TO '<db-user>'@'localhost';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;

Example: open MySQL with sudo mysql, then:

CREATE DATABASE orders_staging CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;
CREATE USER 'orders_app'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY '<output of: openssl rand -base64 24>';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON orders_staging.* TO 'orders_app'@'localhost';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;
EXIT;

The app never connects as root. The user is created for localhost, so set the app's DB host to localhost: MySQL may not match it for a TCP connection to 127.0.0.1.

Step 3. Give the server read access to the repository

Without this, git clone and git pull fail with Permission denied (publickey). Use one key per repository, so this app's key never affects other apps on the server.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "<env>-<app>" -f ~/.ssh/<app> -N ""
cat ~/.ssh/<app>.pub

Add the printed public key to the repository as a read-only key. In Bitbucket: Repository settings, Access keys. In GitHub: Settings, Deploy keys. Then add a host alias to ~/.ssh/config, lock the files down and test.

Example:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "staging-orders-api" -f ~/.ssh/orders-api -N ""
cat ~/.ssh/orders-api.pub
# ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3Nza...  staging-orders-api   <- paste this into Bitbucket

~/.ssh/config:

Host git-orders-api
    HostName bitbucket.org
    User git
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/orders-api
    IdentitiesOnly yes

chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config ~/.ssh/orders-api
ssh -T git@git-orders-api
# authenticated via a deploy key.

Step 4. Get the code 

git clone git@git-<app>:<repo> <app-dir>
cd <app-dir>
git checkout <branch>
npm ci

Example:

git clone git@git-orders-api:acme/orders-api.git /home/ubuntu/orders-api
cd /home/ubuntu/orders-api
git checkout main
npm ci

No repository access yet? Upload src/, package.json, package-lock.json, the build config and ecosystem.config.cjs with SFTP (for example FileZilla) to /home/ubuntu/orders-api. Then check the files landed where expected: ls /home/ubuntu/orders-api/src must list the source files, not another src folder.

Step 5. Create the env file

The env file never goes through git. Create it on the server, or upload it with SFTP, then lock it down. Start from the app's .env.example and follow the Env file rules section below.

nano <app-dir>/<env-file>
chmod 600 <app-dir>/<env-file>

Example:

nano /home/ubuntu/orders-api/.env.staging
chmod 600 /home/ubuntu/orders-api/.env.staging

NODE_ENV=staging
PORT=4000
CORS_ORIGIN=https://staging.example.com
TRUST_PROXY=1

DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=3306
DB_USERNAME=orders_app
DB_PASSWORD=<the password from step 2>
DB_DATABASE=orders_staging

JWT_SECRET=<output of: openssl rand -hex 32>

SMS_PROVIDER=fake
# SMS_API_KEY=

The last two lines show rule 2 below: an unused key is commented out, not left blank.

Step 6. Build, migrate and seed

Prefix every server command with NODE_ENV=<env>. Without it, the app may read the wrong env file or the wrong database. Take a database backup first if the database already holds data.

cd <app-dir>
<build-command>
NODE_ENV=<env> <migration-command>
NODE_ENV=<env> <seed-command>

Example:

cd /home/ubuntu/orders-api
npm run build
NODE_ENV=staging npm run migration:run
NODE_ENV=staging npm run seed:admin

Step 7. Run it once by hand, then under PM2

A hand run shows any startup error directly, instead of hiding it in a PM2 restart loop. Wait for the app's "listening" line, then press Ctrl+C.

cd <app-dir>
NODE_ENV=<env> node <start-file>

Example:

cd /home/ubuntu/orders-api
NODE_ENV=staging node dist/server.js
# orders-api listening on port 4000 (staging)   <- press Ctrl+C

Then start it under PM2, from the app folder. If the app has no ecosystem.config.cjs, create one:

module.exports = {
  apps: [
    {
      name: '<app>',
      script: './<start-file>',
      cwd: __dirname,
      autorestart: true,
      max_restarts: 10,
      restart_delay: 5000,
      max_memory_restart: '512M',
      env_<env>: { NODE_ENV: '<env>', PORT: <port> },
    },
  ],
};

cd <app-dir>
pm2 start ecosystem.config.cjs --env <env>
pm2 save
pm2 startup

Example:

module.exports = {
  apps: [
    {
      name: 'orders-api',
      script: './dist/server.js',
      cwd: __dirname,
      autorestart: true,
      max_restarts: 10,
      restart_delay: 5000,
      max_memory_restart: '512M',
      env_staging: { NODE_ENV: 'staging', PORT: 4000 },
    },
  ],
};

cd /home/ubuntu/orders-api
pm2 start ecosystem.config.cjs --env staging
pm2 save
pm2 startup     # then run the sudo command it prints
pm2 list        # orders-api  online  restarts 0  mem 95mb

In pm2 list, the restart count must stay at 0 and memory must be above 0.

Step 8. Add the DNS record

At the DNS provider, create an A record from the API domain to the server IP, then wait until it resolves. In Route 53, use simple routing with alias off. In Cloudflare, set it to "DNS only" until HTTPS works.

Field Value
Type A
Name subdomain part of <api-domain>
Value <server-ip>
TTL 300 
nslookup <api-domain> 8.8.8.8

Example: in the example.com zone, add type A, name api-staging, value 203.0.113.10, TTL 300. Then:

curl -4 ifconfig.me                          # 203.0.113.10  (run on the server)
nslookup api-staging.example.com 8.8.8.8
# Name:    api-staging.example.com
# Address: 203.0.113.10

Step 9. Add the Nginx site 

sudo nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/<api-domain>

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name <api-domain>;
    client_max_body_size 60M;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:<port>;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}

sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/<api-domain> /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx

Example: /etc/nginx/sites-available/api-staging.example.com:

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name api-staging.example.com;
    client_max_body_size 60M;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:4000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}

sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/api-staging.example.com /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
sudo nginx -t
# nginx: configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf test is successful
sudo systemctl reload nginx

Reload only when nginx -t reports success. Set client_max_body_size above the app's largest upload. Behind Nginx, the app must trust one proxy hop (in Express: app.set('trust proxy', 1)), or rate limits and client IPs will be wrong.

Step 10. Turn on HTTPS

Run this only after step 8 resolves. Certbot gets the certificate, edits the Nginx site, adds the HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect and schedules renewal.

sudo certbot --nginx -d <api-domain>
sudo certbot renew --dry-run

Example:

sudo certbot --nginx -d api-staging.example.com
# Successfully received certificate.
# Successfully deployed certificate for api-staging.example.com
sudo certbot renew --dry-run
# Congratulations, all simulated renewals succeeded

Step 11. Lock down the firewall

Only SSH, HTTP and HTTPS stay open. Never open the app port or the database port to the internet: Nginx is the only way in.

sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
sudo ufw allow 'Nginx Full'
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status

Example: sudo ufw status on a correct server:

Status: active
To                         Action      From
--                         ------      ----
OpenSSH                    ALLOW       Anywhere
Nginx Full                 ALLOW       Anywhere

Port 4000 and port 3306 must not appear in the list. If the server also has a cloud security group, allow only 22, 80 and 443 there too.

Env file rules

A wrong env file is the most common reason a new server fails: the app exits at startup, and PM2 restarts it in a loop. These rules apply to every app and environment.

Rule Example
1. One file per environment, picked by NODE_ENV. Run every command from the folder that holds the file. NODE_ENV=staging reads .env.staging; NODE_ENV=production reads .env.production
2. Blank is not the same as missing. An empty value is an empty string, which strict validation rejects. Wrong: SMS_API_KEY= · Right: # SMS_API_KEY=
3. A real provider needs its credentials. Switching a service from fake to real makes its keys required. SMS_PROVIDER=twilio also needs SMS_API_KEY and SMS_SENDER; SMS_PROVIDER=fake needs neither
4. Env files stay out of git. Keep them on the server with chmod 600, and in a password manager. If one is committed, change every secret in it: git history keeps it. .gitignore holds .env.* and !.env.example; ls -l .env.staging shows -rw-------
5. Each environment gets its own secrets. Staging JWT_SECRET and production JWT_SECRET are two separate openssl rand -hex 32 outputs
6. An encryption key is permanent. Changing it later makes data already encrypted with it unreadable. Set DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEY once, before the first real record is saved
7. Paired settings change together. Where the frontend and the API share a setting, change both. API CORS_ORIGIN=https://staging.example.com and frontend VITE_API_URL=https://api-staging.example.com
8. Restart after every change. A frontend setting needs a rebuild instead, because build tools bake it into the bundle. API: pm2 restart orders-api --update-env · Frontend: npm run build again, then deploy

Verify the deployment

Check from the inside out: the first check that fails tells you which layer to fix. Each example uses the sample values.

Check Example command Expected result If it fails
1. App is running pm2 list, twice, 10 seconds apart orders-api online, restart count unchanged, memory above 0 pm2 logs orders-api --err --lines 60 --nostream
2. App answers locally curl http://127.0.0.1:4000/api/v1/health {"success":true,...} App or database: read the logs
3. DNS nslookup api-staging.example.com 8.8.8.8 Address: 203.0.113.10 Add or fix the A record (step 8)
4. HTTP through Nginx curl -I http://api-staging.example.com/api/v1/health 301 Moved Permanently to HTTPS sudo nginx -t, the site file, port 80
5. HTTPS curl https://api-staging.example.com/api/v1/health Same as check 2 certbot, port 443
6. Frontend reaches the API Browser DevTools, Network tab, make a request Requests to api-staging.example.com succeed Match the error in Troubleshooting
7. Survives a reboot (only on a server you may reboot) sudo reboot, then pm2 list orders-api online pm2 startup, then pm2 save

Troubleshooting

Each row is a real problem from a past setup. Find your symptom, then apply the fix.

The app won't start

Symptom Cause Fix
pm2 list: restart count climbing, blank status, 0b memory The app exits at startup; PM2 restarts it in a loop pm2 logs <app> --err --lines 60 --nostream, fix what it names
pm2 reload or pm2 restart says Process <id> not found The process is dead mid-restart pm2 delete <app>, fix the cause, pm2 start ecosystem.config.cjs --env <env>
pm2 start crashes with Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'pm2_env') PM2 is tripping over the crash-looping process pm2 delete <app>, then start again
Config error: Too small: expected string to have >=1 characters A variable is present but blank Comment the line out with #
Config error: required when <PROVIDER>=... A real provider is set without its credentials Fill the credentials, or use the fake provider where the environment allows it
Config error: fake is not allowed in <env> The environment's safety rules refuse a fake provider, or the server runs an old build Use the real provider, or deploy the build that allows it
EADDRINUSE Another app already uses <port> `sudo ss -ltnp \
{% raw %}Cannot find module .../dist/server.js No build on the server npm ci && npm run build
ECONNREFUSED ...:3306 or Access denied for user Database down or wrong credentials sudo systemctl status mysql; test with mysql -u <db-user> -p <db-name>
Table ... doesn't exist Migrations not run NODE_ENV=<env> npm run <migration-command>

Deploys that don't take effect

Symptom Cause Fix
pm2 start ecosystem.config.cjs started a different app Run from the wrong folder, which held another app's ecosystem file Always cd <app-dir> first
New source uploaded, nothing changed PM2 runs the compiled dist/, not the source npm run build, then pm2 restart <app> --update-env
Env change ignored PM2 kept the old environment pm2 restart <app> --update-env, or delete and start again
git pull fails with Permission denied (publickey) The server has no key the repository accepts Add a deploy key (step 3); meanwhile upload with SFTP

The domain doesn't work

Symptom Cause Fix
Browser: net::ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED No DNS record for the domain Add the A record (step 8)
certbot: DNS problem: NXDOMAIN looking up A certbot ran before DNS resolved Wait for nslookup to return the IP, run certbot again
certbot: timeout or connection error Port 80 is closed Open 80 and 443 in the firewall and security group
502 Bad Gateway Nginx is up but the app is not, or the port is wrong pm2 list; check proxy_pass uses <port>
413 Request Entity Too Large Upload is bigger than Nginx allows Raise client_max_body_size, nginx -t, reload
Browser: CORS error The API doesn't allow the frontend's origin Set the app's CORS origin to <ui-origin>, restart
Frontend shows a blank page after deploy The frontend's own config check fails, for example a provider set with an empty key Fix the frontend env file and rebuild it

Never run on a shared server: pm2 kill (stops every app), pm2 delete all, or sudo systemctl reload nginx without a passing sudo nginx -t first.

Redeploying an update

An update is pull, build, migrate, restart, check. Run it from the app folder.

cd <app-dir>
git pull
npm ci
<build-command>
NODE_ENV=<env> <migration-command>
pm2 restart <app> --update-env
pm2 logs <app> --lines 20 --nostream
curl https://<api-domain>/<health-path>

Example:

cd /home/ubuntu/orders-api
git pull
npm ci
npm run build
NODE_ENV=staging npm run migration:run
pm2 restart orders-api --update-env
pm2 logs orders-api --lines 20 --nostream
curl https://api-staging.example.com/api/v1/health

Not every change needs every command:

What changed What to run Example
Code only Pull, build, restart git pull && npm run build && pm2 restart orders-api
Dependencies (package.json) Add npm ci before the build git pull && npm ci && npm run build && pm2 restart orders-api
Database schema Back up, then migrate before the restart mysqldump orders_staging > ~/backup-$(date +%F).sql, then NODE_ENV=staging npm run migration:run
Env file only Restart with --update-env; no build pm2 restart orders-api --update-env
Nginx site Test, then reload sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx

Without repository access on the server, replace git pull with an SFTP upload of the changed files, and still build.

Environments compared

The setup steps are the same for every environment. What changes is how strict the settings are and what data the server may hold.

Area Development (local) Staging Production
Purpose Building features Testing a release on a real server Real users and real data
Env file .env.local .env.staging .env.production
Third-party services Fake providers Fake where the app allows it, real where testing needs it Real only
Login shortcuts (fixed OTP, test logins) Allowed Only if the app allows it and staging holds no real data Never
Data Seed or test data Test data only Real data
Secrets Local values Own values Own values, never shared
HTTPS Not needed Required Required
Backups None Optional Daily, tested restores, plus one before every migration
Monitoring and alerts None Logs Logs, uptime check, disk and certificate expiry alerts

Production checklist

  • Every provider is real; no fake providers or login shortcuts
  • New secrets, created only for production and stored in the password manager
  • Env file is chmod 600 and not in git
  • Database user has access to its own database only; MySQL is not reachable from the internet
  • Automated daily database backup, with a restore tested once
  • Firewall allows only 22, 80 and 443; SSH by key only
  • pm2 startup and pm2 save done, and the app survives a reboot
  • Log rotation on (pm2 install pm2-logrotate)
  • sudo certbot renew --dry-run passes
  • An uptime check on the health URL alerts someone when it fails

If this saved you a debugging session, leave a comment with the error that cost you the most time on your own setup, and I'll add it to the troubleshooting tables.

title: October 28, 2026
description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI and vector search features and improvements are generally available (GA):

  • The alloydb_scann extension supports four-level tree (4LT) ScaNN vector indexes on PostgreSQL 17 and later, providing support for tables with up to 10 billion vector rows. For more information, see Four-level ScaNN tree indexes.

  • 4LT ScaNN vector indexes support automatic index maintenance. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and Maintain vector indexes automatically.

  • You can enable streaming functionality for ScaNN vector indexes by setting the scann.satisfy_limit parameter to relaxed_order. When enabled, the vector scan continues searching through additional leaf partitions until it finds enough results to satisfy the LIMIT clause of your query, improving recall on filtered searches. Additionally, you can enable this feature for parallel process scans by setting the scann.enable_parallel_satisfy_limit database flag to on. For more information, see ScaNN index reference and Best practices for tuning ScaNN indexes.

  • Vector assist simplifies the deployment and management of your AlloyDB vector workloads by helping you set up production-ready vector search capabilities, including embedding generation, query optimization, and index creation for vector types such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). For more information, see Vector assist overview.

  • For AlloyDB for PostgreSQL instances running PostgreSQL 17 and later, the maximum supported value for num_leaves when building ScaNN vector indexes is increased from 30,000,000 to 104,857,600. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and ScaNN index reference.

  • You can use the external_search_fdw extension to connect to external search clusters and query their data directly from your database using the following search sources:

    • Elasticsearch

    • Solr

    • OpenSearch

  • AlloyDB supports the rum extension for high-performance full-text search operations on PostgreSQL 17 and earlier. The rum extension extends standard GIN indexes by storing positional information directly in the index, letting you perform faster phrase searches and relevance ranking without accessing the table data. For more information, see Create and manage a RUM index.

Fixed

AlloyDB provides more accurate memory usage estimation and prevents out-of-memory (OOM) errors when you build a ScaNN four-level tree index. This feature is in Preview. This update improves the stability of index builds by enforcing memory limits and improving memory estimation under constrained conditions.

Feature

Identity and Access Management (IAM) group authentication is generally available (GA) for new and existing AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 15 and later. With IAM group authentication, you can manage database roles and privileges at the group level across primary instances and read pool instances, including first-time sign-ins directly to read pool instances. You can also preserve individual and IAM group user configurations when you migrate from a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL backup.

For more information, see IAM database authentication overview and Manage IAM authentication.

Security

In response to GCP-2026-071, Google is updating AlloyDB managed components. The fix to the certificate store is shipped in a new maintenance version that AlloyDB applies during scheduled maintenance, so you don't need to manually update AlloyDB managed instances. You can also apply the fix by performing self-service maintenance.

Depending on how you connect to AlloyDB, take the following actions:

  • If you use the AlloyDB Auth Proxy, then upgrade it to v1.17.2 or later. If you run the standalone proxy binary, then also update the host's certificate authority (CA) certificates.

  • If you use the AlloyDB Language Connectors, then update the language runtime and operating system CA certificates (for example, Go 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 or later).

Application Integration

Security

A Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability was discovered in the SubWorkflow task in Application Integration versions prior to September 11, 2026. For more information, see the GCP-2026-074 security bulletin.

Feature

Application Integration agent skills

Application Integration agent skills are available in the public google/skills repository: application-integration-basics, application-integration-authoring, and application-integration-troubleshooting. AI coding agents that use these skills can help you set up Application Integration; build, publish, and run integrations through the REST API; and troubleshoot failed runs. For more information, see Application Integration agent skills and Build an integration with an AI agent.

Bigtable

Feature

You can configure Bigtable tables with microsecond timestamp granularity to capture and store high-frequency data. By supporting microsecond precision for cell timestamps, Bigtable helps you prevent data loss from write collisions in workloads with high event rates. This feature is generally available (GA) for instances in the Enterprise Plus edition. For more information, see Data type enforcement in Bigtable.

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource types are publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, Feed, and Search (SearchAllResources, SearchAllIamPolicies) APIs.

  • Google Cloud Migration Center
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/DiscoveryClient
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Group
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/ImportJob
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/PreferenceSet
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/ReportConfig
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Settings
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Source

Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

Database Migration Service for homogeneous SQL Server migrations now supports Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations in general availability (GA).

With DAG migrations, you can use gcloud CLI and Database Migration Service API to migrate databases from self-managed SQL Server Enterprise Edition instances directly to Cloud SQL for SQL Server over a private network connection. DAG migrations don't require exporting backup or transaction log files to Cloud Storage, and support post-promotion reverse replication for zero-data-loss failback.

For more information, see About Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations and Migrate from self-managed SQL Server using Distributed Availability Groups.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Managed replica indexes for Cloud SQL for MySQL are generally available (GA). This feature lets you automatically retain and restore secondary indexes on read replica instances when Cloud SQL re-creates a replica.

Previously, re-creating a read replica deleted custom secondary indexes because primary backups don't have replica-only index definitions. With managed replica indexes, Cloud SQL tracks secondary index metadata on the primary instance, replicates this metadata to read replicas, and automatically rebuilds secondary indexes after replica re-creation.

Managed replica indexes are supported on instances that are running Cloud SQL for MySQL 8.0 or later, Cloud SQL Enterprise edition or Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition, and maintenance version R20260726.00_05 or later.

For more information, see Read replica indexes overview and Create and manage read replica indexes.

Confidential Space

Announcement

A new Confidential Space image (261001) is available. This image removes compromised CA certificates from the OS trust store. See the security bulletin for more details.

This image also adds support for running workload containers as a non-root user. Workload authors can require non-root execution with the tee.launch_policy.nonroot_container launch policy, and workload operators can enable it with the tee-nonroot-container metadata variable. For more information, see Non-root container execution.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Support for Brazil (br) region (GA with allowlist)

You can use the Gemini Enterprise app in the Brazil (br) in-country region with at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP) in region.

This location is available in GA with allowlist. To get access to this location for use with Gemini Enterprise, contact your Google account team.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Change

Use a single regional Agent Registry instance for Gemini Enterprise apps

For Gemini Enterprise apps, we recommend associating each Agent Gateway with a single regional Agent Registry instance in the same project and region as the gateway. Use the us-central1 registry for global and us apps, and the europe-west1 registry for eu apps.

This note updates the September 9, 2026 entry. For more information, see Register your agents and destination resources.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.17.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Support bundle diagnostics: Introduce cm support-bundle to collect environment metadata, configuration policies, health reports, and session logs into a compressed archive for streamlined troubleshooting.
  • Plain output mode: Add the persistent --plain flag (configurable via the CM_PLAIN environment variable or output.plain in config.yaml) to suppress decorative emojis, ANSI escape sequences, and Unicode borders for compatibility with screen readers and CI/CD log pipelines.
  • Dedicated exit codes for setup failures: Assign distinct exit codes (such as code 10 for credential issues) to configuration and authentication failures, preventing CI/CD pipelines from confusing environment setup issues with security findings.
  • Tailored CI/CD credential guidance: Provide environment-specific authentication guidance when running inside automated CI/CD systems such as GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Buildkite, and Jenkins instead of interactive login prompts.
  • Single-line JSONL statistics: Add the --jsonl flag to cm stats to output single-line JSON records with model and team attribution for seamless integration with Cloud Logging and log aggregation pipelines.
  • Granular sandbox and policy flags: Replace the overloaded --unrestricted flag with orthogonal flags (--sandbox=false) and configurable command policies to decouple container sandboxing from execution safety controls.
  • Sandbox configuration protections: Mount .git/hooks, .git/config, and .codemender read-only within writable execution sandboxes during cm fix and cm verify to prevent modifications to repository security policies.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a security warning when commands are executed with both sandbox isolation disabled and interactive approval skipped.
    • Enforced allowedRoots path boundaries across host discovery and remediation file operations to prevent traversal via dangling symlinks.
    • Supplied exact finding line ranges to remediation agents during cm fix to eliminate manual file scanning overhead.
    • Updated cm report import to properly treat findings without location data as file-level findings rather than defaulting to the first line.
    • Ensured cm session cancel routes requests to the session's original region regardless of local environment overrides.
    • Fixed finding status tracking in cm verify so unexploitable verdicts update the local state database rather than leaving findings open.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google SecOps

Fixed

Tools power-up: Environment filtering in Get Integration Instances

There was an issue where the Get Integration Instances action in the Tools power-up didn't correctly filter environments with names that contain an ampersand (&). This issue has been fixed in version 85.0 of the Tools power-up.

title: howbad: What a Prompt-Injected Coding Agent Could Do With the Credentials on Your Machine
description:
Claude Code, Codex and Cursor run as me. A prompt injection in a README or an issue comment doesn't need a sandbox escape. It gets whatever my shell gets: the gh token, the npm token that publishes packages, the AWS profile from this morning, the Slack token pasted into an MCP config.

I knew roughly what was on my laptop. I didn't know what any of it could do. "There is a GitHub token" and "this token can push to 49 repos and rewrite their CI" are different answers, so I wrote a tool that gives the second one.

  • Source: https://github.com/kanywst/howbad
  • Install: brew install kanywst/tap/howbad or go install github.com/kanywst/howbad@latest

The report

This is the repo's demo harness (go run ./internal/demo): a throwaway home directory with fake tokens, and an httptest server standing in for GitHub, npm and Slack. Same binary, same report code.

  howbad · if a coding agent on this machine got hijacked right now, it could:

  CRITICAL  push code to 49 GitHub repos and rewrite their CI workflows
            e.g. acme/sdk-js (1830★), you/dotfiles (240★), acme/payments (12★)
            ↳ gh CLI · you on github.com · ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml · #e9e4a9d1
  CRITICAL  publish new versions of 3 npm packages (234k downloads/week) unless npm demands 2FA (inferred)
            e.g. @acme/sdk (184k/week), @acme/cli (41k/week), @acme/ui (9.8k/week)
            ↳ npm · you on npm · ~/.npmrc · #f54f870e
  HIGH      change settings on 2 repos (branch protection, deploy keys, webhooks)
            ↳ gh CLI · you on github.com · ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml · #e9e4a9d1
  HIGH      read message history in Acme: public channels, private channels, DMs
  HIGH      search every message you can see in Acme
  HIGH      post messages as you in Acme (trusted-sender phishing)
            ↳ MCP server "slack" (Cursor) · you in Slack workspace Acme · ~/.cursor/mcp.json · #dadd4c65
  MEDIUM    spend money on your OpenAI API account (not verified)
            ↳ $OPENAI_API_KEY · environment variable $OPENAI_API_KEY · #85bd6af8
  MEDIUM    create secret gists, a ready-made exfiltration channel
            ↳ gh CLI · you on github.com · ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml · #e9e4a9d1

  one login away:
    AWS profile prod: likely do anything (role AdministratorAccess) once logged in again

  agents running as you: Claude Code (bypassPermissions), Cursor, Codex
  pasted straight into agent configs: 1 credential
  5 credentials · 3 verified read-only with the issuer · nothing sent anywhere else

Each line is a capability, not a token. The #e9e4a9d1 is the first 8 hex of the token's SHA-256, so you can tell two tokens apart without the secret ever being printed. The AWS profile is an SSO profile whose session expired, so it lands under "one login away" with the role name instead of being dropped. The footer lists which agents are installed and flags Claude Code because its settings set defaultMode to bypassPermissions.

Where it looks and who it asks

It reads env vars, the gh CLI (hosts.yml or keychain), .npmrc, ~/.aws, kubeconfig, gcloud and Application Default Credentials, and the MCP configs of Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, VS Code, Zed, GitHub Copilot, Cline, Continue, Windsurf, Devin Desktop and Claude Desktop.

Each credential goes only to the provider that issued it, and only to read-only endpoints:

Credential Asked with Comes back as
GitHub GET /user, /user/repos, the X-OAuth-Scopes header repos you can push to, CI workflow access, admin repos, gists
npm whoami, token list, package search packages you maintain and their weekly downloads
Slack auth.test scopes history, search, posting as you
AWS sts:GetCallerIdentity, attached policies identity, account, policy or SSO permission set
Kubernetes SelfSubjectAccessReview per context cluster-admin, Secrets, exec, pod creation
GitLab GET /personal_access_tokens/self push, CI/CD, registries, runners, admin
Google Cloud testIamPermissions per project (up to 25) IAM admin, impersonation, Secret Manager, GKE

Stripe, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google API keys, Hugging Face tokens and database URLs are recognized by format and never called. That's why the OpenAI line says "not verified".

Where it can't read permissions

Fine-grained GitHub tokens, GitHub App tokens and npm tokens can't report their own permissions. For those, howbad reports the account's access as an upper bound and marks it inferred. The repo's own rule for this is "under-reporting is the dangerous direction", and it shows up in the code: a GitHub token with no X-OAuth-Scopes gets every repo the user can push to, prefixed with "up to".

--offline shows the same thing without any network calls. Everything becomes an upper bound:

  CRITICAL  likely do anything (role AdministratorAccess) (inferred, not checked)
            ↳ AWS profile prod · ~/.aws/config
  HIGH      use a GitHub token as its owner (inferred, not checked)
            ↳ gh CLI · ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml · #e9e4a9d1
  HIGH      use an npm token as its owner (inferred, not checked)
            ↳ npm · ~/.npmrc · #f54f870e

Being boring with live credentials

A tool that reads every token on the machine is itself a good injection target, so:

  • The secret is an unexported field on cred.Credential, and the type implements fmt.Formatter, so %v, %+v and %#v can't print it either. Tests assert no secret appears in any output.
  • --no-exec skips everything that runs a helper: gh auth token, gcloud auth print-access-token, AWS credential_process, kubeconfig exec plugins.
  • Configs in the current directory are read, but a cloned repo can't steer where a token goes. ${VAR} in a repo's .npmrc isn't expanded, and if both the token and its host come from a repo-local config, nothing is sent: 
case c.RepoLocal && h != "" && h != "github.com":
    // A cloned repo names this host; don't let it make howbad dial out.
    f.Status, f.Detail = finding.Unverified, "token and host both come from a repo-local config; not sent"

In CI

--fail-on high exits 2 if anything at or above that severity is reachable. It also exits 2 when a credential couldn't be checked, because "couldn't check" isn't "safe":

$ howbad --offline --no-exec --fail-on high
  howbad · if a coding agent on this machine got hijacked right now, it could:

  HIGH      use an npm token as its owner (inferred, not checked)
            ↳ npm · ~/.npmrc, ./.npmrc · #f54f870e

  1 credential · 0 verified read-only with the issuer · nothing sent anywhere else
$ echo $?
2

--json gives the same findings with severity, inferred and status per credential. Those fields and the exit code are treated as an API.

Not covered

Custom AWS policies aren't evaluated, only attached policy names. Remote MCP servers using OAuth keep their tokens in the agent's own store, often the keychain, which howbad doesn't read. Claude Code policies pushed through macOS configuration profiles aren't read either.

Source and issues: https://github.com/kanywst/howbad

title: Property Webhook Recovery with Queue Retries, Exponential Backoff, and Delayed Redrive
description:
Short answer: make recovery the design constraint: keep one delivery ID across every attempt, classify failures before retrying, use capped exponential backoff with jitter, and send exhausted work to a dead-letter queue that operators can inspect and redrive safely.

Consider a property-management SaaS sending a lease.payment_recorded webhook to an accounting integration. The useful data flow is event store to queue to delivery worker to recipient, with a delivery ledger recording each transition. A timeout leaves the sender with an uncomfortable fact: the recipient may have applied the payment even though the worker never saw the response. A queue retry policy controls when another request runs. It cannot, by itself, prevent that request from repeating the business effect.

That distinction drives the whole design.

What should a simple queue retry policy preserve for SaaS background jobs?

Start with the recovery record, not the delay formula. For each delivery, preserve the immutable event ID, tenant and property scope, destination, payload version, attempt number, first enqueue time, next eligible time, and final disposition. Keep credentials and sensitive request headers out of this record. The goal is to answer three operational questions without piecing together scattered logs: what should have happened, why did automated delivery stop, and can an operator replay it without creating a second payment entry?

The delivery ID is the anchor. Generate it once and send the same value as an idempotency key on every attempt, including manual redrive. For property prop_204, lease lease_881, and payment pay_7319, delivery whd_01JQ7K6N9M2A remains whd_01JQ7K6N9M2A on attempt two and on a later DLQ replay. Don't replace it with a new job ID when moving between queues. A new audit ID for the replay action is useful, but it is a different identifier with a different job.

There is a hard limit here. If the recipient neither honors an idempotency key nor provides a way to query whether it applied an event, the sender cannot guarantee one business effect after an ambiguous timeout. Local deduplication can stop the queue from processing the same completed delivery twice, but it cannot reverse an unknown remote side effect. In that situation, stick with documented at-least-once delivery and require the recipient to deduplicate by immutable event ID. This pattern is not suitable when the business operation must be exactly-once but the receiving contract offers no deduplication mechanism.

How should the worker choose between retrying and dead-lettering?

Recovery needs an explicit classification before it needs exponential backoff. A retryable result says another attempt may succeed later. A permanent result says more attempts will waste capacity or repeat an invalid request. Delivered means the recipient acknowledged the request according to the integration contract. Keep that protocol-specific mapping in the HTTP adapter rather than spreading status checks through queue code, because authentication rejection, payload rejection, rate limiting, and an ambiguous network outcome have different operational meanings.

Worker result Queue transition Operator meaning
Delivered Record delivery, then acknowledge No redrive is needed for this delivery ID
Retryable with budget remaining Record the next attempt, then schedule it Automated recovery is still active
Permanent or attempts exhausted Record the failure, then dead-letter Human review is required before redrive

This ordering prevents a poison message from spending the retry budget while healthy lease events wait behind it. It also makes the DLQ meaningful: entries arrive because automation made an explicit terminal decision, not because every error followed the same timer until a counter happened to expire.

Implementation starts with an auditable delayed-message state machine

Use a deliberately small policy first: seven total attempts, a one-second base delay, a 15-minute cap, and full jitter. These numbers are operating choices for the example, not universal defaults. A rent-accounting update that remains useful for an hour has a different retry horizon from a door-access event. I'm not sure a fixed schedule can fit every recipient; observed recovery time and delivery age should decide later tuning.

The queue interface below exposes business transitions rather than a particular library. That keeps the worker testable and makes transport changes less invasive. More important, it forces retryAt and deadLetter to carry the original delivery record instead of creating an unrelated message.

type WebhookJob = {
  deliveryId: string;
  propertyId: string;
  destination: string;
  eventType: "lease.payment_recorded";
  payload: { leaseId: string; paymentId: string; amountCents: number };
  attempt: number;
  firstQueuedAt: string;
};

type SendResult =
  | { kind: "delivered" }
  | { kind: "retryable"; reason: string }
  | { kind: "permanent"; reason: string };

interface QueuePort {
  acknowledge(deliveryId: string): Promise<void>;
  retryAt(job: WebhookJob, availableAt: Date): Promise<void>;
  deadLetter(job: WebhookJob, reason: string): Promise<void>;
}

interface DeliveryLedger {
  wasDelivered(deliveryId: string): Promise<boolean>;
  markDelivered(deliveryId: string, deliveredAt: Date): Promise<void>;
  recordRetry(
    deliveryId: string,
    attempt: number,
    availableAt: Date,
  ): Promise<void>;
  recordDeadLetter(
    deliveryId: string,
    reason: string,
    failedAt: Date,
  ): Promise<void>;
}

const policy = {
  maxAttempts: 7,
  baseDelayMs: 1_000,
  maxDelayMs: 15 * 60_000,
};

function nextDelayMs(attempt: number, random: () => number): number {
  const exponential = policy.baseDelayMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1);
  const cap = Math.min(exponential, policy.maxDelayMs);
  return Math.floor(random() * cap);
}

async function processWebhook(
  job: WebhookJob,
  queue: QueuePort,
  ledger: DeliveryLedger,
  send: (job: WebhookJob) => Promise<SendResult>,
  now: () => Date = () => new Date(),
  random: () => number = Math.random,
): Promise<void> {
  if (await ledger.wasDelivered(job.deliveryId)) {
    await queue.acknowledge(job.deliveryId);
    return;
  }

  const result = await send(job);

  if (result.kind === "delivered") {
    await ledger.markDelivered(job.deliveryId, now());
    await queue.acknowledge(job.deliveryId);
    return;
  }

  if (result.kind === "permanent" || job.attempt >= policy.maxAttempts) {
    const reason =
      result.kind === "permanent" ? result.reason : "attempts_exhausted";
    await ledger.recordDeadLetter(job.deliveryId, reason, now());
    await queue.deadLetter(job, reason);
    return;
  }

  const availableAt = new Date(
    now().getTime() + nextDelayMs(job.attempt, random),
  );
  const nextJob = { ...job, attempt: job.attempt + 1 };
  await ledger.recordRetry(job.deliveryId, nextJob.attempt, availableAt);
  await queue.retryAt(nextJob, availableAt);
}

Full jitter selects a delay from zero to the current capped exponential value. Injecting the random function and clock is not ceremony — it makes the schedule deterministic under test. With random fixed at 0.5, the first delay is 500 ms and the second is 1,000 ms. Also test the attempt-seven boundary, a permanent rejection that schedules no retry, and the ambiguous outcome where the recipient applies the payment but the sender does not observe the response. Every execution must retain the same delivery ID.

One ordering detail deserves scrutiny: recording delivery and acknowledging the queue are separate operations. If the worker stops between them, the message can appear again, which is why wasDelivered runs before the send. If it stops after the remote side effect but before markDelivered, only recipient-side idempotency can close the gap. Exactly-once language tends to hide this boundary. Don't use it unless the entire end-to-end contract earns it.

Governance turns dead-letter redrive into a controlled production change

A DLQ is an isolation boundary, not permanent event history. AWS documents that dead-letter queues hold messages that were not successfully consumed, that their retention needs deliberate configuration, and that a redrive policy can restrict which source queues may use them. The portable lesson is to separate environments and event families whenever shared dead-letter storage would blur authorization, retention, or ownership.

Redrive should preserve evidence. Leave the failed delivery record intact, write a separate audit entry for who initiated replay and which selection criteria they used, then enqueue the original delivery identity. Before release, show a dry count grouped by destination and failure reason. Apply a destination rate limit and provide a stop control. Otherwise a recovery action can recreate the pressure that caused the backlog — only faster.

Be conservative.

For the property webhook, an operator might select exhausted deliveries for one accounting destination after its credentials were corrected. The tool should report how many lease.payment_recorded events match, reject a mixed-tenant selection unless authorization permits it, and redrive at a bounded rate. It should not edit the payload, reset the immutable event ID, or erase the old attempts. If the payload itself needs correction, create a new business event through the normal application path; replay is not a hidden data editor.

Dead-letter storage is also the wrong place for compliance history or long-term tenant support records. Keep the authoritative business event and delivery audit in durable application storage when those requirements outlive queue retention. The catch is extra state and another consistency boundary. For very low-volume, noncritical jobs where duplicates have no business impact, a ledger may cost more operational effort than it returns; a basic retry counter and failure log can be the better choice. Property payment webhooks do have a duplicate side effect, so the ledger earns its keep here.

Migration tests belong in the operational recovery rehearsal

Exponential backoff spaces attempts, but many workers can still contend for the same unhealthy recipient. Set a per-destination concurrency budget so one accounting endpoint cannot occupy the whole worker pool, then put a separate limit on global concurrency. Keep queue polling independent from outbound request timeouts. Delay is not recipient protection.

Measure outcomes rather than queue depth alone. Split delivered, retry-scheduled, permanently rejected, and dead-lettered work by destination. Track the age of the oldest eligible message and oldest dead-letter entry, because a stable total depth can conceal one tenant that is no longer making progress. Alerts should point to an operator action such as pausing one destination or reviewing one failure class; a generic “queue high” page creates noise but gives no recovery decision. Deployment belongs in the same runbook. Delayed messages may be decoded by a newer worker, so version the envelope and retain compatible decoders for the maximum delivery window, or explicitly migrate queued records. During rollback, verify that both worker versions derive the same delivery identity, since one small difference in that calculation defeats deduplication even if the backoff math is perfect. Before launch, run one complete recovery rehearsal: enqueue a payment webhook, produce a retryable result, verify a delayed copy with the unchanged ID, exhaust the attempt budget, inspect the dead-letter record, correct the destination configuration, redrive at a limited rate, and confirm one recipient-side effect. Repeat with a permanent rejection and confirm that it never returns to the active queue. Check that logs omit secrets, dashboards expose property and destination scope, and an operator can halt redrive without stopping unrelated tenants. This is the acceptance test for operational recovery; a unit test of nextDelayMs cannot replace it.

The final choice is modest: use the simplest queue in your environment that provides delayed availability, explicit acknowledgement, dead-letter isolation, and controlled redrive. A library-backed queue can fit a team already operating its data store and wanting retry controls in application code. A managed queue can fit a team that would rather hand off queue operations. Neither option supplies idempotency or a recovery contract for you. Keep correctness in delivery identity, keep evidence in the ledger, and tune backoff only after actual destination behavior gives you a reason.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/retrying-failing-jobs
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/jobs/delayed

Further reading

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
