title: Our Chrome extension sat untouched for four months. Review took one day.
description:
MapWit was written over five days in April. It could read a Google Maps search, score every business in it, and export the lot to Excel, and it did — the first exports are dated 21 April. Then nobody touched it for four months.

When we came back to it, the build still worked. It had no tests. It shipped its own source code to anyone who opened DevTools. On the Indian Google domain, where most of its users would land, it installed and did nothing at all — and the change that fixed that introduced a bug that got the most important fact about every business wrong.

It went live on the Chrome Web Store on 14 September, one day after submission and on the first review round. Most of the work between those two states was not adding things. It was finding out what the extension actually did, and removing the parts a reviewer would reasonably object to — including a feature that worked.

This is the full account: how a lead gets from a Maps result to a row in a spreadsheet, what we measured, where it broke the first time it met live Google Maps, and what we cut.

TL;DR

  • The most useful signal was the one we were getting wrong. A business with no website is the best lead MapWit can find, and on google.co.in every business looked like it had one — the extension was reading the listing's own Maps link as the business's site. Those leads lost 5 points out of 10. Seven test cases now fail if it comes back.
  • One of thirty hostile URLs got past our private-address guard. The browser's URL parser rewrites ::ffff:127.0.0.1 into hex before our code sees it, so a dotted-quad check never matches. A throwaway harness found it in minutes; reading the code had not.
  • We went from 0 tests to 171 in one day, and the tests found real bugs. Bulk review analysis lost every business but the first in a batch. A missing setting clamped to 1 instead of the default of 8. Neither would have shown up in a demo.
  • Review passed first time because the review had already happened. We cut outreach drafting to satisfy the single-purpose rule, made website access optional, stopped shipping 2.1 MB of sourcemaps, bundled the fonts, and wrote a packaging script that refuses to zip a build that breaks any of six rules.
  • The first live run of the rebuilt extension found three bugs that 166 tests had not. A year glued to a star rating became a phone number: Est. 2005 next to 4.5(177) read as 20054.5(177.

MapWit, in one paragraph

MapWit is a Chrome side panel for people who sell to local businesses — web studios, agencies, freelancers. You search Google Maps the way you already would ("dentists in Pune"), and the businesses appear in the panel as you scroll. A Deep scan opens each listing to collect its website, phone, address and recent reviews. Enrich visits each business's own website for email addresses, social profiles and a site-quality check. Every lead gets a score from 1 to 10, you can filter to the ones with no website at all, and Analyse reviews writes a one-sentence summary of what customers complain about. Then you export to Excel, written in the browser with SheetJS. There is no server, no account and no subscription; leads live in your browser's storage, and the one AI feature runs on your own OpenRouter key.

The premise is in the product page's first line: a bought lead list is rows somebody has already sold twice. The businesses worth calling are the ones already visible on Maps with no website or a bad one, and the fastest way to find them is to qualify a search you were going to run anyway.

Diagram: Everything above the line happens in the browser. Two things cross it, and both are opt-in: Enrich fetches a business's own website only after you allow website access, and review text goes to OpenRouter only when you click Analyse with your own key. The README used to say nothing leaves the machine. That was never true, and it now says what does. See it in the original post.

How to generate leads from Google Maps with MapWit

The practical version first, in the order the extension's own tour walks through it.

  1. Install it and open the side panel. Add MapWit from the Chrome Web Store (Chrome 114 or later) and click its toolbar icon. The panel opens beside the page and stays open while you use the map.
  2. Search Google Maps the way you would anyway. A category and a place works best: dentists in Pune, interior designers in Indiranagar. Scroll the results and each business appears in the panel as it renders. Load more scrolls the list to the end of the search for you; Google Maps shows about 120 results per search.
  3. Deep scan. It opens each listing and collects the website, phone, address and recent reviews. It is the slow step on purpose, because it paces itself, so start it and let it run.
  4. Enrich (optional). It visits each business's own website for email addresses, social profiles and a site-quality check. Chrome asks once for website access the first time you use it.
  5. Analyse reviews (optional). With your own OpenRouter key, it writes one sentence on what customers praise and complain about, which is often the opening line of a call.
  6. Find the best leads. Sort by lead score, switch on No website only, or search by name or category. The score is built from these signals:
Signal Points What it usually means for a pitch
No website +4 A website build, and the strongest single reason to call
Own website scores 3 or less out of 10 +2 A redesign: no HTTPS, no mobile layout, slow, or visibly stale
Phone number +2 You can call today
Email address +2 You can write first
50+ reviews and no website +1 An established business with an obvious gap, not a new one
Rating between 3.5 and 4.2 +1 Real customers, and room to improve
Missing 4 or more of 7 social platforms +1 A thin presence generally
  1. Export. Choose Excel, sorted by score, with 19 columns including the AI review insight, or JSON for a CRM import.

That is the whole workflow, and it takes one search to see whether the list is worth calling. What you do with the list afterwards is your responsibility. Google's Maps terms and India's data protection law both apply to it; the section near the end says how.

The rest of this post is how each of those steps works, and what it took to ship it.

How MapWit captures leads from Google Maps

There is no Maps API underneath this. MapWit reads the page you are already looking at.

A content script runs on four Maps origins — www.google.com/maps, maps.google.com, and their .co.in equivalents — and watches the results feed as it renders. Each card is a link with a stable place identifier in its URL, which becomes the lead's primary key, plus a few lines of text that hold the name, rating, review count, category and, sometimes, a phone number and an outbound link. Load more scrolls the feed for you to the end of the search. Google Maps shows about 120 results per search; on the live test it reached 106 and stopped where the list stopped.

Deep scan is the slower half. For each captured lead it opens the listing's detail panel and reads the fields Maps exposes there with stable data attributes — website, address, phone — plus up to 15 recent reviews, each cut to 400 characters. Only a panel that has actually finished loading, with a heading that matches the listing that was clicked, counts as scanned. An earlier version marked a lead done as soon as it had clicked it, which meant a slow load produced a lead with nothing in it and no way to tell.

The side panel is a real Chrome side panel, not a popup, which is why the manifest sets minimum_chrome_version to 114: below that the API does not exist, and the toolbar button installs and silently does nothing. A popup would have been simpler and would have closed every time you clicked the map.

The fragile part is worth saying plainly. The result cards use obfuscated class names that Google can change on any deploy, and several of the patterns that pull a rating or an "Open now" out of card text match English interface strings. On a Maps interface set to another language MapWit captures less. The detail panel is sturdier, because the website, address and phone rows carry data-item-id attributes that have been stable for years — which is also why Deep scan is the reliable path and card capture is the fast one.

How MapWit scores a Google Maps lead

A score only earns its place if it sorts the list the way the person calling would. The whole point table is in step 6 above; it is small enough to show in full, and it has no hidden terms. The total is clamped to 1–10, and 8 or above is labelled hot, 5 or above warm. It is a pure function shared by the service worker and the side panel so the two can never disagree about a number.

The site-quality score out of 10 is equally blunt, and deliberately so. It checks five things on the business's home page: served over HTTPS (2), a mobile viewport tag (2), a response under three seconds (2, or 1 under six), a copyright year from this year or last (2), and a mailto: or tel: link somewhere on the page (2). None of that is a design judgement, and all of it is something a salesperson can say out loud on a call: your site doesn't load on a phone.

Two classification rules matter more than the weights. A listing whose only outbound link is a booking platform — Booksy, Fresha, Setmore and twelve others on the list — has no website of its own. That is a pitch, not a site to crawl. And a link back into Google itself is not a website at all, which is the rule the extension broke on google.co.in (below).

Enrichment, and the one address the guard missed

Enrich visits the business's own site to find what Maps does not show: email addresses, social profiles, and the quality signals above. It tries up to six paths — /, /contact, /contact-us, /contactus, /about, /about-us — with an eight-second timeout and a 512 KB cap per page, and stops early once it has two likely email addresses, keeping the best three with contact@ ranked above support@ above info@.

That is the only feature that needs to fetch arbitrary websites, so it is the only one behind the broad website permission — and that permission is optional. The extension installs without it. The first time you click Enrich, Chrome asks. Settings can revoke it, and revoking it mid-run stops enrichment with the leads left pending rather than failed.

Fetching arbitrary URLs has a sharper problem than permissions. The URL comes from a Maps listing, which is data we do not control. A listing whose website field says http://192.168.1.1/ would be fetched from the user's own machine, inside their own network — their router, their NAS, their office intranet. That is server-side request forgery with a browser as the server, and it is exactly the kind of thing a reviewer probes on an extension that can reach any host.

So before any fetch, a guard refuses non-HTTP schemes, ports other than 80 and 443, embedded credentials, single-label names like router or nas, private suffixes like .local and .internal, and every private, loopback, link-local and shared address range, including 169.254.169.254, where cloud providers serve instance credentials. The list follows the OWASP SSRF guidance and the RFC 1918 and RFC 6598 ranges.

Rather than trust the list, we wrote a throwaway harness with thirty hostile inputs and ran the guard against it. Twenty-nine were refused. One got through.

http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]/     allowed   ← loopback, written as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address

The guard checked IPv6 hosts for a dotted IPv4 address inside the mapped prefix. It never saw one, because the browser's URL parser had already rewritten the host before our code read it. The WHATWG URL Standard serialises every IPv6 address as hexadecimal pieces, so [::ffff:127.0.0.1] arrives as [::ffff:7f00:1] — the same address, spelled so that a dotted-quad regex cannot match it. (IPv4-mapped addresses are defined in RFC 4291.) The fix decodes both spellings:

// IPv4-mapped addresses. The WHATWG parser rewrites `::ffff:127.0.0.1` to its
// hex form `::ffff:7f00:1`, so both spellings have to be decoded — checking
// only the dotted form lets ::ffff:127.0.0.1 straight through.
const hex = h.match(/^::(?:ffff:)?([0-9a-f]{1,4}):([0-9a-f]{1,4})$/);
if (hex) {
  const hi = parseInt(hex[1], 16);
  const lo = parseInt(hex[2], 16);
  return isPrivateIpv4(`${hi >> 8}.${hi & 0xff}.${lo >> 8}.${lo & 0xff}`);
}

The same parser is also why three other inputs needed no special code at all. http://2130706433/, http://0x7f000001/ and http://0177.0.0.1/ — loopback in decimal, hex and octal — are all normalised to 127.0.0.1 before the guard looks. The parser that caused the bug fixed three others for free. It is the same lesson as the time six of our agent's seventeen tools turned out never to have run: the code you have read is not the code that runs, and the only way to find the difference is to execute it against something hostile.

There is one residual risk, and it is written down rather than hidden. The fetch follows redirects, so a public site can answer with a redirect to a private address. In a Manifest V3 service worker, redirect: 'manual' returns an opaque response, so the hops cannot be inspected one at a time; instead the final URL is re-checked. That means the request to the internal host is still sent. What the guard prevents is its content reaching the extension — the step that turns a forged request into a leak.

Deduplication, and the write that lost leads

The same business turns up more than once: in two searches, or in a search and then a Deep scan of the same listing. Leads are merged on the Maps place ID first and a normalised phone number second, and a merge only ever fills empty fields. A value we already captured is never overwritten by a later, possibly worse, read of the same page. The score is recomputed after every merge, because a Deep scan can make a lead newly eligible for "50+ reviews and no website".

Merging on phone number has a known cost: two branches of a chain that share one number collapse into a single lead. For the people using this — who call a business, not a branch — that is usually what they want, and it is recorded as a known limit rather than a bug.

The dedup logic was fine. The bug was around it. Every writer to the lead store went through a single write queue, except the enrichment worker, which wrote directly. A lead captured by the content script while enrichment was patching another one could be overwritten by enrichment's stale copy of the list. Nothing crashed; a lead just disappeared. The fix moved the queue into the store module so there is no other way to write — the kind of bug that only exists because two parts of the code were each correct on their own.

Storage had a quieter version of the same problem. chrome.storage.local defaults to 10 MB, which is roughly 1,500 to 3,000 deep-scanned leads with their review text, and quota errors were being swallowed. The extension now holds unlimitedStorage, and a full store is an error you can see.

The AI runs on your key, not ours

The one AI feature reads a business's recent reviews and writes one sentence about them: what customers praise, and what they complain about, which is usually the opening line of a sales call. It shipped in April calling Google's Gemini API directly, with the model name hard-coded:

export const GEMINI_MODEL = 'gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview';

A pre-submission audit flagged it. Nobody had checked that slug still existed; the file had already churned once from a different preview model, and its own error strings said "not available on this API key". The question "does this model still exist?" had no durable answer — any answer would rot the next time Google renamed a preview.

So we removed the question rather than answering it. The direct Gemini integration was deleted. MapWit now talks to OpenRouter, which puts hundreds of models behind one endpoint whose format is very similar to OpenAI's Chat API, and the model is a setting. On the day we switched, the catalogue listed 418. The default is a ~latest alias that always resolves to the newest Gemini Flash, and a stale model is now an error on the Settings page with a named cause instead of every AI feature failing silently.

Bring-your-own-key is also what makes "no server" true. If the requests went through us, we would hold review text for businesses we had never heard of and an API bill tied to a free product. With the user's key, the text goes from their browser to OpenRouter and back, and Settings has a section headed What leaves your browser.

Letting users pick any model found the next bug. One model spent its entire output budget of 1,024 tokens on internal reasoning and returned no answer at all. OpenRouter's reasoning controls fixed most of it — reasoning tokens count against the output budget on most providers, so a model left to think freely can spend all of it: the call now asks for low reasoning effort with 2,048 tokens, and if a model still returns only reasoning, it retries once with four times the room before giving up with a message that suggests a non-reasoning model.

Bulk analysis is where the design had to be deliberate. Analysing one business at a time would mean a hundred requests for a hundred leads, and OpenRouter rate-limits free models to 20 requests a minute. So requests are batched — up to eight businesses, or 24,000 characters of review text, whichever fills first — and paced, one in flight, at least 3.1 seconds apart. A hundred leads is about thirteen requests; twenty is three. If a rate-limit response arrives anyway, the run pauses for as long as OpenRouter says to and retries the same batch, rather than stopping.

Two things about that took tests to find. The first is Manifest V3's service worker lifecycle: Chrome stops an idle extension worker after thirty seconds, and a rate-limit pause can be two minutes of silence. The run makes a cheap extension API call every twenty seconds, which resets the timer. The second was a plain parsing bug. Some models return a batch answer as a bare JSON array instead of an object, and the shared helper that stripped code fences from model output extracted only the first object it found — so every business but the first in a batch silently lost its insight. It passed every manual check, because a manual check is one business.

Being polite to Google Maps

Deep scan opens listings one after another, and Google Maps notices when a session does that quickly. It does not return an error. It slows down: the detail panel keeps spinning, and a naive scanner either records an empty lead or, as ours used to, resets the page and loses its place.

We researched how Maps behaves under load before changing anything, and the conclusion was not to go faster. MapWit now paces itself, rests, and backs off further every time Maps stops answering. It pauses while its tab is hidden, since Chrome throttles background tabs and Maps stalls with them. It keeps its progress in session storage, so a reload picks up with the listings it had not reached. And if Google shows a captcha, it stops and waits for you — it does not try to solve it, and it never will.

That is a product decision as much as an engineering one. MapWit reads the search you ran, in your own signed-in session, at a pace a person clicking through the same results could plausibly keep. It is not a crawler, and the day it needs to behave like one is the day it should not exist.

One piece is still unfinished. Maps' loading spinner in the results feed carries no role="progressbar" and no aria-busy, so Load more cannot yet tell "still loading" from "finished". It stops correctly at the end of a list today, but it cannot wait politely in the middle of one. That is the first item for 1.0.1.

What we deleted to pass review

Chrome Web Store review is a person reading your listing, your permissions and your code. The documented rules are public, and nearly every rejection story we could find was a known rule broken knowingly. So we reviewed MapWit against them before submitting it, and removed what failed.

A working feature. MapWit used to draft cold outreach — an email and a WhatsApp message tailored to each lead. It worked, and it was arguably the most impressive thing in the extension. It was also a second purpose. The store's quality guidelines require an extension to have a single purpose that is narrow and easy to understand, and "scores leads, and also writes sales emails" is two. We first removed the UI, then found the service worker still answered the outreach messages — so a reviewer reading the bundle would still find cold-email generation in a lead-scoring extension. The handlers went too: 237 lines, their prompts, three settings and three spreadsheet columns. The source is kept under a git tag for a later version, where it may be its own product.

The broad permission, as a requirement. Website access became optional, as above. The tabs permission was removed entirely — querying tabs by URL works with host permissions alone, and the only behaviour that changed is one the code already wanted.

2.1 MB of source code. The build shipped sourcemaps, which embed the full original source, comments included. Two of them were web-accessible to google.com pages. They are off.

Anything that loads from somewhere else. Manifest V3 forbids remotely hosted code, and a stylesheet from Google Fonts is not code, but it is a request we did not need to explain. The fonts are bundled, which is why fonts are 62% of the 1.6 MB build: 66 files, about 1 MB. We would rather ship weight than a network dependency on the one page that has to work offline.

A hand-written User-Agent, left over from April, that dressed enrichment requests up as Chrome/latest. The browser sends its own; the invented one only added a question a reviewer would ask. And a button labelled "Scrape more", which is now "Load more" — words in a listing are read as intent.

Then we made the rules executable. npm run package type-checks, runs the tests, builds, and refuses to produce a zip if the build contains any sourcemap, requires a broad host permission, contains any outreach string, uses eval( or new Function(, references Google Fonts, or has a manifest version that disagrees with package.json. Every one of those six has been true of this repository at some point. Its first run failed: two preconnect tags to Google Fonts were still in the HTML after the stylesheet import had gone.

The listing copy got the same treatment. The store description says qualify and capture, never "scrape" or "harvest", carries a line saying MapWit is not affiliated with Google, and answers the privacy questions field by field. The privacy policy and terms went live on this site before submission, not after.

Submitted on 13 September; published on the 14th. No rejection, no resubmission. Google's review documentation says most reviews finish within a few days and that broad host permissions, or a lot of hard-to-review code, can make one take longer. We had neither left.

Where it broke

Every test in the repository runs against pure modules or a mocked Maps page. On 12 September, with 166 tests passing, we ran the rebuilt extension against live Google Maps. It found three bugs.

Signed-out sessions get a limited view. Maps serves a reduced interface to a signed-out browser — "You're seeing a limited view of Google Maps" — and the new throttling code read that banner as a block and refused to scan. Deep scan did nothing at all. It is now a notice in the panel, and the scan runs.

Promo cards moved the end of the list. Maps now places promotional cards after its "You've reached the end of the list." text, so the end-of-list check, which read the last item, never fired. It reads the last five now.

A year became a phone number. A salon card read Est. 2005 followed immediately by its rating, 4.5(177). In the card's flattened text those run together, and the phone pattern matched 20054.5(177. Ratings are stripped before phone matching now, and a candidate with a decimal point between digits is rejected. The regression test uses the real card text.

After those three: Deep scan saved 5 of 5 listings on a live search, and Load more ran to 106 results and stopped where the list ended.

The worst bug, though, was older and quieter, and no live run on google.com would have found it. When we added the Indian Maps domains in August, nobody updated the classifier that decides whether a link is the business's own website or a link back into Google. It only knew google.com. On google.co.in, the card's own /maps/place/ link was taken as the business website, so "No website" never appeared — on exactly the domain an Indian user types — and every one of those leads lost the 4 points for no website and the 1 for "50+ reviews and no website". The product's best signal was silently off for the market it was built in. Any Google country domain now classifies as Google, and seven test cases fail if the old pattern returns.

The two surfaces no automation could reach — Enrich's permission prompt, and Analyse reviews with a real OpenRouter key — were run by hand in real Chrome. Both work.

What 171 tests bought

The test suite did not exist on the morning of 12 September. By the evening it had 171 cases across 16 files, and it had found:

  • the batch parser that dropped every business but the first;
  • a missing "reviews per business" setting clamping to 1 instead of the default of 8, because Number(null) is 0;
  • concurrent writes to the token ledger dropping entries, and an AI cache hit that never wrote its result back to the lead;
  • email parsing that discarded real hello@, hi@ and admin@ inboxes, and a "prefer contact emails" sort that ran after the list had already been cut to three.

None of those would have shown up in a demo. All of them would have shown up in the first week of someone actually using it. The pattern is the same one we hit when our agent passed every red-team probe: a green result from the check you already had tells you very little, and the useful tests are the ones written to try to break a specific claim.

What the suite does not do is also worth stating. It covers pure modules and a mocked Maps page, and the Chrome APIs are faked. There is no CI; the tests run on a laptop and inside the packaging script. The mocked Maps page is our description of Google's markup, which is exactly the thing that changes without notice, and the only real check of that is a person running a search.

What is still true

MapWit is free. The AI feature costs whatever your OpenRouter model costs, and nothing to us. There is no paywall and no telemetry, so the honest answer to "how many people use it" is that we see the store's own counters and nothing else, and they are not yet worth quoting.

It also carries a risk we would rather name than have someone discover. Google's end-user Maps terms say you may not copy Maps content, "mass download or create bulk feeds of the content", or use it to build "a business listings database, mailing list, or telemarketing list" for a service that substitutes for Google Maps. A lead list sits uncomfortably close to that sentence, and the store that lists MapWit belongs to Google. We have built it to be as conservative as we know how — it reads only the search you ran, in your own session, at a human pace, stops at a captcha, and says plainly that it is not affiliated with Google — but that is a posture, not a licence. A product that depends on another company's page, and sits this close to its terms, can be removed by that company. We decided to ship knowing that, rather than not ship.

The same reasoning applies to what you do with the export. Business phone numbers and emails are often a person's details — a sole proprietor's mobile is their mobile — and in India the Digital Personal Data Protection Act applies to how you store and use them. MapWit keeps the data on your machine; what happens after you click Export is on you, and the terms on this site say so.

And the extension is 9,748 lines of TypeScript, a 1.2 MB zip, and five months old, with work on six days of it: three in April, one in August, two in September. That ratio is the most instructive number in this post. The April version did almost everything the published one does. What it lacked was evidence: that it worked on the domain its users would use, that it could not be pointed at a user's own network, that its batch parser did not lose data, that nothing in the bundle contradicted the listing. None of that is a feature, and all of it is why review took a day.

Verdict

A Chrome extension is easy to build and slow to trust. The five April days produced a tool that worked on the machine it was written on. The September days produced one we could describe accurately to a stranger — in a store listing, a privacy policy, a permission prompt and a reviewer's queue — and every one of those descriptions forced a change in the code before it could be true.

If there is one practice to take from this, it is the packaging gate. Every rule a reviewer might apply, and every mistake you have already made once, should be a line in a script that refuses to produce the zip. We wrote it on the last day. It should have been the first.

MapWit is free, and it will tell you which dentists in Pune do not have a website. It is off the Chrome Web Store for now: on 23 October 2026 Google took version 1.2.0 down, citing its branding guidelines, and a fixed version is under appeal. The product page will say when it is back.

Every figure here is first-party, taken from the MapWit repository and its build between 21 April and 14 September 2026 across 16 commits, 11 of them on 12 September. Test counts are vitest runs on the published commit (171 passing, 16 files). Sizes are the store zip (1,259,577 bytes) and the built dist/ directory (1,648,035 bytes). Live-Maps results are from one search session on 12 September and are a smoke test, not a benchmark. Chrome and OpenRouter behaviour is quoted from their documentation as of September 2026. This is one extension, one codebase, one author.

FAQ

What does MapWit do?

MapWit is a free Chrome extension that captures the businesses in a Google Maps search into a side panel, scores each one from 1 to 10 as a sales lead, and exports them to Excel or JSON. It can open each listing for its website, phone, address and reviews, visit the business's own website for email addresses and a site-quality check, and summarise its reviews with AI using your own OpenRouter key. It is built for web studios, agencies and freelancers who sell to local businesses.

How do you generate leads from Google Maps?

Search Google Maps for a business category in a place, such as "dentists in Pune", then qualify the results rather than calling all of them. The strongest signals are a business with no website, a poor website, or a phone number and email you can reach. MapWit does this inside Chrome: it captures the search results into a side panel, scores each business from 1 to 10, filters to the ones with no website, and exports the list to Excel.

Is MapWit free?

Yes. MapWit has no subscription, no account and no paywall. The optional review-analysis feature uses your own OpenRouter API key, so you pay OpenRouter directly for whatever model you choose — and nothing if you never use that feature.

Does MapWit send my data to a server?

No, MapWit has no server. Leads are stored in your browser's own extension storage. Two things leave your browser, and both are opt-in: Enrich fetches a business's own public website after you grant the optional website permission, and Analyse reviews sends review text to OpenRouter using your key. Settings lists both under "What leaves your browser".

How does MapWit score a lead?

MapWit adds points for signals a salesperson cares about: 4 for no website, 2 each for a phone number and an email address, 2 if the business's own site scores 3 or less out of 10 for quality, 1 for a rating between 3.5 and 4.2, 1 for 50 or more reviews with no website, and 1 for missing four or more of seven social platforms. The total is clamped to 1–10; 8 and above is hot.

Why does MapWit need permission to access all websites?

Only the Enrich feature needs it, because it visits each business's own website to look for email addresses and check site quality — and those websites could be anywhere. MapWit installs without that permission and asks for it the first time you click Enrich. It refuses to fetch private, local or internal network addresses even when it has the permission.

Is it legal to extract business leads from Google Maps?

It depends on how you do it and what you do with the data, and this is not legal advice. Google's end-user Maps terms prohibit copying Maps content and mass downloading or creating bulk feeds of it, and business contact details can be personal data under India's DPDP Act. MapWit reads only the search you run in your own session, at a human pace, and stops at a captcha rather than solving it — but responsibility for how an exported list is used stays with the person using it.

Does MapWit work on google.co.in?

Yes. MapWit runs on www.google.com/maps, maps.google.com, www.google.co.in/maps and maps.google.co.in. The Indian domains were added because most users in India land there, and an early version misread every business on google.co.in as having a website — fixed before launch and covered by tests.

Which browsers does MapWit support?

MapWit needs Chrome 114 or later, because it runs in Chrome's side panel, which does not exist in earlier versions. It is published on the Chrome Web Store. An Edge Add-ons submission has not been made yet.

title: Cloudflare Measures the Markdown It Serves to AI Agents
description:
TL;DR

  • Markdown for Agents is a Cloudflare network feature that converts an HTML page into Markdown when a client asks for it in the Accept header, so an AI agent receives a compact document stripped of navigation, footers and scripts.
  • Cloudflare made the feature generally available on 9 November 2026 and added an Analytics tab, sampled Logs, a Playground that compares Markdown against HTML, a GraphQL dataset and a tracing span for each conversion.
  • The mechanism is HTTP content negotiation: Cloudflare fetches the HTML from the origin, converts the body on the fly, streams the result and leaves the origin's security and cache headers in place.
  • A converted response sets Content-Type to text/markdown, adds Accept to Vary, and omits ETag and Last-Modified; the validators used by conditional requests are therefore absent.
  • The dashboard reports conversion attempts, a full conversion rate, partial and failed conversions, top pages, user agents and an estimated token reduction over a seven-day window that is queryable through GraphQL as well.
  • Every token figure is an estimate based on bytes divided by four and sample-weighted counts from full conversions, so a saving describes bytes delivered; a tokenizer-specific count requires running the target tokenizer.
  • A full outcome means no content-limit flag fired. HTML preservation requires a separate assessment, which makes the partial rate the number a content team should watch.
  • User agents are client-supplied strings, and Cloudflare verifies no bot identity behind them, so the breakdown tells a team what callers claim about themselves, and the page URLs exclude query strings and fragments.
  • The feature covers Pro, Business and Enterprise plans plus SSL for SaaS at no cost, converts HTML only, and stops converting above 6 MiB of decompressed HTML.

Cloudflare added measurement tools to the feature it announced in February. Converting pages to Markdown gives agents the requested representation; conversion outcomes, estimated savings and failure locations turn that delivery path into an engineering decision.

Netics visual, 10 November 2026: the request path the reference page describes, where the edge asks the origin for HTML and returns Markdown.

What the Agent Readiness dashboard now counts

The changelog entry is short and unusually concrete about scope. Under Agent Readiness in the dashboard, the Markdown for Agents panel now carries three tabs. Analytics shows conversion outcomes, an estimated token reduction, the top converted pages, the top user agents, failure reasons, content limits and the pages with partial or failed conversions. Logs shows sampled conversion events with an outcome, a failure reason and content-limit filters. The Playground requests Markdown for one path and compares it with the HTML response, including the headers and the estimated token reduction.

The same numbers leave the dashboard through the GraphQL Analytics API as markdownForAgentsAdaptiveGroups, at zone and account scope, and through Cloudflare Traces as a markdown_conversion span on sampled streaming conversions. That span carries the conversion outcome, the input and output bytes, the converter CPU time, the longest processing slice and the content-limit flags. For an operator, the trace is the part that attaches a delivery decision to a request timeline, where a daily total hides it.

Content negotiation is the mechanism underneath

The feature runs at Cloudflare's edge in front of the origin. When a client sends Accept with text/markdown among its options, Cloudflare fetches the HTML version from the origin, converts it and serves the result, adding a Vary on Accept so caches keep separate variants for the two representations. The reference page invites people to test it against Cloudflare's own documentation and blog with a single curl request.

The output has a stable shape, which is the part that matters for anyone consuming it in code. A YAML frontmatter block is prepended when the source page carries supported meta tags, with title, description and image taken from the standard meta form first and the Open Graph form as a fallback. Navigation, footers, scripts and styles are stripped during pre-processing, and any JSON-LD in the source is preserved at the end of the document in a single fenced block. Consumption gets predictable without the consumer writing per-site parsers.

The Analytics tab as published in the reference page: conversion attempts, full conversion rate, estimated token reduction and the partial and failed counts beside them. Image from https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/reference/markdown-for-agents/.

Response headers on a converted page

The header contract is documented with a precision that makes it worth reading twice. Security and cache headers survive conversion, including Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, Set-Cookie, the CORS headers and the caching headers. Cloudflare changes the body-derived headers to match the converted response: Content-Type becomes text/markdown, Content-Length is removed to support streaming, and ETag, Last-Modified, Content-Encoding, Content-Range and Transfer-Encoding are dropped because their values belong to the original HTML body.

Dropping the validators has consequences that reach outside the feature. A conditional request cannot be answered for a converted response, so an agent that polls a page with If-None-Match pays for a full transfer every time and a monitor counting requests sees a different pattern from the HTML side. A team that stores Markdown downstream also loses the cheap way to tell whether the page changed, which pushes change detection back onto a content hash of its own.

Netics visual, 10 November 2026: the split between the numbers the dashboard reports and the questions they leave to the team.

Token savings are byte estimates over seven days

The definition of the saving is worth quoting because it decides how the figure should be read: bytes divided by four, rounded down, weighted by sampling, computed only over full conversions that carry a positive input estimate. Queries cover at most seven days of history, and a single dataset query returns at most 1,000 groups. Cloudflare also publishes the formula for a reduction ratio and warns that the estimated value turns negative when the Markdown output is larger than its HTML input.

An engineering team should treat that number as a bandwidth proxy. Dividing the byte count by four gives a serviceable approximation for English prose, with lower accuracy for code, tables and identifier-heavy pages where a real tokenizer can produce a different count. As a trend line, it shows whether the Markdown variant moves meaningfully less data than the page it replaces. Its use as a cost model introduces an error the team has not measured.

Netics visual, 10 November 2026: the caveat the documentation states in its own words, and the estimate behind every token figure.

Partial conversions are the number worth watching

The outcome vocabulary is where the documentation earns its keep. A full conversion means the content-limit flags are all false. Cloudflare defines this outcome by those flags. Preservation fidelity requires a separate assessment. A partial conversion means a limit truncated the input or dropped the frontmatter or the JSON-LD. Two more outcomes cover a conversion whose limit state cannot be established and a stream that never reached a terminal state.

The limitations explain the flags: the converter accepts HTML input and stops at 6 MiB of decompressed HTML. A large documentation page about a data platform can cross that line, and the failure is quiet in the sense that matters, since the agent receives a document that parses and simply lacks the section it came for. Watching the partial rate by section of a site turns that into a content decision about page size, which is cheaper to fix than a crawl budget.

The changelog entry on 10 November 2026, where the Analytics, Logs and Playground tabs are each described in one line. Page from https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2026-11-09-markdown-for-agents-observability.

Turning the analytics into a crawl budget decision

The remaining caveat is the one no dashboard can fix. Cloudflare says the user agents in the analytics are client-supplied strings, with no verified bot identity behind them, which is a fair statement and a hard limit: a scraper that presents a popular agent's user agent appears in the same bucket as that agent. Read the top-user-agent list as a claim, and pair it with whatever identity signal the zone already has.

What the feature does deliver is a measurable floor for an AI-readiness programme. A team can enable conversion for documentation and blog paths through a configuration rule, leave the application untouched, and then decide with data: the share of full conversions, the pages that keep converting partially, and the byte reduction across the top pages. Measuring the content delivered to a crawler also applies to DevOps pipelines and managed monitoring, where crawler delivery belongs in the pipeline's success criteria.

The reference page on 10 November 2026, where the response-header section lists what a converted response keeps and what it drops. Page from https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/reference/markdown-for-agents/.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: End-to-end testing a phone sign-up with Playwright and a real SMS code
description:
Most end-to-end suites skip the one step that breaks most often in production: the SMS code. They mock the SMS provider, so a wrong sender ID, a template change or a country your provider no longer delivers to only shows up when real users complain.

Here is a small Playwright test (Node.js, built-in fetch) that signs up with a real phone number and types the real code. It uses the Receive SMS HTTP API to get a number and read the SMS. Disclosure: I run that service, but the structure works with any provider that can buy a number and return its messages.

Helper: get a number, wait for the code 

// sms.js
const API = 'https://receive-smss.net/api/v1';
const headers = { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SMS_API_KEY}` };

async function call(path, params) {
  const url = `${API}/${path}?${new URLSearchParams(params)}`;
  const res = await fetch(url, { headers });
  return { status: res.status, body: await res.json() };
}

export async function getNumber(app, country, maxPrice) {
  const { body } = await call('get_number', { app, country, max_price: maxPrice });
  if (!body.success) throw new Error(`get_number failed: ${body.error}`);
  return body.data; // { id, number, deduction, expires_at }
}

export async function waitForCode(id, timeoutMs = 5 * 60_000) {
  const end = Date.now() + timeoutMs;
  while (Date.now() < end) {
    const { body } = await call('get_sms', { n_id: id });
    if (body.success) return body.code;
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 5000));
  }
  await call('reject_code', { n_id: id }); // nothing came: cancel and get refunded
  throw new Error('No SMS received');
}

export const finish = (id) => call('finish', { n_id: id });

get_sms returns HTTP 404 until the first message arrives, so the loop simply polls every 5 seconds.

The test 

// signup.spec.js
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { getNumber, waitForCode, finish } from './sms.js';

test('sign up with a UK number', async ({ page }) => {
  const order = await getNumber('yourapp', 'GB', 0.5);

  await page.goto('https://staging.example.com/signup');
  await page.getByLabel('Phone number').fill(order.number);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send code' }).click();

  const code = await waitForCode(order.id);
  await page.getByLabel('Verification code').fill(code);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Verify' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByText('Welcome')).toBeVisible();
  await finish(order.id);
});

Set a generous timeout for this test (test.setTimeout(6 * 60_000)), because SMS delivery can take a minute or two.

Practical notes

  • Run it against staging and on a schedule, not on every commit. Each run buys a number, so a nightly job per country is usually enough to catch delivery problems.
  • max_price makes get_number fail instead of paying more than you expect. HTTP 503 means no numbers are free right now and you are not charged.
  • Use the service code your provider uses for your app. get_services lists them; for your own product you'd typically use a generic "any other" service.
  • Keep the key in CI secrets and send it in the Authorization header, not in the URL, so it doesn't end up in logs.
  • Test the negative case too. If your app is supposed to reject virtual numbers, this setup is an easy way to check that it does.

API reference: receive-smss.net/api-docs. Questions welcome in the comments.

title: prpr, a Terminal List of Every Open GitHub Pull Request I Can See
description:
My open pull requests are spread out: my own repositories, the 0-draft org, and upstream projects I send patches to. Review requests come from all three. GitHub's pulls page shows what I opened or was asked to review, but not everything open in the orgs I belong to, so checking meant a handful of tabs.

prpr is one terminal screen with all of it. Enter opens the pull request in the browser. When it merges, it leaves the list with a 🎉.

  • Source: https://github.com/kanywst/prpr
  • Install: brew install kanywst/tap/prpr, scoop install prpr (bucket kanywst/scoop-bucket), or go install github.com/kanywst/prpr@latest

The recording runs prpr --demo, which serves a fixed fixture list instead of GitHub, so nobody's real account ends up in a GIF.

No config

prpr reuses gh auth login, so there is no token to set up. At start it asks GitHub for your login and every org you are in, then runs one search per owner plus two more:

is:pr is:open archived:false user:<owner>
is:pr is:open archived:false author:<you>
is:pr is:open archived:false user-review-requested:<you>

The last two catch your patches to other people's projects and review requests from orgs you are not in. Anything outside the watched owners goes in the elsewhere tab, next to all, mine, to review, drafts and bots. Dependabot and Renovate stay in bots unless one asks you for a review by name.

The searches run separately, four at a time, instead of OR-ed into one query. An org that enforces SAML SSO your token is not authorized for then costs only its own pull requests: it is named in the header and the rest of the list stays up.

A config file exists for when you want something else (owners, exclude_owners, interval, issues). Unknown keys are an error, so a typo does not silently do nothing:

$ prpr --config config.yaml
prpr: config.yaml: yaml: unmarshal errors:
  line 2: field intervall not found in type config.Config

Saying goodbye without lying

A pull request missing from a refresh is not necessarily merged, and several of the fix commits in the log are about that. The search that covers it may have failed, hit the 60-result cap, or come back partial because GitHub withheld nodes the token cannot read. Or it only dropped out of user-review-requested because I submitted my review.

prpr handles each case differently:

  • a covering search failed: the pull request is carried over from the last refresh, no lookup
  • a covering search was partial: carried over, and its state is looked up anyway, since a partial answer can repeat on every refresh and would otherwise pin a merged pull request to the list for good
  • a covering search hit the cap: its state is looked up, and nothing is shown if it is still open
  • only the review request held it: it leaves quietly
  • otherwise: one GraphQL lookup asks how it ended, and the banner says so 
┃ 🌸 prpr  kanywst · 0-draft                                                             ⟳ 61s ┃
┃ ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ ┃
┃ ▸ all 3  │  mine 2  │  to review 1  │  elsewhere 0  │  drafts 1  │  bots 0                   ┃
┃                                                                                              ┃
┃ ✨ 🎉 0-draft/api#127 fix: nil deref on empty body merged! nice one 🎊                       ┃

That is the repository's render test (go test ./internal/ui -run TestDumpRender -v) against its fixtures. A closed one gets 🌙, and one that only stopped matching the search gets 👋.

The last list is cached on disk, so prpr shows it instantly on start while the first refresh runs. Anything that merged while it was closed still gets its banner then.

What else changes on the row

Icon Meaning
🟢 / 🟡 / 🔴 / ⚪ Checks passing / running / failing / none
✅ / 🔁 / 👀 Approved / changes requested / review requested
💥 Conflicts with its base branch
🆕 Joined the list since you last looked
🔔 Its checks, review or conflict state changed since you last looked

🆕 and 🔔 clear once the cursor lands on the row, and both count what changed while prpr was closed. 🔔 compares the icon, not the raw state, so a change the row cannot show does not ring.

/ filters by title, repository, author, #number and labels. d opens a detail pane with branch, diff stat, reviewers and body. --issues mixes open issues in as 🎫, and polling pauses while the terminal is not focused.

Source and issues: https://github.com/kanywst/prpr

title: RunsOn GitHub Actions runners explained
description:
RunsOn GitHub Actions runners are ordinary EC2 instances that RunsOn launches inside your own AWS account, so you pay RunsOn a flat annual licence and pay Amazon for every instance-second separately. That split is the whole product decision: the licence does not grow with your minutes, and the compute line does, which makes RunsOn expensive for a small team and hard to beat for a large one.


Where each bill comes from. RunsOn prices a licence by runners launched per month and states that the compute is "your AWS bill, not ours", read from runs-on.com/pricing on 21 September 2026.

Almost every other vendor in this area sells you a minute. RunsOn sells you a control plane and leaves the minute on your own cloud bill, which means the comparison against GitHub-hosted runners is not a rate against a rate. It is a fixed cost against a variable one, and the answer flips at a volume you can calculate.

This page covers what the installation actually puts in your account, how a workflow asks for a machine, what the two bills look like, and the operational work you are taking on by moving the runners inside your own perimeter.

What actually gets installed

RunsOn is deployed as infrastructure, not subscribed to as a service. The quickstart describes Flex as installing "with a single CloudFormation stack in about 10 minutes", which creates "a dedicated, least-privilege IAM role for the service" and a GitHub App that the documentation is explicit about: "this creates a private GitHub App that lives only in your AWS account".

That sentence is the reason this page exists. A private GitHub App means no third party holds a token against your organisation, which is the single strongest argument for RunsOn over any hosted runner vendor, and it is also why nobody else can page themselves when your runners stop launching. The trade is stated plainly on both sides.

There are two shapes. Flex provisions one ephemeral EC2 instance per job, driven by workflow_job webhooks that arrive "through API Gateway and Lambda" and queue in SQS. Fleet is the Terraform-defined version, where a fleetd control plane "runs on ECS Fargate and uses a pull-based connection to GitHub", with "no inbound webhook, API Gateway, or SQS queue in the demand path". Flex is for teams whose jobs want different machines; Fleet is for a platform team that wants the runner shape under review.

How a workflow asks for a machine

The migration is a label change, which is the part RunsOn shares with every managed vendor. The documentation gives the Flex form as a single compound label, and the keys inside it are what you would otherwise express in an autoscaler configuration: family for the EC2 type or family, cpu and ram as fixed values or ranges, image for the AMI, volume as size:type:throughput:iops, and extras for features such as s3-cache, ecr-cache, efs, tmpfs and otel.

Two defaults are worth knowing before the first run. Spot is on by default, documented as "whether to attempt to use spot pricing (default: true)", which is where the low compute cost comes from and also where the interruptions come from. SSH access is off by default. The runs-on=${{ github.run_id }} prefix is not decoration: it namespaces the runner to the run that asked for it.

Platform coverage is Linux on x64 and arm64, Windows, and GPU instances. There is no macOS, which rules RunsOn out of an iOS pipeline entirely and is the clearest single filter on whether this product fits your repository.

# GitHub-hosted
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

# RunsOn Flex: the compound label is the whole migration
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: runs-on=${{ github.run_id }}/cpu=4/ram=16/family=m7a+m7i-flex/image=ubuntu22-full-x64

# RunsOn Fleet: the workflow names a fleet, Terraform owns the shape
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: runs-on/fleet=linux-small/env=production

Label forms and key descriptions quoted from RunsOn: runner labels, read 21 September 2026.

The two bills, and where they cross

The licence is metered by runners launched per month, not by minutes. The published Commercial Starter tier is "from 300 euros / year" and covers "< 50k runners / month"; the Enterprise tier is "3,600 euros / year" for "500k+ runners / mo". Non-commercial use is free, described as "the full product, at no cost", in exchange for a public acknowledgement linking back to the vendor. A commercial trial runs 15 days with payment details collected at checkout.

The compute is separate and RunsOn does not touch it: the pricing page describes "spot or on-demand instances, billed per second by AWS" and says the compute line is "your AWS bill, not ours". So the total is a flat number plus a number you already know how to forecast, and neither half is a per-CI-minute rate you can quote in a comparison table.

Do the arithmetic on your own volume rather than on a headline. Ten thousand Linux minutes a month at GitHub's standard 2-core rate of $0.006 is $60 a month, or $720 a year, and that single line already exceeds the Starter licence before a single instance-hour is added. Run a hundred thousand minutes and GitHub bills $7,200 a year while the licence has not moved. The flat fee is the entire argument, and it is an argument that gets stronger the more CI you run.

What you are taking on

Everything the stack cannot do for itself becomes yours. EC2 service quotas in the region, spot capacity when a family runs short, AMI currency, the VPC and its egress path, and the pager at three in the morning when a workflow queues because an account limit was reached rather than because anything is broken. None of that appears on either bill and all of it appears on somebody's week.

That is the honest line between this product and a managed runner. Latchkey sells the opposite trade: nothing to own in your cloud, a published $0.0025 a minute at 2 vCPU with 8 GB, and no EC2 account of your own in the path between a push and a build. RunsOn genuinely wins on cost at volume, because a flat licence plus spot compute beats any metered rate once the minutes are large enough, and it wins outright when the requirement is that no third party holds credentials against your repositories.

Pick on that axis and not on the rate card. If your constraint is the AWS account you are not allowed to have, or the operations time you do not have, the cheaper line on paper is not the cheaper line in practice. Self-hosted versus managed runners works through the same decision without a vendor attached, and RunsOn against Blacksmith is the head-to-head.

FAQ

Is RunsOn a managed runner service?

No, and the distinction matters for the bill. RunsOn installs a control plane into your own AWS account and launches EC2 instances there, so Amazon invoices you for the compute and RunsOn invoices you for a licence. A managed runner vendor gives you one metered line and owns the capacity behind it.

How much does RunsOn cost?

The published Commercial Starter licence is from 300 euros a year and covers fewer than 50,000 runners a month, rising to 3,600 euros a year at the Enterprise tier for 500,000 or more. On top of that you pay AWS directly for spot or on-demand instances, billed per second, with no RunsOn markup. Non-commercial use is free with a public acknowledgement.

Which operating systems can RunsOn launch?

Linux on x64 and arm64, Windows, and GPU instances, all as EC2 instances. The documented platform list does not include macOS. Any job needing Xcode or the iOS simulator therefore stays on GitHub-hosted macOS or on a vendor that sells Mac hardware, and RunsOn takes the rest of the pipeline.

What does the RunsOn CloudFormation stack put in my AWS account?

A control plane, a least-privilege IAM role for the service, and a private GitHub App that exists only in your account. Flex adds the webhook path through API Gateway, Lambda and SQS; Fleet instead runs its control plane on ECS Fargate with a pull-based connection and no inbound webhook. The runners themselves are ordinary ephemeral EC2 instances.

Is RunsOn cheaper than GitHub-hosted runners?

At volume, yes, because the licence is flat and your compute is at spot prices. Ten thousand Linux minutes a month costs $720 a year at GitHub's $0.006 standard rate, which already exceeds the Starter licence before compute. At a few hundred minutes a month the fixed fee makes it more expensive, and the operational time it adds is not on either invoice.

  • RunsOn quickstart: the CloudFormation stack and the private GitHub App (verified 2026-09-21)
  • RunsOn: runner labels, keys and defaults including spot (verified 2026-09-21)
  • RunsOn: Flex and Fleet, and how each one launches a runner (verified 2026-09-21)

title: Coding Agents Generate Outdated Frontend Code Due to Stale Training Data, Which Real-Time Web Platform Guidelines Fix
description:
Introduction: The Legacy Trap in AI-Generated Code

When you prompt an AI coding assistant to build a UI overlay or an animated modal, the generated code often looks astonishingly retrograde. Despite possessing theoretical knowledge that modern platform primitives exist, models like Claude Code and Codex routinely default to brittle, legacy patterns. They write manual position: fixed click-outside event listeners instead of leveraging the native popover API, and they wire up complex class toggles paired with transitionend and setTimeout statements instead of utilizing @starting-style and transition-behavior.

This failure mode is mechanical rather than accidental. Large language models operate on probabilistic token prediction governed by massive historical datasets. Because the public internet contains billions of lines of legacy code and only a thin veneer of newly standardized code, the statistical weight of historical patterns dominates the neural network's activation paths. When an agent receives a UI prompt, its weights naturally gravitate toward the path of least resistance: code written in 2018. This creates an insidious risk formation: developers inherit technical debt before a single line of application code is written, locking next-generation web applications into legacy behaviors that trigger unnecessary layout thrashing, memory leaks from uncleaned event listeners, and severe accessibility regressions like broken focus management.

Until recently, the industry relied on waiting for model providers to retrain base models—an approach that fails because web standards evolve weekly while training cycles take quarters or years. Relying on static model updates for dynamic platform specifications is structurally broken; it guarantees a permanent lag between browser capabilities and agent output.

The definitive turning point arrived with the release of Modern Web Guidance, a collaborative, open-source coding agent skill spearheaded by engineering teams from Chrome, Microsoft (Edge), Mozilla (Firefox), and MDN (including contributions from Kadir Topal, Patrick Brosset, Jake Archibald, Lea Verou, and technical lead Paul Irish). Rather than waiting for model weights to shift, this initiative attacks the problem at the runtime context level. When an agent receives a frontend task, a local CLI scans and injects human-vetted, Baseline-compliant markdown guides directly into the agent's working context. Evaluated across approximately 2,000 rigorous verification checks, agents running without guidance flounder at a fifty percent pass rate, whereas context-injected agents spike to a ninety percent success rate. By binding real-time browser standards directly into the agent prompt loop, the web development ecosystem has finally established a mechanism to prevent legacy habits from permanently fossilizing the modern web.

The Anatomy of the Problem: Why AI Struggles with Modern Web Standards

When an AI coding assistant generates a frontend interface, it is executing a high-dimensional probabilistic search over a static training corpus. The core mechanical failure of modern web development stems from a fundamental temporal asymmetry: browser standards and platform APIs evolve weekly, whereas base model training cycles require quarters or years. Because historical repositories on GitHub are heavily saturated with pre-2018 patterns written before modern primitives existed, statistical token prediction treats legacy code as the path of least resistance. The model's neural weights are mathematically biased toward what was common yesterday, not what is standard today.

This training lag manifests as concrete architectural degradation in the generated execution paths. Consider three distinct failure modes where coding agents bypass native platform primitives in favor of brittle legacy workarounds:

  • Overlay management: Without real-time awareness of the HTML

popover

API, agents routinely fall back to manual JavaScript event listeners, calculating viewport coordinates and attaching document-level click-outside handlers on

position: fixed

elements. This introduces memory leaks from uncleaned event listeners and layout thrashing as DOM mutations force synchronous style recalculations.

  • Entry animations: To animate an element entering the DOM from

display: none

, agents script complex state machines involving class toggles,

setTimeout

delays, and event listeners listening for

transitionend

. This brittle timing logic frequently desynchronizes under main-thread congestion, causing jarring visual pop-ins instead of leveraging native

@starting-style

and

transition-behavior

.

  • Accessibility and focus pipelines: When spawning a modal or new view, unassisted agents frequently fail to redirect the browser's active focus tree into the container and capture tab navigation within it. Screen reader users are left stranded in the background DOM, breaking WCAG compliance at the state-machine level.

Relying on traditional model updates or fine-tuning to close this gap is fundamentally flawed. Fine-tuning is a lagging indicator; by the time a model weights its parameters against newly stabilized Baseline features, those features have already iterated. Therefore, software engineering workflows must reject static model updates in favor of dynamic runtime context injection—such as local CLI-driven skills that scan and inject human-vetted, Baseline-compliant documentation directly into the agent's working prompt loop during execution.

Cross-Browser Alliance: Inside the Collaboration

For decades, browser vendors—Chrome, Microsoft, and Mozilla—operated as isolated fortresses, shipping standards independently while developers bore the friction of fragmentation. But the rise of LLM coding agents broke this institutional inertia. When AI models like Claude Code and Codex write frontend code, they do not read live specifications; they execute probabilistic pattern-matching over massive historical corpora weighted heavily toward pre-2018 codebases. This temporal asymmetry created a systemic crisis: even as browsers natively implemented advanced primitives like the popover API and @starting-style, AI models continued generating legacy mechanical fallbacks.

To short-circuit this decay, an unprecedented coalition of engineering leads from Chrome (Kadir Topal, Paul Irish), Microsoft (Patrick Brosset), Mozilla (Jake Archibald), and independent standards authority Lea Verou united to engineer a direct countermeasure: Modern Web Guidance. Rather than waiting quarters or years for base model retraining cycles to absorb modern specs—a lagging indicator that guarantees perpetual obsolescence—the alliance built a unified, open-source skill that injects human-vetted, Baseline-compliant architectural constraints directly into the agent execution loop.

The Mechanics of Runtime Context Injection vs. Static Fine-Tuning

When evaluating how to align coding agents with modern web standards, engineering teams face a stark architectural choice: static model fine-tuning versus runtime context injection. Fine-tuning attempts to reweight neural network parameters using curated datasets. However, because web platform standards iterate weekly while model weights remain static post-training, fine-tuned models inevitably drift into obsolescence the moment a new Baseline feature ships. Furthermore, probabilistic generation biases the LLM toward whichever code pattern appears with highest frequency in its training tokens—which, statistically, remains legacy DOM manipulation.

The alliance selected runtime context injection via a local CLI as the optimal solution for a distinct mechanical reason: deterministic constraint enforcement. When a developer triggers a frontend task, the CLI intercepts the prompt loop, searches over 200+ human-written Markdown guides, and injects precise, browser-tested implementation parameters directly into the agent's working memory. This forces the neural network to evaluate explicit, up-to-date syntax constraints rather than relying on statistical memory of obsolete forum threads.

  • Option A (Static Fine-Tuning): Fails because model weights freeze at training cutoff, causing a permanent lag behind weekly browser capability updates.
  • Option B (Unvetted Retrieval-Augmented Generation): Fails because general web scraping pulls conflicting, low-quality legacy code snippets from uncurated sources, amplifying technical debt.
  • Option C (Vendor-Governed Local CLI Injection - Chosen Solution): Succeeds by supplying verified, Baseline-compliant code blueprints with baked-in browser support data, pinned to @latest to eliminate drift.

This chosen architecture stops working under specific edge conditions: if an agent runs in an air-gapped environment without local cache persistence, or if the prompt context window truncates the injected guides due to extreme token length overages, the agent defaults back to unconstrained probabilistic sampling. To prevent this failure mode, the guidance pipeline mandates local execution with pinned package dependencies.

Measurable Mechanical Impact on Agent Output

Without this collaborative governance layer, coding agents systematically introduce high-cost runtime failures into production codebases. For instance, when tasked with building a modal or dropdown menu, unguided agents instantiate manual document-level click-outside listeners on position: fixed overlays. This forces synchronous style recalculations on every pointer move, triggering layout thrashing and creating permanent memory leaks if component teardown fails to unbind the listeners.

Similarly, fade-in entry animations written without native primitives rely on brittle chains of class toggles, setTimeout execution blocks, and transitionend event listeners. When the main thread experiences execution congestion, these timers desynchronize, causing jarring visual pop-ins and rendering UI states unpredictable.

By embedding human-authored guides backed by rigorous browser support data, the alliance's evaluation harness—tested against roughly 2,000 distinct verification checks across Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity—demonstrated a dramatic performance shift. Unguided agents passed only fifty percent of checks, while agents augmented with the Modern Web Guidance skill cleared ninety percent. By replacing legacy state machines with native platform primitives like popover and @starting-style, the collaboration successfully transformed AI assistants from engines of legacy technical debt into active vectors of modern web excellence.

Architecture of the Skill: How AI Learns Modern Standards

AI coding assistants like Claude Code and Codex operate on a foundational mismatch: temporal asymmetry. Model training cycles require quarters or years, while web platform standards iterate weekly. Because neural networks execute probabilistic token prediction over historical training corpora heavily dominated by pre-2018 codebases, their statistical path of least resistance is to generate legacy mechanical fallbacks instead of native platform primitives.

Mechanical Failure Modes of Unguided AI Code

When unguided agents attempt frontend tasks, their reliance on stale training weights triggers specific, measurable runtime defects:

  • The Popover Gap: Lacking awareness of the HTML popover API, agents generate manual document-level click-outside listeners on position: fixed overlays. This leaves uncleaned event listeners in the heap, causing permanent memory leaks and layout thrashing from synchronous style recalculations during DOM mutations.
  • Transition Desynchronization: Instead of utilizing native @starting-style and transition-behavior, agents construct brittle state machines using class toggles, setTimeout delays, and transitionend event listeners. Under main-thread congestion, these timing chains desynchronize, resulting in observable visual pop-ins and layout jank.
  • Focus Tree Abandonment: Spawning modals without explicit focus management leaves screen reader users stranded in the background DOM, violating accessibility compliance at the state-machine level.

Architectural Evaluation: Why Local CLI Injection Succeeds

To solve these failure modes, engineering teams evaluated three distinct architectural approaches:

  • Static Fine-Tuning (Rejected): Fails because model weights freeze at the training cutoff. This guarantees a permanent lag behind weekly browser capability updates and requires expensive, recurring retraining cycles.
  • Unvetted Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Rejected): Fails because generalized web scraping retrieves conflicting, low-quality legacy snippets from uncurated forums, actively amplifying technical debt within the agent's context window.
  • Vendor-Governed Local CLI Injection (Chosen): Succeeds by intercepting the prompt loop locally. A lightweight CLI scans and injects human-vetted, Baseline-compliant Markdown guides directly into the agent's working memory during frontend tasks.

Decision Rule: When feature evolution velocity outpaces model retraining cycles (X), do not rely on parameter updates; deploy runtime context injection via pinned, verifiable blueprints (Y) to enforce deterministic constraints.

Structural Mechanics and Verification

The Modern Web Guidance architecture—stewarded by engineers from Chrome, Microsoft, Mozilla, and MDN—operates through a deterministic runtime pipeline:

  • Local Execution: A small CLI running on the developer's machine searches over 200 human-vetted guides written by browser engineers when a frontend task is initialized.
  • Baseline Enforcement: Every blueprint enforces Baseline Widely Available standards. Newer features include baked-in browser support data, forcing agents to supply fallbacks or progressive enhancements.
  • Dynamic Pinning: CLI commands are pinned to @latest, ensuring weekly updates bypass the model's static training cutoff entirely.

Edge Cases and Failure Conditions

The chosen architecture encounters critical edge conditions when operating constraints break down. In air-gapped environments lacking local cache persistence, or when extreme token length overages truncate the context window, the CLI fails to inject the guides. Under these conditions, the agent defaults to unconstrained probabilistic sampling, reverting immediately to legacy code patterns. Mitigation requires strict local cache persistence and dependency locking.

When evaluated across approximately 2,000 rigorous checks in Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity, unguided agents cleared only 50 percent of the criteria. With the skill's direct context injection bridging the gap between legacy training weights and modern platform primitives, pass rates surged to 90 percent.

Impact and the Future of AI-Assisted Web Development

When engineering teams from Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and MDN united to release Modern Web Guidance, they targeted a foundational structural flaw in AI coding assistants: temporal asymmetry. Because neural network weights freeze at the conclusion of training cutoffs, models like Claude Code and Codex operate on historical corpora heavily weighted toward pre-2018 patterns. Without direct intervention, probabilistic token prediction treats legacy workarounds—such as manual position: fixed click-outside listeners and setTimeout transition chains—as the statistical path of least resistance. This forces the browser rendering engine into mechanical failure modes, including layout thrashing and accessibility regressions.

Quantitative Performance and Verification Benchmarks

To measure the efficacy of runtime context injection, engineering evaluations tested coding agents across approximately 2,000 rigorous automated checks in Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity. The performance delta is stark:

  • Unguided Agents: Cleared only 50% of verification checks, persistently injecting legacy patterns that fail to leverage native platform primitives like the popover API and @starting-style.
  • Context-Injected Agents: Achieved a 90% pass rate when equipped with the local CLI skill, injecting human-vetted, Baseline-compliant blueprints directly into the agent working prompt loop.

Architectural Solution Comparison

When selecting a mechanism to bridge the gap between rapidly evolving web standards and static LLM parameter weights, engineering analysis reveals distinct failure thresholds across competing strategies:
Approach Mechanism Failure Mode & Effectiveness
Static Fine-Tuning Periodic retraining of model parameter weights. Retraining Lag: Web standards iterate weekly while training cycles take quarters or years, guaranteeing perpetual obsolescence. (Rejected)
Unvetted RAG Generalized web scraping across uncurated developer forums and blogs. Noise Injection: Retrieves conflicting, legacy code snippets that pollute the context window and amplify technical debt. (Rejected)
Vendor-Governed Local CLI Injection Local CLI intercepting the prompt loop to inject human-vetted, Baseline-compliant Markdown guides pinned to @latest. Optimal: Deterministic constraint enforcement; breaks down only in air-gapped environments without local cache persistence or extreme token truncation. (Chosen)

Decision Rule for Web Platform Guidance

To eliminate architectural selection errors, engineering workflows must adhere to a strict decision rule:

If feature evolution velocity outpaces model retraining cycles, then avoid parameter updates and deploy runtime context injection via pinned, verifiable blueprints to enforce deterministic constraints and prevent browser rendering degradation.

Failure Edge Conditions and Mitigation Mechanics

Even with runtime context injection, specific edge conditions can trigger degradation in agent output. In air-gapped environments lacking local cache persistence, or when extreme token length overages truncate the agent's working context window, the system drops the injected guides. This forces the neural network to fall back to unconstrained probabilistic sampling over its base weights. Furthermore, default telemetry transmission sends anonymous usage data to Google unless explicitly suppressed via the environment variable DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1.

title: Stripe webhook mistakes that lose or repeat payments
description:
A Stripe webhook endpoint is a public URL that moves money and access. Five coding mistakes let a forged request or a plain retry do the wrong thing.

A Stripe webhook endpoint is an ordinary web address that Stripe calls when something happens in your account: a payment succeeds, a subscription renews, a dispute opens. Whatever your handler does next, such as shipping a product, switching on a plan or crediting a balance, is real. That makes the endpoint a target for two kinds of trouble. Someone outside Stripe can post a made-up event to it, and Stripe itself can legitimately deliver the same event more than once.
