title: Why is my CI so expensive? A diagnostic
description:
Why is my CI so expensive is almost never a mystery once you know which of two meters moved: the rate you are paying per minute, or the number of minutes you are buying. This page names six shapes of GitHub Actions invoice, says what each one usually is, and gives the one check that confirms or clears it before you change any workflow.


The six causes sorted under the two meters they move. Rates and storage prices from docs.github.com, read on 21 September 2026.

A CI bill has exactly two inputs, and every cause below is one of them wearing a different hat. Either the work got more expensive per minute, which is a runner type or a runner size, or there is more work, which is triggers, retries or storage.

Work down the list in order. It is ordered by how much money each cause typically accounts for, not by how likely it is, and the first two together explain most invoices that doubled without anyone deploying anything unusual.

Start by asking which meter moved

Pull the usage report and group it by SKU. If one SKU grew, the rate moved: somebody added a macOS or Windows leg, or switched a job to a larger runner. If every SKU grew together, the volume moved: more triggers, more retries, or more branches. That single grouping saves an afternoon of guessing, and it is the only view that separates the two.

Then check the date the growth started against your own history. A bill that stepped on a specific day is a change somebody made; a bill that has been climbing for six months is your repository growing. The first has a commit behind it and the second does not, and they need entirely different answers.

What the invoice looks like What it usually is The check that settles it
Roughly ten times a Linux baseline macOS minutes Group the usage report by SKU and look for the macOS line
Stepped up on one specific day A larger runner was switched on Search the workflows for a size label, and check how fast it now spends the allowance
Climbs with the size of the team More pushes, no caching, no filters Count runs per week against merged pull requests per week
Minutes high, wall clock low A matrix of short jobs and per-minute rounding Compare billed minutes against summed job durations
A sizeable share of runs are retries Flaky or transient failures Count runs with run_attempt above 1
Grew without any minutes changing Artifact and cache storage Look for the storage SKUs rather than the Actions minutes SKU

SKU names and report fields from GitHub billing reports, read 21 September 2026.

Cause one: the machine, not the workload

A macOS minute is $0.062 and a standard Linux minute is $0.006, so one iOS job is worth ten of anything else on the invoice. Windows is $0.010, a gentler premium that is nonetheless two thirds more than Linux for work that frequently did not need Windows in the first place. If the macOS or Windows line is the tall one, the answer is not to make those jobs faster, it is to run fewer of them.

Larger runners are the version of this that appears overnight. They cost roughly double per doubling of cores, they spend a Team or Enterprise Cloud allowance at that higher rate, and they are billed on public repositories where standard runners are free. A single pull request that changed runs-on to a 16-core label can produce a step change in the bill with no other visible cause, and the allowance running out sooner at the same time makes the step look larger than the rate difference alone.

Confirm by reading the label, not by reading the workflow name. GitHub Actions larger runners pricing has every size and rate, and Windows runner cost prices the matrix leg most teams have forgotten they added.

Cause two: work you did not need to start

Workflows are triggered by pushes, not by relevance. A pull request that edits a README starts the same build as one rewriting the networking layer, and it bills the same. Push twice within five minutes and the first run keeps going, obsolete and fully charged, unless something cancels it.

These are volume causes, so they scale with the team rather than with the product, which is why they show up as a bill that climbs steadily rather than one that steps. The shape to look for is runs per week growing faster than merged pull requests per week.

The fixes are three lines of YAML and they are priced, against one worked month, in how to reduce GitHub Actions costs. This page deliberately does not repeat them, because a tactic list and a diagnostic are different documents and splitting one answer across two pages helps nobody.

Cause three: the same work, billed twice

A retry buys the same minutes again. If a meaningful share of your runs are second attempts, that share of the bill produced no additional information about your code, and it is the one cause on this page that no per-minute discount touches: a 30 percent cheaper runner applied to a pipeline that re-runs 15 percent of its jobs saves less than fixing the flakiness would.

Separate the two kinds before you act. A test that fails on real non-determinism is your code and needs a fix in the test. A job that failed on a registry timeout, a DNS failure or a lost runner is not your code at all, and those minutes are pure waste in both directions: you pay for the failure, you pay for the retry, and the pipeline sits red until a human presses a button.

Count it rather than estimating it. The command is in identifying high cost GitHub Actions workflows, and it is three lines.

Cause four: rounding, and cause five: storage

GitHub rounds the minutes and partial minutes each job uses up to the nearest whole minute. A twelve-leg matrix of 40-second jobs uses eight minutes of machine time and bills twelve, and the gap is invisible in every dashboard that reports duration. If your billed minutes are well above the sum of your job durations, rounding is the difference and the fix is fewer, longer jobs.

Storage is the cause that produces a bill with no minutes behind it at all. Artifacts and packages share an allowance and cost $0.25 per GB-month beyond it; Actions cache has its own 10 GB per repository and costs $0.07 per GB-month above that. Both accrue hourly, which is the part that catches people: deleting an artifact stops future charges and does not refund the hours already recorded.

A retention policy is usually the whole fix, and the default is generous: artifacts and logs are retained for 90 days unless you say otherwise. Cache and artifact storage cost works through the arithmetic and the retention change that lands on 1 October 2026.

Cause six: nothing changed, and that is the answer

Sometimes the bill is correct and the expectation was wrong. Included usage resets monthly, and since 28 October 2026 it is a dollar amount spent at each runner's rate rather than a minute count: $18 on Team buys 3,000 Linux minutes but only about 290 macOS minutes, so how far it goes depends on which runners spent it. A plan change, a new organisation, a change in how the allowance is counted, or a repository moving from public to private will all produce a step with no workflow change behind it.

Private is the big one. Standard runners are free and unlimited on public repositories, so a repository that goes private starts paying full rate for work that was genuinely free the week before, and nothing in the workflow files will show you why.

Once you know which of the six it is, the order of operations is the same every time: stop the work you did not need, then move the work that is on the wrong machine, then and only then argue about the rate. Running out of minutes covers what happens when the allowance goes rather than when the invoice grows.

FAQ

Why did my GitHub Actions bill suddenly double?

A step on a specific date is nearly always a runner change: a macOS or Windows leg added to a matrix, or a job moved to a larger runner. Larger runners double roughly per doubling of cores and spend the included allowance at that higher rate, so it runs out sooner and the step is bigger than the rate difference alone would suggest.

Why is my CI expensive when the jobs are short?

Per-minute rounding. Every job is rounded up to the nearest whole minute, so a wide matrix of 40-second jobs bills roughly a minute and a half for every minute it actually runs. Compare your billed minutes against the sum of your job durations; if there is a large gap, consolidating legs recovers most of it.

Can a cheaper runner fix an expensive CI bill?

It multiplies whatever is left after the other five causes, which makes it the last change rather than the first. It does nothing at all about re-runs, storage, or jobs that should never have started, and those three account for most invoices that surprised somebody.

My repository is public. Why am I being charged for Actions at all?

Standard runners are free on public repositories, but larger runners are always charged there, at their per-minute rate. Storage is the other possibility: artifacts and caches are billed by the GB-month regardless of what kind of repository produced them.

References

  • GitHub: Actions billing, allowances, rounding and storage accrual (verified 2026-11-12)
  • GitHub: Actions runner pricing, every per-minute rate by runner (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub billing reports: grouping usage by SKU, repository and workflow (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub: dependency caching limits and the 7-day eviction policy (verified 2026-09-21)

title: CSS Grid Explained with Simple Examples
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

CSS Grid is a layout system built into CSS that lets you place items in rows and columns at the same time. You turn a parent element into a grid container with display: grid, define the columns and rows, add spacing with gap, and the browser lines everything up for you. In this guide you will learn the core ideas step by step, build a complete card gallery you can copy, and see when Grid beats Flexbox.

What Is a Grid Container?

Every grid starts with a container. Pick the element that wraps your items, a div, a section or a main element, and set display: grid on it. That one line changes how its direct children behave. The children become grid items, and the container controls where they sit.

Think of it like a spreadsheet. Columns run down, rows run across, and each item sits in a cell where a row and a column meet. Lines are the borders between cells, and tracks are the rows and columns themselves. You describe the spreadsheet, and the browser builds it.

If you are still sorting out which language does what on a page, our guide to the difference between HTML, CSS and JavaScript is a friendly place to start. HTML gives the structure, CSS, including Grid, gives the layout.

The MDN guide to the basic concepts of grid layout explains containers, items, lines and tracks in detail, and it is worth bookmarking as you practise.

Step 1: Create Your First Grid

Start with simple HTML and one CSS rule:

<div class="box">
  <div>One</div>
  <div>Two</div>
  <div>Three</div>
</div>

.box {
  display: grid;
}

That is a real grid already. With no columns defined, Grid creates one column and stacks the three items in three rows. The magic starts when you describe the columns and rows yourself.

Step 2: Define Columns and Rows

Two properties do most of the work. grid-template-columns sets how many columns there are and how wide each one is. grid-template-rows does the same job for rows.

.box {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 200px 200px 200px;
  grid-template-rows: 100px 100px;
}

This says: make three columns, each 200 pixels wide, and two rows, each 100 pixels tall. Six items fill it perfectly. A seventh item creates a new row automatically, which is handy and also a common surprise.

Fixed sizes are clear, but they do not adapt to different screens. That is why Grid has a unit made just for this job.

Step 3: Meet the fr Unit

The fr unit means one fraction of the free space. It is Grid only, and it makes columns share space fairly without any maths from you.

grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr;

Here the free space is split into three equal parts. Change it to 2fr 1fr and the first column gets twice the share of the second. It is like slicing a cake where one guest politely, and correctly, gets a bigger slice.

Writing the same value again and again gets dull, so use repeat():

grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);

That line means the same as 1fr 1fr 1fr, but it is shorter and easier to change. The full MDN CSS grid layout reference lists every Grid property you will meet as you grow.

Step 4: Add Space with gap

Items that touch each other look cramped. The gap property adds space between rows and columns, and only between them, never around the outside edge.

.box {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  gap: 16px;
}

One value sets both gaps. Two values set them separately: gap: 24px 16px means 24 pixels between rows and 16 between columns. Before gap, developers used margins and fixed the extra edge space by hand. Grid skips that headache.

Terminal style code listing for this article: the gallery CSS rules, the verified check on the test file, and the layout measurements for a 900 pixel container.

Step 5: Place Items with grid-column

By default, each item takes one cell and they flow in order. Sometimes one item deserves more room, like a featured card at the top of a gallery. Use grid-column on that item:

.featured {
  grid-column: span 2;
}

span 2 means this item stretches across two columns. You can also name exact lines: grid-column: 1 / 3 means start at line 1 and end at line 3, the same width. Beginners usually find span easier, so start there. The row version is grid-row.

Good structure helps Grid too. Using meaningful elements for your sections and cards, as covered in our guide to HTML semantic tags explained with examples, keeps your markup clear while Grid handles the visual placement.

Step 6: A Complete Card Gallery You Can Copy

Now put it all together. This is the exact example tested for this article. It builds a gallery with a wide featured card and four normal cards:

<div class="gallery">
  <article class="card featured">
    <h2>Featured</h2><p>Wide card.</p>
  </article>
  <article class="card"><h2>Card 2</h2><p>Normal card.</p></article>
  <article class="card"><h2>Card 3</h2><p>Normal card.</p></article>
  <article class="card"><h2>Card 4</h2><p>Normal card.</p></article>
  <article class="card"><h2>Card 5</h2><p>Normal card.</p></article>
</div>

.gallery {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  gap: 16px;
  max-width: 900px;
  margin: 0 auto;
}
.card {
  background: #eef6ff;
  padding: 20px;
  border-radius: 8px;
}
.featured {
  grid-column: span 2;
}

Here is what happens. The gallery has three equal columns. In a 900 pixel container, each column is 289.33 pixels wide, because the two 16 pixel gaps use 32 pixels first: (900 minus 32) divided by 3. The featured card spans two columns, so it is 594.67 pixels wide. Row one holds the featured card and Card 2. Row two holds Cards 3, 4 and 5. No floats and no extra wrapper divs.

We verified this example in a standalone HTML file: the CSS braces were balanced, all the Grid properties were present, and the five article elements were correctly opened and closed. Try changing repeat(3, 1fr) to repeat(2, 1fr) and watch the gallery rebuild into two columns.

Grid vs Flexbox: Which One Should You Use?

Grid and Flexbox are friends, not rivals. Flexbox lays items out in one direction, a row or a column. Grid works in two directions at once. If you know the shape of the whole page, Grid usually wins. For a line of items that should wrap and centre, Flexbox is often simpler. Our companion guide to CSS Flexbox explained with simple examples covers that case in the same style.

Question CSS Grid Flexbox
Main job Page layouts in rows and columns Items in a single row or column
Directions Two: rows and columns together One at a time
Best for Galleries, dashboards, whole pages Menus, toolbars, centring items
Item placement You can place items in exact cells Items flow and size by content
Typical start grid-template-columns justify-content and align-items

A common pattern is Grid for the page and Flexbox inside each card.

Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting

Putting display: grid on the wrong element. Grid only controls direct children. If your cards are wrapped in extra divs, the wrapper becomes the item, not the card. Check your HTML nesting first.

Expecting gap around the outside. gap adds space only between tracks. If you want space around the whole grid, add padding to the container.

Confusing columns and rows. grid-template-columns controls widths as you read across. If your layout looks rotated, you probably swapped the two template properties.

Fixed sizes that overflow small screens. Three 200 pixel columns need at least 600 pixels plus gaps. On a phone that overflows. Prefer fr units for flexible columns, and test at a narrow width.

Forgetting that extra items create new rows. Grid adds rows for items you did not plan for. Check your item count when a layout looks taller than expected.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is CSS Grid hard for beginners?

No. Start with display: grid, grid-template-columns and gap. Those three alone build most beginner layouts, and the rest can wait.

What does 1fr mean in Grid?

It means one fraction of the free space left after fixed sizes and gaps are taken away. Three columns of 1fr share that space equally.

Should I learn Grid or Flexbox first?

Learn Flexbox basics first if you mainly centre items and build menus, then learn Grid for full page layouts. In practice you will use both together.

Does Grid work in all modern browsers?

Yes. Grid is supported in all modern browsers, including Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge, so the examples in this article are safe to use today.

How do I make a grid item span two rows?

Use grid-row: span 2 on that item, in the same way grid-column: span 2 spans two columns.

Conclusion

Grid stops being scary once you see it as a described spreadsheet: a container, columns and rows you define, fr units that share space fairly, gap for breathing room, and grid-column when one item needs more space. Copy the gallery, change the numbers, and break it on purpose.

title: Grade once, prove it forever: 46,756 settled calls and the case for an append-only grading ledger
description:
Every prediction system eventually makes a promise like this: "our hit rate is 57%." That is a claim about the past, and it is only meaningful if the past cannot be edited. In almost every system I have audited, the grade is a mutable boolean on the same row as the prediction, updated by whatever job ran last. The row is not a record. It is a cache of the most recent writer's opinion.

The case study: a production system with 46,969 prediction rows, 46,756 of them settled. All figures come from the live database.

What a grade actually contains

A grade is not a boolean. It is a tuple: the frozen inputs, the outcome source, the rule version that mapped outcome to verdict, and the instant the verdict was written. Change any one of the four and you have a different claim wearing the same primary key.

The failure is structural, not a bug. UPDATE ai_predictions SET hit = ... has no memory. When the outcome feed corrects a score ninety minutes after full time, the settle job overwrites the verdict and the previous one ceases to exist. Nobody can prove afterwards whether the row was graded once or nine times.

The evidence: a row that keeps changing

The schema has both settled_at and updated_at. The gap between them is a lower bound on row mutation after grading — not proof of re-grading, because any column write touches updated_at, but it is enough to show the row is not frozen.

SELECT
  count(*)                                                              AS settled,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE updated_at > settled_at + interval '1 minute')  AS late_1m,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE updated_at > settled_at + interval '1 day')     AS late_1d,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE updated_at > settled_at + interval '7 day')     AS late_7d,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE settled_at > updated_at)                        AS impossible,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS NULL)                                    AS settled_no_grade,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE settled_at IS NULL)                             AS settled_no_ts
FROM ai_predictions
WHERE settled;

 settled | late_1m | late_1d | late_7d | impossible | settled_no_grade | settled_no_ts
---------+---------+---------+---------+------------+------------------+---------------
   46756 |   35414 |   26831 |   21145 |         93 |              120 |           329

75.7% of settled rows were written more than a minute after their own settlement timestamp. 57.4% more than a day later. 45.2% more than a week later. And 93 rows carry a settlement timestamp that is later than their last write — an ordering that cannot happen if settlement is a single atomic act.

The trend shows a process problem being fixed by accident:

Cohort (by created_at) settled written >1d after settlement share
2026-06 2,735 2,735 100.0%
2026-07 2,637 2,636 100.0%
2026-08 164 164 100.0%
2026-09 9,752 8,808 90.3%
2026-10 21,865 11,117 50.8%
2026-11 9,603 1,371 14.3%

Older cohorts were re-touched by every downstream backfill: calibration columns, visibility flags, learning timestamps. Each write was legitimate; collectively they destroyed the only audit trail we had.

A 25-row ledger for 35,414 mutations

One table records a re-grade: r132_settle_reverify_log, 25 rows, spanning 2026-09-22 to 2026-11-09. Of those, 8 changed the recorded outcome and 4 flipped the verdict.

Read that ratio again: when a re-grade was logged, 32% of the time the answer changed. That is the real value of an audit trail — it tells you the base rate of your own corrections. And 25 logged events cannot explain 35,414 mutated rows.

There is a quieter signal. The table has two boolean grade columns, hit and hit_1x2, and they disagree on 391 of 46,636 rows. Two fields meant to say the same thing, disagreeing on 0.84% of the corpus, with no documented rule about which wins. When a consumer asks "what is the hit rate", the honest answer is "of which column".

The 342 rows a guard was designed not to see

The system does recompute grades to check itself. A guard compares stored hit against a recomputation from actual_result and prediction_direction: 1,428 runs recorded, 343 flagged abnormal, most recent run 2026-11-15 12:21.

Latest reading: hit_vs_recalc = 0.74%, mismatch = 342 of n = 46,427, against a 2.0% threshold. The guard is green, and stays green while up to ~928 rows are wrong. A percentage threshold turns an integrity question into a tolerance question, and tolerance always wins — nobody wants a red dashboard.

Here is the query that produces the 342, split by whether the call had one label or two:

SELECT
  prediction_direction LIKE '%/%' AS multi_label,
  count(*)                                                              AS n,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit)                                            AS graded_true,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit = (actual_result = split_part(prediction_direction,'/',1)))
                                                                        AS fits_primary_only,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit = (actual_result = ANY(string_to_array(prediction_direction,'/'))))
                                                                        AS fits_any_of_pair
FROM ai_predictions
WHERE settled AND hit IS NOT NULL AND actual_result IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1;

 multi_label |    n  | graded_true | fits_primary_only | fits_any_of_pair
-------------+-------+-------------+-------------------+------------------
 f           | 29389 |       17319 |             29364 |            29364
 t           | 17039 |        9282 |             12171 |            16722

Single-label rows are clean: 29,364 of 29,389 agree with strict equality, a 0.09% residual. Two-label rows are not. The production rule is clearly "hit if the outcome is either label" — that explains 16,722 of 17,039. But 317 rows fit neither reading. They were graded under a rule that no longer exists, or by a code path since rewritten, and the row cannot tell you which.

That is the concrete cost: not that 317 rows move the headline number (0.68% of 46,756), but that you cannot distinguish "wrong" from "graded under an older rule" and therefore cannot fix either. You can only overwrite, which is how you got here.

The hash column that cannot identify a row

odds_snapshot_hash is the right instinct and the wrong implementation. 2,039 rows have it NULL. Among non-null values, 2,511 groups share a value, and the largest single value is shared by 357 rows, because the hash covers the market-price snapshot rather than the row. Coverage also arrived late: 31.9% of June rows, 96.0% of July, 99.9%+ from September. The field cannot answer "which inputs produced this verdict", only "which snapshot was current" — a weaker claim.

The fix: two pieces, both small

Piece one is an append-only grade ledger with a hash chain. Each entry commits to the previous entry's digest, so the history is verifiable by walking it. The canonical serialization matters more than the hash function — if two processes serialize the same grade differently, the chain reports tampering that did not happen.

import hashlib, json

FIELDS = ("prediction_id", "model_id", "direction", "prob_hash",
          "home_score", "away_score", "outcome", "verdict",
          "rule_version", "graded_at")

def canonical(payload: dict) -> bytes:
    body = {k: payload[k] for k in FIELDS}
    # sort_keys + no whitespace + explicit separators = one byte string per grade
    return json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")).encode()

def link(payload: dict, prev_digest: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
    digest = hashlib.sha256(prev_digest.encode() + b"|" + canonical(payload)).hexdigest()
    return digest, prev_digest

def verify(entries: list[dict]) -> dict:
    prev = "0" * 64
    bad = []
    for e in entries:
        if e["prev_digest"] != prev:
            bad.append((e["prediction_id"], "broken_link"))
        expect, _ = link(e, prev)
        if expect != e["digest"]:
            bad.append((e["prediction_id"], "payload_changed"))
        prev = e["digest"]
    return {"entries": len(entries), "violations": bad, "head": prev}

Piece two is a database-level refusal. A trigger that rejects any change to the grading columns once a final entry exists turns "we promise to grade once" into "the database will not let us do otherwise". Corrections then go through a new ledger entry with a reason code, not an UPDATE.

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION reject_regrade() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  IF OLD.hit IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.hit
     OR OLD.actual_result IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.actual_result
     OR OLD.match_home_score IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.match_home_score
     OR OLD.match_away_score IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.match_away_score
     OR OLD.settled_at IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.settled_at THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'grade is immutable; append a correction entry instead (id=%)', OLD.id;
  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER ai_predictions_grade_frozen
BEFORE UPDATE ON ai_predictions
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION reject_regrade();

Rollout order matters

Do not turn the trigger on first. Freeze what you have, label it, then close it.

  1. Backfill one ledger entry per settled row, marked origin = 'backfill'. This deliberately blesses today's values, including the 342 mismatches.
  2. Quarantine the 342 into a disputed column rather than overwriting. A human adjudicates them exactly once.
  3. Resolve hit vs hit_1x2: one canonical, the other derived in a view. Two writable booleans for one fact is a bug on a schedule.
  4. Then enable the trigger, routing every correction through an append-only entry with rule_version and reason.
  5. Run verify() hourly and alarm on any violation, not on a percentage. A chain either verifies or it does not.

The payoff is not tidiness. With a chain you can answer what is currently unanswerable: the published hit rate on 1 October, recomputed from entries that existed on 1 October; how many verdicts changed after the fact; whether a model improved from better calls or from a re-grade. Without it, every historical number is a claim about the current contents of a mutable table — and that claim quietly improves whenever someone cleans the data.

One more reason: this corpus feeds a public leaderboard. One match carries 358 graded calls from 358 model variants, three more carry 120 or more. A single rule change applied to that cluster moves a ranking without any model having changed. Sorting by a number whose rows can be rewritten is not measurement; it is a snapshot of whoever ran last.
Grade once. Keep the receipt. Make the receipt impossible to edit.

title: Designing screens with AI expert roles: what each one caught
description:
AI agents write most of my code. What keeps the screens from looking like a default template is a design phase with separate AI roles and a design gate after the build. This post walks through one real redesign of Seed, role by role, with a link to every catch and an honest list of what did not work.

TL;DR

  • I don't ask one AI to design a screen. A product designer, a product lead, a UX writer and a psychologist advise in parallel, and a lead merges one spec.
  • The spec ends with a table: every recommendation, the role that gave it, and whether it was adopted or dropped. That table is where weak ideas get cut.
  • After the build, a design reviewer opens the screens in a browser at 390 and 1440 px with axe-core and the keyboard. It found a Block dialog that never said who.
  • The roles still miss things: the big calls in this redesign were mine, and a wording rule drifted until a later fix settled it.

dotfiles: Code: github.com/spy4x/dotfiles

I don't ask one AI model to "design a nice screen". When I design UI with AI
agents, four of them, each with a different job description, read the same brief
in parallel: a product designer, a product lead, a UX writer and a psychologist.
A lead agent merges their advice into one spec, with a table of what each
recommendation became. After the build, a separate design reviewer opens the
screens in a real browser and blocks the merge if something is broken.

This post shows what each role caught in one real redesign, of the app in
Seed, my free SaaS starter, in October 2026. Every catch links to
the issue or pull request where it's written down, so you can check me.

It's for founders who wonder why my products look finished when agents write
most of the code, and for developers who run agents and want screens that don't
look like a default template.

What does each role do?

Each role is a Markdown file in my public
dotfiles
repository. Here is each one in a sentence or two:

  • Product designer. The job of the screen, hierarchy, layout "mobile first at 390 px, then 1440 px", every state (empty, loading, error, offline), keyboard paths and contrast. It returns at most ten recommendations and a wireframe at both widths.
  • Product lead. The CEO lens: who it's for, what to cut so it ships sooner, the one number it should move, and the risk (personal data, legal text, abuse).
  • UX writer. Every word on the screen. "Buttons say what happens ("Save note", not "Submit")", and "one term per concept across the app". It returns the final copy for every string, grouped by state.
  • Psychologist. Trust, cognitive load and motivation. It names the framework it uses, says how well established the evidence is, and refuses dark patterns: "no fake urgency, no hidden costs, no forced continuity, no misdirection, no confirm-shaming".
  • Marketing and SEO. Joins only for pages a visitor uses to decide: public pages, pricing, sign-up. It sat out this redesign, which was all signed-in screens.
  • Design reviewer. Comes after the build. Its file tells it, "You did not design or build this screen." It opens every changed screen with Playwright at 390 and 1440 px in every theme, runs axe-core, walks it with the keyboard only, and tries the main task as a first-time user.

None of them writes code. Every file asks for the same strong model tier, so
the difference between them is only the job description. That turns out to be
enough.

The order lives in the
design skill,
the instructions an agent loads before it touches anything a person sees:

  1. Ground truth. Screenshots of the current screens at 390 and 1440 px, in every theme, and one shared brief: the job of the screen, the audience, the constraints.
  2. Roles in parallel, no code. Each returns at most ten recommendations, most important first.
  3. One merged spec, by the lead. Wireframes, the final copy, and a table: "each recommendation, and what it became or why it was dropped".
  4. Build, look, revise. The implementer screenshots its own work and revises it "at least twice" before opening the pull request.
  5. Design gate. The design reviewer checks the result next to the code reviewer. A public page also has to score at least 95 for performance and 100 for the rest in Lighthouse mobile.

What did the roles catch in Seed's redesign?

On 16 October I asked for a redesign of Seed's app: drop the header bar and keep
only the sidebar, and make "New group" open the same editor as editing a group,
instead of a dialog with one Name field. The merged spec is
template#453 (Seed lived in the
spy4x/template repository then; it's archived now). It says: "The design phase
ran the product designer, product lead, UX writer and psychologist." Its
Evidence section has the table of where each recommendation went. Here are some
of its rows.

Product lead: one request, and limits before the form

The old create call carried only an id and a name, so description, colour and
emoji had to be set afterwards. The product lead asked that "create sends every
field in one request", and that plan limits are "checked before the form, not
after", so nobody fills in a form only to be told they're over their plan. It
also asked for "no pre-fill from the URL". All three were adopted. The New group
page at the top of this post is the result: all four fields, one Create group
button.

Psychologist: the row is the link, and opening is not switching

In the old app, clicking a group in /groups opened its notes, and "Open notes"
was promoted as if notes were the only thing in a group. I asked for the row to
open the group's editor instead and for "Open notes" to stop being promoted. The
psychologist added that the whole row be the link, with "Current" written as
text. That's how the list in the demo looks today:

Its second catch was quieter. Opening a group's editor must never change your
current group. The product lead said the same thing, and the lead added one
exception: creating a group does switch to it, "since the person made it to use
it".

Product designer: no danger zone, and secrets shown once

The designer put destructive actions, such as Leave and Delete, in the editor's
"More actions" menu instead of a "danger zone". With the psychologist, it also
asked that a new API token's secret or an invitation link be shown only once, on
its own page. The pull request that built those pages,
template#479, adds a guard: leave
before you press Done and the page asks "Leave without copying?".

UX writer: every string, plus what didn't match

The writer returned the copy for every string on every state, and five notes on
wording elsewhere in the app that no longer matched. For example: tags and notes
said "This group was not found." while the group page said "This group does not
exist.", and delete dialogs said "Keep it" in one place and "Cancel" in another.
The spec's summary of its rules: "Create" replaces "Add", and "…" replaces
"...". #479 applied the table across notes and groups.

What did the design reviewer catch after the build?

The roles above advise before any code. The design reviewer looks at what was
actually built, and it's the one that finds what nobody planned for.

Reviewing the new sidebar in
template#483, it ran axe-core on
the admin screens and found failures that were already
on main too:
heading levels that skip on the Billing page, and on the System page a <dl>
holding <p> children and two scrolling tables that the keyboard can't reach.

Those admin screens were built before the design gate existed, so I had already
asked for an audit of all of them. The reviewer checked every admin screen at
390 and 1440 px, light and dark, and
listed what blocked:

  • Tab panels showed no focus ring, and focus was lost after a token was revoked.
  • At 390 px, the API tokens and audit tables hid the token name, the Revoke button and the event.
  • At 1440 px, addresses in the audit log broke mid-word.
  • There was a card inside a card and dashed empty boxes.
  • The block dialog did not name the person.

The fix, template#502, made each
confirmation name the person ("Block Ada Lovelace") and state the consequence.
The focus ring and the keyboard-scrollable table went into my shared component
library first, so they ship to every app that uses it, not only this one.

What did not work?

Some recommendations didn't survive the merge, and one fix didn't hold.

The designer's 280 characters. Its wireframe gave a group description 280
characters. The API already allowed 500, so the merge dropped it: "Dropped: the
API allows 500 today". You can see "0 of 500 characters" in the first
screenshot. The roles work from the brief and the screenshots, so a limit the
brief doesn't state is a guess.

More than the job needed. The designer also wanted to move the group picker
into the shared library ("Dropped for now: only this template needs it today")
and let the admin edit a group's appearance ("Not built: a feature the owner did
not ask for"). Roles happily invent work. The table is where it gets cut, and
the cut is written down instead of silently lost.

"Create" against "Add". The writer's rule was one term per concept, and its
table said "Create" replaces "Add". In notes, though, only the editor's button
ended up saying "Create note"; the toast, the shortcut and the audit log still
used "add". Two weeks later, seed#586
fixed the mismatch and settled on "Add note" for notes. A test now pins it.
Today the group editor says "Create group" and the note editor says
"Add note",
which is consistent per thing, if not across the app.

What do the roles still miss?

The big calls in this redesign were mine. "Let's only leave a sidebar", "no need
for product logo", and "it must always be THE SAME COMPONENT" for create and
edit: those are my words, quoted at the top of #453. The roles turned them into
details, states and copy, and caught real problems on the way. The direction
came from me.

They also miss what isn't in front of them. A limit the brief leaves out, they
guess. A wording rule isn't a check, so "Create" and "Add" drifted apart without
anything turning red. And the design reviewer only judges the screens in the
diff, which is why the old admin screens needed their own audit.

Where AI did the work: every role, the merged spec, the build and both reviews
in this post were AI agents. I wrote the rules they follow and the request that
started it. How the rest of my setup works, the worktrees and the code reviewer
that breaks the code, is in
my AI coding agent setup, and what that means for
a project with me is on how I work.

If you want to see the result yourself, the
Seed demo has a "Try it without an account" button.
Open Groups, press New group, and count the fields.

First published on antonshubin.com.

title: The Difference Between a Website That Looks Good and One That Actually Sells
description:
A beautiful website is a lovely thing to own. The colours are right, the photos are gorgeous, the layout feels expensive. You show it to friends and they say it looks fantastic. Then you check your enquiries, and there are none. The phone is quiet. The inbox is empty. A website can look wonderful and still fail at the one job that matters, which is bringing in business.

This is one of the most common problems small business owners face, and it usually comes down to a simple confusion. Looking good and selling are two different jobs, and a website needs to do both. A site that only looks good is like a shop with a stunning window display and a locked door. People admire it, then walk on.

The first difference is clarity. A pretty site often hides what the business actually does. The headline is clever but vague. The visitor has to scroll and guess. A selling site says, in plain words, what you do, who you do it for, and why you are worth choosing, right at the top of the page, where it cannot be missed. There is no riddle to solve. Within a few seconds, a visitor knows whether they are in the right place. That clarity feels less artistic, but it works far better.

The second difference is the call to action. A good-looking site might have a small contact link hidden in the corner. A selling site tells the visitor exactly what to do next, and makes it easy. Call now. Book a free consultation. Get a quote. Send a message. That instruction appears more than once, in the places where a visitor is most likely to be ready: after the main headline, after the list of services, and at the bottom of the page. It should be a clear button, in a colour that stands out, with words that describe what happens when you click it. A vague button that says submit or click here does not tell anyone anything.

The third difference is trust. A beautiful site can feel cold, like a showroom nobody lives in. A selling site feels human. It shows real photos of real work, real people, and real customers. It includes honest testimonials with names and places. It mentions how long the business has been running, and what happens after you get in touch. These details do not need to be flashy. A short line about your experience, a photo of your team, or a list of the areas you cover can be the thing that tips a hesitant visitor into making contact. People buy from businesses they trust, and trust is built from small, believable details, not from decoration.

The fourth difference is focus. A site that tries to show everything at once confuses people. Ten services, five special offers, a blog, a gallery, a newsletter sign-up, and a chat box, all competing for attention on one page. A selling site picks one main goal for each page and builds around it. The homepage might aim to get people to call. A service page might aim to get people to request a quote. Everything on that page supports that one goal, and anything that distracts from it is removed or moved elsewhere. Focus feels simple, and simple is what turns visitors into customers.

The fifth difference is speed and ease of use. A site loaded with large images, animations, and fancy effects can look impressive, but if it takes too long to load, or if the buttons are hard to find on a phone, people will leave before they see any of it. A selling site is fast, clean, and easy to use. The menu is short. The text is easy to read. The forms are short. Every page works properly on a phone, because that is where most visitors are. Beauty that slows a site down is not beauty, it is a barrier.

The sixth difference is measurement. A business owner with a pretty site often has no idea how it is performing. They do not know how many people visit, which pages they look at, or where they drop off. A selling site is checked regularly. Simple tools can show how many visitors arrive, how long they stay, and which pages lead to enquiries. That information tells you what to fix. If lots of people visit a service page but nobody contacts you, the page needs a clearer offer or an easier way to get in touch. Without that information, you are guessing.

Copy is another quiet difference. Pretty sites often use vague, polished language that could belong to any business. We are passionate about excellence. We deliver outstanding results. These phrases sound nice and mean nothing. A selling site uses plain, specific words. It says what you do, how long it takes, what it costs, and what the customer gets. It answers the questions a real customer would ask, in the order they would ask them. Plain words sell. Fancy words decorate.

So how do you tell which kind of site you have? Ask a few honest questions. Can a stranger understand what you do within five seconds of landing on your homepage? Is there a clear next step on every page? Can a visitor find your phone number without hunting? Does the site work well on a phone? Have you had an enquiry from the site in the last month? If the answer to several of these is no, your site may look good but it is not selling, and that is a fixable problem.

Fixing it does not always mean starting again. Sometimes a few changes are enough: a clearer headline, a stronger button, a shorter form, a few real testimonials in the right places. Sometimes the structure needs more work, because the whole site was built around looking good rather than bringing in business. A good designer will look at the site the way a customer does, not the way an artist does, and rebuild the pages around the actions you want visitors to take.

That is the shift that matters. A website is not a brochure, and it is not a piece of art. It is a tool for your business, and it should be judged by the enquiries it brings in, not just by how it looks. Studios like DezignLoop build sites with that balance in mind, pairing clean design with clear messages, visible contact details, and pages that guide visitors towards getting in touch. The result still looks good, but it works hard too.

If your site looks lovely and the phone is quiet, do not assume the problem is your business. It may simply be that your website is dressed up for a party when it should be dressed for work. Make it clear, make it easy, make it trustworthy, and give people a reason to act. That is what turns a good-looking website into one that actually sells.

title: November 11, 2026
description:
Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

On November 11, 2026, we began releasing Edge UI updates for Apigee Edge for Public Cloud.

Fixed

Bug ID Component Description
392653797, 399185014 Edge UI Fixed an issue where navigating to the App Details or New App pages in organizations with a large number of API products experienced slowness or UI freezing during the initial page load. The Edge UI now fetches API products on demand when you open the Add Product dialog, improving initial page load performance.
576859695 Edge UI Fixed an issue in the Analytics Error Code Analysis dashboard where 504 Gateway Timeout responses caused by target timeouts were excluded from the Proxy errors charts. Target timeout 504 responses are now counted under Proxy errors.
188163219 Edge UI Fixed a UI formatting issue in the Analytics Custom Reports list view so that dimensions display without overlapping.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.16.14

On November 11, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.16.14.

  • For information about upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to v1.16.14.
  • For information about new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release. The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch by using the Helm chart automatically updates the images. You don't typically need to make manual image changes. For information about container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse policies now support function calling

The SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse policies now handle LLM function calling (tool use) flows. Two new optional XML elements extract function calling content for Model Armor sanitization:

  • <FunctionResponseSource> in SanitizeUserPrompt: extracts function/tool response data from user turns. Used as a fallback when <UserPromptSource> returns empty on function calling turns.
  • <FunctionCallSource> in SanitizeModelResponse: extracts function call arguments from model responses. Used as a fallback when <LLMResponseSource> returns empty.

Default templates target the Gemini format and require no additional configuration. For OpenAI and Anthropic formats, configure custom JSONPath templates. For more information, see FunctionResponseSource and FunctionCallSource.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
575563262 Updated the Google Cloud client library stack to match Apigee hybrid 1.17 (protobuf 4.x, gRPC 1.82, GAX 2.83, Guava 33.5). With this update: (1) a malformed inbound gRPC request frame is now reported to the client as grpc-status INTERNAL (13) and recorded in analytics as x-apigee.grpc.status=13, instead of an Apigee ServiceUnavailable fault (UNAVAILABLE, 14) with no x-apigee.grpc.status; (2) an ExternalCallout policy whose Google service account does not exist now fails with gRPC UNAUTHENTICATED (16) instead of UNAVAILABLE (14); and (3) Gson parse-error messages, such as in proxy validation errors, now end with a link to Gson's troubleshooting guide.
572875915 Fixed an issue where the apigee-env Helm chart and Apigee operator ignored the synchronizer pollInterval configuration (synchronizer.pollInterval, envs[].pollInterval, and envs[].components.synchronizer.pollInterval); configured values now take effect, and values below 60 seconds are raised to 60.
572025634 Fixed an issue where responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow returned a corrupted body; compressed text/event-stream responses now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact.
560272924 Apigee hybrid now supports continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Fixed an issue where Model Armor policies did not honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: when set, Model Armor callouts now bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic, while streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
549779897 Apigee analytics now reports the Model Armor template, verdict, and matched filters for each request on both the prompt and model-response directions.
524115876 Fixed an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests under load.
519116013 Disabled weak Diffie-Hellman (DH) TLS cipher suites on port 7070 (Prometheus jmx_exporter) in the apigee-hybrid-cassandra container.
500345401 The apigee-telemetry Helm chart now supports independent tolerations and nodeSelector configuration for the OpenTelemetry Collector (metrics.collector), Prometheus Adapter (metrics.adapter), and Stackdriver Exporters (metrics.proxyStackdriverExporter and metrics.appStackdriverExporter).

CodeMender updates (v0.21.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Sandboxed build commands and patch refresh: When sandboxing is enabled, cm build and cm fix build validation now run build.command inside the sandbox, and cm fix refreshes stored patch diffs after build validation finishes.
  • Read-only host toolchains and isolated caches: Sandboxed cm build, cm fix, and cm verify runs now mount host toolchain and package-manager directories read-only and redirect supported compiler and package caches to session-scoped temporary directories.
  • Command environment isolation: Disabled repository Git hooks, isolated host Git configuration, and ignored repository Python bytecode caches (__pycache__) during command and build runs.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a 30-minute timeout for silent active turns so stalled sessions cancel and recover cleanly.
    • Preserved proof-of-concept execution output when reproducer errors occur, retaining stdout and stderr to help diagnose build failures, timeouts, and setup issues.
    • Fixed an issue where patch generation failed on mid-run sandbox failures by automatically retrying with a fresh sandbox environment.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Gemini 4 Carbon in CodeMender (Preview)

Your agents keep running where they are, but you govern them from one place: give each agent a verifiable identity, register agents and MCP servers in Agent Registry, and route their LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic through local Agent Gateway proxies by using your existing service mesh or network stack. Those proxies enforce access and Model Armor safety policies, and send access logs and agent traces to Cloud Logging and Cloud Trace.

Agent Gateway for cross-cloud is available at no charge during Limited Preview. Other products that you configure with it, such as Model Armor, Cloud Logging, and Cloud Trace, are billed at their standard rates. To request access, complete the access request form.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Issue

On nodes that have Linux syscall auditing enabled, such as Container-Optimized OS nodes where you enabled Linux auditd logging, mounting Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver volumes can hang indefinitely. Pods that use these volumes don't start and remain in a status such as Init:0/1 or ContainerCreating. Pods that are being deleted remain in the Terminating state, and node drains, including drains during node pool upgrades, might not complete. Pod events show errors similar to the following:

MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "VOLUME_NAME" : rpc error: code = DeadlineExceeded desc = context deadline exceeded
MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "VOLUME_NAME" : rpc error: code = Aborted desc = An operation with the given volume key TARGET_PATH already exists

The following GKE versions are affected:

  • 1.31.14-gke.2963000 and later
  • 1.32.13-gke.2714000 and later
  • 1.33.13-gke.1973000 and later
  • 1.34.12-gke.1209000 and later
  • 1.35.8-gke.2014000 and later
  • 1.36.5-gke.1817000 and later
  • 1.37.1-gke.1777000 and later

In these versions, the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver uses a Debian 13 base image whose mount utility uses the newer Linux mount API. When syscall auditing is active, the mount operation can hang in the kernel before the FUSE file system is initialized. Restarting the gcsfusecsi-node Pod doesn't resolve the issue. Nodes that don't have syscall audit rules loaded aren't affected.

Workaround: Disable Linux auditd logging in clusters that use the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver, and then re-create the affected nodes to clear the audit rules that are loaded on them. If you must keep auditd logging enabled, contact Cloud Customer Care.

A fix is in progress.

title: A small test for the denominator in a research results table
description:
A table says a study enrolled 120 participants and reports 24 events. The numerator is easy to spot. The tricky part is whether those 24 events were measured among all enrollees or among the 96 participants with observed outcomes.

In this synthetic example, 24 of the 96 participants with observed outcomes had an event. The observed-case percentage is 25%. If you use 120 as the denominator and report 20%, readers can wrongly infer that the other 24 participants had no event.

Put the population in the table

Quantity Count
Enrolled 120
Outcome observed 96
Outcome missing 24
Events among participants with an observed outcome 24

A regression fixture can catch the accidental denominator swap before an export:

def observed_rate(enrolled, observed, events):
    if not 0 <= events <= observed <= enrolled:
        raise ValueError("Counts must reconcile")
    return events / observed if observed else None

assert observed_rate(120, 96, 24) == 0.25
assert observed_rate(120, 0, 0) is None

Keep the source column and time point next to each of the three counts. This check catches inconsistent bookkeeping. It leaves open how to handle missing outcomes for the actual study: decide that separately using the protocol and the assumptions that fit the data.

For reporting an observational study, consult the STROBE checklists, including the items on participants and missing data. RigorMed can organize a protocol, a results table, and the manuscript draft in one research project for review. The numbers above are for teaching and came from no participant records.

Disclosure: This article was generated with AI and checked for the numbers, code, and example boundaries.

title: How to Scrape Workday Job Postings from any myworkdayjobs.com Site
description:
How to Scrape Workday Job Postings from any myworkdayjobs.com Site

A surprising number of large employers — from NVIDIA and Adobe to retailers and banks — host careers on Workday. The public site lives under a myworkdayjobs.com URL. If you recruit against those companies, or you want their openings in a spreadsheet, clicking through the career portal does not scale. This guide shows how to scrape Workday job postings from any public myworkdayjobs.com site.

You will use the Workday Jobs Scraper on Apify. Paste one or more career-site URLs and get titles, locations, country, remote flag, time type, posting date, job ID and the full description. Keyword, location, remote and recency filters are built in.

By the end of this article you will have a CSV or JSON file on your machine, and a short Python snippet you can rerun or schedule. The same Actor is also callable from JavaScript and from AI agents through the Apify MCP server.

What you need

  • An Apify account. The Free plan is enough to try a small run.
  • A list of inputs for the Actor (URLs, IDs or search terms — details in the steps below).
  • Optional: Python 3 with the apify-client package if you want to automate the run.

You do not need a Workday employee login or an internal tenant ID. The public career site URL is enough.

How to run it in the Apify Console

Step 1: Open the Actor

Go to https://apify.com/veenkes/veenkes-workday-jobs and click Try for free.

Step 2: Paste the career site URL

Example: https://nvidia.wd5.myworkdayjobs.com/NVIDIAExternalCareerSite. You can add several employers in one run.

Step 3: Filter and cap

Use search text, location, remote-only or posted within N days if you only want fresh roles. Set max jobs per site low for a first run. Leave details on to get full descriptions.

Step 4: Export

Start the run and download CSV or JSON. Job IDs plus posting dates make incremental watches easy.

The same company can have more than one Workday site (for example a student site and a professional site). Add each URL you care about. You pay for saved jobs.

How to run it from Python

Install the official client and call the Actor by its Store id veenkes/veenkes-workday-jobs. Replace YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN with a token from Apify Console > Integrations. Do not commit the token to a public repository.

pip install apify-client

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("veenkes/veenkes-workday-jobs").call(run_input={
    "careerSites": [
        "https://nvidia.wd5.myworkdayjobs.com/NVIDIAExternalCareerSite"
    ],
    "maxJobsPerSite": 50,
    "includeDetails": True
})

# Write every dataset item, then export from the Console or keep going in code.
for item in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(item)

The JavaScript client (apify-client on npm) uses the same Actor id and the same input object. You can also start the run with a plain HTTP POST to the Apify API if you prefer.

Sample output

Here is a shortened example of one dataset record (field values are illustrative of the schema, taken from a real sample run shape):

{
  "company": "nvidia",
  "careerSite": "NVIDIAExternalCareerSite",
  "jobId": "JR2026556",
  "title": "Firmware Engineer",
  "url": "https://nvidia.wd5.myworkdayjobs.com/NVIDIAExternalCareerSite/job/Israel-Tel-Aviv/Firmware-Engineer_JR2026556",
  "location": "Israel, Tel Aviv",
  "postedOn": "Posted Today",
  "publishedAt": "2026-11-12",
  "allLocations": [
    "Israel, Tel Aviv",
    "Israel, Beer Sheva"
  ],
  "country": "Israel",
  "countryCode": "IL",
  "remote": false,
  "remoteType": null,
  "timeType": "Full time",
  "validThrough": null,
  "hiringOrganization": "IL00 Mellanox Technologies, Ltd.",
  "applyUrl": "https://nvidia.wd5.myworkdayjobs.com/NVIDIAExternalCareerSite/job/Israel-Tel-Aviv/Firmware-Engineer_JR2026556",
  "descriptionText": "NVIDIA is seeking a dedicated Firmware Engineer to join our NIC Firmware Core team in Beer-Sheva/Tel-Aviv. You will contribute to the development of brand-new networking adapter te…",
  "descriptionHtml": "<p>NVIDIA is seeking a dedicated Firmware Engineer to join our NIC Firmware Core team in Beer-Sheva/Tel-Aviv. You will contribute to the development of brand-new networking adapter…",
  "scrapedAt": "2026-11-12T22:14:14.812Z"
}

Once the run has finished, open the dataset in the Console and use Export > CSV if a spreadsheet is your destination. JSON is usually better for code and for language models.

What to use the data for

Agency recruiters watch a roster of enterprise clients. In-house talent teams benchmark how competitors write similar roles. Researchers study location and remote patterns at large employers. A scheduled daily run with posted within 1 day is a simple new-jobs alert.

Pricing

Pay-per-result pricing starts at $1.50 per 1,000 saved jobs on the Apify Free plan, with lower unit prices on paid Apify plans, plus a small per-run start fee. Always check the live pricing on the Actor page, because plans and unit prices can change. For a first test, keep the input tiny so you can inspect the schema before you scale up.

Scheduling and automations

In the Apify Console you can schedule the Actor (daily or hourly) and leave the same input in place. For incremental jobs, prefer a "since" or "posted after" style filter when the Actor offers one, so you are not paying to re-collect old rows. When a run finishes you can send a webhook, or connect the Actor in Zapier, Make or n8n. AI agents can discover and call veenkes/veenkes-workday-jobs through Apify's MCP server using the same input.

Good practices and limits

Job descriptions belong to the employer. Use them for search, analysis or applications, not to clone a careers site. Follow the employer's terms. The Actor is not affiliated with Workday or any employer mentioned as an example.

If a run returns fewer rows than you expected, check the input caps, language or country filters, and the Actor log. A zero-row run is usually a filter or an unavailable source, not a silent crash — read the log before you increase limits.

Next step

Open the Actor and run a small job: Workday Jobs Scraper: Any myworkdayjobs.com Career Site.

If you later want this on a schedule, save the input that worked, add a date filter where it applies, and export CSV automatically from the dataset or from the API snippet above.

title: New connections failed, old ones worked: the failover that sent writes to a read-only database
description:
On Wednesday 28 October 2026, the RIPE Database started failing updates. Not all of them. Some went through fine. Others were refused. The same service, the same hour, the same kind of request, and nobody could tell from the outside which ones would fail.

That is the worst kind of outage. A service that is fully down is easy to understand. A service that works for some people and not others, with no pattern you can see, makes everyone doubt their own code first.

The people who run the RIPE Database are the RIPE NCC, the registry that hands out IP addresses across Europe, the Middle East and parts of Central Asia. Their database, usually called Whois, is the record of who holds which block of addresses. If you want to change who owns a block, or set up reverse DNS for it, you send an update to this database. Reverse DNS is the record that maps an IP address back to a name, and mail servers use it to check that the server sending them email is who it claims to be. So when updates to this database fail, address records stop changing, and reverse DNS changes stop going through.

The failure ran from 11:42 to 19:40 UTC, just under eight hours, and it was intermittent the whole time. The postmortem, published on 3 November, is short. Three sentences of cause, and they are worth reading slowly, because the bug is not where you would expect it.

The clue that did not fit

Start with what the operators could see. Updates were failing intermittently. Not every update, and not in a steady pattern. If the database had been down, everything would have failed. If the update service had been down, everything would have failed. Intermittent failure, spread across eight hours, points somewhere else: something in the path between the application and the database was different for different requests.

The postmortem gives the answer in one sentence. There had been a short interruption on the network link to the primary load balancer, and the system failed over to the standby load balancer. Because of a misconfiguration, new Whois update connections that went through the newly elected load balancer were sent to the read-only database instead of the primary database. Existing connections from the application stayed connected to the primary database and were unaffected.

Read that again, because it contains the whole story. Two groups of connections, two different destinations, one working and one not.

A short glossary, because the jargon hides the mechanism

A load balancer is a machine whose job is to stand in front of a service and hand each incoming connection to a server behind it. You run two of them, a primary and a standby, so that if one dies the other takes over. That takeover is called a failover, and it is supposed to be the boring part of the system, the part that works without anyone thinking about it.

A database primary is the one copy that accepts writes. A read-only replica is a copy that keeps itself up to date by copying from the primary, and exists so that read queries can be spread across machines without loading the primary. It can answer questions. It cannot accept changes. Sending a write to a read-only replica is like posting a letter to a library: the building is real, the address is correct, and nothing you send there will ever be filed.

So the failover did its job. Traffic moved to the standby balancer. The standby balancer then sent new connections to the wrong database. And the old connections, the ones opened before the failover, were still sitting on the primary, happily accepting writes. That is why the failure was intermittent. It depended on when your connection was opened, and nobody looking at the service from the outside could see that.

Why the old connections masked the fault

This is the part that should worry you, because it is the part that repeats in other systems.

Every check the operators had would have looked reassuring. The standby balancer was up and answering. The database was up and answering. The application was connected and processing some updates. If your monitoring asks "is the balancer alive" and "is the database alive", both answers were yes. The system was green on every dashboard that measured liveness, and broken on the one thing that mattered: could a new update actually land?

The old connections made it worse. They were proof, visible to anyone watching, that the system worked. An operator seeing successful updates would reasonably conclude the problem was elsewhere, maybe with the people submitting the updates, maybe with a bad batch of requests. The healthy connections were not just unaffected. They were camouflage.

There is a second quiet detail in the postmortem. On 30 October, two days after the incident, RIPE NCC reported that none of the failed requests would have changed a reverse delegation anyway, because they either contained no changes or failed their pre-delegation checks. That is good news for the internet, and it is worth stating plainly: no valid reverse DNS change was lost, as far as the published evidence shows. It is also luck. The mechanism did not care what was in the requests. The next time a misrouted write path fails, the requests it drops might be the ones that matter.

RIPE NCC has not published how many updates failed, or which configuration setting was wrong, or a trace through the standby path. So this article does not guess at those numbers. The mechanism is enough.

The test that would have caught it

Here is the uncomfortable question. The standby balancer existed for exactly this moment, and the misconfiguration in its path had presumably been sitting there since it was set up. How do you catch a fault in a path that only runs during a failover?

You test the failover the way the system will actually use it: with a write.

Most health checks do not do this. A typical database health check opens a connection and runs SELECT 1, which is a read. A read succeeds on a read-only replica. A read succeeds on a primary. It tells you the database is alive and says nothing about whether it can accept a write. It is the exact check that would have passed on both sides of this incident.

A write-path check is different. It writes a small probe row to a scratch table, reads it back, and deletes it. If the connection is pointed at a read-only replica, the write fails at once, and you learn the truth in milliseconds. Here is the idea in Go, using the standard database package and Postgres:

// ProbeWrite checks that this connection can actually write,
// not just that the database answers. Run it against the
// connection your application will use for updates, including
// after a failover.
func ProbeWrite(ctx context.Context, db *sql.DB) error {
    _, err := db.ExecContext(ctx,
        `INSERT INTO write_probe (id, checked_at) VALUES (1, now())
         ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET checked_at = now()`)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("write probe failed: %w", err)
    }
    return nil
}

And the same check in Python:

def probe_write(conn):
    """Fail fast if this connection cannot write.
    A read-only replica will reject the INSERT at once."""
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute(
            "INSERT INTO write_probe (id, checked_at) VALUES (1, now()) "
            "ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET checked_at = now()"
        )
    conn.commit()

There is also a cheaper check that belongs in any code that opens a database connection and assumes it can write. Postgres can tell you whether the connection you hold is on a replica:

SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();

If that returns true, you are talking to a replica, and any write you attempt will fail. In Go or Python, run it once when a connection is opened for writes, and refuse to proceed if the answer is not what you expect. It costs one query. It catches exactly this class of mistake: the connection is healthy, the database is healthy, and the role is wrong.

The third guard is a habit, not code. When you test a failover, do not test that traffic moves. Test that a write lands. Fail over, submit a real update through the new path, read it back from the authoritative record, and only then call the test a pass. A balancer that answers pings is not a balancer that routes writes correctly. The RIPE incident is a case study in the difference.

What to take away

The failover worked. The standby took over, the traffic moved, and the system stayed up. Every part of the safety machinery did its job except the one line that said where the writes go. And because the old connections kept working, the fault hid behind partial success for eight hours.

If you run a primary and a replica, the question is not whether your failover works. It is whether you have ever watched a write travel the standby path and land. If the answer is no, you have the same untested configuration RIPE NCC had: a spare route that has never carried a real update, waiting for the day it has to.

When was the last time you failed over on purpose and proved a write landed on the other side?

Sources: RIPE NCC status page, "Intermittent RIPE Database update failures", postmortem posted 3 November 2026, incident window 28 October 2026, 11:42 to 19:40 UTC. The 30 October update on failed reverse-delegation requests is from the same incident record.

title: Prisma Migrations When AI Features Touch Your Database
description:
This post was created with AI assistance and reviewed for accuracy before publishing.

AI features arrive with a distinctive database footprint. You need somewhere to keep conversations, the messages inside them, the tool calls each message triggered, and the feedback users leave. Individually these look like ordinary tables. Collectively they are the fastest-growing thing in your schema, because a single user session writes dozens of rows where a normal feature writes one.

That growth rate is what makes migrations on these tables different. A schema change that is instant on your users table can lock a messages table with fifty million rows for long enough to take the product down.

Model messages as append-only from the start

The most useful early decision is treating message rows as immutable:

model Message {
  id             String   @id @default(cuid())
  conversationId String
  role           String   // user | assistant | tool
  content        String   @db.Text
  createdAt      DateTime @default(now())

  conversation Conversation @relation(fields: [conversationId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)

  @@index([conversationId, createdAt])
}

Append-only tables are far easier to migrate. There are no in-place updates to contend with, backfills can run in ranges without racing live writes, and you can archive old partitions without touching application logic.

The compound index on [conversationId, createdAt] is the one query this table actually serves: fetch a conversation's messages in order. A single-column index on conversationId still requires a sort afterwards, which on a long conversation is the difference between a fast read and a slow one.

Expand and contract, never rename

Prisma will happily generate a migration that renames or retypes a column. On a large table under load, that is how you cause an outage. The safe pattern splits it into steps that are each individually harmless.

Suppose Message.content needs to become structured JSON:

  1. Expand. Add contentJson as a nullable column. Nullable additions do not rewrite the table.
  2. Dual-write. Deploy code that writes both columns and reads the old one.
  3. Backfill. Populate contentJson for existing rows in batches.
  4. Switch reads. Deploy code that reads the new column, still writing both.
  5. Contract. Once nothing reads it, drop content.

Every step is independently reversible, and at no point does a deploy require the schema and the code to change simultaneously. That last property is the real prize: it means a rollback never leaves you with code expecting a column that no longer exists.

Backfills should run in bounded batches rather than one statement:

let cursor: string | undefined;
for (;;) {
  const batch = await prisma.message.findMany({
    where: { contentJson: null },
    select: { id: true, content: true },
    take: 1000,
    ...(cursor && { cursor: { id: cursor }, skip: 1 }),
    orderBy: { id: 'asc' },
  });
  if (batch.length === 0) break;
  await Promise.all(batch.map((m) =>
    prisma.message.update({ where: { id: m.id }, data: { contentJson: parse(m.content) } })
  ));
  cursor = batch.at(-1)!.id;
}

A single UPDATE across fifty million rows holds locks and generates enough WAL to cause its own problems. Batching keeps each transaction short and lets you stop partway without losing work.

Watch for the index build that locks

Adding an index to a growing table is the other common outage. By default Postgres takes a lock that blocks writes for the duration of the build.

Prisma Migrate generates plain CREATE INDEX. On a large table you want the concurrent form, which requires editing the generated SQL by hand:

-- Edit the generated migration before applying it.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY "Message_conversationId_createdAt_idx"
  ON "Message" ("conversationId", "createdAt");

CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction, so the migration file needs its transaction wrapper removed as well. It is slower and it can fail partway, leaving an invalid index you have to drop and retry. Both are better than blocking writes on your busiest table.

This is the strongest argument for reading generated migration SQL rather than applying it unseen. The Prisma schema is a good abstraction, and the SQL it produces is where the operational consequences live.

Plan the retention policy before you need it

Conversation data grows without bound and most of it is never read again. Decide early what happens to it, because retrofitting deletion onto a table with foreign keys pointing at it is considerably harder.

onDelete: Cascade on the relation, as in the model above, means deleting a conversation removes its messages automatically. That is convenient and it is also a large transaction if the conversation is long, so batch deletions by conversation rather than by date range across the whole table.

Retention is also frequently a compliance requirement rather than a housekeeping one. If users can request deletion of their data, the tool call log is easy to forget: it often contains the prompt text, which is the thing they are asking you to delete.

Review the SQL, especially when it is generated

The practical rule that prevents most of the above: no migration reaches production without a person reading the SQL.

This matters more now that schema changes are often drafted by an assistant. A generated migration is usually correct in the sense that it produces the described schema. Whether it does so without locking a table for four minutes is a different question, and not one the generator is reasoning about.

Read the file, check for table rewrites, index builds, and NOT NULL additions on existing columns, and confirm each one is safe at your current row counts. That review takes a minute and is the cheapest insurance available.
