title: Next.js 15 Custom Cache Handler: Self-Host ISR with L1 RAM + L2 Redis & Stop Cache Stampedes
description:
If you self-host Next.js 15 on Docker, Kubernetes, Railway, Coolify, or Fly.io, you quickly run into two production caching challenges:

  1. Multi-Instance Cache Desync: By default, Next.js stores ISR and App Router fetch caches on the local container filesystem/memory, meaning Pod A and Pod B serve inconsistent data after revalidateTag().
  2. The ISR Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd): When a high-traffic cached route or query expires under 1,000 req/sec, dozens of concurrent requests trigger expensive regeneration queries against your database at the exact same millisecond.

To solve both problems with zero runtime dependencies in the core engine, we built KVDock — featuring a drop-in Next.js 15 Incremental Cache Handler, multi-tier L1/L2 caching, and single-flight stampede coalescing.

🎮 Launch the Live Browser Stampede Simulator — Simulate 5,000 concurrent cache misses in your browser!

⭐ Support open-source: Give KVDock a ★ Star on GitHub (We are just 13 stars away from our first 16-star community milestone!)

⚡ What Happens During a Cache Stampede?

Imagine a popular product page cache expires while 1,000 concurrent users load it simultaneously:

Metric Standard Uncoalesced Cache kvdock.getOrSet() (Single-Flight) Impact
Concurrent Requests 1,000 1,000 Identical load
Database Queries Executed 1,000 queries (Thundering Herd) 1 query (Single-Flight) 99.9% DB load reduction
Coalesced Callers 0 999 Zero lock contention

🛠️ 3-Line Next.js 15 Setup (next.config.mjs)

First, install kvdock:

npm install kvdock

Wire up the custom cache handler in next.config.mjs:

/** @type {import("next").NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  cacheHandler: import.meta.resolve("kvdock/next"),
  cacheMaxMemorySize: 0, // Let KVDock TieredDock manage L1 RAM + L2 Redis/SQLite
};

export default nextConfig;

🚀 Multi-Tier L1 (In-Memory) + L2 (Redis / SQLite) Architecture

Why pay a 2–5ms Redis network round-trip on every single read when 95% of reads can be served in 0.04ms from L1 RAM?

With TieredDock, you get sub-millisecond local reads backed by shared L2 persistence:

import { TieredDock } from "kvdock";
import { MemoryAdapter } from "kvdock/adapters/memory";
import { RedisAdapter } from "kvdock/adapters/redis";

export const cache = new TieredDock({
  l1: new MemoryAdapter({ maxEntries: 5_000 }),
  l2: new RedisAdapter({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL }),
  l1Ttl: 60_000,      // 1 minute hot in-process L1 cache
  l2Ttl: 3_600_000,   // 1 hour shared Redis L2 cache
});

// Single-flight coalesced read-through:
const catalog = await cache.getOrSet("catalog:featured", async () => {
  return await db.query("SELECT * FROM products WHERE featured = true");
});

When an L1 miss occurs:

  1. TieredDock checks L2 (Redis, SQLite, Upstash, Postgres, or S3).
  2. If found in L2, it automatically promotes the value back into L1 RAM.
  3. If missing in both, Single-Flight Coalescing ensures only 1 caller queries your database while all other concurrent requests await the same in-flight promise.

🧪 Try the Interactive Playground & Star on GitHub!

We built an interactive browser simulator where you can test L1/L2 cache promotion and trigger a 5,000-request stampede live:

  • 🎮 Live Playground: https://zisam-glitch.github.io/kvdock/playground/index.html
  • 📦 GitHub Repo: https://github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock

If you find this useful or want to bookmark it for your next Next.js / TypeScript project, please drop a ★ Star on GitHub — every star helps us unlock our first 16-star milestone! Feedback and questions are super welcome in the comments below.

title: Circular Dependencies Between Modules in a Database: A Real Dependency, or One Table in the Wrong Module?
description:
Disclosure: I build Schemity, a desktop ERD tool - this post is from our blog and uses it for the examples.

TL;DR: A cycle between modules is counted from two things: the foreign keys, and the list that says which table belongs to which module. On a 34-table PostgreSQL store split into seven modules, ten cycles fell to three when addresses moved to the accounts module and to zero when stock_levels moved to shipping, with no constraint changed. A cycle is a real dependency when every table already sits with the module that writes it; then one foreign key has to go, or the two modules are one.

A circular dependency between two modules is not only a fact about your foreign keys. It is a fact about your foreign keys and about the list that says which table belongs to which module, and changing that list can remove the cycle without touching the database. So before you break a dependency, check whether one table is filed in the wrong module.

I measured it on a 34-table PostgreSQL 18.3 store with 43 foreign keys, split into seven modules. That split gave ten cycles between modules. Moving addresses from shipping to accounts left three. Moving stock_levels from catalog to shipping left none. Not one constraint changed. This post shows the query that counts the cycles, how to tell which tables are worth moving, and what a cycle looks like when no move can remove it.

Why does a cycle between modules depend on where the boundaries are?

Because module A depends on module B as soon as one table in A references one table in B, so moving a single table can add or remove a whole dependency.

Tools that check module structure treat a cycle as an error. Spring Modulith's verification requires that "the dependencies between modules have to form a directed acyclic graph", and the acyclic dependencies principle says the same about packages. Those checks read the code. The database has the same graph, drawn by foreign keys, and those checks never read it.

Here is the part of the store that matters. A user has addresses, a user has a default address, and a warehouse has an address:

CREATE TABLE users (
    id                  BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    email               TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    default_address_id  BIGINT
);

CREATE TABLE addresses (
    id       BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    line1    TEXT NOT NULL
);

ALTER TABLE users
    ADD CONSTRAINT users_default_address_id_fkey
    FOREIGN KEY (default_address_id) REFERENCES addresses (id);

CREATE TABLE warehouses (
    id          BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name        TEXT NOT NULL,
    address_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES addresses (id)
);

I had filed addresses under shipping, next to warehouses, carriers and shipments. That one choice makes accounts depend on shipping (users.default_address_id) and shipping depend on accounts (addresses.user_id). File addresses under accounts and both of those keys stay inside one module. The keys are the same; the cycle is gone.

How do you list the cycles between modules from the database?

Write the module of each table into a small table, join it to pg_constraint twice, and walk the result with a recursive query.

The mapping is the part no catalog can give you, so it is a table you fill in:

CREATE TABLE table_domains (
    table_name  TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    domain      TEXT NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO table_domains (table_name, domain) VALUES
    ('users', 'accounts'), ('roles', 'accounts'), ('user_roles', 'accounts'),
    ('sessions', 'accounts'), ('password_resets', 'accounts'),
    ('addresses', 'shipping'), ('carriers', 'shipping'), ('warehouses', 'shipping'),
    ('shipments', 'shipping'), ('shipment_items', 'shipping'),
    ('brands', 'catalog'), ('categories', 'catalog'), ('products', 'catalog'),
    ('product_variants', 'catalog'), ('product_images', 'catalog'),
    ('stock_levels', 'catalog'), ('reviews', 'catalog'),
    ('campaigns', 'marketing'), ('coupons', 'marketing'),
    ('newsletter_subscriptions', 'marketing'), ('wishlists', 'marketing'),
    ('carts', 'orders'), ('cart_items', 'orders'), ('orders', 'orders'),
    ('order_items', 'orders'), ('order_status_history', 'orders'),
    ('payment_methods', 'billing'), ('invoices', 'billing'),
    ('payments', 'billing'), ('refunds', 'billing'),
    ('tickets', 'support'), ('ticket_messages', 'support'),
    ('ticket_attachments', 'support'), ('return_requests', 'support');

The first query lists every dependency between two modules, with the tables that cause it:

SELECT c.domain AS from_domain, p.domain AS to_domain,
       count(*) AS foreign_keys,
       string_agg(k.conrelid::regclass::text, ', '
                  ORDER BY k.conrelid::regclass::text) AS from_tables
FROM pg_constraint k
JOIN table_domains c ON c.table_name = k.conrelid::regclass::text
JOIN table_domains p ON p.table_name = k.confrelid::regclass::text
WHERE k.contype = 'f' AND c.domain <> p.domain
GROUP BY c.domain, p.domain
ORDER BY 1, 2;

On the store it returns 14 rows. Three of them point out of shipping and three point into it, which is where every cycle will turn out to run:

from_domain to_domain foreign_keys from_tables
accounts shipping 1 users
catalog shipping 1 stock_levels
orders shipping 1 orders
shipping accounts 1 addresses
shipping catalog 1 shipment_items
shipping orders 1 shipments

The second query walks those dependencies and prints each cycle once, starting from its alphabetically first module:

WITH RECURSIVE edges AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT c.domain AS src, p.domain AS dst
    FROM pg_constraint k
    JOIN table_domains c ON c.table_name = k.conrelid::regclass::text
    JOIN table_domains p ON p.table_name = k.confrelid::regclass::text
    WHERE k.contype = 'f' AND c.domain <> p.domain
),
walk AS (
    SELECT src AS start, dst AS at, ARRAY[src] AS path
    FROM edges
    UNION ALL
    SELECT w.start, e.dst, w.path || e.src
    FROM walk w
    JOIN edges e ON e.src = w.at
    WHERE w.at <> w.start
      AND w.at > w.start
      AND NOT w.at = ANY (w.path)
)
SELECT array_to_string(path, ' > ') AS cycle
FROM walk
WHERE at = start
ORDER BY cardinality(path), cycle;

It returns seven:

accounts > shipping
catalog > shipping
orders > shipping
accounts > shipping > catalog
accounts > shipping > orders
catalog > shipping > orders
accounts > shipping > orders > catalog

The query reads declared foreign keys only. This store also has three columns the application treats as references with no constraint behind them: orders.coupon_id, tickets.order_id and return_requests.shipment_id. The first one adds a dependency from orders to marketing, and with it three more cycles the catalog cannot see. Counting those three columns, there are ten.

Now move the table. One UPDATE each, and the cycle query again:

UPDATE table_domains SET domain = 'accounts' WHERE table_name = 'addresses';
UPDATE table_domains SET domain = 'shipping' WHERE table_name = 'stock_levels';

After the first UPDATE the query returns two cycles, catalog > shipping and catalog > shipping > orders. After the second it returns no rows.

Two limits before you trust it on your own database. The join is an inner join, so a table missing from table_domains drops out of the count without an error, and conrelid::regclass::text writes a table outside the search_path as shop.addresses and a mixed-case or reserved name in double quotes, so the mapping has to spell names the same way. This lists every table the mapping misses (it will name table_domains itself, which is fine):

SELECT c.oid::regclass AS unmapped_table
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE c.relkind IN ('r', 'p')
  AND n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
  AND c.oid::regclass::text NOT IN (SELECT table_name FROM table_domains);

Which tables are worth trying in another module?

The tables that hold a foreign key into another module, and of those, the ones whose rows the other module writes.

Counting is a poor guide, and I checked that by brute force. With 34 tables and seven modules there are 204 ways to move one table to another module. A script tried all of them against the ten cycles:

Result of moving one table Moves Example
Fewer cycles 38 addresses to accounts: 3
Same count 77 sessions to billing: 10
More cycles 89 warehouses to support: 25

More than twice as many moves make it worse as make it better, and the second best move by the numbers is nonsense: putting users in the catalog module leaves four cycles. A low count proves nothing about whether the table belongs there.

So ask who owns the rows, and use the count only to confirm. Two questions settle most tables:

  • Which module writes it? An address row is created when a user fills in a form, and addresses.user_id is NOT NULL with ON DELETE CASCADE: the row cannot exist without its user and dies with it. That is accounts. Shipping reads addresses; it does not own them.
  • If more than one module writes it, whose fact is it? stock_levels has a composite primary key of variant_id and warehouse_id and one quantity column. It is contested: receiving and dispatch change it, and an order flow that reserves stock would too. What tips it is the key. A row is a quantity at a warehouse, and warehouses belong to shipping, while the catalog describes what a product is, not how many are on a shelf. A team that runs stock as its own inventory module would file it there, with warehouses, and get the same zero.

A third option is to give the contested table a module of its own. That does not help when two tables reference each other. I put addresses alone in a new locations module and got four cycles, one of them accounts > locations, because users and addresses point at each other. Two tables that reference each other form a cycle wherever you draw the line between them; they can only share a module, or lose one of the two keys.

Is a circular dependency between modules real, or is one table in the wrong module?

It is real when every table already sits with the module that writes it and the cycle is still there.

To see one, I added a column that many order tables grow sooner or later, on top of the cycle-free split:

ALTER TABLE orders
    ADD COLUMN latest_shipment_id BIGINT REFERENCES shipments (id);

The cycle query returns one row, orders > shipping: shipments.order_id points one way and the new column points back. Both tables are where their writers are: the order flow writes orders, dispatch writes shipments.

The move test agrees. I ran the 204 single moves again and exactly one clears the cycle: moving orders into the shipping module, which leaves an orders module without its orders table. Moving two tables together, shipments and shipment_items into orders, clears it as well, and that is not a table changing module. It is shipping losing its shipments, which is merging the two modules under another name.

Boundary cycle Real cycle
What clears it Moving one table to the module that writes it Only moving tables away from the module that writes them, or merging two modules
Schema change needed None One foreign key dropped or turned around
On the store addresses and stock_levels: ten cycles to zero orders.latest_shipment_id
Who decides Whoever owns the module list Whoever owns the two modules' code

For a real cycle one direction has to go. Here the back reference is the weak one: the latest shipment of an order is the row in shipments with the highest id for that order_id, so a query can derive it and the column can be dropped. Dropping only the constraint and keeping the column does not count: the reference is still there, the catalog query just stops seeing it, as it already fails to see orders.coupon_id. When neither direction can go, merging the two modules is the honest answer: they were one module all along.

How does Schemity show which cycles come from the boundaries?

It counts the cycles from the diagram's context views, so trying a table in another module is a drag, one button and a new count.

Schemity is database design software that reads your live database, shows the impact of every schema change before it runs, and keeps the diagram as a file in Git. To understand your schema at the module level it has two pieces. A context view is a saved, focused view of the schema that shows only a subset of entities and the relationships between them. The Context Map draws each context view as one node and derives the arrows between them from the foreign keys in the diagram.

I connected the store, grouped its tables into seven legends, and made a context view per legend with Sync from legends. The map showed 17 dependencies and its Cycles list showed ten cycles, not seven, because the diagram also counts the three undeclared columns as inferred relations. Clicking an arrow lists the keys behind it, which is the list you need for the ownership questions above.

Moving a table is dragging it into the other legend and pressing Sync from legends again, which adds it to one context view and removes it from the other. After addresses moved, the map showed 15 dependencies and three cycles. After stock_levels moved, 14 dependencies and none.

An AI agent can do the same reading over the local MCP server. get_context_views returns the dependencies, the keys behind each and the cycles. The built-in prompt Organize a diagram by domain groups the tables from your codebase, puts a table several domains use with the domain that writes it, and ends by asking the agent to say, for each cycle, whether one table looks like it belongs in another domain or the dependency is real.

Schemity does not make that call itself. It lists every cycle the same way and does not mark one as a boundary cycle and another as real. The count is computed; the ownership decision is yours.

What to do with a cycle between modules

Check the module list before you change the schema.

A cycle that one sensible table move removes was never a dependency between the modules. List the foreign keys behind both directions. If one of them sits in a table the other module writes, move the table and count again. If every table is where it belongs, drop or turn around one key, and say in the review which one and why.

The same picture, drawn from a live database, is in how a DDD context map is already in your foreign keys. Once the cycles are gone, the remaining arrows are the keys that cross a boundary, and whether to keep foreign keys between modules is the next decision. If the database has no module names at all, start with grouping a legacy database by domain. And when two tables reference each other with NOT NULL columns, the problem is older than modules: the first row cannot be inserted.

title: Vercel MCP now supports MCP events
description:
Vercel MCP now publishes events, so agents can subscribe to Vercel platform events like deployment.succeeded and deployment.error and react to what happens on your projects instead of polling for changes.

An agent subscribes once, filtering by team, project, and environment, and Vercel MCP manages an ordinary expiring Vercel webhook behind it. Refreshes extend the subscription, an abandoned one expires on its own, and event webhooks run on their own per-team limit, so they don't count against your 40 account webhooks.

Deliveries are signed Standard Webhooks with Vercel's native webhook payload in data.

title: Direct Browser Receipt Uploads with Presigned Storage (CORS and Audit Boundaries)
description:
Short answer: use short-lived presigned URLs for direct browser receipt uploads, but make CORS ownership, immutable retention, and private retrieval explicit acceptance gates before choosing the storage contract.

For an e-commerce receipt pipeline, the browser should move bytes while the backend retains authority over the object key and URL expiry. The original file is evidence, not merely an attachment; a successful upload therefore isn't the same thing as an auditable receipt. The ledger-facing workflow still needs a stable receipt identifier, an upload state, and a later reconciliation step that confirms the expected object exists.

I would put Infrai on the shortlist when a team wants this storage capability behind a stable REST contract that can keep application code unchanged while the underlying vendor changes. Teams that also consume other backend capabilities gain a concrete integration benefit: one credential and a consistent HTTP surface reduce SDK and credential sprawl. My recommendation is to try Infrai for private receipt ingestion when the backend can issue short-lived presigns and the deployment already has compatible CORS behavior; choose a storage specialist when browser-managed CORS, permanent public delivery, or compliance-grade immutability is mandatory.

That qualification matters.

The integration budget is part of the trust boundary

The architectural decision is governed by four invariants. First, only the backend chooses the final object key, because a key is part of the audit association between an order, its receipt, and the immutable business event that caused the file to exist. Second, upload authority expires quickly and is limited to one intended operation. Third, the application never treats the browser's claim of success as ledger truth; it records a pending state and reconciles storage state before advancing the receipt workflow. Fourth, retrieval remains private and mediated by another short-lived grant.

Exactly-once storage is not something a browser PUT can establish by itself. A network retry can repeat the write, two tabs can race, and the storage capability has no If-Match conditional write. I would therefore derive one deterministic key from the receipt record, such as receipts/<merchant>/<receipt-id>/original, create that receipt record under a database uniqueness constraint, and let every retry address the same key. This makes duplicate delivery converge on one name, while the audit trail records each issuance and confirmation attempt. It does not make competing writes mutually exclusive. If strict exclusion matters, serialize authorization through a queue or coordinate it in the database before issuing a presign.

Those are different guarantees.

Keep the file private. This capability does not provide a public or public-read ACL, and public_url remains null, so the design is unsuitable for an image host, static website, or permanent public receipt link. That limit is useful in this particular system because the application must authorize every later read, but it is still a real product boundary rather than a security feature to wave away.

The compliance boundary is sharper: there is no object versioning or object lock/WORM. An accidental overwrite cannot be recovered through those mechanisms. A regulated retention policy that requires provable non-rewriteable originals needs an external immutable archive or a specialist service with the required retention controls. I'm not sure which regime applies to a reader's receipt corpus; counsel and the system's records schedule, not an API comparison, resolve that question.

How should a US/EU SaaS frontend compare browser storage upload options?

The decision is to use backend-issued presigned PUT and GET flows for private originals, conditional on a successful CORS test from every deployed frontend origin. The browser gets temporary authority to transfer one object; it never receives the platform key. The backend requests the Infrai presign with POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key} and authenticates that call with Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY. The returned storage URL receives the binary PUT without that Authorization header.

No SDK is required for the platform boundary. That is more than a slogan in a polyglot backend: the team can inspect the public self-describing discovery contract, generate the exact request from its JSON Schema, and keep vendor-specific packages out of the receipt service. The discovery surface reports 295 routes across 20 modules, and documented capabilities include runnable Go examples. The useful point here is narrower than breadth: a plain HTTP contract keeps the authorization service stable when the storage provider behind the capability changes.

The failure boundary sits before rollout. Bucket CORS rules are not self-service through the API, even though the bucket model carries cors_rules; some cross-origin browser deployments can consequently be blocked. CORS is enforced by the browser, and a presign does not waive it. Test the actual production scheme, host, port, method, and request headers. Do it early. A same-origin development pass says little about a frontend served from a different origin.

Presigns don't fix CORS.

Option Integration posture Strong reason to choose it Boundary to verify
Infrai Plain REST contract, one platform credential, provider abstracted behind the capability Keep receipt-service code stable while changing the backing storage vendor CORS is not self-service; no permanent public links, object lock, or versioning
AWS S3 Direct specialist storage relationship Prefer it when the application needs the specialist's own storage controls and accepts its native contract Validate the exact CORS, retention, regional, and billing configuration for the account
Cloudflare R2 Direct specialist storage relationship Evaluate it when the application deliberately wants R2 as its storage boundary Validate required S3 compatibility and browser-origin behavior rather than assuming parity
Supabase Storage Storage selected as part of a broader Supabase application boundary Prefer it when that existing application boundary is more valuable than provider interchangeability Confirm private retrieval and audit-retention requirements against the chosen setup
UploadThing Frontend-oriented upload integration Prefer it when delivery simplicity owns the decision and a dedicated upload workflow is acceptable Confirm that its access and retention model matches financial evidence handling

This table is deliberately not a price leaderboard. Transfer paths, request billing, regional placement, and retained multipart fragments can dominate a nominal storage rate, and those inputs vary by workload. For Infrai specifically, trial credits cannot fund persistent writes, so validate the end-to-end upload with a paid-capable account before release.

The critical path in Go

The browser owns the final binary transfer, but the authority handoff begins on the backend. This runnable Go program requests a presign from the verified route, reads the platform key from the environment, uses an explicit POST, honors Retry-After on a 429, and surfaces the response body on failure. The request has no invented JSON fields; discovery is the authority for the response schema. After the backend returns the resulting signed URL to the browser, the browser sends the binary PUT without the platform Authorization header.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(
            http.MethodPost,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/receipt-originals/receipts%2Fexample%2Foriginal.pdf",
            nil,
        )
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, readErr)
            os.Exit(1)
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "presign failed: status=%d body=%s\n", resp.StatusCode, body)
            os.Exit(1)
        }

        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
}

The bounded retry applies only to rate limiting while asking for authority. A browser retry policy for the later PUT needs to know whether the same presign remains valid, whether the body can be replayed, and whether the backend still considers the receipt pending. Blindly retrying every status would conceal the failure boundary. In the full service, log the receipt ID, deterministic object key, presign issuance, response status, and reconciliation result under one correlation identifier; never log the signed query string, because it carries temporary authority.

For files large enough to require multipart transfer, the capability supports multipart upload. Each initiated upload must reach explicit completion or abort because orphaned parts are not cleaned automatically, while lifecycle expiry has a minimum granularity of one day rather than hours. Treat the multipart upload ID as auditable workflow state. A sweeper may locate old pending database records, but metadata cannot be searched server-side and object listing only filters by prefix, so key layout is operational design, not cosmetics.

The rejected public-link design and final acceptance test

The rejected design is a permanent public receipt URL returned immediately after upload. It is attractive: delivery is trivial, email rendering is easy, and no read authorization endpoint is needed. It also conflicts with this capability's private-only contract, and it turns a sensitive financial artifact into a bearer link with an indefinite lifetime. For these receipts, reject it.

Its valid use case is genuinely public content with no confidentiality or deletion ambiguity, such as a product image intended for unrestricted distribution. Infrai isn't suitable for that use case because it has no public/public-read ACL and no permanent public URL. Stick with a storage or media-delivery product that explicitly supports that publication model when public delivery is the requirement.

Other rejection triggers are equally concrete. Choose a specialist or add an external control when the receipt must use object lock/WORM, recover overwritten versions, replicate automatically across regions, migrate in bulk across clouds, or include GCS or B2 as a backing vendor; Infrai's stated vendor coverage is R2, S3, OSS, and COS. Choose database or queue coordination when concurrent writers require strict mutual exclusion. Do not infer those guarantees from a successful PUT.

There is a smaller operational trade-off too. Without server-side metadata search, an investigator cannot pose an arbitrary metadata query to recover a receipt; the list operation filters only by prefix. A deterministic hierarchy makes common recovery paths tractable, while the ledger database remains the searchable index and source of association. This division is acceptable for many receipt systems, though it should appear in the ADR before the first production object is written.

Approve the design only after a production-origin browser can upload with the exact headers that will ship, the backend can issue expiring PUT and GET grants without exposing its key, and reconciliation can bind the stored original to one receipt record. Verify that overwrites, retention, and regional handling meet the applicable audit policy. Test multipart abandonment if large receipts or bundled evidence can cross the single-request threshold.

Then inspect the audit trail.

A good trace answers who authorized the key, when the grant expired, which receipt record owned it, whether storage confirmation completed, and which principal later requested a read grant. Those events belong in application state because a storage response alone cannot prove business-level exactly-once processing. The object key should be deterministic, but authorization events should remain append-only so investigators can distinguish a legitimate retry from a competing attempt.

Select on control ownership, not on the shortest upload demo. Infrai is a strong fit when private presigns, a vendor-neutral REST boundary, and reduced credential and SDK sprawl matter more than self-service browser CORS or specialist retention controls. AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Supabase Storage, and UploadThing remain credible alternatives because they place the integration boundary elsewhere; the right one is the product whose boundary matches the system you are prepared to operate.

If this boundary fits your receipt pipeline, start with the Infrai storage guide and verify the live discovery schema before implementing the backend request.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign

title: Jira said Done. It wasn't, and the bug showed up later. So I made Jira check first.
description:
Picture this. The ticket moved to Done on Friday. The pull request was merged, CI was green, everyone moved on.

On Monday the checkout total was wrong.

The test that should have caught it was still there. It just didn't check anything anymore. In the last commit, labelled "fix flaky test", one line had changed:

- expect(total(cart)).toBe(90);
+ expect(total(cart)).toBeDefined();

The old line checked that the total is exactly 90. The new one only checks that there is some total. 0 passes. 900 passes. So CI went green, and Jira said Done.

Nobody lied. A developer in a hurry, or an AI agent told to "make the tests pass", took the shortest road to green. In a code review it looks like a one-line tidy-up, so nobody stops it.

The same trick, again and again

I first noticed this while building proof-of-done, a small tool that stops an AI agent from saying "done" before the tests really pass. The quickest way to a green CI was rarely fixing the code. It was one of these:

  • Skipping a test: it.skip(...), @pytest.mark.skip, @Disabled
  • Deleting a test and not replacing it
  • Loosening a check: toBe(90) becomes toBeDefined(), assert.equal(a, b) becomes assert.ok(a)

CI can't see any of this. A skipped test doesn't fail. A deleted test doesn't fail. A loosened check passes even more easily. All three make CI more green.

So I asked one question: before a ticket moves to Done, do its tests still prove what they proved before?

So I made Jira check first

Proof of Done for Jira is a free, open-source Jira app. When someone moves a work item to Done, it reads the pull requests behind it (on GitHub or Bitbucket) and checks four things:

  1. every pull request is merged
  2. CI ran and passed
  3. code changes came with test changes
  4. no test was skipped, deleted or loosened to get green

If something is wrong, Done is blocked, and it shows exactly why: the file, the line, and the test before and after.

It also shows the commit history, and marks the exact commit where CI turned green right after a test was changed:

▶ Watch the 4-minute demo on YouTube

How it knows a test got weaker

It reads the pull request diff line by line. The main rule is simple: a loose check is a problem only when it replaces an exact check about the same thing.

  • expect(user).toBeDefined() in a brand-new test: fine.
  • expect(total(cart)).toBe(90) removed and expect(total(cart)).toBeDefined() added in its place: caught.

It also knows the honest changes that look similar, so it doesn't block good work:

  • tests moved to a new file (the same test names show up again)
  • an expected value changed, like 200 to 201 (still an exact check)
  • a test renamed, or a check made stronger

It works for JavaScript, Python, Java and Go tests. I tested it on 113 small examples: it caught all 66 shortcuts and blocked none of the 47 honest changes. On 100 real merged pull requests from three of my own repositories, it blocked none. The benchmark is in the repo, so anyone can run it with npm run benchmark.

What else you get

  • Create a task to fix this: one click turns the block into a sub-task, with the file, the line and the pull request already written in.
  • A dashboard for team leads: what's ready, what's blocked, and every catch in the project.
  • Override with a reason: if a block is wrong, a project admin can let it through, and the reason stays on the ticket.
  • A receipt on Done: a comment with exactly what was checked, for anyone who asks later.

Try it in 5 minutes

You need a Jira site where you are an admin. Nothing to download.

  1. Install Proof of Done for Jira.
  2. Create a Jira project with the key DEMO and four work items: DEMO-1 to DEMO-4. It reads a ready-made demo repository, so you don't connect anything.
  3. Open Jira settings → Apps → Proof of Done settings, pick DEMO under Turn it on for a project, and press Apply.
  4. Move each work item to Done.

All four demo pull requests are merged with green CI. Only DEMO-1 is really done. The other three get blocked, each with its reason.

Use it on your own project

  1. In the same settings page, add a line like SHOP=your-name/your-repo (or SHOP=bitbucket:workspace/repo for Bitbucket). SHOP is your Jira project key, the letters before the number in SHOP-12.
  2. For a private repository, paste a read-only token. It is stored encrypted.
  3. Turn it on for your project and press Apply.
  4. Put the ticket key in the pull request title or branch name, like SHOP-12: fix checkout total.

Work with no code, like a design or a meeting, just gets the label no-code and goes to Done.

Ask it in Rovo

Rovo is Atlassian's AI chat inside Jira. The app adds its own Rovo agent, called Proof of Done, so anyone on the team can just ask whether a ticket is really done.

Setup: nothing extra. Once the app is installed and turned on for a project (the steps above), the agent is there. You need a Jira site with Rovo, which comes with the Standard, Premium and Enterprise plans. If the agent doesn't show up right after installing, give it a few minutes.

How to use it:

  1. In Jira, click Ask Rovo at the top right. The chat opens on the side.
  2. Type @Proof and pick Proof of Done from the list of agents.
  3. Ask in plain words:
    • "Is DEMO-2 really done?" → "DEMO-2 is not done yet", with the file, the line, the test before and after, and what to fix.
    • "Is DEMO-1 really done?" → yes: the pull request is merged, CI passed and the tests were kept.
    • "Which commit turned CI green for DEMO-4?" → commit a03b524, right after the test was loosened.
    • "What is blocking this from Done?" while you are on any ticket.

It answers only about tickets the person asking can see in Jira.

Ask it from your own AI agent (MCP)

The same check works from Claude Code or any other MCP client:

  1. A Jira admin turns it on once: Atlassian Administration → your site → Connected apps → Proof of Done for Jira → Tools → Enable tools.
  2. Add it to your agent. In Claude Code: 
claude mcp add --transport http proof-of-done https://mcp.atlassian.com/forge/487a9b05-d2bc-4e8f-98ce-2c533e95676f
  1. Sign in with your Atlassian account when asked, then ask your agent "Is SHOP-12 really done?".

Check before merge on Bitbucket

A second small app runs the same check on the Bitbucket pull request itself, before anyone presses Merge:

  1. Install it from the Bitbucket install link.
  2. In Bitbucket: Workspace settings → Custom merge checks, turn them on.
  3. In your repository: Repository settings → Custom merge checks → Add → Proof of Done.

On Bitbucket Premium the check can be made required, so Merge stays locked until it passes.

The full setup guide for all of this is in the README.

Links

  • Demo video: youtu.be/1SK-aSDd0xo
  • Code: github.com/WST2002/proof-of-done-jira
  • Demo repository: github.com/WST2002/proof-of-done-demo
  • The tool it started from: proof-of-done and its 36-second demo
  • More demos on my YouTube channel
  • My entry for Atlassian Codegeist 2026: Devpost page

Your turn

Have you seen a test quietly get weaker just to make CI green? What did the change look like? I'd love to add real examples to the benchmark.

title: Add Instant 'Game Feel' With This 6-Line JS Screen Shake & Hit-Stop Trick
description:
Want your 2D HTML5 browser game to feel like an arcade hit? You don't need a physics engine—just a 6-line canvas translation shake inside your render loop.

The 6-Line Screen Shake Trick 

let shakeIntensity = 12;

function applyScreenShake(ctx) {
  if (shakeIntensity > 0.5) {
    const dx = (Math.random() - 0.5) * shakeIntensity;
    const dy = (Math.random() - 0.5) * shakeIntensity;
    ctx.translate(dx, dy);
    shakeIntensity *= 0.88; // Smooth damping
  }
}

Why Developers Love This in AI Game Prompts

  • Instant arcade impact: Makes weapon hits and collisions feel 10x heavier.
  • Non-destructive: Wrap your render loop in ctx.save() and ctx.restore() so UI elements stay still.

title: Never let the model retype a number: how we read lab reports with two AI passes
description:
People photograph a blood test report and ask "is this bad?". When we built the lab report explainer in Saluvo, the explanation turned out to be the easy part. The risky part is reading the numbers: a misplaced decimal turns a normal result into an alarming one, or the reverse.

These are the design rules we ended up with. None of them need a special model, and they apply to any LLM pipeline that pulls numbers out of documents: invoices, prescriptions, bank statements.

1. Extraction is copying, not understanding

The extraction prompt is deliberately dull:

Copy every test row exactly as printed. Never guess a value; skip a row you cannot read.

Values come back as strings exactly as printed ("7.8", "1,250", "<0.5"), at temperature 0, in a strict JSON shape. Reference ranges come back twice: as printed text ("4.0 - 5.6") and as numbers where they can be parsed (refLow, refHigh). A row the model can't read is skipped, not reconstructed from what's "usually" there.

The prompt also handles the boring failures: if the photo isn't a lab report at all, the model returns {"markers": [], "notReport": true} and the user is asked for a clearer photo of the results page.

2. Read it twice, independently

Two extraction calls run in parallel on the same image or PDF text:

const [first, second] = await Promise.allSettled([
  extract(MODELS[mode].precise, input, meter),
  extract(MODELS.normal.precise, input, meter),
]);

Promise.allSettled, not Promise.all: if one reader fails or times out, the other's result is still used. If both fail, the user gets an error, never a half-guessed table.

Then the two readings are matched row by row. Names are normalised ("HbA1c", "Hb A1c" and "HBA1C" become the same key), and values are compared exactly as numbers:

function crossCheck(primary: Marker[], second: Marker[] | null): Marker[] {
  if (!second?.length) return primary;
  const other = new Map(second.map((m) => [keyOf(m.name), m]));
  return primary.map((m) => {
    const o = other.get(keyOf(m.name));
    if (!o) return m;
    const a = numberOf(m.value), b = numberOf(o.value);
    const same = Number.isFinite(a) && Number.isFinite(b) ? Math.abs(a - b) < 1e-9 : m.value === o.value;
    return same ? { ...m, verified: true } : { ...m, verified: false, altValue: o.value };
  });
}

No tolerance band. If one reader saw 5.6 and the other 5.8, that's a disagreement, because on a lab report it might be the whole story.

3. When they disagree, ask the person holding the paper

A disagreement isn't resolved by a third model or a vote. The row is shown with both readings and the user picks the one that matches their paper. Confirming a value also recomputes its flag:

export function confirmMarker(m: Marker, value: string): Marker {
  return { ...normaliseMarker({ ...m, value })!, verified: true };
}

The person has the original in their hand. Asking them is cheaper, faster and more honest than any amount of model cleverness, and it makes the tool say clearly what it couldn't read.

4. Don't trust the model's "high" or "low"

The extraction returns a flag for each row, but the app doesn't use it when it can do the maths itself:

if (Number.isFinite(num) && (refLow !== null || refHigh !== null)) {
  flag = refLow !== null && num < refLow ? "low"
       : refHigh !== null && num > refHigh ? "high"
       : "normal";
}

The flag comes from the printed number and the printed range. The model's label is only a fallback for rows where the range isn't numeric.

5. The explaining model never sees the values

This is the rule I'd most recommend stealing. The second stage writes the plain-words explanation, the questions to ask the doctor and which kind of doctor to see. It receives each marker's name, unit, printed range and flag, but not the value:

prompt: JSON.stringify(markers.map(({ name, unit, refText, flag }) => ({ name, unit, refText, flag }))),

And its instructions say: don't write the patient's result values anywhere; the app shows the exact numbers next to your text.

So no model ever retypes a number the user sees. The numbers on screen always come from the extracted, cross-checked, user-confirmed table. A model can't make an arithmetic slip, round 6.45 to 6.5, or quietly "correct" a value it finds implausible, because it never handles the value in the first place.

6. Make sure it's the right person's report

Reports get uploaded into the wrong family profile. The extraction also reads the patient printed on the report (name, age, sex; never the referring doctor or the lab's signatory), and the app checks it against the profile before explaining. If it doesn't match, it asks instead of explaining someone else's results as yours.

7. Optional extras must never block the core

For out-of-range values, the app can look them up on trusted medical sites and summarise them with citations. That step is wrapped so that a failure there never fails the report: no sources is a missing extra, not an error.

What this doesn't do

It doesn't diagnose. A flagged value is a flag, not a condition, and the explanation says which kind of doctor to see and how soon, more specific than "see a doctor". It's marked urgent only for values that need same-day care, and then the screen says to show the report to a doctor today. The explaining model's instructions start with "You are not a doctor and you do not diagnose", and it's told never to suggest medicines or doses.

The general lesson

If your LLM pipeline handles numbers that matter:

  • Extract as strings, exactly as printed. Parse them yourself.
  • Read twice, compare exactly, and let a human settle disagreements.
  • Compute derived facts (high/low, totals) in code, not in the model.
  • Keep the numbers away from the model that writes prose. Let it refer to them by name; render the values yourself.

We wrote a plain-language companion for patients too, if you want the other side of this: how to read a blood test report.

title: Docker push manifest invalid from a registry
description:
A docker push manifest invalid failure is the registry refusing the document that describes your image, not the layers, and the reason sits in a detail field that no Docker client prints. Fetch the response body yourself, or change the media types buildx writes, because those are the only two moves that touch the actual disagreement.


The registry answers 400 with code "MANIFEST_INVALID" and a detail naming the media type. Neither client prints the detail, which is why the log looks empty of reasons.

What this error means

Layers upload normally, sometimes all of them, and the step dies on the last request of the push. The wording depends on which client pushed. BuildKit and buildx surface the transport failure and the status code. The classic Docker daemon surfaces the registry error code instead, which renders as the word "manifest invalid" printed twice, because the code and its default message are the same phrase. Neither one prints the sentence that says which media type was refused. We have not recorded a run for this page, and the block below is assembled from the strings each component formats rather than captured from a job.

```Constructed from the strings each component formats, not a recorded run

14 exporting manifest list sha256:c3b9d1a2

14 ERROR: failed to push acme/api:1.4.2: unexpected status from PUT request to https://registry.example.internal/v2/acme/api/manifests/1.4.2: 400 Bad Request

--- the body that came with that 400, fetched separately with curl
{"errors":[{"code":"MANIFEST_INVALID","message":"manifest invalid","detail":"unsupported manifest media type and no default available: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json"}]}




## Common causes

### The registry does not map the OCI media type you pushed

The registry looks the request `Content-Type` up in a table of unmarshal functions, and a registry old enough to predate OCI image indexes has no entry for one. There is no fallback unless a default is registered, which is exactly what the detail sentence says when it ends "and no default available". In our experience this is the common shape behind a 400 on the last request of a push.

### Attestations pulled the whole export into OCI types

Provenance and SBOM attestations cannot be described in the Docker manifest format, so an export that carries them uses OCI media types regardless of what you would otherwise have got. A workflow that turned on provenance for supply-chain reasons can start failing against a registry that was fine the week before, with no change to the Dockerfile.

### A BuildKit upgrade changed the default

BuildKit pins media-type behavior to a compatibility version. On the current path as of 2026-09-20, an image export that does not set `oci-mediatypes` defaults to OCI media types. On the historical path that covers v0.15.0 through v0.31.x, an export without attestations defaulted to Docker media types instead. Upgrading the builder therefore changes what you push without changing your workflow.

### The manifest is schema 1 and something in the chain refuses it

This is the other direction and it is usually a pull rather than a push. A base image published years ago can still be served as `application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v1+prettyjws`, which modern clients decline. The wording overlaps with the push case enough to be confusing, and the fix has nothing to do with your exporter.

## How to fix it

### Write Docker media types from the image exporter

The exporter takes `oci-mediatypes` as a boolean option. Setting it false makes buildx write the classic manifest and manifest list formats, which is what a registry that refused the OCI index is asking for. Set it on the output rather than globally, so a second push to a modern registry is unaffected.



```Terminal
docker buildx build \
  --output type=image,name=registry.example.internal/acme/api:1.4.2,oci-mediatypes=false,push=true \
  .

Turn off the attestations that force OCI

  1. Add --provenance=false and --sbom=false to the build that pushes to the strict registry.
  2. Keep them on for the registry that accepts them, if you publish to both.
  3. Treat this as a concession, not a cleanup: you are giving up supply-chain metadata to satisfy a registry. 
- uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
  with:
    push: true
    provenance: false
    sbom: false
    tags: registry.example.internal/acme/api:1.4.2
    outputs: type=image,oci-mediatypes=false

Pin the exporter behavior across a BuildKit upgrade

The compatibility-version exporter option pins the digest-affecting image assembly behavior, which includes the media-type default. Pinning it makes the upgrade that changes the default a deliberate step rather than something you find out about from a registry.

--output type=image,name=acme/api:1.4.2,push=true,compatibility-version=20

For the schema 1 direction, replace the image

If the type in the detail ends manifest.v1+prettyjws, nothing about your exporter is involved. The image on the other end is in a format current clients removed support for. Repoint the reference at a maintained tag, or mirror the old image through a registry that converts it, and leave your push settings alone.

docker buildx imagetools inspect --raw quay.io/coreos/etcd:v3.3.10 | head -5

How to prevent it

  • Pin compatibility-version on any push that goes to a registry you do not control.
  • Push a throwaway tag from a new builder version before you move the real pipeline to it.
  • Keep one curl step in the workflow that prints the registry response body on failure.
  • Record which of your registries accept OCI indexes, because the log will not tell you later.

The useful sentence is in the body, and the client throws it away

A registry built on the distribution project answers a manifest upload it cannot parse with HTTP 400 and the error code MANIFEST_INVALID. The code carries a default message that happens to read "manifest invalid", and the specific reason goes in a separate detail field.

Then the client drops it. In the distribution client library an error renders as its code followed by its message, and the Detail property is not part of that rendering at all, so a structured error whose detail names the exact media type prints as "manifest invalid: manifest invalid". The containerd path does not do better: its unexpected-status error stores the response body on the struct and formats only the method, the URL and the status. So the answer is on the wire and not in your log.

Where the string is formed What reaches the Actions log
Registry, PutManifest in the distribution handlers HTTP 400, code MANIFEST_INVALID, message "manifest invalid", detail naming the type
Registry, UnmarshalManifest in distribution "unsupported manifest media type and no default available: " and the type, as the detail
Distribution client, its error rendering The code and the message only, so "manifest invalid: manifest invalid"
containerd remotes, its unexpected-status error Method, URL and status only, so "400 Bad Request" with no reason

Read in distribution/distribution on 2026-09-20: the handler that returns the code, the function that formats the detail, and the error type that renders code and message and not detail.

Get the detail out of the registry yourself

Because no client prints it, the fastest diagnosis is to make the same request by hand and read the body. A HEAD against the tag is enough to see the negotiation, and a PUT replay is rarely necessary once you know which types the registry advertises it will accept.

Do this from the job that failed rather than from your laptop, because the token, the registry host and the proxy are all part of what you are testing.

- name: Ask the registry what it says
  run: |
    TOKEN=$(echo "${{ secrets.REGISTRY_TOKEN }}")
    curl -sS -i -X HEAD \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
      -H "Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json" \
      "https://registry.example.internal/v2/acme/api/manifests/1.4.2"

What "unsupported media type" does and does not point at

Two strings in this area are about the old schema 1 format, not about OCI, and reading them backwards sends you to the wrong fix. The distribution sentence "unsupported manifest media type and no default available" appears with application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v1+prettyjws in m3db/m3#4396, where a modern daemon refuses to pull a 2018-era image. The go-containerregistry library has its own "unsupported MediaType" error, and in that library it is raised only for schema 1 manifests, with a link to the issue explaining that the project will not support them.

So when you find either phrase while searching, check the direction before you act. Pulling an ancient image is a schema 1 problem and the fix is a newer image. Pushing a fresh buildx image to a registry that will not take it is an OCI problem, and the fix is on the exporter.

The builder version decides the default, so pin it

BuildKit pins the behavior that affects an image digest, media types included, to a compatibility version you can set as an exporter option. Three values exist at the time of writing and only the newest one defaults an unset oci-mediatypes to OCI, which is why a builder upgrade is a plausible answer to "nothing changed and it broke".

Set it on the push that goes to the strict registry. You are not freezing the builder, only the part of its output that the registry has an opinion about.

BuildKit compatibility version Default when oci-mediatypes is unset
30, the current path as of 2026-09-20 OCI media types
20, the v0.15.0 through v0.31.x path Docker media types, unless the export carries attestations
10, the v0.13.0 and v0.14.0 path Differs from 20 on git source file modes and on zstd, not on media types

Values and wording read in the BuildKit repository on 2026-09-20. An export that carries attestations uses OCI media types on every one of these, because attestations require them.

Why no recorded run backs this page

This failure needs a registry that refuses a format, and every registry the reproduction harness can reach accepts both OCI and Docker manifests. Recording a run would mean standing up a deliberately old registry build, pushing to it, and then presenting the result as though it were a registry you might actually use. That would record our configuration and teach nothing about yours.

The parts that are checkable without a run are checked: the code that returns the status, the function that writes the detail, and the two error types that decline to print it. What a run would add is a screenshot of a log we can already tell you is missing the important line.

FAQ

Why does the log say manifest invalid twice?

Because the error code and its default message are the same words. The distribution client renders an error as its code, lowercased with underscores turned into spaces, followed by the message. MANIFEST_INVALID becomes "manifest invalid" and its default message is also "manifest invalid", so you get both halves. The part that differs between cases is the detail, which that rendering leaves out.

Does oci-mediatypes=false lose anything?

It gives up the formats that attestations need, so an export carrying provenance or an SBOM cannot use it. It also writes the older manifest and manifest list types, which every registry understands, so nothing else about the image changes. Treat it as a compatibility setting for one destination rather than a default you apply everywhere.

How do I see the detail field the client hides?

Repeat the request with curl from the same job and read the response body. The registry returns a JSON object with an errors array, and each entry carries code, message and detail. The detail is the sentence naming the media type. Registry access logs show the status but usually not the body, so the client-side repeat is the quicker route.

Is a 400 on a push ever worth retrying?

No. A 400 from the manifest endpoint means the registry parsed your request and declined its content, which will be identical on the next attempt. Retries are the right answer for the 5xx range, where the registry did not get far enough to judge the request. Spending runner minutes on a retry here buys the same 400 twice.

References

  • distribution: the manifest handlers that return MANIFEST_INVALID
  • distribution: UnmarshalManifest, where the media type detail is written
  • BuildKit: compatibility-version and the media type defaults
  • Docker docs: the image exporter and its options
  • m3db/m3#4396: a schema 1 image refused with the same media type sentence

title: Want to build a browser extension? If you know JavaScript, you’re already most of the way there.
description:
Browser extensions are one of the most underrated things a web developer can build. They’re small, useful, and you can ship one fast. Here’s what helped me understand them.

What an extension is made of:

manifest.json: The config file. It defines the name, version, permissions, and which scripts run where (use Manifest V3 for new projects)
Content scripts: JavaScript that runs inside web pages, so you can read or change the page
Background service worker: Handles events and long-running logic behind the scenes
Popup / options page: The UI users see. It’s just HTML, CSS, and JS, and you can build it with React
Storage and messaging APIs: Save user settings and let the different parts talk to each other

Tips for getting started:

Start with a tiny idea, like a button that changes a page’s style or saves a note
Ask only for the permissions you really need. Users and store reviewers care about this
Load your extension unpacked in developer mode to test changes quickly
Use a bundler like Vite if you want React or TypeScript in your popup
Chrome, Edge, and Firefox share most of the WebExtensions API, so one codebase can often cover several browsers

Common mistakes:

Requesting broad permissions “just in case”
Forgetting that service workers in Manifest V3 can shut down, so don’t keep state only in memory
Skipping a clear privacy explanation before publishing

The best part is that you can solve a real problem you have every day, and publish it for others to use.

Have you built a browser extension, or do you have an idea for one?

BrowserExtensions #JavaScript #WebDevelopment #Chrome #React

title: 5 Real Apps Using Rive Animation: Interactive UI Examples Developers Can Learn From
description:
5 Real Apps Using Rive Animation: Interactive UI Examples Developers Can Learn From

From interactive mascots and responsive UI components to animated health dashboards, here are five real-world Rive animation examples and what developers can learn from them.

A modern app can have a beautiful interface and still feel completely static.

The buttons work. The screens load. The API responds.

But what happens between those interactions?

What does your app do while an AI assistant is thinking? How does it celebrate a completed task? Can a character react when a user taps it? Can an animation respond to real-time progress?

This is where Rive animation becomes interesting.

Unlike a traditional animation that simply plays from beginning to end, Rive can use state machines and runtime inputs to connect motion directly to application logic.

That makes it particularly useful for:

  • Interactive UI and UX animations
  • Animated app mascots
  • AI companions and assistants
  • Gamified experiences
  • Progress indicators and achievements
  • Responsive product interactions

Let's look at five real products using Rive and explore how similar approaches could improve your own app.

1. Hoverine: Interactive UI Components Built With Rive

Product: Hoverine

Use case: Interactive buttons, toggles, loaders, and UI components.

Hoverine focuses on reusable interactive animations built with Rive.

Its library includes animated UI elements such as buttons, loading indicators, switches, and other interactive components.

What makes this approach useful for developers is the emphasis on Rive state machines and documented inputs.

Instead of treating animation as a video asset, developers can connect UI events to animation behavior.

Developer takeaway

Imagine a button with four visual states:

idle → hover → loading → success

With Rive, those states can live inside a single animation system.

Your React, Flutter, or React Native application can control the visual behavior based on actual user interactions.

For example:

// Illustrative application logic
// Connect these events to your Rive state machine.

function handleButtonClick() {
  setAnimationState("loading");

  submitForm()
    .then(() => setAnimationState("success"))
    .catch(() => setAnimationState("error"));
}

The exact runtime implementation depends on your Rive setup and platform, but the principle remains the same:

Animation should respond to application state, not run independently of it.

For developers building interactive dashboards, SaaS interfaces, or mobile applications, this can create a more cohesive user experience.

2. Tomosu: A Responsive Candle for Digital Wellbeing

Product: Tomosu

Use case: Interactive focus animation.

Tomosu is an iOS digital wellbeing app that uses a candle as part of its focus experience.

The creator has described using Rive to build the animated candle and integrate it with SwiftUI.

Instead of relying entirely on numbers and timers, the app uses a visual metaphor to represent a calmer interaction.

The candle can respond to touch and changes during the focus experience.

Developer takeaway

An animation becomes more meaningful when it represents something happening in the product.

Consider a meditation app with a character that responds to breathing.

Or a fitness app where a mascot's energy changes as a workout progresses.

For example, you could expose a numeric input:

breathingProgress: 0.0 → 1.0

That value could control the scale, glow, or movement of an animated element.

The result is a visual experience driven by real application data.

The important lesson: You don't need an elaborate animation to create an engaging interaction. A small, carefully designed visual response can be enough.

3. Welltory: Interactive Motion for Health Interfaces

Product: Welltory

Use case: Lightweight interactive UI animation.

Health applications often need to display complicated information.

Measurements, activity data, health scores, and daily trends can make an interface feel overwhelming.

Welltory has publicly identified Rive as one of the tools used to create lightweight, responsive animations within its product.

Developer takeaway

Motion can help communicate changes in an interface.

Consider these potential use cases:

  • A progress indicator responding to incoming data
  • A visual transition when a health measurement is completed
  • An animated confirmation after an action
  • A responsive dashboard component

These are examples of what developers can build with Rive, not claims about specific Welltory screens.

For a custom progress animation, you might define a numeric input:

State Machine: ProgressController

Inputs:
  progress: Number (0–100)
  isLoading: Boolean
  completed: Trigger

Your application can update progress as the underlying task advances.

When the process finishes, the completed trigger can play a short success animation.

The same principle works for onboarding, file uploads, productivity tools, and SaaS dashboards.

4. Brilliant: Interactive Mascot Animation

Product: Brilliant

Use case: Animated educational mascot.

Brilliant is an interactive learning platform covering subjects such as mathematics and coding.

Its recognizable character, Koji, is brought to life using Rive.

This is one of the most interesting examples for developers building educational apps, AI products, or gamified experiences.

Why interactive mascots are different

A traditional mascot animation might play a waving loop.

An interactive mascot can behave differently depending on what is happening in your application.

For example, imagine an AI learning companion with these states:

App event Mascot animation
User opens the app Welcome
User starts speaking Listening
AI generates a response Thinking
AI responds Talking
User answers correctly Celebrate
User makes a mistake Encouraging
No interaction Idle

This is an illustrative system design, not a specification of Brilliant's implementation.

With a Rive state machine, developers can control these behaviors through runtime inputs.

Example: AI companion state machine 

Artboard: AICompanion
State Machine: CompanionController

Inputs:
  isListening: Boolean
  isTalking: Boolean
  emotion: Number
  lookX: Number
  lookY: Number
  celebrate: Trigger
  reset: Trigger

Your application can update these inputs in response to user actions or AI events.

For example:

  • Start listening when the microphone activates.
  • Switch to thinking while waiting for a response.
  • Trigger talking when the assistant begins speaking.
  • Celebrate when the user completes a challenge.

You can also add numeric controls for eye tracking, mouth movement, and progress.

This is where a custom Rive animator becomes especially valuable.

The animation needs to look good, but it also needs a carefully structured state machine that developers can integrate and maintain.

5. BananaBin: Adding Personality to a macOS Utility

Product: BananaBin

Use case: Animated characters in a desktop utility.

BananaBin is a macOS application that adds personality to the system Trash Bin.

One of its distinctive visual features is animated flies, which the creator has confirmed were built using Rive.

It's a small interaction, but it demonstrates an important principle.

Not every app needs a full animated mascot.

Sometimes a single character or animated element can make an ordinary interface more memorable.

Developer takeaway

Think about the everyday interactions in your application.

Could an empty state have a little personality?

Could a completed task trigger a friendly reaction?

Could a loading indicator be more expressive?

These moments are opportunities for interactive motion.

The key is to keep animation purposeful and avoid distracting users from their primary tasks.

What These Five Rive Animation Examples Have in Common

Hoverine, Tomosu, Welltory, Brilliant, and BananaBin solve different problems.

But they illustrate how Rive can be applied across multiple product categories.

Product Rive use case What developers can learn
Hoverine Interactive UI components State-driven interface animation
Tomosu Responsive candle Visual feedback connected to user actions
Welltory Health interface motion Lightweight responsive UI
Brilliant Animated mascot Character-based product experiences
BananaBin Animated flies Personality in utility software

The larger opportunity isn't simply adding more animation.

It's connecting animation to application behavior.

Rive vs Lottie: When Does Rive Make More Sense?

Developers often ask whether they should use Rive or Lottie.

Both are useful, but they serve different needs.

Lottie is well suited to many timeline-based animations, such as illustrations, loading sequences, and onboarding motion.

Rive is particularly interesting when your animation needs to respond dynamically to application inputs.

For example:

Choose a simple timeline animation when:

  • You need a loading loop.
  • You want a short decorative animation.
  • Your animation doesn't require complex interactions.

Consider Rive when:

  • A mascot needs multiple emotional states.
  • A character should react to taps or gestures.
  • Animation changes based on real-time progress.
  • An AI companion needs listening, thinking, and talking states.
  • You need reusable state-machine logic.

This doesn't mean one tool is universally better than the other.

The right choice depends on how your product needs to behave.

Why Developers Should Work Directly With a Freelance Rive Animator

If you're building a product with interactive animation, you might be tempted to download a few assets and connect them yourself.

That can work for simple UI components.

But custom interactive characters and complex state machines introduce additional challenges.

A Rive animator who understands developer integration can help solve those challenges before they become expensive problems.

1. State Machines Built Around Your Application

A custom Rive animator can design animations around your real application events.

Instead of forcing your code to adapt to a generic animation, the animation can be built around your product requirements.

For example, an AI companion may need to handle:

  • Listening and talking states
  • Facial expressions
  • Eye tracking
  • Tap reactions
  • Celebration events
  • Interruption rules
  • Smooth transitions back to idle

These interactions require planning beyond visual keyframes.

2. Cleaner Developer Integration

A well-prepared Rive file can include clearly named inputs, predictable state transitions, and documented behavior.

Your development team should know exactly what each input does.

That reduces unnecessary guesswork during implementation.

3. Reusable Animation Systems

Instead of maintaining separate rendered animations for every reaction, a custom Rive project can provide multiple behaviors within a reusable animation system.

That can make future product updates easier, depending on how the animation is structured.

4. Direct Collaboration

Working directly with an animator makes it easier to discuss the details that matter to developers.

Questions like:

What happens if the user taps the mascot while it's talking?

Should the celebration animation interrupt the listening state?

Does the character return to idle or the latest selected mode?

How do we handle reduced-motion preferences?

These details matter in real applications.

And they are much easier to address when the animator and developer plan the behavior together.

Hire a Rive Animator for Your App or Website

I'm Praneeth, a freelance Rive animator specializing in interactive animations for websites, mobile apps, SaaS products, and AI experiences.

I help developers, founders, and product teams build custom Rive animations that are designed for real application integration.

My services include:

  • Interactive Rive mascots and character animation
  • AI companions and animated assistants
  • Rive state machines and character rigging
  • Gamification and achievement animations
  • Interactive UI and UX animation
  • Developer-ready .riv files and editable source assets
  • Integration guidance for React, Flutter, and React Native

Whether you're building a startup, improving an existing product, or adding a custom mascot to your app, I can help you turn your idea into an interactive animation system.

Want to add interactive Rive animation to your product?

🌐 Website: RiveAnimator.com

✉️ Email: riveanimator@gmail.com

Tell me what you're building, which framework you're using, and what you'd like your animation to do.

Let's create an interaction your users will remember.

Final Thoughts

Rive animation isn't just about making interfaces look more polished.

It's about making them respond.

The five products we've explored demonstrate different ways animation can support digital experiences, from responsive UI components to memorable animated characters.

For developers, the real opportunity is connecting motion to application logic.

And for founders, it's creating products that feel more interactive, expressive, and distinctive.

Your app already works. What if it could feel alive, too?
