title: Rerunnable Domain Provisioning in 2026 — 3 Checks for Marketplace Mail Intent
description:
Make the whole domain provisioning flow rerunnable by storing the tenant's zone identifier and intended SPF, DKIM, and DMARC record set before publishing anything, then make every retry reconcile that saved intent and repeat verification. Advance the marketplace's mail-readiness state only when the current intent passes all three checks: correct zone, matching records, and successful verification.

TL;DR: Make the whole domain provisioning flow rerunnable by converging on durable intent. Upsert every intended record on every run, accept an existing match as success, and keep verification inside the reconciliation loop. An interrupted sequence of completed steps is a poor recovery contract because its progress marker can disagree with the records it was supposed to publish.

For a marketplace onboarding sellers, the operational question is whether the published mail configuration still matches the seller's approved configuration. Finishing a worker job is insufficient evidence. DNS configuration is also only one part of delivery; this experiment evaluates publication and verification, without treating them as an inbox-placement guarantee.

How can the whole domain provisioning flow converge after interruption?

Consider a deliberately constructed test: seller A has three intended mail records, the worker publishes two, and execution stops before publishing the third. A checkpoint saying that provisioning started cannot reconstruct the missing record, while a checkpoint saying that two writes succeeded becomes misleading as soon as the approved configuration changes. The recovery input must therefore be the intended record set in the tenant database, together with its zone identifier, rather than whichever arguments survived in a particular worker invocation.

Keep intent durable.

The same reasoning applies after publication. If the worker stops before recording verification, the next run must repeat verification against current intent; it cannot infer readiness from a previous write response. Treat a record match as success so that restarting the entire operation is ordinary behavior, rather than a special recovery procedure with a second set of rules.

For a platform team already coordinating several backend services, I recommend trying Infrai for the DNS upsert and verification leg of seller onboarding: one API key and a single bill reduce the credentials and invoices the team must coordinate across that workflow. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas without requiring a key, which gives the implementation team a concrete way to inspect the integration contract before building the adapter. Those are reasons to include it in the experiment, not evidence that it wins the experiment.

Infrai offers one key, one bill across backend services through a single REST API, with no SDK required. The tenant database still owns intent. A shared API doesn't replace that responsibility.

Implement recovery as a repeatable reconciliation

Save an intent revision with the zone identifier and complete desired record set before scheduling the worker. On each execution, read that revision, upsert its records, and verify them; if intent changes during the run, reconcile the new revision before declaring readiness. A per-tenant serialization rule or an equivalent revision check belongs in the application's design, because a stale worker should not overwrite a newer readiness decision merely because it finished later.

The following runnable Go program exercises the recovery contract locally. Its record values are opaque test fixtures, not publishable SPF, DKIM, or DMARC configurations. The in-memory provider deliberately stops after its second write; the saved tenant object stands in for the database row that a production worker reloads. This is a state-machine demonstration, so it makes no network calls and assumes no undocumented request fields.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "os"
)

type Tenant struct {
    Zone string
    Intent map[string]string
}

type Provider struct {
    Records map[string]map[string]string
    Writes int
    StopAt int
}

func (p *Provider) upsert(zone, name, value string) error {
    if p.Records[zone] == nil {
        p.Records[zone] = make(map[string]string)
    }
    p.Records[zone][name] = value
    p.Writes++
    if p.Writes == p.StopAt {
        return fmt.Errorf("injected interruption after write %d", p.Writes)
    }
    return nil
}

func (p *Provider) verify(t Tenant) bool {
    for name, value := range t.Intent {
        if p.Records[t.Zone][name] != value {
            return false
        }
    }
    return true
}

func reconcile(p *Provider, t Tenant) error {
    for name, value := range t.Intent {
        if err := p.upsert(t.Zone, name, value); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    if !p.verify(t) {
        return fmt.Errorf("intent verification failed")
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    t := Tenant{Zone: "seller-a-zone", Intent: map[string]string{
        "spf": "fixture-spf-A",
        "dkim": "fixture-dkim-A",
        "dmarc": "fixture-dmarc-A",
    }}
    p := &Provider{Records: make(map[string]map[string]string), StopAt: 2}
    if err := reconcile(p, t); err == nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "expected an injected interruption")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    p.StopAt = 0
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 2; attempt++ {
        if err := reconcile(p, t); err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
    }
    if len(p.Records[t.Zone]) != len(t.Intent) || !p.verify(t) {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "recovery did not converge")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println("recovered and repeated without changing intended state")
}

Map iteration order is irrelevant to this test: it interrupts after two writes regardless of which records were selected first. Repeating reconciliation then repairs the incomplete state and demonstrates that a matching run can succeed again. The program does not prove remote DNS behavior, database durability, concurrent-worker safety, or actual mail delivery. Those require separate checks.

For the remote adapter, inspect the published schemas and examples before supplying record parameters. This separate runnable Go program retrieves the real Infrai discovery manifest and prints the DNS capability entries, preserving their published paths instead of guessing request fields. It reads an optional credential from INFRAI_API_KEY; discovery also works without authentication. Save it separately from the local recovery example.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("GET", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil { return err }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer " + key)
        }
        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return err }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return readErr }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            if attempt == 3 { return fmt.Errorf("rate limited: %s", body) }
            wait := time.Second * time.Duration(1 << attempt)
            value := res.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if delay := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; delay > wait { wait = delay }
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                if delay := time.Until(deadline); delay > wait { wait = delay }
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", res.StatusCode, body)
        }
        var manifest struct { Capabilities []json.RawMessage `json:"capabilities"` }
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &manifest); err != nil { return err }
        for _, entry := range manifest.Capabilities {
            var capability struct { Path string `json:"path"` }
            if err := json.Unmarshal(entry, &capability); err != nil { return err }
            parts := strings.Split(capability.Path, "/")
            if len(parts) > 2 && parts[2] == "dns" { fmt.Println(string(entry)) }
        }
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The 20-second HTTP timeout and four-attempt retry budget are example choices, not provider guarantees. The discovery call is read-only. For writes, preserve a client idempotency key across retries of the same operation; distinguish that operation from a later intent revision. Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window, so application convergence must remain correct after that window expires.

Request deduplication and state convergence solve different problems. Neither should carry the other's entire recovery burden.

Run the same experiment against each candidate

Use two test sellers with distinct stored zone identifiers and three intended records each. Obtain the actual SPF, DKIM, and DMARC values from the approved mail configuration; do not substitute the fixture strings above. Save the intent revision, initial observed state, attempt count, and final verification result for each seller. This is proposed evaluation data, not a report of measured production results.

The buy-versus-build comparison should preserve those inputs while changing the publication adapter. Include at least these candidates, and apply the same acceptance criteria to all of them:

Candidate What to evaluate for this marketplace Operating trade-off and selection boundary
Infrai DNS upsert and verification within the shared backend API Try it when credential and billing consolidation matter; require the same recovery evidence as every other candidate.
Cloudflare DNS A direct DNS integration against the same saved intent Prefer the direct candidate when this zone already belongs in that platform and its documented controls match the team's requirements; account for a separate integration contract.
Amazon Route 53 A direct DNS integration within the team's AWS operating model Prefer it when existing AWS ownership makes the direct path easier to operate; include its authentication and change workflow in the evaluation.
DNSimple A specialist domain and DNS integration Prefer the specialist when its documented domain workflow best matches the team's needs; evaluate the additional service relationship explicitly.
Application-owned reconciliation The worker and durable intent store around any of these adapters Build this control loop when the marketplace needs its own readiness contract; budget maintenance and on-call ownership alongside adapter work.

These are selection criteria, not claims of benchmark superiority or identical feature coverage. Check each candidate's documentation for the exact operations needed before running the test. A specialist or an existing direct integration is the better choice when consolidation offers little operational benefit and the team's required DNS controls are already supported there.

The experiment has four interruption points: before any write, after a partial write set, after all writes but before verification, and after verification but before the readiness decision is persisted. At each point, stop execution and restart from the saved tenant intent. Also deliberately alter one owned test record between successful runs and confirm that reconciliation restores its intended value. Use a separate case for an intent revision arriving during execution; the older revision must never mark the newer revision ready.

Pass means that every restarted run targets the stored zone, restores all intended records, and reaches a verification result tied to the current revision, while the other seller's configuration stays unchanged. A repeated successful run must leave the intended state unchanged. Fail the candidate if it needs manual reconstruction of missing intent, mistakes an old verification for current readiness, or changes the wrong seller's records. Do not silently delete unrelated records to make a comparison look clean: upserting the owned set does not establish an ownership policy for everything else in the zone.

Decide from evidence.

For capacity planning, count every intended upsert plus verification on each attempt, including the extra attempts introduced by interruptions. Two sellers with three records mean six intended record upserts in one complete sweep, before verification and retries; this is a workload definition, not a throughput measurement. Put a bound on concurrent reconciliations and retry attempts, then measure how long drift remains unresolved under that workload. Define a publication SLO separately from a delivery SLO, with the publication clock beginning when approved intent is saved and ending when that revision is verified. Choose the target from the marketplace's requirements rather than inventing an availability promise for a provider.

Verify the revision, then prepare rollback

Keep evidence for three checks: the worker used the tenant's saved zone, the owned record set matches the saved intent, and verification succeeded for that revision. An API acknowledgment alone cannot stand in for all three. Repeat the loop when verification is incomplete; retain the pending state and schedule another bounded attempt instead of declaring onboarding finished.

Rollback should be another explicit intent revision containing the previous approved record set. Reconcile it through the same upsert and verification path, and retain both revisions so operators can explain which configuration was requested and which one passed verification. Record removal needs an explicit ownership and deletion decision; restoring old values by upsert alone does not remove a record introduced by a later revision. Avoid using zone deletion as a shortcut for reversing a mail configuration change.

The release criterion is narrow: current publication intent has converged and passed verification. Evaluate delivery separately, including the mail authentication policy described by DMARC, before promising sellers that a DNS readiness indicator means their messages will reach recipients.

References

  • DMARC specification
  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Amazon Route 53 documentation
  • DNSimple API documentation

If this integration boundary fits your marketplace, start with the schemas and runnable examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Why Passing Tests Doesn't Mean Your Software Is Correct
description:
A Go pricing example show my green tests and high coverage can still miss a business rule defect.

Imagine a checkout service that gives customers a 10% discount on orders of $200 or more. The change has passed code review. The CI pipeline is green and the unit tests report 100% statement coverage.

Then a customer places a $150 order and recieves the discount. The service is working as written but it is not following the business rule.

How could the tests pass ?

The answer is simple

a test can run the code without checking whether the result is correct.

To understand this problem we need to seperate test execution, passing tests, code coverage, assertion quality and software correctness.

A small Go service with a real defect

Our business rule is

Apply a 10% discount only when the order subtotal is at least $200, Otherwise return the original subtotal.

The example stores money as integer cents. It assumes a non negative subtotal and rounds the discount down to a thole cent through integer division. We will focus on the discount threshold, not input validation.

Create a go module

mkdir pricing-demo && cd pricing-demo
go mod init example.com/pricing

Add pricing.go

package pricing

// FinalPrice returns the price in cents after any eligible discount.
func FinalPrice(subtotalCents int) int {
    if subtotalCents >= 10_000 { // BUG: the rule says 20_000.
        return subtotalCents - subtotalCents/10
    }
    return subtotalCents
}

The code gives the discount starting at $100 instead of $200 This matters for any subtotal from 10,000 to 19,999 cents.

For example, FinalPrice(15_000) return 13_500. The correct result is 15_000 because a $150 order should not recived a discount.

Test execution is not the same as verification

Now add pricing_test.go

package pricing

import "testing"

func TestFinalPrice_Weak(t *testing.T) {
    for _, subtotal := range []int{9_000, 20_000} {
        got := FinalPrice(subtotal)
        if got < 0 {
            t.Fatalf(
                "FinalPrice(%d) = %d, want a non-negative amount",
                subtotal, got,
            )
        }
    }
}

This test execute both path in FinalPrice one order without a discount and one with a discount. It also has an assertion, which is a check that compares an observed result with an expected condition.

But the assertion is too weak. It only checks that result is not negative. A wrong price of 13_500 would satisfy that condition, just as the correct price of 15_000 would.

Run

go test -count=1 -cover ./...

For this isolated example the test passes and Go report

coverage: 100.0% of statements

Both branches have run. Every statement in this small function has been exercised. The business rule defect is still present.

Figure 1. Passing tests confirm only the checks the suite actually makes

  1. Test Execution
    Running tests confirms that the test code was executed. However, it does not mean the tests checked important behavior.

  2. Passing Tests
    Passing tests mean all executed checks succeeded. However they do not prove that every requirement was tested.

  3. Code coverage
    Code coverage shows which parts of the source code were executed duting testing. However, high coverage does not mean the results were correct.

  4. Assertion Quality, Can the tests detect incorrect behavior ?
    Good assertions help tests catch wrong results. However strong assertions do not guarantee that every possible scenario was tested.

  5. Software Correctness, Does the software work as expected ?
    Software correctness means the system meets it requirements under relevant conditions. Passing tests provide edividence of correctness, but they cannot prove it on thier own.

Running tests, passings test and achieving high code coverage are not the same as proving software correctness. What matters is whether the tests can detect meaningful defects.

Thesese concepts support each other, but they are not interchangeable.

Go coverage tooling measures executed statement. It does not judge the quality of your expectations. The official

go.dev

explains how instrumentation redcords which parts of the source code are exercised.

Stornger tests use the business rule as expeceted result

A better test starts from the rule, not from what the implementation happens to return.

Add pricing_rule_test.go

package pricing

import "testing"

func TestFinalPrice_BusinessRule(t *testing.T) {
    tests := []struct {
        name     string
        subtotal int
        want     int
    }{
        {"ordinary order", 9_000, 9_000},
        {"below threshold", 15_000, 15_000},
        {"just below threshold", 19_999, 19_999},
        {"at threshold", 20_000, 18_000},
        {"above threshold", 25_000, 22_500},
    }

    for _, tt := range tests {
        t.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {
            got := FinalPrice(tt.subtotal)
            if got != tt.want {
                t.Errorf(
                    "FinalPrice(%d) = %d, want %d",
                    tt.subtotal, got, tt.want,
                )
            }
        })
    }
}

This test use a test oracle, meaning a source of expected results. Here the oracle is the written business rule, expressed as exact amounts in the test cases.

go test -count=1 -cover ./...

The stronger suite fails on two cases

FinalPrice(15000) = 13500, want 15000
FinalPrice(19999) = 18000, want 19999

Notice what changed. We did not need more statement coverage to find this defect. We needed test inputs near the rule boundary and assertions that checked the actual price.

Fix the condition in pricing.go

if subtotalCents >= 20_000 {

Now both test files pass. The coverage number remaings 100% in this small example, but the tests provide stronger evidence about the discount rule.

Why 100% coverage is not 100% correctness

Figure 2. Equal statement coverage does not mean equal defect-detection ability.

Coverage answer an execution question

Which parts of this code ran while tests were running ?

it does not answer a requirements question

Did the program produce the right result ?

Coverage is useful when it points to a path that no test exercises. It is much less useful as a score for test quality. Martin Fowler makes this distinction in his article on

Test Coverage

martinfowler.com

Even 100% statement coverage leaves important gaps. A test might check only that a function returns without an error. It might use the wrong expected value. It might miss an input boundary. And a rule missing from the implementation cannot be discovered merely by measuring execution of the code that exists.

Go's coverage report is also about instrumented source statements, not a guarantee that every possible input, condition or execution order has been explored. The Go command documentation describe the available coverage options and test behavior.

Use coverage to find places that need attention. Do not treat its percentage as proof that the service meets its contract.

A pasing test it evidence, not a proof

A test has a limited claim for these inputs, in this environments, the observed result met these expectations.

That is valuable edividence, it can prevent regressions, document an example of expected behavior and detect defects early. But its strength depends on the selected cases, the correctness of the expected results and the reliability of the test environment.

A services has many more possible situations than a small test suite can usally exercise. Inputs can change dependencies can fail and concurrent requestes can arrive in difference orders. Passing tests cannot by themselves, establish that every possible behavior is correct.

This does not make testing pointless. It means we should be precise about what our tests demonstrate. Formal verification can esablish specific properties under stated assumptions, but an orinary green go test result its not that kind of mathematical proof.

How to make test result more meaningful

When reviewing a unit test, begin with the requirement. Ask what result should occur and which mistake the test should catch. In the pricing example, the key condition is the threshild at 20,000 cents, so the values just below and at that boundary are more useful than two arbitary positive amounts.

Prefer assertions about observable behavior. Checking got != want for the final amount is more informative than checking that the amount is non-negative. When a function returns an error, check both the error and relevant result, according to its contract.

Next, use coverage reports to find the code that has not been exercised. in Go, these command produce and inspect a statement coverage profile

go test -count=1 -coverprofile=coverage.out ./...
go tool cover -func=coverage.out
go tool cover -html=coverage.out

The HTML view makes it easier to see which statements ran. It does not mark wak assertions or missing business requirements.

Finally review failure cases as carefully as success cases. For services, that may include invalid input dependency timeouts, retries and concurrent updates. Choose these cases based on the service's actual contract not on a target coverage percentage.

Conclusion

Passing tests are useful, but thier meaning is narrower than the green status suggests. Coverage tells us what ran Assertions tell us what was checked. Correctness depends on whether those checks reflect the real requirements.

The important question is not only whether we have tests, but whether those tests whould fail when the behavior becomes wrong. Mutation testing explores this by deliberately changing code and checking whether the tests notice.

Further reading

  • Go: Add a test, an introduction to the built-in test workflow.
  • Go: The cover story, an explanation of statement coverage and reports.
  • Go command documentation, including go test and coverage flags.
  • Martin Fowler: Test Coverage, on using coverage to find gaps rather than treating it as a quality score.

title: AP CS A, USACO or coding interviews: why a structured path beats random practice
description:
Students learning to code usually fail the same way: they jump between YouTube videos, random LeetCode problems and half-finished courses. They work hard, but nothing builds on anything else.

What works better, whether you're aiming for AP Computer Science A, USACO or a first job interview, is a path: one topic at a time, practice straight after each lesson, and a clear "what's next".

What a good path looks like

  1. Short lessons in order. Variables → loops → methods → arrays → classes → collections. Don't skip ahead.
  2. Practice immediately. 3–5 problems after every lesson, while it's fresh.
  3. Run real code. Type it, run it, break it. Reading isn't learning.
  4. Revisit what you got wrong a few days later.
  5. Know the target. AP CS A rewards the four FRQ shapes (methods, a class, ArrayList, 2D arrays). USACO Bronze rewards simulation and complete search. Interviews reward ~15 DSA patterns.

What learners tell us

We built MentorNxt around exactly this idea, and the feedback keeps coming back to structure:

"The course is really well structured — everything is laid out clearly, so I always know what to learn next. It's helped me a lot with AP Computer Science A."
— Ali, United States

— Bala, India

"Both my kids are learning Python and Java basics and they're doing very well. They're also using it to prepare for competitive exams here in Canada."

title: A CSS Grid Column Set to 1fr Still Overflows? The Minimum Is Not Zero
description:
We built a simple two-column page. The side menu had a fixed width. The main column was 1fr, which we read as "take whatever width is left." Then we put a long, unwrapped line of code in the main column. The page grew a horizontal scrollbar. The main column was wider than the leftover space. The 1fr did not shrink.

This is a CSS Grid issue. It is close in spirit to a flex item's automatic minimum, but the property that surprises people here is the track size itself.

The layout 

<div class="page">
  <nav class="side">Menu</nav>
  <main class="main">
    <pre>npm install some-long-package-name-and-then-another-one</pre>
  </main>
</div>

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 120px 1fr;
  width: 400px;
}

.main pre {
  margin: 0;
  white-space: nowrap;
}

The page is 400 pixels wide. The menu is 120 pixels. You would expect the main column to be the rest, about 280 pixels. You would also expect the long line to sit inside it, or to scroll inside it. That is not what happens.

What we measured

We pasted this layout into Chrome and measured the boxes on November 13, 2026, in Chrome 156.

The long line in this snippet measured about 430 pixels. The main column grew to that same width, about 430 pixels. The 400-pixel page then overflowed. The 1fr track did not stay in the leftover space.

Why a bare 1fr has a content minimum

fr means a fraction of leftover space. MDN's page on grid-template-columns adds a key detail. When fr is used on its own, not inside minmax(), it implies an automatic minimum. MDN writes this as minmax(auto, <flex>). So 1fr is minmax(auto, 1fr).

The 1fr is only the maximum. The minimum is auto. For a grid item, that automatic minimum is based on its content when the item is not a scroll container. The CSS Grid specification covers this in section 6.6. A single long line that cannot wrap sets a floor for the track: the track will not get narrower than that line.

So the track will not go below that line's width, even when the line is wider than the leftover space. The page overflows.

Two direct fixes

The first fix is to set the minimum to zero in the track list:

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 120px minmax(0, 1fr);
  width: 400px;
}

In the same Chrome test, the main column shrank to the leftover space: 280 pixels, after the 120-pixel menu. The long line no longer forced the column open.

The second fix leaves 1fr as it is and puts min-width: 0 on the grid item in that column:

.main {
  min-width: 0;
}

That also gave a 280-pixel main column in our test.

If you want the long line to scroll inside the main column, add overflow: auto on .main as well. In a third test, overflow: hidden on .main also let the column shrink to 280 pixels. It clipped the leftover content, so the page itself no longer overflowed. We prefer minmax(0, 1fr) or min-width: 0, and overflow: auto when the content should scroll inside the column.

Equal columns have the same trap

grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr looks like two equal halves. It is two tracks that each have a content minimum. In our 400-pixel page, we put the same long line in the left column and a short word in the right. The left column grew to the full width of the line. The right column was only 37 pixels wide. They were not equal.

grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) minmax(0, 1fr) made both columns 200 pixels, which is half of the 400-pixel page.

If you want equal, shrinking columns, write the zero minimum on each track.

A short checklist

  • A bare 1fr is minmax(auto, 1fr). The auto is a content minimum.
  • Long unwrapped text, a wide table, or a large image can hold that track open.
  • Use minmax(0, 1fr) on the track, or min-width: 0 on the item.
  • Do this for every 1fr track that should be allowed to shrink.
  • If the content is still wider than the column, set overflow on the item so the extra scrolls or clips inside it.

Browser support is broad. On MDN, grid-template-columns and minmax() are marked Baseline widely available from October 2017.

Sources

  • MDN, grid-template-columns: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/grid-template-columns
  • MDN, minmax(): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/minmax
  • W3C CSS Grid Layout Module Level 1, section 6.6 (automatic minimum size) and section 7.2.4 (fr unit): https://www.w3.org/TR/css-grid-1/#min-size-auto

title: Node.js API Storage: Expire Generated Promo Videos After Verified Copy
description:
An e-commerce API must store generated promo videos at useful quality, then expire redundant copies before storage and bandwidth grow without a policy. A Node.js service should therefore decide quality tier and retention at ingestion, before a temporary download URL quietly becomes its archive strategy.

TL;DR: fetch the generated video's download URL, copy the bytes into a private bucket you control, verify the copy, switch customer re-downloads to short-lived presigned URLs from that bucket, and only then delete the generated asset. Retain an approved high-quality master when later crops or encodes are plausible. Expire rejected candidates and redundant renditions on separate schedules. This makes quality versus bandwidth an explicit product decision rather than an accident of provider retention.

The ordering is the durable part. A generation provider's asset is governed by a retention policy the application does not control, so it should never be the source for a customer's later download. Generated video also tends to become the fastest-growing storage line; a deletion schedule belongs in the design from day one, not in a cleanup ticket six months later.

How Should an API Store and Expire Generated Promo Videos?

Start with business states, not bucket vendors. A generated candidate is evidence of an attempt. An approved master is the best available source for a future square crop, subtitle change, or new delivery encode. A delivery rendition is what the storefront should actually serve. Those objects have different value, and giving them one expiration rule either wastes bytes or destroys future options.

For a concrete catalog launch, suppose a job produces 12 candidates, the merchandiser approves one, and the channel requires two delivery renditions. The number 12 is an example policy input, not a performance claim. The important ratio is structural: candidate volume follows experimentation, while approved-master volume follows published products. Keeping every candidate at master quality makes storage grow with the noisier curve.

I would make the application record four fields before it copies anything: asset_id, role, approved, and expires_at. Add a content length or checksum when the source and destination expose one that can be compared; do not manufacture equivalence between unlike checksum schemes. A database flag named copied is weak evidence by itself. The deletion gate needs evidence that the destination operation completed and that the stored object is the one the application intends to serve.

Wait.

Small files conceal this mistake, because an inefficient policy remains cheap long enough to look correct; video removes that disguise, and a catalog that generates 12 candidates for each accepted creative can retain eleven times as many rejected sources as approved ones before counting renditions. That is why role assignment happens at ingestion rather than during a later cost review. The application should be able to explain, for any stored object, which product or campaign owns it, why its quality tier exists, which policy version selected its expiration, and what condition blocks deletion. If it cannot answer those questions, a lifecycle rule will automate ambiguity rather than resolve it.

The quality rule should be narrow. Keep a master only if another transformation is reasonably expected or regeneration would lose an approved creative. For ordinary playback, serve a delivery rendition through the CDN path rather than repeatedly moving master-quality bytes. This adds a rendition object, but it prevents routine customer traffic from paying the bandwidth cost of editing headroom that a browser cannot use.

Asset class Why it exists Access path Expiration posture
Rejected candidate Review and short dispute window Internal, signed access only Short and explicit
Approved master Future crop, encode, or text revision Restricted worker access Long enough for the reuse case
Delivery rendition Storefront playback and re-download CDN or short-lived presigned URL Aligned with the listing or campaign
Thumbnail or poster Catalog browsing Derived delivery path Rebuildable, but not necessarily free to rebuild

The table deliberately contains no universal day counts. Return windows, legal holds, campaign reuse, and the ability to reproduce the same creative determine those numbers. Storage governance fails when an example such as 7, 90, or 365 days is copied into production without an owner for the decision.

Make deletion a consequence, not a timer

A timer can identify work that is due. It cannot prove custody. The state transition should run generated -> copying -> verified -> serving -> source_delete_due -> source_deleted, with deletion eligibility depending on verified and serving, not merely on age.

That distinction handles the ugly interval between systems. If the copy succeeds and the metadata update fails, reconciliation can discover a private destination object that is not yet referenced. If metadata points at the destination before verification, a customer can receive a broken object. If source deletion succeeds but the worker dies before recording it, the next run must reconcile the already-completed action without treating absence alone as evidence that custody is safe. At-least-once execution turns each of those intervals into a normal state, so the worker needs a stable asset identifier and idempotent transitions.

The generation-side flow uses two verified operations: obtain GET /v1/video/download_url/{id}, then, after the controlled copy has been verified and the serving pointer has changed, call DELETE /v1/video/delete/{id}. Do not attach the API's Authorization header to the returned presigned download URL. That URL carries its own temporary authorization; forwarding a bearer credential to another host crosses an authentication boundary for no benefit.

Destination objects must remain private or signed-only. Customer re-downloads should receive fresh, short-lived presigned URLs from the application-owned bucket, never a public object URL and never a fresh dependency on the generation provider. The provider copy becomes disposable only after the customer path no longer depends on it.

Here is a compact API client suitable for a Python worker behind a Node.js orchestration service. It obtains the transfer URL through the verified route, uses an environment variable for the key, sets the method explicitly, surfaces non-2xx response bodies, and honors Retry-After on HTTP 429. It deliberately prints the documented response rather than guessing an undeclared response field; the copy worker can map the response through the live discovery schema it has pinned and reviewed.

import json
import os
import sys
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.parse import quote
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def get_download_metadata(asset_id: str) -> dict:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    safe_id = quote(asset_id, safe="")
    api_host = ".".join(("api", "infrai", "cc"))
    url = f"https://{api_host}/v1/video/download_url/{safe_id}"

    for attempt in range(5):
        request = Request(
            url,
            method="GET",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                body = response.read().decode("utf-8")
                if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"unexpected status {response.status}: {body}")
                return json.loads(body)
        except HTTPError as error:
            body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 4:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"download metadata failed ({error.code}): {body}"
                ) from error
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(min(delay, 60))

    raise RuntimeError("retry budget exhausted")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(get_download_metadata(sys.argv[1]), indent=2))

Do not reuse this request's bearer header when the worker fetches the returned presigned URL. In a production schema, store the selected retention policy version beside expires_at; otherwise a later configuration change can silently rewrite the meaning of old rows.

Compare control planes after defining the boundary

Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, and Cloudflare R2 can all be evaluated as the application-owned custody layer. The selection should happen after the states above are agreed, because a lifecycle feature cannot repair an application that serves a provider URL or deletes before verification. Their official documentation describes lifecycle management, but the operational fit differs around identity, eventing, replication choices, signed access, and the network path to the storefront.

Product Sensible shortlist condition Question that can disqualify it
Amazon S3 AWS identity, event, and data controls already govern the service Can the team test lifecycle, replication, and presigned delivery as one recovery path?
Google Cloud Storage The workload already uses Google Cloud projects and service identities Does signed delivery fit the existing identity boundary and CDN route?
Azure Blob Storage Commerce workloads are operated through Azure identity and policy Are lifecycle rules and delegated access observable by the same on-call team?
Cloudflare R2 The storefront delivery path already runs through Cloudflare Have API assumptions, residency needs, and the complete read path been validated?

This is not a feature-equivalence claim. Read each product's current lifecycle and signed-access documentation, then run deletion and restore drills against the exact configuration. Marketing pages tend to flatten the distinction between an object being durably stored, an object being reachable through the intended identity path, and an object being recoverable after an operator mistake. Storage architecture cannot afford that flattening.

The managed-media comparison is different. Cloudinary fits when transformation and delivery should live in the same media control plane. imgix is a stronger candidate when the primary job is dynamic delivery from an existing source, while ImageKit belongs on the shortlist when image and video optimization workflows are central. Cloudflare Stream is the more direct alternative when managed video upload, encoding, and playback matter more than retaining raw object-store control. Each choice adds a vendor-specific transformation or delivery contract, so export, private-source access, deletion semantics, and original-file retention need verification in current documentation.

Infrai is a reasonable generation-side option when a team wants plain REST calls without installing or tracking a client SDK. Its API is self-describing: a public discovery endpoint requires no key and exposes full request and response JSON Schema. Infrai puts its verified 295 routes across 20 modules behind one key and one bill, avoiding the platform pattern of juggling 30 SDKs, 30 keys, and 30 invoices. In this workflow, that single credential and consolidated billing reduce key rotation and invoice reconciliation across generation and adjacent backend jobs. Every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. The limitation is equally clear: it does not fit a team seeking one managed product to own transformation, encoding, playback, and media delivery; Cloudinary or Cloudflare Stream should be evaluated instead, while a team already committed to an external origin may prefer imgix or ImageKit. These are integration advantages and trade-offs, not reasons to leave the sole durable video copy with the generation service.

Price does not settle this decision. The durable cost model is stored bytes over time, write and read operations, transformation copies, and network transfer along the real customer path. A team should measure approved masters, rejected candidates, renditions per listing, re-download frequency, and retention days in its own workload; a volatile unit-price table cannot substitute for those counts.

Roll out the custody change without a flag day

First, dual-write only the metadata: record the intended bucket key and quality role while the existing download behavior remains unchanged. Next, copy newly completed assets into a private prefix, verify them, and shadow-check that a presigned destination read is possible without exposing that URL to customers. Do this for a bounded cohort.

Then switch re-downloads for verified rows to the controlled bucket. Track rows stuck in copying, objects with no matching row, rows whose destination object is absent, and source deletions that remain due. These are reconciliation counts, not invented service-level objectives; establish thresholds from observed traffic and the business tolerance for delayed cleanup.

Only after that path has operated correctly should scheduled source deletion begin. Keep the deletion worker independently stoppable. A rollback should restore the serving pointer for assets whose source still exists, while the durable bucket copy remains the preferred recovery asset.

Finally, enable bucket lifecycle rules for object classes whose application retention has already been proven. Lifecycle expiration is a backstop, not the primary state machine. Preserve legal holds and explicit exceptions outside the default clock, sample restore procedures, and review policy versions when merchandising changes its reuse horizon.

The compact decision is this: preserve quality where it retains future creative value, spend delivery bandwidth only on renditions customers can use, and let deletion follow verified custody. Everything else is vendor selection.

Sources and References

  • Amazon S3 object lifecycle management
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Google Cloud Storage object lifecycle management
  • Google Cloud Storage signed URLs
  • Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management
  • Azure Storage shared access signatures
  • Cloudflare R2 object lifecycles
  • Cloudinary video transformations
  • imgix video API
  • ImageKit video API
  • Cloudflare Stream documentation

title: GitHub-hosted vs self-hosted vs managed runners
description:
The github hosted vs self hosted runners question has a third answer that did not exist when the question was first asked, and for most teams it is the right one: managed runners. Stay GitHub-hosted while your minutes fit the included allowance or your repositories are public, go self-hosted when you need hardware, network position or persistent state that nobody rents, and take managed runners for everything in between, which is most CI.


The same job under three models, with the published rates read 20 September 2026. The self-hosted column has no per-minute rate because GitHub charges nothing for it.

Every GitHub Actions job runs on a runner, and there are exactly three places that runner can come from: GitHub, you, or a vendor who operates it for you. That choice is the largest single lever on what CI costs and how much of your week it takes.

They are not a ladder you climb but three trades: GitHub-hosted trades money for zero setup, self-hosted trades your time for control, and managed runners trade a vendor relationship for most of the self-hosted economics without the pager. Plenty of mature teams run all three at once, because runner selection is per job.

Every rate and limit below was read from docs.github.com or the named vendor's own page on 20 September 2026, and GitHub's included allowance, now a dollar amount, was read again on 12 November 2026. The self-hosted column has no published per-minute rate, and says so rather than carrying a made-up figure.

Comparison

GitHub-hosted Self-hosted Managed (Latchkey shown)
Price per minute, 2 vCPU Linux x64 $0.006 on a private repo (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD); free and unlimited on public repos Not published, because GitHub does not charge for it: its billing page states Actions usage is free for self-hosted runners. You pay your cloud bill, including the idle minutes between jobs $0.0025 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Price per minute, 4 vCPU Linux x64 $0.012 as a larger runner; the free public-repo standard runner is already 4 vCPU and 16 GB Your instance rate. A 4 vCPU cloud VM is cheap per hour and expensive per idle hour, which is the whole economic argument $0.005 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Free tier $12 of included compute a month on Free, $18 on Team, $300 on Enterprise Cloud (2,000, 3,000 and 50,000 standard Linux minutes at $0.006), private repos only; on Team and Enterprise Cloud larger runners can draw on it, and they are billed on public repos Unlimited from GitHub. Your cloud provider has opinions 30-day trial, then 2,000 included minutes a month on Developer, 4,000 on Launch, 6,000 on Scale
Billing granularity Every job is rounded up to the nearest whole minute Your cloud provider's, which is usually per second with a minimum, applied to instance uptime rather than job time Per minute
Runner sizes and OS Linux x64 and arm64, Windows x64 and arm64, macOS on M-series and Intel; larger runners to 96 vCPU x64 and 64 vCPU arm64 Anything you can boot and install the runner agent on, including hardware nobody rents: GPUs, bare metal, an on-premises box next to the license dongle Varies by vendor. Latchkey is 2 to 16 vCPU on Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64 only; Blacksmith and Depot add arm64, Windows and macOS
Cache: type, limit, persistence actions/cache, 10 GB per repository, entries removed after 7 days without access, restorable only from the same or the default branch actions/cache still goes to GitHub and keeps the same 10 GB limit, unless you run your own cache server. What you do get free is a warm local disk between jobs Vendor-provided and usually larger: Latchkey publishes no size and keeps entries 14 days, 25 GB per repo per week on Blacksmith, metered storage on Depot and Namespace
Docker build acceleration None built in. cache-to: type=gha writes into the same 10 GB store Whatever you build. A persistent BuildKit cache on a long-lived host is the single best reason to self-host, and it is also the thing that fills the disk Vendor actions with a managed layer cache: latchkey-dev/docker-cache-action@v1, or Blacksmith's builder on a sticky disk
Concurrency limits 20 concurrent jobs on Free, 40 on Pro, 60 on Team, 500 on Enterprise Cloud. macOS is capped separately at 5, or 50 on Enterprise Your fleet size, and your autoscaler's reaction time. Unlimited in theory, queued in practice Not published by most vendors; Blacksmith states it imposes none. Latchkey sets 20, 40 or 80 busy runners per workspace by plan
Where jobs run GitHub's own hosted fleet Your infrastructure, your VPC, your network position. This is the reason most regulated teams are here The vendor's cloud, or your own account on the vendors that offer a bring-your-own-cloud mode
Self-healing or retries None. A failed job waits for a person, or for retry logic you wrote yourself None, and the runner host is now also yours to fix when it wedges, fills up or goes offline mid-job Latchkey diagnoses and retries transient failures inside the run; most managed vendors do not offer this
Setup change required None; this is the default Runner agents, an autoscaler, images, patching, secrets rotation, disk cleanup, plus a runs-on label A runs-on label change, and for some vendors a GitHub App install

GitHub-hosted: the default, and why it stops being free

The standard runner is the whole story. On a private repository it is 2 vCPU, 8 GB of RAM and 14 GB of SSD; on a public repository the same ubuntu-latest label gives 4 vCPU and 16 GB, free and unlimited. That asymmetry is why a workflow gets slower the week a repository is made private.

The bill arrives from two directions. Minutes are rounded up per job, so a matrix of forty 70-second jobs bills as 80 minutes rather than 46.7. And the included allowance is a dollar amount, deducted at each runner's per-minute rate, so a Team plan's $18 covers 3,000 standard Linux minutes at $0.006 but only about 290 macOS minutes at $0.062.

The ceilings are the other half: 14 GB of disk is why no space left on device is so common, and 8 GB of RAM is why exit code 137 turns up on builds that were fine last quarter.

Self-hosted: cheap compute, expensive attention

GitHub charges nothing for self-hosted Actions usage; its billing page says so in as many words. What you pay instead is your cloud bill plus the part nobody costs in advance: the autoscaler that has to be right, the images that drift, the disk that fills because a persistent BuildKit cache is why you self-hosted, and the runner that goes offline halfway through a release.

The economics only work at high utilisation. A fleet sized for your worst hour is mostly idle for the other twenty-three, and idle bills. Ephemeral autoscaled runners fix that and reintroduce the cold start you were avoiding, in exchange for the strongest security posture of the three models, because nothing survives between jobs.

None of this argues against self-hosting. It argues for being honest about why. There are four good reasons: hardware nobody rents, a network position you need, a compliance answer that requires jobs inside your own account, and volume large enough that a flat cloud commitment beats any metered rate. "It is cheaper" is not one of them on its own, because it is only cheaper once you refuse to count your own time.

Managed runners: the model that did not exist for the original question

A managed runner vendor operates the fleet and sells you the minutes. To the workflow it is indistinguishable from GitHub-hosted: same actions, same secrets, same matrix, one different label. To the invoice it is closer to self-hosted, because you pay compute rates rather than platform rates.

The category is crowded enough to have shape. Blacksmith and Depot sell runners on their own hardware with arm64, Windows and macOS. Namespace sells shapes and cache volumes on a prepaid plan. RunsOn and the bring-your-own-cloud modes run the fleet inside your AWS account, a hybrid of this model and the last. Latchkey sells Linux x64 only and adds what none of the others do: diagnosing a transient failure and retrying it inside the run.

The honest cost of this model is vendor risk, and it is not theoretical: BuildJet shut down in March 2026 and Cirrus CI followed in June. The mitigation is the thing that makes adoption cheap. Because it is a label, leaving is a label.

Cost: the same month under all three models

Ten thousand Linux minutes at 2 vCPU plus two thousand macOS minutes a month, on a private repository. The self-hosted row is the only one where the published price is not the price.

Linux compute macOS compute What else you pay Monthly total
GitHub-hosted $60 at $0.006/min $124 at $0.062/min Nothing $184
Self-hosted Your instance rate for the hours the fleet is up, not the minutes jobs run Apple hardware or a licensed Mac cloud; the most expensive thing to self-host Autoscaler, images, patching, disk cleanup, and the pager Not publishable: it is your cloud bill plus your time
Managed (Latchkey) $25 at $0.0025/min Not offered: $124 on GitHub-hosted $5 to $49 a month for the plan, plus seats past the plan's own at $5 $149 plus the plan

The row that will not resolve to a number is the point of the table, not a gap in it. Self-hosted cost is dominated by utilisation and by engineering hours, and both of those are yours. Measure it rather than guess: the hours your fleet was up last month times your instance rate, plus the hours your team spent on it. Teams that do this honestly find the compute was the small half. Two things make self-hosting look better than that sounds: GitHub charges nothing for the Actions usage itself, and a warm disk with a persistent build cache is worth real minutes on a Docker-heavy pipeline. The managed row is gross too: its plan fee is separate from the compute, and its 2,000 to 6,000 included minutes are not netted off.

Speed

Not benchmarked yet; the runner benchmark report will replace this section. There is no honest ranking without running the same workload on all three, and the number everyone quotes is a vendor multiple measured on a workload the vendor chose.

What the published specifications do say: a standard private-repo GitHub-hosted runner is the smallest machine of the three at 2 vCPU and 8 GB, a self-hosted runner is as fast as whatever you buy and starts warm if it is long-lived, and managed vendors sell larger sizes at lower rates than GitHub's larger runners.

Reliability

Each model fails differently, and that is more useful than any uptime number. GitHub-hosted fails as an opaque platform incident you wait out. Self-hosted fails as your infrastructure: a full disk, a wedged agent, a runner that lost communication mid-job and took the run with it. Managed runners fail as a vendor incident, plus the risk the vendor leaves the market.

All three behave the same on a bad job: a registry timeout or an out-of-memory kill bills, and the re-run bills again. Self-hosting makes this worse rather than better, because host state joins your failure surface. To size that line item before you pick a model, count the runs in your Actions history that passed on a second attempt with no code change in between.

When to choose each

  • GitHub-hosted when your repositories are public, when your minutes fit the included allowance, when your bill is mostly macOS (it is the cheapest macOS of the three), or when adding a vendor would mean redoing a compliance answer.
  • Self-hosted when you need hardware nobody rents, a network position inside your own VPC, jobs inside your own account for compliance, or a persistent build cache on a long-lived host. Budget the fleet as infrastructure, because that is what it is.
  • Managed when the answer to "why are we self-hosting" is only ever cost, when your Linux bill has outgrown the included allowance, or when you want larger machines without operating them. Check the vendor's OS coverage first: Latchkey is Linux x64 only, so a macOS or Windows job stays where it is.

Switching: the exact diff

Moving between GitHub-hosted and managed is one line per job. Moving to self-hosted is one line per job plus a fleet, which is the asymmetry the table cannot show.

jobs:
   test:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: latchkey-medium      # managed: label only

   gpu-eval:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, gpu]   # plus an agent, an image and an autoscaler

   ios:
     runs-on: macos-latest        # left alone: cheapest macOS of the three

The verdict

Stay on GitHub-hosted if your repositories are public or your minutes fit the allowance, because nothing paid competes with free and the default costs you no decision. Self-host when you have a reason that is not cost, which means hardware, network position, compliance or a persistent cache, and budget it as infrastructure with a person attached rather than as a saving. For everyone else, and that is most teams, managed runners are the model the original question did not have: self-hosted economics, no fleet, and a runs-on line you can revert in a minute if it disappoints. The caveats are real and worth saying out loud. Managed vendors leave the market, most of them cover only some operating systems, and none of the three models, on its own, does anything about the job that failed at 2am for a reason that had nothing to do with your code.

FAQ

When should you use self-hosted runners vs GitHub-hosted runners?

Self-host when you need something GitHub does not rent: GPUs or other specific hardware, a network position inside your own VPC, jobs in your own account for compliance, or a persistent build cache on a long-lived host. Stay GitHub-hosted when your repositories are public, your minutes fit the allowance, or your bill is mostly macOS. Choosing self-hosted purely to save money usually means the ops time has not been counted.

Per minute charges for self hosted runners?

GitHub's billing page states that Actions usage is free for self-hosted runners, as read on 20 September 2026. What you pay is your cloud provider's instance rate for the whole time the fleet is up, not just the minutes jobs run, which is why utilisation rather than rate decides whether self-hosting is cheaper.

Which GitHub Actions services let you run jobs on faster hardware without self-hosting?

Managed runner vendors: Blacksmith, Depot, Namespace, WarpBuild, Ubicloud, RunsOn and Latchkey, plus GitHub's own larger runners, which go to 96 vCPU on x64. All of them are adopted with a runs-on label change, and the vendors are typically cheaper per minute than GitHub's larger runners at the same size.

What hardware do GitHub-hosted runners actually give you?

On a private repository the standard Linux runner is 2 vCPU, 8 GB of RAM and 14 GB of SSD. On a public repository the same label gives 4 vCPU and 16 GB, free and unlimited. Windows matches Linux, and macOS on Apple silicon is 3 vCPU with 7 GB. The 14 GB of disk is the same on all of them, which is why disk-full failures appear on jobs with plenty of memory.

References

  • GitHub Actions billing, including self-hosted runners and cache allowance
  • GitHub Actions runner pricing: per-minute rates
  • GitHub-hosted runner specifications
  • GitHub Actions usage limits and concurrency
  • Latchkey runner sizes and rates

title: BrowserRouter in React
description:
1. What is React Router?

React Router is a library that helps us navigate between different pages or views in a React application.

For example:

  • / displays the Home page.
  • /products displays the Products page.
  • /about displays the About page.
  • /cart displays the Cart page.

We can move between these pages without reloading the entire website.

2. What is BrowserRouter?

BrowserRouter is a component provided by React Router.

It uses the browser's URL to manage navigation in our React application.

In simple words, BrowserRouter helps React understand which page should be displayed based on the URL.

3. Installing React Router

Before using React Router, we need to install it.

Open your terminal inside your React project and run:

npm install react-router-dom

Now we can use React Router in our application.

4. Creating Different Pages

First, let's create three simple components.

Home.jsx

function Home() {
  return <h1>Welcome to Home Page</h1>;
}

export default Home;

About.jsx

function About() {
  return <h1>This is About Page</h1>;
}

export default About;

Contact.jsx

function Contact() {
  return <h1>This is Contact Page</h1>;
}

export default Contact;

Each component represents a different page in our application.

5. Setting Up BrowserRouter

Now let's connect these pages using React Router.

In main.jsx, write:

import React from "react";
import ReactDOM from "react-dom/client";

import { BrowserRouter } from "react-router-dom";
import App from "./App";

ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render(
  <BrowserRouter>
    <App />
  </BrowserRouter>
);

Here, we wrap our App component inside BrowserRouter.

This allows the components inside App to use React Router features.

6. Using Routes and Route

Now open App.jsx.

import { Routes, Route } from "react-router-dom";

import Home from "./Home";
import About from "./About";
import Contact from "./Contact";

function App() {
  return (
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />

      <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />

      <Route path="/contact" element={<Contact />} />
    </Routes>
  );
}

export default App;

Let's understand the important parts.

  • Routes: Holds all the route definitions.
  • Route: Connects a URL path to a component.
  • path: Defines the URL.
  • element: Defines which component should be displayed.

For example:

<Route path="/about" element={<About />} />

This means whenever the user visits /about, React displays the About component.

7. Navigating Between Pages Using Link

We have created different pages, but how can users move between them?

We can use the Link component provided by React Router.

Let's update our App.jsx:

import { Routes, Route, Link } from "react-router-dom";

import Home from "./Home";
import About from "./About";
import Contact from "./Contact";

function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <nav>
        <Link to="/">Home</Link>

        <Link to="/about">About</Link>

        <Link to="/contact">Contact</Link>
      </nav>

      <Routes>
        <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />

        <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />

        <Route path="/contact" element={<Contact />} />
      </Routes>
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;

Now we can click the links to move between pages.

Important: Link is similar to an HTML anchor tag, but it handles navigation through React Router without a full page reload.

8. Where Do We Use React Router?

React Router is useful when building applications with multiple pages or views.

For example, in an e-commerce application:

URL Page
/ Home
/products Products
/cart Shopping Cart
/login Login
/profile User Profile

When a user clicks the Cart link, React Router displays the Cart component.

We don't need to create a separate HTML file for every page.

9. Important Things to Remember

  • React Router helps us navigate between pages in React.
  • BrowserRouter manages navigation using the browser URL.
  • Routes contains our route definitions.
  • Route connects a URL path to a component.
  • Link allows users to navigate between pages without a full page reload.

title: One of our 76 pages has animations on it, and the 45-leaf one in the hero is not in the list
description:
document.getAnimations() is the most underused line in front-end debugging. It returns every animation the document currently knows about, each with a playState, a currentTime and the name of the keyframes driving it. One call tells you what is actually moving, as opposed to what your stylesheet says could move.

I ran it across all 76 public pages of Nakodo expecting a spread. The site is drawn rather than photographed, it has 24 @keyframes blocks in its stylesheet, and the landing page has a hero full of blowing leaves.

Here is the whole result:

Pages Animation objects
75 0
1 15

Every guide, every glossary entry, every pricing table, every hub: nothing. One page animates, and it is the home page.

24 keyframes, 8 of which ever reach the public

The stylesheet declares 24 keyframe blocks:

live-pulse illo-river illo-current illo-pencil illo-ink illo-hop illo-alcy-hop
illo-peck-body illo-peck-head illo-drum-body illo-drum-head illo-drum-chip-1
illo-drum-chip-2 grow-x grow-y draw-in illo-scan-head illo-blink illo-dive-bird
illo-dive-ripple illo-notice-sheet illo-notice-roll stamp-land row-arrive

Eight of those names appear in a live animation on a public page. The other sixteen belong to screens behind the login: a bird drumming on a log while a job runs, a blink, a dive with a ripple, a sheet of paper rolling into a notice, a stamp landing, a row arriving in a table. They cost nothing to a visitor beyond their share of the stylesheet, and they are the reason a census of the CSS would have told me the wrong thing. Declared motion and running motion are different populations, and only one of them is measurable from the outside.

4 running, 11 paused, before you scroll

On the home page at the top of the document:

document.getAnimations().length;                                     // 15
document.getAnimations().filter((a) => a.playState === "running");    // 4
document.getAnimations().filter((a) => a.playState === "paused");     // 11

The four that run are two pairs: illo-peck-body and illo-peck-head, twice over. That is the kingfisher in the hero, pecking.

The eleven that exist but do not run are the illustrations further down the page, and they are paused by design. Each one is wrapped in a component whose only job is to decide whether its drawing should move:

export function IlloPlay({ className, children }: { className?: string; children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const ref = useRef<HTMLLIElement>(null);
  const [onScreen, setOnScreen] = useState(false);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = ref.current;
    if (!el) return;
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => setOnScreen(entry.isIntersecting));
    observer.observe(el);
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, []);

  return (
    <li ref={ref} data-play={onScreen ? "" : undefined} className={cn("illo-play", className)}>
      {children}
    </li>
  );
}

The animations are declared paused in CSS and a data-play attribute set by an IntersectionObserver is what starts them. Hovering one pauses it again, on the theory that if you have stopped on a drawing you would like to look at it rather than watch it loop.

Scroll and you can watch the arithmetic change. Measured at 1280 by 900:

Scroll position Objects Running
0 15 4
900 15 15
1,800 32 18
2,700 34 6
4,309 (bottom) 32 4

Two things in that table surprised me.

The first is that the object count goes up and does not come back down. At 1,800 pixels, seventeen new animations appear: seven grow-x and seven grow-y and a few others. Those are the bars of the two small example charts, which grow once when they come into view. They are one-shot animations with a fill, and a finished animation with a fill stays in getAnimations() rather than disappearing from it. So the list is a record of everything that has animated, not a snapshot of what is animating, and playState is the only part of it that answers the question you probably meant to ask.

The second is the bottom row. The hero is long gone off the top of the screen, and its four animations are still running. The pecking bird is the one drawing on the page that is not wrapped in the component above, so nothing ever tells it to stop. It is small, it is cheap, and it is still work being done for a bird nobody can see. That is going on the list.

Reduced motion takes it to zero, not to paused

With prefers-reduced-motion: reduce emulated, the same page returns:

document.getAnimations().length; // 0

Not fifteen paused objects. Zero objects, because they never exist. The stylesheet puts the rules that use those keyframes inside the positive query rather than switching them off in the negative one:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  /* the rules that attach illo-* animations */
}

There are 13 reduced-motion queries in the CSS the site serves, 10 of them no-preference and 3 of them reduce. Writing it this way round means reduced motion is the default state of the site and motion is the enhancement, which is both the accessible way round and the cheaper one: there is nothing to create and nothing to pause.

You can check this in a few seconds without any tooling. Open DevTools on the home page, open the Rendering panel, set "Emulate CSS prefers-reduced-motion" to reduce, reload, and run document.getAnimations().length.

The hero animation is not in any of these numbers

The thing a visitor is most likely to call "the animation on that site" is the gust of autumn leaves that whirls around the hero plate. It has 45 leaves at desktop width, 34 on a tablet and 22 on a narrow phone.

It appears in none of the counts above, because it is not a CSS animation and it is not a Web Animations API animation. It is 318 lines of component that writes transforms on a requestAnimationFrame loop, and getAnimations() has no idea it exists.

That is the catch worth knowing about the API. It lists animations the browser is driving. Anything you drive yourself is invisible to it, so "zero animations" never means "nothing is moving".

It does have the two gates that matter, written as plain early exits rather than as CSS:

if (!svg || window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches) return;

and

frame = onScreen ? requestAnimationFrame(step) : 0;

A reduced-motion visitor never starts the loop at all, and scrolling the hero out of view cancels it until an IntersectionObserver brings it back. The same two decisions as the CSS illustrations, taken twice in two different languages, which is the honest cost of having both kinds of motion in one page.

A note on what I could not measure

I wanted to put a frame rate in this post, so I ran a requestAnimationFrame loop on the home page and on a static page and compared the gaps. The numbers were nonsense: around 30 callbacks a second on the animating page and about 2 a second on the static one, with the tab visible and focused in both cases.

That is not the site. That is how a headless browser produces frames. Without anything damaging the screen there is no reason to produce a frame at all, so an idle page gets a trickle, and a page with a running animation gets whatever cadence the compositor settles on. A real display on a real machine would give you 60 of them a second on both pages.

So there is no frame rate in this post. The census is solid, because getAnimations() reports document state rather than compositor behaviour, and the moment a measurement starts describing the harness instead of the thing, it belongs in a paragraph like this one rather than in a table.

What came out of it

  1. Gate the hero bird. Four animations keep running after the hero has scrolled away. The component that fixes it already exists and is used eleven times on the same page.
  2. playState, not length. Anything that watches animation counts has to filter by state, or a finished bar chart will make a quiet page look busy for ever.
  3. The 16 unused keyframes are fine. They are app motion, they are in the same stylesheet as everything else, and splitting the stylesheet to save a visitor a few hundred bytes of text they never parse into an animation would be the wrong trade.

The counts in this post are reproducible on nakodo.app as it stands. Load the home page, run document.getAnimations().length, scroll to the three-step section, run it again, and then try it on the pricing page for the number that 75 of the 76 pages give.
