title: Empresia Scraper in Python: Company Reports and Daily New Incorporations from the BORME
description:
Empresia.es is a free Spanish company directory built on the Commercial Registry. Every company has a report with its CIF, CNAE activity code, share capital, sales band, employees, address, phones, board, officers and the announcements it published in the BORME (Spain's Official Gazette of the Commercial Registry). It also lists, day by day and province by province, every company that was incorporated, dissolved or changed its capital. For lead generation, KYC or market research, that is a clean B2B dataset. Here is how to pull it into Python, and what to watch out for.

Why not plain requests 

import requests

r = requests.get("https://www.empresia.es/empresa/mercadona/")
print(r.status_code)  # 200, for now

Empresia renders everything on the server, so a single request works. The problem starts at volume: the site sits behind Cloudflare, and a crawl of thousands of company pages from one IP is exactly what gets throttled. Sending each request through Scrape.do rotates the IP on every call and retries failures. A plain request is enough, no extra parameters: 1 credit per page, about 2 seconds.

TOKEN = "<your_token>"

def fetch(url):
    r = requests.get("https://api.scrape.do/", params={"token": TOKEN, "url": url}, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.text

Where the data is on a company page

There is no JSON-LD and no API behind the page. The data sits in a few predictable blocks:

  1. div.datos-ident: name, phones, fax, address, websites and e-mail, then label/value pairs (span.list-group-item-heading followed by p.list-group-item-text) for CIF, incorporation date, share capital, sales band, registry, last filed accounts, employees, governing body and auditor.
  2. #organigrama: the board, one li per person with the role after the link.
  3. #ListaRelaciones: officers with appointment and removal dates.
  4. #ListaEventos: the BORME timeline (changes of address, appointments, capital increases), each with a link to the official PDF.

Two details catch people out. The e-mail is not in the HTML as text: Cloudflare replaces it with [email protected] and a data-cfemail attribute, a hex string whose first byte is the XOR key for the rest. And the sales figure is a band ("Superior a 2.500.000 euros"), kept in the title of a tooltip, not in the visible text.

from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

def decode_cfemail(hex_str):
    data = bytes.fromhex(hex_str)
    return bytes(b ^ data[0] for b in data[1:]).decode()


def company(slug):
    soup = BeautifulSoup(fetch(f"https://www.empresia.es/empresa/{slug}/"), "html.parser")
    box = soup.select_one("div.datos-ident")
    fields = {}
    for label in box.select("span.list-group-item-heading"):
        value = label.find_next_sibling("p", class_="list-group-item-text")
        if value:
            fields[label.get_text(strip=True)] = value
    purpose, _, cnae = fields["Objeto social"].get_text("\n", strip=True).partition("\nCNAE ")
    sales = fields["Ventas"].select_one("[title]")
    email = box.select_one("[data-cfemail]")
    return {
        "name": box.select_one("span.bolder").get_text(strip=True),
        "cif": fields["CIF"].get_text(strip=True),
        "cnae": cnae,
        "purpose": purpose,
        "capital": fields["Capital social"].get_text(strip=True),
        "sales_band": sales["title"] if sales else "",
        "employees": fields["Número empleados"].get_text(strip=True),
        "registry": fields["Registro"].get_text(strip=True),
        "email": decode_cfemail(email["data-cfemail"]) if email else "",
        "board": [(a.get_text(strip=True), a.find_next_sibling(string=True).strip())
                  for a in soup.select("#organigrama li a")],
    }

In a live run on Mercadona this returned the CIF, CNAE 4711, the sales band, 108,742 employees, the registry (Valencia), the decoded e-mail and 13 board members, from one request. Values Empresia shows as - (Mercadona's share capital, for example) come back as -, so clean them before loading the data anywhere.

Every new company, every day

The most useful part of Empresia for lead generation is the BORME by day. Each weekday the gazette publishes every incorporation, and Empresia lists them by act and province:

/borme/fecha/2026-11-13/acto/constitucion/provincia/barcelona/

Change constitucion to disolucion, ampliacion-de-capital, cambio-de-domicilio-social or nombramientos for other acts. On 13 November 2026 there were 41 act types across 34 provinces, and Barcelona alone had 71 new companies. Each row links to the announcement, which has a small table with the registry, start date, share capital, corporate purpose and registered address:

import csv

BASE = "https://www.empresia.es"


def new_companies(date, province):
    url = f"{BASE}/borme/fecha/{date}/acto/constitucion/provincia/{province}/"
    soup = BeautifulSoup(fetch(url), "html.parser")
    for row in soup.select("#contenido table tbody tr"):
        name = row.select_one("a.lk")
        event = row.select_one('a[href*="/evento/"]')
        yield name.get_text(strip=True), BASE + event["href"]


def announcement(url):
    soup = BeautifulSoup(fetch(url), "html.parser")
    cells = [td.get_text(" ", strip=True) for td in soup.select("div.eventonly table td")]
    return dict(zip(cells[::2], cells[1::2]))


with open("new_companies.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["company", "registry", "start", "capital", "purpose", "address"])
    for name, link in new_companies("2026-11-13", "barcelona"):
        d = announcement(link)
        writer.writerow([name, d.get("Registro"), d.get("Fecha inicio"), d.get("Capital"),
                         d.get("Objeto social"), d.get("Domicilio")])

That is one request for the list plus one per company: 72 credits for a full day of Barcelona incorporations. Run it on a schedule and you have a daily feed of companies that did not exist last week.

Search, and its ceiling

Search is /busqueda/?q=<text>&pagina=<n>. Results mix companies (EMPRESA), officers (DIRECTIVO) and trademarks (DISTINTIVO), and Empresia stops at 100 results: past the last page it quietly sends page 1 again, so compare the "Mostrando del X al Y" counter before trusting a page. For anything broader than a name, the BORME lists by province are the better entry point.

Skip the code

The same scraper is an open-source package with a CLI:

pip install empresia-scraper
export SCRAPEDO_TOKEN=<your_token>
empresia-scraper telefonica mercadona -f csv -o companies.csv
empresia-scraper --borme 2026-11-13 --province madrid --details -o new_companies.json

Source and tests: github.com/bugrahansss/empresia-scraper

Use the data responsibly

The data comes from public registers, but officers are real people and their names are personal data under the GDPR. Use it for legitimate purposes such as B2B research or KYC, keep only what you need, honour objection requests and respect Empresia's terms.

Run it at scale with Scrape.do

Every page is one plain Scrape.do call with a rotating IP: no proxy pool, no Cloudflare handling, no headless browser. 1,000 company reports cost 1,000 credits. Get 1000 free credits and start scraping with Scrape.do.

title: Why is my AWS bill so high when traffic is flat?
description:
An AWS bill that climbs while traffic stays flat usually has one of three causes: data nobody deletes keeps piling up, a discount has ended, or a new charge started on a set date. To see why your AWS bill is so high, compare the month before the climb with the latest one in Cost Explorer.

Compare two months in Cost Explorer

Open the free Compare view under Report parameters, pick two of the last 13 months and group by service. According to the cost comparison documentation, Compare shows the three biggest changes and names the reason for each: usage, discounts, or other charges and credits.

Usage rising by a similar amount every month points to data that only grows. If traffic is flat and AWS puts a jump down to discounts or credits, a Savings Plan or reservation has usually expired, or your credits have run out. Then filter to the growing service in the normal Cost Explorer view and group it by Usage type.

The chart for this part is in the original post.
A slow climb usually triggers no alert. According to the Cost Anomaly Detection FAQ, the default setup alerts only when an anomaly exceeds both 40% of expected spend and $100. A budget with a lower threshold warns sooner; see the post on AWS budget alerts.

S3 versions, ECR images and RDS storage

With versioning on, S3 keeps every version of a file as a separate, full object at the normal rate. Deleting a file frees nothing, because S3 only adds a delete marker. Incomplete multipart uploads grow the same way and are billed until someone completes or aborts them. S3 Storage Lens shows both in two free metrics, Noncurrent version bytes and Incomplete multipart upload bytes.

ECR, the container image registry, also fills up when every deploy pushes a new image. A lifecycle policy removes old images by count or age. Check it in the lifecycle policy preview first, as AWS advises, and keep enough recent images to roll back.

On RDS the disk grows. With storage autoscaling on, AWS enlarges it by itself when space runs low but never shrinks it, so you keep paying for the added gigabytes after the data is deleted. Manual RDS snapshots ignore the retention period and stay until you delete them.

CloudWatch logs never expire by default. I cover them, and EBS snapshots left behind by old scripts, in what I check in an AWS cost audit.

A lifecycle rule for S3

The rule below covers the whole bucket: it deletes versions that have been noncurrent for 30 days and aborts uploads older than 7 days. The put command replaces every existing rule on the bucket, so read the current rules first and copy any you want to keep into the file. If one of them keeps old versions longer than 30 days, leave this rule out: where rules overlap, S3 honours the shorter expiration. The commands are for AWS CLI v2.

aws s3api \
  get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration \
  --bucket my-bucket

Save the rule as lifecycle.json:

{
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ID": "cleanup",
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Filter": { "Prefix": "" },
      "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": {
        "NoncurrentDays": 30
      },
      "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": {
        "DaysAfterInitiation": 7
      }
    }
  ]
}

aws s3api \
  put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration \
  --bucket my-bucket \
  --lifecycle-configuration \
  file://lifecycle.json

Deleted versions cannot be recovered, so if you reach for old files months later, raise NoncurrentDays.

When a Savings Plan or reservation ends

Neither a Savings Plan nor a reservation renews itself. Once an RDS reservation ends, the database is billed at the on-demand rate. Before a Savings Plan ends, you can queue a new plan or click Renew Savings Plan. Turn on the expiry email under Manage alert subscriptions on the Savings Plans page.

Year three of RDS Extended Support

RDS adds an Extended Support charge for MySQL and PostgreSQL versions whose standard support has ended, and doubles it in year three. According to RDS pricing on 11 November 2026, a 2-vCPU database on MySQL 5.7 in Frankfurt (eu-central-1) paid about $178 a month for support alone, and since 1 March 2026 it has paid about $356. A Multi-AZ standby is charged too.

For PostgreSQL 11, year three began on 1 April 2026, and PostgreSQL 12 follows on 1 March 2027. The charge stops after an upgrade to a version with standard support. MySQL 8.0 has been in Extended Support since 1 August 2026, as I covered in the post on the MySQL 8.0 charge.

Old EBS snapshots cost less in the archive

The only snapshot left from a deleted server can go to the EBS snapshot archive. EBS pricing for Frankfurt on 11 November 2026 puts a snapshot holding 500 GB of data at $27 a month in the standard tier and $6.75 in the archive. One restore costs $16.20.

An archived snapshot must stay at least 90 days, or you pay for the remaining days. Restoring it takes up to 72 hours, and only then can you create a volume from it.

Never archive a daily, weekly or monthly snapshot of a disk that is still in use and has newer copies. The archive bills it at full size, while the standard tier barely gets cheaper because the newer copies share most of its blocks, so according to AWS guidelines the total cost usually rises.

What it means for a small team

Once a month, after the invoice arrives, run Compare on the last month and the one six months earlier. This week, check the two S3 metrics above in Storage Lens and add the lifecycle rule wherever they are not zero. Then check which engine versions your RDS databases run, when your Savings Plans and reservations end and whether the expiry emails are on.

If a database runs PostgreSQL 12, upgrade it before 1 March 2027: from that day RDS charges it the doubled Extended Support rate.

Originally published on codelevel.pl. Prices are net, for businesses. AWS, Hetzner and OVH are trademarks of their owners; CODELEVEL is not a partner, reseller or representative of any of them.

title: Building a touchscreen macro deck on an ESP32-P4 with LVGL 9.6
description:
I wanted a Stream Deck-style macro pad without paying for a Stream Deck, so I built one on a GUITION JC1060P470C. It is a 7-inch, 1024 x 600 capacitive touchscreen on an ESP32-P4. The project is called Tessera Deck. It is MIT licensed, it runs on Windows 10 and 11, and the panel UI is LVGL 9.6 on ESP-IDF 6.1.

This post covers the design choices behind the panel firmware and the host protocol, for anyone building something similar on an embedded display.

The cover image is a Blender render made from the CAD model of the desk console. I have no photo of a printed one yet. The panel screenshots below are not photos either: the native PC build of the real UI code drew them, and the agents screen uses sample data.

1. Build the UI for the PC first

The UI code compiles natively on the PC against the same LVGL sources as the firmware. A test feeds it touch input and renders 1024 x 600 frames.

A layout bug shows up in seconds, with no flashing and no cable. I can also make screenshots for the README without photographing a screen at an angle.

The catch is that the native build does not exercise the display driver, the touch controller or PSRAM limits. Those still need the board. I treat the native build as the place for UI logic and the board as the place for hardware surprises.

2. Keep the panel dumb

The panel only draws and reports touches. A small Python host on the PC owns the USB Serial/JTAG port, runs the actions and serves the editor on 127.0.0.1. The two talk over a line protocol at 115200 baud.

Each message is one UTF-8 line. The host sends text commands or one JSON object. The panel answers, and it also sends its own events as JSON lines. A key press looks like this, copied from the protocol page at v0.9.0:

{"type":"deck_event","id":N,"button":N,"label":"…","hold":true}

hold is only present for a long press. Everything else about what the key does lives on the PC. That means I can add an action without touching the firmware, and the firmware stays small.

There are limits to this design. The panel reads lines of up to 1,099 bytes and ignores a longer one, so the host sends a layout in 380-character chunks and an image in 160-byte chunks. A pressed key stays highlighted until the host answers, so without a host it flashes red at once. If the PC is off, the panel keeps the last layout on screen and the keys do nothing.

3. Update objects in place

A touchscreen punishes rebuilds. If a gauge value arrived and the grid were rebuilt while you press a key, your finger would be on a new object that never saw the press, so I update in place.

Now labels, colours and gauge values change on the existing LVGL objects. The grid is only rebuilt when the page or its layout changes. A key is never rebuilt under your finger.

The same idea covers widgets. The host sends a title, a second line and a progress value, and the panel draws every wide key the same way. A new widget is a new host-side feature and needs no new firmware.

4. Treat icons as a cache problem

Icons are the one thing that is too big to treat like text. The host sends each icon as RGBA with a CRC32 check, using these lines:

AD_IMG_BEGIN <id> <bytes> <crc32>
AD_IMG_DATA <offset> <hex>
AD_IMG_END

The panel only answers at the end: OK, INVALID or FULL. FULL means the cache cannot hold the image.

The cache is 8 MiB in PSRAM. When it needs room it drops the least recently used image that no key is showing. If the panel needs an image it no longer has, it sends {"type":"image","id":"im:…"} and the host sends it again. Animated icons arrive as frames with a duration each.

The CRC32 lets the panel answer INVALID for a corrupt image instead of showing it, and a corrupt icon is more annoying than a missing one.

5. Let the panel answer your AI agent

When Claude Code wants permission to run something, the question appears on the panel with Allow and Deny buttons. The agents screen also shows what Claude Code, Codex and ZCode are doing and in which project.

Setup adds hooks to ~/.claude/settings.json. It keeps your other hooks and makes a backup first. The hook waits up to 25 seconds for a touch. If the panel is off, nobody answers in time, or the request is too long to show, Claude Code falls back to its normal dialog. Tessera never allows anything on its own. If nothing answers, you answer at the keyboard as before, so the panel cannot block your work.

The screenshot below is drawn by the native PC build and uses sample data.

6. Plan the memory

The panel uses two partial draw buffers of 1024 x 240 pixels in PSRAM, one software draw unit and a 15 ms refresh period. The 6 x 3 key grid is placed by hand because the shape is fixed. Fonts are compressed. The icon cache takes its 8 MiB from the same PSRAM as the draw buffers.

What it does not do

  • It runs on Windows 10 and 11 only. The host is Python and the actions are Windows actions.
  • It supports one board. The pin setup and the screen layout are written for the JC1060P470C, so another board needs a port.
  • There are no physical keys. You lose the feel of a real button.
  • It is not code-signed. Windows SmartScreen may warn on first start. The release includes SHA256SUMS so you can compare the zip before you run it.
  • The agents and mixer screenshots show sample data, and the console images are renders.

In the release the panel has no network and speaks only to the host over USB. The editor and the control API listen on 127.0.0.1 only.

Links

  • Code and releases: github.com/catorendal-a11y/tessera-deck (v0.9.0)
  • Website: catorendal-a11y.github.io/tessera-deck

I would like feedback on the in-place updates and the icon cache. If you want to port it to another ESP32-P4 display, CONTRIBUTING.md says what it takes.

This post was written by an AI agent (Claude Code) from the Tessera repo, and every fact in it was checked against the code. Tessera itself was also built with help from Claude Code.

title: Crypto-shredding Agent Sessions: Deleting What Your Backups Remember
description:
Deleting data is one of the first things any compliance work asks of you. GDPR calls it storage limitation, ISO 27001 has a control just for it (8.10, information deletion), and most B2B contracts say some version of the same thing: data has an expiry date, and when a customer leaves, everything that belongs to them goes with them. Deleting their rows from the live database is the easy part. What I never had a good answer for was everything else, because if a customer is gone but their data is still sitting in thirty days of snapshots, there's no way to open a snapshot and take one tenant out of it, since the whole point of a backup is that nobody can change it.

The answer I ended up with is to stop trying to delete the data and make it unreadable instead, by destroying the key it was encrypted with. To check that it really works, I built a small demo for this post with two made-up tenants, acme and globex, took a real backup of their database and then deleted globex. When I restore that old backup now, every globex session comes back as bytes nobody can read, including the password one of their tools had read from a .env file, while acme's sessions are still there in clear. This post is how I got there, and the questions I had to answer along the way.

What the frameworks fixed

The same question came back when I started looking at agent sessions. Last month I wrote that the frameworks store every turn of a conversation, tool output included, and that giving us a way to delete it was their job. Since then part of that has moved. My fix for ADK's SQLite delete was merged on November 5, so when ADK deletes a session now its events go with it. On Genkit, a maintainer answered my issue that you can already delete through the store, but that they had no objection to an API for it, and since then two PRs that add Agent.DeleteSession have been waiting for review, one for JS and one for Go.

What caught my eye in those PRs is what they leave out on purpose. The author writes that "Retention/TTL isn't in here" and that "Traces, logs and streams live outside the store and aren't touched", and I think they're right to draw the line there, because a framework can only delete what's in its own store. How long your data lives, and the copies your infrastructure makes of it, were never something a framework could reach. So I owe last month's post a correction: deleting a session is the framework's job, and the frameworks are doing it, while retention and copies belong to whoever runs the infrastructure.

Where a deleted session still lives

If I follow a single agent session through a normal production setup on Postgres, the live table is only the first place it lands. Cloud SQL takes a daily backup of it, or, on Kubernetes, CloudNativePG ships base backups and the WAL archive to a bucket through Barman, and point-in-time recovery exists precisely so you can go back to a moment when that row was still there. Then there's the export somebody set up to BigQuery for analytics, and the dump a colleague took before a risky migration and forgot in a bucket. A DELETE reaches the first of these and none of the others, and some of them can't be modified even if you go looking for them.

Encrypt per tenant, then destroy the key

Crypto-shredding solves this by turning it around. If the content is never stored in clear, then every copy of the database, backups and dumps and exports included, only ever carries ciphertext. Each tenant gets its own key, everything they write is encrypted with it before it reaches Postgres, and when the tenant has to go I don't chase the copies at all: I destroy the key, and every copy becomes unreadable at the same moment, wherever it ended up.

The keys live in Cloud KMS, which never hands them out. Calling KMS for every single message would be slow and would cost money on every read, so I use envelope encryption. Each tenant has a data key (a DEK) that does the actual work locally with AES-256-GCM, and KMS only ever encrypts that data key. The wrapped DEK is stored in Postgres, right next to the data it protects:

CREATE TABLE tenant_deks (
    tenant_id   text  NOT NULL,
    month       date  NOT NULL,
    kms_version text  NOT NULL,
    wrapped_dek bytea NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, month)
);

That table ends up in the backups along with everything else, and that's fine, because a wrapped DEK is useless without the KMS key version that wrapped it. The backup holds the locked boxes and the locks, while the only thing that opens them is in a place the backup can't reach.

KMS wraps the data keys, Postgres holds them with the events, and the backups copy Postgres but never KMS.

Writing an event goes through a small wrapper around the session store (the full code is on GitHub):

store.go

func (s *Store) Append(ctx context.Context, e Event) error {
    month := monthOf(e.At)
    if err := s.ensurePartition(ctx, month); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    dek, err := s.dek(ctx, e.Tenant, month, true)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    ct, err := seal(dek, e.Content, eventAAD(e))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    _, err = s.db.Exec(ctx,
        `INSERT INTO session_events (tenant_id, session_id, seq, created_at, content)
         VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5)`,
        e.Tenant, e.Session, e.Seq, e.At, ct)
    return err
}

I do the encryption in the application rather than in the database, because with pgcrypto the key has to travel inside the SQL statement, and from there it ends up in the statement logs and in any error message Postgres decides to print. eventAAD passes the tenant, the session and the position of the event as associated data, so if someone copies an encrypted row into another tenant's session, it simply fails to decrypt.

The tenant, the session ID and the timestamps stay in clear, because I need them to partition the table and to find a session at all. A backup still tells you who talked to the agent and when, even if it can't tell you what they said, and I'd rather say that up front than let you discover it.

I wrote the encryption with the standard library's AES-GCM because I wanted the code in the post to be readable. In production I'd use Tink, which takes care of key formats and nonces for you and already knows how to talk to Cloud KMS.

Data that has to stay, and then go

Offboarding a whole tenant is the easy case, because you destroy every key they have and you're done. The question I had next is the one that comes up more often in practice: how do you handle data that has to be deleted after a certain time, but also must not be deleted before it, because an auditor, a contract or an incident investigation might still need it?

The answer turned out to be in how Cloud KMS handles keys. A key can have many versions, and every ciphertext remembers which version produced it, so instead of giving each tenant a single key I give each tenant one key with a new version every month. September's data key is wrapped by September's version and October's by October's, which means that when September falls out of retention I can destroy that one version and September becomes unreadable everywhere, backups included, while October is left alone.

One key version per month: expiring September means destroying one version.

I choose the version explicitly every time I wrap a key, rather than letting KMS rotate on a schedule. With automatic rotation, which version ends up wrapping a month depends on when the rotation happened to run, and destroying one version could take part of the following month down with it.

In the live database each month is its own Postgres partition, so expiring a month is a DROP TABLE instead of a huge DELETE that leaves the table full of dead rows for vacuum to deal with. The retention job destroys the key versions first and only then cleans up, because the versions are what reaches the backups, and the partition is just housekeeping:

retention.go

for _, r := range expired {
    if err := s.kms.Destroy(ctx, r.version); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
}
for _, m := range months {
    if _, err := s.db.Exec(ctx, fmt.Sprintf(`DROP TABLE IF EXISTS %s`, partitionName(m))); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if _, err := s.db.Exec(ctx, `DELETE FROM tenant_deks WHERE month = $1`, m); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
}

The other half of the rule, the "not before", I enforce through who is allowed to destroy anything. The application can create a tenant's key, add a version each month, and encrypt and decrypt with it, but it has no permission to destroy a version. Only the retention job has that, and the job refuses to touch a month that's still inside the window. This is the part I wanted in infrastructure as code, so here is the split as two custom roles in Pulumi:

infra/main.go

keyUser, err := projects.NewIAMCustomRole(ctx, "session-key-user", &projects.IAMCustomRoleArgs{
    RoleId: pulumi.String("sessionKeyUser"),
    Title:  pulumi.String("Session key user"),
    Permissions: pulumi.ToStringArray([]string{
        "cloudkms.cryptoKeys.create",
        "cloudkms.cryptoKeys.get",
        "cloudkms.cryptoKeyVersions.create",
        "cloudkms.cryptoKeyVersions.useToEncrypt",
        "cloudkms.cryptoKeyVersions.useToDecrypt",
    }),
})

shredder, err := projects.NewIAMCustomRole(ctx, "session-key-shredder", &projects.IAMCustomRoleArgs{
    RoleId: pulumi.String("sessionKeyShredder"),
    Title:  pulumi.String("Session key shredder"),
    Permissions: pulumi.ToStringArray([]string{
        "cloudkms.cryptoKeys.list",
        "cloudkms.cryptoKeyVersions.list",
        "cloudkms.cryptoKeyVersions.get",
        "cloudkms.cryptoKeyVersions.destroy",
    }),
})

Each role is bound on the key ring to its own service account, so a bug in the application, or someone holding the application's token, can't shred even a single month. The stack doesn't declare the tenants' keys themselves, since tenants come and go while the system is running and onboarding is what creates them. What I want the IaC to pin down is the rules those keys live under: who can do what to them, and where every operation gets logged.

Cloud KMS also adds a safety net of its own. When you destroy a version it doesn't disappear on the spot but goes into a "scheduled for destruction" state for a period you choose when you create the key, anywhere from 24 hours to 120 days and 30 days by default. During that period nobody can use the version, so the data is already unreadable, but you can still restore it, which means that if the retention job ever destroys the wrong month you have a few weeks to notice.

That safety net is also why, when someone asks me when their data is actually deleted, I give them more than one date. It stops being readable the moment the version is destroyed, the key is gone for good when the waiting period ends, and after that Google takes up to another 45 days to remove the key material from its own systems and backups, so a customer who asks for proof of deletion should get all three dates.

When is it deleted? It depends on which of the three dates you mean.

What if someone steals the key?

Once the design was on paper, this was the first thing I worried about, and the answer was not the one I expected. With KMS nobody can steal the key itself, because it never leaves KMS, not even for me. What an attacker can steal is the ability to use it, meaning the credentials of a service account that's allowed to call Decrypt, and with those they can decrypt everything, old months included, since the old versions have to stay usable for their data to stay readable.

So rotating the keys every month doesn't protect you here, even though it's tempting to think that a stolen key is only worth one month. The attacker didn't steal a version, they stole an identity that can use every version you haven't destroyed yet. What actually helps is less exciting: no exported service account keys lying around (Workload Identity instead), decrypt permission only where it's really needed, and the KMS data access logs turned on, so that every decrypt leaves a trace and a sudden spike is visible. The Pulumi stack in the repo turns those logs on.

Rotation still matters in this design, only for different reasons. It's what gives retention its granularity, and it limits the damage when a data key leaks, because the DEK does live in the application's memory, and if it ends up in a heap dump it opens one tenant's month and nothing more.

Why not keep the keys myself?

The next question was whether I could do all this without KMS and keep the keys myself. You can, but it helps to look at what a key store for crypto-shredding has to guarantee. It has to be durable, because losing a key by accident means you've deleted that tenant by accident. At the same time it can't have copies you don't control, because a key that ends up in a backup can never really be destroyed, and then shredding destroys nothing.

The most common way to get this wrong is to keep the keys in a table in the same Postgres. When you delete the tenant's key from the live database, the backup still has both the data and the key that opens it, and you've moved the problem without solving it. Vault running on your own infrastructure has the same tension one level down, because its storage needs backups too, and those backups hold the keys.

What KMS sells you is exactly that combination: a key that is durable and replicated, and a destruction with a documented timeline and an entry in an audit log. When a customer asks you to prove their data is gone, being able to say "we destroyed version 12 on November 3, and here is the log" is a much better answer than "we ran DELETE on the keys table". In my setup I manage every key except one: the data keys live wrapped in Postgres and can go wherever the backups go, while the one key that really has to die lives somewhere it can.

People often bring up Cloud SQL's customer-managed encryption keys at this point, so it's worth saying that CMEK solves a different problem. It encrypts the instance's disk with your key, which is a good idea, but the database decrypts transparently for anyone who can run a query, and destroying that key takes down the whole instance rather than one tenant. CMEK protects you from someone walking off with a disk, and it has nothing to say about deleting a customer.

What it costs

My first worry about performance was that decrypting every event on every read would be slow, and the benchmark put that to rest quickly. On my laptop, an Apple M5 Pro, encrypting a 4 KiB event takes about 1.2 µs and decrypting it about 1 µs, so somewhere around 3 to 4 GB/s, which is far less time than the query spent fetching the row.

The expensive part would be KMS, since every call is a network round trip with its own quota and price, and that's why the unwrapped data keys stay in memory for a few minutes. With that cache, reading a 50-event session costs one KMS call instead of fifty, and there's a test in the repo that checks exactly that. The cache has a cost of its own that I want to be upfront about: a process that already had a data key in memory can keep using it until the cache expires, even after the key version has been destroyed. Shredding takes effect within the cache TTL rather than instantly, and five minutes is an acceptable delay for most of us, as long as you know it's there.

Encryption also takes away some things you probably rely on. You can't filter, index or search on encrypted content, and Postgres can't compress it either, because ciphertext doesn't compress, so if size matters you have to compress before you encrypt. Each value also grows by 28 bytes of nonce and authentication tag.

The bill turned out to be what settled how fine-grained the keys should be. Cloud KMS charges $0.06 per active key version per month for software keys, plus $0.03 per 10,000 operations, so a tenant with twelve months of retention keeps twelve versions alive and costs 72 cents a month, and a thousand tenants cost $720. Last month I wrote that the most promising direction was one key per user, and running the same numbers on 100,000 users gives $72,000 a month. The cheaper version of per-user, with one data key per user wrapped by the tenant's key, doesn't work either: when you delete a user's wrapped key from the table it's still in the backups, next to the tenant key that opens it, which is the same key store problem from the previous section. For a B2B product the tenant is the right unit, and per-user keys make sense for consumer products or for a handful of users with unusually strict requirements.

What it doesn't reach

All of this protects what goes through the wrapper and nothing else. If a prompt gets logged in clear before it's encrypted, or ends up in a trace, destroying the key doesn't touch it, and the only fix is upstream, by logging a session_id instead of the content. Embeddings have the same problem in a harder form, because a vector is derived from the text and a good part of the text can be reconstructed from it, but once you encrypt it you can no longer search it, which was the reason to compute it in the first place.

Then there's the memory an agent builds about a user over time: the summaries, the facts it extracts, the notes it keeps across sessions. That's data about the tenant that no longer looks like the tenant's data, and I don't have a good answer for it yet. It's also where this series goes next, because what an agent remembers is only the first boundary, and the second one is what it sends out.

Try it

The code is on GitHub and runs on your machine with Docker, without a cloud account. A local stand-in for KMS keeps its keys in a file of its own (never in the database), and -kms gcp switches to the real Cloud KMS. The demo writes sessions for two tenants, takes a real pg_dump, offboards one tenant, expires a month, restores the old backup and shows you what's left, and the Pulumi stack for the GCP side is in infra/.

If you've found a way to make an agent's long-term memory forgettable per tenant, I'd really like to hear how you did it.

This post was first published on davideimola.dev. If you want the next one in your inbox, subscribe to the newsletter.

title: Why Ctrl+P Truncates ChatGPT & Claude Threads — Purifying SPA DOMs into Crisp Vector PDFs
description:
Try opening a 20-turn architecture or debugging conversation in ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, or DeepSeek right now and pressing Cmd+P (Ctrl+P) to save a PDF reference for your team wiki or tablet.

Three things almost always go catastrophically wrong:

  1. Only Page 1 Prints (The 100vh Flex Scroll Trap): Everything above or below the current viewport disappears because modern single-page chat apps lock html, body to height: 100vh; overflow: hidden and scroll an inner flex: 1; overflow-y: auto container. Browser print engines paginate the root document viewport—not nested scrollboxes!
  2. Code Blocks & Tables Get Sliced Horizontally: <pre><code> blocks styled with overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre clip the right 40% of your SQL queries or TypeScript types, and page breaks slice single lines of code vertically in half.
  3. Dark Mode Torches Printer Toner: Terminal dark slate backgrounds (#0f172a), sticky composer drawers, sidebar thread histories, and low-contrast #94a3b8 text produce muddy, ink-soaked pages.

Many existing "ChatGPT to PDF" tools work around this by rasterizing the DOM onto an HTML5 <canvas> (html2canvas) and wrapping giant PNG screenshots inside a PDF container—resulting in 25 MB files where you cannot Cmd+F search or copy-paste a single line of code, or worse, requiring terrifying <all_urls> "Read and change all your data on all websites" permissions.

We built and open-sourced CleanPrint & AI-Chat to PDF Studio (live on Mozilla Firefox Add-ons and unpacked for Chrome/Edge/Brave) to produce true 80 KB selectable vector PDFs in <50ms locally. Here is how the DOM purification and @media print architecture works under the hood.

1. Escaping the 100vh Scroll Container Trap Non-Destructively

If you try to mutate ChatGPT or Claude's live React/Next.js Fiber tree in-place—stripping overflow: hidden and deleting sidebar nodes—two bad things happen: CSS specificity wars with Tailwind utility classes break layout unpredictably, and the moment React reconciles state, your mutated DOM crashes with hydration/removeChild errors when the user returns to their chat.

Instead, CleanPrint treats the live SPA DOM as read-only input, extracts a clean semantic AST, mounts an isolated sibling root (#cleanprint-studio-root) directly under document.body, and hides sibling app shells purely via a reversible root class:

html.cleanprint-studio-active,
html.cleanprint-studio-active body {
  background: #e2e8f0 !important;
  height: auto !important;
  overflow: visible !important;
  margin: 0 !important;
  padding: 0 !important;
}

html.cleanprint-studio-active body > *:not(#cleanprint-studio-root) {
  display: none !important;
}

Why is body > *:not(#cleanprint-studio-root) { display: none !important; } so effective?

  • Every nested 100vh React wrapper (#__next, main, sticky navbars, composer inputs) stays completely intact in memory—preserving scroll position, React event listeners, and streaming state.
  • #cleanprint-studio-root sits in normal document block flow with height: auto, allowing Blink, Gecko, and WebKit's native print pagination engine to lay out 1 to 100+ vector pages effortlessly.
  • Clicking Restore Original Web View simply removes html.cleanprint-studio-active and unmounts #cleanprint-studio-root, restoring window.scrollTo(0, savedScrollY) with zero page reload.

2. Multi-Platform AI Turn Extraction + Density Fallback

Different LLM interfaces mark up conversation turns differently, and those selectors evolve. In src/purifier.js, our parser cascades through three tiers before falling back to an article link-density scorer (for GitHub READMEs, MDN docs, and engineering blogs):

// Tier 1: OpenAI / ChatGPT semantic author role attributes
var roleNodes = doc.querySelectorAll('[data-message-author-role]');

// Tier 2: Claude, Copilot & Gemini custom elements / test IDs
var combinedTurnNodes = doc.querySelectorAll(
  '[data-testid="user-message"], .font-claude-message, ' +
  '[data-content="user-message"], [data-content="ai-message"], ' +
  'user-query, model-response, .copilot-chat-message'
);

// Tier 3: Generic turn wrappers & link-density article root fallback

Inside each turn, a recursive walker normalizes headings (h1–h6), inline formatting runs (code, strong, em, resolved a[href]), Markdown tables, blockquotes, lists, and fenced <pre><code> blocks—automatically detecting the programming language either from language-* classes or adjacent header pills (sql, python, typescript) while ignoring UI buttons like "Copy" or "Edit".

3. Passing Mozilla AMO Security Review: Zero innerHTML & Least-Privilege MV3

If you have ever submitted an extension to Mozilla Add-ons (AMO), you know their automated linter and human security reviewers strictly flag any assignment to .innerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, or outerHTML inside privileged scripts due to DOM XSS risks when parsing untrusted web pages.

CleanPrint contains zero .innerHTML calls across the entire codebase (enforced automatically by our build script before running syntax checks in JavaScriptCore). Every purified card, table cell, inline code badge, and multi-tab Table of Contents entry is constructed through a tiny 25-line hyperscript helper using document.createElement and textContent:

function el(tag, attrs, children) {
  var node = document.createElement(tag);
  if (attrs) {
    Object.keys(attrs).forEach(function (k) {
      if (k === 'className') node.className = attrs[k];
      else if (k === 'textContent') node.textContent = attrs[k];
      else if (k.indexOf('on') === 0 && typeof attrs[k] === 'function') {
        node.addEventListener(k.slice(2).toLowerCase(), attrs[k]);
      } else if (attrs[k] != null) {
        node.setAttribute(k, String(attrs[k]));
      }
    });
  }
  (children || []).forEach(function (ch) {
    if (ch == null) return;
    node.appendChild(typeof ch === 'string' ? document.createTextNode(ch) : ch);
  });
  return node;
}

Equally important is Manifest V3 permission hygiene. CleanPrint requests strictly:

"permissions": ["activeTab", "scripting", "storage"]

No <all_urls>. No persistent content scripts slowing down every page load. purifier.js is injected strictly on-demand via scripting.executeScript when—and only when—you click the toolbar icon. For cross-browser compatibility between Chromium (service_worker) and Firefox MV3 (background.scripts + browser_specific_settings.gecko with data_collection_permissions.required: ["none"]), we maintain clean target manifests sharing 100% of the runtime JS.

4. Print-Media CSS That Never Cuts Off Code Blocks or Wastes Toner

To ensure exported PDFs read like typeset technical handouts rather than broken web dumps, our print stylesheet combines four rules:

/* 1. Wrap long code lines cleanly instead of clipping horizontally */
#cleanprint-studio-root .cp-pre {
  white-space: pre-wrap;
  word-break: break-word;
  overflow-x: visible;
  line-height: 1.5;
}

/* 2. Keep code blocks, tables, figures & headings anchored across page breaks */
#cleanprint-studio-root .cp-heading,
#cleanprint-studio-root .cp-qa-header {
  break-after: avoid;
  page-break-after: avoid;
}

#cleanprint-studio-root .cp-avoid-break,
#cleanprint-studio-root pre,
#cleanprint-studio-root table {
  break-inside: avoid;
  page-break-inside: avoid;
}

/* 3. Eco Low-Ink Mode: strip dark terminal fills into crisp monochrome hairlines */
#cleanprint-studio-root.cp-low-ink .cp-code-block {
  background: #ffffff !important;
  color: #0f172a !important;
  border: 1.25px solid #334155 !important;
}

Toggling Eco Low-Ink Mode replaces solid #1e293b code backgrounds and tinted prompt cards with pure #ffffff paper fills and sharp #334155 borders—cutting black toner/ink usage by roughly 65%–75% on code-heavy LLM threads while boosting laser-print legibility.

Install or Inspect the Source (MIT Licensed)

  • 🦊 Firefox Official Add-on (1-Click Install): CleanPrint & AI-Chat to PDF Studio on Mozilla Add-ons
  • 📦 Chrome / Edge / Brave Release .zip & MIT Source: github.com/963239327/cleanprint-ai-chat-to-pdf
  • 👀 Interactive Web Preview: Try CleanPrint Formatting in Browser
  • 📚 CleanPrint Pro ($5.99 Lifetime Offline Key): Unlocks our Multi-Tab Print Queue Binder (combine 10+ ChatGPT threads & docs into one research PDF with an auto-generated Table of Contents), Academic Serif / 2-Column Study / 2-Up Booklet themes, and marginless URL header removal via Gumroad.

Happy printing—and may your <pre><code> blocks never get chopped at column 80 again!

title: Estimating Proxy Bandwidth for Public Data Collection in Kazakhstan with Python
description:
Collecting public data responsibly is not only a question of writing faster code. Before increasing concurrency, you need to estimate the traffic volume, the available time window, retry overhead, and the throughput your workload can actually sustain.

This guide builds a small Python model for that calculation. It is intended only for requests you are authorized to make. Respect applicable law, the target website's terms, robots directives, and rate limits.

1. Start with the theoretical minimum

For decimal terabytes, the average throughput required to transfer a given volume is:

required_Mbps = traffic_TB × 8,000,000 ÷ seconds
seconds = days × 86,400

For example, moving 100 TB evenly over 30 days requires:

100 × 8,000,000 ÷ 2,592,000 = 308.6 Mbps

That is only the theoretical average. It assumes continuous transfer, no retries, no pauses, and no protocol overhead.

2. Add utilization and retry overhead

A practical estimate should reserve capacity for variable latency, connection setup, retries, and quiet periods. The function below makes those assumptions explicit.

from dataclasses import dataclass

SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86_400
BITS_PER_TERABYTE = 8_000_000  # Mbps-seconds in one decimal TB


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BandwidthEstimate:
    theoretical_mbps: float
    planned_mbps: float


def estimate_bandwidth(
    traffic_tb: float,
    days: int,
    utilization: float = 0.70,
    retry_fraction: float = 0.10,
) -> BandwidthEstimate:
    if traffic_tb <= 0:
        raise ValueError("traffic_tb must be positive")
    if days <= 0:
        raise ValueError("days must be positive")
    if not 0 < utilization <= 1:
        raise ValueError("utilization must be between 0 and 1")
    if retry_fraction < 0:
        raise ValueError("retry_fraction cannot be negative")

    seconds = days * SECONDS_PER_DAY
    theoretical = traffic_tb * BITS_PER_TERABYTE / seconds
    planned = theoretical * (1 + retry_fraction) / utilization

    return BandwidthEstimate(
        theoretical_mbps=round(theoretical, 1),
        planned_mbps=round(planned, 1),
    )


estimate = estimate_bandwidth(traffic_tb=100, days=30)
print(estimate)

With 70% utilization and 10% retry overhead, the result is approximately:

BandwidthEstimate(theoretical_mbps=308.6, planned_mbps=485.0)

The gap between 308.6 Mbps and 485.0 Mbps is not wasted bandwidth. It is operational headroom for a workload that does not run perfectly every second of the month.

3. Compare the result with standard throughput levels

The following table shows the maximum theoretical transfer volume when a connection runs continuously at the listed rate.

Throughput 1 day 7 days 30 days
100 Mbps 1.08 TB 7.56 TB 32.4 TB
200 Mbps 2.16 TB 15.12 TB 64.8 TB
400 Mbps 4.32 TB 30.24 TB 129.6 TB
600 Mbps 6.48 TB 45.36 TB 194.4 TB
800 Mbps 8.64 TB 60.48 TB 259.2 TB
1 Gbps 10.8 TB 75.6 TB 324 TB

For the 100 TB example, 400 Mbps covers the theoretical average but leaves limited room for retries and idle periods. A 600 Mbps tier provides more practical headroom under the assumptions above.

4. Measure latency instead of guessing

A bandwidth plan alone does not guarantee application throughput. Measure representative endpoints before selecting concurrency.

import statistics
import time
import requests


def measure_latency(url: str, samples: int = 20) -> dict[str, float]:
    durations = []

    for _ in range(samples):
        started = time.perf_counter()
        response = requests.get(url, timeout=15)
        response.raise_for_status()
        durations.append((time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000)
        time.sleep(0.5)

    ordered = sorted(durations)
    p95_index = max(0, int(len(ordered) * 0.95) - 1)

    return {
        "p50_ms": round(statistics.median(ordered), 1),
        "p95_ms": round(ordered[p95_index], 1),
        "mean_ms": round(statistics.mean(ordered), 1),
    }

Use an endpoint you control or have permission to test. Do not benchmark a third-party website aggressively.

P95 latency is especially useful because the slowest requests often determine how much concurrency is needed. If P95 rises sharply as concurrency increases, adding more workers may reduce reliability instead of increasing useful throughput.

5. Treat 429 and 403 responses as control signals

A high rate of HTTP 429 or 403 responses is not a reason to push harder. Reduce concurrency, apply bounded exponential backoff, and verify that the collection is permitted.

import random
import time


def backoff_seconds(attempt: int, cap: float = 30.0) -> float:
    base = min(cap, 2 ** attempt)
    return base + random.uniform(0, base * 0.2)

Set a retry limit. Record status codes and failure reasons. A successful collection pipeline optimizes valid responses, not raw request volume.

6. Consider Kazakhstan-specific network conditions

For workloads operated from or targeting services in Kazakhstan, test from the actual deployment region. International routing, time-of-day congestion, target hosting location, and regional availability can change both P50 and P95 latency.

A useful capacity test should therefore include:

  • the same cloud region or server location used in production;
  • representative response sizes;
  • realistic concurrency;
  • separate measurements during peak and off-peak hours;
  • an explicit retry and timeout policy;
  • logs for 429, 403, 5xx, DNS, and connection failures.

Do not choose a throughput tier from theoretical volume alone. Combine the formula with real latency and success-rate measurements.

7. Reusable planning checklist

  1. Estimate the project's total authorized traffic volume.
  2. Convert the available duration to seconds.
  3. Calculate the theoretical average Mbps.
  4. Add retry overhead and a realistic utilization factor.
  5. Measure P50 and P95 latency from the production region.
  6. Run a small controlled test before scaling concurrency.
  7. Stop or slow down when the target signals rate limiting.
  8. Review the target's terms and data-handling requirements.

For quick scenario testing, use the interactive residential proxy bandwidth calculator. A Kazakhstan-focused reference in Kazakh also summarizes the available throughput levels and durations.

The important distinction is simple: a plan with no data cap still has a throughput rate. Capacity planning determines whether that rate fits the workload within the available time window.

title: copilot-setup-steps.yml: the rules, runners and limits
description:
copilot-setup-steps.yml is a workflow at .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml with one job, named copilot-setup-steps, whose steps GitHub runs before Copilot cloud agent starts work, so the agent begins with your toolchain and dependencies installed. It applies only to sessions that run on GitHub Actions, and GitHub honors only six keys of that job.


What happens between assigning a task and Copilot's first edit. The setup job only exists on the Actions path.

GitHub's documentation now calls the Copilot coding agent Copilot cloud agent, and the setup steps file is now one of three places a session can get its environment from. That is the first thing to check when setup steps seem to be ignored: the file can be fine while the session never ran on Actions.

Where Copilot fits beside other agents is on CI for Cursor and Copilot coding agents. Here it is only the file: what GitHub runs, in what order, on which runners, with which secrets, and what it ignores.

First, check the session runs on Actions

GitHub now runs a Copilot session in one of two hosted environments. Cloud is a sandbox GitHub hosts; Actions is a GitHub Actions job on a GitHub-hosted runner or one you configure. Where a client lets you choose, Cloud is the default, the choice is made when the session starts and cannot be changed afterwards, and a different environment means a new session.

Setup steps, larger runners, self-hosted runners and the Windows environment all exist only on the Actions path. So do Agents variables: in a cloud sandbox only Agents secrets are available. If your repository depends on any of these, choose Actions when you delegate the task, or the agent starts in a sandbox that never read your file. A third option, a custom environment, registers a Linux machine or codespace you manage yourself.

The rules for the file

The path is fixed and the job name is the mechanism: GitHub's own example carries the comment that the job MUST be called copilot-setup-steps or it will not be picked up. The file also has to be on the default branch before it triggers at all, so a branch that adds it changes nothing until it merges.

Only six job keys count: steps, permissions, runs-on, services, snapshot and timeout-minutes, the last capped at 59. Anything else is ignored rather than rejected. A fetch-depth on actions/checkout is overridden so the agent can roll back commits, and if you do not check out the code at all, Copilot clones it after your steps finish. Give the job contents: read only if a step clones; Copilot gets its own token for its own work.

The push and pull_request path filters are what make the file testable: a pull request that edits it runs it as an ordinary check, and once merged you can run it from the Actions tab.

name: Copilot Setup Steps
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
jobs:
  # The job MUST be called `copilot-setup-steps` or it will not be picked up by Copilot.
  copilot-setup-steps:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    permissions:
      contents: read
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
        with:
          node-version: "22"
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci

What happens when a step fails

This is the behavior that surprises people most, because nothing goes red. GitHub documents that if any setup step returns a non-zero exit code, Copilot skips the remaining setup steps and begins working with the environment in whatever state it reached. The session continues; the agent just has less than you meant to give it, and it falls back to discovering dependencies by trial and error, which GitHub's own documentation calls slow and unreliable.

Two habits follow. Order the steps so the one that matters most, usually the dependency install, comes first after checkout and toolchain setup, rather than after an optional cache warm-up. And treat the file's own pull_request run as its test: a failure there is visible as a check, whereas a failure inside a session only shows up in the session logs.

Secrets are Agents secrets, not Actions secrets

Copilot cloud agent does not receive Actions, Codespaces or Dependabot secrets. It has its own type, Agents secrets and variables, set at repository or organization level under Settings, Secrets and variables, Agents. On the Actions path they are exposed as environment variables, including to the steps in copilot-setup-steps.yml; names prefixed COPILOT_MCP_ go only to MCP servers. Secrets you once put in a repository's copilot environment were migrated to the repository-level Agents type automatically.

Because they arrive as environment variables, a private registry needs no secrets. expression in the workflow. An .npmrc that reads the token from the environment is enough for npm ci in the setup steps and for every install the agent runs afterwards.

# .npmrc, committed; NPM_TOKEN is an Agents secret
@your-org:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com
//npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}

Runners: larger, self-hosted and Windows

runs-on moves the agent off the default ubuntu-latest, and each destination comes with conditions. Copilot cloud agent is only compatible with Ubuntu x64 and Windows 64-bit runners; macOS is not supported anywhere. Organization owners can also set a default runner type and switch off repository overrides, in which case your runs-on has no effect.

Runner What GitHub requires Example runs-on
Larger GitHub-hosted Larger runners set up for the organization; with Azure private networking, outbound access to the Copilot hosts ubuntu-4-core
Self-hosted Ephemeral single-use runners recommended (ARC or the Runner Scale Set Client); integrated firewall disabled, or the agent is blocked; your own network controls your ARC scale set name
Windows Self-hosted or larger runners; the integrated firewall is not compatible with Windows your Windows runner label

The hosts a self-hosted or privately networked runner must reach, besides the standard Actions hosts, are uploads.github.com, user-images.githubusercontent.com, and whichever of api.individual.githubcopilot.com, api.business.githubcopilot.com and api.enterprise.githubcopilot.com match the Copilot plans in use, per the GitHub Docs page read on 2026-11-12.

services and snapshot

services works as it does in any job, which is the cleanest way to give the agent a real database or cache to run integration tests against instead of letting it mock one. snapshot is the less obvious key: in workflow syntax it generates a custom image, with each successful run of a job carrying it producing a new image version. It belongs to GitHub's custom images feature for larger runners, so read that documentation before relying on it here.

The same file also configures Copilot code review's environment, which reuses copilot-setup-steps.yml unless you add a separate copilot-code-review.yml. Split them when review needs less than the agent does.

```.github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml, a larger runner with Git LFS
jobs:
copilot-setup-steps:
runs-on: ubuntu-4-core
timeout-minutes: 45
permissions:
contents: read
steps:
- uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
with:
lfs: true




## Where these rules come from

GitHub's Copilot documentation, read on 2026-11-12, and nothing else: the environment pages, the secrets and variables page, the organization runner page and the workflow syntax reference listed below. No recorded run backs this page, and neither evidence file in this repository has an entry for it. A session's setup log belongs to one repository and one Copilot plan, so the rules are quoted from the pages that define them rather than inferred from a log.

## FAQ

### Why is my copilot-setup-steps.yml not being used?

Three causes cover nearly every case. The file is not on the default branch yet, the job is not named exactly `copilot-setup-steps`, or the session ran in a cloud sandbox, where setup steps do not apply. Check the session logs: when the setup job runs, its steps appear there.

### Can Copilot coding agent use self-hosted runners?

Yes, through `runs-on` in the setup steps file, on Ubuntu x64 or Windows 64-bit runners. GitHub recommends ephemeral single-use runners, requires you to disable the integrated firewall for self-hosted use, and asks you to allow the Copilot API hosts through your own network controls.

### How do I give Copilot coding agent access to secrets?

Add them as Agents secrets, at repository or organization level. They reach the agent as environment variables, including inside `copilot-setup-steps.yml`, while names starting with `COPILOT_MCP_` are passed only to MCP servers. Actions secrets are not passed to the agent.

### What is the maximum timeout for copilot-setup-steps?

59 minutes. `timeout-minutes` is one of the six keys GitHub honors on the `copilot-setup-steps` job, and the documentation gives 59 as its maximum value.

## References

- [GitHub Docs: configure the development environment for agents on GitHub Actions (read 2026-11-12)](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/customize-copilot/customize-cloud-agent/customize-the-agent-environment)
- [GitHub Docs: about cloud sandboxes, choosing where Copilot runs](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/about-cloud-sandboxes)
- [GitHub Docs: configure secrets and variables for Copilot cloud agent](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/customize-copilot/customize-cloud-agent/configure-secrets-and-variables)
- [GitHub Docs: configuring runners for Copilot cloud agent in your organization](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/administer-copilot/manage-for-organization/configure-runner-for-coding-agent)
- [GitHub Docs: workflow syntax, jobs.<job_id>.snapshot](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax)

title: Measuring PR Cognitive Load with Deterministic Python AST Heuristics
description:
AI-assisted code generation is not inherently a software defect—most engineering teams rely on coding assistants daily to accelerate boilerplate, test scaffolding, and migrations.

The real architectural bottleneck is review throughput versus generation velocity. When pull requests grow from 150 lines to 1,200+ lines, human reviewers hit cognitive fatigue. Two failure modes tend to slip past fatigued code reviews:

  1. Loss of Cognitive Ownership: Deeply nested control flow, redundant defensive wrappers, or silent exception swallowing (except Exception: pass) that compile cleanly and pass happy-path tests while obscuring failure states.
  2. Unverified Dependency Surface: Unfamiliar or hallucinated package imports introduced during rapid iteration without supply-chain verification.

Rather than relying on probabilistic "AI text detectors" (which are noisy and largely irrelevant to production reliability), teams get far higher signal from deterministic AST heuristics wired directly into PR triage.

Minimal AST Heuristics in Pure Python (stdlib)

Using Python's built-in ast module, we can flag review-friction hotspots in milliseconds before a human reviewer even opens the diff:

import ast

class ReviewFrictionVisitor(ast.NodeVisitor):
    def __init__(self):
        self.max_depth = 0
        self._depth = 0
        self.silent_broad_excepts = 0

    def _enter_branch(self, node):
        self._depth += 1
        self.max_depth = max(self.max_depth, self._depth)
        self.generic_visit(node)
        self._depth -= 1

    visit_If = visit_For = visit_While = _enter_branch
    visit_Try = _enter_branch

    def visit_ExceptHandler(self, node):
        is_broad = node.type is None or (
            isinstance(node.type, ast.Name) and node.type.id == "Exception"
        )
        if is_broad and len(node.body) == 1 and isinstance(node.body[0], ast.Pass):
            self.silent_broad_excepts += 1
        self.generic_visit(node)

Why Deterministic Structural Signals Beat Authorship Guessing

For Engineering Leads, CISOs, and Staff Reviewers, who (or what) typed a function matters much less than how expensive it will be to debug at 3 AM:

  • Control-flow nesting depth > 5 correlates strongly with missed edge cases during code review.
  • Silent broad except blocks mask upstream timeouts and schema drift.
  • Dependency delta gates force explicit justification whenever a PR adds a package outside the organization's verified lockfile baseline.

I put together a small zero-dependency reference snippet here if you want to experiment with custom AST checks in CI: evan-mercer-dev/ast-review-signals.

How is your team adapting PR review gates as commit volume scales up? Curious what deterministic checks have given you the highest signal-to-noise ratio.

title: I Couldn't Find a Spring Boot 4 ELK Tutorial, So I Wrote One
description:
Most ELK + Spring Boot tutorials I found had one of these problems:

  • Built for older Spring Boot versions
  • Missing Elasticsearch security setup
  • Ignored Logstash authentication
  • Didn't cover Zipkin integration
  • Broke the moment TLS certificates entered the picture

I wasn't looking for a fancy setup.

I just wanted this:

Request
   ↓
Spring Boot Microservice
   ↓
Structured Logs
   ↓
Logstash
   ↓
Elasticsearch
   ↓
Kibana

And...

Request
   ↓
Trace ID
   ↓
Zipkin

Simple.

Reality was... not simple.

The Rabbit Hole 🕳️

While building my E-Commerce Microservices Project, I ran into:

  • Elasticsearch security configuration
  • Enrollment tokens
  • Logstash authentication failures
  • SSL/TLS certificate headaches
  • Spring Boot 4 compatibility issues
  • Missing trace correlation between logs and traces
  • Reactive Gateway logging challenges

I spent hours debugging issues that most tutorials completely skipped.

Instead of keeping scattered notes, I decided to document the entire process from start to finish.

What You'll Learn

✅ ELK Stack Setup with Docker

✅ Elasticsearch 9.x Security Configuration

✅ Kibana Integration

✅ Logstash Pipelines

✅ Structured JSON Logging with Logback

✅ Zipkin Distributed Tracing

✅ TraceId Correlation Between Kibana and Zipkin

✅ Troubleshooting Real Errors

✅ Spring Boot 4.1.1 + Spring Cloud Gateway Setup

Why I Wrote This

I wanted a guide that explained what actually goes wrong and how to fix it, not just a happy-path tutorial.

So this article contains:

  • Real screenshots
  • Real configuration files
  • Real Docker setup
  • Real errors
  • Real fixes

Everything comes from a working implementation, not a toy project.

Architecture 

Client
  ↓
API Gateway
  ↓
Microservices
  ↓
JSON Logs
  ↓
Logstash
  ↓
Elasticsearch
  ↓
Kibana

Trace IDs
  ↓
Zipkin

The result is a complete observability workflow where you can:

  1. Find an error in Kibana
  2. Copy the Trace ID
  3. Open Zipkin
  4. View the full distributed request journey

The Full Guide

👉 Read the complete walkthrough on Medium:

🔗 https://medium.com/@ashaw8176/elk-stack-with-zipkin-in-a-spring-boot-4-microservices-project-a-docker-setup-guide-for-2026-4cc94ecc5993

If you're learning:

  • Spring Boot
  • Microservices
  • Docker
  • ELK Stack
  • Observability
  • Distributed Tracing

I'd love to hear your feedback and experiences.

Happy debugging! 🚀

Built while working on my E-Commerce Microservices project and learning production-style observability one bug at a time.

title: Analysing UK Retail Sales and Profitability Using Python and SQL
description:
Tags: #dataanalytics #python #sql #datascience

Revenue tells us how much a business sells. Profit tells us how much value it keeps.

Understanding the difference is an important part of business data analysis.

I explored this through my UK Retail Sales Performance Analysis project.

Project Overview

The project analyses 2,500 synthetic UK retail transactions from 2025.

The dataset covers five regions, four product categories and two sales channels.

My objective was to practise transforming transaction records into meaningful business metrics.

Analytical Workflow

The workflow includes:

  1. Importing raw transaction data.
  2. Checking missing values and duplicates.
  3. Standardising inconsistent fields.
  4. Calculating revenue and profitability metrics.
  5. Running SQL queries.
  6. Creating visualisations.
  7. Interpreting business results.

The raw dataset intentionally contains minor data-quality issues to demonstrate cleaning techniques.

Key Results

The repository reports:

KPI Result
Total revenue £320,707
Total profit £116,331
Profit margin 36.3%
Return rate 9.2%
Top revenue region Midlands
Top profit category Electronics

These are results from simulated transactions, not real UK retail market statistics.

Example SQL Query

One of the included queries calculates regional revenue:

SELECT
    region,
    ROUND(SUM(revenue_gbp), 2) AS revenue
FROM retail_sales
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

This produces a ranked view of revenue contributions by region.

Turning Analysis into Decisions

The analysis raises several business questions.

Should management investigate why the Midlands performs strongly?

Are high-revenue products also generating strong profits?

Do discounts improve sales volume at the expense of profitability?

Could high return rates reduce the value of certain product categories?

The synthetic dataset cannot establish real-world answers, but it provides a useful environment for practising analytical reasoning.

Future Improvements

I would like to extend this project with Power BI, customer segmentation, forecasting and automated reporting.

Conclusion

This project helped me connect Python and SQL analysis with business decision-making.

The most useful takeaway was that revenue, profit, returns and discounts need to be examined together.

GitHub: https://github.com/tasnem-tech/uk-retail-sales-analysis

title: Build a Weekly Lead Quality Dashboard from CRM Data
description:
A weekly lead quality dashboard should show accepted enquiries, qualified enquiries, disqualifications and pending reviews by campaign. Pair the qualification rate with its denominator and the amount of work still pending. This makes campaign comparisons easier to interpret.

A manager sees that one campaign has a 75% qualification rate and another has 45%. The first had four reviewed enquiries. The second had twenty. Both figures describe real observations, but they carry different amounts of evidence and may be affected by how quickly sales reviewed each cohort.

Pick one cohort and define each count

Group enquiries by acceptance date in an explicit timezone. Include records accepted during that week and evaluate their current status at a recorded cutoff time. Each enquiry should be counted once, using its stable ID.

For the example below, reviewed enquiries are those with a qualified or disqualified decision. A pending enquiry is still awaiting a decision. Confirmed spam can be tracked as a disqualification reason or a separate bucket, depending on where review happens. State your policy and apply it consistently.

Metric Calculation
Review coverage Reviewed enquiries ÷ accepted enquiries
Qualification rate among reviewed Qualified enquiries ÷ reviewed enquiries
Qualified share of accepted Qualified enquiries ÷ accepted enquiries
Pending review Accepted enquiries − reviewed enquiries

Show a dash when a denominator is zero. A campaign with no reviewed records has no observed qualification rate yet.

Worked example with three campaigns

Campaign Accepted Qualified Disqualified Pending Qualification among reviewed Review coverage
Paid search 30 9 11 10 45% (9/20) 67% (20/30)
Partner email 5 3 1 1 75% (3/4) 80% (4/5)
Unknown 8 2 2 4 50% (2/4) 50% (4/8)
Total 43 14 14 15 50% (14/28) 65% (28/43)

The partner campaign has a higher observed rate across a small set. Paid search already has nine qualified enquiries and ten still pending. A practical next step is to finish reviewing the oldest pending enquiries and inspect the most frequent reasons among the eleven paid-search disqualifications.

Compute the total rate using total qualified divided by total reviewed. Averaging the three campaign percentages would give equal weight to campaigns with very different review volumes.

Add fields that explain the weekly numbers

Show the most common disqualification reasons, oldest pending age and the share of enquiries with unknown attribution. Use those fields to choose the next investigation. For instance, a rise in unsupported requests can prompt a landing page review, while a rise in unknown attribution can prompt a check of form payloads and CRM mapping.

Keep recent weeks visible as provisional until they reach your agreed review cutoff. If a week's figures can change when sales updates a record, either preserve snapshots or label the report with its calculation time.

What should the weekly review produce?

Record one action, an owner and a date for each recurring issue. An example is “Review the five unsupported service requests from paid search, compare them with ad copy, and update the landing page by Friday.” Then check whether the next comparable cohort shows a change in the same reason.

Before sharing the dashboard, verify that the status counts add up, duplicate submissions are excluded according to policy, and campaign totals match the underlying enquiry records. A dashboard earns its place when people can trace the numbers and agree on what to do next.
