title: I Tested My SMS Parser Against 200 Real-World Edge Cases — Here's What I Found
description:
Writing a regular expression to parse a clean, standard banking SMS is easy.

Any junior developer can write a regex that matches:

"Debited Rs. 500.00 from A/C 1234 to CAFE"

The real engineering challenge begins when the telecom provider delivers the messy, ambiguous, adversarial alerts that real banks generate every single day:

  • The OTP Trap: "Your OTP is 4921 for transaction of Rs. 1,450.00 at AMAZON. Valid for 10 mins. Do not share with anyone."
  • The Failed Transaction Alert: "Transaction of Rs. 2,500.00 on Card ending 8012 at STARBUCKS was DECLINED due to insufficient balance."
  • The Bill Generation Alert: "Your monthly statement for Credit Card XX4321 is Rs. 38,450.00 due on 15-NOV-26. Min due Rs. 2,000.00."
  • The Ambiguous Reversal: "Refund of Rs. 499.00 credited to A/C **1092 for failed UPI order."

If your parsing engine fails to differentiate between an actual expense and an OTP alert, your ledger will record an expense before the user has even authorized the payment. If it fails on a declined alert, it logs an expense for money that never left the account!

Here is how FinLedger constructed an automated test harness (SMSParserEngineTest.kt, SMSParserFailureReproductionTest.kt) to guarantee safety across hundreds of banking edge cases.

The Taxonomy of SMS Parser Failure Modes

In financial software, there are two distinct categories of parser bugs:

flowchart TD
    subgraph FalseNegative["Type 1: False Negative (Inconvenient)"]
        SMS1["Valid Bank Alert"] --> Missed["Parser Fails to Recognize Format"]
        Missed --> UserEnters["User Manually Enters Transaction:
        Minor friction, zero ledger corruption."]
    end

    subgraph FalsePositive["Type 2: False Positive (CATASTROPHIC)"]
        SMS2["OTP / Declined Alert / Bill Notice"] --> BadParse["Parser Incorrectly Detects 'Expense'"]
        BadParse --> CorruptLedger["Phantom Expense Injected into Ledger:
        Balance is wrong, budgeting breaks, trust destroyed!"]
    end

A False Negative (failing to detect an unusual format) is a mild inconvenience; the user can manually enter the transaction or adjust their settings.

A False Positive (logging an OTP, declined charge, or statement balance as a live expense) is an accounting catastrophe. It silently corrupts balances and destroys user confidence.

Therefore, our automated test suites prioritize Negative Assertions above all else: proving that non-transactional messages are rejected 100% of the time.

The Automated Test Architecture

To safeguard the parsing pipeline against regressions, FinLedger maintains a comprehensive test suite in app/src/test/java/com/finance/app/data/sms/:

flowchart TD
    subgraph TestSuites["FinLedger Automated SMS Test Harness"]
        direction TB
        Suite1["SMSParserEngineTest:
        Parameterized matrix of 200+ real bank formats across 50+ institutions"]

        Suite2["SMSParserFailureReproductionTest:
        Dedicated regression tests for every user-reported parsing failure"]

        Suite3["SmsPipelineComprehensiveSafetyTest:
        Negative assertion harness for OTPs, balance queries, and declined alerts"]

        Suite4["ConsentFirstSmsAutomationTest:
        Verification that pipeline never executes without user permissions"]
    end

Let's examine the specific edge cases covered by this harness:

1. The OTP and Security Code Guard

Banking OTP messages frequently mention the transaction amount:

"Use 829104 as your secret OTP to authorize payment of Rs. 1,299.00 to FLIPKART."

In SmsPipelineComprehensiveSafetyTest.kt, the suite asserts that any message containing keywords like OTP, verification code, one time password, secret code, or valid for immediately returns null or TransactionValidationResult.Invalid.

The test verifies that this rejection occurs in less than 50 microseconds, preventing expensive regex evaluation on authentication codes.

2. Declined and Failed Transactions

When a card transaction fails at a POS machine due to a network glitch or insufficient funds, the issuing bank sends an alert:

"Your transaction of Rs. 500.00 on ICICI Bank Card 4921 has DECLINED. Reason: Exceeded daily limit."

If a parser merely searches for Rs. 500.00 and Card 4921, it records an expense.

Our test harness exercises a dedicated keyword blocklist: declined, failed, unsuccessful, cancelled, rejected, and insufficient funds. The test asserts that messages containing these failure markers are discarded without touching ledger balances.

3. Credit Card Statement Notifications

Once a month, credit card issuers send billing summaries:

"Statement for your HDFC Card ending 1042 generated. Total Amt Due: Rs 42,190.00. Min Amt Due: Rs 2,500.00. Due Date: 12-NOV-26."

This is not a new transaction; it is an aggregate bill for transactions that occurred over the preceding thirty days.

The test harness asserts that keywords like total amt due, min amt due, statement generated, and payment due date are recognized as billing statements, preventing the app from double-counting thirty days of spending in a single catastrophic Rs. 42,190 entry.

4. Non-Breaking Spaces and Unicode Currencies

Telecom gateways often transmit messages using non-standard character encodings:

  • Non-breaking spaces (\u00A0) instead of standard ASCII spaces (\u0020).
  • Mathematical bold unicode characters (₹ vs Rs vs INR).
  • Zero-width non-joiners inserted between letters.

In SMSParserFailureReproductionTest.kt, every string undergoes unicode normalization (Normalizer.Form.NFC) and whitespace sanitization before regex matching. The test suite verifies that messages with hidden control characters parse with identical precision to clean ASCII text.

Continuous Regression Prevention

Whenever an edge case is discovered in real-world testing:

  1. The raw, anonymized SMS text is added directly to SMSParserFailureReproductionTest.kt.
  2. A failing test case is committed to the repository, proving the reproduction.
  3. The deterministic extraction pipeline is adjusted until the test passes.
  4. The test remains in the suite permanently, ensuring that future performance optimizations or feature additions can never reintroduce the regression.

Key Takeaway

You cannot build a reliable financial parser by testing a handful of happy-path strings on your own phone.

Real-world banking alerts are filled with security codes, declined alerts, billing summaries, and malformed encodings. By constructing a rigorous, parameterized test harness with strict negative assertions, FinLedger guarantees that automated parsing makes life easier without ever compromising the mathematical integrity of your ledger.

FinLedger is a privacy-first, offline-first personal finance application for Android that models bank accounts, credit cards, and cash without double-counting.

Explore FinLedger on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.devanshufinance.app

title: Creating 3D-printable business cards with React Three Fiber
description:
Recently, I've been looking into ways in which we can connect both the web and the physical world. As a web engineer who sometimes does IoT-related projects, such as a lamp that changes colours when you send a message to a Bluesky account, I know that using microcontrollers is a common approach for this. And, of course, this can be great fun, both to develop and use! But, what about creating new things instead of just connecting to existing ones?

In this guide, we'll explore how to create an app that can make business cards which can be customised and 3d printed. We go from scratch: starting with a design and setting up the project, creating its UI using DaisyUI, adding all the interactive elements, and then creating the body and elements of the business card with React Three Fiber. Finally, we connect everything through a Zustand store to let us download the model.

Let's get started!

Notes:

  • This guide assumes that you already know how to use React and have a notion of how Tailwind works.
  • Some code blocks include comments to make it easier to understand and follow what's going on in them.
  • The code of the UI was partially created using Claude. The design and React Three Fiber sections of the code were done by hand.

What we will create

Throughout this guide we will be making the following app, which you can also try here:

It will consist of two parts:

  • The left part will contain a form that controls all the different properties that will make up our model: positions, widths, heights, contents of text and QR code, etc.
  • The right part will contain a 3d preview of the business card model and a download button for the result. Using the button, we'll be able to download the model as a .stl file, one of the standards for 3d printing.

As for the technologies we'll be using, we'll control the shared state of our application through Zustand, use DaisyUI for the User Interface, generate QR codes with node-qrcode, and React Three Fiber to create our models. For this guide, we will be packing everything into a Next.js application, but this can be done with any other React-based framework as we won't be using any Next.js-specific features. Additionally, you can use the final repository for guidance if you need some support.

Project setup

Let's start the development of this project by setting up our dev environment. For this first step you have two options: you can download the starting repo, which is part of the full repository, or follow the manual setup steps described below. If you decide to go for the first option, make sure you are using it in its initial status, the one labelled with the initial-commit tag.

Manual Setup

Packages installation

To prepare our files for the project we will need to create the Next.js app we will be using, install our dependencies, and set up some files. We can do the first two steps by using the following commands:

# Create a Next.js app
npx create-next-app@latest rtf-cards --empty --use-npm --ts --tailwind --react-compiler --eslint --app --src-dir --yes
cd rtf-cards

# Install our dependencies. This is all one single line.
npm i @react-three/csg @react-three/drei @react-three/fiber qrcode daisyui  zustand three @tailwindcss/postcss

# Install qrcode types
npm i -D @types/qrcode

Adding DaisyUI's config

Now, let's configure our project so DaisyUI's styles are added properly. Add a postcss.config.mjs file into the root of your project and paste the following content in it:

/** @type {import('postcss-load-config').Config} */
const config = {
  plugins: {
    '@tailwindcss/postcss': {},
  },
};
export default config;

Next, make sure your app/global.css looks like this:

@import "tailwindcss";

/* Add this line */
@plugin "daisyui";

Note: If you would like to add any custom theming using DaisyUI so your app looks just how you want it, you can do so in this file! Check out DaisyUI's Theme Generator to personalise the look and feel of your app.

Now we're ready to start creating our UI! You can start the app by using npm run dev in the root folder of your project.

Creating the UI for the form

The form will be the source of truth for our application. It will control the model, its texts, dimensions, and every other part of it. On its side, the 3d scene will only have to read the form's values to generate and render the final model.

Let's start by creating our types and configuring the default values of the application. For this, we'll create a src/types/cardFormTypes.ts in our project, where we will add the following:

export interface CardDimensions {
  width: number;
  height: number;
  thickness: number;
}

export interface TextBlockState {
  enabled: boolean;
  xPosition: number;
  yPosition: number;
  thickness: number;
  fontSize: number;
  content: string;
}

export interface QrCodeState {
  enabled: boolean;
  xPosition: number;
  yPosition: number;
  thickness: number;
  moduleSize: number;
  qrContent: string;
}

/** Shape of the whole card form. */
export interface CardFormState {
  card: CardDimensions;
  textBlock: TextBlockState;
  qrCode: QrCodeState;
}

export const initialCardFormState: CardFormState = {
  card: { width: 84, height: 53, thickness: 1 },
  textBlock: {
    enabled: true,
    xPosition: -40,
    yPosition: 14,
    thickness: 1,
    fontSize: 14,
    content: "Name Lastname\n\nSoftware Engineer\n\nMaker",
  },
  qrCode: {
    enabled: true,
    xPosition: 20,
    yPosition: -5,
    thickness: 1,
    moduleSize: 1.2,
    qrContent: "https://example.com/",
  },
};

The 84 by 53 represent something close to the standard size of a card in mm. Although the standard size is closer to 85.6 x 53.98 mm, making it a bit smaller will give us a bit of leeway for the card to fit in a wallet without issues due to its thickness. In addition, the application will always start with something realistic whenever a new user tries it out.

We'll save these as initial values in a Zustand store. This store will include not only these values, but also several functions that will help us manage them to make our life easier later. In the code below, note how we're creating this store and wrapping it in persist, which will save the values to localStorage so they are constantly saved after any changes happen. Additionally, the merge function fills in all the values that a returning visitor's saved data doesn't have.

Add the following content in src/stores/formStore.ts:

import { create } from "zustand";
import { persist } from "zustand/middleware";
import type { CardFormState } from "@/types/cardFormTypes";
import { initialCardFormState } from "@/types/cardFormTypes";

interface FormStateStore {
  form: CardFormState;
  setForm: (form: CardFormState) => void;
}

export const FORM_STATE_STORAGE_KEY = "formState";

/**
 * Merges a persisted form over the defaults, group by group, so fields added
 * in later versions still get their default value for returning users.
 */
export function mergePersistedForm(persisted: unknown): CardFormState {
  const saved = (persisted as { form?: Partial<CardFormState> } | null)?.form;
  if (!saved || typeof saved !== "object") return initialCardFormState;
  const d = initialCardFormState;
  return {
    card: { ...d.card, ...saved.card },
    textBlock: { ...d.textBlock, ...saved.textBlock },
    qrCode: { ...d.qrCode, ...saved.qrCode },
  };
}

const useFormStateStore = create<FormStateStore>()(
  persist(
    (set) => ({
      form: initialCardFormState,
      setForm: (form) => set({ form }),
    }),
    {
      name: FORM_STATE_STORAGE_KEY,
      partialize: (s) => ({ form: s.form }),
      merge: (persisted, current) => ({
        ...current,
        form: mergePersistedForm(persisted),
      }),
      skipHydration: true,
    },
  ),
);

export default useFormStateStore;

If you, like me, are using Next.js, we need to ensure that the first render is done without access to localStorage. This is to avoid any mismatches that could happen between the server and the client. For this, we're using the following component on src/components/FormStateHydrator.tsx:

"use client";

import { useEffect } from "react";
import useFormStateStore from "@/stores/formStore";

/** Restores the saved form from localStorage once mounted in the browser. */
export function FormStateHydrator() {
  useEffect(() => {
    void useFormStateStore.persist.rehydrate();
  }, []);
  return null;
}

Next up is the form. For this, we'll create a series of small, reusable components that will make up our inputs. We'll be using some custom implementations to make them look exactly how we want while keeping their standard HTML behaviour. Add the following under src/components/FormInputs.tsx:

"use client";

import { useId, useState } from "react";
import type { ReactNode } from "react";

interface FieldShellProps {
  label: string;
  htmlFor: string;
  className?: string;
  children: ReactNode;
}

function FieldShell({ label, htmlFor, className, children }: FieldShellProps) {
  return (
    <div className={`fieldset min-w-0 ${className ?? ""}`}>
      <label htmlFor={htmlFor} className="label">
        {label}
      </label>
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}

export interface NumberFieldProps {
  label: string;
  value: number;
  onValueChange: (value: number) => void;
  unit?: string;
  className?: string;
}

const STEP = 1;
const SHIFT_STEP = 10;

/** What the field accepts while typing: optional minus sign, digits, one point. */
const NUMERIC_DRAFT = /^-?\d*\.?\d*$/;

function parseDraft(draft: string): number {
  return /^-?\.?$/.test(draft) ? 0 : Number(draft);
}

/**
 * Controlled number input with a trailing unit.
 *
 * Keeps the text being typed in a local draft: a controlled `type="number"`
 * input would re-render "1." as "1" and drop the decimal point before the
 * user can type the fractional digits. Both "." and "," work as the decimal
 * separator; the parsed number is reported through `onValueChange`.
 *
 * Being a text input, it restores the number-input behavior by hand
 * (WAI-ARIA spinbutton pattern): `role="spinbutton"` with `aria-valuenow`,
 * and ArrowUp / ArrowDown step by 1 (10 with Shift).
 */
export function NumberField({
  label,
  value,
  onValueChange,
  unit = "mm",
  className,
}: NumberFieldProps) {
  const id = useId();
  const [draft, setDraft] = useState(String(value));

  // The value changed from outside (e.g. restored form state): show it.
  if (parseDraft(draft) !== value) {
    setDraft(String(value));
  }

  function commit(nextDraft: string) {
    setDraft(nextDraft);
    onValueChange(parseDraft(nextDraft));
  }

  return (
    <FieldShell label={label} htmlFor={id} className={className}>
      <label className="input w-full">
        <input
          id={id}
          type="text"
          role="spinbutton"
          aria-valuenow={value}
          inputMode="decimal"
          value={draft}
          onKeyDown={(e) => {
            if (e.key !== "ArrowUp" && e.key !== "ArrowDown") return;
            e.preventDefault();

            const step = e.shiftKey ? SHIFT_STEP : STEP;
            const delta = e.key === "ArrowUp" ? step : -step;
            // Round away float noise
            commit(String(Math.round((value + delta) * 1e10) / 1e10));
          }}
          onChange={(e) => {
            const next = e.target.value.replace(",", ".");
            if (!NUMERIC_DRAFT.test(next)) return;

            commit(next);
          }}
        />
        {unit && <span className="label">{unit}</span>}
      </label>
    </FieldShell>
  );
}

export interface TextFieldProps {
  label: string;
  value: string;
  onValueChange: (value: string) => void;
  placeholder?: string;
  className?: string;
}

export function TextField({
  label,
  value,
  onValueChange,
  placeholder,
  className,
}: TextFieldProps) {
  const id = useId();
  return (
    <FieldShell label={label} htmlFor={id} className={className}>
      <input
        id={id}
        type="text"
        className="input w-full"
        value={value}
        placeholder={placeholder}
        onChange={(e) => onValueChange(e.target.value)}
      />
    </FieldShell>
  );
}

export interface TextAreaFieldProps {
  label: string;
  value: string;
  onValueChange: (value: string) => void;
  className?: string;
}

export function TextAreaField({
  label,
  value,
  onValueChange,
  className,
}: TextAreaFieldProps) {
  const id = useId();
  return (
    <FieldShell label={label} htmlFor={id} className={className}>
      <textarea
        id={id}
        className="textarea h-24 w-full"
        value={value}
        onChange={(e) => onValueChange(e.target.value)}
      />
    </FieldShell>
  );
}

For the sections that can be hidden, we use a small wrapper around a fieldset. When the switch that controls these sections is off, the fieldset gets disabled and hidden, so the corresponding section disappears. Create the following component on src/components/PropertyGroup.tsx:

"use client";

import type { ReactNode } from "react";

export interface PropertyGroupProps {
  label: string;
  legend: string;
  children?: ReactNode;
  checked: boolean;
  onToggleChange: (checked: boolean) => void;
  className?: string;
}

/**
 * A DaisyUI toggle with a label, controlling a fieldset of input fields.
 * While the toggle is off the fieldset is disabled and hidden.
 */
export function PropertyGroup({
  label,
  legend,
  children,
  checked,
  onToggleChange,
  className,
}: PropertyGroupProps) {
  return (
    <div className={`flex flex-col gap-3 ${className ?? ""}`}>
      <label className="flex cursor-pointer items-center gap-2 text-sm">
        <input
          type="checkbox"
          role="switch"
          className="toggle"
          checked={checked}
          onChange={(event) => onToggleChange(event.target.checked)}
        />
        <span>{label}</span>
      </label>
      <fieldset
        disabled={!checked}
        hidden={!checked}
        className="fieldset bg-base-300 border-base-300 rounded-box border p-4"
      >
        <legend className="fieldset-legend">{legend}</legend>
        {children}
      </fieldset>
    </div>
  );
}

And, finally, the form that ties it all together. To make sure that all the fields read only from a single group, we create and use a helper with all the different inputs of the form. Add this onto a new src/components/CardForm.tsx file:

"use client";

import { NumberField, TextAreaField, TextField } from "./FormInputs";
import { PropertyGroup } from "./PropertyGroup";
import useFormStateStore from "@/stores/formStore";

export interface CardFormProps {
  className?: string;
}

const GRID = "grid grid-cols-1 gap-x-2 gap-y-2 md:grid-cols-2";

export function CardForm({ className }: CardFormProps) {
  const state = useFormStateStore((s) => s.form);
  const onChange = useFormStateStore((s) => s.setForm);
  const { card, textBlock, qrCode } = state;

  const setCard = (patch: Partial<typeof card>) =>
    onChange({ ...state, card: { ...card, ...patch } });
  const setText = (patch: Partial<typeof textBlock>) =>
    onChange({ ...state, textBlock: { ...textBlock, ...patch } });
  const setQr = (patch: Partial<typeof qrCode>) =>
    onChange({ ...state, qrCode: { ...qrCode, ...patch } });

  return (
    <form
      className={`bg-base-200 border-base-300 rounded-box flex flex-col gap-6 border p-6 ${className ?? ""}`}
      onSubmit={(e) => e.preventDefault()}
    >
      <fieldset className={GRID}>
        <legend className="sr-only">Card</legend>
        <NumberField
          label="Width"
          value={card.width}
          onValueChange={(width) => setCard({ width })}
        />
        <NumberField
          label="Height"
          value={card.height}
          onValueChange={(height) => setCard({ height })}
        />
        <NumberField
          label="Thickness"
          value={card.thickness}
          onValueChange={(thickness) => setCard({ thickness })}
        />
      </fieldset>

      <PropertyGroup
        label="Include text block?"
        legend="Text Properties"
        checked={textBlock.enabled}
        onToggleChange={(enabled) => setText({ enabled })}
      >
        <div className={GRID}>
          <NumberField
            label="X Position"
            value={textBlock.xPosition}
            onValueChange={(xPosition) => setText({ xPosition })}
          />
          <NumberField
            label="Y Position"
            value={textBlock.yPosition}
            onValueChange={(yPosition) => setText({ yPosition })}
          />
          <NumberField
            label="Font size"
            unit=""
            value={textBlock.fontSize}
            onValueChange={(fontSize) => setText({ fontSize })}
          />
          <NumberField
            label="Thickness"
            value={textBlock.thickness}
            onValueChange={(thickness) => setText({ thickness })}
          />
          <TextAreaField
            className="md:col-span-2"
            label="Text content"
            value={textBlock.content}
            onValueChange={(content) => setText({ content })}
          />
        </div>
      </PropertyGroup>

      <PropertyGroup
        label="Include QR Code?"
        legend="QR Code Properties"
        checked={qrCode.enabled}
        onToggleChange={(enabled) => setQr({ enabled })}
      >
        <div className={GRID}>
          <NumberField
            label="X Position"
            value={qrCode.xPosition}
            onValueChange={(xPosition) => setQr({ xPosition })}
          />
          <NumberField
            label="Y Position"
            value={qrCode.yPosition}
            onValueChange={(yPosition) => setQr({ yPosition })}
          />
          <NumberField
            label="Thickness"
            value={qrCode.thickness}
            onValueChange={(thickness) => setQr({ thickness })}
          />
          <NumberField
            label="Module Size"
            value={qrCode.moduleSize}
            onValueChange={(moduleSize) => setQr({ moduleSize })}
          />
          <TextField
            className="md:col-span-2"
            label="QR code text (can be a link)"
            placeholder="https://example.com/"
            value={qrCode.qrContent}
            onValueChange={(qrContent) => setQr({ qrContent })}
          />
        </div>
      </PropertyGroup>
    </form>
  );
}

Let's add all of these elements into our page by modifying our homepage on src/app/page.tsx. We can add a layout, and prepare the rest of the app for all the components we'll be creating:

"use client";

import RTFContainer from "@/components/3d/RTFContainer";
import { CardForm } from "@/components/CardForm";
import { Visualizer } from "@/components/Visualizer";
import { FormStateHydrator } from "@/stores/FormStateHydrator";

export default function Home() {
  return (
    <div>
      <FormStateHydrator />
      <main className="bg-base-100 mx-auto flex min-h-screen w-full max-w-[1600px] flex-col gap-6 px-4 py-6 lg:px-6">
        <div className="grid min-h-0 flex-1 grid-cols-1 gap-6 lg:grid-cols-2">
          <CardForm />
          <div>Our 3d visualizer will go here!</div>
        </div>
      </main>
    </div>
  );
}

Once you have added this content, your application should look like this:

Setting up the 3d space

Let's now get to the most fun part of the project: the 3d space and its objects. For this part, we can use React Three Fiber, as it lets us create 3d objects using React's jsx syntax.

We'll start by both creating a Canvas object for our 3d space and adding Drei's OrbitControls to handle camera movement, panning, and zoom. In a new file called src/components/RTFContainer.tsx add the following:

"use client";

import { OrbitControls } from "@react-three/drei";
import { Canvas } from "@react-three/fiber";

const RTFContainer = () => {
  return (
    <div className="h-full w-full bg-white/10">
      <Canvas camera={{ position: [0, 0, 100], fov: 70 }}>
        <OrbitControls makeDefault />
        <directionalLight color="white" position={[0, 0, 5]} />
      </Canvas>
    </div>
  );
};

export default RTFContainer;

Here, we're doing three things:

  1. We're adding a camera and positioning it 100 units away from the centre of our 3d scene
  2. We're adding a set of controls to move the camera around the scene and setting them as the default using makeDefault
  3. And we're adding illumination to the scene, so we can actually see the objects in it once we have them

Next, let's add this scene into our page. For this, we can modify page.tsx like we did previously and replace our placeholder div with the following:

"use client";

import { CardForm } from "@/components/CardForm";
import { FormStateHydrator } from "@/components/FormStateHydrator";
// Add this import:
import RTFContainer from "@/components/RTFContainer";

export default function Home() {
  return (
    <div>
      <FormStateHydrator />
      <main className="bg-base-100 mx-auto flex min-h-screen w-full max-w-[1600px] flex-col gap-6 px-4 py-6 lg:px-6">
        <div className="grid min-h-0 flex-1 grid-cols-1 gap-6 lg:grid-cols-2">
          <CardForm />
          {/* We add the following elements: */}
          <div className="bg-base-300 rounded-box flex min-h-96 flex-1 overflow-hidden border border-base-content/10 p-6">
            <RTFContainer />
          </div>
        </div>
      </main>
    </div>
  );
}

You might have noticed that we are missing the download button that was part of our initial layout. Don't worry! We haven't forgotten about it yet, we'll just add it later :)

At this point our app is ready to show all of its 3d contents. However, with no objects to show, we just see an empty canvas!

Let's now focus on creating and adding our first object: the body of the card.

Rendering the card body

To render the body of our card we'll go for the simplest 3d shape: a box! For this, we can use a box geometry that's part of the standard tools that Three.js gives us. Its center will lie at 0, 0, 0, and it will take in the height, width, and thickness props of our form. Afterwards, we'll apply a white material, so the box will be visible on screen. Do the following in src/components/CardMesh.tsx:

import type { CardDimensions } from "../cardFormTypes";

const CardMesh = ({ cardProps }: { cardProps: CardDimensions }) => {
  return (
    <mesh>
      <boxGeometry
        args={[cardProps.width, cardProps.height, cardProps.thickness]}
      />
      <meshBasicMaterial color="white" />
    </mesh>
  );
};

export default CardMesh;

And add this new component into our RTFContainer:

"use client";

import { OrbitControls } from "@react-three/drei";
import { Canvas } from "@react-three/fiber";

// We add these two new imports
import useFormStateStore from "@/stores/formStore";
import CardMesh from "./CardMesh";


const RTFContainer = () => {
  // We add this line to extract the card props from the form state
  const { card } = useFormStateStore((s) => s.form);

  return (
    <div className="h-full w-full">
      <Canvas camera={{ position: [0, 0, 100], fov: 70 }}>
        <OrbitControls makeDefault />

        <directionalLight color="white" position={[0, 0, 5]} />

        {/** And finally add this group with the card mesh */}
        <group>
          <CardMesh cardProps={card} />
        </group>
      </Canvas>
    </div>
  );
};

export default RTFContainer;

With this added, you should be able to see the first object on the canvas: a simple, white box. Because this card is connected to our Zustand store, you can even change the values present in the form to alter the size of the card in real time. And, thanks to the OrbitControls we added, we can move the camera around, even on mobile. Pretty neat, huh?

But, of course, this gives us no information whatsoever about the person that owns the card. So let's proceed by adding another element to the mix: the owner's text.

Rendering text content

We'll be drawing the text using Drei's Text3D component, which takes a typeface JSON file and manages its geometry automatically for us. For this project, I've prepared a file for Roboto Extra Bold, which you can download here from the GitHub repo. Once you have downloaded it, make sure to store it under your public assets, /public for Next.js, and call it Roboto_ExtraBold.json.

I created this file by downloading the font files from Google Fonts, picking the boldest one available, and then converting it using Facetype.js, a free, online converter you can use for these cases. You can follow this same process to customise your card even further, choosing whichever font you like.

To render the text object, let's now create a src/components/TextBlockMesh.tsx file and add the following content into it:

import { CardDimensions, TextBlockState } from "@/types/cardFormTypes";
import { Text3D } from "@react-three/drei";

// The name of the font file you added
const TEXT_FONT = "Roboto_ExtraBold.json";

const TextBlockMesh = ({
  textBlockProps,
  cardProps,
}: {
  textBlockProps: TextBlockState;
  cardProps: CardDimensions;
}) => {
  return (
    <Text3D
      font={`/${TEXT_FONT}`}
      size={textBlockProps.fontSize / 4}
      position={[
        textBlockProps.xPosition,
        textBlockProps.yPosition,
        cardProps.thickness / 2,
      ]}
      height={textBlockProps.thickness}
    >
      {textBlockProps.content}
      <meshBasicMaterial color="black" />
    </Text3D>
  );
};

export default TextBlockMesh;

If you read the code, you might have noticed a few interesting things. First, we're scaling down the size of the text by doing fontSize / 4 so it doesn't change as drastically when altering this value. This way, if you go from font size 14 to 15, its size will just slightly change, making it so you don't have to play around with decimals that much. Second, the text sits at thickness / 2 on the Z axis. While this might seem confusing, this is due to us wanting to position our text directly on the face of our card. By making it so the text is raised by half the card's thickness, we make sure it's always resting on top of the frontal face of our card.

Now, let's add it to our scene by modifying our RTFContainer:

"use client";

import { OrbitControls } from "@react-three/drei";
import { Canvas } from "@react-three/fiber";

import useFormStateStore from "@/stores/formStore";
import CardMesh from "./CardMesh";

// We add Suspense, as Text3D suspends while the font data is loading.
// You can read more about it here: https://drei.docs.pmnd.rs/abstractions/text3d
import { Suspense } from "react";
import TextBlockMesh from "./TextBlockMesh";

const RTFContainer = () => {
  // We destructure the textBlock values from the form state
  const { card, textBlock } = useFormStateStore((s) => s.form);

  return (
    <div className="h-full w-full">
      <Canvas camera={{ position: [0, 0, 100], fov: 70 }}>
        <OrbitControls makeDefault />

        <directionalLight color="white" position={[0, 0, 5]} />
        <group>
          <CardMesh cardProps={card} />

          {/** And we add the text block with Suspense without a fallback 
           * and control its visibility based on form props */}
          <Suspense fallback={null}>
            {textBlock.enabled && textBlock.content.length > 0 && (
              <TextBlockMesh textBlockProps={textBlock} cardProps={card} />
            )}
          </Suspense>

        </group>
      </Canvas>
    </div>
  );
};

export default RTFContainer;

As mentioned in the code, we're controlling the visibility of our text block using the enabled prop we created for the form. If you play around with the values of the form, they should automatically be reflected into our application.

The current app should look like this:

Rendering the QR code

The QR code will be the most complex but fun mesh we'll create here. We'll need to start by making a matrix of 1s and 0s, representing the final result. We can use qrcode to generate this matrix, which we'll then utilise to make every individual module — the squares that make up our QR code.

Similar to the text, the QR is placed at (thickness of card + thickness of QR) / 2 on the Z axis, so it's positioned on top of the card's front face. Add the following into a new src/components/QRCodeMesh.tsx file:

import { useMemo } from "react";
import QRCode from "qrcode";
import * as THREE from "three";
import { CardDimensions, QrCodeState } from "@/types/cardFormTypes";

/**
 * We use a low level of error correction. As defined in the type, possible
 * values are L for Low, M for Medium, Q for Quartile, and H for High. A bigger
 * level of error correction will make it easier for your QR code to be scanned
 * if it gets damaged, but it will also take more space.
 */
type ErrorCorrectionType = "L" | "M" | "Q" | "H";
const ERROR_CORRECTION: ErrorCorrectionType = "L";

const makeModuleSquare = (col: number, row: number, moduleSize: number) => {
  const x = col * moduleSize;
  const y = -row * moduleSize; // flip y: matrix rows go down, 3D y goes up

  // We form the square shape for each QR code module using simple lines.
  const shape = new THREE.Shape();
  shape.moveTo(x, y);
  shape.lineTo(x + moduleSize, y);
  shape.lineTo(x + moduleSize, y + moduleSize);
  shape.lineTo(x, y + moduleSize);
  shape.closePath();
  return shape;
};

const QRCodeMesh = ({
  qrCodeProps,
  cardProps,
}: {
  qrCodeProps: QrCodeState;
  cardProps: CardDimensions;
}) => {
  // This process is quite complex, so we memoize it.
  const qrCode = useMemo(
    () =>
      QRCode.create(qrCodeProps.qrContent, {
        errorCorrectionLevel: ERROR_CORRECTION,
      }),
    [qrCodeProps.qrContent],
  );

  const geometry = useMemo(() => {
    const { size, data } = qrCode.modules;

    const shapes: THREE.Shape[] = [];
    data.forEach((value, index) => {
      if (value) {
        const yCoord = Math.floor(index / size);
        const xCoord = Math.floor(index % size);
        // Shift the grid so the QR code is centred on the origin.
        shapes.push(
          makeModuleSquare(
            xCoord - size / 2,
            yCoord + 1 - size / 2,
            qrCodeProps.moduleSize,
          ),
        );
      }
    });

    const geometry = new THREE.ExtrudeGeometry(shapes, {
      depth: qrCodeProps.thickness,
      bevelEnabled: false,
      curveSegments: 24,
    });

    geometry.center();

    return geometry;
  }, [qrCode, qrCodeProps.moduleSize, qrCodeProps.thickness]);

  return (
    <mesh
      position={[
        qrCodeProps.xPosition,
        qrCodeProps.yPosition,
        (cardProps.thickness + qrCodeProps.thickness) / 2,
      ]}
      geometry={geometry}
    >
      <meshPhongMaterial color="black" />
    </mesh>
  );
};

export default QRCodeMesh;

And, similar to our other meshes, we add the object to our RTFContainer:

"use client";

import { OrbitControls } from "@react-three/drei";
import { Canvas } from "@react-three/fiber";

import useFormStateStore from "@/stores/formStore";
import CardMesh from "./CardMesh";
import { Suspense } from "react";
import TextBlockMesh from "./TextBlockMesh";

// We import the mesh
import QRCodeMesh from "./QRCodeMesh";

const RTFContainer = () => {
  // We destructure the form values
  const { card, textBlock, qrCode } = useFormStateStore((s) => s.form);

  return (
    <div className="h-full w-full">
      <Canvas camera={{ position: [0, 0, 100], fov: 70 }}>
        <OrbitControls makeDefault />

        <directionalLight color="white" position={[0, 0, 5]} />
        <group>
          <CardMesh cardProps={card} />

          <Suspense fallback={null}>
            {textBlock.enabled && textBlock.content.length > 0 && (
              <TextBlockMesh textBlockProps={textBlock} cardProps={card} />
            )}
          </Suspense>

          {/** And add the QR Code mesh into our group similar to how we 
           * did with the text block
           */}
          {qrCode.enabled && qrCode.qrContent.length > 0 && (
            <QRCodeMesh qrCodeProps={qrCode} cardProps={card} />
          )}
        </group>
      </Canvas>
    </div>
  );
};

export default RTFContainer;

With this, our app should look like this:

This now has almost all the elements of our original design. The only thing we're missing is a way to export the model. So, let's add that button!

Exporting our model as an STL

Now that our model is created and customisable, our last step will be to find a way to download it from the browser. Luckily, Three.js includes an STLExporter that can help us do exactly that. It exports any object that contains meshes, but it needs a way to reach the group that wraps all the models of our scene. So, to make our lives easier, we'll create a small Zustand store that will help us hold a reference to this group so we can handle the download.

To make this store, create meshStore.ts in our stores folder and add the following code:

import { create } from "zustand";
import * as THREE from "three";
import { STLExporter } from "three/examples/jsm/exporters/STLExporter.js";

interface MeshStoreState {
  jointMesh: THREE.Object3D | null;
  setJointMesh: (jointMesh: THREE.Object3D | null) => void;
  downloadModel: () => void;
}

function downloadBlobAsFile(blob: Blob, filename: string) {
  const blobUrl = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
  const link = document.createElement("a");
  link.href = blobUrl;
  link.download = filename;
  link.click();

  URL.revokeObjectURL(blobUrl);
}

const useMeshStore = create<MeshStoreState>()((set, get) => ({
  jointMesh: null,
  setJointMesh: (jointMesh) => set({ jointMesh }),

  downloadModel: () => {
    const { jointMesh } = get();
    if (!jointMesh) {
      console.error("The model is not ready yet. Try again in a moment.");
      return;
    }

    // Make sure every child's world transform is updated before exporting.
    jointMesh.updateMatrixWorld(true);

    // We convert the model to STL
    const exporter = new STLExporter();
    const data = exporter.parse(jointMesh, { binary: true });
    const blob = new Blob([data], { type: "model/stl" });

    // And we download it
    downloadBlobAsFile(blob, "joint-model.stl");
  },
}));

export default useMeshStore;

Now we just need to pass our group to the store, which we'll do by using a React ref. For this, we'll change our RTFContainer like so:

const RTFContainer = () => {
  const { card, textBlock, qrCode } = useFormStateStore((s) => s.form);
  // Add this line. Don't forget to import the store!
  const setJointMesh = useMeshStore((s) => s.setJointMesh);

  return (
    <div className="h-full w-full">
      <Canvas camera={{ position: [0, 0, 100], fov: 70 }}>
        <OrbitControls makeDefault />

        <directionalLight color="white" position={[0, 0, 5]} />

        // And make sure to connect the group with the store, here
        <group ref={setJointMesh}>

        // Rest of the code

And, finally, we'll add the download button to our page. To do this, we'll modify the layout of our page.tsx a bit and add a few elements to it:

"use client";

import { CardForm } from "@/components/CardForm";
import { FormStateHydrator } from "@/components/FormStateHydrator";
import RTFContainer from "@/components/RTFContainer";

// First, we import our mesh store
import useMeshStore from "@/stores/meshStore";

export default function Home() {
  // We then get the helper function from the mesh store
  const downloadModel = useMeshStore((s) => s.downloadModel);

  return (
    <div>
      <FormStateHydrator />
      <main className="bg-base-100 mx-auto flex min-h-screen w-full max-w-[1600px] flex-col gap-6 px-4 py-6 lg:px-6">
        <div className="grid min-h-0 flex-1 grid-cols-1 gap-6 lg:grid-cols-2">
          <CardForm />

          {/* And we change this bit, adding the download model function to our button: */}
          <div className="border-base-content/10 bg-base-300 flex flex-col overflow-hidden rounded-box border">
            <div className="bg-base-200 flex items-center justify-center p-6">
              <button
                type="button"
                onClick={downloadModel}
                className="btn btn-primary"
              >
                Download .stl
              </button>
            </div>
            <div className="flex min-h-96 flex-1 items-center justify-center p-6">
              <RTFContainer />
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>
      </main>
    </div>
  );
}

And, with that, the application is done! The final result should look like this:

In our application, the form controls the store, which in turn controls the card 3d model. We can modify the model in real time, move it around in its 3d space, and even download the result! If you have a 3d printer, you can then print this model as a real business card and show it around. Isn't that neat?

Conclusion

As mentioned in the description, this project started as a way for me to explore ways in which we can connect the web with the physical world using 3d prints. For this, we first set up a form to control the properties of our 3d objects and then created a Zustand store to save its values. We then learned how to create a 3d space with React Three Fiber and move it around with Drei's helpers. Afterwards, we learned how to create 3d objects, give them simple textures, and position them in our 3d space. We added these objects using three different methods: standard geometries, Drei's Text3D components, and our own custom geometry. Finally, we created another Zustand store to let us download our model, and we added a download button to let our users export the final result.

While this project started as something similar to what we created here, I then decided to further expand it into a full application with some more complexity, which I decided to call g3co. Although it's still in early test versions, it allows for more customisation than what we created in this guide, and I plan to include some updates in the future to add more features and interesting parts. Moreover, it's open source! And you can find its repository on GitHub.

Apart from the exploration I wanted to do in this project and post, I wanted to use this app to learn something. See, I'm constantly looking to improve my design and development skills. For this, I figured out that creating an app about a topic that I'm already passionate about, 3d printing, was a great path to follow. And I hope you also learned some new things from it, and that you had fun while doing so.

So, if you learned something, please take what you've learned and made, and make it better!

title: Recording screen, system audio and mic to MP4 in the browser (WebCodecs + mp4-muxer)
description:
I built a small meeting recorder that runs as a PWA in Edge. It records the screen, the other people's voices (system audio) and my own microphone into one MP4. This post is about how it works, including the parts that took me a while to get right.

What I wanted:

  • one MP4 with screen + system audio + mic
  • hours of recording without holding the file in memory
  • files that seek properly in any player

Setup: Windows 11, Microsoft Edge (Chrome behaves the same). APIs: getDisplayMedia, Web Audio, MediaStreamTrackProcessor, WebCodecs, File System Access API. MP4 muxing is done by mp4-muxer (MIT).

Why not MediaRecorder

MediaRecorder is the easy option, but I wanted control over a few things:

  • Seeking. WebM files from MediaRecorder have no duration or cues, so some players can't seek in them.
  • Frame rate and keyframes. Meeting screens barely move, so I record at 8 fps to keep files small, but still want a keyframe every 5 seconds so seeking is quick and accurate.
  • Pause. Paused time should be cut out, not left as a gap.

WebCodecs gives you all of that. The price is that you manage timestamps yourself.

1. Screen and system audio 

const displayStream = await navigator.mediaDevices.getDisplayMedia({
  video: { frameRate: { ideal: 8, max: 8 }, height: { max: 1080 }, displaySurface: 'monitor' },
  audio: { suppressLocalAudioPlayback: false, echoCancellation: false, noiseSuppression: false, autoGainControl: false },
  systemAudio: 'include',
  selfBrowserSurface: 'exclude',
  monitorTypeSurfaces: 'include',
});
displayStream.getVideoTracks()[0].contentHint = 'text';
  • On Windows, you only get system audio if the user picks Entire screen and ticks Also share system audio in the share dialog. Sharing a single window gives you no audio. Users won't guess this, so the app says it in one line under the button.
  • Echo cancellation and friends are for microphones. They do nothing useful on system audio, so they're off.
  • contentHint = 'text' tells the encoder to favor sharp detail over smooth motion. Slide text stays readable.

2. Mixing in the microphone

Two separate audio tracks in one MP4 confuse some players (they play only the first). I mix them into one with Web Audio:

const audioCtx = new AudioContext({ sampleRate: 48000 }); // create inside the click handler
const dest = audioCtx.createMediaStreamDestination();
dest.channelCount = 2;

const sys = displayStream.getAudioTracks();
if (sys.length) audioCtx.createMediaStreamSource(new MediaStream(sys)).connect(dest);

const mic = await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ audio: { echoCancellation: true, noiseSuppression: true } });
audioCtx.createMediaStreamSource(mic).connect(dest);

const mixedTrack = dest.stream.getAudioTracks()[0];

Create the AudioContext in the click handler. If you create it on page load it can start suspended, and you get a silent file.

3. Encoding video yourself

MediaStreamTrackProcessor hands you frames one by one, which you feed to a VideoEncoder:

const reader = new MediaStreamTrackProcessor({ track: videoTrack }).readable.getReader();
const first = (await reader.read()).value;
const w = even(first.displayWidth), h = even(first.displayHeight); // H.264 needs even sizes

// try H.264 profiles from best to most compatible
const common = { width: w, height: h, bitrate: 500_000, bitrateMode: 'variable', framerate: 8, latencyMode: 'realtime', avc: { format: 'avc' } };
let cfg = null;
for (const codec of ['avc1.640033', 'avc1.4d0033', 'avc1.42e033', 'avc1.640028']) {
  if ((await VideoEncoder.isConfigSupported({ ...common, codec })).supported) { cfg = { ...common, codec }; break; }
}

const venc = new VideoEncoder({
  output: (chunk, meta) => muxer.addVideoChunk(chunk, meta),
  error: e => console.error(e),
});
venc.configure(cfg);

The loop does three things:

const FRAME_US = 1e6 / 8, KEYFRAME_US = 5_000_000;
const base = first.timestamp;  // recording start
let lastTs = -1, lastKeyTs = -Infinity;

for (let frame = first; frame; ) {
  const ts = Math.max(frame.timestamp - base, lastTs + 1);           // 1. keep timestamps increasing
  if (lastTs < 0 || (ts - lastTs >= FRAME_US * 0.75 && venc.encodeQueueSize < 4)) { // 2. drop extras
    const out = new VideoFrame(frame, { timestamp: ts, duration: FRAME_US });
    const key = ts - lastKeyTs >= KEYFRAME_US;                       // 3. keyframe every 5 s
    if (key) lastKeyTs = ts;
    venc.encode(out, { keyFrame: key });
    out.close();
    lastTs = ts;
  }
  frame.close();
  const r = await reader.read();
  frame = r.done ? null : r.value;
}
  1. Timestamps. When nothing on screen changes, frames stop coming for a while. I take each frame's own timestamp minus the start time, and force it to be strictly increasing.
  2. Dropping frames. max: 8 is a hint, not a promise. Frames that arrive too soon, or while the encoder is backed up (encodeQueueSize), get dropped.
  3. Keyframes. Without regular keyframes, seeking is slow and lands in the wrong place.

And close every frame. Forget frame.close() and you run out of memory within seconds.

4. Audio timestamps from the sample count

For audio, I compute the timestamp from how many samples I've written. Paused time simply never gets counted.

let samples = 0;
// inside the loop (ad is an AudioData)
const n = ad.numberOfFrames, ch = ad.numberOfChannels;
const buf = new Float32Array(n * ch);
for (let c = 0; c < ch; c++) ad.copyTo(buf.subarray(c * n, (c + 1) * n), { planeIndex: c, format: 'f32-planar' });
const out = new AudioData({
  format: 'f32-planar', sampleRate: ad.sampleRate, numberOfFrames: n, numberOfChannels: ch,
  timestamp: Math.round(samples / ad.sampleRate * 1e6), data: buf,
});
samples += n;
aenc.encode(out);
out.close(); ad.close();

While paused, incoming AudioData is just thrown away. On resume, the video side recalculates its base time. The result is a file with the paused section cut out.

The audio encoder tries AAC (mp4a.40.2) first and falls back to Opus.

5. Writing to disk as you go

This made the biggest difference. mp4-muxer has FileSystemWritableFileStreamTarget, which writes straight into a File System Access stream:

// ask for a folder once; keep the handle in IndexedDB for next time
const dir = await showDirectoryPicker({ id: 'rec', mode: 'readwrite', startIn: 'videos' });
const file = await dir.getFileHandle('recording.mp4', { create: true });
const writable = await file.createWritable();

const muxer = new Mp4Muxer.Muxer({
  target: new Mp4Muxer.FileSystemWritableFileStreamTarget(writable),
  fastStart: false,               // streaming, so the moov box goes at the end
  firstTimestampBehavior: 'offset',
  video: { codec: 'avc', width: w, height: h },
  audio: { codec: 'aac', numberOfChannels: 2, sampleRate: 48000 },
});

// on stop
await venc.flush(); await aenc.flush();
muxer.finalize();
await writable.close();

With ArrayBufferTarget, the whole recording sits in memory until you stop. A long meeting in high quality can run out of memory and lose everything. I started that way and switched to streaming. In an automated test that records and saves 100 times in a row, memory doesn't grow (renderer process went from 86 MB to 57 MB).

A FileSystemDirectoryHandle can be stored in IndexedDB as-is. Next time you only check queryPermission / requestPermission and reuse the same folder.

6. Smaller gotchas

  • Static screen = short video. If the last frame came long before you pressed stop, the video track ends early. On stop, I encode the last frame once more with the stop time as its timestamp.
  • Double-clicking Start. Users can click again while the share dialog is open. A simple flag prevents two recordings at once.
  • Folder picker uses up the click. showDirectoryPicker consumes the user activation, so calling getDisplayMedia right after it fails. The app asks the user to click once more.

7. Shipping it to the Microsoft Store

PWABuilder turns the URL into a .msixbundle you can submit. The package is just a shell that opens the site, so code updates are a web deploy with no Store re-review (remember to bump the service worker cache name).

A side effect I didn't plan for: because it installs from the Store like any standard app, with no drivers or virtual audio devices, it also works on locked-down work PCs where you can't install regular desktop software. (Some companies block the Store itself, and please follow your company's policy and tell people when you record.)

The app is called LiteRec, and I'm the developer. 10 recordings are free, then it's $0.99/month.
https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9ntvppczz2gf

Happy to answer questions about any of the WebCodecs bits in the comments.

title: overflow: hidden breaks position: sticky. overflow: clip doesn't.
description:
Someone reports a bug: the "jump to section" bar at the top of a long settings page used to stick to the top of the viewport while you scrolled. Now it doesn't. It just sits there in normal flow like position: sticky was never applied.

You open devtools. The CSS is untouched — position: sticky; top: 0;, same as it's been for months. No typo, no overridden rule, nothing crossed out in the inspector. The element is exactly as sticky as it was yesterday. Except it isn't sticking.

The actual change shipped in a different file entirely: a shared <Card> component picked up overflow: hidden last week, to stop a decorative background image from spilling past its rounded corners. Nobody touched the settings page. Nobody touched the sticky bar. And yet here we are.

The rule nobody reads until it bites them

position: sticky doesn't stick to the viewport by default. It sticks to its nearest scroll container — the closest ancestor whose overflow isn't visible. Usually that's the page itself, so sticky behaves exactly like you'd expect: pinned to the window as you scroll.

But "nearest ancestor with non-visible overflow" doesn't check whether that ancestor actually scrolls. It just checks the computed overflow value. Set overflow: hidden anywhere between the sticky element and the page — for any reason, clipping an image, trimming a shadow, stopping an accidental horizontal scrollbar — and that element becomes the sticky container instead of the viewport.

.card {
  border-radius: 16px;
  overflow: hidden; /* so the thumbnail respects the rounded corner */
}

.card .jump-bar {
  position: sticky;
  top: 0; /* now relative to .card, not the page */
}

.card never scrolls — its content fits. So the sticky bar's "scroll container" never moves, which means the bar never has a reason to detach from its normal spot and pin anywhere. Visually: it just looks broken. There's no console warning, no deprecation notice, nothing that points back to a border-radius fix in an unrelated component.

Try it before you keep reading: open your own devtools on any sticky element that's misbehaving and check getComputedStyle on each ancestor for overflow. It's almost always hidden, and it's almost always there for a reason that has nothing to do with scrolling.

The fix that doesn't ask you to restructure anything

overflow: clip looks, on paper, like a quieter synonym for hidden. It clips content at the element's padding edge the same way. The difference is in what it refuses to become: the CSS Overflow spec defines clip so that it never creates a scroll container. There's no scrollport to establish, so nothing can be scrolled into it — not by the user, not by element.scrollTop = 40 in your own code. hidden still lets that second one through, which is exactly the mechanism it uses to qualify as scrollable in the first place.

.card {
  border-radius: 16px;
  overflow: clip; /* clips the same, isn't a scroll container */
}

Swap the one keyword and the sticky bar starts looking straight past .card again, up to the real scroll container — the page. Nothing else in the component changes. No wrapper <div>, no position: relative hack, no JavaScript recalculating offsets on scroll.

Two details worth knowing before you reach for it everywhere:

  • It's independent per axis. overflow-x: clip; overflow-y: visible; does what you'd want. Try that with hidden and the browser forces the other axis to auto for you, which is its own long-running source of surprise scrollbars.
  • overflow-clip-margin lets clipped content bleed a few pixels past the box before it's cut — useful when a focus ring or a shadow would otherwise get sheared off exactly at the edge.

The one thing overflow: clip can't do that hidden can is be scrolled at all — if that container is genuinely meant to scroll its own content (a chat panel, a code block with a max-height), hidden paired with a real scrollbar is still the right tool. clip is for the much more common case: an element that clips for layout reasons and was never supposed to be a scroll container in the first place.

Play with the before/after below — flip .card between hidden and clip and watch the sticky bar inside it react in real time.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The part worth remembering

overflow: hidden was never just "clip this." It was always "clip this, and also: this now scrolls, even if you never intended that and nothing inside it ever moves." Every position: sticky bug report that starts with "it worked until I touched a totally unrelated component" is worth checking against exactly that rule before you touch the sticky declaration at all.

overflow: clip separates the two meanings that hidden always bundled together. If you only wanted the first one, it's the one to reach for now.

Next time a sticky element goes dead for no visible reason, what's the first ancestor you check — and how far up the tree did the real culprit turn out to be last time?

title: Marq: run coding agents in parallel, and keep everything as Markdown
description:
I'm building Marq, a desktop app that is a Markdown knowledge base and an IDE for coding agents at the same time. It's still early, and I'd like to hear what people think.

Features, file formats and keybindings may change without notice. I develop on macOS. Linux and Windows build, but I haven't tested them.

Why I made it

Running several coding agents at once is easy. Finding out later what each of them did is harder. Prompts, transcripts and results end up spread over terminals and chat histories.

In Marq, all of that is a plain Markdown file in your vault, next to your notes: requests, session logs, results, boards and crews. You can open them in any editor, grep them, or query them with mq, a jq-like language for Markdown that I also maintain.

Queue work and run agents in parallel

Requests wait in an inbox. They start one after another, or several at once if you allow it. Each task gets its own git worktree and branch, so agents working on the same repository don't overwrite each other's files.

Review in the app

The Changes panel shows the diff against the base commit. You can comment on diff lines and send the review back to the agent. When you're happy, commit, push and open a PR from the same place. When a session finishes, its result is written back into the request note.

Kanban boards

I wanted a board to plan work on, but I didn't want another tool with its own database. A board in Marq is a Markdown note. Each ## heading is a list and each checklist item is a card:

## Todo

- [ ] **T1** Write docs — @me
  - start with the README

## Done

- [x] **T2** Add logo

Editing the Markdown edits the board. If you move an item under another heading, the card moves. If you move it under Done, it gets checked. The board tab shows the same file as columns, and you drag cards between them.

The board is also where work starts. Open a card and you can:

  • Start a session with the card as the prompt. It includes the card's text and linked notes, and the agent is told where the card lives so it can update it with board_update_card. The card moves to Doing when the session starts.
  • Queue the card in the inbox, and it runs when there's room.

Agents can read and change boards too. Marq also has a spec workflow: an agent writes a spec, and Break down turns each open item into a card that links back to the spec.

Crews

Several sessions can work on one project as a team, split by role (lead, implementer, reviewer and so on). The lead sets up the team, you approve each member, and they talk to each other by role and share a task list. That task list is a board, so it's the same Markdown as above.

Crews have guardrails. A hop limit stops members from messaging each other forever, and a message over the limit is held until you let it through. A route can forward a member's final reply to someone else automatically, for example every implementation result to the reviewer.

Not only Claude

Claude Code is the main agent, and it's the one that supports everything. Marq can also run a task on other agents:

  • Codex, through its own app-server (codex app-server), so no adapter is needed. The New task dialog has a model and reasoning effort field for it.
  • Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Qwen Code and Goose, through ACP (Agent Client Protocol). You can add any other ACP agent in Settings.
  • Ollama, to run Claude Code against a local model.

You install and log in to these agents yourself, and Marq launches them with the command it finds in your login shell. The vault tools reach them over MCP, and their permission requests show up as the same approval cards. Each task still gets its own worktree, and the session is saved as Markdown like any other.

They come with limits. Crews and the sandbox are Claude only. You can pick Codex's model in the New task dialog, but the other ACP agents don't get a model picker and run on whatever model they're configured with. Other agents also work as a run in a comparison, so you can give the same task to Claude and Codex and keep the diff you prefer.

Markdown in, Markdown out

A request is just a note. Its body is the prompt, and context: attaches pieces of other notes picked with mq:

---
type: request
status: todo
project: ~/dev/git/mq
context:
  - query: 'import "section" | nodes | section::find("Design") | section::body()'
    from: notes/design.md
---

# Show types on hover

Implement what the design note says.

Sessions are Markdown as well, so you can query your agents' history:

# Learnings from every session
mq -A 'import "section" | section::find("Learnings") | section::body()' sessions/*.md

# Every command the agent ran
mq 'select(.code.lang == "tool:Bash") | .code.value' sessions/*.md

Other things in there

  • Compare 2 to 4 runs of the same task (Claude models, Codex and others) side by side
  • Checks that run after each turn, with failures sent back to the agent
  • Approval cards for tool calls, and resume for interrupted sessions
  • Notifications when a session finishes, fails or needs approval
  • Built with Rust and Tauri

Try it 

git clone https://github.com/harehare/marq
cd marq
pnpm install
pnpm tauri dev

You need Rust, Node.js, pnpm and a logged-in claude CLI. Open any folder of Markdown files as the vault. Then hover a heading and choose Ask, or press ⌘N for a new task.

I'm still working out which parts are useful and which aren't. If something breaks or is missing, please open an issue or leave a comment.

Repo: https://github.com/harehare/marq

title: Three UX Choices That Make a Chinese Astrology Chart Easier to Enter
description:
I tested a Chinese astrology product called Taibu with a synthetic birth record: 1992-09-18 14:30, Shanghai, male. The goal was not to compare interpretations. It was to see how the product handles inputs, chart output, and the first-run experience.

This is an AI-assisted draft, reviewed and edited by me. The test was run on 2026-11-15.

1. No login before the first chart

The BaZi page does not require login. The form asks for an optional name, gender, calendar type, birth date/time, and an optional birthplace.

After submit, the result page opens immediately. For a first-time user, that is a low-friction path: see the chart before creating an account.

2. A professional view and a basic view

The default result is a “professional chart”: four pillars, ten gods, hidden stems, growth phases, void branches, na-yin, and shen-sha, followed by decade luck, annual luck, and monthly luck.

That is the right density for someone who already knows BaZi. For a first-time user, the product also has a “basic information” tab. It starts with the day master and explains the ten gods in plain language, marking which ones appear in the chart.

The lesson is simple: if a chart has two audiences, give them two entry points. Do not make the expert view carry the onboarding burden.

3. Palace-level interaction for Ziwei

The Ziwei result starts with the key facts: five-element bureau, life palace, body palace, and current decade. Below that is a twelve-palace grid with natal, period, and flying-star tabs.

Clicking a palace updates the triangle and opposite palace, and the side panel shows the main stars, auxiliary stars, minor stars, and decade range for that palace.

This is the strongest part of the product. A static twelve-palace table is hard to read; a palace-level detail panel gives the user a path through the chart.

The result page keeps the next step close

Save, share, copy, and ask-follow-up actions are all on the result page. The deeper notes view asks the user to save the chart first, which makes sense as a follow-up entry point rather than the first step.

Cross-check note

I ran the same synthetic sample through the Liki astrology engine and compared the four pillars and key Ziwei fields. They matched on this sample. That is one sample, not a claim about overall accuracy.

The product is complete and the interaction model is clear. The three choices above are worth keeping.

Boundary: traditional culture perspective, for reference only, not professional advice. 传统文化视角，仅供参考，不构成专业建议。

title: cryptship | Part 2 — Air-Gapped, On-Prem, Cloud: One Loader, Three Key Providers
description:
Customers run software in very different places: a disconnected network, their own data centre, or a cloud account. cryptship handles all three with one loader and one license format. The only thing that changes is how the content key is obtained.

🔌 Key providers

That choice is a single pluggable interface, pkg/keyprovider:

Mode Provider Binding Revocation
Air-gapped offline machine fingerprint, or none expiry only
On-prem / cloud online a per-license secret held by your server real: the server declines
Confidential attested SEV-SNP / TDX attestation gates the key planned: interface and mock only today

🛫 offline: no network, ever

Everything needed to unwrap the key is in the license and the machine. Revocation is by expiry: issue short-lived licenses and renew them. Binding policies none, strict and pool all work offline.

🌐 online: revocation that works

With online, the per-license binding secret stays on your server. The reference cryptship-server is a stateless key broker: the loader fetches the secret, and the server answers with a signed, nonce-bound response, so replaying an old answer does not work. Revoke a license on the server (--revoke) and its next start fails; instances already running keep running.

If the key server is unreachable, an online-bound app does not start. Separately, a license can carry an optional revocation_url; for that check alone you choose what happens on a network error: open, closed, or grace:<duration>.

🔐 attested: for when the host is not trusted

The attested provider releases the key only to a guest that proves, through hardware attestation, that it is running the expected code in a confidential VM (AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX). In v0.1.0 it is built behind an Attester interface and tested with a mock key broker; real quote generation needs confidential-compute hardware and is on the roadmap.

☸️ Deploying it

The repo's deploy/ folder has a seccomp profile and documented Docker and Kubernetes snippets for a hardened run: a non-root user (set in the Kubernetes example), dropped capabilities, a read-only root filesystem and a tmpfs for the decrypted app. More on what those do and do not stop in Part 3.

🔁 Keys change; licenses keep working

Signing keys live in a key ring identified by signing_key_id, so you can rotate your signing key without invalidating licenses already in the field.

🔗 cryptship

  • 📦 Release: v0.1.0

title: Pagination Testing: Can a Peer Find the Record Beyond Page One?
description:
Pagination testing should show whether someone can find the right record beyond the first page and return to their work without losing context. A public SaaS demo that only opens page one leaves that question unanswered, even when the pagination controls look finished.

For a developer building in public, this is a useful task to share with founder peers. Give them a safe dataset, a specific record to locate and a reason to open it. Then observe where the route becomes unclear. You get a more concrete conversation than asking whether the new table looks good.

The following test plan uses a fictional invoicing product. It is a proposed workflow, not a report of testing a real product. All customer names, records and situations should be synthetic in any public version you create.

Start with a record that is not immediately visible

Create enough sample invoices to require several pages at the page size used in the demo. Put a known target somewhere beyond the first page, and record its identity in your private test notes so you can check what the peer eventually opens.

The task might be: find the unpaid invoice for a named fictional customer, open its details and return to the invoice list to continue checking overdue work. Do not tell the reviewer which page contains it. That would remove part of the navigation question.

Include plausible distractors. Two invoices might belong to the same sample customer but have different dates or payment states. The point is to see whether someone identifies the correct record, not merely whether they can operate a Next button.

Before inviting anyone, confirm that the task is possible with the supplied account and data. A reviewer should not need access to your development tools, private database or personal explanation to complete the route you are asking them to assess.

Establish what pagination is doing

The U.S. Web Design System's pagination guidance describes pagination as dividing content across pages. Its guidance also covers navigation labels, the current page and testing an implementation in its own context. Using a familiar component does not verify the surrounding product flow.

In your demo, explain what one page contains. Is the list filtered to unpaid invoices, or does it show every invoice? Does the page indicator refer to the current filtered set? Can the reviewer tell whether additional results exist?

Avoid adding implementation detail that the reviewer cannot use. They do not need a description of your database cursor to say that they expected another page of unpaid invoices. Developers can investigate the technical cause after the task exposes the confusing behavior.

If the list has a changing or unknown total, describe that honestly. Do not display a precise final page merely because a static mockup had room for one. The interface should reflect what the product actually knows about the available results.

Change the filter while away from page one

After the reviewer has moved forward, ask them to limit the list to a different payment state. Observe what happens to the current page and the visible explanation of the results.

A useful question is whether the new view makes sense on its own. If the filter leaves fewer pages than the previous view, does the product show a useful result or an unexplained empty table? If it moves to the first page, can the reviewer understand that they are viewing a new set?

Do not assume there is one correct page-reset behavior for every product. Write the intended behavior for your workflow, then compare it with the actual experience. The test should expose a mismatch between the chosen design and the task, rather than enforce a rule you never considered.

Repeat with a filter that deliberately matches no records. A legitimate empty result needs a different explanation from a failed request. Ask the peer what they think happened before you explain it. Their answer may reveal whether the state communicates the distinction.

Sort the collection, not just the visible rows

Give the reviewer a task that depends on ordering across pages, such as finding the oldest unpaid sample invoice. Then ask them to change the sort order and explain which record they expect to appear first.

Check whether the behavior matches the product's stated scope. If a control is presented as sorting the whole list, sorting only the currently loaded rows would create a misleading route through the collection. A polished arrow beside the column name would not resolve that problem.

Include records with equal values in the chosen sort field. Watch for records appearing twice or disappearing while the reviewer moves between pages. These observations are reasons to investigate ordering and page boundaries; they are not enough by themselves to diagnose a particular backend defect.

Record the relevant conditions with the observation: the selected filter, sort direction, page and target record. A report that simply says pagination is broken gives a collaborator far less to reproduce.

Open details and follow the return path

Once the reviewer finds the target, ask them to open it, inspect a safe detail and return to the list. Let them choose the return control they naturally notice. That may be a product link or the browser's Back button.

Look at what survives: the filter, sort order, page and enough position context to continue the task. The product may deliberately reset some state, but that choice should fit the work rather than happen accidentally because the list remounted.

Now ask the reviewer to locate the next invoice they intended to inspect. If they must rebuild the previous view from memory, note the extra work and ask what context they expected to keep. Avoid coaching them through the return route while claiming they completed it independently.

Check the same path after reloading the details page when that is a supported product action. A navigation flow that works only when entered from one particular demo sequence can be fragile for someone following a shared link later.

Notice keyboard access and changing data

Run a separate pass using the keyboard. Check whether the pagination controls can be reached and operated, whether their labels explain the action, and whether the current page is conveyed. Inspect your rendered implementation instead of assuming the component library guarantees the result.

Also decide what the test should do when the sample collection changes. You can add or remove a synthetic record between page visits and observe the outcome. Keep that controlled change separate from the first usability pass so you know which conditions produced the observation.

A moving collection may need different behavior from a stable report. The test's purpose is to understand the tradeoff you have implemented, including whether someone can still find a known record. It does not require promising that every list will remain identical while other users change it.

Share the task and the limits of the result

Buildside is a place for founders to share progress, questions and lessons. A public-building update about pagination can include the task, a safe demo link and one question about the route through the records.

Publish what you changed after reviewing the observations. Distinguish a peer finding the right invoice from a peer saying that the list looks clean. Both can be encouraging, but only one directly answers the retrieval question you set.

Preserve useful uncertainty. One founder completing the task does not establish that every customer, browser or access method can do so. A failed attempt may reveal an interface problem, an unsuitable task or a broken demo account. Investigate before generalizing.

Your next release note can be concrete: what navigation behavior changed, why it mattered to the task and which paths you rechecked. That gives developers and potential users a visible account of the work. Pagination becomes more than a row of controls when the public demo follows a real task all the way back to the list.
