title: Get South Korea's CPI, unemployment, base rate and KRW/USD in English with Python
description:
If you model Asian economies, build a macro dashboard, or give an AI assistant a "what's inflation in Korea?" tool,
you eventually need South Korea's official numbers. They live in two places:

  • KOSIS — Statistics Korea's portal (CPI, employment, population, births…)
  • ECOS — the Bank of Korea's database (base rate, exchange rates, money supply, GDP…)

Both have free official APIs. In practice two things slow people down: you register for a key on each portal, and
KOSIS returns table, item and category names in Korean, so you end up building your own translation and parsing
layer before you can plot anything.

This post shows a shortcut: two small Apify actors that call those official APIs for you and return clean,
English-labelled time series — no Korean account or API key on your side.

What you get back

One row per observation, with English labels, a numeric value, the unit and the source:

table period item value unit
KOSIS DT_1J22003 2026-10 CPI, whole country 120.73 2020=100
KOSIS DT_1DA7001S 2026-10 Unemployment rate, total 2.0 %
ECOS 722Y001 2026-10 Bank of Korea base rate 3.0 % per annum
ECOS 731Y001 2026-11-13 KRW per USD 1332.4 Won

A small sanity check I like: CPI comes from Statistics Korea in KOSIS and is mirrored by the Bank of Korea in ECOS.
Pulled independently, both returned 120.05 / 120.43 / 120.73 for Aug–Oct 2026.

Every row also carries an attribution block (source, table, the official table URL, retrieval date), so a chart
or an AI answer can cite where the number came from.

1. Python: several KOSIS tables in one call 

# pip install apify-client pandas
from apify_client import ApifyClient
import pandas as pd

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")

run = client.actor("kdata-hub/kosis-korea-stats").call(run_input={
    # ORGID/TBLID from the kosis.kr table URL; up to 20 tables per run
    "tables": ["101/DT_1J22003", "101/DT_1DA7001S"],
    "periodType": "M",
    "startPeriod": "202401",
    "endPeriod": "202610",
})
df = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

cpi = df[(df.table_id == "DT_1J22003") & (df.item_id == "T") & (df.category_code == "T10")]
unemp = df[(df.table_id == "DT_1DA7001S") & (df.item_id == "T80") & (df.category_code == "0")]
print(cpi[["period", "value"]].tail(3))
print(unemp[["period", "value"]].tail(3))

Note on size: this pulls every item and category of both tables — 1,634 rows for this period (about $3.27).
To fetch only what you need, run one table at a time with "itemId" and "classL1" set (CPI total:
"itemId": "T", "classL1": "T10"; unemployment rate total: "itemId": "T80", "classL1": "0") — 34 rows each.

Any table you can open on kosis.kr works — the address bar shows orgId=…&tblId=…. You don't need to know how many
classification levels a table has; the actor detects that. If one table id is wrong, the other tables still return
and the bad one is named in the run log (a failed table produces no rows, so it isn't charged).

2. Python: Bank of Korea rates and FX 

run = client.actor("kdata-hub/ecos-korea-stats").call(run_input={
    # STATCODE or STATCODE/ITEMCODE1 — item codes differ per table
    "statCodes": ["722Y001/0101000", "901Y009/0"],   # base rate, CPI
    "frequency": "M",
    "startPeriod": "202401",
    "endPeriod": "202610",
})
rates = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
print(rates.pivot(index="period", columns="stat_code", values="value").tail(3))

For daily KRW/USD use "statCodes": ["731Y001/0000001"], "frequency": "D". All tables in one run share the
frequency. Not sure about codes? Run the actor with "mode": "items" and a table code to list its items.

3. From an AI assistant (MCP)

Apify's MCP server (https://mcp.apify.com) exposes public actors as tools for Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor,
VS Code and other MCP clients. After adding it, a prompt like this works:

Use the Apify actor kdata-hub/kosis-korea-stats to get South Korea's monthly CPI and unemployment rate
(tables 101/DT_1J22003 and 101/DT_1DA7001S) from 2024-01 to 2026-10 and chart them.

Because rows are already in English with units and a source URL, the assistant can answer and cite in one step.

Ready-made examples (one click)

  • Korea CPI, monthly — https://apify.com/kdata-hub/kosis-korea-stats/examples/korea-cpi-monthly
  • Korea unemployment rate, monthly — https://apify.com/kdata-hub/kosis-korea-stats/examples/korea-unemployment-rate-monthly
  • Bank of Korea base rate, monthly — https://apify.com/kdata-hub/ecos-korea-stats/examples/korea-base-rate-monthly
  • KRW/USD, daily — https://apify.com/kdata-hub/ecos-korea-stats/examples/krw-usd-exchange-rate-daily

Cost and limits

  • Pay per result: $2 per 1,000 rows. A 34-month CPI series filtered to the headline index is 34 rows (about $0.07); a whole multi-item table costs more, so filter items when you can.
  • Up to 20 tables per run; maxRecords caps rows per table and the run reports truncation.
  • The numbers are the official KOSIS / ECOS values, not estimates; if the official source has a gap, the row says so (value_status) instead of inventing a value.

When not to use this

If you only need one or two headline series and are happy with a monthly lag, a free aggregator may be enough.
This is for when you want any Korean table, in English, with sources, from code or an AI tool — without
setting up Korean accounts and translation yourself.

Data: Statistics Korea (KOSIS) and Bank of Korea (ECOS). The actors are independent tools that call the official
open APIs; they are not affiliated with or endorsed by those institutions.

title: Webhook Retry Queue: Delayed Jobs and Idempotency in Node.js
description:
Short answer: treat a webhook retry queue as an at-least-once transport, and make the durable business change idempotent with a stable event identity and a database transaction.

The deciding constraint is the gap between doing work and acknowledging it. A worker can commit a change, lose its process before the acknowledgement is recorded, and receive the same job again. No reasonable retry policy can infer whether that first change happened. Delayed jobs help recovery; they do not close that gap.

For an AI application, that distinction matters twice. A repeated state change can corrupt customer state, while a repeated call to a model or external API can consume latency and usage budget without producing a new result. Keep the queue simple, but make its boundaries explicit.

Why do webhook retry queues create duplicate processing with delayed jobs and at-least-once delivery?

There are usually two independent retry loops. The webhook sender retries when it does not receive a timely success response. The receiving system may then retry its queued work after a timeout, a process restart, or an unavailable dependency. Both loops are valid, and either can place the same logical event in front of a handler more than once.

Consider a delivery carrying evt_482. The receiver accepts it and places it in durable work storage. A worker charges ahead: it writes the new subscription status, commits the transaction, and is interrupted before its queue acknowledgement becomes durable. On recovery, the queue sees an unacknowledged attempt and makes evt_482 runnable again. The second worker is not seeing a new customer action. It is seeing an unresolved delivery outcome.

That is why "exactly once" is a misleading promise for most distributed systems. The sender, queue, worker, database, and any downstream service do not share one atomic commit. The useful target is one durable business effect for each logical event, even though execution can repeat.

A scheduled retry introduces a separate ordering question. If an older account update waits in a delayed set while a newer update completes, blindly applying the older message later can roll state back. Put a producer version, sequence, or monotonic timestamp in the event when the domain has an ordering rule. The transaction that claims the event should also reject a stale transition.

The small failures are the dangerous ones. A 200 response proves that a hop responded; it does not prove that an intended state exists after a crash boundary.

Put the idempotency boundary around the business effect

Start with an event key that is stable across every delivery. A producer-supplied event ID is ideal. When the protocol does not offer one, derive a deterministic key from immutable business identifiers, the event type, and a source version. Generating a random key on receipt defeats deduplication because each retry looks unrelated.

Then claim that key in durable storage. An in-memory Set vanishes on restart and cannot coordinate multiple Node.js processes. A read followed by an insert is also insufficient: two workers can both observe an absent row before either write wins. A unique constraint or equivalent conditional insert gives the database one clear arbitration point.

One key, one ledger.

Here is the full decision path worth testing before calling a handler safe. A signed delivery with evt_482 arrives twice because the sender did not observe the receiver's first response; both requests validate to the same identity, and both attempts try to enqueue work. Queue-level deduplication may collapse those attempts, but it is an efficiency optimization rather than proof, since one request may have reached the queue through a different path or after queue history has been cleaned up. A worker claims evt_482 and writes the account status. If that worker finishes normally, it acknowledges the job. If it exits after the transaction and before the acknowledgement, another worker can later receive the same job. Its conditional claim sees the existing event record and does no second business mutation. If version 12 has already changed the account, an older delayed version 11 must likewise fail the state transition check even if it has an event identity never seen before. Finally, if applying the change creates outbound work, that work is written as an outbox record in the same transaction. A separate dispatcher can make repeated delivery attempts visible against that outbox identity. Each step has a different purpose: request authentication establishes trust, event identity groups repeated deliveries, a unique claim stops duplicate effects, a version rule protects ordering, and an outbox prevents a committed state change from being forgotten before follow-up work is scheduled. Folding them into a single "retry" setting makes incidents hard to explain.

This focused TypeScript sketch uses generic interfaces deliberately. The queue can reduce redundant scheduling with an event-derived job key, but the transaction owns correctness because redelivery can originate upstream of the queue as well.

type Delivery = {
  eventId: string;
  accountId: string;
  version: number;
  status: "active" | "paused";
};

type Queue = {
  enqueue(name: string, delivery: Delivery, options: {
    key: string;
    attempts: number;
    delayMs: number;
  }): Promise<void>;
};

type Transaction = {
  claimEvent(eventId: string): Promise<boolean>;
  updateAccountIfNewer(input: Delivery): Promise<void>;
};

declare const queue: Queue;
declare const database: { transaction<T>(work: (tx: Transaction) => Promise<T>): Promise<T> };

export async function acceptDelivery(delivery: Delivery): Promise<void> {
  await queue.enqueue("apply-account-status", delivery, {
    key: delivery.eventId,
    attempts: 6,
    delayMs: 1_000,
  });
}

export async function applyDelivery(delivery: Delivery): Promise<void> {
  await database.transaction(async (tx) => {
    if (!(await tx.claimEvent(delivery.eventId))) return;
    await tx.updateAccountIfNewer(delivery);
  });
}

The required behavior of claimEvent is a durable, unique claim. updateAccountIfNewer enforces the domain's ordering rule in the same transaction. In some domains, such as adding an immutable audit record, version ordering is unnecessary; in others, such as a mutable subscription state, it is central. Don't invent an ordering rule where the producer cannot support one.

External side effects need a further decision. A database transaction cannot atomically commit an email, payment request, or model call owned by another system. Persist an outbox record with the business mutation, then have a worker deliver that record using the same idempotency identity when the destination supports it. If the destination has no idempotency mechanism, the remaining ambiguity should be documented and monitored rather than hidden behind a retry count.

Which retry failures should become delayed work?

Retry only failures that can change with time. A transient network timeout, a rate limit, or a temporary dependency overload may merit exponential backoff with jitter. Invalid signatures, malformed payloads, and prohibited state transitions will not become valid because they wait longer. Record them as terminal outcomes with a reason an operator can inspect.

Set a finite attempt budget. Without one, a bad event becomes permanent background activity and can repeat expensive downstream calls. The right limit depends on the business deadline, the retry schedule, and the recovery expectation; it is not a universal queue setting. I'm not sure a generic default will fit a payment update and a low-priority analytics event equally well, because their consequences and freshness requirements differ.

For inbound webhooks, authenticate before accepting work, validate the payload shape, write the acceptance record durably, and return promptly. For outbound webhooks whose destination is user-controlled, the dispatcher is also an SSRF boundary. Restrict allowed schemes and destinations, validate resolved addresses, and control network egress as OWASP recommends. URL parsing alone is not a security policy.

The catch is operational ownership. A database-backed work table is often enough for modest volume, but its leases, polling behavior, and cleanup remain application work. A separate queue can give delayed work clearer lifecycle states, but it introduces another service to monitor. A workflow runtime can fit long-lived, multi-step compensation, yet it adds a mental model that is excessive for one database update. Choose the smallest system whose acknowledgement and recovery behavior the on-call engineer can explain.

Shape Fits best when Responsibility that stays with the team
Database work table Work volume is modest and state lives in one database Leasing, polling, and cleanup
Dedicated queue Delayed work needs explicit lifecycle states Queue operations and worker capacity
Workflow runtime Work has timers, compensations, and several durable steps Runtime model and operational visibility

Test the acknowledgement gap, then measure the outcome

Happy-path tests do not exercise the reason queues redeliver. Use a real database in an integration test and run two handlers for the same event identity concurrently. Assert that one durable transition results. Then repeat the handler after the first transaction has committed, simulate a delayed version 10 arriving after version 11, exhaust the attempt budget for an invalid event, and verify that replay retains its original identity.

The test should distinguish duplicate execution from duplicate effect. The former is expected under at-least-once delivery. The latter is a defect.

Production metrics should make that distinction visible. Track oldest runnable-job age, ready and delayed counts, attempt distribution, terminal outcomes, worker duration, and the number of duplicate claims. Pair those transport signals with a business completion marker. Queue depth alone is weak evidence: a large delayed backlog may be planned, while a small set of old runnable jobs may indicate an urgent processing gap.

Carry the event ID, job identifier, attempt number, and a non-secret destination identifier through logs and traces. Do not log signing secrets or whole sensitive payloads. Also count calls per logical event, particularly where a handler invokes token-metered work. The ledger claim belongs before an expensive action, and reusable output should be persisted when the business operation allows it.

Before copying this design, measure duplicate executions, duplicate business effects, recovery time, oldest-job age, and calls per event. Those numbers reveal whether a delayed-job policy is buying recovery or just postponing an unsafe handler.

References

  • OWASP SSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • BullMQ documentation: https://docs.bullmq.io/

title: Sephora API Example: A Price and Stock Check Tool for an AI Agent
description:
Ask an AI agent what Rare Beauty's Soft Pinch Liquid Blush costs at Sephora, and the first thing it sees is the search result: "listPrice": "$16.00 - $25.00". Which number goes in the answer? The $16 is a 3.2 mL mini. The $25 is the 7.5 mL full size. Per millilitre, the mini costs 50% more.

That is not a rare case. I asked the Sephora API 15 shopping questions, typed the way a shopper types them, and 11 of the 15 products came back with a range instead of a price. Search itself did well: the first result matched the product named in 15 of 15 questions. The trouble starts after that, when the agent has to pick a size, a shade and a store.

What I asked, and how

The questions were the plain kind: "dior lip glow oil", "tatcha water cream", "ysl libre perfume", "dyson airwrap", "olaplex no 3", and ten more across makeup, skincare, hair and fragrance. For each one I ran what an agent connected to the Sephora API would run, on 4 November 2026:

  1. /search-by-keyword with the question, 10 results.
  2. /product-details for the product the shopper meant, which lists every size and shade as a SKU.
  3. /product-availability for that product's default SKU, within 10 miles of one of five US cities (New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, Houston, Seattle).

Over MCP, these are three tools: RapidAPI's gateway turns every endpoint of the API into one (how to connect it). So the raw responses below are exactly what a model would read. In all that was 116 search rows, 15 product records with 140 SKUs, and 204 store rows.

The search price is usually a range

Product Search says Default SKU Best value Smallest size pays
Rare Beauty Soft Pinch Blush $16.00 - $25.00 7.5 mL, $25 7.5 mL, $3.33/mL +50%
Drunk Elephant Protini $24.00 - $99.00 50 mL, $72 100 mL, $0.99/mL +62%
Glow Recipe Dew Drops $20.00 - $49.00 40 mL, $36 80 mL, $0.61/mL +118%
The Ordinary Niacinamide $6.00 - $10.80 30 mL, $6 60 mL, $0.18/mL +11%
Sol de Janeiro Bum Bum Cream $24.00 - $48.00 240 mL, $48 240 mL at $44, $0.18/mL +75%
Olaplex No.3PLUS $34.00 - $68.00 100 mL, $34 250 mL, $0.27/mL +25%
Tatcha The Water Cream $25.00 - $93.00 50 mL, $74 75 mL, $1.24/mL +34%
YSL Libre Eau de Parfum $38.00 - $225.00 90 mL, $185 100 mL, $1.40/mL +171%
Huda Beauty Easy Bake $24.00 - $42.00 2 x 6.5 g, $42 20 g, $2.00/g +100%

In 9 of the 11 ranges, the low end is the price of the smallest size. An agent that reports "from $24" for Drunk Elephant's Protini is quoting a 15 mL jar of a cream most people buy at 50 mL. An agent that reports the high end is often quoting the biggest bottle. Neither is what the shopper meant by "how much is it".

The product record does not settle it either. Each product has a default SKU (the currentSku in /product-details, the same SKU the search row points to for 13 of the 15), and it is often neither the cheapest nor the most common size. For YSL Libre it is the 90 mL bottle at $185. For Glow Recipe it is the 40 mL at $36, a size the search range never mentions.

Per millilitre or gram, the smallest size cost more in all 9 products with a real choice of sizes, a median of 62% more than the best-value size. YSL Libre is the extreme: the 10 mL spray works out at $3.80/mL, the best value is $1.40/mL. And that best value is not the biggest bottle. The 100 mL at $140 costs less than the 90 mL at $185, and it is the one SKU with isOnlineOnly: true. An agent comparing sizes by eye would miss it. An agent that computes price per mL finds it at once.

Shades and models have prices too

11 of the 15 products carried more than one list price across their SKUs. Sizes explain most of it, but not all. Laneige's Lip Sleeping Mask costs $24 in most flavours and $25 in three, two of them limited editions. Charlotte Tilbury's Matte Revolution costs $37, except in two shades at $39. So "how much is the Pillow Talk lipstick" has a right answer only after the agent resolves the shade to a SKU.

Dyson is the other kind of ambiguity. The search for "dyson airwrap" returned 7 different multi-stylers in the top 10, at $649, $699 and $749, plus attachments. The first one, the agent's natural pick, had isOutOfStock: true on its only SKU, and none of the 6 stores near Houston had it. A good answer there is a question back to the user: which Airwrap?

Store stock: read the units, not the label

Across the 204 store rows, 160 said "In Stock", 18 "Limited Stock" and 26 "Out of Stock". 14 of the 15 products were on a shelf somewhere near their city. Three details matter for an agent:

The label is not a unit count. 4 store rows said "In Stock" with exactly 1 unit on hand. 4 said "Limited Stock" with 5 or more, up to 21 for The Ordinary's serum in Houston. If the user is about to drive somewhere, inStoreAvailability is the number to pass on.

Some stores are inside Kohl's. 24 of the 204 rows were Sephora counters inside Kohl's stores (storeType is not SEPHORA), and 15 of them had the item. That is worth saying in the answer, because a shopper heading to "the Sephora in Jersey City" will not find a standalone store.

The search row's pickup flag says nothing about stores. pickupEligible was false on all 116 search rows, including the 14 products that were in stock nearby. It describes the search context, not shelves. Only /product-availability answers "can I pick it up today?"

The tool

None of this needs a model to reason about it. It needs a tool that does the arithmetic and hands the model a short answer: every size once with its price per mL or gram, the SKU for the shade the user named, and the nearest stores with units. Here is that tool, runnable as printed with a RapidAPI key:

"""A price and stock check tool for an AI agent, over the Sephora API on RapidAPI.

Three calls (search, product record, store stock) in, one small answer out: every size with
its price per mL or gram, the shade or size the shopper asked for, and the nearest stores
that have it.

    RAPIDAPI_KEY=... python3 sephora_price_check.py "rare beauty soft pinch liquid blush" Happy 40.758 -73.9855
"""
import json
import os
import re
import sys

import requests

HOST = "real-time-sephora-api.p.rapidapi.com"
BASE = os.environ.get("API_BASE", "https://" + HOST)


def headers():
    if "API_BASE" in os.environ:
        return json.loads(os.environ.get("API_HEADERS", "{}"))
    return {"x-rapidapi-host": HOST, "x-rapidapi-key": os.environ["RAPIDAPI_KEY"]}


def get(path, **params):
    r = requests.get(BASE + path, params=params, headers=headers(), timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()


def dollars(text):
    m = re.search(r"\$([\d,]+(?:\.\d+)?)", text or "")
    return float(m.group(1).replace(",", "")) if m else None


def amount(size):
    """'0.25 oz/ 7.5 mL' -> (7.5, 'mL'), '0.21 oz/6 g' -> (6.0, 'g'). None if neither is given."""
    m = re.search(r"([\d.]+)\s*ml", size or "", re.I) or re.search(r"([\d.]+)\s*g\b", size or "", re.I)
    if not m:
        return None
    return float(m.group(1)), "mL" if "ml" in m.group(0).lower() else "g"


def sku_row(k):
    price = dollars(k.get("salePrice")) or dollars(k.get("listPrice"))
    a = amount(k.get("size"))
    return {
        "sku": k["skuId"],
        "option": k.get("variationValue"),
        "size": (k.get("size") or "").strip() or None,
        "price_usd": price,
        "was_usd": dollars(k.get("listPrice")) if k.get("salePrice") else None,
        "per_unit": "%.2f/%s" % (price / a[0], a[1]) if a and price else None,
        "online_only": k.get("isOnlineOnly"),
        "sold_out_online": k.get("isOutOfStock"),
    }


def check_price(query, option=None, lat=None, lon=None):
    rows = get("/search-by-keyword", keyword=query, pageSize=10)
    full_size = [r for r in rows if not r["displayName"].lower().startswith("mini ")]
    if not full_size:
        return {"error": "no product found for %r" % query}
    product = full_size[0]
    details = get("/product-details", productId=product["productId"])

    skus, seen = [], set()
    for k in [details["currentSku"]] + details.get("regularChildSkus", []):
        if k["skuId"] not in seen:
            seen.add(k["skuId"])
            skus.append(sku_row(k))
    chosen = skus[0]  # the product's default SKU
    if option:
        chosen = next((s for s in skus if option.lower() in (s["option"] or "").lower()), chosen)

    # Many shades share a size and a price, spelled several ways: list each size and price once
    sizes = {}
    for s in skus:
        key = (amount(s["size"]) or s["size"], s["price_usd"])
        sizes.setdefault(key, dict(s, options=0))["options"] += 1
    answer = {
        "product": "%s %s" % (product["brandName"], product["displayName"]),
        "url": details.get("fullSiteProductUrl"),
        "chosen": chosen,
        "sizes": [{"size": v["size"], "price_usd": v["price_usd"], "per_unit": v["per_unit"],
                   "online_only": v["online_only"], "options": v["options"]} for v in sizes.values()],
    }
    if lat is not None:
        stock = get("/product-availability", skuId=chosen["sku"], latitude=lat, longitude=lon, radius=10)
        stores = stock["data"]["stores"]
        answer["stores"] = [{"store": x["displayName"], "miles": x["distance"], "units": x["inStoreAvailability"],
                             "status": x["availabilityStatus"], "inside_kohls": x["storeType"] != "SEPHORA"}
                            for x in stores if x["inStoreAvailability"] > 0][:5]
        answer["stores_checked"] = len(stores)
    return answer


if __name__ == "__main__":
    q = sys.argv[1]
    opt = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None
    lat, lon = (float(sys.argv[3]), float(sys.argv[4])) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else (None, None)
    result = check_price(q, opt, lat, lon)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=1))
    print("answer: %d characters" % len(json.dumps(result, separators=(",", ":"))))

For the blush in the shade Happy, near Times Square, it chose SKU 2362085 (7.5 mL, $25, $3.33/mL), listed the two sizes once each (14 shades of the full size, 8 of the mini at $5.00/mL), and returned the five nearest stores with units, Times Square first with 97. The whole answer was 1,007 characters. The three raw responses behind it run to about 199,000 characters in my test calls (13,228 for the search, 129,780 for the product record, about 55,700 for the stores), roughly 49,700 tokens at four characters a token. That is an estimate, since every model's tokenizer differs, but the gap is the point.

To give it to Claude or another agent, wrap check_price as one tool with three inputs (query, option, and a location), in whatever framework you use, or as a tool of your own MCP server next to the gateway's endpoint tools.

Pitfalls in the data

Size strings are free text. Fenty's Gloss Bomb has 10 SKUs and 7 spellings of its size, among them 0.3 oz/ 9 mL, 0.30 oz, 0.3 oz/9 oz and 0.30 oz/9 g. Huda Beauty's powder has 7. Parse the mL or gram figure, and treat a size with neither as unknown. Four SKUs had no size at all.

Same size, different price. Sol de Janeiro's Bum Bum Cream has two 240 mL SKUs, at $48 and $44, and nothing in the size field says how they differ. Tatcha and Drunk Elephant list refills of the 50 mL at $68 and $63 next to the jars at $74 and $72; there the size says "Refill". Show the user both.

Minis live in two places. A mini is often both a SKU of the main product and a separate "Mini ..." product in search. 39 of the 116 search rows were minis or sets. The tool skips the "Mini" products in search and gets the mini sizes from the main record, so each size appears once.

Sales are rare and live in salePrice. Only 1 of the 116 search rows was on sale (a Charlotte Tilbury mini lipstick set, $26 down to $18.20). When salePrice is set, it is the price, and listPrice is the was-price.

The range and the record can disagree. For 14 of the 15 products, the search range matched the lowest and highest SKU prices exactly. For Laneige's mask, the range started at $23 while every SKU in the product record cost $24 or $25. Quote the record.

What I would do next

Add a size preference to the tool ("the usual size", "the best value", "travel size") so the agent can answer the question the user asked without asking back, and cache product records for a day, since prices change less often than stock.

The Sephora API is on RapidAPI with a free plan for testing. More examples are in the Sephora API repo on GitHub, and the Sephora API overview on LinkedIn covers what the data includes. Building a shopping agent on beauty data, or need the catalog as a dataset? Get in touch.

title: Call controls that match the app: one floating-control component
description:
Floating call controls in Flutter get built twice: once for the call screen, and once more for whatever surface shows the call after the user leaves that screen. Ours had been built three times. The live control row was a set of solid grey discs with a red one at the end, the end card used stock Material filled and outlined buttons, and the top-left collapse button was a semi-transparent black circle with a white arrow. Each was individually reasonable. Together they made an active call look like a different app from the one that had started it.

The fix was one circular control component with two accents, plus a keyboard problem in the collapsed window that had nothing to do with styling at all.

Three surfaces, three dialects

The call screen is the most visually exposed state in the app: it covers everything, it usually sits over live video, and the user is holding the phone one-handed while looking at somebody's face. It is also the state where the buttons must be found without reading.

The old row was hand-rolled: a circle, a fixed colour, an icon, a gesture detector. That pattern is fine once; copied three times it produces three slightly different measurements and three ideas of what "off" looks like.

Meanwhile every other floating control — the navigation dock's destinations, the friends list actions, the profile edit button — had settled on a different vocabulary: a surface-filled circle with a two-pixel accent outline. The call screen was written before that vocabulary existed and nobody had a reason to revisit it.

Floating call controls in Flutter should not fork

The shared piece is CircleSurface: a circle filled with the theme's surface colour, outlined at two pixels, with the icon tinted to match. AppCircleButton wraps it in an IconButton and splits the visible circle from the tap target around it.

Container(
  width: size,
  height: size,
  decoration: BoxDecoration(
    shape: BoxShape.circle,
    color: colors.surface,
    border: Border.all(
      color: selected ? color : color.withValues(alpha: 0.6),
      width: 2,
    ),
  ),
  child: IconTheme(
    data: IconThemeData(color: color),
    child: child,
  ),
)

Two properties do the real work. The fill is the theme's surface, so the circle sits on glass, video or a photo rather than vanishing into a translucent overlay. And the outline is drawn at full strength for active controls instead of the muted sixty per cent used by inactive dock items. Over a bright video call, a muted outline is an invisible button.

The call screen composes CallActionButton: that circle at a call-specific size, plus a semantics label. The end card uses the same widget. The collapse control uses plain AppCircleButton at its default size, because it belongs to the top bar rather than the thumb row.

Why the call row is 72 dp and the dock is 40

CallActionButton defines one number: a 72 dp diameter, circle and tap target together. The app's mini floating button is 40 dp, and it is the right size for a list row you tap while looking at it.

A call is different. The user is often not looking at the controls at all; they are looking at the person, or at something in the room, and reaching by muscle memory. A 40 dp target over live video is a miss-tap magnet, and a miss-tap on a call row can mean hanging up on someone. Seventy-two is roughly the difference between aiming and hoping.

The glyph follows the size: 32 px icons inside the 72 dp circle, which keeps the visual weight close to the text-free dock buttons instead of turning them into tiny icons in big rings.

An audio call gets three controls, not four: mute, speaker, end. The camera switch only exists for video, so hiding it leaves the row evenly spaced rather than gapped where a fourth button would have been.

One shape, two accents

The destructive action should be recognisable, and the three usual ways are all worse than colour. A different shape breaks the row's rhythm; a bigger button makes the row unstable; a different material makes it look borrowed from another component library.

So the end call keeps the exact circle, outline weight and icon size, and changes only the accent: the theme's error colour replaces the primary one. A muted microphone does the same, because "your mic is off" is also a state the user needs to notice at a glance. Everything else stays primary. Shape carries identity; colour carries state.

This is why the accent is an optional parameter on the shared surface rather than a second widget. The dock, the chat header and the send button use the primary default, so the override touched nothing they rely on.

Accessibility labels did not change, deliberately. Mute and Unmute, Switch camera, Speaker on and Speaker off, End call — the icons are ambiguous by nature, and the labels are what makes the row usable with a screen reader. A visual refactor that quietly renamed them would be a regression dressed as a redesign.

The end card moves to where the thumb already is

The end card placed its two actions mid-column: a filled button and an outlined one under the call summary. Legible, and in the wrong place — the hand that just ended a call is at the bottom of the screen.

Both actions are now CallActionButtons in the same bottom row, with the same 24 dp padding and the same spaceEvenly, so redialling or leaving occupies the coordinates the user's thumb already knows. The icons are a phone and an arrow; the words "Call again" and "Back" survive as semantics labels rather than as visible text.

One ordering detail matters more than it sounds. The row is painted above the card's dismiss layer, so a press on either button acts immediately. If it sits below that layer, the first tap only dismisses the overlay and the user has to tap twice — a bug that looks like latency.

The collapsed window keeps its own smaller pair

The floating window an active call collapses into is a deliberately different surface. It is 132 by 180 logical pixels, it floats over whatever the user is doing, and it holds a peer video, a name, a running duration and two quick actions: mute and hang up.

A 72 dp circle does not fit in that card, and pretending otherwise would eat the video. So the window keeps two compact 36 dp discs. They use the same red for hang-up and the same semantics labels, and the mute button turns red when muted. It is the one place where the call controls are not the shared component, and that is a size decision rather than a style one.

The more interesting part of that window is its placement.

The keyboard is occupied space

Collapse a call, go back into a chat, and tap the composer. The software keyboard rises — and the floating call window was still where it had been left, sitting under the keyboard with its buttons and the peer's video hidden behind the keys.

The window lives above the navigator, mounted at the app level so it survives route changes while a call is running. That also means the keyboard never resizes it: the inset belongs to a different subtree, and the window has to notice and move itself.

The fix starts by treating the keyboard as part of the area that is no longer available:

final padding = MediaQuery.paddingOf(context);
final keyboard = MediaQuery.viewInsetsOf(context).bottom;
final bottomInset = keyboard > padding.bottom ? keyboard : padding.bottom;

That bottomInset is subtracted from the height the window may occupy, so the top-left corner it is allowed to reach stops where the keyboard begins. Dragging, clamping and edge snapping all keep working against the reduced rectangle.

The comparison is deliberately max, not a sum. The keyboard inset already extends down through the system's bottom padding, so adding the two would float the window far higher than the keyboard's actual top edge — technically clear, visually wrong, and worst on phones with a large home-indicator area.

Because both insets are read as MediaQuery dependencies, the window rebuilds as the keyboard animates and the safe area changes — no listener to leak, no controller to sync with an animation the system owns.

A lift that is not a position

The subtle half of the fix is that the lift must not be remembered.

The window stores its position as a fraction of the usable area — which side, how far down — and restores it on the next call. If the keyboard-driven lift wrote into that stored value, a user who typed one message mid-call would come back to a window pinned to the middle of the screen forever. The remembered position would be a fossil of a transient layout.

So the lift is display-only. The stored position is written by exactly one thing: a drag. While the keyboard is up, the window is resolved from its remembered fraction inside the shrunken area, which naturally puts it above the keyboard. When the keyboard closes, the area grows back and the window returns to the side and fraction it remembered.

Dragging while the keyboard is visible is the deliberate exception. That is a real decision by the user about where the window should live, so it saves the new spot — and it is saved as a fraction of the temporarily smaller area, which means it lands somewhere sensible in both states.

Because the remembered position is a fraction of the usable area rather than a pixel coordinate, the window lands proportionally: near the bottom of that area it lifts clear of the keyboard, and near the top it barely moves. Edge snapping still happens on release, measured against the reduced width.

The test that fakes a 300 px keyboard

Widget tests cannot summon a real keyboard, but they can set the inset that one produces. The test sets the device pixel ratio to one so physical and logical pixels agree, sizes the surface, pumps the overlay the same way the app mounts it, and records the window's rectangle.

It then asserts the bottom edge at one margin above the safe area in the default bottom-right spot, sets a 300 px bottom inset, and asserts that the window's bottom edge has moved above the keyboard — still one margin clear. Clearing the inset returns it to the original rectangle, which is the part that proves the lift was display-only rather than a new remembered position.

That last assertion is the one I would keep in any app with a floating surface. "It moves correctly" is easy to get right by accident; "it goes back" is the part that regresses silently.

The short version

  • One circle, one outline weight, one icon size: identity comes from shape, state comes from accent.
  • Size the row for the hand, not for the grid. 72 dp over live video is a feature; 40 dp is a gamble.
  • Keep semantics labels stable through a visual refactor; they are part of the contract.
  • Put the post-call actions where the controls were, and paint them above any dismiss layer.
  • Treat viewInsets.bottom as occupied space, and inset by max(bottom padding, keyboard) rather than their sum.
  • Never let a transient layout push write into remembered state; drag is the only author of position.
  • Test the return trip, not just the lift.

Both halves of this came from the same question: what does this surface need in order to be correct? For the buttons it was a size and a shape. For the window it was a rectangle that shrinks and a position that does not. The floating dock taught us the same thing about chrome: geometry first, then colour.

If you have a floating surface that has to survive a keyboard, I would like to hear which half bit you — the inset arithmetic or the remembered position.

title: Compare Cloud Storage Providers for Direct Browser Uploads — Node.js Retention Rules
description:
Property management teams should choose browser-upload storage by its trust boundary and retention controls, not by whether its SDK can mint a presigned URL. For training artifacts, the browser should receive permission for one object, for a short window, with a server-owned key and a separately enforced retention policy. The storage provider matters after those rules are clear.

A useful design has three planes: a Node.js service authorizes an upload, the browser sends bytes directly to object storage, and a worker records completion and applies retention metadata. That separation keeps credentials out of the browser, but it does not make the browser trustworthy. It can still retry, abandon a multipart upload, or send an unexpected content type. I treat those as normal states, not exceptional ones.

Ownership decides the boundary.

No exceptions.

What is the real trust boundary for a training upload?

A presigned URL is a bearer capability. Anyone who obtains it can use it until it expires or its constraints stop matching the request. The API should therefore decide the archive identity before it signs anything: property, course, employee or cohort, artifact type, maximum size, and an immutable object key. Do not accept a client-provided path such as training/finished.pdf and then try to sanitize it later.

For a property management system, an upload record might begin as pending, include the policy version that selected its retention class, and contain a digest once the object is verified. The browser gets an upload URL and an opaque upload ID. It does not get a storage access key, a bucket-wide listing permission, or permission to choose a retention date.

CORS is part of this boundary, but it is not authorization. It controls which browser origins may read or send certain cross-origin requests; it does not stop a non-browser client from using a valid bearer URL. Keep the allowed origins narrow, expose only the headers the upload flow needs, and test preflight behavior with the actual headers used by the browser. A permissive wildcard can hide a broken design during development.

How should the retention policy shape the upload path?

Start with the record, not the bucket. A policy table can map annual_safety_training to a retention class such as 7_years, while draft_course_material maps to 90_days. Store the selected class and policy version with the pending upload. At completion, the service verifies the object and queues the archive event. A later policy change should affect new records unless governance explicitly schedules a migration; silently rewriting old decisions is a difficult audit story.

The object key should be uninteresting and collision-resistant, for example properties/42/training/2026/10/opaque-id. The human filename belongs in metadata or the application database. This makes retries idempotent and prevents a filename from becoming an authorization primitive. It also gives the cleanup worker a stable query key when an employee uploads the same certificate twice.

S3 lifecycle rules are useful for expiration and transitions, but they are not a substitute for the policy record. The lifecycle documentation describes rules that can act on objects by prefixes, tags, or object age. Those selectors are operational tools. The application still needs to explain why this object received a particular tag and which policy version produced it.

How should cloud storage providers handle direct browser uploads?

The comparison becomes clearer after the contract is fixed. Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, and Wasabi all present S3-compatible patterns that can support direct uploads, but compatibility is not sameness. Check the exact signing behavior, multipart limits, CORS configuration surface, checksum support, lifecycle selectors, and event delivery available in the region and account you will use. For a property management archive, I would put that contract in a test matrix before anyone debates a default provider.

Provider Direct upload path Useful fit Main verification work
Amazon S3 Presigned requests and multipart APIs Teams that want a widely documented object API Check signing, lifecycle selectors, checksums, and abandoned-part cleanup
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible presigned requests Systems already organized around Cloudflare endpoints Check endpoint signing, CORS behavior, lifecycle rules, and events
Wasabi S3-compatible presigned requests Teams evaluating S3-compatible archive storage Check multipart completion, retention behavior, and verification metadata

Amazon S3 has the deepest reference material for multipart upload and lifecycle behavior, which reduces ambiguity when the team needs a long-lived archive. Cloudflare R2 emphasizes an S3-compatible API at Cloudflare's edge, so the relevant question is how its endpoint, CORS rules, and lifecycle behavior fit the existing signing and network path. Wasabi also exposes an S3-compatible API, but its operational fit should be tested against the same multipart-abort, retention, and verification cases rather than inferred from the shared API vocabulary.

That is three different engineering trade-offs, not a leaderboard. S3 may reduce specification uncertainty for a team already using its APIs. R2 may fit a system whose data path already depends on Cloudflare's network model. Wasabi may fit a team evaluating S3-compatible archive storage. None of those statements answers whether a seven-year training record is governed correctly. The table is a test plan, not a ranking: each row needs the same artifact set, the same browser origin, the same expiration window, and the same application-side verification before the result means anything.

I would put the provider adapter behind a small interface and run the same contract tests against each candidate. The test suite should create a presigned single-part upload, exercise an expired URL, upload a deliberately wrong content type, complete and abort a multipart upload, verify a checksum, and confirm that the lifecycle rule selects the intended class. A green SDK example is not enough.

How do you keep incomplete browser uploads from becoming archive debt?

Multipart upload is where direct browser flows become operational. It lets a large object upload in parts and be completed later, but an initiated upload that never completes can consume storage until it is explicitly aborted or cleaned up by a lifecycle rule. The browser can disappear when a laptop sleeps. Mobile networks can switch. Users close tabs. Plan for that.

The Node.js service should issue an upload session with a deadline and persist the expected part count or size range. A completion request must identify the application upload ID, not merely trust a list of object parts posted by the browser. The worker can then inspect object metadata, compare size and checksum where supported, and transition the record to verified. A timeout job marks abandoned sessions and relies on provider cleanup for unfinished multipart state.

Here is the shape of the authorization decision. The storage client is intentionally abstract; the point is the policy boundary, not a vendor SDK tutorial.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from uuid import uuid4


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class UploadGrant:
    upload_id: str
    object_key: str
    expires_at: datetime
    max_bytes: int
    retention_class: str


def create_training_grant(property_id: int, artifact_type: str) -> UploadGrant:
    policy = policy_for(artifact_type)  # Reads a versioned, server-owned policy.
    upload_id = str(uuid4())
    object_key = f"properties/{property_id}/training/2026/{upload_id}"
    expires_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(minutes=15)

    save_pending_upload(
        upload_id=upload_id,
        object_key=object_key,
        policy_version=policy.version,
        retention_class=policy.retention_class,
        expires_at=expires_at,
    )
    return UploadGrant(
        upload_id=upload_id,
        object_key=object_key,
        expires_at=expires_at,
        max_bytes=policy.max_bytes,
        retention_class=policy.retention_class,
    )

The real adapter would sign only the operation and headers the browser needs. It should not sign a broad prefix, accept arbitrary metadata that later drives retention, or treat a successful HTTP response as proof that the application record is complete. The completion endpoint owns that state transition.

What should a rollout prove before archive traffic moves?

Use a small corpus of synthetic artifacts: a 4 MB PDF, a near-limit video, an empty file, a duplicate filename, and a multipart upload abandoned after its second part. Include an origin that should pass CORS and one that should fail. Repeat the tests after rotating signing credentials and after changing the retention policy version. These cases expose more than a dashboard showing upload success.

Observe grant creation, upload completion, verification failures, expiration, abort cleanup, and lifecycle actions with the opaque upload ID. Do not put signed URLs in logs. Alert on pending uploads older than their grant window and on verified objects missing a retention class. For an audit, you want the policy decision and the object result without retaining a reusable capability. In a property management rollout, that means an auditor can start with a course record, follow its policy version to the pending upload, match the opaque key to the verified object, and see the cleanup outcome for an abandoned attempt. If any link in that chain exists only in a provider console, the archive is harder to explain and harder to migrate. The log should prove the decision without becoming another place where a bearer capability can leak.

The migration can be staged: shadow the policy decision, upload test artifacts to each candidate, compare verification and cleanup results, then move one property or training class at a time. Keep the application database as the source of business identity. Storage is the byte holder and the enforcement point for object operations; it should not become the only place where the organization remembers why a training record exists.

The decision rule is compact: pick the provider whose tested behavior matches your required signing, multipart, CORS, lifecycle, and verification contract. Then keep authorization and retention decisions in your service. Direct browser upload is a delivery optimization. It is not a governance model.

title: Before You Ship an AI-Built Web Feature, Test the Browser Fallback
description:
Imagine you're building a workshop registration page. An AI coding tool adds a polished session picker. You open the page, pick the afternoon slot, and register. Good enough to send to the client?

Not yet. You know the picker worked in the browser you opened. You don't know what a visitor sees when their browser can't apply the styling or positioning the picker relies on.

This article was prepared with AI assistance. The workshop example is hypothetical.

On November 10, Chrome for Developers announced Modern Web Guidance 1.0, with Firefox and Edge joining the effort. The project gives coding agents web platform guidance that includes browser compatibility data. Its fallback guide makes a distinction worth keeping even if you never install it: sometimes an unsupported feature can disappear harmlessly, and sometimes you need a second way to complete the task.

Here's the release checklist I'd use for that session picker.

1. Name the browsers before you name the solution

Write down the browser and device combinations the feature needs to support. Use the client's known requirements or product traffic when you have it. If you're starting from scratch, pick a reasonable initial support target and label it as an assumption. Don't let the coding tool infer the target from whichever browser happens to be on your laptop.

Baseline is a useful starting point. Newly available means a feature works across its core browsers; widely available means 30 months have passed since that point. Neither tells you which versions your particular visitors run. Ask the assistant to name the exact feature it wants to use and explain how it fits your targets. Check that answer before you approve the approach.

2. Define what must work without the enhancement

For the workshop page, I'd start with a labeled native select and a submit button. If the decorative layout doesn't apply, a user should still be able to see the available sessions, select one, submit, and read which session they booked. The native control doesn't have to look like the enhanced control. It has to finish the same job.

Make that difference explicit in the ticket: "If the enhanced picker isn't supported, show the regular session field. Submitting either version must use the same session identifier and show the same confirmation." Keep the enhancement separate from the submission logic so both paths don't drift into maintaining their own rules for a sold-out slot.

3. Run the same task through both paths

Try a registration in a supported browser, then repeat it where the feature isn't supported. Use test data and check the confirmation, not just whether the button was clickable. On both paths, try submitting without a selection and make sure the error tells you what to fix. Check that you can choose and submit with the keyboard without losing track of focus.

If you can't get the target browser right away, exercising the fallback in a test build can catch a logic error. Record that as fallback-path evidence, not proof that the target browser works. A smaller viewport is useful for layout testing, but it doesn't change which features the browser implements.

My handoff would be two short rows: browser and version, picker path, session chosen, confirmation observed, and any failure. If only one row has results, that's the honest state of the release.

The question isn't whether the enhanced picker looks good. It's whether someone can still register when that enhancement isn't there.

title: Analysing 68 Years of Atmospheric CO Data with Python
description:
Tags: #python #datascience #climatechange #dataanalytics

One of the most interesting things about data analysis is the opportunity to explore real scientific questions.

For my Keeling Curve Climate Data Analysis project, I worked with historical atmospheric carbon dioxide measurements and global temperature data.

What Is the Keeling Curve?

The Keeling Curve records the long-term increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations, using measurements that began at Mauna Loa in 1958.

The project explores data from March 1958 through May 2026, alongside global temperature anomaly data.

Project Objectives

I wanted to investigate:

  • How atmospheric CO₂ concentrations changed over time
  • Whether the average growth rate increased
  • How seasonal patterns appear in the data
  • How CO₂ and global temperature trends compare
  • How to communicate scientific findings through visualisations

Tools and Data

The project uses Python, Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib and Jupyter Notebook.

Its documented data sources include NOAA atmospheric CO₂ measurements and NASA GISS temperature anomaly data.

Key Findings

The repository reports:

Measure Result
CO₂, March 1958 315.7 ppm
CO₂, May 2026 432.3 ppm
Total increase 116.6 ppm
Percentage increase 36.9%
1960s annual growth 0.86 ppm/year
2020s annual growth 2.67 ppm/year

The analysis also reports a correlation of r = 0.966 between overlapping CO₂ and temperature time series.

This correlation should be interpreted carefully. Two strongly trending series can produce a high correlation, and correlation alone does not establish causation.

A Data-Quality Challenge

One interesting challenge involved the imported CO₂ dataset.

The expected column structure did not match the retrieved data fields.

Instead of immediately analysing the imported table, the project involved inspecting the structure, correcting column mappings and validating the results.

This reinforced an important lesson:

Never assume that imported data is analysis-ready.

Limitations

Mauna Loa is a monitoring location, not a direct measurement of every location on Earth.

The comparison also uses different observational datasets with their own measurement and modelling assumptions.

Further analysis could examine detrended relationships, uncertainty and seasonal adjustment.

Conclusion

This project helped me practise time-series analysis, data validation and scientific visualisation using real environmental data.

GitHub: https://github.com/tasnem-tech/keeling-curve-climate-data-analysis

title: I built a decision graph on HydraDB that learns from corrections. Here's what broke.
description:
Agents keep acting on engineering decisions that were reversed years ago. A 48-hour HydraDB build, the bugs I hit, and an honest baseline.

Every engineering team writes its decisions down. Then it changes its mind and writes another one. Two years later, search finds the old decision as easily as the new one, and an AI coding agent will happily build on a choice the team reversed long ago.

For the HydraDB hackathon I built DecisionGraph to fix that. It links each architecture decision record (ADR) to the records that replaced it. When an agent asks "what did we decide about X?", it walks those links to the decision that still stands and hands back that decision and its history, in about 130 tokens instead of 590. When someone corrects an answer, the correction is written into the graph, so the next question on that topic lands right even in different words.

  • Live app: https://decisiongraph-latest.onrender.com
  • Code: https://github.com/0xNexuz/decisiongraph
  • Video walkthrough: https://youtu.be/ChWL-frv5v8

The problem in one picture

Asked "Does each business unit get its own Cloud Platform cluster now?", vector search returns the closest text: a 2019 decision to run one shared cluster, which has been replaced three times since. DecisionGraph starts at the same record, then follows the "replaced by" links to the decision that stands today.

The data is about 130 real, public ADRs from three UK government engineering teams: MoJ Cloud Platform, MoJ Modernisation Platform and GOV.UK on AWS (all MIT licensed). The test set is 50 questions I wrote, scored before each correction is applied.

How it works

  1. Find the decision. Vector similarity, distinctive terms and hints from past corrections each vote for where the question starts.
  2. Walk to what replaced it. One HydraDB path query follows trusted "replaced by" links until it reaches a decision nothing has replaced.
  3. Learn from the correction. The links on the right path are confirmed, the wrong ones rejected, and the question is stored as a node so the next one like it starts in the right place.

Where HydraDB earned its place

Trust lives in the path cost

Every REPLACED_BY link has a cost: 1 if trusted, 100 if not. Walking only trusted links is then a single algo.MSpaths call with maxCost set to the path length, so one untrusted hop rules the path out:

CALL algo.MSpaths({
  sourceLabel: 'Decision', sourceProperty: 'key',
  sourceValues: ['cloud-platform:12'], targetValues: [...],
  relTypes: ['REPLACED_BY'], relDirection: 'outgoing',
  maxLen: 5, pathCount: 1, pairwise: false,
  weightProp: 'cost', costProp: 'cost', maxCost: 5
}) YIELD path RETURN path

"Follow only what we trust" stopped being a loop in my Python and became one query inside the database.

Learning is a write, not a retrain

Links come from rules: an ADR's status line naming its replacement, a body that cites an older ADR next to "replace" or "migrate", and so on. Each rule has a trust score (a Beta count). When a correction proves a rule right or wrong, the new trust flows to every link that rule proposed that nobody has judged yet, in one statement:

MATCH (x:Decision)-[r:REPLACED_BY]->(y)
WHERE r.rule = $rule AND r.state = 'candidate'
SET r.w = $w, r.cost = $c

The graph that answers the next question is already the corrected one.

Memory is part of the graph

Every corrected question becomes a Question node with a RESOLVED_TO edge to the right decision, an ABOUT edge to the topic and IN_QUESTION edges from its distinctive terms. "Has someone asked this before?" is a two-hop walk from the new question's terms, not a separate cache.

Two cells, two worlds

The public demo runs on one HydraDB cell. The "replay all 50 corrections" demo runs on a second cell, so a visitor pressing replay never resets anyone else's graph.

Self-hosted for $0

HydraDB is built from source into one Docker image with the app. GitHub Actions builds the image and pushes it to GitHub's container registry, and it runs on Render's free tier.

What broke, and how I fixed it

1. Building from source. My Rust toolchain was a version behind what the build asked for, and a dependency (LAGraph) wouldn't download as a release archive. I built LAGraph from a git clone, pinned the HydraDB commit, and used a two-stage Docker build so the final image carries only the graph-node binary.

2. A 500 on every startup. On a small (512 MB) config, graph-node refused to serve until the unflushed-write limit was larger than the first-level SST file size:

GRAPH_L0_SST_SIZE_BYTES=8388608      # 8 MB
GRAPH_MAX_UNFLUSHED_BYTES=33554432   # 32 MB, must be bigger than the line above

Obvious once you know it, painful until you do.

3. Restarts broke writes. HTTP query ids start again from 1 in each new process, so a restarted node pointed at an old store hit idempotency-key conflicts. My graph is derived from the records anyway, so the fix was to start from an empty store on every boot and rebuild it (about 20 seconds).

4. Writing the queries. HydraDB speaks a subset of OpenCypher. What made loads fast and predictable: batch everything through UNWIND, merge nodes by id and then set labels, and create edges between ids.

UNWIND $rows AS row
MERGE (n {id: row.id})
SET n:Decision, n.key = row.key, n.title = row.title

5. One bad correction poisoned the graph. Early on, a single wrong correction confirmed a whole chain of wrong links, and answers for unrelated questions got worse. Now a correction only confirms a link if the two decisions are actually related (similar text or a shared distinctive term) or the link was stated in the record itself. A brand-new link the rules never proposed stays "proposed" until a second correction agrees.

The numbers

Test-then-train over 50 questions, 5 question orders, with 95% intervals from resampling the questions:

Right Outdated Tokens
Vector search 52% 28% 588
DecisionGraph, learning off 74% 18% 135
DecisionGraph, learning on 80% 10% 129
  • When a topic comes back in new words, learning adds 23 points over the same graph with learning off (interval +7 to +40).
  • On 24 held-out questions written by an independent reviewer: 96% against 42% for vector search.
  • It says "no decision on record" for 92% of out-of-scope questions instead of guessing.

The hardest lesson: be honest about the baseline

My first "plain store" baseline was too easy to beat. An outside reviewer built a much stronger one with no graph database: the same starting points, chasing each record's "superseded by" note in a Python dictionary, plus a memory of corrections. It scored 78% to DecisionGraph's 80%. On about 130 records that mostly state their own replacements, you don't need a graph database to win on accuracy.

What the graph does give you is everything it learned, in the open: every link, how far it trusts it, and the question that changed it, all queryable by an agent (/api/learned).

That matters more as the records get bigger and messier, where replacements have to be worked out rather than read off a status line. I put the stronger baseline and its numbers in the README, because a result nobody else can reproduce isn't a result.

Use it from an agent

The repo ships an MCP server with three tools: current_decision(question), find_decisions(search) and correct_decision(question, correct_decision_id).

pip install -r agent/requirements.txt
claude mcp add decisiongraph -e DECISIONGRAPH_URL=https://decisiongraph-latest.onrender.com -- python agent/decisiongraph_mcp.py

Try it

  • Live app: https://decisiongraph-latest.onrender.com (free host, so the first visit after a quiet spell takes about a minute to wake up)
  • Code: https://github.com/0xNexuz/decisiongraph
  • HydraDB: https://github.com/hydra-db/hydradb

If your team keeps ADRs and lets agents work in your repos, I'd like to hear whether the "outdated decision" problem bites you too.

title: I forced the WCAG text-spacing override onto all 76 of our pages, and the line-height rule made them shorter
description:
Of all the WCAG success criteria, 1.4.12 Text Spacing is the one most often waved through. It asks that nothing be lost when a reader overrides four properties: line height at least 1.5 times the font size, space after a paragraph at least 2 times the font size, letter spacing at least 0.12em and word spacing at least 0.16em. People who need those settings use an extension or a user stylesheet to get them, and if your layout assumes its own leading, their reading experience is text sliced in half by a box that will not grow.

It is also one of the few criteria you can test exhaustively with no judgement calls at all. Four declarations, injected, then measure. So I ran it over all 76 public pages of Nakodo and compared each page with itself.

The injection

One stylesheet, appended to the head, with the four properties at !important so nothing in the cascade can refuse them:

const s = document.createElement("style");
s.textContent = `*,*::before,*::after{
  line-height:1.5 !important;
  letter-spacing:0.12em !important;
  word-spacing:0.16em !important
}
p{margin-bottom:2em !important}`;
document.head.appendChild(s);

Applying it to * rather than to body text is deliberate. The criterion is about what a reader's override does, and a reader's override does not politely skip your buttons, badges and table cells. If a 36px high button holds text that suddenly wants 1.5 line height, I want to know.

Then, before and after on each page, I collected two things. First, every element that is clipping: a computed overflow of hidden, clip, auto or scroll combined with a scrollHeight greater than its clientHeight, or the same in the horizontal. Second, every element whose text escapes its own box, found by selecting the element's contents with a Range and comparing the range's rect with the element's rect, which catches content spilling out of a box that is not clipping it.

Comparing before with after is the part that matters. A site always has a few elements that clip on purpose, and a tool that reports those as failures teaches you to ignore it.

The result

Zero newly clipped elements across 76 pages. No page gained a horizontal scrollbar. None had one to begin with.

The count of clipping elements went the other way, from 105 down to 29. The reason is pleasing. 76 of those 105 are one element: the site footer, which has overflow-hidden because a drawn landscape sits behind it at 10 per cent opacity and must not stick out of the bottom of the page. When every paragraph above it grows, the footer grows, the scenery fits, and the only element on the page whose clipping was doing real work stops clipping at all.

The 29 that remain were clipping before the override as well:

  • 10 are sr-only, which is a 1px box with clipping as its entire mechanism. Flagging those is the tool working correctly on a pattern that is correct.
  • 18 are a metadata row with leading-none, over by a pixel or two in both measurements.
  • 1 is a display heading in the same state before and after.

The escape check came back identical before and after: three per page, every page. Two of them are the wordmark, whose text range is 37px tall in a 33px box because the font's ascenders exceed the line box, and one is a decorative illustration positioned against the bottom of a section. Neither moves when the spacing changes.

69,833 extra pixels

Passing does not mean nothing happened. Added up across the site, the documents went from 423,816 pixels of height to 493,649. That is 69,833 more pixels, or 16.5 per cent more page.

Per page, the median growth is 16.2 per cent. The spread is wide:

Page Growth
/glossary 6.6 per cent
median of 76 16.2 per cent
/guides 29.5 per cent

That spread is the interesting part, because it is not about how much text a page has.

Which of the four properties actually costs anything

I ran the four declarations separately on three pages. The results were not what I expected from a criterion everybody files under "line height".

Override /guides /glossary a guide page
line-height: 1.5 2.1 per cent shorter 8 per cent shorter 4.7 per cent shorter
letter-spacing: 0.12em 12.6 per cent taller 14 per cent taller 10.9 per cent taller
word-spacing: 0.16em 1.8 per cent taller 3.2 per cent taller 1.7 per cent taller
p { margin-bottom: 2em } 16.8 per cent taller 1 per cent taller 9.7 per cent taller

The line-height rule shrinks every page it touches. 1.5 is a floor, and this site is already well above it. Sampling 40 paragraphs in one guide's main, the computed metrics are 15px text on a 28px line in 15 of them and 15 on 24 in another 16, which is a ratio of 1.87 and 1.6. Forcing 1.5 is a reduction, not an increase, for 31 of 40 paragraphs. The ones it genuinely helps are the 11 and 12px captions sitting at 1.33 and 1.45.

That is worth saying plainly, because the way the criterion is usually described ("make sure 1.5 line height does not break your layout") implies the test adds vertical space. On comfortable typography it removes some, and the real cost lands elsewhere.

Letter spacing is the expensive one. 0.12em on every character reflows paragraphs into more lines, and that is 10 to 14 per cent of page height on every page measured. It is also the property least likely to be in anyone's test setup, because adding tracking looks harmless written down.

The paragraph rule explains the whole spread. The guides hub has 68 p elements, so 2em after each one is 16.8 per cent of its height. The glossary has 11 paragraphs and 27 dd elements, because a glossary is a description list rather than a sequence of paragraphs, and p { margin-bottom: 2em } barely touches it. The least affected page on the site is the one that is not built out of paragraphs.

Why it passes

There is no clever work behind this result, which is the useful thing to report. Three ordinary habits did it:

  1. Almost nothing on the site has a fixed height with text inside it. Buttons are 36px with 14px text, so a 21px line box still fits. Cards and panels size to content. The one fixed-height thing with text inside is the metadata row that was already a pixel over.
  2. overflow: hidden is on decoration, not on text. The footer clips a drawing. Nothing on the site clips a sentence, so there is nowhere for text to be lost.
  3. Containers cap width, not height. Pages are flow layout inside max-w-* containers, so the only thing that happens when the text gets bigger is that the page gets longer, which is the thing a browser is actually good at.

Try it on this site

Paste this into the console on any page of nakodo.app and watch the document grow without anything being cut off:

const h = document.documentElement.scrollHeight;
document.head.insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend",
  `<style>*,*::before,*::after{line-height:1.5!important;letter-spacing:.12em!important;word-spacing:.16em!important}p{margin-bottom:2em!important}</style>`);
setTimeout(() => console.log(h, "->", document.documentElement.scrollHeight), 300);

For the version that finds failures, add the clipping check and run it before and after:

[...document.querySelectorAll("body *")].filter((el) => {
  const cs = getComputedStyle(el);
  return ["hidden", "clip", "auto", "scroll"].includes(cs.overflowY)
    && el.scrollHeight > el.clientHeight + 1;
}).map((el) => el.className);

On the guides hub that returns one element before the override, which is the footer, and none after.

What I am taking away

Nothing to fix, which is the rarest outcome of a sweep like this. Two things to keep, though.

Put the four declarations in a snippet and run them when you build anything with a fixed height around text. The failures this criterion catches are specific: pill badges with hardcoded heights, single-line truncated labels, tab bars, anything with leading-none and a h- class in the same string.

And stop thinking of 1.4.12 as the line-height criterion. On this site the line-height clause gave pages back 2 to 8 per cent of their height, and the one that cost real layout was letter spacing, which nobody tests.
