title: Postgres to DuckDB with CDC: One ATTACH Instead of a Nightly Export
description:
DuckDB makes analytics on a laptop feel free, right up to the point where the data has to come from somewhere. For a lot of people that somewhere is Postgres. The first Postgres to DuckDB setup is usually a pg_dump or a CSV export loaded into a DuckDB file, and that file is stale by the time anyone opens it.

The usual ways to put Postgres data in front of DuckDB:

  • The DuckDB postgres extension. DuckDB logs in to the live database and reads the current rows. Nothing is copied and there is nothing to operate, but every query lands on Postgres.
  • pg_dump or COPY TO, then COPY into DuckDB. A script and a scheduler rebuild a DuckDB file. Freshness is hours to daily, and it does full reloads only, so updates and deletes never arrive as changes.
  • Debezium and Kafka, with a consumer that writes Parquet. Changes show up within seconds. You operate Kafka, Kafka Connect, Debezium and the consumer, and the merge logic for updates and deletes is yours to write.
  • Managed extract, load, transform (ELT) into a warehouse, with DuckDB reading the warehouse. Nothing to host, and freshness in minutes by plan. Pricing is per row, per GB or per connector, and the warehouse tables are a second copy you pay to move and store.

This walkthrough takes a fifth route. OLake Go, an open source (Apache 2.0) replication tool, does change data capture (CDC) on the Postgres write-ahead log (WAL) and commits the rows as Apache Iceberg tables into Apache Polaris. Polaris is an open source Iceberg Representational State Transfer (REST) catalog that you host next to a bucket you own.

DuckDB then attaches the whole catalog with one ATTACH and queries the tables where they sit. There is no DuckDB file to rebuild or pass around, and ClickHouse and Trino can read the same tables.

I ran this on one laptop: Postgres 16, Polaris 1.8.0 and MinIO in Docker, OLake Go v1.1.0, and DuckDB 1.5.5 in a local shell. The first sync copied 48 records in 22 seconds, and the second replayed 12 changes in 12 seconds. All the figures below come from that run.

What you need

  • Docker, plus curl, jq and the AWS command line tool for the catalog script in step 2.
  • Postgres 12 or later. Mine was Postgres 16, in a container.
  • DuckDB 1.4 or later. It installs the iceberg and httpfs extensions the first time you ask for them.
  • About 40 minutes.

Step 1: Prepare Postgres for CDC

Pointing at tables you already have? Skip the sample rows and go straight to the settings. To follow along with my exact data, connect with psql to a database named shop and create two tables:

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(100), email VARCHAR(200), city VARCHAR(100), tier VARCHAR(20),
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
  updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW());

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT REFERENCES customers(id), product VARCHAR(100), amount NUMERIC(10,2), status VARCHAR(20),
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
  updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW());

INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city, tier) VALUES
  ('Aarav Mehta','aarav@example.com','Mumbai','gold'),   ('Priya Sharma','priya@example.com','Bengaluru','silver'),
  ('Liam Carter','liam@example.com','Austin','bronze'),  ('Sofia Rossi','sofia@example.com','Milan','gold'),
  ('Kenji Tanaka','kenji@example.com','Tokyo','silver'), ('Emma Schulz','emma@example.com','Berlin','bronze'),
  ('Noah Kim','noah@example.com','Seoul','gold'),        ('Zara Ali','zara@example.com','Dubai','silver');

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, product, amount, status)
SELECT 1 + (n % 8), (ARRAY['Laptop','Headphones','Monitor','Keyboard','Mouse','Webcam'])[1 + n % 6],
       ROUND(20 + ((n * 7919) % 120000) / 100.0, 2), (ARRAY['placed','shipped','delivered'])[1 + n % 3]
FROM generate_series(1, 40) AS n;

That is 8 customers and 40 orders. Next come the replication settings. wal_level only takes effect after a restart, and on managed Postgres it is a parameter group or server setting instead of ALTER SYSTEM.

ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_level = 'logical';
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_replication_slots = 10;
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_wal_senders = 10;
ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_sender_timeout = 0;   -- so a long first snapshot is not cut off

After the restart, create a role for OLake Go, a publication for the two tables and a replication slot on the built-in pgoutput plugin:

CREATE ROLE olake WITH LOGIN REPLICATION PASSWORD '<password>';
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO olake;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO olake;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO olake;

CREATE PUBLICATION olake_pub FOR TABLE customers, orders;
SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('olake_slot', 'pgoutput');

-- check
SHOW wal_level;                                        -- logical
SELECT slot_name, plugin, active FROM pg_replication_slots;
SELECT pubname, puballtables FROM pg_publication;

⚠️ One slot and one publication per job. Two jobs on the same slot read each other's changes, and both lose data.

Both sample tables have a primary key, so they need nothing more. A table without one needs ALTER TABLE <table> REPLICA IDENTITY FULL; so that its updates and deletes carry the old row.

Step 2: Run Polaris and MinIO, then create the catalog

Three things must exist before OLake Go can write: a Polaris server, a catalog in it that points at a bucket, and a principal allowed to manage that catalog. A principal is a client id plus a secret. Save this as docker-compose.yml, pick a root secret and run docker compose up -d:

services:
  minio:
    image: minio/minio
    hostname: lake-minio
    command: server /data --console-address ":9001"
    environment: { MINIO_ROOT_USER: minioadmin, MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD: minioadmin }
    ports: ["9000:9000", "9001:9001"]
  polaris:
    image: apache/polaris:latest
    depends_on: [minio]
    ports: ["8181:8181", "8182:8182"]
    environment:
      AWS_REGION: us-east-1
      AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: minioadmin
      AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: minioadmin
      POLARIS_BOOTSTRAP_CREDENTIALS: POLARIS,root,<root-secret>
      polaris.realm-context.realms: POLARIS

In this form Polaris holds its own state in memory, so it is empty after every restart. A production deployment points it at Postgres.

With both containers up, the management API creates everything else. Give the aws command the MinIO keys (minioadmin above) as its credentials first, so it can make the bucket.

P=http://localhost:8181

# 1. A bucket for the tables
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3 mb s3://lakehouse

# 2. A root token
TOKEN=$(curl -s $P/api/catalog/v1/oauth/tokens -H 'Polaris-Realm: POLARIS' \
  -d grant_type=client_credentials -d client_id=root -d client_secret=<root-secret> \
  -d scope=PRINCIPAL_ROLE:ALL | jq -r .access_token)
H=(-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Polaris-Realm: POLARIS' -H 'Content-Type: application/json')

# 3. The catalog: where the files go, and how Polaris and the engines reach the store
curl -s "${H[@]}" $P/api/management/v1/catalogs -d '{"catalog": {
  "name": "olake", "type": "INTERNAL", "readOnly": false,
  "properties": {"default-base-location": "s3://lakehouse/olake"},
  "storageConfigInfo": {"storageType": "S3", "allowedLocations": ["s3://lakehouse/olake"],
    "endpoint": "http://<minio-host>:9000/", "endpointInternal": "http://lake-minio:9000",
    "pathStyleAccess": true, "region": "us-east-1"}}}'

# 4. A principal for OLake Go and the engines. The response holds clientId and clientSecret: keep them.
curl -s "${H[@]}" $P/api/management/v1/principals -d '{"principal": {"name": "olake"}}'

# 5. Roles and the grant that lets the principal create namespaces and tables in the catalog
curl -s "${H[@]}" $P/api/management/v1/principal-roles -d '{"principalRole": {"name": "olake_role"}}'
curl -s "${H[@]}" $P/api/management/v1/catalogs/olake/catalog-roles -d '{"catalogRole": {"name": "olake_catalog_role"}}'
curl -s -X PUT "${H[@]}" $P/api/management/v1/principals/olake/principal-roles -d '{"principalRole": {"name": "olake_role"}}'
curl -s -X PUT "${H[@]}" $P/api/management/v1/principal-roles/olake_role/catalog-roles/olake -d '{"catalogRole": {"name": "olake_catalog_role"}}'
curl -s -X PUT "${H[@]}" $P/api/management/v1/catalogs/olake/catalog-roles/olake_catalog_role/grants -d '{"type": "catalog", "privilege": "CATALOG_MANAGE_CONTENT"}'

Three details in that script matter later:

  • There are two store addresses. endpoint is what Polaris hands to engines together with short-lived credentials, and endpointInternal is what Polaris uses itself. MinIO needs both, and on AWS S3 you leave both out. In my run <minio-host> was host.docker.internal.
  • The secret appears once. The response to call 4 holds clientId and clientSecret. OLake Go and DuckDB both log in with that pair.
  • Hostnames must not contain underscores. Polaris is a Java service, and a store host such as lab_minio makes every table creation fail. That is why the MinIO container is called lake-minio.

Step 3: Start OLake UI and connect Postgres 

curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datazip-inc/olake-ui/master/docker-compose-v1.yml | docker compose -f - up -d

Open http://localhost:8000 and log in with admin / password. Under Sources, click Create Source and choose Postgres.

  1. Under Change data capture (CDC), keep Enable CDC on. Enter olake_slot as the Replication Slot and olake_pub as the Publication.
  2. Under Connection details, fill in the host, port, database name, username and password. My Postgres ran in another container, so the host was host.docker.internal, with database shop and user olake.
  3. Click Set up source.

The test runs before anything is saved. OLake Go checks the connection, then wal_level, the replication privilege, the slot and the publication, and shows the current and recommended value for anything that fails.

Step 4: Add the Polaris destination

Under Destinations, click Create Destination. Choose Apache Iceberg as the connector, Polaris as the catalog type and OAuth2 as the authentication type. Polaris and MinIO were containers too, so both addresses below go through host.docker.internal.

Field Value
REST Catalog URI http://host.docker.internal:8181/api/catalog
Polaris Catalog Name olake
REST Auth URI http://host.docker.internal:8181/api/catalog/v1/oauth/tokens
REST Credential <client_id>:<client_secret> from step 2
REST scope PRINCIPAL_ROLE:ALL
AWS Region us-east-1
S3 Endpoint http://host.docker.internal:9000
AWS Access Key, AWS Secret Key the MinIO keys

Click Create. OLake Go trades the credentials for a token, creates a namespace and a test table through Polaris, writes to the bucket and then drops the test table.

Step 5: Create the job and run the first sync

  1. Open Jobs and click Create Job. Name it postgres_to_duckdb and set a schedule.
  2. Pick the source and the destination from steps 3 and 4.
  3. Under Advanced Settings, set Target Query Engines to DuckDB, and add Trino if it will read the tables too.
  4. Click Next. On the Streams page, tick customers and orders.
  5. For each table, set the sync mode to Full Refresh + CDC and the ingestion mode to Upsert.
  6. Click Create Job, open the job's menu and choose Sync Now.

The schedule is how often the change stream is drained, not how often a full copy runs. With DuckDB and Trino as the target engines, OLake Go offers the delete formats both can read. My job ran with Positional Deletes, the format DuckDB documents, and OLake UI stores the small index that format keeps between runs.

The first sync copied 8 customers and 40 orders, 48 records and 2.23 KB, in 22 seconds with container start included. It notes the WAL position through the slot and then reads each table in parallel chunks. Nothing written during the copy is lost, and there is no separate backfill job.

Step 6: Query the tables in DuckDB

There is no registration step and no CREATE TABLE. Open a DuckDB shell and run this with the client id and secret from step 2:

INSTALL iceberg; LOAD iceberg;
INSTALL httpfs;  LOAD httpfs;

CREATE SECRET polaris_secret (
  TYPE iceberg,
  CLIENT_ID '<client_id>', CLIENT_SECRET '<client_secret>',
  OAUTH2_SERVER_URI 'http://<polaris-host>:8181/api/catalog/v1/oauth/tokens',
  OAUTH2_SCOPE 'PRINCIPAL_ROLE:ALL'
);
-- MinIO, or any store whose address differs from the one Polaris vends
CREATE SECRET store_secret (
  TYPE s3, KEY_ID '<access key>', SECRET '<secret key>',
  ENDPOINT '<minio-host>:9000', URL_STYLE 'path', USE_SSL false, REGION 'us-east-1'
);

ATTACH 'olake' AS polaris (
  TYPE iceberg,
  ENDPOINT 'http://<polaris-host>:8181/api/catalog',
  SECRET polaris_secret,
  ACCESS_DELEGATION_MODE 'none'
);

SHOW ALL TABLES;

SELECT id, name, city, tier FROM polaris.postgres_to_duckdb_shop_public.customers ORDER BY id;

Here <polaris-host> and <minio-host> are the addresses as DuckDB sees them. From the laptop that runs the containers, both are localhost, the same address the step 2 script used.

Two notes on that block:

  • store_secret and ACCESS_DELEGATION_MODE 'none' are there for the laptop. Polaris vends the store address from the catalog, and that address may not resolve outside Docker. With Polaris on AWS S3 you drop both, and DuckDB reads with the credentials Polaris vends.
  • The schema name is built for you. OLake Go joins the job name, the source database and the schema, which gave postgres_to_duckdb_shop_public. The Iceberg DB field at the top of the Streams page changes it before the first sync.

DuckDB fetches the OAuth2 token itself, and the attached catalog is read-only from its side. OLake Go is the writer.

Step 7: Change rows in Postgres and sync again

A nightly export has no answer for this part. Back in psql, I made 12 changes, 7 inserts and 5 updates:

INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city, tier) VALUES
  ('Maya Patel', 'maya@example.com', 'Pune', 'silver'),
  ('Lucas Silva', 'lucas@example.com', 'São Paulo', 'bronze');
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, product, amount, status) VALUES
  (9, 'Laptop', 1299.00, 'placed'), (9, 'Mouse', 25.50, 'placed'),
  (10, 'Monitor', 349.99, 'placed'), (3, 'Keyboard', 89.00, 'placed'), (7, 'Webcam', 79.90, 'placed');
UPDATE customers SET tier = 'gold', updated_at = NOW()      WHERE name = 'Liam Carter';
UPDATE customers SET city = 'Abu Dhabi', updated_at = NOW() WHERE name = 'Zara Ali';
UPDATE orders    SET status = 'delivered', updated_at = NOW() WHERE id IN (1, 4, 7);

Choose Sync Now again. The second sync read 12 records (594 bytes) from the slot and finished in 12 seconds.

For customers, OLake Go wrote one data file holding 4 rows: the 2 inserts and the new versions of the 2 updated rows. One small positional delete file retires the 2 old versions. orders has the same shape with 8 rows and 3 deletes, and the commit report in the sync log spells it out.

Run the SELECT again. DuckDB shows the result on its next query, with no refresh: Liam Carter is gold, Zara Ali is in Abu Dhabi, and Maya Patel and Lucas Silva have arrived.

DuckDB returns 10 rows, one per key, because it applies the positional deletes while reading. Add _op_type to the column list to see how each row got there: r for the snapshot, c for an insert and u for an update.

Read the same tables from ClickHouse and Trino

This is what open tables buy you over an exported DuckDB file. Both engines read the files OLake Go wrote, through the same Polaris endpoint, and nothing is exported for them.

ClickHouse attaches the catalog as one database:

SET allow_database_iceberg = 1;

CREATE DATABASE polaris
ENGINE = DataLakeCatalog('http://<polaris-host>:8181/api/catalog')
SETTINGS
  catalog_type = 'rest',
  warehouse = 'olake',
  catalog_credential = '<client_id>:<client_secret>',
  oauth_server_uri = 'http://<polaris-host>:8181/api/catalog/v1/oauth/tokens',
  auth_scope = 'PRINCIPAL_ROLE:ALL',
  vended_credentials = true,
  region = 'us-east-1';

SELECT id, name, city, tier
FROM polaris.`postgres_to_duckdb_shop_public.customers`
ORDER BY id;

ClickHouse has one level of namespace, so the Iceberg namespace and the table name go inside one pair of backticks. Trino needs a single file, etc/catalog/polaris.properties:

connector.name=iceberg
iceberg.catalog.type=rest
iceberg.rest-catalog.uri=http://<polaris-host>:8181/api/catalog
iceberg.rest-catalog.warehouse=olake
iceberg.rest-catalog.security=OAUTH2
iceberg.rest-catalog.oauth2.credential=<client_id>:<client_secret>
iceberg.rest-catalog.oauth2.scope=PRINCIPAL_ROLE:ALL
iceberg.rest-catalog.oauth2.server-uri=http://<polaris-host>:8181/api/catalog/v1/oauth/tokens
iceberg.rest-catalog.vended-credentials-enabled=true
fs.native-s3.enabled=true
s3.region=us-east-1
# MinIO or another S3-compatible store only:
s3.endpoint=http://<minio-host>:9000
s3.path-style-access=true

ClickHouse 26.8.36, a long-term support (LTS) release, and Trino 484 returned the same 10 rows as DuckDB. A roll-up of orders by status matched Postgres to the cent in all three: 16 delivered for 8659.68, 18 placed for 10522.26 and 11 shipped for 6397.25.

Tips from the run

  • Expect three type changes. numeric shows up in DuckDB as DOUBLE, so round at query time when you need exact decimal arithmetic. timestamptz becomes TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), and json and jsonb arrive as VARCHAR for DuckDB's json extension.
  • Copy a hot table locally. DuckDB reads Parquet over the network on every query. For a table you hit all day, run CREATE TABLE local AS FROM polaris... once and query the local copy.
  • New columns arrive on their own. Add a column in Postgres and OLake Go adds it to the Iceberg table on the next sync. Widening changes such as int to bigint are applied, and narrowing ones fail the sync instead of corrupting the table.
  • Watch the slot. It pins WAL on the Postgres server until OLake Go has read it. Keep the job on a schedule, alert on pg_replication_slots lag, and drop the slot when you retire a job.
  • Plan for compaction. Nothing compacts the tables for you, and a CDC table gets a new small data file and delete file on each sync. Spark's rewrite_data_files works through the same Polaris endpoint.

How the Postgres to DuckDB methods compare

Method Freshness Updates and deletes Where the data lands What you run
DuckDB postgres extension live, on every query reads the current row nowhere; each query hits Postgres a Postgres login for DuckDB
pg_dump or COPY TO, then COPY hours to daily no, full reloads a DuckDB file you rebuild a script and a scheduler
Debezium, Kafka and a Parquet consumer seconds yes, with merge logic you write Parquet files, then DuckDB Kafka, Kafka Connect, Debezium, the consumer
Managed ELT into a warehouse minutes, by plan varies by tool warehouse tables, a second copy nothing; per-row, per-GB or per-connector pricing
OLake Go to Polaris (this post) CDC on a schedule, down to one minute yes, as Iceberg row-level deletes Iceberg tables DuckDB, ClickHouse, Trino and Spark all read one Docker Compose stack, open source, plus your bucket

The postgres extension is the simpler choice for a one-off query against a small table you can reach directly. The route in this post is worth its setup when you want production Postgres out of the query path, or when more than one engine needs the same rows.

Where it is the wrong tool:

  • One analyst, one laptop, one small table. The postgres extension or a nightly COPY is less to run than a catalog and OLake Go.
  • Tables with no primary key. Inserts replicate, but updates and deletes cannot be matched to a row and are not applied. Add a key or set REPLICA IDENTITY FULL first.
  • A reader that depends on equality deletes in DuckDB. Keep the job on positional deletes or deletion vectors.

FAQ

Can DuckDB write to the tables it attached?

No. The attached Polaris catalog is read-only from DuckDB, and OLake Go is the writer. For scratch work, copy a table into a local DuckDB table and change that copy.

How often can the sync run?

The schedule goes down to one minute. It sets how often the change stream is drained, so each run moves only the rows that changed. Every sync ends with one commit to Polaris, and DuckDB sees it on the next query.

Can I use Amazon S3 in place of MinIO?

Yes. Use an S3 bucket and an Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, and leave endpoint and endpointInternal out of the catalog. In DuckDB, drop store_secret and the ACCESS_DELEGATION_MODE line, because on AWS S3 the address Polaris vends resolves everywhere.

Do I have to attach the catalog again after every sync?

No. New and changed rows show up on the next query against the attached catalog. A column added in Postgres is the exception, since DuckDB shows it on the next ATTACH.

Where to go from here

  • Point the source at a real database. Hosted Postgres on Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS), Aurora, Cloud SQL, Azure, Neon or Supabase exposes the same settings through a parameter group or a dashboard toggle.
  • Prefer a terminal? The same pipeline runs from the OLake Go Docker images with JSON config files in place of the forms.
  • The full guide, with the command line configuration, the troubleshooting section and the cost notes, is on olake.io.

If a step prints something different on your machine, leave the exact message in the comments and I will look into it.

title: The fx adapter now runs the harness on the host
description:
The fx adapter for the AI SDK’s HarnessAgent now uses libfx, the TypeScript library for fx. The harness and model requests run in your application’s process, while built-in filesystem and shell operations remain isolated in the sandbox.

This simplifies sandbox setup: you no longer need to install fx inside the sandbox, run a sandbox bridge, or expose a sandbox port. Model credentials stay on the host, outside the environment where the agent runs commands.

The rewrite also adds:

  • Built-in tool filtering: choose which built-in tools the agent can use

  • Mid-turn steering: send new instructions while a turn is running

  • Structured output: generate responses that match a schema

  • Image tool results: return images to the model through toModelOutput()

Sessions can be saved and resumed in a new host process.

Update @ai-sdk/harness-fx to the latest version to use the new adapter. Learn more in the fx harness documentation.

title: Unsubscribe'ı doğru kurmak: Tek tık çıkış, suppression listesi, kanal bazlı izin ve gönderim öncesi kontrol
description:
Bir pazarlama otomasyonu projesinde en az konuşulan ama en çok sorun çıkaran parça, "abonelikten çık" bağlantısıdır. Kampanya akışları, segmentler, şablonlar ve raporlar uzun uzun tartışılır; çıkış ise e-posta altbilgisine konan küçük bir link olarak görülür. Sonra bir gün müşteri, aylar önce çıktığı listeden hâlâ mesaj aldığını söyleyerek şikâyet eder. İncelendiğinde çıkışın bir araçta kaydedildiği, ama CRM'den gelen bir yeniden senkronun kişiyi listeye geri eklediği ortaya çıkar.

Ben Koray Yalçın; lead yönetimi, CRM ve pazarlama otomasyonu altyapıları kuruyorum, ağırlıklı olarak gayrimenkul ve PropTech tarafında. Bu yazıda unsubscribe konusunu hukuk metni olarak değil, bir yazılım tasarımı problemi olarak ele alacağım: çıkış olayı nasıl modellenir, tek tık çıkış nasıl uygulanır, suppression listesi neden ayrı bir tablo olmalıdır, kanal bazlı izinler nasıl tutulur ve her gönderimden önce hangi kontrol mutlaka çalışmalıdır.

Not: Bu yazı teknik bir tasarım rehberidir, hukuki görüş değildir. KVKK, ticari ileti mevzuatı ve İYS yükümlülükleri için hukuk danışmanınızla çalışın.

Unsubscribe bir alan değil, bir olaydır

En yaygın hata, kişi tablosuna is_subscribed boolean gibi tek bir alan eklemektir. Bu alan üç soruyu cevaplayamaz: Kişi ne zaman çıktı? Hangi kanaldan ve hangi listeden çıktı? Bu bilgiyi hangi sistem yazdı? Daha kötüsü, tek bir boolean her senkronda üzerine yazılabilir. Dış sistemden true gelirse, kişinin kendi iradesiyle yaptığı çıkış sessizce silinir.

Bu yüzden çıkışı bir olay olarak, yalnızca eklenen (append-only) bir tabloda tutuyorum. Güncel durum bu olaylardan türetilir.

CREATE TABLE consent_event (
  id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  contact_id    bigint      NOT NULL REFERENCES contact(id),
  channel       text        NOT NULL CHECK (channel IN ('email','sms','whatsapp','call')),
  topic         text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'all',   -- 'newsletter', 'launch', 'all' ...
  action        text        NOT NULL CHECK (action IN ('opt_in','opt_out')),
  source        text        NOT NULL,                 -- 'one_click', 'preference_center', 'reply_stop', 'agent', 'import'
  evidence      jsonb       NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',    -- ip, user_agent, message_id, kayıt formu sürümü
  occurred_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  recorded_by   text        NOT NULL                  -- servis veya kullanıcı kimliği
);

CREATE INDEX ON consent_event (contact_id, channel, topic, occurred_at DESC);

Burada iki ayrıntı önemli. Birincisi topic: kişi lansman duyurularından çıkıp aylık bültende kalmak isteyebilir. Tek bir "çık" butonu her şeyi kapatıyorsa insanlar ya hepsinden çıkar ya da spam olarak işaretler; ikisi de sizin için kötüdür. İkincisi evidence: bir gün "bu kişi izin vermiş miydi, ne zaman çıktı?" diye sorulduğunda cevabın kanıtıyla birlikte veritabanında olması gerekir.

Güncel durumu türetmek

Olay tablosundan güncel izni okumak için her kanal ve konu için son olayı almak yeterlidir. Kanal genelindeki all çıkışı, konu bazlı her izni ezmelidir.

CREATE VIEW consent_state AS
SELECT DISTINCT ON (contact_id, channel, topic)
       contact_id, channel, topic, action, occurred_at, source
FROM consent_event
ORDER BY contact_id, channel, topic, occurred_at DESC, id DESC;

-- Belirli bir konuda gönderim izni var mı?
CREATE FUNCTION can_send(p_contact bigint, p_channel text, p_topic text)
RETURNS boolean LANGUAGE sql STABLE AS $$
  SELECT
    NOT EXISTS (                       -- kanal genelinde çıkış var mı?
      SELECT 1 FROM consent_state
      WHERE contact_id = p_contact AND channel = p_channel
        AND topic = 'all' AND action = 'opt_out')
    AND EXISTS (                        -- bu konu için açık izin var mı?
      SELECT 1 FROM consent_state
      WHERE contact_id = p_contact AND channel = p_channel
        AND topic IN (p_topic, 'all') AND action = 'opt_in')
    AND NOT EXISTS (                    -- bu konu için çıkış var mı?
      SELECT 1 FROM consent_state
      WHERE contact_id = p_contact AND channel = p_channel
        AND topic = p_topic AND action = 'opt_out');
$$;

Dikkat edilirse fonksiyon varsayılan olarak "hayır" der. Kaydı olmayan kişiye gönderim yapılmaz. Bu, "izin yoksa gönderme" ilkesinin koddaki karşılığıdır ve içe aktarılan eski listelerin otomatik olarak gönderime girmesini engeller.

Hacim büyüdüğünde bu görünümü her gönderimde hesaplamak pahalı olabilir. O durumda olaylar yazıldıkça güncellenen bir consent_current tablosu tutulabilir; ama kaynak gerçek her zaman olay tablosu olarak kalmalı ve güncel tablo istenildiğinde olaylardan yeniden üretilebilmelidir.

Suppression listesi neden ayrı durur

İzin tablosu "bu kişi ne istiyor?" sorusunu cevaplar. Suppression listesi ise "bu adrese ne olursa olsun gönderim yapılmayacak" sorusunu. İkisi aynı şey değildir. Kalıcı geri dönen (hard bounce) bir adres, spam şikâyeti yapan bir alıcı, silme talebinde bulunan bir kişi ya da yasal nedenle engellenen bir numara suppression listesine girer.

Önemli nokta, suppression listesinin kişi kaydına değil iletişim adresine bağlanmasıdır. Kişi kaydı silinebilir, birleştirilebilir (deduplication) ya da yeni bir form doldurularak yeniden oluşturulabilir. Adres ise aynı kalır. Bu yüzden normalleştirilmiş adresin hash'ini saklıyorum:

CREATE TABLE suppression (
  channel      text        NOT NULL,
  address_hash bytea       NOT NULL,   -- sha256(normalize(address))
  reason       text        NOT NULL CHECK (reason IN
                 ('hard_bounce','complaint','global_opt_out','erasure_request','legal_block')),
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  note         text,
  PRIMARY KEY (channel, address_hash)
);

Hash kullanmanın bir faydası da silme talebinden sonra ortaya çıkar. Kişinin kişisel verilerini sildiğinizde, açık adresi saklamadan "bu adrese bir daha yazma" bilgisini koruyabilirsiniz. Aksi halde silinen kişi bir sonraki toplu içe aktarmada listeye geri döner ve silme talebi fiilen anlamsızlaşır. Bu dengeyi kendi veri saklama politikanız ve hukuk danışmanınızla birlikte netleştirmeniz gerekir.

Normalleştirme kuralı tek bir yerde tanımlanmalıdır: e-postada boşlukları kırpmak ve küçük harfe çevirmek, telefonda ülke koduyla E.164 biçimine getirmek gibi. Form, içe aktarma ve gönderim servisi farklı normalleştirme yaparsa hash'ler eşleşmez ve suppression listesi delik deşik olur.

Tek tık çıkış: List-Unsubscribe ve RFC 8058

E-posta tarafında altbilgideki linke ek olarak List-Unsubscribe başlığını göndermek, posta kutusu sağlayıcılarının kendi arayüzlerinde bir "abonelikten çık" düğmesi göstermesini sağlar. RFC 8058 bunun tek tık versiyonunu tanımlar: sağlayıcı, kullanıcı düğmeye bastığında sizin URL'nize gövdesinde List-Unsubscribe=One-Click bulunan bir POST isteği atar. Google ve Yahoo, 2024'ten bu yana toplu gönderen göndericilerden tek tık çıkışı desteklemelerini istiyor.

List-Unsubscribe: <https://mail.example.com/u/7f3a...c91>, <mailto:unsubscribe@example.com?subject=u-7f3a...c91>
List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click

Uygulamada dikkat edilecek noktalar:

  • URL'deki token tahmin edilemez ve imzalı olmalı; içinde kişi kimliği, kanal, konu ve mesaj kimliği bulunur. Düz contact_id=123 gibi bir parametre, başkasının herkesi listeden çıkarabilmesi demektir.
  • POST uç noktası oturum, CAPTCHA ya da onay sayfası istememeli. Sağlayıcı bu isteği arka planda atar; bir yönlendirme veya giriş ekranı çıkışın gerçekleşmemesi anlamına gelir.
  • GET isteği çıkış yapmamalı. Bazı güvenlik tarayıcıları e-postadaki linkleri otomatik açar; GET ile çıkış yapan bir sistem, kişiyi hiç tıklamadan listeden düşürebilir. GET bir tercih sayfası göstermeli, çıkışı POST yapmalıdır.
  • Uç nokta idempotent olmalı. Aynı istek iki kez gelirse ikinci olay yazılmaz ya da zararsızdır. 
@app.post("/u/<token>")
def one_click_unsubscribe(token):
    claims = verify_signed_token(token)          # imza + son kullanma kontrolü
    if claims is None:
        return "", 400
    with db.transaction():
        already = db.fetch_one("""
            SELECT 1 FROM consent_event
            WHERE contact_id=%s AND channel=%s AND topic=%s
              AND action='opt_out' AND evidence->>'message_id' = %s
        """, claims.contact_id, claims.channel, claims.topic, claims.message_id)
        if not already:
            db.execute("""
                INSERT INTO consent_event
                  (contact_id, channel, topic, action, source, evidence, recorded_by)
                VALUES (%s, %s, %s, 'opt_out', 'one_click', %s, 'unsubscribe-api')
            """, claims.contact_id, claims.channel, claims.topic,
                 json.dumps({"message_id": claims.message_id,
                             "ip": request.remote_addr,
                             "ua": request.headers.get("User-Agent")}))
            outbox.publish("consent.opted_out", claims.as_dict())
    return "", 200

Son satırdaki outbox.publish önemlidir. Çıkış yalnızca e-posta aracında kalmamalı; CRM, reklam kitleleri, SMS sağlayıcısı ve WhatsApp şablon gönderimi gibi diğer tüketicilere de bir olay olarak dağıtılmalıdır.

Kanal bazlı çıkış: SMS, WhatsApp ve telefon

E-posta dışındaki kanallarda çıkış genellikle bir link değil, bir yanıttır. SMS'te "RET" ya da "STOP", WhatsApp'ta "artık yazmayın" gibi serbest bir cümle, telefonda ise danışmana söylenen bir "beni bir daha aramayın" olabilir. Bunların her biri aynı consent_event tablosuna, kendi source değeriyle düşmelidir.

  • SMS ve WhatsApp yanıtları: Gelen mesaj webhook'unda anahtar kelime eşleşmesi yapılır. Serbest metinde emin olunamayan durumlar otomatik çıkışa değil, bir insan görevine dönüştürülür; ama şüpheli durumda kişi incelenene kadar pazarlama gönderimlerinden geçici olarak çıkarılır. Yanlışlıkla bir mesaj daha göndermek, yanlışlıkla bir gün beklemekten daha pahalıdır.
  • Telefon görüşmeleri: Çağrı sonucu kodlamasına "aranmak istemiyor" gibi bir sonuç kodu eklenir ve bu kod seçildiğinde arka planda channel='call', action='opt_out', source='agent' olayı yazılır. Danışmanın ayrıca bir not girmesini beklemek, o kaydın çoğu zaman hiç oluşmaması demektir.
  • Türkiye'de İYS: Ticari elektronik ileti izinleri İleti Yönetim Sistemi'nde de tutulur. İYS'den gelen ret kayıtları ayrı bir source='iys' ile içe alınmalı, sizin tarafınızdaki ret kayıtları da İYS'ye aktarılmalıdır. İki yönlü senkronda kural basittir: ret her zaman kazanır.

Gönderim öncesi kontrol: son kapı

Bütün bu tablolar, gönderimden hemen önce kontrol edilmedikçe işe yaramaz. Segment oluşturulurken izin kontrolü yapmak yetmez; segment ile gönderim arasında saatler, bazen günler geçebilir ve bu arada kişi çıkmış olabilir. Bu yüzden her kanalın gönderim işçisinde, mesaj sağlayıcıya gitmeden hemen önce çalışan tek bir kontrol fonksiyonu bulunur.

def guard_send(contact_id, channel, topic, address):
    h = sha256(normalize(channel, address))
    if db.exists("SELECT 1 FROM suppression WHERE channel=%s AND address_hash=%s", channel, h):
        return Decision.block("suppressed")
    if not db.fetch_value("SELECT can_send(%s, %s, %s)", contact_id, channel, topic):
        return Decision.block("no_consent")
    if is_transactional(topic):
        return Decision.allow("transactional")
    return Decision.allow("marketing")

Bu fonksiyonun üç kuralı var:

  1. Gönderim yapan her kod yolu bu fonksiyondan geçer. Kampanya motoru, otomasyon akışları, danışmanın CRM'den tek tek attığı şablonlu mesajlar ve "tek seferlik" toplu gönderim script'leri dahil.
  2. Engellenen her gönderim gerekçesiyle loglanır. "Bu kampanya neden 400 kişi eksik gitti?" sorusunun cevabı tahmin değil, sorgu olmalıdır.
  3. İşlemsel (transactional) mesaj istisnası dar tutulur. Randevu teyidi veya sözleşme bilgilendirmesi işlemseldir; "randevunuz yaklaşıyor, bu arada yeni projemize de göz atın" ise artık pazarlama mesajıdır.

Senkronlarda çıkışı korumak

Başta anlattığım sorun, yani çıkmış kişinin bir senkronla listeye geri eklenmesi, genellikle iki sistemin aynı alanı birbirine yazmasından doğar. Bunu önlemek için üç kural uyguluyorum:

  • İzin alanları için tek bir kaynak sistem belirlenir; diğer sistemler bu alanı okuyabilir ama doğrudan yazamaz, yalnızca olay gönderebilir.
  • Dış sistemden gelen opt_in, kaynakta daha yeni bir opt_out varsa yok sayılır. Zaman damgası karşılaştırması yapılır, son yazan kazanmaz.
  • Toplu içe aktarmalar hiçbir zaman çıkış kaydını ezemez. İçe aktarılan listede izinli görünen bir kişi suppression listesinde ya da olay tablosunda çıkmış görünüyorsa, içe aktarma o satırı reddeder ve raporlar.

Bu kuralları otomatik testlerle de güvenceye almak iyi bir fikirdir: "çıkış yap, ardından eski tarihli bir opt_in senkronu gönder, can_send hâlâ false dönmeli" gibi bir test, en pahalı hata sınıfını erken yakalar.

Ölçüm: çıkışları sorun olarak değil sinyal olarak okumak

Çıkış oranı kendi başına bir başarısızlık göstergesi değildir; liste sağlığının doğal bir parçasıdır. Asıl değerli olan, çıkışların nerede yoğunlaştığıdır. Olay tablosu zaten elinizde olduğu için şu sorular basit sorgularla cevaplanır: Hangi konu ya da kampanyadan sonra çıkışlar artıyor? Lead'ler ilk temastan kaç gün sonra çıkıyor? Tek tık çıkış ile tercih merkezi arasındaki dağılım nasıl? Tercih merkezinde konu bazlı çıkış seçeneği sunmak, toptan çıkışları azaltıyor mu?

Gayrimenkul tarafında sık gördüğüm bir örüntü, lansman döneminde yoğun mesaj gönderilmesi ve ardından gelen toplu çıkışlardır. Konu bazlı izin modeli burada işe yarar: kişi lansman duyurularından çıkar ama teslim ve aidat bilgilendirmeleri gibi işlemsel iletişimde kalır.

SSS

Unsubscribe ile opt-out aynı şey mi?
Pratikte çoğu zaman aynı anlamda kullanılır. Ben unsubscribe'ı e-postadaki çıkış eylemi, opt-out'u ise tüm kanallar için genel izin geri çekme olayı olarak modelliyorum. Veritabanında ikisi de aynı consent_event tablosunda action='opt_out' olarak durur.

Çıkış ne kadar sürede işlenmeli?
Teknik hedefim, çıkışın anında, yani bir sonraki gönderim denemesinden önce geçerli olmasıdır. Google ve Yahoo'nun toplu gönderen kuralları en geç iki gün içinde işlenmesini istiyor; yerel mevzuattaki süreler için hukuk danışmanınıza danışın. Gönderim öncesi kontrol doğru kurulduysa süre zaten pratikte sıfırdır.

Silme talebinde bulunan kişiyi suppression listesinde tutmak çelişki değil mi?
Amaç kişiyi takip etmek değil, ona tekrar yazmamaktır. Açık adres yerine hash saklamak bu amacı daha az veriyle karşılar. Yine de bu kararı veri saklama politikanızda açıkça tanımlayın.

Danışmanların CRM'den tek tek gönderdiği WhatsApp mesajları da bu kontrole tabi mi?
Evet. Pazarlama içerikli her mesaj, kim gönderirse göndersin, aynı gönderim öncesi kontrolden geçmelidir. Arayüzde gönder düğmesinin izin yoksa pasif olması ve nedenini göstermesi, danışmanın hem hatadan korunmasını hem de durumu anlamasını sağlar.

Tercih merkezi şart mı?
Zorunlu değil ama çok faydalı. Tek tık çıkış yasal ve teknik tabanı karşılar; tercih merkezi ise kişiye "her şeyden çık" yerine "sadece bunu istemiyorum" deme imkânı verir. İkisini birlikte sunmak en sağlıklı yaklaşımdır.

Kapanış

Unsubscribe'ı küçük bir link olarak değil, kendi veri modeli, olayları ve kontrol noktası olan bir alt sistem olarak tasarladığınızda, şikâyetler azalır, gönderici itibarı korunur ve "bu kişi neden hâlâ mesaj alıyor?" sorusu tahmin yerine bir sorguyla cevaplanır. Ben yeni bir CRM veya otomasyon kurulumuna başlarken izin olay tablosunu, suppression listesini ve gönderim öncesi kontrolü ilk sprintte kuruyorum; çünkü sonradan eklendiğinde geriye dönük olarak temizlenmesi gereken veri her zaman beklenenden fazladır.

title: Show your working: why an online calculator should print its formula
description:
Most online calculators give you one number and nothing else. You type the area of a room and get "53 tiles". If you want to know where 53 came from, you are on your own.

We built Calc around the opposite idea: the result is only half of the answer. The other half is the working.

The formula with your numbers in it

Under every result, the page prints the formula with your values already substituted. For tiles it looks like this:

12 m² × 1.10 ÷ 0.25 m² = 52.8, round up to the next whole tile.

That one line answers the questions people actually ask. Where did the 10% go? Why 53 and not 52? Is the tile area right? Anyone can check it with a phone calculator.

Assumptions as a list, not a footnote

A calculation is only as good as its assumptions. Calc shows them as a list next to the result: the waste margin, the rounding rule, what the calculator does not account for. If a number depends on a rate or a standard, the constant has a source and the date it was checked. If we cannot back a number with a source, the field stays empty and asks for your own value instead of inventing a default.

"I don't know this value"

The hardest part of a calculator is often not the maths but the input. Next to fields where a number is hard to know, there is a card that tells you where to find it: the device spec sheet, your contract, a label, or another calculator.

Nothing leaves the browser while you calculate

The calculation runs in the browser. The only exception is the "calculation receipt" link: it writes the values into the address so you can send the whole scenario to a colleague or come back to it later. Because the values are in the address, the page says plainly that they end up in the server log when someone opens the link.

Checked outside the code

Each formula is checked against test cases by a separate calculation that does not call the site's code. If the two disagree, the calculator is wrong, not the test.

That is the whole philosophy: no ads inside the result, no "AI estimates" where arithmetic will do, and a formula you can redo by hand. Calc has calculators for energy and backup power, money, small business and e-commerce, home renovation, cars, shipping and dates. They are available in Ukrainian, and most of them also in English, Polish, German and French:

https://calc.uk.app/en/

title: Stop Spawning Threads: Building a Lock-Free Work-Stealing Scheduler in Rust
description:
When you first learn concurrent programming in Rust, the std::"thread"::spawn function feels like magic. Got 10,000 URLs to parse? Just wrap the scraper function in a loop, spawn 10,000 threads, and let the operating system figure it out.

But as your systems scale, that magic quickly turns into a nightmare.

Spawning more OS threads than you have physical CPU cores forces the Linux kernel into heavy context switching. The OS frantically pauses and resumes threads, thrashing your CPU caches and wasting precious clock cycles just figuring out who gets to run next.

To achieve maximum throughput for a high-performance Web-to-Markdown extraction engine I am building, I needed a system that keeps the CPU cores pinned at 100% execution, bypassing the OS scheduler entirely.

Here is how I built a 1:1 hardware-mapped, lock-free, work-stealing job scheduler from scratch in Rust using crossbeam-deque.
The Architecture: Silicon Over Syscalls

The goal of a custom scheduler is to spawn exactly as many OS threads as you have logical CPU cores (e.g., 8 cores = 8 threads). These threads boot up once, live forever, and constantly hunt for tasks.

But how do you distribute the work safely without wrapping everything in a massive, slow Mutex? We use a Chase-Lev work-stealing deque.

Instead of fighting over a single locked queue, every thread gets its own private queue.

The thread operates on the bottom of its own queue. This requires zero locks.

If a thread runs out of work, it becomes a "thief". It uses hardware-level Compare-And-Swap (CAS) atomic instructions to rip jobs from the top of a peer's queue. No system calls, no OS intervention—just pure silicon arbitration.

Step 1: Mapping the Memory Boundaries

We need to define three layers of state: the public API, the synchronization primitives, and the internal worker context.


use crossbeam_deque::{Injector, Stealer, Worker, Steal};
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex, Condvar};
use std::thread::JoinHandle;

// The payload: a heap-allocated closure that owns its data and is thread-safe
pub type Job = Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send + 'static>;

// The Intercom: Used to wake up starving threads
pub(crate) struct SleepSignal {
    keep_running: Mutex<bool>,
    cvar: Condvar,
}

// The Manager: Lives on the Main Thread
pub struct JobStealer {
    global_queue: Arc<Injector<Job>>,
    sleep_signal: Arc<SleepSignal>,
    workers: Vec<JoinHandle<()>>,
}

// The Worker Brain: Moved permanently into the OS Thread
struct WorkerContext {
    id: usize,
    local_deque: Worker<Job>,
    stealers: Vec<Stealer<Job>>,
    global_deque: Arc<Injector<Job>>,
    sleep_signal: Arc<SleepSignal>,
}

Notice the separation of concerns: The JobStealer manager holds the handles to shut the system down, while the WorkerContext holds the Stealer keys to access its peers.
Step 2: The Execution Loop (The Hunt)

Once we spawn the OS threads and move the WorkerContext into them, they get trapped in an infinite loop {}. The threads execute a strict hierarchy of operations to find work, optimizing for cache locality.


impl WorkerContext {
    fn run(self) {
        loop {
            // Priority 1: Check the local, lock-free queue
            if let Some(job) = self.local_deque.pop() {
                job();
                continue;
            }

            // Priority 2: Global Batch Steal
            // Take a chunk of jobs, put them in local, return one to run now
            if let Steal::Success(job) = self.global_deque.steal_batch_and_pop(&self.local_deque) {
                job();
                continue;
            }

            // Priority 3: Peer Stealing (Hardware Atomics)
            let mut stole_job = false;
            for stealer in &self.stealers {
                if let Steal::Success(job) = stealer.steal_batch_and_pop(&self.local_deque) {
                    stole_job = true;
                    job();
                    break;
                }
            }
            if stole_job { continue; }

            // Priority 4: All queues are empty. Time to sleep.
            self.sleep(); 
        }
    }
}

Step 3: Navigating the Sleep Trap

If all queues are empty, a thread must yield its CPU cycle back to the OS, otherwise it will burn 100% CPU spinning in a loop {}.

We use a POSIX Condvar to sleep. But sleeping in systems programming comes with two notorious traps:

The Lost Wakeup: If the Main Thread signals new work a microsecond before the Worker goes to sleep, the Worker will miss the signal and sleep forever. We fix this by tying the Condvar to a Mutex. It makes the state-check and the sleep-command one unbreakable atomic transaction.

The Spurious Wakeup: The Linux scheduler can randomly wake up parked threads even if no one pressed the alarm. We fix this by putting the sleep command inside a while loop.




impl WorkerContext {
    fn run(self) {
        loop {
            // Priority 1: Check the local, lock-free queue
            if let Some(job) = self.local_deque.pop() {
                job();
                continue;
            }

            // Priority 2: Global Batch Steal
            // Take a chunk of jobs, put them in local, return one to run now
            if let Steal::Success(job) = self.global_deque.steal_batch_and_pop(&self.local_deque) {
                job();
                continue;
            }

            // Priority 3: Peer Stealing (Hardware Atomics)
            let mut stole_job = false;
            for stealer in &self.stealers {
                if let Steal::Success(job) = stealer.steal_batch_and_pop(&self.local_deque) {
                    stole_job = true;
                    job();
                    break;
                }
            }
            if stole_job { continue; }

            // Priority 4: All queues are empty. Time to sleep.
        let mut keep_running_guard =   self.sleep_signal.keep_running.lock().unwrap();

        // The while loop protects against Spurious Wakeups
        while *keep_running_guard && self.global_deque.is_empty() {
            // wait() safely hands the Mutex key to the OS, goes to sleep, 
            // and catches the new key when it wakes up.
            keep_running_guard = self.sleep_signal.cvar.wait(keep_running_guard).unwrap();
        }

        // If we woke up because the factory is closing, shatter the loop
        if !*keep_running_guard {
            std::process::exit(0); // In actual code, we break the outer loop
        }
    }
}

Step 4: The Graceful Shutdown

If the main program finishes and exits, the OS will violently murder the sleeping worker threads, potentially corrupting memory. We implement Rust's Drop trait on the manager to politely fire the workers instead.


impl Drop for JobStealer {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        {
            let mut keep_running = self.sleep_signal.keep_running.lock().unwrap();
            *keep_running = false; 
            self.sleep_signal.cvar.notify_all(); // BLAST THE FIRE ALARM
        } // Mutex auto-unlocks here

        // Wait for threads to cleanly pack their desks
        let handles = std::mem::take(&mut self.workers);
        for worker in handles {
            worker.join().unwrap();
        }
    }
}

By flipping the boolean and calling notify_all(), the kernel makes all sleeping threads awake. They see the boolean is false, break out of their infinite loops, and peacefully return their memory to the OS.
The Benchmark: 1 Million Jobs

To prove the efficiency of bypassing the OS scheduler, I wrote a benchmark that blasts 1,000,000 CPU-bound tasks into the Global Injector.

Running this in --release mode on my machine with a 4-core processor yields incredible throughput:
Bash

==================================================
BENCHMARK COMPLETE
Total Execution Time : 2.450011653s

Throughput : 408161.32 jobs / second

Instead of the Linux kernel drowning in 1,000,000 thread context switches, exactly 4 threads are spun up. They ruthlessly steal batches of work from the global queue and each other, relying entirely on L1/L2 CPU caches and silicon atomic instructions to synchronize.
Conclusion

This scheduler will serve as the concurrency backend for my Rust-based Web-to-Markdown extraction engine, allowing it to parse thousands of DOM trees across multiple cores without dropping a single frame.

The full source code for this scheduler is available in my systems_engineer workspace on GitHub https://github.com/14elias/zero-copy-protocol/tree/main/thread-pool.

Understanding how to construct your own thread pool forces you to learn what happens when your code crosses the boundary into the operating system.

title: cryptship | Part 1 — Binding the Decryption Key to the License and the Machine
description:
Most license checks look like this somewhere in the binary:

if !license.Valid() {
    os.Exit(1)
}

Find that branch, flip one instruction, and the check is gone. cryptship moves the most important part of that check, which machine and which license, out of if statements and into the cryptography.

🔑 The key comes from the license

The content key that decrypts your app is never stored in the image. It is wrapped inside the license, and it can only be unwrapped with a key-encryption key (KEK) derived from the machine and the license's own claims:

KEK         = HKDF(machine_fingerprint, license_id, bound claims)
content_key = unwrap(license.wrapped_key, KEK)
plaintext   = aead_open(payload.enc, content_key)   # wrong key => AEAD tag fails

Run on a machine the license is not bound to, or edit a bound claim (license and customer id, product, payload id, binding policy, issue or expiry date), and the unwrap produces a wrong key. AES-256-GCM's authentication tag then refuses to decrypt. Stretching the expiry date by editing the license does not work.

⚖️ What is still an ordinary check

Being precise matters here. Two checks are still normal code in the loader:

  • The signature check. Claims outside the KEK context (edition, entitlements, revocation_url) are protected only by the signature.
  • The expiry check. An unedited license past its date still unwraps on its machine if someone patches that check out or turns the clock back. If expiry must hold against a patched loader, use the online provider (Part 2).

And with binding none, the license itself carries everything needed to unwrap the key: treat that license like a secret.

📄 What a license looks like

Signed claims, canonically JSON-encoded, with a detached Ed25519 signature:

{
  "claims": {
    "v": 1,
    "license_id": "lic_ab12cd34",
    "customer_id": "acme-corp",
    "product": "widget-server",
    "edition": "enterprise",
    "payload_id": "f3a9…",            // binds the license to one build
    "entitlements": ["module.reporting"],
    "issued_at": 1762905600,
    "not_after": 1765497600,          // expiry drives offline revocation
    "binding": { "policy": "strict", "max": 1, "fingerprint_hashes": ["…"] },
    "wrapped_keys": ["base64…"],       // one per bound machine (pool), else one
    "revocation_url": "https://…",     // optional online check
    "signing_key_id": "v1"             // key rotation
  },
  "sig_alg": "ed25519",
  "sig": "base64…"
}

The signature is over the exact stored claim bytes. The loader rejects unknown fields, so a license with newer fields needs a newer loader.

🖥️ Binding to machines

  • none: any machine; the key is unwrapped from a secret in the license
  • strict: one machine
  • pool: a set of machines, with one wrapped key per machine (that is how migrations work)

The machine fingerprint is derived from readable host identifiers such as /etc/machine-id and the DMI UUID. The hostname is deliberately excluded, because in a container it is the container ID and changes every run. Bind-mount /etc/machine-id:ro into the container for a stable identity.

Next, Part 2: the same loader for air-gapped, on-prem and cloud.

  • 📦 Release: v0.1.0
  • 📚 Docs: HOWTO · Architecture · Diagrams
  • 🌐 Website: ai2th.github.io/cryptship.html
  • 💬 Discussion: AI2TH Google Group

title: How I built 2,300 static pages of calculators in 8 languages without a framework
description:
I work in operations at a factory in Bangladesh. In my spare time I built LifeEasyTools, a site with 515 free calculators and everyday tools in 8 languages. It has no framework and no database for the tools: one Node.js script turns plain JavaScript objects into 2,359 static pages.

Here is how it works, what went wrong, and what I would do again.

Why static pages

Most of my users are on low-cost Android phones and slow mobile data. A calculator should show up instantly and never wait for a server to do maths that the phone can do itself.

So every page is plain HTML. Calculations run in the browser, and the PDF and image tools process files locally, so nothing is uploaded. A typical tool page is about 50 KB of HTML (13 KB gzipped), plus one shared stylesheet and one shared script.

One file per tool

Each tool is a JavaScript object:

module.exports = {
  slug: 'concrete-calculator', cat: 'everyday',
  title: 'Concrete Calculator: Volume, Bags, Cement, Sand & Stone',
  form: `${seg('units', 'Units', [['m', 'Metric (m)'], ['ft', 'Feet']], 'm')}
         ${row(num('L', 'Length', 5), num('W', 'Width', 4), num('T', 'Thickness', 0.125))}`,
  js: `DN.init(function (v) {
         var vol = v.L * v.W * v.T;
         return DN.result({ answer: { label: 'Concrete needed', value: DN.fmt(vol, 3) + ' m³' } });
       });`,
  content: `<h2>How to calculate concrete volume</h2> ...`,
  faq: [['How many bags of cement are in 1 cubic metre?', '...']]
};

seg, num and row are tiny helpers that return form HTML. DN is a small shared runtime (about 25 KB gzipped) that reads the form, formats numbers for the visitor's locale, and draws the result card, tables and charts.

The build script loops over every tool and writes the page with its title, description, breadcrumbs, JSON-LD (WebApplication, FAQPage, BreadcrumbList), hreflang links and a sitemap entry. A full build of all 2,359 pages takes about 35 seconds.

Translations without a framework

Each language has a translation file per tool: title, description, intro, content and a ui map of the English strings used in the form and the script.

The build translates the form HTML text nodes and every single-quoted string in the tool's script through that map. When a sentence is built from pieces ('in ' + days + ' days'), a small jsFix list replaces that expression with a properly ordered one, because word order differs between languages.

The catch: it is easy to leave English behind. So a test runs every translated tool in headless Chromium, clicks Calculate, and lists any English phrase left in the visible result. That test found things I would never have spotted by hand, such as holiday names in English on Bangla pages, or a chart legend that still said "Part / Rest".

Testing the maths

For a calculator site, a wrong answer is the worst bug. I keep a "golden" test file: 36 real cases, each with a reference value computed independently from the published formula, not copied from the tool's code.

const pmt = (P, r, n) => P * r * Math.pow(1 + r, n) / (Math.pow(1 + r, n) - 1);
const CASES = [
  ['emi-calculator', { p: 500000, r: 9.5, t: 5, tu: 'y' }, [pmt(500000, 0.095 / 12, 60)], 'EMI 5 lakh 9.5% 5y'],
  ['bmi-calculator', { units: 'metric', kg: 70, cm: 175 }, [22.9], 'BMI'],
  // ... net salary in France, Spain, Italy, Netherlands and Poland, due dates, unit converters
];

Playwright fills each form, runs it, and checks the result contains the expected number. When a test failed the first time, it was usually my test input that was wrong (a mortgage down payment is a percentage, not an amount), which is a good reason to write the reference values independently.

Layout shift on file tools

Chrome's layout-shift measurement showed 0.077 on the PDF tools on phones. The file drop zone gets extra buttons (link, camera, paste, Drive, Dropbox) from JavaScript after the first paint, and on narrow screens they wrapped onto two lines and pushed everything down.

The fix was two parts: show the extra sources as one row of fixed-height tiles on phones, and reserve their height in CSS until the script marks the zone as ready:

@media (max-width: 600px) {
  .fstart .drop:not(.dready) .dbtn { margin-bottom: 87px; }
}

Layout shift went to 0 on every page I measured.

SEO lessons from a site with 2,000+ pages

  • Link siblings around each page, not the first few. Pages in long families (land units, US state paycheck calculators, currency pairs) linked to the first ten items of the list, so items later in the list got almost no internal links. Linking each page to its neighbours on both sides fixed 161 weakly linked pages.
  • Keep titles under about 65 characters. Dropping the brand suffix on long titles let Google show the words that matter.
  • One canonical per page and full hreflang sets for 8 languages, generated from the same data so they never drift apart.
  • Answer first. Converter pages now start with the factor ("1 foot = 0.3048 metres") before anything else.

Numbers

  • 515 tools, 2,359 pages, 8 languages (English, Bangla, Hindi, Spanish, Arabic, Portuguese, Indonesian, French)
  • Build: about 35 seconds for all pages
  • Hosting: one small VPS behind Cloudflare; deploys upload only changed files and notify IndexNow

What I would do again

Plain objects plus a build script were enough for 500 tools. The two things that paid off most were the golden tests and the "find leftover English" test. Both caught real problems before users did.

If you want to try a tool or tell me what is missing, the site is lifeeasytools.com. I am happy to answer questions about the build in the comments.

title: PocketBase for Beginners: A Whole Backend in One Small File
description:
PocketBase is a backend that fits in a single file. One executable gives you a database, user authentication, file storage, and an admin dashboard — no setup, no separate services, no configuration files. If you want a backend for a side project and you do not want to run a server farm, PocketBase is the simplest honest option.

The pitch is that most small apps need the same things: users who can log in, data that can be stored, and files that can be uploaded. PocketBase provides all three out of the box. Download the binary, run it, and you have an admin dashboard at localhost:8090/_/ where you can create collections, define fields, and set access rules with a visual editor.

Your frontend talks to it over a simple REST API, with SDKs for JavaScript and Dart. A login looks like this:

import PocketBase from 'pocketbase';

const pb = new PocketBase('http://127.0.0.1:8090');

await pb.collection('users').authWithPassword('user@example.com', 'password123');
console.log('Logged in as', pb.authStore.model.email);

const posts = await pb.collection('posts').getList(1, 20);
console.log(posts.items);

That is the whole backend for a blog, a todo app, or a small shop. PocketBase also handles realtime updates, so your UI can refresh when data changes, and it stores files on disk with no extra service.

The limits are honest. PocketBase is a single SQLite database in one file, so it is not built for massive scale or for teams that need complex queries across many tables. It is written in Go, so extending it means writing Go. And for a large production app with millions of users, a dedicated database and a separate auth service will fit better. But for a side project, a prototype, or a small business tool, it is hard to beat.

Start today with one step: download PocketBase, run it, create a posts collection in the admin dashboard, and fetch it from a tiny HTML page. When your app has a working backend in fifteen minutes, you will understand the appeal.
