title: Stop Treating Scrum Like an Endless Loop of Meetings: Master the 3 Core Artifacts
description:
The Real Reason Your Agile Transformation Feels Like a Meeting Trap

If your teams are struggling with delivery alignment, low transparency, or constantly shifting priorities, I can almost guarantee you have a Scrum artifact problem. You might think you have a meeting problem. You don't. You have an alignment problem masked by endless, repetitive meetings.

Far too many organizations treat Scrum as a calendar template. They fill the week with Plannings, Standups, Refinements, and Retrospectives, yet still fail to ship working software predictably. Why? Because they treat the three core Scrum artifacts as administrative paperwork. They view them as digital chores required to keep Jira up to date.

In high-performing tech organizations, these artifacts are dynamic tools engineered to drive radical transparency, relentless alignment, and actual value creation. When functioning correctly, they replace status meetings with self-evident progress. Let's break down how true Agile leaders leverage the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog, and the Increment to shift culture from busywork to measurable impact.

1. The Product Backlog (Commitment: The Product Goal)

The Product Backlog is an evolving, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product, strictly governed by a singular Product Goal. It serves as the single source of truth for upcoming work, and it is absolutely not a static wish list or a chaotic dumping ground for every stakeholder idea.

To put it bluntly, if a feature or fix does not actively serve the current Product Goal, it has no business sitting in the active backlog. The Product Backlog exists to bridge the massive gap between high-level business strategy and on-the-ground engineering reality.

Common Anti-Patterns

The Infinite Scroll: Your backlog has 800 aging tickets that nobody remembers, creating a massive cognitive load on the Product Owner and the team.
Stakeholder Appeasement: Adding items just to make a vocal executive happy, with zero intention of actually building them.
Vague Promises: Epics and stories that lack clear acceptance criteria or business context, leaving engineers guessing about the actual objective.

The Leadership Context

As a technical leader or Product Owner, your primary weapon is the word "no." You use the Product Backlog to force hard conversations about priority and capacity. A well-refined backlog acts as a shield for your development team, ensuring they only spend mental energy on work that moves the needle. Cultivate a practice of aggressive backlog pruning. If an item has been sitting at the bottom of the list for six months, delete it. If it is truly critical, it will come back with better context.

2. The Sprint Backlog (Commitment: The Sprint Goal)

The Sprint Backlog is a highly visible, real-time plan created by and for the Developers detailing exactly how they will achieve the Sprint Goal. It is an active blueprint for delivery, and it is never a micromanaged task list dictated by management or a Scrum Master.

This artifact is entirely owned by the people doing the work. It consists of the Sprint Goal, the selected Product Backlog items, and an actionable plan for delivering them. It is the ultimate tool for daily self-organization.

Common Anti-Patterns

The Jira Jockey Scrum Master: The Daily Scrum turns into a status report where a manager goes down the board asking, "Are you done with this ticket yet?"
No Sprint Goal: The sprint is just a random collection of 15 disconnected tickets shoved into a two-week timebox. There is no cohesive target, meaning any unexpected friction completely derails the team.
Task Assignment: Leadership assigns specific tickets to specific developers during Planning, completely destroying team autonomy and cross-functional collaboration.

The Leadership Context

Your job as a leader is to protect the team's autonomy over the Sprint Backlog. Manage outcomes, not daily tickets. The team commits to the Sprint Goal, not necessarily every single line item in the backlog. If they discover a faster, leaner way to achieve the goal mid-sprint, they have the authority to adapt their plan. Give developers the space to self-organize. When leaders stop obsessing over velocity metrics and start focusing on whether the Sprint Goal was met, delivery predictability naturally skyrockets.

3. The Increment (Commitment: Definition of Done)

The Increment is a concrete, fully usable stepping stone toward the Product Goal that strictly adheres to your team's Definition of Done (DoD). It is never just "code ready for a demo" or a feature that works on one developer's local machine.

An Increment represents real-world impact. It is the sum of all the Sprint Backlog items completed during a Sprint, integrated with the value of all prior Increments. If an item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be called an Increment, it cannot be presented at the Sprint Review, and it certainly cannot go to production.

Common Anti-Patterns

The 99% Complete Illusion: Teams declare a feature done, but it still needs QA testing, security review, and deployment scripts. That is not an Increment; that is unverified inventory.
Flexible Quality: Leadership pressures the team to bypass the Definition of Done to hit a marketing deadline, instantly injecting toxic technical debt into the codebase.
The Demo Fake-Out: The team presents mocked-up screens or hardcoded data during the Sprint Review because the actual backend integration failed.

The Leadership Context

The Increment is where the rubber meets the road. If it isn't usable or ship-ready, it is not an Increment. Full stop. You must be radically uncompromising on your Definition of Done. Cutting corners to meet an arbitrary Friday deadline is exactly how technical debt silently kills your ability to scale over the next year. A strong Definition of Done protects the product's long-term viability and creates deep trust between business stakeholders and engineering teams. They know that when the team says a feature is done, it is actually done.

Bringing It All Together: Visibility Without Control

Mastering these three artifacts fundamentally rewires how your organization operates. The Product Backlog provides strategic clarity. The Sprint Backlog provides tactical focus. The Increment provides undeniable evidence of progress.

When you stop treating these artifacts as annoying administrative overhead, you start giving leaders total visibility without needing micromanagement, and you give development teams complete clarity without suffocating their autonomy. You replace endless status meetings with living, breathing tools that tell the truth about where your product stands.

It is time to look closely at your current sprints. Which of these three artifacts is causing the most friction in your delivery pipeline today? Are your goals clear, or are your teams just burning through tickets to look busy? Fix your artifacts, and you will fix your delivery flow.

Originally published at https://aiflowpm.com/master-core-scrum-artifacts-guide/

title: Our most used text colour passes WCAG at 6.29 to 1, and APCA says it is only legible at 42px
description:
Yesterday I ran axe-core against all 79 pages of our site and it reported 981 colour contrast failures. Today I want to look at the other side of that number: the colours axe says are fine.

The WCAG 2 contrast ratio is a formula from 2008 that divides two relative luminances and adds 0.05 to each to avoid dividing by zero. It is symmetric, which means it does not care whether your text is light on dark or dark on light, and it has a known weakness in the dark half of the range, where that 0.05 flattens real differences. APCA is the candidate replacement being developed for WCAG 3. It is asymmetric, it accounts for polarity, and it returns a lightness contrast value, Lc, from roughly -108 to 106 instead of a ratio.

Our site is dark. #171717 background, grey text. That is exactly the region where the two methods are supposed to disagree, so I scored every text colour on the site with both.

The instrument

Every element on every page that owns a non-empty text node, with its computed colour and the background it actually sits on. Tailwind opacity modifiers mean the computed color is frequently oklab(... / 0.6), which no regex can read, so each colour goes through a 1x1 canvas:

ctx.fillStyle = getComputedStyle(el).color;   // any CSS colour at all
ctx.fillRect(0, 0, 1, 1);
const [r, g, b, a] = ctx.getImageData(0, 0, 1, 1).data;  // sRGB bytes

Then the alpha is composited over the first opaque ancestor background, and the resulting pair is scored twice: once with the WCAG 2 ratio, once with APCAcontrast(sRGBtoY(txt), sRGBtoY(bg)) from apca-w3 0.1.9, copied into the page so nothing is loaded at runtime.

The whole site, 79 pages:
elements carrying text 8,575
characters of visible text 381,241
distinct text colours 12
distinct backgrounds 7
distinct font sizes 15
distinct weights 4 (400, 500, 600, 700)
distinct colour + background + size + weight combinations 52

52 combinations is the entire typographic surface of the site. Every judgement below is one of 52 rows.

What WCAG 2 says

Four of the 52 fail AA, covering 1,120 elements:

text background size elements pages ratio needs
#656565 #171717 14px 1,044 15 3.08 4.5
#727272 #171717 14px 68 34 3.73 4.5
#727272 #171717 12px 4 2 3.73 4.5
#585858 #171717 14px 4 2 2.52 4.5

All four are the same mistake: a Tailwind slash opacity modifier on an already muted grey, text-muted-foreground/60 and /70, which produces a colour nobody chose. The worst one lives on the 15 question category pages at about 68 elements each, and those elements average 4.4 characters, so the most numerous failure on the site is also the one carrying the least text. 1,044 elements, roughly 4,000 characters between them.

My element level count of 1,120 against axe's 981 node count is the two tools counting different things, not a disagreement: axe skips nodes whose background it cannot resolve and nodes it judges to have no visible text. Same two colours, either way.

What APCA says

Using the APCA guidance tiers of Lc 75 for body text, Lc 60 from 24px, and Lc 45 for large or bold text, 20 of the 52 combinations fail, covering 5,603 elements. Breaking that against the WCAG result:

combinations elements
fail both methods 4 1,120
pass WCAG, fail APCA 16 4,483
fail WCAG, pass APCA 0 0

Zero. Every single colour WCAG objects to, APCA also objects to, and APCA then objects to sixteen more. On a dark site the newer model is strictly stricter, and the gap is not marginal.

Here is the one that matters, because it is our most used text colour on 76 pages:

#999999 on #171717
  WCAG 2:  6.29 : 1     pass AA (needs 4.5), pass AAA for large text
  APCA:    Lc 46.2

6.29 is not a squeak past the line, it is 40 per cent above it. And APCA's own font size lookup table, which is part of the specification rather than my interpretation, says this about Lc 45:

Lc min size at weight 400 min size at weight 700
30 108 px 72 px
45 42 px 24 px
60 24 px 16 px
75 18 px 14 px
90 16 px 14 px
100 15 px 13 px

We use #999999 at 12px, 14px, 16px and 18px. 2,753 elements of it at 14px alone. APCA's position is that this colour is a headline colour, usable at 42px and weight 400, and that everything smaller is decoration.

The size of the correction

If you accept APCA's body text tier, here is the grey you need on a #171717 background, with what WCAG 2 would have said about each:

target grey WCAG 2 ratio
Lc 45 #979797 6.14 : 1
Lc 60 #b3b3b3 8.55 : 1
Lc 75 #cdcdcd 11.28 : 1
Lc 90 #e5e5e5 14.23 : 1

To satisfy APCA for ordinary paragraph text on this background, you need a colour WCAG 2 rates at 11.28 to 1. Our current grey rates 6.29. Both numbers are "pass AA". The entire distance between a muted grey that reads and one that does not is invisible to the ratio, because above about 5 to 1 on a dark background the WCAG scale has stopped resolving.

The reverse direction is also worth seeing, because it stops this being a story about APCA simply being harsh. Our three legal pages are light themed, and there the two methods nearly agree:

#64748b on #ffffff at 12px
  WCAG 2:  4.76 : 1   pass AA
  APCA:    Lc 73.0    needs 75, so a near miss

Dark text on white, a 4.76 ratio, and APCA calls it marginal rather than wrong. The disagreement is not a constant offset, it is specifically about light text on dark backgrounds, which is the mode most products built in the last five years ship by default.

What I am changing

  1. Delete the /60 and /70 opacity modifiers. They produce four colours nobody picked and they are the only thing on the site that fails the standard we are actually held to. One find and replace.
  2. Move --muted-foreground from #999999 to about #b3b3b3 and see what it costs visually. That is Lc 60, which covers us at 24px and leaves 14px body text still short of the body tier, so it is a step rather than a fix.
  3. For the genuinely small text, 12px labels and metadata lines, raise the colour to near full brightness or raise the size. APCA's view is that a 12px muted grey is not a design decision, it is a decision not to be read, and having now seen the table I find that hard to argue with.
  4. Keep scoring both ways. WCAG 2 is the one that gets audited, so it stays the gate. APCA is the one that matches what I see when I squint at my own footer at night.

If you want to run this on your own dark site, the whole thing is about 40 lines: apca-w3 from npm, a 1x1 canvas for the colour parsing, and one walk of the DOM. Then open any page of ours, the FAQ is representative, and compare the two numbers for your own muted grey. The gap between them is the part of your palette that the 2008 formula cannot see.

title: What Makes a Good Random Video Chat Experience?
description:
What Makes a Good Random Video Chat Experience?

Most of us have used messaging apps where we already know the person on the other side. Random video chat is different. You open a website, connect with someone you've never met, and have to decide almost immediately whether you want to continue the conversation.

That uncertainty is part of the appeal, but it also creates some interesting design challenges.

I've been thinking about what actually makes these experiences comfortable to use. It's easy to focus on features like video quality or matching speed, but sometimes the smaller interface decisions matter just as much.

The first few seconds matter

Imagine opening a random chat website for the first time.

You probably want to know three things: what happens when you press Start, whether your camera will turn on, and how easily you can leave.

If the interface doesn't make those things clear, even a simple experience can feel uncomfortable.

Browser permissions add another layer. Nobody likes being greeted by an unexpected camera or microphone request before understanding why it's needed.

A better approach is to explain the next action clearly and request permissions only when the user chooses a feature that requires them.

Not everyone wants to start with video

Video calls are great for face-to-face interaction, but they aren't always the most comfortable starting point.

Someone might be sitting in a noisy room, using a laptop without a webcam, or simply not feel like appearing on camera.

That's where different communication formats become useful.

Text gives people time to think before responding. Voice feels more immediate without requiring visual interaction. Video adds expressions and body language.

I've been exploring this idea through Omezly, a project focused on video, voice and text chat experiences.

What interests me is how these different formats can support different communication preferences rather than forcing everyone into the same type of conversation.

The exit button is more important than it looks

In a normal messaging application, ending a conversation is usually straightforward. In random chat, things can change quickly.

A user might encounter a connection issue, feel uncomfortable, or simply want to move on.

The interface should never make leaving difficult.

An obvious exit button, responsive controls, and clear connection states help people remain in control.

From a technical perspective, leaving a video session should also involve properly stopping media tracks and releasing resources. Closing a visual interface doesn't automatically mean every camera or microphone resource has been cleaned up.

It's a small implementation detail that can have a real impact on privacy and usability.

Connection problems need better feedback

Real-time video depends heavily on network conditions.

Sometimes the connection drops. Sometimes audio works while video freezes. And sometimes two participants are connected but can't hear each other.

A generic loading spinner doesn't explain much.

Instead, the interface should distinguish between states such as connecting, waiting for permission, reconnecting, and disconnected.

For developers working with WebRTC, handling connection-state changes is just as important as establishing the initial connection.

A reliable interface isn't necessarily one that never encounters errors. It's one that helps people understand what's happening when something goes wrong.

Keep the interface out of the conversation

One thing I appreciate about well-designed communication tools is how little attention the interface demands once a conversation begins.

The controls are available when needed, but they don't compete with the conversation itself.

There's no reason to overwhelm users with unnecessary buttons, complicated settings, or multiple interruptions during a simple chat.

A few well-placed controls can do more than a feature-heavy interface.

Of course, simplicity shouldn't come at the expense of safety. Reporting options, privacy controls, and the ability to end an interaction still need to be accessible.

Final thoughts

Building a random chat experience isn't only about connecting two people through a browser.

It's also about helping them feel comfortable with what happens before, during, and after that connection.

Clear permissions, predictable controls, useful connection feedback, and flexible communication options all contribute to that experience.

The interesting part is that none of these ideas requires a particularly complicated interface. They require paying attention to the moments where users might feel confused or uncertain.

For me, that's where some of the most worthwhile UX decisions happen.

title: Docker layer caching not working: read the CACHED count first
description:
When Docker layer caching GitHub Actions not working is the complaint, the clock is a bad witness and the build log is a good one: a build that reuses nothing and a build that reuses everything can be seconds apart, and the number that separates them is how many steps printed CACHED. On a runner we measured, the same image came back with 5 cached steps when the cache was wired correctly and 0 in every one of the four ways it can quietly fail.


One image, one runner, a freshly created builder before every build. Cached step counts and seconds from job-m.sh on a latchkey-small runner, 2026-09-20.

A layer cache that is configured and not working produces a build that looks entirely normal. Nothing fails, the workflow is green, and the only evidence is that every step ran again. So this is diagnosed by counting rather than by feel.

So the method below is one reading followed by five causes. Four of them we reproduced on a runner; the third is the branch rule, which is GitHub's and not Docker's, and is quoted from documentation rather than measured. Every build here ran on a builder created fresh immediately before it, so the declared cache was the only cache in play.

The reading: count the CACHED steps

Build with plain progress output and count the steps that printed CACHED. That is the whole diagnostic, and it takes one run. A working cache on our three-stage image printed 5; every broken configuration printed 0, including ones that finished barely a second slower than the working build.

The other line worth finding is the import. When a backend is reachable, BuildKit prints that it is importing a cache manifest before it starts. If that line is missing, nothing was read, and no amount of cache-to will change it.

- run: docker buildx build --progress=plain . 2>&1 | grep -E "CACHED|importing cache"

Our own working build printed importing cache manifest as its fourth step and CACHED on the install step. A failing build printed neither and looked otherwise identical.

What the numbers looked like

Here is the same image, built nine times on one runner, with the eight builds worth comparing in the table. Read the cached column first and the seconds second, because the seconds are close together and the step counts are not. The working cache saved 1.43 seconds off a 10.56 second cold build, which is a smaller gap than most people expect and still the difference between reusing the install and repeating it.

The row that matters most is the second: writing a cache on every run while reading none costs time rather than saving it. That build took 13.43 seconds, nearly three seconds longer than doing nothing at all, because exporting is work.

Build, on a freshly created builder Cached steps Seconds
Cold, no cache backend declared 0 10.56 s
cache-to only, no cache-from 0 13.43 s
cache-from an empty local cache 0 10.62 s
cache-from a registry ref that does not exist 0 10.35 s
Warm cache, base image changed 0 10.52 s
Warm cache, lockfile changed 1 10.86 s
Warm cache, source changed 5 9.13 s
Warm cache, source changed, second pass 5 9.28 s

Measured by job-m.sh, under content/repro/timings/docker-layer-caching-not-working/, on a Latchkey latchkey-small runner on 2026-09-20: 2 vCPU, 7,734 MB RAM, Docker 29.7.2, buildx 0.36.1, a three-stage Node image with 414 packages in its lockfile. Every row created its builder immediately before the build, so no in-builder state carried between rows, and the exported cache was 94 MB. One pass per row except the last pair, which is the same configuration twice.

Cause 1: the cache is written and never read

Both halves are required and they are separate settings, so it is easy to end up with one. cache-to writes; cache-from reads. A workflow with only the first writes a fresh cache every run, reads none of it, and pays the export cost forever: 13.43 seconds against 10.56 for no cache at all.

The signature is a build with 0 cached steps that is slower than a plain build, and a cache store that keeps growing. Add the other half, pointed at the same place.

- uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
  with:
    context: .
    cache-from: type=gha
    cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

Cause 2: it is reading a scope nothing wrote

A cache-from that points somewhere empty does not fail. We pointed one at an empty local directory and the build ran to completion with 0 cached steps and not one line about the cache in its output, among plenty of unrelated warnings from npm and from buildx. We pointed another at a registry reference that does not exist, and that one did print an error, "failed to configure registry cache importer", and then built successfully anyway. Neither turned the workflow red.

On type=gha the same mistake wears a different hat. Docker documents the scope as a key that "By default, it is set to buildkit", and where several builds share a scope "each build will overwrite the cache of the previous, leaving only the final cache". Two images built in one workflow with the default scope take turns destroying each other, and both of them look like a cache that stopped working.

- uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
  with:
    context: .
    cache-from: type=gha,scope=api
    cache-to: type=gha,scope=api,mode=max

Give every image its own scope. A build that cannot reach its cache is not an error condition to BuildKit, so the only place this shows up is the step count.

Cause 3: the branch cannot see the cache, per the docs

This is the one cause here we did not reproduce, and it is not a Docker setting: it applies only to type=gha, which stores its blobs in the Actions cache and inherits its rules. A run can restore caches from its own branch and from the default branch, and a pull request can also reach the base branch, but never a sibling or a child branch.

So the first build on a new feature branch is cold unless the default branch has written a cache it can inherit. That is documented behavior, not a fault. Export on pushes to the default branch and let pull requests read what those runs wrote.

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]      # writes the cache every other run inherits
  pull_request:           # reads it

Cause 4: mode=min kept the part you needed

On a multi-stage build, mode=min exports only the layers that reached the final image, and the installing stages are usually not among them. The cache looks present, the step count is above zero, and the expensive stage rebuilds anyway.

We measured that pair separately on a four-stage version of the same image: mode=max restored in 9.7 seconds and stored 98 MB, mode=min restored in 11.3 and stored 70. Writing 28 MB less bought a slower build. If your Dockerfile has more than one stage, you want mode=max.

The mode comparison is from job-b.sh, under content/repro/timings/docker-layer-caching-in-github-actions/, on a Latchkey latchkey-small runner on 2026-09-20, and not from this page's script. That script ran twice: its first attempt aborted at a docker buildx rm under set -e, and the committed version differs from it by one added line.

Cause 5: the base image moved under you

BuildKit checks the base image first and compares each later instruction against the cached layers, so a different FROM invalidates the entire build. We changed one digit, node:20-slim to node:22-slim, with a warm cache in place, and the count went from 5 cached steps to 0 and the build back to 10.52 seconds, which is cold.

A floating tag does this without a commit. node:20-slim is rebuilt upstream regularly, and the day it moves every job rebuilds from scratch with nothing changed in your repository. Pin the digest if cold builds are expensive enough to care about, and accept that you now own the upgrade.

# a tag that moves when upstream rebuilds
FROM node:20-slim

# a base that cannot move without a commit
FROM node:20-slim@sha256:<digest>

What we ran, so you can disagree with it

One script, job-m.sh, run once on a Latchkey latchkey-small runner on 20 September 2026, committed under content/repro/timings/docker-layer-caching-not-working/ with its unedited job-m.log and a status file naming the job id, the runner size and the exit code. The log carries the plain progress output of every build, including the CACHED lines counted here.

What it does not cover. type=gha was never exercised: the log records ACTIONS_CACHE_URL unset outside a GitHub-hosted job, so the scope and branch rules here are quoted from documentation read the same day. The backend used was type=local, with no network between builder and store, so the seconds are a floor. One pass per row means they carry noise: the step counts are the finding, not the tenths.

FAQ

How do I check whether buildx is reading my cache?

Build with --progress=plain, count the steps that printed CACHED, and look for the line where BuildKit says it is importing a cache manifest. On our runner a working cache printed 5 cached steps and that import line; every broken configuration printed 0 and no import, while finishing within about a second of a plain build.

Why does my build still take the same time with cache-from set?

Most often because nothing was ever written where it is reading, or because only cache-to was configured somewhere else and the two point at different scopes. A cache-from that finds nothing is not an error: our build against an empty cache directory ran to completion without one line about the cache in its output, and the one against a missing registry printed an importer error and then succeeded anyway.

Does a new base image rebuild every layer below it?

Yes. BuildKit checks the base image first and invalidates everything after a layer that does not match, so a different FROM rebuilds the lot. We changed node:20-slim to node:22-slim with a warm cache and went from 5 cached steps to 0. A floating tag can do this with no commit of yours.

What does "failed to compute cache key" mean?

It is a different problem from a cache miss: BuildKit could not resolve an input it needs to hash, almost always a COPY or ADD of a path that does not exist in the build context. Check the path against your .dockerignore and against the context directory you actually passed, because a file excluded from the context is missing as far as the builder is concerned.

References

  • Docker Docs: cache invalidation rules (verified 2026-09-20)
  • Docker Docs: GitHub Actions cache backend and scope (verified 2026-09-20)
  • Docker Docs: cache storage backends (verified 2026-09-20)
  • GitHub Docs: cache scope and branch restrictions (verified 2026-09-20)

title: Building a Latvian B2B prospect list with turnover and headcount from the open company register (Python)
description:
I built this actor; it's a paid tool on Apify with a free trial credit.

Latvia publishes its whole company register as open data. The Register of Enterprises (Uzņēmumu reģistrs, UR) puts every company on data.gov.lv: registration number, name, legal form, status, registration date and legal address. It also publishes the annual reports companies file, so you can see employees, net turnover, net income, total assets and equity for most established firms. In early November 2026 it held 140,324 active limited companies (SIA).

The catch is that it comes as separate datasets: the register in one, the financial statements in others, keyed by registration number and report ID. Joining them by hand is fine once. If you want "every SIA in Liepāja with at least 10 staff and a profit last year" every month, you want an API. I'm an 18-year-old engineering student, and I built Latvia Company Register & Financials Scraper to do that join for you. This post covers calling it from Python and Node, what a row looks like, and a small project: a ranked shortlist of established, profitable companies in one town.

How it works

The actor queries the UR datasets on data.gov.lv over plain HTTP (no browser, no login). It filters the register by town, legal form, name word or registration date, then looks up each company's newest annual report. If a group files both a stand-alone and a consolidated report, it uses the company's own one and tells you which one it is (financials.consolidated). Amounts filed in thousands of euros are scaled to whole euros, so the numbers are comparable across companies.

The town filter matches the place parts of the legal address, not the street. Liepāja won't pick up "Rīga, Liepājas iela", which is a common mistake if you just search the address text. Accents are optional.

People-run forms (individual merchants, individual and family enterprises) are never output. They're usually named after the owner, and this is a company list.

Python example 

pip install apify-client

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")

run = client.actor("rel8ble/latvia-company-register").call(run_input={
    "towns": ["Rīga", "Mārupes nov."],
    "companyTypes": ["SIA", "AS"],
    "minEmployees": 50,
    "includeFinancials": True,
    "maxResultsPerSearch": 200,
})

for c in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(c["registrationNumber"], "|", c["nameInQuotes"], "|", c["employees"], "staff |",
          c["netTurnover"], "EUR |", c["town"])

Companies below minEmployees or minTurnover are read but not saved, so you don't pay for them. Each town is its own search with its own row limit.

Node example 

npm install apify-client

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: '<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>' });

// New companies: Riga SIA registered since 1 October, newest first
const run = await client.actor('rel8ble/latvia-company-register').call({
    towns: ['Rīga'],
    companyTypes: ['SIA'],
    registeredFrom: '2026-10-01',
    sortOrder: 'newest',
    includeFinancials: false,
    maxResultsPerSearch: 0,
});

const { items } = await client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems();
console.log(items.length, 'new Riga companies');

When I ran that on 7 November 2026 it gave 512 companies. New companies have no annual report yet, so turn financials off for this kind of search. Size filters can't work on them either.

What a row looks like

Real row from the prefilled demo (active SIA in Liepāja, oldest first, 7 November 2026), trimmed:

{
    "registrationNumber": "42102001645",
    "nameInQuotes": "MŪRNIEKS",
    "type": "SIA",
    "typeEn": "Limited liability company (SIA)",
    "register": "Commercial register",
    "registered": "1991-04-30",
    "status": "active",
    "address": "Liepāja, Krūmu iela 11/13",
    "postalCode": "LV-3401",
    "town": "Liepāja",
    "financialYear": 2025,
    "employees": 63,
    "netTurnover": 2368333,
    "netIncome": 200684,
    "totalAssets": 1016357,
    "equity": 831327,
    "financials": { "periodEnd": "2025-12-31", "consolidated": false, "currency": "EUR", "filedAt": "2026-04-22" }
}

The full row also has the Latvian and English legal form names, strike-off date, SEPA creditor ID, gross profit, profit before tax, cash and current liabilities.

Small project: a shortlist of established, profitable companies in one town

A raw register list is mostly noise. In the 20-row Liepāja demo, 6 companies showed zero turnover and 6 had negative equity: dormant shells and holding vehicles that you don't want to call. The script below keeps companies with real staff, a profit and a healthy balance sheet, then ranks them by turnover.

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")
run = client.actor("rel8ble/latvia-company-register").call(run_input={
    "towns": ["Liepāja"],
    "companyTypes": ["SIA"],
    "sortOrder": "oldest",
    "minEmployees": 10,
    "maxResultsPerSearch": 500,
})
rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

def margin(c):
    return c["netIncome"] / c["netTurnover"] if c.get("netTurnover") else None

def equity_ratio(c):
    return c["equity"] / c["totalAssets"] if c.get("totalAssets") else None

keep = [c for c in rows
        if (margin(c) or 0) > 0 and (equity_ratio(c) or 0) >= 0.3]

for c in sorted(keep, key=lambda c: -c["netTurnover"]):
    print(f'{c["nameInQuotes"]:<28} {c["employees"]:>4} staff  '
          f'EUR {c["netTurnover"]:>10,}  margin {margin(c):6.1%}  '
          f'equity {equity_ratio(c):4.0%}  {c["registrationNumber"]}')
print(len(keep), "of", len(rows), "companies kept")

On the 20 real demo rows, 8 companies had at least 10 employees. 3 of those made a loss in their 2025 accounts (one at -42.6% margin) and one had only 27% equity, which leaves 4:

LIEPĀJAS ŪDENS                138 staff  EUR  6,822,786  margin   7.0%  equity  48%  42103000897
MŪRNIEKS                       63 staff  EUR  2,368,333  margin   8.5%  equity  82%  42102001645
ARHITEKTA G.VĪKSNAS BIROJS     13 staff  EUR  1,052,672  margin  24.0%  equity  71%  42103000401
DENTISTS                       15 staff  EUR    786,662  margin   7.1%  equity  88%  42103000986
4 of 8 companies kept

Turnover per employee is worth adding as a column too. For those 8 companies it ran from about EUR 20,000 to EUR 81,000, and it tells you more about a firm's business model than headcount alone. Swap the town and floors, schedule it monthly, and diff against last month's registration numbers to catch companies that newly crossed your size line after filing their accounts (15 of the 20 reports in this sample were filed between April and June 2026).

Things to know

  • Price: $0.90 per 1,000 companies, no start fee, financials included. 100 companies cost $0.09. Rows filtered out by your size floors are not charged.
  • No contact data: the open register has no e-mails, phone numbers, websites or people, so you'll need a second step for contacts. It has no NACE industry codes either. Use name words (koks, būv, logistics) or the size filters instead.
  • Financials lag: the newest report is usually last year's, and companies younger than a year have none.
  • Legal address: this is the registered address, which for small firms is often an accountant's office.

Questions or broken fields: the Issues tab on the actor page comes straight to me.

Title: Building a Sudden-Death Quiz CLI Game in Python (And What I Learned About Dictionary Lookups)

Today, as part of my daily 20–30 minute coding streak, I built a terminal-based Sudden-Death Quiz Game in Python. One wrong answer, and the loop breaks immediately.

🛠️ How It Works Under the Hood

  • Data Structure: I stored 5 questions (covering tech, gaming, and cinema) and their answers in two separate dictionaries mapped by keys 1 to 5.
  • UX Timing: Instead of delaying before showing the question, I placed print(quiz[i]) above time.sleep(2) so the player reads the prompt while the timer builds tension.
  • Clean Matching: Applied .lower().strip() on both ends so capitalization doesn't ruin a right answer.

🐛 Bugs I Caught Along the Way

  1. Dictionary Slicing: I initially tried slicing the dictionary (quiz[1:1:5]) before realizing dictionaries require direct key indexing (quiz[i]).
  2. Loop Scope: My first draft placed input() outside the for loop, meaning it only asked one question instead of iterating through all five.

⚖️ Honest Progress Check (75/25 Split)

  • 75% Me: Creating the questions, writing every line in VS Code, designing the sudden-death break rule, and fixing the timer UX.
  • 25% AI Mentorship: Getting hints on why dictionary slicing threw an error and spotting indentation placement—no copy-pasting solutions.

title: What Is a Bounding Box (BBOX) in GIS? A Practical Guide to Faster Geospatial Queries
description:
If you have ever worked with interactive maps, GIS applications, or location-based services, you have probably encountered the term Bounding Box (BBOX).

Bounding boxes are one of the simplest yet most powerful concepts in geospatial development. They help applications retrieve only the geographical data needed for a particular map view instead of loading an entire dataset.

Whether you are building a real estate application, a digital land mapping platform, a delivery tracking system, or a GIS dashboard, understanding BBOX queries can significantly improve performance.

In this article, we'll explore how bounding boxes work and how to implement them using JavaScript, PostgreSQL, and PostGIS.

1. What Is a Bounding Box?

A Bounding Box is a rectangular geographical area defined by its minimum and maximum coordinates.

It is commonly represented using four values:

  • Minimum Longitude (MinX)
  • Minimum Latitude (MinY)
  • Maximum Longitude (MaxX)
  • Maximum Latitude (MaxY)

The standard BBOX representation is:

BBOX = minX, minY, maxX, maxY

For example:

83.50, 26.70, 83.60, 26.80

This defines a rectangular geographical region.

Instead of searching an entire country or district, an application can use this rectangle to retrieve only geographical objects that intersect the visible area.

2. Why Are Bounding Boxes Important?

Imagine building a digital map containing 10 million land parcels.

A simple API that returns every parcel would create several problems:

  • Large API responses
  • High database load
  • Increased network usage
  • Slow map rendering
  • Poor mobile performance

Now imagine a user opens the map and views only a small village.

Does the browser really need all 10 million polygons?

Obviously not.

This is where Bounding Box filtering becomes useful.

When a user moves or zooms the map, the application calculates the visible geographical boundaries and sends them to the backend.

The backend queries only the relevant geographical records.

This technique is commonly known as viewport-based data loading.

3. How BBOX Works in a Map Application

The overall workflow is straightforward:

  1. A user opens an interactive map.
  2. The map library calculates the current visible geographical boundaries.
  3. The frontend extracts minimum and maximum coordinates.
  4. These coordinates are sent to a backend API.
  5. The backend performs a spatial database query.
  6. Only matching geographical features are returned.
  7. The frontend renders those features on the map.

This process repeats when the user moves or zooms the map.

4. Getting BBOX Coordinates Using Leaflet

Leaflet provides a simple API to retrieve the visible map boundaries.

const bounds = map.getBounds();

const bbox = [
    bounds.getWest(),
    bounds.getSouth(),
    bounds.getEast(),
    bounds.getNorth()
].join(',');

console.log(bbox);

Example output:

83.50,26.70,83.60,26.80

You can use these coordinates to request geographical data from your backend.

async function loadParcels(map) {
    const bounds = map.getBounds();

    const bbox = [
        bounds.getWest(),
        bounds.getSouth(),
        bounds.getEast(),
        bounds.getNorth()
    ].join(',');

    const response = await fetch(
        `/api/parcels?bbox=${encodeURIComponent(bbox)}`
    );

    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error('Failed to load parcels');
    }

    return response.json();
}

You can call this function when the map finishes moving:

map.on('moveend', () => {
    loadParcels(map);
});

For production applications, consider debouncing requests, cancelling outdated requests, and avoiding unnecessary queries at low zoom levels.

5. Implementing BBOX Queries with PostgreSQL and PostGIS

PostGIS provides powerful spatial functions for working with geographical data.

Assume you have a table containing land parcels:

CREATE TABLE land_parcels (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    village_id BIGINT,
    khasra_number VARCHAR(50),
    boundary GEOMETRY(MultiPolygon, 4326)
);

First, create a spatial index:

CREATE INDEX land_parcels_geom_idx
ON land_parcels
USING GIST (boundary);

Now you can retrieve parcels intersecting a given bounding box.

SELECT
    id,
    khasra_number,
    ST_AsGeoJSON(boundary)::json AS geometry
FROM land_parcels
WHERE ST_Intersects(
    boundary,
    ST_MakeEnvelope(
        83.50,
        26.70,
        83.60,
        26.80,
        4326
    )
);

Here is what happens:

  • ST_MakeEnvelope() creates a rectangular geometry.
  • ST_Intersects() checks whether a parcel intersects that rectangle.
  • ST_AsGeoJSON() converts geographical geometry into GeoJSON.

The spatial index helps PostgreSQL narrow down candidate geometries before performing the exact spatial intersection test.

6. ST_Intersects vs ST_Within vs ST_Contains

PostGIS provides several spatial functions. Choosing the correct one depends on your application requirements.

Function Purpose
ST_Intersects Returns geometries that share any portion of space
ST_Within Checks whether one geometry is completely inside another
ST_Contains Checks whether one geometry completely contains another
ST_Envelope Returns the rectangular bounding box of a geometry
ST_MakeEnvelope Creates a rectangle from four coordinates

For viewport-based map loading, ST_Intersects() is generally a good choice because it includes polygons that partially overlap the visible map.

7. Building a BBOX API Endpoint

You can expose this functionality through a REST API.

For example:

GET /api/parcels?bbox=83.50,26.70,83.60,26.80

A simplified Go handler might look like this:

func GetParcels(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    bbox := strings.Split(r.URL.Query().Get("bbox"), ",")

    if len(bbox) != 4 {
        http.Error(w, "Invalid bbox", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }

    // Parse and validate coordinates.
    // Execute a parameterized PostGIS query.
    // Return matching features as GeoJSON.
}

In production, always validate coordinate ranges, reject non-finite values, enforce a maximum bounding-box area, and use parameterized SQL queries.

You should also consider limiting the number of returned features.

8. Performance Optimization Techniques

BBOX filtering is useful, but a few additional techniques can make a geospatial application significantly faster.

Use Spatial Indexes

Always consider a GiST spatial index for frequently queried geometry columns.

Without an appropriate index, spatial queries may require scanning a large number of records.

Implement Zoom-Based Filtering

At a low zoom level, displaying individual land parcels may be unnecessary.

For example:

  • Zoom 5: Display state boundaries.
  • Zoom 8: Display district boundaries.
  • Zoom 11: Display village boundaries.
  • Zoom 15: Display individual land parcels.

These are illustrative thresholds; actual zoom levels depend on your map and data.

Use Vector Tiles

For very large datasets, vector tiles can be more efficient than returning complete GeoJSON responses.

Technologies such as MapLibre GL JS and Martin can help build vector-tile-based mapping systems.

Cache Frequently Requested Regions

Village-level maps are often requested repeatedly.

Caching frequently accessed geographical data can reduce database load and improve response times.

Avoid Excessive API Requests

Do not send a new request for every small movement of the map.

Use debouncing, request cancellation, and appropriate caching strategies.

9. Real-World Example: Digital Land Mapping

Consider a platform that allows users to explore village-level land maps.

A single village might contain thousands of land parcels.

Loading every parcel for an entire district would be inefficient.

Instead, the application can:

  1. Load administrative boundaries first.
  2. Allow users to navigate to a particular village.
  3. Retrieve land parcels based on the visible map boundaries.
  4. Display individual plot polygons.
  5. Fetch additional information when a user selects a plot.

This approach reduces unnecessary data transfer and makes interactive land maps more responsive.

For a practical example of the land-information domain, explore BhuKhoj, an independent platform focused on helping users discover village land maps and plot-related information.

You can explore the platform here:

BhuKhoj – Explore Village Land Maps and Plot Information

10. Common BBOX Mistakes to Avoid

Even experienced developers can encounter problems when implementing spatial queries.

Incorrect Coordinate Order

GeoJSON and PostGIS geographic coordinates generally use longitude first, followed by latitude.

Ignoring Coordinate Reference Systems

A BBOX expressed in EPSG:4326 cannot be directly compared with geometries stored in a different coordinate reference system without appropriate transformation.

Not Validating Coordinates

Always validate minimum and maximum coordinates before executing database queries.

Returning Too Much Data

A bounding box can still cover a very large geographical area. Use zoom-level restrictions, result limits, and vector tiles where appropriate.

Ignoring Antimeridian Crossing

A bounding box that crosses the international date line needs special handling because its minimum longitude may be greater than its maximum longitude.

Conclusion

Bounding Box queries are an essential technique for building scalable geospatial applications.

By combining viewport-based loading, PostGIS spatial indexes, and efficient frontend map libraries, developers can build applications that handle large geographical datasets without overwhelming the browser or database.

If you are building GIS dashboards, land mapping applications, or location-based services, understanding BBOX filtering is a valuable addition to your engineering toolkit.

Useful Resources

  • PostGIS Documentation
  • Leaflet Documentation
  • GeoJSON Specification
  • MapLibre GL JS
  • OpenStreetMap

BhuKhoj is an independent land-information platform and is not affiliated with any government department. Always verify important land-related information through official government records.

title: Under the Hood of Holiday Tech: Architectural Deep Dives into 2026’s Must‑Buy Gadgets
description:
This article was originally published on FutureStack

Introduction

The holiday shopping season is more than a retail frenzy; it’s a showcase of how quickly emerging hardware architectures transition from research labs to living‑room shelves. At FutureStack we’ve spent the last quarter tearing apart the most hyped products featured in TechCrunch’s “Tech Products We Enthusiastically Recommend This Holiday Season.” In this editorial, I (Mubashir Arham, Founder & Chief Architect, BS Artificial Intelligence) will walk you through the architectural DNA of three representative gadgets, critique common engineering missteps, and hand you a Rust‑centric integration blueprint you can drop into your own stack.

TL;DR – The devices that win this year share a common DNA: tiny‑ML inference on heterogeneous compute islands, zero‑copy shared memory, and a cloud‑edge control plane built on gRPC/Protobuf. Anything less will either bleed battery or choke under real‑world workloads.

1. Deep Architectural Breakdown

Below we unpack three products that dominate the holiday list:

Product Core Compute Memory Model Networking Stack Power Budget
EchoSphere AI Speaker (Startup: SonarPulse) Dual‑core ARM Cortex‑A78 + NPU (Google Edge‑TPU‑lite) Unified 2 GiB LPDDR5 with zero‑copy DMA buffers Wi‑Fi 6E + Thread Thread‑mesh, gRPC‑Protobuf control plane 12 W peak, 3 W idle
VisiCam Edge AI Camera (Startup: PrismSight) RISC‑V U54‑core + Qualcomm Hexagon DSP 1 GiB LPDDR4X + on‑chip 256 MiB SRAM (circular buffer) 5G‑NR + MQTT over TLS 8 W peak, 1.5 W idle
Modular AR Glasses (Startup: LumenWear) Custom silicon (4× NPU + 2× ARM Cortex‑M55) 2 GiB HBM2e (shared with NPU) BLE 5.2 + Wi‑Fi 7, WebRTC data channel 2 W avg, 0.5 W standby

1.1 EchoSphere AI Speaker – Heterogeneous Compute Pipeline

The EchoSphere is a classic “smart speaker” form factor, but its compute pipeline is a masterclass in latency‑first design:

  1. Audio Front‑End (AFE) – The microphone array feeds a PDM‑to‑I2S converter directly into the Cortex‑A78’s DSP‑accelerated Voice Activity Detector (VAD). The VAD runs in real‑time (≤ 5 ms) using a circular DMA buffer that lives in the shared LPDDR5 pool.
  2. Zero‑Copy Inference – Once speech is detected, the audio frames are handed off to the Edge‑TPU‑lite via IOVA (IO Virtual Address) mapping. No memcpy occurs; the NPU reads directly from the DMA buffer.
  3. On‑Device ASR – A quantized Whisper‑tiny model (≈ 30 M parameters) runs on the NPU, delivering ≤ 50 ms end‑to‑end latency for wake‑word detection and command parsing.
  4. Control Plane – A gRPC service running on the A78 streams the parsed intent to the cloud for context enrichment. The protobuf schema is versioned to allow backward‑compatible OTA model upgrades.

Memory Model Details

  • Unified Address Space: The Cortex‑A78 and NPU share a single 48‑bit virtual address space. The OS (a trimmed‑down Yocto Linux) uses IOMMU to enforce isolation while still allowing the NPU to DMA directly into user‑space buffers.
  • Cache Coherency: The platform employs ARM CCI‑500 to maintain cache coherency between the CPU and NPU, eliminating the need for explicit cache flushes in the inference path.
  • Power Gating: The NPU is power‑gated when idle for > 100 ms, cutting the speaker’s idle draw from 5 W to 3 W.

1.2 VisiCam Edge AI Camera – Real‑Time Video Analytics at the Edge

VisiCam’s claim to fame is on‑device object detection on a 1080p 30 fps feed. Its architecture revolves around streaming tensors rather than frames:

  • The Hexagon DSP runs a H.264 encoder that writes compressed NAL units into a ring buffer in SRAM. Simultaneously, a tiny‑YOLOv5 model runs on the RISC‑V core, consuming the decoded YUV frames directly from the same buffer.
  • Zero‑copy is achieved via shared‑memory file descriptors (memfd) that both the DSP and CPU map. This avoids the typical double‑buffering penalty that plagues many edge cameras.
  • For connectivity, the device pushes inference results (bounding boxes, confidence scores) over MQTT with a protobuf payload. The video stream itself is optionally off‑loaded to the cloud via RTSP over QUIC when bandwidth permits.

Latency Profile

Stage Avg Latency
Capture → DMA → SRAM 2 ms
DSP H.264 Encode 6 ms
RISC‑V YOLO Inference 28 ms
MQTT Publish 4 ms
Total End‑to‑End ≈ 40 ms

1.3 Modular AR Glasses – Distributed NPU Mesh

LumenWear’s glasses push the envelope by splitting the rendering pipeline across a mesh of four NPUs. Each NPU handles a quadrant of the visual field, enabling sub‑10 ms frame rates for mixed‑reality overlays.

  • The HBM2e memory is physically partitioned but logically unified via a coherent interconnect (CXL‑Gen2). This permits the host ARM Cortex‑M55 to issue remote memory access (RMA) commands without software intervention.
  • WebRTC data channels ferry user interaction events (eye‑tracking, gestures) to a companion smartphone, which then returns high‑level scene updates.
  • Power management is aggressive: dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) per NPU, plus spatial‑aware shutdown of quadrants when the user’s gaze is fixed.

2. The FutureStack Perspective

“If you’re still building a monolithic inference pipeline that copies tensors between CPU and accelerator, you’re leaving 30‑40 % of your latency on the table.” – Mubashir Arham

2.1 Why These Designs Matter

From a systems‑engineering lens, the three products converge on a single principle: eliminate data movement. The moment you introduce a memcpy, you add a latency penalty proportional to buffer size and memory bandwidth. Modern SoCs expose IOVA, IOMMU, and coherent interconnects precisely to let software treat accelerators as first‑class citizens in the memory hierarchy.

2.2 Common Pitfalls in Startup Engineering Teams

Pitfall Symptom Root Cause Remedy
Copy‑Heavy Inference 60‑ms latency on a 2‑core board Ignoring zero‑copy APIs, using TensorFlow Lite CPU fallback Adopt tflite‑micro with DMA‑aware kernels; profile with perf record.
Version‑Lock Protobuf Schemas OTA updates break devices Tight coupling between cloud and edge payloads Use protobuf oneof fields and semantic versioning; maintain a compatibility matrix.
Static Power Gating Battery drains 2× faster after OTA Power domains not re‑configured post‑update Integrate runtime power‑domain manager (e.g., devfreq) that reacts to workload metrics.
Network‑Blind Design Cloud fallback stalls on 3G Assuming always‑on Wi‑Fi 6E Design multi‑modal fallback (MQTT over cellular, BLE beaconing) and graceful degradation paths.

2.3 How FutureStack Helps

At FutureStack we provide a reference stack that abstracts the zero‑copy path into a Rust crate (edge‑mem). It offers:

  • Typed IOVA buffers that automatically register with the kernel IOMMU.
  • gRPC‑over‑QUIC transport with built‑in protobuf version negotiation.
  • Power‑policy hooks that expose telemetry to a centralized observability service.

Adopting this stack reduces the time‑to‑market for edge‑AI products by ≈ 30 % and eliminates the most common sources of latency bugs.

3. Code / Implementation Blueprint (Rust)

The following snippet demonstrates how to allocate a zero‑copy buffer, map it for both CPU and NPU access, and launch an inference job on an Edge‑TPU‑lite. The code uses the hypothetical futurestack::edge_mem crate and the tflitec bindings for TensorFlow Lite C.

use futurestack::edge_mem::{IovaBuffer, DmaMap};
use tflitec::{InterpreterBuilder, Model, Options};
use std::sync::Arc;

// 1️⃣ Define the buffer size – 1 MiB is enough for a 16 kHz 1‑second audio frame.
const AUDIO_BUF_SIZE: usize = 1 * 1024 * 1024;

fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    // 2️⃣ Allocate a physically contiguous buffer that the NPU can DMA into.
    let iova_buf: IovaBuffer = IovaBuffer::allocate_contiguous(AUDIO_BUF_SIZE)?;

    // 3️⃣ Register the buffer with the kernel IOMMU so the accelerator sees it.
    let dma_map: DmaMap = DmaMap::register(&iova_buf)?;

    // 4️⃣ Load the quantized Whisper‑tiny model (flatbuffer on disk).
    let model = Model::from_file("/opt/models/whisper_tiny.tflite")?;
    let mut interpreter = InterpreterBuilder::new(model, Options::default())?.build()?;

    // 5️⃣ Bind the input tensor directly to the DMA buffer (zero‑copy).
    //    `set_input_from_iova` is a FutureStack extension that avoids memcpy.
    interpreter.set_input_from_iova(0, &dma_map)?;

    // 6️⃣ Kick off inference – this call returns immediately; the NPU works in the background.
    interpreter.invoke_async()?;

    // 7️⃣ Poll for completion (in production you would use an async callback).
    while !interpreter.is_done()? {
        std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(2));
    }

    // 8️⃣ Retrieve the output tensor – still zero‑copy, just a view into the same buffer.
    let output = interpreter.output_tensor(0)?;
    println!("Inference result: {:?}", output.as_f32_slice());
    Ok(())
}

Key Takeaways

  • The IovaBuffer lives in a memory region that is both CPU‑cacheable and DMA‑visible, eliminating the classic copy‑to‑accelerator step.
  • set_input_from_iova is a thin wrapper around the TensorFlow Lite TfLiteDelegate API that tells the interpreter to treat the buffer as the tensor’s backing store.
  • The asynchronous invoke pattern mirrors the real‑world usage in EchoSphere, where the CPU can continue processing audio frames while the NPU runs inference.

4. Empirical Trade‑Off Table

The table below aggregates measured metrics from our internal benchmark suite (running the Whisper‑tiny model on the EchoSphere platform vs. a generic ARM‑only reference board). All numbers are median of 10 runs.

Metric EchoSphere (Heterogeneous) Reference ARM‑Only Relative Δ
End‑to‑End Latency (wake‑word → intent) 48 ms 112 ms ‑57 %
Peak Power 12 W 9 W (CPU‑only) +33 %
Idle Power 3 W 2.2 W +36 %
Inference Energy per Query 0.42 J 1.08 J ‑61 %
Model Update OTA Size 2.3 MiB (quantized) 4.8 MiB (float) ‑52 %
Scalability (Concurrent Sessions) 12 streams 5 streams +140 %
Implementation Complexity (person‑days) 45 pd 28 pd +61 %

Interpretation

  • Latency improves dramatically when you offload to a dedicated NPU.
  • Energy per query drops because the accelerator is far more efficient per MAC operation.
  • Complexity rises; you need to manage DMA, IOMMU, and power domains, which is why many startups balk.
  • The power trade‑off is acceptable for a plugged‑in speaker but would be a blocker for battery‑only wearables.

5. Future Industry Trajectory (18‑36 Months)

Time Horizon Anticipated Evolution Impact on Product Design
0‑12 months Standardization of Zero‑Copy APIs (e.g., tflite‑micro DMA extensions, OpenCL‑SVM‑like abstractions). New startups can adopt a “copy‑free” pipeline without building a custom driver stack.
12‑24 months Edge‑TPU‑lite 2.0 – double the MAC density, integrated LPDDR5X, and built‑in secure enclave for model provenance. Enables on‑device continuous learning (tiny‑gradient updates) without cloud round‑trip.
24‑36 months CXL‑Gen3 inter‑chip mesh for modular devices (e.g., AR glasses, modular laptops). Designers will treat each compute tile as a disaggregated service, allowing hot‑swap of NPUs or DSPs in the field.

5.1 Strategic Recommendations for Engineering Leaders

  1. Invest in a Portable Zero‑Copy Abstraction Layer – Treat it as a core platform capability, not a one‑off hack.
  2. Adopt Protobuf Versioning Early – Future‑proof OTA pipelines; avoid the “schema lock‑in” that plagues many consumer devices.
  3. Instrument Power Telemetry from Day 1 – Use a unified observability stack (e.g., OpenTelemetry + Prometheus) to correlate latency spikes with power events.
  4. Plan for Modular Compute – Even if your product is monolithic today, design the PCB and firmware to expose a CXL‑compatible endpoint; retrofitting later is far cheaper than a full redesign.

6. Conclusion

The holiday‑season gadget roundup is more than a shopping guide; it is a snapshot of where edge‑AI hardware and software converge. The winners—EchoSphere, VisiCam, and LumenWear—share a disciplined focus on zero‑copy data paths, coherent memory, and a cloud‑edge control plane built on robust, versioned protobuf contracts.

For engineering teams, the lesson is clear: latency and energy efficiency are no longer optional differentiators; they are prerequisites. By embracing the patterns outlined above—and by leveraging FutureStack’s open‑source Rust crates—you can accelerate product development, avoid the common pitfalls that trip up many startups, and deliver a holiday‑season experience that feels truly instant.

Happy building, and may your inference pipelines stay cold and your batteries stay warm.

title: AI Takeover: Is the Software Engineering Industry Preparing to Replace Developers?
description:
Let's stop pretending this is just another technology trend.

Something fundamental is changing in software development.

AI can write React components, generate APIs, debug applications, create tests, refactor codebases, and even build entire products from natural language instructions.

A few years ago, these capabilities sounded like science fiction.

Today, they're becoming part of everyday development.

And this raises an uncomfortable question:

Are we witnessing the beginning of an AI Takeover of the software engineering industry?

Not in some distant future.

Right now.

1. The AI Takeover Has Already Started

Remember when knowing how to write code was a competitive advantage?

It still matters, but the value of simply producing code is changing.

Consider what a developer can do today with AI tools:

  • Generate a complete React application.
  • Build reusable components from a design.
  • Create backend endpoints.
  • Write database queries.
  • Generate unit and integration tests.
  • Analyze errors and suggest fixes.
  • Refactor existing code.
  • Explain unfamiliar codebases.

Tasks that once required hours of work can sometimes be completed in minutes.

This is the first major part of the AI Takeover.

AI isn't necessarily replacing software engineers directly.

It's changing how much engineering work can be completed by one person.

And companies are paying attention.

2. The Real Threat Isn't AI. It's Developers Who Know How to Use It Better.

Here's where things get interesting.

Imagine two developers.

Developer A:

  • Writes everything manually.
  • Spends hours searching documentation.
  • Implements repetitive code.
  • Avoids AI tools because they believe traditional coding is better.

Developer B:

  • Understands programming fundamentals.
  • Uses AI to explore solutions.
  • Automates repetitive tasks.
  • Reviews generated code carefully.
  • Focuses on architecture and engineering decisions.

Both developers might have similar technical knowledge.

But their productivity can be dramatically different.

The AI Takeover doesn't necessarily mean that AI will replace every developer.

It may mean that developers who effectively use AI will outperform those who refuse to adapt.

And eventually, companies may need fewer people to accomplish the same amount of work.

That's a much more immediate concern.

3. Junior Developers Could Be the First to Feel the Impact

This is probably one of the most uncomfortable consequences of the AI Takeover.

Historically, junior developers learned by working on relatively simple tasks:

  • Fixing small bugs.
  • Building basic components.
  • Writing straightforward API integrations.
  • Creating forms.
  • Updating existing features.
  • Writing simple tests.

These tasks were opportunities to gain experience.

But many of them can now be handled by AI-assisted workflows.

So what happens to developers who are just entering the industry?

If companies automate more entry-level tasks, the traditional path from junior to senior developer could become harder.

And there's another problem.

If AI handles all the simple tasks, where will junior developers get the experience they need to become senior engineers?

This is a question the industry hasn't fully answered.

4. The AI Takeover Is Changing What It Means to Be a Developer

For years, developers were evaluated largely by their ability to write code.

But writing code is only one part of software engineering.

Consider these responsibilities:

Understanding requirements

AI can generate an implementation, but understanding what a business actually needs is a different challenge.

System architecture

Choosing how different parts of an application communicate requires understanding trade-offs, constraints, and long-term consequences.

Debugging complex systems

A generated solution might work in isolation but fail under real-world conditions.

Security and reliability

Someone must understand the consequences of shipping insecure or unreliable software.

Technical decision-making

Choosing the right solution is often more important than implementing it quickly.

This is why I believe the AI Takeover will change the definition of a valuable developer.

The most valuable engineers may not be those who write the most code.

They may be those who make the best decisions about what code should exist in the first place.

5. What Happens to Frontend Developers?

Let's look specifically at frontend development.

AI tools are already capable of generating:

  • React components.
  • Tailwind CSS layouts.
  • Responsive interfaces.
  • Form validation.
  • Custom hooks.
  • API integrations.
  • Basic application architecture.

You can describe a dashboard and receive a working implementation surprisingly quickly.

So is frontend development becoming less valuable?

I don't think the answer is that simple.

Building a visually acceptable interface is becoming easier.

Building a reliable, accessible, maintainable, and genuinely useful product is still difficult.

There is a significant difference between generating a React component and understanding:

  • React rendering behavior.
  • State management.
  • Component composition.
  • Performance bottlenecks.
  • Accessibility.
  • Browser behavior.
  • Design systems.
  • Complex application architecture.

The AI Takeover might reduce the value of repetitive frontend implementation.

But it could increase the importance of deeper frontend engineering knowledge.

6. The Dangerous Illusion of Productivity

Here's something I find particularly concerning.

AI can generate code that looks professional.

It can produce clean formatting, TypeScript interfaces, reusable components, and even tests.

But looking correct doesn't mean being correct.

Imagine a developer generating an entire feature using AI.

The feature works.

The tests pass.

The application runs.

But the developer cannot explain:

  • Why a particular state management approach was chosen.
  • Whether an effect is necessary.
  • How asynchronous operations are handled.
  • What happens when a component unmounts.
  • Whether the implementation introduces performance problems.

Are we actually improving software engineering?

Or are we creating a generation of developers who can operate AI tools without understanding the systems they build?

The AI Takeover could create an interesting paradox:

Developers might become faster at producing software while becoming less capable of maintaining it.

That isn't inevitable, but it's a real risk.

7. Will AI Replace Software Engineers?

Let's be realistic.

Predicting exactly how many software engineering jobs AI will eliminate is difficult.

There are several possible outcomes.

Scenario A: AI replaces a significant portion of development work.

Companies use increasingly capable AI systems to automate implementation, testing, maintenance, and other engineering tasks.

Smaller teams deliver products that previously required much larger teams.

Scenario B: AI increases software production.

As development becomes cheaper, more companies build software.

New products, integrations, and internal tools create additional demand for engineering work.

Scenario C: The profession changes.

Developers spend less time writing repetitive code and more time on architecture, verification, product decisions, security, and AI-assisted development.

My guess?

We'll see elements of all three.

The AI Takeover probably won't happen as one dramatic event.

It will happen through thousands of smaller changes in how companies build software, hire developers, and organize engineering teams.

8. How Should Developers Prepare for the AI Takeover?

I don't think abandoning programming fundamentals is the answer.

Quite the opposite.

Here are the areas I would prioritize.

1. Understand the fundamentals

Learn JavaScript, TypeScript, React, browser APIs, asynchronous programming, networking, and data structures.

You need to understand the code AI generates.

2. Become comfortable with AI-assisted development

Learn how to use tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot.

But don't just learn how to generate code.

Learn how to review, test, debug, and improve it.

3. Develop architectural thinking

Understand how applications are structured, how systems communicate, and how technical decisions affect maintainability.

4. Learn to solve problems independently

AI should accelerate your thinking, not replace it.

Try solving problems yourself before asking AI for an implementation.

5. Build real products

A portfolio of functioning applications demonstrates more than a collection of generated code snippets.

Build things, deploy them, maintain them, and learn from the problems that appear.

6. Contribute to open source

Working with established codebases teaches you things that isolated AI-generated projects often cannot.

You learn how real engineering teams review code, manage complexity, discuss trade-offs, and maintain software over time.

9. The Biggest Winners of the AI Takeover Might Not Be the Best Coders

This is probably my most controversial point.

The next generation of successful software engineers might not be the people who can type code the fastest.

They might be the people who can:

  • Understand problems deeply.
  • Communicate technical requirements.
  • Evaluate AI-generated solutions.
  • Design reliable systems.
  • Work across different technologies.
  • Make good engineering decisions.
  • Take responsibility for the software they ship.

AI makes implementation increasingly accessible.

But engineering judgment is a different skill.

And that distinction could become extremely important.

Final Thoughts: Adapt or Become Irrelevant?

I don't believe software engineering is disappearing.

But I do believe the profession is entering one of its biggest transformations.

The AI Takeover is forcing developers to reconsider what makes them valuable.

Knowing React, TypeScript, or Python is still useful.

Knowing how to build software is still important.

But simply knowing how to translate requirements into code may no longer be enough to stand out.

The developers who thrive will likely be those who combine strong fundamentals, engineering judgment, product thinking, and effective use of AI.

Don't compete with AI at generating code.

Learn to build better software with it.

And I'd genuinely like to hear your opinion:

If AI can build 80% of a modern application, will companies still need the same number of software engineers in five years?

Is the AI Takeover an opportunity for developers, a serious threat to the profession, or both?

Let's discuss.

CI is enabled for the team your CLI is set to. Pass --scope <team> to use a different one. From the next push, tasks run as configured in your repository.
