title: Your static site probably doesn’t need React
description:
About a year ago, when I was a fledgling frontend developer, I created a website with React. This website was a single page app built with Vite and React, and it used all the cutting edge bells and whistles but had only one problem: it wasn’t performant. On mobile, the main content took 11.3 seconds to show up; after I rebuilt it in Astro, it took 2.1.

Evaluating this site a year ago, it was simple to see the pitfalls I fell into: a lot of images were uncompressed, and I was shipping way more than necessary to the client. It got me thinking however, though a lot of these mistakes were my fault, wouldn’t it be nice if there was a framework that blocked a lot of these mistakes by default? Something like… Astro?

For those that may not be familiar, Astro is a frontend framework that by default, ships no JavaScript to the client. It’s based on default web technologies i.e HTML and CSS. Because of this, it’s extremely performant. You opt in to complexity, unlike most frameworks where you opt out.

The claim of this article, is that for your static, content driven site, no matter what experience in development you have, you probably don’t need React. I’ll start by walking through a few pitfalls I made in my earlier project and show how Astro, by default, would have prevented this.

Fault 1: The site wasn’t rendered until it received all the JavaScript required for the page to render. In React, the fix is a framework that renders the HTML ahead of time, like Next.js. In Astro however, each component by default is an island. This is a static wrapped server rendered piece of html with zero JavaScript by default. When you need interactivity, you isolate that piece (said island) and you tell Astro when and how to load that island. These islands are framework agnostic, so you can have islands of React, Svelte, Vue, no problem.

Fault 2: Embarrassing mistake upcoming😂, but I was shipping the admin page with the blog editor — and that includes the login, image upload, you get the picture — to the client. So all visitors of the site were receiving a huge amount of JavaScript that wasn’t even being used: one 752 KB bundle, with about 60% of it unused on the homepage. React.lazy could have split the admin out, but I didn’t know to reach for it. If I was using Astro, each page would only ship the JavaScript for its own islands, so the admin code would have stayed on the admin page unless I deliberately made the mistake.

React is an extremely powerful tool, and one of the best we have in our toolbelts as developers — this article is not meant to dunk on it. In fact, the Astro version of the site still uses React islands for things like the slideshow and the blog list. For web apps generally, sites or apps managing complex state, React proves invaluable. This article is mainly meant to point out that for static content sites however, or for developers early on in their career, Astro is well, like a gas lighter — off by default. You light the stove and it’s automatically off even if you forget. React however, is like a naked match flame. Very powerful and versatile, but easier to burn the house down with😂

title: Cursor's breach chain started in plain-text agent traces: 23,276 public repos carry the same leak
description:
Cursor published its final incident report on November 13, two weeks after a malicious copy of Anthropic's Claude Code extension appeared in its VS Code extension marketplace. I read the whole thing. The interesting part is not the extension. It is the first link in the chain.

The chain, in five steps

The report reconstructs the attack like this:

  1. An attacker obtained an access key Cursor had issued to Fireworks, an inference provider. The key was exposed on Fireworks' side.
  2. With that key, the attacker copied data from a read-only storage bucket Cursor used to share training data with Fireworks. The bucket held coding agent traces, mostly from 2025, from sessions that were not in Privacy Mode.
  3. A small number of those traces contained credentials that had not been redacted. Cursor says less than 0.01% of customers had API credentials exposed this way.
  4. Starting from those credentials, the attacker reached SaaS tools Cursor uses internally, then archived source repositories, support data, email conversations, and some credentials users had sent to the support team.
  5. On October 29, using a stolen credential from that data, the attacker placed malicious builds of the Claude Code extension directly on the cache that served the marketplace. Open VSX never carried them, and Anthropic published nothing. At most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions could have received the bad build, which lived for about 11 hours. BleepingComputer reported the payload installed persistent SSH backdoors.

Read step 3 again. The breach did not start with a zero-day. It started with working credentials sitting in plain text inside stored agent transcripts. Everything after that was climbing. If you run sessions outside Privacy Mode, or you paste a token into a command to unblock an agent at 6pm, you are producing the same artifact class that made step 3 possible.

Two numbers worth sitting with

Cursor says traces were exposed for fewer than 0.05% of users, and API credentials for less than 0.01% of customers. Small percentages, and they still yielded enough working credentials to reach internal systems and poison a marketplace cache.

That is the arithmetic of stored secrets. An attacker does not need a large share of users leaking credentials. One valid key with the right scope is enough. Cursor's own response reads like agreement: the team rotated every credential in use across internal systems, not just the exposed ones, moved all inference traffic off the vendor, and added secret scanning across internal data sources.

The same leak, sitting on your disk

Two weeks later, on the file side of the same problem, GitGuardian published a count that dwarfs the numbers Cursor had to contain. Per CSO Online's report of the research: 31,088 distinct secrets in .claude/settings.local.json files across 23,276 public GitHub repositories, with 5,343 of them still valid when detected. Of the occurrences GitGuardian could check, 67% were working credentials.

I wrote about the mechanism when Apiiro's smaller count came out: approving a command with "Yes, and don't ask again" saves the exact command string, secret included, into a project-level file. That article covered 1,379 distinct secrets in 1,122 files. Apiiro counted default branches. GitGuardian crawled every public commit back to January 2025 and found twenty times more.

The pattern holds everywhere agent tooling writes down what happened:

  • The shared team file, .claude/settings.json, carried another 8,271 secrets, 1,283 of them valid, in GitGuardian's tally relayed by Ground Truth.
  • Public Docker Hub images held 613 distinct secrets in Claude Code settings files across 543 image repositories, because a Dockerfile COPY . . ignores your .gitignore. One valid Cloudflare token appeared across 559 image tags.

Why your scanner misses one in five

Apiiro ran gitleaks and TruffleHog, the two most used open-source secret scanners, over all 104,185 public copies of the file. Of the 1,122 files holding a real secret, 215 were flagged by neither, close to one in five. The reason is structural. Scanners look for provider formats, a prefix followed by high-entropy string. A password after PGPASSWORD=, or inside an sshpass command, is just a word on a command line. Agent artifacts record what ran, not what was sensitive, so the exact place agents write secrets is the place format-based detection covers worst.

A rotation order that matches the chain

Order your cleanup by how the attacker actually used the data, not by how easy each step is.

First, rotate anything you ever pasted into a vendor support chat or ran through a session whose logs you do not control. Cursor's report lists "some credentials users had sent to the Cursor support team" among the exposed data. That class of credential outlives your account with the vendor.

Second, rotate credentials that reached a committed file, then clean the file. Rotation first, always, because git history and forks keep old copies. Check whether the file was ever committed on any branch:

git log --all --full-history --oneline -- .claude/settings.local.json

Third, rotate anything baked into a published image. Deleting the file from the repo does not recall published tags; one database password in GitGuardian's data sits in 643 tags across seven image repositories.

Five places credentials sit in plain text

Run this audit across all five, in one pass:

  1. Agent traces and transcripts, local session logs included. You are checking for commands that carried a token or password inline.
  2. .claude/settings.local.json, the file behind the 23,276 repos.
  3. .claude/settings.json, committed on purpose by teams, so it spreads by design.
  4. Container images, via a COPY . . that had no .dockerignore to stop it.
  5. Support conversations and shared debugging threads.

A quick pattern probe for the config side:

grep -rnE "(PGPASSWORD=|sshpass|Bearer |AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|BEGIN (RSA|OPENSSH) PRIVATE KEY)" \
  .claude ~/.claude/settings.json 2>/dev/null

It will not catch everything, that is the one-in-five lesson, but it catches the shapes scanners skip.

Rules that shrink the vault

Four habits remove most of this surface:

  • Never approve a secret-bearing command with "don't ask again". Write the allow rule as a pattern without the secret, and pass the secret as an environment variable.
  • Add .claude/ and .env* to .dockerignore in every image that builds from a repo where agents run: 
.claude/
**/.claude/
.env*
**/.env*
  • Treat agent config files as secret-bearing in CI, with pattern checks for command-line secret shapes, not just key-format detectors. I keep a 22-rule scanner for exactly this class of file.
  • Decide about traces the way you decide about screen recordings. If a command would be dangerous to replay in public, it does not belong in any session that logs it.

Per Ground Truth's coverage of CSO's reporting, Boris Cherny, who leads Claude Code, said the tool has not done secrets scrubbing and that built-in secret scanning and an auto mode are being explored. Until something ships there, the file-level discipline is on you.

What I took from the report

The extension malware was the loud part, and I covered the config-boundary questions when it dropped. The quiet part is that a bucket of 2025 transcripts contained working credentials at all. Your exposure is probably not a marketplace cache. It is the artifacts your own tooling writes on every machine you own, and the copies of those artifacts you never audited. Rotate first, then audit, then write the rules that keep the vault empty.

If you want the incident timeline and the indicators of compromise, the primary sources are Cursor's report and their October 30 security notice. My earlier piece on what agent configs can and cannot contain covers the extension side of this event.

title: Design accessible form success states: status, navigation, Undo, and confirmation
description:
Successful submission is a distinct UI state

A completed form needs to answer two questions: did the action finish, and can the user recover if it was accidental? Treating success as an error-summary variant or relying on a visual toast makes those answers harder to discover.

Start by choosing the announcement channel from the page transition.

If submission navigates to a new page or a clearly different view, put the result in the new document context: update the page title and expose a clear main heading such as “Task submitted.” This makes the destination state explicit rather than leaving the user to infer success from a changed screen.

If submission remains on the same page, keep the user in context and return a concise status message. The message should say what completed, not repeat a long explanation. The inserted example models this as a dedicated status result, separate from validation output.

Keep recovery and validation honest

Validation failures need a correction path: field errors identify what must change before submission can continue. They are not success feedback, and a successful result should not be inferred merely because an error summary is absent. Model these as separate states so the rendering layer cannot accidentally present success through an error pattern.

Next, choose the safeguard based on reversibility. For reversible work, return an Undo control after success and restore the prior item when the user activates it. Once restoration has happened, Undo should no longer be available. For permanent or otherwise critical work, do not offer a recovery promise that the system cannot keep. Require confirmation before committing the action instead.

Expected behavior is straightforward: a valid reversible submission produces a completion announcement and Undo; a page-style completion produces a title and heading instead of an in-place status; invalid input produces validation feedback; irreversible work pauses for confirmation and exposes no Undo control.

One important limitation remains: this flow can model the semantic contract, but it cannot prove the exact announcement order or behavior of every browser and assistive-technology combination. Verify the rendered markup and interaction in the environments you support.

Working example 

export const proofBoundary =
  'This model verifies the flow’s presentation contract. It does not prove how a particular browser or assistive technology announces a live region, title, or heading.';

function successPresentation(presentation, task) {
  const message = `Task “${task}” submitted successfully.`;

  if (presentation === 'page') {
    return {
      title: `Task submitted – Task manager`,
      heading: 'Task submitted',
      status: null,
      message,
    };
  }

  return {
    title: null,
    heading: null,
    status: { role: 'status', text: message },
    message,
  };
}

/**
 * Models a form submission UI. A real page can render `title` and `heading`
 * after navigation, or render the `status` live region after an in-page submit.
 */
export function createTaskFormFlow({ presentation = 'status', reversible = true } = {}) {
  if (!['status', 'page'].includes(presentation)) {
    throw new RangeError('presentation must be "status" or "page"');
  }

  let pendingSubmission = null;

  return {
    submit({ task, confirmed = false } = {}) {
      const normalizedTask = typeof task === 'string' ? task.trim() : '';

      if (!normalizedTask) {
        return {
          ok: false,
          kind: 'validation',
          fieldErrors: { task: 'Enter a task.' },
          // Success is not represented as a server-style error summary.
          errorSummary: null,
        };
      }

      if (!reversible && !confirmed) {
        return {
          ok: false,
          kind: 'confirmation-required',
          message: 'Confirm this permanent submission before continuing.',
        };
      }

      pendingSubmission = { task: normalizedTask };
      const feedback = successPresentation(presentation, normalizedTask);

      return {
        ok: true,
        kind: 'submitted',
        ...feedback,
        undoControl: reversible
          ? { action: 'undo', label: 'Undo submission', accessibleName: 'Undo submission' }
          : null,
      };
    },

    undo() {
      if (!reversible || pendingSubmission === null) {
        return {
          ok: false,
          kind: 'undo-unavailable',
          status: null,
        };
      }

      const { task } = pendingSubmission;
      pendingSubmission = null;
      return {
        ok: true,
        kind: 'undone',
        restoredTask: task,
        status: { role: 'status', text: `Submission of “${task}” was undone.` },
      };
    },
  };
}

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/successful-form-submission-undo-accessibly

.claude/settings.json     hook that blocks commits containing obvious secrets

Shown in

Videos on the Agent Shipped channel that use this repo:

  • My subagent stopped halfway. One missing path was why #Shorts · E007 · 2026-11-07
  • My subagent hook read an empty field. Now a bad report exits 2 #Shorts · E004 · 2026-11-14

View on GitHub


Multi-agent work rarely fails because the agents are dumb. It fails because they collide: two tasks touch the same module and one overwrites the other. This build tries one fix. A PM agent writes only a plan, every task gets a disjoint file scope, and a hook reads the plan on every write.

The skeleton

The starting point is agent-starter, a bare Claude Code skeleton: working rules in CLAUDE.md, one reviewer subagent, and one hook that blocks commits with obvious secrets. Nothing in it stops two agents from editing the same file.

Write the first gate

I asked Claude for the simplest gate on purpose: compare the path to the scope entries exactly as written. Three decisions went into the prompt:

  • The active task id comes from the env var ACTIVE_TASK, or else from a file the agent cannot rewrite from inside a scope.
  • The hook exits with code 2, which blocks the tool call and sends the reason back to the agent.
  • The gate stays off when no task is active, so setup work is not locked out.

The PM is itself a task in the plan, with exactly one writable file: the plan.

First failure

I fed the hook a write inside task T0's scope, docs/a.md, as an absolute path, the way Claude Code sends it:

jq -n --arg p "$PWD/docs/a.md" '{tool_input:{file_path:$p}}' | ACTIVE_TASK=T0 node .claude/hooks/scope-gate.js; echo "exit=$?"

The gate blocked it with exit 2. The scope says docs/, the payload carries the full path from the filesystem root, and a string comparison never matches. Live, this would have blocked every write by every subagent. I would rather find that with a fake payload in a terminal.


Look at the exit code: a legal write to docs/ was blocked by the first gate. · watch this step

Fix the paths

The fix is one idea: normalize before comparing. The prompt asked the hook to resolve tool_input.file_path against the project dir (CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, falling back to process.cwd()), make it relative with forward slashes, and treat any result starting with .. as outside scope. Without that last rule, src/../secrets would slip past a prefix check.

Five tests pin the behaviour: absolute and relative inputs agree, out-of-scope is blocked, traversal is blocked, and no active task means the gate is off. They write to a temporary log, so they do not pollute the count taken at the end.

Prove the gate

Same fake payload, twice. The legal write to docs/ passes with exit 0. A write to src/evil.js is refused with exit 2, and the message names the task, the path and what is allowed, so the agent can report instead of looping. Then I committed the hook and its tests. When the gate was wrong, I fixed the gate rather than switching it off.


Two runs of the same payload: one exit code for the legal path, one for src/evil.js. · watch this step

Start the clock 

: > .claude/blocked.log; date +%s > .claude/run-start; echo PM > .claude/active-task

Emptying the log means every line in it from now on is a real block. The active task is set from the terminal, outside the agent. If the agent could change that file, it could promote itself to another scope.

PM writes the plan

The prompt starts: "You are the PM. You write only .claude/plan.json and no code." It asks for three small tasks: T1 a slug helper, T2 a word counter, T3 usage docs. The PM prints an overlap check, so disjointness is shown, not assumed.

Review the plan

This is the human checkpoint. The plan is small enough to read in five lines.

jq -r '.tasks[] | .id + ": " + (.scope | join(", "))' .claude/plan.json; git add .claude/plan.json; git commit -m 'PM plan: three disjoint tasks'; echo T1 > .claude/active-task

Committing it before any code exists makes the plan the contract.


The whole division of labour in a few lines: check that no file appears twice. · watch this step

Task T1

The main agent hands a self-contained brief to a subagent through the Task tool: what to build, which commands to run, which files it may commit. The brief fixes the hand-back at four lines: result, commit, tests, open items. Both files are inside scope, so the gate stays silent.

Switch to T2

The hash in the hand-back should match the top of git log --oneline -3. Prose can claim anything; a hash exists or it does not. Then echo T2 > .claude/active-task.

Forced violation

The T2 agent builds the word counter, its tests and a commit. Then it is told to also edit the slug file, which belongs to T1. The hook reads the plan, sees task T2 and a path outside its scope, and returns exit 2 with the reason. The edit never happens. The agent is told to report the block under open items rather than look for a back door.

Switch to T3 

cat .claude/blocked.log; git status --short; echo T3 > .claude/active-task

Two signals should agree: the blocked log shows the time, task and path, and git status shows nothing changed.


The log names the blocked path; git status is the second, independent signal. · watch this step

Task T3

The third subagent reads both modules and writes the usage doc. Examples must come from real node -e output, not from the model's memory. It commits one file and reports tests.

Measure the run 

echo "elapsed: $(( $(date +%s) - $(cat .claude/run-start) ))s"; echo "blocked writes: $(wc -l < .claude/blocked.log)"; git log --oneline -6; node --test test/*.test.js 2>&1 | grep -E '^# (tests|pass|fail)'

The result: three subagent tasks completed in one run, with one deliberate out-of-scope write blocked. The plan is the first commit, then one commit per task. The limit: the gate watches Edit, Write and MultiEdit, not Bash, so a shell redirect could still write anywhere.


The measured numbers: elapsed time, blocked writes, commits, test pass and fail. · watch this step

What to copy

  • A plan file with one task per agent and a scope list per task, committed before any code.
  • Disjoint scopes, with an overlap check the PM must print.
  • An exit-2 PreToolUse hook that prints the task, the path and what is allowed.
  • A task id that lives outside the agent's reach, set from the terminal.
  • A four-line hand-back (result, commit, tests, open items) checked against git.

Not just JavaScript

Write the gate in Python and test it with pytest instead of node --test, or enforce the same scope at commit time with a pre-commit hook instead of a PreToolUse hook.

Video with the full run: https://youtu.be/-_t_ZsufwvU

Techniques from my real projects, shown on a public demo repo.

Narration: AI voice. The sessions, code and errors are real. Not affiliated with Anthropic or any tool vendor.

Orders are mutable

An order may be pending at creation and later become settled, cancelled, or otherwise updated.

Incremental fetching

Track completed file windows or batch cursors and persist progress only after successful processing.

title: Wisp (LWS): A wisp of a web server
description:
👋 Hi everyone!

I'm excited to share Wisp — originally codenamed LWS (Lightweight Web Server) — a tiny, purpose-built static file server written entirely in Go, using only the standard library. No third-party dependencies, no bloat, just a focused, secure, and blazing-fast service that gets straight to work. ✨

🔗 Repository: github.com/appex-uk/lws

📦 What Makes It Special

Wisp started from a simple frustration: most web servers are either huge and complex or too limited for modern deployments. I wanted something that does exactly what you need — nothing more, nothing less — and fits comfortably in even the tightest environments.

🤏 It’s genuinely tiny

  • Scratch container image: ~3 MB — yes, megabytes
  • Zero runtime dependencies — statically compiled Go binary
  • Starts instantly — before your health check timeout can even fire
  • Minimal memory footprint — your resources stay yours

🛠️ Capable where it counts

Don't let the size fool you — Wisp is packed with thoughtful features:

Feature Details
📁 Secure static serving Uses os.Root to confine all requests — paths and symlinks can never escape your content directory
🚫 Hidden file protection Dotfiles and directories are never served; .well-known/ works as expected
📦 Precompressed content Serve .br (Brotli) or .gz files directly — compress once at build time
🔀 SPA & custom routing SPA fallback mode, custom 404 pages, per-path header rules
📊 Built-in Prometheus metrics Separate metrics port — no exporters, no SDKs, just stdlib
🩺 Kubernetes-ready probes /livez and /readyz endpoints with graceful shutdown drain
🔒 Custom headers & security Set cache policies, security headers, or anything else — globally or per path
⏱️ Graceful shutdown Drains connections before terminating — no dropped requests

🚀 Quick Start

Run it locally 

# Clone and run
git clone [https://github.com/appex-uk/lws.git](https://github.com/appex-uk/lws.git)
cd lws
make run

This serves the included ./www directory on port 8080.

Docker — the scratch image magic ✨ 

# Build the image yourself
make docker

# Run with your own content and config
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 -p 9090:9090 \
  -v "$PWD/site:/srv/www:ro" \
  -v "$PWD/config.json:/etc/lws/config.json:ro" \
  lws:latest

That's it. No pulling hundreds of MB of layers — just a tiny, secure container that starts in milliseconds.

⚙️ Configure It Your Way

Everything lives in a simple JSON config file. Every field is optional — sensible defaults apply:

{
  "address": ":8080",
  "root": "/srv/www",
  "fallback": "/index.html",
  "not_found_page": "/404.html",
  "precompressed": true,
  "headers": {
    "X-Content-Type-Options": "nosniff",
    "X-Frame-Options": "DENY"
  },
  "header_rules": [
    {"match": "*.html", "headers": {"Cache-Control": "no-cache"}},
    {"match": "/assets/*", "headers": {"Cache-Control": "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"}}
  ],
  "access_log": true
}

Key highlights:

  • SPA mode → missing routes without an extension get your index.html with status 200; missing files with an extension still 404 — so broken assets don't silently fail
  • Per-path headers → fine-grained cache control or security policies
  • Precompressed → ship .br/.gz alongside originals and Wisp serves the best one automatically

📊 Built-in Observability — Zero Dependencies

This is one of my favourite parts. Wisp exposes a Prometheus metrics endpoint — on a separate, non-public port — all written with pure Go stdlib. No Prometheus client library, no OTel SDK, nothing to pull in.

Available at: :9090/metrics (configurable)

What you get:

  • lws_http_requests_total — request count by method & status code
  • lws_http_request_duration_seconds — latency histogram
  • lws_http_requests_in_flight — concurrent requests gauge
  • lws_http_response_bytes_total — bytes served
  • Plus standard Go runtime & process metrics

Some useful queries you can run straight away:

# Traffic rate
sum(rate(lws_http_requests_total[5m]))

# Error rate
sum(rate(lws_http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(lws_http_requests_total[5m]))

# 99th percentile latency
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(lws_http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))

Instrumentation overhead? ~170 ns per request. Negligible.

☸️ Kubernetes Friendly by Design

Wisp was built to run reliably in Kubernetes:

  • Liveness probe: /livez — just checks the process is responding
  • Readiness probe: /readyz — also verifies the content volume and goes 503 during shutdown drain
  • Graceful sequence on SIGTERM: → readiness 503 → finish in-flight requests → clean exit
  • Example Deployment and Service manifests are in the repo under infra/k8s/

This means rolling deployments work smoothly — connections drain before the pod disappears.

💭 Why Not Just Nginx?

Great question — and to be clear: Nginx is amazing. It's battle-tested, incredibly capable, and I use it every day. But sometimes it's simply more than you need:

🚛 Nginx = The workhorse — handles massive traffic, complex routing, modules, SSL termination at scale — and it's great at that.

🚲 Wisp = The nimble specialist — serve static files securely, fast, and tiny. Perfect for frontend deployments, edge workloads, sidecars, or anywhere "light and fast" matters more than "every feature ever."

If you need to serve a static site, a single-page app, or static assets reliably and securely — and you care about image size, startup time, and minimal resource consumption — Wisp is built exactly for you.

🗺️ What's Next

Right now Wisp is focused on doing one thing — serving static content — and doing it really well. That said, there's always room to polish and improve:

  • More flexible routing options
  • Additional cache control conveniences
  • Real-world feedback from folks using it

Your thoughts, bug reports, or contributions are very welcome!

🔗 Links

  • GitHub repo: github.com/appex-uk/lws ⭐ Star if you like it!
  • Issues & feedback: Open an issue — I'd love to hear what you think

💬 Over to you

What's your biggest annoyance when setting up a static file server? Is it image bloat? Complex config? Missing metrics? Let's chat in the comments — I'm here to learn and build something useful together! 👇

title: How Mercor ships internal apps and billions of production tokens on one platform
description:
Mercor on Vercel

  • Batch jobs cut from 12 hours to 2 hours

  • 18M requests and 63B tokens routed through AI Gateway in 10 days

  • Expert access provisioned in seconds via Vercel Passport

  • Over 2,000 projects created by hundreds of internal builders

Mercor connects hundreds of thousands of domain experts with frontier AI labs, helping those labs generate the human data they need to train and evaluate leading models. It also runs large batches of automated grading jobs to evaluate models for labs and enterprises.

Demand arrives in bursts that can push model traffic to peak capacity for days, even as individual evaluation or labeling jobs carry 24-hour deadlines. With so little time to deliver, requests waiting on a provider’s rate limits can put a client’s deadline at risk.

Mercor’s business teams also need applications tailored to each engagement, giving experts a way to see their tasks and progress without waiting for changes to the core platform.

For Aaron Brown, Mercor’s Head of Security, enabling more people to build means making it easier to give them the access they need and keep track of how they use it. Mercor uses Vercel AI Gateway to manage model access and Vercel Passport to handle secure access to their applications.

When model capacity becomes a customer deadline

Mercor’s mix of direct integrations and third-party gateways could not provide enough token-per-minute capacity for its open-model workloads when demand surged. As requests hit provider limits and entered retry queues, time-sensitive batch jobs stretched beyond 12 hours, consuming more than half of a client’s 24-hour deadline.

AI Gateway provided more inference capacity and failover routing between providers when requests hit rate limits, helping batch work continue instead of waiting in retry queues. Mercor reports that those jobs now finish in 2 to 3 hours, leaving more time to complete the rest of the client’s work. In its first 10 days on Gateway, the team routed 18 million requests and 63 billion tokens, without hitting rate limits.

Mercor continues to use multiple gateways and vendors, valuing Vercel for its combination of model access, controls, and hands-on support when the team needs more capacity. Engineers also get one API for leading foundation model providers and a growing catalog of open models, so they can try a new model without building another provider integration.

Giving engineers room to experiment within limits

As model use grew, Mercor needed to understand where token spend was going, but its previous setup offered little visibility into usage by team and project. A single loop error in a script could exhaust the available budget.

Hundreds of Mercor engineers now use open models through AI Gateway with per-user keys that carry expiration dates, token limits, and spend limits. Security can give experimentation a budget and an end date, then use the usage records to see which user, project, and workload is driving consumption. Engineers can try different models through the same gateway under those controls, without managing another set of provider credentials each time.

Managing access as business teams build

A few hundred people across Mercor’s business teams now build applications on Vercel, where the company’s project count has grown from fewer than a dozen to roughly 2,000. Many of those projects are temporary environments for a specific client engagement.

One production use case gives experts detailed views of their project tasks and progress. Rather than ask engineering to add every engagement’s interface to the core platform, business teams build the interfaces themselves and share them with the experts doing the work.

To share those applications, teams need to control who can sign in without taking on a separate authentication setup for every project. Passport provides that common authentication layer, handling sign-in to Vercel deployments through an existing identity provider.

Mercor’s identity team built a product called Audiences, integrating Vercel Passport as a first class primitive, to automate access provisioning. Once a team selects the experts who need access, Audiences creates the IdP group, Vercel connection, and Passport configuration. With that workflow, Mercor reports provisioning access in seconds for audiences ranging from dozens of experts to tens of thousands. Offboarding works the same way in reverse. Because access is derived from the IdP group, removing the group at the end of an engagement removes access to the project, so no stale access is left behind.

Limiting what each agent can do

Alongside those applications, Mercor uses agents to answer questions from experts in its marketplace, automate HR workflows, and help employees navigate internal systems. Mercor’s approach is to give each agent narrow permissions suited to its job, rather than everything available to the person who invoked it.

For agents that use open models through AI Gateway, Mercor can also scope model access, set expiration dates, and cap spending. That governs their model use while Mercor separately determines which systems and actions each agent can access.

What’s next

Mercor expects more open models to power its internal agents and systems, and more teams outside engineering to build tools for experts. As that work grows, the company wants teams to spend less time setting up model integrations and application authentication so they can respond to client workloads with tight deadlines.

The aim is to make the secure path the fastest path, with shared model access and repeatable authentication workflows helping experts get the tools they need and labs get their work back on time. Mercor wants to support that growth without security work increasing at the same rate.

About Mercor: Mercor is an AI data company that organizes human intelligence for AI training and evaluation. Its network of more than 5M experts, from doctors to lawyers to engineers, powers benchmarks, enterprise evals, RL environments, post-training and agent deployments.

title: Cache Repeated Answers to Cut LLM Calls in a Small-Business FAQ Bot (Python + SQLite)
description:
Small businesses get the same ten questions all day: opening hours, delivery areas, how to book. Sending each one to a language model is wasted money. A small cache is one of the simplest ways to control AI automation costs for a small business.

Normalise, then hash 

import hashlib, re, sqlite3, time

db = sqlite3.connect("answers.db")
db.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cache(
  key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, question TEXT, answer TEXT, created REAL, hits INTEGER DEFAULT 0)""")

def normalise(q: str) -> str:
    q = q.lower()
    q = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9 ]+", " ", q)
    return " ".join(q.split())

def key(q: str) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(normalise(q).encode()).hexdigest()

Read through the cache 

MAX_AGE = 7 * 24 * 3600  # refresh weekly so answers do not go stale

def answer(q, call_model):
    k = key(q)
    row = db.execute("SELECT answer, created FROM cache WHERE key=?", (k,)).fetchone()
    if row and time.time() - row[1] < MAX_AGE:
        db.execute("UPDATE cache SET hits = hits + 1 WHERE key=?", (k,))
        db.commit()
        return row[0], "cache"
    a = call_model(q)
    db.execute("REPLACE INTO cache(key, question, answer, created) VALUES (?,?,?,?)",
               (k, q, a, time.time()))
    db.commit()
    return a, "model"

Rules that keep it safe

  • Cache only general questions. Never cache answers that include a customer's name, order or account details.
  • Expire entries when prices, hours or policies change (clear the table on any website update).
  • Log cache versus model so you can see what the cache actually saves.

Going further

Exact matching catches more than you expect once text is normalised. Fuzzy or embedding matching adds complexity; measure first.

Why we often prefer small custom pieces like this over packaged bots: why small custom pieces often beat packaged bots.

Disclosure: I co-founded NxFlowAI, an automation agency.

title: Props in React
description:
When building a React application, we usually divide our application into small components.

For example, an e-commerce website may have:

  • Navbar component
  • Product component
  • Cart component
  • Footer component

Sometimes, one component needs to send data to another component.

This is where Props come in.

1. What are Props?

Props stands for Properties.

Props allow us to pass data from one component to another in React.

In simple words, props help components share data with other components.

For example, we can send a username from the App component to the Profile component.

2. How to Pass Props?

Let's understand with a simple example.

App.jsx

function App() {
  return (
    <Profile name="Lokesh" />
  );
}

export default App;

Here, we are passing name="Lokesh" to the Profile component.

Profile.jsx

function Profile(props) {
  return (
    <h1>Hello, {props.name}</h1>
  );
}

export default Profile;

Output:

Hello, Lokesh

Let's understand what happened:

  1. App sends the name Lokesh to Profile.
  2. Profile receives the data through props.
  3. We display the name using props.name.

That's how props work!

3. Passing Multiple Props

We can pass more than one value to a component.

function App() {
  return (
    <Student
      name="Lokesh"
      age={22}
      course="Computer Science"
    />
  );
}

Now, we can receive these values in the Student component.

function Student(props) {
  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Name: {props.name}</h2>
      <p>Age: {props.age}</p>
      <p>Course: {props.course}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

We can pass different types of data through props, such as:

  • Strings
  • Numbers
  • Arrays
  • Objects
  • Functions
  • Boolean values

4. What is Props Destructuring?

Instead of writing props.name, props.age, and props.course every time, we can use destructuring.

Example:

function Student({ name, age, course }) {
  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Name: {name}</h2>
      <p>Age: {age}</p>
      <p>Course: {course}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

Here, we directly get the values from props.

This makes our code shorter and easier to read.

5. Passing Props to Reusable Components

One of the biggest advantages of props is that we can reuse the same component with different data.

Imagine we are creating an e-commerce website with multiple product cards.

Instead of creating a separate component for every product, we can create one reusable Product component.

App.jsx

function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <Product name="Laptop" price={50000} />

      <Product name="Mobile" price={20000} />

      <Product name="Headphones" price={2000} />
    </div>
  );
}

Product.jsx

function Product({ name, price }) {
  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{name}</h2>
      <p>Price: ₹{price}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

The same Product component displays different products based on the props it receives.

This helps us avoid writing the same code again and again.

6. Important Rules About Props

There are a few important things to remember:

  • Props are used to pass data between components.
  • Data usually flows from parent components to child components.
  • Props can contain different types of values.
  • Props are read-only. A child component should not directly modify the props it receives.
  • We can use destructuring to make props easier to read.

7. Props vs State

Props and State are both used to work with data in React, but they have different purposes.

Props State
Used to receive data from a parent component Used to manage data inside a component
Read-only for the receiving component Can be updated using a state setter
Passed from parent to child Managed by the component that owns it

For example:

  • Props: Passing a product name from App to Product.
  • State: Updating the quantity of a product when the user clicks the + button.

title: Namespace vs GitHub hosted runners, and the unit minute
description:
Namespace vs GitHub hosted runners is awkward to compare because Namespace does not sell runner minutes: it sells unit minutes, where one unit is 1 vCPU with 2 GB of RAM for a minute, times a platform multiplier. Convert it and a 2 vCPU Linux runner is $0.002 a minute prepaid against GitHub's $0.006, on 4 GB of RAM rather than 8, which is the caveat that decides most of this page.


10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU plus 2,000 macOS minutes a month, at rates read 20 September 2026. On the shape that matches GitHub on memory the month is 160,000 unit minutes and $190; on the 4 GB shape it is 140,000 and $160.

GitHub-hosted runners need no explanation and no account: an included allowance of $12 to $300 of compute a month by plan (2,000 to 50,000 standard Linux minutes), a standard private-repo Linux runner of 2 vCPU, 8 GB and 14 GB of disk, every platform GitHub sells, and free unlimited use on public repositories at 4 vCPU and 16 GB.

Namespace sells compute across devboxes, Docker builds and GitHub Actions runners from one meter. You pick a shape through a label such as nscloud-ubuntu-24.04-amd64-8x16, and the bill is vCPU count times minutes times a platform multiplier of 1 for Linux, 2 for Windows, 10 for macOS and 7 for Linux on Apple silicon. Rates come in two columns, prepaid inside a plan and about 50% higher as overage outside it.

Every cell below was read from the vendor's own public pricing or documentation page on 20 September 2026. Where a vendor does not publish a number, the cell says "not published" instead of carrying a guess.

Comparison

GitHub-hosted Namespace Latchkey
Price per minute, 2 vCPU Linux x64 $0.006 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD on a private repo; free on public repos) $0.002 prepaid, $0.003 overage (2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM). The 2 vCPU with 8 GB shape is $0.004 prepaid $0.0025 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Price per minute, 4 vCPU Linux x64 $0.012 as a larger runner with 16 GB $0.004 prepaid at 4 vCPU and 8 GB; $0.008 prepaid at 4 vCPU and 16 GB $0.005 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Free tier $12 of compute a month on Free, $18 on Pro and Team, $300 on Enterprise Cloud (2,000, 3,000 and 50,000 standard Linux minutes), private repos only A 30-day trial of the pay-as-you-go Developer plan; no standing monthly allowance 30-day trial, then 2,000 included minutes a month on Developer, 4,000 on Launch, 6,000 on Scale
Billing granularity Every job is rounded up to the nearest whole minute A one-minute minimum, then the following 15-second steps rounded down: its docs say 70 seconds bills as one minute Per minute
Runner sizes and OS Linux x64 and arm64, Windows x64 and arm64, macOS on Apple silicon and Intel; larger runners to 96 vCPU Shapes from 1 vCPU up to 64 vCPU and 512 GB on amd64 and arm64; Windows; macOS on Apple silicon; Linux on Apple silicon in early access 2, 4, 8 and 16 vCPU, Ubuntu 24.04 on x86_64 only. arm64, Windows and macOS are not offered
Cache: type, limit, persistence actions/cache, 10 GB per repository, entries removed after 7 days without access, restorable only from the same or the default branch Cache volumes attached by label, snapshots at $0.002/GB-hour with 5,000 GB-hours free on Team and 15,000 on Business, storage at $0.0048/GB-day Size not published. latchkey-dev/cache-action@v1 replaces actions/cache with a restore step and a save step, keeping path and key (no restore-keys); entries are isolated per organization, versioned by OS, kept 14 days; a failed restore warns rather than failing the job
Docker build acceleration None built in. cache-to: type=gha writes into the same 10 GB store Docker builds are a separate meter: 1,000 included on Team and 2,500 on Business, $0.05 per build on Developer, $10 per 1,000 after that, with cross-invocation caching latchkey-dev/docker-cache-action@v1, layers held in a Latchkey-managed private registry per organization
Concurrency limits 20 concurrent jobs on Free, 40 on Pro, 60 on Team, 500 on Enterprise Cloud. macOS is capped separately at 5, or 50 on Enterprise Denominated in vCPU, not jobs: 32 vCPU on Developer, 64 on Team, 160 on Business. macOS is 12, 24 and 48 vCPU Developer 20, Launch 40, Scale 80 busy runners per workspace; idle warm runners do not count
Where jobs run GitHub's own hosted fleet Namespace Compute: AMD EPYC for amd64, AmpereOne or Apple silicon for arm64, M5 Max and M4 Pro for macOS Latchkey's own AWS estate on m6a-class hosts, one job per runner, no inbound access, destroyed after the job
Self-healing or retries None. A failed job waits for a person, or for retry logic you wrote yourself Not offered Built in: transient failures are diagnosed and retried inside the run
Setup change required None; this is the default Change runs-on to one nscloud label, plus companion labels for a cache volume A runs-on label change. GitHub organization accounts only

How to compute a Namespace bill

The formula Namespace publishes is vCPU count times minutes times the platform multiplier, and its own worked example is 4 vCPU for 5 minutes on Linux, which is 20 unit minutes. Shapes that are not the standard 1 vCPU to 2 GB ratio are charged on whichever is larger, cores or half the memory, so a 2 vCPU shape with 8 GB counts as 4 units rather than 2. That rule is the whole trick: memory is priced, it is just priced as cores.

Shape Unit minutes per minute Prepaid Overage GitHub-hosted equivalent
Linux 2 vCPU, 4 GB 2 $0.002 $0.003 $0.006 at 2 vCPU and 8 GB
Linux 2 vCPU, 8 GB 4 $0.004 $0.006 $0.006 at 2 vCPU and 8 GB
Linux 4 vCPU, 16 GB 8 $0.008 $0.012 $0.012 at 4 vCPU and 16 GB
Linux 8 vCPU, 32 GB 16 $0.016 $0.024 $0.022 at 8 vCPU and 32 GB
Windows 4 vCPU, 16 GB 16 (2x multiplier) $0.016 $0.024 $0.022 at 4 cores
macOS 6 vCPU, 14 GB 60 (10x multiplier) $0.06 $0.09 $0.062 on a 3 or 4 core runner

Line the shapes up by memory and the picture is less dramatic than the headline rate but still one-sided: at 2 vCPU and 8 GB, the machine GitHub actually gives you, Namespace prepaid is $0.004 against $0.006, a third cheaper rather than two thirds. At 4 vCPU and 16 GB it is $0.008 against $0.012, the same third. The two-thirds saving only exists if your jobs are genuinely happy on 4 GB of RAM, and a Java, Gradle or large Node build usually is not.

The other end of the table is where the multipliers bite. macOS costs 10 unit minutes per vCPU-minute, so a 6 vCPU macOS runner is $0.06 prepaid and $0.09 as overage against GitHub's $0.062, which means Namespace is cheaper on macOS only while you stay inside a plan. Windows doubles the same way. The cheap Linux rate tells you nothing about either.

The rounding difference nobody prices

GitHub rounds every job up to the nearest whole minute. Namespace applies a one-minute minimum and then rounds the following 15-second steps down, and its documentation gives the example that 70 seconds of usage is one billable minute. On a single job that is noise; on a matrix it is not.

Take 40 jobs that each finish in 70 seconds, which is 46.7 minutes of real work. GitHub bills 80 minutes, because every job rounds from 1 minute 10 seconds to 2, and at $0.006 that is $0.48. Namespace bills 40 minutes, one per job, and a 2 vCPU 4 GB shape is 2 unit minutes each, so 80 unit minutes at $0.001 prepaid is $0.08. Most of that $0.40 gap is the rate: billing the same 80 minutes at $0.002 would be $0.16. The remaining $0.08, a fifth of the gap, is rounding, and rounding is the part you cannot optimize away by buying a smaller runner.

Speed

Not benchmarked yet; the runner benchmark report will replace this section. We have not run the same workload on these runners ourselves, and until we have, there is no number here worth quoting.

The cheap way to get a real answer is to point one slow job at each candidate for a week, because runner selection is per job and the Actions run log gives you the timings for free.

Cost: the same month, priced three ways

The usual workload, 10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU plus 2,000 macOS minutes a month on a private repository. For Namespace the arithmetic runs in unit minutes, and the shape decides it: matched to the machine GitHub gives you, a 2 vCPU runner with 8 GB is 4 units a minute and the Linux half is 40,000 unit minutes; the 4 GB shape is 2 units a minute and 20,000. The macOS half is 2,000 times 60 units either way, and the $100 Team plan covers the first 100,000 unit minutes.

10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU 2,000 macOS minutes Monthly total
GitHub-hosted $60 at $0.006/min $124 at $0.062/min $184
Namespace on Team, 2 vCPU and 8 GB 40,000 unit minutes 120,000 unit minutes $190: the $100 plan plus 60,000 overage unit minutes at $0.0015
Namespace on Team, 2 vCPU and 4 GB 20,000 unit minutes 120,000 unit minutes $160: the $100 plan plus 40,000 overage unit minutes at $0.0015
Latchkey $25 at $0.0025/min Not offered: $124 on GitHub-hosted $149 plus $5 to $49 a month for the plan

On the machine that matches GitHub's, Namespace is $190 against $184, so on this particular mix it is six dollars dearer rather than cheaper, and the cheaper row underneath it buys half the memory. What moves the total is macOS: 120,000 of those unit minutes are 2,000 macOS minutes at a 10x multiplier, which swamps a Linux rate that is a third lower. Note also what the $100 buys. It is not a fee on top of the compute, it is the compute, so the comparison holds only if you would actually use 100,000 unit minutes; a team that burns 30,000 pays $100 for 30,000. Latchkey's own plan is $5 to $49 a month on top of that compute, and its 2,000 to 6,000 included minutes are not netted off, so the figure is gross on both counts.

What GitHub-hosted still wins on

  • Public repositories, where standard runners are free and unlimited on a 4 vCPU and 16 GB machine.
  • An included allowance with no plan decision: $12 of compute on Free, $18 on Team, $300 on Enterprise Cloud (2,000, 3,000 and 50,000 standard Linux minutes), and no commitment to reach the best rate.
  • Memory per core. GitHub pairs 4 GB with each vCPU on its standard Linux runner; Namespace standard shapes pair 2 GB, and you buy cores to get memory.
  • A concurrency limit you can reason about. GitHub counts jobs, 20 to 500 by plan; Namespace counts vCPU, 32 on Developer and 64 on Team, so one 32 vCPU job can consume the whole Developer allowance.
  • Job duration. GitHub allows 6 hours per job; Namespace publishes a maximum instance duration of 3 hours on Developer and 5 on Team, rising to 24 on Business.
  • One vendor, one bill, one status page, and the reference images every action in the marketplace is tested against.

Switching: the exact diff

Namespace is a label change like everything else in this category, with one rule to remember: only one nscloud label is allowed in runs-on, and cache volumes arrive as companion labels rather than as inputs on a step. That makes the diff slightly longer than the usual one-liner and still nothing like a migration.

jobs:
   test:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: nscloud-ubuntu-24.04-amd64-4x8

   build:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on:
+      - nscloud-ubuntu-24.04-amd64-8x16-with-cache
+      - nscloud-cache-tag-my-repository
+      - nscloud-cache-size-50gb

The verdict

Namespace is genuinely cheaper than GitHub-hosted on private-repo Linux, by a third at matched memory and by two thirds if your jobs fit in 4 GB, and its billing rounds in your favor where GitHub rounds against you. A cheap Linux rate is not the same as a cheap month, though: the worked example above, on the matched 8 GB shape, lands at $190 against GitHub's $184, because 2,000 macOS minutes at a 10x multiplier are most of the bill. The price of that is a model you have to do arithmetic in, a plan you have to commit to for the prepaid rate, and two ceilings that GitHub states differently: concurrency measured in vCPU rather than jobs, and a maximum instance duration of 3 hours on the entry plan against GitHub's 6. On public repositories the comparison does not start, because free and unlimited on a bigger machine beats every rate on this page. Neither vendor does anything about a job that fails for a mechanical reason, which is the line item both rate cards leave out.

FAQ

How much does Namespace cost per minute?

There is no single per-minute price, because Namespace bills unit minutes: one unit is 1 vCPU plus 2 GB of RAM for a minute, at $0.001 prepaid or $0.0015 as overage on Linux. A 2 vCPU shape with 4 GB is therefore $0.002 a minute prepaid, a 2 vCPU shape with 8 GB is $0.004, and a 4 vCPU shape with 16 GB is $0.008. Windows consumes units at 2x and macOS at 10x.

Is Namespace cheaper than GitHub-hosted runners?

On private repositories, yes, at every Linux shape: $0.004 against $0.006 at 2 vCPU and 8 GB, $0.008 against $0.012 at 4 vCPU and 16 GB, and $0.016 against $0.022 at 8 vCPU. On public repositories no, because standard GitHub-hosted runners are free and unlimited there. On macOS it depends on the plan: $0.06 prepaid beats GitHub's $0.062, and the $0.09 overage rate does not.

What is a unit minute?

One unit is 1 vCPU and 2 GB of RAM running for one minute, multiplied by a platform factor of 1 for Linux, 2 for Windows, 10 for macOS and 7 for Linux on Apple silicon. Shapes with more memory than the standard ratio are charged on half their memory instead of their cores, so 8 vCPU with 32 GB counts as 16 units a minute rather than 8. Namespace's own example is 4 vCPU for 5 minutes on Linux, which is 20 unit minutes.

What are the Namespace runner labels?

The machine label is nscloud-{os}-{arch}-{shape}, for example nscloud-ubuntu-24.04-amd64-8x16 for 8 vCPU and 16 GB, and only one nscloud label is allowed in runs-on. Cache volumes are added with a -with-cache suffix plus companion labels naming the cache tag and its size in gigabytes, which is also how you keep two repositories from sharing one volume by accident.

References

  • Namespace pricing: unit minutes, shapes, plans and concurrency
  • Namespace runner labels, shapes and cache volumes
  • GitHub Actions per-minute rates by runner
  • GitHub-hosted runner specifications
  • GitHub Actions usage limits and concurrency

title: PostgreSQL and pgvector: When Should AI Applications Use a Separate Vector Database?
description:
An AI application can keep business records, embeddings and searchable documents in PostgreSQL, or introduce a dedicated vector system. The right decision depends on retrieval quality, access controls, scaling requirements and the cost of keeping multiple data stores synchronized.

An organization building an AI knowledge assistant may already store its documents, users and permissions in PostgreSQL. To make those documents searchable by meaning, the application needs embeddings. These are numerical representations of content that allow software to find semantically related passages.

One option is to store embeddings alongside application data using the pgvector extension. Another is to maintain a separate vector-search system. Both architectures can support retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

The question is whether a separate database solves a measurable problem or introduces complexity that the application does not yet need.

What pgvector adds to PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL already provides relational storage, transactions, joins, indexing and full-text search. pgvector adds vector data types, similarity operators and approximate nearest-neighbor indexes, which find close matches quickly without checking every vector.

An application can store document chunks, their embeddings and associated metadata in PostgreSQL. When a user asks a question, the application creates an embedding of that question and searches for similar document embeddings. The retrieved passages can then provide context to a language model generating an answer.

pgvector does not generate embeddings, enforce the correctness of model-generated answers or automatically determine whether a document is safe for a particular user to read. Those remain responsibilities of the application and its security architecture.

Importantly, pgvector is an extension, not a PostgreSQL 19 feature. Its existing capabilities work across supported PostgreSQL versions, and the pgvector README lists support for PostgreSQL 13 and later, so check which versions your release supports. For what changes in PostgreSQL itself, see our article on PostgreSQL 19 and its release candidate.

Source: pgvector official documentation.

How an enterprise RAG application retrieves documents

Consider a hypothetical internal knowledge assistant used by Finance and Human Resources employees. The organization stores documents and access metadata in PostgreSQL. Each document is divided into searchable passages, with an embedding associated with each passage.

A typical retrieval operation has several stages.

1. Authenticate the user. The application establishes the user’s identity and authorized organizational context.

2. Determine the permitted document scope. The server identifies which documents the user is entitled to access, using trusted authorization data rather than user-supplied instructions.

3. Generate the question embedding. An embedding model converts the user’s question into the same compatible vector representation used for the stored passages.

4. Retrieve matching passages. PostgreSQL searches for semantically similar content while applying the appropriate document-access conditions.

5. Enforce the access boundary. The application verifies that only permitted content can be passed to the model. Database-side row-level security can provide another enforcement layer where correctly configured.

6. Generate the response. The language model uses authorized passages as supporting context. The application can retain source references for traceability.

Interactive figure: view it in the original article

Suppose a Finance employee asks about an expense-approval policy. A Human Resources document might be semantically similar, but similarity does not make that document authorized. The database query and surrounding application controls must prevent restricted material from entering the model’s context.

PostgreSQL row-level security

PostgreSQL row-level security (RLS) can restrict which records a database role may read or modify. It can help enforce tenant or document boundaries independently of ordinary application filtering.

However, enabling RLS does not automatically make every connection safe. Superusers and roles with BYPASSRLS bypass policies. Table owners normally bypass RLS unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is configured. Applications also need to establish authorization context safely, especially when connections are pooled or reused.

RLS should be tested with realistic user roles, including negative tests proving that unauthorized documents cannot be retrieved. An ordinary WHERE tenant_id = ... clause is useful for query filtering, but should not be treated as a complete security boundary when the calling application can alter or omit it.

Source: PostgreSQL, Row Security Policies.

Exact search and approximate indexes solve different problems

By default, pgvector performs exact nearest-neighbor search. This finds the nearest matching vectors under the selected distance measure, providing a useful baseline against which approximate results can be evaluated. As vector collections and request volumes grow, exact search may become more expensive.

pgvector supports two principal approximate indexing methods.

Index How it works Important trade-off
HNSW Organizes vectors into a navigable graph Strong speed and recall characteristics for many workloads, with additional build time and memory requirements
IVFFlat Groups vectors into lists and searches selected lists Requires suitable training data and tuning of search breadth

Approximate indexes can return different results from exact search. That is why latency alone is an insufficient performance measure. Teams should also measure recall, which indicates how many expected nearest-neighbor results were retrieved compared with an exact-search baseline.

For an AI assistant, a faster result may be less useful if an important document is consistently omitted.

Source: pgvector, Indexing.

Filtering can affect retrieval quality

Enterprise searches rarely depend on vector similarity alone. Results may also be filtered by organization, document type, project or access scope. With approximate indexes, PostgreSQL can apply filtering after the index scan has selected candidates, and this can return fewer results than requested.

For example, if a search examines 40 candidates and only 10% satisfy a category filter, approximately four may remain on average. That is an illustration of selectivity, not a guaranteed outcome for every search.

pgvector introduced iterative index scans in version 0.8.0 on October 30, 2024. Iterative scans can continue examining more index candidates when filtering removes too many results, subject to configured resource and scan limits. Other approaches include ordinary PostgreSQL indexes, partial vector indexes and table partitioning, depending on query patterns. These mechanisms should be selected through measurement.

Tenants that share one approximate index can also affect each other. The pgvector documentation says vectors from one tenant can change recall and speed for other tenants, and recommends list partitioning or separate tables for tenant isolation.

A correctly enforced authorization filter must never be weakened merely to increase the number of search results. A retrieval system returning fewer authorized passages may produce a less complete answer. Returning unauthorized passages is a different and more serious failure.

Sources: pgvector changelog, pgvector filtering guidance and pgvector multitenancy.

Hybrid search combines different forms of relevance

Semantic similarity is useful when users describe a concept without using the exact wording found in a document. Keyword search remains important for identifiers, product names, policy numbers and technical terms.

PostgreSQL supports full-text search through facilities such as tsvector and tsquery. Applications can combine those results with pgvector similarity search. For example, a knowledge assistant searching for a specific incident number may benefit from exact text matching, while a broader troubleshooting question may benefit from semantic retrieval.

Ranked results can be combined using techniques such as reciprocal rank fusion, which merges two ranked lists by position, then optionally reranked using another relevance model. However, hybrid search does not guarantee better retrieval in every application. Teams should evaluate representative questions, expected documents and final ranking quality.

Sources: PostgreSQL full-text search and pgvector hybrid search.

When does a separate vector database become useful?

A dedicated vector system may become worthwhile when an application’s retrieval requirements exceed what its existing PostgreSQL environment can support effectively. Examples include independently scaling vector-search traffic, specialized distributed indexing, very large search collections or retrieval features that are unavailable in the chosen PostgreSQL deployment.

But moving embeddings to another system creates additional responsibilities.

Consider a document update. The application changes the source document in PostgreSQL. It must also regenerate affected embeddings and update the vector index. Until synchronization finishes, searches may retrieve outdated content.

Deletion creates a related problem. Removing a document from the transactional database must also remove or invalidate its vector representations.

Permission changes are particularly important. If a user’s access is revoked, stale access metadata in another search system must not allow restricted content to reach the model.

An architecture with two data stores therefore needs a reliable way to propagate changes, handle failures, retry safely and determine when search data is current. Change-data capture, which streams changes out of the database, transactional outbox patterns, which record the change event in the same transaction as the data, and event processing can help, but each requires implementation and operational ownership. The authoritative permission check should remain enforceable even when the search index is delayed.

These synchronization boundaries are part of the cost of adopting a separate vector system.

Embedding models introduce another migration boundary

An embedding is generated using a particular model and representation. Changing the embedding model may change vector dimensions, distributions and similarity behavior. Embeddings produced by incompatible models should not be combined as though their distances were directly comparable.

Organizations should record embedding-model identifiers, versions and relevant generation settings. A model migration may require generating new embeddings, rebuilding indexes and evaluating retrieval quality before switching production queries. During a transition, old and new representations may need to coexist.

pgvector also has indexing limits that depend on the representation. Its documented HNSW support includes vector values up to 2,000 dimensions and halfvec values up to 4,000 dimensions. These limits concern the relevant index representation, not a universal restriction on every possible storage or search strategy. The application’s embedding-model choice therefore affects index design.

Source: pgvector, Vector Types and Indexing Limits.

How should a team choose?

A useful evaluation compares the existing PostgreSQL approach with a separate vector system using the same representative workload.

Evaluation area Question to answer
Retrieval quality Are expected relevant passages consistently found?
Authorization Can unauthorized documents ever reach the model context?
Performance Does search latency meet the target under realistic concurrency?
Filtering Do selective tenant and metadata conditions preserve acceptable recall?
Updates and deletions How quickly does the search index reflect source changes?
Operations What are the indexing, backup, monitoring and recovery requirements?
Scaling Can retrieval demand grow without harming transactional workloads?
Cost What is the combined infrastructure and maintenance expense?

The comparison should not assume that the most specialized technology is automatically the most suitable. A small or moderately sized application may find that PostgreSQL with pgvector meets its needs with fewer systems to manage. A larger application may justify an independent search tier when workload isolation, specialized features or independent scaling delivers measurable benefits. Those outcomes are workload-dependent and should be established through tests, not generic database-size thresholds.

Operations also include keeping the extension patched. The pgvector changelog records fixes for possible index corruption during HNSW vacuuming in version 0.8.3 on June 17, 2026, and for buffer overflows during IVFFlat index builds in versions 0.8.6 on July 29 (on 32-bit systems) and 0.8.7 on October 1, 2026. Teams should run a current patch release and test index maintenance, such as vacuuming and rebuilds, before relying on an index in production.

Source: pgvector, Changelog.

What the architecture decision comes down to

PostgreSQL and pgvector allow application records, embeddings, metadata and text search to remain within one database environment. This can simplify AI applications that already depend heavily on relational data. A separate vector system may provide valuable capabilities, but requires attention to synchronization, deletions, authorization and operational ownership.

Neither architecture automatically guarantees search relevance or secure retrieval.

Start with verified retrieval and access-control requirements. Use PostgreSQL with pgvector when it meets them effectively, and introduce a separate vector system when measurements justify the additional complexity.

References and further reading

  1. pgvector, Official Repository. Supported vector types, similarity search, indexing, filtering and multitenancy.
  2. pgvector, Changelog. Version history, iterative index scans and patch releases.
  3. PostgreSQL, Row Security Policies. Database authorization behavior and bypass conditions.
  4. PostgreSQL, Full Text Search. Keyword retrieval and ranking.
  5. PostgreSQL, Full Text Search Introduction. The tsvector and tsquery types.
  6. PostgreSQL, EXPLAIN. Execution-plan inspection and performance evaluation.
  7. pgvector, Release and Security History. Extension releases and maintenance updates.

Sources verified November 6, 2026. pgvector releases often, and the 0.8.7 release on October 1, 2026 fixed an IVFFlat index build bug and is not presented as introducing the architectural capabilities discussed here, so check the sources above before you act. Performance and architecture guidance are analytical recommendations, not independent TechiesJournal benchmark results.

Originally published on TechiesJournal.

title: I Was Shipping Five Font Files. One Variable Font Replaced Them All.
description:
Open the network tab on a site with a half-decent type system and count the font requests. Four is normal. Six isn't rare. Every one of them is a separate .woff2 file for a separate weight — Regular, Medium, Semibold, Bold — sitting in the critical path before the browser can paint text in anything but a fallback font.

Our design system had five: four weights plus a bold italic for pull-quotes. Nobody had decided that on purpose. It accumulated — a designer added Semibold for one component, Bold Italic followed for another, and eighteen months later the font folder looked like a weight had been added every time someone liked how it looked in Figma.

The fix everyone reaches for first

When this shows up in a performance audit, the fix is almost always the same: cut weights. Drop from five down to three. Merge Semibold into Medium. Ship Bold Italic as a font-style: oblique of regular Bold instead of a dedicated file.

@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/fonts/inter-regular.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 400;
}
@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/fonts/inter-medium.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 500;
}
@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/fonts/inter-bold.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 700;
}

This genuinely helps — three requests beat five. It also doesn't touch the actual shape of the problem: every weight you keep is still its own file, its own request, its own round trip. Cut too aggressively and you lose the weight your design actually needs; cut too little and you're back where you started with a slightly smaller number.

Before you keep reading — guess how many of those weights the browser actually downloads on a page that only uses Regular body text and one Bold heading. The honest (and slightly surprising) answer is: two. Browsers don't fetch an @font-face file the moment it's declared — the CSS Fonts spec requires user agents to download only the faces a page's rendered text actually calls for, so Medium, Semibold, and Bold Italic never leave the server for this particular page. That's the one thing "cut weights" already gets right, mostly by accident. What it doesn't fix: those two downloads are still two separate round trips, and the moment any other page in the same design system reaches for a third weight — a Semibold stat callout, a Bold Italic pull-quote — that page pays for a third file, one request at a time, because nothing about a static setup can serve more than the single weight baked into each one.

It's not about how many weights — it's about how many files

Here's what the "cut weights" fix never addresses: a static font file is a fixed snapshot. One file draws letterforms at exactly 700 and nothing else. Want 650 for a hover state that should feel "almost bold but not quite"? You can't — 650 doesn't exist unless you shipped a sixth file for it. The weight scale looks continuous in your design tool and is actually a handful of hardcoded stops in production.

A variable font isn't a set of snapshots. It's one file that encodes the whole range as interpolation data — the letterforms at 100 and the letterforms at 900, with the browser computing everything in between on the fly. Ask for font-weight: 538 and you get a real, rendered 538, not a browser fallback or a rounded guess.

@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/fonts/inter-variable.woff2") format("woff2-variations");
  font-weight: 100 900; /* a range, not a single value */
  font-stretch: 75% 125%;
}

That's the whole type system. One @font-face block. One network request. Every weight from thin to black, plus every stop in between, available from the same file:

h1   { font-weight: 700; }
h2   { font-weight: 600; }
body { font-weight: 400; }
.btn:hover { font-weight: 538; } /* yes, this is a valid value now */

Five requests become one. The five-weight design system from the top of this post could have shipped as a single file from day one — nobody needed to decide anything about which weights to keep, because the weight is no longer a file, it's a number.

When font-variation-settings is the wrong tool

Variable fonts expose more than weight. The OpenType spec registers five standard axes: weight (wght), width (wdth), slant (slnt), italic (ital), and optical size (opsz) — plus whatever custom axes an individual typeface adds on top (a "grade" axis some foundries ship for tuning contrast in dark mode is a common one). The low-level way to reach any axis by its tag is font-variation-settings:

.headline {
  font-variation-settings: "wght" 650, "opsz" 32;
}

It works, but it's the wrong default for four of those five registered axes — wght, wdth, ital, and slnt already have real CSS properties (font-weight, font-stretch, font-style: italic / oblique <angle>) that do the same job and play better with the rest of CSS: they animate and transition the way you'd expect, they interact correctly with font-weight: bolder/lighter inheritance, and they don't silently override each other the way two font-variation-settings declarations on the same element do. opsz is the odd one out — CSS only gives you an on/off switch for it (font-optical-sizing: auto, which is also the default), not a property that sets a specific number — so pinning an exact optical-size value, or reaching a font's own custom axes, is what font-variation-settings is actually for.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The part worth being honest about

A variable font file is not automatically smaller than a single static one. It has to encode interpolation data for the entire range it covers, so a variable file is often larger than any one static weight on its own — sometimes close to the size of two or three static files combined, especially once a large character set (Cyrillic, Greek, a wide set of Latin diacritics) is involved. The win isn't "smaller file." It's "one request instead of several," and that trade only pays off once you're actually using three or more weights. A page that only ever renders Regular text has nothing to gain from swapping to a variable font — a single static .woff2 is still the smallest, fastest thing you can ship.

The other honest caveat: this isn't new. Safari and Chrome shipped variable font support in 2017; Firefox and Edge followed in 2018. There's no legacy-browser excuse here — the fix has been sitting in every evergreen browser for the better part of a decade, available the moment you swap the font file and the @font-face block that points at it.

What changed

Our five-weight type system is now one file and one @font-face block, and the button hover state finally gets the in-between weight it always should have had instead of jumping straight from 400 to 700. Nothing about the design changed. The number of HTTP requests it took to render it did.

Open your own network tab and count the font requests on something you shipped this year. If it's more than two, how many of those files are actually different weights of the exact same typeface — and what would happen to your render time if they were one?

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.
