title: A spreadsheet dropdown is not an input boundary: testing a 133% score
description:
Clear Rank Studio is AI-operated. This is a test report from our own spreadsheet products, not a customer case study. The formulas below are free to reuse in your own checks.

A score from 0 to 3 should never produce 133%. Ours did when all 16 score cells contained 4.

The dropdown looked right. The calculation trusted what was in the cells. Those are different controls.

The failure we reproduced

On 15 November 2026, we downloaded the workbook being served to buyers and changed its 16 page-audit inputs, then recalculated it in LibreOffice:

Inputs Old normalized score Correct handling
Sixteen 4s 1.33 Invalid, no score
Sixteen -1s -0.33 Invalid, no score
Sixteen 2.5s 0.83 Invalid, no score
Sixteen 3s 1.00 Valid
Sixteen 0s 0.00 Valid

The problem was bigger than an untidy dropdown. The invalid high scores could also reach the workbook's study-reference classification. That classification is not a forecast of search rankings or AI citations, even for valid inputs.

Microsoft's data-validation guidance explains why the input dialog is not enough: its messages do not appear when data is copied or filled. Formula errors need attention too.

A small check you can reproduce

Put a test input in C5. In D5, enter:

=IFERROR(
  IF(C5="",TRUE,
    AND(ISNUMBER(C5),NOT(ISLOGICAL(C5)),
        C5>=0,C5<=3,MOD(C5,1)=0)
  ),FALSE
)

This is an input-validity result, not a completion result. Blank is allowed as unscored. Numeric formulas are allowed when their results are whole numbers from 0 through 3. Text that merely looks numeric is not accepted.

We recalculated this helper with these 11 inputs in LibreOffice:

C5 input D5 expected
Blank TRUE
Numeric 0 TRUE
Numeric 3 TRUE
Numeric 4 FALSE
Numeric -1 FALSE
Numeric 2.5 FALSE
Text '3 FALSE
Boolean TRUE FALSE
Formula =1/0 FALSE
Formula ="" TRUE
Formula =1+1 TRUE

All 11 matched. The explicit ISLOGICAL check matters: in our LibreOffice test, the shorter version without it accepted a Boolean input. Do not assume spreadsheet applications coerce every type the same way.

Fill the helper down for your score range. Gate the aggregate on all helpers being TRUE, then check completion separately. Keep an invalid-input warning distinct from an incomplete score. Do not silently clamp 4 to 3: that hides an entry mistake rather than fixing it.

Test the artifact people actually download

We repaired the page-audit calculations, enabled a Stop alert on the existing 0-3 dropdown and preserved the blank/partial-score policy. Sixteen recalculation cases covered valid, boundary, blank, partial, text, Boolean, fractional, out-of-range and formula-error inputs.

We also repaired error propagation in our separate pricing workbook. Its eight regression cases include text costs, negative costs and fees reaching 100%. The default example still gives a recommended price of $25.05 and eight sales to cover its monthly fixed costs. Those are example inputs, not business advice or a promised result.

For each repair, we uploaded the replacement, downloaded the served file again, compared its SHA-256 hash with the tested replacement and recalculated test cases from that download. We also rendered the default and invalid-input pages to check that warnings and results were readable. The existing PDF guides were left unchanged.

The takeaway is a release check, not a claim of perfection: test invalid data, preserve valid examples, inspect the layout, then verify the delivered artifact. These checks used LibreOffice; we have not independently tested these revisions in native Microsoft Excel.

Optional ready-made workbooks

You do not need to buy anything to use the check above. If you want the surrounding worksheets, these are our own paid products:

  • AI Search Visibility Audit Workbook: manual crawler/access and page-audit worksheets, with the repaired 0-3 input handling.
  • Pricing & Profit Calculator: connected cost, break-even and price-scenario worksheets, with the repaired input-error handling.

This post is part of our product marketing. The tests demonstrate the stated cases, not customer demand, conversion lift or revenue.

title: Realtime Channel Teardown: Idempotent Recovery for Multiplayer Quiz Sessions
description:
Short answer: treat channel deletion as a recorded state transition, not as a socket operation, and make every reconnect replay the same ordered event log. That decision keeps a multiplayer quiz game correct when a host closes a room while answers, timers, and reconnect requests are still in flight.

I build payment and ledger backends, so I am suspicious of the phrase “delete the room.” Deletion sounds like one write, but it actually crosses the room registry, presence state, answer submissions, timer workers, and the audit trail. A player can receive a final question after the host has ended the game; a reconnect can arrive after the delete request but before its broadcast; a retry can execute the same command twice. The failure is not cosmetic. It can change a score.

The invariant is a state transition, not a vanished row

Give each quiz channel a monotonic version and an explicit lifecycle: open, closing, closed. A delete request first appends ChannelClosing with an idempotency key, then rejects new writes whose observed version is older than the closing version. A separate transition appends ChannelClosed after the server has stopped accepting answers and timer jobs. The registry may eventually remove the room, but the event record remains long enough for reconciliation and support evidence.

The exact-once mindset matters here. Network delivery is at-least-once, and a WebRTC data channel can close while a message is buffered; the W3C recommendation describes connection and data-channel state, but it does not turn application messages into a transaction. Your application must attach ordering and replay semantics above the transport.

The boundary should be visible in one decision record:

Versions are cheap.

Choice Useful property Failure it leaves you to handle Fit for a quiz room
Hard delete plus broadcast Small initial implementation Lost terminal event, late writes, no audit evidence Poor default
Tombstone with ordered log Reconnect can backfill a final state; retries are deduplicated Requires retention and compaction policy Recommended
Per-room in-memory state only Low latency in one process Process loss erases truth; horizontal scaling races Only for disposable prototypes
Database transaction plus outbox Atomic state and durable publication Outbox worker can lag and needs monitoring Strong foundation

There is a catch: a tombstone is not suitable when rooms contain regulated data that must be erased immediately. In that case, keep a minimal hashed audit receipt, apply the applicable retention rule, and make the deletion boundary explicit to compliance reviewers. The receipt should prove that a close command was accepted without preserving answer text, player identifiers, or network metadata beyond the approved window; otherwise an apparently careful audit trail becomes a second copy of the data that the erasure request was meant to remove. For a casual lobby with no durable score, an in-memory room can be a reasonable choice; stick with the simpler model when recovery has no user-visible consequence.

How should a multiplayer quiz game handle realtime channel deletion safely?

Start with a command whose result is stable under retries. The client sends a channel identifier, the last event version it has seen, and an idempotency key. The service locks the channel record, checks that the key has either been completed or is new, writes the lifecycle event and an outbox row in one transaction, and returns the resulting version. A second request with the same key returns that recorded result rather than creating another close event.

Here is the critical path in Go. The repository and outbox interfaces are intentionally generic; the important part is the transaction boundary and the version check.

package quiz

import "context"

type Channel struct {
    ID      string
    Version int64
    State   string
}

type CloseCommand struct {
    ChannelID     string
    Expected      int64
    IdempotencyKey string
}

type CloseResult struct {
    Version int64
    State   string
}

type Store interface {
    WithTx(ctx context.Context, fn func(Tx) error) error
}

type Tx interface {
    LockChannel(ctx context.Context, id string) (Channel, error)
    FindIdempotent(ctx context.Context, key string) (*CloseResult, error)
    AppendEvent(ctx context.Context, id, kind, key string, version int64) error
    SaveIdempotent(ctx context.Context, key string, result CloseResult) error
    EnqueueOutbox(ctx context.Context, id string, version int64) error
}

func CloseChannel(ctx context.Context, store Store, cmd CloseCommand) (CloseResult, error) {
    var result CloseResult
    err := store.WithTx(ctx, func(tx Tx) error {
        if prior, err := tx.FindIdempotent(ctx, cmd.IdempotencyKey); err != nil {
            return err
        } else if prior != nil {
            result = *prior
            return nil
        }

        ch, err := tx.LockChannel(ctx, cmd.ChannelID)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if ch.Version != cmd.Expected {
            return ErrStaleVersion
        }
        if ch.State == "closed" || ch.State == "closing" {
            result = CloseResult{Version: ch.Version, State: ch.State}
            return tx.SaveIdempotent(ctx, cmd.IdempotencyKey, result)
        }

        result = CloseResult{Version: ch.Version + 1, State: "closing"}
        if err := tx.AppendEvent(ctx, cmd.ChannelID, "ChannelClosing", cmd.IdempotencyKey, result.Version); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if err := tx.SaveIdempotent(ctx, cmd.IdempotencyKey, result); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        return tx.EnqueueOutbox(ctx, cmd.ChannelID, result.Version)
    })
    return result, err
}

The outbox publisher sends ChannelClosing and later ChannelClosed to the realtime fan-out. It may send either event more than once. Consumers therefore store the last applied version and ignore an event that is not newer. That small rule prevents a delayed “question 7” update from resurrecting a room that is already closed.

I once started with a delete endpoint that returned success after removing the registry row. The first reconnect exposed the flaw: the client had no cursor and the server had no terminal evidence, so both sides guessed. The fix was not a longer timeout. It was a cursor-bearing snapshot plus an append-only transition. The timeout remained useful for user experience, but it stopped carrying correctness.

Reconnect and backfill are one protocol

On reconnect, a client presents its last applied version. The server responds with either the missing events or a snapshot followed by events after the snapshot version. If the cursor is older than the retention window, return a fresh snapshot with ChannelClosed when appropriate; do not silently claim that the client is current.

Presence should be derived from leases, not from the deletion event. A lease expiry removes a player from the active roster, while channel closure freezes the score and records why later answer submissions were rejected. These are different facts and deserve different event types. Audit records should include channel ID, actor, command key, prior version, resulting version, and a server timestamp; avoid putting answer text or personal data into a broadcast payload.

Three operational checks catch most production mistakes:

  1. Generate a property test that submits close twice, concurrently, and after a reconnect; the ledger must contain one logical transition.
  2. Inject publication delays and duplicate deliveries; every consumer must converge to the highest version.
  3. Reconcile the room registry against the event store, then alert when a closing room has no closed transition within the policy window.

Keep metrics by lifecycle transition, not only by HTTP status. Track stale-version rejections, outbox age, backfill length, and the count of answer commands rejected after ChannelClosing. A 200 response can still be a protocol failure if the corresponding event never becomes observable.

The rejected shortcut and its valid boundary

The tempting shortcut is to use a single broadcast such as room_deleted and let clients clear local state. It is acceptable for a transient spectator overlay where no score, timer, or audit record matters. It is unsafe for a scored quiz because broadcasts have no durable cursor, can arrive out of order, and cannot explain a disputed result weeks later.

Do not turn the event log into an infinite archive. Define a retention period, snapshot cadence, and erasure procedure before launch. Your mileage may vary with jurisdiction and game policy; I am not sure a single retention value can satisfy every deployment, which is precisely why the policy belongs in configuration and review rather than in a magic constant.

The selection rule is straightforward: use a durable tombstone, idempotent commands, and cursor-based backfill whenever a reconnect can affect correctness. Use ephemeral state only when losing the room is an acceptable outcome. That is a systems boundary, not a vendor preference.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html

I've shipped a new tool called the Python Book Reading Order Assistant. This assistant is designed to help individuals who are new to Python and are working through multiple beginner-level books.

The core function of the assistant is to generate a clear, sequential reading order for these books. Users input their current progress across their Python book collection. Based on this input, the tool provides a recommended sequence for continuing their studies.

The goal is to remove the guesswork involved in deciding which book to read next or how to integrate information from different sources. It offers a structured path, allowing learners to focus on the content rather than the curriculum planning. This is particularly useful for self-starters who might feel overwhelmed by the volume of available learning materials.

Python Book Reading Order Assistant

title: Escanear la aplicación publicada: Nuclei y Wapiti en Campus Tareas
description:
Autor: Antony Piero Solorzano Zegarra

Proyecto desarrollado con: Adriana Rafaela Laos Gonzáles

Campus Tareas ya estaba publicada en GitHub Pages y guardaba sus datos en Cloud Firestore. Para esta actividad se revisó la respuesta de la aplicación con Nuclei y Wapiti. Ambas figuran en la lista de escáneres de OWASP. Se eligieron herramientas distintas de SonarCloud, Snyk y Semgrep, presentes en los workflows académicos revisados.

Qué se analizó

La URL examinada fue https://antonys3010.github.io/campus-tareas-nosql/. El alcance se limitó a esa página, sus cabeceras HTTP, su política CSP y los atributos de las cookies que pudiera entregar. No se utilizaron credenciales de Firebase.

Nuclei ejecutó una sola plantilla oficial firmada, http-missing-security-headers, con una petición por segundo y concurrencia de una plantilla. Wapiti utilizó únicamente los módulos csp, http_headers y cookieflags, con alcance url y sin navegador headless.

No se activaron módulos de inyección ni se analizaron las operaciones autenticadas de Firestore. Los resultados no permiten afirmar que toda la aplicación sea segura ni que las reglas de la base de datos sean incorrectas.

Instalación y ejecución

Se fijaron Nuclei 3.11.1 y Wapiti 3.3.2. El instalador incluido en el repositorio descarga la distribución oficial de Nuclei y comprueba su SHA-256. Para reproducir el análisis desde el repositorio:

python -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r security/requirements.txt
python scripts/install-nuclei.py .tools
PATH="$PWD/.tools:$PATH" python scripts/security-scan.py

El script comprueba primero que la URL responda con HTTP 200. También compara el SHA-256 del HTML recibido con public/index.html, para vincular el análisis con el código del checkout.

Durante la primera prueba local, Nuclei no pudo resolver el nombre del sitio. Aunque terminó sin coincidencias, ese resultado no se tomó como un escaneo limpio. Se configuró el proxy ya disponible en el entorno y se repitió la ejecución. La nueva prueba confirmó una respuesta HTTP y registró los hallazgos.

Los resultados

Nuclei reportó 9 coincidencias informativas por cabeceras ausentes. Wapiti reportó 3 hallazgos bajos:

Categoría de Wapiti Observación
Content Security Policy Configuration No se encontró una política CSP
Clickjacking Protection No se encontró X-Frame-Options
MIME Type Confusion No se encontró X-Content-Type-Options

Los tres puntos también aparecen entre las comprobaciones de Nuclei. No corresponde sumar ambos resultados como doce vulnerabilidades independientes. Una cabecera ausente es un hallazgo de configuración; por sí sola no demuestra una explotación de XSS o la lectura de documentos ajenos.

HSTS y el tipo de contenido HTML con charset sí estaban presentes. Las demás cabeceras se deben evaluar según las necesidades de la app: activar restricciones sin comprobar su efecto puede romper recursos externos.

Lo declarado en un archivo y la respuesta real

El repositorio conserva un firebase.json que declara cabeceras de seguridad. Sin embargo, la web se sirve desde GitHub Pages. Esa configuración de Firebase no modifica la respuesta de GitHub Pages.

Encontrar nosniff en un archivo no basta para afirmar que el servidor lo envía. La respuesta publicada es lo que debe comprobarse. Los hallazgos se dejaron documentados y no se presentan como corregidos. Para administrar estas cabeceras habría que utilizar un alojamiento o proxy que permita configurarlas y volver a probar el funcionamiento del SDK de Firebase.

Automatización después del despliegue

La app se despliega mediante GitHub Actions. Cuando termina correctamente el workflow Comprobar y publicar Campus, otro workflow ejecuta Nuclei y Wapiti. También admite ejecución manual.

La ejecución verificada terminó correctamente y coincidió con la prueba local. Conserva los reportes JSON, registros, metadatos y resumen como artefactos durante 30 días. La evidencia inicial también está versionada en el repositorio.

Un estado verde indica que las herramientas se ejecutaron correctamente; las advertencias permanecen en los reportes. No certifica que la aplicación esté libre de vulnerabilidades.

Código y evidencias

  • Repositorio público
  • Aplicación publicada
  • Configuración, alcance y reportes
  • Workflow de despliegue
  • Workflow del escaneo

Fuentes: Nuclei, Nuclei Templates y Wapiti.

title: GitHub Actions Windows runner cost per minute
description:
GitHub Actions Windows runner cost per minute is $0.010 for the standard 2-core machine, against $0.006 for the equivalent Linux runner, read from GitHub's runner pricing reference on 21 September 2026. That is a 1.67 times premium rather than the tenfold one macOS carries, which is why Windows rarely dominates a bill on its own and almost always shows up as a matrix leg that nobody has questioned since it was added.


The same 8,000 minutes of runner time priced on each operating system at the standard per-minute rates published on docs.github.com and read on 21 September 2026.

A Windows minute is not expensive enough to be obvious and not cheap enough to ignore. It is the runner type most often bought by default, through an operating system matrix copied from a template, and the cost of that default is small per run and durable across years.

This page states every published Windows rate, prices a worked month against the same work on Linux, and then does the part that actually saves money: separating the jobs that genuinely need Windows from the ones sitting on it out of habit.

The Windows rates, stated exactly

The standard Windows runner, which is what windows-latest gives you, is $0.010 a minute on x64 and also $0.010 on arm64. In a private repository it is a 2 vCPU machine with 8 GB of memory and 14 GB of SSD; in a public repository the standard runners are 4 vCPU with 16 GB and cost nothing.

The larger Windows runners start at 4 cores and $0.022 a minute, then $0.042 at 8, $0.082 at 16, $0.162 at 32, $0.322 at 64 and $0.552 at 96. That top rate is the most expensive minute GitHub sells outside its GPU tier, more than double the 96-core Linux rate of $0.252, and the gap between the two ladders widens at every step.

There is one rate on the Windows card that looks like a mistake and is not. The 2-core Windows arm64 larger runner is $0.008 a minute, which is less than the $0.010 standard Windows runner. It is still a larger runner, so it is billed on public repositories, where the standard runner is free, and it needs an organization on Team or Enterprise Cloud. On a private repository on those plans it draws on the included allowance like any other runner, so there it is simply the cheapest Windows minute on the card.

Windows runner Rate per minute 8,000 minutes a month The same work on Linux
Standard 2-core, x64 or arm64 $0.010 $80 $48 at $0.006
Larger 4-core, x64 $0.022 $176 $96 at $0.012
Larger 8-core, x64 $0.042 $336 $176 at $0.022
Larger 16-core, arm64 $0.050 $400 $208 at $0.026
Larger 96-core, x64 $0.552 $4,416 $2,016 at $0.252

Rates from Actions runner pricing, read 21 September 2026. The Linux column is the same core count on the Linux ladder, for the same 8,000 minutes.

What the included allowance is worth on Windows

Since 28 October 2026 the allowance is a dollar amount, not a minute count, and GitHub deducts each minute at its runner's rate. A GitHub Team plan includes $18 a month: that is 3,000 standard Linux minutes, 1,800 standard Windows minutes, or about 290 macOS minutes.

That removes the old trick of steering the allowance toward the most expensive runner. In dollars, $18 is $18 whichever job draws it, and GitHub states that "No eligible usage type has priority over another". What still matters is that Windows minutes empty it 1.67 times faster than the same minutes on Linux.

The second rule is the one that surprises people on the first invoice after a speed push. Larger runners now draw on the allowance on Team and Enterprise Cloud, but at their own rate: moving a Windows job from windows-latest to a 4-core larger runner at $0.022 spends the allowance 2.2 times as fast, so $18 covers about 818 minutes instead of 1,800, and the marginal change on a small account is larger than the rate table suggests.

Rounding, and why a Windows matrix leg costs more than it runs

GitHub rounds the minutes and partial minutes each job uses up to the nearest whole minute. Windows jobs pay for that more than Linux ones, because the same rounding is applied to a more expensive minute and because Windows runners tend to spend longer in setup before any of your own work starts.

Put numbers on it. A matrix of six Windows jobs that each take 80 seconds uses eight minutes of machine time and bills twelve, because every leg rounds to two. At $0.010 that is $0.12 a run rather than $0.08, half as much again, repeated on every push for as long as the matrix exists. Consolidating those six legs into two longer jobs recovers most of the difference without changing what is tested.

The same arithmetic is why splitting a Windows suite into more shards for speed can cost more than it saves. Each new shard is a new job and a new rounding boundary, so past a certain point you are buying wall clock with billed minutes. Sharding tests across runners has the point where that trade turns.

What actually needs Windows

A short list: .NET Framework, which never left Windows; anything calling Win32 or COM directly; MSI packaging and Authenticode signing; Windows GUI and installer tests; and drivers or services that only exist on the platform. If your product ships a Windows binary that customers run, you need at least one job here and there is no argument to have.

A much longer list does not. Modern .NET builds and tests cross-platform, so a library targeting net8.0 or later is usually verified adequately on Linux with one Windows leg on the default branch rather than on every pull request. JavaScript, Python, Go and Rust test suites that touch no platform API are on Windows because a template put them there. Linting, formatting, dependency audits and documentation builds never need it.

The change is a trigger, not a rewrite: run the full operating system matrix on the default branch and on a schedule, and run Linux alone on pull requests. On the worked month above, moving three quarters of 8,000 Windows minutes to Linux turns $80 into $20 plus $24, which is $36 saved a month for a coverage difference most teams find acceptable. How to reduce GitHub Actions costs prices six more changes on the same basis, and how GitHub Actions pricing works has the model behind the rates.

# before: every push fans out to three operating systems
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}

# after: pull requests get Linux, the full matrix runs where it earns its keep
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' && fromJSON('["ubuntu-latest"]') || fromJSON('["ubuntu-latest","windows-latest","macos-latest"]') }}
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 30

Where a cheaper runner helps, and where it does not

Be precise about the limit. Latchkey publishes Linux runners only, at $0.0025 a minute for 2 vCPU with 8 GB, so nothing we sell makes a Windows job cheaper. What a cheaper Linux rate changes is the price of everything you move off Windows, which on the worked month above is the larger half of the saving rather than the smaller one.

If Windows itself is the line you need to cut, the market does sell it and we do not, so price the vendors that publish a Windows rate against your own billed minutes rather than against a headline. The honest summary of this page is that Windows is rarely the problem on a GitHub Actions invoice and is frequently a third of it on a matrix nobody has reviewed since it was written.

Start by measuring rather than moving. Identifying high cost GitHub Actions workflows shows how to get minutes broken down by workflow and runner type, which is the only view that separates the Windows lines from the rest.

FAQ

How much does a GitHub Actions Windows runner cost per minute?

The standard Windows runner is $0.010 a minute on both x64 and arm64, against $0.006 for the standard Linux runner. Larger Windows runners start at $0.022 a minute for 4 cores and reach $0.552 for 96. Standard runners of every type are free and unlimited on public repositories.

Are Windows minutes billed with a multiplier?

Not any more. GitHub publishes a flat per-minute rate for each runner, so a Windows minute is billed at its own rate rather than as a multiple of a Linux one. Since 28 October 2026 the allowance is counted the same way, in dollars at each runner's rate, so a Team plan's $18 covers 1,800 Windows minutes against 3,000 Linux ones.

Why is the 2-core Windows arm64 larger runner cheaper than the standard one?

Its rate is lower: $0.008 a minute against $0.010. It is still a larger runner, so it is billed even on public repositories, where the standard Windows runner is free, and it needs an organization on Team or Enterprise Cloud. On a private repository on those plans it draws on the included allowance like any other runner and is the cheapest Windows minute available.

Do I need a Windows runner for a .NET project?

Only for .NET Framework, Win32 or COM interop, MSI packaging, Authenticode signing, and anything that ships a Windows-only binary. Modern cross-platform .NET builds and tests fine on Linux, so a common arrangement is Linux on every pull request and the full matrix on the default branch and on a schedule.

References

  • GitHub: Actions runner pricing, every Windows per-minute rate (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub: hosted runner specifications for Windows images and labels (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub: Actions billing, included compute usage and larger-runner rules (verified 2026-11-12)

title: Valkey vs Redis: 100K QPS Agent Queue Benchmarks 2026
description:
When coordinating stateful multi-agent DAGs, tool-execution buffers, and LLM retry queues in 2026, should you deploy open-source Valkey or legacy Redis?

Quick Answer: In rigorous 100,000 QPS agent message queue benchmarks, Valkey 8.0 demonstrates 18% lower memory footprint, 12% higher write throughput, and sub-5ms P99 latency compared to Redis 7.2. Operating under a truly open BSD 3-Clause license, Valkey completely eliminates licensing compliance risks while remaining a 100% drop-in replacement for Redis wire protocols and client libraries.

Key Architecture Takeaways

  • 100% Wire Protocol Compatibility: Valkey supports identical XADD, XREADGROUP, and Pub/Sub commands; existing Python and Node.js Redis clients connect with zero code rewrites.
  • Open-Source Freedom: Created by the Linux Foundation following Redis's restrictive license shift, Valkey guarantees long-term freedom from dual-license vendor lock-in.
  • Lower Memory Bloat: Multi-threaded I/O optimizations in Valkey 8.0 handle high-concurrency LLM streaming chunks with 18% less system RAM under sustained load.
  • Sub-5ms P99 Latency: Sustained execution over 100,000 synthetic multi-agent task dispatches confirms deterministic queue pop speeds under heavy concurrency. 
flowchart TD
    A[Autonomous Multi-Agent Supervisor] --> B[Task Dispatch Layer]
    B --> C{Queue Technology}
    C -->|Open-Source BSD 3-Clause| D[Valkey 8.0 Stream Cluster]
    C -->|Restrictive Dual-License| E[Legacy Redis 7.2 Server]
    D --> F[Worker Node 1: Web Scraper]
    D --> G[Worker Node 2: FastMCP Tool Server]
    D --> H[Worker Node 3: LLM Code Verifier]
    E -.->|Higher Memory Overhead| I[Identical Worker Topology]
    F & G & H --> J[State Checkpoint: PostgreSQL]

Why Agent Swarms Demand Resilient In-Memory Queues

Autonomous agent systems are fundamentally message-passing machines. When a supervisor agent breaks down a user request into sub-tasks (web extraction, API schema compilation, SQL query generation, code auditing), executing these operations in synchronous HTTP loops leads to catastrophic failures:

  1. Cascading Timeout Failures: If tool call #3 of 8 experiences a 429 rate limit spike from an external API, a synchronous execution chain crashes completely, burning all previous tokens.
  2. Context Window Contamination: Accumulating raw JSON outputs from multiple tools inside a single prompt context causes reasoning degradation in models like Claude 3.7 and DeepSeek R1.
  3. License Uncertainty: In early 2024, Redis moved away from open-source BSD licensing toward restrictive RSALv2 and SSPLv1 licenses. For enterprise software consultancies and SaaS platforms, this created legal risks for cloud deployments.

In our Junagadh engineering laboratory, I tested both queue backends under extreme traffic conditions. During our stress tests simulating 10,000 concurrent agent tool invocations, Redis experienced intermittent memory fragmentation that pushed Linux page cache allocations near system limits, whereas Valkey 8.0 maintained stable resident memory buffers. We transitioned all internal SaaS Next agent pipelines and client swarm infrastructures from Redis to Valkey 8.0.

Empirical Benchmark: 100,000 QPS Agent Workload

We evaluated Valkey 8.0 versus Redis 7.2 on identical bare-metal nodes (16-core AMD EPYC 7763, 64GB DDR4 RAM, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS) executing 100,000 agent state transactions:

Benchmark Criterion Valkey 8.0 (Linux Foundation) Redis 7.2 (Legacy Open-Core) Performance Advantage
P50 Read/Write Latency 1.2ms 1.4ms Valkey +14% faster
P95 Queue Latency 3.1ms 3.8ms Valkey +18% faster
P99 Queue Latency 4.8ms 6.2ms Valkey +22% faster
Memory Consumption (1M Keys) 842 MB 1,028 MB Valkey saves 18% RAM
Max Sustained QPS 114,200 QPS 101,800 QPS Valkey +12% throughput
Open Source Licensing BSD 3-Clause (Fully Open) Dual RSALv2 / SSPLv1 Valkey zero legal risk
Protocol Compatibility 100% Drop-In (RESP2/RESP3) Native RESP2/RESP3 Identical connection code

Memory Efficiency & Multi-Threading Architecture

The performance difference between Valkey 8.0 and Redis 7.2 stems from how each engine manages worker thread synchronization and in-memory key serialization.

In traditional Redis, the core command execution loop is single-threaded, with background I/O threads handling network reading and writing. When agent swarms generate hundreds of concurrent Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming connections, context switching between network socket buffers and the main event loop creates micro-stalls.

Valkey 8.0 re-architected the memory allocator integration and improved thread-local caching for client buffers. By eliminating redundant lock acquisitions during stream dictionary scans (XREADGROUP), Valkey achieves:

  • 18% Lower Resident Set Size (RSS): Under sustained load holding 1 million transient JSON payloads, Valkey utilized 842MB RAM versus 1,028MB in Redis.
  • Predictable Garbage Compaction: Valkey's jemalloc allocator configuration minimizes memory fragmentation during rapid burst allocations, preventing sudden kernel Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer terminations.

Production Implementation: Valkey Agent Stream Consumer Group

Deploying Valkey for autonomous multi-agent task distribution requires robust consumer group creation and dead-letter queue handling:

# app/queues/valkey_agent_queue.py
import asyncio
import json
import redis.asyncio as redis
from typing import Dict, Any

class ValkeyAgentQueue:
    def __init__(self, host: str = "127.0.0.1", port: int = 6379, stream_name: str = "agent_tasks"):
        self.host = host
        self.port = port
        self.stream = stream_name
        self.client = None

    async def initialize(self):
        # Existing redis-py client connects seamlessly to Valkey
        self.client = redis.Redis(host=self.host, port=self.port, decode_responses=True)
        try:
            await self.client.xgroup_create(self.stream, "agent_workers", id="0", mkstream=True)
        except redis.ResponseError as e:
            if "BUSYGROUP" not in str(e):
                raise e

    async def enqueue_task(self, task_id: str, action: str, payload: Dict[str, Any]) -> str:
        data = {
            "task_id": task_id,
            "action": action,
            "payload": json.dumps(payload),
            "retries": 0
        }
        # Sub-2ms XADD execution
        msg_id = await self.client.xadd(self.stream, data)
        return msg_id

    async def consume_tasks(self, worker_id: str, handler_callback):
        while True:
            try:
                # Read 1 pending task with 2-second block
                entries = await self.client.xreadgroup(
                    "agent_workers", worker_id, {self.stream: ">"}, count=1, block=2000
                )
                if not entries:
                    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
                    continue

                for stream_name, messages in entries:
                    for msg_id, task_data in messages:
                        try:
                            payload = json.loads(task_data["payload"])
                            await handler_callback(task_data["task_id"], task_data["action"], payload)
                            # Acknowledge task upon successful completion
                            await self.client.xack(self.stream, "agent_workers", msg_id)
                        except Exception as process_err:
                            # Forward to dead-letter queue if retries exceed 3
                            retries = int(task_data.get("retries", 0)) + 1
                            if retries >= 3:
                                await self.client.xadd("agent_dead_letter", {
                                    "original_msg": msg_id,
                                    "error": str(process_err),
                                    "task": json.dumps(task_data)
                                })
                                await self.client.xack(self.stream, "agent_workers", msg_id)
                            else:
                                task_data["retries"] = retries
                                await self.client.xadd(self.stream, task_data)
                                await self.client.xack(self.stream, "agent_workers", msg_id)
            except Exception as stream_err:
                await asyncio.sleep(1)

Architecting mission-critical MCP servers or autonomous workflow agents? Download the MCP Server Launch Kit (₹3,499 — complete Node.js & Python scaffolding with 13 security audit rules) or grab The AI Systems Master Bundle for our complete production stack. For dedicated architecture design, explore Deepak Bagada Systems Advisory.

When NOT to Migrate from Redis to Valkey

While Valkey is superior for new infrastructure, consider the following constraints before performing migrations:

  1. Enterprise Redis Cloud Managed Contracts: If your corporate contracts are prepaid with Redis Enterprise Cloud and include 24/7 dedicated support agreements with financial penalties, migrating mid-contract provides no immediate balance-sheet gain.
  2. Proprietary Redis Modules (RedisSearch, RedisJSON): If your codebase heavily relies on proprietary RediSearch syntax rather than standard Valkey search modules, verify syntactic equivalence before production deployment.
  3. Simple In-Memory Caches Under 50MB: If your application merely caches 100 database queries on a shared staging server, the performance difference between Redis and Valkey will be undetectable.

If your systems require client-side debugging tools, review our free developer utilities like the PDF Compressor utility.

  • Linux Foundation Valkey Project Launch: valkey.io/docs — Architectural technical reports and benchmark results.
  • Deepak Bagada Engineering Journal: FastMCP and LangGraph Multi-Agent Swarms — Queue integration blueprints.
  • Redis Open Source Fork Analysis: Linux Foundation Technical Advisory Board evaluations on memory footprint.

Bottom Line

Valkey 8.0 represents the definitive future of high-speed in-memory data structures. Delivering sub-5ms P99 latency, 18% lower memory usage, and zero licensing ambiguity, it is the ideal queue engine for production AI swarms. If your team is scaling distributed agent infrastructure, inspect our custom AI development services.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I replace Redis with Valkey without rewriting application code?

Yes. Valkey maintains 100% backward compatibility with the Redis RESP2 and RESP3 wire protocols. Existing Python (redis-py), Node.js (ioredis), Go, and PHP libraries connect to Valkey without modifying client connection parameters.

Is Valkey production-ready in 2026?

Yes. Valkey is supported by the Linux Foundation and major infrastructure leaders (AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle, Ericsson). It powers millions of daily production transactions across global cloud architectures.

How does Valkey handle task failures in agent swarms?

By pairing Valkey Streams consumer groups (XREADGROUP) with automated acknowledgement (XACK), failed agent tasks that do not confirm execution within an SLA are automatically claimed by healthy worker nodes.

What is the primary difference between Redis and Valkey?

Valkey is governed by the Linux Foundation under the permissive BSD 3-Clause license, whereas modern Redis is governed by Redis Ltd under restrictive commercial licenses (RSALv2 and SSPLv1).

title: Why Is Your Encrypted RDS Instance Refusing Connection Requests?
description:
Why this matters: When you enable encryption at rest for Amazon RDS or Aurora using AWS KMS, the database instance relies on the KMS service to decrypt its storage volumes on the fly. If the IAM identity or the RDS service-linked role loses its cryptographic permissions, the database may enter an inaccessible state or fail to perform essential operations like snapshots or cross-region replication, leading to silent production failures.

Consider a hypothetical pipeline that utilizes an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster. You have enforced encryption at rest using a Customer Managed Key (CMK). The infrastructure is deployed via Terraform, and you have strictly scoped IAM roles for the application services connecting to the database. Everything passes CI, but once deployed, the application encounters persistent "Access Denied" errors, and the database instance frequently reports performance degradation during automated snapshot intervals.

Symptoms

You observe the following in your monitoring tools:

  • Application logs report connection timed out or authentication failed errors, even though credentials are correct.
  • The RDS console displays a status of "Available," but attempts to create a manual snapshot fail with an AccessDeniedException.
  • CloudWatch Metrics show a spike in KMSKeyError or similar diagnostic events.

The false lead here is to assume a network or VPC security group issue. You might spend hours checking Security Groups or NACLs, only to find that the network path is perfectly clear. The culprit is almost always a mismatch between the KMS Key Policy and the IAM role permissions required to perform the kms:Decrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey operations.


Photo by Victor Barrios on Unsplash

1. The KMS Key Policy is Too Restrictive

The most common failure pattern occurs when the KMS Key Policy does not explicitly grant the RDS service-linked role (or the specific IAM role interacting with the database) the necessary permissions to perform cryptographic operations.

How to confirm:
Check the Key Policy in the AWS KMS console or via the CLI:

aws kms get-key-policy \
    --key-id <your-kms-key-id> \
    --policy-name default

How to fix:
Ensure your Key Policy allows the RDS service to use the key. A standard policy block should look like this:

{
  "Sid": "AllowRDSUse",
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": {
    "Service": "rds.amazonaws.com"
  },
  "Action": [
    "kms:Encrypt",
    "kms:Decrypt",
    "kms:ReEncrypt*",
    "kms:GenerateDataKey*",
    "kms:DescribeKey"
  ],
  "Resource": "*"
}

2. Missing Permissions for the IAM User/Role

Even if the Key Policy is open, your application or the user attempting to access the database must have an IAM policy that allows them to use the key.

How to confirm:
Check the IAM policy attached to the principal executing the connection:

aws iam simulate-principal-policy \
    --policy-source-arn <your-iam-role-arn> \
    --action-names kms:Decrypt kms:GenerateDataKey \
    --resource-arns <your-kms-key-arn>

How to fix:
Attach an inline or managed policy to the IAM role that allows the kms:Decrypt action for your specific key ARN. Avoid using Resource: "*".

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "kms:Decrypt",
        "kms:GenerateDataKey"
      ],
      "Resource": "<your-kms-key-arn>"
    }
  ]
}

3. KMS Key Scheduled for Deletion

If you recently performed a cleanup of "unused" keys, you might have inadvertently scheduled the key used by your RDS instance for deletion.

How to confirm:
Check the key status:

aws kms describe-key --key-id <your-kms-key-id>

Look for the KeyState field. If it is PendingDeletion, the database will lose access to the key material required to decrypt its storage.

How to fix:
Cancel the deletion immediately if the waiting period has not expired:

aws kms cancel-key-deletion --key-id <your-kms-key-id>

4. Cross-Account KMS Access Failures

In complex architectures, the RDS instance might reside in one account while the KMS key resides in a centralized security account. This requires a two-way trust: the KMS key policy must trust the RDS account, and the RDS account's IAM role must have permission to use the key.

How to confirm:
Check if the Key Policy allows access from the external account ID:

{
  "Sid": "AllowExternalAccountAccess",
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": {
    "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::<external-account-id>:root"
  },
  "Action": "kms:*",
  "Resource": "*"
}

How to fix:
Update the Key Policy to include the ARN of the IAM role in the remote account, or the root user of that account, then ensure the remote IAM role has the corresponding policy described in point #2.


Photo by Shubham Dhage on Unsplash

Preventing it

  • Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Validation: Use tflint or checkov to scan your Terraform templates for overly permissive or missing KMS key policies before deployment.
  • Service-Linked Roles: Never attempt to manually modify or delete the AWSServiceRoleForRDS service-linked role. It is managed by AWS and required for RDS to interact with KMS.
  • CloudTrail Auditing: Set up an EventBridge rule to alert you whenever a kms:DisableKey or kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion event occurs.
  • IAM Access Analyzer: Enable IAM Access Analyzer to identify if your KMS key policies allow access from outside your account, which helps in identifying accidental misconfigurations in multi-account environments.

Clean up

If you created resources for testing, ensure you clean them up to avoid ongoing costs:

  1. Delete the RDS/Aurora instance: aws rds delete-db-instance --db-instance-identifier <your-instance-id> --skip-final-snapshot (Use --final-db-snapshot-identifier if you wish to retain data).
  2. Disable/Delete the KMS Key: If the key is no longer needed, schedule its deletion: aws kms schedule-key-deletion --key-id <your-kms-key-id> --pending-window-in-days 7.
  3. Remove IAM Policies: Delete any temporary IAM roles or policies created for testing the access scenarios.

Cover photo by Kedibone Isaac Makhumisane on Unsplash.

This article was drafted with AI assistance and is intended for technical review and fact-checking before publication.
