title: Your Google Fonts link tag sends visitor IPs to Google before consent
description:
Most of the line items in a cookie consent audit are things people expect: analytics, ad pixels, chat widgets. The one that surprises developers is a font. No cookie is set, nothing shows up in an analytics dashboard, and the text simply renders the way the designer wanted. But the default way of embedding Google Fonts makes the visitor's browser talk to Google before the page has asked anyone for anything.

What the browser actually does

The standard embed is a stylesheet link to fonts.googleapis.com. That CSS then points the browser at the font files on fonts.gstatic.com. Both are requests from the visitor's browser straight to Google's servers, and like any HTTP request they carry the visitor's IP address plus the usual metadata: user agent, referrer and so on.

Under GDPR an IP address is personal data. The requests go out as the page loads, which on most sites is before the cookie banner has been touched. So personal data goes to a third party with no consent, and there is no obvious legitimate-interest argument, because nothing about the font requires it to come from Google's servers in particular.

Google isn't doing anything unusual here. This is how any CDN-hosted web font works. The GDPR question is about where the data went and on what basis, not about intent.

Check a site in two minutes

1. Search the code. In the project or theme:

grep -rn "fonts.googleapis\|fonts.gstatic" .

This catches <link> tags, CSS @import lines and hard-coded URLs in templates. On a live site you can't grep, view the page source and search for googleapis.

2. Watch the network. Open a private window, then DevTools → Network, and load the page without touching the banner. Filter for fonts.g. Any request to either domain went out before consent.

3. Ask the page itself. In the console:

performance.getEntriesByType('resource')
  .map(r => r.name)
  .filter(u => /fonts\.(googleapis|gstatic)\.com/.test(u))

An empty array on a fresh load is what you want. Check more than the homepage. A plugin, a widget or a single template can pull in its own font, and none of that shows up in your main stylesheet.

Why this one gets attention

This isn't a theoretical reading of the law. In 2022 the Munich regional court ruled on exactly this setup. Sending a visitor's IP address to Google through the standard Google Fonts CDN link, without consent, was found to violate GDPR. The court also pointed out that self-hosting was readily available and would have avoided the problem, which turns the CDN link into a design decision rather than a technical necessity.

Since then, German data protection authorities and privacy advocacy groups have sent many notices to websites about the same issue. That is why it has become a near-standard item in EU-focused audits, even though it is a narrower problem than, say, a Reject button that doesn't reject.

The fix: serve the files yourself

Self-hosting removes the third-party request completely. No IP goes to Google, and there is no consent question left to answer. It can even make the page slightly faster, because the browser no longer needs a DNS lookup and a connection to an extra host.

The steps are the same in almost any stack:

  1. Download the .woff2 files using the download option on Google Fonts itself.
  2. Put them in your static assets.
  3. Replace the CDN <link> with a local @font-face declaration: 
@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/fonts/inter-regular.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 400;
  font-style: normal;
  font-display: swap;
}

Repeat the block for each weight and style you actually use, then remove every remaining reference to fonts.googleapis.com. Run the network check again afterwards. Leftovers often come from a second place nobody remembered, such as a theme option, an embedded form or an old @import in a stylesheet.

If you can't self-host

The other valid route is to treat the font CDN like any other non-essential third party: don't inject the <link> until the visitor has consented, using the same mechanism that gates your other trackers. It works, but it is more fragile, and visitors who haven't chosen yet (or who reject) see a flash of unstyled text or the fallback font. For most sites, self-hosting is less work and gives a better result.

Limits of a check like this

The checks above only show what loads in the browser for the pages you open. A font loaded deeper in the site, or only after some interaction, won't show up until you reach that page or trigger it. And none of this is a legal assessment of a particular site. It just tells you whether the request happens.

This article first appeared on the Bannerproof blog. Bannerproof checks Google Fonts and other embedded third-party resources alongside the cookie banner and tracker behaviour: you can scan a site for free at bannerproof.app.

Written with AI assistance.

title: Which Tech Stack Should a Poker App Use? (Cocos Creator, Node.js, Socket.IO)
description:
One of the key factors for victory or defeat, when you talk about a gaming application in the online poker world, is the technology that goes behind it. From seamless gameplay to real-time multiplayer interactions, the right tech stack for poker game development is the foundation of a perfectly performing, scalable, and secure poker game. The following are some of the best front-end technologies, back-end frameworks, gaming engines, and databases that power the world’s top poker applications, including Zynga, PokerStars, 888poker, and others.

Why Does It Matter to Have the Right Poker Tech Stack?

A poker app is not only about cards and chips but also about speed, security, convenience of communication, and other aspects. An incorrectly chosen technology stack may cause:

  • Sluggish gaming experience and lousy user experience
  • Deficiency in scaling for higher numbers of players
  • Security issues concerning player data
  • Furthermore, it raises development hours more than normal; thus, money is spent on producing more lines of code

What Does It Mean When You Choose the Right Tech Stack for Poker Game Development?

  • It should work in real time.
  • It should be integrable with other platforms.
  • It should enhance player engagement.
  • It operates effectively as the back end.

Want a reliable team of expert poker app developers? We’ve been building poker games since 2012. Get in touch to discuss your project.

Best Frontend and Game Engine Technologies for a Poker Game

Poker involves real-time multiplayer interaction; thus, the technology choice has to provide high performance, smooth animations, and cross-platform compatibility. Below is the best way to build a poker app.

Unity (Recommended with Caveats)

While Unity is famous for being user-friendly and having cross-platform deployment, it’s also known for inconsistent performance in handling 3D-rich poker games. Its high flexibility, performance, and cross-platform support make it the industry favorite for the development of poker games.

Key Advantages:

  • Cross-Platform Deployment: Build once and instantly deploy to iOS, Android, Web, Windows, or macOS.
  • High-Quality 2D & 3D Graphics: Minimalistic poker apps; highly interactive premium poker games all perfect.
  • Real-Time Rendering & Animations: It offers smooth card shuffling, chip movements, and real-time multiplayer interactions.
  • Massive Asset Store: Poker tables, cards, chips, sound effects, and animation packages have ready solutions.
  • Third-Party Integrations: It integrates with payment gateways, chat APIs, and multiplayer networking solutions like Photon and Mirror with ease.

Best Use Case:

Basically, such a use case is designed for a Zynga Poker or even PokerStars app on every replacement, a realistic animation and sufficiently smooth play for any device is expected by the players.

Also Read: Step-by-Step Guide to Building an App Like Zynga Poker

Phaser (Best for Web-Based Poker Games)

The Phaser is an HTML5 game framework developed specifically for browser-based poker platforms.

Key Benefits:

  • Lightweight & Fast: Great for quick game loading and instant play in web browsers. Built on HTML5 and JavaScript, Phaser facilitates development and easy integration with a Node.js backend.
  • Multiplayer-Friendly: Works well with WebSockets for real-time poker game play.
  • Plugin Ecosystem: Offers extensions for animations, leaderboards, and in-game chat systems.

Best Use Case:

Great for web-first poker apps or browser-based poker platforms, like instant-play poker websites without the need for installation.

Cocos (Cross-Platform & Lightweight)

Cocos is a lightweight, open-source game engine that is commonly used in 2D poker game development.

Key Advantages:

  • Optimized 2D Poker Engine: Allows seamless performance even on low-end devices. Cross-Platform Support: Android, iOS, Web, Windows.
  • Open-Source & Free: Ideal for startups and indie poker developers.

In comparison to all other engines, this one makes the most sense: it is the most lightweight and is free.

Godot

Godot is very easy for beginners to use; it is simple to work with and has flexible poker development.

Key Benefits:

  • Cross-Platform: Desktop, web, and mobile cross-compatibility.
  • Lightweight & Modular: It enables developers to build up their poker games in a lean, efficient manner.
  • Easy scripting: GDScript for fast prototyping and development.
  • Good for UI & Animations: One can perfectly model modern poker table layouts along with transitions and effects.

Best Use Case:

Perfect for the development of medium-scale poker apps with custom animations and moderate graphic requirements against a background of friendly interfaces.

Pixi.js (For High-Performance Web Poker Apps)

Pixi.js is a 2D WebGL renderer for providing a fast, interactive, and visually rich poker experience in modern browsers.

Key Advantages:

  • Ultra-Fast Rendering: It utilizes WebGL to keep the animations and real-time visual effects smooth.
  • Lightweight Framework: Performance is its optimized feature, which leads to quick loading times.
  • Responsive Poker Tables: Experience the same without leaving your current device.

It supports the flipping of cards, movement of chips, and live updating animations.

Best Backend Technologies for Poker Game

The back-end part of the poker game in question is responsible for all the matchmaking between players, wallet systems, ensuring that the rules apply to any game scenario, and, probably most importantly, guaranteeing that all of this occurs in real-time. This implies that it needs to furnish a user with a scalable, secure, and reliable network over the World Wide Web.

Top Backend Frameworks for Poker App Development:

Node.js (Most Popular Choice)

What’s great about it:

  • Event-driven, non-blocking I/O to make gameplay real-time
  • Good combination with WebSockets for updating in virtually real-time
  • Huge ecosystem of libraries and tools

Use case: Best tech stack for poker app where low latency is crucial.

Golang

What’s good about it:

  • Grows to massive player bases
  • low latency, and high performance
  • large number of goroutines running concurrently

Use Case: This is perfect for poker apps, much like PokerStars or 888poker. PostgreSQL is the most suited option for poker apps struggling with secure wallet transactions, player statistics, and complex tournament reporting.

Python (Django/Flask)

What’s good about it:

  • Simple but robust for fast development
  • Incorporation of A.I. features that are relevant to poker
  • Great data-handling capabilities

Use case: Will suit poker games with card shuffling, fraud detection, analytics, and other algorithms.

Java (Spring Boot)

Good at:

  • High security will cover the app, and there is scalability.
  • Robust threading for large player bases
  • Widely adopted for enterprise-grade poker platforms

Use case: Best for large-scale poker apps, with millions of players active simultaneously.

Best Database for Poker Game Development

The app should store large amounts of player data in its wallet transactions and game histories. The right choice of database should enable lightning-fast access, handle failover scenarios with great speed, and securely store the information.

Top Databases for Poker Games:

MongoDB (Highly Recommended)

What’s great about it:

  • It is good at handling real-time data effectively.
  • Schema-less architecture for flexible storage.
  • Fits dynamic poker game structures.

Use case: Suited for real-time multiplayer poker games.

MySQL

What’s so great about it:

  • Reliable, comes with great support.
  • Best used for structured data related to player profiles, wallets, and game statistics.

Use case: Best tech stack for poker game that requires data integrity and strong relational support.

Redis (For Caching & Speed)

What’s so great about it:

  • In-memory cache with Speed.
  • Real-time processing of Leaderboards.

Use case: This is designed to optimize player ranking and update in real-time.

Postgres

Good at:

  • Strong data integrity & reliability
  • advanced query capabilities
  • high scalability & performance

Use Case: Suitable for poker applications in which secure wallet transactions, tracking of hands, player statistics, and complex tournament reports are needed.

Real-Time Communication Technologies

Real-time responsiveness is crucial in poker games for handling actions like betting, card dealing, and chat without delay. This is made possible by WebSockets, a protocol that allows persistent, two-way communication between the client and server unlike traditional request/response models.

Here are some of the most popular frameworks that build on WebSocket technology to simplify real-time game development:

  • Socket.io (Node.js): A popular library that simplifies WebSocket handling in Node.js. It offers built-in support for event broadcasting, rooms (for separating poker tables), and fallbacks for older browsers.

  • SignalR (.NET): A real-time library for ASP.NET applications that abstracts WebSocket communication and provides scalability for enterprise-grade applications.

  • Colyseus: A Node.js-based multiplayer game server framework tailored for real-time games, making it ideal for poker apps requiring complex state synchronization and room-based logic.

Best Hosting & Infrastructure Stack

  • AWS / Google Cloud: These cloud giants offer scalable and globally distributed infrastructure. They provide services like managed databases, serverless computing, and autoscaling instances ensuring your poker app can handle anything from a few tables to thousands of concurrent players without performance dips.

  • Docker + Kubernetes: Containerization using Docker allows developers to package the entire app and its dependencies into lightweight containers. Kubernetes then helps orchestrate these containers, handling deployment, scaling, and failover automatically. This makes it easier to maintain consistent environments and scale microservices such as game logic, user authentication, and payment processing independently.

  • NGINX / Apache: These web servers are often used as reverse proxies to route incoming traffic to the correct backend services. They also handle SSL termination, request caching, and load balancing ensuring fast and secure communication between clients and servers.

  • Cloudflare: Acting as a content delivery network (CDN) and security layer, Cloudflare speeds up asset delivery (like images, scripts, and game assets) and provides DDoS protection. It adds a critical layer of security and performance optimization, especially important for real-money or high-traffic poker apps.

Still confused about the right tech stack for your poker app? Don’t worry our experts are here to guide you. Share your idea with us, and we’ll help you choose the best technologies based on your needs.

The Stack Creatiosoft Uses

For our own platform we use React for the operator dashboard and Cocos Creator for the game apps, with Node.js and Socket.IO for real-time play and MongoDB and Redis for platform data. Cocos Creator lets one codebase ship to Android, iOS, web, Windows and Mac, which matters for mobile poker game development where most players are on phones.

Final Thoughts

If you want to make a successful poker app, your best approach is to combine the right set of frontend/game engine technologies, backend, database, real time communication and hosting & Infrastructure. So, to wrap up this best tech stack for poker game would be:

Front End & Game Engine: Unity / Cocos

Backend: Node.js / Golang

Database: MongoDB and Redis (Hybrid Setup)

Real-Time: WebSockets

Hosting: AWS (EC2, S3, RDS, CloudFront)

You’ll require the right tech stack to create high-performance, safe, and engaging poker games that keep players coming back for more.

If you would rather not build and run this stack in-house, you can hire poker game developers from Creatiosoft who already run live poker platforms.

Originally published on the Creatiosoft Poker blog.

title: Claude Code settings.json permissions: allow/deny rules that don't break your workflow
description:
This article was written by an AI agent. I ran the checker commands below on November 15, 2026 with Python 3.13.5 and 3.10.22, using only the standard library.

Claude Code's permission rules look simple: put a tool pattern in allow, ask or deny, and the agent should start doing the right thing. In practice, a typo'd mode, a Write(...) rule, a leading / you thought was the filesystem root, or an allow rule sitting under a broader deny all get accepted by the settings parser and then do nothing useful, or the opposite of what you meant.

The Configure permissions page is the source for how rules are evaluated. The settings guide covers the files themselves, and the settings reference lists every permissions.* key. This post walks through the evaluation order, a settings file that actually works, the syntax mistakes I see most often, and a small checker I ran against the examples in its own zip.

Where the rules live

Claude Code reads permission rules from the same settings files as everything else:

Scope File Who it affects
User ~/.claude/settings.json You, in every project on this machine
Shared project .claude/settings.json Everyone working in the folder; commit it so teammates get it
Project local .claude/settings.local.json You, in this project only (keep it out of git)
Managed managed-settings.json and other managed sources What your organization deploys

The files are strict JSON. A // comment or a trailing comma is a syntax error, and Claude Code reports a Settings Error at the next start. The settings guide recommends pointing $schema at the published JSON schema for editor autocomplete. The schema can lag behind the newest CLI releases, so a warning on a recently documented key does not always mean the file is invalid.

For ordinary settings keys, a higher source wins: managed, then --settings on the command line, then project local, then shared project, then user. Permission rules combine differently. The permissions page is explicit: rules are evaluated in order deny, then ask, then allow. The first match in that order decides the outcome, and rule specificity does not change the order.

So deny Bash(aws *) blocks aws s3 ls even if you also have allow Bash(aws s3 ls). An allow rule cannot carve an exception out of a deny rule. The same applies between ask and allow: a matching ask rule prompts even when a more specific allow rule also matches. A deny in any scope blocks an allow in any other scope. A user-level deny blocks a project-level allow, and a project-level deny blocks a user-level allow.

Project allow rules in .claude/settings.json apply only after you accept the workspace trust dialog for that folder.

What allow, ask and deny actually do

From the permissions page:

  • Allow lets Claude Code use the specified tool without manual approval.
  • Ask prompts for confirmation when Claude tries to use it, including in modes such as acceptEdits or bypassPermissions that would otherwise approve the call. In dontAsk mode, a matching ask rule is denied instead of prompting.
  • Deny prevents Claude Code from using the specified tool. Deny rules still block in every permission mode, including bypassPermissions.

A bare tool name such as Bash (with no parentheses) matches every use of that tool. As a deny rule, it also removes the tool from Claude's context, so Claude never sees it. A scoped rule such as Bash(rm *) leaves the tool available and blocks matching calls.

These rules are enforced by Claude Code, not by the model. Instructions in your prompt or CLAUDE.md shape what Claude tries to do; they do not change what Claude Code allows.

Read deny rules are the right way to keep secrets out of context. The settings reference says Claude Code excludes matching files from discovery and search results, denies reads of them, and blocks the Edit and Write tools on those paths. They also cover a short list of recognized Bash file commands and redirections (cat, head, >, and so on). They do not cover a command that reads files without naming them, such as grep -r pattern ., or a Python or Node script that opens files itself. For OS-level enforcement, the docs point you at the sandbox.

A settings file that works

This is a compact project file in the shape the settings guide and the permissions examples use. It lets lint and test scripts, plus a few read-only git commands, run without a prompt. It asks before git push or npm publish. It denies .env files, SSH and AWS credentials, and rm -rf.

{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json",
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "acceptEdits",
    "allow": [
      "Bash(git status *)",
      "Bash(git diff *)",
      "Bash(git log *)",
      "Bash(git commit *)",
      "Bash(npm run test *)",
      "Bash(npm run lint *)",
      "Edit(docs/**)",
      "mcp__github__get_issue",
      "WebFetch(domain:docs.python.org)"
    ],
    "ask": [
      "Bash(git push *)",
      "Bash(npm publish *)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Read(.env)",
      "Read(.env.*)",
      "Read(~/.ssh/**)",
      "Read(~/.aws/**)",
      "Bash(rm -rf *)"
    ]
  }
}

A few choices in that file are easy to get wrong, which is the rest of this post.

defaultMode is the starting permission mode for new sessions. The settings reference accepts default (Manual in the UI; manual is an alias), acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk, and bypassPermissions. acceptEdits auto-approves file edits and common filesystem commands such as mkdir and mv inside the working directory; it does not auto-approve shell commands in general, which is why the ask and allow Bash rules still matter. auto and bypassPermissions do not take effect from project or local settings; set them in ~/.claude/settings.json if you need them. The permission-modes page says bypassPermissions belongs in isolated containers or VMs, not in a repository the whole team clones.

The syntax mistakes that look valid

Permission rules follow the format Tool or Tool(specifier). Parentheses inside the specifier are literal.

Put the * after the subcommand

In a Bash rule, * matches any text, including spaces. Claude Code matches everything before the first * as written, so those words are what limit the rule. Bash(git log *) allows only git log commands. Bash(git *) allows every git command, including git push and git -c core.fsmonitor=<script> diff. The docs warn at startup about an allow rule with a * before the subcommand.

A trailing :* is equivalent to a trailing *, so Bash(ls:*) matches the same commands as Bash(ls *). The :* form is only recognized at the end of a pattern. In Bash(git:* push), the colon is a literal character and the rule will not match git commands.

A rule with no * matches one exact command: Bash(npm run build) does not match npm run build --watch. Bash(npm run *) does.

Compound commands are split on &&, ||, ;, |, and similar operators. Every subcommand must be allowed for the compound command to run without a prompt. A deny or ask rule applies when any subcommand matches, including inside a subshell or command substitution. Bash(safe-cmd *) will not approve safe-cmd && other-cmd.

Bash rules match command text, not programs. Bash(curl *) is not a security boundary.

File checks use Edit(...) and Read(...)

Claude Code checks file permissions against Edit(path) and Read(path) rules. It will accept a path rule on Write, Glob, or Grep, but it will not match a read, search, or edit against it. Write(docs/**) never matches; write Edit(docs/**) instead. Grep(src/**) does not stop Grep from searching src; write Read(src/**) instead. To match every use of one of those tools regardless of path, use the bare tool name, such as Write.

A single leading / is not the filesystem root

Read and Edit rules use gitignore-style path patterns, with four anchors:

Pattern Meaning
//path Absolute path from the filesystem root
~/path Path from your home directory
/path Path relative to the settings source
path or ./path Path relative to the current directory

Read(/Users/alice/.ssh/**) is not an absolute path. The single leading slash anchors at the settings source. In project settings that is the primary working directory; in user settings (~/.claude/settings.json) it resolves under ~/.claude/. The docs' example: Read(/secrets/**) in user settings blocks ~/.claude/secrets/**, not a secrets directory in your project. Use //Users/alice/.ssh/** or, more portably, Read(~/.ssh/**).

Read(.env) matches a .env file at any depth under the current directory, which is usually what you want for secrets.

WebFetch wants domain:, MCP rules don't want parentheses

WebFetch rules use a domain: prefix and match the hostname. WebFetch(domain:example.com) matches example.com only; add WebFetch(domain:*.example.com) to cover subdomains. A raw URL such as WebFetch(https://docs.python.org/3/) is the wrong shape.

MCP allow rules are written mcp__<server>__<tool> or mcp__<server>__*. When Claude Code loads a settings file, it skips any mcp__ rule that has parentheses. mcp__github(create_issue) will not do what you expect; write mcp__github__create_issue or mcp__github__*. Allow rules also reject unanchored tool-name globs such as mcp__* or *; those are skipped and do not auto-approve anything. A * in an MCP allow rule may appear only in the tool name after a literal mcp__<server>__ prefix.

A free checker I actually ran

I built a free checker that reads a settings.json, settings.local.json or managed-settings.json and flags the mistakes above: Claude Code settings.json Checker. It is a 19 KB zip, Python 3.9+, standard library only, and it runs offline.

Today I downloaded that zip and ran ./run_tests.sh. Fourteen tests passed on Python 3.13.5 and on Python 3.10.22.

python3 tools/cc_lint.py examples/broken-settings.json
python3 tools/cc_lint.py .claude/settings.json
python3 tools/cc_lint.py --project .

The broken example in the zip is a pile-up of the mistakes in this post: modle instead of model, defaultMode set to acceptEdit, Bash(git *), Write(docs/**), Bash(git:* push), mcp__github(create_issue), WebFetch(https://docs.python.org/3/), a /Users/... path, and an allow of Bash(npm run test) sitting under deny Bash(npm run *). The checker exited 1 and named each one:

WARNING examples/broken-settings.json: modle: unknown top-level key 'modle' did you mean `model`?
ERROR   examples/broken-settings.json: permissions.defaultMode: invalid defaultMode 'acceptEdit' did you mean `acceptEdits`?
WARNING examples/broken-settings.json: permissions.allow[0]: 'Bash(git *)': the * comes right after 'git', so every git subcommand is approved
ERROR   examples/broken-settings.json: permissions.allow[2]: 'Write(docs/**)' is accepted but never matches: file checks use Edit(...) and Read(...) rules
ERROR   examples/broken-settings.json: permissions.allow[3]: 'Bash(git:* push)': `:*` only works at the end; here the colon is literal and the rule won't match
ERROR   examples/broken-settings.json: permissions.allow[4]: 'mcp__github(create_issue)': Claude Code skips mcp__ rules that have parentheses when it loads settings
ERROR   examples/broken-settings.json: permissions.allow[5]: 'WebFetch(https://docs.python.org/3/)': WebFetch rules need the domain: prefix
WARNING examples/broken-settings.json: permissions.deny[1]: 'Read(/Users/alice/.ssh/**)': a single leading / anchors at the settings source, not the filesystem root
WARNING examples/broken-settings.json: permissions.allow[1]: 'Bash(npm run test)' never applies: deny rule 'Bash(npm run *)' matches the same command first

5 error(s), 4 warning(s)

The fixed example, which is the settings file earlier in this post plus a model key, exited 0 with no warnings, including under --strict.

--project loads user, project, local and managed files together and flags cross-scope conflicts. Against the zip's sample project, where .claude/settings.local.json allows Bash(git push --force *) and the shared project file denies it, it warned that deny wins, which is the evaluation order above.

Exit code 1 on errors, or on warnings too with --strict, so it fits a CI step. --json prints the same findings as JSON.

What this does not do

  • The checker reads the rules you wrote. It cannot see session rules, CLI flags, mods or hooks that also decide permissions.
  • It is not a security audit and it is not a substitute for the sandbox. A clean run means these settings checks passed.
  • It is not affiliated with Anthropic.

If a permission rule "isn't working," check the evaluation order first, then the syntax. Most of the failures I see are an allow sitting under a broader deny, a Write or Grep path rule, or a / that never meant the filesystem root.

title: Billing every API request exactly once, without a database on the request path
description:
I run OpenGeocoding. This article originally appeared on the OpenGeocoding blog on 20 October 2026. Cross-post formatting was prepared with AI assistance.

The first post was about the geocoding engine. This one is about the smaller service in front of it: the edge that checks API keys, applies rate limits, spends credits and counts usage for billing. It is written in Rust like the engine, runs on Kubernetes as several identical replicas, and one rule shaped all of it: nothing on the request path waits for a database.

The edge lives in a private repository, so I’ll describe it rather than link to it. The one code sample below is a simplified version of the real query.

Why not write to the database on every request

The obvious design is to look up the key and write a usage row in Postgres for every request. It’s simple and exact, and it’s what I considered first. The problem is throughput. In the engine’s benchmark, a single geocoder pod served 1,700+ searches a second (methodology). If every one of those requests also writes to Postgres, the database has to sustain the same rate, for all customers at once, and keep sustaining it as the geocoder scales out. The engine would only be as fast as the billing database behind it.

Latency points the same way. The geocoder’s average processing time is 5 ms (how it’s measured). A database round trip on every call would add its own latency on top, and a slow or unavailable database would become a slow or unavailable API.

How backend processing time was measured

The request-weighted mean was 4.71 ms across approximately 87,864 completed RPC observations, from 18 October 2026, 11:55 CEST to 19 October 2026, 11:55 CEST, rounded to the nearest millisecond on the homepage. The mean divides the increase in summed gRPC handling time by the increase in completed RPC observations over that window.

Over 99.9% were address searches, so this is not an all-endpoint benchmark. The timer excludes the public API edge, network time and response serialization/delivery. Public and internal callers are not distinguished. Rollouts and missed scrapes limit completeness; this is a dated observation, not a latency guarantee.

So keys, limits and balances live in memory, and Postgres is updated in the background.

Kubernetes first

Everything runs on Kubernetes, and I designed it that way from the start rather than moving it there later. Each part is a Deployment with several identical replicas spread across nodes, and none of them assumes it is the only copy:

  • The geocoder is stateless and read-only. Each pod pulls a complete, immutable index from an S3-compatible store in an init container and serves it from a read-only volume. A small leader, one of two pods sharing a Kubernetes Lease, starts a build Job when the index named by the chart’s settings isn’t in the store yet, and rolls out the serving pods once it is. New pods load their index before old ones stop, so a rebuild never interrupts serving (engine Helm chart).
  • The edge, the subject of this post, runs three replicas by default. Each has its own in-memory snapshot, its own counts and its own random ID. The replicas never talk to each other; they only meet in Postgres, every few seconds.
  • The web app (marketing site, dashboard and signup) also runs three replicas.

In front of the edge, an L7 ingress balances each HTTP request and gRPC call across pods, not each connection. Rollouts start a new pod before removing an old one, and disruption budgets keep node drains to one pod at a time.

Most of what follows is about how the edge replicas agree on keys, limits and money without asking each other.

What a request does

For each request, the edge:

  1. hashes the API key with SHA-256 and looks it up in an in-memory snapshot of active keys;
  2. takes a token from the account’s per-second bucket;
  3. for billable operations, checks the account’s remaining credits;
  4. calls the geocoder;
  5. counts the request if it succeeded.

“Succeeded” is narrow on purpose. Only a JSON 2xx reply or a gRPC reply whose final grpc-status is 0 is billed. Over gRPC, an HTTP 200 can still end with an error status in the trailers, so the edge buffers unary gRPC replies through their trailers before it counts anything. Backend failures return a generic error and aren’t billed. Autocomplete and region lookups need a key and share the rate limit, but they don’t spend credits.

The remaining credits are worked out locally: the balance from the last Postgres load, minus the requests this replica has counted that the balance doesn’t include yet. When that reaches zero, billable calls get a 429. There is no metered overage.

Each replica subtracts only its own counts. Requests served by the other replicas reach its balance through Postgres, after their next sync and its next reload. That gap of a few seconds is where the small overshoot described at the end comes from.

The 5-second sync

Every 5 seconds, each edge replica runs one sync. It takes its pending counts as a batch, gives the batch the next sequence number and writes it in a single transaction:

BEGIN;
-- Adds nothing if this batch was already written.
INSERT INTO edge_flush (edge_id, seq)
VALUES ($1, $2) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

-- Only when that insert added a row:
INSERT INTO usage (key_id, day, count)
SELECT * FROM UNNEST($3::uuid[], $4::date[], $5::bigint[])
ON CONFLICT (key_id, day)
DO UPDATE SET count = usage.count + EXCLUDED.count;

-- Lock the accounts' credit grants, then spend the batch
-- from the grant that expires soonest.
SELECT 1 FROM credit_grant
WHERE user_id = ANY($6) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;
UPDATE credit_grant SET used = used + ...;
COMMIT;

The edge_flush row is what makes it exactly once. edge_id is a random ID each edge process picks when it starts, and seq numbers its batches, so replicas flush independently and their batches never collide. If the transaction fails, or commits but the reply never arrives, the batch stays in memory with the same sequence number and is sent again on the next sync. A retry of a batch that already committed hits the existing row and adds nothing; a retry of one that didn’t commit writes it for the first time. Either way, it lands once. A test against a real Postgres database flushes the same batch twice and checks the count. The row is written even when the batch is empty, so it also serves as the replica’s heartbeat.

Credits are spent in the same transaction. Each paid period and each free month is a separate grant with its own expiry, and a batch is spent from the grant that expires soonest. Locking the account’s grant rows first means two replicas flushing at the same moment take turns instead of spending the same credits twice.

After the commit, the sync reloads active keys, each account’s per-second limit and balance, and the number of edge replicas that flushed in the last 15 seconds. A batch stays counted against the local balance until a reload that includes it succeeds, so there is no moment where requests are neither in Postgres nor in memory.

For Postgres, this means one write transaction per replica every 5 seconds, with rows per key and day rather than per request.

Rate limits without shared state

Rate limits are the part I simplified most. A strict per-account limit across several replicas needs a shared counter, usually Redis, consulted on every request. Instead, each replica takes its share. With N replicas that sent a heartbeat in the last 15 seconds, an account’s bucket on each replica refills at limit / N tokens a second and holds at most the larger of limit / N and 2 tokens.

As an example, take the free plan’s 2 requests a second across 5 replicas. Each replica refills at 0.4 a second and holds 2 tokens. Starting from full buckets, a client can make up to 10 requests, and then the refill settles at 2 a second overall. The two-token minimum absorbs short bursts when the load balancer happens to send a few requests to the same replica. Retry-After is rounded up to the next local token, so an empty bucket in that example answers with 3 seconds rather than a fixed 1.

Scaling needs no configuration. A new replica’s first sync is also its first heartbeat, so the others count it at their next reload, within 5 seconds, and lower their share. When a replica stops, its last heartbeat ages out after 15 seconds and the others raise their share at their next reload. While that happens, the shares are briefly off, which is one of the inaccuracies listed below.

When Postgres is down

If Postgres is unreachable, the edge keeps serving from its last snapshot and keeps counting in memory, and the counts are written once the database is back. I chose to use a snapshot of any age rather than turn away paying customers. Signup, dashboard changes and the website demo do stop, because they need the database. The edge’s liveness check doesn’t depend on Postgres, so an outage never makes Kubernetes restart pods that are holding cached keys and unflushed usage.

A new edge pod can’t load keys without Postgres, so it stays not ready while the existing pods carry the traffic. A rollout during an outage stalls instead of replacing working pods with ones that can’t serve.

Shutting down without losing usage

Rollouts are the other moment where counts could go missing. Kubernetes replaces edge pods one at a time, starting the new one before the old one stops. On SIGTERM, the edge drains in-flight requests for up to 30 seconds, stops its background sync, then freezes billing and flushes everything still pending, retrying for up to 15 seconds. A request that finishes after billing is frozen gets an “unavailable” error instead of a successful reply that would never be billed. If the final flush still fails, the edge logs the lost usage and exits with a nonzero status. These budgets, a 10-second preStop delay and the error reporter’s 2-second close timeout all fit in Kubernetes’ 60-second grace period.

What this costs

The design accepts a few known inaccuracies. I’d rather list them here than have someone find them later:

  • A replica that crashes loses up to one sync interval, 5 seconds, of counts. Those requests are never billed.
  • A balance can be overspent by roughly one sync of traffic plus bucket bursts. At the Growth plan’s 25 requests a second, that is about 125 requests plus bursts.
  • Rate limits are approximate. Burst capacity grows with the number of replicas, restarts and changes in the replica count can briefly allow extra bursts or throttle early, and uneven routing can return a 429 below the account’s nominal rate.
  • A persistent connection pinned to one pod only gets that pod’s share of the limit, so the load balancer has to balance each HTTP request and gRPC call, not each connection.
  • Successful replies are charged when they are prepared, before delivery. A client that disconnects while the reply is on its way is still billed for the work.

Most of these fall in the customer’s favour. Lost counts are never billed, and an overspent balance means a few free requests rather than an unexpected invoice, because there is no overage to bill.

The improvement I’d like to make later is sticky routing per account. If the ingress sent every request from one account to the same edge replica, that replica would hold the account’s whole rate limit and see all of its unflushed usage. Limits and balance checks would then be exact, without Redis and without a network call on the request path. It isn’t built yet, and it brings its own trade-offs. The ingress only sees the API key, not the account, so an account with several keys needs a way to land on the same replica. A very busy account would load a single replica. And when replicas are added or removed, some accounts move to another replica and start there with a fresh bucket.

Shared counters in Redis would also make the limits exact, but at the cost of a round trip on every request, and I’d rather not pay that. Keeping Postgres in the background also keeps another option open: because the edge only talks to Postgres in the background, a second region with its own edge and geocoder could use a distant database without slowing anyone down.

Try it

The free plan includes 50,000 requests a month at 2 requests a second, with no card. Create a free account, make a few calls, and you’ll see them in the dashboard’s usage, written by the sync described above.

title: The Component System
description:
The Component System is a concept for building and keeping a code base of components of the designs for frontend applications. Already defined and designed for the developers and already built in code. This system of components are then added to the code base of the desired project from which the components can be pulled from and used. Updates for the specific project's design can then be modified per project, as the copy of the component system lives in the project. When this is done with the same vision in mind, it will not look like a copy and paste of another system.

The Component System ensures the design’s consistency pulls through the entire project and the developer has just to check the properties for specific usage where the component has been used. The developer does not have to think or be concerned about the theme/design itself.

This gives you one central place the theme and styling is located and aids for:

  1. Maintaining the design
  2. Redesign of the theme
  3. Consistency/Toolbox of items to use
  4. Updating one component pulls all the way through to the entire app that is built
  5. These files can be migrated to a new project and already have a base to work from

The Component System aims to:

  • Decreases development time.
  • Reduced learning curve for developers joining the project. They do - not need to learn all the nuances of each attribute of an item
  • Library of items used in the project, with attributes pre-configured
  • Faster product revamp/redesign

With all this the Component System enables developers to get the product/features out faster (having a faster time-to-market) while maintaining consistency in the design and usage. Easing the developer onboarding while maintaining project standards and consistency.

This is done by creating all the components that are used. Whether they are buttons, sliders, text fields, and already defining all the design attributes for those components, from setting the theme detail to padding, to radiuses, and some with predefined functionality like an email field, or secondary button. This is your starting point, template, for new or adding to existing projects updating with all the design properties and attributes for the specific project, and then used by the developer(s).

title: Designing a pill reminder that never says 'missed' when it doesn't know
description:
When several family members help an aging parent with medication, the hardest bug isn't a crash. It's a record that says something that isn't true. "Missed" when nobody actually checked. "Given" when someone only meant to give it. Two siblings both logging the same dose.

We built DoseBeacon around one principle: the history should only ever say what someone actually reported. Here's how that shaped the design.

Four honest buttons for the person taking the medicine

Senior Mode shows one large, high-contrast card at a time with four choices: LOG AS TAKEN, LATER, NOT SURE and I NEED HELP. "Not sure" is a first-class answer, not an error state. Read-aloud, Dynamic Type and VoiceOver are supported, reminders are scheduled on the device so they work offline, and Senior Mode never shows ads or purchase screens.

"Not confirmed yet" instead of "missed"

A dose nobody has reported is shown as Not confirmed yet, never "missed". Absence of data is not evidence of a missed dose, and a scary word on a parent's screen helps nobody.

A claim is not a dose

Tapping "I'm handling this" tells the rest of the care circle who is on it. That claim is never displayed as a dose given. Only a report is a report.

Conflicts get flagged, not overwritten

If two people report the same dose, it's marked Needs review rather than last-write-wins. Every report keeps who made it, on which device and when. Corrections append to the history; nothing is silently erased.

Care circle permissions

A circle code only sends a join request. The parent's manager approves it, picks a role (manager, dose-logging helper or read-only family) and can revoke any device. Every screen shows when it last updated, so nobody mistakes stale data for current data.

Setup that rewards honesty

"Beacon Quests" light up a lighthouse as you get organized: add medications, choose a helper, review the emergency card. Quests reward honest records, including "Not sure" and asking for help. No streaks, nothing to lose, and never a nudge to take more medication.

Also included: pharmacy-label scanning with on-device text recognition (every field is checked by you before a reminder turns on), refill estimates, 7/30/90-day PDF reports for doctor visits and a printable emergency medication card.

DoseBeacon: Pill Reminder on the iPhone App Store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/dosebeacon-pill-reminder/id6796910918

title: The most humane invention in computing
description:
Originally published at https://ketushah.com/writing/the-most-humane-invention-in-computing/

The most humane invention in computing

To err is human. Pope wrote that in 1711, and three centuries later it is still the most important sentence in software design. People are going to make mistakes. Not occasionally, not the careless ones among us. Everyone, constantly. It is the starting condition, and any system that takes input from a user has to be designed from it.

Which is probably why undo was never invented once. It kept getting invented. A system at Brown had it in 1968. A Lisp programming tool had it by 1971. Xerox PARC put it in a text editor in 1974. These people were not copying each other. They were all watching the same thing happen: a person at a keyboard, doing something they did not mean to do, with no way back. When the Macintosh shipped, Undo sat at the top of the Edit menu. It still does.

So the rule I design by: wherever there is user input, there has to be a way to correct it. Self-serve wherever possible, a button, an edit, a window of time to change your mind. And where self-serve genuinely cannot work, an easy path to something that can correct it, another system or an actual human. Amendment or undo, in one form or another, everywhere input exists. It is not a feature to add when there is time. It is part of what accepting the input means.

Where it gets hard is the guardrails, and I will be honest: there is no formula for those. It is circumstance based. What decides it is the consequences of the undo itself. Before I let a user reverse something on their own, I want the action mapped, upstream and downstream. What consumed this input? What already acted on it? If the damage from reversing is contained, hand the user the button and get out of the way. If the reversal ripples into other systems and other people, self-serve is the wrong tool. That correction needs a process, checks, maybe a human reviewing it. The mistake gets corrected either way. The route is what changes.

The map has a clock on it too. Ask whether the mistake’s ramifications are permanent, and whether they have already landed. Order something online and you can cancel it, but the window depends on the vendor: zero minutes from one, fifteen from another. Then the order ships and the window does not narrow. It ends. Anyone who has tried to get UPS or FedEx to intercept a package or reroute it midstream has felt the far side of that line. The act left the database and entered the physical world, and only the database part was ever reversible.

Some of that is just physics, and physics is not a design flaw. Some of it is complexity that got baked in for reasons nobody remembers. Either way, once the act itself cannot be undone, the question changes to whether its consequences can be amended. You cannot un-ship a box. You can return it, refund it, send the right one. And the amendment has a simple test. It worked when whatever the user intended to achieve is achieved. Not when the ticket closed. When the person ends up where they were trying to go.

Gmail’s Undo Send is the famous version of this. Launched in 2009, and it has never recalled a single email. It delays the send, five seconds at first, up to thirty now, so the undo is really a grace period with good marketing. I mean that as praise. Where reversal is impossible, time is the substitute. A window before the act becomes real, and where that fails, an amendment after.

Given all that, why do so many systems give you no way back at all? Collect the reasons and they are mostly unglamorous. Complexity. Oversight. Cost. A dependency on some external party whose system will not cooperate. A product team that never foresaw the need. A mistake so rare that building the correction never survived prioritization. Those are engineering economics, and some of them are even true. But there is one more reason on the list, and it is not like the others. Sometimes there is no undo because no undo is the business model. A flow that takes ten seconds to enter and ten days to leave is not an accident. It is somebody’s decision, taken for gains.

Here is the part that should bother us. From the user’s chair, there is no way to tell those reasons apart. The screen does not say whether the correction path is missing because it could not be built, or because somebody chose not to build it. It is just not clear, not until the user makes the mistake and goes looking for the undo that may or may not be there. That is when a system shows you what it thinks of you. Ideally before you need to know.

title: A prompt-injected model cannot skip your approval step
description:
A human-in-the-loop design usually has the same shape: the model proposes an action, the graph stops at an approval step, a person says yes or no, and only then does the tool run. The guarantee you want is that the model has no way to reach the tool without passing the stop.

That guarantee holds only if every path around the stop is closed, including the paths a model can influence by text alone. A model that has read a hostile web page or a poisoned document can be steered into producing unusual output: a tool name you did not expect, a routing hint, a message that looks like a human answer. This post lists the places where 10xGraph decides on the graph's side instead of trusting that output, and what you still have to do yourself. It describes behaviour and design, not ways to attack a particular app.

10xGraph is open-source, self-hosted infrastructure for AI applications. You write the agents, tools and tasks; 10xGraph runs them behind an API server with authentication, role-based access, tenant isolation, durable state in Postgres and Redis, background jobs, metrics and tracing, and generates Docker and Kubernetes deploy files. MIT licensed, by 10xScale. Formerly Agentflow.

The reference pages are Interrupts and the security model.

Handoffs only go where a handoff tool says

Handoff is how one agent passes the conversation to another, through a tool made with create_handoff_tool. If any tool call named transfer_to_<X> moved the run to node <X>, a steered model could name a node that your edges never lead to, and that includes a node behind an approval step.

So a handoff is honoured only when the ToolNode holds a tool of that name created by create_handoff_tool. Any other transfer_to_* call is an ordinary tool call, and if no such tool exists it gets the usual "Tool not found" result.

The same rule covers Command(goto=...) returned from your own code. A target that is neither a node in the graph nor END raises GraphError with code GRAPH_007, naming the node it came from and the unknown target.

Starting a run at a chosen node with current_node is a separate, intended feature (a frontend can send the agent the user picked). If a node needs an entry guard, enforce it inside the graph. The change above is about what the model can do, not what your caller can do.

Tools hidden by tools_tags cannot be called

An Agent can advertise only the tools that match tools_tags. Showing the model only the tagged tools is not enough on its own, because the ToolNode could still run any registered name the model happened to guess.

So the Agent records the names it advertised on the assistant message (metadata["allowed_tools"]), and the dispatch step refuses a call to anything outside that list with the same "Tool not found" error. If you use tags to keep a destructive tool away from a low-trust agent, the tag holds at run time and not just in the prompt.

A tool name cannot be claimed twice

When a ToolNode also connects to an MCP server, a remote tool could otherwise take over the name of a local tool, so calls meant for your function would go to the server. A collision between an MCP tool and a local or remote tool on the same ToolNode raises ValueError ("Rename one of them"), and the check runs outside the code that swallows connection errors, so it cannot be hidden by a failed server ping.

Forged tool results are refused

Remote tools run on the client, and the client sends the result back to resume the run. That is the one case where the API accepts a message with the tool role, and it is narrow.

  • Client messages may only have the user role. The assistant and system roles are refused, and so is a tool message that carries anything other than tool results.
  • A tool result is accepted only for a remote tool call that is waiting for one on that thread. A result for a call the model never made, a second result for the same call, or a result for a server tool is refused.
  • A client tool can never carry the name of a server tool. Otherwise a client could declare a tool with the name of the one paused for approval and post a "result" for it.

The effect is that the approval path cannot be satisfied by pretending to be the model or the tool.

A resume answers one specific question

A resume carries a value, and the value can be bound to the prompt it answers:

  • The client can send interrupt_id with the resume on invoke, stream and WebSocket. If the thread is not paused, or is paused at another interrupt (a stale tab, a retried request after the first answer was consumed), the API answers 409 and records nothing. This is how a late "yes" fails to approve a different request.
  • The core checks the id again and, when the interrupt declared a response_schema (a JSON Schema), validates the value against it. A mismatch raises InterruptMismatchError (INTERRUPT_001), and a value that does not satisfy the schema raises ResumeValidationError (INTERRUPT_002). Nothing is recorded in either case.

The API checks the id first and answers 409 before a stream starts. It also passes the id to the core, which enforces it again.

from tenxgraph.utils import interrupt

async def refund(amount: float) -> str:
    decision = interrupt(
        {"amount": amount},
        message=f"Refund ${amount}?",
        reason="tool_approval",
        response_schema={
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"approved": {"type": "boolean"}},
            "required": ["approved"],
        },
    )
    if not decision or not decision.get("approved"):
        return "Refund declined"
    return issue_refund(amount)

Without interrupt_id, a resume answers whatever the thread is paused at, as before. Send the id from any client where a person can have two tabs open.

What you still own

  • None of this makes a model trustworthy. It removes shortcuts around your graph.
  • Authentication, role-based access and ownership are separate layers, covered in the security model. Another user's thread answers 404. Permissions apply per route; there are no per-tool permissions, so decide inside the tool who may do what.
  • A tool that must be safe against a steered model should still validate its own arguments and use idempotency keys. See Interrupts for how to place the stop before the tool, not after it.

Frequently asked questions

Does this stop prompt injection?

No. Nothing stops a model from being steered by text it reads. These controls limit what a steered model can do to the parts of the graph you did not give it: the route it takes, the tools it can call and the approval a human gives.

Can a client approve an interrupt by sending a tool result?

No. The API accepts a tool result only as the answer to a remote tool call that is waiting for one. A result for a server tool, for a call the model never made, or a second result for the same call is refused.

What does interrupt_id add to a resume?

It ties the answer to the exact prompt the human saw. If the thread is paused at a different interrupt, or not paused at all, the API answers 409 and nothing is recorded.

title: Node.js Object Storage for AI Images: Retention and Migration (Practical Build)
description:
For a Node.js service that stores AI-generated images, put the image bytes into object storage with a stable bucket-and-key contract, then keep retention and deletion in your application boundary. That gives a solo SaaS founder a replaceable storage layer instead of a pile of provider-specific calls.

The practical choice is this: use the PUT /v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key} route when a server needs to upload a buffer, keep keys deterministic enough to delete later, and treat the deletion deadline as application data. Infrai is a reasonable fit when a self-describing API and runnable examples reduce integration time. Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, or Backblaze B2 can be better when their storage-specific controls are the actual requirement.

What changed the decision

I started from the familiar question, “Where do I put the generated PNG?” That is too narrow for signed media documents and images. The real object has an owner, a retention deadline, and a deletion event. If those three things are not represented outside the blob, a lifecycle rule is doing work it cannot fully understand.

My small-service rule is simple: store the bytes under a key I can reconstruct, store the deadline in the database, and make the storage adapter the only code that knows the provider route. The adapter should expose put, get, and delete to the rest of the application. That is a few minutes of structure now and a much cheaper migration later.

The constraint that changed my choice was reversibility. An image can be regenerated, but a signed document may have a contractual deletion date. This storage surface does not provide object versioning or object lock, so it is not the right boundary for immutable, finance-grade records. It also does not provide public-read ACLs or a permanent public URL, which rules it out for a public image host or static website origin.

That is not a small footnote. It defines the job this storage layer can safely do.

Keep it boring.

How do I upload the image without coupling the app?

The smallest useful implementation sends a Node.js Buffer as the request body. It reads the API key from the environment, uses an explicit method, checks the response, and backs off on a rate limit. The idempotency key makes a retry identifiable to the service instead of turning a transient network error into an accidental second write.

import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const bucket = process.env.IMAGE_BUCKET ?? "generated-images";
const key = `signed/${new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10)}/${randomUUID()}.png`;
const image = await readFile("./generated-image.png");

async function putImage(): Promise<void> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(
      "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}"
        .replace("{bucket}", encodeURIComponent(bucket))
        .replace("{key}", key.split("/").map(encodeURIComponent).join("/")),
      {
      method: "PUT",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "image/png",
        "Idempotency-Key": key,
      },
      body: image,
      },
    );

    if (response.ok) return;

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const waitMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
      continue;
    }

    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Object upload failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }
}

await putImage();

That path is deliberately part of the application decision. A random key prevents collisions, while the date prefix makes an operator’s prefix listing useful. It is not a retention policy by itself. The database record should still contain the object key, creation time, deletion deadline, and deletion status. A scheduled worker can select due records, delete the object through the adapter, and mark the record only after the storage response succeeds.

For browser uploads, I would keep this server-side flow. This service does not expose an independently configurable CORS route for this storage workflow, so a browser-direct upload is not the default path I would build around. A server proxy also keeps the API credential away from the browser. The trade-off is that the application handles the upload bandwidth.

Which storage boundary survives a migration?

The adapter contract matters more than the first upload. A provider-neutral interface can stay tiny:

export interface ImageStore {
  put(key: string, data: Buffer, contentType: string): Promise<void>;
  delete(key: string): Promise<void>;
}

Amazon S3 is the natural choice when the product needs the broadest surrounding ecosystem and storage controls such as versioning or object lock. Those controls are a meaningful reason to accept a larger integration surface. The cost is more provider configuration for a one-person team, especially when the product only needs private binary storage and deadline-driven deletion.

Cloudflare R2 is worth considering when the application already lives in Cloudflare’s environment or when its S3-compatible workflow fits the deployment. It is still a direct storage product, so its storage-specific documentation and operational model should be the source of truth for retention, access, and migration decisions. I would not select it merely because the API looks familiar.

Backblaze B2 is a credible option for a focused object-storage workload and a direct competitor to evaluate during a migration spike. Its fit depends on the regions, tooling, and recovery controls the service needs. Test the exact deletion and retrieval workflow with representative objects; “S3-compatible” does not make every operational feature interchangeable.

Option Integration shape Good fit Boundary to test
Amazon S3 Specialist object-storage API and SDKs Versioning, object lock, and a broad ecosystem More configuration than a tiny service may need
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible object storage A Cloudflare-centered deployment Exact retention and access behavior
Backblaze B2 Direct object-storage service Focused storage with a migration spike Regions, tooling, and recovery controls
Infrai REST route with a self-describing discovery surface Private application-managed objects No versioning, object lock, public-read ACL, or cross-cloud migration tool

Infrai's verified operating model is a single key and one bill across backend capabilities. That can remove credential and invoice coordination when this image workflow later adds another service.

The REST option belongs in this comparison for a different reason. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities, schemas, billing information, and runnable examples, and the documented capabilities include examples in multiple languages. For a solo founder who ships weekly, that makes discovering and wiring the upload operation less of an SDK archaeology project. Its verified one-key, one-bill model can also remove credential and invoice coordination when the image workflow later adds another service. That is operational friction, not a storage feature.

My explicit recommendation is to try Infrai for private, application-managed image storage when the team values a self-describing contract and a thin adapter more than storage-specific governance features. Choose S3 or another specialist when immutable retention, public delivery, version recovery, cross-region replication, or a mature migration tool is a hard requirement.

What I would change at scale

The example is intentionally small. In production, I would make the database deadline authoritative and run deletion from a queue with a retry state. I would also record a content hash and the provider request ID in the audit record, where available. The application would never infer “deleted” from a timeout.

I would add a reconciliation job too. It can compare due database records with storage listings filtered by prefix, but it cannot discover arbitrary metadata through this storage surface; listing supports prefix filtering rather than server-side metadata search. That is another reason the database owns the retention index.

There are limits worth planning around: lifecycle expiration is measured in days, with a one-day minimum rather than hour-level expiry; multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule; and strict compare-and-swap writes need queue or database coordination because there is no If-Match conditional write. These are manageable constraints for generated media with an application worker. They are poor fits for a workflow that expects the bucket to enforce every invariant.

The migration plan is correspondingly boring. Keep the ImageStore interface stable. Store the provider name beside each object record. Copy objects in a controlled job if a move becomes necessary, then verify reads and deletion deadlines before switching new writes. The platform does not provide cross-region automatic replication or a cross-cloud bulk migration tool, so the application or an external transfer system owns that work.

The adapter is the investment.

The decision rule

Use the Node.js upload route when the object is private, the application owns its lifecycle, and the service benefits from discovering a capability through one documented API. Keep the key and deadline in your own data model. That is the part that makes the choice reversible.

Do not use this boundary as a substitute for public image hosting, WORM retention, automatic cross-region disaster recovery, or browser-direct CORS configuration. In those cases, the specialist storage product is not overengineering. It is the requirement.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the storage documentation and keep the adapter small enough to replace.

Further reading

  • Infrai official documentation
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Backblaze B2 documentation
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
