title: Uma transferência em Go com arquitetura hexagonal
description:
Publiquei um mini tutorial guiado de arquitetura hexagonal em Go. Para mostrar como as fronteiras aparecem no código, montei uma pequena API de transferência e organizei a explicação em nove etapas.

Uma chamada a POST /transfers chega ao handler HTTP como JSON. O handler converte a entrada em uma chamada para o serviço da aplicação. O serviço busca as contas usando a porta AccountRepository. No domínio, Withdraw recusa valores menores ou iguais a zero e saldos insuficientes. Em seguida, Deposit soma o valor à conta de destino. O serviço pede ao repositório que grave as duas contas.

HTTP → handler → serviço de aplicação → domínio
                         ↓
                 porta AccountRepository
                         ↓
                 adaptador em memória

O papel da porta e do adaptador

A aplicação conhece o contrato AccountRepository, que define Get e Save. O repositório em memória implementa esses métodos. Em Go, essa implementação é implícita: o tipo que possui os métodos com as assinaturas exigidas satisfaz a interface, sem declarar explicitamente que a implementa.

Essa direção ajuda a manter as regras do domínio independentes do protocolo HTTP e do armazenamento concreto. O handler traduz entrada e erros HTTP; o serviço coordena o caso de uso; o bootstrap escolhe as implementações e monta a aplicação. O router recebe handlers que registram as próprias rotas, enquanto /health é compartilhado pelo servidor.

O que o exemplo cobre

O projeto expõe GET /health e POST /transfers, com duas contas de demonstração. O adaptador protege o map com sync.RWMutex; Save valida as duas contas antes de atualizar o armazenamento. Essa proteção cobre o acesso ao map, mas a sequência completa de leitura, alteração e gravação não é uma transação. Os dados ficam em memória e desaparecem quando o processo termina. O exemplo também não tem banco de dados, autenticação ou regras de moeda.

A página do mini tutorial percorre as nove etapas, da introdução à arquitetura e ao mapa do projeto até a composição e inicialização da aplicação. Se quiser seguir cada parte, acesse:

https://bendevoficial.com/learning/aprendendo-hexagonal-em-go

O código está disponível em https://github.com/bendevjunior/hexagonal-architecture-go.

Se você acompanhar o exemplo, me conta se a separação entre aplicação, domínio e adaptadores ficou clara. Pode deixar dúvidas ou sugestões nos comentários. Quero conversar sobre arquitetura hexagonal e outros temas técnicos para os próximos conteúdos.

title: Accept crypto payments in Python
description:
A minimal Moonvex integration in Python with Flask and requests: create a checkout, send the customer to the Moonvex page where they pick the coin and network, receive the webhook and verify its HMAC-SHA256 signature with the standard library. Works for any WSGI app.

Step by step

1. Get an API key and a webhook secret

In the Moonvex dashboard go to “Integration” → “Create key” → type “Secret” (sk_live_…). The key is shown only once: store it on your server as MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY. On the same page add a webhook pointing to an https URL on your server and store its signing secret as MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET.

pip install flask requests

# environment variables on the server
export MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_...
export MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_...

2. Create a checkout

POST /v1/payments with requests: Authorization: Bearer and Idempotency-Key in the headers; orderId, amount as a string and currency (USD, EUR, UAH, RUB or a coin) in the body. Without network the API creates a checkout and the customer picks the coin and network on the Moonvex page. description is shown as “You are paying for”, returnUrl (https only) is where the Back buttons lead. A 201 response returns an object with object: "checkout", id (inv_…) and paymentUrl.

# app.py
import os
import sqlite3
from contextlib import closing

import requests
from flask import Flask, abort, redirect

app = Flask(__name__)
API = "https://api.moonvex.org"


def db() -> sqlite3.Connection:
    conn = sqlite3.connect("shop.db")
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    return conn


def create_checkout(order_id: int, amount: str, attempt: int = 1) -> dict:
    r = requests.post(
        API + "/v1/payments",
        headers={
            "Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY"],
            # a retry with the same key never creates a second checkout
            "Idempotency-Key": f"order-{order_id}-{attempt}",
        },
        json={
            "orderId": str(order_id),
            "amount": amount,
            "currency": "USD",  # no network: the customer picks the coin on the checkout page
            "description": f"Order #{order_id}",  # shown as “You are paying for”
            "returnUrl": f"https://shop.example.com/orders/{order_id}",  # the Back buttons
        },
        timeout=15,
    )
    checkout = r.json()
    if r.status_code >= 400:
        raise RuntimeError(checkout["error"]["code"] + ": " + checkout["error"]["message"])
    return checkout  # {"object": "checkout", "id": "inv_…", "paymentUrl": …}


@app.post("/orders/<int:order_id>/pay")
def pay(order_id: int):
    with closing(db()) as conn:
        order = conn.execute("SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE id = ?", (order_id,)).fetchone()
    if order is None:
        abort(404)
    # total is stored as TEXT "25.00", so the amount is sent as a string
    checkout = create_checkout(order["id"], str(order["total"]))
    return redirect(checkout["paymentUrl"], code=303)

3. Send the customer to paymentUrl

paymentUrl is the Moonvex checkout page: the customer picks the coin and network, then sees the exact amount including the fee, the address, a QR code, the official token contract and a timer, with a status that updates by itself. Your description is shown as “You are paying for”, and the Back and “Back to the shop” buttons lead to returnUrl. If you know the customer's language, add ?lang=ru, ?lang=uk or ?lang=en to paymentUrl; otherwise the page picks the language itself. Open the page with a redirect or in a new tab; it cannot be embedded in an iframe. A customer returning to your site is not proof of payment: mark the order paid only from a webhook. In Flask: redirect(payment["paymentUrl"], code=303).

4. Receive the webhook and verify the signature

Moonvex sends a POST with a Moonvex-Signature header: t=,v1=. The signature is a hex HMAC-SHA256 of the string “t.raw_body” keyed with the webhook secret. Compute it over the body bytes before parsing JSON, compare in constant time and reject events older than 5 minutes. For 24 hours after a secret rotation the header carries two v1 values; either one is valid. In Flask the raw body is request.get_data(), and hmac.compare_digest compares signatures in constant time.

# moonvex_signature.py
import hashlib
import hmac
import time


def verify_moonvex(raw: bytes, header: str, secret: str, tolerance: int = 300) -> bool:
    """Checks Moonvex-Signature: t=<unix>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256(secret, t + "." + raw)>"""
    parts = [p.split("=", 1) for p in (header or "").split(",") if "=" in p]
    t = next((v for k, v in parts if k == "t"), None)
    if t is None or not t.isdigit() or abs(time.time() - int(t)) > tolerance:
        return False
    expected = hmac.new(secret.encode(), t.encode() + b"." + raw, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    # compare_digest is constant-time; during a secret rotation there are two v1 values
    return any(hmac.compare_digest(expected, v) for k, v in parts if k == "v1")

# app.py (continued)
import json

from flask import request

from moonvex_signature import verify_moonvex


@app.post("/moonvex/webhook")
def moonvex_webhook():
    raw = request.get_data()  # raw bytes, before JSON parsing
    if not verify_moonvex(raw, request.headers.get("Moonvex-Signature", ""), os.environ["MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET"]):
        return "bad signature", 400
    event = json.loads(raw)
    if event["type"] in ("payment.confirmed", "payment.overpaid"):
        mark_paid_once(event["id"], event["data"]["orderId"])
    # payment.cancelled also arrives when the customer switches coins: do not cancel the order on it
    return "", 200

5. Mark the order paid exactly once

A redelivered event keeps the same id, so store it in a table with a unique key in the same transaction as the order update: a duplicate then changes nothing. Fulfil on payment.confirmed and payment.overpaid, never on payment.detected. Events arrive for the payment the customer starts: data.id is its pay_… id and data.orderId is your order number. If the customer switches coins, the previous payment gets payment.cancelled: do not cancel the order on it while the checkout is open. In SQLite that is INSERT OR IGNORE plus a cursor.rowcount check in one transaction.

# app.py (continued)
# CREATE TABLE processed_events (event_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, created_at TEXT DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP);


def mark_paid_once(event_id: str, order_id: str) -> None:
    # the second "conn" is a transaction: commit on success, rollback on error
    with closing(db()) as conn, conn:
        cur = conn.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES (?)", (event_id,))
        if cur.rowcount == 1:  # first delivery of the event
            conn.execute("UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = ? AND status <> 'paid'", (int(order_id),))

6. Test the integration

Moonvex has no test network: everything runs on mainnets. The “Send test” button under “Integration” sends a webhook.test event, which is how you check the signature. Then pay a small invoice, for example 1 USDT on TRON: it is a regular payment and the money lands on your balance. The delivery log with response codes and a “Retry” button is on the same page.

Pitfalls

  • Use request.get_data(), not request.json: the signature covers the original bytes and re-serialising changes them.
  • Keep amounts as Decimal or strings. 0.1 + 0.2 in float is not 0.3, and in payments that is an error in cents.
  • Always pass a timeout to requests.post; without it a hung request holds the worker forever.
  • verify_moonvex accepts every v1 value in the header, so a secret rotation causes no downtime.
  • Need one fixed coin instead of the customer's choice? Add network (and asset when currency is USD) to the same request, for example "network": "TRON", "asset": "USDT": that is the classic payment in one coin. The checkout above is the recommended flow.

FAQ

Is there an official Python SDK?

The official SDK is for Node.js (@moonvex/node). In Python requests or httpx is enough: the API is plain HTTPS with JSON, and signature verification is the dozen lines shown in this guide.

What if the customer does not pay in time?

The checkout is valid until expiresAt; the window is set with expiresInMinutes, 5 to 1440 minutes, 30 by default. If the customer started a payment and did not pay it in time, it moves to EXPIRED and you receive payment.expired. To let them try again, create a new checkout with a new Idempotency-Key (for example, bump the attempt number at the end of the key); if the API answers DUPLICATE_ORDER, that order number is closed, so use a new orderId such as 1001-2.

Is there a test mode or a sandbox?

No, there is no test network: Moonvex runs on mainnets only. Check the signature with the “Send test” button (a webhook.test event) and the whole payment flow with a real payment of a small amount, for example 1 USDT on TRON.

Originally published at: moonvex.org/en/guides/python

title: 5 commands that list every deprecated call your code still makes (Python, TS, Go, Java, Kotlin)
description:
Don't upgrade Python or Java until you run 5 commands. Each one below lists the deprecated calls your code still makes, and deprecated today usually means removed in the next major.

The problem with deprecations isn't that tools hide them. It's that they're warnings, and warnings scroll past in CI where nobody reads them. So the trick in every language is the same: make them errors once, on a branch, and read the list.

Python 

pytest -W error::DeprecationWarning

Every DeprecationWarning raised while your tests run becomes a failure with a traceback pointing at your line. Run it on a branch; don't leave it on in main until the list is empty.

TypeScript / JavaScript

typescript-eslint has a rule that uses type information to flag anything marked @deprecated:

// eslint.config.js, with typed linting enabled
rules: { "@typescript-eslint/no-deprecated": "error" }

tsc alone won't fail on deprecations; your editor's strike-through is the only other hint.

Go 

staticcheck -checks SA1019 ./...

SA1019 reports uses of identifiers whose doc comment starts with Deprecated:.

Java 

javac -Xlint:deprecation ...

In Maven, add -Xlint:deprecation to the compiler plugin's compilerArgs; in Gradle, options.compilerArgs << "-Xlint:deprecation". Add -Werror for the one run where you want the list to fail the build.

Kotlin

The compiler already warns on calls to @Deprecated declarations. For one build, make warnings fatal:

kotlin { compilerOptions { allWarningsAsErrors.set(true) } }

Kotlin deprecations often carry a ReplaceWith(...), and the IDE can apply it for you.

Then what

Fix the list before the upgrade, while the old and new names both still work. During the upgrade you're fixing deprecations and breaking changes at once, and you can't tell which is which.

This is also the check Versyka runs inside every fix: before editing, it reads the new version's deprecation notes for the functions your code calls, in all five languages.

Which language in your stack hides the most deprecation warnings?

title: GitHub Actions arm64 runners pricing, size by size
description:
GitHub Actions arm64 runners pricing is a discount that grows with the machine: 16.7 percent below x64 on the standard 2-core Linux runner, and 39.5 percent below it at 64 cores, read from GitHub's runner pricing reference on 21 September 2026. The standard Windows runner is the exception that catches people out, because arm64 and x64 are both $0.010 a minute there, so switching a small Windows job to arm64 saves nothing at all.


The arm64 discount at each Linux size, computed from the per-minute rates published on docs.github.com/en/billing/reference/actions-runner-pricing and read on 21 September 2026.

There is one arithmetic question on this page and everything else serves it: how much slower is your job allowed to be on arm64 before the cheaper minute stops being cheaper? The answer is the ratio of the two rates, it is different at every size, and at the standard size it is tighter than most people expect.

The rates below are GitHub's published ones. They changed from a multiplier model to flat per-minute rates, so nothing here needs a conversion step, and since 28 October 2026 the included allowance is a dollar amount spent at each runner's rate, so an arm64 minute spends less of it than an x64 one.

Every arm64 rate, against the x64 rate beside it

Standard Linux arm64 is $0.005 a minute against $0.006 for standard Linux x64. That is the rate most workflows would move to, and it is the smallest discount on the page: one tenth of a cent a minute, or $10 a month on ten thousand minutes.

The larger runners are where the money is. Linux arm64 at 4 cores is $0.008 against $0.012, at 8 cores $0.014 against $0.022, at 16 cores $0.026 against $0.042, at 32 cores $0.050 against $0.082, and at 64 cores $0.098 against $0.162. The discount widens monotonically from a third to just under 40 percent, and there is no arm64 runner at 96 cores, so the top of the x64 ladder has no cheaper twin.

Windows behaves differently at both ends. The standard Windows runner is $0.010 a minute on arm64 and $0.010 on x64, an identical rate, so the arm64 discount does not exist at standard size. On the larger Windows runners it reappears and is the largest on the rate card: $0.014 against $0.022 at 4 cores, rising to $0.194 against $0.322 at 64. There is also a 2-core Windows arm64 larger runner at $0.008 with no x64 counterpart at that size.

Machine arm64 rate x64 rate arm64 discount Slower it may run and still pay
Linux 2-core, standard $0.005 $0.006 16.7% 20%
Linux 4-core, larger $0.008 $0.012 33.3% 50%
Linux 16-core, larger $0.026 $0.042 38.1% 61%
Linux 64-core, larger $0.098 $0.162 39.5% 65%
Windows 2-core, standard $0.010 $0.010 none not at all
Windows 16-core, larger $0.050 $0.082 39.0% 64%

Rates from Actions runner pricing, read 21 September 2026. The break-even column is the x64 rate divided by the arm64 rate, rounded down to a whole percent.

What the break-even column actually means

Read the last column as a permission rather than a promise. On the standard Linux runner, arm64 costs five sixths of x64, so an arm64 job may take up to 20 percent longer and cost exactly what the x64 job cost. Beyond that the cheaper minute buys you a more expensive job, and you have also made every pipeline slower.

Twenty percent is not a lot of headroom. It is comfortably inside the range an interpreted test suite moves by between two architectures, and it is well inside what an emulated container costs, so on the standard runner the switch has to be measured rather than assumed. On a 16-core larger runner the same job is allowed to be 61 percent slower before it stops paying, which is enough headroom that the decision usually goes the other way.

Rounding shortens the odds again at the small end, because GitHub "rounds the minutes and partial minutes each job uses up to the nearest whole minute". A 65-second job bills two minutes on either architecture, so the whole saving on that job is $0.002, and a matrix of twenty short jobs saves four cents a run. The arm64 discount is a large-job and large-machine instrument.

Where the saving lands on a real month

Take ten thousand Linux minutes a month in private repositories. On the standard x64 runner that is $60 and on standard arm64 it is $50: a real ten dollars, and not a number anyone will notice on an invoice. Put the same work on a 4-core larger runner and it is $120 against $80, which is a $40 difference on the same ten thousand minutes, and on a 16-core runner it is $420 against $260.

Two rules move that number more than the architecture does. Larger runners draw on the included allowance at their own rate on Team and Enterprise Cloud, so an $18 Team allowance covers 2,250 minutes of a 4-core arm64 runner at $0.008 before every minute bills, and larger runners are not free on public repositories while standard runners are. An open source project running on ubuntu-24.04-arm pays nothing; the moment it switches to a larger arm64 runner for speed, it starts paying for every minute.

None of this is a rate you can improve by moving vendor on the arm64 line specifically, and it would be dishonest of us to imply otherwise: Latchkey sells Linux x64 managed runners at $0.0025 a minute for 2 vCPU with 8 GB and does not sell arm64 at all. Ubicloud does, publishing $0.00125 a minute for a 2 vCPU arm64 runner on its own pricing page read the same day, which is below every rate on this page. What Ubicloud CI is works through what that rate comes with.

Before you move the label

The labels are ubuntu-24.04-arm, ubuntu-22.04-arm and ubuntu-26.04-arm on Linux, and windows-11-arm on Windows. In a private repository they give you 2 vCPU with 8 GB of memory and 14 GB of SSD, the same shape as the x64 standard runner; in a public repository the standard runners are 4 vCPU with 16 GB.

The cost of getting this wrong is not a failed build, it is a slow one that still bills. Anything that pulls a container image without an arm64 variant will either fail to pull or quietly run under emulation, and an emulated job is several times slower, which turns a 16.7 percent discount into a large net loss. The compatibility work is the subject of running GitHub Actions on ARM; this page is only the rate card behind it.

Measure one workflow at both labels for a week before you move the rest, and compare billed minutes rather than wall clock, because rounding is what you are actually charged on. For the model behind the whole rate card, see how GitHub Actions pricing works, and for the larger-runner ladder in full, GitHub Actions larger runners pricing.

# x64 today
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

# arm64, same 2 vCPU and 8 GB in a private repo, $0.005 against $0.006
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04-arm

# both, for one week, so you can compare billed minutes rather than guess
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        runner: [ubuntu-latest, ubuntu-24.04-arm]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}

FAQ

How much cheaper are GitHub arm64 runners than x64?

It depends entirely on the size. Standard Linux arm64 is $0.005 against $0.006, a 16.7 percent discount. Larger Linux runners run from 33.3 percent cheaper at 4 cores to 39.5 percent at 64. Standard Windows arm64 is the same $0.010 as x64, so there is no discount there at all.

How much slower can an arm64 job be before it costs more?

Divide the x64 rate by the arm64 rate. On the standard Linux runner that is 1.2, so a 20 percent slowdown is break-even. On a 4-core larger runner it is 1.5, and at 64 cores it is about 1.65. The bigger the machine, the more slowdown the discount absorbs.

Are arm64 runners free on public repositories?

The standard arm64 runners are, because the use of standard GitHub-hosted runners is free and unlimited on public repositories, and ubuntu-24.04-arm is a standard runner. Larger runners of any architecture are billed even on public repositories, so switching a public project to a larger arm64 runner starts a bill that did not exist before.

Is there a 96-core arm64 runner?

No. The published arm64 Linux ladder stops at 64 cores and $0.098 a minute, while x64 continues to 96 cores at $0.252. If a job genuinely needs 96 cores there is no cheaper architecture available for it, and the question becomes whether the job parallelises well enough to justify the top of the x64 ladder at all.

Which arm64 runner labels does GitHub publish?

On Linux, ubuntu-24.04-arm, ubuntu-22.04-arm and ubuntu-26.04-arm; on Windows, windows-11-arm and windows-11-vs2026-arm. In private repositories they are 2 vCPU with 8 GB of memory and 14 GB of SSD, and in public repositories the standard runners are 4 vCPU with 16 GB.

References

  • GitHub: Actions runner pricing, every arm64 and x64 per-minute rate (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub: hosted runner specifications and the arm64 workflow labels (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub: Actions billing, included compute usage and the larger-runner rules (verified 2026-11-12)
  • Ubicloud pricing: a second published arm64 runner rate card (verified 2026-09-21)

title: Give your AI coding agent an IDE for Java and Kotlin jars (with jdx)
description:
AI coding agents are good at writing JVM code. Reading it is another story.

Ask an agent what a method in one of your dependencies does and watch the transcript: it unzips the jar, runs javap, greps the output, and then reads an entire source file into its context window. javap gives it erased signatures and raw opcodes, so it fills the gaps by guessing.

In this tutorial we'll give the agent the answers an IDE gives a human, using jdx, an open-source CLI and MCP server I built for exactly this. Every output below comes from the jdx quickstart, which is generated by actually running the commands.

What you need

  • A Java 21+ runtime (Linux, macOS or Windows)
  • An MCP-capable agent if you want the integration step (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, OpenCode, Cline, Kilo Code, Antigravity, or anything else that speaks MCP)

1. Install 

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MohammadMD1383/jdx/main/install-release.sh | bash
jdx version

It installs per user (no root) into ~/.local/share/jdx and links ~/.local/bin/jdx. On Windows, use the PowerShell installer from the installation guide. jdx doctor checks your environment if anything looks off.

Releases are unsigned, so macOS Gatekeeper and Windows SmartScreen will warn on first run. The installation guide shows how to clear it.

2. Ask the JDK something, with zero setup

The running JDK is always on the classpath:

$ jdx members java.util.HashMap --limit 5
members of java.util.HashMap
constructors declared on java.util.HashMap:
  constructor public HashMap()
  constructor public HashMap(int initialCapacity)
  constructor public HashMap(int initialCapacity, float loadFactor)
  constructor public HashMap(java.util.Map<? extends K, ? extends V> m)
methods declared on java.util.HashMap:
  method public V compute(K key, java.util.function.BiFunction<? super K, ? super V, ? extends V> remappingFunction)
+ 7 from java.lang.Object (--from java.lang.Object to expand)
5 of 53 members shown (--limit 53 to see more)
source: java.base (jrt)

Two things matter here for an agent. The output is bounded, and the footer says exactly what was cut and how to get the rest. And the source: line says where the answer came from.

Now read one method, and only that method:

$ jdx body 'java.util.HashMap#get(java.lang.Object)'
java.util.HashMap#get(java.lang.Object)
  source: src.zip · java.base/java/util/HashMap.java:562-565
    public V get(Object key) {
        Node<K,V> e;
        return (e = getNode(key)) == null ? null : e.value;
    }
next: jdx show java.util.HashMap

Quote references in your shell: #, ( and $ are shell syntax.

3. Ask about a library by its Maven coordinate

--coord resolves a library from your local Gradle and Maven caches. --fetch allows downloading it (and its -sources.jar) from Maven Central once:

$ jdx body 'com.google.gson.Gson#toJson(Object)' --coord com.google.code.gson:gson:2.14.0
com.google.gson.Gson#toJson(java.lang.Object)
  source: gson-2.14.0-sources.jar · com/google/gson/Gson.java:542-547
  public String toJson(Object src) {
    if (src == null) {
      return toJson(JsonNull.INSTANCE);
    }
    return toJson(src, src.getClass());
  }
next: jdx show com.google.gson.Gson

(Gson is a multi-release jar, so on JDK 21 jdx also prints a warning MULTI_RELEASE_VARIANT line; I've trimmed it from the outputs in this article.)

If there is no sources jar, jdx decompiles the method with Vineflower and marks the output ⚠ reconstructed, so the agent knows it's reading a reconstruction. (--engine javap gives raw bytecode instead.)

4. Let it refuse to guess

toJson has eight overloads. jdx won't pick one:

$ jdx body 'com.google.gson.Gson#toJson' --coord com.google.code.gson:gson:2.14.0
ambiguous: 8 candidates for com.google.gson.Gson#toJson
  com.google.gson.Gson#toJson(com.google.gson.JsonElement)
  com.google.gson.Gson#toJson(com.google.gson.JsonElement, com.google.gson.stream.JsonWriter)
  com.google.gson.Gson#toJson(com.google.gson.JsonElement, java.lang.Appendable)
  com.google.gson.Gson#toJson(java.lang.Object)
  com.google.gson.Gson#toJson(java.lang.Object, java.lang.Appendable)
  com.google.gson.Gson#toJson(java.lang.Object, java.lang.reflect.Type)
  com.google.gson.Gson#toJson(java.lang.Object, java.lang.reflect.Type, com.google.gson.stream.JsonWriter)
  com.google.gson.Gson#toJson(java.lang.Object, java.lang.reflect.Type, java.lang.Appendable)
hint: re-run with one of the refs above
[exit 2]

Exit code 2 means "ambiguous", and every candidate is a paste-ready reference. An agent can branch on the exit code without parsing prose, and the next call is a copy-paste, not a reconstruction. Other outcomes (not found, no index, bad usage) have their own exit codes, and every command has --json.

5. Navigate: hierarchy and callers 

$ jdx hierarchy com.google.gson.JsonElement --coord com.google.code.gson:gson:2.14.0
hierarchy of 'com.google.gson.JsonElement'
  supertypes
    extends java.lang.Object  java.base
  subtypes in workspace (4)
    class com.google.gson.JsonArray  gson-2.14.0.jar
    class com.google.gson.JsonNull  gson-2.14.0.jar
    class com.google.gson.JsonObject  gson-2.14.0.jar
    class com.google.gson.JsonPrimitive  gson-2.14.0.jar

$ jdx callers 'com.google.gson.JsonParser#parseReader(com.google.gson.stream.JsonReader)' --coord com.google.code.gson:gson:2.14.0
callers of 'com.google.gson.JsonParser#parseReader(com.google.gson.stream.JsonReader)'
  call com.google.gson.JsonParser#parse(com.google.gson.stream.JsonReader)  gson-2.14.0.jar
  call com.google.gson.JsonParser#parseReader(java.io.Reader)  gson-2.14.0.jar

--depth N follows the call graph transitively (cycle-safe). jdx usages and jdx implementors work across every jar on the classpath, not just one. More in Usages, hierarchy & calls.

6. Ask what a dependency upgrade breaks 

$ jdx diff com.google.code.gson:gson:2.11.0 com.google.code.gson:gson:2.14.0 --fetch
api diff com.google.code.gson:gson:2.11.0 -> com.google.code.gson:gson:2.14.0 (public surface)
info  TYPE_ADDED  com.google.gson.internal.GsonTypes
...
info  MEMBER_ADDED  com.google.gson.stream.JsonReader#setNestingLimit(int)
info  FIELD_CONSTANT_VALUE_CHANGED  com.google.gson.internal.GsonBuildConfig#VERSION: "2.11.0" -> "2.14.0"
0 breaking · 0 suspicious · 17 informational · 2 types added · 0 types removed

Every finding names a rule (MEMBER_REMOVED, RETURN_TYPE_CHANGED, KOTLIN_NULLABILITY_CHANGED, …) at breaking, suspicious or info. Add --fail-on breaking and it becomes a CI gate. See API diff for upgrades.

7. Name your classpath once 

jdx ws create gson --coord com.google.code.gson:gson:2.14.0
jdx -w gson usages com.google.gson.TypeAdapter
jdx ws use gson        # make it the default

Inside a Gradle or Maven project you often need nothing: jdx discovers the project's sources and dependency jars from the local caches, without running the build.

8. Hand it to your agent 

jdx setup --agent claude-code --scope project   # then restart Claude Code
# or: cursor, codex, copilot, opencode, cline, kilo, antigravity, windsurf, aider

Any other MCP client takes one line of config:

{"mcpServers":{"jdx":{"command":"jdx","args":["mcp"]}}}

The MCP server exposes each query as a typed tool (jdx_members, jdx_body, jdx_usages, jdx_callers, jdx_diff, …) and keeps the index warm, so queries take about 20 ms instead of about 250 ms for a cold CLI call. If you'd rather use the CLI from your agent, jdx help --agent prints a compact block to paste into CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md.

Per-agent setup pages: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, all integrations.

New in v1.7.0: the questions IDEs don't answer

Agents also ask things an IDE never made easy. v1.7.0 adds commands for them (see the command reference for every flag):

  • jdx literals — search string constants (LDC loads and ConstantValue fields) and .properties keys/values across the workspace: "where does this log message / resource key come from?"
  • jdx services — META-INF/services SPI providers: "who provides com.foo.Spi?"
  • jdx modules — JPMS module-info (requires / exports / opens / uses / provides).
  • jdx manifest and jdx resources — MANIFEST.MF attributes and non-class resources (--cat prints a text resource).
  • jdx annotated — classes and members carrying an annotation, with recipes such as deprecated, forRemoval, test and bean; jdx usages --where filters on annotation values.
  • callers is now override-aware by default (--exact for invoke-owner matching), bytecode usages carry file:line, and usages --context shows inline snippets.
  • Kotlin nullability is rendered from @Metadata, and there's a PowerShell installer for Windows.

Does it actually save context?

On one task from the README, "list Gson's API, then show only toJson(Object)" on gson-2.14.0:

Approach Calls Output in context
unzip + javap + grep + sed 5 ~17.5 KB (~4.4k tokens), and head -200 missed the method entirely
jdx members + jdx body 2 ~4.6 KB (~1.2k tokens)

The method body alone is 267 bytes, against 60,590 for javap -c and 58,251 for the full Gson.java. That's one task, not a benchmark suite, but you can rerun it yourself with sh docs/bench-compare.sh from the repo.

A note on safety

jdx parses bytecode with ASM and never loads the classes it inspects, so no static initialiser or other code from those jars runs. It only touches the network when you pass --fetch, run jdx upgrade, or run jdx kotlin install.

Kotlin

Kotlin binaries are read through @Metadata, so the agent sees nullability, suspend functions, properties, default arguments and @JvmName mappings instead of the JVM projection. Reading Kotlin sources needs a one-time jdx kotlin install. Details in Reading code.

Wrapping up

jdx is free and open source (Apache-2.0). Start with the quickstart, browse the docs, and if it gives your agent a wrong answer, please open an issue with the command and what you expected.

Source: github.com/MohammadMD1383/jdx

title: I Log Every Movie I Watch as a Markdown File, Filed Through GitHub Issues
description:
I keep a diary of every film I watch: score, where it streams, a one-line impression. It lives in a git repo as markdown, and a small React site reads it.

  • Source: https://github.com/kanywst/i-watched-movies
  • Live: https://kanywst.github.io/i-watched-movies/

One file per film

Every entry is movies/<slug>.md. This is the current top of the diary, trimmed (the cover URL and EN/JA summaries are cut):

---
title: 'Kingsman: The Secret Service'
title_ja: 'キングスマン'
published: true
tags:
  - 'Action'
  - 'Comedy'
national: 'UK'
streaming:
  - 'Disney+'
  - 'Prime Video'
checked: '2026-09'
release_date: '2015-01-29'
watch_date: '2026-09-23'
point: 8.9
---

Titles are stored in the original language (기생충, 無間道), with title_en and title_ja underneath when they differ. A build script walks movies/, writes one JSON file for the React app, plus an RSS feed, a sitemap and a static page per film so a shared link unfurls as that film.

Four flags split the files into five lists, and the precedence is fixed in src/partition.ts: dropped beats watching beats seen beats rated. Right now the 245 files break down like this (computed from the repo with that same function):

watched (rated)  76
seen (unrated)   60
dropped          76
watchlist        32
in progress       1

Yes, I have given up on as many films as I have rated. Dropped gets its own tab and stays out of the stats, so it does not drag anything down.

Adding a film is an issue

I almost never edit the files by hand. The repo has an "Add a movie" issue form. Submitting it starts movie-from-issue.yml, which parses the form, writes the file, runs lint, tests and build, opens a PR, squash-merges it and dispatches the Pages deploy. Progress shows up as labels on the issue: status: queued, processing, pr-opened, merged, or failed with a link to the run.

Filing an issue for a slug that already exists updates that entry, which is how a film moves from Watchlist to Watched. An empty field keeps the old value. Issue #1498 only bumped a watchlist rank, so its body is two fields:

### Title

九龍城寨之圍城

### List

Watchlist

### Recommend rank

32

Running the same parser locally against that body:

$ ISSUE_BODY="$(gh issue view 1498 --json body --jq .body)" ISSUE_NUMBER=1498 \
    node scripts/build-movie-from-issue.js
slug=twilight-of-the-warriors-walled-in
path=movies/twilight-of-the-warriors-walled-in.md
title=九龍城寨之圍城
list=Watchlist
watchlist=true
action=update

It found the existing file by title, merged, and wrote nothing new because the rank was already 32. The repo has 672 issues now. When I file a batch, they run in parallel, and a merge that loses the race to main retries up to five times with backoff.

The Stats page argues with me

The Stats tab compares genre, country and era averages against my personal average. From the current data:

baseline 7.65  median 7.85  spread 1.09
Crime     28 films  7.96  +0.31
Mystery   19 films  7.98  +0.33
Comedy    11 films  7.52  -0.13
Japan     23 films  7.35  -0.30
On release 29 films 7.38  -0.27
Catch-up   47 films 7.82  +0.17

Films I see within 90 days of release score lower than ones I catch up on later. A catch-up is usually something I already heard was good, so that gap measures picking as much as taste.

It also ranks the watchlist by the score the profile predicts. One rating broke that early. 新解釈・幕末伝 got a 1.0, and on its own it pulled Period to -3.04, which put Kingsman: The Golden Circle 42nd of 44 on the watchlist while the first Kingsman sat at the top. Now any score more than two standard deviations from the mean is capped before predicting. The averages on the page stay raw.

The page also backtests itself: predict every rated film from the other 75 and compare the miss against just guessing the average.

model error     0.71
baseline error  0.71

That is 0.705 against 0.711, and the page prints "That is 1% closer." Genre and country explain almost nothing about how I score a film. The page prints both numbers live, so the ranking never claims more than it has.

"Top of the diary" replays the #1 spot in watch order. 28 Years Later held it for 313 days, until The Devil Wears Prada 2 took it for nine.

Running it 

npm install
npm run dev

I ran npm test on a fresh clone: 21 files, 316 tests, all pure logic, no component tests. The README has a short list of what to change if you want to fork it for your own log.

title: Kubecost vs. OpenCost in 2026: Production Architecture & Setup for Kubernetes FinOps
description:
As containerized workloads scale across enterprise production clusters, understanding where container spend goes is one of the hardest challenges in cloud financial management. Traditional cloud billing tools like AWS Cost Explorer or Azure Cost Management stop at the node level. They can tell you how much an EC2 instance or an EKS node pool costs, but they are entirely blind to what is happening inside the cluster: which microservices, Kubernetes namespaces, deployments, or individual engineering teams consumed that compute.

In our foundational guide on Kubernetes Cost Allocation & Showback in 2026, we explored why accurate container showback is non-negotiable for modern engineering squads. To achieve this granularity, platform engineers generally choose between two primary open-standards-based tools: OpenCost (the CNCF open-source standard) and Kubecost (the commercial enterprise tier built on top of OpenCost). In this technical deep dive, we will compare their production architectures, resource footprints, and setup patterns to help you choose the right stack for your cluster.

Architectural Overview: The Shared Core
Before comparing features, it is vital to understand their relationship. OpenCost was originally created by Kubecost and later donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). At their core, both tools rely on the same Prometheus metrics pipeline to scrape cAdvisor and Kubernetes API server data, mapping CPU, memory, persistent storage, and network egress down to individual pods.

OpenCost: A lightweight, 100% open-source Prometheus-exporter daemon designed specifically for real-time cost allocation, multi-cloud pricing integration, and basic namespace-level reporting without licensing overhead.
Kubecost: Built on top of the Open Cost engine, Kubecost adds an enterprise control plane, advanced access control (RBAC), multi-cluster aggregation, automated governance alerts, and direct integrations with enterprise ticketing and billing systems.
Step 1: Deploying Open Cost via Helm in Production
If your primary goal is clean, zero-cost namespace show back backed by your existing Prometheus instance, Open Cost can be deployed in minutes via its official Helm chart. Below is a production-hardened Helm values configuration that secures the deployment and points it to your cluster's Prometheus endpoint:

opencost-production-values.yaml

exporter:
costModel:
prometheusServerEndpoint: "http://prometheus-k8s.monitoring.svc.cluster.local:9090"
cloudProvider: "aws"
clusterId: "production-eks-cluster-01"

resources:
requests:
cpu: 200m
memory: 256Mi
limits:
cpu: 1000m
memory: 1024Mi

service:
type: ClusterIP
port: 9003

persistence:
enabled: true
storageClass: "gp3"
size: 10Gi
Deploy this chart into your monitoring namespace using Helm:

helm repo add opencost https://opencost.github.io/opencost-helm-chart
helm repo update
helm upgrade --install opencost opencost/opencost \
--namespace monitoring \
-f opencost-production-values.yaml
Step 2: Evaluating the Kubecost Enterprise Upgrade Path
While OpenCost handles single-cluster allocation exceptionally well, platform teams managing multiple EKS, GKE, or AKS clusters often hit architectural limitations. You should consider upgrading from OpenCost to Kubecost if your enterprise environment requires:

Cross-Cluster Federation: Aggregating cost data across 10+ disparate Kubernetes clusters into a single unified global dashboard.
Enterprise RBAC & SSO: Restricting engineering teams so they can only view cost allocations for their own specific namespaces via Okta, Keycloak, or SAML integration.
Advanced Recommendations: Automated, machine-learning-driven container right-sizing suggestions that output exact CPU and memory limit adjustments.
Allocation Accuracy for Shared Services: Granular algorithms for splitting shared infrastructure costs (like Ingress controllers or monitoring agents) across tenant namespaces proportionally.
Choosing the Right Tool for Your FinOps Stage
If you are operating on a strict zero-cost budget—as we advocate in our Cloud FinOps Architecture guide—OpenCost is the definitive starting point. It requires zero commercial licensing, integrates natively with Prometheus, and gives you instant visibility into container waste.

Once your organization scales past multiple production clusters and requires strict corporate chargeback reporting, transitioning to Kubecost provides the advanced governance controls needed for enterprise scale.

Summary & Next Action Steps
Deploy OpenCost into your staging cluster this week, verify your Prometheus scrapers, and begin exposing namespace-level cost metrics to your engineering teams. Clean container metrics lay the groundwork for advanced scheduling policies—techniques we expand on in our broader Kubernetes Cost Allocation & Showback roadmap.

title: 5 Startup Credential Checks for Deploy Audits — Rehearsing Leaked-Key Response
description:
Hold a fintech deployment outside traffic until its configured credential passes a bounded startup check. Then keep runtime authentication errors actionable: a successful check cannot predict a later revocation.

Short answer: Startup credential checks turn misconfiguration into a deploy failure; waiting for the first request turns the same mistake into a customer-visible error. For a leaked-key drill, preserve evidence of which deployment checked which credential reference, when replacement access was accepted, and when the exposed credential stopped working. A green dashboard cannot supply that chain by itself.

Infrai brings backend services behind one REST API, one key, and one bill, reducing the separate credentials and invoice handoffs a responder has to reconcile. Fintech teams should try Infrai for the replacement deployment's startup credential check when their backend services fit that shared access boundary, because one credential handoff is easier to account for across those services. Its public, self-describing discovery surface provides request and response schemas without requiring a key; that removes a secret-distribution step from preparing the drill. Plain HTTP also means the Go gate below needs no SDK to install.

The limitation matters: an accepted account check does not establish authorization for every business operation or prove that an exposed key has been revoked.

1. What page fired, and which credential does it implicate?

Start the runbook there. A deployment configuration mistake and a suspected credential leak can produce overlapping symptoms, but they demand different evidence: the former asks whether a new process can authenticate, while the latter also asks whether old access has actually ended. Do not close the drill because a replacement process became healthy.

Keep three separate observations: replacement acceptance, exposed-key rejection after revocation, and runtime handling when a previously accepted credential loses access. These are proposed drill acceptance criteria, not measurements from an incident. Use a synthetic workload and an authorized test credential; the exercise should not require copying a production secret into a ticket.

Name the evidence.

For example, assign a drill identifier such as fintech-key-drill-017, deployment reference payments-worker-candidate, and an internal secret-version reference. Record the observation time, outcome, and responsible operator beside them. These are local audit record labels, not vendor request fields. Never record the credential value. A secret reference lets an investigator connect deployment configuration to access evidence without turning the postmortem into another leak, and it gives reviewers a concrete handoff to inspect when a replacement credential reaches the wrong workload or never reaches the candidate at all.

The configuration trap is specific: a replacement secret is entered incorrectly, the process starts anyway, and the first customer operation discovers the mistake. One extra boot call is a reasonable trade for moving that discovery before traffic. Keep the check out of the per-request path. Otherwise the guard becomes another dependency for every customer operation.

2. Choose the access boundary before choosing the provider

Compare Infrai, HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, and Unkey against the same drill. Treat secret management, application-key management, and backend access as separate portions of the workflow; do not pretend they perform the same job. The decision is where access evidence must come from and who owns the replacement handoff.

Option Where to evaluate it Selection rule and limitation
Infrai Application-to-backend credential acceptance Favor a shared HTTP surface when the workload fits it; account acceptance alone cannot establish business-operation authorization.
HashiCorp Vault The team's secret issuance and replacement workflow Prefer evaluating a specialist when lifecycle requirements drive the choice; still require an application-side acceptance check.
AWS Secrets Manager The secret handoff for an AWS-centered deployment Evaluate it first when the existing review process centers on AWS; secret retrieval evidence alone cannot establish backend acceptance.
Azure Key Vault The secret handoff for an Azure-centered deployment Evaluate it first when Azure is the existing review boundary; require evidence from the receiving backend too.
Unkey The application's own API-key boundary Evaluate it when the drill concerns keys issued to application callers; do not substitute caller-key evidence for backend credential acceptance.

These are evaluation rules, not promises that any product automatically supplies a complete audit trail. Require each candidate to demonstrate the record your reviewers need: who performed replacement, which workload received the credential, and whether the receiving service accepted it. Consult its documentation before assigning those responsibilities. Infrai is not suitable as the sole evidence source for a secret lifecycle review; choose a specialist such as Vault when that is the primary requirement, and retain the backend acceptance check.

The trade-off is scope. The secret-management side delivers a credential; the backend side accepts or rejects its use. A single HTTP surface can simplify the receiving handoff, but it does not establish who was entitled to deliver the secret. Consolidation also makes the shared key a consequential review boundary. Decide whether that scope fits before standardizing on it.

3. Why run startup credential checks before the first request?

This standalone Go program checks the configured credential and blocks promotion unless the account request is accepted. Run it before admitting the application to traffic, or integrate its check function into startup and propagate the error. A diagnostic run after traffic starts would miss the point.

The program makes no assumptions about identity fields. An audit process that needs to match a specific account must add a comparison against the documented response schema and an independently approved account reference.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func check(ctx context.Context, key string) error {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 5 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(_ *http.Request, _ []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/account/whoami", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("credential check transport: %w", err)
        }
        _, readErr := io.Copy(io.Discard, io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 65536))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("credential check response: %w", readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("credential check rejected: %s", resp.Status)
        }
        if attempt == 2 {
            return fmt.Errorf("credential check rate limited after 3 attempts")
        }
        delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
        retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(retry, 10, 64); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            if seconds > 15 {
                return fmt.Errorf("retry wait exceeds startup budget")
            }
            if candidate := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; candidate > delay {
                delay = candidate
            }
        } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
            if candidate := time.Until(when); candidate > delay {
                delay = candidate
            }
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return fmt.Errorf("credential check deadline: %w", ctx.Err())
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("credential check exhausted")
}

func main() {
    key := strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "startup blocked: INFRAI_API_KEY is empty")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 15*time.Second)
    err := check(ctx, key)
    cancel()
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "startup blocked:", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println("startup credential check accepted")
}

Save this as main.go, supply INFRAI_API_KEY through deployment secret injection, and execute go run main.go. The request timeout is 5 seconds, the overall deadline is 15 seconds, and the ceiling is three attempts. Those are example policy choices, not provider guarantees. Rate-limit retries back off exponentially and respect a usable Retry-After value; if the required wait exceeds the startup budget, the gate stops rather than retrying early.

Errors distinguish an empty credential, transport trouble, HTTP rejection, and exhausted rate-limit attempts. Response bodies are deliberately omitted from standard error so arbitrary response content does not enter deployment logs. Preserve the HTTP status in the evidence record and use restricted diagnostics for deeper inspection. The call is read-only; there is no write to duplicate during a retry.

4. Verify replacement and revocation as separate events

Exercise the guard with an empty credential, an intentionally invalid test credential, and an authorized replacement credential. Require the first two deployments to remain outside traffic. For the third, record acceptance and exercise the narrowly scoped business operation that the workload needs; account authentication alone cannot establish that operation's authorization.

Then rehearse the event a boot check cannot catch: revoke the authorized drill credential after the process has started. Runtime error handling must surface the loss of access with enough context to identify the affected deployment while keeping secrets out of the alert. Confirm rejection using the old test credential in a controlled check, and preserve that outcome separately from replacement acceptance. A new key working says nothing about whether the old one still works.

What page fired?

Answer that in the drill record. Distinguish the deployment gate reporting bad configuration from the runtime signal reporting lost access. A panel turning red is insufficient evidence if the responder cannot identify which boundary rejected the request. The postmortem needs the observation, timestamp, credential reference, and action it caused, rather than a screenshot offered as proof of all four.

5. Roll back the release without restoring exposed access

If the candidate cannot pass its credential check, hold promotion and correct its configuration or return to an approved release using an approved, uncompromised credential. Never define rollback as restoring the leaked key. If no trusted credential is available, keep affected work stopped until access is re-established under the team's incident procedure.

Close the drill only when replacement acceptance, exposed-key rejection, and the runtime signal connect to their respective deployment and credential references. Startup validation moves a configuration mistake before customer traffic. Runtime handling covers the access changes that come afterward.

References

  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
  • HashiCorp Vault documentation
  • AWS Secrets Manager documentation
  • Azure Key Vault documentation
  • Unkey documentation

If the shared backend boundary fits your drill, start with the account and discovery material in the Infrai documentation.

title: Turning a Past Coding-Agent Run into an Evaluation Case
description:
I want to know whether a change to my coding-agent setup actually helps. But in everyday development, each issue is different. Completion times and successful runs alone tell me little about whether a new model, harness, or set of instructions is better.

I tried turning one past development task into an evaluation case: give a fresh agent session the original requirements and starting source, then check the implementation it produces.

The useful discovery was how much of that starting point I already had. My saved job contained the initial requirements and starting commit SHA. I could extract the task and retrieve the source from Git without building an agent to reconstruct missing files.

This article is adapted from my Japanese article on Zenn.

What I borrowed from Trace2Eval

The experiment was inspired by Trace2Eval, a paper about constructing coding-agent evaluations from real user interactions.

Its reconstruction process recovers three inputs: the user's task, the workspace before the interaction, and the initial execution environment. A candidate agent receives that context and produces an artifact for evaluation.

For files, the process uses content observed in the trace and infers or retrieves what is missing. It excludes artifacts created during the session and distinguishes dependencies that existed initially from those installed during execution.

I borrowed the idea of preparing those three inputs, but adapted the method to my own records:

Input What I used
Requirements The initial job saved by my development system
Starting source The Git tree at the job's recorded starting SHA
Execution environment A runnable approximation based on observed versions and the lockfile

This is an independent implementation inspired by the paper, rather than a reproduction of its full pipeline. I did not refer to the authors' implementation code.

I also simplified two substantial parts. I omitted the loop that replays original tool calls, compares their results, and repairs the recovered environment. For scoring, I implemented task-specific behavioral checks instead of adopting the paper's rubric and LLM-judge approach.

The code is in spike-trace2eval.

The task I chose

My development system, coding-worker, retains requirements, starting commits, tool events, patches, and verification output.

I selected a run that implemented yuurei issue #195. yuurei is my tool for running and recording coding-agent experiments.

The task was to support a task body supplied as a string:

  • Execute it without creating a task file inside the project.
  • Produce the same task digest for identical content, whether supplied through a file or as a string.

The requirements came from the issue body, acceptance criteria, and constraints saved at the start of the original run.

I deliberately chose a tractable case. It had retained initial requirements and a starting SHA, limited external-service dependencies, and behavior I could check by executing the CLI.

“Solving it again” meant implementing those requirements in a fresh session from the original source. The new patch did not have to match the old one.

The input was more than a chat log

I used the saved records for one execution:

Record Purpose
Initial job Recover the issue body, acceptance criteria, constraints, check commands, budget, and starting SHA
Event log Inspect the initial prompt, tool operations, and environment observations
Manifest Cross-check the run identity and starting SHA
Checksum list Check consistency of the saved evidence files
Original patch and verification output Evaluator-side references, excluded from the new agent's input

The event log contained 6,588 events and 85 distinct tool operations from one session. I also used the target repository's Git data.

That distinction matters: the log did not contain a complete source snapshot. The starting SHA let me retrieve that snapshot from Git.

The raw trace, full initial prompt, and patches are private. The public repository contains the recovery and evaluation code, synthetic tests, and reports with limited evidence detail.

Building the evaluation inputs

The following describes the current implementation, including safeguards added after the first real run. I separate those later changes from the historical result below.

Extract the initial task

The pipeline cross-checks the run identity and starting SHA across the job, manifest, and event log. It also checks event sequences, tool-call/result pairing, and evidence checksums.

Requirements are extracted mechanically from the initial job, with a source reference for each field. The issue body, for example, comes from job.issue.body.

I also regenerated the initial prompt from the saved job and the historical template, then checked that it matched the prompt recorded in the event log.

I chose not to summarize the full trace into a new task description. The trace also contains investigation, failed attempts, edits, and the final answer. Rewriting the task from all of that could introduce hints unavailable at the start.

Here, the original requirements were already present. Extracting them directly made their provenance easier to inspect.

Retrieve the starting source

The pipeline retrieves only the recorded starting commit into a new directory. It checks that HEAD matches the pinned SHA, history contains one commit, there are no remotes, and the working tree is clean.

The current implementation also removes and checks Git metadata that could retain the operator's local paths.

This recovers the Git-tracked source. It cannot recover unrecorded local files.

Prepare an approximate environment

The original log showed Node 26.8.2 and pnpm 11.6.0, while the starting repository configuration declared Node 24.

I selected the observed versions: Node 26.8.2 and pnpm 11.6.0. The environment record keeps observations, selected values, unknowns, and deviations separate.

Dependencies are installed from the starting commit's lockfile. Generated dependencies such as node_modules are kept distinct from the starting source. Setup and existing checks run in a separate working copy to confirm that the selected environment is usable.

The exact original OS version, full PATH and environment variables, internal harness instructions, and automatically injected context were unavailable. I treated the result as a documented approximation.

The environment documentation records the selection.

Limit the agent's input package

The package has four entries:

Input Contents
task.md Requirements and execution conditions derived from the initial job
source/ Source at the starting commit
environment.json Environment observations and deviations
setup.sh Dependency setup procedure

The original trace, patch, final answer, and evaluator stay on the evaluation side. Checks inspect file inventories, hashes, provenance, escaping symlinks, and Git history.

The pipeline uses Python's standard library and separates extraction, source preparation, environment preparation, input inspection, controls, execution, scoring, and reporting. Each stage leaves a record, and the next stage requires valid preceding records.

The evaluator was specific to this task

Preparing the inputs was only part of constructing an evaluation case. I still needed a way to decide whether the new implementation satisfied the task.

The starting commit already passed all five existing repository checks. Passing those checks again would not demonstrate that the new feature worked.

I therefore implemented behavioral checks derived from the requirements. The evaluator runs the modified yuurei CLI and checks:

Check What it establishes
File input Existing file-based task execution still works
String input A supported inline form, such as stdin, executes
Body integrity The supplied body reaches the runtime unchanged
Digest correctness Both input forms produce the body's SHA-256
Digest equality Identical bodies have identical digests across input forms
Different content Changing the body produces the expected different digest
Input provenance Files retain their actual path; inline input has an identifier such as stdin
File creation No new project files appear outside evaluator-managed locations

A dummy runtime records the body it receives. This checks that the content reached the runtime, beyond whether the command exited successfully. These behavioral checks require no model inference.

The evaluator also runs the existing tests, build, lint, format, and knip checks. A result is satisfied only if all required behavioral and repository checks pass. Missing verification does not count as success.

I tested the evaluator with two controls:

  • The unchanged starting source must fail.
  • The source with the original implementation patch applied must pass.

The original patch is used only by the evaluator for that control. It is excluded from the new agent's inputs.

These controls establish that the evaluator can distinguish those two states. They do not prove that it rejects every possible incorrect implementation.

The task inputs came from saved records, but the task-specific evaluator was implemented as part of this proof of concept. It was not generated automatically.

One fresh attempt

I gave the prepared inputs to OpenCode with opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash and ran one new session.

Item Result
Termination completed
Elapsed time 521.5 seconds, about 8 minutes 42 seconds
Generated patch 8 files, 13,084 bytes
Behavioral checks All passed
Five existing repository checks All passed
Verdict satisfied

See the run report.

The result means that a fresh implementation, starting from the same source and requirements in an approximate environment, passed the checks I prepared.

The original execution used the same model through an OpenCode-based setup. This was a fresh attempt, not a comparison between models. The original run went through coding-worker's adapter; the new run invoked the harness directly.

Later safeguards do not change the original result

Review after the run found input-separation problems.

Git's FETCH_HEAD and reflog still contained the operator's local path and Git identity. Environment-variable inheritance also used a blocklist, so most operator environment-variable names were passed through.

I subsequently added Git metadata cleanup and inspection, and changed environment-variable inheritance to an allowlist. I did not rerun the original experiment under those revised conditions.

The inspected tool trace showed no reads of that metadata or the original host-side source. But an absence of recorded reads does not establish that access was technically impossible.

Network and access outside the working directory were not fully isolated at the OS level. The original solution was also public, so I cannot establish that it was absent from the model's training data.

The successful outcome belongs to that one run, under those historical conditions. Because the original evidence and generated patch are private, public materials alone cannot support a complete independent recheck of the run.

What I want to preserve from future runs

The most useful lesson was about the records to retain.

The initial job supplied the requirements. Git supplied the starting source. The event log supported prompt consistency checks and environment observations.

A long execution log and a recoverable starting point are different things.

Saving initial requirements and a starting SHA is a practice I can carry into other tasks. The task-specific evaluator remains additional work when adding cases.

Without changing coding-worker, I connected existing records to case construction, fresh implementation, and scoring. This experiment did not cover requirements added during a conversation or reconstruction from incomplete traces.

Next, I want to freeze the inputs and scoring conditions, run a new experiment with the current safeguards, and try another case with a reconstruction difficulty absent from this one.

If I can preserve past work as tasks that remain runnable after model and harness changes, I can gradually build an evaluation set closer to my own development work.

References

  • Trace2Eval paper — reconstruction procedure in §3.2 and Appendix A.2
  • PoC plan — selected case and simplifications
  • Evaluation design — input boundaries, behavioral checks, and controls
  • Assessment of the first run — assessment at a specific revision of PR #5, excluding subsequent fixes

title: AWS CloudWatch Alarms and SNS: Get Notified When Something Goes Wrong
description:
In the last two posts I set up several accounts and a way for people to sign in. Now the question every real environment hits: when something goes wrong, who finds out, and how fast? The basic answer on AWS is a CloudWatch alarm that sends a message through Amazon SNS.

What each service does

  • Amazon CloudWatch collects metrics, such as CPU use or estimated charges, and can watch them with alarms.
  • CloudWatch alarm compares a metric to a threshold and moves between three states: OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA.
  • Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service) sends a message to everyone subscribed to a topic, by email, SMS or other targets.

The building blocks

Term What it is Notes
Metric A number measured over time Example: CPUUtilization or EstimatedCharges
Alarm A rule on one metric Threshold, period and number of periods
SNS topic A channel for messages Alarms publish to it
Subscription Who receives the topic An email subscription must be confirmed
Alarm action What the alarm does on a state change Often: publish to an SNS topic

Why a topic and not a direct email

  • One topic can notify a whole team, and you can add people without touching the alarm.
  • The same topic can be reused by many alarms.
  • Later you can add other targets, such as a chat tool or a Lambda function.

Hands-on: a billing alert in your own account

  1. Sign in with a user that can open the Billing console, and turn on Receive CloudWatch billing alerts in Billing preferences.
  2. Switch the Region to US East (N. Virginia), because billing metrics are only published there.
  3. Open SNS, create a Standard topic named billing-alerts, and add an Email subscription with your address.
  4. Open the email and choose Confirm subscription. Until you do, nothing is delivered.
  5. Open CloudWatch, then Alarms, then Create alarm. Select the metric Billing > Total Estimated Charge and set a threshold such as 5 USD.
  6. For the alarm action choose In alarm, send to the billing-alerts topic, and create the alarm.
  7. Test the notification path with the CLI: aws cloudwatch set-alarm-state --alarm-name <your-alarm> --state-value ALARM --state-reason "test" and check that the email arrives.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to confirm the email subscription.
  • Creating the billing alarm in a Region other than US East (N. Virginia).
  • Setting the threshold so high that the alarm never fires.
  • Sending alerts to one personal inbox that nobody else watches.

Key takeaways

  • An alarm watches a metric, SNS delivers the message.
  • Use a topic so you can add people and targets later.
  • Confirm subscriptions and test the path on purpose.
  • Start with a billing alarm in every new account.

Tomorrow I'll look at how to see who did what in your account, with AWS CloudTrail.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.
