title: Wanted a Dictation App, Got Three Libraries
description:
I swapped my M2 MacBook with the old design for a new fanless M5 Air. A new computer feels like a clean start. So instead of dragging all my old apps and settings along, I went looking for lighter and more native alternatives. For example, I replaced VS Code with Zed and Chrome with Helium.

To talk to agents, I used a dictation app called Handy. But I really didn't like that it's built on Tauri, and I wanted something native. I asked an agent to find an alternative, but nothing it found worked for me. So I decided to write my own.

People on X are rewriting everything in GPUI Kit right now, so I decided to try it too. The author of Handy had also moved the speech recognition engine into a separate project called transcribe.cpp. So the task looked easy, especially with agents.

Week 1. Picking a GUI and prototypes

So I took GPUI Kit, the one everyone on X was hyping, and quickly built the first version of the UI with agents. It came out pretty well: the app with an open window used about 80 MB of RAM. But compiling was painfully slow. Part of it was GPUI Kit itself, and part was linking transcribe.cpp, which took about a minute on every rebuild.

I also didn't like that GPUI Kit pulls in over 400 dependencies, just like Node.js. Who knows what malware might be hiding in there? Besides, GPUI from Zed isn't a finished library with stable releases. So GPUI Kit depends on a dev version from the Zed repo, and the API can change at any moment. Another problem is integration with the system, like a tray icon or a native context menu. GPUI Kit doesn't have it, so all of that has to be written by hand.

I decided to look at other options in the Rust ecosystem. Back in the pre-agent era, I played with egui for UIs, and it left a good impression. It really was faster and lighter on memory, and it pulled in fewer crates. But all the native integrations still have to be written by hand, and the components need a lot of customizing to look nice.

I also tried native controls: Rust bindings to the system UI libraries (AppKit on macOS, Win32 on Windows and GTK on Linux). The idea came from another project I saw on X, mygo, which builds native desktop UIs in Go. But in practice I had to write a huge pile of integration code and repeat it at least three times. The app looked native on each platform, but so different that some features couldn't be done properly. And that's for a dictation app, which is literally a settings menu, a list of models and a history.

The most annoying thing the whole time was rebuilding: every launch meant waiting almost a minute for transcribe.cpp to link. And I didn't really get why there should be C++ in my Rust toolchain at all. So I decided to look at what's going on inside.

Week 2. My own speech recognition engine

Inside transcribe.cpp there was ggml, which has separate code for each GPU backend (Metal, Vulkan and CUDA). Each one needs its own tools to build. Rust has wgpu, where shaders are written once in WGSL and run on any GPU. And everything builds with a plain cargo build.

I got curious whether I could run at least one model on WGSL, though I had no plans to rewrite anything yet. I took GigaAM v3, which I use most often, and made a small demo with it. To my surprise, the agent wrote the shader code easily, and the results were close to the original library.

That's when it became a challenge for me. I remembered optimizing math on the secp256k1 curve in ecloop and optimizing RIPEMD-160, and kept digging. The first model was GigaAM v3 e2e RNN-T, which outputs punctuation and capital letters. I also decided to add other models from the same family to see how hard it would be. They differ in the decoder. CTC recognizes each piece of audio on its own, while RNN-T also looks at the text it has already written, so it's more accurate but slower. Each of them also has a version with punctuation (e2e) and one without.

I dictate in two languages, Russian and English. Since adding Russian was easy, I thought English wouldn't be a problem either. NVIDIA's Parakeet v2 is a good fit for English because it's accurate and fast. But when I started adding it, I found out that models come in different architectures, and each one needs its own compute code.

I took the models already packed into GGUF by the author of transcribe.cpp. It turned out that GGUF stores only the weights and some metadata about the model: the architecture name, layer sizes and vocabulary. The computations aren't in the file, so they have to be written by hand. That's the difference from TensorFlow or Apple's Core ML, where the model file describes a graph of operations and the runtime just executes it.

So I had to sit down and figure it out by reading and watching YouTube videos about how speech recognition models work. In short, long audio is cut into chunks (Whisper, for example, uses 30-second windows). Each chunk goes through a fast Fourier transform (FFT) and becomes a spectrogram (which frequencies sound at each moment). The encoder (a stack of neural network layers that mostly multiply matrices) takes the spectrogram and turns it into a sequence of vectors. The decoder reads them and outputs tokens (pieces of words) one step at a time, and these tokens make up the text. Most of the work is matrix multiplication in the encoder layers, and that's what the GPU computes.

Once I understood how it works, I added support for Parakeet v2. Codex wrote the first version overnight, but the code was messy, so I threw it away and rewrote it cleanly with Claude Code. In the end I got a pretty fast speech-to-text program that beat transcribe.cpp in my tests. Since I was on a roll, I right away added Parakeet v3, a multilingual model from the same family (I barely had to write anything new). Right after it came Whisper, as a reference model to compare the others against.

Parakeet differs from GigaAM in plenty of ways. The model is bigger (24 layers vs 16, and each one is wider). It compresses audio twice as much (one vector per 80 ms instead of 40). It also has a different way to mark when each word was said. But the main difference is the decoder (TDT): along with each token, it predicts how many of the next audio frames it can skip.

The program was turning out so well that I decided to release it as a separate project in the style of ollama. I named it wavo, kind of from WAV, and the name was free. Besides, I had needed local audio transcription before, and there was nothing good for it in the terminal. I tried whisper.cpp, but it's slow and inconvenient (it has to be compiled from source, and the audio has to be cut into chunks by hand).

Before publishing, I decided to clean up the code. The rustfft crate was still slowing down the build. People can use wavo as a library, so everyone who builds it would get that delay too. Once I found the cause, I wrote my own FFT just for this task. It came out at 176 lines of code vs 55,000 in rustfft, and rebuilds went from 11.9 down to 2.1 seconds. The crate itself is good, it's just built for every case, and I needed only one.

The last step before publishing was testing. Luckily, I have a few Macs at hand, an N100 box with Linux and an x86 machine with a GeForce card and a good CPU. I had the agent run the final tests and compare the speed with other libraries. On Macs my library crushed everyone on speed, no question (I'm still shocked it was that easy). But on Windows with an NVIDIA card it was a big failure. Again I had to dig in, and it turned out there's a thing called flash attention.

Attention is the part of the model where each vector is compared with all the others in the same audio chunk. For Whisper that's 1,500 vectors per 30 seconds, so more than two million comparisons in each layer. Regular code writes this whole table to GPU memory and then reads it back. Flash attention computes the same thing in small pieces in fast memory next to the GPU cores and never stores the whole table.

On Macs, the agent had already made such shaders earlier, but for Apple's matrix units (hardware acceleration). NVIDIA's units have a different size, so on NVIDIA wavo computed everything with generic code. After I added shaders for NVIDIA's matrix units, wavo on Windows caught up with transcribe.cpp and in some cases beat it. A short Whisper turbo recording now takes 201 ms vs 226 ms for transcribe.cpp, down from 637.

I made all the measurements on an RTX 4060 and didn't test on AMD Radeon at all. So I'd be glad to see results from other GPUs in issues.

During testing I also found that on M5, wgpu uses only the old matrix units. The M5 got a neural accelerator in each GPU core, which multiplies matrices three times faster (0.60 ms vs 1.89 ms). But it's only available through Metal 4, and wgpu doesn't support it yet. I worked around this with a separate Metal shader just for M5 and opened an issue in wgpu.

I also taught wavo to run on the Neural Engine (a separate part of Apple chips for neural networks), but that's another story. At the end, I ran a final comparison of Parakeet v3 in English against other engines, and the numbers looked impressive.

Engine Runs on 5 s phrase 1 h recording
wavo Neural Engine 0.12 s 200×
FluidAudio Neural Engine 0.13 s 175×
wavo GPU 0.14 s 160×
transcribe.cpp GPU 0.12 s 107×
parakeet.cpp GPU 0.77 s 90×
parakeet-mlx GPU 0.63 s 61×
sherpa-onnx CPU 0.83 s 39×

The table shows the time for a 5-second phrase and how many times faster than real time a one-hour recording gets transcribed (MacBook Pro on M5). In Russian with GigaAM v3 the gap is similar: wavo is 330 times faster than real time, and transcribe.cpp is 262 times faster.

Week 3. My own renderer

While I worked on wavo, another agent was experimenting with a UI library in the background. Every approach still needed a lot of hand-written wrappers to talk to the OS, so I decided I could write the renderer myself too. I also had some experience with UIs in video games, so the task seemed simple.

I've long been a fan of Sublime Text, and especially Sublime Merge, and their approach to UI. I thought that if the authors of these apps and of the Zed editor could write their own UI framework, then I, armed with an agent, could too. Armed with strings and nm, we looked at which system functions Sublime Merge uses and figured out the idea behind it. It was an interesting one ;)

The text there is drawn by the system itself (CoreText on macOS, DirectWrite on Windows, Pango on Linux), so it looks native everywhere. That's unlike egui, for example, which draws glyphs on its own. The system draws each glyph once and it goes into a cache, and after that the screen gets ready glyphs from the cache. Context menus work the same way and come from the system (GPUI Kit draws them itself by default).

So it turned into a kind of Frankenstein. The edges are system stuff, and in the middle, like the filling in a sandwich, is my library, which lays out elements in the window and builds components from them.

Rendering uses immediate mode (the frame is built from scratch every time, without a complex event system). Regular apps don't have that much interactivity, and a settings window doesn't need to be redrawn 60 or 120 times per second. Besides, the frame is rebuilt only when something changes, and an idle window draws nothing.

I decided to draw the frame itself on the CPU. It's the simplest code, and it works the same everywhere, without shaders, drivers and other junk that has to be integrated and then tested too. The finished frame goes to the system's regular 2D window output. For an app without complex animations, that's more than fast enough.

3D acceleration pulls in extra libraries, and the program starts eating more memory (on Windows a simple window with D3D11 takes 27 MB instead of 5.1). But if it's ever needed, I can always add it later.

The renderer itself came out at about 3,000 lines of Rust, and the agent quickly put together the basic components on top of it (around 6,000 more lines). Everything worked, and it seemed like the job was almost done.

Next I needed a context menu and a small popup that shows the text being dictated. That's where the pain and suffering began, especially when I ran everything on real computers with Linux and Windows instead of VMs.

Now I understand why there were so few GUI frameworks in the pre-agent era. The hard part isn't writing a renderer and a component system at all. The hard part is wiring all of it together on different platforms so that it works. Each cross-platform feature can easily take several thousand lines for three systems:

  • windows (open them, drag them and draw in them): 5,000 lines;
  • text fields and IME: 4,000;
  • tray, hotkeys and autostart: 7,000;
  • accessibility on macOS: 3,000;
  • native context menu: 2,000.

Of course the agent writes the code, but someone still has to read it, check it and test it on each system, and that's a lot of work.

For example, a context menu can be drawn by the app's own renderer, and that's how GPUI in Zed does it. But it looks janky, and more importantly, such a menu can't go outside the window. I had never thought about this before, but once I started writing, I realized it matters. Sublime Merge can do it, and I give it credit for that.

As expected, Linux was the biggest pain. On macOS and Windows everything goes through one system API, but Linux is a damn zoo. At first I tried to draw separately on X11 and Wayland to make the program as optimized as possible, but the amount of code grew exponentially. So I made a compromise and took GTK 3, which is on almost every distro. Sublime Merge does the same.

I named the library nimbo. A simple counter window built with it pulls in 14 crates on macOS, 5 on Windows and 3 on Linux. Almost all of them are system bindings, like objc2 on macOS and windows-sys on Windows. It builds from scratch in 11 seconds, and the binary is 1.3 MB. For comparison, here is the same counter on other frameworks (the number of crates on each system, a clean release build on M2 and the binary size):

macOS Windows Linux Build Binary
nimbo 14 5 3 11 s 1.3 MB
iced 152 159 237 59 s 10.9 MB
Tauri¹ 217 223 265 64 s 9.9 MB
Xilem 157 177 257 65 s 12.2 MB
egui 177 178 279 74 s 14.3 MB
Slint 248 244 345 84 s 12.5 MB
GPUI 300 270 322 86 s 8.6 MB
GPUI Kit 411 395 518 144 s 19.4 MB

¹ Plus the system WebView, which isn't part of the binary.

In the era of personal software and endless hacks, I want my own foundation for this kind of program, without depending on other people's frameworks. So I decided to finish nimbo properly. There's no first release yet because I'm still working on the API, so I have no time to make cool videos for X. But if you need something minimal in Rust, you're welcome to try it.

The library is built in three layers. At the bottom is a common API for system stuff (windows, tray, context menu and so on), so the app code never has to touch it at all. Above it are headless components (behavior without styling), and any design can be built on top of them. On top is a base design in the style of system controls. The model for the library's API is SwiftUI.

Week 4. Release: signing, packaging, updates

The program is ready and tested, and all that's left is to ship a release. But that turned out to be not so simple either. There were three problems: signing, packaging and auto-update, and they took the last week.

Signing

In recent versions of macOS and Windows, unsigned apps just don't run. Windows is easier: SmartScreen shows a warning on the first launch, and once the user accepts it, the app starts. On macOS, though, the quarantine has to be removed from an unsigned app by hand with /usr/bin/xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Wavo.app, and a regular user is unlikely to do that.

I had to pay Apple $99 a year. And their payment form is straight from the early 2000s: I had to type in my card details by hand, and Apple charged the card on its own sometime later. In the end the charge failed on 3-D Secure. I had to temporarily lower the protection on my card and ask support to retry the payment, and the whole thing dragged on for several days. I can't remember the last time I saw something like that.

Packaging

A program for three systems needs installers for all three. On macOS the standard is a DMG. On Windows it's a setup.exe that installs the program, usually made with NSIS. On Linux it's an AppImage and a .deb package. Linux actually has more formats, but for now I picked these two.

At first it seemed easy to do with a Python script, so I gave that to the agent. There was one requirement: build and signing are separate. The build step downloads and compiles other people's code, so it must not have access to the signing keys. The second step only signs the finished files.

The script quickly grew to almost 2,000 lines. That surprised me, and I went looking for ready solutions, since after so many years someone must have solved this. I found a few (Velopack, cargo-packager and the Tauri bundler), but each has its own problems. Some can't separate build from signing. The worst part is that almost none of them can do everything on one machine (DMG and signing for macOS only on a Mac, deb and AppImage only on Linux, and Windows also needs NSIS). Velopack can build everything at once, but only on a Mac. In my opinion this is crazy. Packaging and signing should work on one computer, and ideally on any computer.

I looked through other people's repos, and from what I saw, only Mozilla does it properly. They package Firefox on Linux, even the DMG for macOS, but with wild hacks. For DMG they have their own fork of the C library libdmg-hfsplus, which has no prebuilt releases, and their CI builds it straight from the repo at a specific commit. To use it myself, I would have to pull an artifact out of someone else's unversioned build, and I didn't want that. Well, I had an agent, so I gave this job to it too.

At first I wanted to make it part of nimbo. Then I realized it's a completely separate program and moved it to its own crate, shipo.

The main idea of shipo is that all installers can be built on any machine, even on Linux. Everything that exists on only one system (hdiutil on macOS, makensis for Windows, apt packages on Linux) is replaced with its own code. The other tools are downloaded at a pinned version and hash.

For macOS, shipo writes the DMG itself, together with the HFS+ file system per Apple's spec. It even includes the Unicode tables HFS+ uses to normalize file names. It also writes the .DS_Store that places the app icon and the /Applications shortcut in the window. It builds the .icns icon itself too, without sips and iconutil. Signing and notarization outside a Mac go through rcodesign and Apple's notarization service.

For Windows, the installer is custom too. It's a small prebuilt setup.exe in Rust with an empty marker inside. The packager replaces the icon, version and manifest in the app's exe and compresses the files into one archive. Then it appends the archive to the end of setup.exe and writes into the marker where that archive is. The uninstaller is the same setup.exe, just without the files.

For Linux, AppImage (a prebuilt runtime with a squashfs image of the app appended to it) and deb are built right in memory.

Auto-update

The third thing actually has nothing to do with packaging, but I had to do it too. On macOS many apps update with Sparkle, but it works only on macOS. For Windows there's WinSparkle, which has a similar idea but is a different library. I wanted one thing for all systems, but didn't find anything here either. I decided that building and updating are close things and can live in one crate, so I made them together.

The idea of auto-update is simple. Each release also includes a small file that describes the latest version. The app reads it from time to time, and if the version is newer, it downloads and installs the update by itself.

In shipo it's one text file, update.txt, in the latest release on GitHub:

version 1.2.0
notes https://github.com/me/hello/releases/tag/v1.2.0
macos-aarch64 394788 <sha512> https://github.com/me/hello/releases/download/v1.2.0/Hello-v1.2.0-macos-aarch64.dmg
windows-x86_64 285930 <sha512> https://github.com/me/hello/releases/download/v1.2.0/Hello-v1.2.0-windows-x64-setup.exe
linux-x86_64 412204 <sha512> https://github.com/me/hello/releases/download/v1.2.0/Hello-v1.2.0-linux-x86_64.AppImage
sig <signature>

It has the version, a link to the release notes, and a line for each platform (size, SHA-512 hash and file URL). At the end is an Ed25519 signature of everything above. No separate update server is needed. The app just downloads the file from the latest GitHub release by a permanent link (releases/latest/download/update.txt).

The app checks the downloaded file by size and hash. It has two signing keys, a main one and a backup. If the main one leaks, the next release is signed with the backup.

The update uses the same installer as the first install. On macOS the library mounts the DMG, copies the app from it and replaces the old one. On Windows it runs setup.exe without a window. On Linux it replaces the AppImage file.

shipo has no separate HTTP library. Instead it has three short wrappers over the system ones (NSURLSession on macOS, WinHTTP on Windows, libcurl on Linux). So the updater has few dependencies: signature checking, errors and system bindings.

So in a week I got shipo, about 12,000 lines of code. Roughly 10,000 of them are the packager (with the setup.exe stub), and 2,400 are the library that goes into the app. Its packager builds installers for all three systems on one machine. The updater adds only 8–15 crates to the app depending on the system (Velopack and cargo-packager have over a hundred). In the end, releasing an app properly and setting up CI turned out to be harder than writing a UI renderer.

Wrap up

A program for a couple of days turned into a month of work. In that time there were about 850 commits and 167,000 changed lines (including prototypes and code I later threw away). Working with agents took about 90 active hours and 3.7 billion tokens, which is roughly $2,700 at API prices. The numbers are approximate because some agent logs got lost.

Most of the code was written by Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra did the reviews. Copilot on GitHub did about 390 more reviews until I hit its limit. Codex drew the graphics and images.

The work didn't end there. For anyone besides family and friends to hear about the program, I have to write about it on Reddit, X and other places, and that's a big separate job too. While doing it, I found a lot of similar programs. If I had seen them at the start, I probably wouldn't have built mine at all. But what's done is done. In the end I got my own cross-platform stack, and I hope to reuse it for other things.

All the programs from the post once more:

  • Wavo: local dictation for macOS, Windows and Linux;
  • wavo: CLI and Rust crate for speech recognition in the style of ollama;
  • nimbo: native UI library with almost no dependencies;
  • shipo: installers and auto-update for three systems from one machine.

I wanted to make one small dictation app, and got an app and three libraries for it.

title: From Beginner to Full-Stack Developer: What I'm Learning Along the Way
description:
From Beginner to Full-Stack Developer: What I'm Learning Along the Way

Becoming a full-stack developer is more than just learning how to write code. It's about understanding how different technologies work together, solving problems, and continuously improving your skills.

As someone building projects and exploring modern web development, I've learned that the journey is not always easy—but every challenge brings an opportunity to grow.

1. Learning the Frontend

The frontend is where users interact with an application.

I've been exploring technologies such as:

  • React for building interactive user interfaces.
  • JavaScript and TypeScript for application logic.
  • Tailwind CSS for responsive and modern designs.

One important lesson I've learned is that a good interface should not only look attractive but also provide a smooth user experience.

2. Understanding Backend Development

A frontend application needs a reliable backend to manage data, authentication, and business logic.

Laravel has become one of the technologies I'm interested in using for backend development.

Some of the concepts I'm continuously learning include:

  • RESTful API development.
  • Authentication and authorization.
  • Database relationships.
  • CRUD operations.
  • Request validation and error handling.

Understanding these concepts helps me build applications that are more organized, maintainable, and scalable.

3. Working With Databases

Databases are an essential part of almost every application.

I've been working with technologies such as MySQL and SQLite while learning how to structure tables, establish relationships, and manage application data.

A well-designed database can make an application easier to maintain and improve as it grows.

4. Learning Git and Team Collaboration

One of the most valuable skills I've been developing is using Git and GitHub.

Working with branches, commits, pull requests, and code reviews has helped me understand how developers collaborate on real-world projects.

I've also learned that communication and teamwork are just as important as technical skills.

5. Exploring AI-Powered Development Tools

AI tools are becoming useful companions for developers.

They can help explain unfamiliar code, identify potential bugs, generate ideas, and improve development workflows.

However, I believe developers should still understand the code they write. AI should support learning and problem-solving rather than replace critical thinking.

6. Every Project Is an Opportunity to Learn

Building projects has taught me that real learning happens when theory meets practice.

Not every feature works on the first attempt. Sometimes there are dependency conflicts, unexpected errors, database problems, or confusing bugs.

But debugging those problems is part of becoming a better developer.

Final Thoughts

My journey toward becoming a full-stack developer is still ongoing.

I'm continuously learning, experimenting with different technologies, and building projects that challenge my current knowledge.

My biggest takeaway so far is simple:

You don't have to know everything to start building. You just have to be willing to learn something new every day.

If you're also learning software development, keep building, keep experimenting, and don't be afraid of making mistakes.

Every experienced developer was once a beginner.

What technology are you currently learning, and what has been your biggest challenge so far? Let's connect and learn together!

AI Hypercomputer

Feature

Generally available: Pathways on Cloud is now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Major features include the following:

  • Single-controller execution model: Coordinate multi-slice and multi-host Cloud TPU workloads from a single Python client process. Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and centralized scheduling to support both Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) and Multiple Program, Multiple Data (MPMD) workloads. For example, training and reinforcement learning (RL) loops.
  • Resilient and elastic training: Keep training jobs running across hardware interruptions with resilient training, including the following capabilities:
    • Elastic training: Dynamically scale down to healthy Cloud TPU slices during unplanned hardware failures and scale back up when replacement slices rejoin without restarting the entire job.
    • Suspend-resume: Automatically save and restore high-bandwidth memory (HBM) state to Cloud Storage during planned GKE preemption events.
    • Hot-swapping: Remap interrupted workloads onto standby or lower-priority Cloud TPU slices.
  • Colocated Python sidecar containers: Run custom Python code directly on Cloud TPU host VMs alongside Pathways workers. For example, multi-host data loading with Grain or RemoteIterator, and distributed asynchronous checkpointing with Orbax.
  • Interactive mode and Shared Pathways Service: Run, inspect, and debug JAX workloads interactively from a notebook or terminal using interactive mode, or share a long-running pool of Cloud TPU slices on demand across multiple users and jobs with the Shared Pathways Service.
  • Cluster Director, Cluster Toolkit, and GKE integration: Launch JAX workloads on the Pathways runtime using Cluster Director or Cluster Toolkit (gcluster with --pathways and --pathways-headless), or by deploying Kubernetes JobSet manifests on GKE.
  • pathwaysutils utility package: Use the pathwaysutils Python package for advanced features such as the Shared Pathways Service, elasticity, and experimental.reshard for device-side data transfers across hosts over Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) or Data Center Network (DCN).
  • Standard libtpu.so layering and custom libtpu.so support: Pathways is layered over the standard libtpu.so shared library and provides a way to dynamically link in a user-provided libtpu.so at runtime using PathwaysJobSet.with_custom_libtpu in pathwaysutils.
  • Single-process profiling, observability, and compilation cache: Capture end-to-end JAX profiler traces across the client, proxy, resource manager, and Cloud TPU hosts from a single process. Reuse compiled XLA modules with a persistent compilation cache on Cloud Storage, and view Pathways control and data plane metrics in Cloud Monitoring.
  • Agentic workload debugging: Troubleshoot failed, crashing, or stalled Pathways workloads on GKE using the pathways-workload agent skill. With this skill, AI agents can inspect Cloud Logging container logs, node kernel logs, and GKE events to help identify root causes and fixes.
  • Supported Cloud TPU versions, JAX versions, and container images: Supports TPU7x (Ironwood), TPU v6e (Trillium), TPU v5p, and TPU v5e for JAX versions 0.12.0.1, 0.12.0, 0.11.2, 0.11.1, 0.11.0, 0.10.2, and 0.10.1, with container images published in Artifact Registry:
    • Image locations:
      • Pathways resource manager and worker: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/server:TAG
      • IFRT proxy server: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/proxy_server:TAG
      • Colocated Python sidecar: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/colocated_python_sidecar:TAG
    • Image tags: Replace TAG with one of the following tags, which are created automatically when a Pathways build passes qualification tests and is promoted to production:
      • YYYYMMDD-jax_JAX_VERSION: Pinned tag created by combining the UTC promotion date (YYYYMMDD) with -jax_ and the verified JAX version (JAX_VERSION) after per-version qualification tests pass. For example, 20261108-jax_0.12.0.1.
      • jax-JAX_VERSION: Rolling tag updated after per-version qualification tests pass to point to the most recent verified image for that JAX release. For example, jax-0.12.0.1 or jax-0.12.0.
      • latest: Rolling tag updated when a build passes qualification tests against the most recent supported JAX release.

For more information, see Introduction to Pathways on Cloud.

They're served on the global endpoint through the OpenAI-compatible Responses API. All three models accept text and image inputs and support reasoning, function calling, structured output, and a 1M-token context window.

For more information, see Muse models from Meta.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

GKE Gateway now supports Server Name Indication (SNI)-based routing with TLS passthrough. You can use TLS protocol-specific rules to route incoming TLS streams from the Gateway to Kubernetes Services based on SNI without terminating TLS at the GKE Gateway load balancer. Application developers can create TLSRoute resources to expose secure TLS traffic to applications that run in the GKE cluster.

Creating TLSRoute resources requires the Gateway API version 1.5.0 or later CRDs (Standard channel), which are installed in GKE version 1.35.2-gke.1842000 or later.

This feature supports single-cluster and multi-cluster GKE Gateway load balancers by using the following GatewayClass resources:

  • gke-l7-rilb
  • gke-l7-regional-external-managed
  • gke-l7-rilb-mc
  • gke-l7-regional-external-managed-mc
  • gke-l7-cross-regional-internal-managed-mc

For more information, see Deploy a TLS passthrough Gateway.

Feature

Agent Substrate on GKE is now Generally Available (GA) for GKE Standard clusters running version 1.37 or later.

Agent Substrate is an infrastructure layer designed for large-scale, high-density AI agent workloads, such as personal assistants and coding agents. Because interactive agents often remain idle while waiting for user input, running them on traditional microservice infrastructure can underutilize CPU and memory resources. Agent Substrate uses a lightweight control plane that bypasses standard Kubernetes Pod scheduling limits to provide fast sandbox provisioning and efficient suspend-and-resume capabilities.

For more information, see About Agent Substrate on GKE.

Managed Service for Apache Spark

Announcement

Managed Service for Apache Spark (formerly Google Cloud Serverless for Apache Spark): Runtime version 4.0 is generally available (GA). This version includes the following components:

  • Apache Spark 4.2.0
  • BigQuery Connector 0.46.0
  • Cloud Storage Connector 4.0.7
  • Java 25
  • Python 3.13
  • Scala 2.13.17

Runtime 4.0 also introduces the following changes:

  • Batch workloads run in the premium tier and use Lightning Engine by default.
  • Memory shapes determine the memory of drivers and executors. The default highmem memory shape provides 7.75 GiB of memory per vCPU.
  • Premium tier workloads that use the default driver configuration are eligible to run the driver on a fast-startup VM, which reduces startup time.
  • The Lakehouse runtime catalog is the default Spark catalog for batch workloads and interactive sessions.
  • Workloads that don't use GPUs consume the Data Compute Units quota instead of Compute Engine CPU and disk quotas.

Runtime 4.0 doesn't support some features of earlier runtimes, such as SparkR batches, Jupyter sessions, and the Persistent History Server. For more information, see Unsupported functionality and behavior changes.

Memorystore for Redis

Feature

Memorystore for Redis supports the CLIENT command and the following subcommands:

  • CLIENT | CACHING
  • CLIENT | GETNAME
  • CLIENT | GETREDIR
  • CLIENT | HELP
  • CLIENT | ID
  • CLIENT | INFO
  • CLIENT | KILL
  • CLIENT | LIST
  • CLIENT | NO-TOUCH
  • CLIENT | REPLY
  • CLIENT | SETNAME
  • CLIENT | TRACKING
  • CLIENT | TRACKINGINFO

For more information about the CLIENT command and its supported subcommands, see Supported and blocked commands. This feature is generally available (GA).

SAP on Google Cloud

Announcement

Google Cloud's Agent for SAP version 3.16

Version 3.16 of Google Cloud's Agent for SAP is generally available (GA). This version introduces enhancements for the agent's configureinstance command, support bundle feature, and some framework level updates.

For more information, see What's new with Google Cloud's Agent for SAP.

Security Command Center

Feature

Security Command Center predefined roles are modified. For information about the changes and how to migrate your custom roles, see Migrating custom roles.

Feature

Preview: Security Command Center Vulnerability Assessment for Google Cloud helps you detect vulnerabilities and exposed secrets in the container images of your Cloud Run services, jobs, and worker pools with Vulnerability Assessment for Cloud Run (Preview).

For more information, see Enable and use Vulnerability Assessment for Google Cloud.

Java

Feature

General Availability: You can create an internal range with the INTERNAL_ADDRESS purpose to allocate global internal IPv4 addresses for Private Service Connect endpoints that access global Google APIs.

For more information, see Internal ranges for Private Service Connect endpoints.

title: How to talk to users who leave at the paywall without paying
description:
This guide was originally published on the Hailbell blog.

Short answer: Put a small "Questions?" link next to the paywall that opens a chat inside the app, answer within minutes, and look at what the person already did before you reply. Make an offer only when price is the reason, and follow up once with a push at a decent local time. If you're a solo developer with a few hundred new users a week, a support email link on the paywall that you answer yourself is enough to start. If you use Superwall or RevenueCat and want in-app chat, purchase history, offers that open your paywall and push in one SDK, Hailbell does that from $29 a month. If you're a funded team that also needs a full help center and many channels in one inbox, Intercom is the better fit.

Hailbell is our product, built by an indie app developer who uses it in his own apps. This guide works with or without it. The steps come first, and the section on where Hailbell fits, including what it doesn't do, is near the end.

Why most people leave the onboarding paywall

Superwall analyzed more than 40 million onboarding paywall opens from February to May 2026. Single-page paywalls converted 9.07% of viewers into a trial or purchase, and multi-page paywalls 12.41% (Superwall; paywalls with no sales were left out). Put the other way, about 9 in 10 people close it.

Most paywall advice is about the other 10%: layout, trial length, A/B tests. That work matters. But the people who leave usually aren't saying "no forever". They leave with something unresolved:

  • a question the paywall didn't answer ("does it sync to my iPad?", "can I cancel the trial in settings?", "is there a student price?")
  • a price that's a bit too high for them, or a plan length they don't want
  • a bug or a confusing step in onboarding that made them doubt the app
  • no reason yet to pay today

The first three can be fixed in a conversation. The fourth can't, and you shouldn't try. The trouble is that most apps give these people no way to talk to anyone. They close the paywall and you never hear from them.

The same problem shows up later from the cancel side. A founder on r/SaaS was weighing a stricter refund policy: refunds within a week of each charge for now, maybe no refunds at all after the first month. A rule like that decides who gets money back. It doesn't tell you why they wanted out, and a conversation does.

Seven steps to talk to the people who didn't buy

  1. Record that they left. When someone closes the paywall without buying, log an event such as paywall_decline with the placement name. Superwall's presentation handler and RevenueCat's paywall views both call your code when the paywall is dismissed, so you can tell whether it ended in a purchase. Without this event you can't tell the difference between "never saw the paywall" and "saw it and said no".
  2. Give them a way to ask, next to the paywall. A small "Questions? Chat with us" link under the plans, or a quiet help button after they close it. Don't make it a popup that blocks the screen. An email link works too, but people rarely switch to their mail app in the middle of onboarding, so a chat that opens inside the app gets more messages.
  3. Answer while they're still in the app. A reply four hours later reaches someone who already moved on. Write a short note with your prices, plans, trial terms, refund policy and known issues, and let an AI answer first from that note, labelled as AI. It should hand the chat to you when it doesn't know. You finish the hard ones from wherever you already are during the day.
  4. Read what they did before you reply. Did they start a trial last month and cancel? Get a refund? Close this paywall three times today? Is a billing retry failing? A person who closed the paywall three times probably wants it, and the price or a missing answer is in the way. Your purchase tool already has this history; put it next to the conversation so you don't reply blind.
  5. Make an offer only when it fits the reason. If they say "too expensive", send a button that opens a second paywall: an annual plan with a lower monthly cost, a shorter plan, or a one-time discount you've set up in your paywall tool. If they asked a question, answer it and stop. A discount in reply to "does it work offline?" just teaches people to close the paywall.
  6. Follow up once with a push, and respect the rules. If they asked something and left before your answer arrived, the reply should come back as a push that opens the chat. For a promotional follow-up, send it only to people who opted in to promotional pushes, at a sensible hour in their time zone, with a daily cap so nobody gets three in a day. One message. If they don't respond, leave them alone.
  7. Ask for a review only after you've fixed something. Someone whose problem you just solved is your happiest user that day. That's the moment to show the App Store or Play review sheet. Never ask someone who is still upset, and never offer anything for a review.

A worked example

Say a meditation app shows its paywall at the end of onboarding: $59.99 a year with a 7-day trial. Someone closes it and taps "Questions?" with "is there a monthly plan? I don't want to commit to a year". The AI knows there's a $9.99 monthly plan from the note and says so. The person still leaves. Next evening, around the hour they usually open the app, they get one push: "The monthly plan is $9.99 and you can cancel anytime. Tap to see it." The push opens a paywall with only the monthly plan. Whether or not they buy, that's the last promotional message they get this week.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Discounting everyone who closes the paywall. Your full-price buyers learn to close it first. Keep offers for people who said price was the problem.
  • A chat nobody answers. An unanswered chat feels worse than no chat. If you can't reply within a few hours, turn on AI first replies or set an away message that says when you'll be back.
  • A chain of win-back pushes. Three "come back!" messages in three days get your app's notifications turned off, and then you can't reach them even when you have something good to say.
  • Asking for the review too early. Asking during onboarding, or right after a complaint, gets you the review you don't want.
  • Answering without context. Offering a trial to someone who already used one, or a discount to someone who just got a refund, wastes the one message you get.

Tools for this

Approach Chat inside the app Purchase history next to the chat Offer that opens a paywall Promotional push Cost
Email link on the paywall No No Send a link by hand No Free
Hailbell Yes: iOS, Android, web Yes, from Superwall and RevenueCat webhooks Yes Yes, included $29/mo for 10,000 MAU, unlimited seats
Intercom Yes: iOS, Android, web Custom attributes you send A link or deep link in a message Proactive Support Plus add-on, $99/mo for 500 messages $29 per seat/mo (monthly billing), plus $0.99 per Fin AI outcome

When a plain email is enough: if you get a few hundred new users a week, you're the only person answering, and you check email often, a "Questions? hello@yourapp.com" line on the paywall costs nothing and teaches you what people ask. Start there. Move to an in-app chat when you notice people don't bother switching apps to write, or when the same five questions eat your mornings.

Pick Intercom if you have a support team, need a help center with collections and translations, ticketing and email, social and chat in one inbox, and the per-seat price is fine for your budget. It's a mature product and it does those things well.

Where Hailbell helps

Hailbell is in-app support chat and push notifications for iOS, Android and web apps in one SDK. For this job, that means:

  • Recording the decline. Hailbell.track("paywall_decline") records a signal that shows next to the chat. You can also build a push segment from it, such as "declined in the last 48 hours".
  • Context. Connect your Superwall or RevenueCat webhook and each conversation shows the person's plan, purchases, trials, cancellations, refunds and billing problems, along with their device and country.
  • Fast answers. AI replies answer first from your notes and help articles, in the user's language, labelled as AI, and hand the chat to you when they can't help. You reply from the dashboard, a Discord forum thread (one per customer) or Telegram. The customer gets a push when you answer, and if they don't see it in the app, the reply goes to their email.
  • Offers. An offer is a message with a button that opens one of your paywall placements, through Hailbell.onPaywall. A new offer needs no app update. See offers and reviews in the docs.
  • Follow-up push. Campaigns go out at each person's local time or their usual hour, with quiet hours and a daily cap on promotional pushes. Promotional pushes are opt-in, and marketing sends skip people who opted out.
  • Reviews. A review request button in the chat opens the App Store review sheet, or your Play Store listing on Android.
  • Agents. An AI agent can do this over the MCP server: read the chat with the person's purchases, draft a reply your team sends from the dashboard, and plan the follow-up push. Broadcasts need a preview first.

Price Pro is $29 a month for 10,000 monthly active users, Scale $79 a month for 100,000. Every plan includes unlimited apps and seats, and AI replies. Free for 14 days, no card.

What it doesn't do Hailbell is new. You answer from the dashboard, Discord or Telegram; there's no Slack, SMS or social inbox, and the help center is basic: articles with search, suggested in the web chat but not yet in the iOS and Android chat. A Hailbell iPhone app for answering on the go is coming soon. Native chat needs iOS 16 or Android 8 or later. It doesn't run A/B tests on the paywall itself; keep using your paywall tool for that.

Fits Solo developers, studios and agencies running several client apps that already sell through Superwall or RevenueCat. See pricing or read the docs.

Questions

What share of people buy at an onboarding paywall?

Superwall looked at more than 40 million onboarding paywall opens from February to May 2026. Single-page paywalls converted 9.07% of viewers and multi-page paywalls 12.41%. So roughly 88 to 91 people in 100 leave without starting a trial or buying.

Should I show a discount to everyone who closes the paywall?

No. People learn that closing the paywall gets them a lower price, and the ones who only had a question would have paid full price. Answer the question first and make an offer only when the reason they gave is price.

Can I ask for an App Store review in a support chat?

Yes, after you've solved the person's problem and they're happy. Don't offer anything in return for a review, and don't ask people who are still upset.

Is it allowed to send a promotional push to people who didn't buy?

Only to people who opted in to promotional pushes. Apple's guidelines require that consent. Keep it to one message, at a sensible local time, and stop if they don't respond.

title: How do you move RunPod training jobs over to Nodus?
description:
You move a Runpod training job to Nodus by running the same container image and script with nodus run, with datasets in a Nodus Volume and checkpoints written to /nodus/state. Nodus saves that directory while the job runs and restores it on a new machine if capacity is lost, so most single-node jobs need one changed path and one command. Serverless endpoints and multi-node Instant Clusters are the parts to leave on Runpod for now.

Runpod is still written RunPod in many older guides and searches; we use its current spelling. We build Nodus, so weigh our view accordingly. If you are still deciding whether to move, read Nodus vs RunPod or the RunPod alternatives list first. This post covers only the move, and every Nodus command in it is copied from our docs.

What does each Runpod concept become on Nodus?

A Runpod Pod used for a training run becomes a Nodus Job, and almost everything around it has a direct counterpart. We built this table from Runpod's storage, templates, secrets, CLI and Pod pricing docs, and our Jobs, Volumes, Secrets, Images and Workspaces guides.

On Runpod On Nodus What changes
Pod running a training script Job, started with nodus run The Job ends when your command exits, so nothing idles afterwards
Pod you SSH or Jupyter into Workspace Home directory lives on a Volume and is saved every time it stops
Template (a Docker image plus settings) --image with any public or private registry image Or upload a local image with nodus image push
Container disk (lost on stop) The Job's local disk, sized with --disk Scratch space, as before
Checkpoints on the /workspace volume disk The state directory, /nodus/state Nodus copies it and restores it on the next attempt
Network volume Volume, mounted with --volume NAME:/path[:ro] Every change is a numbered revision
Env vars in a template --env K=V Same idea
{{ RUNPOD_SECRET_name }} nodus secret create, then --secret Values arrive as env vars and as files under /run/secrets/
runpodctl pod create nodus run One command uploads code, launches, streams logs and prints the cost
Account spend limit (default $80/hour) --max-cost per run, plus Budgets The cap is on each run, not only the account

Runpod's own CLI overview launches a Pod from a template with runpodctl pod create --template-id runpod-torch-v21 --gpu-id "NVIDIA RTX 4090". That Pod then runs until you stop it. The Nodus equivalent runs one command to completion and releases the machine, which is the change that matters most for cost.

What is the smallest real job submission on Nodus?

The smallest submission is one line, copied from the nodus run reference:

  nodus run --gpu L4 --image nodus/pytorch -- python train.py

It uploads your current directory, creates a Job on one NVIDIA L4, streams the logs and ends with a cost line. Install and sign in first with pip install nodus-compute and nodus login. Our quickstart adds the habits worth keeping from day one, a dry run and a spending cap:

nodus run --name cli-quickstart --gpu L4 --image nodus/pytorch \
  --max-cost 1 --timeout 10m --no-warm --dry-run \
  --output metrics=/nodus/outputs/metrics.json -- python train.py

--dry-run prints the estimate without creating the Job. Drop it to start paid compute, then fetch the declared output with nodus cp job/cli-quickstart:outputs/metrics metrics.json, which checks the file against its SHA-256 digest. Finished Jobs keep their logs and outputs for 30 days.

How do you bring your image, data and secrets over?

Bring the image first, because it carries your environment. If your Runpod template points at a registry image, pass the same reference to --image. For a private registry, store a Registry Secret and name it under imagePullSecrets, as the Images guide describes. For an image you only have locally, upload it straight to your project:

IMAGE=$(nodus image push my-app:latest --name my-app:trial -p my-project)

Nodus resolves the tag to a digest when you submit, so a retry or recovery runs exactly the same bytes.

Data comes next. Runpod's S3-compatible API reads network volumes in select data centers without launching a Pod, so you can download a volume without paying for a GPU. Then upload it to a Nodus Volume; uploads only send what changed, so a second attempt moves almost nothing:

nodus create volume data --size 100Gi
nodus volume put data ./data /data

If the dataset or base model came from Hugging Face, skip the round trip. A Volume can import from a pinned Hugging Face revision, a git repo, an https:// URL or an S3 bucket, and the import runs on Nodus (Volumes guide). An S3 Connection also takes an s3.endpoint field, which in principle covers Runpod's endpoint, but we have not tested that path.

Secrets last. Each {{ RUNPOD_SECRET_name }} reference in your template becomes a Nodus Secret, created once:

nodus secret create hf-token --from-literal HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx

Name it with --secret hf-token and every key arrives as an env var and as a read-only file under /run/secrets/hf-token/. Nodus never returns a value through the API, console or CLI and redacts secret values from logs (Secrets guide).

How do you carry a checkpoint over without losing progress?

Upload your last Runpod checkpoint to a Volume, mount it read-only, and resume from it only when the Nodus state directory is empty. After the first Nodus checkpoint, the state directory wins. We wrote this Hugging Face Trainer version from the recipe in our checkpoints guide and have not run it end to end on a real model. The /workspace fallback keeps the script working on a Runpod Pod:

import os
from transformers import Trainer, TrainingArguments

STATE = os.environ.get("NODUS_STATE_DIR", "/workspace/ckpt")  # /workspace on Runpod
SEED = "/seed/checkpoint-12000"                                # last Runpod checkpoint

def has_checkpoint(d):
    return os.path.isdir(d) and any(n.startswith("checkpoint-") for n in os.listdir(d))

args = TrainingArguments(output_dir=STATE, save_steps=500, save_total_limit=2)
trainer = Trainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train_ds)

if has_checkpoint(STATE):
    trainer.train(resume_from_checkpoint=True)   # Nodus restored the state directory
elif os.path.isdir(SEED):
    trainer.train(resume_from_checkpoint=SEED)   # first start after the move
else:
    trainer.train()

We check for a checkpoint- folder rather than only NODUS_RESTORED, because Trainer refuses to resume from an empty directory. Upload the seed with nodus volume put into a Volume named seed, then review the estimate and launch:

nodus run --dry-run --gpu H100:4 --image "$IMAGE" --secret hf-token \
  --volume seed:/seed:ro --expected-duration 18h -- torchrun --nproc_per_node 4 train.py
nodus run --gpu H100:4 --image "$IMAGE" --secret hf-token \
  --volume seed:/seed:ro --max-cost 210 -d -- torchrun --nproc_per_node 4 train.py

What you gain is recovery. The checkpoints guide says a Job gets at least four checkpoints over its expected run time, plus one when capacity gives notice it is about to be reclaimed. An empty state directory never replaces an earlier checkpoint.

Setting recovery.checkpoint.integration: HFTrainer in a Job manifest also makes Trainer save when Nodus asks, with no change to your image. Why this matters on Runpod is covered in keeping training alive without spot Pods.

What does the same job cost on Runpod and on Nodus?

At list prices, the 4 x H100, 18-hour fine-tune above costs $187.20 on Nodus, against $316.08 on Runpod Secure Cloud and from $193.68 on Runpod Community Cloud. That is 72 GPU-hours on each. Runpod lists the H100 SXM at $4.39/hr on Secure Cloud and from $2.69/hr on Community Cloud, billed per second (Runpod pricing). The H100 SXM is listed at $2.60/hr on the Nodus pricing page.

4 x H100 SXM, 18 hours (72 GPU-hours) Hourly rate per GPU Total
Runpod Secure Cloud $4.39 72 x $4.39 = $316.08
Runpod Community Cloud from $2.69 72 x $2.69 = $193.68
Nodus $2.60 72 x $2.60 = $187.20

Prices checked November 15, 2026. Storage is extra on both and is left out.


At list prices, the same 72 GPU-hour fine-tune costs 41% less on Nodus than on Runpod Secure Cloud.

The gap is not the same on every GPU. Runpod lists the H200 at $5.29/hr on Secure Cloud and from $3.59/hr on Community Cloud (Runpod pricing), while the H200 SXM is listed at $3.593/hr on the Nodus pricing page. On H200 Community Cloud, Runpod is a fraction of a cent cheaper per hour. For a longer breakdown of Runpod's storage and idle costs, see Runpod pricing explained.


To the tenth of a cent: H100 SXM is $4.390, from $2.690 and $2.600; H200 is $5.290, from $3.590 and $3.593. Nodus leads on H100, and H200 on Community Cloud is a near tie.

Which training jobs should you move first?

Move a job first when it passes four checks. We use this rule because each failed check adds manual work to the move:

  1. It runs on one machine. Multi-node training on Nodus is in Beta.
  2. A script starts it, not a person typing in a shell.
  3. It can resume from checkpoint files, or can be made to with the pattern above.
  4. Its inputs can be fetched again: Hugging Face, git, a URL, a bucket or one volume put.

A job that passes all four needs only the steps above. A job that fails only the second check belongs in a Workspace first, then becomes a Job once its steps are scripted. Jobs that fail the first check stay where they are until you have tested multi-node on Nodus with a small run.

Can you keep using your Runpod account through Nodus?

Yes, in Beta: Nodus can connect to a Runpod account with its API key, and it does this in two separate steps (connect your cloud accounts). The default, view existing resources, lists the CPU and GPU Pods in the account and never creates, changes or deletes anything. Read-only observation is free.

Running work there is an explicit Beta upgrade, and the docs say no internal enablement or operator qualification step is required. It needs an execution credit limit and a fresh check of the key.

Nodus then places your Jobs, Workspaces and other single-node work in that account first, within its limits. Sandboxes and multi-node runs use Nodus capacity. The nodus cloud connect reference reads the API key from standard input, so a Runpod connection looks like this:

  printf '%s' "$RUNPOD_API_KEY" | nodus cloud connect runpod my-runpod --credit-limit 200

For a GPU Job in your own account, the estimate shows a Route fee of $0.02 per device-hour, and Runpod bills the machine and disk separately. On the 72 GPU-hour job above, that fee is 72 x $0.02 = $1.44 on top of your Runpod bill. --burst decides what happens when the account is full or out of credit: use Nodus capacity (the default), ask for approval, or deny. Nodus's spending limit uses its own estimate of cloud cost, which can differ from what Runpod actually charges.

When should you stay on Runpod?

Stay on Runpod for the workloads Nodus does not yet cover as well:

  • Multi-node clusters. Runpod Instant Clusters offer managed multi-node compute with 1600 to 3200 Gbps between nodes and managed Slurm. Multi-node training on Nodus is in Beta.
  • Inference endpoints. Runpod Serverless bills inference workers based on usage (Runpod pricing). Hosted inference on Nodus is in Beta, so a working Serverless endpoint is a poor first candidate.
  • Data-heavy work. Runpod states no fees for data ingress or egress on Pods (Pod pricing).
  • H200 on Community Cloud, where Runpod's listed rate already matches ours.

None of these require an all-or-nothing choice. The account connection above lets single-node jobs move while clusters and endpoints stay put.

FAQ

Do I have to rewrite my training code to run it on Nodus?

Usually not. Code that runs in a container with a command line runs as a Nodus Job; the one change worth making is writing checkpoints to NODUS_STATE_DIR so Nodus can restore them.

Can I SSH into a Nodus machine like a Runpod Pod?

Yes, through a Workspace, which offers SSH, VS Code in the browser and JupyterLab. While it is stopped you pay only for the saved files in its home directory.

What happens to a migrated job if my Nodus credit runs out?

Nodus warns you, stops work gracefully and resumes it when credits, a raised Budget or a raised cap return, as described in when money runs out. Setting --max-cost on each run keeps one job from using the whole balance.

Does Nodus run my work on Runpod capacity?

Only if you connect your own Runpod account and enable running work there. Otherwise your Jobs run on Nodus capacity, and the job page's Attempts view says where each attempt ran.

Can a coding agent do this migration?

Yes. Once connected with nodus mcp install claude or the hosted server, Claude Code, Codex or Cursor can review an estimate and run a Job through MCP (MCP guide).

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: How Java Synchronization Works: A Quick Walkthrough
description:
One keyword - synchronized - and two threads stop corrupting each other's data. But what did the keyword actually buy you? The JVM spec has a surprisingly small answer: one mechanism, the monitor, and a handful of bytecode instructions. Let's open it up with real javap output, a live look at a blocked thread, and the Linux primitive the JVM leans on when a thread truly has to wait.

One construct: the monitor

The JVM spec (JVMS 2.11.10) is blunt: "The Java Virtual Machine supports synchronization of both methods and sequences of instructions within a method by a single synchronization construct: the monitor."

Every object can act as a monitor. synchronized (lock) { ... } means: enter the monitor associated with lock; only one thread can own it at a time; everyone else waits. That is the entire mechanism - everything else is how it is compiled and what waiting costs.

Here is the journey of two threads and one monitor, animated:

Two forms, two very different bytecodes

A synchronized block and a synchronized method look alike in Java. In bytecode they are nothing alike. This class:

public class SyncBytecode {
    private final Object lock = new Object();
    private int count;

    public void incrementBlock() {
        synchronized (lock) {
            count++;
        }
    }

    public synchronized void incrementMethod() {
        count++;
    }
}

javap -c on the block form - real output:

  public void incrementBlock();
    Code:
       0: aload_0
       1: getfield      #7        // Field lock:Ljava/lang/Object;
       4: dup
       5: astore_1
       6: monitorenter
       7: aload_0
       8: dup
       9: getfield      #13       // Field count:I
      12: iconst_1
      13: iadd
      14: putfield      #13       // Field count:I
      17: aload_1
      18: monitorexit
      19: goto          27
      22: astore_2
      23: aload_1
      24: monitorexit
      25: aload_2
      26: athrow
      27: return
    Exception table:
       from    to  target type
           7    19    22   any
          22    25    22   any

Read it closely - there are two monitorexit instructions. One on the normal path (offset 18), one inside a compiler-generated cleanup (offset 24) guarded by an exception-table row of type any. If count++ somehow threw, control would jump to offset 22, the monitor would still be released, and then athrow would rethrow. That is the spec's promise, made visible: "the executing thread enters a monitor, invokes the method itself, and exits the monitor whether the method invocation completes normally or abruptly." A forgotten unlock on the exception path is impossible by construction.

The method form? javap -v shows there are no monitor instructions in its code at all - just a flag on the method:

  public synchronized void incrementMethod();
    flags: (0x0021) ACC_PUBLIC, ACC_SYNCHRONIZED

Per the same spec section, "method-level synchronization is performed implicitly, as part of method invocation and return... the ACC_SYNCHRONIZED flag... is checked by the method invocation instructions." The entering and exiting still happen; they are just the JVM's job at the call boundary rather than explicit bytecodes.

What waiting looks like

A thread that wants a held monitor doesn't spin visibly - it changes state. The Thread.State JavaDoc defines BLOCKED as: "A thread that is blocked waiting for a monitor lock is in this state." You can watch it happen. Two threads, one lock, the holder sleeping inside its critical section:

before start: holder=NEW waiter=NEW
while contended: holder=TIMED_WAITING waiter=BLOCKED
waiter got the lock
after finish: holder=TERMINATED waiter=TERMINATED

Real output, one run. The holder is TIMED_WAITING (it is inside Thread.sleep - a timed wait, holding the monitor the whole time; sleep never releases locks). The waiter is BLOCKED - parked on the monitor, making zero progress, until the holder's monitorexit lets it in. Note the distinction the states encode: BLOCKED means "waiting for a monitor"; WAITING/TIMED_WAITING mean "waiting for something else" (a notify, a sleep, a join).

Where the kernel genuinely appears

If nobody else wants the monitor, entering it is pure user-space work in the JVMs we know: an atomic compare-and-swap in the runtime's own code, no system call, no scheduler, no kernel. That is an implementation strategy, not a spec promise - the JVMS defines the monitor's behavior, not how a JVM parks threads.

Contention changes the story. When a thread genuinely cannot proceed, it must stop running, and stopping a thread so it can be woken later is an operating system service. On Linux, the primitive built for exactly this is the futex. From futex(2): "The futex() system call provides a method for waiting until a certain condition becomes true... When using futexes, the majority of the synchronization operations are performed in user space. A user-space program employs the futex() system call only when it is likely that the program has to block for a longer time until the condition becomes true."

And this is not just theory on the machine that ran the demo above. Tracing the same BlockedState run with strace on this Linux sandbox counted the real syscalls:

% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ----------------
100.00    0.036076          49       728        55 futex

728 futex calls across the JVM's threads in that one short, contended run. Two honest readings of that number. What it shows: this JVM, on this OS, reaches for the futex syscall routinely - the user-space-plus-kernel design from the man page is really in use. What it does not show: strace -c aggregates process-wide, so we cannot attribute individual calls to our two threads' monitor contention specifically - some of that traffic is the JVM's ordinary internal bookkeeping, and a handful of EAGAIN errors are normal futex races. Treat it as a process-level observation, not causal proof about the monitor's internals. And the scope stands as before: this is the HotSpot-based OpenJDK 21 on Linux that we measured - other JVMs and other operating systems park threads differently, and the spec guarantees none of it.

What it costs

How much does an uncontended synchronized cost? Honestly: more than a plain call, less than folklore says, and pinning down the number is genuinely hard. An uncontended monitor enter/exit is real extra work around your code - an atomic operation, bookkeeping on the object, a memory barrier's worth of ordering guarantees - where a plain call has none of that. Under contention it gets more expensive in a different way: threads stop and sleep on the OS path from the previous section, and waking them later costs far more than any single instruction.

Why not just show you a number here? Because a quick nanoTime loop cannot produce a fair one. The JIT treats a synchronized empty-ish method and a plain one differently: it can fold, coalesce or eliminate work in one path but not the other, so a homegrown loop ends up measuring the optimizer as much as the monitor. JVM engineers use JMH, the OpenJDK benchmarking harness built to defend against exactly those artifacts. So take the qualitative version, which is solid: synchronization costs something even when nobody competes, contention costs a lot more, and both are worth paying exactly where correctness requires them - nowhere else.

The free bonus: visibility

Mutual exclusion is only half of what a monitor gives you. The Java memory model adds a guarantee (JLS 17.4.5): "An unlock on a monitor happens-before every subsequent lock on that monitor." Everything thread A wrote before releasing the monitor is visible to thread B after it acquires the same monitor. No stale caches, no half-seen objects - this is why synchronized fixes both races and visibility bugs at once.

Habits worth keeping

  • Lock on a private final object, like the lock field above - never on this (callers can grab it too) and never on a String (the string pool means unrelated code may share your monitor - see the strings walkthrough).
  • Keep critical sections tiny. Every nanosecond inside is a nanosecond every other thread waits.
  • Never sleep while holding a monitor unless that is genuinely the intent - sleeping holds the lock.
  • Reach for java.util.concurrent (locks with timeouts, concurrent collections, atomics) before building anything elaborate out of raw synchronized.

Sources

  • JVMS 2.11.10: Synchronization
  • Java 21 API: Thread.State
  • JLS 17.4.5: Happens-before Order
  • Linux man-pages: futex(2)

Written with AI assistance; every bytecode listing, thread state and syscall trace above comes from real compiles, runs and strace counts on JDK 21 (Temurin 21.0.13) on this Linux sandbox - the trace is a process-wide observation, and HotSpot's internal lock implementation is version-specific. The animation is an illustration of the monitor's logical behavior.

title: Printable LEGO instructions from a three.js viewer: cqw units, headless Edge and a page count
description:
A 3D viewer is great on a laptop. On the living-room floor, with a kid and a pile of bricks, you want paper. So every guide on Mister Blocks prints as a real instruction booklet, comes as a PDF, and works offline once you've opened it.

This is how that works, with no PDF library and no server-side rendering of 3D.

The booklet is just a web page

/builds/<name>-lego-build/print lays the guide out like a LEGO booklet: a cover, one step per page (the number, a blue box of the pieces it needs, what to do, and the model so far as big as the page allows), then the parts list.

The trick that makes it look the same on screen and on paper: everything inside a page is sized in cqw, 1% of the sheet's width (CSS container query units). The sheet on screen and the sheet in the print dialog are the same shape, so the text and pictures land in the same places.

Paper size is a toggle. US Letter landscape is the default and A4 is one click away. The toggle swaps an @page rule and a class on <html>, and remembers your choice.


Ladder 9 Fire Engine: 127 pieces, 15 steps, 18 printed pages. More LEGO trucks.

Every picture is drawn in your browser

There are no stored step images. The print page runs the same three.js viewer off screen and takes snapshots:

  • The cover: the finished model in its own lighting, framed a little wider than tight.
  • Each step: the model so far, on white, framed on what's built so far. The camera is never closer than 60% of the distance that fits the whole model, so step 1 (four plates) doesn't fill the page like a close-up. Then the white edges are cropped off.
  • Each kind of piece: drawn on its own, all from the same camera distance, so a 1×1 plate looks small next to a 2×4 brick, just like in a real booklet.

Wheels are the exception: they're drawn flat in 2D, because the viewer can't draw a wheel without the plate it sits on.

PDFs: headless Edge and a page count

A PDF is the print page printed by headless Edge:

msedge --headless=new --no-pdf-header-footer --virtual-time-budget=<ms> --print-to-pdf=out.pdf <url>?paper=a4

The time budget grows with the model (40 s plus a bit per piece and per step), because a 1,400-piece sculpture takes a while to draw 120 times.

Before anything is uploaded, the script counts the pages in the PDF: it should be 1 cover + 1 page per step + 1 page per 40 kinds of piece. If the count is off, a picture didn't finish drawing, so that PDF is skipped instead of shipping a booklet with a blank step. Good ones go to Cloudflare R2, Letter and A4, in English and Ukrainian, and only get redone when the guide changes.


Sky Hook Tower Crane: 112 pieces, 12 steps. One of the easy builds.

Offline: guides you've opened keep working

The site is a PWA. The service worker uses a different strategy per kind of request:

Request Strategy
Pages network first; the saved copy if offline or after 4 s with no answer
A build's data network first, saved copy offline: a guide opened once works offline
/app.js?v=<deploy> cache first (that address never changes)
three.js, fonts cache first, but only CORS responses (opaque ones can cost ~7 MB of quota each)
New designs, chat network only

If you open a page that isn't saved, the offline page lists the guides that are, newest first, titled from their cached pages.

The bug that taught me to version everything

One morning a fan build wouldn't open on my phone. The page was new, but the phone still had yesterday's build.js cached (Cloudflare's browser cache keeps it for hours), and yesterday's script didn't know the new /builds/<name> addresses.

Now every script and stylesheet is linked as /<file>?v=<deploy id>, the deploy id taken from the commit SHA. The service worker is served from an API route with the same id baked in, so every deploy changes the worker, browsers install the new one, and it deletes the old deploy's caches. Pages themselves are never served stale.

Pick any guide, press Print or save as PDF, and see how it comes out: trucks, robots, cars or the full list of LEGO build ideas. Everything is free at misterblocks.com.
