title: SQL Server Query Store: A Practical Beginner's Guide
description:
Originally published at SQL & Cloud Lab.

This post was drafted with AI assistance.

Query Store is like a flight recorder for your database. It keeps a history of the queries that ran, the execution plans they used and how they performed, so you can answer questions such as "what changed since yesterday?" without having caught the problem live. If you use SQL Server 2016 or later, or Azure SQL, it is one of the most valuable features you are probably not using enough.

Is Query Store already on?

Query Store is enabled by default in Azure SQL Database and for new databases created in SQL Server 2022. Older databases, including those upgraded from earlier versions, may have it off. Check with:

SELECT actual_state_desc, desired_state_desc,
       current_storage_size_mb, max_storage_size_mb,
       query_capture_mode_desc
FROM sys.database_query_store_options;

If actual_state_desc shows READ_ONLY when you expected READ_WRITE, the most common reason is that it has reached its maximum size and stopped collecting.

Turn it on with sensible settings 

ALTER DATABASE [YourDb]
SET QUERY_STORE = ON (
    OPERATION_MODE = READ_WRITE,
    QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE = AUTO,          -- skip trivial, rarely run queries
    MAX_STORAGE_SIZE_MB = 2048,
    SIZE_BASED_CLEANUP_MODE = AUTO,
    CLEANUP_POLICY = (STALE_QUERY_THRESHOLD_DAYS = 30)
);
  • QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE = AUTO avoids filling Query Store with one-off ad hoc statements.
  • MAX_STORAGE_SIZE_MB should be big enough for your workload; busy databases with many distinct queries need more.
  • SIZE_BASED_CLEANUP_MODE = AUTO removes old data as it approaches the limit, so it does not flip to read-only.

The four reports worth knowing

In SSMS, expand the database, then Query Store. These reports cover most day-to-day needs:

  • Top Resource Consuming Queries: the heaviest queries by CPU, duration, reads or executions over the time window you choose. Start here for general tuning.
  • Regressed Queries: queries that got worse compared with an earlier period. Ideal for "it was fine last week".
  • Queries With High Variation: queries whose performance swings a lot, often a sign of parameter sniffing.
  • Overall Resource Consumption: a timeline of total load, useful to find when a problem started.

Click any query to see each plan it has used as a coloured dot on a chart. Different colours mean different plans, so a jump in duration that lines up with a new colour usually means a plan change caused the slowdown.

Compare plans and force the good one

When a query has a good plan and a bad plan, you can select both in the report and click Compare Plans to see what changed, such as a seek turning into a scan or a different join type.

To stop the problem quickly, force the good plan, either with the Force Plan button or in T-SQL:

EXEC sp_query_store_force_plan @query_id = 1234, @plan_id = 56;

-- Later, to remove it:
EXEC sp_query_store_unforce_plan @query_id = 1234, @plan_id = 56;

Plan forcing is an excellent emergency fix. Treat it as temporary: find the root cause, such as statistics, parameter sniffing or a missing index, and unforce the plan once it is fixed. Forced plans can also fail if an index they rely on is dropped, so check the Queries With Forced Plans report occasionally.

Query the data yourself

The reports are built on catalog views you can query directly. For example, the slowest queries by average duration in the last 24 hours:

SELECT TOP (10)
    q.query_id,
    qt.query_sql_text,
    SUM(rs.count_executions)  AS executions,
    AVG(rs.avg_duration) / 1000.0 AS avg_duration_ms
FROM sys.query_store_runtime_stats rs
JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats_interval i
     ON rs.runtime_stats_interval_id = i.runtime_stats_interval_id
JOIN sys.query_store_plan p        ON rs.plan_id = p.plan_id
JOIN sys.query_store_query q       ON p.query_id = q.query_id
JOIN sys.query_store_query_text qt ON q.query_text_id = qt.query_text_id
WHERE i.start_time >= DATEADD(HOUR, -24, SYSUTCDATETIME())
GROUP BY q.query_id, qt.query_sql_text
ORDER BY avg_duration_ms DESC;

Query Store stores times in UTC and durations in microseconds, which is why the script divides by 1,000.

Good habits

  • Check Query Store after every deployment or upgrade, using the Regressed Queries report.
  • Before changing database compatibility level, make sure Query Store has a baseline. It makes it much easier to spot and fix regressions afterwards.
  • Watch its size and state; a read-only Query Store silently stops recording.
  • Prefer fixing the cause over leaving plans forced forever.

Related reading:

  • How to Find Slow Queries in SQL Server
  • SQL Server Parameter Sniffing: What It Is and How to Fix It
  • How to Read a SQL Server Execution Plan

More SQL Server guides on my blog, SQL & Cloud Lab.

title: Catching PostgreSQL Double-Spends in 60ms on the Wire Protocol (Without Touching App Code)
description:
Imagine a classic wallet withdrawal endpoint in Go, Python, Node, or Rust. Everything is wrapped inside a database transaction:

tx, _ := pool.Begin(ctx)
defer tx.Rollback(ctx)

var balance int64
_ = tx.QueryRow(ctx, "SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE id = $1", walletID).Scan(&balance)
if balance < amount {
    return ErrInsufficientFunds
}

_, _ = tx.Exec(ctx, "UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2", amount, walletID)
_ = tx.Commit(ctx)

Your unit tests pass. Your sequential integration tests pass. Code review looks clean.

Then in production, a mobile client retries on a flaky network or a webhook fires twice in the same millisecond. Wallet 1 starts with balance = 100. Both POST /withdraw requests for 100 return 200 OK. The database now says balance = -100.

Why? Because PostgreSQL defaults to READ COMMITTED, where each statement sees a snapshot of data committed before that statement began. Most critical concurrency bugs in backend systems aren't memory data races inside one process. They are interleavings of SQL transactions across the network:

  • Check-then-act double spends
  • Lost updates (SET balance = $computed overwriting a concurrent write)
  • Write skew across multiple rows or aggregate checks (SELECT COUNT(*))
  • Phantom inserts before uniqueness or quota checks
  • Lock-order deadlocks when two endpoints touch rows in opposite order

Load tests (k6, wrk) only hit that microsecond race window by luck and give you no deterministic way to replay the failure. Thread model checkers like tokio-rs/loom only see threads and atomics inside a single Rust binary, stopping at the socket boundary.

So I built PgLoom, an open-source (Apache-2.0) deterministic race-condition model checker written in Rust that operates directly on the PostgreSQL v3 wire protocol.

Voskan / pgloom

Deterministic race-condition testing for PostgreSQL-backed services. A wire-protocol proxy explores how transactions interleave and finds double spends, lost updates and deadlocks, with exact replay. No code changes, any language.

PgLoom

Deterministic race-condition testing for anything that talks to PostgreSQL.

PgLoom is a model checker that sits between your service and PostgreSQL as a wire-protocol proxy. It fires concurrent requests at your service, holds every database round trip at a gate, and systematically explores how the transactions can interleave. When an interleaving breaks an invariant (a double spend, a lost update, a negative balance, a deadlock), it prints the exact schedule, explains the root cause, and writes a file that replays the bug deterministically in milliseconds.

No SDK, no code changes, no sleeps: point the service's DATABASE_URL at the proxy. It works the same for Go, Rust, Python, TypeScript, Java or anything else that speaks the PostgreSQL v3 protocol.

$ pgloom demo

Plain-text transcript 
✗ RACE CONDITION DETECTED  [demo-wallet-withdraw]
  Explored 3/50 schedules in 66ms (1-preemption trace)
  Violated Invariants:
    • no_negative_balance: Wallet balance must never drop below zero
      Observed DB state:
…
View on GitHub

How PgLoom Works Without SDKs or Code Changes

Every database-backed service already funnels its state transitions through one narrow choke point: DATABASE_URL.

Instead of instrumenting your application code, PgLoom sits as a stateful TCP proxy between your unmodified service and a real PostgreSQL instance (tested across PostgreSQL 12 through 17):

  1. Wire-Turn Gating (pgloom-wire): PgLoom speaks the PostgreSQL v3 frontend/backend protocol, parsing Simple Query, Extended Query pipelines (Parse, Bind, Describe, Execute, Flush, Sync), and COPY streams. Whenever a worker completes a protocol round trip, PgLoom holds that turn at a gate before forwarding it upstream. Because it works at the wire level, it doesn't care whether your app is written in Go (pgx), Python (psycopg / asyncpg), TypeScript (pg / Prisma), Java (JDBC / Hibernate), or Rust (sqlx / tokio-postgres).
  2. Source-DPOR Schedule Exploration (pgloom-engine): Blindly permuting every query across workers blows up factorially. PgLoom extracts read/write footprints from SQL statements, enriches them with pg_catalog metadata (foreign keys and triggers), and uses Source-DPOR (dynamic partial-order reduction with sleep sets) to skip Mazurkiewicz-equivalent schedules that are guaranteed to produce the exact same database state.
  3. Parking Row-Lock Waiters via pg_blocking_pids() (pgloom-pgctrl): What happens when Worker B executes UPDATE (or SELECT ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE) on a row already locked by Worker A? Postgres blocks Worker B inside the lock manager, so ReadyForQuery won't come back until Worker A finishes. A naive proxy would hang. PgLoom polls pg_blocking_pids(), recognizes that Worker B is blocked by Worker A, parks Worker B, hands control back to Worker A, and flags true lock cycles as deadlocks.
  4. Real COMMITs + Sub-Millisecond Resets: A tempting shortcut in test harnesses is wrapping each run in BEGIN / SAVEPOINT / ROLLBACK. Unfortunately, faking commits with savepoints silently changes READ COMMITTED visibility semantics and hides real bugs. PgLoom executes genuine COMMITs against PostgreSQL on every schedule and restores dirty tables in <1ms from an UNLOGGED snapshot schema.

What a Scenario Looks Like

Pointing PgLoom at an existing service takes a single pgloom.yaml file. Here is a complete double-spend scenario against an HTTP wallet service:

version: 1
name: "wallet-withdraw-double-spend"

database:
  upstream: "postgres://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:5432/postgres"
  proxy_listen: "127.0.0.1:15432"
  setup_sql: |
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS wallets (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, balance BIGINT NOT NULL);
    TRUNCATE wallets;
    INSERT INTO wallets (id, balance) VALUES (1, 100);

target:
  command: "go run ."
  env:
    DATABASE_URL: "postgres://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:15432/postgres?sslmode=disable"
    LISTEN_ADDR: "127.0.0.1:18080"
  ready_http: "http://127.0.0.1:18080/healthz"

workers:
  - id: "req_a"
    http:
      method: "POST"
      url: "http://127.0.0.1:18080/withdraw"
      headers: { Content-Type: "application/json" }
      body: '{"wallet_id": 1, "amount": 100}'
  - id: "req_b"
    http:
      method: "POST"
      url: "http://127.0.0.1:18080/withdraw"
      headers: { Content-Type: "application/json" }
      body: '{"wallet_id": 1, "amount": 100}'

invariants:
  sql:
    - name: "no_negative_balance"
      description: "Wallet balance must never drop below zero"
      assert_true: "SELECT COALESCE(MIN(balance), 0) >= 0 FROM wallets"
      diagnostic_query: "SELECT id, balance FROM wallets"
  responses:
    - name: "at_most_one_successful_withdrawal"
      max_2xx_count: 1

Running pgloom run explores the interleavings in ~60ms, prints the exact step-by-step execution trace, runs the built-in SQL Fix Advisor, and writes .pgloom-repro.json so anyone on your team (or CI) can replay that exact schedule deterministically via pgloom replay:

[FAIL] RACE CONDITION DETECTED  [wallet-withdraw-double-spend]
Explored 3/50 schedules in 66ms (1-preemption trace)
Observed DB state: id=1, balance=-100 (req_a=200, req_b=200)

+------+------------------------+------------------------+
| Step | Worker req_a (pid 205) | Worker req_b (pid 204) |
+------+------------------------+------------------------+
|  t3  | SELECT balance -> 100  |                        |
|  t4  | UPDATE balance - 100   |                        |
|  >>  |       --- context switch (preempt) ---->        |
|  t5  | [paused before COMMIT] | SELECT balance -> 100  |
|  t6  |                        | UPDATE balance - 100   |
|      |                        | [blocked by req_a]     |
|  t7  | COMMIT -> HTTP 200 OK  |                        |
|  t9  |                        | lock granted -> UPD 1  |
| t10  |                        | COMMIT -> HTTP 200 OK  |
+------+------------------------+------------------------+

Fix Option A (Pessimistic Lock):
  SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE id = $1 FOR NO KEY UPDATE;
Fix Option B (Atomic Guarded Update):
  UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND balance >= $1;

"Why Not Just Set SERIALIZABLE Everywhere?"

Whenever transaction anomalies come up, someone reasonably asks: why not turn on SERIALIZABLE (Postgres SSI) globally?

If you have low write contention and clean transaction-retry boundaries from day one, SSI is awesome. In practice, two things push most high-throughput production backends back toward READ COMMITTED with targeted locking or atomic predicates:

  1. Hot-row 40001 retry storms: On hot merchant accounts, fee pools, or shared inventory counters, SERIALIZABLE aborts concurrent writers with SQLSTATE 40001 instead of queuing them cleanly in Postgres's lock manager. Under load bursts, that turns into retry loops and p99 tail-latency spikes, whereas FOR NO KEY UPDATE or a guarded UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= $1 serializes just that row in one pass.
  2. Legacy codebases & side-effect hazards: Most existing services and ORMs aren't structured around pure, side-effect-free retry closures. Forgetting a 40001 retry handler leaks HTTP 500s under contention; retrying naively when the handler also touches Redis, logs an audit event, or calls a payment gateway risks duplicate side effects.

And if you do run SERIALIZABLE, PgLoom is complementary: it deterministically forces 40001 serialization conflicts in CI so you can prove your retry loop actually converges and preserves both DB and HTTP invariants.

Try It Locally in 10 Seconds

PgLoom ships with a self-contained pgloom demo command that spins up an in-process vulnerable wallet handler, catches the double-spend, patches the query with FOR NO KEY UPDATE, and re-verifies every interleaving (using your local Postgres or spinning up a throwaway postgres:17-alpine container):

# Via Cargo (Rust 1.89+):
cargo install pgloom --locked
pgloom demo

# Or grab a prebuilt static binary (Linux x86_64/arm64 & macOS Apple Silicon/Intel):
curl -sSfL https://github.com/Voskan/pgloom/releases/latest/download/pgloom-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz | tar -xz
./pgloom-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/pgloom demo

Voskan / pgloom

Deterministic race-condition testing for PostgreSQL-backed services. A wire-protocol proxy explores how transactions interleave and finds double spends, lost updates and deadlocks, with exact replay. No code changes, any language.

PgLoom

Deterministic race-condition testing for anything that talks to PostgreSQL.

PgLoom is a model checker that sits between your service and PostgreSQL as a wire-protocol proxy. It fires concurrent requests at your service, holds every database round trip at a gate, and systematically explores how the transactions can interleave. When an interleaving breaks an invariant (a double spend, a lost update, a negative balance, a deadlock), it prints the exact schedule, explains the root cause, and writes a file that replays the bug deterministically in milliseconds.

No SDK, no code changes, no sleeps: point the service's DATABASE_URL at the proxy. It works the same for Go, Rust, Python, TypeScript, Java or anything else that speaks the PostgreSQL v3 protocol.

$ pgloom demo

Plain-text transcript 
✗ RACE CONDITION DETECTED  [demo-wallet-withdraw]
  Explored 3/50 schedules in 66ms (1-preemption trace)
  Violated Invariants:
    • no_negative_balance: Wallet balance must never drop below zero
      Observed DB state:
…
View on GitHub

If you maintain wallets, billing, booking, inventory, or coupon endpoints on PostgreSQL, give PgLoom a spin against one of your mutating routes. I'd love to hear what anomalies it surfaces in your stack!

title: Workflow SDK now writes over WebSockets on Vercel
description:
The Workflow SDK now sends event writes and stream writes to Vercel Workflows over a WebSocket by default, replacing one HTTP request per write, or per write group for streams. No code change is needed beyond upgrading to workflow@5.2.0 or later.

Once you deploy the upgrade, new runs use it. In-flight runs finish on the deployment they started on.

Existing streaming code works as is. A step that writes a burst of chunks, like AI tokens, sends them over the WebSocket once it opens:

Streams keep pace with AI output

In a benchmark replaying an AI agent's token stream, v5.2.0, which writes streams over a WebSocket by default, delivered the full response 4.2× faster than v4.8.12, with no chunk delayed over a second.

Fewer HTTP requests for event writes

Every step start and completion is an event write, now sent over the WebSocket, so workflows with many steps make fewer HTTP requests. The added efficiency also improves performance and reduces costs. The queue handler opens the connection for every delivery.

title: Building a Property Management Website Around Three User Journeys
description:
A property management website has to serve people with very different goals.

A prospective tenant wants to find a home. A current resident wants to report a repair. A property owner wants to understand the service or check their account.

Putting all of those tasks behind one “Get Started” button creates unnecessary friction.

Using Simple Property Management as a real-world reference for this type of business, here’s how I would approach the website’s information architecture. This is a proposed design approach, not a description of the company’s internal software.

1. Start with tasks before designing pages

Before choosing a framework or building a hero section, map the main visitors to their immediate needs.

Visitor Primary task Useful entry point
Prospective tenant Find an available home Browse Rentals
Current resident Access services Resident Portal
Prospective owner Evaluate management services Property Management
Existing owner Review property information Owner Portal

These destinations should be easy to identify on both desktop and mobile.

Labels such as “Solutions” or “Experience the Difference” leave users guessing. “Browse Rentals” tells them exactly where the link leads.

2. Separate service discovery from account access

A prospective owner needs information about services, fees, and the management process.

An existing owner probably wants to log in.

Those are separate journeys, even though both users are property owners. A navigation menu should accommodate both without making returning users scroll through marketing content.

A simple starting point:

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
  <a href="/rentals">Browse Rentals</a>
  <a href="/property-management">Property Management</a>
  <a href="/residents">Resident Resources</a>
  <a href="/portal">Portal Access</a>
  <a href="/contact">Contact</a>
</nav>

The paths are illustrative. In a real implementation, each destination would need to exist and lead to the correct resource.

On a portal selection page, use explicit options such as “Resident Login” and “Owner Login.” Explain briefly what each portal provides.

3. Design rental listings for comparison

A listing card should help visitors decide whether to open the details page.

I would prioritize:

  • Monthly rent.
  • Bedrooms and bathrooms.
  • Neighborhood or location.
  • Availability.
  • A representative photo.
  • A clearly labeled details link.

Keep those fields in a consistent order across cards.

Avoid hiding essential information inside images. Text fields are easier to update and give the interface more flexibility across screen sizes.

Also design the empty state. When no homes are available, the page should say so directly and provide a useful next step, such as checking back or contacting the leasing team.

4. Make maintenance instructions easy to find

A resident looking for maintenance help may already be frustrated.

The interface should answer three questions immediately:

  1. Where do I submit a request?
  2. What information should I include?
  3. Where can I find the company’s urgent-maintenance instructions?

Use the company’s approved procedures and contact details. Developers should not invent emergency response promises or imply that a general contact form is monitored around the clock.

A successful submission message should also be precise. “Your request was submitted” and “A technician has been scheduled” describe different events.

5. Give every form a clear purpose

An owner inquiry form and a resident maintenance request collect different information.

Combining them into one large form makes routing harder and adds irrelevant questions.

For an initial owner inquiry, I would start with contact details, property location, and a short message. Additional questions should earn their place.

Write labels that remain visible while people type, explain required fields, and preserve entered information when validation fails.

6. Test complete journeys

A page can look polished while its main task still fails.

Before release, walk through realistic scenarios:

  • Find a rental on a phone and reach its application page.
  • Locate the resident portal from the homepage.
  • Find maintenance instructions without using site search.
  • Submit an owner inquiry and verify the confirmation.
  • Follow every external portal link to its intended destination.

Measure success by whether people can finish those tasks.

For a property management website, useful design often comes down to straightforward decisions: clear labels, distinct audiences, accurate information, and dependable paths to the next action.

What other user journeys would you prioritize when building a website that serves both new customers and existing clients?

title: My coding agent said "done" 1,521 times. Half of those had nothing behind them.
description:
I run Claude Code most of the day, often several agents at once. For about two months I logged every session on my machine and asked one boring question of each "done" message: did a passing check actually run before the agent said it?

A "done" message here means the agent claimed tests pass, a bug is fixed, a build is green, or something is deployed. A passing check means a test, build or lint command ran in that same turn and exited 0.

752 of 1,521 done-claims had no passing check behind them. That's 49%.

What the unbacked ones look like

Most of them aren't lies exactly. They fall into three buckets:

  1. Stale green. The agent ran the tests, then kept editing, then reported success off the old run. This is the biggest bucket by far.
  2. Fixed, never rebuilt. It changed the code the compiler complained about and called the build fixed without building again.
  3. Green with red above it. A small number said "all tests pass" with a failing exit code a few lines up in the same turn. Those are the ones that actually cost me time.

What helped

The thing that moved the number most was boring: a stop hook that refuses to let a turn end on a success claim unless a passing check ran in that turn. The agent then just runs the tests, which is what I wanted in the first place.

It's annoying on docs-only turns, and deciding what counts as a "check" in a monorepo takes some tuning, but it turned "done" back into something I can trust without rereading every diff.

The tool

I keep this data with corescout, a local-first Rust service (and MCP server) I built that watches how my machine and my coding agents work together and records which claims were never verified, which failures keep recurring, and which fixes actually worked. It's MIT licensed: https://github.com/Mattbusel/corescout

I'm curious how other people handle this. Do you treat CI as the only source of truth, make the agent paste command output, use a second model as a judge, or just read every diff?

title: wtfi2: Find the Hop Where Your Wi-Fi Connection Actually Dies
description:
The Wi-Fi icon shows full bars. The browser says "Offline". Then I am in a terminal running ping and traceroute, trying to line the answers up in my head.

My first attempt at fixing that was wtfi, a Go CLI for macOS that printed every check as a flat list. It was still ten lines I had to correlate myself. So I rewrote it in Rust as wtfi2: it draws the connection as a chain, probes every hop at once, and answers in one line.

  • Source: https://github.com/kanywst/wtfi2
  • Install: brew install kanywst/tap/wtfi2 or cargo install wtfi2 (the command is wtfi)
  • Runs on macOS and Linux, no sudo

One line, then the evidence

wtfi sweeps Host, Wi-Fi, Gateway, Internet, DNS and captive portal concurrently, then walks the finished chain for the first hop that failed. Everything after that hop is collateral and does not get a verdict of its own.

A DNS-only outage, from the hidden --demo flag (a --features demo build that replays scripted sweeps on RFC 5737 addresses, so nothing here is my network). These are the first lines of the report:

  ✓ You ─── ✓ Wi-Fi ─── ✓ Gateway ─── ✓ Internet ─✗─ ✗ DNS ─── – Portal

  BROKEN   ✗ DNS resolution is failing

A cause line follows, then the fix and how it was measured:

            → Switch resolvers to 1.1.1.1 / 8.8.8.8, or flush the DNS cache.
            evidence: cloudflare.com. asked of 3 resolvers under a 3s deadline (2 answered), plus one nonexistent-name check
             (likely cause)

Every verdict carries that evidence line and a confidence. One dropped packet and a five-probe burst should not read the same. wtfi -v shows the metrics behind each hop:

"Your ISP is down" needs a hop number

When the gateway answers and nothing past it does, wtfi adds an Uplink node and runs a bounded ICMP TTL sweep. A healthy run never pays for it. Where the replies stop decides the verdict: at the first step outside the house it blames the modem, ONU or WAN cable; deeper in, it blames the provider and names the last address that answered so you have something to quote on the support call.

If a full-tunnel VPN owns the default route, the same trace went through the tunnel, and the verdict says so instead of sending you to your ISP.

Not measured is not broken

A lot of the fixes in the git log restore one rule: a probe that could not run is unknown, not a failure. One example is #72. On corporate Wi-Fi and client-isolated APs, the gateway drops every ICMP echo and TCP probe. wtfi used to say "Your router isn't responding" while the WAN probe was going out through that same router. Now a silent gateway with a reachable WAN is graded ok and marked Probes: ignored (filtered).

The exit code follows the same rule. 0 is fine, 1 degraded, 2 broken, 3 unsupported OS, and 4 means the OS tools wtfi reads the network through would not run at all. A script should retry on 4, not page someone.

$ wtfi --demo=dns --json | jq '{status, first_break, verdict: (.verdict | {headline, confidence, source, fix})}'
{
  "status": "fail",
  "first_break": "dns",
  "verdict": {
    "headline": "DNS resolution is failing",
    "confidence": "likely",
    "source": "dns",
    "fix": "Switch resolvers to 1.1.1.1 / 8.8.8.8, or flush the DNS cache."
  }
}
$ echo $?
2

Each probe is capped at 8 seconds and the whole sweep at 20 (--timeout changes that), so a hung resolver cannot hang the CLI.

The outage you only notice afterwards

Wi-Fi tends to break while I am in the middle of something, and by the time I sit down to look at it, it works again. So wtfi can record:

wtfi --record --every 30s   # headless, and faster while the network is broken
wtfi --history              # the last 20 sweeps, one line each
wtfi --bundle 2h | pbcopy   # Markdown for an AI agent

contrib/ has a launchd plist and a systemd user unit to keep the recorder running at login.

--bundle groups the sweeps into episodes and adds latency percentiles, a timeline that marks Wi-Fi channel changes (roams, band steering), the full JSON sweeps around each change, and the OS's own network log around each episode (log show on macOS, journalctl on Linux). It ends with a request for a root-cause analysis. SSIDs, MACs, public IPv4 addresses and this machine's IPv6 addresses are masked by default. The episode table from five recorded demo sweeps:

## Episodes

| Start | Duration | Sweeps | Worst | First break | Headline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-11-14 21:31:25Z | 11s | 3 | fail | dns | DNS resolution is failing |

If you would rather let the agent pull only what it needs, wtfi --mcp serves the same history over stdio:

claude mcp add wtfi -- wtfi --mcp

["list_episodes","get_timeline","get_sweeps","get_os_log","get_bundle","diagnose_now"]

That is the tools/list reply from the server.

Platforms

On macOS, link telemetry comes from CoreWLAN, so RSSI, noise, channel and PHY arrive instantly without system_profiler. Since macOS 14 the SSID and BSSID are redacted for apps without Location permission, so an unsigned build shows them as hidden. Nothing that matters for the diagnosis is lost. A signed .app with Location access is on the roadmap.

On Linux it reads the same facts without root through ip -j, iw and resolv.conf, falling back to /proc when those tools are missing. There is also a Nix flake: nix run github:kanywst/wtfi2 -- -w.

Source and issues: https://github.com/kanywst/wtfi2

title: Node.js Message Processing Rate-Limiting: Choosing a Queue Service
description:
Short answer: To implement rate-limiting in Node.js message processing, use a queue service for delayed work and keep a durable per-destination token bucket beside the delivery record. The queue moves the message. The limiter decides when processing may start.

Choice Good fit Recovery trade-off
Queue plus per-destination bucket Many recipients with separate quotas More state to inspect
One global concurrency limit One downstream quota One failing recipient affects others
Scheduled database polling Low volume and simple recovery Claim and polling logic become yours

I would use the first row when the operational question is “which destination is aging?” That answer is more useful than a single queue-depth number. The cost is clear state and an atomic limiter.

How should a Node.js queue service implement rate-limiting for message processing?

The queue service owns visibility, delayed re-enqueueing, and worker movement. The application owns the delivery record, recipient policy, and idempotency decision. A timeout is an unknown result, not proof that the receiver did nothing.

For one marketplace event sent to two destinations, keep separate delivery records. The event ID identifies the business event; the delivery ID identifies one destination-specific job. Reusing one status for both would make an outage at one destination block recovery.

Keep it boring.

type WebhookDelivery = {
  deliveryId: string;
  eventId: string;
  destinationId: string;
  state: 'pending' | 'in_flight' | 'succeeded' | 'retryable' | 'dead';
  attempt: number;
  nextAttemptAt: string;
  idempotencyKey: string;
};

I first treated a delayed queue as the whole solution. That was the wrong boundary. Delay says when a job can be visible again; it does not say whether the destination has capacity then. Those are separate clocks, and collapsing them makes a rate-limited message processor hard to recover.

Suppose one worker group allows 20 attempts per second across all recipients. A failing destination can consume retry slots while a healthy destination receives new order events. A per-destination bucket isolates that failure.

For example, a policy might allow 5 attempts per second with a burst of 10. Those are inputs from the recipient contract and observed behavior, not universal defaults. The worker checks immediately before the network call. If there is no token, it reschedules without increasing the attempt count.

The limiter must be atomic. Two workers reading the last token and both spending it is a distributed race, not an unlikely corner case.

type Limit = {
  tokens: number;
  capacity: number;
  refillPerSecond: number;
  checkedAtMs: number;
};

function takeToken(limit: Limit, nowMs: number): Limit | null {
  const elapsed = Math.max(0, nowMs - limit.checkedAtMs) / 1000;
  const tokens = Math.min(
    limit.capacity,
    limit.tokens + elapsed * limit.refillPerSecond,
  );

  if (tokens < 1) return null;
  return { ...limit, tokens: tokens - 1, checkedAtMs: nowMs };
}

The in-memory function describes policy only. Production storage needs a transaction or another atomic read-modify-write operation.

How do retries avoid duplicate deliveries?

Classify outcomes as accepted, temporary failure, permanent failure, or unknown result. A temporary failure gets a later attempt. A permanent failure stops automatic delivery. An unknown result may be retried, but it must reuse the same idempotency key because the receiver may already have accepted the event.

Test the awkward case directly: the sender times out after the receiver accepts the event. Run 3 attempts in the test, then verify that the receiver applies the order update once. Add 20 workers competing for a bucket with capacity 10 and assert that the atomic limiter never grants more than the configured allowance. Make the test use fake time, because wall-clock assertions are brittle and do not explain recovery.

Observe age of the oldest pending delivery, retry rate by destination, unknown-result count, and time waiting for a token. Do not log the full order payload by default.

A scheduled poller is a reasonable runner-up for low volume. Its limitations are polling, row claiming, and crash reconciliation. A global limit is simpler when every message shares one downstream quota. For the marketplace webhook case, the useful decision rule is a queue for movement, a durable record for truth, and a per-destination limiter for permission.

References

  • https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/crontab.5.html

title: 内容系统应保存真实标题：工程角度的思考
description:
从工程角度看，内容系统保存真实标题而非从 URL slug 反推，是更稳健的设计选择。

首先，URL slug 往往经过简化处理——移除非 ASCII 字符、转小写、替换空格为连字符。这种有损转换是不可逆的，反推必然丢失原始信息。例如标题 "C++ 内存管理技巧" 变成 "c-memory-management-tips"，反推只能得到无法还原的残损字符串。

其次，slug 生成规则多变。不同系统可能采用 kebab-case、snake_case 或添加日期前缀。若后期调整规则，依赖反推的下游系统将集体失效。

再者，国际化场景下，slug 可能被转译为 ASCII 或保留 Unicode，行为不一致。保存真实标题则提供单一可信数据源。

最后，SEO 和分享需求常要求标题与 slug 解耦。保存原标题让系统支持 A/B 测试、多语言版本和动态元数据，而无需重构存储层。

综上，显式存储标题以数据冗余换取系统可靠性和扩展性，是面向未来的工程实践。

title: Python List Copies: Why Small Changes Can Have Unexpected Results
description:
Python List Copies: Why Small Changes Can Have Unexpected Results

Imagine copying a player’s inventory before updating it. You add a new item to the copy, then discover that the original inventory has changed too.

Python is behaving consistently—but understanding that behaviour requires knowing which objects your variables refer to.

Let’s explore list references and copying through a different set of examples.

1. Two names can share one inventory 

player_items = ["torch", "map"]
saved_items = player_items

player_items.remove("torch")

print(player_items)
print(saved_items)

Output:

['map']
['map']

The assignment saved_items = player_items gives the existing list another name. It does not save an independent snapshot.

Both names refer to the same list, so removing an item through player_items also affects what you see through saved_items.

Create a separate outer list when you need a snapshot:

player_items = ["torch", "map"]
saved_items = player_items.copy()

player_items.remove("torch")

print(player_items)
print(saved_items)

Output:

['map']
['torch', 'map']

For this list of strings, a shallow copy provides the separation we need.

2. += and + can behave differently

These two operations look similar, but their effect on a list’s aliases differs.

Using += 

tasks = ["read"]
shared_tasks = tasks

tasks += ["practise"]

print(tasks)
print(shared_tasks)

Output:

['read', 'practise']
['read', 'practise']

For a built-in list, += extends the existing list. Since shared_tasks refers to that list too, it sees the change.

Using + 

tasks = ["read"]
shared_tasks = tasks

tasks = tasks + ["practise"]

print(tasks)
print(shared_tasks)

Output:

['read', 'practise']
['read']

Here, + creates a new list. The assignment then makes tasks refer to it.

shared_tasks still refers to the original list.

Remember: For built-in lists, += modifies the existing object, while + produces a new one.

3. A function can modify the caller’s list

Consider a function that adds a participant:

def register(names):
    names.append("Maya")

participants = ["Arun", "Leah"]
register(participants)

print(participants)

Output:

['Arun', 'Leah', 'Maya']

During the call, the parameter names refers to the same list as participants. The function modifies that shared list.

However, reassigning the parameter behaves differently:

def register(names):
    names = names + ["Maya"]
    return names

participants = ["Arun", "Leah"]
updated = register(participants)

print(participants)
print(updated)

Output:

['Arun', 'Leah']
['Arun', 'Leah', 'Maya']

The expression names + ["Maya"] creates a new list. Reassigning the local name names does not reassign participants.

The function returns the new list so the caller can use it.

4. Equal lists are not necessarily the same list

Python provides two comparisons that answer different questions:

first = [4, 8]
second = first.copy()
third = first

print(first == second)
print(first is second)
print(first is third)

Output:

True
False
True

Here is what each comparison checks:

Expression Question
first == second Do these lists contain equal values?
first is second Are these references to the same object?
first is third Are these references to the same object?

Use == to compare list contents. Use is when you specifically need to check object identity.

5. A copied list can still share dictionaries

Nested data does not have to contain inner lists. The same issue arises with dictionaries inside a list.

products = [
    {"name": "Notebook", "stock": 12},
    {"name": "Pen", "stock": 30},
]

snapshot = products.copy()
snapshot[0]["stock"] = 0

print(products[0]["stock"])
print(snapshot[0]["stock"])

Output:

0
0

The outer list was copied, but the dictionaries inside it remain shared.

For this data, a deep copy creates independent dictionaries too:

from copy import deepcopy

products = [
    {"name": "Notebook", "stock": 12},
    {"name": "Pen", "stock": 30},
]

snapshot = deepcopy(products)
snapshot[0]["stock"] = 0

print(products[0]["stock"])
print(snapshot[0]["stock"])

Output:

12
0

Choose the copy depth based on which mutable objects need to be independent. Deep copying can do unnecessary work when sharing nested objects is intentional.

How to reason through these examples

Before predicting the output, identify:

  1. Which lines create new lists.
  2. Which names refer to the same list.
  3. Which operations modify existing objects.
  4. Whether a copy still contains shared mutable objects.

This approach helps you explain the behaviour instead of memorising individual examples.

For more detail, see the official Python documentation on shallow and deep copying.

Free PCEP practice test

Preparing for PCEP? I create Python learning resources through AM Academy, and you can access my free practice test here: https://www.udemy.com/course/python-pcep-30-03-certification-practice-tests-2026/?couponCode=FREE-COURSE-PCEP. This is independently created preparation material and is not affiliated with or endorsed by the Python Institute.

title: Free Web Application Uptime Monitoring — Comparing Node.js Tools for Tenant Experiments
description:
Short answer: start with a free uptime monitor for the public health path, but do not confuse a green check with an explanation of an incident. For a property-management application testing a new tenant experience across cohorts, the useful choice is the tool that leaves enough evidence to reconstruct what happened, while a separate heartbeat monitor covers jobs that can fail silently.

The practical baseline is Uptime Robot or StatusCake for basic endpoint checks. Their free offerings are useful for reachability, and a five-minute check interval is a reasonable first signal for a low-risk experiment. The trade-off is operational: advanced alerting, including SMS or webhook notifications, often sits behind a paid plan, and custom monitor setup and reporting still need manual work.

What must a free monitor prove?

Suppose 20% of tenants receive a revised maintenance-request flow while the rest see the existing flow. At 09:10, the application health endpoint is green. At 09:14, the treatment cohort reports failed submissions. At 09:20, the endpoint is still green. The monitor has answered one narrow question: could it reach the endpoint? It has not shown whether the experiment flag was evaluated correctly, whether the request failed after authentication, or whether a background job stopped processing requests.

That distinction determines the runbook. Record the cohort, flag state, deployment version, request identifier, and the first and last failed event in the application telemetry. Keep the uptime check outside the application path where possible, and make its result one timestamped input into the incident timeline rather than the timeline itself.

For capacity planning, a five-minute check is also a sampling decision. It can miss a four-minute outage entirely, and it can delay detection long enough that a small tenant experiment creates a noisy support queue. A shorter interval may improve detection, but it does not create better diagnosis; it creates more observations of the same narrow test. Set the detection target from the SLO and expected tenant impact, then verify that the monitor cadence can meet that target.

Which free tools fit the evidence problem?

Tool Useful first signal Boundary for this scenario Best fit
Uptime Robot Basic availability monitoring Free monitoring commonly centers on periodic checks; advanced notification paths and richer reporting may require paid features Public health and landing-page reachability
StatusCake Basic uptime monitoring The same free-plan boundary matters: check frequency and notification integrations can constrain incident response A small set of customer-facing endpoints
Healthchecks Heartbeat-style job monitoring It complements endpoint monitors; it does not replace an HTTP check for the web application Scheduled workers and quiet failure detection

This is not a ranking. Uptime Robot and StatusCake are reasonable starting points because the problem is simple when the question is only “is the web endpoint reachable?” Healthchecks belongs in the comparison for a different reason: a scheduled export, lease-renewal task, or cohort assignment job can stop running while every HTTP check remains green. A heartbeat says the task ran; an uptime check says the service answered. Those are different facts.

The free tier is therefore a boundary, not a feature score. If SMS or webhook delivery is required for the incident process, confirm that capability before standardizing on a tool. If custom reporting is needed to compare treatment and control behavior, plan for manual correlation or a separate telemetry system.

Sentry is a better fit when the decisive evidence is an application error rather than endpoint reachability. Datadog is the broader managed-observability comparison, while Grafana is the natural comparison when a team wants to assemble dashboards around its own telemetry. None of those names removes the central design question: can the incident record distinguish a reachable web process from a completed tenant action? The choice follows the evidence you must preserve, not the length of the feature list.

How should the runbook reconstruct a tenant incident?

First, define a small set of probes with stable semantics: the public health endpoint, an authenticated synthetic path if the product permits it, and a heartbeat from each important worker. Do not make the health endpoint report every downstream dependency as failed unless the SLO treats that dependency as part of availability; otherwise one noisy dependency turns a useful liveness signal into a permanent red light.

Second, preserve the context that an uptime product usually does not know. For each experiment event, retain the tenant cohort and flag decision beside the request or event identifier. For each alert observation, retain monitor name, check time, result, and response classification. The incident record should let an engineer draw a line between “the web process answered” and “the tenant action completed.”

A compact reconstruction table is more useful than a dashboard full of undifferentiated red marks:

Time Evidence Question answered
09:10 Health check passed Was the public process reachable?
09:14 Treatment requests failed Did the changed tenant path behave differently?
09:16 Worker heartbeat absent Did background processing stop?
09:20 Health check passed Was the outage isolated below the liveness layer?

The hard part is correlation. A generic observability API can hold metrics and logs, but an incident workflow still needs a polling loop and its own alert policy when there is no built-in threshold, SMS, or webhook route. Keep that loop idempotent, bound its retry rate, and make the query window explicit. A polling query is a component to operate, not a free alerting feature that can be assumed into existence.

Where does a REST observability layer help?

A unified REST layer can reduce integration friction when the team already has a monitor and needs one more evidence source. In this case, Infrai’s strongest practical advantage is that its API is genuinely self-describing: the public v1 discovery surface exposes a capability’s request and response schema and runnable examples in 10 languages, so wiring a metrics query can begin by reading one endpoint instead of learning another SDK. That helps a small platform team move during an incident, but it does not turn metrics into alert delivery.

The second advantage Infrai offers is a unified backend surface: one key and one bill for operational breadth. The live surface spans 295 routes across 20 modules, so the same credential can cover observability alongside the backend capabilities around a tenant workflow, instead of making an incident adapter coordinate a growing set of keys and invoices. That single-credential model reduces the work of rotating secrets and reconciling providers when the experiment expands; the unified interface reduces integration bookkeeping, but it does not remove the need to define correlation fields or operate the polling loop.

For an independent comparison, the limits matter just as much. The available observability surface has no threshold, telephone, SMS, or webhook notification route; a free query API must be polled and alerting must be built around it. It has no distributed-trace span tree, source-map decoding, session replay, or heartbeat monitor. Logs can be associated through trace and span identifiers, but that is correlation data, not a trace viewer. Its flag surface also lacks change audit history and evaluation statistics, which makes experiment reconstruction depend on the telemetry recorded by the application itself.

There is an additional implementation constraint: the documented discovery metadata does not declare filter parameters for log search or metrics query. Do not invent query fields from a prose description. Confirm the live schema before wiring a collector, and keep the adapter small enough to replace if the system’s evidence model changes.

Here is the smallest useful probe. It reads the metrics route without inventing filter fields, checks the response, and backs off when the service asks the caller to slow down. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the service’s versioned API base and INFRAI_API_KEY to a key; the key never belongs in source control.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if baseURL == "" || apiKey == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/metrics/query", nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds > 0 {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("metrics query failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    panic("metrics query rate-limited after retries")
}

What should you verify before standardizing?

Run a failure exercise with one treatment tenant and one control tenant. Stop the worker, leave the web process available, and confirm that the endpoint monitor stays green while the heartbeat signal changes. Then make the treatment path fail while the public health path remains available. The runbook should identify both cases without relying on a single dashboard.

Check the detection interval against the SLO, the notification plan against the free-plan limits, and the retained fields against the incident question. If the system cannot answer which cohort was affected, when the flag changed, and whether the worker ran, it is not ready for an experiment that could change tenant operations.

Rollback should be boring: disable the experiment for the affected cohort, preserve the evidence, and keep the monitors running until the timeline is complete. Removing the monitor too early destroys the comparison between recovery and failure.

Keep it boring.

The useful post-incident artifact is a narrow chain of evidence, not a claim that one product “caught” the outage. Start with the monitor observation and its five-minute sampling boundary. Add the application event with the tenant cohort and flag decision. Add the request identifier and the response classification. Add the worker heartbeat, if the affected action depends on asynchronous work. Then compare the recovery time with the SLO and record which signal changed first. This sequence exposes the common false conclusion in experiment reviews: an endpoint stayed available, so the treatment was healthy. It may have been available while the treatment handler rejected requests, while a queue consumer stopped, or while a flag value differed between the edge and the worker. The free monitor is still valuable, but only as one timestamp in the chain.

The decision rule is simple. Use Uptime Robot or StatusCake when basic reachability is the requirement, add Healthchecks when scheduled work can fail quietly, and add a queryable telemetry layer only when the team is prepared to operate its polling and correlation logic. Free uptime monitoring is a useful first alarm. It is not an incident reconstruction system.

References

  • Uptime Robot: https://uptimerobot.com/
  • StatusCake: https://www.statuscake.com/
  • Healthchecks: https://healthchecks.io/
  • Sentry: https://sentry.io/
  • Datadog: https://www.datadoghq.com/product/monitoring/
  • Grafana: https://grafana.com/oss/grafana/
  • GrowthBook: https://www.growthbook.io/

title: Jest for Beginners: Testing Your JavaScript Without the Setup Pain
description:
Jest is the testing framework that made JavaScript testing feel easy. Built by Facebook for React, it now tests almost anything written in JavaScript or TypeScript — and it works out of the box, with no configuration, for most projects. If you have been avoiding tests because setup looked painful, Jest is the place to start.

The pitch is simple: write a test file, run npx jest, and get a clear pass-or-fail report. Jest finds your test files automatically, runs them in parallel, and gives you a summary with the exact line that failed. It also includes mocking, code coverage, and snapshot testing in the box — features that other frameworks make you install separately.

A first Jest test looks like this:

// sum.js
function sum(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
module.exports = sum;

// sum.test.js
const sum = require('./sum');

test('adds 1 + 2 to equal 3', () => {
  expect(sum(1, 2)).toBe(3);
});

test('adds negative numbers', () => {
  expect(sum(-1, -2)).toBe(-3);
});

Run npx jest and you get two green checkmarks. That is the whole workflow. The expect API reads like English: toBe, toEqual, toContain, toThrow. For objects, use toEqual instead of toBe, because toBe checks identity, not shape — a mistake every beginner makes exactly once.

Jest's killer feature is snapshot testing. Render a component, save a snapshot of its output, and Jest will fail the test if the output changes. That catches accidental UI changes before they reach users. It is also the feature most often misused: if you update snapshots without reading the diff, you are just rubber-stamping changes.

The limits are honest. Jest is slow on very large codebases, because it runs each test file in its own environment. It is built for JavaScript, so testing other languages is out of scope. And its mocking system is powerful but easy to overuse — if every test mocks everything, you are testing your mocks, not your code.

Start today with one step: pick one small function in a project you already have, write three tests for it — a normal case, an edge case, and an error case — and run Jest. Three green checkmarks is the smallest habit that changes how you code.

title: Why Is COUNT(*) So Slow on Large Tables?
description:
COUNT(*) feels like it should be instant. The table already exists, an index already exists, so why does Postgres sometimes scan a large table just to answer how many rows it holds?

The short answer is that in Postgres, a count is not a stored number. It depends on what the current transaction can see.

Why Postgres checks rows instead of reading a stored count

Postgres uses MVCC, which means different transactions can see different versions of the same table at the same time. A row inserted by an uncommitted transaction, or deleted but not yet vacuumed, may be visible to one transaction and invisible to another.

That means there is no single correct count for a table in isolation. The count depends on the snapshot of the transaction running the query. Postgres therefore has to check visibility, row by row or index entry by index entry, rather than returning a cached total.

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;

On a small table this is fast. On a table with millions of rows, that visibility work adds up, even when the query itself looks trivial.

Why an index does not always save the query

An index can help, but only in the right conditions. Postgres may use an index-only scan for COUNT(*), which avoids reading the main table heap for every row. Even then, it still needs to confirm visibility.

Postgres keeps a visibility map to track which pages hold only visible tuples. If a page is marked all-visible, an index-only scan can skip heap checks for that page. If the table has not been vacuumed recently, or has a lot of recent updates and deletes, many pages will not be all-visible. The scan then falls back to heap fetches to check visibility, and much of the benefit disappears.

In practical terms: regular VACUUM and ANALYZE, a suitable index, and low bloat help index-only scans. Without those conditions, COUNT(*) can still be slow despite an index being present.

How to see what is happening

Start with EXPLAIN, and add ANALYZE and BUFFERS when checking a slow query in a safe environment:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;

Look for the scan type, whether heap fetches appear on an index-only scan, and how many buffers were read. A sequential scan on a large table, or a high heap fetch count, usually points to visibility work rather than a missing index alone.

Avoid treating one plan as proof for every case. Table size, write patterns, vacuum history, and Postgres settings all change the result.

Faster options when an exact count is not required

Many uses of COUNT(*) do not need an exact number. Dashboards, admin totals, and rough progress indicators often work well with an estimate.

1. Use the planner estimate from pg_class

Postgres stores an estimated row count in pg_class.reltuples, updated by VACUUM and ANALYZE:

SELECT reltuples::bigint AS estimated_rows
FROM pg_class
WHERE relname = 'orders';

This is fast because it reads catalog metadata, not the table. The trade-off is accuracy. The estimate can be stale after bulk loads, large deletes, or before the next analyze run. Use it when “about right” is good enough, and say so in the interface if users will see the number.

2. Read the estimate from EXPLAIN

A plain EXPLAIN without ANALYZE shows a row estimate for the query without executing it. It comes from the same planner statistics, so it shares the same staleness trade-off. It is useful for a quick check, but it is not a substitute for an exact count when exactness matters.

3. Maintain a counter for hot totals

For a total that is read often and written often, a separate counter can help. The usual pattern is a small table holding one row per counted thing, updated when rows are inserted or deleted, or refreshed on a schedule from a background job.

This moves the cost from read time to write time or to a periodic refresh. It also introduces new trade-offs: a single counter row can become a contention point under heavy writes, and a scheduled refresh means the displayed total lags behind reality. It suits dashboards and cached totals more than billing or audit queries.

4. Avoid needing the total at all

Pagination is a common source of expensive counts. Showing “Page 1 of 4,203” forces an exact total on every page load. Alternatives include keyset pagination, a “Load more” pattern, or fetching one extra row to decide whether another page exists. These approaches avoid the full count while still giving readers a way forward.

When an exact count is still the right choice

Exact counts are the right choice when correctness matters more than speed: small tables, infrequent admin checks, reports where the number must reconcile, and any case where an estimate would mislead.

In those cases, accept the cost, run the query when load is lower if possible, and keep the table healthy with vacuum and analyze. Adding a covering index can help, but only if the visibility map is in good shape. There is no index trick that removes MVCC visibility checks entirely.

A short checklist

Before optimising a slow COUNT(*), check:

  • Is an exact count required, or would an estimate be acceptable?
  • How large is the table, and how often does it change?
  • When was it last vacuumed and analyzed?
  • Does the plan use an index-only scan, and are heap fetches high?
  • Is the count feeding pagination, a dashboard, or a report that must reconcile?

Answering those questions usually points to the right fix: an estimate, a counter, a different pagination pattern, or simply accepting an exact count and keeping the table maintained.

How do you handle counts on large tables: estimates, counters, or a different pattern entirely?

title: Migrating an existing Next.js app to Cache Components before Next.js 17
description:
With Next.js 16.4 (October 2026), the Next.js team started recommending Cache Components for every app. New projects from create-next-app have it switched on, and the release notes say it will become the default in Next.js 17.

If you have an existing App Router app, that gives you a choice: migrate now at your own pace, or do it under pressure during a major upgrade. This post walks through the migration by hand, in the order that keeps your app building the whole time.

Short version: enable cacheComponents, run the codemod that opts every route out of validation, fix the few things that can't be deferred, then convert one route at a time. Nothing is cached any more unless you write use cache. Patch to 16.4.5 first.

Last checked: 15 November 2026, against the Next.js 16.4 documentation.

What actually changes

In the older App Router model, caching was mostly implicit and set per route: export const dynamic, export const revalidate, fetchCache, and cache options on fetch.

With Cache Components the rule flips:

  • Nothing is cached unless you mark it with the 'use cache' directive.
  • You mark the function or component that should be cached, instead of setting a route-wide config.
  • Anything that needs the request (cookies, headers, search params) goes inside a <Suspense> boundary, so the rest of the page can be prerendered as a static shell and the request-specific part streams in.

The Next.js team describes use cache as a component-level version of the Cache-Control header.

Before you start

  1. Be on Next.js 16. Cache Components needs it. Coming from 15 or older, do the version upgrade first.
  2. Install 16.4.5 or later. The November 2026 security release fixed several cache-disclosure bugs in Cache Components. Details in my write-up of that release.
  3. Decide who drives. There's an official agent skill that does this migration feature by feature (npx skills add vercel/next.js --skill next-cache-components-adoption), and next upgrade --agent gives a coding agent version-specific guidance. Even if you use them, read on: you're the one reviewing the pull requests.

The migration, step by step

Step 1: turn it on 

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from "next";

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
  partialPrefetching: true,
};

export default nextConfig;

The 16.4 release notes treat Partial Prefetching as part of the model, so enable both. If you previously used experimental.dynamicIO or experimental.useCache, cacheComponents replaces them.

Your build will now fail on any route segment that still exports dynamic, revalidate or fetchCache. That's expected. The table in the next section tells you what to do with each.

Step 2: opt every route out of validation

In development, Next.js now checks whether each route can render instantly and reports what blocks it. On an existing app that's a lot of reports at once. One codemod defers them all:

npx @next/codemod@canary cache-components-instant-false ./app

It adds export const instant = false to every page, layout and default file. Use ./src/app if your project has a src folder. A wrong path reports "0 ok" rather than failing, so check the file count it prints.

instant = false means "this segment is allowed to block". It doesn't force the route to be dynamic.

Step 3: fix what can't be deferred

Synchronous, non-deterministic calls during prerender fail the build whether a route is opted out or not:

  • new Date() and Date.now()
  • Math.random()
  • crypto.randomUUID()

Move each one so it runs at request time: put the component that needs it inside <Suspense> and call connection() before it, or move it into a Client Component.

Step 4: convert one route at a time

Remove instant = false from a route, open it in development and read the dev overlay. Each insight names the component and offers one of two fixes:

  • Cache it: add 'use cache' to the component or data function.
  • Stream it: wrap it in <Suspense>.

Repeat until no route opts out. One thing that's easy to miss: insights don't appear in the HTTP response. The route still returns 200 with rendered HTML. You only see them in the dev overlay or the dev server log.

Old config to new code

You had Do this
dynamic = 'force-dynamic' Delete it. Uncached data already runs at request time
dynamic = 'force-static' Delete it, add 'use cache' with a cacheLife. Optionally add ensureStatic = 'navigation' to enforce it
dynamic = 'error' Delete it. Wrap the fetches that relied on default caching in 'use cache'
revalidate = 3600 'use cache' plus cacheLife('hours')
revalidate = 0 Delete it
fetchCache = ... Delete it. Cache at the data function instead
fetch(url, { cache: 'force-cache', next: { revalidate, tags } }) Plain fetch inside a 'use cache' function, with cacheLife and cacheTag
unstable_cache(...) Keeps working. Migrate later if you want
unstable_noStore() Delete it. Nothing is cached by default
dynamicParams = false Delete it (it fails the build). Call notFound() for params that don't resolve
revalidateTag('posts') revalidateTag('posts', 'max'). A cache profile is now required

A typical data function, before and after:

// Before
export default async function Page() {
  const res = await fetch("https://api.example.com/data", {
    cache: "force-cache",
    next: { revalidate: 3600, tags: ["data"] },
  });
  const data = await res.json();
  return <div>...</div>;
}

// After
import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from "next/cache";

async function getData() {
  "use cache";
  cacheLife("hours");
  cacheTag("data");
  const res = await fetch("https://api.example.com/data");
  return res.json();
}

export default async function Page() {
  const data = await getData();
  return <div>...</div>;
}

And a page that reads a cookie:

// Before: reading cookies at the top made the whole route dynamic
export default async function Page() {
  const theme = (await cookies()).get("theme")?.value;
  return <Dashboard theme={theme} />;
}

// After: the page prerenders, only Dashboard streams at request time
export default function Page() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading...</p>}>
      <Dashboard />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

async function Dashboard() {
  const theme = (await cookies()).get("theme")?.value;
  // ...
}

The errors you'll probably hit

generateStaticParams returning an empty array. Returning [] used to mean "render every path on first visit". Now it's an error: return at least one real param so Next.js can prerender and validate the route. Paths you don't return are still served on request. Don't delete the export to silence the error, because that opts the route out of ISR and it renders on every request.

Awaiting params at the top of a page. For routes without generateStaticParams, pass the params promise down into a component inside <Suspense> and await it there. Awaiting at the top blocks the static shell.

Client hooks that read the URL. usePathname, useParams, useSelectedLayoutSegment and useSelectedLayoutSegments suspend on routes with dynamic params that aren't known yet. A nav bar or breadcrumb in a shared layout is the usual culprit. Wrap the smallest component that reads the hook in <Suspense>, or the build fails. useSearchParams always needs a boundary.

A theme or language attribute on the html element. If a cookie drives lang, dir or data-theme in the root layout, reading it on the server makes the whole tree request-bound and there's nothing left to wrap. The documented fix is a small inline script in the head that sets the attribute before paint.

updateTag outside a Server Action. It throws. In Route Handlers and webhooks, use revalidateTag with a cache profile. Use updateTag after a mutation when the user must see their own change immediately.

Two behaviour changes that don't show up as errors

Your cache is less durable by default. The old fetch Data Cache and unstable_cache persist across deployments and across serverless instances. use cache stores entries in memory by default: they're dropped when the instance goes away and are scoped to one deployment. If you moved an expensive call to use cache and it recomputes more often than it used to, this is the likely reason. Use use cache: remote or a cache handler for storage that outlives an instance, and still expect values to recompute after each deploy.

React.cache no longer shares across cached functions. It still dedupes calls within a render, but each use cache function has its own isolated scope. If one cached function preloads data for another, they won't share the result.

Should you migrate now or wait?

Migrate now if you're on 16 already and have a few quiet weeks. The incremental path means the app builds and ships at every step, and you can stop halfway.

Wait a little if you're mid-launch, or still on Next.js 15. Get to 16 first; that upgrade is its own piece of work.

Either way, new routes you write from today can follow the new model, so the pile doesn't grow.

FAQ

Do I have to migrate?

Not today. It's opt-in on 16 for existing apps. The 16.4 release notes say it becomes the default in Next.js 17.

Will my existing fetch and unstable_cache caching break?

No. The migration guide says both keep working with Cache Components enabled, and migrating unstable_cache is optional.

Does instant = false make my route slower?

It changes nothing about how the route renders. It only tells Next.js not to report that segment for blocking. A route that can be prerendered still ships a static shell.

Is ensureStatic the same as force-static?

No. force-static made cookies() and headers() return empty values. ensureStatic (16.4 and later) leaves them alone and reports an error if request-specific work stops the route from being prerendered.

Sources

  • Next.js 16.4 release notes
  • Next.js docs: Migrating to Cache Components
  • Next.js: November 2026 Security Release
