title: Databricks AI Tools: The SQL Commands Your Coding Agent Should Use
description:
What databricks experimental aitools is, the five commands that matter, why it changes how coding agents and scripts talk to Databricks SQL, and the sharp edges I found while testing it.

Suppose you ask your coding agent a simple question: "Which pickup zip codes have the most taxi trips?"

The data is in a Databricks table, the agent has the Databricks CLI, it should take one command... right?

Without help, it takes many!

The agent lists the SQL warehouses to find an ID, it writes a JSON body for the Statement Execution API and it sends it with databricks api post.

It polls until the state is SUCCEEDED, then it parses result chunks or it skips all of that and writes a Python script with a SQL connector.

Each step is a place to make a mistake, and each mistake costs tokens and time.

The Databricks CLI now has a command group built for exactly this job. It is called aitools.

We run every important command against a real workspace, we look at the sharp edges, and then I explain why I think you should pay attention to it.

Databricks AI Tools in one minute

The Databricks CLI is the command-line tool for Databricks.

You install it on your laptop or in continuous integration (CI), and you sign in with a profile from ~/.databrickscfg.

Data engineers use it to deploy Declarative Automation Bundles, run Lakeflow Jobs, and call the Databricks REST APIs.

aitools is two command groups inside the Databricks CLI:

Command group What it does Who uses it
databricks aitools Installs Databricks skills and plugins into coding agents You, once per machine or project
databricks experimental aitools tools Runs SQL and reads table metadata, with output that an agent can parse Your coding agent, your scripts, and you

A coding agent is an AI assistant that runs commands in your terminal, such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex CLI.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions that tells the agent how to do a task. The Databricks skills come from the databricks-agent-skills repository.

A SQL warehouse is the Databricks compute that runs SQL and every tools command below needs one.

The Statement Execution API is the Databricks REST API that runs SQL on a SQL warehouse and the databricks api post is the Databricks CLI command that sends a raw POST request to a REST API, these two are the manual path from the story above.

The second group sits under experimental, and the Databricks CLI is honest about it:

CLI tools to be used by AI agents. These tools are optimized for AI coding agents
like Claude Code and Cursor. The tools can change at any time. There are no
stability guarantees for these tools.

Keep that warning in mind. We come back to it in the negatives.

Our example

Everything in this guide uses one workspace profile and one public table:

Profile:   aws-workspace
Table:     samples.nyctaxi.trips
CLI:       Databricks CLI v1.26.0

samples is a catalog that Databricks ships with every Unity Catalog workspace, so you can run every command here without creating data.

To keep the commands short, I define a small shell function first:

# ~/.zshrc (or paste into your terminal)
ait() { databricks experimental aitools tools "$@"; }

From now on, ait query ... means databricks experimental aitools tools query ....

Add -p <profile> if your profile is not the default.

Command 1: get-default-warehouse

Every tools command needs a SQL warehouse, if you do not give one, the Databricks CLI picks one for you.

To see which one it picks:

ait get-default-warehouse --output json

{
  "id": "9810e746a2babb0b",
  "name": "Serverless Starter Warehouse",
  "state": "RUNNING"
}

That is all it does, and that is the point!

The agent does not need to list SQL warehouses and guess.

If you want every command to use a specific SQL warehouse, set an environment variable:

export DATABRICKS_WAREHOUSE_ID=9810e746a2babb0b

Or pass --warehouse <id> on each query and statement submit command.

Command 2: query

This is the main command, it runs SQL, waits for the result, and prints it.

ait query "
  SELECT pickup_zip, count(*) AS trips, round(avg(fare_amount), 2) AS avg_fare
  FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips
  GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 3"

When an agent runs it (a non-interactive terminal), the output is JSON:

[
  { "avg_fare": "10.62", "pickup_zip": "10001", "trips": "1227" },
  { "avg_fare": "10.98", "pickup_zip": "10003", "trips": "1181" },
  { "avg_fare": "10.91", "pickup_zip": "10011", "trips": "1129" }
]

The help text says that in an interactive terminal it renders a table, and large results open an interactive table browser.

I only ran it non-interactively, so I have not seen the browser.

Look at the values again: "1227" is a string, not a number, every value comes back as a string.

That is fine for an agent that reads the text, but a script that sums the column must cast it first.

Many ways to send SQL

query accepts SQL from four places:

ait query "SELECT 1"                    # positional argument
ait query --file report.sql             # a file (-f)
ait query report.sql                    # a positional argument that ends in .sql and exists
echo "SELECT 1" | ait query             # stdin

Parameters, not string building

This is the feature I like most!

Use :name markers in the SQL and bind values with --param:

ait query --output csv \
  --param zip:INT=10001 \
  --param since:DATE=2016-02-14 \
  "SELECT tpep_pickup_datetime, fare_amount
   FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips
   WHERE pickup_zip = :zip AND tpep_pickup_datetime >= :since
   ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 3"

tpep_pickup_datetime,fare_amount
2016-02-14T00:10:08.000Z,7.5
2016-02-14T00:17:38.000Z,23.0
2016-02-14T00:23:36.000Z,30.0

name=value binds a string, name:TYPE=value binds a typed value, such as DATE or INT.

The Databricks CLI sends an empty value as NULL, it does not support positional ? markers.

Why does this matter? An agent that builds SQL by gluing strings together can, one day, glue in a quote character from your data.

Parameters remove that whole class of bug.

--output csv is useful on its own, you can export a result to a file without a notebook:

ait query --output csv "SELECT * FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips LIMIT 1000" > trips.csv

Many queries in parallel

Pass more than one SQL statement and the Databricks CLI runs them at the same time, up to --concurrency statements (default 8).

I passed two queries, the second one has a typo on purpose:

ait query \
  "SELECT count(*) AS n FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips" \
  "SELECT nope FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips"

Error: multiple queries require --output json (got "text"); pass --output json to
receive a JSON array of per-statement results

The help text says "Multi-query output is always JSON".

In v1.26.0, it is not always JSON: you must ask for it, so add --output json:

ait query --output json \
  "SELECT count(*) AS n FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips" \
  "SELECT nope FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips"
echo "exit=$?"

[
  {
    "sql": "SELECT count(*) AS n FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips",
    "statement_id": "01f1e012-704d-163a-b2d2-17ed3cd4c4f2",
    "state": "SUCCEEDED",
    "elapsed_ms": 1348,
    "columns": ["n"],
    "rows": [["21932"]]
  },
  {
    "sql": "SELECT nope FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips",
    "statement_id": "01f1e012-7052-197a-a61c-dedd88e64047",
    "state": "FAILED",
    "elapsed_ms": 1276,
    "error": {
      "message": "[UNRESOLVED_COLUMN.WITH_SUGGESTION] A column, variable, or function parameter with name `nope` cannot be resolved. Did you mean one of the following? [`dropoff_zip`, `pickup_zip`, `fare_amount`, `trip_distance`, `tpep_dropoff_datetime`]. SQLSTATE: 42703; line 1 pos 7",
      "error_code": "BAD_REQUEST"
    }
  }
]
exit=1

Three things to notice:

  1. The good query still returns its result: One failure does not hide the other answers.
  2. The error carries the suggestion: An agent reads "Did you mean pickup_zip" and fixes its own SQL on the next try.
  3. The exit code is 1: Any failed query makes the whole command fail, so CI checks and scripts can trust it.

Also, notice the shape changed!

A single query returns a list of objects ({"trips": "1227"}), a batch returns columns and rows as arrays.

If you parse the output in a script, you must handle both shapes.

Command 3: discover-schema

Before an agent writes SQL against a table, it needs to know the columns.

Without this command, it runs DESCRIBE, then a sample SELECT, then maybe a null check... that's three round trips per table!

discover-schema does all of it in one command:

ait discover-schema samples.nyctaxi.trips

COLUMNS:
  tpep_pickup_datetime: timestamp
  tpep_dropoff_datetime: timestamp
  trip_distance: double
  fare_amount: double
  pickup_zip: int
  dropoff_zip: int

SAMPLE DATA:
  Row 1:
    tpep_pickup_datetime: 2016-02-13T21:47:53.000Z
    tpep_dropoff_datetime: 2016-02-13T21:57:15.000Z
    trip_distance: 1.4
    fare_amount: 8.0
    pickup_zip: 10103
    dropoff_zip: 10110
  ...

NULL COUNTS:
  total_rows: 21932
  tpep_pickup_datetime_nulls: 0
  ...

For each table you get the column names and types, five sample rows, the null count per column, and the total row count.

Pass many tables in one call, use the full CATALOG.SCHEMA.TABLE name:

ait discover-schema samples.tpch.orders samples.tpch.customer samples.tpch.lineitem

All the probes share one budget of --concurrency statements (default 8), however many tables you pass.

The help text says that Ctrl+C cancels the running statements on the server.

A small warning: the sample rows are real data. If a table holds personal data, the agent now has five rows of it in its context. Point the agent at tables it is allowed to see.

Command 4: statement submit, status, get, cancel

query waits for the result, that is what you want most of the time.

Sometimes you do not want to wait, a large OPTIMIZE, a long backfill, or a heavy report can run for minutes.

An agent that blocks on it cannot do anything else.

The statement commands split the work into steps:

Command What it does Blocks?
statement submit Sends the SQL and returns a statement_id at once No
statement status <id> Reads the current state one time No
statement get <id> Waits until the statement finishes, then prints the result Yes
statement cancel <id> Asks the server to stop the statement No

Here is the full cycle:

ait statement submit "
  SELECT pickup_zip, sum(fare_amount) AS total
  FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips
  GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 2"

{
  "statement_id": "01f1e012-7467-1656-b3f5-73910324e0d2",
  "state": "PENDING",
  "warehouse_id": "9810e746a2babb0b"
}

STATEMENT_ID=01f1e012-7467-1656-b3f5-73910324e0d2

ait statement status "$STATEMENT_ID"
ait statement get "$STATEMENT_ID"

{
  "statement_id": "01f1e012-7467-1656-b3f5-73910324e0d2",
  "state": "SUCCEEDED"
}
{
  "statement_id": "01f1e012-7467-1656-b3f5-73910324e0d2",
  "state": "SUCCEEDED",
  "columns": ["pickup_zip", "total"],
  "rows": [["11422", "19209.5"], ["11371", "14798.84"]]
}

To stop a statement, use cancel, I submitted a slow self-join on the same table, then cancelled it at once:

ait statement cancel "$STATEMENT_ID"
ait statement status "$STATEMENT_ID"

{
  "statement_id": "01f1e01e-4981-1152-92c5-79b495d9e88a",
  "state": "CANCELED"
}
{
  "statement_id": "01f1e01e-4981-1152-92c5-79b495d9e88a",
  "state": "CANCELED",
  "error": {
    "message": "statement reached terminal state CANCELED"
  }
}

The first CANCELED is optimistic, the API returns no body on cancel, so the Databricks CLI assumes it worked. The second one comes from the server.

If you need to be sure, always run status after cancel, a statement get on a cancelled statement prints the same error and exits with code 1.

One difference is easy to miss: The help text says that Ctrl+C on query cancels the statement on the server, but Ctrl+C on statement get only stops waiting. The statement keeps running, and the SQL warehouse keeps working.

If an agent stops waiting, it must also run statement cancel.

Command 5: aitools install

The tools commands are useful, but the agent must know they exist, that is the job of the other command group.

I noticed this the first time I listed my profiles, the Databricks CLI printed a hint before the list:

Databricks skills are not installed. To work with Databricks reliably, first run: databricks aitools install

databricks aitools install finds the coding agents on your machine and installs the Databricks skills for them.

For Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot, it installs a plugin through the agent's own CLI, for the others (Cursor, OpenCode, Antigravity, Pi, Gemini CLI, Goose, Kiro), it writes raw skill files.

To install for one agent, in the current project only:

databricks aitools install --agents claude-code --scope project

Useful flags:

Flag What it does
--agents claude-code,cursor Act only on the named agents
--scope project or global Install for this repository, or for your user
--skills name1,name2 Install only the named skills (with --skills-only or --path)
--experimental Include experimental skills
--path <dir> Write the skill files to a folder, so you can read them first

The group also has list, update, uninstall, and version.

I did not run install for this article, if you want to know what the skills tell your agent before you trust them, use --path and read the files.

The sharp edges

So far so good... right?

Mostly... here is what can hurt you.

It runs any SQL, not only SELECT, the same command that reads a table can drop a catalog:

ait query 'DROP CATALOG IF EXISTS `my_catalog` CASCADE'

The Databricks CLI does not ask "are you sure?". The only guard is the permissions of the identity behind the profile.

If an agent uses your admin profile, the agent has admin rights.

So give the agent its own identity, such as a service principal (an identity for automation, not for a person), and its own profile.

Grant it only what it needs to read:

GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG main TO `agent-readonly`;
GRANT USE SCHEMA, SELECT ON SCHEMA main.reporting TO `agent-readonly`;

It also needs CAN USE on one SQL warehouse, with these grants, a DROP fails on the server, however the agent writes it. Then keep the agent's own approval rules for anything that is not a read.

Quote carefully in zsh and bash: Backticks inside double quotes run a shell command. Use single quotes around SQL that has backtick identifiers, as above.

It can start a SQL warehouse: If the default SQL warehouse is stopped, the first query starts it. That costs money. Pin a small SQL warehouse with DATABRICKS_WAREHOUSE_ID for agent work.

Values are strings in JSON: Cast before you do maths in a script.

Batches need --output json: At least in v1.26.0.

It is experimental: Flags, output shapes, and command names can change in any Databricks CLI release. Do not build a production pipeline on the exact JSON shape.

Why you should pay attention

I see three reasons.

  1. Databricks now treats coding agents as real users of the Databricks CLI: Databricks wrote these commands for agents, said so in the help text, and ships the skills that teach agents to use them. I read that as a signal about where the tooling is going. That part is my opinion, not a fact from the docs.
  2. One command replaces a fragile chain: Find a SQL warehouse, submit, poll, parse, handle errors: query does all of it. Fewer steps means fewer wrong guesses and fewer wasted tokens.
  3. It is useful without an agent. Parameter binding, CSV export, parallel batches with a correct exit code, and asynchronous statements are good tools for shell scripts and CI checks too.

Positives

  • One command for "run this SQL and give me the result", with structured output.
  • Named, typed parameters instead of string building.
  • discover-schema gives columns, samples, and nulls for many tables in one call.
  • Parallel batches return per-query results and a non-zero exit code on any failure.
  • Asynchronous statement commands for long work.
  • aitools install puts the instructions where the agent can find them.

Negatives

  • Experimental, no stability guarantee, and I already found one gap between the help text and the behaviour.
  • Two output shapes, and every value is a string.
  • No built-in guard against destructive SQL, safety depends on your identity and agent permissions.
  • Auto-detection can pick, and start, a SQL warehouse you did not expect.
  • Sample rows from discover-schema put real data into the agent's context.

My default recommendation: install the skills in one project, pin a small SQL warehouse, give the agent a read-only profile, and let it use query and discover-schema for a week.

Wrapping up

If your coding agent talks to Databricks SQL through databricks api post or a one-off Python script, it is working too hard.

databricks experimental aitools tools gives it one command to run SQL, one to understand tables, and a small set to handle long work.

databricks aitools install tells the agent those commands exist.

Treat it as experimental, because it is, give it a narrow identity, because it can run any SQL.

If you already use it in CI or with a coding agent, please tell me in the comments what worked and what broke.

Then try one command today:

databricks experimental aitools tools discover-schema samples.nyctaxi.trips

title: I turned forced colours on for all 76 of our pages, and 39,617 drawing colours ignored it completely
description:
Forced colours mode is the setting behind Windows High Contrast. When it is on, the browser throws away most of your colour decisions and repaints the page in a palette the user chose: one colour for text, one for background, one for links, one for buttons. It is not a dark theme. It is a user saying "I will decide what things look like, thank you".

What makes it interesting to test is that the override is partial. The browser forces some properties and leaves others alone, and the ones it leaves alone are exactly the ones a drawn interface relies on.

Nakodo is a drawn interface. Its public pages contain no photographs and no raster images, just line art. So I turned forced colours on for all 76 pages and counted what changed.

Running it

Chrome can emulate the mode, which means you can test it without a Windows machine:

await page.cdp("Emulation.setEmulatedMedia",
  { features: [{ name: "forced-colors", value: "active" }] });

By hand it is DevTools, the Rendering panel, "Emulate CSS media feature forced-colors", set to active. Readers can follow along on any page of the site.

Then on each page I walked every element and recorded its computed color, backgroundColor, fill and stroke, and whether each had become a system colour or kept its own.

The counts

Across 76 pages:

Measure Count
Elements 59,700
of which SVG elements 34,175, or 57 per cent
color values replaced by the system palette 57,607
color values that kept their own value 2,093
SVG strokes untouched 23,733
SVG fills untouched 15,884
Declarations of forced-color-adjust on the site 0

The first line of the result is good news. Text is the thing forced colours is for, and 57,607 of 59,700 elements hand their text colour straight over. Paragraphs go white, links go yellow, buttons become outlined boxes. The pricing page in this mode is entirely readable: three plan cards as black boxes with white borders, every feature line legible, every price legible.

The one thing it loses there is emphasis. In normal colours the recommended plan is an inverted dark card that pulls your eye across the row. In forced colours all three cards are identical, and the only reason you can still tell which one is recommended is that the word "RECOMMENDED" is text rather than a colour. That is the rule this mode teaches, and it is worth writing on a wall: any distinction carried by colour alone does not survive, and any distinction also carried by a word or a shape does.

The 57 per cent the mode does not touch

More than half of every page here is SVG, and forced colours mode does not override fill or stroke. That is per spec, not a Chrome bug: the forced properties are things like color, background-color, border-color and outline-color. Paint on a shape is left to the author.

So 39,617 colour values across the site carry on exactly as they were, on top of a background the user has just changed to black. Whether that is fine or catastrophic depends entirely on which colour each shape was drawn in. Measured against the forced background:

Drawing colour Contrast against the forced canvas
paper 0 (the fill inside drawings) 20.63:1
ochre 400 (the spot colour) 11.46:1
cyano 800 (the brand mark) 2.23:1
ink 900 (every outline) 1.33:1

The top two are better in forced colours than they are in daylight. The bottom two are the problem, and the bottom one is the whole line system.

Every outline in every drawing on the site is --illo-line, which is ink 900, which lands at 1.33:1 against black. A line at 1.33:1 is not a faint line. It is not there.

What saves the screenshots from being empty is that the drawings are not outlines alone. They are shapes filled with paper and spotted with ochre, with ink outlines on top. The birds on the home page are still perfectly clear in forced colours: white bodies, ochre wings, and outlines you cannot see but do not need. The autumn leaves in the hero, which are mostly ink with a little ochre, are mostly gone.

The clearest single failure is the brand mark in the header. It is one path filled with var(--primary), which is cyano 800, which is 2.23:1 against the forced background. That is below the 3:1 that WCAG 1.4.11 asks of a meaningful non-text graphic, and it sits in the top left corner of all 76 pages.

The one thing that was already handled

There is exactly one rule in 154 KB of CSS that anticipates this mode:

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .hatch {
    background-image: none;
    border: 1px dashed CanvasText;
  }
}

Hatching means "locked" or "not recorded yet" in this interface. It is a repeating background image, and forced colours drops background images, so the meaning would have gone with the pattern. The fallback turns it into a dashed border instead.

It works. Measured on the home page in forced colours, the hatched elements report background-image: none and a 1px dashed border in the system text colour, and in the screenshot the hatched avatar circles are dashed rings exactly as intended.

It is also the only public page that has a .hatch element on it, which is a good reminder of how these things go: the one rule somebody wrote for this mode protects the one component they were thinking about at the time.

The fix is three lines

This is where an earlier decision paid off. Every drawing on the site reads its colours from three custom properties rather than hardcoding them:

:root {
  --illo-line: var(--color-ink-900);
  --illo-fill: var(--color-paper-0);
  --illo-spot: var(--color-ochre-400);
}

There are already two overrides of that trio in the stylesheet, one for the dark theme and one for inverted panels, and each is three lines. So the forced colours version is three more, using the system keywords that are the whole point of the mode:

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  :root {
    --illo-line: CanvasText;
    --illo-fill: Canvas;
    --illo-spot: CanvasText;
  }
}

That maps every outline on the site to the user's text colour and every fill to the user's background, which is precisely what they asked for. The brand mark needs one more rule of its own, since it is painted with --primary rather than with the drawing variables.

Worth saying: forced-color-adjust: none would also make the drawings "work", by exempting them from the mode entirely. That is the wrong tool here. It is for things like a colour picker, where the colours are the content. A kingfisher is not content, it is decoration, and decoration should do as the user says.

Try it

Open any page on nakodo.app, open DevTools, Rendering panel, set forced-colors to active. Then this will tell you how much of the page the mode did not reach:

[...document.querySelectorAll("body *")]
  .filter((el) => {
    const cs = getComputedStyle(el);
    const sys = /^rgba?\((0, 0, 0|255, 255, 255|255, 255, 0)/;
    return (cs.stroke && cs.stroke !== "none" && !sys.test(cs.stroke))
      || (cs.fill && cs.fill !== "none" && !sys.test(cs.fill));
  }).length;

The home page returns the largest number, because it has 860 SVG elements on it. The glossary returns one of the smallest. Neither of them will return zero until I ship those three lines.

The short version

  1. Forced colours is mostly a text feature, and text came through fine. 57,607 of 59,700 colours replaced, no layout damage, every page readable.
  2. SVG paint is yours to handle. fill and stroke are not forced, so more than half of this particular site ignored the mode, and only the lightness of the fills kept it legible by luck.
  3. Measure contrast against the forced background, not against your own. Ink on paper is 15.74:1 and the same ink on the user's black canvas is 1.33:1. It is the same colour. It is a different page.
  4. A theme that runs on a few variables is cheap to extend. Three lines, because somebody avoided hardcoding ink into 26 drawings two months ago.

title: Google pairs confidential TPU 8tx with AMD EPYC hosts instead of Axion
description:
Originally published on The Daily Flare.

Google announced on November 9 that its new TPU 8tx confidential-AI system will pair its accelerator with fifth-generation AMD EPYC host CPUs, rather than its Axion processor.

The announcement came six days before TechRadar published its analysis on November 15. The TPU 8tx uses the same accelerator silicon as Google’s TPU 8t, which is designed for training, but changes the host processor and network configuration for confidential workloads.

Google introduced the eighth-generation TPU 8t and TPU 8i in April 2026. The 8t targets large-scale model training, while the 8i is intended for inference, sampling and reasoning. Both systems use Google’s Arm-based Axion CPU as their host. The new 8tx configuration is designed for confidential inference and small-scale training, including work for regulated businesses and government customers.

Taiwanese outlet INSIDE reported that the 8tx retains the TPU 8t’s 12.6 petaflops of FP4 compute and 216GB of high-bandwidth memory, while adopting the Boardfly network used by the 8i. Google says the revised system can deliver up to twice the 8t’s latency performance with a near-zero performance penalty. Those figures describe Google’s claims, not independently reported test results.

AMD says its EPYC processors coordinate workloads, prepare data and provide high-throughput communication with the TPU accelerators. They do not replace the TPUs’ AI processing role. The host-and-accelerator arrangement is central to the system’s confidential-computing design: AMD says its Secure Encrypted Virtualization technology works with the TPU environment to extend protections to connected accelerators.

In AMD’s description, the system checks an accelerator’s identity and security configuration before granting it direct access to protected memory. AMD says prompts, model weights and intermediate data remain encrypted in host memory and while moving between the host and accelerators, with hardware isolation during accelerator execution. Google described the system as “keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use.”

TechRadar pointed to Google’s existing confidential-computing support as a likely explanation for using EPYC rather than Axion. Google’s documentation lists Confidential VM configurations based on AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization and Intel Trust Domain Extensions. It does not list Axion-based C4A or N4A instances among those configurations, and states that TPUs cannot currently be attached to Confidential VMs.

That evidence suggests Google’s established confidential-computing trust chain is currently built around x86 processors. Axion, which Google unveiled in 2024 as its first data-center processor, is based on Arm’s Neoverse V2. Qualifying a separate Axion-based security stack would require establishing and reviewing that chain for a product whose purpose is to protect sensitive data in use. Google has not confirmed that this is why it chose EPYC, so the explanation remains an inference from its documented support.

AMD said Google security specialists have conducted deep reviews of its security-processor firmware. The company also said SEV already supports Google services including Confidential VMs, Confidential GKE, Confidential Space, and confidential Spark and Dataflow. That existing use gives EPYC a role in extending Google’s confidential-computing offering to TPU workloads.

Google Cloud infrastructure chief Mark Lohmeyer told reporters that selected customers would be able to deploy the 8tx in their own data centers. The system is therefore intended to protect workloads not only in Google-operated facilities but also when customers run it in third-party locations. Hardware attestation, which checks a system’s identity and security state, is part of the mechanism for allowing model owners to place sensitive data and model weights on hardware operated elsewhere.

The host choice is also tied to the accelerator’s interface, according to ServeTheHome. It reported that Google selected AMD’s Turin-generation EPYC processors to match the TPU 8t’s PCIe Gen5 x16 connection; a newer PCIe Gen6 host would not provide additional bandwidth to the accelerator. The outlet also connected that choice to Google’s 2027 qualification schedule.

AMD cautions that its Infinity Guard security features vary by EPYC generation and processor series, and require enablement by a server manufacturer or cloud provider. The protections available in a particular 8tx deployment therefore depend on the configuration enabled by its provider.

title: One database, four dialects: MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server and PostgreSQL clients on one server
description:
Count the databases your team runs. If you got to one, congratulations. Most of us get to three or four, and not because we wanted to:

  • the web app was written for MySQL,
  • the reporting tool wants PostgreSQL,
  • the vendor product you bought last year ships with SQL Server,
  • the CMS is still on MariaDB.

Four installers, four backup scripts, four monitoring setups, four upgrade days.

I have been working on a database server called Raft DB that tries to give that back: one install that speaks all of those protocols, so you keep your drivers and your SQL and change only the address in the connection string.

What it looks like

After the install, each protocol has its usual port:

Client Port
MySQL / MariaDB 3306
SQL Server (T-SQL) 1433
PostgreSQL 5432
Raft DB native protocol, HTTP API, web studio 7480

(If a port is taken, the installer uses the next free one and prints which.) And you connect with the tools you already have:

mysql -h 127.0.0.1 -P 3306 -u admin -p
psql "host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 user=admin dbname=postgres"
sqlcmd -S 127.0.0.1,1433 -U admin -C

Same for the drivers behind your app (JDBC, ODBC, .NET, Python, PHP, Node.js) and the ORMs on top of them. The front-ends run side by side, so your MySQL app, your PostgreSQL reporting tool and the SQL Server vendor product can use the same install at the same time.

What is underneath

One engine: JSON documents with a schema, a write-ahead log, row versions so readers get a consistent snapshot, and replication using the Raft consensus algorithm (hence the name). The front-ends are separate programs in front of it, one per dialect.

If you are starting something new you do not have to use anybody's dialect: there is a native protocol and an HTTP API, connectors for 16 languages, and a web studio at http://127.0.0.1:7480/ to look at the data.

The honest part

I would rather you hear these from me than find them on a Friday.

Each dialect sees its own databases. Create a table through the MySQL port and \dt in psql will not show it. They share the engine, the disk, the replication and the studio, not the tables. If a tool in one dialect has to read what an app in another dialect wrote, go through the native HTTP API, which can read all of it.

Compatibility is partial, and different per dialect. Every front-end has an "Errors and limits" page that lists what is refused or different. Some things will not come at all, for example add-ons written in native code. Read that page for your dialect before you move anything real.

MySQL and MariaDB share one front-end. It serves one of the two dialects at a time, chosen in a setting. The other front-ends run next to it regardless.

It is version 0.0.1. Pre-release. Windows (Intel/AMD and ARM) and Linux (x86-64 and ARM64) only, no macOS yet. It is free to use and closed source.

Try it, and tell me what breaks

Download: https://raftdb.com (one installer for Windows, one script for Linux, both for Intel/AMD and ARM). Connectors, docs and the limits pages are there too, and there is a short project page at https://github.com/developerfowlguard/raftdb.

The most useful thing you can do is point one real client of yours at it, run what your app actually runs, and report what does not work. I especially want to hear about drivers and ORMs I did not test.

Raft DB is independent software and is not affiliated with, endorsed or sponsored by Oracle, MariaDB, Microsoft or the PostgreSQL project. MySQL and Oracle are registered trademarks of Oracle and/or its affiliates; MariaDB is a trademark of MariaDB plc; Microsoft and SQL Server are trademarks of the Microsoft group of companies; PostgreSQL is a trademark of the PostgreSQL Community Association of Canada. The names are used only to say which protocols Raft DB works with.

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.22

We've released version 6.22 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

Feature

Transcript separation for chat

You can now configure Google Cloud CCaaS to deliver a separate transcript file for each participant segment in a chat, instead of one combined transcript per session. Under Settings > Chat > Chat Transcript, select Per Segment in Transcript Separation to generate individual transcript files for each agent, virtual agent, or supervisor who joins the chat—helpful for identifying which participant handled each part of a transferred or escalated conversation. Your consumers still receive a single, full-chat transcript regardless of this setting.

For more information, see Chat transcripts and chat history.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Campaign-based scheduled callbacks

Agents can now schedule a callback during an outbound campaign call. The callback belongs to the campaign, not to an individual agent, and the dialer calls the consumer back in the time slot they chose. Administrators set slot length, capacity, booking window, and expiry for each campaign, and supervisors can track upcoming, completed, and expired callbacks from the campaign list.

For more information, see Campaign management.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where direct access point (DAP) greeting messages played twice when a call was deflected to an internal phone number due to queue overcapacity.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata for top-level menu paths and selected menus was incorrectly displayed in English instead of the user's configured language.

  • Fixed an issue where a failed Salesforce lookup was incorrectly treated as having no matches, which resulted in the creation of duplicate records.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound transfer restrictions remained in force even after being hidden in the administrator interface, causing queues to become silently unreachable for transfers.

  • Fixed an issue where hold music continued to play throughout a call recording after a warm transfer was completed.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound virtual agent audio was prematurely truncated during multi-message turns.

  • Fixed an issue where the Real-time Monitoring Queues report didn't accurately count skill-matched agents for skills-based queues, often displaying zero available agents despite their availability.

  • Fixed an issue where calls deflected to an external phone number after entering a queue were incorrectly recorded as abandoned by the customer.

  • Fixed an issue where the credit card tokenizer was missing from the SmartActions menu during outbound callback calls.

  • Fixed an issue where mandatory call dispositions were discarded if an agent's voice connection dropped but their session remained active.

  • Fixed an issue where the text resize menu in the chat widget wasn't scrollable at 400% browser zoom, which prevented users from accessing all available text size options.

  • Fixed an issue where the system incorrectly prevented saving automatic call redirection settings when the target was a virtual agent-operated queue.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate call records were created for a single inbound call, causing incorrect wait times to appear in the real-time queue view.

  • Fixed an issue where empty data attributes caused an error in the agent interface during call connections.

  • Fixed an issue where the Transfer Restrictions destination picker provided no feedback when a queue was ineligible, making it indistinguishable from a typo or search error.

  • Fixed an issue where incoming calls were rejected with a SIP 603 error due to high database latency and connection timeouts.

  • Fixed an issue where the documentation for the Apps API and call session metadata schema didn't define the top-level parentId and finishReason fields.

  • Fixed an issue where certain inbound call failures were incorrectly reported as a busy signal.

  • Fixed an issue where the event processor service crashed during scaling or rebalancing of the system.

  • Fixed an issue where the conversation ID was missing from chat events during active sessions.

  • Fixed an issue where report exports didn't download or remained stuck in a processing state indefinitely.

  • Fixed an issue where agents could transfer calls to queues that were already closed if their transfer list was loaded while the queue was still open.

  • Fixed an issue where queued chats were assigned to agents after the end-user had become unresponsive without being prompted to check in.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls cold-transferred to an over-capacity queue generated duplicate reporting records and incorrect queue wait times if the callback leg failed.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls deflected to voicemail during after-hours played three separate audio prompts sequentially.

  • Fixed an issue where a single call was simultaneously assigned to two different agents if the pickup coincided with the cascade timer expiry.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls weren't projected to agents in a breakthrough-enabled status if another call was already waiting in their queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a gray empty area appeared below the chat container in the agent adapter when the iframe width was narrower than 449px.

  • Fixed an issue where several Kubernetes and Google Cloud service accounts were granted overly broad permissions, which could have allowed for unauthorized privilege escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's status sequence was recorded in the incorrect order following a brief connection loss during an active chat.

  • Fixed an issue where selecting a contact during a native campaign call didn't automatically open the corresponding record in the CRM.

  • Fixed an issue where AI-generated Smart Disposition suggestions were inconsistently displayed for outbound calls during the wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings became distorted or garbled when multiple holds were placed during a call.

  • Fixed an issue where audio uploads were accepted based on the file extension rather than the actual file content, which caused call disconnections when incompatible formats were played.

  • Fixed an issue where the call duration timer in the external call adapter didn't match the In-call status timer in the agent desktop for inbound calls.

  • Fixed an issue where the sentiment score was incorrectly displayed in the call adapter for calls escalated from a virtual agent, even when the Sentiment Analysis setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate reporting rows were generated for call and wrap-up durations due to concurrent system events.

  • Fixed an issue where agents couldn't sign in or refresh their status if their account was linked to a deleted or unknown status.

  • Fixed an issue where the Manager API documentation for agent activity logs omitted 17 chat routing and activity values, leading to incomplete reporting data for customers.

  • Fixed an issue where IVR custom callback numbers for certain international regions, including Norway and Denmark, were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix.

  • Fixed an issue where metadata for calls deflected between virtual agent assignment and connection wasn't exported to the Cloud Storage bucket.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent to human chat escalations experienced delays of up to 300 seconds during agent assignment.

  • Fixed an issue where the Answer button didn't appear for dial-by-extension calls when other calls were already waiting in an agent's queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a supervisor's name didn't appear in the chat widget when joining a conversation using the monitor then barge workflow.

title: Vercel Container Registry now supports 2 GB compressed image layers
description:
Vercel Container Registry now supports compressed image layers of up to 2 GB each, up from 500 MB, the total image size limit stays 15 GB.

The registry works with standard workflows like docker push, docker pull, and docker tag, and pushing an image creates the repository on the fly.

Repositories can be made public for read-only pull access by any Vercel team, or shared with specific teams up to 100 from the dashboard or with vercel vcr permissions. The Vercel Managed Images that Vercel Sandbox runs on are served from ordinary public repositories, built with the same public-repository feature any team can use for its own images.

Manage repositories, images, and tags with the vercel vcr CLI commands in Vercel CLI v58.3.0 or later, and log CI workflows in from GitHub Actions with the vercel/vcr-action/login action using GitHub OIDC, which removes the need for long-lived registry credentials. If background optimization of a pushed image fails, the image shows an error status in the dashboard, and pushing the same image again retries the conversion.

See the documentation for the full setup.

title: Let your coding agent start from a real component instead of writing one from scratch
description:
Ask Claude Code, Codex or Cursor for "a hotel date picker with a price under each night" and you will get a calendar written from zero. It renders. It usually misses the details a mature component already handles: check-out on a night that is booked by the next guest, a minimum stay, the total under the selected range, keyboard navigation.

We built Clay UI so the agent looks in established component libraries first, then adapts real code to your project.

Demo videos and the site: https://clayui.behavio.one

What the agent does with it

Install the skill in a project:

npx @behavio1/clayui init

Then ask in plain words, in any language. The skill tells the agent to translate the request into a concrete English search and run the CLI:

clayui search "date range picker booking nightly price" --available-only --json

For that request the top three results are:

kokonut/stay-picker     A date range picker for booking stays. Every night shows its price...
kokonut/team-selector   Seat picker with a scrubbable number, generated avatars and a price line
shadcn/calendar         Select a date or a range of dates (react-day-picker)

The agent shows you the options with preview links. You pick one, and it downloads the source:

clayui get kokonut/stay-picker --out .clayui-examples --json

The folder holds the component files exactly as the library publishes them, the usage notes from its docs, and a clayui.json. Here is part of the real one:

{
  "id": "kokonut/stay-picker",
  "sourceUrl": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kokonut-labs/kokonutui/main/public/r/stay-picker.json",
  "sourceRef": "main",
  "license": "MIT",
  "dependencies": ["lucide-react", "motion"],
  "gaps": ["local-imports-missing"],
  "missingLocalImports": [
    { "file": "components/kokonutui/stay-picker.tsx", "import": "@/lib/utils" }
  ],
  "files": ["components/kokonutui/stay-picker.tsx"]
}

It also stores a SHA-256 for every file. The gap here is the usual cn helper from @/lib/utils, which most shadcn-style projects already have. The agent sees it and either reuses yours or adds it.

The agent then rewrites the example into your codebase: your tokens, your data, your naming. Clay UI never runs npm install and writes only into the examples folder.

Where the components come from

shadcn/ui, Radix, Base UI, Sonner, Vaul, cmdk, NumberFlow, Beautiful UI, RareUI, Magic UI, Aceternity UI, 21st.dev and Kokonut UI. The CLI keeps a local index of them and refreshes it from each library's registry or repository.

Two decisions that mattered

Be honest about what is missing. A component that imports ../utils/foo you did not get is not a working example. get resolves every relative and alias import against the delivered files and reports the ones that are missing as local-imports-missing. Paid or deleted items exit with code 3 instead of writing a half-empty folder. The agent reads those gaps before it starts adapting.

Search without a key, better with one. Out of the box the search is BM25 over names, descriptions and synonyms, with no account needed. Set a Gemini API key and it adds semantic search with gemini-embedding-001, which handles loose requests like "this checkout feels cheap" much better. Query embeddings are cached for 30 days.

Try it

  • Install: npx @behavio1/clayui init
  • Code and docs (MIT): https://github.com/behavio1/clay-ui
  • How we measure search quality: https://github.com/behavio1/clay-ui/blob/main/docs/search-tuning.md
  • Short demos: https://www.youtube.com/@BehavioOne

The CLI is a small Rust binary, shipped through npm for macOS, Linux and Windows. If a search returns the wrong component for your request, open an issue with the query. That is the most useful feedback we can get.

Disclosure: this account belongs to Behavio One, the team that built Clay UI.

title: Refactoring in Java 21+: Records and Pattern Matching for Readable Code
description:
Introduction to Legacy Code in Java

For years, Java developers have relied on extensive class hierarchies, multiple type checks using the instanceof operator, and explicit type casting to model data and handle complex conditional structures. This traditional approach not only increases the volume of source code but also introduces latent runtime risks, such as ClassCastException, while severely hindering long-term software maintainability.

With the release of Java 21, the language has matured significantly thanks to stable, high-impact features such as Records and Pattern Matching for switch. These modern tools allow architects and developers to write highly expressive, safe code aligned with Google Java Style standards. Below, we will analyze a real refactoring case from a legacy design to a modern, self-documenting design.

The Problem: Legacy Code with Verbose Checks

Let's consider a typical enterprise application processing network or database operation responses using abstract classes and multiple subclasses along with chained if-else blocks to determine the received response type:

// BEFORE: Verbose and error-prone legacy code
public abstract class Response {
}

public class SuccessResponse extends Response {
    private final String data;
    public SuccessResponse(String data) { this.data = data; }
    public String getData() { return data; }
}

public class ErrorResponse extends Response {
    private final String errorCode;
    public ErrorResponse(String errorCode) { this.errorCode = errorCode; }
    public String getErrorCode() { return errorCode; }
}

public class ResponseProcessor {
    public static String process(Response response) {
        if (response instanceof SuccessResponse) {
            SuccessResponse success = (SuccessResponse) response;
            return "OK: " + success.getData();
        } else if (response instanceof ErrorResponse) {
            ErrorResponse error = (ErrorResponse) response;
            return "FAIL: " + error.getErrorCode();
        } else {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown response type");
        }
    }
}

This traditional pattern presents several drawbacks: it requires writing manual constructors, getters, equals, hashCode, and toString methods, while duplicating unnecessary casting logic inside conditional structures.

The Solution: Records and Pattern Matching in Java 21

We can radically refactor this design using sealed interfaces, Records to model immutable data concisely, and Pattern Matching applied to the switch statement. This combination completely eliminates explicit casting and ensures exhaustiveness of analyzed cases.

// AFTER: Clean, modern, and safe code in Java 21
public sealed interface Response permits Response.Success, Response.Error {
    record Success(String data) implements Response {}
    record Error(String errorCode) implements Response {}

    /**
     * Processes the response safely using pattern matching.
     *
     * @param response the response received from the server
     * @return a formatted string with the processing result
     */
    static String process(Response response) {
        return switch (response) {
            case Success(var data) -> "OK: " + data;
            case Error(var code) -> "FAIL: " + code;
        };
    }
}

Architectural Advantages and Maintainability

  1. Boilerplate Reduction: Records automatically generate the canonical constructor, accessors, string representations, and equality contracts.
  2. Type Safety (Exhaustiveness): The Java compiler validates that all subtypes of a sealed interface are covered in the switch, preventing runtime errors from forgotten branches.
  3. Extreme Readability: Deconstruction patterns allow direct access to internal record components inside the pattern itself.

Auto-Documentation with Artificial Intelligence (Auto-Doc AI)

Using modern standards like Java 21 drastically facilitates the task of Auto-Doc AI tools. Thanks to the clear semantics of sealed interfaces and records, automated documentation generators can infer precise contracts without requiring redundant annotations. By integrating automatic formatters under the Google Java Style standard, we guarantee that code structure remains uniform across the entire development team, reducing friction in code reviews and elevating the overall quality of the corporate repository.

Try it interactively: Format, validate, and auto-document your java directly in JW Solutions Code Formatter & Auto-Doc AI.

title: KiviDB 1.2.2: A Redis-Compatible Rust Database With Built-In Vector Search
description:
Why KiviDB is worth a look now

Redis-compatible databases are easy to describe and harder to evaluate. A new server may speak RESP and support familiar commands, yet still differ in scripting, clustering, persistence, modules, or operational behavior. KiviDB combines a Redis-style interface with built-in JSON, full-text search, vector search, time-series commands, and other data structures in a Rust server.

The immediate reason to examine it is release 1.2.2, published on November 12, 2026. It fixes a medium-severity server-availability issue affecting versions 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 when a search index was being changed while a multi-key write encountered an expired key. The server could stop answering, including PING, until restarted. This was not a data-loss issue, but it matters when evaluating a database for real workloads.


Maintainer-published benchmark overview for KiviDB 1.2.0. Read the benchmark methodology before comparing the numbers.

What KiviDB provides

KiviDB is a standalone database server that accepts Redis clients over RESP2 and RESP3. Its compatibility target is Redis 8.10 for commands it implements. That wording matters: it does not mean every Redis feature, module, or operational workflow is supported.

The feature set includes:

  • Familiar strings, lists, hashes, sets, sorted sets, streams, transactions, and pub/sub.
  • JSON commands and Redis Stack-style full-text search.
  • Vector indexing using FLAT or HNSW, with configurable distance metrics.
  • Time-series commands, built-in Bloom filters, and vector sets.
  • Native snapshots that can preserve keys, index schemas, and populated HNSW graphs.

The workflow is simple: an application uses its existing Redis client, connects to KiviDB's RESP endpoint, and sends supported commands. A service that needs caching, structured documents, and semantic retrieval can evaluate one process instead of immediately adding a separate vector database. The trade-off is that more workloads now depend on the same database process.

Install KiviDB 1.2.2

The official README provides packages for Debian and Ubuntu, Fedora and compatible distributions, Homebrew, Cargo, and Docker. For an isolated test, Docker is the shortest route.

docker run -d \
  --name kividb \
  -p 6380:6380 \
  -v kividb-data:/home/kividb \
  kividb/kividb:v1.2.2

The volume is important. KiviDB stores its data under /home/kividb; without a persistent volume, removing or recreating the container can remove the data directory with it.

Check that the server is responding:

redis-cli -p 6380 PING
redis-cli -p 6380 SET greeting hello
redis-cli -p 6380 GET greeting

The expected responses are PONG, OK, and the stored value. Notice the port: KiviDB listens on 6380 by default, not Redis's usual 6379. That allows both servers to run side by side.

The package installation starts a systemd service bound to 127.0.0.1:6380. Protected mode is enabled by default, so do not expose the server to a network until you have configured authentication, binding, and transport security.

A practical vector-search example

KiviDB implements Redis Stack-compatible FT commands. The official quick start creates a hash index with an HNSW vector field:

redis-cli -p 6380 FT.CREATE idx ON HASH PREFIX 1 doc: SCHEMA \
  vec VECTOR HNSW 10 TYPE FLOAT32 DIM 128 DISTANCE_METRIC COSINE M 16 EF_CONSTRUCTION 128

Vectors are stored as raw little-endian FLOAT32 bytes in a hash field. A vector with 128 dimensions therefore needs 512 bytes. Use a binary-safe Redis client and generate the vector with your application or a library such as NumPy.

The search documentation shows the K-nearest-neighbor query shape:

FT.SEARCH idx '*=>[KNN 10 @vec $q]' PARAMS 2 q <binary-vector> DIALECT 2

Creating an index is easy; producing consistent embeddings, storing binary vectors correctly, choosing an index configuration, and measuring recall versus latency are the real engineering work.


Vector-search chart from the project's 1.2.0 benchmark assets. It is a maintainer-produced result, not an independent cross-vendor certification.

Compatibility and trade-offs

KiviDB's compatibility document is essential reading. It lists several boundaries:

  • Sentinel is not implemented.
  • Redis modules cannot be loaded with MODULE LOAD. Some Redis 8 module functionality is built in, but arbitrary module compatibility is not.
  • Lua scripting is absent from the default build. Choose the Lua or full binary variant if your workload depends on EVAL or functions.
  • Scripts run on Lua 5.4, which can differ from Redis's Lua 5.1 behavior.
  • Some cluster operations and hybrid-search cases have specific limitations.
  • KiviDB has no REST API; it is a Redis-protocol server.

The project is licensed under AGPL-3.0-only. That is a strong copyleft license, so teams should review the obligations for their deployment and distribution model rather than treating it as interchangeable with BSD or MIT software.

Alternatives depend on the job. Valkey is a natural choice when you want an open Redis-compatible server. Redis remains strong when its ecosystem and operational familiarity matter most. Dragonfly and Garnet are worth benchmarking for high-throughput workloads. Qdrant or Weaviate may be a better fit when vector retrieval is the primary workload rather than one feature in a general-purpose store.

How to read the performance claims

KiviDB publishes a benchmark suite for throughput, latency, memory, snapshots, and vector search. The maintainers document their hardware, workloads, and cases where KiviDB loses. That is useful, but it is still a project-produced benchmark.

Use the same client, payload sizes, pipeline depth, persistence mode, hardware, and network path when comparing systems. Measure p50 and p99 latency under mixed reads and writes, restart behavior, and the cost of rebuilding indexes after a restart.

The 1.2.2 release is a patch, not a reason to assume every earlier release is unsafe in every configuration. The advisory says the lockup affected 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 when a search index was present; 1.1.x and servers without a search index were not affected. If you run 1.2.0 or 1.2.1, upgrade to 1.2.2.

Who should evaluate it?

KiviDB is worth testing if you already use Redis clients and want to experiment with a single server for caching, structured data, full-text search, and vectors. It is not yet a universal replacement for Redis, especially if your deployment relies on Sentinel, arbitrary modules, or exact scripting compatibility.

Start with a disposable dataset, run your application's integration tests, test persistence and restart behavior, and review the license before adopting it for a commercial service.

Would you rather keep vector search beside your cache, or split those responsibilities between a Redis-compatible store and a dedicated vector database?

Sources and further reading

  • KiviDB repository
  • KiviDB 1.2.2 release notes
  • Security advisory GHSA-8rm8-p5c5-g3mr
  • Compatibility matrix
  • Vector search guide
  • Performance methodology
  • Earlier project walkthrough

Author links: GitHub · LinkedIn · StackShade on YouTube

AI disclosure: This article was prepared by an autonomous AI editorial agent from public sources. The setup and command syntax were checked against upstream documentation; no benchmark was run for this article.

title: How OpenEvidence scales medical search for 650K doctors
description:
OpenEvidence on Vercel

  • Serves 650,000 doctors with medical search

  • Completes production deployments in about five minutes

  • Absorbs traffic spikes without additional capacity provisioning

  • Reduced serverless spend by 90% with Fluid compute

  • Updates doctor- and patient-facing applications independently

OpenEvidence helps physicians find medical evidence during care, whether they’re checking a dosage on intensive care rounds or handling a case outside their specialty without a specialist nearby. Answers draw on peer-reviewed literature and include citations, so doctors can examine the sources behind them.

OpenEvidence’s small team began using Vercel to get early experiments online and kept that workflow as the product grew, relying on the platform to handle web deployments and capacity.

Building software physicians depend on

The stakes are different when software helps inform medical decisions. An incorrect answer can affect how a doctor treats a patient, while an unavailable application can cut off access to evidence when it is needed.

OpenEvidence supported more than 20 million clinical consultations in January 2026. The company also reported that more than 100 million Americans were treated by doctors using OpenEvidence in 2025.

"Honestly, life or death is not inaccurate," says Kush Khosla, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. "We operate in situations where it's an ER and they really need to know what's going on. Uptime is very, very important to us."

"A lot of doctors and medical professionals are used to really outdated software," says Andy Yoon, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. A more modern experience still needs to meet physicians' expectations of speed, stability, clarity, and information they can trust. The small team needs a way to test updates to the web application before putting them into production and to roll back if something goes wrong.

Keeping releases simple as the audience grows

Andy recalls why Vercel suited the team he joined at OpenEvidence. "I was pretty much the only engineer on our team coming from an actual frontend background," he says. "Most of our team works in Python and machine learning." He adds, "Given the makeup of our engineering team, Vercel really scaled with our needs so well."

The team builds its physician-facing web application with the Next.js framework. When engineers push changes to a development branch, Vercel builds and deploys a preview, giving them a link they can use for live demos and share with colleagues to try new features. Pushing or merging into the production branch then triggers the production build and deployment. If a release needs reverting, the team can roll back to a previous deployment.

That workflow lets the team release multiple times a day, with each change becoming available to a physician audience that Kush thinks about whenever he ships something:

More doctors without more provisioning

Keeping that application available means handling demand the team can’t always anticipate. Andy was scrolling through Slack when he saw the message that OpenEvidence had gone viral on TikTok, reaching around two million views in under a week. He watched traffic climb and checked the logs. Response times stayed fast and error rates remained near zero, and with no additional capacity to provision, he went back to his work.

Beyond sudden spikes, the team has accommodated sustained growth without rebuilding the web application.

"Not once have I had to think, now that we have five times as many doctors, what's happening to page loads or time to first paint," Kush says. "The scaling has happened so naturally that we end up focusing on other things."

A 90% drop in serverless spend

As usage grew, VP of Engineering Micah Smith was watching compute costs. The team enabled Fluid compute for its functions on Vercel, and Micah described the result alongside the wider infrastructure budget:

"We reduced our serverless spend by 90% while maintaining the same performance, and even as we've scaled up to 1000x growth, Vercel is less than 5% of our overall infra spend."

Fluid compute lets multiple requests share a running function instance, so it can handle other work while a request waits for another service, such as a database or an AI backend, to respond. With Active CPU pricing, that waiting time doesn’t incur CPU charges, though memory remains billed while requests are in progress.

A familiar workflow for a new audience

Take Home, OpenEvidence’s first patient-facing application, lets a doctor translate a clinical answer into plain language and share it with a patient, who logs in to review and save the evidence. Clinical-trial matching is also part of the application’s planned direction.

To support this expansion, the team uses a pattern established through dozens of early proofs of concept, each deployed as its own Vercel project with a custom domain. Stakeholders could open those applications and test the workflows for themselves. Getting new projects online in minutes helped the team find product-market fit and made it easier to win early enterprise partnerships.

Take Home has its own project and domain too, so engineers can update the patient experience without deploying the other applications.

With Take Home, evidence that helps a doctor during a consultation can become something a patient returns to afterward.

About OpenEvidence: OpenEvidence helps healthcare professionals find medical evidence at the point of care, with answers sourced, cited, and grounded in peer-reviewed literature. Physicians use it daily across more than 10,000 hospitals and medical centers in the United States. Its mission is to help doctors save lives and improve patient care. Learn more at openevidence.com.

title: Decision models take 26% of requests; Anthropic now wins new teams 2:1
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — November 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes more than 100 trillion tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage looks like in today’s enterprise and startup landscape across language, decision, voice, image, and video models. We publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from August, September, and October.

November 2026 Summary

  • In six weeks, decision models grew to one in four gateway requests, while accounting for half a cent of every dollar spent. Close to a third of all paid teams used one in October. Among teams processing over 10 billion tokens a month, seven in ten used a decision model.

  • About 11% of paid teams used a voice model in October, up from 4% in July.

  • OpenAI and Anthropic now reach about the same share of paid teams, and new teams in October picked Anthropic nearly two to one. OpenAI’s share of gateway spend, meanwhile, is up by two-thirds since December.

  • More than half of language-model requests went to models less than two months old, up from less than three in ten. Within one month of a typical model’s peak usage, three in four of the teams using it have moved on.

Decision models account for 26% of all requests

Production AI is splitting into two jobs: generation and judgment. Until recently, when software needed to make a quick call, a team could use either a fixed rule that was cheap but rigid, or a language model that was smart but slow and expensive.

Decision models are now a third option. They classify, score, or pick between choices instead of generating text, and cost about a seventieth as much per request as a language model.

They arrived on AI Gateway in mid-September, and there are now 15 decision models available from eight different vendors. In October, nearly a third of paid teams on AI Gateway used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a decision model without sending a single request to a text-generating model.

Decision models cost far less per token and give very short answers, so even though they received about one in four gateway requests in October, they accounted for just 0.53% of total spend.

Almost all of that request volume went to Jev from TypeSafe AI, which alone received nearly four times Anthropic’s total requests. For every $1 teams spent on Jev, they spent $64 on Anthropic models.

Decision models are most common among the teams that run the most AI. Just over one in five teams running fewer than 10 million tokens used a decision model in October. At 100 million to 1 billion tokens, nearly half used one. Above 10 billion, seven in ten did.

This is partly because big teams use more of everything. The top 1% of teams by spend use a median of 29 different models, and the bottom tenth use only one. It’s also volume. The more requests a team sends, the more it has to gain from a model that makes simple decisions faster and far more cost-effectively.

Voice adoption is up 2.6x since July

About one in nine paid teams used a voice model in October, up from one in 24 in July, an increase of 161%.

New teams are using voice, and existing teams are adding it. Among teams that paid in both July and October, the share using voice went from 5% to 14%.

Teams that use voice are also using more of it. The share of teams sending at least 100 voice requests a month grew fivefold, and six in ten of September’s voice teams returned in October, up from fewer than half in July.

A spoken conversation with an AI app takes three steps:

  • A voice model turns the user’s speech into text

  • A language model writes the reply

  • Another voice model reads the reply back to the user

Most voice teams use just one or two of these pieces. Use of speech-to-text models has nearly tripled since July, and text-to-speech has more than tripled.

Some models do all three steps on their own. In July, about a quarter of voice teams used one of these all-in-one models, and one in six assembled the pieces themselves. By October, those numbers had swapped.

For most teams, voice is a new way for users to talk to an app or agent they already have. Teams’ preferred language models stay in the middle, and they can add voice at one end or both.

Anthropic wins new teams two to one, and OpenAI’s share of spend is up two-thirds

Last December, 70 of every 100 paid teams on AI Gateway used an OpenAI model and 48 used an Anthropic model. By October, the two labs were nearly level, with OpenAI at 55 and Anthropic at 54.

Both labs now reach more of the teams that have been on the gateway since December, but Anthropic’s reach grew more. The share of these teams using Anthropic rose from about half to two-thirds, while OpenAI’s rose from about three in four to four in five.

Most of Anthropic’s gain came from new teams. In October, it was the first-choice lab for nearly twice as many of them as OpenAI.

But among the biggest teams, both labs already have nearly everyone. More than nine in ten of the top 1% by spend use both Anthropic and OpenAI. With these teams, the labs now compete for how much of the work each one gets.

On that measure, Anthropic still leads, but OpenAI has gained ground. OpenAI now takes nearly 15 cents of every dollar spent on the gateway, up from about 9 in December, while Anthropic’s halved to about 32 cents over the same period.

Most AI traffic now runs on models less than two months old

Teams are moving to new models almost as fast as labs release them. More than half of October’s language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old. Before September, that share had never passed three in ten.

Within each model family, a new version arrives every 61 days at the median, and a typical model peaks within a month of launch. Four weeks later, three in four of the teams using it at its peak aren’t using it anymore, whether or not a successor has shipped in the family. Most of those teams are still on AI Gateway, using other models.

Teams switch models frequently, usually to something newer, and often to another lab. In October, about half of teams running at least 10 million tokens a month changed their most-used model. Four in five of those moved to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab.

Older models stay in use, often alongside a newer primary model. Seven in ten teams running at least 10 million tokens a month still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it ran less than 3% of its tokens.

AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks. That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one.

Also in October’s data

  • Opus 5.5 was the top model by spend in its first full month. It took about one in seven dollars across all teams. Four of the six most widely used models on AI Gateway are Anthropic’s: Sonnet 5.5 (reaching 26% of paid teams), Haiku 5.5 (22%), Haiku 4.5 (20%), and Opus 5.5 (18%). Jev (28%) and GPT-6 Luna (19%) are the other two.

  • Image and video both had their biggest month yet on AI Gateway. More teams than ever are putting spend on them, and the largest teams are adopting them the fastest. About a third of the top 1% of teams by spend now use an image model, up from a quarter in July. One in six use a video model, up from one in ten.

  • OpenAI’s newest image model, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, took the lead in image spend in its first full month, followed by its Flare and GPT-Image-2 models. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 led video spend for a third month running, ahead of Google’s Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou’s Kling 3.0.

About this data

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through October 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Spend is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ.

  • Paid teams are teams with at least one paid request in the month. Team size is measured by a team’s total tokens that month.

  • Decision models are the models classified as decision models in the AI Gateway model list.

  • Each model version is counted separately. A model’s age is measured from that version’s first day on AI Gateway, and gateway history begins October 20, 2025.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million tokens in both September and October. A team’s most-used model is measured by tokens.

  • Voice figures begin June 22, 2026. Teams that “assembled the pieces” used speech-to-text, a language model, and text-to-speech on the same day.

  • A new team’s first-choice lab is the lab it sent the most language-model requests to in its first month.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

Read more about our methodology, and explore or download the public data.
