title: Are You a CSS Developer or a CSS Expert? 9 Tests I Failed Styling a 12,400-Line Photo Editor
description:
Most developers can make a button blue, centre a div and copy a flexbox cheat sheet.

CSS experts know what happens when the browser disagrees with you: when the page flashes white before it turns dark, when a phone's address bar eats the bottom of your layout, when a "simple" gradient border refuses to follow rounded corners, and when your grey text looks elegant on your monitor and invisible in sunlight.

I found out which one I was while styling APIC, a free photo editor that runs entirely in your browser: edit, convert, compress, resize and remove backgrounds, with no sign-up. It is one HTML file of about 12,400 lines, and its whole look lives in just ~1,100 lines of CSS inside it. This post is about those 1,100 lines (and the HTML around them).

Every test below is a real decision or a real bug from that file. The code is trimmed for reading, but the ideas are exactly what ships. 👇

New here? Good. This post is written for you too. Every test has a plain English part first, then the code, then the "what is really going on" part. If you only read the plain English parts, you will still learn something true. If you are an expert, skip straight to the code and the last line of each test.

🧰 Five words you will see (read this once)

Word What it means, no jargon
Custom property (--bg) A variable for CSS. Define a colour once, use it everywhere with var(--bg).
Pseudo-element (::before) A free extra box the browser lets you attach to any element, with no extra HTML.
Stacking context A "layer fence". Things inside it can be ordered among themselves, but cannot escape it.
Viewport The part of the page you can currently see on screen.
Paint The moment the browser actually draws pixels on your screen.

📊 APIC's CSS by the numbers

These are counted straight from the file:

  • ~1,100 lines of CSS
  • 666 uses of var(--...): the whole design runs on variables
  • 33 @media queries
  • 20 uses of color-mix()
  • 12 @keyframes animations
  • 18 :focus-visible rules (keyboard users get a visible outline)
  • 8 prefers-reduced-motion: reduce guards (people who get dizzy from animation get less of it)
  • 20 <details> elements (accordions with no JavaScript)

Now the tests. Score yourself honestly.

Test 1: Does your dark site flash white before it turns dark?

In plain English. You choose "light mode", you reload the page, and for a split second the screen is dark before it switches. That flash is the browser drawing the page with the wrong colours, then fixing them. It looks cheap, and it hurts if you are in a dark room.

Why it happens. The browser paints as soon as it has your HTML and CSS. If the code that picks your theme runs after that, the first frame is already wrong.

The fix. Pick the theme in a tiny script in the <head>, so it runs before the first paint:

<head>
<script>
  // Runs before anything is drawn
  (function () {
    var mode = 'system';
    try {
      var m = localStorage.getItem('apic_theme');
      if (m === 'light' || m === 'dark' || m === 'system') mode = m;
    } catch (e) {}                       // storage can be blocked, so never trust it

    var t = mode === 'system'
      ? (matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: light)').matches ? 'light' : 'dark')
      : mode;

    document.documentElement.setAttribute('data-theme', t);
  })();
</script>

And the CSS only has to change a handful of variables:

:root {                                   /* dark is the default */
  --bg: #07070a;   --bg-2: #0d0d13;   --bg-3: #14141c;
  --line: rgba(150, 255, 210, .14);
  --text: #eef1f6; --text-muted: #8b8fa3;
}
html[data-theme="light"] {                /* light only overrides the values */
  --bg: #f2f3ee;   --bg-2: #e8e9e1;   --bg-3: #dcded2;
  --line: rgba(10, 40, 25, .14);
  --text: #0c0e0a; --text-muted: #5b5f52;
}
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--text); }

APIC's light theme overrides 8 variables. The other 600+ places that use colours never needed to know a second theme exists.

Three small details separate "it works" from "it works every time":

  1. try/catch around localStorage. Private modes and strict settings can make it throw. A theme script that crashes leaves you with no theme at all.
  2. Three modes, not two: light, dark and system. "Follow my device" is a real choice, so it gets stored as one.
  3. The script is inline and in the head. A script loaded from a file, or placed at the bottom, runs too late. Being render-blocking is exactly what you want here.

Developer: toggles a class after the page loads.
Expert: decides the theme before the first pixel exists.

Test 2: Can one line make a see-through header that works in both themes?

In plain English. A sticky header that is slightly see-through, so content blurs underneath it as you scroll, looks premium. The trap: "slightly see-through" needs a colour with transparency, and you have two themes with two different background colours.

The old way: write rgba(7, 7, 10, .82) for dark, then write a second rgba(...) for light. Now you have two numbers to keep in sync forever.

The expert way: color-mix() takes the colour from your variable and mixes it with "nothing":

header.top {
  position: sticky; top: 0;
  background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--bg) 82%, transparent);  /* 82% bg, 18% see-through */
  backdrop-filter: blur(12px);                                  /* blur what's behind it */
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--line);
}

/* when you scroll, the border quietly turns slightly green */
header.top.scrolled {
  border-bottom-color: color-mix(in srgb, var(--green) 22%, var(--line));
}

Switch the theme and --bg changes, so the header changes with it. No second rule. APIC uses this trick 20 times: hover glows, drag-and-drop highlights, active buttons, the lot.

rgba() cannot do this, because it wants raw numbers, not "whatever --bg currently is". color-mix() works in all current major browsers.

Developer: copies a colour and lowers its alpha, twice.
Expert: derives colours from the tokens, so there is only one source of truth.

Test 3: Why does my glow lag, or vanish behind the wrong thing?

In plain English. APIC's main card has a soft rainbow glow behind it. When you open a photo, the glow fades out so the picture is easy to see. Simple idea. Two things can go wrong: the glow ends up in the wrong layer, and the animation stutters on cheap phones.

.studio {
  position: relative;
  isolation: isolate;                    /* 1. build a layer fence around this card */
}
.studio::before {                        /* the glow is a free extra box */
  content: "";
  position: absolute; inset: -1px;
  z-index: -1;                           /* behind the card's content... */
  border-radius: inherit;
  background: var(--grad-brand);         /* green → cyan → pink */
  opacity: .28;
  filter: blur(18px);
  will-change: opacity, transform;
  transition: opacity .9s var(--ease-out), transform 1.1s var(--ease-out);
}
.studio.has-image::before {              /* JS adds .has-image; CSS does the animation */
  opacity: 0;
  transform: scale(.94);
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .studio::before { transition: none; }  /* 3. respect people who opt out of motion */
}

1. isolation: isolate creates a stacking context, the "layer fence" from the glossary. Without it, z-index: -1 means "go behind whatever the page decides", and that can change when some ancestor gets a transform or opacity later. With the fence, it means "behind this card's content", always.

2. Only cheap properties animate. Fading (opacity) and moving or scaling (transform) are the two things browsers can usually animate on the GPU without re-measuring the page. The expensive part is the blur, and the blur never changes, so it is drawn once and then just faded. Animating box-shadow, width or filter itself would redo that work on every frame.

3. Reduced motion. Some people get dizzy or distracted by animation, and their system tells your site so. One @media line is the whole accommodation.

Notice who does what: JavaScript only flips a class (has-image). CSS owns every pixel of the animation. That split keeps both sides small.

Developer: animates box-shadow and wonders why it is janky.
Expert: animates only opacity and transform, and builds a fence first.

Test 4: Can you put a gradient on a rounded border?

In plain English. You want a thin rainbow outline around a rounded floating bar. Sounds like one line: border: 1px solid <gradient>. It is not. A border can only be a flat colour, and the tool made for fancy borders, border-image, ignores border-radius. Your corners come out square.

The trick: don't use a border at all. Draw a gradient box, then cut a hole in the middle, so only a 1px ring is left:

#apicDock::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute; inset: -1px;
  border-radius: inherit;               /* the ring follows the rounded corners */
  padding: 1px;                         /* 1px = the thickness of the ring */
  background: var(--grad-brand);
  opacity: .55;
  pointer-events: none;                 /* never block clicks on the real bar */

  -webkit-mask: linear-gradient(#000 0 0) content-box, linear-gradient(#000 0 0);
  -webkit-mask-composite: xor;          /* older browsers */
  mask: linear-gradient(#000 0 0) content-box exclude, linear-gradient(#000 0 0);
  mask-composite: exclude;              /* standard */
}

How to read it. A mask says "show the element only where the mask is solid". Here are two solid masks:

  • one covers the content box (the middle),
  • one covers the whole box.

exclude means "show where they don't overlap". The only place the two masks differ is the thin padding strip around the edge. That strip is your ring, and because the element itself has rounded corners, so does the ring.

APIC ships both the -webkit- version and the standard one, because older browsers only know the prefixed one.

Developer: gives up and uses a wrapper <div> with a gradient background and a smaller <div> on top.
Expert: subtracts one shape from another with a mask.

Test 5: How do you animate something to "gone", when display: none can't be animated?

In plain English. When you open a photo, APIC's tagline fades and slides up, and its space collapses so the editor moves up smoothly. When you close the photo, it comes back. You cannot animate display, and you cannot animate height: auto. So how?

.eyebrow {                                /* visible state */
  max-height: 40px;  overflow: hidden;
  opacity: 1;        transform: none;
  visibility: visible;
  transition: max-height .5s var(--ease-out),
              opacity .35s ease,
              transform .5s var(--ease-out),
              visibility 0s linear 0s;    /* flip to visible immediately */
}

body.studio-active .eyebrow {             /* hidden state */
  max-height: 0;
  opacity: 0;
  transform: translateY(-12px);
  visibility: hidden;
  pointer-events: none;
  transition: max-height .5s var(--ease-out),
              opacity .35s ease,
              transform .5s var(--ease-out),
              visibility 0s linear .5s;   /* ...but wait .5s before hiding */
}

Two ideas hold this up:

  • max-height instead of height. Browsers can animate between two numbers (40px → 0px) but not between a number and auto. Pick a ceiling that is safely bigger than the content, and animate to it.
  • The delayed visibility flip. That last line is the expert part. visibility: hidden makes an element unclickable, unfocusable and invisible to screen readers, which is what you want eventually. But if it flipped instantly, the fade would never be seen. So when hiding, it waits .5s (the length of the animation) and then flips. When showing, it flips right away so the fade-in can be seen.

Without this, you get one of two bad endings: an invisible tagline that keyboard users can still tab into, or a tagline that vanishes with no animation at all.

Developer: display: none and a jump.
Expert: fades first, then removes it from the page's reach.

Test 6: Why does 100vh hide the bottom of my layout on a phone?

In plain English. On a phone, the browser's address bar slides away as you scroll. 100vh means "the screen height with the bar hidden", so when the bar is showing, the bottom 60 or so pixels of your layout are tucked underneath it. Buttons you can't tap. That is not your imagination.

Modern CSS has three honest heights:

Unit Meaning
lvh the large viewport: bars hidden
svh the small viewport: bars showing, so it always fits
dvh the dynamic viewport: follows the bars live

APIC uses them on purpose. The photo area must never push the tools off screen, so it uses svh:

:root {
  --apic-header: 66px;
  /* Old browsers: vh. Photo is never smaller than 260px, never taller than 60% of the screen,
     and always leaves 330px for the title bar, tabs and first controls. */
  --apic-img-max: max(260px, min(60vh, calc(100vh - 330px - (var(--apic-header) - 62px))));
}
@supports (height: 100svh) {              /* Browsers that understand svh override it */
  :root {
    --apic-img-max: max(260px, min(60svh, calc(100svh - 330px - (var(--apic-header) - 62px))));
  }
}

body.studio-active .studio-wrap {
  min-height: calc(100vh  - var(--apic-header));   /* fallback */
  min-height: calc(100svh - var(--apic-header));   /* wins if understood */
}

Read max(260px, min(60svh, …)) as a sandwich: "at least 260px, at most 60% of the screen, and never so tall that the controls fall off." APIC's full-screen design studio (a position: fixed; inset: 0 overlay) is different: it should fill the screen exactly, and keep doing so as the bar slides in and out, so it uses dvh: #dsApp { height: 100vh; height: 100dvh; }.

The pattern is also worth stealing: write the old value first, then the new one on the next line. A browser that doesn't understand the second line ignores it. No JavaScript, no feature detection.

Developer: height: 100vh, tests on desktop, ships.
Expert: knows which of three heights each element actually means.

Test 7: Is a small screen the same thing as a finger?

In plain English. No. A small laptop window is small but has a precise mouse. An iPad is big but has a thumb. If your "mobile layout" is triggered by width, both get the wrong thing.

CSS can ask about the pointer instead:

@media (pointer: coarse) {                       /* "the main input is a finger" */
  html { -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent; -webkit-text-size-adjust: 100%; }
  .btn, .tool-btn, .quick-btn { min-height: 44px; }          /* finger-sized targets */
  select, input[type=number], input[type=text], textarea {
    font-size: 16px;                                         /* stops the iPhone zoom-in */
    min-height: 44px;
  }
  input[type=range] { min-height: 32px; }
}

/* the area you draw on with a finger or mouse */
#overlay.active {
  cursor: crosshair;
  touch-action: none;                  /* drawing must not scroll or zoom the page */
  -webkit-touch-callout: none;
  user-select: none;
}

Three small rules, three real problems:

  • 44px is the size Apple's guidelines recommend for a tappable thing. Smaller, and people hit the wrong button.
  • 16px inputs. On iPhone Safari, tapping a text field with a font smaller than 16px makes the whole page zoom in. Annoying, and it does not zoom back out on its own.
  • touch-action: none on the drawing layer. Without it, dragging your finger across a photo to erase a background scrolls the page instead. The browser has to be told "this area is mine".

Developer: @media (max-width: 600px) and hope.
Expert: designs for the input device, not the screen size.

Test 8: Is your "stylish" grey text actually readable?

In plain English. Dark themes love soft grey text. It looks calm in a design tool. Then someone opens your site outdoors, or is tired, or is 55, and the secondary text turns into fog.

You do not have to guess. Readability has a number: the contrast ratio. WCAG, the accessibility standard, asks for 4.5 or more for normal text (level AA), and 7 or more is the gold level (AAA). Here is the whole calculation, in 5 lines of JavaScript:

const lin = c => (c /= 255) <= 0.03928 ? c / 12.92 : ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4;
const lum = hex => {
  const [r, g, b] = [1, 3, 5].map(i => lin(parseInt(hex.slice(i, i + 2), 16)));
  return 0.2126 * r + 0.7152 * g + 0.0722 * b;      // how bright the eye sees it
};
const ratio = (a, b) => { const [x, y] = [lum(a), lum(b)].sort((p, q) => q - p); return (x + .05) / (y + .05); };

ratio('#8b8fa3', '#07070a');   // 6.28
ratio('#a3a9bd', '#07070a');   // 8.59

APIC's first dark theme used #8b8fa3 for muted text. That is already a pass. But a late "dark-mode legibility pass" lifted it anyway, and it started with one line of variables:

html:not([data-theme="light"]) {
  --text-muted: #a3a9bd;                 /* was #8b8fa3 */
  --line: rgba(160, 255, 220, .20);      /* was .14: borders you can actually see */
  --btn-text: #d9deec;
}
Muted text on Before After
page background #07070a 6.28 8.59
card #0d0d13 6.05 8.27
raised panel #14141c 5.72 7.82

That moves every one of them from "passes" to "gold level", with three variable changes, not 200 selector edits. This is the quiet payoff of Test 1: when your colours live in variables, an accessibility fix is a small diff.

(The bright green of the main buttons is easy: #39ff9d against the page is 15.3.)

Developer: "it looks fine on my monitor."
Expert: measures it, and fixes it where the colour is defined.

Test 9: How much can your HTML do before you write any JavaScript?

In plain English. CSS gets the glory, but a lot of "interactive" features are already built into HTML. Using them means fewer bugs, less code, and a page that works for people using keyboards and screen readers.

1. An accordion in four lines. APIC's FAQ and its advanced tool sections are 20 <details> elements:

<details class="faq-item">
  <summary>Is APIC really free?</summary>
  <p>Yes. APIC is a free online photo editor that runs in your browser…</p>
</details>

.faq-item summary:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--cyan); outline-offset: 2px; }

You get open and close, keyboard support (Tab, Enter, Space) and screen readers announcing "expanded" or "collapsed", for free. CSS only adds a focus outline so keyboard users can see where they are. That is the whole component.

2. Landmarks. The page uses <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section> ×7 and <footer> instead of a pile of <div>s. Screen reader users can jump straight to "main content". Search engines also understand the page's shape.

3. One honest security line. In the <head>:

<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'">

It does two small things: no old-style plugins (object-src 'none'), and nobody can sneak in a <base> tag that redirects your relative links elsewhere (base-uri 'self'). It is a small policy and I will not pretend it is a full shield. Honest, narrow rules are better than a big one nobody maintains.

4. A page that explains itself to machines. A short block of JSON-LD in the head tells crawlers "this is a free photo-editing app, here is its feature list, here are the questions people ask". Plus Open Graph tags so a pasted link shows a proper preview card instead of a bare URL.

Developer: builds an accordion with divs, an onclick and an isOpen variable.
Expert: uses the element that already exists.

🎁 Bonus: a checkerboard with zero image files

When you open a transparent PNG in an image editor, you see the grey checkerboard behind it. APIC draws it with one declaration:

.has-alpha {
  background-image: repeating-conic-gradient(#8a8a8a 0% 25%, #5c5c5c 0% 50%);
  background-size: 18px 18px;
}

A conic gradient sweeps around a centre point like a clock hand. This one says "grey A for the first quarter turn, grey B for the second quarter, then repeat". Each stop starts at 0%, which is earlier than where the previous one ended, so the browser snaps it up to the previous stop, which gives hard edges instead of a blend. Four quarters make two light squares and two dark ones. Shrink it to an 18px tile, repeat it, and you have a checkerboard.

No PNG to download, no extra request, and it stays sharp on any screen.

😬 Two tests I still fail in APIC's own code

A post called "tests I failed" would be dishonest if it only covered the ones I fixed. I audited the shipping file for this article and found two:

Fail 1: smooth scrolling ignores reduced motion. The file has html { scroll-behavior: smooth; } and no matching opt-out. So someone who asked their device to minimise motion still gets animated scrolling on anchor links. The fix is to only turn it on for people who haven't asked otherwise:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  html { scroll-behavior: smooth; }
}

Fail 2: safe-area insets that do nothing. APIC writes bottom: calc(18px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)) for its back-to-top button, so it should clear the iPhone's home bar. But env(safe-area-inset-*) only returns real values if the page asks to draw edge to edge:

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0, viewport-fit=cover">

The file's viewport tag doesn't have viewport-fit=cover, so in that file those env() lines quietly resolve to their 0px fallback. The CSS half was written; the HTML half was missing. The lesson fits this whole series: a line of code that never errors can still never run.

🔍 Check my work in 60 seconds

Don't trust me, trust DevTools. Open APIC, press F12, then:

  1. Elements → <html>. Watch data-theme flip when you change the theme (Test 1).
  2. Styles panel → search isolation, mask-composite, color-mix. Every technique above is in there (Tests 2 to 4).
  3. Toolbar → device icon. Pick a phone, then look at the layout with the address bar showing (Test 6).
  4. Rendering tab → "Emulate CSS media feature prefers-reduced-motion". Watch the glow animation switch off (Test 3).
  5. Pick any grey text → click the colour swatch. DevTools shows the contrast ratio for you (Test 8).

🏆 Your score

Tests you already knew You are…
0–3 A CSS developer. You build things that work. Pick one test above and recreate it from scratch. That is how this stuff sticks.
4–6 Solid. You have shipped real interfaces and met real browsers.
7–9 A CSS expert. Come argue with me in the comments.

And the part nobody puts in a score table: the experts in this post aren't people who memorised more properties. They're people who stopped asking "what does this line do?" and started asking "what will the browser do before, after and instead?"

Which test did you fail first? Mine is in the "Two tests I still fail" section, so you already know. Tell me yours below 👇 (and if you spot a mistake in my code, say so. That's the point of this series.)

Try APIC, and break it

Open APIC is free, runs in your browser, and (per its own description) processes images on your device rather than uploading them. Try the background remover, drag in a transparent PNG for the checkerboard, switch themes for Test 1, then open DevTools and hunt for every technique above.

Not just try it: break it too. I want feedback, because feedback is what makes the next version better.
Desktop version:
[APIC DESKTOP]🖥️💻
-----> https://github.com/Akhouri-Systems/APIC/releases/download/APIC/APIC.zip

📢 remove.bg is shutting down on December 1. Here is a free alternative

If you use remove.bg, you have a deadline. The service has announced that its standalone website and self-serve API close on 1 December 2026 at 9:00 am CET. Background removal is moving into Canva, the developer API is moving to Leonardo.Ai, and unused pay-as-you-go credits expire the same day. (Always check remove.bg's own notice for the latest details.)

If what you actually need is "drop in a photo, get a transparent PNG", APIC does that for free, and everything you just read about is how it is built:

  • 🔒 Runs in your browser. The AI model runs on your own device using WebAssembly. Per APIC's own description, your photos are not uploaded to a server.
  • ⚡ Three model sizes. Lite (about 5 MB), Fast (about 44 MB) and Maximum (about 176 MB). The model downloads once, is cached on your device, and later runs start much faster.
  • 🆓 No paid tiers and no credits. There is nothing to run out of on December 1. You can edit without an account, and the site signs you in with Google only when you export.
  • 🧰 More than a remover. Resize, compress to a target file size, convert between PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, ICO and PDF, remove objects, social media size presets, and a batch studio for many images at once.

What APIC is not: it is a web tool, not an API and not a Photoshop plugin. If a script or a plugin depends on remove.bg, you need a developer replacement (remove.bg points API users to Leonardo.Ai). And no tool is perfect on every photo, so try your hardest images (hair, glass, fine edges) before you switch a real workflow.

Do these before December 1, whatever you choose:

  1. Use up any remove.bg credits. They do not roll over.
  2. Download your invoices and usage reports while the account still exists.
  3. Test APIC on 5 of your real photos. It takes two minutes: apic-online.vercel.app

title: How We Built a 10-Language Bulk QR Generator (And Handled RTL Layouts)
description:
When we first launched the RahaLune Batch QR Code Generator, it was a fully functional, client-side React application capable of generating up to 100 custom QR codes from a single CSV file.

But it had one limitation: the entire interface was available only in English.

For a tool intended for businesses, event planners, and inventory managers worldwide, that wasn't ideal.

So, we decided to make it multilingual.

Our latest update brings support for 10 languages, including full Right-to-Left (RTL) support for Arabic and Urdu.

In this article, I'll share some of the challenges we encountered and how we approached localization while keeping everything client-side.

1. Building a Client-Side Translation System

Our first decision was to avoid external translation APIs.

Since RahaLune is entirely client-side, introducing an external service just to handle translations would add unnecessary complexity and potentially affect performance.

Instead, we created separate translation files for each supported language.

When a user selects a language from the header dropdown or visits the tool through a localized URL, the application automatically loads the corresponding translations.

This approach helped us achieve three things:

  • Keep the initial application bundle lightweight.
  • Load translations only when needed.
  • Allow users to switch languages without reloading the entire application.

The result is a straightforward localization system that doesn't require a translation backend.

2. The Biggest Challenge: Right-to-Left Layout Support

Translating the interface was relatively straightforward. Making the entire application work properly in RTL languages was a different challenge.

Arabic and Urdu aren't simply English interfaces with translated labels. Their reading direction changes, which affects the overall layout and user experience.

We wanted the application to feel native to RTL users.

That meant adapting:

  • Navigation and interface alignment.
  • Input sections and tabs.
  • Buttons and form elements.
  • The three-step generation wizard.
  • QR code preview layouts.

We also made the layout direction change automatically when users switch between languages.

One important lesson from this process was to avoid relying on fixed left-to-right spacing throughout the application.

Using flexible, direction-aware layouts made it much easier to support both LTR and RTL languages without maintaining completely separate designs.

3. Dealing with Longer Translations

Another challenge was handling text that takes up more space than its English equivalent.

For example, German and French translations can be considerably longer than English labels.

This becomes particularly noticeable in compact UI components such as our input tabs:

  • Paste List
  • Upload CSV
  • Manual Entry

Longer translations can cause text overflow, inconsistent button heights, and alignment problems.

To address this, we made the interface more flexible.

Instead of forcing every label into a fixed-size container, we allowed buttons and tabs to grow naturally. We also adjusted spacing and minimum heights to maintain visual consistency when text wraps onto multiple lines.

This helped us maintain a clean interface across all 10 languages.

4. Making Multilingual SEO Work

Adding multiple languages also introduced an SEO consideration.

We wanted search engines to understand that the application was available in different languages and direct users to the appropriate version.

To achieve this, we implemented language-specific page titles, meta descriptions, and social sharing metadata.

We also added hreflang information to help search engines identify the available language versions.

For example, users searching in French should be able to discover the French version of the tool rather than always landing on the English interface.

This is an important part of building multilingual web applications. Translating the interface is only one part of localization; making those translations discoverable is equally important.

5. Keeping Everything Client-Side and Private

Throughout this update, one requirement remained unchanged: user privacy.

RahaLune doesn't need a backend to process QR codes.

Even after introducing support for 10 languages, all major operations continue to happen directly in the browser:

  • Loading translations.
  • Processing CSV files.
  • Generating multiple QR codes.
  • Creating ZIP downloads.
  • Rendering QR code previews.

We don't need users to upload their CSV files to an external server to perform these operations.

Your files stay on your device.

Adding multilingual support didn't require compromising the privacy-first architecture of the application.

6. What's Next?

The Batch QR Code Generator now supports 10 languages and automatically adapts its layout for RTL users.

This update was a good reminder that internationalization involves much more than translating interface text.

It requires thinking about layout direction, text length, accessibility, SEO, performance, and the overall user experience.

We're happy to make RahaLune more accessible to people around the world while keeping it free and entirely browser-based.

Try It Yourself

You can explore the updated Batch QR Code Generator here:

RahaLune Batch QR Code Generator

Try switching to Arabic or Urdu to see the RTL layout in action.

If you're building a multilingual React application, we'd also love to hear about your approach to handling localization and RTL layouts.

title: Eliminating Redis & Valkey Hot-Key Bottlenecks in Multi-Region Distributed Rate Limiters
description:
When a single enterprise tenant fires 250,000+ requests per second across US, UK, and European API gateways, the failure mode rarely looks like an obvious cluster crash. More often, aggregate Redis or Valkey CPU sits comfortably below 25%, yet P99 gateway latency jumps from 1.2ms to nearly 190ms.

In a standard distributed token-bucket setup, an atomic Lua script runs against one central key—such as ratelimit:tenant_9841. Because Redis and Valkey execute Lua scripts single-threaded on the primary node owning that CRC16 hash slot, dozens of edge gateway pods end up queuing behind a single CPU core.

(You can explore the complete architectural walkthrough and production implementation in our full guide on AI Dev Toolkit.)

Why Single-Key Rate Limiters Stall at Scale
Three compounding bottlenecks trigger this sudden latency cliff during heavy traffic surges:

Single-Slot Serialization: Wrapping {tenant_id} inside hash tags pins every request for a high-volume customer to one primary shard, leaving the rest of the cluster mostly idle.

Cross-Region NTP Clock Skew: Passing edge proxy timestamps into Lua causes inconsistent token refills across us-east-1, eu-central-1, and London edge nodes.

Per-Request Network Round-Trips: Paying an inter-AZ network hop on every single HTTP request caps throughput and inflates tail latency.

The 3-Layer Architecture Fix (1.45M+ RPS)
To eliminate hot-key stalls while keeping strict quota accuracy, high-throughput API gateways combine three architectural shifts:

Virtual Key Sharding: Place the shard index inside the hash tag (rl:tenant_882:{shard_0..15}) instead of the tenant ID so token buckets distribute evenly across 16 independent primary slots.

Server-Authoritative Millisecond Timing: Anchor elapsed refill math directly to Redis or Valkey server time (redis.call('TIME')) inside Lua so edge clock drift never causes burst leaks or negative deltas.

Two-Tier Hybrid Lease Batching (Edge L1 + Cluster L2): Have Go or Rust edge proxies lease micro-batches of tokens (for example, 50 tokens per lease with a short local TTL) in memory. Most checks resolve locally in nanoseconds, cutting cluster round-trips by up to 98%, backed by a fail-open local sliding window if inter-region RTT spikes.

What Multi-AZ Benchmarks Show
In multi-AZ edge tests simulating a single hot tenant at 300,000 RPS:

A single key with per-request Lua execution saturates one primary thread and pushes P99 overhead to 188.4 ms (~285k RPS).

Distributing across 16 virtual shards balances CPU load across primaries and drops P99 overhead to 4.8 ms (~920k RPS).

Combining 16-shard keys with edge L1 lease batching cuts rate-limit overhead to 0.42 ms while sustaining 1.45M+ RPS with linear horizontal scale.

Read the Complete Production Guide
For the full Lua token-bucket implementation, EVALSHA deployment checklist, deterministic PEXPIRE memory bounds, and complete multi-region failover playbook, read the full engineering guide on AI Dev Toolkit:

👉 Read the full guide: https://aidevtoolkit.blogspot.com/2026/11/distributed-systems-api-gateway-redis.html

title: Why a cloud range list is refused at load, not at verify
description:
An operator's published IP range file is evidence because it lists the addresses that operator's crawlers send from, and nothing else. A general cloud provider list (AWS's ip-ranges.json, Google's cloud.json, Azure's service tags) lists every address a customer can rent, so a match there tells you only that the request came from a datacenter. Let both kinds of file become a range snapshot and every instance on a public cloud verifies as whatever crawler it claims to be, with the verdict carrying the same word, range, that a real verification does.

That is the problem the identity package in crawlwarrant has to solve before it does anything else. A vendor's robots.txt group governs a request only when evidence ties the request to that vendor; a request that merely names a product token is a claimant, and the * group governs it. The whole design rests on evidence actually being evidence. One misconfigured range file quietly converts the strict path into the permissive one.

Two files with identical shape and opposite meaning

Both are JSON documents full of CIDR prefixes. Fetch them, parse them, and you hold the same Go value either way:

type Snapshot struct {
    Operator     string
    Tokens       []string
    URL          string         // URL the file was requested from
    FinalURL     string         // URL that answered, set when it differs
    CreationTime time.Time      // creationTime the operator put in the file
    FetchedAt    time.Time      // when we read it
    MaxAge       time.Duration  // how long it may be used, DefaultMaxAge when zero
    Prefixes     []netip.Prefix // ranges the file listed
}

Nothing in Prefixes tells you which claim the publisher was making. A crawler operator publishes a range file to say these are the addresses our crawler sends from. A cloud provider publishes one to say these are the addresses we rent out. The first narrows the world to one sender. The second narrows it to roughly everyone who can run a container.

The only place that distinction survives is the URL the file came from. So the URL is the thing you have to check, and the moment to check it is when the snapshot is built.

Refusing at the boundary

Load is the one constructor that turns a fetched file into a usable snapshot. It is also where the refusal lives:

// Load records a fetched range file as a snapshot. A general cloud provider
// list is refused here, at load, rather than left to verify requests it cannot
// speak for, and so is one a redirect led to.
func Load(s Snapshot) (Snapshot, error) {
    if s.URL == "" {
        return Snapshot{}, errors.New("identity: a range snapshot needs the URL it was fetched from")
    }
    for _, u := range []string{s.URL, s.FinalURL} {
        if u == "" {
            continue
        }
        if c, ok := cloudRangeList(u); ok {
            return Snapshot{}, fmt.Errorf("identity: %s: %s: %w", u, c.note, ErrCloudRangeList)
        }
    }
    if s.MaxAge == 0 {
        s.MaxAge = DefaultMaxAge
    }
    return s, nil
}

The alternative, letting the snapshot exist and adding a reason at verify time, looks more informative and is worse in practice. A bad range file is a configuration mistake, not a property of any request. Catch it at load and it surfaces once, at startup or at refresh, as an error with the offending URL in it, and somebody fixes the config. Catch it at verify and it surfaces as a line in an evidence chain, once per request, forever, and the chain now has to carry a kind of doubt that has nothing to do with the client being judged.

There is a second reason, which I learned from years of payment reconciliation rather than from crawler work: anything that can produce a false positive in a decision path will eventually be read by code that only checks the boolean. EvidenceKind.Verifies() returns true for EvidenceSigned, EvidenceRange and EvidenceFCrDNS. Some caller, somewhere, will branch on that and never look at the reasons. The reasons are for auditing. The refusal has to be structural.

Note also the missing-URL case, the same principle in a smaller form: a snapshot nobody can re-fetch cites nothing, so it is not a snapshot.

A redirect is part of the fetch

FinalURL is set when a different URL answered for the published one. That field is not cosmetic. If a vendor's range URL 301s to a cloud provider's list, the bytes you ended up with are the cloud provider's bytes, and having started somewhere respectable changes nothing about what they prove. So both URLs go through the same check, and the test says why:

func TestLoadRefusesACloudListARedirectLedTo(t *testing.T) {
    _, err := Load(Snapshot{
        Operator:  "Example",
        URL:       "https://crawler.example.com/ranges.json",
        FinalURL:  "https://ip-ranges.amazonaws.com/ip-ranges.json",
        FetchedAt: fetched,
    })
    if !errors.Is(err, ErrCloudRangeList) {
        t.Fatalf("error = %v, want %v: where the fetch ended decides what the file proves", err, ErrCloudRangeList)
    }
}

Where the fetch ended decides what the file proves. That sentence is the entire redirect policy.

Matching the list, and the limits of doing it this way

The match itself is deliberately dull: a small table, compared by lowercased host with either an exact path or a path fragment:

var cloudLists = []cloudList{
    {host: "ip-ranges.amazonaws.com", path: "/ip-ranges.json", note: "AWS lists every address its customers can rent"},
    {host: "www.gstatic.com", path: "/ipranges/cloud.json", note: "Google Cloud lists the addresses of customer workloads"},
    {host: "www.gstatic.com", path: "/ipranges/goog.json", note: "this file lists Google's whole address space, not its crawlers"},
    {host: "download.microsoft.com", fragment: "servicetags", note: "Azure service tags cover every tenant in a region"},
}

func cloudRangeList(rawURL string) (cloudList, bool) {
    u, err := url.Parse(rawURL)
    if err != nil {
        return cloudList{}, false
    }
    host, path := strings.ToLower(u.Hostname()), strings.ToLower(u.Path)
    for _, c := range cloudLists {
        if host != c.host {
            continue
        }
        if c.path != "" && path == c.path {
            return c, true
        }
        if c.fragment != "" && strings.Contains(path, c.fragment) {
            return c, true
        }
    }
    return cloudList{}, false
}

Two things are worth saying plainly about this. The fragment case exists because Azure's download path carries a dated filename, so an exact path would stop matching on the next publication; the test fixture is a path containing ServiceTags_Public_20261019.json. And the goog.json entry is there because it is the trap most likely to be set by accident: Google publishes it, it sits next to a file that is genuinely about Google Cloud, and it lists Google's whole address space rather than its crawlers.

The honest limitation: this is a denylist. It names four files. It will not catch a regional mirror, a smaller provider, or a vendor file that has quietly become a reverse proxy for one. A denylist of known-bad sources cannot be complete, and the note on each row is as much documentation of why this class is wrong as it is an error message.

What the snapshot still refuses after it loads

Passing Load is not the end of the scepticism. A zero MaxAge becomes DefaultMaxAge, 24 hours, and Verify builds its evidence in a fixed order, with the staleness check placed before any prefix is read:

if age := now.Sub(s.FetchedAt); age > s.maxAge() {
    e.Reasons = append(e.Reasons, Reason{ReasonSnapshotStale, ...})
    return e
}
if !s.contains(ip) {
    e.Reasons = append(e.Reasons, Reason{ReasonOutOfRange, ...})
    return e
}
e.Kind = EvidenceRange

The early return is the point. Past its age the snapshot verifies nothing at all: Kind stays EvidenceAnonymous, Verifies() is false, and the message names the file, when it was fetched, how many hours ago that was, and how many hours it may be used. An expired file is not weaker evidence to be weighed. It is not evidence.

Two more reasons ride along without blocking anything. A Redirected() snapshot adds ReasonSnapshotRedirected even when the final URL was fine, because the file is re-verified at its published URL before it is trusted again. A zero CreationTime adds ReasonNoCreationTime, since without it you know when you read the file but not how old the operator's own data was when they published it.

And when len(s.Tokens) > 1, a successful match still adds ReasonOperatorOnly. One file shared across several products proves the operator sent the request, not which of its products did. That matters directly, because the next step applies a robots.txt group chosen by product token, and the address did not establish the token.

What I would do differently

I would make the allowlist the primary mechanism and keep the denylist as the second line. The purpose package already stores, per product token, the RangeFileURL its operator publishes, read from a cited SourceURL on a recorded VerifiedOn date. A Load that took the token and required the snapshot's URL to be the published one would refuse every wrong file, not just the four I thought of, including the regional mirror and the proxied vendor path that the current table misses.

The denylist would still earn its place, because an allowlist fails closed in a way that is annoying to operate: a vendor changes a URL, the row goes stale, and verification stops. When someone reaches for a manual override in that moment, the four note strings are probably what stop them from pasting in ip-ranges.json because it was the only range file they could find.

Close

A verification is only as good as the claim the source file was making. The cheapest way to keep that straight is to decide what a file can speak for once, where it enters the system, and to let everything downstream assume the question was already settled.

Originally published on polycratia.com — where I write about payment systems, crypto rails and marketplace backends.

title: Write the test plan before your coding agent writes code
description:
When a coding agent writes code faster than you can read it, reading every line stops working as review, and approved tests have to carry most of that load. So define the tests before the agent writes any implementation, read them yourself, and require every commit to pass them. Your attention moves from reading diffs to deciding what "done" means.

Anush Elangovan is Corporate VP of AI Software at AMD. Before we recorded his April 2026 episode, he told me he was generating 250,000 lines of code a week with AI agents. Lines of code isn't a measure of success, but it shows the throughput problem: no human reviews that volume line by line. By the time we talked, he said a week had earlier come to about 4.2 billion tokens, a check that morning showed 6.5 billion consumed, and he could no longer keep track of lines.

Why write tests before the agent writes code?

Because the tests are the only fixed point while the implementation churns. Anush held this view before agents existed:

Yeah, so my philosophy is, even before agentic coding, I used to advise people and friends and colleagues, 80% of your time should be spent on tests and writing tests. Even before you write your first line of code, you should have a test framework.

With agents, the tests also do the job a reviewer used to do. When he doesn't like something about the output, he turns it into a stronger gate instead of arguing with the agent:

Yep, testing is the code review and testing is kind of the gate of your sandbox. If you have a complaint about anything in the box, fix the sandbox, right?

Anush Elangovan, Corporate VP of AI Software at AMD, on Chain of Thought ep 56

That includes non-functional requirements. For his virtual GPU simulator he set a performance metric, each dispatch executing in 50 microseconds of simulator time. When a change fails that test, the agent has to find another approach.

How do you check the tests an agent proposes?

Read them before you approve them. Anush's example: an agent wanted to implement GPU demand paging in one go. He stopped it and told it to write 100 tests covering combinations and corner cases first. Some of the tests were repetitive, with parameters changed but not the thing being tested. After reading them, he was satisfied that if the set passed, the feature was good.

Things to look for in an agent-written test list:

  • The same assertion with only literal values changed.
  • Missing negative cases, or platforms you named in the plan but no test covers.
  • Mocks that remove the behavior you care about, which make passing cheap.

His reason for the scrutiny is that agents optimize for the gate:

they try to just reward hack their way towards that test. So all you have to think of is like, they cannot reward hack that, right? Like you're putting up gates that they have to pass through.

Anush Elangovan, Corporate VP of AI Software at AMD, on Chain of Thought ep 56

A minimal sketch to adapt. Test cases are plain records with a content hash, so an agent can't keep an approved test ID while weakening its assertions.

def near_duplicates(cases):
    """cases: list of dicts with 'id', 'target' and 'params' keys."""
    seen, dups = {}, []
    for c in cases:
        # same target, same parameter names: probably only values changed
        key = (c["target"], tuple(sorted(c["params"])))
        if key in seen:
            dups.append((seen[key], c["id"]))
        else:
            seen[key] = c["id"]
    return dups

def may_implement(proposed, approved):
    """approved: {test_id: sha256 of the test's source}, frozen at human approval."""
    if not approved:
        return False, "a human has not approved the test list yet"
    current = {c["id"]: c["sha256"] for c in proposed}
    changed = [t for t, h in approved.items() if current.get(t) != h]
    return (not changed), f"approved tests missing or edited: {sorted(changed)}"

def commit_passes(approved, current_hashes, ran_ids, failed_ids):
    # all inputs come from your CI runner, not from the agent's report
    unchanged = all(current_hashes.get(t) == h for t, h in approved.items())
    return bool(approved) and unchanged and set(approved) <= ran_ids and not failed_ids

near_duplicates only surfaces candidates for you to read. It won't decide whether two tests cover different behavior.

What should gate every commit?

The approved suite, plus a test for whatever the commit fixes. Anush rewrote Slurm in Rust as a project called Spur, and he runs an agent that monitors its issue tracker. It picks up filed issues, fixes them, tests and deploys. If CI is green, it ships. His rule is that every commit it makes must include a test for the fix before it's committed.

How do you run several agents without losing track?

Give each one a job you can describe in a sentence. He doesn't give agents free rein to go off in the weeds or spawn their own thread pools. The Spur agent's job is to wake up at 5 a.m., check for issues, fix what it can and go back to sleep. When it finds an issue it can't fix, he steps in. On the simulator, each ISA transpilation target is its own sub-agent.

FAQ

Does this mean you never read agent-written code?
No. You still read the plan and the tests closely, and you step in when an agent hits an issue it can't fix. What changes is where review effort goes first.

Aren't token counts or lines of code a sign the workflow works?
No. Both measure throughput. A green run of tests you approved before implementation is the measure that matters.

How many tests should you ask for?
Enough to cover the corner cases you can name. Anush asked for 100 for demand paging, then read them and found repeats. The count matters less than reading the list.

Takeaway

  • Write a short plan, then ask the agent for test cases before any implementation prompt.
  • Read the list, merge near-duplicates, and store the approved IDs where the agent can't change them.
  • Gate every commit on the approved suite passing, and require a test with every fix.
  • Put performance and platform requirements in the suite, not in chat.
  • Give each agent one job, and own what it can't resolve.

The full conversation, with the transcript, is on Chain of Thought.

Subscribe to the Chain of Thought newsletter for new episodes and write-ups like this one.
