title: Flisk: run a multi-service app on your laptop with one command (and what it does not do)
description:
Flisk is an open-source command-line tool that runs every part of a multi-service app (API, website, worker, database) on your own computer with one command. The README says a small app starts "as two local processes in about a second", with no Docker.

  • Repo URL: https://github.com/flisk-sh/flisk
  • Language: TypeScript CLI (Ink terminal UI). Runs on Node.js 22.12+. Your own services can be Node, Python, Go, Rust, JVM, Ruby or PHP.
  • Try it: npx @flisk-sh/flisk demo. No signup, no global install. With Docker and Tilt it starts a six-service restaurant demo with Postgres, one gateway and live reload. Without them it starts a small menu app as two local processes and prints their URLs (usually http://localhost:3000; it picks a free port if that one is busy), and flisk down stops it.
  • CLI:
    • flisk create asks a few questions and writes a project that runs.
    • flisk import . reads a docker-compose.yml and writes one service.json per Compose service, keeping ports, names and env values.
    • flisk up starts services in health-checked dependsOn order and prints a *.localhost URL for each.
    • flisk status, flisk logs and flisk doctor show what is running and what is wrong.
    • flisk down stops everything.
  • Config: One small service.json per service. From it Flisk writes the Dockerfile, the Compose entry, the Traefik route, the health check and DATABASE_URL. It refuses to start if a generated file was edited by hand, and flisk config verify reports drift.
  • Docker: Optional. Services that each declare a command run as plain local processes. A database, one gateway URL for every service, or the same container you deploy need Docker (Engine 25+) and Tilt 0.25+.
  • For AI helpers: flisk mcp is an MCP server with 24 tools for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. flisk connect claude (or cursor, codex) adds it. The idea is that the helper writes your app and Flisk writes the setup around it, the same way every time.
  • Speed (from the repo's own benchmarks):
    • A plain Compose app (a Node API and Postgres) answered through Flisk's router 49 s after flisk import on a clean Ubuntu CI runner, images pulled and built from scratch.
    • With warm image layers, a one-backend stack is healthy in 12.8 to 13.8 seconds.
    • An 8-service stack settles in 32 to 42 seconds warm and about 4.5 minutes on its first cold build.
  • Licence: MIT. flisk up needs no key. Premium extras are optional.
  • Maturity: The npm package is at 1.4.x and the repo has thousands of commits. The README lists five teams that run flisk up on their own code, with their consent. The timings above come from CI runs the README links, not from an independent benchmark.
  • Not a deploy tool: It does not emit Kubernetes manifests and does not replace Helm, Kustomize, Flux or Argo. The one export scope is opt-in: flisk export render, wrangler and compose write render.yaml, wrangler.toml or a standalone docker-compose.yml. They write files only. They never deploy and never call a cloud API.
  • Windows: flisk demo and local processes work natively. The full Docker stack runs in Ubuntu on WSL2.
  • Not mentioned: Memory use compared with plain Compose, support for apps that need a local Kubernetes cluster, and any third-party benchmark.

When it fits, and when it does not

It fits when you run 3 to 10 services locally, you are tired of keeping a Compose file, a Tiltfile and a gateway config in sync by hand, or you want an AI helper to start and fix your stack without rewriting a Dockerfile each time.

It does not fit when your app is a single process, when your local setup already needs a real cluster, or when you want a tool that also ships to production.

Try it in 30 seconds 

npx @flisk-sh/flisk demo

Already have a Compose file?

npx @flisk-sh/flisk import .
npx @flisk-sh/flisk up

Add --dry-run to import to preview first.

Repo: https://github.com/flisk-sh/flisk · Site: https://flisk.sh

title: Depot vs WarpBuild for GitHub Actions runners
description:
Depot vs WarpBuild used to be a tie on price and is not one today: Depot lists a 2 vCPU Linux runner at $0.006 a minute, which is GitHub-hosted list price to the cent, and WarpBuild lists the same shape at $0.004. WarpBuild is a third cheaper at every Linux size both sell, so the case for Depot now has to be made on what the extra money buys.


10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU plus 2,000 macOS minutes a month, at rates read 20 September 2026. The macOS halves are identical, so the Linux rate is the whole difference; the dashed band is the Latchkey plan the compute bars exclude.

Depot sells ephemeral EC2 runners with a RAM disk in front of the root disk, 2 GB at 2 vCPU rising to 32 GB at 64 vCPU, and a cache its documentation describes at up to 1,000 MiB/s. Usage is tracked by the second with no one-minute minimum, and minutes come bundled into a plan, $20 a month with 2,000 or $200 with 20,000, rather than a standing free tier.

WarpBuild sells three things from one account: managed cloud runners at $0.004 a Linux minute, remote Docker builders priced separately from $0.06 a minute, and a bring-your-own-cloud mode at $0.002 a minute where runners execute inside your own AWS, GCP or Azure account and the compute lands on your cloud bill. Billing is per minute, and cache is a line item rather than an allowance.

Every cell below was read from the vendor's own public pricing or documentation page on 20 September 2026. Where a vendor does not publish a number, the cell says "not published" instead of carrying a guess.

Comparison

Depot WarpBuild Latchkey
Price per minute, 2 vCPU Linux x64 $0.006 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk, 2 GB RAM disk) $0.004 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM) $0.0025 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Price per minute, 4 vCPU Linux x64 $0.012 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 130 GB disk, 4 GB RAM disk) $0.008 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM) $0.005 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Free tier None standalone: 2,000 minutes with the $20/month Developer plan, 20,000 with the $200/month Startup plan Not published. Sign-up needs no card until you reach a usage or credit limit 30-day trial, then 2,000 included minutes a month on Developer, 4,000 on Launch, 6,000 on Scale
Billing granularity Per-second usage tracking, with whole minutes billed at the end of the month and no one-minute minimum Per minute, in its own words: "CI runners are billed on a per-minute basis" Per minute
Runner sizes and OS 2 to 64 vCPU on Linux x64 and arm64 (Graviton4); Windows Server 2022 and 2025 from 2 vCPU, with no Hyper-V; macOS at 8 vCPU 2 to 32 vCPU on Linux x64 and arm64; Windows from 4 vCPU; macOS M4 Pro at 6 and 12 vCPU; Linux on Apple silicon at 6 and 12 vCPU 2, 4, 8 and 16 vCPU, Ubuntu 24.04 on x86_64 only. arm64, Windows and macOS are not offered
Cache: type, limit, persistence Depot Cache, 25 GB included on Developer and 250 GB on Startup, then $0.20/GB/month; not isolated by branch Cache storage $0.20 per GB-month plus $0.0001 per write or restore; snapshot restore $0.04 per job and $0.025 per hour of snapshot storage Size not published. latchkey-dev/cache-action@v1 replaces actions/cache with a restore step and a save step, keeping path and key (no restore-keys); entries are isolated per organization, versioned by OS, kept 14 days; a failed restore warns rather than failing the job
Docker build acceleration A RAM disk on every runner, plus remote container builds as a separate product Remote Docker builders billed separately, 16 vCPU at $0.06/min up to 192 vCPU at $0.88/min, driven by Warpbuilds/build-push-action@v7; cache TTL 10 days latchkey-dev/docker-cache-action@v1, layers held in a Latchkey-managed private registry per organization
Concurrency limits Not published Advertised as unlimited job concurrency, with an explicit no-queue guarantee only on Enterprise Developer 20, Launch 40, Scale 80 busy runners per workspace; idle warm runners do not count
Where jobs run Ephemeral EC2 instances in Depot's AWS account, or in your own account on Depot Managed WarpBuild's own cloud, or your AWS, GCP or Azure account under BYOC at $0.002/min Latchkey's own AWS estate on m6a-class hosts, one job per runner, no inbound access, destroyed after the job
Self-healing or retries Not offered Not offered Built in: transient failures are diagnosed and retried inside the run
Setup change required Change the runs-on label. The repository must be owned by a GitHub organization Sign up, install the WarpBuild bot from its dashboard rather than the GitHub marketplace, then change the runs-on label to a runner ID A runs-on label change. GitHub organization accounts only

The rate cards, size by size

This is the table the two vendor sites no longer agree on, and it is the reason this page needed rewriting. WarpBuild doubles its rate with every vCPU step from $0.004, and so does Depot from $0.006, so the gap stays at a third all the way up.

Linux x64 Depot WarpBuild GitHub-hosted Latchkey
2 vCPU $0.006 $0.004 $0.006 $0.0025
4 vCPU $0.012 $0.008 $0.012 $0.005
8 vCPU $0.024 $0.016 $0.022 $0.01
16 vCPU $0.048 $0.032 $0.042 $0.02
32 vCPU $0.096 $0.064 $0.082 Not offered
2 vCPU arm64 $0.006 $0.003 $0.005 Not offered

Two things fall out of that table that neither vendor page says out loud. The first is that Depot matches GitHub-hosted list price at 2 and 4 vCPU and then passes it: at 8 vCPU it is $0.024 against GitHub's $0.022, and at 32 vCPU $0.096 against $0.082, because GitHub's ladder flattens as it climbs and Depot's does not. The second is arm64, where WarpBuild charges $0.003 and Depot charges its x64 rate of $0.006, so the architecture that is usually the cheap one costs twice as much on Depot.

Speed

Not benchmarked yet; the runner benchmark report will replace this section. We have not run the same workload on these runners ourselves, and until we have, there is no number here worth quoting.

The cheap way to get a real answer is to point one slow job at each candidate for a week, because runner selection is per job and the Actions run log gives you the timings for free.

Cost: the same month, priced three ways

The usual workload: 10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU plus 2,000 macOS minutes a month, on a private repository, at the rates above.

10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU 2,000 macOS minutes Monthly total
Depot $60 at $0.006/min $160 at $0.08/min $220 before plan fees
WarpBuild $40 at $0.004/min $160 at $0.08/min on a 6 vCPU M4 Pro $200
Latchkey $25 at $0.0025/min Not offered: $124 on GitHub-hosted $149 plus $5 to $49 a month for the plan

The macOS half is identical, which is why the Linux rate decides it: $20 a month on this mix, and $200 a year at three times the volume. Depot also starts from a plan fee of at least $20, where WarpBuild publishes no monthly fee at all, so the gap on a small account is wider than the table shows. Latchkey's own plan is $5 to $49 a month on top of that compute, and its 2,000 to 6,000 included minutes are not netted off, so the figure is gross on both counts.

BYOC is the line that makes WarpBuild structurally different rather than just cheaper. At $0.002 a minute, the same 10,000 Linux minutes cost $20 in WarpBuild fees, and then your own cloud account pays for the instances, which is a number WarpBuild cannot publish because it is yours. That is the right buy if you hold committed spend or need jobs inside your VPC, and the wrong one if nobody on the team wants another AWS footprint to own.

Then the cache meters, which are easy to miss on both. WarpBuild charges $0.20 per GB-month of cache storage plus $0.0001 for every write or restore, so a 50 GB cache is $10 a month plus roughly $1 per 10,000 operations, and a snapshot restore is $0.04 a job on top. Depot includes 25 GB on the Developer plan and charges $0.20 per GB-month after that, so the same 50 GB is $20 of plan plus $5 of storage. Cheap either way at this size, and worth checking before a monorepo pushes it to 500 GB.

Reliability

An Actions SLA appears on these pages only as something you buy: WarpBuild lists a contractual 99.9% uptime SLA and unlimited concurrency under Enterprise, and Depot publishes no figure on its pricing page. Depot does publish one honest constraint worth repeating, which is that Apple licensing makes its macOS capacity inelastic, so macOS jobs can queue at busy times.

On both, a job that fails for a reason unrelated to your code fails, bills the minutes it burned, and waits for a person. That is the whole category of work these rate cards do not price, and it is measurable in your own history: count the runs that passed on the second attempt with no code change between them. Exit code 137 and npm network errors in CI are the two that most often look like a runner problem and are not.

When to choose Depot

  • Your jobs are short and numerous, so per-second tracking with no one-minute minimum beats a lower per-minute rate on a wide matrix.
  • Your jobs are disk-bound: 100 GB at 2 vCPU with a RAM disk in front of it is more machine than the rate suggests.
  • You need 64 vCPU Linux, or Windows at 2 vCPU, neither of which WarpBuild publishes.
  • You want container builds and runner minutes from one vendor, with a cache the docs rate at up to 1,000 MiB/s.

When to choose WarpBuild

  • Your bill is mostly Linux minutes. A third off at every size is the plainest saving on this page.
  • You build on arm64: $0.003 against Depot's $0.006 at 2 vCPU is half price, and below GitHub's own arm64 rate of $0.005.
  • You want runners inside your own cloud account. BYOC at $0.002 a minute plus your compute is a different cost structure, not a discount.
  • Your Docker builds want a dedicated remote builder you size yourself, from 16 vCPU at $0.06 a minute up to 192 vCPU at $0.88.
  • One caveat: Windows starts at 4 vCPU on WarpBuild, and at 4 vCPU the two vendors are level at $0.016 a minute.

Switching: the exact diff

Both are a label change on top of one account step: Depot needs the repository to be owned by a GitHub organization, and WarpBuild needs its bot installed from the WarpBuild dashboard rather than the GitHub marketplace. Nothing else in the workflow moves, and because runner selection is per job you can run this exact diff on two jobs in the same file and compare a fortnight of real runs.

jobs:
   test:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4

   build:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: warp-ubuntu-latest-x64-4x

   build-arm:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04-arm
+    runs-on: warp-ubuntu-latest-arm64-4x

The verdict

On published rates this is now WarpBuild's comparison to lose: a third off Depot at every Linux size, half price on arm64, no plan fee to clear first, and a BYOC mode that changes the cost structure rather than the discount. Depot is not overpriced so much as differently priced, and the two things it sells that WarpBuild does not publish are per-second metering and a genuinely large disk under every runner, both of which matter more than the rate if your matrix is wide or your jobs thrash the filesystem. Price them against your own billed-to-elapsed ratio rather than against each other. Neither of them does anything about the run that failed on a registry timeout at 2am, which is the line item that never appears on a rate card.

FAQ

Is WarpBuild cheaper than Depot?

On Linux, yes, and by a consistent third: $0.004 against $0.006 at 2 vCPU, $0.008 against $0.012 at 4, and $0.064 against $0.096 at 32, read 20 September 2026. On arm64 it is half: $0.003 against $0.006. macOS is level at $0.08 a minute, and Windows is level at $0.016 for 4 vCPU. Depot can still win on a matrix of very short jobs, because it tracks usage by the second and WarpBuild bills per minute.

Are Depot runners 3x faster than GitHub-hosted?

That is Depot's own claim, published as "up to 3x faster than a GitHub-hosted runner", and it is not a benchmark you can reproduce from the page: it names no workload. What is checkable is the hardware behind it, which is a larger disk, a RAM-disk accelerator and a cache Depot rates at up to 1,000 MiB/s. We have not run our own comparison yet, so we are not repeating a multiplier as though it were measured.

What is WarpBuild BYOC and what does it actually cost?

BYOC runs the runners inside your own AWS, GCP or Azure account while WarpBuild keeps the control plane. The published fee is $0.002 a minute for Linux and for Windows on AWS and Azure, with add-ons free, and the instances themselves appear on your cloud bill at whatever you pay for them. For 10,000 Linux minutes that is $20 in WarpBuild fees plus your own compute, against $40 on its managed runners and $60 on Depot.

Do Depot and WarpBuild support arm64 runners?

Both do, at very different prices. WarpBuild publishes arm64 from $0.003 a minute at 2 vCPU up to $0.048 at 32 vCPU, a 25% discount against its own x64 rate. Depot runs arm64 on Graviton4 and charges the same as x64, $0.006 at 2 vCPU. GitHub-hosted arm64 sits between them at $0.005. Latchkey has no arm64 runner at all, which is a real gap on this page and not one worth papering over.

References

  • Depot GitHub Actions runner types and per-minute prices
  • Depot pricing and plan inclusions
  • WarpBuild pricing: runners, Docker builders, BYOC and add-ons
  • WarpBuild cloud runner IDs and shapes
  • GitHub Actions per-minute rates by runner

title: Our pages render identically at 1280px and at 4K, and our prose runs 78 characters to the line
description:
Every typography guide gives you the same number. Bringhurst says 66 characters a line is ideal for single-column text. The looser version of the advice is 45 to 75. CSS has had a unit for this since forever, ch, and the advice usually arrives as max-width: 65ch.

What almost nobody does is measure what their site actually renders. I had never measured mine, so I did it across all 76 public pages of Nakodo, at four viewport widths, two different ways.

The second part of that sentence turned out to be pointless, and that is the first finding.

The site stops responding at 768 pixels

I ran the sweep at 1280, 1920, 2560 and 3840 pixels wide. Here is the result in full:

Width Paragraphs Median measure p90 Longest
1280 1,755 78ch 82ch 136ch
1920 1,755 78ch 82ch 136ch
2560 1,755 78ch 82ch 136ch
3840 1,755 78ch 82ch 136ch

Not similar. Identical. All 76 pages have the same paragraph line counts at 3840 as at 1280, and every paragraph box is the same number of pixels wide.

That is because the widest element inside main is 768 pixels on 68 of the 76 pages, 1024 on six of them and 1152 on one. The only thing that grows past that is a full-bleed panel on the home page, which stretches the whole width because it is a background.

So at 4K, the readable part of a content page is a 768 pixel ribbon down the middle of a 3840 pixel screen. One fifth of the display. Everything above 1280 is wallpaper.

I am not going to pretend that is a bug. A guide is a column of prose, and prose does not want to be 3840 pixels wide. But it was worth knowing that the site has no design above lg, that nothing was decided for those widths, and that the measurement is therefore a single number rather than a curve.

Two ways to measure a line

The empirical way is to count rendered lines. A Range over a paragraph's contents returns one client rect per line box, so the distinct rect tops give you the real line count after the browser has done its wrapping:

const range = document.createRange();
range.selectNodeContents(p);
const tops = new Set([...range.getClientRects()]
  .filter((r) => r.height > 4 && r.width > 2)
  .map((r) => Math.round(r.top)));
const charsPerLine = text.length / tops.size;

That gives the median 77 characters a line across the site. It has a known bias: the last line of a paragraph is usually short, so the average is lower than the typographic measure. A two-line paragraph whose second line holds three words drags the number down a long way.

The typographic way is to measure the box in characters, which is what ch is for. There is no getComputedStyle property for it, so you ask the browser by making an element one ch wide inside the paragraph you are measuring, so it inherits the right font, and reading its rect back:

const probe = document.createElement("span");
probe.style.cssText = "position:absolute;visibility:hidden;width:1ch";
p.appendChild(probe);
const ch = probe.getBoundingClientRect().width;
probe.remove();
const measure = p.getBoundingClientRect().width / ch;

That gives 78. The two methods landing one character apart was more reassuring than either number on its own.

A caveat on ch: it is the advance width of the digit zero, which in most proportional fonts is wider than the average lowercase letter. So a box of 78ch typically fits rather more than 78 characters of real English. Both of my numbers are estimates of the same thing from opposite directions, and the honest conclusion is "somewhere around 78", not "78.0".

The distribution, which is where the problem is

1,755 paragraphs of at least 40 characters inside main. Grouped by measure:

Measure Paragraphs
20 to 29ch 7
30 to 39ch 334
40 to 49ch 74
50 to 59ch 20
60 to 69ch 161
70 to 79ch 528
80 to 89ch 625
130ch and over 3

11 per cent of the paragraphs on this site sit in the 45 to 75 range. 628 of them are over 80.

The shape is two humps, and each hump is a component rather than a decision about reading.

The big hump at 70 to 89 is the prose column. 626 paragraphs are in a box exactly 704 pixels wide and 351 are in one 672 pixels wide, which is max-w-3xl and max-w-2xl with padding taken off. At the body size of 15 pixels, 704 pixels is 78ch.

The hump at 30 to 39 is card blurbs: 267 paragraphs in a 302 pixel box, which are the two-line summaries in the grids on the hub pages like /guides and /youtubers. The narrowest-measure pages on the site are those hubs, at a median of 33ch, because they are not pages of prose at all.

The three paragraphs over 130ch are a measurement artefact worth describing, because it is the kind of thing that makes a sweep lie. They are single-line paragraphs of 46 to 48 characters sitting in a 1,088 pixel box. The box is wide, the text is short, and no line ever gets near the width, so the measure is a fact about the container and not about anything anybody reads. Measure is only meaningful for text that wraps.

Three more paragraphs came back with a box width of one pixel, which turned out to be sr-only text: the 1px clipped box is the mechanism, so those are correctly excluded rather than a bug.

15 pixels is the actual cause

The font sizes in that paragraph set are 15px for 1,245 of them, 14px for 351, 17px for 77 and 26px for 72.

That is the lever. A measure is a ratio of box width to character width, so there are two ways to pull 78ch down into the range, and only one of them is any good.

Narrowing the column from 704 to 640 pixels gets you to about 71ch and makes the page feel thinner without making anything easier to read.

Raising the body text from 15px to 16px gets you to about 73ch, and the text is also bigger. The counterintuitive version of the typography advice is that when your measure is too long, the first thing to try is larger text rather than a narrower column, because the reader gets both improvements from one change.

I am going to do the second one. 15px was a choice made for density on the app side of the product that leaked into the marketing pages, where there is nothing to be dense about.

Check it yourself

On any page of nakodo.app, this prints the measure of every wrapping paragraph:

const range = document.createRange();
console.table([...document.querySelectorAll("main p")]
  .filter((p) => p.textContent.trim().length > 40 && p.getBoundingClientRect().width > 5)
  .map((p) => {
    const probe = document.createElement("span");
    probe.style.cssText = "position:absolute;visibility:hidden;width:1ch";
    p.appendChild(probe);
    const ch = probe.getBoundingClientRect().width;
    probe.remove();
    range.selectNodeContents(p);
    const lines = new Set([...range.getClientRects()].filter((r) => r.height > 4).map((r) => Math.round(r.top))).size;
    return { measure: Math.round(p.getBoundingClientRect().width / ch), lines,
             perLine: Math.round(p.textContent.trim().length / lines) };
  }));

Then make the window 3840 pixels wide, or set that width in the device toolbar, and run it again. Nothing in the output moves, which is the whole of the first half of this post.

A guide page is the clearest place to see the long measure, the guides hub the clearest place to see the short one, and both of them will still say 78 and 33 until I ship the font size change.

What I took from it

  1. Measure, do not assume. I would have guessed this site was at 65 to 70 characters, because the column felt right. It is at 78, and 89 per cent of its paragraphs are outside the range every typography book recommends.
  2. Measure in two units. Characters per rendered line and box width in ch have opposite biases. They agreed here, and if they had not, that disagreement would have been the finding.
  3. A sweep needs an exclusion rule before it needs a chart. Six of my 1,755 paragraphs were single lines in wide boxes or 1px screen-reader text, and all six sat at the extremes of the distribution.
  4. Having no design above 1280 is a decision, so decide it. Right now the answer to "what does this site look like on a 4K monitor" is "exactly like a 1280 monitor with more wallpaper", which is defensible for prose and a waste for the home page.

title: UPI MDR Is Back: What NPCI's Supreme Court Defence of the 0.4% Merchant Discount Rate Means for Payment Engineers
description:
For six years I never had to build a fee line for UPI. Every card integration I have shipped carries a fee column in its ledger; every UPI one carried a zero, and most teams eventually dropped the column to tidy the schema. If the reporting is accurate, that tidy-up is about to cost somebody a bad month-end.

I will say my position up front. Most merchants will never compute this fee, because their gateway deducts it. The teams that must build real fee logic are PSPs, aggregators and platforms that settle to sub-merchants. Everyone else needs a place to store the fee and a reconciliation check that understands it. I would not build a full engine unless I sit on the settling side of the flow.

The first sections explain the concept; the later ones cover the design and code. Payment engineers can jump to Part 4.

What I am relying on, and what I have not seen

My inputs are press coverage of NPCI's 3 November 2026 submission to the Supreme Court and the RBI's 5 November 2026 cyber-resilience Master Directions for non-bank payment system operators. The affidavit itself I have not read. The Rs 2,000 threshold and the 0.4% ceiling are the reported numbers; confirm slabs and the effective date against primary documents before shipping. Coverage of the Vyapaar Saksham incentive scheme contradicted itself, so it stays out of every calculation below. It is also the reason the code keeps each number in configuration rather than constants.

Part 1: The plain-language version

UPI (Unified Payments Interface) is India's instant bank-to-bank payment system, used through QR scans or phone-number handles. NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India) is the non-profit entity that operates it.

MDR (Merchant Discount Rate) is the cut a merchant gives up on each electronic payment. Cards make the idea familiar: pay Rs 1,000 by card and the shop may receive about Rs 980, the remainder being split between the card network and the two banks. Cards have typically sat around 1.8-2%, depending on category and card type, which is why the proposed ceiling of 0.4% is a fifth of that.

UPI has charged merchants nothing since 2020. Small shops had no reason to refuse it, which is a big part of why it spread so fast. The running cost did not vanish, though; banks and the operator carried servers, fraud tooling and support, partly offset by government incentives.

As reported, NPCI told the court a revised MDR framework is needed for the system to stay financially sustainable. The proposal is narrow:

  • It applies only to P2M payments, i.e. person-to-merchant.
  • P2P, person-to-person, stays free.
  • It applies only above Rs 2,000 per transaction.
  • It is capped at up to 0.4%.
  • Merchants cannot pass it on to customers.

A Rs 1,500 grocery bill is untouched. A Rs 10,000 electronics bill at the full 0.4% costs the merchant Rs 40, and the customer still pays Rs 10,000.

Scale is what makes it matter: UPI has been running at well over 20 billion transactions a month, so even a fraction of them above the threshold adds up to a real revenue line. This would be the first time the rail has carried an explicit price.

Part 2: Why this is hard even though the rule sounds simple

The rule fits in five bullets, but each one conceals an engineering choice.

"Only person-to-merchant." The UPI protocol carries merchant category information, but not every payment arrives labelled cleanly. A neighbourhood tea stall may collect on a personal QR code. A freelancer may use a personal handle for business. Whether a payment is P2M depends on how the receiver is registered in your system, and you may have to treat the registration as the source of truth instead of the payer's app.

"Above Rs 2,000." Is that strictly above, or at or above? Is it measured on the transaction amount or on the order total when an order is split across payments? Does the fee apply to the entire amount or only to the portion above Rs 2,000? Reporting so far does not settle these questions, so I model them as policy options. Card pricing is the closest precedent: interchange is applied to the whole transaction amount, not an excess over a slab, and slab edges are defined per category in the network's own rules. My bet is the same here: full amount, strictly above the threshold, measured per transaction rather than per order. I would still keep the other combinations switchable, since a split cart paying Rs 1,200 twice is exactly the case someone will try to game.

"Up to 0.4%." The words "up to" mean the effective rate may vary by merchant category or by agreement. Your engine needs a rate lookup, not a global constant.

"Cannot be passed on." This is a checkout rule. If your platform has ever offered a "convenience fee" line for certain payment methods, that logic now becomes a compliance risk for UPI. You need a technical guard, not just a policy document.

Refunds and reversals. This is the case I would settle before any other, because it is where fee logic goes wrong most often. If a Rs 10,000 payment is refunded, is the Rs 40 returned to the merchant? Card networks usually return interchange on a full reversal, but nothing I have read says what UPI will do. Model it as a policy flag, and post the fee reversal as its own ledger line linked to the original, so a partial refund can prorate it. Dispute outcomes through NPCI's UDIR process need the same treatment.

On a payment integration I worked on earlier, fee rules ended up in three places: a spreadsheet finance maintained, a controller constant and a database trigger. Nobody planned that; each was a quick fix at the time. Within a few months they disagreed on edge cases, and we spent a painful stretch working out which of the three the bank's numbers actually matched. That is why I now insist on one fee engine, one source of truth and one audit trail. My wider background is in the experience section.

Part 3: The money flow, step by step

Follow a UPI merchant payment and note where the fee enters.

  1. The customer approves the payment in their UPI app. The customer's bank debits the full amount, with no deduction.
  2. NPCI routes the instruction and the merchant's acquiring side receives a credit notification. The acquirer is the bank or provider that onboards the merchant.
  3. Your payment backend, whether you are a PSP (payment service provider) or a merchant platform, records a successful collection for the gross amount.
  4. At settlement time, the money that reaches the merchant is the gross amount minus the MDR, and possibly minus tax on that fee. Taxes on fees are another reason to keep the fee as its own record.
  5. Reconciliation compares what your ledger expects against what the bank statement and the NPCI settlement file actually show.

Step 1 is identical to today: the customer sees the same debit. Everything new sits on the merchant side, in steps 3 to 5, so this is back-office work rather than anything a user would notice. Note too who does the deducting. If you collect through a payment aggregator or gateway, it takes the MDR before paying you out, and your system only needs to mirror what it was told. Settlement cycles are typically T+1 or similar, and the aggregator's settlement report, not your own estimate, is the authority on what was deducted. Only if you are the settling party do you compute the fee yourself.

A ledger entry for a Rs 10,000 payment should end up as three lines instead of one:

Account Debit Credit
Customer collection (gross) 10,000.00
Merchant payable 9,960.00
MDR income / expense 40.00

A single net number is not enough. If you store only Rs 9,960, you cannot later prove to the merchant or an auditor why it was not Rs 10,000.

Part 4: Architecture of a fee engine

For anyone who does settle, this is the design I would use: four small components, deliberately kept apart.

Classifier. Takes the payment event and decides P2M or P2P, with a reason string. The reason matters when a merchant disputes a charge six months later.

Policy resolver. Given the merchant, category and date, returns the active fee policy: threshold, rate, whether the fee applies to the full amount or the excess, rounding mode, and an effective-from date. Policies are versioned, never edited in place.

Calculator. A pure function. Amount plus policy in, fee out. No database calls, no clock reads. Pure functions are cheap to test with thousands of edge cases.

Ledger writer. Writes the gross, fee and net lines atomically with the policy version that produced them.

The pure calculator is what lets me sleep. In the market-data systems I run, I use the same discipline to make results replayable, which I wrote about in deterministic market data replay. For fees the payoff is the same: given the same inputs and the same policy version, you get the same paise every time, even years later.

Money rules I do not bend

  • Use BigDecimal, or integer paise. Never double.
  • Pick one rounding mode, record it in the policy, and apply it once per transaction.
  • Store the fee at the time of the transaction. Do not recompute it later from the current policy, or old data will change when rates change.
  • Make the write idempotent. UPI callbacks get retried, and a duplicate callback must not charge a duplicate fee. The pattern I use is the one in my post on the transactional outbox and idempotent consumers.

Part 5: A Spring Boot sketch of the fee engine

Treat this as a sketch to adapt, not a drop-in. Every threshold, rate and mode comes from a policy record, because the final slabs and effective date are not mine to hard-code.

public enum PayeeType { P2P, P2M }

public enum FeeBasis { FULL_AMOUNT, EXCESS_OVER_THRESHOLD }

public record FeePolicy(
        String version,
        BigDecimal threshold,        // e.g. 2000.00, from config
        boolean thresholdInclusive,  // is exactly 2000.00 charged?
        BigDecimal rate,             // e.g. 0.004 for 0.4%, or lower per category
        FeeBasis basis,
        RoundingMode rounding,
        LocalDate effectiveFrom) {}

public record FeeResult(BigDecimal fee, String policyVersion, String reason) {}

public final class MdrCalculator {

    public FeeResult compute(PayeeType type, BigDecimal amount, FeePolicy p) {
        if (type == PayeeType.P2P) {
            return new FeeResult(BigDecimal.ZERO.setScale(2), p.version(), "P2P_EXEMPT");
        }
        int cmp = amount.compareTo(p.threshold());
        boolean charged = p.thresholdInclusive() ? cmp >= 0 : cmp > 0;
        if (!charged) {
            return new FeeResult(BigDecimal.ZERO.setScale(2), p.version(), "BELOW_THRESHOLD");
        }
        BigDecimal base = p.basis() == FeeBasis.FULL_AMOUNT
                ? amount
                : amount.subtract(p.threshold());
        BigDecimal fee = base.multiply(p.rate()).setScale(2, p.rounding());
        return new FeeResult(fee, p.version(), "P2M_ABOVE_THRESHOLD");
    }
}

The service around it loads the policy that was active on the transaction date, not today's, and posts the ledger lines in one database transaction:

@Service
class SettlementPostingService {

    private final PolicyRepository policies;
    private final LedgerRepository ledger;
    private final MdrCalculator calculator = new MdrCalculator();

    SettlementPostingService(PolicyRepository policies, LedgerRepository ledger) {
        this.policies = policies;
        this.ledger = ledger;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void post(UpiCollection c) {
        if (ledger.existsByUpiRef(c.upiRef())) {
            return; // retried callback, already posted
        }
        FeePolicy policy = policies.activeOn(c.merchantCategory(), c.txnDate());
        FeeResult fee = calculator.compute(c.payeeType(), c.amount(), policy);

        BigDecimal net = c.amount().subtract(fee.fee());
        ledger.save(LedgerEntry.collection(c.upiRef(), c.amount()));
        ledger.save(LedgerEntry.mdr(c.upiRef(), fee.fee(), fee.policyVersion(), fee.reason()));
        ledger.save(LedgerEntry.merchantPayable(c.upiRef(), net));
    }
}

The unique constraint on upiRef in the database is the real idempotency guard. The existsBy check is a cheap shortcut, and the constraint catches the race when two callbacks arrive at once.

Blocking surcharges at checkout

The no-pass-through rule needs a guard at the point where the cart total is built. I prefer to make it structurally impossible instead of relying on code review:

public CheckoutQuote quote(Cart cart, PaymentMethod method) {
    BigDecimal base = cart.total();
    BigDecimal methodFee = feeSchedule.customerFeeFor(method, base);

    if (method == PaymentMethod.UPI && methodFee.signum() != 0) {
        // The merchant bears MDR. A customer-facing fee on UPI must never exist.
        audit.record("UPI_SURCHARGE_BLOCKED", cart.id(), methodFee);
        methodFee = BigDecimal.ZERO;
    }
    return new CheckoutQuote(base, methodFee, base.add(methodFee));
}

Silently zeroing the fee is a choice. In a stricter setup, I would throw and fail the quote so the misconfiguration is noticed in testing rather than papered over in production. Either way, the audit event is the part a regulator will ask for.

Part 6: Reconciliation, where fee bugs actually show up

Calculating the fee correctly is half the job. The other half is proving that what you calculated matches what actually arrived. A reconciliation check compares three sources: your ledger, the acquirer's settlement file, and the bank credit.

The check I would run nightly, per merchant per settlement cycle:

public ReconReport reconcile(String merchantId, LocalDate cycle, SettlementFile file) {
    BigDecimal expectedGross = ledger.sumCollections(merchantId, cycle);
    BigDecimal expectedFee   = ledger.sumMdr(merchantId, cycle);
    BigDecimal expectedNet   = expectedGross.subtract(expectedFee);

    BigDecimal reportedFee = file.totalFee(merchantId);
    BigDecimal reportedNet = file.totalNet(merchantId);

    List<Break> breaks = new ArrayList<>();
    if (expectedFee.compareTo(reportedFee) != 0) {
        breaks.add(Break.feeMismatch(expectedFee, reportedFee));
    }
    if (expectedNet.compareTo(reportedNet) != 0) {
        breaks.add(Break.netMismatch(expectedNet, reportedNet));
    }
    // Transaction-level diff only when totals disagree, to keep the job cheap
    if (!breaks.isEmpty()) {
        breaks.addAll(txnLevelDiff(merchantId, cycle, file));
    }
    return new ReconReport(merchantId, cycle, breaks);
}

Raw settlement data from NPCI and the acquirer arrives as files, and the column layout differs by bank, so write one adapter per source that maps into a common SettlementFile shape rather than scattering parsing through the job. Two practical points from experience. First, compare fee totals separately from net totals. If only the net differs, you cannot tell whether the cause is a wrong fee, a missing transaction or a timing cut-off. Splitting them narrows the search immediately. Second, a difference of a few paise across thousands of rows is almost always rounding. If the acquirer rounds per transaction and you round per batch, you will drift. Match their rule exactly and record it in the policy.

The threshold boundary deserves its own test. I would add test cases at 1,999.99, 2,000.00 and 2,000.01, with both inclusive and exclusive settings. That is where an off-by-one in a comparison quietly turns into a recurring mismatch on exactly the payments people round to, like a Rs 2,000 bill.

If you want to see how I approach large volumes with predictable behaviour, the projects section and my write-up on high-throughput Java under virtual threads cover the throughput side of reconciliation jobs.

Part 7: The second half of the news, RBI's cyber-resilience Master Directions

The same week brought a second development that affects the same operators. On 5 November 2026 the RBI issued cyber-resilience Master Directions for non-bank payment system operators, often shortened to PSOs. These are the non-bank companies that run wallets, payment gateways and similar services under RBI authorisation.

I have not memorised every clause, and you should read the text itself, but the direction of travel matches what I have seen in other regulated sectors: stronger security controls, incident reporting, and evidence that you can prove what happened. For a fee engine this matters in concrete ways:

  • Audit trails. Every fee decision should be reconstructible: which policy version, which inputs, which result. The reason and policyVersion fields above exist for this purpose.
  • Change control. A rate change is a financial change and a security-relevant one. Policies should be versioned, approved by two people and logged.
  • Access control. Who can edit fee policies, and who can view merchant settlement data? Keep those roles separate.
  • Resilience. If the fee engine is down, do you fail closed and hold settlement, or fail open and post later? Decide deliberately and document it.

I wrote about producing this kind of evidence automatically in DORA and NIS2 policy-as-code. The regulators differ, but the engineering habit is shared: make compliance a by-product of how the system runs, not a quarterly scramble.

What I would do this week

Rules like these tend to arrive with short notice and a long tail of clarifications. Rather than wait for every detail, I would prepare the parts that will not change:

  1. Put a fee field in your ledger. Gross, fee and net as separate lines, even if the fee is zero today.
  2. Tag every payee as P2P or P2M with a stored reason, and decide who owns corrections when the tag is wrong.
  3. Move all thresholds, rates and rounding rules into versioned policy records. No constants in code.
  4. Add the surcharge guard to checkout and alert on any attempt.
  5. Add the fee-versus-net split to nightly reconciliation.
  6. Read the primary texts. Confirm the slabs, the basis of calculation, the effective date and any carve-outs against the NPCI affidavit and the RBI Master Directions, and treat unconfirmed items such as the Vyapaar Saksham scheme as unknown until a primary source says otherwise.

My honest view is that the 0.4% itself is the least interesting number. What matters is that India's flagship public digital rail now has a price signal in it, and every system that touched it assumed that price was zero. Systems built on a hidden assumption break in surprising places, usually in a reconciliation report at month end.

If you are planning this change and want a second pair of eyes on a fee engine, ledger design or reconciliation job, reach me through the contact section. Before that, open your current UPI ledger schema today and check whether it has a place to store a fee next to the gross amount. If it does not, that is your first ticket.

Related Articles

  • Commercial VRP in the UK: Spring Boot mandates and recurring payments
  • Transactional outbox and idempotent consumers for Spring Boot payment systems
  • ASEAN cross-border QR payments: an EMVCo router in Spring Boot

title: I built interview prep games where you write real CSS and JavaScript
description:
Interview prep has a habit problem. You open a list of questions, read a solution, and close the tab feeling productive. A week later the idea is gone, because you never used it.

I wanted something I would actually open for ten minutes. That is how Playhire started: interview topics turned into short browser games, with no sign-up required to play. There are 13 games live, grouped into six Masters — CSS, DSA, JavaScript, OOP, system design, and interview English — and 181 levels in total. I want to talk about a design rule we refused to break, and what it taught me about teaching hard ideas.

The rule: write the real thing

A lot of learn-to-code games hide the language behind arrow keys or a custom mini-language. That can be delightful, and it is also a step away from the interview. On Playhire, when the topic is CSS, you type CSS. When it is JavaScript, you type JavaScript. The page's own engines decide if you are right. That sounds obvious. It is also the whole product.

How Flexbox becomes a game you cannot fake

Take Flex Escape. A horde is closing in on a building site. The steel beams are flex items; the gap you need to cross only closes when they sit in the right place. You type into an editor and watch the beams move. There are 14 sites.

The mechanic forces a mental model interviewers care about: the main axis and the cross axis. With flex-direction: row, justify-content works left to right and align-items works top to bottom. Change the direction to column and those properties appear to swap, because the axes rotated. Once you think in axes instead of "move it up", most Flexbox puzzles get easier. Putting justify-content on the item instead of the container also fails in public, which is the most common real-world bug.

Flex Strike uses the same language in a tighter loop: 24 waves across Easy, Hard, and Pro. Hostiles sit in fixed lanes. Your turrets sit on a flex rail. Guessing does not work, because the alignment has to be exact. That is how we drill the spacing tools people mix up: space-between versus space-evenly versus gap, margin: auto to push one item to the far end, order, and flex-grow. You can feel why flex-grow: 2 is twice the leftover space, not twice the total width.

Later CSS games keep the "real CSS, live preview" contract and change the question:

  • In Drone Dock (18 levels) the hangar is the container and the drones are items. Levels start with single-line Flexbox and move into Grid, including place-items: center as the short way to center a child on both axes.
  • Blueprint (11 levels) shows a dashed target layout. You edit real CSS until the live preview sits on the dashed lines. Early levels are Flexbox classics — centering, space-evenly, flex: 1. Later ones are Grid: fr units, grid-template-areas, auto-fit, dense packing. When two tools can solve the same level, that is the interview: knowing which one fits.
  • Selector Quest (18 chambers) runs your selector through the page's own query engine. The vault opens only if you matched exactly the right elements, no more and no fewer — through combinators, attribute selectors, :has(), and specificity duels.
  • Position Ninja (15 missions) is checked by the browser's layout engine, so the traps are real. position: sticky that silently fails inside overflow: hidden, or fixed that stops being relative to the viewport because an ancestor has a transform, fails in the game the same way it fails in production.

HTML Lab, which starts the CSS Master path, applies the same idea to markup: 16 lessons where you write real HTML and watch the rendered page, the DOM tree, and a screen-reader view update together.

Mapping a mechanic to a concept

The event loop is hard to lecture about and easier to play if you design the loop correctly.

Event Loop Express has ten levels. You read a short snippet, predict the console.log order, then watch the call stack, the microtask queue, and the task queue run the code step by step. Every answer is checked against real Node output. Level 3, "The VIP lane", is the classic rule in game form: promise callbacks are microtasks, setTimeout even with 0 ms is a task, and the engine drains every microtask before it takes the next task.

console.log("A");
setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("C"));
console.log("D");
// A, D, C, B

The important design choice is the order of play: predict first, then watch. If we only animated the queues, people would nod along. A wrong prediction is what makes the rule stick.

Sorting and graph search needed a different trick: either you do the comparison with your hands, or your algorithm has to work on a map it has never seen.

In Duck Pond you send each duck left or right of a party-hat pivot — that is quick sort. Web Sort lets you tap boxes through merge sort, or write merge() yourself. Every comparison is a move you make, which is why the O(n log n) / O(n²) trade-off is easier to explain afterwards.

Code Arena is closer to a real interview: six turn-based puzzles, one turn(state) function, three test cases, and a replay of what your code did each turn. A solution only counts when it passes every test, not just the example. Because turn is called again every turn, any memory you need has to live outside the function or in the state you are given — the same idea as a visited set during a graph search.

Rover Protocol pushes that further. Twelve missions, from loops up to BFS, Dijkstra, DFS, and flood fill, each tested on maps your code has never seen. A path hard-coded for the first map dies on the second. The game only lets a general algorithm through. That is a more honest teacher than a green check on the sample input.

What I learned about making learning games fun

A few things we kept running into.

One idea at a time. If a level also sneaks in a new API, failure becomes ambiguous. You do not know whether you missed the concept or the syntax.

Make the feedback visual and immediate. Beams moving, drones landing, queues emptying, a rover taking a wrong turn — that loop is the reason you try one more level.

Do not rely on a single metaphor. Flexbox is more interesting when it is an escape route, a turret rail, a hangar, and a dashed blueprint, not fourteen screens of the same animal.

After a win, explain the interview angle in a few lines — the complexity, the trap, the one-liner you should be able to say out loud. Blueprint and Code Arena do this on purpose. The Blockchain labs go further: each of the 16 topics ends with a three-question quiz and a typical interview question with a model answer. The hashing and signatures are real SHA-256 and ECDSA from the browser's WebCrypto API.

Keep the door open. Every game works as a guest; progress stays in the browser. Optional Google sign-in keeps progress across devices, puts you on the weekly leaderboard (it resets every Monday at 00:00 PKT), and unlocks a Certificate of Mastery with a unique ID and a public verify link when you clear every live game in a Master. XP is simple on purpose: +50 per level, +20 per star, and a 1.2× daily streak. Ads appear on some pages, but they never block a game, and you never pay to unlock a level.

Fun, here, is not jokes on the loading screen. It is a problem small enough to finish, a check you cannot argue with, and a reason to start the next one.

Try it

Playhire is free at playhire.online. If you want a CSS session, start with Flex Escape or Drone Dock. If you want JavaScript, start with Event Loop Express. You can play the first level in the time it takes to read a blog intro — which was the point.

title: One editor per entity: why Add and Edit share one screen
description:
Seed's New group button used to open a dialog with one field, while editing a group showed four: description, colour and emoji besides the name. This post is for developers and product people who keep building a create form and an edit form for the same thing, and wonder whether they should.

TL;DR

  • In my apps, Add and Edit are one screen: New group opens the group's editor at /groups/new, and an existing group opens the same component at /groups/:id.
  • One component means one set of fields, one check and one place for the loading, error and offline states, so create and edit cannot drift apart.
  • A real address beats ?new: you can link to it and reload it, and after a create the address is replaced, so Back does not reopen an empty form.
  • Ids made on the device let Seed create tags and notes offline and send them later with the same id. Groups still need a connection.

Seed: Live: Open the live demo · Code: github.com/spy4x/seed

In my apps, Add and Edit are one screen. "New group" opens the group's editor at
/groups/new in create mode, and an existing group opens the same editor at
/groups/:id: the same component, the same fields, the same checks. One screen
for add and edit, never a one-field dialog for create and another form for edit.

This post is for developers and product people who build a create form and an
edit form for the same thing. I'll show the before and after from
Seed, my SaaS starter: why one component, why a real address
beats ?new, what offline-first adds, and where Seed does not do that part yet.

What was wrong with a "New group" dialog?

On 16 October I wrote down what annoyed me in Seed's app, and it became
an issue. One item:

Always make "Add/New " button to open the entity's editor (in "create"
mode), not a dialog with only one field "name". [...] it must always be THE
SAME COMPONENT.

Here is what it was about. "New group" opened a dialog with one field (trimmed
from
the pull request that removed it):

<Modal open title="New group" cancelLabel="Close" onClose={closeCreate}>
  <ScreenForm pending={creating} onSubmit={onCreate}>
    <Field id="group-name" label="Name" error={error} required>
      <Input name="name" maxLength={100} value={name} required autoFocus />
    </Field>
    {/* Cancel and "Create group" */}
  </ScreenForm>
</Modal>

Editing a group was a different thing: the name was renamed in place, and a
separate "Details" dialog held the description, colour and emoji. So a group was
born with a name only, and you had to find the second dialog to finish it. Tags,
API tokens and invitations repeated the same dialog pattern.

Nothing in it was broken. It just looked like two features that happened to
share a database table.

Why one component instead of two forms?

Because two forms for one thing drift. A new field has to be added twice. A
check has to be written twice. The loading, error and offline states have to be
drawn twice, and one of them gets forgotten. The person sees two different
screens for the same group and learns two layouts.

Seed's routes now point both addresses at one view
(app.tsx):

"/groups/new": () => <GroupEditorView key="new" />,
"/groups/:groupId/:tab?": (params) => <GroupPage groupId={params.groupId} tab={params.tab} />,

GroupPage renders the same GroupEditorView with the group's id, and the view
picks the mode
(GroupEditorView.tsx):

{
  groupId === null
    ? <NewGroup />
    : <ExistingGroup groupId={groupId} tab={tab} />
}

Both branches draw one GroupEditorScreen. Create mode passes creating; edit
mode passes the saved group. What that buys:

  1. One set of fields. Name, description, emoji, colour and, since November, the group's time zone, in both modes. A create sends them all in one request.
  2. One check. checkGroupDraft checks the draft with the server's own parsers, so a typo is caught before the round trip, and both create() and save() call it (groups.ts).
  3. One place for every state. Loading, "this group does not exist", errors under their field, saving, the offline notice. Written once, so create cannot forget one.
  4. Small, visible differences. Create mode says "New group" with Cancel and "Create group". Edit mode is titled with the saved name, and Discard and "Save group" show only after you change something. Leaving with unsaved changes asks first, in both.

The fields themselves come from my own
Preact component library, so
the editor is mostly wiring. The note editor already worked this way; it was the
model. Seed's UI rules now say it as rule 2,
"One editor per entity",
so the next entity an app adds starts right.

Why /groups/new and not ?new?

Before, "New group" in the group switcher went to /groups?new, and the groups
page opened the dialog when it saw new in the query. A dialog over a list is
not a place. /groups/new is: you can link to it, reload it, and leave it with
Back, and the browser's history makes sense.

The interesting moment is right after the create. The address /groups/new is
now wrong: the group exists. So Seed swaps it for the group's page instead of
pushing a new entry
(GroupEditorView.tsx):

const group = await groups.create()
if (!group) return false
// The group is in the list before the address changes, so its page draws at once.
navigate(GROUP_PATHS.settings(group.id), { replace: true })
void selection.select(group.id)

replace: true is the whole trick. Back from the new group goes to where you
were before, the groups list in my case, not to an emptied "New group" form. The
new group also becomes your current one, since you made it to work in it, and a
toast says so. No reload: the route changes inside the app, and the same editor
draws again in edit mode, now with the Members, Billing and Activity tabs.

What does offline-first add?

In an offline-first app the device makes the id, not the database. Seed gives
every new record a UUID version 7 on the client
(newId: () => uuidV7())
and sends it with the create. Since the id exists before the server answers, the
editor's address exists too.

Tags and notes go one step further: you can create them with no connection. Here
is a tag I created in the demo with the network off:

What happened there:

  1. "Create tag" put the create into a queue on the device, with the tag's id.
  2. The tag showed up in the list, and the editor moved from /tags/new to /tags/<id> in edit mode, exactly as it does online.
  3. When the network came back, the queue sent tag.create with the same id (new-ids.test.ts checks exactly this).
  4. If the queue sends a create again because an answer got lost, the server sees that the id already holds this tag and answers with it, so a retry cannot make a copy. Only a different tag under the same id is refused ("Tag id is already in use").

One editor helps here too: the group editor's offline notice is written once,
with one sentence for creating and one for saving, and both modes show it.

Now the honest part. Groups don't do this yet. Creating a group needs the
server. With no network, the group editor lets you fill in the form and says
"You can fill this in now, but you need a connection to create the group." A
create that fails keeps what you typed. Each try at a group also gets a fresh
id, so the same-id protection covers tags and notes, not groups. The rest of
Seed's offline layer is in the Seed post.

What else did one editor drag along?

The same issue had more in it, and my AI agents built it in four pull requests
in Seed's previous repository, on 16 and 17 October (how I run them is in
my AI coding agent setup):

  • Tags got /tags/new and /tags/:tagId first, with one TagEditorScreen.
  • Groups got the editor above. Clicking a group in the list now opens its editor, not its notes, and the "Open notes" button is gone: notes are not the only thing an app will ever have.
  • API tokens and invitations are created on pages too, at /tokens/new and /groups/:groupId/invitations/new. They are never edited, so their pages are create-only, in two steps: the form, then the token or link shown once, with "Leave without copying?" if you try to leave first. A dialog that shows a secret once is very easy to close by accident.
  • The header bar went away, and the sidebar is now the app's only frame. Not about editors, but the same issue.

So the next time a "New something" button opens a dialog with one field, ask
what the edit screen looks like. If the answer is "different", you have two
forms, and they have already started drifting.

First published on antonshubin.com.

title: When 75% Is Not the Whole Score: Auditing Predictions by Denominator
description:
A 75% score over four rows

Put one number on the table and break it open. Suppose an eight-row inventory and its predictions show 75% correct. That fraction covers four records: id0, id1, id4, and id6. id2 abstains, id3 has no prediction line, id5 is invalid because of conflicting duplicates, and id7 has null gold. None enters the A/C=3/4 numerator or denominator, but the inventory still has eight rows. The number itself does not say which rows left, so the per-row filters belong next to it.

prediction-metric-desk is a local audit desk that compares an inventory with saved predictions and counts them. It trains nothing, infers nothing, and does not rewrite invalid rows. The eight-row fixture is a fixed fault set included in the package. The inventory has N=8 records, with K=7 known gold and null gold for id7. The predictions file has 11 physical lines, including one broken JSON line, one extra ID, and duplicate id5 lines. These rows stay in the report.

The screenshot comes from the standalone App page and is uncropped. The App renders NLL as ∞ and notes zero true-class probability. The exported JSON writes the same condition as value:null and infinite:true, two representations with no change to the metric definition.

Record-level map

One clarification first: labels are ["a","b","missing"], and "missing" is a legitimate taxonomy string, not a missing value. id4 has gold label "missing" and predicted label "missing", so this line counts as correct. That is separate from id3's missing state, which means there is no prediction line at all.

id gold prediction line C D E
0 a predicted a, probabilities [0.8,0.1,0.1] yes yes yes
1 a predicted b, probabilities [0,1,0] yes yes yes
2 b predicted null, probabilities [0.1,0.8,0.1] no yes no
3 b no prediction line no no no
4 "missing" predicted "missing", no probabilities yes no yes
5 "missing" two lines: a and typo, invalid no no no
6 a predicted a, probabilities [0.1,0.8,0.1] yes yes yes
7 null predicted b, probabilities [0.1,0.8,0.1] unscored no yes

From the table: C contains id0, id1, id4, and id6; three of them are correct, so A=3, C=4, and A/C=75%. id2 has probabilities but a null predicted_label, so it is abstained and enters D but not C or E. id4 has a decision and no probabilities, so it enters C/E and not D. id5 has two conflicting physical lines, so the record is invalid and stays out of C/D/E; both original lines remain visible in prediction_lines, while line_accounting carries counts such as invalid_lines and not the raw rows themselves. id7 has null gold, is not scored, and enters E only. The extra ID is separate from inventory cases.

C and D both equal 4 in this fixture by coincidence, but their members differ: id2 is in D and not C, id4 is in C and not D. Reading 4 as the same filter misses that difference.

Coverage needs three rates

E counts a single valid prediction line with a non-null predicted_label, regardless of gold, so id7 qualifies and E=5. C counts decided rows among known gold, so C=4. C/K=4/7 asks what share of known-gold rows decided; E/N=5/8 asks what share of inventory emitted a label; A/C=3/4 asks what share of those decisions were correct. Treating A/C as overall accuracy drops the first two denominators.

U=K-C=3. If I force all three undecided rows to answer, completed accuracy runs from A/K=3/7 to (A+K-C)/K=6/7. The range assumes all three are wrong or all three are right. It is not a confidence interval and not a promise. It shows how sensitive the current 0.75 is to those rows.

Probability support and decision labels

D counts known-gold rows with one valid prediction line and a non-null probabilities vector, four in this fixture. Label order is a, b, "missing"; id1 has true class a and vector [0,1,0], whose first term for a is zero. Mean NLL is therefore infinite. The exported report writes value:null, infinite:true, zero_probability_rows:1, and support:4; the page renders ∞. I do not clip the value, renormalize the vector, or fabricate a one-hot output. predicted_label may also differ from probabilities argmax: id6 has predicted_label a while its argmax is b. The report records that mismatch and does not override the policy label.

Reproduce the fixture with one command

From the package root, with Node 22 or newer and no existing output file:

node audit_cli.mjs data/fault-inventory.json data/fault-predictions.jsonl my-audit.json

stdout is JSON. This block is an excerpt of key fields, not the full stdout; the full report is written to my-audit.json with cases as record-level status, prediction_lines as original physical lines with line errors, and line_accounting as a physical-line summary.

{
  "denominators": {"N": 8, "K": 7, "E": 5, "C": 4, "A": 3, "U": 3, "D": 4},
  "metrics": {
    "coverage": 0.625,
    "known_gold_coverage": 0.5714285714285714,
    "conditional_accuracy": 0.75,
    "completion_bounds": [0.42857142857142855, 0.8571428571428571],
    "nll": {"value": null, "infinite": true, "zero_probability_rows": 1, "support": 4}
  }
}

That command verifies the table without recomputing the 3080-row result. Entry points and fixed version:

  • Standalone App page
  • HF Space
  • Fixed source commit cb003655f55c5a9153bceaa7fde897ec598d7011

I still recommend the standalone App page as the stable entry point. The inline Hub view appeared blank in a minimized Edge environment on 2026-11-13, and that cause remains unproven. On 2026-11-14, a signed-out inline browser environment previewed and applied the fault fixture and showed N=8, C=4, A=3, D=4, conditional accuracy 3/4, known-gold coverage 4/7, and infinite NLL. That success is limited to the new signed-out context; it does not show the original Edge issue is fixed, the root cause is known, or every browser and entry point works.

What the report carries

Active audit work and newly imported inputs live in browser memory and clear on refresh. There is no autosave and no crash checkpoint. A downloaded JSON report itself remains on disk, but it cannot be reimported as a checkpoint, and refreshing does not reload it automatically. The exported report contains full original inventory and predictions, so I check what is inside before sharing. SHA256 proves byte consistency, not provenance, authorization, or gold-label reliability.

The 3080-row BANKING77 predictions were generated from saved int8 logits and frozen temperature 0.75 by the earlier work; prediction-metric-desk audits that saved result. It gives 2779 correct and 301 incorrect while retaining the original seven normalized train/test overlaps. The tool does not regenerate logits, fit a temperature, or perform new calibration. That is not new training, inference, blind evaluation, or generalization evidence. The implementation and synthetic fixture are Apache 2.0. The BANKING77 source data and derived outputs stay CC BY 4.0 with attribution to PolyAI and Casanueva et al. 2020.

By Renchao Wu.

title: Identify high cost GitHub Actions workflows
description:
To identify high cost GitHub Actions workflows you need three numbers that the billing dashboard does not give you: minutes by workflow, minutes by job inside the worst workflow, and the share of your runs that are retries of a previous attempt. All three come from the REST API and the usage report, and the third one is the one almost nobody measures and frequently the largest.


The three measurements and where each one comes from. Endpoint paths from the GitHub REST API reference for Actions workflow runs, read on 21 September 2026.

The billing page shows a total. A total tells you that CI costs money and nothing about where it goes, and optimisation aimed at the wrong job is the most common way a team spends a sprint and saves nothing.

Everything below is read-only and takes under an hour on a repository you already have a token for. Do it before you change a single workflow file, and rank what you find by money rather than by minutes, because a Linux job and a macOS job of the same length are not the same line on the invoice.

One: minutes by workflow

The workflow timing endpoint returns billable milliseconds per operating system for a single workflow, which is exactly the breakdown the billing dashboard will not give you. Loop it over the workflow list and you have a ranked table in a few seconds.

Read the result as a ranking rather than as an invoice. The figure is machine time in milliseconds, and the bill rounds the minutes and partial minutes each job uses up to the nearest whole minute, so a workflow made of many short jobs will cost more than this endpoint suggests and a workflow made of a few long ones will cost about what it says.

There is one answer that looks like a broken script and is not. On a public repository the billable object comes back empty, because the use of standard GitHub-hosted runners is free and unlimited there. If you get nothing back from a public repository, nothing is wrong: there is nothing to bill. Larger runners are the exception and are charged on public repositories too.

# per-workflow billable time, ranked
gh api /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows --paginate \
  --jq '.workflows[] | "\(.id)\t\(.name)"' |
while IFS=$'\t' read -r id name; do
  ms=$(gh api "/repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/$id/timing" \
        --jq '[.billable[]?.total_ms] | add // 0')
  printf "%8.1f min  %s\n" "$(echo "$ms/60000" | bc -l)" "$name"
done | sort -rn

Run this first. It almost always shows one or two workflows dominating, which turns an open-ended optimisation project into a specific one.

Two: where the minutes go inside that workflow

Once you know which workflow is expensive, the question is which job inside it. The run timing endpoint gives billable milliseconds per operating system for a single run along with the total run duration, and the jobs endpoint gives you the start and completion timestamps of every job in that run.

Average across the last fifty runs rather than reading one. A single run tells you about one moment of registry weather; fifty tell you which job is structurally slow. The pattern that comes back most often is that dependency installation, not compilation and not the tests, is the largest single block of time in the pipeline.

Keep the two operating systems separate while you do it. A five-minute macOS job and a five-minute Linux job are $0.31 and $0.03 respectively, so a ranking by duration puts them side by side and a ranking by cost puts them ten rows apart. Sort by minutes multiplied by that runner type's published rate, never by minutes alone.

# average per-job duration across the last 50 runs of one workflow
gh run list --workflow=ci.yml --limit 50 --json databaseId --jq '.[].databaseId' |
while read -r id; do
  gh api "/repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/$id/jobs" \
    --jq '.jobs[] | [.name, (((.completed_at|fromdate) - (.started_at|fromdate))/60)] | @tsv'
done | awk -F'\t' '{s[$1]+=$2; n[$1]++} END {for (k in s) printf "%8.1f min avg  %4d runs  %s\n", s[k]/n[k], n[k], k}' | sort -rn

Three: the number nobody measures

Every workflow run carries a run_attempt field, and it is 1 on a first attempt. Count how many of your recent runs are at attempt 2 or higher and you have the share of your bill that bought the same work twice.

This is the measurement that changes what you do next, because no per-minute discount touches it. A pipeline that re-runs a meaningful share of its jobs is paying for the failure, paying again for the retry, and paying a third time in the hour between the failure and somebody noticing. If that share is more than a few percent, reliability is your cost problem and the rate is a distraction.

Look at what the retries are for while you are there. Retries of registry timeouts, DNS failures and runner losses are a different problem from retries of a genuinely flaky test, and they are the ones with nothing to do with your code at all.

# what fraction of recent runs are attempt 2 or later?
gh run list --limit 200 --json databaseId --jq '.[].databaseId' |
while read -r id; do
  gh api "/repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/$id" --jq '.run_attempt'
done | awk '{t++; if ($1>1) r++} END {printf "re-runs: %d of %d (%.1f%%)\n", r, t, 100*r/t}'

The one report the API cannot replace

The API is per repository. The usage report is per account, and it is the only surface that attributes spend to a workflow file across an organisation. GitHub offers a summarized report covering up to a year and a detailed report covering up to 31 days, and the detailed one adds two fields that matter here: username and workflow_path.

Read discount_amount before you read anything else. That field carries the usage that was discounted, including your included allowance and the discounts for standard runners in public repositories and for self-hosted runners. Reading gross_amount without it is how a team concludes that its open source project costs thousands of dollars a month.

The reports are delivered by email to the address on the account and you can only request one at a time, so start the request before you begin the API work rather than after. Group the result by sku first: that single grouping usually answers the question, because the expensive SKU is rarely the one people name when you ask them to guess.

Question Where the answer is What that source cannot tell you
Which workflow costs most? Workflow timing endpoint, per repository Anything about rounding, or about other repositories
Which job inside it? Run timing and jobs endpoints Money, until you multiply by the runner rate yourself
How much is re-runs? run_attempt on recent runs Why they were re-run
Who and what across the org? Detailed usage report, 31 days Anything older than 31 days
Is storage the problem? Usage report, grouped by SKU Which artifact or cache is responsible

Report types and field names from GitHub billing reports, read 21 September 2026.

Turn the measurement into a decision

Five findings, five different next moves. If installation dominates, cache the dependency directory and key it to the lockfile hash. If a wide matrix of short jobs dominates, the rounding is the cost and consolidation is the fix. If one long job dominates, shard it or size it up, and check the break-even first. If re-runs dominate, nothing about runner choice helps you. If macOS dominates, move everything that does not need Xcode, because that minute is more than ten times a Linux one.

Only after that is the rate worth touching. A cheaper runner multiplies whatever is left, so it is the last change rather than the first, and it is worth the most to the team that has already removed the work it was never going to need. How to reduce GitHub Actions costs prices seven changes against one worked month, and the cost calculator prices your own month at two rates.

If the numbers came back surprising rather than clarifying, why is my CI so expensive works through what each shape of invoice usually means.

FAQ

How do I see GitHub Actions minutes by workflow?

Call the workflow timing endpoint for each workflow id, which returns billable milliseconds broken down by operating system, and sort the result. The billing dashboard does not provide this breakdown. Treat the numbers as a ranking, because the invoice rounds every job up to a whole minute and this endpoint does not.

Why does the timing endpoint return nothing for my repository?

Almost certainly because the repository is public. Standard GitHub-hosted runners are free and unlimited on public repositories, so there are no billable milliseconds to report. Larger runners are billed even on public repositories, so a public repository using those will still return figures.

What is the biggest hidden GitHub Actions cost?

Re-runs. A retry buys the same work a second time, and the failure is often unrelated to the code that triggered it. Measure the share of runs with a run_attempt above 1 before optimising your per-minute rate; above a few percent it dominates any rate difference on the market.

What is the difference between the summarized and detailed usage reports?

The summarized report covers up to a year and sums usage by date, SKU, repository and cost centre. The detailed report covers a maximum of 31 days and adds username and workflow_path, which is what lets you attribute spend to a specific workflow file. Both arrive by email and you can only request one at a time.

References

  • GitHub REST API: Actions workflow runs, timing and jobs endpoints (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub billing reports: usage report types and every field (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub: Actions runner pricing, the rates to multiply minutes by (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub: Actions billing, rounding, allowances and public repositories (verified 2026-09-21)

title: MongoDB vs PostgreSQL: how I choose between them
description:
I use both in my projects, so people often ask me which one is better. My answer is that it depends on the shape of your data.

I reach for PostgreSQL when:

Data is highly relational (users, orders, payments, invoices)
I need strict consistency and transactions
I want complex queries with joins and aggregations
The schema is fairly stable and I want the database to enforce it

I reach for MongoDB when:

Data is flexible or changes shape often (content, logs, product catalogs)
I’m prototyping and want to move fast without migrations
Documents are naturally nested and read together
I’m working with Node.js and want JSON-like data end to end

Common mistakes I see:

Choosing MongoDB because it feels easier, then fighting relationships later
Choosing PostgreSQL for everything without thinking about whether the data really needs that structure
Picking based on hype instead of how the data will be queried

Neither one is “better.” The right choice comes from your data and your queries, not from trends. And sometimes using both in one project is perfectly fine.

Which one do you use most, and why?
