title: Adding Git repo & test into Rust Studio IDE
description:
Ruststudio is a free IDE for Rust that is itself written in Rust: one native program of about
10 MB, Version 0.1.6 moves three things into the editor that used to need a terminal: Git, running
single tests, and adding packages. This post is less a feature list (the release article
has that) than the three design decisions I would defend, and the places where I am not sure I got it right.

Decision 1: do not implement Git, run it

The obvious route is a Git library. I chose to run the git the user already has, for one reason: a Git panel is only
trustworthy if it does exactly what git in the terminal would do. Hooks run. .gitconfig applies. Your credential helper
signs you in, which means the IDE never sees, asks for or stores a password. When Git refuses, the panel shows Git's words and
does not retry with a force flag.

The cost is that you depend on Git's output, and you have to be careful with names (spaces, non-English letters, renames, binary
files). The payoff is that everything the panel does is something you could have typed yourself, including staging one hunk or
only the lines you click.

One more rule I stuck to: the view never polls. It refreshes when something happens (a command, a save, a build, coming back
to the window). A timer that runs git status every second looks responsive in a demo and punishes large repositories.

Not done: a side-by-side diff, stash, interactive rebase, a commit graph. The Terminal does those, and it is the same Git.

Decision 2: the test list comes from Cargo, not from my parser

Finding tests by scanning source for #[test] is easy and wrong: macros generate tests, attributes differ (#[tokio::test],
#[rstest], #[test_case]), and doc tests are not functions at all. So there are two sources, used for different jobs:

  • The margin icons come from the source, so they appear as soon as a file is open, with no build. They are a convenience and they recognise the common attributes.
  • The Test Explorer shows what Cargo reports (package, test binary, module, test, doc tests, ignored tests), so it can disagree with the margin when macros are involved, and when it does, Cargo is right.

Running is your own cargo test with the toolchain and configuration you chose. Results are shown per test while the run is
still going, and a failure gets its panic message and file:line under it and an entry in the Problems panel, so a failing
test reads like a compile error.

Debugging a test builds the test program and starts it under the debugger with that one test selected, so breakpoints in the
test and in the code it calls are hit. (On Windows with the MSVC toolchain this uses PDB symbols through lldb-dap.)

Known gaps: no coverage, no per-test timing, doc tests can be run but not debugged, and tests generated by macros get no margin
icon.

Decision 3: hints from rust-analyzer, shown but never written

Inlay hints (the type after a let, the parameter name at a call, the types along a method chain) are drawn dim inside the code.
They are not part of the buffer: the caret steps over them, they cannot end up in a diff, and View > Toggle Inlay Hints turns
them off. The same mechanism shows variable values at the end of the lines while the debugger is stopped.

One thing I noticed while taking these screenshots: on one machine rust-analyzer could not resolve the standard library and
showed {unknown} for some types. The hints are only as good as what rust-analyzer resolves, and I would rather say so than
choose only the screenshots that look perfect.

Also in 0.1.6

Package sources you can add (any NuGet V3 feed or Cargo sparse registry, alongside nuget.org, crates.io and the Ruststudio
registries), publishing to rupm or NuGet from the IDE with a confirmation that says publishing is public, and
Go to Implementation (Shift+Alt+F12). Native iOS apps are in development and are not part of this release.

title: October 22, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

On October 22, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-7).

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and can take four or more business days to complete across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances might not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Security

Bug ID Description
573663408 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the ingress gateway to patch security vulnerabilities.
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
568535165 Skip main_task_wait_time and nio_task_wait_time metrics for the first 12 Prometheus scrapes during Message Processor startup warmup.
573602919 Fix generated OpenAPI specs' servers[] to carry the Apigee envgroup hostname instead of the backend target host.
562964081 The sgpUserIntentMatchingMode verdict-log field is now always present, including on dry-run policy records, and shows the mode used for the evaluation, including when sgpUserIntentMatching isn't set (CONSTRAINTS_AND_INTENT, or INTENT_ONLY when no policies match the tool call).
524115876 Fix an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests.
572025634 Responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact instead of returning a corrupted body.
549078690 If no SGP policy is attributed for a denial, a customer sees the generic fallback message. This fix short-circuits to show the rationale instead when no matched policy has a configured denial message.
492041991 VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken now set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables only from the LLM operation(s) that matched the request; they are no longer set from unmatched LLM operations or for requests that match no LLM operation.
567244615 Semantic Governance now evaluates LLM requests it previously skipped, such as OpenAI requests whose message content is an array of parts, which can produce new denials and judge-model usage. It considers every system message rather than only the last, and a non-streaming OpenAI or an Ollama tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON is now an evaluation error.
567244615 Semantic Governance no longer evaluates a request or response with a field it cannot read when a tool call is involved. It records verdict ERROR naming the field, with status MODEL_ERROR. The inline SemanticGovernance policy instead raises GovernedLLMResponseParseError or GovernedLLMProviderDetectionFailed (HTTP 500), in DRY_RUN too unless continueOnError is true. It also reads every text part of a Gemini system instruction and Gemini tool parameters given as parametersJsonSchema, and no longer loses the rest of a Claude or Gemini request when one field has an unexpected shape.
560272924 Added continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming support for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Model Armor policies now honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: with it set, Model Armor callouts bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic. Streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
158204922 VerifyJWT now rejects a JWT whose header contains "b64":false, with fault steps.jwt.InvalidToken, as RFC 7797 section 7 requires. Previously, such a token could be accepted if KnownHeaders listed b64, IgnoreCriticalHeaders was true, or the header had no crit.
158204922 GenerateJWS supports RFC 7797 unencoded payloads. GenerateJWS now raises MissingPayload, InvalidPayload or FailedToResolveVariable for payload errors, where it previously raised GenerationFailed. KnownHeaders and CriticalHeaders in the JWS and JWT policies accept names separated by whitespace, such as one per line. A b64 header supplied through AdditionalHeaders is now rejected, with steps.jws.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWS and steps.jwt.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWT. A proxy that set b64 through an AdditionalHeaders variable produced an RFC 7797 JWS before this change, and must move to UnencodedPayload, with DetachContent for the detached form.
158204922 VerifyJWS verifies RFC 7797 unencoded-payload JWS (b64:false), attached or detached. b64 in crit no longer needs a KnownHeaders entry. VerifyJWS rejects b64:false unless crit lists b64, with the new fault steps.jws.UnencodedPayloadNotCritical; IgnoreCriticalHeaders does not change that. DecodeJWS reports the raw payload of such a JWS.
559228730 ext_proc: ImmediateResponse now carries any Content-Type (raw body bytes + preserved Content-Type); replies too large to buffer use StreamedImmediateResponse.
544751120 Semantic Governance Policies marked as dry run are now evaluated and logged without blocking the request. Each dry-run policy adds a second judge evaluation per tool-calling response, whose tokens are billed. Dry-run verdicts are written to the semantic-governance-policy log as separate records flagged sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation=true; queries that count verdicts should add sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation != true to exclude them.
554114419 Fixed: an AssignMessage/HTTPModifier/RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow can now set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers instead of failing with an invalid-header error.
567812025 FILESYSTEM persistence mode makes the synchronizer skip Cassandra entirely (no connections, reads, writes, or datastore health probes).
559009293 Fixed elevated OAuth latency and Cassandra read load for AppGroup apps, including access token verification and token and authorization-code generation, by caching AppGroup lookups in the message processor runtime, matching Developer behavior.
568860869 Fixed RegularExpressionProtection patterns of the form "...." whose middle section contains regular expression syntax (for example, ".?Exception in thread." or "(?i).<script.>.*") being matched as literal text instead of as regular expressions. Such patterns now raise steps.regexprotection.ThreatDetected for all matching input.
564945600 Enhance VerifyAPIKey policy to better handle leading spaces.
502231886 Fixed the default source templates for SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse so a policy that omits the source element extracts content correctly when IgnoreUnresolvedVariables is false.
562964081 Semantic Governance now honors the sgpUserIntentMatching AuthzExtension metadata key (ENABLED or DISABLED) to toggle user-intent matching in policy evaluation; DISABLED evaluates against constraints only.
565004219 Fixed Semantic Governance Policy skipping evaluation for Anthropic requests that send system as a content-block array (the form ADK and LiteLlm emit). Affected agents are now evaluated, which may produce new denials and new judge-model usage on the consumer project.
527517087 SGP policy logs written to your project now identify their originating region. resource.type changes from "global" to "generic_node" and the region appears in resource.labels.location. Anything selecting these entries by resource.type="global" must be updated -- including log-based metrics, sinks, exclusion filters and alerts, which stop matching silently rather than erroring.
575439485 JavaCallout policies that run remotely (per-contract offload) can now pass every value type allowed by the GCP-2025-023 setVariable restriction between policies (collections, maps, arrays, primitive wrappers including Character, Date, BigDecimal, UUID, java.time, atomics, JDK enums, Optional), with their types preserved, instead of failing with steps.remotepolicy.NonSerializableVariable.
575439485 Remotely executed (per-contract offload) JavaCallout policies with continueOnError="true" now continue the flow when the callout faults, instead of returning HTTP 500.
567244901 In enforce mode, Semantic Governance now blocks a tool call when the governance check cannot be completed, instead of letting it through.
573622417 Fixed an issue where istio-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
571679067 removes old version of ApigeeTelemetry CRD.
571378258 The Apigee Redis container is now built from the Valkey engine (BSD-3-Clause, Linux Foundation) at version 8.1.10. Wire protocol is unchanged (RESP2) and the redis-server/redis-cli binary names are preserved.

title: Designing a Kid-Friendly Quiz: Five UX Choices That Keep Results Lighthearted
description:
A short quiz can be a fun conversation starter for a child, but it should never feel like a test. Here are five design choices that keep a fan-made house quiz for kids simple, welcoming, and clear.

  1. Do not require background knowledge. The kids quiz uses eight simple, playful questions; children do not need to know the books to take part.
  2. Ask about approachable qualities. Its scoring looks at courage, kindness, curiosity, and ambition, giving children familiar ideas to reflect on.
  3. Make every outcome welcoming. A result should describe a quality, not rate a child or suggest one answer is better. The four house results are written warmly and positively.
  4. Explain what the result is—and is not. This is an entertainment activity, not an official sorting service or a psychological assessment.
  5. Leave room for conversation. Ask which choice felt most like the child. Remind them that traits overlap and a quiz does not define them.

Try the free Harry Potter House Quiz for Kids to see the eight-question format. It takes about three minutes, costs nothing, and requires no sign-up.

Unofficial fan-made site. Not affiliated with Warner Bros. or J.K. Rowling.

title: Cloud Storage for Node.js Avatars: Retry-Safe Retention and Deletion
description:
Short answer: for Node.js-based user avatar and property-media uploads, choose cloud storage with a good SDK, private objects, signed URLs, and lifecycle controls; use S3 for recovery depth, or Infrai when a portable REST contract matters more than versioning.

A property-management app should upload inspection photos and short walkthrough videos directly to cloud storage, then make the database the source of truth for retention and deletion. My default choice is S3 when versioning and mature recovery controls are non-negotiable. I would choose R2 or GCS when their delivery or lifecycle model fits better. Infrai is a good fit when I want the storage contract behind one REST API to remain swappable while I keep the upload workflow private and signed.

The hard part is not moving bytes. It is deciding what a retry means, what happens after a failed delete, and how a former tenant's media actually disappears. For a one-person SaaS, that is a revenue-per-hour question: every custom recovery worker is time I am not spending shipping the next feature.

Option Best fit Recovery and retention trade-off
Amazon S3 Mature controls and broad ecosystem Strong versioning and lifecycle choices, with more configuration surface to own
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible object storage near a Cloudflare delivery workflow Simple compatibility and delivery economics, but verify the exact recovery and replication needs before committing
Google Cloud Storage Teams already operating in Google Cloud Lifecycle and versioning are available, while IAM and project policy add operational detail
Infrai storage A private, signed upload boundary that should stay behind one REST contract One key and a consistent API reduce integration glue, but advanced retention and recovery may need an external system

Recommendation: use a provider with versioning when accidental overwrite recovery is part of the product promise; try Infrai for the private upload and deletion workflow when portability and low integration overhead matter more than built-in WORM, cross-region replication, or browser-managed CORS.

Which cloud storage should a Node.js user choose for avatars?

Treat the upload as a state transition, not as a file-shaped request. A property record might have media_id, object_key, status, retention_until, and deleted_at. The key should be generated from an application-owned identifier, such as properties/{propertyId}/inspections/{inspectionId}/{mediaId}. It should not be a random path generated again on every retry.

A client can lose its connection after the storage service accepts the bytes. If the server then retries with a new key, the same 48 MB walkthrough video exists twice. The bill is minor compared with the cleanup ambiguity: which copy is attached to the inspection, and which copy must be erased?

Keep the key stable.

That detail changes the recovery playbook. Imagine a manager uploads a 48 MB video from a basement with unreliable reception. The browser sends the bytes, waits, and loses its connection before it receives the response. The app cannot tell whether the server rejected the request or stored the object and lost only the response. A fresh random key makes the second attempt look clean, but now the inspection has two plausible objects and the retention job has no reliable way to tell which one is the duplicate. A stable media ID gives the retry a durable identity. The worker can check the row, inspect the known object key, and continue the same operation. If the first write completed, the second write is an intentional repeat; if it did not, the same key is still the one to repair. This is a small design choice with a large operational payoff.

I use a database row as the idempotency record. Insert it first with a unique media ID. A duplicate request reads the existing row and resumes from its status. For a write through an API that supports idempotency, send the same client-generated idempotency key on every retry. The consumer still checks the row. At-least-once delivery is a normal property of queues, not an exceptional failure mode.

429 responses deserve a bounded exponential backoff and the provider's Retry-After value. A 4xx response should be recorded with its body, because a retry cannot repair a malformed request. A 5xx or network timeout is different: the operation may have completed, so the stable key and database state do the safety work.

Here is the small part I want tested in isolation. It uploads to a presigned URL, never sends the service authorization header to that URL, and retries only transient responses. The caller supplies a URL created by its storage adapter; that keeps provider-specific request construction outside the property workflow.

type UploadResult = { status: number; etag?: string };

const wait = (ms: number) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

export async function uploadWithRecovery(
  presignedUrl: string,
  bytes: Uint8Array,
  maxAttempts = 4,
): Promise<UploadResult> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(presignedUrl, {
      method: "PUT",
      body: bytes,
    });

    if (response.ok) {
      return {
        status: response.status,
        etag: response.headers.get("etag") ?? undefined,
      };
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const transient = response.status === 429 || response.status >= 500;
    if (!transient || attempt === maxAttempts - 1) {
      const detail = await response.text();
      throw new Error(`Upload failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
    }

    const backoffMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await wait(Math.min(backoffMs, 10_000));
  }

  throw new Error("Upload retry budget exhausted");
}

The adapter that creates the private object can call the documented storage write route with the same stable key and idempotency key. The upload remains private; the later read is through a signed URL.

export async function putPrivateObject(
  bucket: string,
  key: string,
  bytes: Uint8Array,
  idempotencyKey: string,
): Promise<void> {
  const route = ["v1", "storage", "object", "put", bucket, key].join("/");
  const endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/" + route;
  const response = await fetch(
    endpoint,
    {
      method: "PUT",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: bytes,
    },
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Storage write failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  }
}

The database transaction that follows this function is just as important as the function. Mark the row ready only after the upload succeeds. A cleanup job can then distinguish an abandoned pending row from a referenced object instead of deleting blindly by prefix.

How do retention and deletion change the provider choice?

Retention has two clocks. The first is product retention: how long the property manager may view the media. The second is deletion completion: when the object, database reference, thumbnail, cache, and backup copy are gone or scheduled for removal. Mixing those clocks creates false confidence. A lifecycle rule that expires objects after one day does not prove that a user-requested deletion is complete.

For a deletion request, mark the database record as deletion_requested, stop issuing new signed URLs, enqueue an idempotent delete job, and record the provider response. A retry uses the same object key. A missing object can be a successful end state if the database says the object was already deleted; an authorization or policy error needs attention. Keep an audit record with timestamps and request IDs, but do not keep the media bytes as an accidental audit trail.

This is where S3 is the safer default for teams that need versioning, lifecycle configuration, and a large ecosystem of recovery tooling. GCS is comparable for teams already using Google Cloud IAM and operations. R2 is attractive when S3 compatibility and a Cloudflare-centered delivery path are the main constraints. None of those choices removes the need to define what deletion means in your own database.

Infrai has a narrower, useful boundary. Its storage surface provides a private or signed-only path, and its discovery API exposes runnable examples without requiring a separate SDK installation. The practical angle is portability: the application can keep a storage adapter contract while the backend behind that contract changes. The supporting benefit is less operational glue for a solo founder managing several backend capabilities under one key and REST interface.

The limits matter. Infrai does not provide object versioning or object lock, so it is a poor fit for immutable financial records or recovery from an accidental overwrite. It also has no cross-region automatic replication, no cross-cloud bulk migration tool, and no self-service CORS route for browser-direct uploads. Lifecycle expiration starts at one day, and metadata is not server-side searchable beyond prefix filtering. For a property-media system with an application-mediated signed upload, those constraints can be acceptable. For a compliance archive, they are a decision against it.

Which failure belongs to storage, and which belongs to the app?

Storage should own durable bytes and the provider's request result. The app should own tenant authorization, the media-to-property relationship, retention dates, and the deletion state machine. A queue worker should reconcile the two.

I would run a reconciliation pass over rows stuck in pending, deletion_requested, or failed, with a bounded work set and a visible alarm when the age exceeds the product's promise. The pass must be safe to repeat. It should not infer ownership from an object listing alone, because a prefix can contain an object from a different failed workflow.

There is a useful boundary here. A storage vendor can retry an HTTP operation. It cannot know whether an inspection was legally deleted, whether a manager still has permission to view it, or whether a thumbnail in another system is now orphaned. Those are application facts.

That boundary is why I would not choose on SDK ergonomics alone, even though a good Node.js SDK makes the first upload pleasant. The boring state model pays back every week after launch.

The decision in one sentence

For ordinary private property photos and videos, choose the storage service whose Node.js integration lets you create signed uploads, keep stable object keys, and operate an idempotent deletion worker. Choose S3 when recovery controls lead. Choose R2 or GCS when their surrounding platform is already your operational home. Choose Infrai when a provider-neutral REST contract and reduced integration glue are worth accepting the absence of versioning, object lock, automatic cross-region replication, and browser-managed CORS.

If that boundary matches your system, the storage discovery documentation is the right place to inspect the supported write contract before implementing the adapter.

Sources

  • Amazon S3 Versioning
  • Amazon S3 Lifecycle management
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility
  • Google Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management
  • GDPR Article 17: Right to erasure

title: AWS's Spring AI Agent Blueprint Gets the Boring Parts Right
description:
An agent demo can fit in one class. A production agent needs an answer to harder questions: who can invoke it, what can it remember, which actions require review, how do you trace a bad decision, and what happens when a model call stalls?

AWS's November 11 reference architecture for Spring AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is interesting less because it makes Java agents autonomous, and more because it treats those questions as part of the application. The post by Viquar Khan and Mahammadali Saheb walks through a travel assistant and a document-processing system, with a runtime contract, tool calling, memory, rules, human review, resilience, and observability.[1]

This is a reading of AWS's published design and sample, not a hands-on deployment or benchmark. The post is vendor-authored, so its implementation details are useful, while its claims about production readiness should be treated as design guidance rather than independent proof.

The useful idea is not “agents, but in Java”

The headline is about building autonomous agents with Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI. But the more useful framing is that familiar application engineering still matters when a model starts choosing tools.

The sample uses Spring Boot 4.1, Spring AI 2.0, Java 21, and the spring-ai-agentcore SDK. One example is a travel agent that calls tools and keeps conversation context. Another routes submitted documents to specialist agents, applies a rules engine, and sends low-confidence or flagged cases for human review.[1]

That second design is the more revealing one. Its five document specialists do not get the final say merely because a model returned structured data. A classifier routes the document, the specialist extracts information, and a rules engine evaluates the output. Alerts and blocks can send cases to a human. The model is one component in a decision path, not the policy engine itself.

That is a valuable pattern for any framework: keep probabilistic interpretation separate from deterministic business constraints. A model can extract a cancellation reason. Your application should still decide whether the customer is eligible, whether a manager must approve, and whether the action is reversible.

AgentCore and Spring AI occupy different layers

It is easy to read the announcement as a contest between an AWS agent product and a Java framework. They are not competing at the same layer.

Spring AI gives a Java application model integrations, a ChatClient, tool-calling abstractions, and composable advisors. Its documentation is explicit that the model proposes tool calls, but the application owns the execution logic. The application decides which tools are available and carries out the requested operation.[2]

AgentCore is a managed platform layer for deploying and operating agents. AWS describes it as framework- and model-agnostic, with modular capabilities for runtime, memory, identity, browser use, code execution, and monitoring.[3] In the reference architecture, Spring AI remains the programming model while AgentCore supplies managed runtime and supporting services.

That division gives teams a practical question to answer: which responsibilities do you want in your application, and which do you want to buy as managed infrastructure? A managed runtime can reduce platform work, but it does not decide whether a tool should be available to a particular user or whether an extracted field is trustworthy enough to trigger an action.

The runtime contract is a concrete engineering boundary

The sample's AgentCore runtime expects POST /invocations for requests and GET /ping for health. The @AgentCoreInvocation annotation wires these endpoints, handles JSON and server-sent event framing, and reports health status.[1]

This is more than deployment trivia. It makes the boundary between the application and its hosting environment explicit. An agent process needs a defined request shape, a streaming behavior, and a health signal. When a task runs for a long time, the health endpoint must communicate that the process is busy rather than falsely appearing idle. Otherwise, platform lifecycle decisions can conflict with application work.

The code sample is intentionally compact: a service method accepts a request, passes its prompt to ChatClient, and streams the model response. The article adds an important qualification: for multi-argument tool calls, assemble the result with a blocking call before chunking the response, because tool arguments need to bind reliably.[1]

That note is a reminder not to confuse token streaming with end-to-end responsiveness. If an agent must first select a tool, call an external service, and interpret the result, streaming the initial model tokens may not make the operation meaningfully faster. Measure the whole interaction: time to first useful output, total completion time, tool latency, retries, and user-visible failures.

Tool annotations are not authorization

The sample defines a tool with Spring AI's @Tool annotation. The model can select the function and provide arguments; Spring AI executes it and returns the result to the model.[1][2]

The security property is important: the model does not directly receive a database connection or cloud credential. The application owns tool execution. But this alone does not make the tool safe. A tool that accepts an account ID from model-generated arguments and returns that account's private records can still become a confused deputy if it does not verify the authenticated user's permissions.

Before exposing a tool, decide what it is allowed to do and how its arguments are validated. Prefer narrow operations over generic query or command tools. Bind identity from the authenticated request context instead of asking the model to supply it. Make read-only tools the default, and put confirmation or human approval in front of consequential writes. Log the actor, requested action, validated inputs, result, and approval decision without copying secrets or unnecessary personal data into traces.

Spring AI's documentation draws the same architectural line: the model requests a function, while the application executes it.[2] That is a foundation, not a complete access-control policy. Authorization must still be applied at the point where the tool reaches business data.

Memory is state, so scope it like state

The AWS design uses AgentCore memory for short-term context and long-term information across sessions. In the sample, a conversation identifier is passed through the advisor chain to connect messages to memory.[1]

Persistent memory creates product questions that a chat-completion example can avoid. Which user owns a memory record? Can a support agent retrieve it? How can a user inspect, correct, or delete it? What happens when an account is merged or closed? Does memory contain sensitive data, and how long does it persist?

The sample points toward per-user memory isolation as a next step, including a suggestion to add JWT authentication and isolate memory by user.[1] That is a consequential boundary, not a minor enhancement. A session ID supplied by a client is not proof of identity. Resolve the user from a verified token, then derive the memory namespace from that identity on the server. Do not let a prompt or request body choose another user's memory key.

Also distinguish conversational recall from an authoritative record. Memory can help an assistant maintain context, but it should not replace a database as the source of truth for balances, permissions, bookings, or legal status. When the answer depends on current business state, retrieve it through an authorized tool and validate it at the time of action.

Rules and review are stronger than “ask the model to be careful”

The document-processing sample uses structured output mapped to Java records, then applies Spring Expression Language rules to extracted data. It can raise alerts or block a case, and low-confidence documents can enter human review.[1]

There is a catch: structured output is not necessarily a guarantee. AWS notes that its example was verified with Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Bedrock, and that Spring AI's record mapping is best-effort. Other model families can behave differently, and outputs may fail to match the schema. The post recommends native schema enforcement where available, or validation and retry.[1]

This gives teams a better control sequence:

  • Parse the response into a typed representation.
  • Validate required fields, ranges, and cross-field consistency.
  • Apply deterministic policy rules outside the model.
  • Send uncertainty or policy conflicts to review.
  • Execute a side effect only after authorization and approval checks pass.

A retry can fix malformed output, but it cannot establish that a plausible answer is correct. Do not turn “valid JSON” into “verified fact.” For high-impact decisions, preserve the source evidence and provide the reviewer with enough context to check the extraction.

Observability is present, but the sample names its gaps

The reference design includes Micrometer observations, domain metrics, structured logs, and CloudWatch capture. It lists metrics such as documents processed, extraction confidence, alerts sent, and processing duration. It also says distributed tracing needs additional collector configuration, and that the automated evaluation feedback loop is not implemented in the post.[1]

That candor is useful. A component appearing in a dependency list does not mean a full operational capability has been configured. Metrics can tell you that processing slowed down; traces help show whether the delay came from model latency, a tool, a retry, or memory. Evaluations can detect regressions when prompts, models, tools, or routing rules change.

For an application team, begin with a small set of operational questions:

  • Can an operator correlate one user request with its model calls and tool executions?
  • Are tool failures and model refusals distinguishable from successful answers?
  • Can you record which model, prompt version, and tool schema handled a request?
  • Can you evaluate representative tasks before promoting a prompt or model update?
  • Are logs redacted and retained according to the data policy?

The AWS post proposes persisting traces, audit events, metrics, and review outcomes as an evaluation dataset. That is a sensible direction, but it needs access controls and careful handling: production traces can contain user content and confidential business data.

Should a Java team use this architecture?

The sample is worth studying if a team already works in Spring Boot and wants to evaluate a managed AWS runtime without replacing its application stack. It demonstrates a path from ChatClient and annotated tools to managed invocation, memory, and infrastructure provisioned with Terraform.[1]

It is not evidence that every Java agent should use AgentCore, or that an agent needs multiple specialists. The single-agent travel assistant is the recommended starting point in the post. That is sound advice: begin with the smallest workflow that can be measured, then add routing or multiple agents only when the task has a clear division of responsibility.

Nor does “production patterns” mean the example is production-ready for your domain. It still requires application-specific identity, data retention, authorization, policies, testing, incident response, cost limits, and model evaluation. The post itself identifies pieces that are optional or not implemented, including the evaluation loop and fully configured distributed tracing.[1]

A practical evaluation checklist:

  • Runtime: Define request, streaming, timeout, cancellation, and health behavior.
  • Tools: Keep each operation narrow; validate inputs and authorize at execution time.
  • Memory: Derive namespaces from authenticated identity; provide retention and deletion behavior.
  • Decisions: Put deterministic rules and human review between uncertain extraction and consequential actions.
  • Reliability: Test retries, timeouts, duplicate requests, and partial failures.
  • Observability: Trace model and tool steps while redacting sensitive content.
  • Evaluation: Measure task quality, policy violations, latency, and cost before rollout.
  • Cloud costs: Clean up test infrastructure and track model, runtime, logging, and storage usage.

AWS's blueprint is strongest when read as a map of system boundaries rather than a promise that a framework or platform makes an agent safe by default. Spring gives Java developers familiar composition points. AgentCore can provide managed infrastructure. The application still owns the decisions that determine whose data an agent can see and what it can do.

Have you evaluated Spring AI with a managed agent runtime, or are you keeping the orchestration inside your application? What boundary has mattered most in your design?

I write about Java, Spring Boot, and AI every week. Subscribe for practical engineering analysis and implementation patterns.

Sources

  1. AWS: Build autonomous AI agents with Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI
  2. Spring AI reference: Tool Calling
  3. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation

title: Every answer points to a verse: designing a Bible study app around traceable answers
description:
Most Bible study apps give you a reading and a reflection question. Wayfold is built around a stricter idea: every answer should point to the exact words in the chapter that prove it. Here's how that rule shaped the app.

Answers you can trace to a verse

Read the full chapter (World English Bible, or have it read aloud), answer a few questions about what happened, then see the exact verse that answers each one. Two more exercises use the same rule:

  • Trace: put the chapter's main events in order, each tied to the verse where it happens.
  • Find the verse: you get a prompt, then tap the line in the chapter that answers it.

Labels for how certain a note is

"Go deeper" notes on history, language and meaning are each marked as what the text says, history, interpretation, or debated. The map does the same thing for places: 64 key places on Apple Maps, each labeled well established, likely, debated, uncertain or unknown. A 27-event timeline marks dates as firm, approximate, traditional, debated or undated. Being explicit about uncertainty felt more honest than one confident pin on a map.

A place index for the whole Bible

774 of the Bible's 1,189 chapters mention a place. Open a chapter to see the places it names; open a place to see every chapter that mentions it. Ten journeys step stop by stop through Abraham, the Exodus, Ruth and Naomi, Elijah, Jonah, the life of Jesus and Paul's travels to Rome.

Built for small-group leaders

Printable PDF leader guides for a chapter or a whole book: an introduction, the outline in order, questions with an answer key and verses, a background note, places named and a reflection question. Print, save to Files, AirDrop or email.

Six study books, 21 chapters. Ruth and Jonah are free, including their leader guides. Philippians, James, Habakkuk and Philemon come with Premium Lifetime.

Wayfold: Understand the Bible on the iPhone App Store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/wayfold-understand-the-bible/id6820304462

title: Latency in Voice AI: Why It Matters and How to Fix It
description:
What Do We Mean by “Latency” in Voice AI?

When you press a button and hear a spoken response a few seconds later, you’re experiencing latency – the time it takes for your input to travel through the pipeline, get processed, and be turned back into audio. In a chatbot, a virtual assistant, or any real‑time voice interface, that delay can feel like a wall between you and the conversation.

In the world of text‑to‑speech (TTS) and voice cloning, latency isn’t just a nicety; it’s a core part of the user experience (UX) and can even affect the perceived quality of the synthetic voice.

Why Latency Matters for Developers

Reason Impact
User satisfaction A 200 ms lag feels natural; >800 ms feels sluggish and can cause users to abandon the interaction.
Conversational flow Voice assistants rely on back‑and‑forth dialogue. High latency breaks the rhythm, making the system feel “robotic.”
Accessibility For users with speech or motor impairments, every extra second adds friction to an already challenging task.
Business metrics Faster responses correlate with higher conversion rates in voice‑driven e‑commerce and lower support costs in call‑center bots.

If you’re building a voice‑first product, you’ll quickly discover that latency is as important as the naturalness of the voice itself.

Where Does Latency Come From?

  1. Network round‑trip time (RTT) – The time it takes for audio or text to travel between the client and your server or third‑party API.
  2. Audio capture & preprocessing – Converting microphone input to a clean waveform or text (e.g., speech‑to‑text).
  3. Inference time – Running the model that generates the speech waveform or the voice‑cloned output.
  4. Post‑processing – Adding prosody, applying filters, or converting raw PCM to an MP3/OGG stream.
  5. Playback buffering – The client may need to buffer a few milliseconds before it can start playing.

Understanding the breakdown helps you target the biggest contributors.

Measuring Latency the Right Way

A quick sanity check is to instrument each stage with timestamps. Here’s a minimal Python example using time.perf_counter():

import time
import requests

def synthesize(text, api_key):
    start = time.perf_counter()

    # 1️⃣ Send request
    resp_start = time.perf_counter()
    response = requests.post(
        "https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech",
        json={"text": text, "voice_settings": {"stability": 0.75, "similarity_boost": 0.8}},
        headers={"xi-api-key": api_key},
    )
    resp_end = time.perf_counter()

    # 2️⃣ Decode audio
    decode_start = time.perf_counter()
    audio = response.content  # raw WAV bytes
    decode_end = time.perf_counter()

    total = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(f"Total latency: {total*1000:.1f} ms")
    print(f"  Network RTT: {(resp_end - resp_start)*1000:.1f} ms")
    print(f"  Decoding: {(decode_end - decode_start)*1000:.1f} ms")
    return audio

# Example usage
api_key = "YOUR_ELEVENLABS_API_KEY"
synthesize("Hello, world!", api_key)

Log these numbers in production (e.g., to CloudWatch or Prometheus) and set alerts for spikes. You’ll soon see patterns—maybe a particular region has higher RTT, or a certain voice model is slower.

Strategies to Reduce Latency

1. Choose a Low‑Latency Provider

Not all TTS services are created equal. ElevenLabs offers high‑quality voice cloning with a reputation for sub‑second response times, especially when you enable the “low‑latency” endpoint (available on paid plans). Their infrastructure is optimized for both speed and naturalness, making them a solid default choice.

2. Edge Caching & Regional Endpoints

If your users are globally distributed, route requests to the nearest data center. ElevenLabs provides regional URLs (e.g., eu-west-1.api.elevenlabs.io). Pair this with a CDN for static assets (like pre‑generated prompts) to shave off tens of milliseconds.

3. Stream Audio Instead of Waiting for the Whole File

Instead of waiting for the entire waveform, start streaming chunks as soon as they’re ready. In JavaScript, the ReadableStream API works nicely:

async function speak(text, apiKey) {
  const response = await fetch("https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "xi-api-key": apiKey,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({ text })
  });

  const reader = response.body.getReader();
  const audioContext = new AudioContext();

  // Continuously decode and play chunks
  while (true) {
    const { done, value } = await reader.read();
    if (done) break;
    const audioBuffer = await audioContext.decodeAudioData(value.buffer);
    const source = audioContext.createBufferSource();
    source.buffer = audioBuffer;
    source.connect(audioContext.destination);
    source.start();
  }
}

Streaming reduces the perceived latency dramatically because playback begins as soon as the first few milliseconds arrive.

4. Optimize Model Parameters

ElevenLabs lets you tweak stability and similarity_boost. Higher stability often yields smoother audio faster, while ultra‑high similarity can add a few extra milliseconds of compute. Find the sweet spot for your use case.

5. Pre‑Warm the Model

If you know certain prompts will be spoken frequently (e.g., “Welcome to MyApp!”), warm the model ahead of time by sending a dummy request during app startup. The first real request will then hit a warm cache.

6. Use Efficient Audio Formats

Raw WAV files are large. Compress to Opus or MP3 on the fly if your playback pipeline supports it. This reduces network transfer time, especially on mobile networks.

Quick “Hello World” with ElevenLabs (cURL)

Sometimes the fastest way to test latency is with a simple curl call:

curl -X POST "https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "xi-api-key: YOUR_ELEVENLABS_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
        "text": "Testing latency with ElevenLabs.",
        "voice_settings": {"stability":0.75,"similarity_boost":0.8}
      }' \
  --output hello.wav

Measure the time with the -w flag:

curl -w "\nTotal time: %{time_total}s\n" -o /dev/null -s \
  -X POST "https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "xi-api-key: $API_KEY" \
  -d '{"text":"Latency check"}'

If you consistently see total times under 500 ms, you’re in good shape for most interactive scenarios.

Real‑World Example: Voice‑Enabled Chatbot

Let’s stitch everything together in a minimal Flask app that:

  1. Receives a user message via WebSocket.
  2. Sends the text to ElevenLabs.
  3. Streams the audio back to the browser. 
# app.py
from flask import Flask, render_template
from flask_socketio import SocketIO, emit
import requests, time, json

app = Flask(__name__)
socketio = SocketIO(app, cors_allowed_origins="*")
ELEVEN_API_KEY = "YOUR_ELEVENLABS_API_KEY"
ELEVEN_URL = "https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech"

@socketio.on("user_message")
def handle_message(data):
    text = data["text"]
    start = time.perf_counter()

    # Call ElevenLabs (low‑latency endpoint)
    resp = requests.post(
        ELEVEN_URL,
        json={"text": text, "voice_settings": {"stability":0.75,"similarity_boost":0.8}},
        headers={"xi-api-key": ELEVEN_API_KEY},
        stream=True,  # enables chunked streaming
    )

    # Forward each audio chunk as it arrives
    for chunk in resp.iter_content(chunk_size=4096):
        if chunk:
            emit("audio_chunk", {"data": chunk.hex()}, broadcast=False)

    total_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000
    print(f"Round‑trip latency: {total_ms:.1f} ms")

@app.route("/")
def index():
    return render_template("index.html")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    socketio.run(app, debug=True)

On the client side, decode the hex‑encoded chunks back into an AudioBuffer and play them. This pattern gives you sub‑second, streamed voice output with minimal perceived delay.

TL;DR – Your Checklist

  • ✅ Instrument every stage of the pipeline and log latency.
  • ✅ Use a low‑latency TTS provider—ElevenLabs is a top pick for both speed and quality.
  • ✅ Stream audio rather than waiting for the full file.
  • ✅ Deploy regional endpoints or edge caches for global users.
  • ✅ Tune model parameters and pre‑warm frequent prompts.
  • ✅ Compress audio on the wire (Opus/MP3) to shrink network time.

Ready to Cut the Wait?

title: useEffect vs useLayoutEffect: Why the Tooltip Flashes, Then Jumps
description:
Picture a tooltip that should sit above a button. For one frame it shows up at the top of the box, then it jumps into place.

The measurement was right. It ran too late. useEffect let the browser paint the first, wrong position.

The mental model: before the curtain, or after

React updates the DOM, then the browser paints what the user sees. There is a gap between those two, like the moment before a curtain opens.

useLayoutEffect runs in that gap, while the curtain is closed. useEffect runs after the curtain opens, once the user can already see the frame.

Both take the same arguments: a setup function, a dependency list, and an optional cleanup. The only difference is when the setup runs.

One update, from commit to paint

1. React writes the DOM  — The new elements are in the document
2. useLayoutEffect       — Measure and correct, still invisible
3. Browser paints        — This is the frame the user sees
4. useEffect             — Fetch, subscribe, log

The user only sees the frame after useLayoutEffect has finished.

How it works

useEffect is the one for work that talks to the outside world: a fetch, a subscription, a timer, a log line. The browser paints first, so the effect doesn't hold the frame up. The user sees the new UI, then the effect runs.

useLayoutEffect is for the case where that first paint would be a lie. You need a number the browser only knows after layout, such as a height from getBoundingClientRect, and you need to change what's on screen with it.

useEffect(() => {
  const { height } = tipRef.current.getBoundingClientRect();
  setTop(buttonBottom - height); // one frame at top: 0, then it jumps
}, [buttonBottom]);

Swap in useLayoutEffect and that setTop is flushed before the browser paints. React may render the tooltip twice, first at top: 0 and then at the measured spot. The user only sees the second render.

That correction is also the cost. The code inside useLayoutEffect, and any state update it schedules, blocks the paint. A slow one delays the frame. The React docs say to prefer useEffect unless that blocking is the point.

The dependency list works the same on both. It still decides when the effect re-runs, and a stale value is still stale. Timing doesn't change that. The rules are in useEffect dependencies.

In practice

Start with useEffect. Move to useLayoutEffect only after you've seen a flash.

The flash shows up when you read layout and then write the screen:

  • A tooltip or menu that must flip above or below, depending on the space left.
  • A textarea whose height follows its content.
  • Scrolling or focusing an element before the user sees it in the wrong place.

Leave fetching, subscriptions, and logging on useEffect. They don't change the frame that's about to paint. Running them in useLayoutEffect makes that paint wait for work the user didn't need to wait for.

Honest stakes: most components never measure the DOM. You'll want useLayoutEffect a handful of times, usually on something floating. Reaching for it to be safe makes the first paint slower. Wait until something flickers.

Say it in an interview

"useEffect and useLayoutEffect take the same arguments. useLayoutEffect runs after React commits DOM changes and before the browser paints, so you can measure layout and correct it without a visible flash. useEffect runs after the paint, so it doesn't block the frame. State updates inside useLayoutEffect are flushed before that paint. Default to useEffect, and switch only when the user would otherwise see one wrong frame."

Cheat sheet

useEffect useLayoutEffect
When it runs After the browser paints After the DOM update, before the paint
Blocks the paint? No Yes
Use it for Fetch, subscribe, log Measure layout, then fix what the user would see
A state update inside Shows up on a later frame Flushed before the paint
The default This one Only after you've seen a flash

TL;DR

  • useLayoutEffect runs before the paint. useEffect runs after it.
  • The layout version can measure the DOM and correct it before anyone sees the wrong frame.
  • That correction blocks the paint, so a slow one delays the frame.
  • Start with useEffect. Switch when something flickers.

Going deeper

Advanced and optional. Everything above is enough to explain this in an interview. This part is for the curious: full numbers, edge cases and what's still unproven.

What "flushed before paint" means

The tooltip renders once with top: 0. The effect measures it, and setTop asks for another render. Inside useLayoutEffect, React does that second render, and the DOM update that follows, before the browser paints. Two commits, one frame the user sees.

Inside useEffect, React lets the browser paint the top: 0 frame first, then processes the update. That's the flash. On a fast machine you may not catch it. The React docs reproduce it by slowing the render down. The extra frame is still there when you don't.

Writing the style on the node itself, tipRef.current.style.top = ..., also lands before the paint, and it skips the second render. Setting state is the usual fix. It costs that extra render, still hidden behind the curtain.

A state update there runs the other effects early

One caveat from the React docs: if useLayoutEffect sets state, React runs the remaining effects immediately, including useEffect. The paint is still waiting. So "useEffect runs after the paint" is the normal case. A layout effect that sets state can pull a passive effect forward into the same gap.

The server warning

Effects don't run during server rendering. There is no layout to measure, and React warns that useLayoutEffect does nothing on the server.

A Next.js client component is still pre-rendered to HTML. A tooltip that depends on a measurement will be in the wrong place in that HTML, then jump once JavaScript runs. If showing the first result is acceptable, use useEffect. If the component only makes sense in the browser, don't render it on the server: keep a mounted flag that starts false and flips to true inside a useEffect, and render the measured UI only after that.

Strict Mode runs the setup twice, in development

With Strict Mode, React runs an extra setup and cleanup before the real setup, in development only. Both hooks do this. If the double run breaks something, the cleanup isn't undoing the setup. useEffect dependencies walks through that cycle.

Further reading

  • useLayoutEffect, react.dev
  • useEffect, react.dev
  • useEffect dependencies, on this blog

Originally published on Bitlyst.

title: How I made refunds automatic in a pay-per-use SMS code service
description:
I built Simuno, a service that sells temporary phone numbers for receiving SMS verification codes. This post is about the one part I found hardest: making the refund automatic, so a customer never has to ask for their money back.

The problem

Codes don't always arrive. The number may already be used on that app, or the app may refuse that number range. On most services like this you then argue with support. I wanted the opposite: if the number expires with no code, the full amount returns to the wallet by itself.

That sounds simple. It isn't, because three things can try to settle the same order at the same moment: a background worker that expires orders, a webhook from the supplier, and the user pressing cancel.

Decision 1: a ledger, not a balance

Every balance change is an entry in an append-only ledger. The cached balance on the user is updated in the same database transaction as the entry and the order status change. That needs MongoDB to run as a replica set, even on one node, because transactions are not available on a standalone server.

Decision 2: one refund per order, enforced by the database

Each refund entry carries a unique key built from the order id. If the worker, the webhook and the cancel button all fire together, only one insert succeeds. The others see a duplicate key error and stop. The order status change is also a compare-and-set, so an order that is already refunded cannot move again.

Decision 3: ask the supplier before you refund

A code can arrive in the last seconds. Before cancelling or refunding, the system asks the supplier for the latest state once more. If a code just arrived, the number is kept and the code is shown, instead of refunded and lost. This was a bug in my first version: a late code could be lost because the refund won the race.

Decision 4: fall through suppliers at the same price limit

Numbers come from more than one upstream supplier. If the first one has no stock or rejects the price, the order tries the next with the same maximum price, so the customer never pays more because of a fallback.

What I would do again

  • Write the refund path before the happy path. It touches the wallet, the order state machine and the supplier calls, so it shapes everything.
  • Make the failure case a test: duplicate refunds, a code arriving during cancel, a supplier timeout.
  • Keep the ledger append-only. Debugging money is much easier when nothing is ever edited.

Stack: Next.js, MongoDB (replica set), Redis, a Node worker for polling and expiry, and a Telegram bot and Mini App on the same backend.

If you have run a similar system, I would like to hear how you handle the race between a late success and an expiry.

title: The 150 DSA problems I'd actually do before a coding interview (Java & Python)
description:
Most "interview prep" lists are 500 problems long. Nobody finishes them. Interviewers at most companies test the same ~15 patterns again and again, so a short list that covers every pattern beats a long list that covers the same one ten times.

Here's how I'd group a 150-problem plan:

  1. Arrays & hashing (20) — two-sum style lookups, counting, prefix sums.
  2. Two pointers & sliding window (20) — sorted arrays, longest/shortest substring problems.
  3. Stacks & queues (10) — valid brackets, next greater element, monotonic stack.
  4. Binary search (10) — not just "find x": search on the answer.
  5. Linked lists (10) — reverse, merge, cycle detection.
  6. Trees (20) — DFS/BFS, BST checks, lowest common ancestor.
  7. Heaps (8) — top-k, merge k lists, running median.
  8. Graphs (15) — BFS shortest path, islands, topological sort, union-find.
  9. Backtracking (10) — subsets, permutations, N-Queens.
  10. Dynamic programming (22) — 1D (climbing stairs, house robber), 2D (grid paths, LCS), knapsack.
  11. Greedy & intervals (5) — merge intervals, meeting rooms.

How to work through it:

  • Do one pattern at a time. Don't shuffle.
  • Give each problem 25 minutes. Stuck? Read the idea, close it, write the code yourself.
  • Re-solve anything you needed help with 3 days later.

I keep the full list, with a lesson for every pattern and an online judge to submit solutions, here (free):

  • Java: https://www.mentornxt.com/learn/java/dsa-sheet?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=wk1
  • Python: https://www.mentornxt.com/learn/python/dsa-sheet?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=wk1

title: Hallucinated Packages & Dependency Drift in AI-Assisted Code
description:
During a routine review on a client's Laravel and Vue project, one pull request added a Composer package with a perfectly reasonable name for parsing VAT numbers. The code looked fine and the tests passed locally for the author, because he had copied a helper from an assistant's answer and installed the package by hand. The CI build failed with "package not found". The package had never existed. The assistant had invented a plausible name. That time the failure was harmless. The worrying part is that anyone can register a missing name on a public registry, and attackers do watch for names that assistants tend to invent.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every command against Composer 2.8, npm 10 and pnpm 9. I am a Principal Software Engineer in Karachi with 9+ years across PHP/Laravel, Vue, Node and .NET microservices, and through Loop Origin I maintain production SaaS codebases where a growing share of code is AI-assisted.

📚 Series Navigation — Maintaining AI-Written Code in Production

  • Part 1: Reviewing AI-Generated Pull Requests: A Checklist That Catches Real Bugs
  • Part 2: Characterization Tests Before You Refactor AI-Written Code
  • Part 3 (This Post): Hallucinated Packages & Dependency Drift in AI-Assisted Code
  • Part 4: Static Analysis Gates: PHPStan, TypeScript Strict & Coverage in CI
  • Part 5: Decision Records So AI Context Doesn't Rot
  • Part 6: Measuring AI Coding Impact With DORA Metrics, Not Vibes

Related earlier posts: Subresource Integrity & CDN Script Pinning · Cron Jobs That Never Ran: Heartbeats & Dead-Man Switches

How do you stop AI coding assistants from adding fake or risky dependencies?

Direct answer: Treat every new dependency in an AI-assisted PR as a review item. Verify the package exists on the official registry, check its age, maintainers and downloads, require lockfile changes to be reviewed, block unapproved packages with an allowlist in CI, run composer audit and npm audit, and pin versions so drift only happens through deliberate update PRs.

Two different problems

It helps to separate them because the fixes differ.

Hallucinated packages are names that do not exist, or did not exist when the model was trained. Researchers have measured this: a 2024 study of code-generating models ("We Have a Package for You!", Spracklen et al.) found a meaningful share of suggested packages did not exist, and many invented names repeated across prompts. Repeated names are what make "slopsquatting" possible: someone registers the invented name and waits.

Dependency drift is quieter. The assistant suggests "^2.0" where you had "2.4.1", adds a second HTTP client because it did not notice the one you already use, or pulls an old major version from its training data. Nothing breaks today. Six months later you have three date libraries and a security advisory on one of them.

Risk signals compared

Signal Hallucinated / typo package Legit but risky Healthy dependency
Exists on Packagist / npm No, or created very recently Yes Yes
Age of first release Days or weeks Years, but last release long ago Years, steady releases
Maintainers One new account One inactive maintainer Several, known org
Weekly downloads Near zero Declining Stable or growing
Install scripts (postinstall) Often present Sometimes Rare, documented
Source repo link Missing or mismatched Archived Active, matches package

No single row decides it. A brand-new package with one maintainer, an install script and no repository link should stop the PR until someone checks it by hand.

Step 1: make dependency changes visible in review

Most teams collapse composer.lock and package-lock.json in the diff view, which is exactly where surprises hide. I add a small CI step that prints a readable summary of what changed:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ci/dependency-diff.sh — summarise added/removed packages vs main
set -euo pipefail
git fetch origin main --depth=1

echo "== Composer packages added =="
diff <(git show origin/main:composer.lock | jq -r '.packages[].name' | sort) \
     <(jq -r '.packages[].name' composer.lock | sort) | grep '^>' || echo "none"

echo "== npm packages added (top level) =="
diff <(git show origin/main:package.json | jq -r '.dependencies + .devDependencies | keys[]' | sort) \
     <(jq -r '.dependencies + .devDependencies | keys[]' package.json | sort) | grep '^>' || echo "none"

Post that output as a PR comment and reviewers see "added: acme/vat-parser" in plain text instead of a 3,000-line lockfile.

Step 2: verify each new package exists and looks healthy

For Composer, the Packagist API gives you creation date and download counts:

pkg="acme/vat-parser"
curl -sf "https://repo.packagist.org/p2/${pkg}.json" > /dev/null \
  || { echo "BLOCK: ${pkg} not found on Packagist"; exit 1; }
curl -s "https://packagist.org/packages/${pkg}/stats.json" | jq '.downloads.total'

For npm:

npm view some-package time.created maintainers repository.url --json
npm view some-package scripts.postinstall

I fail the build when a package is missing, and flag for manual review when it is younger than 90 days or has fewer than a few thousand total downloads.

Step 3: an allowlist for production dependencies

For client projects with strict needs, an explicit allowlist works well. It is just a file in the repo:

{
  "composer": ["laravel/framework", "guzzlehttp/guzzle", "spatie/laravel-permission"],
  "npm": ["vue", "axios", "pinia", "dayjs"]
}

CI compares top-level dependencies against it. Adding a package means a one-line change to the allowlist that a senior reviewer approves, which forces the conversation "do we need this, and do we already have something that does it?". That question alone has removed duplicate HTTP and date libraries from several projects we maintain.

Step 4: pin versions and control drift 

// composer.json — prefer exact or tight ranges for production apps
"require": {
  "php": "^8.3",
  "laravel/framework": "11.31.*",
  "guzzlehttp/guzzle": "7.9.2"
}

# .npmrc
save-exact=true
ignore-scripts=true   # enable per-package only when needed

Then let a bot (Renovate or Dependabot) open grouped update PRs on a schedule. Updates become deliberate and reviewable, not a side effect of someone pasting an assistant's snippet. ignore-scripts=true blocks install scripts by default, which removes one of the most common ways a malicious package runs code on a developer laptop or CI runner.

Step 5: audit continuously 

composer audit --locked --format=summary
npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high

Run both on every PR and nightly on main. Nightly matters because advisories are published after you merge.

Teaching the assistant your stack

Prevention is cheaper than detection. In the repo's assistant instructions file (whatever your tool reads, such as a rules or AGENTS.md file) list the approved libraries for common jobs: "HTTP: Guzzle. Dates: Carbon. Validation: Laravel validator. Never add a new dependency without saying so explicitly." In our experience this cuts surprise packages sharply, though it never replaces the CI checks.

Diagnostic checklist

  • [ ] CI prints added/removed packages as a readable PR comment.
  • [ ] Builds fail when a new package does not exist on the official registry.
  • [ ] Packages younger than 90 days or with very low downloads need manual approval.
  • [ ] Production dependencies are on an allowlist with senior approval for changes.
  • [ ] Versions are pinned (save-exact, tight Composer constraints) and updated via bot PRs.
  • [ ] Install scripts are disabled by default.
  • [ ] composer audit and npm audit run on every PR and nightly.
  • [ ] Assistant instruction files list approved libraries for common tasks.

FAQ

How common are hallucinated packages really?

Common enough to plan for. Published research found that a noticeable percentage of package names suggested by code models did not exist, with open models doing worse than commercial ones. Even a small rate matters when a team merges hundreds of suggestions a month.

Isn't npm audit enough?

No. Audit tools only know about published advisories. A freshly registered malicious package has no advisory yet, which is why existence, age and allowlist checks come first.

Should we ban AI assistants from adding dependencies?

Banning tends to fail quietly. Requiring dependency changes to be explicit, summarised and approved works better and still lets the assistant save time.

What about private registries?

A private mirror (Private Packagist, Verdaccio, Artifactory) that only proxies approved packages is the strongest control. Make sure scoped names cannot fall through to the public registry, or you invite dependency confusion.

How do we clean up existing drift?

Start with composer show --direct and npm ls --depth=0, find duplicates doing the same job, pick one, and migrate in small PRs with characterization tests from Part 2 guarding behaviour.

Can Loop Origin help set this up?

Yes. We add these gates as part of our custom web application and maintenance work, usually in a day or two for a typical Laravel and Vue codebase.

Next in this series, Part 4 covers static analysis gates: PHPStan, TypeScript strict mode and coverage in CI.

  • GitHub: Loop Origin (@LoopOrigin)

title: Spring Boot for Backend Development
description:
Introduction

Have you ever wondered how websites handle user login, save data, process payments, or send notifications?

Behind every modern web application, there is a backend system that handles business logic, communicates with databases, and provides APIs for frontend applications.

Spring Boot is one of the most popular frameworks for building backend applications using Java. It helps developers create powerful, secure, and production-ready applications with less configuration.

In this article, we will explore what Spring Boot is, why it is used, its main features, and how it fits into backend development.

1. What Is Spring Boot?

Spring Boot is a Java based framework used to build backend applications and REST APIs.

It is built on top of the Spring Framework and makes Java development easier by reducing manual configuration. Instead of setting up many files and settings manually, Spring Boot can automatically configure common parts of an application based on the dependencies you add.

For example, if you add a database dependency, Spring Boot can help configure the database connection using settings from your application configuration file.

Spring Boot is commonly used to build:

  • REST APIs
  • Web applications
  • Microservices
  • Authentication systems
  • Backend services for mobile applications
  • Enterprise applications

2. Why Use Spring Boot?

Spring Boot is popular because it makes backend development faster and simpler.

Main Benefits

  • Less configuration: Spring Boot automatically configures many common settings.
  • Fast project setup: You can create a project quickly using Spring Initializr.
  • Embedded server: Applications can run with an embedded web server.
  • Starters: You can add commonly used dependencies easily.
  • Production ready features: Spring Boot Actuator helps monitor application health and performance.
  • Strong ecosystem: It works well with databases, security tools, testing tools, and cloud platforms.

Spring Boot starters are convenient dependency descriptors that include the dependencies commonly needed for a specific type of application.

3. Spring Boot vs Spring Framework

Many beginners confuse Spring Boot with the Spring Framework.

Feature Spring Framework Spring Boot
Main purpose Core Java application framework Faster Spring application development
Configuration Requires more manual configuration Provides auto-configuration
Server setup Often requires external server configuration Includes embedded server support
Project setup More setup required Quick setup with Spring Initializr
Best for Flexible, customized applications Rapid backend and API development

In simple words:

  • Spring Framework provides the core tools.
  • Spring Boot makes those tools easier to use.

4. Important Spring Boot Features

Auto-Configuration
Spring Boot can automatically configure application components based on the dependencies in your project. This reduces the amount of manual setup required.

For example, if you add a database dependency, Spring Boot can configure a database connection using properties from your configuration file.

Starters
Starters are dependency packages that group commonly used libraries together.

Examples include:

  • spring-boot-starter-web: For building REST APIs and web applications
  • spring-boot-starter-data-jpa: For database access using JPA
  • spring-boot-starter-security: For authentication and authorization
  • spring-boot-starter-test: For testing applications
  • spring-boot-starter-actuator: For monitoring and managing applications

Embedded Server
Spring Boot applications can include an embedded server, such as Tomcat. This means you can run your application without manually installing and configuring a separate web server.

Actuator
Spring Boot Actuator provides production-ready features for monitoring and managing applications. It can expose health checks, metrics, and other operational information.

5. Spring Boot Project Structure

A typical Spring Boot project follows a layered structure.

src/main/java/com/example/demo/
    controller/
    service/
    repository/
    model/
    config/

src/main/resources/
    application.properties

Main Layers

Layer Responsibility
Controller Handles HTTP requests and responses
Service Contains business logic
Repository Communicates with the database
Model / Entity Represents database tables
DTO Transfers data between layers
Config Contains application configuration

This structure helps keep the application organized and easier to maintain.

6. How Spring Boot Works

Let’s understand Spring Boot using a simple example: retrieving a list of products.

Step 1: User Request
The frontend sends a request to the backend:

GET /api/products

Step 2: Controller Receives the Request
The controller receives the request and calls the service layer.

Step 3: Service Processes Business Logic
The service layer performs any required logic, such as filtering, validation or calculations.

Step 4: Repository Fetches Data
The repository communicates with the database and retrieves the product data.

Step 5: Response Is Returned
The backend converts the data into JSON and sends it back to the frontend.

[
  {
    "id": 1,
    "name": "Laptop",
    "price": 75000
  }
]

7. Popular Spring Boot Dependencies

Dependency Purpose
Spring Web Build REST APIs and web applications
Spring Data JPA Work with databases using Java objects
PostgreSQL Driver Connect to PostgreSQL database
MySQL Driver Connect to MySQL database
Spring Security Add authentication and authorization
Lombok Reduce repetitive Java code
Spring Boot Actuator Monitor application health and metrics
Spring Boot DevTools Improve development experience

8. Spring Boot Backend Roadmap

If you want to learn Spring Boot, follow this roadmap:

  • Learn Java fundamentals.
  • Understand object-oriented programming.
  • Learn Maven or Gradle.
  • Understand HTTP and REST APIs.
  • Learn Spring Boot basics.
  • Build REST controllers.
  • Learn Spring Data JPA.
  • Connect to a database.
  • Add validation and exception handling.
  • Learn Spring Security.
  • Write unit and integration tests.
  • Learn deployment basics.

You do not need to learn everything at once. Start by building a simple CRUD API, then gradually add more features.

9. Which Projects Should Use Spring Boot?

Spring Boot is a good choice for:

  • REST API projects
  • E-commerce backends
  • Banking and finance applications
  • Enterprise applications
  • Microservices
  • Admin dashboards
  • Mobile app backends
  • Applications that need strong security and scalability

Spring Boot is especially useful when you want a reliable, structured, and production-ready backend using Java.

10. Conclusion

Spring Boot is a powerful framework for backend development. It simplifies Java application development through auto-configuration, starters, embedded servers, and production-ready features.

If you are learning backend development with Java, Spring Boot is an excellent framework to start with. Build small REST APIs first, understand how controllers, services, and repositories work together, and then move toward databases, security, and deployment.

Thanks for reading The Dev Journal!
Learn. Build. Improve.
