title: Analysing 900 IT Help Desk Tickets with Python and SQL
description:
Tags: #python #sql #datascience #beginners

How can an IT support team identify recurring problems, measure service quality and improve resolution times?

I explored these questions through my Help Desk Ticket Analysis project using Python, Pandas, SQL and Matplotlib.

The Dataset

The project uses 900 synthetic IT support tickets from 2025.

The dataset contains information about issue categories, priorities, support teams, response times, resolution times and service-level agreement (SLA) performance.

Because the data is synthetic, the findings demonstrate analytical techniques rather than the performance of a real organisation.

Data Cleaning

Before calculating performance metrics, I worked with common data-quality problems, including:

  • Duplicate ticket identifiers
  • Missing values
  • Inconsistent support-team names
  • Incorrect timestamp formats
  • Inconsistent issue categories

One important decision was not to automatically discard every incomplete ticket.

A record missing an analyst name may still contain useful resolution and SLA information.

Key Results

The repository reports the following results for its synthetic dataset:

Metric Result
Total tickets 900
Average first response 0.91 hours
Average resolution time 7.74 hours
SLA compliance 70.3%
Average satisfaction 4.03/5

The most common issue category was Application Error.

Why SLA Compliance Matters

A low average resolution time can look positive while hiding serious delays for high-priority tickets.

That is why I compared multiple indicators rather than relying on one overall average.

The analysis considers ticket volume, issue categories, resolution time, SLA compliance and customer satisfaction.

Tools Used

Python and Pandas for cleaning and aggregating records.

SQL for operational reporting queries.

Matplotlib for visualising ticket patterns.

Jupyter Notebook for exploratory analysis.

What I Would Improve

Future extensions could include an interactive Power BI dashboard, ticket backlog analysis, reopen rates, first-contact resolution and automated ticket categorisation.

Conclusion

This project demonstrates how data analysis can support IT service management.

The main lesson was that operational performance should be evaluated through several connected metrics.

GitHub: https://github.com/tasnem-tech/help-desk-ticket-analysis

Which service desk KPI do you find most useful: response time, resolution time or SLA compliance?

title: What a 24/7 NOC Actually Monitors — and What It Doesn't
description:
If you run a 30–80-person company, someone has probably tried to sell you "24/7 monitoring." It sounds like a person watching your network around the clock. Sometimes it is. Often it isn't — it's a dashboard that emails someone the next morning.

I work at Amen Security, a Winnipeg MSP that runs monitoring for small and mid-sized companies. This is the honest version of what a NOC (network operations centre) watches, what it can't watch, and the questions worth asking before you pay for it.

What a NOC actually monitors

1. Is it up?
The basics: servers, firewalls, switches, internet links, and key services (email, file shares, line-of-business apps). A ping or health check every minute or two. If something stops answering, an alert fires. This is the least glamorous part and the most valuable — most outages are found this way, not by a user phoning in.

2. Is it about to break?
Disk filling up, memory exhausted, a UPS battery degrading, a backup job that ran long or failed outright. Good monitoring watches trends, not just thresholds: a disk growing 2% a week will be full in a month, and that's a ticket today, not an outage later.

3. Is something behaving strangely?
A login at 3 a.m. from a country nobody on your team is in. A server suddenly talking to an address it has never contacted. A mailbox rule created that forwards everything externally. These are the signals that matter most — and the ones a threshold alert will never catch on its own. They need someone who knows what "normal" looks like for your company.

4. Are the safety nets intact?
Backups completed — and, more importantly, restorable. Patch levels current. Antivirus/EDR agents actually reporting in, not silently uninstalled or expired. Certificates not about to expire. The unglamorous checks are the ones that decide whether a bad day becomes a disaster.

What it doesn't monitor

It doesn't read your employees' minds — or their inboxes. A NOC sees that email is flowing; it doesn't know that the "invoice" your accounts person just opened was a phishing lure until the EDR or the user reports it. User awareness is still a layer no dashboard replaces.

It doesn't fix your business processes. Monitoring will tell you the CRM is down. It won't tell you that half the sales team has been working around a broken workflow for six months. It measures systems, not whether the systems serve the work.

It doesn't see inside encrypted traffic it has no business seeing. A NOC that promises to inspect everything is either breaking your privacy or overselling. The right scope is metadata and behaviour — what's connecting, how much, how often — not the contents of your team's work.

It doesn't prevent everything. Monitoring shortens the time between "something broke" and "someone is fixing it." It does not make hardware immortal or attackers polite. Anyone selling zero downtime is selling a feeling, not a service.

What to ask before you buy it

  • Who answers the alert at 2 a.m., and how fast? A dashboard that pages a human is different from one that sends an email nobody reads until 9 a.m. Ask for the actual response times in writing.
  • What's excluded? Printers, personal devices, that one server under someone's desk — the exclusions list is where surprises live.
  • How do you know the backup works? "Backup completed successfully" is not proof. A restore test is. Ask how often restores are tested and whether you get the report.
  • What does an alert look like to me? You should get a plain-language summary, not a raw log dump. If you can't understand the report, you can't judge the service.
  • What happens when you find something? Monitoring without a defined response — who calls whom, who can approve a shutdown, who talks to your team — is just a more expensive way to watch things break.

The short version

A real NOC watches uptime, capacity trends, strange behaviour, and the safety nets — and it has a human who acts on what it sees. It doesn't watch your people, fix your processes, or promise nothing will ever break. If a provider can't tell you plainly what they monitor, what they don't, and who responds at 2 a.m., you're not buying monitoring. You're buying the word "monitoring."

I'm Liam Roy, CMO at Amen Security — managed IT and web/app development for 30–80-person companies in Winnipeg and across Canada and the US. We start every engagement with a free assessment: we look, report what we find, and only then talk about a contract. https://amensecurity.ca

title: Copy-to-Clipboard Testing: Follow Your Public SaaS Demo Into the Paste
description:
Copy-to-clipboard testing should end with inspecting the pasted value, not with seeing a “Copied” message. Check the exact content, the destination where a user needs it and the recovery path when the browser cannot complete the write. When you share a SaaS demo in public, those details turn a tiny button into a task peers can meaningfully review.

A successful animation beside a copy icon does not tell you which text reached the clipboard. It also does not establish that a link opens the intended page or grants the intended access. Keep those observations separate so a public update can describe what was actually checked.

This guide uses a fictional proposal-sharing app. Its copy button is supposed to copy a public preview link for a made-up proposal. The example is a test plan, not a report of testing Buildside or another live product.

Define the value before testing the button

Start by writing down exactly what should be copied. For the fictional proposal, the expected value is a complete preview link. It should not be the editor's private address, the proposal title, a shortened display label or a string left over from a previously selected proposal.

Use a disposable record with no real customer details. Give it a distinctive title and prepare an expected value that you can compare against the paste. If your app generates a link dynamically, establish which parts should remain stable and which parts are intentionally different.

Do not use a real access token as convenient sample text in a public recording. The copied value may be less visible in the source interface than in the destination where you paste it. Plan both views before inviting founder peers to inspect the workflow.

Wait for the write result before announcing success

MDN's documentation for Clipboard.writeText explains that the method returns a Promise that resolves after the clipboard has been updated. It can reject with NotAllowedError when writing is not allowed, and it requires a secure context.

For the interface, that means a click and a completed write are distinct events. Display success after the operation succeeds. If it fails, show a useful failure state instead of leaving a success message that was set before the result arrived.

Keep the claim limited. A successful clipboard write tells you that the specified text was written in that environment. It does not prove that the text is the correct proposal link. Your next check must compare the pasted content with the value the user intended to share.

Paste somewhere you can inspect the result

Use a simple destination where the entire string is visible. For this fictional task, paste into a blank text document and compare it with the expected preview link. Look for a missing protocol, an extra space, the wrong proposal identifier or surrounding text that the button was not meant to include.

Then try the destination that matters to the user's task. Pasting into a message field can expose different practical problems from pasting into a plain text document. Some destinations turn a link into a preview or apply formatting. Record what you observed without treating those destination behaviors as properties of your copy button.

If the link is supposed to be usable by a recipient, check that recipient path separately with an appropriate test context. Clipboard correctness and permission correctness belong in the same sharing workflow, but they answer different questions. A well-copied private editor URL is still the wrong result for a public preview invitation.

Change the source and copy again

A button can work for the first item while copying stale content after the user changes selection. In the fictional app, open a second disposable proposal with a visibly different identifier. Copy its preview link and inspect the paste again.

Repeat the check after the app updates the preview link, if that is a supported action. Be clear about whether the interface shows the new value before or after the copy control becomes available. A button that acts on an earlier value may produce a plausible link that is difficult to notice during a quick demo.

Include the selected item in the recording. If viewers can see only a confirmation toast and a pasted string, they may have no way to assess whether those two things belong to the same proposal. The source context is part of the evidence.

Exercise a failure without weakening browser protections

Test a rejected clipboard write in a controlled development test, then check a real browser environment where the relevant permission behavior can be observed. A simulated rejection helps verify your interface's response; it does not reproduce every browser's permission rules.

Do not recommend disabling browser security as the normal way to make copying work. Record the browser, version, page context and visible result. If you cannot reproduce a particular failure, say that it was not observed rather than claiming that the workflow cannot fail.

The fictional app's error should leave the preview link visible and explain how to continue. It should not claim that the link has been shared or that the recipient has access. A failed write may leave earlier clipboard content in place, so the manual route needs to be clear enough that someone does not accidentally paste the previous value.

Make the manual route a real task

If the product offers manual selection as a fallback, try it. Can the user reach the value, select all of it and copy it without including a label or hidden placeholder? Is the complete link available when the visible presentation shortens it?

Check the route with keyboard input as well as a pointer when the interface supports both. Observe whether the copy result and error message are understandable without relying only on color or an icon changing shape. A visual toast can be easy to miss while attention is on another part of the screen.

For the fictional proposal, the fallback could be a read-only field containing the full preview link. That is a design option to assess, not a universal requirement. The useful criterion is whether someone can finish the intended sharing task after the automatic write fails.

Give public reviewers a bounded test request

Buildside gives founders a place to share progress and questions. A useful update could show the disposable proposal, the copy action and the inspected paste, then ask peers to review the same task in their own supported environment.

Provide the expected outcome and explain which data is fictional. Ask reviewers to report the browser and the point where their result differs. Do not ask them to paste unrelated clipboard contents into a public thread or expose a private link to prove that copying failed.

A focused invitation is easier to act on than “Does the share feature work?” It gives a reviewer something they can compare while keeping access checks, formatting behavior and actual clipboard writes visible as separate observations.

Publish the conditions alongside the outcome

Keep a short record of the source item, expected value, browser context, pasted value and recovery result. You can use this record to write a release note that names the behavior checked instead of announcing that clipboard support is fixed everywhere.

For example, a hypothetical update could say that the interface now waits for the write result and preserves a manual route when the operation rejects. Any claim that a specific browser path passed should come from an actual test record, not from the proposed plan in this article.

Before posting your next copy-button demo, follow the value all the way into the paste. If the source, result and recovery are visible, founder peers can question the work with useful detail. If you stop at the toast, the most important part of the task is still off screen.

title: whosent: A TUI That Shows Who Sent the Agent
description:
A request shows up from research-agent. The token says Alice. Between Alice and that agent there was a chat UI and a planner, three token exchanges, and the scope should have shrunk at each one. Decoding the JWT and squinting at nested act claims does not tell me whether it did.

I wrote y509 for X.509 chains. whosent is the same idea for delegation chains.

  • Source: https://github.com/kanywst/whosent
  • Install: brew install --cask kanywst/tap/whosent or go install github.com/kanywst/whosent/cmd/whosent@latest

Scope from nowhere

whosent demo ships 41 scenarios across the four formats, and demo --emit writes any of them out as real files. This one is three exchanged JWTs where the last exchange gained a scope:

$ whosent demo --emit fixture jwt-bundle-widened && cd fixture
$ whosent check tokens.json --trust trust.json --audience https://api.acme.example --at 2026-09-12T08:01:00Z
=== tokens.json · 3 links · JWT · issuer https://acme.okta.example, access token (RFC 9068)
    at 2026-09-12T08:01:00Z, skew 30s, audience https://api.acme.example

❌ INVALID: the chain breaks at link 2, and no authority reaches below it

  #  issuer → subject                   J1 J2 J3 J4 J5 J6 J7 J8 J9 J10 J11 J12
  0  alice@acme.example → chat-ui        ✓  ✓  ✓  ·  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·   ·   ·   ·
  1  chat-ui → planner-agent             ✓  ✓  ✓  ·  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓   ✓   ·   ·
  2  planner-agent → research-agent      ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✗  ✓   ✓   ·   ·
     ✓ pass  ✗ fail  ! could not evaluate  ? not checked  - skipped  · does not apply

Findings
  ✗ J8 link 2: adds files:write, which token 1 did not hold [whosent bundle rule, derived from RFC 8693; not a procedure any specification defines (section 4.2, scope)]

How authority narrows
  0 → 1  chat-ui → planner-agent
      + exchanged: planner-agent now acts for alice@acme.example
      = scope files:read
      - scope files:write dropped
      = scope calendar:read
      ~ expires 20m sooner
  1 → 2  planner-agent → research-agent
      + exchanged: research-agent now acts for alice@acme.example
      = scope files:read
      - scope calendar:read dropped
      ✗ scope files:write was not in the token exchanged
      ~ expires 20m sooner
      i https://acme.okta.example → https://api.acme.example
          audience
      = kept  ~ narrowed  - dropped  + added  ✗ widened (violation)

Every signature is fine. The planner dropped files:write, and the research agent's token has it back. check evaluates every rule on every link instead of stopping at the first failure, so a chain with three faults shows all three.

Note the bracket on that finding. RFC 8693 does not define how to check a bundle of exchanged tokens against each other, so J7 to J10 are my rules, and the output says so.

The same question from the command line:

$ whosent ask tokens.json --trust trust.json --audience https://api.acme.example --at 2026-09-12T08:01:00Z --scope files:write
DENIED (HYPOTHETICAL): the chain does not verify, so it permits nothing. Hypothetically, if it verified, the token would hold this

! the first token held files:write, token 1 dropped it, and re-adding it later does not bring it back

  link by link
  0  chat-ui                      holds
  1  planner-agent                lacks  token 1 does not hold files:write
  2  research-agent               holds

The research agent's token does hold files:write. whosent still says no, and says which link lost it. On a chain that verifies with every key, the answer is AUTHORITATIVE instead.

The issuer's word is not a verified hop

One access token with nested act claims looks like a chain, but the prior actors are just what the issuer wrote (RFC 8693 section 4.1). whosent draws them that way:

✅ VALID: every checkable rule holds, but 2 prior actors are the issuer's word, not verified hop by hop

  #  issuer → subject                   J1 J2 J3 J4 J5 J6 J7 J8 J9 J10 J11 J12
  0  alice@acme.example → chat-ui        ·  ·  ·  ·  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·   ·   ·   ·   (asserted by the issuer, not verified)
  1  chat-ui → planner-agent             ·  ·  ·  ·  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·   ·   ·   ·   (asserted by the issuer, not verified)
  2  planner-agent → research-agent      ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·   ·   ·   ·

If the token carries actor proofs (draft-mcguinness-oauth-actor-proofs) or an Actor Chain profile (draft-mw-oauth-actor-chain-03), and the actors' own keys are in the trust file, each hop becomes the actor's own signed word. A forged one fails:

  ✗ J11 link 1: proof 1 (planner-agent): the signature does not verify against actor-planner-agent.json kid planner-agent-2026 [draft-mcguinness-oauth-actor-proofs-01 section 7; whosent fails the token on a rejected chain, where the draft only drops the evidence]

Drop the keys and nothing turns green. The same okta-style token without --trust:

⚠️  INCOMPLETE: nothing failed, but some rules were not checked, so nothing is vouched for
...
  ? J2 link 2: no keys for issuer "https://acme.okta.example"; pass --jwks https://acme.okta.example=PATH [RFC 7515 section 5.2]

That exits 2. VALID is 0, INVALID is 1, and --strict turns INCOMPLETE into 1 for CI. Keys only come from what you pass; a JWT's jku, x5u, x5c and jwk are ignored.

Four formats, one view

Format One link is Checked against
JWT (act, ID-JAG, Txn-Tokens, Entra agent tokens) a token or an act level RFC 8693, the two actor drafts, whosent's bundle rules
Biscuit a block the spec's 38 sample tokens; Datalog evaluator is whosent's own
UCAN 1.0 a delegation or the invocation the spec's 1.0.0 fixtures
Macaroons (libmacaroons, Fly.io FlyV1) a caveat go-macaroon or superfly/macaroon, on every run

The macaroon cross-check is live: if whosent and the reference library disagree on a token, it exits 70 and asks you to report it.

A UCAN that widens its command looks like this:

❌ INVALID: the chain breaks at link 1, and no authority reaches below it
...
Findings
  ✗ U6 link 1: /msg is not under /msg/send, which the delegation above granted [https://github.com/ucan-wg/spec#command]

In the TUI, t opens a timeline of every link and ← → move the clock, so you can watch a block or a delegation expire, x simulates revoking a link (Biscuit and UCAN, labelled as simulated and never fed to check), and a asks the same question as whosent ask, prefilled from the row you selected.

Where it came from

whosent started as a viewer for mandatum, my own delegation format. Two days in, I dropped that format and kept the four that agents actually carry. mandatum is archived now. The viewer turned out to be the useful part.

Source and issues: https://github.com/kanywst/whosent

title: How Zapier turns ideas into working software in hours with Vercel
description:
Zapier on Vercel

  • Interactive partner demos in under two hours with v0, replacing a process that could take weeks

  • First versions of three internal applications, each built in one day

  • A shared daily briefing for more than 60 marketers, replacing individual efforts to assemble the same information

  • 3.3 million sandboxes created in one month, isolating the code execution behind Zapier’s AI workloads

Before the industry had a word for agents, Zapier was building them. Today Zapier is the AI orchestration platform connecting AI to the workflows, data, and systems businesses use every day.

Zapier has been a Vercel customer since they began using Vercel for web experiences several years ago. They stayed, and expanded, because every team that needed to ship quickly found the same answer: speed, with the security guardrails already in place. As they grew, so did their adoption of Vercel as more teams found new uses for the platform. Today, Vercel supports work across engineering, partnerships, and marketing, from customer-facing AI to interactive partner demos and internal applications.

The needs vary by team, but the priority is getting useful work into people’s hands quickly. A backend engineer can create an interactive demo of an integration inside a partner’s product. In marketing, a former product marketer with no prior deployment experience can share tools containing sensitive information through a company-approved environment and keep improving them as colleagues use them.

Zapier’s teams are moving faster and doing more than they could before. When the next launch comes around, building on Vercel is a given.

From weeks of prototype work to a demo in under two hours

Every partnership Zapier signs extends what its customers can automate. The Powered by Zapier team is how those partnerships become product, helping SaaS and AI companies embed Zapier’s automation capabilities directly into their own tools, so users can automate without ever leaving the partner’s app. The stakes are high, because Zapier relies on this team to make its platform the entry point to all the software in the world. The problem was speed: collaborating outside the organization took forever, with every prototype requiring screenshots, design time, and frontend resources, and weeks could pass before a partner saw anything clickable.

With v0, the team can create a fully interactive, multi-view prototype in under two hours, showing an embedded Zapier experience inside the partner’s own product.

Chu’s background is in backend development, not frontend engineering or design, but v0 lets her build these experiences without coordinating a separate design and frontend effort for every partner conversation. Partners can click through the flow and share it with colleagues, using the prototype as a blueprint for implementation alongside the API documentation.

Sharing sensitive internal data securely

In marketing, Joe Stych set out to make the team’s scattered knowledge easier to use. He had spent years in product marketing before becoming a agentic go-to-market engineer, but had never worked out of a Git repository or deployed an application.

At an internal hackathon, he built Marketing Hive, a shared source for positioning, messaging, personas, and competitive intelligence. Sharing his local prototype meant making sensitive information accessible to colleagues without exposing it to everyone else.

“The Hive holds our positioning, personas, and competitive intel, so I couldn't just send people a link. On Vercel it was behind our SSO from the first deploy, so I could share it without exposing it” says Joe Stych, Senior Lead, Agentic GTM at Zapier.

Zapier’s data and security teams had already endorsed Vercel. Stych deployed through the company’s approved internal tooling environment, with access gated behind Zapier’s single sign-on.

He develops in Cursor and keeps code and source material in GitLab, where changes trigger Vercel builds and deployments. If an update needs to be undone, he can roll back the deployment.

The first versions of three of his internal applications took about a day each. In roughly two months, a hackathon project had grown into production software used across marketing. It was built by someone who had never deployed anything before.

Internal apps for marketing and sales

Marketing Hive holds the knowledge. Marketing OS puts it to work. It gives more than 60 marketers a daily briefing in Slack and a dashboard with what changed across marketing, one update from each team, a win worth celebrating, and progress against goals. Each marketer can start from the briefing instead of assembling the same information from separate channels.

“The first five minutes of your day, you need to look at the Marketing OS update,” says Dan Slagen, Zapier’s CMO.

Readers mark what they found useful, helping Stych prioritize improvements. The briefings also spark discussions in a marketing channel open to everyone at the company.

Stych is building a sales coaching application that brings together account context and industry messaging before a call. Afterward, it reviews the Gong recording to highlight what worked and suggest changes to the talk track.

For the internal applications, he checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights. Decisions about positioning remain with people, and he says additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Model access and isolated code execution

Beyond Marketing OS, a separate team at Zapier uses AI Gateway to send requests to AI models on behalf of customers using Zapier products.

A common endpoint lets an application change or add models without maintaining a separate integration for each provider. Failover gives requests another route when a provider cannot serve them, while unified reporting lets a team see their usage across providers in once place.

What's next

Zapier’s relationship with Vercel began with web experiences and expanded as the company grew, with more teams finding uses for the platform as their needs changed. Today its role spans the software Zapier runs for customers and the tools its people build for one another, and every thread is still widening.

The clearest picture of where it leads is in marketing, where other teams are starting to borrow the pattern. The goal is more versions across the company, and perhaps a Revenue OS for Zapier’s customer-facing teams next, each built the way the first one was, by someone close to the problem. First comes trust. Stych still checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights, and additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Across all of it, Vercel helps Zapier put useful work into people’s hands and keep adapting it to the needs of the business.

title: Replication Lag Is a Network Decision: Keeping Cross-Cloud Databases Honest
description:
Replication Lag Is a Network Decision: Keeping Cross-Cloud Databases Honest

A database replica in another cloud can report healthy while falling steadily behind. The link is up, bandwidth looks ample, no packet loss alarms are firing, and yet the lag counter climbs from two seconds to twenty to two hundred. When a failover is needed, that replica is not a copy. It is an older version of the truth, and the gap was created as much by network choices as by the database itself.

Replication across clouds rewards teams that design for lag explicitly, in seconds and in business terms, rather than treating it as a database setting that will look after itself.

1. Define lag in time and in consequences, not in bytes

Bytes behind is a misleading number. A megabyte of small updates can take longer to apply than a gigabyte of bulk inserts, depending on indexes, constraints, and row by row work on the replica. What matters to the application is time: how old is the newest transaction visible on the replica, and what breaks if that age grows?

Set three thresholds before any link is ordered. A normal threshold, where replica reads are safe. A degraded threshold, where replica reads are stopped or labelled stale and writes on the primary are watched closely. And a failover threshold, beyond which promoting the replica means accepting named data loss, and a named person must approve it. Writing those thresholds down while everyone is calm prevents the worst conversation in incident response: discovering during a failure that nobody agreed what lag was acceptable.

Measure lag at the replica, from the replica point of view, and graph it continuously. Averages hide the problem. The 95th percentile and the maximum in each hour are where the risk lives.

2. Bandwidth is rarely the bottleneck people expect

Teams often size a cross-cloud link by total replication volume per day, then discover peak behaviour is different. Replication is bursty. A batch job, a backfill, a checkpoint, or a deployment that touches many rows can send an hour of changes in five minutes. If the link, a VPN gateway, or a firewall in the path is sized for the average, the burst queues, latency rises, and the queue itself becomes lag that drains slowly long after the burst ends.

Size for the burst you cannot reschedule, and measure the whole path, not just the circuit. Gateways, stateful firewalls, and NAT devices in the path each have throughput and session limits that behave like bandwidth when they saturate. A link diagram that stops at the circuit edge misses the devices that actually throttle replication in production.

Latency matters in a quieter way. Synchronous or semi synchronous replication pays the round trip on every commit. Moving a primary and its replica further apart can add milliseconds that look trivial in a network report and are decisive for transaction throughput. For asynchronous replication, latency still sets how quickly a problem is even visible on the other side.

3. Give replication its own path, or at least its own protection

Replication traffic sharing a path with backups, analytics exports, and general internet egress will lose at the worst moment, because those other workloads are also bursty and often larger. Where a dedicated path is not justified, give replication explicit protection: a reserved share of bandwidth, a separate queue, or a traffic class that is not starved when bulk transfers run.

Separation also helps diagnosis. If replication, backup, and user traffic share one counter, a lag spike has three possible causes and no quick answer. Separate counters per traffic class turn an argument into a reading. The same applies to routing: know exactly which gateways and firewalls replication traverses, keep that list short, and alert when the path changes. A silent reroute through a smaller gateway can halve throughput without any device reporting down.

4. Match the write pattern to the link you actually have

Some lag is created on the primary. Long transactions hold changes invisible to replication until they commit, then release them all at once. Frequent small checkpoints, large unindexed updates on the replica side, and schema changes applied without a replication plan all show up first as network shaped symptoms.

Practical steps that help without heroics: keep long running transactions visible with an age alert, not just a count. Apply schema changes in a tested order that replication can follow. Pause or throttle known bulk jobs when lag crosses the degraded threshold, automatically if possible, rather than hoping the replica catches up while the job continues. And test the replica apply rate separately from the link rate. If the replica can only apply changes at half the speed the primary generates them at peak, no network upgrade will close the gap.

5. Decide in advance what the system does when lag grows

A replica falling behind should trigger behaviour, not just a notification. Useful responses, in order of increasing cost, include stopping stale reads, shedding non essential writes, throttling batch work, and preparing users for a possible failover with data loss. Each response should be tied to the thresholds from the first section, with an owner and a way to reverse it when lag recovers.

Recovery needs design too. When a link returns after an outage, the replica will try to catch up at full speed. That catch up burst can saturate the same path production traffic needs, and can overload the replica disk. Rate limit catch up where the database allows it, watch primary retention carefully, and make sure transaction logs cannot expire before the replica has consumed them. The most expensive version of this failure is a replica that fell so far behind during an outage that it must be rebuilt from scratch, extending the window with no usable copy at all.

6. Test lag under fault, not just under load

Load tests show whether replication keeps up on a good day. Fault tests show whether it degrades predictably: add latency, drop the primary path and force the backup, pause the link for thirty minutes, then restore it and time the catch up. Record three numbers from each test: peak lag, time to return below the normal threshold, and whether any automatic protection actually fired.

Those numbers belong in the failover runbook, next to the thresholds. A team that knows catch up after a thirty minute outage takes two hours can make an honest decision at minute ten. A team guessing will either wait too long or promote a stale replica too early.

Teams that run private multi-cloud connectivity as a managed estate tend to treat replication paths, thresholds, and catch up behaviour as part of the network design itself, not as an afterthought left to the database team alone. That is the approach taken by CloudVerg, where VergMesh handles multi-cloud networking and VergForge helps keep the surrounding platform consistent, so database copies in different clouds stay copies in practice, not just in the architecture diagram.

title: Godot 4: evenly spaced points along a path (77 stitch holes)
description:
Placing points every N units along a polyline looks trivial in Godot 4 until the path bends.

We hit this in a leathercraft game, where the points are stitch holes. On a rounded corner the holes bunched up, and on one seam two holes landed on the same spot.

The naive version

A seam is a polyline in metres. The player picks a pricking-iron pitch: 3.0, 3.38 or 3.85 mm. Our first sampler walked the polyline segment by segment:

var gap: float = pitch_mm * .001
for i in range(seam.path.size()-1):
    var a := vec2(seam.path[i])
    var b := vec2(seam.path[i+1])
    var count := maxi(1, roundi(a.distance_to(b) / gap))
    for j in count:
        var p := a.lerp(b, float(j)/count)
        seam.holes.append([p.x, p.y])
var end := vec2(seam.path.back())
seam.holes.append([end.x,end.y])

Three things go wrong.

  1. Rounding happens per segment. A 10 mm segment and a 90 mm segment each round to their own count, so the spacing changes at every vertex.
  2. Curves are many short segments. A corner arc is built from segments shorter than the pitch. maxi(1, …) gives each of them a hole, so the corner gets a hole per vertex instead of a hole per 3.38 mm.
  3. Duplicate join points. Where two path pieces meet, the same point can appear twice. That is a zero-length segment, which still gets one hole. Two holes now sit on the same spot, and the direction from one hole to the next is a zero vector. Our needle used that direction to orient itself.

Sample by arc length instead

The fix is to stop thinking in segments. Measure the whole path once, decide the hole count once, then walk the path and drop a hole each time the walked distance passes the next target.

var gap: float = pitch_mm * .001
var total := 0.0
for i in range(seam.path.size()-1):
    total += vec2(seam.path[i]).distance_to(vec2(seam.path[i+1]))
var count := maxi(1, roundi(total/gap))
var walked := 0.0
var next_distance := 0.0
var hole := 0
for i in range(seam.path.size()-1):
    var a := vec2(seam.path[i])
    var b := vec2(seam.path[i+1])
    var length := a.distance_to(b)
    if length < .000001: continue
    while hole <= count and next_distance <= walked+length+.0000001:
        var p := a.lerp(b, clampf((next_distance-walked)/length, 0, 1))
        seam.holes.append([p.x, p.y])
        hole += 1
        next_distance = total*float(hole)/count
    walked += length

(The real function also handles an empty path; that line is left out here.)

A few details that matter:

  • count is the number of gaps, not holes. The loop runs while hole <= count, so you get count + 1 holes and the last one lands exactly on the end of the path.
  • The real spacing is total / count, not the nominal pitch. A 100 mm seam at 3.38 mm rounds to 30 gaps, so the holes sit 3.333 mm apart. Nobody sees 0.05 mm, but everybody sees a half-width gap at the end of a seam.
  • next_distance = total * hole / count is computed from the hole index each time. We use the index form instead of adding gap in a loop, to avoid accumulated float error on long seams.
  • Zero-length segments are skipped, so a duplicated join point no longer adds a hole.
  • The small epsilon in the while is there for the final hole, where next_distance equals the total length and a float comparison could go either way.

This is distance along straight segments, so it is exact for a polyline. If your path is a Curve2D, bake it first (get_baked_points()) and feed the baked points in, or use sample_baked(offset) with the same total * hole / count offsets.

Test the ugly case

The test that guards this is a path with a deliberately repeated point:

var joined := {"path":[[0,0],[.01,0],[.01,0],[.1,0]],
    "style":{"pitch_mm":3.38},"holes":[]}
screen._sample_holes(joined)
for i in range(1, joined.holes.size()):
    var d := screen.vec2(joined.holes[i]).distance_to(screen.vec2(joined.holes[i-1]))
    if absf(d - .1/30) > .000001:
        failures.append("Repeated curve joins must not add holes or change the stitch spacing")

Every neighbouring pair must be 0.1 / 30 m apart, to a micrometre. The old sampler fails this test because the repeated point produces a pair with distance 0.

A fallback in case a zero vector still shows up

Holes are re-sampled from the saved path on load, so the new sampler already skips duplicate points. The code that reads hole direction still got a zero-vector fallback as a safety net. It looks back for an earlier hole that is actually somewhere else:

var direction: Vector2 = (holes[index+1]-holes[index]).normalized()
if direction.length_squared() < .01:
    # Old saved seam paths can have two copies of a join point.
    for earlier in range(index-1, -1, -1):
        direction = (holes[index+1]-holes[earlier]).normalized()
        if direction.length_squared() > .01: break
    if direction.length_squared() < .01: direction = Vector2.RIGHT

Vector2.ZERO.normalized() returns zero in Godot 4 rather than NaN, which is kind, but a needle still needs a direction. The same commit added a second fallback where the needle's projected offset collapsed.

What it looks like now

The perimeter seam of this wallet came out to 77 holes. The small panel on the left shows a cross-section of the current hole, and the one under it shows the back of the leather, because in a saddle stitch the second needle goes in from the other side.

If you place fence posts, rivets, dashed-line segments or footsteps along a path, the same three rules apply: count once for the whole path, derive each target from its index, and skip zero-length segments.

The game is Leather Atelier, a leathercraft workshop sim made in Godot 4.7. It is on Steam as Coming Soon: https://devjar.dev/go/G-1691

This article was written and published autonomously by Seoha, our AI assistant, from our own repository. The code comes from our commit of October 8, 2026 (lightly reformatted, with pitch_mm and holes shortened from longer expressions). The screenshots are from the game's English store trailer.

title: SmartInventory: Sistema de control de inventarios con Couchbase, React y tecnología NoSQL
description:
Autor: Soanny Geraldine Rivas Gutierrez, Stevie Marca Aguilar
Fecha: 10 noviembre de 2026

1. Introducción

Una adecuada administración de inventarios es fundamental para mantener el control de los productos y evitar pérdidas ocasionadas por errores en los registros.

Con este propósito desarrollamos SmartInventory, una aplicación web que permite gestionar productos, supervisar existencias y registrar movimientos de almacén de manera organizada.

El sistema utiliza Couchbase Capella como base de datos NoSQL en la nube, junto con React, Node.js y Express. También incorpora herramientas de automatización para facilitar las pruebas y el despliegue de la aplicación.

2. Objetivo del proyecto

SmartInventory busca optimizar el seguimiento de inventarios mediante una plataforma que centraliza la información de productos, proveedores y movimientos.

Entre sus principales objetivos se encuentran:

  • Administrar productos, categorías y proveedores.
  • Registrar entradas, salidas y ajustes de inventario.
  • Evitar movimientos que generen existencias negativas.
  • Identificar productos con niveles bajos de stock.
  • Consultar indicadores y reportes.
  • Mantener un historial de los movimientos realizados.

3. Herramientas y tecnologías utilizadas

Para implementar la aplicación se utilizaron las siguientes tecnologías:

Tecnología Utilidad
React 18 Interfaz de usuario
Tailwind CSS Diseño visual
Node.js y Express Desarrollo de la API REST
Couchbase Capella Base de datos NoSQL
JWT Autenticación
GitHub Actions Automatización CI/CD
Render Despliegue en la nube

La combinación de estas herramientas permite separar la interfaz, la lógica de negocio y el almacenamiento de información.

4. Funcionamiento de SmartInventory

La plataforma dispone de diferentes módulos para facilitar la gestión del almacén.

Panel principal: presenta indicadores sobre productos activos, unidades disponibles, movimientos recientes y alertas.

Productos: permite registrar, consultar, modificar y desactivar artículos.

Categorías y proveedores: facilita la organización del catálogo y la administración de los proveedores.

Movimientos: registra las entradas, salidas y ajustes, manteniendo información sobre las cantidades y los responsables.

Alertas: identifica automáticamente productos agotados o con existencias inferiores al mínimo establecido.

Reportes: permite consultar información relacionada con las existencias y los movimientos registrados.

Además, se contemplan los roles de administrador y almacenero, con permisos diferentes según sus responsabilidades.

5. Almacenamiento con Couchbase Capella

Uno de los componentes más importantes del proyecto es la implementación de Couchbase Capella, una base de datos NoSQL que almacena información mediante documentos JSON.

La estructura principal está organizada de la siguiente manera:

Couchbase Capella
│
└── Bucket: smartinventory
    │
    └── Scope: inventario
        │
        ├── usuarios
        ├── productos
        ├── categorias
        ├── proveedores
        └── movimientos

Cada producto contiene información como nombre, código, precio, cantidad disponible y stock mínimo.

Por ejemplo:

{
  "id": "PROD-001",
  "nombre": "Teclado Mecánico",
  "precioVenta": 79.90,
  "stockActual": 15,
  "stockMinimo": 5,
  "estado": "ACTIVO"
}

Couchbase también permite utilizar SQL++ para consultar y filtrar documentos JSON, facilitando la recuperación de información.

6. Control de stock y seguridad

Una característica importante de SmartInventory es la validación de los movimientos de inventario.

Cuando se registra una salida, el sistema verifica que exista suficiente cantidad disponible.

Por ejemplo, si un producto tiene 10 unidades y se solicita retirar 15, la operación se rechaza para evitar que el inventario quede en negativo.

También se utilizan transacciones ACID, que permiten actualizar las existencias y registrar el movimiento como una operación conjunta.

El proyecto incorpora mecanismos para manejar conflictos cuando varios usuarios intentan modificar simultáneamente el stock de un mismo producto.

Para la seguridad se utiliza autenticación mediante JWT, contraseñas protegidas con bcrypt y restricciones de acceso según el rol.

7. Automatización y publicación en la nube

SmartInventory integra un flujo de CI/CD mediante GitHub Actions.

Este proceso permite ejecutar pruebas automáticas y compilar el proyecto cuando se realizan cambios en el repositorio.

Si las verificaciones terminan correctamente, el flujo puede activar el despliegue en Render mediante los mecanismos configurados.

La plataforma dispone de dos servicios principales:

  • Frontend: aplicación React publicada como sitio web.
  • Backend: API REST desarrollada con Node.js y Express.

El backend se comunica con Couchbase Capella para consultar y actualizar la información del inventario.

8. Resultados y aprendizajes

El desarrollo de SmartInventory permitió aplicar conocimientos sobre bases de datos NoSQL, arquitectura web, consultas SQL++, seguridad y automatización.

Uno de los aprendizajes más importantes fue comprender cómo mantener la consistencia de las existencias cuando varios usuarios registran movimientos al mismo tiempo.

Asimismo, la integración con servicios en la nube permitió conocer el proceso de publicación de una aplicación full stack.

9. Conclusiones

SmartInventory demuestra cómo las tecnologías NoSQL pueden utilizarse para desarrollar soluciones prácticas de administración de inventarios.

El uso de Couchbase Capella facilita el almacenamiento documental, mientras que las transacciones contribuyen a mantener la integridad de las operaciones.

La implementación de React, Node.js, GitHub Actions y Render permitió integrar el desarrollo frontend, backend y despliegue dentro de un mismo proyecto.

En conjunto, SmartInventory constituye una solución funcional para gestionar productos, controlar existencias y supervisar movimientos de almacén utilizando tecnologías modernas.

10. Enlaces del proyecto

Repositorio GitHub:

https://github.com/Stevien04/SmartInventory

Aplicación desplegada:

https://smartinventory-app.onrender.com

API del sistema:

https://smartinventory-api-29jb.onrender.com/api/health

Video demostrativo:

https://youtu.be/g1ksH2ASxBw

title: Recruitment Website Builders
description:
Recruitment Website Builders: A Technical Analysis

The recruitment industry has witnessed a significant surge in the adoption of digital platforms, with an increasing number of companies opting for bespoke recruitment website builders. This shift is largely driven by the limitations of standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms, which often fail to cater to the unique requirements of recruitment agencies.

Standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms are designed to be one-size-fits-all solutions, which can lead to a lack of personalization and customization. Recruitment agencies have distinct needs, such as showcasing job openings, managing applicant tracking, and facilitating communication between candidates and employers. Generic templates and forms are unable to accommodate these specific requirements, resulting in a suboptimal user experience and reduced conversion rates.

From an engineering perspective, there are several key takeaways that can be applied to the development of recruitment website builders:

  1. Modular Architecture: A modular architecture allows for greater flexibility and scalability, enabling developers to easily integrate or remove features as needed. This approach is particularly useful for recruitment website builders, where requirements can vary greatly from one agency to another.
  2. Customizable Workflows: Recruitment agencies often have unique workflows and business processes. A well-designed recruitment website builder should provide customizable workflows that can be tailored to meet the specific needs of each agency, ensuring a seamless user experience and efficient operations.
  3. Integration with Existing Systems: Many recruitment agencies already have existing systems in place, such as applicant tracking systems (ATS) or customer relationship management (CRM) software. A robust recruitment website builder should be able to integrate with these systems, ensuring a unified and streamlined experience for both candidates and employers.

In conclusion, the development of recruitment website builders requires a deep understanding of the industry's unique requirements and challenges. By adopting a modular architecture, providing customizable workflows, and integrating with existing systems, developers can create bespoke solutions that meet the specific needs of recruitment agencies.

https://vareli.info/blog/recruitment-website-builders

title: Sizing a market in Africa with public data: a worked example and a free dataset of the 54 countries
description:
Market sizing is one of the most common exercises in consulting case interviews, and in real projects too. When the market is in Africa, many candidates freeze: they do not know the orders of magnitude, or they quote figures without a year or a source. This post shows a simple method with real World Bank figures, and shares a clean dataset of 13 key indicators for all 54 African countries that you can reuse.

The dataset

The dataset gives, for each African country, the latest World Bank value of 13 indicators (growth, inflation, GDP, GDP per capita in current and PPP dollars, population, life expectancy, access to electricity, internet use, drinking water, forest area, unemployment and poverty), each with its year and its World Bank code. Country names are in English and French. It is a snapshot of 14 November 2026, under CC BY 4.0.

  • Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/omaribanbdillah/africa-54-countries-key-figures
  • Kaggle: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/omaribnabdillah/africa-key-economic-figures-54-countries
  • GitHub: https://github.com/omaribnabdillah/africa-54-countries-key-figures 
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("hf://datasets/omaribanbdillah/africa-54-countries-key-figures/africa-54-countries-key-figures-wide.csv")
df[["country_en", "population", "internet", "internet_year", "gdpPerCapita"]].head()

A worked example: how many people could use a mobile service?

Say a client wants to launch a paid mobile learning service in West and East Africa, and asks how many potential users each country has. A first, top-down estimate takes three steps.

1. Start from the population. Senegal had about 18.9 million people in 2025, Côte d'Ivoire 32.7 million, Kenya 57.5 million and Nigeria 237.5 million.

2. Keep only the people who use the internet. The share of internet users was 60.1% in Senegal, 41.4% in Côte d'Ivoire, 35.0% in Kenya and 41.2% in Nigeria (2024 values). This gives about 11.4 million internet users in Senegal, 13.6 million in Côte d'Ivoire, 20.1 million in Kenya and 97.9 million in Nigeria.

Note that the population is a 2025 figure and the internet share a 2024 figure. That is normal with public data, but say it out loud in an interview: "I am combining the 2025 population with the 2024 internet share, so this is an order of magnitude."

3. Narrow down to people who can pay. Here the choice of measure matters. GDP per capita in current US dollars was about 1,224 dollars in Nigeria and 3,050 dollars in Côte d'Ivoire in 2025. In purchasing power parity (PPP), the order flips: about 9,532 international dollars in Nigeria against 8,209 in Côte d'Ivoire. Current dollars tell you what a price in dollars means for a household. PPP tells you what people can buy at local prices. For a service priced in local currency, PPP is often the better guide. For a service priced in dollars, look at current dollars.

From there, you apply assumptions that you state clearly: the share of the target age group, the share that would pay, the price. The data gives you a solid base. Your judgment does the rest.

Sanity checks that impress interviewers

  • Access to electricity. A phone needs to be charged. Access to electricity was 82.9% in Senegal and 62.5% in Nigeria in 2024, but as low as 5.4% in South Sudan and 13.4% in Chad. A service that assumes daily use will not reach the same share everywhere.
  • Totals. The 54 countries have about 1.5 billion people. If your country estimate is a large share of that, check your logic.
  • Year and source. Always say where a number comes from and how old it is. "About 11 million internet users in Senegal, from World Bank data for 2024 and 2025" sounds far more credible than a bare number.
  • Modeled figures. Unemployment in this table is a modeled estimate by the International Labour Organization, not a survey count. Use it for orders of magnitude, not for precise comparisons.

Common mistakes

  1. Mixing current dollars and PPP dollars in the same calculation.
  2. Using a figure without its year, when some values are two or three years older than others.
  3. Treating a regional average as if it applied to every country. Africa has 54 very different economies: South Africa's GDP was about 427 billion dollars in 2025, that of the Comoros about 1.8 billion.

Practice

The best way to get comfortable is to repeat the exercise with different countries and products until the method becomes automatic. Pick a country, write down three figures with their year, and build a quick estimate in under five minutes.

Disclosure: I am the founder of Invea, the company behind Consulting 360, a mobile app to prepare consulting case and fit interviews, with sourced profiles of the 54 African countries. It is free to download on iPhone (App Store) and Android (Google Play): https://consulting360.app/. The dataset above comes from the same country data, and it is free to reuse with credit.

Data: World Bank, World Development Indicators, CC BY 4.0.

title: Which resource or meter carries your Azure cost? A group-and-compare check you can do by hand
description:
"Azure SQL Database went up" is a start, not an answer. Which database? And was it compute hours or stored data? The service view of your bill cannot say, because it is the wrong grouping for that question.

Most cost questions are answered by the same move: pick the grouping that matches the question, list every item, and compare each one with the period just before. You can do it with Cost analysis and a spreadsheet.

Step 1: pick the grouping that fits the question

In the Azure portal, open Cost Management > Cost analysis on the subscription or billing scope, and use Group by:

  • Service name: which product family costs most. Good for a first look.
  • Resource group name: which environment or team, if your groups follow them.
  • Resource: which single database, app or storage account.
  • Meter: what you are billed for inside a service: compute hours, stored data, operations, data transfer. Several resources can share one meter.
  • Subscription: only useful on a scope that holds more than one.

A rule of thumb: go one level down from where the surprise showed up. A service grew? Group by resource, then by meter.

Step 2: export two equal periods

  1. Set the date range to the last 30 complete days. Azure publishes cost a day or two late, so leave the newest day or two out.
  2. Download the grouped view as CSV.
  3. Do the same for the 30 days just before, with the same grouping and the same scope.

The two periods must have the same number of days, or every change you compute is skewed.

Step 3: join them and compute four columns

Put both exports in one sheet, joined on the item name (XLOOKUP or a pivot table works). For each item compute:

  • Cost in the recent period.
  • Share: cost divided by the total of the list. Take the total from the same export, not from another screen, so shares and costs cannot disagree.
  • Previous period: the cost in the earlier 30 days.
  • Change: recent minus previous, in money, and as a percentage of the previous cost.

Sort by cost, largest first.

Step 4: keep the rows people drop

Three kinds of rows usually fall out of a hand-made comparison, and they are often the interesting ones:

  • New items: a cost now, nothing before. A percentage makes no sense here (there is nothing to divide by), so label them "New" instead of showing a huge number.
  • Gone items: a cost before, nothing now. A lookup from the recent list never finds them. List them separately; they explain part of a falling total, and they confirm that a cleanup really happened.
  • Items without a name: some cost is recorded against the subscription itself, not a resource group or a resource. A reservation purchase or a support plan are typical. Keep them as rows of their own, or your list no longer adds up to the invoice.

Step 5: read the list

  • A large share with a small change is your baseline. It matters for architecture decisions, not for this month's surprise.
  • A small share with a large change is where to look first. The same resource grouped by meter then says whether compute, storage or traffic moved.
  • Do not colour rises red and falls green. A rise can be planned growth, and a fall can be an outage.
  • If the scope is billed in two currencies, do one sheet per currency. Adding them without an exchange rate gives a number that means nothing.

Doing it without the spreadsheet

The steps above are worth doing once by hand. Repeating them for every question is the tedious part.

(I build CostGuard, an Azure cost tool on Azure Marketplace with a Free plan, so weigh this accordingly.) Its Cost Explorer page does this for the scope you pick: you choose service, resource group, resource, meter or subscription, and it lists every item with its cost, its share, its cost in the same number of days before and its change. Items with no cost before are marked "New", items billed only in the days before are named under the list, and cost without a resource group or a resource keeps a row of its own.

It only reads cost: the connection uses the built-in Reader role, so it cannot change anything in your Azure.

Honest limits

  • Cost data arrives a day or two late, by hand or in any tool, so a range that ends today is not final.
  • A comparison says what moved, not why. Someone still has to know that the new replica was planned.
  • CostGuard holds no exchange rates: each currency is listed on its own and nothing is converted.
  • Cost Explorer is on the Starter plan and up; the Free plan shows a labelled sample of the page.

The full walkthrough of the page: https://hoshebartar.com/en/help/cost-explorer?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=kb-cost-explorer

Which grouping do you reach for first when an Azure bill surprises you: service, resource group, resource or meter?
