title: Rust 1.100 Is Out. I Installed It This Morning and Tried the Three Things That Actually Matter
description:
Rust 1.100.0 landed on Thursday, November 12. Three days later I upgraded my own machine from 1.99.1 and spent the morning putting the headline features through their paces: the never type, custom allocators, and Cargo's two new supply-chain features. Everything below ran on my machine, and the numbers are the ones I actually saw.

The upgrade itself

One command, about ninety seconds, and rustc --version went from 1.99.1 (58cf8f9c3 2026-10-13) to 1.100.0 (0ef1bc386 2026-11-09). Nothing broke on the way up. That matters, because this release does carry one change the release notes flag as potentially breaking, and I'll get to it.

The never type, ten years later

The headline is !, the never type. It's the type of an expression that never produces a value. A panic!(), an endless loop, a function that exits the process. People have been able to use it for years. But naming it anywhere a type goes, writing Result<u32, !> for a result that can never fail, took ten years and five failed stabilization attempts to land.

The first thing I tried was the obvious one:

let ok: Result<u32, !> = Ok(42);

It compiles, and it reads the way you'd hope. This result has no error case, and the type system now says so out loud. Infallible is now just an alias for !, which tidies up a decade of Result<T, Infallible> signatures.

The part worth paying attention to is the fallback change, because it's the one that can bite existing code. When the compiler can't work out what type a ! expression should be, it used to fall back to (). On 1.100 it falls back to ! instead, on every edition, not just 2024. I checked this directly with a snippet where the type is genuinely unconstrained: a closure that never runs, collecting into a Vec of unknown element type:

let v: Vec<_> = (0..0).map(|_| panic!()).collect();
println!("element type: {}", std::any::type_name_of_val(&v));

On 1.99.1 that prints alloc::vec::Vec<()>. On 1.100.0 it prints alloc::vec::Vec<!>. Same code, different inferred type. Most code will never notice. The fallback only matters where a type was left completely unspecified. But if your build breaks after this upgrade and the error mentions ! where you expected (), this is the change to look at. The other two things the release notes flag for the same reason: closures now capture variables used in if let more precisely, and some Box implementations were generalised to arbitrary allocators, which can surface as new inference errors.

Custom allocators: Vec in my own arena

The second big item is the core of the allocator API, first proposed years ago and unstable until now. Vec and Box can live in an allocator you define, instead of the global one. I wrote a tiny bump allocator: a fixed 64 KiB buffer, a cursor, nothing else. Then I put a Vec inside it:

let bump = Bump::new();
let mut v: Vec<u32, &Bump> = Vec::new_in(&bump);
for i in 0..1000 {
    v.push(i * i);
}

It ran first try. The output:

Vec in bump arena: len=1000, sum=332833500, arena used=8176 bytes
Box in bump arena: 0xdeadbeef, arena used=8184 bytes

A thousand squares, 8,176 bytes of arena used. The Vec's four allocations (it grows 4, 8, 16… up to 4,096 bytes, plus alignment padding) land exactly where you'd expect, and a Box::new_in next to it takes 8 more bytes. The sum checks out against the closed form (999 × 1000 × 1999 / 6 = 332,833,500), so the Vec really holds what I think it holds.

Who is this for? Not most of us, honestly. If you're writing a game engine, an embedded runtime, or anything where allocation patterns are part of the design, this is the release you've been waiting for. Vec::new_in, Vec::with_capacity_in and Box::new_in are the whole story. If you're writing a web service, you'll probably never touch it, and that's fine. It's a foundation, not a feature you have to use.

Two smaller additions from the same release that I will use: bool::toggle() (finally, no more flag = !flag) and core::mem::DropGuard, which runs a closure when it drops while keeping the value usable in the meantime. Both worked exactly as documented.

Cargo's two supply-chain features

Cargo gets the most practical upgrade in this release, and both parts are about the same worry: the dependencies you pull in.

Unused dependency warnings. Cargo now tells you when a dependency in your manifest is never used, through the new cargo::unused_dependencies lint. I added itoa to a test project and used nothing from it:

warning: unused dependency `itoa`
  --> Cargo.toml:10:1
   |
10 | itoa = "1"
   | ^^^^^^^^^^
   |
   = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default
help: consider removing the dependency on `itoa`

Warn by default, and it becomes a hard error if you set it to deny in [lints.cargo]. I tried both, and the deny version fails the build with the same message as an error. This is the kind of lint that pays for itself the first time it catches a dependency someone added "just in case" three years ago.

Dependency cooldowns. Set registry.global-min-publish-age and the resolver skips crate versions published more recently than that age, unless they're already in your lockfile. The idea is simple. Most malicious crate versions get caught within days of publication, so waiting a week before adopting anything new closes that window. One gotcha I hit while setting it up: "7d" is rejected. The value has to read like "7 days":

error: invalid value for `registry.global-min-publish-age`:
expected a value of the form "N seconds/minutes/hours/days/weeks/months",
got: "7d"

With "7 days" in place, the build passed with the locked versions untouched. I should be honest about the limit of what I tested here: the protection only bites on a fresh resolve, when the resolver is choosing versions. My test project already had a lockfile, so I watched the config get accepted, not the resolver refuse a version. The next fresh project I start will be the real test.

Did anything get faster?

I timed clean release builds of a small project (serde, serde_json, clap) on both toolchains, twice each:

Toolchain Run 1 Run 2
1.99.1 29.1s 29.4s
1.100.0 31.1s 29.9s

No measurable difference. The 1.100 numbers sit inside the same noise band as 1.99.1, and a two-second spread on a 30-second build of a small project is not a finding. It's the machine breathing. Nobody should upgrade for compile speed. (The release does stabilise -Cprofile-sample-use, sample-based PGO, which is a real performance lever for production binaries. But that's a profiling setup, not something a clean-build timer would show.)

Should you upgrade?

Yes, and the checklist is short. Run your test suite on 1.100 before you commit to it. The fallback change is narrow but real, and it's exactly the kind of thing that shows up in one weird corner of a big codebase rather than everywhere at once. If you maintain a library, the Box generalisation is the other one to watch for. Everything else in this release is additive: the never type, the allocator API, the Cargo lints and the cooldowns are all things you can adopt when they fit, not things you have to deal with on upgrade day.

The round number is a coincidence, mostly. Rust 1.100 is not a new era and not a rewrite. It's a solid release with one ten-year-old feature finally landing, one genuinely useful Cargo upgrade, and a small breaking change hiding in the compatibility notes. Read those notes, run your tests, then upgrade. That's the whole plan.

Sources

  • Rust 1.100.0 release notes: dev-doc.rust-lang.org/stable/releases.html (Version 1.100.0, 2026-11-12)
  • Never type, custom allocators, Cargo lints and cooldowns, compatibility notes: same page, sections Language / Libraries / Stabilized APIs / Cargo / Compatibility Notes
  • Every number in this article comes from runs on my own machine on 2026-11-15: rustc 1.100.0 (0ef1bc386 2026-11-09), upgraded from rustc 1.99.1 (58cf8f9c3 2026-10-13)

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: Designing the first 10 seconds of a quit-vaping app: one button for a craving
description:
A vaping craving usually peaks and passes within minutes. The problem is those minutes. CraveBreaker is built around one button, "I have a craving", and what happens in the first few seconds after you tap it.

The craving screen: no account, no paywall, no questionnaire

  • A 90-second reset: slow breathing plus a quiet 5-4-3-2-1 grounding exercise.
  • Pattern Break: a small puzzle to pull your attention somewhere else.
  • A craving timer: 1, 3 or 5 minutes or your own length. Stop early or add time.
  • Your reasons: the words you wrote for yourself, shown back to you.
  • Change the routine: practical swaps for coffee, driving, stress and work breaks.
  • Reach out: text someone you trust, or find free quitline support (U.S. and Canada).

Every craving tool is free, always. That was a deliberate decision: the moment someone needs help is the worst moment for a purchase screen.

Data that only says what you recorded

Log a craving in seconds: situation, intensity, what you tried, and whether you vaped. Patterns only appear once you've logged enough to be meaningful, and they're shown as observations, not causes. The app doesn't claim to measure your body; progress is your quit date, your vape-free stretch, total vape-free days and cravings handled.

A lapse doesn't erase progress

Vaped? Record it without judgment. Your original quit date, total vape-free days and milestones stay. You look at what happened, adjust the plan and pick a next step. Resetting everything to zero after one slip is a common design choice, and we think it pushes people to quit the app instead of the vape.

Savings, with the formula shown

Enter what you spent per week or month and see estimated spending avoided, with the calculation visible. You can also record money you actually set aside.

Guides on cravings, withdrawal, triggers and lapses are short and sourced from Smokefree.gov and Health Canada guidance. Everything runs privately and offline.

CraveBreaker: Quit Vaping is free on the iPhone App Store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/cravebreaker-quit-vaping/id6787461078

Have you designed for a "moment of need" screen? What did you remove to make it faster?

title: How to cut token costs without dropping Claude 3.7
description:
API bills eat up project budgets. Processing text through Claude 3.7 Sonnet at $3 per million input tokens or renting AWS H100 instances directly at $6.88 per hour makes mass generation unprofitable. Rewriting production from the familiar PyTorch and CUDA stack to JAX just to save money takes too long. Free engineering hands for such massive tasks are usually unavailable.

We will break down the pricing mechanics in the hardware market and set up hybrid routing through a single gateway to redirect routine tasks to cheap TPU chips.

Where the graphics card shortage came from and the 108 billion dollars behind it

The market long believed in a natural shortage of computing power. A Wall Street Journal investigation showed the hidden mechanics of price formation. Nvidia management forced circular financing deals with cloud providers and AI startups in the second half of 2026 under the leadership of former CEO Jensen Huang. The scheme worked directly. The chipmaker gave startups loans or invested money in them on the condition of buying Nvidia equipment. The company actively absorbed the excess of semiconductor wafers from TSMC. This helped artificially keep graphics processor prices at a consistently high level. Startups received hardware while Nvidia showed record revenue.

Sharp conflicts began inside the company around the scale of guaranteed deals. Jensen Huang criticized CFO Colette Kress after her appointment as interim CEO. She demanded a sharp reduction in financial obligations and the termination of the agreement with OpenAI. The contract included guarantees of 250 billion dollars to build the largest data center.

Nvidia's official financial report for the quarter ending July 26, 2026, recorded a maximum volume of credit and lease guarantees to customers totaling 108.5 billion dollars. Out of this amount, 105 billion dollars went to support the OpenAI data center campus in Ohio. Such financial injections created the illusion of endless demand for equipment. Legal consequences have not yet arrived. The US Department of Justice and the SEC have not officially charged Nvidia with cartel collusion or stock market manipulation. Inside the company, such deals are classified as standard vendor project financing.

Redirecting TSMC silicon wafers and memory chips toward data center AI accelerators caused an instant spike in consumer prices. Memory manufacturers switched their assembly lines to produce HBM chips for servers. Regular DDR5 RAM went up in price right after graphics cards. GeForce graphics cards exceeded 160 percent of the recommended retail price. The flagship RTX 5090 model became practically unavailable for open purchase. Gamers and independent researchers lost the ability to build local workstations at a reasonable price.

Market rates for renting graphics chips were artificially inflated. The annual lease of an H100 accelerator rose from $1.70 per hour in October 2025 to $2.35 in March 2026. The median on-demand price reached $2.70 by June 2026. Rates for the Blackwell B200 generation fluctuate from $5.30 to $7.05 per hour of chip operation. On the AWS platform, renting an H100 instance reaches $6.88 per hour. A typical AI startup stack generating a million tokens a day became 40 percent more expensive in just one year.

How much a million tokens cost across different vendors

The difference in hardware costs directly reflects on API prices. We collected current rates for November 2026 for popular text generation models. Vendors factor the cost of equipment depreciation into every generated token.

Model name Price per 1M input tokens Price per 1M output tokens
Claude 3.7 Sonnet $3.00 $15.00
Claude Sonnet 5.5 $2.00 $10.00
GPT-4o-mini $0.15 $0.60
Claude Haiku 5.5 $0.10 $0.50
Gemini 2.0 Flash $0.10 $0.40

The Gemini 2.0 Flash model is 30 times cheaper than Claude 3.7 Sonnet on input tokens. The price gap on output tokens between these same models reaches 37.5 times. Calls to the lightweight OpenAI GPT-4o-mini model cost $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output. Cached context for GPT-4o-mini costs developers $0.075.

The flagship reasoning model Claude 3.7 Sonnet in the Anthropic API costs $3.00 per million input tokens and $15.00 per million output tokens. This amount includes the mandatory generation of thinking tokens. Hitting the cache lowers the input cost to $0.30. The Claude Haiku 5.5 model is priced at $0.10 per million input and $0.50 per million output tokens for prompts up to 100,000 tokens.

The blended rate for Gemini 2.0 Flash is $0.50 per million input and million output tokens combined. This is 33 percent cheaper than the previous Gemini 1.5 Flash generation. The difference in rates is explained by data center architecture and the cost of the chips used.

The exact internal margin per token remains unknown. Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic publicly disclose their profit and loss regarding the cost price of each specific token. You cannot say exactly what share of the $15 per million Sonnet tokens goes to amortizing Nvidia clusters and what covers research or electricity bills. Cartel markup estimates are calculated by analysts through the hourly chip rental cost and throughput.

Why TPU inference costs less

Chip economics rely on power consumption and production costs. The sixth-generation TPU Trillium consumes 300W TDP. The Nvidia H100 accelerator requires 700W TDP, while the power consumption of the Blackwell B200 generation reaches 1200W. The difference provides 2.3 times higher energy efficiency per watt during continuous inference. A cluster of tens of thousands of chips saves megawatts of electricity every hour. Lower heat output reduces the cost of liquid cooling systems in data centers. Cooling infrastructure takes up to a third of the budget when building a server farm based on Blackwell.

The hourly rental of a TPU v5e in Google Cloud is $1.20 per chip on demand and $0.54 with a three-year contract. Renting a TPU v6e Trillium will cost $2.70 on demand and $1.22 with long-term reservation. Renting an AWS H100 instance costs about $6.88 per hour. Thanks to full hardware stack optimization on their own TPU accelerators, Google's unit cost for Gemini model inference dropped by 78 percent in 2025.

The full cost price of Google TPU chips for third parties is also unpublished. Google sells Gemini API tokens with a subsidized margin inside its ecosystem. The exact production cost of TPUs at TSMC factories and Google's net savings per generated token remain a commercial secret of Alphabet.

Where specialized chips lose to graphics processors

Inference on specialized ASIC chips does not automatically win in speed on every request. With single interactive queries featuring low parallelism and a batch size of 1 to 4, modern Nvidia graphics processors deliver comparable or lower time to first token. The massive TensorRT and vLLM ecosystem perfectly optimizes single calls. GPU architecture with high memory bandwidth is ideal for an instant response to a single user. Graphics processors load model weights into memory faster during frequent context switching.

TPUs provide a 50 to 70 percent price advantage only on large batches starting from 32 requests. This requires high cluster utilization and a constant stream of tokens. With a three-year reservation of TPU Trillium capacity, the cost of generating a million tokens using dense 70B models drops to $0.42. The same task on AWS H100 instances on demand costs $0.91 or $0.94. Developers of low-load chatbots might not notice the speed difference, but they will see a difference in their bills.

The creators of Claude are also moving away from the CUDA monopoly

Dependence on graphics cards hits the profit margins of AI developers themselves. There is a widespread belief that advanced labs depend exclusively on the CUDA stack. In practice, the situation is changing very quickly.

Anthropic historically trained its models on Nvidia clusters. In November 2025, the company signed the largest deal in Google Cloud history. The developers of Claude reserved hundreds of thousands of TPU Trillium chips for 2026. The agreement includes scaling capacity to a million chips by 2027.

Anthropic uses this capacity to reduce infrastructure dependence on Nvidia GPUs during inference. Scaling a commercial API solely on graphics cards proved unprofitable even for market leaders. Switching to other chips became a matter of business survival.

Hybrid routing through a single API replaces rewriting code

Moving from PyTorch and CUDA to JAX and XLA on your own requires hundreds of engineering hours. For a single company, such a step is often economically pointless. Using different SDKs for different vendors is also inconvenient. Developers have to maintain several data contracts and handle different error formats.

The problem of library zoos is solved by model routing at the level of a single API gateway like AltRouter. The application sends standard JSON requests, and the router directs large contexts to the ultra-cheap Gemini Flash. Expensive GPU models are kept only for critical final output.

We can send a 50,000-token text to the Gemini 2.5 Flash model to extract facts. We pass the filtered data of 2,000 tokens to Claude Sonnet 5.5 for final formatting. Without a single gateway, a developer has to write integration with two different libraries. The code grows with extra type checks and network failure handlers for each vendor separately. Maintaining such a zoo of dependencies takes time away from the product team. In code, a manual cascade looks like a sequential call to two different APIs.

from google import genai
import anthropic

gemini_client = genai.Client(api_key="YOUR_GEMINI_API_KEY")
claude_client = anthropic.Anthropic(api_key="YOUR_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")

raw_documents = "Very long text from the knowledge base spanning 50,000 tokens..."

# Step 1: Draft processing on a cheap model
draft_response = gemini_client.models.generate_content(
    model='gemini-2.5-flash',
    contents=f"Extract only key facts and numbers:\n{raw_documents}"
)
extracted_facts = draft_response.text

# Step 2: Final output on a smart model
final_response = claude_client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5.5",
    max_tokens=1000,
    system="Write an analytical report based on the facts.",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": extracted_facts}
    ]
)

print(final_response.content[0].text)

Looking at the price list, sending 50,000 tokens directly to Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs $0.10. Processing 50,000 tokens through Gemini 2.5 Flash costs $0.0135 at the rate of $0.27 per million. The subsequent sending of the compressed 2,000 tokens to Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs another $0.004. Total expenses amount to $0.0175.

Using Gemini 2.5 Flash for draft fact extraction lowers the cost of processing long context by 82.5 percent compared to sending it directly to Claude Sonnet 5.5. With a volume of ten thousand requests a day, the savings reach 825 dollars. The difference covers the salary of several developers for a month.

How to split traffic in a production application

Model selection depends on context size and latency requirements. Routing rules in the code help avoid overpaying for routine tasks.

Use case Batch size Recommended model
Interactive chat with a user 1 to 4 Claude 3.7 Sonnet
Mass background log parsing 32+ Gemini 2.0 Flash
Complex agents with function calling 1 to 4 Claude Sonnet 5.5
Context filtering for RAG 32+ Claude Haiku 5.5

Mass background log parsing requires processing millions of lines. Sending such a volume to Claude 3.7 Sonnet will bankrupt a project in a couple of days. Gemini 2.0 Flash handles the task for pennies. Complex agents with function calling require strict logic. Here Claude Sonnet 5.5 pays off its price through a minimal hallucination rate.

Background tasks and large texts go to models with a low input token price. Flagship solutions remain for tasks with a high cost of error. Splitting the streams cuts token costs without losing the quality of the final response. Set up cascade processing once to permanently untie your project budget from the cost of renting graphics cards.

title: I built an AI agent that turns scattered recipes into a print-ready cookbook
description:
Every family has one: a drawer of handwritten recipe cards, a Word doc from years ago, a few PDFs, and a camera roll full of dishes. Turning that into a real book usually means weeks of retyping and fighting with layout tools.

I built Cookbook AI so that takes minutes instead.

How it works

  1. Drop in your recipes. Paste text or upload PDFs, Word docs, or photos. The agent reads them first and drafts a page-by-page outline. Your recipes go in as-is; it doesn't rewrite them.
  2. Confirm the outline and pick a style. Review the plan, choose a look, and watch each page get designed and illustrated live. You can also just tell it what you want in chat — it asks questions, then designs the pages.
  3. Refine, then print or share. Edit any page, then export a print-ready A4 PDF or send a share link.

A few details I cared about:

  • Clean recipe layout — ingredients, steps and servings laid out clearly on every page, no manual formatting.
  • No bare pages — if a dish has no photo, the agent generates or finds an image for it.
  • Print that actually fits — every page fits A4 without overflow, so it's easy to print and bind at home.

Why an agent instead of a template

Templates still leave you with the tedious middle step: copying text into boxes and deciding what goes where. The agent takes over that part — reading unstructured input, planning the book, and laying out every page — so you only make the decisions that matter: which recipes, and which look.

Who's using it

  • Families turning grandma's cards into a keepsake recipe book
  • Private chefs and small kitchens making a recipe book or menu
  • Health and food creators turning a meal plan into a downloadable cookbook

Try it

It's free to start at cookbookai.io. I'd love feedback from other builders — what would you want an AI agent to handle when turning your own notes into a book?

title: 🧱 A Java Architecture Stack, Layer by Layer: From APIs to Availability and Recovery
description:
A Java Architecture Stack, Layer by Layer: From APIs to Availability and Recovery

A production system is rarely one application. It is a stack of concerns that must work together: an API that accepts requests, a database that stores state, identity that decides who may do what, infrastructure that runs the code, pipelines that ship it, and mechanisms that keep it standing when traffic spikes or something breaks. Each concern has a layer, and a weakness in any layer shows up as an outage somewhere else.

This article walks through twelve layers of a typical Java architecture, from APIs and backend logic down to availability and recovery. For each layer we look at the purpose, the Java and Spring Boot tooling that usually fills it, and the decisions that matter most. The goal is a shared checklist you can use in design reviews.

1. APIs and Backend Logic

This is where requests enter the system and business rules run. In Java, the common choice is Spring Boot with Spring Web MVC for blocking workloads or WebFlux for reactive ones. Keep controllers thin, put business rules in services, and return stable DTOs rather than persistence entities.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/orders")
public class OrderController {

    private final PlaceOrderUseCase placeOrder;

    public OrderController(PlaceOrderUseCase placeOrder) {
        this.placeOrder = placeOrder;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request) {
        Order order = placeOrder.execute(request.toCommand());
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(OrderResponse.from(order));
    }
}

Decisions here include versioning, idempotency for writes, and explicit validation at the boundary.

2. Database and Storage

Choose storage by access pattern, not habit. Relational databases such as PostgreSQL suit transactional data with integrity rules. Spring Data JPA or jOOQ provide the Java access layer. Use migrations with Flyway or Liquibase so schema changes are versioned and repeatable.

public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<OrderEntity, UUID> {

    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
    @Query("select o from OrderEntity o where o.id = :id")
    Optional<OrderEntity> findForUpdate(@Param("id") UUID id);
}

Plan for connection pooling with HikariCP, indexes that match real queries, and backups you have actually restored at least once.

3. Auth and Permissions

Authentication answers who the caller is. Authorization answers what they may do. In Spring, Spring Security with OAuth2 and JWT is the usual combination. Validate tokens at the edge and enforce fine-grained permissions close to the business operation, not only at the URL level.

@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('ORDER_CANCEL') and #order.ownerId == authentication.name")
public void cancel(Order order) {
    order.cancel();
}

Keep roles and scopes minimal, and rotate signing keys through a JWKS endpoint.

4. Hosting and Deployment

Decide how the artifact reaches production. A typical path packages the service as a container image with a multi-stage Dockerfile, then deploys it to a runtime such as Kubernetes, a managed container service, or a virtual machine managed with systemd. Configuration belongs in the environment, not in the image. Use readiness and liveness probes so the platform knows when an instance can take traffic.

5. Cloud and Compute

Compute decisions shape cost and resilience. Right-size JVM heaps against container memory limits. Set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage rather than a fixed heap so the JVM adapts to its environment. Choose between instance types, serverless functions, and managed containers according to workload shape, and prefer horizontal scaling for stateless services.

6. CI/CD and Version Control

Every change should flow through the same automated path: commit, build, test, scan, package, deploy, verify. Git provides history and review. Jenkins, GitHub Actions, or GitLab CI runs the pipeline. Gate merges on unit and integration tests, and gate releases on contract tests and a smoke test against the deployed environment.

Keep pipelines reproducible by pinning JDK and dependency versions, and treat the pipeline definition itself as code under review.

7. Security and Row-Level Security

Defense in depth means no single control is trusted alone. Validate inputs, encode outputs, keep secrets out of source control, and enforce data access at the database when the platform supports it. PostgreSQL row-level security (RLS) lets the database filter rows by tenant or owner, so a missed where clause in application code does not expose another customer's data.

ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders
    USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid);

In Spring, set the session variable per request so the policy applies to every query.

8. Rate Limiting

Rate limits protect shared resources from abuse and accidental overload. Apply them at the edge with nginx, an API gateway, or a managed firewall, and add per-user or per-key limits inside the application when business rules require them. Return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header so well-behaved clients back off.

Libraries such as Bucket4j implement token-bucket limits in Java when you need them inside the service.

9. Caching and CDN

Caching removes repeated work. A CDN serves static assets and cacheable responses close to users. Inside the service, Spring Cache with Caffeine or Redis reduces database load for hot reads. Every cache needs an explicit invalidation strategy and a time to live. A cache without invalidation is a bug waiting for a customer to find it.

@Cacheable(cacheNames = "products", key = "#id", unless = "#result == null")
public Product findProduct(String id) {
    return productRepository.findById(id).orElse(null);
}

10. Load Balancing and Scaling

Distribute traffic across instances with a load balancer or an nginx upstream block. Choose a strategy such as least connections when request durations vary. Scale stateless services horizontally, and keep session state in a shared store or in signed tokens. Scale stateful components, such as databases, with replicas, partitioning, or managed services, not by adding application instances.

11. Error Tracking and Logs

When something fails, you need to know quickly and understand why. Log structured JSON with a correlation ID on every request, and send exceptions to an error tracker such as Sentry or a centralized logging stack. Avoid logging secrets or personal data. Alert on symptoms customers feel, such as error rate and latency at the percentile level, rather than on every exception.

12. Availability and Recovery

Availability is a design target, not a feature. Define service level objectives for each customer-facing path, then design failure behavior to meet them. Use timeouts, retries with backoff, and circuit breakers through Resilience4j so one slow dependency does not exhaust threads. Run regular backups and restore drills, and document a recovery runbook with a measured recovery time objective.

@CircuitBreaker(name = "paymentService", fallbackMethod = "queuePayment")
public PaymentResult charge(PaymentRequest request) {
    return paymentClient.charge(request);
}

Using the Stack as a Checklist

You do not need every layer on day one. A small internal service might need only layers one through four, plus logs. A customer-facing platform needs all twelve, with the most attention on security, rate limits, and recovery. Walk through the stack in every architecture review and ask, for each layer: what is the decision, who owns it, and how would we know if it failed?

Common Mistakes

  • Skipping the layers you find boring. Backups, logs, and rollbacks decide how bad an incident becomes.
  • Enforcing security in one place only. Edge checks, application checks, and database policies each catch different mistakes.
  • Caching without invalidation. Stale data is harder to debug than slow data.
  • Retrying without limits. Unbounded retries turn a partial outage into a full one.
  • Treating the pipeline as an afterthought. A deployment you cannot repeat is a deployment you cannot trust.

Best Practices Checklist

  • Keep controllers thin and DTOs stable.
  • Version the schema and test restores of backups.
  • Separate authentication from authorization, and enforce both.
  • Build once, configure per environment, and probe health.
  • Size the JVM for its container and scale stateless services out.
  • Gate every change through the same automated pipeline.
  • Use defense in depth, including database-level isolation where possible.
  • Limit request rates and cache only with explicit invalidation.
  • Log structured events with correlation IDs and alert on customer symptoms.
  • Define service level objectives and practice recovery.

Conclusion

Architecture is the sum of its layers. Each one answers a question the business will eventually ask: can it handle requests, keep data safe, let the right people in, run reliably, grow under load, ship changes safely, and recover when things break. Java and Spring Boot provide mature tools for every layer. The discipline is in deciding what each layer must guarantee, and in checking that the guarantees hold before the next incident checks for you.

Key takeaways

  • Treat the stack as twelve concerns that must all be designed, not as twelve tools to install.
  • Enforce security and limits at more than one layer.
  • Cache, retry, and scale only with explicit limits and invalidation.
  • Practice recovery as often as you practice deployment.

title: Stop the jump when a web font loads, measured with three Google fonts
description:
With font-display: swap, the browser shows text in a fallback font first and swaps in the web font when it arrives. If the two fonts take up different space, the text reflows and everything below it moves. CSS has four descriptors to make a local fallback font take up the same space: size-adjust, ascent-override, descent-override and line-gap-override.

I wanted to know how big the jump really is for the fonts I use on demo sites, and whether the fix works, so I measured it.

The setup

One paragraph of 250 characters at 17px, set in three Google fonts: Hanken Grotesk, Manrope and Space Grotesk. The fallback is Arial. I ran this in headless Chromium on Linux, where Arial isn't installed, so I used Liberation Sans, which was made to have the same metrics as Arial.

Two column widths: 343px (a phone with 16px margins) and 560px. Two line heights: 1.6 and normal.

How far the text moves with a plain fallback

Paragraph height, real font vs. plain fallback:

Font 343px, line-height: 1.6 343px, normal 560px, 1.6 560px, normal
Hanken Grotesk 163.1 vs 163.1 132 vs 120 108.8 vs 108.8 88 vs 80
Manrope 163.1 vs 163.1 138 vs 120 108.8 vs 108.8 92 vs 80
Space Grotesk 190.3 vs 163.1 154 vs 120 108.8 vs 108.8 88 vs 80

Two different things are going on.

With line-height: normal, every font shifts, even when the line breaks are identical. "Normal" means "use the font's own ascent, descent and line gap", and those differ: Manrope's ascent and descent add up to 1.37 times the font size; Arial's ascent and descent are 1.12, about 1.15 with its line gap. So every line grows when Manrope arrives. Here that's 12 to 18px for one paragraph, more on a page of them.

With a fixed line-height: 1.6, only the line count matters. Each line is 27.2px whatever the font, so Hanken and Manrope don't move the paragraph at all. Space Grotesk does: it's about 8% wider than Arial, so at 343px the text needs 7 lines instead of 6 and the paragraph grows by one line, 27.2px.

So the first fix is free: set a unitless line height on body text. That removes the line-box part of the shift for every font; what's left comes from line breaks.

Writing the fallback @font-face

For the width, size-adjust scales the fallback's glyphs. For the line box, the three overrides set the ascent, descent and line gap the fallback should report. Both can be measured in the console once the web font has loaded:

async function fallbackFor(family, localName = 'Arial') {
  await document.fonts.load(`100px "${family}"`);
  const sample = 'Small-batch beans roasted every Tuesday in our Portland shop, shipped the same week so they reach you while the flavor is still bright.';
  const ctx = document.createElement('canvas').getContext('2d');
  const measure = (font) => { ctx.font = `100px ${font}`; return ctx.measureText(sample); };
  const web = measure(`"${family}"`);
  const local = measure(`"${localName}"`);
  const sizeAdjust = web.width / local.width;
  const pct = (n) => (n * 100).toFixed(1) + '%';
  return `@font-face {
  font-family: "${family} Fallback";
  src: local("${localName}");
  size-adjust: ${pct(sizeAdjust)};
  ascent-override: ${pct(web.fontBoundingBoxAscent / 100 / sizeAdjust)};
  descent-override: ${pct(web.fontBoundingBoxDescent / 100 / sizeAdjust)};
  line-gap-override: 0%;
}`;
}

Two details:

  • The overrides are divided by sizeAdjust. They're percentages of the font size, and the font size of the fallback is already scaled by size-adjust, so without the division the line box comes out too tall by the same factor.
  • The width ratio comes from a real sentence, not the alphabet. Letter frequency matters: a font with a wide "m" and narrow "i" averages differently on prose than on "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz".

What it printed (with 'Liberation Sans' as the local name):

Font size-adjust ascent-override descent-override
Hanken Grotesk 100.8% 99.2% 29.7%
Manrope 102.4% 104.5% 29.3%
Space Grotesk 109.3% 89.6% 26.5%

Then use the fallback right after the web font:

body {
  font-family: "Space Grotesk", "Space Grotesk Fallback", sans-serif;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

After

Same paragraph, real font vs. adjusted fallback:

Font 343px, 1.6 343px, normal 560px, 1.6 560px, normal
Hanken Grotesk 163.1 vs 163.1 132 vs 132 108.8 vs 108.8 88 vs 88
Manrope 163.1 vs 163.1 138 vs 138 108.8 vs 108.8 92 vs 92
Space Grotesk 190.3 vs 190.3 154 vs 154 108.8 vs 108.8 88 vs 88

Every height matches, including line-height: normal, and Space Grotesk's fallback now wraps to 7 lines like the real font.

What it doesn't fix

Widths only match on average. At 100px, the adjusted fallback for Space Grotesk set my test paragraph on one line within 0.5% of the real font's width (12213px vs 12157px). At 17px, on this Linux machine, it came out 6% wider (2163px vs 2038px on one line), while the plain fallback was 7% narrower. I suspect font hinting rounding each glyph's width to whole pixels at small sizes, but I didn't dig into it. Line breaks matched for my paragraph; a different paragraph can still break on a different word. The fix makes a reflow much smaller and much rarer, not impossible.

The local font has to exist. local("Arial") matches nothing on a machine without Arial; then the fallback face is skipped and the next font in the stack is used, unadjusted. Mac and Windows ship Arial. Many Linux systems don't, but often have Liberation Sans, so src: local("Arial"), local("Liberation Sans"); covers both with the same numbers. A system with only DejaVu Sans would need its own fallback face.

Headings need their own check. A display serif against Georgia or Times needs a separate fallback face and separate numbers.

Short version

  1. Use a unitless line height for body text. That alone removed the vertical shift for two of the three fonts.
  2. For the rest, generate a fallback @font-face with size-adjust and the three overrides, measured on real text, with the overrides divided by size-adjust.
  3. Measure the result: paragraph heights at a phone width and a desktop width, real font vs. fallback.

If you're doing this for a site you didn't build, you first need to know which fonts it renders and which weights. I made a Chrome extension, Stylasso, that lists every font a page actually renders, with its role, weights and where it loads from; there's a guide here: what font is this website using. DevTools' Rendered Fonts gives you the same for one element at a time.

Written with help from an AI assistant. Every number comes from running the snippet and layout tests described above in headless Chromium.

title: Token Pass credit now applies automatically across AI Gateway
description:
Token Pass credit now applies automatically to included model usage through AI Gateway, whether a request authenticates with an API key, OIDC token, or fx login. No dedicated Token Pass API key is required, though you can still create one from the dashboard or the CLI for keys scoped only to featured models and providers.

When Token Pass credit runs out for the billing period, requests from a standard key or OIDC token fall back to your team's AI Gateway credits. Token Pass keys still stop until the next billing period.

Requests served through the Token Pass provider remain Zero Data Retention (ZDR). Fallback requests follow your team's setting. With team-wide ZDR enabled, they route only to ZDR providers.

Available now for Token Pass subscribers on Pro teams. If you created a Token Pass key during setup, switch to a standard API key or OIDC token to get fallback. Learn more in the Token Pass documentation.

title: Letting AI agents query production databases without giving them a database account
description:
The problem

Once a company has an AI assistant, someone asks whether it can answer questions over production data. I do data consulting for companies that keep everything on-premises, and I kept hearing that question.

The usual answer is a read-only database account plus a text-to-SQL prompt. That leaves three things unsolved:

  • The account sees every row. Other tenants, other regions and personal data are all in reach.
  • The model writes joins from column names it has to guess at.
  • Nobody can say afterwards who read what.

I built Truejoin to close those three, on your own servers, with Oracle and SQL Server included.

What Truejoin is

Truejoin is an open-source (Apache 2.0) data gateway. It connects to PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQL Server and Oracle, and serves them three ways from one Python process and one config file:

  • MCP: 18 tools for agents, over streamable HTTP or stdio
  • REST: an API per table with a typed OpenAPI schema
  • Analytical SQL: in-memory OLAP on DuckDB

Every query, whoever wrote it, runs under the caller's row rules and column masks and leaves one audit event. It is not a warehouse, an ETL tool or a BI dashboard. It reads the databases you already have, live.

Rules are applied by rewriting the query

Filtering the result is too late. An aggregate over rows the caller may not see has already leaked, and so has a masked column read through an alias, a join or a subquery.

So Truejoin rewrites the query before it runs. Each table the query names is replaced by a subquery that carries that caller's row conditions and masks. Aliases, joins, CTEs and aggregates then all read the restricted view, because there is nothing else to read.

The rules are a few lines of config (trimmed here; the full nesting is in config/reference.yaml):

row_filters:
  orders: [{column: tenant_id, value: "${tenant}"}]
row_filter_exempt_roles: [dpo]

masking:
  enabled: true
  rules: {email: partial, national_id: hash}

Three things follow from doing it this way:

  • It fails closed. Anything that cannot be wrapped, a table function for example, refuses the query.
  • Model-written SQL gets no special path. It goes through the same rewrite as a person's.
  • The audit event never holds the SQL. It records who asked, which tables, how many rows, and which columns were masked.

A model drafts the catalog, a person approves it

A model reads the schema and drafts table and column descriptions, PII labels, relationships and business terms (truejoin catalog analyze). Sample values are masked before they reach it, and with Ollama nothing leaves your network.

A person then reviews, approves and certifies the draft. Nothing unapproved is used.

The approved catalog does two jobs. Masks key off its semantic types, and questions are read against its business terms.

Questions in words, without a model at query time

answer_question first reads a question against the approved vocabulary, with no model involved. It returns the request it understood and the SQL it compiled, so you can check what was asked before you trust the answer. Joins follow declared foreign keys, so a request cannot write a wrong join.

Only a question the vocabulary cannot read goes to a model, and that answer is marked as model-written.

I benchmarked the approaches on a banking-shaped schema with qwen2.5-coder:7b, graded by result set against a gold query. On the 16 held-out questions:

Approach Correct (of 16) Hallucinated
Model writes SQL from the DDL 8 31.2%
Model writes SQL from the catalog 10 18.8%
Approved terms, no model 12 0%

Sixteen questions is a small set and the intervals are wide. The table in the repo shows 13 for the last row; one of those was right by luck and is now refused, so I count 12. The method and every caveat are in bench/README.md.

Where it came from: Warp, Fusion and Stargate

Truejoin merges three earlier projects of mine into one package and one process:

  • Warp: database to governed REST, with the catalog
  • Fusion: DuckDB OLAP and the agent tools
  • Stargate: OpenAPI to MCP. It lives on as truejoin mcp convert, which turns an OpenAPI or Postman description into an MCP server definition.

Their code moved over with its history. The query rewriter is the one component with no ancestor in the three, and it carries the privacy promise, so its tests were written first.

Try it

You need Python 3.12+ and uv.

git clone https://github.com/yasinyaman/truejoin.git
cd truejoin
uv sync --all-extras

export TRUEJOIN_SECRET_KEY=$(uv run python -c 'from cryptography.fernet import Fernet; print(Fernet.generate_key().decode())')
uv run truejoin config validate -c config/database.yaml
uv run truejoin users add admin --permission all -c config/database.yaml
uv run truejoin serve -c config/database.yaml

The console is at http://localhost:8000/ui. Any MCP client can connect over HTTP at http://<host>:8000/mcp with an API key in X-API-Key. For a desktop client such as Claude Desktop, run the tools over stdio:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "truejoin": {
      "command": "uv",
      "args": ["run", "--directory", "/path/to/truejoin", "truejoin", "serve",
               "--transport", "stdio", "-c", "config/database.yaml"]
    }
  }
}

Limits, and what I'd like to hear

  • 1.0.0 is still in development. It installs from source and is not on PyPI yet.
  • SQL Server and Oracle connect through ODBC.
  • A restricted caller's analytical queries always run locally in DuckDB, and one that is not a flat SELECT loads whole tables for that caller.
  • The benchmark is small, and it is one schema.

The feedback I want most is on the rewriter. Try to read around a row rule or a mask. If a query gets through, please report it privately through a GitHub security advisory rather than a public issue.

The code is at github.com/yasinyaman/truejoin and the docs are at yaman.dev/truejoin.

title: Data Center Power Distribution: Best Practices for Reliability, Efficiency, and Scalability
description:
Data centers form the foundation of today's digital economy, and the way organizations build and run them varies considerably depending on business needs. Some operators own their infrastructure outright in enterprise data centers, others lease space in colocation facilities, many rely on cloud and hyperscale providers for on-demand capacity, and still others deploy edge computing sites positioned close to end users or specific points of interest.

The explosive growth of artificial intelligence and machine learning workloads is forcing a rethink of how data centers manage power, pushing operators toward new strategies that can satisfy tomorrow's energy demands. No matter the size or category of facility—whether it draws a few tens of kilowatts or scales into the gigawatt range—every data center shares one constant: a network of electrical power distribution paths that keeps IT equipment running.

This article outlines proven practices for designing and operating these electrical distribution systems, with an emphasis on meeting the scalability, flexibility, resilience, and efficiency demands that define modern data center operations.

Plan for Both Present and Future Requirements

Every data center project begins with design work, but before drafting a single line, engineers need a solid estimate of the electrical load generated by individual components, subsystems, and the facility as a whole. Power sizing isn't the only concern—floor space must also be managed carefully, since real estate directly affects an operator's bottom line. The relationship between floor layout and IT load shapes how power distribution gets sized; get this wrong, and the facility either hits a growth ceiling prematurely or becomes an operational headache to run efficiently.

Consider a common scenario: an operator wants to add more IT capacity, only to discover that upstream infrastructure—a transformer or a molded-case circuit breaker, for instance—can't handle the increased load. Swapping out these components after the fact is expensive and risky, potentially threatening uptime across the entire site. This is why balancing today's needs against tomorrow's growth from the outset is so critical.

Several concrete strategies help operators avoid these pitfalls. Building with modular systems allows capacity to expand incrementally as demand rises, rather than forcing a disruptive overhaul later. Major equipment like transformers and generators should be sized for the facility's ultimate build-out, with an additional 10-20% buffer beyond that final capacity target.

Physical planning matters just as much as electrical planning. Reserving floor space and pathways now for equipment that will be installed years down the line saves enormous cost and disruption compared to retrofitting later. Similarly, oversizing cable trays, busways, and conduits during initial construction creates room for additional distribution infrastructure without having to rip out existing pathways.

Operators also need to keep an eye on where technology is heading. Rack power densities continue to climb, particularly as AI and high-performance computing workloads become more common, and facilities designed without this trend in mind risk obsolescence. Rather than constructing an entire facility in one massive push, many operators now favor phased deployment—building and commissioning sections incrementally so that each completed phase can start generating revenue while later phases are still under construction. This approach spreads capital expenditure over time and reduces the financial risk of overbuilding capacity that may not be needed for years.

Define a Suitable Electrical Architecture

Every power distribution design must comply with regional regulations, which vary depending on where the facility sits. North American installations follow UL and ANSI standards, while European facilities adhere to IEC standards. These frameworks dictate voltage levels throughout the system, particularly for the low-voltage segment that delivers power to IT equipment.

Power Connection and Grid Voltage Levels

The journey from utility grid to server rack starts with selecting an appropriate voltage tier based on facility size and location. Small edge deployments typically operate at low voltage internally, while mid-sized enterprise and colocation facilities—generally in the 1-50 MW range—connect at medium voltage. Hyperscale campuses and AI-focused facilities exceeding 50 MW require high-voltage connections to handle their massive power draw.

Since IT racks ultimately run on low voltage, incoming power must be stepped down through transformers. Regional standards shape this process differently: IEC-based systems commonly use 230V/400V three-phase configurations, while North American facilities are increasingly adopting 240V/415V setups that eliminate an extra transformation stage, cutting losses and supporting denser racks. Traditional UL-based systems still rely heavily on 120/208V and 277/480V configurations. Some cutting-edge AI facilities with GPU-heavy racks are now experimenting with 800V DC distribution to squeeze out additional efficiency.

Choosing the right voltage comes down to a few guiding principles: favor higher voltages to shrink current levels and copper usage, minimize the number of transformation stages to reduce cumulative losses, and standardize on one voltage throughout the facility to simplify spare parts and maintenance. Fault levels also deserve attention, since the chosen voltage must support straightforward protection coordination.

Power Distribution Paths and Resilience Tiers

Resilience depends on building redundant pathways from the grid to the IT load, guided by frameworks from the Uptime Institute, BICSI, and EN 50600. These bodies define resilience "tiers," ranging from Tier I facilities with a single non-redundant path to Tier IV facilities featuring fully fault-tolerant, dual independent paths with no single point of failure. Selecting the right tier requires weighing business criticality, acceptable risk, and cost against the operational benefits of higher resilience.

Single- and Dual-Corded Loads

IT equipment connects to power through either single or dual power cords. Dual-corded devices draw from two independent sources, providing built-in redundancy, while single-corded equipment requires a static transfer switch to seamlessly swap between power sources during a failure. Choosing dual-corded equipment where possible eliminates single points of failure and reduces the number of supporting components needed.

Specify Appropriate Power Equipment

Selecting the right hardware for each stage of the power chain directly impacts a facility's reliability, efficiency, and environmental footprint. This spans everything from high-voltage switchgear at the utility connection down to the rack-level distribution units that feed individual servers.

Switchgear and Transformers

At the point where data centers connect to high or medium voltage grids, switchgear equipped with vacuum circuit breakers offers a more sustainable alternative to older gas-insulated designs, though gas-insulated switchgear remains necessary at higher voltage tiers where arc suppression is more demanding. Transformers require careful attention to impedance, thermal behavior, and insulation ratings, since these factors determine how the system responds to short circuits. Dry-type transformers have become the preferred choice for reducing maintenance burden, and operators must also account for harmonic distortion—an increasingly important consideration given the heavy harmonic content generated by AI workloads.

Backup Generators

Diesel generators remain the traditional backup power source, valued for fast startup and proven reliability, though natural gas alternatives are gaining ground for their lower emissions and continuous fuel supply. Gas turbine generators, while carrying higher upfront costs, deliver very low emissions and can sustain long continuous runtimes, making them attractive for hyperscale operations focused on sustainability.

Uninterruptible Power Supplies and Energy Storage

UPS systems protect IT loads from power disturbances, with online double-conversion models offering the strongest protection through continuous power conditioning, making them the standard choice for mission-critical data center environments. Behind these systems, energy storage technology has traditionally relied on valve-regulated lead-acid batteries, though lithium-ion options are gaining traction for their smaller footprint and built-in cell monitoring, despite carrying greater fire risk that often pushes operators to house them outside the main building. Flywheel systems offer an eco-friendly alternative but only bridge short gaps of up to fifteen seconds before generators must take over.

Distribution Units

Power moves through several distribution layers between the utility connection and the server rack, including main switchgear, floor-level power distribution units, remote power panels, and rack-mounted units. Best practices at this stage include balancing electrical loads evenly across all phases, coordinating protection settings so faults get isolated without cascading failures, and building in spare capacity to accommodate future expansion without costly rework.

Conclusion

Building and running power systems for a critical facility demands relentless attention to detail, from the earliest design decisions through years of ongoing operation. As data centers grow more sophisticated and power-hungry, operators must weigh not just performance and reliability, but also the environmental consequences of every component they choose.

Getting data center power distribution right means addressing planning, architecture, equipment selection, maintenance, and monitoring as interconnected pieces of a single system rather than isolated tasks. Skipping attention in any one area creates weaknesses that ripple through the entire facility, whether that means outgrowing capacity too soon, facing unplanned downtime, or losing efficiency gains that could have been captured with better foresight.

Data center infrastructure management software ties all these efforts together, functioning as the operational backbone that gives facility teams visibility across every layer of the power chain. Rather than managing transformers, UPS systems, generators, and distribution panels as disconnected components, a well-implemented DCIM platform consolidates monitoring, maintenance tracking, and capacity planning into a single actionable view.

The payoff for this integrated approach is substantial: better use of existing capacity, clearer visibility into how power flows through the facility, faster response to equipment issues, and smoother maintenance scheduling. These operational improvements translate directly into higher uptime, stronger energy efficiency, leaner spare parts inventories, and greater flexibility to adapt as demands shift. For data center owners, the result is a facility that not only performs reliably today but remains financially and operationally sound as requirements evolve in the years ahead.
