title: Hexagonal architecture: ports and adapters, step by step
description:
"Does the controller implement the incoming port?" "Where do I put the
repository interface?" When you start with hexagonal architecture, or
when you come from a layered application, the direction of the arrows
is easy to get wrong.

This post explains the ideas one at a time, with one example: create
an order with Spring Boot. At each step, one question guides you:
here, who calls? who implements? The full code is in the public
repository
hexagonal-architecture-demo
(tag v1). For a more real case, with Kafka and several use cases,
see
Hexagonal architecture with Spring Boot: a simple example.

The problem

In a layered application, each layer calls the layer below it: the
controller calls the service, the service calls the repository, and
the repository talks to the database. The dependencies go down. So the
business service depends on JPA: to test it, you need a database, or a
lot of mocks.

Hexagonal architecture turns some of these arrows around. In the
center is the core: the domain and the use cases, in plain Java. Around
it are the adapters: REST, JPA, Kafka, and so on. All dependencies
point to the core. The core knows no adapter.

See the diagram in the original post.

The name comes from Alistair Cockburn (2005). He also calls it "Ports
and Adapters". Its goal: "Allow an application to equally be driven by
users, programs, automated test or batch scripts, and to be developed
and tested in isolation from its eventual run-time devices and
databases." The hexagon shape has no special meaning: "The hexagon is
not a hexagon because the number six is important".

Here: in layers, each layer calls the one below and depends on
it. In hexagonal architecture, the adapters depend on the core, never
the other way.

The big picture

Here is the whole example in one diagram. There are two kinds of
arrows: full line = "calls", dotted line = "implements".

See the diagram in the original post.

It all fits in two rules:

  • incoming side: an adapter (here the REST controller) calls an incoming port; the core implements it;
  • outgoing side: the core calls an outgoing port; an adapter (here JPA) implements it.

A port is an interface that belongs to the core. Cockburn defines it
like this: "A port identifies a purposeful conversation." An adapter
translates between this port and a technology. Cockburn also talks
about "driving adapters and driven adapters": the adapters that drive
the application (incoming), and the ones the application drives
(outgoing).

In the repository, each part has its own package:

Package Content Knows Spring?
domain Order, OrderLine, InvalidOrderException no
application.port.in CreateOrderUseCase, CreateOrderCommand no
application.port.out OrderRepository no
application CreateOrderService no
adapter.in.web the REST controller and its DTOs yes
adapter.out.persistence the JPA entity, the adapter, the mapper yes
config the Spring wiring yes

Here: the incoming adapter calls, the core implements. The core
calls, the outgoing adapter implements.

The domain

The domain holds the business rules, and nothing else. In the example,
the rule is simple: an order has at least one line, each quantity is
between 1 and 99, and the domain computes the total.

public final class Order {

    private final UUID id;
    private final List<OrderLine> lines;

    public Order(UUID id, List<OrderLine> lines) {
        if (id == null) {
            throw new InvalidOrderException("an order needs an id");
        }
        if (lines == null || lines.isEmpty()) {
            throw new InvalidOrderException("an order needs at least one line");
        }
        this.id = id;
        this.lines = List.copyOf(lines);
    }

    public static Order create(List<OrderLine> lines) {
        return new Order(UUID.randomUUID(), lines);
    }

    public BigDecimal total() {
        return lines.stream()
                .map(OrderLine::amount)
                .reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add);
    }
    // id(), lines()
}

OrderLine is a record that checks the quantity in its constructor.
The rules are checked when the object is created, so an Order is
always valid.

Why no JPA annotation here? Because the shape of the database is not a
business rule. A renamed column must not change Order. Why no DTO?
For the same reason: the JSON format of the API belongs to the REST
adapter.

In this post, the domain knows nobody: not Spring, not the ports,
not the application. This is a common choice, not a rule from
Cockburn: his page talks about "the application" in the center, and
does not split it into a domain and use cases. Other code bases put
interfaces in the domain (see "Common mistakes").

Here: the domain calls no port and implements no port. The use
case calls it.

The ports and the use case

The incoming port says what the application offers to the outside
world. It is an interface, in application.port.in:

public interface CreateOrderUseCase {

    Order create(CreateOrderCommand command);
}

public record CreateOrderCommand(List<OrderLine> lines) {
}

The command has no JSON and no HTTP in it. Another adapter (a Kafka
listener, a batch job, a test) can use it in the same way.

The outgoing port says what the application needs. It is also an
interface, in application.port.out:

public interface OrderRepository {

    void save(Order order);
}

The core writes this interface, with its own words: save, not
persist or insertInto. It does not know that JPA is behind it.

The use case implements the incoming port and calls the outgoing
port:

public class CreateOrderService implements CreateOrderUseCase {

    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;

    public CreateOrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
    }

    @Override
    public Order create(CreateOrderCommand command) {
        Order order = Order.create(command.lines());
        orderRepository.save(order);
        return order;
    }
}

Why an interface for the incoming port, when it has only one
implementation? It gives the contract a name, and the adapter depends
only on this contract. This is also a choice: a lot of code calls the
use case class directly. For the outgoing port, the interface is
required: it is what lets the core not depend on JPA.

Here: CreateOrderService implements the incoming port and calls
the outgoing port. Both interfaces are in the core.

The adapters

The outgoing adapter: JPA

The JPA adapter implements the outgoing port:

@Component
class OrderPersistenceAdapter implements OrderRepository {

    private final OrderJpaRepository jpaRepository;

    OrderPersistenceAdapter(OrderJpaRepository jpaRepository) {
        this.jpaRepository = jpaRepository;
    }

    @Override
    public void save(Order order) {
        jpaRepository.save(OrderMapper.toEntity(order));
    }
}

OrderJpaRepository is a Spring Data interface
(JpaRepository<OrderJpaEntity, UUID>). Only the adapter knows it.

The JPA entity is a different class from Order:

@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
class OrderJpaEntity {

    @Id
    private UUID id;

    @ElementCollection
    @CollectionTable(name = "order_lines", joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "order_id"))
    private List<OrderLineEmbeddable> lines = new ArrayList<>();

    protected OrderJpaEntity() {
        // for JPA
    }
    // constructor and getters
}

It has the JPA constraints (a constructor with no arguments, fields
that are not final), and the domain does not have them. The mapper
goes from one to the other:

static OrderJpaEntity toEntity(Order order) {
    List<OrderLineEmbeddable> lines = order.lines().stream()
            .map(line -> new OrderLineEmbeddable(line.productCode(), line.quantity(), line.unitPrice()))
            .toList();
    return new OrderJpaEntity(order.id(), lines);
}

Here, the mapper goes in one direction only, because the port has only
save. A read use case would add the other direction (entity →
Order).

The database is H2, in memory. The Spring Boot docs say: "Spring Boot
can auto-configure embedded H2, HSQL, and Derby (deprecated)
databases. You need not provide any connection URLs." The tables are
also created at startup for an embedded database. You do not need
Docker to try the example.

The incoming adapter: REST

The controller does not implement the incoming port. It calls
it:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
class OrderController {

    private final CreateOrderUseCase createOrderUseCase;

    OrderController(CreateOrderUseCase createOrderUseCase) {
        this.createOrderUseCase = createOrderUseCase;
    }

    @PostMapping
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    OrderResponse create(@RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request) {
        Order order = createOrderUseCase.create(request.toCommand());
        return OrderResponse.from(order);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(InvalidOrderException.class)
    ProblemDetail invalidOrder(InvalidOrderException exception) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, exception.getMessage());
    }
}

The DTOs CreateOrderRequest and OrderResponse are records, in the
adapter package. The DTO-to-command conversion happens here
(request.toCommand()), not in the core. A broken rule
(InvalidOrderException) becomes a 400 response.

The HTTP direction is not the architecture direction. In HTTP, the
request comes in and the response goes out. But for the architecture,
the controller does one thing only: it calls the incoming port, and the
response is the return value of this call. It is still an incoming
adapter.

A test run, with the application started (mvn spring-boot:run):

$ curl -X POST localhost:8080/api/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"lines":[{"productCode":"BOOK-1","quantity":2,"unitPrice":12.50},{"productCode":"PEN-7","quantity":3,"unitPrice":1.20}]}'
{"id":"45e27a15-2bce-454b-83a4-3b770cf674b3","lines":[{"productCode":"BOOK-1","quantity":2,"unitPrice":12.50},{"productCode":"PEN-7","quantity":3,"unitPrice":1.20}],"total":28.60}

$ curl -X POST localhost:8080/api/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"lines":[{"productCode":"BOOK-1","quantity":0,"unitPrice":12.50}]}'
{"detail":"quantity must be between 1 and 99, got 0","instance":"/api/orders","status":400,"title":"Bad Request"}

The domain computes the total (28.60). The error message comes from
the domain, and the REST adapter turns it into a 400.

Here: the controller calls the incoming port; the JPA adapter
implements the outgoing port. The DTOs and the JPA entity stay in
their adapters.

The Spring wiring

The core does not know Spring. So who gives an OrderRepository to
CreateOrderService? Spring does, through the constructor. The Spring
Framework docs recommend it: "The Spring team generally advocates
constructor injection, as it lets you implement application components
as immutable objects and ensures that required dependencies are not
null." And with a single constructor, you do not need @Autowired:
"An @Autowired annotation on such a constructor is not necessary if
the target bean defines only one constructor."

To create the use case with no annotation in the core, a
@Configuration class declares the bean:

@Configuration
class OrderConfiguration {

    @Bean
    CreateOrderUseCase createOrderUseCase(OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        return new CreateOrderService(orderRepository);
    }
}

Spring finds the bean that implements OrderRepository (the JPA
adapter, marked @Component) and passes it to the method. The
controller gets the use case in the same way, through its constructor.

The common variant is shorter: @Service on CreateOrderService, and
no configuration class. It works too. Its limit: the core then depends
on a Spring annotation. In the repository, an ArchUnit test forbids
this. With @Service on the use case, the build fails:

Architecture Violation [Priority: MEDIUM] - Rule 'no classes that reside in any package ['..domain..', '..application..'] should depend on classes that reside in any package ['org.springframework..', 'jakarta..', '..adapter..', '..config..']' was violated (1 times):
Class <dev.aymenjamaaoui.hexagonal.application.CreateOrderService> is annotated with <org.springframework.stereotype.Service> in (CreateOrderService.java:0)

Here: Spring calls nothing and implements nothing in the core. It
creates the objects and connects them: the JPA adapter into the use
case, the use case into the controller.

Testing without Spring

This is the real gain. The use case depends only on interfaces, so you
can test it with a fake outgoing port, in memory.

class InMemoryOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {

    private final List<Order> saved = new ArrayList<>();

    @Override
    public void save(Order order) {
        saved.add(order);
    }

    List<Order> saved() {
        return saved;
    }
}

class CreateOrderServiceTest {

    private final InMemoryOrderRepository repository = new InMemoryOrderRepository();
    private final CreateOrderService service = new CreateOrderService(repository);

    @Test
    void savesAValidOrder() {
        Order order = service.create(new CreateOrderCommand(
                List.of(new OrderLine("BOOK-1", 2, new BigDecimal("12.50")))));

        assertThat(repository.saved()).containsExactly(order);
        assertThat(order.total()).isEqualByComparingTo("25.00");
    }

    @Test
    void savesNothingWhenTheOrderIsInvalid() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.create(new CreateOrderCommand(List.of())))
                .isInstanceOf(InvalidOrderException.class);

        assertThat(repository.saved()).isEmpty();
    }
}

No Spring, no database, no mock: just new. On my machine,
two runs of mvn verify give:

Test class What it tests Time
OrderTest the domain alone 0.002 s
CreateOrderServiceTest the use case, with the fake port 0.032 to 0.034 s
OrderApiTest HTTP → controller → use case → JPA → H2 (@SpringBootTest) 1.94 to 2.08 s

The end-to-end test is still useful: it checks the wiring. But you can
test the rules without starting Spring.

Here: the test calls the incoming port (through the use case),
and the fake repository implements the outgoing port, in place of the
JPA adapter.

Common mistakes

Wrong Right
The REST controller implements the incoming port. The controller calls the incoming port; the use case implements it.
The domain gets the DTO or the JPA entity. The DTO and the JPA entity stay in their adapters; the conversion happens at the border.
The controller is both incoming and outgoing, because the HTTP response "goes out". The response is the return value of the call to the incoming port. The controller is an incoming adapter.

One point depends on the team's choices: where the repository
interface lives. In this post, it is in application.port.out, and
the domain knows nobody. In many DDD projects, it is in the domain.
Microsoft's .NET guide on DDD says: "it's recommended that you define
and place the repository interfaces in the domain model layer". Both
ways work. What matters: the interface belongs to the core, and the
implementation is outside.

Here: in both variants, the core calls the interface and the
adapter implements it. Only the package of the interface changes.

When not to use it, and a summary sheet

This structure has a cost. For one feature (create an order), the
repository has 17 classes in src/main, with 3 for the ports, plus a
JPA entity and a mapper next to the domain. For a simple CRUD, with no
real business rule, a layered application is enough: there is nothing
to protect in the center.

It pays off when the rules grow, when a technology changes (another
database, Kafka messages next to REST), or when you want to test the
rules fast and often.

Summary sheet

Element Package Who calls it Who implements it
Order (domain) domain the use case — (a class)
CreateOrderUseCase (incoming port) application.port.in OrderController CreateOrderService
CreateOrderService (use case) application the controller, through the incoming port —
OrderRepository (outgoing port) application.port.out CreateOrderService OrderPersistenceAdapter
OrderController (incoming adapter) adapter.in.web Spring, for each HTTP request —
OrderPersistenceAdapter (outgoing adapter) adapter.out.persistence the use case, through the outgoing port —

Three rules to keep:

  1. dependencies point to the core;
  2. on the incoming side, the adapter calls and the core implements; on the outgoing side, the core calls and the adapter implements;
  3. DTOs and JPA entities do not cross the border.

To keep rule 1 true over time, an ArchUnit test checks it at each
build: see the part "The rule, checked by the build" in
the example with Kafka.

Tested with

Java 25 (Temurin 25.0.5), Maven 3.10.0, Spring Boot 4.1.2 (Hibernate
7.4.13), H2 2.4.240 and ArchUnit 1.5.1, on macOS. The code is frozen by
the tag
v1
of the demo repository.

Sources

  • Alistair Cockburn, Hexagonal architecture (2005)
  • Microsoft Learn, Designing the infrastructure persistence layer (.NET guide, DDD part)
  • Spring Framework, Dependency Injection, Using @Autowired, @Bean and @Configuration
  • Spring Boot, SQL Databases
  • ArchUnit User Guide

Further reading

  • Hexagonal architecture with Spring Boot: a simple example: the same ideas on a real service, with Kafka, a sealed result and ArchUnit.
  • Kafka and Spring Boot: a complete local project

title: What stack would you choose for a matching platform?
description:
I’m working on a matching platform and considering Next.js, Tailwind CSS and Supabase/PostgreSQL. I’d like to hear from people who’ve built applications with similar technical requirements, particularly where this combination works well and where it starts to get awkward.

It’s a web-first application with a fairly complex backend. The main requirements are:

  • Reliable editing and relational data. Multi-step forms, autosave and resume across devices, with users potentially editing in multiple tabs. Some transactions affect several related records or users. Concurrent updates, retries and lost responses need to be handled without overwriting newer data or repeating an operation.

  • Matching and search. Deterministic, rules-based calculations rather than ML. Results need to track the versions of their inputs and rules, with recalculation when those change. Search includes filtering, pagination and geographical queries.

  • Authentication. Passwordless email sign-in, phone verification, account recovery and admin MFA. Verification codes need to remain single-use even when requests overlap. Revoked sessions and replaced codes must stop working.

  • Access control. Permissions depend on account status, role, the relationship between users and its current state. They can differ for each participant, resource and field, with separate rights to read history, send messages, edit data or access shared files. Changes must take effect during active sessions and govern protected responses, cached content and queued work.

  • Private media. Upload validation, image processing and asynchronous content screening. Files remain access-controlled, and a delayed processing result must not replace a newer version.

  • Messaging, jobs and integrations. Private messaging, timely updates, notifications, payment integration and scheduled work. Jobs and webhooks need to cope with duplicate or out-of-order delivery, restarts and partial failures. Time-based access rules need to stay correct across timezones and daylight-saving changes, even if a scheduled job runs late.

  • Privacy and administration. Scoped admin permissions, audit trails, aggregate reporting, retention rules, data export and deletion. Deletion and access changes also need to be accounted for in derived data, queues, external services and backup recovery.

I’d prefer managed database, authentication and storage services where possible. I also want a straightforward way to test the complete stack locally and in staging, including concurrency and failure recovery. Safe migrations, monitoring and tested backups matter, and the application needs to behave correctly with multiple instances and workers.

Would you choose Next.js and Supabase for this? Which parts would you handle within that setup, and where would you introduce a separate API, worker or service?

If you’d choose a different stack, what makes it a better technical fit? I’m particularly interested in limitations or tradeoffs you’ve encountered in production.

title: Turning Your Python AI Agent Into an Asynchronous FastAPI Backend with Server-Sent Events (SSE)
description:
After building our standalone Python agent in Post #27, Post #28 wraps our reasoning loop inside an asynchronous FastAPI microservice with Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming.

Why FastAPI for AI Agents?

FastAPI leverages native ASGI async/await to prevent thread blocking during slow I/O waits (such as GitHub REST API calls or vector database queries). Because FastAPI is built natively around Pydantic, your agent tool input schemas double as FastAPI request validation bodies.

Streaming SSE via StreamingResponse

Using Python generator functions (async def agent_event_stream()), you can yield custom W3C-compliant SSE frames (event: tool-start, event: text-delta, event: done) directly through FastAPI's StreamingResponse with media_type='text/event-stream' and anti-buffering headers.

Read the full tutorial with complete Python source code on my blog: https://zahidhasantonmoy.vercel.app/blog/fastapi-ai-agent-backend-streaming-python

title: 17 Reasons Booking Systems Go Unused on the Shop Floor: Notes From a Barber Who Codes
description:
The premise: it's not about technology, it's about who decides

I'm a barber, and I'm also an engineer. I built the booking system for my own shop, and I use it on the floor every day.

When I look at specs and screens for salon software from that position, I get stuck at almost the same places every time. It isn't a technical problem. The assumption about who decides is the reverse of how a shop works.

Developers build on "the system decides." Fix the slots, assign staff automatically, handle exceptions in the admin screen. As a design it looks rational. But on the floor there is a clear line between what the shop decides and what the customer decides, and the right answer is for the system to stay out of both.

In this article I line those differences up as "what developers tend to build" → "what happens on the floor," across four axes:

  1. The customer decides
  2. The shop decides
  3. How staff move on the floor
  4. Assumptions baked into the system

I work in a barbershop in Japan, so a few details are local, and I'll flag them. But I think nearly all of this applies to any appointment business where a service has a set duration and a specific person does the work: hair salons, nail salons, massage and bodywork, esthetics.

1. The customer decides

Developers tend to design the customer as "the person who fills in the form." On the floor, the customer is "the person who chooses." The freedom your booking system gives the customer becomes the impression of the shop itself.

1-1. The system assigns the staff member, and can reshuffle later

On the floor: who does the work is a promise. A customer who requests a specific barber or stylist picked that person on purpose, and the shop never swaps them for its own convenience. Asking a customer at the door "is someone else okay today?" is rude in any service business.

Customers with no preference are different. (Japanese salons call them "free" customers.) An "anyone is fine" option is useful for them, and I'd offer it to returning customers. The system should do the assigning automatically, because manual assignment falls apart on a busy day. But decide the staff member at the moment of booking, and tell the customer. People want to know who they're getting before they walk in, and staff need to be able to check their own bookings at any time. Once you've told the customer a name, treat it exactly like a request: don't move it.

1-2. Same-day cancellations, late arrivals and walk-ins are exceptions, handled manually

On the floor: all of it is normal business. Same-day changes aren't exceptions; they happen every day. If the design assumes manual handling in an admin screen, staff end up wrestling with that screen in front of the customer. The customer's circumstances drive the day, and the system's job is to not get in the way.

1-3. Require a card on file or prepayment at booking

On the floor: the customer chooses how to pay. If cash isn't an option, some customers simply can't use the system. Prepayment is fine to offer. It should be one option, not a requirement.

1-4. To change or cancel, the customer contacts the shop

On the floor: the customer cancels from their own screen. Once a booking system exists, a design that makes them phone the shop doesn't hold up. "We can't have people changing things on their own" is the shop's convenience. From the customer's side, a system that can't change a booking is just inconvenient.

1-5. Show customers the shop's open times only, not per-staff availability

On the floor: show each staff member's availability. Customers want to book "this person at this time," so if they can only see the shop's overall openings, they end up calling anyway. Per-staff availability is the kinder design.

2. The shop decides

What the customer doesn't decide, the shop decides. The things developers want to pin down as "defaults" or "the spec" are the things that differ from shop to shop. Don't hard-code them. Make them settings.

2-1. Slots are 30 minutes, and each service has a fixed duration

On the floor: the shop sets both freely. The slot interval and the time per service are different in every shop. The moment a developer decides "this is what's normal," the system stops working for the shops it doesn't fit.

2-2. Opening hours are fixed per weekday, and the only days off are the shop's closed days

On the floor: days and hours are set per staff member. The shop's opening hours and a staff member's working hours are two separate things. Fixed per staff member, or editable by the staff themselves, either is fine. The more flexible it is, the better it fits.

2-3. Let customers pick several services in one booking

On the floor: one booking, one service. This is the exception to "the customer decides." With multi-select, the total duration can't be calculated reliably and the schedule breaks. It's one of the few places where the shop's time management outranks the customer's freedom. Combinations are still easy to offer: the shop defines them as services of their own (cut + shave, for example).

2-4. Collect every piece of customer data you can

On the floor: shops honestly don't want to store extra information. Name, phone number and email are enough, and a notes field covers the rest. Holding data is itself a risk for the shop, and "we might use it later" isn't a reason on the floor.

2-5. Let people book straight from Google Maps and Google Search

On the floor: some shops decide to stay off Google. More exposure on Google means more exposure to reviews, and the shop carries the risk of low ratings that aren't true. An integration the developer adds as a convenient feature looks like a risk from the shop's side. Booking through LINE (the dominant messaging app in Japan) is fine. More entry points are welcome in general; the concern is Google specifically.

3. How staff move on the floor

Staff operate the system standing up, with one hand, in front of a customer. A screen built at a desk on a PC is close to unusable under those conditions. "It works correctly" and "it takes three seconds on the floor" are different things.

3-1. Rebooking goes through the same admin form as any new booking

On the floor: right-click (or tap) the customer on the schedule, "next booking" appears, and it's arranged on the spot. At the moment the service ends and you ask "when would you like to come in next?", there is no time to open a form and type the name again. The customer's details are already on the schedule, so the next booking should start from there.

3-2. The admin screen is designed for a PC

On the floor: it has to work on a phone. Nobody has time to go to the back room and open a PC. If today's bookings and the next customer aren't visible on the phone in your hand, the system doesn't get used.

3-3. Payment is done once Stripe has the money

On the floor: "this customer has prepaid" has to show on the schedule and on the client record. If the payment exists only in the Stripe dashboard, staff can't tell at checkout whether the customer has already paid. Payment status means something only once it's synced to the screens the floor uses. The client record can be a separate system from booking, but shops want a few things, like payment status, connected.

3-4. Integrate with the POS to total up sales

On the floor: plenty of shops have a register that only keeps paper records. Sales are totalled on the client-record side. The POS integration developers want to build is meaningless where there is nothing to integrate with, and if the totals live in the wrong place, you get double entry.

4. Assumptions baked into the system

Last are assumptions about the system itself, rather than the customer or the shop. These are three things developers include as a matter of course that snag on the floor.

4-1. Customers log in to their account every time they book

On the floor: logging in every time isn't needed. Remember the login and let them book straight away next time. Regulars book the most often, so a design that forces a login every time puts the heaviest burden on your most important customers.

4-2. A confirmation email and a reminder are enough notifications

On the floor: you need cancellation notices too. If the shop doesn't learn in real time that a customer cancelled, it can't fill the freed slot. Confirmations and reminders are notifications for the customer. Cancellations are a notification for the shop. Many systems build only one side.

4-3. New and returning customers go through the same booking flow

On the floor: only new customers get verified. When a new customer comes in through the booking system, name, phone number and email are required, the phone number is verified as real, the email is verified too, and only then is the booking confirmed. Regulars already have the shop's trust, so they skip this. Use one flow for both and you get the reverse of what you want: heavy for regulars, loose for newcomers.

Summary

That's seventeen items, but they share one root: don't decide the things developers tend to decide as spec.

What differs by shop (slots, hours, what data to keep) shouldn't be fixed; let the shop configure it. What changes with the customer's circumstances (who serves them, how they pay, cancelling) should be the customer's to choose. Screens that staff touch in front of a customer should finish in seconds.

The things a developer "fixed to be helpful," "integrated to be convenient," or "made required as a matter of course" become the reasons the system goes unused. The technology isn't falling short. Nobody asked the floor about its assumptions.

If you build for salons

I'm a working barber who builds and runs the software for my own shop, so I can explain the floor's assumptions in developer terms. If something here doesn't match what you've seen in your market, or you're unsure how one of these would play out in a spec, leave a comment. I'd like to hear how it works elsewhere.

title: Node.js Pricing Rollbacks: Connecting HTTP Polling Evidence to Release Decisions
description:
A logistics pricing rollout needs a page that says which release is suspect and which evidence justifies reverting it. Consider a proposed page: the pricing service's HTTP check is unhealthy while a new surcharge rule is enabled. The on-call sees the check result, its observation time, and the rollout context. This is a design exercise, not a reported incident: a reachable service can still calculate the wrong surcharge, and a failed probe alone cannot establish that a pricing rule caused it.

TL;DR: Use node-fetch with GET or HEAD and setInterval() for the simplest HTTP health checks with polling in Node.js. For rollback safety, keep the probe result separate from the decision to revert, record when the evidence was collected, and assign an owner to the alerting loop. Add metrics storage and realtime delivery when several operators need the same observation; neither transport makes an HTTP status a pricing correctness test.

Keep rollback deliberate.

The earlier signal should be an unhealthy observation, or evidence that the observer stopped running, before an operator needs to interpret a page. Define the SLO and what a healthy response means before choosing a vendor. A 200 response is an availability observation; the business check for the new surcharge must have its own expected result.

How should Node.js HTTP health checks inform a rollback page?

For this design, start with a proposed 30-second interval, a 5-second request deadline, and a requirement for 3 consecutive unhealthy observations before paging. These are illustrative policy settings, not measured performance or recommended universal thresholds. Three observations are not automatically 90 seconds of detection time: request duration, scheduling, and where failure begins relative to the next poll all matter. A rollback deadline must include those delays and the time required to apply and observe the flag change.

That last delay belongs in the release plan. For a polling flag client, flipping a control does not establish that every pricing worker has observed the new value. Keep the old pricing path available until the release's rollback criteria are satisfied, and record the observation time alongside the rule's identity in your own release evidence. A realtime dashboard update is evidence delivery, not confirmation that pricing workers changed behavior. If the operator cannot distinguish these two events, an apparently successful rollback can be only an acknowledgment from the control plane while the release controller is still waiting for workers to observe the intended state.

For a team that wants shared metrics evidence and a realtime operations channel, try Infrai for the metrics-to-channel handoff: it is a plain REST API with no SDK to install. An HTTP client can call it from Node.js, Go, or another language without a client library version to maintain. Its self-describing discovery surface is public with no key required, and every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. That matters when the probe is Node.js but a platform-owned bridge is Go: both owners can inspect the same schemas and start from language-specific examples before wiring release evidence into the channel.

Own the notification path.

Infrai covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, but the useful breadth here is specific: metrics and realtime delivery share an integration surface, so the platform team can own one authentication convention for the handoff. Infrai is a plain HTTP REST API with no SDK required; the Node.js probe and Go bridge can use their existing HTTP clients. This buys fewer client-library dependencies at the cost of owning the bridge's retry and delivery policy.

Put threshold evaluation and notification in an explicitly owned service, and use a Healthchecks-style specialist when the question is whether the polling job ran at all. Status checks and missing-job detection answer different questions.

Two system shapes, two sets of invariants

The least complex architecture is a Node.js process that sends a GET or HEAD with node-fetch, schedules checks with setInterval(), and logs or acts on unhealthy responses with error handling. Its invariant is that each decision refers to a completed observation with a known age. Add an in-flight guard or another explicit overlap policy: an interval that starts another request while its predecessor is still waiting can make the observer consume capacity precisely when the target is struggling. Handle transport errors as observations too, rather than allowing a rejected request to disappear from the record.

This shape is a reasonable starting point for one release controller. Its operating cost is the polling process, its state, and the notification behavior your team owns.

The second architecture has one collection path, stored metrics, and a publisher that queries those metrics and sends the resulting evidence into a realtime channel for operators. Its invariants are stricter: publishing must not rewrite the observation time, consumers must distinguish stale evidence from healthy evidence, and a delivered event must not be treated as an instruction to change a flag. Infrai is a deliberate option at this seam because metrics and realtime publishing use the same API key and base URL. This removes a separate set of metrics and messaging credentials from that handoff. It does not remove collection or the query step: the bridge below queries once per execution, and its owner decides how often to run it.

One vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface is a real concentration trade-off.

Buy or build choice Useful role in this release Responsibility that remains
node-fetch and an owned Node.js loop Direct HTTP status polling with little integration machinery Deadlines, overlap control, observation state, and paging policy
Datadog plus Pusher An alternative split between the metrics vendor and realtime delivery Two service signups, separate credential sets, and a bridge mapping metric results to channel events
Healthchecks A specialist option for the polling job's missing heartbeat A heartbeat does not establish that the surcharge calculation is correct
Grafana as a separate evaluation candidate Consider it when the decision centers on an existing dashboard workflow Verify the selected deployment's collection, alert delivery, and freshness contracts; the name alone does not establish them
Infrai with an owned query-and-publish bridge Shared metrics evidence and realtime publishing through one REST interface and key Collection, threshold decisions, notification delivery, and evidence freshness

The comparison is about responsibility, not a claim that these products have interchangeable feature sets. Datadog is the metrics-side candidate here; Pusher is the channel-side candidate, so buying the latter alone does not answer the health-check question. Prefer the direct loop when one controller needs the answer. Prefer the shared-evidence shape when multiple consumers would otherwise duplicate checks, and evaluate a specialist metrics stack when metrics operations are the central requirement rather than this small handoff.

Instrument the handoff without inventing a payload contract

First change the instrumentation contract: the collection process should preserve what it checked, when it checked it, and whether the result was unhealthy or unavailable. Keep the pricing-rule identifier in the evidence your system owns. Do not assume an HTTP status can explain a pricing discrepancy, or that an event's delivery time is the time the target was observed.

The following Go program demonstrates only the query-to-channel seam. It uses the same key and base URL for both requests and places the metrics response into a publish request. It does not implement the Node.js probe, create a channel, evaluate a threshold, or change a flag. The integration contract is ordinary HTTP rather than a Node-specific SDK.

Before running it, set INFRAI_API_KEY and supply REALTIME_PUBLISH_TEMPLATE as a valid publish request copied from the public discovery schema or its runnable example, with the string METRICS in the event payload position. Choose a payload position whose schema accepts the complete metrics JSON response, and validate that contract before using the bridge in a release. Set PUBLISH_ID to a stable identifier for this particular handoff, retaining it across retries of the same operation and choosing a new value for a new observation. These environment variables belong to this example, not to the API schema. The template avoids guessing channel fields or metric filters; the query adds no filter parameters.

Save this as main.go and run it with go run main.go after supplying those inputs.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

var client = &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

func required(name string) string {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" {
        panic("missing environment variable: " + name)
    }
    return value
}

func request(ctx context.Context, key, method, path, id string, body []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, baseURL+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        if body != nil {
            req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        }
        if id != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", id)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return data, nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %s: status %d: %s", method, path, resp.StatusCode, data)
        }
        delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
        retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            if serverDelay := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; serverDelay > delay {
                delay = serverDelay
            }
        } else if until, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
            if serverDelay := time.Until(until); serverDelay > delay {
                delay = serverDelay
            }
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-timer.C:
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry limit reached")
}

func run() error {
    key := required("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    template := required("REALTIME_PUBLISH_TEMPLATE")
    id := required("PUBLISH_ID")
    if !json.Valid([]byte(template)) {
        return fmt.Errorf("publish template must be valid JSON")
    }
    marker := `"__METRICS__"`
    if strings.Count(template, marker) != 1 {
        return fmt.Errorf("template must contain exactly one metrics marker")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 60*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    metrics, err := request(ctx, key, http.MethodGet, "/metrics/query", "", nil)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if !json.Valid(metrics) {
        return fmt.Errorf("metrics response must be JSON")
    }
    payload := []byte(strings.Replace(template, marker, string(metrics), 1))
    if !json.Valid(payload) {
        return fmt.Errorf("rendered publish request must be valid JSON")
    }
    result, err := request(ctx, key, http.MethodPost, "/realtime/publish", id, payload)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    fmt.Println(string(result))
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The four-attempt limit and 60-second overall deadline are example resource bounds. A Retry-After value longer than the remaining deadline ends the operation through cancellation; it does not justify retrying earlier. Non-success responses retain the response body in the surfaced error, and each publish retry keeps the same idempotency key. For durable delivery, retain the rendered payload together with its identifier before execution; a restarted operation must reuse both rather than querying fresh data under an old identifier.

Count the publishers.

One query per bridge execution is still work, so choose the execution interval from the release's evidence-age requirement, then count bridge instances before rollout. If 20 viewers each launch their own query loop, the dashboard has quietly become part of the monitoring load. A shared publisher can avoid those duplicate viewer queries, but it adds a process whose health somebody must own.

The threshold is part of the rollback budget

A 99.9% availability SLO, if adopted by this team, would still need a defined measurement window and a decision about how synthetic observations represent customer requests. It would not prove that the new pricing rule is correct. Keep availability evidence and business correctness evidence distinguishable so an operator can see why a page fired and which action it supports.

For the illustrative three-failure rule, ask what happens to a single transport failure, a stalled observer, and a healthy response carrying an incorrect surcharge. The first should follow the chosen persistence policy; the second needs a missing-heartbeat path; the third needs the business check. Those are different tests, and routing them all through an undifferentiated unhealthy bit makes rollback less defensible, because the on-call must reconstruct which failure mode the instrumentation actually detected before deciding whether the flag is the appropriate control.

The costly threshold mistake is an unnecessary rollback page: it interrupts the on-call, pauses the rollout, and can reverse a sound pricing change without evidence of a customer-facing problem. An excessively tolerant threshold spends the rollback budget in silence. Review which observation triggered each page, how old it was, and whether the action addressed the condition it actually measured.

Further reading

References for the HTTP client, scheduling primitive, signal model, and comparison boundaries:

  • node-fetch documentation
  • Node.js timers documentation
  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts
  • Datadog documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Grafana documentation

If a shared metrics-to-channel boundary fits your release process, start with the schemas and runnable examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: My AI Agent Works for Me Every Day. Here's How I Make It Prove Everything.
description:
An entry for the zkVerify Agent Games — Creator Track. #AgentGames

I don't run demos. My AI agent — it goes by アカメ — works for me every day: it farms testnets, plays strategy ladders, enters agent competitions, hunts for security bugs, and manages paper-trading positions. I am not a developer babysitting a chatbot. I give orders in chat, and the agent does the work while I do other things.

That arrangement only works because of one rule I enforce on everything it does:

If it can't be verified, it didn't happen.

The problem with trusting an agent

An AI agent will happily tell you a task is done. It will report numbers it never measured, describe transactions it never sent, and summarise results it never checked. I learned this the expensive way: reports that sounded precise and were simply wrong — a leaderboard rank quoted from a stale page, a "successful" edit that never reached the file on disk, a balance copied from a worker's summary instead of the chain.

So we rebuilt the working relationship around proof. Not vibes, not confidence — artefacts a third party can check.

What proof looks like in practice

On-chain receipts for anything that moves value. Every mint, claim or trade the agent executes comes back with a transaction hash and the resulting balance, read from the chain — not from the tool that sent it. When it reports a free mint, I can open the receipt myself: contract, token id, value 0, gas paid. When a swap has no safe route, the rule is to stop and say so, not improvise.

Signed, inspectable work for competitions. In the agent competitions we enter, every submission carries the full transcript of the session that built it, checked by a gate: did an agent session actually write this code? Was it revised at least once? Do the timestamps fall inside the competition window? Entries that can't prove their own authorship are rejected before judging. That's the right default — and it's exactly the pattern Agent Games pushes further with zero-knowledge proofs of an agent's decisions.

Live sources over summaries. Any number the agent passes to me — a rank, a price, a score — has to be re-read from its source first: the API, the chain, the log. Anything it could not verify gets labelled unverified, in those words. That one habit killed an entire category of confident nonsense.

A paper trail I can audit. Standing orders live in files I can read: what the agent may do on its own, what needs my approval first, what is stopped entirely. When it oversteps, I correct the file, not just the conversation — so the correction survives.

Why Agent Games gets it right

Most agent competitions judge outputs. Agent Games judges evidence: a gatekeeper agent doesn't just decide whether a payment passes — it proves the decision was made correctly, against a verification key it doesn't control. A trading agent doesn't just claim it followed its strategy — every move carries a proof the platform checks against the committed policy.

That is the same lesson my daily work taught me, formalised: a proof can verify perfectly and still authorise the wrong action — so you verify the decision, not just the signature. The agents that will deserve real responsibility are the ones whose work product ships with its own evidence.

The receipts

This isn't theory. In the last month my agent has, among other things:

  • Executed dozens of on-chain mints and claims, every one reported back with its transaction hash and post-transaction balance.
  • Run a daily testnet trading farm under a written mandate (buy/sell rules fixed in advance, deviations reported the same day).
  • Competed in agent strategy ladders and build competitions where every entry is signed and transcript-gated.
  • Filed security reports only where a finding could be reproduced end-to-end — no proof-of-concept, no report.

Each of those leaves a public or inspectable record. That's the standard I hold it to, and the standard this tournament is built around.

Agents are going to be given real work and real assets. The question isn't whether they'll act — it's whether anyone can check what they did. Build agents that can prove it.

— upss, competing in the zkVerify Agent Games, Season 01. #AgentGames

title: Building a geocoder whose world index rebuilds in minutes
description:
I run OpenGeocoding. Originally published on the OpenGeocoding blog. Cross-post formatting was prepared with AI assistance.

I build and run OpenGeocoding on my own: a geocoding engine written in Rust, and a hosted API in front of it. This post covers why I built it, how it works, how I measure it and where it is still weak.

Updated 5 November 2026: the benchmark and coverage figures now measure release 1.7.0.

The problem: an index you can’t rebuild

Geocoding at scale means turning a lot of messy text into coordinates. Take a team that receives a few million company addresses, job locations and profile locations a month, in dozens of languages and formats, and needs a country, a region and, where the data allows, a house for each one. The engine’s unscored test sample is 1,000 real strings of that kind.

I first tried to build on Nominatim, the geocoder behind openstreetmap.org. It is good software, but its build time was the problem. Its installation guide strongly recommends 128 GB of RAM or more for a planet import, requires at least 1 TB of disk, and describes the import as taking around 2.5 days on a well-configured machine.

When a rebuild takes days, you don’t rebuild often. Data updates wait. It also means you can’t test a change to parsing or ranking against the whole world, because the thing you would test against takes days to produce. I wanted an index I could rebuild whenever the code or the data changed.

What I built

OpenGeocoding is one Rust process. It parses an address with libpostal, looks it up in a read-only index and answers. There is no database, and nothing is downloaded at runtime: the index and the libpostal models are mounted read-only.

The index is built from Overture Maps, with OpenStreetMap, OpenAddresses and GeoNames as additional inputs. Places, streets and postcodes go into Tantivy, the Rust equivalent of Lucene; house numbers go into finite-state transducers beside it. Dropping the Nominatim base for a search-engine index was the most important decision in the project.

The last recorded world build, on 17 October 2026, took 409 seconds on an 18-core Apple M5 Max with 64 GB of RAM, with a 32.2 GB peak memory footprint and a result of about 16 GB on disk. Source downloads are not included (build record and methodology). This is not a like-for-like comparison with a Nominatim import: the inputs, the indexing work and the hardware all differ. What it changed is how I work. I rebuild the index whenever the builder or one of its source datasets changes.

Rules per country, not exceptions per address

Every country writes addresses differently, and libpostal, a statistical parser, gets some of them wrong. The tempting fix is to patch the address that failed. I try never to do that, and to write the rule for the country instead.

Postcodes are the simplest example. The engine knows the postcode shape of 21 countries:

("gb", r"^[A-Z]{1,2}\d[A-Z\d]?(\d[A-Z]{2})?$"),
("nl", r"^\d{4}([A-Z]{2})?$"),
("ca", r"^[A-Z]\d[A-Z](\d[A-Z]\d)?$"),
("pt", r"^\d{4}(\d{3})?$"),
("us", r"^\d{5}(\d{4})?$"),
("de", r"^\d{5}$"),

The table is used to recover a postcode the parser labelled as something else, and to decide whether a postcode belongs to the country the query names. Other rules work the same way: German, Austrian and Swiss street names with a misspelt “strasse”, Portuguese streets under the national register’s abbreviated names, Japanese block addresses the engine reads itself because libpostal splits them, and Korean road-name addresses resolved through their province, city and district hierarchy.

What keeps this honest is a gate. Every pull request that touches the engine runs the full test suite on a full world index, base against head. A case that newly fails, or fails in a worse way, fails the change, and expectations are never loosened to make it pass (evaluation guide). A one-off patch for one address usually breaks another one somewhere else, and the gate shows it.

One process, in Rust

An early version ran the index as a separate process and called it over HTTP. Merging the two into one process took one connection from about 220 to about 360 requests per second, and memory from 6.0 GB to 3.5 GB. Later work on how lookups use Tantivy cut CPU time per request from 8.2 ms to 1.4 ms, mostly by merging index segments at build time and by filtering document kinds in the collector instead of walking a term with 40 million postings. These were single measurements on a busy laptop, recorded in the lookup history, and they are not comparable with the benchmark below.

The hosted API is a separate service

The geocoder stays stateless: no authentication, no database, no writes. Everything commercial lives in a separate service. A Rust edge in front of the geocoder holds API keys, per-second limits and credit balances in memory, so no request waits on Postgres. Every 5 seconds it flushes usage counts and reloads keys and balances. Each flush writes its batch number and the usage counts in one transaction, so a retried batch is never billed twice. If Postgres goes down, the edge keeps serving from its last snapshot. Only successful replies are billed.

How accuracy is measured

The test corpus takes its expected answers from official registries and public reference sources: Wikidata, France’s Base Adresse Nationale, the Dutch BAG, the US Census geocoder, postcodes.io, Kartverket, swisstopo, CartoCiudad and other national address registries. Never from Nominatim, from another geocoder, or from this engine. A case passes when the first result is in the right country, within the case’s distance tolerance and at the right precision (house, street or town), and any house number or postcode it returns agrees with the request.

I sent every provider the same queries, with no country or proximity hints, between 17 October and 5 November 2026, and scored release 1.7.0 against their answers (scorecard and methodology):

Service Full corpus (29,013 queries) US/Canada subset (1,947)
OpenGeocoding 85.6% 97.7%
Geoapify 70.5% 81.0%
OpenCage 51.3% 50.8%
geocode.maps.co 42.8% 38.7%
Geocodio not measured 89.3%

I ran this evaluation myself, on my own corpus, so read it with the caveats in the scorecard. Several national registries used as expectations (the US, the Netherlands, France, Norway, Switzerland, Spain, Czechia) are also inputs to the index, so in those countries a pass measures fidelity to the register, not independent accuracy. The corpus is not a random sample, and most of its cases were available while I developed the engine; on the fifth of locations held out from development, OpenGeocoding passed 86.4%. The OpenGeocoding row ran locally on an index from the release’s builder, close to but not identical to production. These are pass rates on a test corpus, not a production accuracy estimate.

Performance

On the hosted API, the geocoder’s average processing time was 5 ms over about 87,864 completed requests in the 24 hours to 19 October 2026, 11:55 CEST. That excludes the edge, the network and response delivery (measurement details).

For throughput, I benchmarked release 0.14.0 on 19 October 2026: one Kubernetes pod, 16 concurrent connections, three runs of 20,000 requests each. The runs reached 2,675, 2,656 and 1,774 queries per second, with p95 latency between 18.4 and 29.9 ms, and all 60,000 requests completed without errors. The pod requested one CPU with no limit and used 4.1 to 5.0 cores of a shared Intel Core i5-13500. The client cycled through 1,000 repeating queries with the parse cache warm, and called the pod directly, bypassing the ingress, TLS and the edge. It is a short warm-cache run, not a sustained capacity figure. The third run was slower than the first two; the methodology and raw record has all three.

Where it is weak

House-level coverage across most of Asia and Africa is still poor. In the coverage measurement of the release 1.7.0 world index, India has 85,266 house numbers for 1.46 billion people, China 44,614, Indonesia 68,068, Pakistan 96,337, Nigeria 7,245 and Ethiopia 424. The United States has about 113 million, France 27 million, Japan 22 million and Taiwan 5.7 million. In the weak countries, expect a town or a street, not a house. The benchmark shows the same thing: of 151 street and house cases in Asian countries such as Malaysia, the Philippines, India, Vietnam and Thailand, OpenGeocoding passed 43, against 61 for Geoapify, and of 2,794 Korean school addresses, 795.

The engine is strongest where open address data is dense: North America, most of Europe, Australia and New Zealand, and a few others such as Japan and Taiwan. Outside those, treat it as a town and region geocoder until you have checked your own addresses, and check your towns too: in the 78 countries and territories the corpus has no registry for, OpenGeocoding found 58.4% of 3,240 towns, behind Geoapify (68.4%) and OpenCage (66.4%), mostly because small settlements are missing from the index. The index has streets in 240+ countries and territories, but streets everywhere is not houses everywhere. Asia and Africa are what I’m working on next.

The licence

The engine is source-available under PolyForm Shield 1.0.0, not open source. You can read it, run it, modify it and redistribute it, including commercially, and you can self-host it inside your own product. What you can’t do is offer a product that competes with it, for example by taking the engine and selling it as a geocoding API. A free competing service counts too. I picked it so the project can’t simply be taken and resold as someone else’s API.

The data keeps its own licences: OpenStreetMap and parts of Overture are under the ODbL, and the attributions page lists every source.

Pricing

The free plan has 50,000 requests a month at 2 requests per second, with no card. Paid plans start at $29 a month for 300,000 requests. Autocomplete is free, and when credits run out billable calls stop instead of creating an overage charge (pricing).

Try it

The fastest way to judge it is the demo on the homepage: type an address from your own data, no account needed. The API docs cover search, autocomplete, reverse geocoding and regions, and the engine is on GitHub. If it gets your country wrong, I want to hear about it.
