title: Flutter on Edge Robotics: Adapting UI Workloads to Jetson Thermal Pressure
description:
Edge systems share a thermal and power envelope across inference, networking, video, and application services. The Flutter client should degrade gracefully when telemetry indicates resource pressure.

Observe before adapting

Collect temperature, throttling state, CPU/GPU use, memory pressure, inference latency, and frame age through supported interfaces. Do not infer thermal state from one slow frame.

Define graceful degradation

Lower chart refresh rates, reduce decorative animation, request lower preview resolution, or reduce noncritical diagnostics. Keep essential alarms and controls available.

Use explicit policy and hysteresis

A small state machine prevents mode flapping near thresholds. Separate signal collection, policy, and presentation.

Coordinate with the edge service

The Jetson service owns model and accelerator scheduling. Flutter can request supported quality profiles but hiding widgets does not directly reduce GPU inference load.

Test recovery

Simulate pressure and verify gradual recovery after metrics stabilize. Log adaptation decisions and their triggering measurements.

Example implementation

This Dart snippet illustrates one part of the design. Adapt types, transport behavior, timestamp semantics, and platform APIs to your actual system before production use.

`enum UiLoadMode { full, reduced, minimal }


UiLoadMode chooseMode({

  required double frameAgeMs,

  required double cpuPercent,

}) {

  if (frameAgeMs > 500 || cpuPercent > 90) return UiLoadMode.minimal;

  if (frameAgeMs > 200 || cpuPercent > 75) return UiLoadMode.reduced;

  return UiLoadMode.full;

}

`




Performance checklist

  • Measure p95/p99 behavior on target hardware, not only a desktop simulator.
  • Bound queues and buffers; define what may be coalesced or dropped.
  • Keep heavy parsing, image processing, and inference away from the Flutter UI thread.
  • Track source timestamps, sequence numbers, stale-data rate, and dropped updates.
  • Test network degradation, reconnects, sustained operation, and resource pressure.
  • Keep control commands and critical alerts separate from replaceable telemetry.

title: Build a WooCommerce to Shopify redirect map with 40 lines of Python
description:
When a WooCommerce store moves to Shopify, nearly every URL changes. WooCommerce lets you shape permalinks; Shopify doesn't. Products always live under /products/, collections under /collections/, pages under /pages/ and posts under /blogs/<blog-name>/. Shopify treats those prefixes as fixed.

That means the SEO side of a migration comes down to one file: a list of every old URL that gets traffic or has links, each pointing at its new Shopify address with a 301. Shopify's URL redirect import takes a CSV with two columns, Redirect from and Redirect to, so the job is to produce that file and check it before launch.

Here is the small script we use as a starting point, and the checks we run around it.

Step 1: collect the old URLs

Don't rely only on the sitemap. Combine three sources:

  • The WordPress sitemap (Yoast, Rank Math or core wp-sitemap.xml).
  • Search Console: Performance → Pages, last 16 months, exported to CSV. These are the URLs Google actually shows.
  • Your backlink tool or Search Console's Links report: pages other sites link to.

Put them all in one text file, one URL per line, and de-duplicate.

Step 2: map them by pattern

WooCommerce's default bases are /product/ and /product-category/. Check Settings → Permalinks in WordPress first, because many stores change them (/shop/, /item/, /category/), and adjust the patterns below.

import csv, re, sys
from urllib.parse import urlparse

RULES = [
    (r"^/product/([^/]+)/?$",                lambda m: f"/products/{m[1]}"),
    (r"^/product-category/(?:.+/)?([^/]+)/?$", lambda m: f"/collections/{m[1]}"),
    (r"^/product-tag/([^/]+)/?$",            lambda m: f"/collections/{m[1]}"),
    (r"^/shop/?$",                           lambda m: "/collections/all"),
    (r"^/\d{4}/\d{2}/([^/]+)/?$",             lambda m: f"/blogs/news/{m[1]}"),
    (r"^/(about-us|contact|shipping|returns)/?$", lambda m: f"/pages/{m[1]}"),
]

def map_path(path):
    for pattern, target in RULES:
        m = re.match(pattern, path)
        if m:
            return target(m)
    return None

def main(infile, outfile):
    unmapped = []
    with open(outfile, "w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["Redirect from", "Redirect to"])
        for line in open(infile):
            path = urlparse(line.strip()).path or "/"
            if path == "/":
                continue
            new = map_path(path)
            if new:
                w.writerow([path.rstrip("/") or "/", new])
            else:
                unmapped.append(path)
    print(f"{len(unmapped)} URLs need a manual decision:")
    print("\n".join(unmapped))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])

Run it with python map_redirects.py old-urls.txt redirects.csv. Everything it can't match is printed so a person decides where it goes. That list is usually short but important: landing pages, old campaign URLs and posts without a date in the path.

A few notes on the patterns:

  • Nested categories flatten. /product-category/clothing/hoodies/ becomes /collections/hoodies, because Shopify has no nested collection paths. If two child categories share a slug under different parents, the script will map them to the same collection: check for duplicates.
  • Tags only map if you actually build matching collections. Otherwise send them to the nearest real collection.
  • Blog posts land under /blogs/news/ because Shopify's default blog is called News. Change it if you create a different blog.
  • Keep slugs identical where you can. If blue-hoodie stays blue-hoodie, the map is easy to read and easy to audit.

Step 3: check the targets exist

A redirect to a 404 is worse than no redirect. Before importing, request every target on the Shopify development store (with the storefront password, or from an admin session) and flag anything that isn't a 200. If you used Shopify's Store Migration app or a CSV import, remember imported products start as drafts, so publish them on the dev store before testing.

Step 4: import, then re-test on launch day

Import redirects.csv under Online Store → Navigation → URL Redirects → Import. On launch day, after DNS points at Shopify, request each old URL and confirm it returns a single 301 to the expected path, not a chain. Then watch Search Console's Pages report for new 404s for the next few weeks and add redirects as they appear.

What the script doesn't cover

Redirects keep link equity flowing, but rankings also depend on the content that loads at the new address. Carry over titles and meta descriptions from Yoast or Rank Math, image alt text and product descriptions. Customer passwords can't move at all, so plan the customer communication too. If you'd rather hand the whole move to a team, Dzimark runs WooCommerce to Shopify migration projects for stores in the US, UK, Canada and Australia.

FAQ

Does Shopify let me keep /product/ URLs?
No. Product URLs always start with /products/, which is why every product needs a redirect.

Do I need an app for redirects?
No. Shopify's built-in URL Redirects page imports a CSV. Apps help mainly with bulk editing and monitoring 404s after launch.

Should I redirect URLs that get no traffic?
Redirect anything with traffic, links or that appears in Search Console. Thin, empty archives can go to the closest collection.

Can I import historical orders at the same time?
Not with a CSV. Shopify points to apps such as Matrixify or LitExtension for order history.

Further reading: the full WooCommerce to Shopify migration guide on the Dzimark blog.

title: How to fix net::ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT (when an ad blocker breaks your images, scripts and links)
description:
Scheduled broken-link and redirect checks that tell you the moment a link breaks — linkbruno.com

You open the console on your own site and see a column of red:

GET https://example.com/static/ads/hero-banner.webp net::ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT
GET https://example.com/js/analytics-consent.js net::ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT

Nothing is wrong with your server. The request never left the browser. ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT means something running inside the browser, almost always an extension, cancelled it. For your visitors who use ad blockers (a large share on developer-focused and tech sites), that image, script or link target simply doesn't exist.

This matters most when the blocked thing isn't an ad at all. Here's how to find out why it's blocked and how to fix it without asking anyone to turn off their blocker.

Step 1: confirm it's an extension

Open the same page in an Incognito or private window with extensions disabled (Chrome disables them in Incognito unless you've allowed them). If the errors disappear, an extension is the cause.

To find which extension, re-enable them one at a time, or check the obvious candidates first: uBlock Origin, AdBlock Plus, AdGuard, Ghostery, Privacy Badger, and the blockers built into Brave and Opera. Brave's shields block requests without any extension installed, and show up the same way.

Step 2: find the rule that matched

Content blockers use filter lists such as EasyList, EasyPrivacy and Fanboy's lists. Rules match on URL patterns, so the file name or path is usually what triggered the block, not the content.

In uBlock Origin, open the dashboard's logger (the "list" icon in the popup, or the extension's logger page). Reload your page and find the red entries. Each one shows the rule that matched and the list it came from, for example:

||example.com^*/ads/       EasyList
/analytics-               EasyPrivacy

AdGuard and AdBlock Plus have similar request logs. Once you know the rule, you know what to rename.

Step 3: the usual innocent victims

These are the patterns that most often catch legitimate files:

  • /ads/, /ad/, -ad-, _ad_, adserver, banner in paths or file names. A folder called static/ads/ holding product images for your "advertise with us" page gets blocked wholesale.
  • analytics, tracking, track, pixel, beacon, collect, stats. Including your own first-party code with those words in it: analytics-consent.js, track-order.js (an order tracking page!), stats-chart.js.
  • share, social, facebook, twitter, linkedin in file names, caught by social-widget and annoyance lists.
  • popup, modal-promo, newsletter-overlay, caught by annoyance lists.
  • Common third-party hosts: tag managers, analytics endpoints, ad networks, many chat and feedback widgets, and some font and CDN hosts on stricter lists.

The track-order case is a good example of why this is a broken-link problem as much as a script problem. If a page's important link or button is rendered by a blocked script, that link doesn't exist for a large slice of visitors.

Tired of hunting blocked assets one URL at a time? linkbruno.com crawls the site and flags the images, scripts and links that fail to load.

Step 4: fix it

Rename first-party files and folders

For your own assets, the fix is boring and effective: rename them so they don't match ad or tracker patterns. static/ads/ becomes static/promo-images/ (check that one too; "promo" appears in some lists), track-order.js becomes order-status.js, stats-chart.js becomes dashboard-chart.js.

Then search your codebase and build output for the old names, so nothing still references them. And keep redirects from the old URLs if any of them were ever linked from outside.

Don't build core features on blocked third parties

If your checkout, sign-up form or main navigation depends on a third-party script that's on a common block list, some users can't complete those flows. Load essential functionality from your own domain, and treat third-party widgets as optional enhancements: the page should work, and the links should be visible, if they fail to load.

Make blocked loads fail softly

When you do load optional third-party scripts, handle the failure:

const s = document.createElement("script");
s.src = "https://widget.example-chat.com/loader.js";
s.async = true;
s.onerror = () => {
  // Blocked or unreachable: show a plain contact link instead
  document.querySelector("#chat-fallback").hidden = false;
};
document.head.appendChild(s);

A plain <a href="/contact"> fallback means the visitor still has somewhere to go.

Don't try to evade blockers for tracking

Renaming your own product images and order-status script is fixing a false positive. Disguising tracking scripts so blockers miss them is something else, it's against your visitors' explicit choice, and filter list maintainers usually catch up anyway.

Find blocked files across the whole site

Checking pages one at a time in a browser is slow. If you have a list of your own asset URLs (from your build manifest, or a crawl), you can test them against a downloaded copy of EasyList and EasyPrivacy with a filter-matching library, such as the adblock Python bindings for Brave's Rust engine or the @cliqz/adblocker package in Node. Load the lists, run every URL through the matcher with the right request type (image, script, stylesheet), and print the ones that match a blocking rule along with the rule. It takes a few minutes to set up and turns "some users say the chart is missing" into a precise list of files to rename before the next release.

Step 5: test with a blocker on

Add a blocker to your regular testing. A browser profile with uBlock Origin and default lists, used for a quick click-through before each release, catches most of these issues. For automated tests, you can load an unpacked extension in Playwright using a persistent Chromium context, which lets you run your link and smoke tests with the blocker active.

Link checkers that request URLs directly, including linkbruno.com, see these files as healthy, because the server returns them fine. The blocker-on browser test is the check that sees what those visitors see.

Related reading

  • How to find and fix broken images on a website
  • '0 broken links found' is a myth: 7 places link checkers don't look
  • How to find mixed content (http:// links) on an HTTPS site
  • Moving docs from a GitHub wiki to a docs site? An 11-point checklist so the links survive

What's the most innocent file you've had blocked? I've seen a recipe site lose its whole "Add to shopping list" feature because the script was called list-tracker.js.

title: I Built Aven App Agent to Help Users Find Their Next Click
description:
I Built Aven App Agent to Help Users Find Their Next Click

Suggested DEV tags: ai, webdev, ux, showdev

Paste the title into DEV's title field and the article below into the body. The YouTube embed uses DEV's supported embed syntax.

A user opens your app with a simple goal.

“Invite someone to my workspace.”

They look at the dashboard. Open a menu. Try a different tab. Somewhere in your product, the right button exists. Finding it is the problem.

I'm the founder of Aven App Agent, and I'm building an AI assistant that connects questions like this to guidance inside the product.

Users can ask for help, read an answer, and choose a walkthrough that points them toward the controls they need.

Start with the task the user wants to finish

Take an invitation flow that crosses several parts of a website.

  1. Open Settings.
  2. Switch to Team.
  3. Select Invite members.
  4. Enter the details and send the invitation.

Each individual screen can be straightforward while the complete path still takes effort to discover. The user thinks about inviting a person. The application organizes that task into pages, tabs, and fields.

That gap is where Aven fits.

The user asks, “How do I invite a teammate?” Aven can offer a guide that highlights the next relevant control. The user follows the steps in the application where the task happens.

Here's an overview of the product.

The engineering detail that shapes the experience

A useful guide needs to know which page the user is on, which element a step refers to, and when that element is ready.

Aven uses context the product team registers, including pages, elements, and workflows. The host application handles navigation and UI behavior. That gives developers explicit places to connect guidance to the routes and controls they own. How Aven's guided workflows work

For a developer trying this in a product, I'd start with one complete task. Register its context, test the question that should lead to it, and walk through every step as a user would.

Pay particular attention to route changes, loading states, permissions, and responsive layouts. A button that exists in one state may be absent in another. Those conditions deserve the same care as the instruction shown beside it.

The Web SDK is available through npm.

npm install @avenappagent/web

The setup flow is to initialize the SDK, register the relevant pages, elements, and workflows, then test the question and guide against your application's current state. The Web SDK documentation covers the configuration and registration methods. Aven Web SDK

Knowledge Chat handles the questions that need an explanation

Some questions are about understanding the product.

“What is a workspace?” needs an explanation. “How do I invite someone?” may benefit from a guide.

Aven's Knowledge Chat uses connected documentation, pages, and files to answer questions and show supporting sources. The aim is to keep relevant help close to the user's task, with a source they can consult for more detail.

Give product teams several ways to build guides

Writing a guide means choosing a target, explaining the action, and checking how the step appears in the product. Aven offers several authoring paths for that work.

  • Chrome Visual Builder. Select an element on the live website and edit the guide through a left sidebar with templates and settings. Preview the tooltip against the actual page before publishing.
  • GitHub import. Connect a selected repository with read-only access to generate draft guides. Review their content and targets on the site before publishing them.
  • Mobile editor. Connect a test device, capture an app screen, and select a target in the editor. Build the guide step and preview it on the connected device.

Each path brings the author back to the experience the user will see. Checking the target and the instruction together is part of building the guide.

Watch the demos in different applications

We've recorded Aven integration demos using three open-source projects with different interfaces.

  • Dolibarr shows Aven in an ERP and CRM application. Watch the Dolibarr demo
  • Memos shows it in a note-taking application. Watch the Memos demo
  • TodoMVC shows it in a focused task-list interface. Watch the TodoMVC demo

These demos give developers concrete examples to compare with the workflows in their own products.

Which task would you guide first?

I'm looking for feedback from developers and product teams building apps where users regularly ask, “Where do I find this?”

You can explore the product and its demos on the Aven website. Explore Aven App Agent

What's one task in your app that users keep asking you to explain? Share the task in the comments, especially if it spans several screens. I'd like to understand where guidance would help and what would make it practical for your team to maintain.

title: cryptship — Ship Encrypted, License-Gated Code Inside Docker Images
description:
The problem

A Docker image ships your code in the clear. Anyone with the image can do this:

docker save your/app:latest -o app.tar
tar -xf app.tar   # unpack the layers and read everything

For interpreted languages such as Python, Node or Ruby, that means your entire source. If you sell software that customers run on their own servers, air-gapped networks or private clouds, that is a problem.

What cryptship does

cryptship ships your application encrypted, with a thin loader that decrypts and runs it only when a valid license is present.

  • One tool, one license format
  • Three deployment modes: air-gapped, on-prem and cloud
  • Written in Go, licensed GPLv3, first release v0.1.0

The 30-second version

Build time (you):

  1. cryptship keygen: an Ed25519 signing keypair, once
  2. cryptship pack: encrypt your app directory with a random key (AES-256-GCM) into payload.enc
  3. cryptship issue: a signed license that wraps that key to a machine, a pool of machines, or nothing
  4. Build an image with the loader, payload.enc, the license and your public key. No source, no content key.

Run time (customer): the loader verifies the license, checks expiry and revocation, derives the key, decrypts into tmpfs and execs your app.

An honest promise

Code that runs on hardware the customer controls can never be made perfectly extraction-proof: at some instant the plaintext is in memory. cryptship is not DRM snake oil. It makes casual copying impossible and makes serious reverse engineering cost more than a license. Part 3 is all about where that line is.

Try it

You need Docker, plus python3 for the demo's tamper step; the tools compile in a Go container.

git clone https://github.com/AI2TH/cryptship && cd cryptship
bash scripts/demo.sh

The demo packs a small Python app, issues a license and builds the image. It then docker saves the image, unpacks it and searches it for the source (it is not there), runs it to show it works, and tampers with the license to show the loader refuse it.

The series

  1. Part 1: binding the decryption key to the license and the machine
  2. Part 2: air-gapped, on-prem and cloud with one loader and three key providers
  3. Part 3: an honest threat model, and the hardening that raises the cost
